en: Auspiciousness.

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The First Book, named "The Foundation of Stories. This nectar of stories, it is said, formerly emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth when churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the daughter of the King of Mountains (Pārvatī). Those who forcibly swallow it, having attained their goal free from obstacles, bear upon this earth the burden of the status of the gods through the grace of Bhava (Śiva).

First Wave: May the dark throat of Śambhu bestow prosperity upon you—his throat which seems as if it were entwined by the nooses of the glances of Pārvatī resting in his lap, [glances] that are like the god of love himself.
May the Conqueror of Obstacles protect you, who, at the festival of the supreme twilight, raises the stars with his trunk and seems to fashion others with the spray from his *sītkāra* sounds.
Having prostrated, I compose this compendium of the essence of the *Bṛhatkathā*, a speech that serves as a lamp illuminating all categories of reality without exception.
Herein, first is the *Kathāpīṭha*; after that is the *Kathāmukha*; then follows the third section, named the *Lāvānaka*.
After that comes the birth of Naravāhanadatta; then follows the one called Caturdārika, and after that, Madanamañcukā.
Then there shall be the seventh book, named Ratnaprabhā; and then the eighth book shall be that entitled Sūryaprabha.
Then Alaṃkāravatī shall become Śaktiyaśas, and thereafter the eleventh will be known as Velālambaka.
Then there shall be the Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka, and likewise the Madirāvatī-lambaka; following these shall be the Pañcalambaka, which follows the Mahābhiṣeka.
Then Suratamañjarī shall likewise become Padmāvatī; thereafter, the eighteenth chapter, named Viṣamaśīla, shall follow.
Just as it is in the root text, so it is here; there is not even the slightest deviation. There is merely a difference in the expansion or brevity of the composition, and the language differs.
Preservation of propriety and consistency is maintained to the best of one's ability, and the composition of the poetic portion is joined together without interrupting the flavor of the narrative.
This effort of mine is by no means for the sake of proclaiming my own cleverness; rather, it is for the purpose of facilitating the recollection of the various networks of stories.
There exists the Himavat, renowned as the sovereign of mountains, frequented by Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas.
The majesty of that mountain has reached such a height that Bhavānī, the mother of the three worlds, attained the state of being his daughter.
Its northern peak is the great mountain named Kailāsa, which stands having ascended many thousands of yojanas.
Even when the ocean was churned, Mount Mandara did not attain the whiteness of nectar; yet I, through no effort at all, have done so—thus it seems to laugh, as it were, with its own splendors.
There dwells Maheśvara, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, accompanied by Ambikā and attended by his hosts, the Vidyādharas, and the Siddhas.
Upon his high, tawny mass of matted hair, the moon enjoys the pleasure of resting upon the peak of the eastern mountain, which is reddened by the twilight.
It is marvelous that by him, while fixing a trident in the heart of the Asura Andhaka alone, the trident was extracted from the hearts of even these three worlds.
Upon their crest-jewels, the gods and asuras shine as if they have attained a crescent moon, marked by the reflection of the tips of his toenails.
Once, having developed confidence, his beloved wife, in private, gratified the Lord, the husband of Bhavānī, with hymns of praise.
Delighted by her words of praise, the moon-crested Lord placed her upon his lap and said, "What pleasing thing shall I do for you?"
Then Girijā said: "If you are pleased, O Lord, tell me today some beautiful and new story, O God."
"O beloved, what could there be in this world—past, present, or future—that you would not know? Thus even Śarva spoke to her.
Then his beloved made a persistent request to her lord, for the mind of a proud woman is devoted to the affection of her lover.
Then, with the very intent of pleasing her, Śiva described to her a brief account concerning his own power as follows.
Formerly, Brahmā and likewise Nārāyaṇa came to behold me; wandering over the earth, they both arrived at the foot of the Himalayas.
Then they both saw there before them a great flaming linga; one set out to see its upper limit, while the other went downward.
Having failed to reach their goal through ascetic penances, the two of them pleased me; appearing before them, I said, "Choose whatever boon you desire."
Upon hearing that, Brahmā said, "May you become my son. Because of that, he was born unworthy of honor and censured for his lack of self-restraint.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa requested a boon from me, saying: "O Blessed One, may I be intent upon serving you."
Therefore, he has become my very body through your self; for you who are Nārāyaṇa are that power belonging to me, the possessor of power.
When Śaṅkara said, "Why are you my wife from a former birth? Pārvatī replied, "How could I be your wife from a former birth?"
Then Bharga replied: "O Goddess, in former times many daughters were born to the Prajāpati Dakṣa, both you and others."
He gave you to me, and those other daughters of his—Dharmā and the rest—to others; once, when invited to a sacrifice, all of them became my sons-in-law.
But I alone was excluded from that; therefore, he was questioned by you: "Father, tell me, why was my husband not summoned by you?"
Then he uttered these words, which were like a poison-needle to your ears: "How can your husband, who wears a garland of skulls, be summoned to the sacrifice?"
"Since this body was born from such a wicked man, what use have I for it?"—thus, out of anger, that body was cast away by you, O beloved.
And that sacrifice of Dakṣa was destroyed by me through that wrath; from that you were born from the Himālaya mountain, like a digit of the moon from the ocean.
Then, O Smara, I came to the Snowy Mountain for the sake of asceticism; both my father and you were appointed by him to serve me as a guest.
Sent by the gods to obtain a son who would be the destroyer of Tāraka, the God of Love found his opportunity there and pierced me; thus was he consumed.
Therefore, O wise one, I have been won by you through your intense asceticism; and that [asceticism], my beloved, was endured by me solely for the sake of acquiring you.
"In this way you were my wife in a former birth; what more need be said to you? When Śambhu had spoken thus and ceased, the Goddess, agitated with anger, replied:
"You are a rogue; even when entreated, you do not tell a heart-pleasing tale. Have you not been defeated by me, who carries the Gaṅgā yet does not bow during the twilight?"
Having heard that, Hara, having offered his apologies, consented; she then released her anger so that he might tell the divine tale.
When she herself had said, "No one is to enter here," and Nandin had closed the door, Hara proceeded to speak.
The gods are exclusively happy, while humans are perpetually suffering; yet the conduct of gods and humans alike is not captivating when viewed from a distance.
"Therefore, I shall describe to you the life of the Vidyādharas"—as Hara was saying this to the Goddess, [another] arrived.
Puṣpadanta, the best of the Gaṇas, who possessed the wealth of Śambhu’s grace, was stopped at the gate by Nandin as he stood there.
Thinking, "Today there is a prohibition against me as well, for no reason," he entered that very moment, unobserved through the power of yoga, out of curiosity.
Having entered, he heard everything being described by the wielder of the Pināka bow—the unprecedented and wondrous life-stories of the seven Vidyādharas.
Having heard this, he went and described it to his wife Jayā; for who indeed is able to conceal wealth or a secret from women?
Overcome with wonder at that, the female doorkeeper Jayā went before the Daughter of the Mountain and sang: "Among women, where is there any restraint of speech?"
Thereupon Girijā became enraged, saying, "You have not described what has never been told before," and she addressed the Lord, "For even Jayā knows this."
Then, having understood this through his power of resolve, the Lord of Umā spoke thus; and Puṣpadanta, having become a yogin and entered therein, heard it.
"O beloved, who else indeed knows what was described by him regarding Jayā? Having heard this, the goddess, filled with great wrath, summoned Puṣpadanta.
She cursed him, who was distraught at being called a mortal and ill-behaved, and she also cursed the attendant Mālyavān, who was pleading on his behalf.
Having prostrated at their feet, Śarvāṇī, being exhorted by Jayā, spoke these words slowly regarding the end of the curse.
In the Vindhya forest, a yakṣa named Supratīka, having attained the state of a piśāca due to the curse of Kubera, lived under the name Kāṇabhūti.
"When you see him and, remembering your former birth, recount this story to him, O Puṣpadanta, then you shall be released from the curse."
When Mālyavat hears that story of Kāṇabhūti, he will eat his meal at Kāṇabhūti's house after having related the story, and then he will depart.
Having spoken thus, the daughter of the mountain ceased; and at that very moment, those two hosts vanished from sight like flashes of lightning.
Then, after some time had passed, the compassionate Gaurī asked Śaṅkara: "O Lord, where on earth have those two excellent Pramathas been born, who were cursed by me?"
And the Moon-crested Lord said: "There is a great city called Kauśāmbī; in it, my dear, that Puṣpadanta was born under the name Vararuci."
Moreover, O Queen, that Mālyavat was also born in the excellent city named Supratiṣṭhita under the name Guṇāḍhya; such is the account concerning those two.

Having thus informed her, the Lord dwelt, delighting his beloved in pleasure-palaces fashioned from wish-fulfilling creepers upon the slopes of Mount Kailāsa—she who was filled with remorse at the thought of having insulted a servant who had always been devoted to him.

Thus ends the first wave in the Kathāpīṭha-lambaka of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave. Then Puṣpadanta, wandering about in human form, was known by the names Vararuci and also Kātyāyana.
Having mastered the sciences and fulfilled his duties as a minister, he once, feeling weary, went to visit the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhya mountains.
Propitiated by his ascetic penance, the Goddess, through a command in a dream, sent him to the Vindhya forest to visit Kāṇabhūti.
Wandering there through a place crowded with tigers and monkeys, where the trees were waterless and harsh, he beheld a tall banyan tree.
And nearby he saw that Piśāca Kāṇabhūti, surrounded by hundreds of Piśācas, his body resembling a sal tree in its bulk.
Having been seen by Kāṇabhūti and having performed the ritual salutation at his feet, Kātyāyana sat down and after a moment spoke to him.
"How is it that you, who were always of such virtuous conduct, have come to this state? Having heard that, Kāṇabhūti, showing his friendship, said to him:
"I possess no knowledge of my own; however, I have heard everything from Śarva. Listen, and I shall tell you what I heard in the cremation ground at Ujjayinī."
"Why, O Lord, do you take delight in skulls and cremation grounds? When thus questioned by the Goddess, the Blessed One then spoke as follows:
Long ago, when the destruction of the eon had occurred, the world became composed of water; then, having pierced my thigh, a drop of blood was cast down by me.
Within the water, that egg came into being; from it, when divided into two parts, a Person emerged. Then, for the sake of creation, Prakṛti was projected by me.
And those two created other Prajāpatis and their progeny; therefore, O beloved, that Puruṣa is called the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) in the world.
Having thus created the universe of moving and non-moving beings, he became arrogant; therefore, I severed his head.
Then, out of remorse, I undertook the great vow; henceforth, my hand has held a skull-bowl and I have taken delight in the cremation ground.
Moreover, O Goddess, why is this world, whose nature is a skull-cup, held in my hand? For it is said that the two previously mentioned egg-shells are known as heaven and earth (rodasī).
When Śambhu had spoken thus, and I remained there full of curiosity, thinking "I shall hear it," Pārvatī then spoke further to her husband.
"In how much time will that Puṣpadanta come to us? Having heard this, Maheśvara spoke to the Goddess concerning me:
This piśāca who is seen here is indeed a follower of Vaiśravaṇa; he was a yakṣa named Sthūlaśiras who became his friend.
Having observed that he was joined with that sin, the Lord of Wealth, the master of riches, ordained that he should become a Piśāca in the Vindhya forest.
Then his brother Dīrghajaṅgha, having fallen at his feet, entreated him regarding the end of the curse; thereupon, the Lord of Wealth spoke.
Having heard the Great Tale from Puṣpadanta, who had descended due to a curse, and having related it to Mālyavat, who had likewise attained mortal status through a curse;
"Accompanied by those two hosts, he shall cross over this curse"—thus was the end of his curse ordained here at that time by Dhanada.
"And remember, my beloved, that he is indeed Puṣpadanta; having heard these words of Śambhu, I have come here filled with joy."
"This curse of mine shall last until the arrival of Puṣpadanta"; having said this, Kāṇabhūti ceased speaking at that very moment.
Having remembered his former birth, Vararuci spoke as if waking from sleep: "I am that very Puṣpadanta; hear that story from me."
Having said this, Kātyāyana recounted seven hundred thousand verses and seven great narratives; thereafter, Kāṇabhūti spoke.
O Lord, you are an incarnation of Rudra; who else knows this story? By your grace, that curse has for the most part departed from my body.
Therefore, O Lord, tell me your own life-story from birth onwards; purify me once again, provided that it is not something to be hidden from one such as me.
Then, out of consideration for him who had bowed down, Vararuci related this entire account of his life from birth in full detail.
In Kauśāmbī, there was a twice-born man known by the name Somadatta, also called Agniśikha; his wife was named Vasudattā.
And that daughter of a sage, due to a curse, descended into her; from that best of the twice-born, I was born of her because of that curse.
Then, while I was still very young, my father passed away; my mother, however, remained, rearing me through arduous labors.
Then, on one occasion, two brahmins, dust-covered from a long journey, came to our house for the purpose of staying for a single night.
And as the two of them stood there, the sound of a drum arose; remembering her husband, my mother spoke to me in a faltering voice because of it.
"O son, this dancer Nanda, your father’s friend, is dancing. I too said, "Mother, I shall go to see this."
"I shall show all of that to you as well, along with the recitation. Upon hearing these words of mine, those two Brahmins were filled with wonder.
And my mother said to them both, "O sons, there is no doubt in this matter: having heard it but once, this boy shall indeed retain everything in his heart."
Then, for the sake of inquiry, the Prātiśākhya was recited to me by these two; likewise, I recited it all while they were looking on.
Then, having gone with them and witnessed that very same dance, I returned home and showed it all in its entirety before my mother.
Having ascertained me to be one who retains everything heard only once, one of those two, named Vyāḍi, bowed to my mother and said this story.
O Mother, in the city named Vetasā, there were two brothers, Devaśvāmin and Karambhaka; they were both brahmins and held great affection for one another.
Of those two, this Indradatta was born as the son of one, and I, Vyāḍi, was born as the son of the other; my father then departed for him.
Out of grief for him, Indradatta’s father departed upon the great path; and then, due to that sorrow, the hearts of our two mothers burst asunder.
Therefore, although we possess wealth, we are destitute; desiring knowledge, we have come from there to seek the Prince through ascetic penance.
And while we were established there in asceticism, that Lord commanded us in a dream: "There is a city named Pāṭalika belonging to King Nanda."
"There is a certain brahmin there named Varṣa; from him you two shall obtain the entirety of knowledge. Therefore, you two must go there."
Then we two went to that city, and when we asked there, the people said to us, "There is a foolish Brahmin here named Varṣa."
Then, having traveled that very moment with a mind mounted upon a swing, we two beheld the house of Varṣa in a state of desolation.
It was a dwelling built by mice, dilapidated by the crumbling of its walls, lusterless, and deprived of its roof—like the very field of origin for calamities.
Then, having observed that he was established in meditation within for a year, his two wives approached him and were offered the honors of hospitality.
With a body emaciated and greyish, wearing tattered and soiled garments, she was like his own misfortune personified, having come to him out of love for his virtues.
Then, preceded by a salutation, he reported to her our own account as well as the news regarding her husband's folly that we had heard.
"You two are my sons; what shame is there? Listen, and I shall tell you both this story," having said this, that virtuous woman related this tale to them.
In this city there was an excellent brahmin named Śaṃkarasvāmin; my husband was Upavarṣa, and these two are both his sons.
This man was foolish and poor, while his younger brother was the opposite; therefore, the brother entrusted his own wife to him for the maintenance of their household.
Then, at one point, the rainy season arrived; and during that time, a woman [offered him] a loathsome, secret substance made of flour mixed with molasses.
Having prepared them, they indeed give them to a foolish Brahmin; for when they are given, they remove the distress and fatigue of bathing during both the cold season and the summer heat.
"It is a contemptible custom that they do not accept what has been given; therefore, let this gift, along with its sacrificial fee, be given by me to him as the wife of my brother."
Having taken that, he arrived here; though I rebuked him severely, he was consumed by inner resentment born of his foolishness.
Then he went to the feet of Svāmikumāra; pleased by his asceticism, the latter revealed all the sciences to him.
"Having found a Brahmin who can retain what he hears but once, you shall reveal these [teachings] to him. Thus commanded by him, he has come here with joy.
Having arrived, he reported the entire account to me; since that time, he has remained there, incessantly chanting and meditating.
Therefore, you two should search for and bring back someone who possesses the learning of the scriptures; by that means, the accomplishment of all goals will surely come to pass, without a doubt.
Having heard this from the wife of Dharṣa, they quickly gave her a hundred pieces of gold to eliminate her poverty, and then departed from that city in well-being.
Then we wandered over the earth, yet we did not find anyone anywhere who had mastered the scriptures; consequently, exhausted, we have arrived at your home today.
Your son Bāla has now become a possessor of a single hearing; therefore, give him to us so that we may go for the sake of attaining knowledge, wealth, and supernatural powers.
Having heard these words of Vyāḍi, my mother spoke with respect: "All this is indeed most excellent; I have full confidence in this matter."
For instance, previously, when this only son of mine was born, a disembodied voice clearly arose from the sky in this manner:
This one has been born as Śrutadhara; he will acquire knowledge within a year, and furthermore, he will cause grammar to attain a firm foundation in the world.
"By name he is Vararuci, for whatever may be excellent indeed pleases him"; having said this, Speech ceased.
Therefore, now that this boy has grown, I think day and night about where that preceptor Varṣa might be.
Having learned this today from your own lips, my joy is supreme; therefore, take him away as your brother—what loss is there for you two?
Having heard these words of my mother, Vyāḍi and Indradatta, filled with joy, passed that night as if it were a mere moment.
Then, desiring that I should become worthy of the Vedas, Vyāḍi quickly gave his own wealth for my mother’s festival and brought me back.
Then, having somehow been permitted by my mother, whose tears were suppressed, I took him with me, his entire distress having been quelled by my own resolve.
And considering that youthful favor to be like a flower in bloom, Vyāḍi and Indradatta then departed swiftly from the city.
Then, in due course, having reached my teacher’s house at the end of the year, he regarded me as Skanda himself approaching in bodily form.
On another day, having seated us in front on pure ground, the teacher Varṣa uttered the syllable *oṃ* with a divine voice.
Immediately thereafter, the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences appeared before him; from that point on, he set about teaching us.
I heard it there once, Vyāḍi likewise heard it twice, and Indradatta heard it thrice; thus was the word spoken by the teacher grasped.

Then, having suddenly heard that unprecedented and divine sound, the assembly of brahmins, their inner wonder instantly flashing forth, approached from all sides to see what this could be; with the beauty of their faces resounding with praise, they honored the rain-god with prostrations.
Upon beholding that wonder there, Upavarṣa was not merely overcome by joy; indeed, the entire populace of Pāṭaliputra became immersed in a grand and widespread festival.

King Nanda also, beholding that power of the boon granted by the Son of Giriśa and attaining great satisfaction, he of exalted glory, with due respect, immediately filled the house of Varṣa with riches.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Kathāpīṭha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. Having spoken thus while Vararuci listened with a one-pointed mind, Kāṇabhūti spoke these words once more in that forest:
Once, when some time had passed and the duty of Vedic recitation was completed, we questioned the teacher after he had performed his daily rites regarding the rainy season retreat.
"O teacher, tell me why this city of such a kind has become a sacred field (kṣetra) for both Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī."
Having heard that, he said to us, "Listen to this story: there is a purifying sacred site named Kanakhala at Gaṅgādvāra."
There, by means of the fall of his golden spear, Devadatta caused the Ganges to descend, having split open the plateau of the Uśīnara mountain.
A certain twice-born man from the Deccan was performing austerities there together with his wife, and three sons were born to him right there.
When he had passed away to heaven along with his wife, those sons of his went to the place named Rājagṛha, desiring to acquire knowledge.
And there, having completed their studies, those three, suffering from the misery of being without a protector, went to the Deccan to see the prince, their master.
Having gone there to the city named Ciñcinī on the shore of the ocean, they dwelt in the house of a Brahmin known as Bhojika.
And that Bhojika, having given his three daughters and wealth to them, went to the Ganges for asceticism, being without any other offspring.
Now, while they were living there in their father-in-law’s house, a severe famine caused by drought broke out.
Therefore, having abandoned their virtuous wives, those three departed; for kinship-feelings do not touch the hearts of the cruel.
Then, among them, the middle one became pregnant; thereupon, they took refuge in the house of Yajñadatta, the friend of their father.
There they remained, their conduct distressed as they meditated upon their own husbands; for what noble women would ever abandon the conduct of virtuous wives, even in times of calamity?
In due time, that middle one among them gave birth to a son; and because of their mutual excellence, their affection for him increased.
Once, seeing Maheśvara traveling through the path of the sky with the mother of Skanda seated upon his lap, she spoke to him with compassion:
"O King, behold: even these three women have conceived an affection for this child and harbor the hope that he might bring us back to life."
"Act in such a way that even this child may live," said his beloved; thus addressed, the boon-granting god spoke to her.
"I favor this man first because he, together with his wife, propitiated me; therefore, for the sake of enjoyment, he has been manifested upon the earth."
And she shall be born as the daughter of King Mahendravarman, named Pāṭalī, and she will become his very wife.
Having spoken thus, the Lord addressed those three virtuous women in a dream: "This young son of yours is indeed named Putraka."
Day by day, at the end of his head as he awakens from sleep, there shall be a hundred thousand pieces of gold; and he shall become a king.
Then, when that boy had risen from sleep, those virtuous daughters of Yajñadatta obtained the gold and rejoiced, their vows having borne fruit.
Then, by means of that gold, King Putraka’s treasury soon became full; for the riches of those devoted to austerity are indeed under their own control.
Then once, Yajñadatta spoke privately to his son: "O King, due to the calamity of famine, your ancestors have gone away somewhere."
Therefore, always give to the Brahmins so that they may enter [heaven]; and here I shall tell you this story of Brahmadatta—listen to it.
Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. One night, he saw a pair of swans traveling through the sky.
Shimmering with the luster of gold and surrounded by hundreds of royal swans, it was like a mass of lightning encircled by sudden white clouds.
Then his longing to see him increased so greatly that he no longer found delight anywhere in the pleasures of royalty.
Having consulted with his ministers, that king then had a lake constructed according to his own design, and he granted safety from fear to all living beings.
Then, in the course of time, the king saw those two swans who had arrived; he questioned them, for they were full of confidence, as to the cause of their golden bodies.
Then those two swans, speaking clearly, said to the king: "O lord of the earth, in a former birth we were both born as crows."
And while fighting for the sake of a sacrificial offering in a sacred, deserted temple of Śiva, they both fell down and perished within the hollow of that very spot.
"Then we were born as two golden swans with the memory of our former births. Having heard that, the king was delighted as he gazed upon them according to his desire.
"Therefore, you shall obtain [the desired fruit] from a gift to the ancestors that is not otherwise. Having been told this by Yajñadatta, the young son did exactly so.
Having heard that news of the gift, those twice-born ones arrived; once they were recognized, they obtained supreme fortune along with their wives.
It is a marvel that the innate nature of wicked-souled men—whose intellects are blinded by a lack of discernment—is never abandoned, even when their visible fortunes have vanished.
In due course, those twice-born men, desiring the kingdom and wishing to kill that son, took him away under the pretext of showing him the sights to the Vindhya-dwelling goddess.
Having stationed the executioners within the inner sanctum of the queen's chamber, they said to him: "First, you alone must go inside and look upon the queen."
Then, having entered out of trust, Putraka saw men prepared to kill him and asked, "Why are you killing me?"
"We have been sent by our fathers to give gold," they said; then the wise Putraka spoke to those who were deluded by the goddess.
"I give you this priceless jewel-ornament of my own; release me, for I shall not cause a disturbance here, but will go far away."
Saying "So be it," the executioners accepted that and departed; they spoke falsely before the boy's father, saying, "The son has been killed."

Then those twice-born men, who had been slain while seeking the kingdom, returned; having learned that they were traitors, the ministers turned them back—for how can there be welfare for the ungrateful?
In the meantime, that king, his little son, true to his promise and detached from his own kinsmen, entered the Vindhya forest.
While wandering there, he saw two men intent solely on a wrestling match; he then asked them, "Who are you two?"
"We two are the daughters of the asura Maya, and this wealth belongs to us: this vessel, this staff, and these sandals."
"This is the condition for our battle: whoever is stronger shall take [the prize]. Having heard these words of his, the son laughed and said:
"How much wealth is required for this? they both replied; "By wearing these sandals, one attains the power of moving through the air."
Whatever is written with a stick indeed becomes true; whatever food is thought of in a vessel, that very food remains there.
Having heard that, the son said: "What is the use of fighting? Let this be the wager: whoever is superior in speed while running shall take this."
"So be it," said those two fools, and they ran; he too, having mounted his sandals and taken up his staff and bowl, flew up into the sky.
Then, having traveled a great distance in an instant, he beheld a beautiful city named Ākarṣikā, and there he descended from the sky.
Prostitutes are prone to deception, as are brahmins like my fathers, and merchants are greedy for wealth; in whose house, then, shall I dwell?
Reflecting thus, the king reached a deserted house; within it, he saw an old woman in a dilapidated dwelling.
Having first gratified that old woman with gifts and being honored by her, the son lived there in a dilapidated house, unobserved.
Once, being well-pleased, that old woman said to her son: "I have a concern, my son: that your wife is nowhere suitable for you."
In this place, the king has a daughter, a maiden named Pāṭalī; she is guarded as a jewel within the inner apartments.
As he listened with attentive ear to these words of the old woman, Smara entered his heart by that very same path, having found an opening through it.
Having resolved, "I must see that beloved this very day," he traveled through the sky by means of his two sandals there during the night.
Having entered through a high window at the peak of the mountain, he beheld Pāṭalī sleeping in secret within the inner apartments.
Constantly attended by the moonlight clinging to her limbs, she was like the personified power of the god of love, exhausted from having conquered this entire world.
While he was thinking, "How shall I awaken her?", a watchman outside suddenly called out.
That alone is the fruit for young men in this life: to awaken their beloved while she sleeps in secret, embracing her as she utters sweet murmurs and opens her languid eyes.
Upon hearing this introduction, with his limbs trembling and distressed, he embraced that beloved woman; and then she woke up.
As she watched the king, a mutual conflict arose in her eyes between shame and curiosity as they moved back and forth.
Then, when conversation had taken place and the Gandharva marriage ceremony was completed, the affection of that couple increased, but not the night.
Then, having taken leave of his eager bride with a mind fixed solely upon her, the young man returned to the house of his parents in the western quarter.
While he was thus making his comings and goings there every night, the guards once beheld a sign of sexual enjoyment upon a trumpet-flower tree.
This was reported by them to her father, and he, in turn, appointed a woman to observe secretly within the inner apartments there during the night.
And by her, for the sake of achieving supernatural power (*abhijñāna*) over him who had arrived there, lac-dye was applied to the garment of her sleeping son.
Informed by her in the morning, the king dispatched spies; and by means of those tokens, they found Putraka in the house of the old woman.
Having been brought into the presence of the king, and seeing that monarch enraged, he leaped into the air with his two sandals and entered the Pāṭalī palace.
"O lady, they have been discovered; arise, let us go by means of the sandals. Having thus placed Pāṭalī upon his lap, he then departed through the sky.
Then, descending from the sky near the bank of the Gaṅgā, he gladdened his weary beloved with foods produced by the power of his alms-bowl.
Then, having been entreated by Pāṭalī’s son, who possessed the power of vision, he drew there with his staff a city equipped with a fourfold army.

There, having become that king when great power and truthfulness had been attained, he caused his father-in-law, Śaśākha, to bow before him, [extending his rule] over the earth as far as the ocean's edge.
This very divine city, fashioned by illusion along with its citizens, is therefore known by the name Pāṭaliputra, a field of fortune and eloquence.
Thus, having heard this unprecedented and exceedingly wonderful tale beginning with Varṣamukha, we remained for a long time with our hearts overflowing with wonder and joy, O Kāṇabhūti.

Thus ends the third wave in the Kathāpīṭha-lambaka of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave. Having related this story to Kāṇabhūti while they were within the Vindhya mountains, Vararuci once again described the matter at hand to him.
Thus, dwelling there with Vyāḍi and Indradatta, I gradually reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge as my childhood passed away.
Once, having gone out to witness the festival of Indra, we beheld a maiden who was the bowless weapon of the God of Love.
Then I asked Indradatta, "Who might this woman be? and he replied, "This is Upakośā, the daughter of Upavarṣa."
Recognizing me, she, with a gaze tender with affection, drew my heart toward her even as she proceeded with difficulty to her own home.
Her face was like the full moon, her eyes were like the finest blue lotuses, her arms were as graceful as lotus stalks, and she was radiant with full breasts.
With a neck like a conch shell, beautiful with lips as radiant as coral, she was like another goddess Lakṣmī in the palace of the beauty of King Smara.
Then, my heart having been pierced by the falling arrows of Kama, I had no sleep that night due to my thirst for her bimba-like lips.
Having somehow obtained sleep, I saw at the end of the night a divine woman wearing white garments; she spoke to me.
Your former wife Upakośā, who recognizes your virtues, does not desire any other husband; therefore, my son, you should have no anxiety on this account.
"I am Sarasvatī, always dwelling within your body; I cannot bear to see your suffering," she said, and then vanished.
Then, having awakened and regained my composure, I went slowly and stood beneath a young mango tree near the chamber of my beloved.
Then, having arrived, her friend related to me how Upakośā was experiencing the intense blossoming of the new god of love.
Then, my grief redoubled, I spoke to her thus: "How can I enjoy Upakośā, whom my elders have not given to me of their own accord?"
Death is indeed better than infamy; for if your heart were to be discovered by your elders, it might perhaps lead to some calamity.
"Therefore, do this, O blessed lady: restore life to that friend of mine and to me. Having heard that, she went and reported everything to her friend's mother.
She related that at once to her husband Upavarṣa; he told it to his brother Varṣa, and he in turn rejoiced in it.
When the marriage was settled, Vyāḍi went to Kauśāmbī and, by the command of his teacher Varṣa, brought my mother there.
Then Upakośā was formally bestowed upon me by my father; thereafter, I lived there happily together with my mother and my wife.
Then, in the course of time, the circle of disciples became great; among them, one named Pāṇini was the dullest in intellect.
Wearied by his service and sent away by the wife of Varṣa, he went to the Himalayas for asceticism, distressed and desiring knowledge.
There, having propitiated the Moon-crested Lord with intense austerity, he obtained a new grammar that serves as the gateway to all branches of knowledge.
Then, having arrived, he challenged me alone to a debate; and as our debate proceeded, seven days passed away.
On the eighth day, immediately after he had been conquered by me, Śambhu, standing in the sky, uttered a most terrible *huṃkāra*.
Because of that, our Aindra grammar was lost from the earth; we have all been defeated by Pāṇini, and we have become fools once again.
Then, having conceived a sense of world-weariness, he placed his own wealth for the maintenance of his household into the hands of the merchant Hiraṇyagupta.
Having said that to Upakośā, I went to Śaṅkara on the Himalayas to propitiate him with austerities while remaining without food.
For Upakośā, desiring my welfare, remained in her own palace every day, bathing in the Gaṅgā with her vows strictly observed.
Once, when spring had arrived, she—emaciated, pale, yet beautiful, like the crescent moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight—captivated the eyes of the people.
As she was going to the triple-pathed river to bathe, she was seen by the royal priest, the commander-in-chief, and the prince’s counselor.
At that very moment, they all became targets for the arrows of the God of Love; she too, while bathing on that day, somehow lingered there for a long time.
As she was returning in the evening, the prince’s minister seized her by force; then she, being possessed of great eloquence, spoke to him.
This is agreeable to me, O noble one, just as it is to you and to myself; however, I am born of a virtuous family and my husband is currently away on a journey.
"How might I act in such a way that someone might see me at any time? For then, surely misfortune would befall me along with you."
Therefore, since the citizens will be distracted by the honey-festival, you must certainly come to my house during the first watch of the night.
Having spoken thus and made her promise, she was released by him; but as soon as she had gone a short distance, she was stopped by the priest through the power of destiny.
On that very same day, she likewise arranged a secret rendezvous with him for the second watch of the night.
Having somehow escaped from him as well, she traveled a short distance when the third, the commander of the army, blocked her as she was utterly overwhelmed.
Then, on that very same day, she likewise made an appointment with him for the third watch of the night.
By chance, she was released by him and returned home trembling; there she spoke privately to her own maidservants regarding what must be done.
For a woman of noble family, death is better while her husband is away on a journey than becoming an object for the glances of men who prize their own beauty.
Reflecting thus and remembering me, that virtuous woman passed that night in grief for her own body, without even taking food.
In the morning, she dispatched a maidservant to Hiraṇyagupta’s merchant to seek some wealth for the purpose of honoring the Brahmins.
Having arrived, he too spoke thus to her in private: "Accept me; then I shall give you that which was entrusted to you by your husband."
Having heard that and perceiving the status of her husband’s wealth to be without witnesses, she was tormented by grief and indignation upon seeing the merchant’s wickedness.
On that very night, during its final watch, she made an appointment with him; then, while the remaining watch passed, he arrived.
Then, with many maidservants, he prepared a large quantity of collyrium mixed with oil and combined with musk and other ingredients, which was kept in small jars.
She prepared four pieces of cloth smeared with [sandalwood paste], and a large chest was made, complete with an external bolt.
Then, on that day of the spring festival, during the first watch of the night, the prince’s minister arrived, disguised in grand attire.
When he had entered unobserved, Upakośā said this to him: "I will not touch you unless you have bathed; therefore, bathe and enter within."
Accepting that, the fool was led by female servants into the inner house, which was secluded and filled with darkness.
Having taken from there her inner garments and ornaments, and having given that single piece of cloth for the sake of an undergarment;
From head to foot, upon his limbs, he saw that thick oil and collyrium applied by them in the guise of anointing, as if it were the very sin of the man who did not perceive it.
While they remained there massaging each of his limbs, in the second watch of the night, that priest arrived.
"This priest has arrived as a friend of Vararuci; therefore, let him enter here," said those maidservants to him as he was in that state.
Then, in great haste, they placed the naked minister into a chest, fastened it shut, and secured it from the outside with a bolt.
Under the pretext of bathing, that domestic priest was likewise led into the darkness and stripped of his garments and other belongings by means of massages with oil and collyrium.
The wearer of the rag-robe remained thus infatuated by the maidservants until the third watch, when the chief magistrate arrived.
And because of the sudden fear arising from his arrival, the maidservants likewise placed that priest into a chest, just as they had done with the first one.
Having given him the key, those women brought the commander-in-chief inside under the pretext of bathing; and there, he too was subjected to the rubbing of soot for that same duration.
Deceived as if by another, he was clad only in a single rag of cloth; meanwhile, during the final watch of the night, a merchant arrived there.
Then, having instilled fear by showing him that sight, the magistrate was cast into a chest, and the slave-girls bolted it from the outside.
And those three, as if exerting themselves to escape from the Andhatāmisra hell, did not speak to one another even after obtaining mutual contact within the chest, out of fear.
Then, having offered a lamp in this house and ushered that merchant inside, Upakośā said to him, "Give me back that wealth which was entrusted to you by my husband."
Hearing that and seeing the house empty, that rogue also said: "I have already stated that I will indeed give whatever wealth was deposited by my master."
Upakośā also, making the casket resound, then said: "O deities, hear these words of Hiraṇyagupta."
Having spoken thus and extinguished the lamp, he, like any other merchant, was smeared with collyrium by the maidservants for a long time under the pretext of bathing.
Then, at the end of the night, he was told, "Go; the night has passed," and though he was unwilling, he was driven out from there by them with a forceful grasp of the neck.
Then, clothed in a single tattered garment, smeared with soot, and being bitten by dogs at every step, he reached his own home in deep shame.
There, even as a servant washed that ink, he was unable to stand before him; for the course of ill-mannered conduct is indeed painful.
Then, early in the morning, Upakośā also went to the palace of King Nanda, accompanied by her maidservant, without having informed her elders.
"The merchant Hiranyagupta wishes to seize the wealth deposited with him by my husband," she informed the king herself.
Therefore, in order to ascertain that matter, he had a merchant brought right there; and the merchant declared, "O King, she has nothing whatsoever in my hands."
Then Upakośā said: "O King, I have witnesses; O household deities, my husband was cast into a chest and thrown away."
"In their presence, he has acknowledged this wealth by his own speech; therefore, have that chest brought here and let the deities be questioned by you."
Having heard that, the king, out of wonder, ordered her to be brought; then, in an instant, that casket was brought by many people.
Then Upakośā said: "O deities, speak the truth! Since this merchant has spoken thus, depart now for your own homes."
"If you do not give it to me, I shall kill you all or open the chest. Hearing this, they became terrified and, remaining inside the chest, spoke.
"In our presence, he has admitted that the wealth belongs to us; therefore, being left without a defense, let that merchant surrender it all."
Then, at the king's extreme curiosity, Upakośā was requested, and there the chest was opened and its bolts were broken.
Those men, having been extracted, were like three lumps of darkness; they were recognized with great difficulty by the ministers and likewise by the king.
Then, while everyone was laughing out of curiosity as to what this could be, Upakośā, being questioned by the king, related everything that had happened.
"The conduct of noble women who guard their virtue is inconceivable"—thus did the members of the assembly applaud Upakośā.
Then, having been stripped of all their possessions and found guilty of adultery, they were all banished from the country by the king; for to whose prosperity does immorality lead?
Having said, "You are my sister," and having affectionately given her much wealth, Upakośā was sent away by the king and returned home.
Having learned of this, Varṣa and Upavarṣa congratulated that virtuous woman; and all the people in that city were filled with wonder and smiles.
In the meantime, having performed most intense penance on the Snowy Mountain (Himavat), I propitiated the boon-granting Lord, the husband of Pārvatī.
That very treatise of Pāṇini was thus revealed by him to me; and by his grace alone, it has been brought to completion by me.
Then I returned home, unaware of the fatigue of the journey, overflowing with the nectar of the grace of Him whose crown is adorned with a digit of the moon.
Then, having performed prostrations at the feet of my mother and my elders, I heard there that most wonderful account concerning Upakośā.
Because of that, supreme joy and wonder arose within me, and in that state, natural affection and great respect for him were born.
Then Varṣa desired to hear a new grammar from my mouth; thereupon, that very [grammar] was revealed to him by Svāmikumāra himself.
Then, having been requested regarding the sacrificial fee by Vyāḍi and Indradatta, the teacher Varṣa said, "Let ten million gold pieces be given to me."
Accepting the words of their preceptor, the two of them said this to me: "Come, friend, with the king to request the teacher's fee from Nanda and the others."
"Let us go; we cannot obtain more gold than this from anyone else, for he is the lord of ninety-nine billion."
Because Upakośā was previously made a co-wife by him through his speech, he has now become your brother-in-law; yet, he is won over somewhat by your virtues.
Having thus resolved, the three of us, fellow students, went from Ayodhyā to the camp of King Nanda.
As soon as we had arrived, that king passed away; a great outcry arose throughout the kingdom along with our own despair.
Then Indradatta, who had attained perfection in yoga, said: "I shall now enter the body of this deceased king."
"Let Vararuci be my petitioner; I shall give him gold. And let Vyāḍi protect my body until my return."
Having spoken thus, Indradatta entered the body of Nanda; and when the king was restored to life, a great festival took place there in the kingdom.
At that time, while a snake remained in an empty temple to guard the body of Indradatta, I went to the royal palace.
Having entered and performed a respectful salutation, I offered a teacher’s fee to Yogananda there and requested ten million gold pieces from him.
Then he commanded Satyananda’s minister, named Śakaṭāla, saying, "Cause ten million gold pieces to be given to him."
Seeing life restored to the dead and the immediate attainment of his goal by the seeker, that mantra-master realized the truth; for what indeed is unknowable to the wise?
Having said, "O King, let it be given," that minister reflected: "Nanda’s son is but a child, and the kingdom is full of many enemies."
"Therefore, I shall now protect even his body in such a state. Having thus resolved, he then had all the corpses cremated.
Having searched for him with spies and found him there among them, they dragged Vyāḍi from that temple; he then burned the body of Indradatta.
In the meantime, Śakaṭāla, reflecting deeply, spoke to the king who was hurrying to offer ten million gold pieces.
"All these attendants are standing here with their minds distracted by the festival; let this Brahmin wait for a moment while I give [the gift]."
Then, having approached King Yogananda, Vyāḍi cried out before him: "This twice-born man, established in yoga and whose life-force has not yet departed, is committing an act of sacrilege!"
"Today, at your rise, the corpse of the helpless man was forcibly cremated. Upon hearing that, Yogananda fell into a certain state of profound grief.
When that [gold] had become stable through the burning of his body, the highly intelligent Śakaṭāla emerged and then gave me ten million gold pieces.
Then Yogananda, sorrowful in that solitary place, said to Vyāḍi: "Though I am a Brahmin, I have become a Śūdra; what use is prosperity to me, even if it were stable?"
Having heard that, Vyāḍi comforted him and spoke what was appropriate for the occasion: "You have been discovered by Śakaṭāla; therefore, consider this now."
For this great minister, acting according to his own will, would soon destroy you and instead make Candragupta, the son of the former Nanda, the ruler of the earth.
Therefore, appoint Vararuci as your chief minister, so that by means of his divine insight, your kingdom may become stable.
As soon as Vyāḍi had spoken thus and departed, Yogananda brought her and gave her to me as that very teacher’s fee, having first consecrated her with mantras.
Then I said to that king: "Even though your Brahminhood has been taken away, I do not consider your kingdom to be secure as long as Śakaṭāla remains in his position."
Therefore, when I uttered the mantra, "Destroy him by means of logic," Yogananda cast Śakaṭāla into the depths of a blind well.
Moreover, he cast his hundred sons right there, proclaiming the fault: "This brahmin was burned alive by him."
A single bowl of barley meal and a single bowl of water were placed there daily for Śakaṭāla and his son.
Then he said to his sons: "O sons, even one person might with difficulty subsist on these barley-meals; what talk can there be of many?"
Therefore, let that one who is capable of taking revenge upon Yogananda consume these men along with their water every single day.
"You alone are capable; eat this," his sons said to him; for to the wise, the retaliation against an enemy is dearer even than their own lives.
Then Śakaṭāla, being alone, maintained his livelihood day after day with those waters mixed with barley meal; alas, those who desire victory are cruel.
One who desires their own welfare should not act according to their own whims toward powerful persons, without having understood their minds or gained their confidence.
Thus did Śakaṭāla reflect there, fallen into a blind well, as he beheld the agony of the departure of life from his sons who were tormented by hunger.
Then, as he watched, his hundred sons perished; surrounded by their skeletons, he alone remained alive.
Then Yogananda became firmly established in his empire; subsequently, Vyāḍi approached him and gave a sacrificial fee to his preceptor.
Having approached him, he said: "O friend, may your kingdom remain secure for a long time; you have been bid farewell, for I am going somewhere to perform ascetic penance."
Hearing that, Yogananda, though his throat was choked with tears, said to him: "Enjoy the pleasures of my kingdom; having enjoyed them, do not ever leave me."
Then Vyāḍi said: "O King, what wise person indeed would immerse himself in such things as these—insubstantial bodies that perish in an instant?"
"Fortune does not delude the wise man, for she is like a mirage in the desert"—having said this, he departed at that very moment, resolved upon asceticism.
Then Yogananda returned to his own royal city, Pāṭaliputra; accompanied by me and joined by his entire army, he went there for the sake of enjoyment with Kāṇabhūti.
There, being attended by Upakośā and bearing the burden of ministering to him, I dwelt for a long time, having attained prosperity along with my mother and my elders.

On that day, the celestial river Ganges, pleased by his asceticism, bestowed much gold upon the earth; and Sarasvatī herself, appearing in bodily form, always spoke directly to him regarding his duties.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the Kathāpīṭha-lambaka of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave. Having spoken thus, Vararuci further described this: "In the course of time, Yogananda then fell under the sway of passion and the like."
Like a rutting lordly elephant, he paid no heed to anything; for whom does fortune not delude when she arrives with such sudden descent?
Then I thought: "As long as the king is unrestrained, he will be overwhelmed by the anxiety of state affairs, and my own duty will fall into neglect."
Therefore, it is better that you rescue that ally Śakaṭāla; for if something hostile were done, what could he do while I am present?
Having decided this, I entreated the king, and Śakaṭāla was then pulled out from the blind well; for the twice-born are indeed gentle.
"Since this Yogananda is difficult to conquer while Vararuci remains here, we must adopt the behavior of a reed and wait for the right time."
Having reflected thus, the wise Śakaṭāla, having once again attained the position of minister by my will, performed the affairs of state.
Once, Yogananda, having gone outside the city, beheld in the middle of the Ganges a hand with its five fingers clasped together.
"What is this? he asked me, calling me at that very moment; and I pointed two of my fingers toward that direction.
When that hand had thus disappeared, the king, out of great astonishment, questioned me once more; thereupon, I spoke to him.
"What is there in this world that cannot be accomplished by these five joined together? said that hand, pointing to its five fingers.
Then, O King, these two fingers were shown by me to him, thinking: "When even two [fingers] are joined as one city, what could there be that is impossible?"
When this secret knowledge had been spoken, the king was then thoroughly satisfied; yet Śakaṭāla despaired upon seeing that my intellect was invincible.
Once, Yogananda saw his own queen at the window, looking up with her face turned toward a Brahmin guest.
At that very moment, the king became enraged and ordered the execution of that Brahmin; for envy is indeed the enemy of discernment.
While that brahmin was being led to the execution ground to be slain, even the fish situated in the midst of the marketplace laughed, though its life had departed.
At that very moment, the king, having learned of this, forbade his execution; he also questioned the brahmin regarding the cause of the fish's smile.
Having said, "I shall tell you this after investigation," as I was departing, Sarasvatī herself appeared before me in a secluded spot and spoke thus.
"Stay behind this palm tree at night, unobserved; here you will undoubtedly hear the reason for the fish's laughter."
Having heard that, I went there at night and, standing atop a palm tree, I beheld a terrible rākṣasī who had arrived with her young sons.
To those who were begging for food, she said: "Wait; tomorrow morning I will give you the flesh of a Brahmin, for he has not been killed today."
When asked by them, "Why was he not killed today?", she replied again, "Indeed, upon seeing him, even though dead, the fish laughed here."
When her sons asked her again, "Why did he smile?", that Rākṣasī replied, "All the kings, even the king himself, have fallen into ruin."
"For here in the entire inner palace, men stand in the form of women; yet a Brahmin is being killed despite being innocent"—at this, Timi laughed.
For these transformations indeed occur among all beings who move within the body, when they lose their discernment due to excessive attachment to earthly things.
Having heard these words of hers, I then dismounted from my vehicle and, having arrived, reported the cause of the fish's laughter to the king.
Then, having discovered from the women's quarters that those men were actually women in disguise, the king held me in high regard and released the brahmin from execution.
Having observed such unrestrained behavior of that king, and while I was weary, a new painter once arrived there.
He painted the Great Queen and Yogananda upon a canvas; that painting was as if alive, yet it remained devoid of speech and movement.
The king, being pleased, rewarded that painter with wealth and had him paint that picture on the wall of his bedchamber.
And once, when I had entered that dwelling, that goddess of mine, endowed with every auspicious mark, appeared as if depicted in a painting.
Inferring it from its connection with other characteristics by the power of intuition, I then applied a tilaka-mark upon her at the place of the girdle.
Having thus made her possess all the auspicious marks, I departed; then Yogananda entered and beheld that forehead mark.
And he asked the elders, "By whom was this composed? and they informed him that I was the author of the *Tilaka*.
"No one other than I knows this [mantra] located in the secret place of the Goddess; how then has this Vararuci come to know it?"
"Surely this man has brought about a scandal in my inner apartments; for that very reason he saw those men there in the form of women."
Thus Yogananda reflected, burning with rage: "Alas! Even such conversations arise among fools."
Then, having summoned Śakaṭāla at his leisure, he commanded him: "Vararuci is to be executed by you on account of his destruction of the Queen."
Having said, "I shall do as you instruct," Śakaṭāla went outside and thought, "It will not be possible for me to kill Vararuci."
He possesses the power of divine intellect and is the deliverer from my misfortunes; I shall now accept that secret boon of the Brahmin.
Having thus resolved, Śakaṭāla approached and told the king that his anger was groundless; then, after describing my situation ending in execution, he spoke as follows:
"Having incited someone else against me, I shall kill him; you, however, must remain hidden in my house to protect me from this wrathful king."
Thus, at his word, I remained concealed in his house; and he killed another person during the night in order to report my own death.
When he had thus employed such a stratagem, I then said to him with affection: "Become my sole minister, so that no one else might form the intent to kill me."
This Rākṣasa cannot be slain by me, for he is my friend; as soon as he is thought of, he arrives and, by my will, devours the universe.
"But here, O King, there is a Brahmin named Indradatta who is my friend; he must not be executed by me. Hearing this, the minister said, "Then let that Rākṣasa be shown to me."
Then, through meditation, I caused that Rākṣasa to see me there; and upon seeing me, he became both terrified and astonished.
When that Rākṣasa had vanished, Śakaṭāla asked me again, "How did that Rākṣasa become your friend?"
Then I said: "Previously, while I was wandering through the city for the sake of protection, one lord of the city perished every single night."
Having heard that, Yogananda made me the lord of the city; and while wandering about at night, I saw a Rākṣasa wandering there.
And he said to me, "Tell me, is there any beautiful woman in this city? Hearing that, I laughed and said to him:
"O fool, whichever woman is pleasing to anyone, she shall belong to him. Upon hearing this, he said to me, "By you alone have I been conquered."
After I had escaped from death by answering his question, he spoke to me again: "I am pleased; you are my friend, and I shall remain near you whenever I am remembered."
When he had vanished after saying this, I went back the way I had come; thus did that Rākṣasa, my companion in calamity, become my friend.
Having spoken thus, and being further entreated by Śakaṭāla, I caused him to see the Gaṅgā, who had appeared in bodily form through the power of my meditation.
Pleased by my hymns of praise, that goddess vanished; and Śakaṭāla became my devoted ally.
And once, while I was staying in hiding and distressed, that minister said to me: "Why do you give yourself over to grief, even though you are omniscient?"
Do you not know that the minds of kings delight in acting without deliberation? Yet purity will soon be attained; listen now to how this is so.
In former times, there was a king named Ādityavarman, and he had a minister of great intelligence named Śivavarman.
Once, one of that king's queens became pregnant; having learned of this, the king questioned the guards of the inner apartments as follows:
"Two years have passed since I entered this inner apartment; therefore, tell me now, from where has this conception of a fetus arisen?"
Then they said, "O Lord, there is no entry here for any other man; however, your minister Śivavarman may enter without being hindered."
Having heard that, the king thought: "Surely he is my very own betrayer; and if he were killed openly, public scandal would fall upon me."
Having reflected thus, the Lord Śivavarman sent him by a clever stratagem into the presence of his friend, the vassal Bhogavarman.
Immediately after sending that letter commanding his execution, the king secretly dispatched a messenger there to deliver it.
When seven days had passed after the minister had departed, that queen fled out of fear; she was captured by the guards along with a man in the form of a woman.
Upon learning of this, Ādityavarman was then filled with remorse, thinking: "Why have I caused such a minister to be slain without cause?"
In the meantime, Śivavarman reached the vicinity of Bhogavarman, and that man arrived, carrying the letter.
And having read that letter in private to Śivavarman, Bhogavarman, by the power of fate, informed him of the order for his execution.
Śivavarman, the best of ministers, also said to that feudal lord: "Kill me; otherwise, I shall kill myself by my own hand."
Hearing that, Bhogavarman was filled with astonishment and said to him: "Tell me, O Brahmin, what is this? You are under a curse if you do not speak."
Then the minister said to him: "O King, in whatever land I am killed, for twelve years the god will not send rain upon that country."
Having heard that, Bhogavarman reflected with his ministers: "That wicked king desires the destruction of our country."
For are there not indeed assassins lurking in hiding there? Therefore, this minister must not be killed; he must be protected even from his own death.
Having deliberated thus and provided him with guards, Śivavarman was then dispatched from that country by Bhogavarman in an instant.
Thus, by his own wisdom, that minister returned alive; moreover, his purification was achieved through another means, for dharma does not change otherwise.
"In this way, you too shall attain purification; stay for now in my house, Kātyāyana, and this king as well will come to feel remorse."
Having been addressed thus by Śakaṭāla, I remained concealed in his house, passing those days while awaiting the opportune moment.
Then, at one time, the son of that Yogananda Kāṇabhūti, named Hiraṇyagupta, went out for a hunt.
Having traveled a considerable distance at the speed of a horse, the day passed for him as he remained alone in the forest.
Then, in order to pass that night, he climbed a tree; but in an instant, while still upon it, he was terrified by a lion that had climbed up there as well.
Seeing that prince terrified, he spoke in human speech, saying, "Do not fear; you are my friend," and thus rendered him fearless.
Then, trusting the words of the bear, the prince fell asleep; the bear, however, remained awake, and then the lion spoke.
"Throw this human bear away from me while I am still departing. Thereupon the bear said, "O wicked one, I will not cause my friend to be killed."
When the bear had gradually fallen asleep and the prince was awake, the lion spoke again to that bear: "O man, throw me down!"
Having heard that, although he was thrown by him out of fear for his own life in order to propitiate the lion, the bear did not fall, for he was awakened by destiny.
And he pronounced this curse upon that prince: "You shall become a betrayer of friends and insane," with the condition that it should last until he learned of this very account.
As soon as he reached his own home in the morning, the prince became insane; and Yogananda, seeing that, suddenly fell into despair.
And he said at that time: "If Vararuci were alive now, all of this would be known; shame on my skill in his murder!"
Having heard those words of the king, Śakaṭāla reflected: "Ah! This is the opportune moment to reveal Kātyāyana."
"He would not remain here as one who is proud, nor would he place his trust in me. Having reflected thus, he, having requested immunity from fear, spoke to the king.
"O King, enough with despair; Vararuci remains alive. Thereupon Yogananda said, "Let him be brought here quickly!"
Then I was forcibly brought into the presence of Yogananda by Śakaṭāla, and I beheld that prince in such a state.
"O King, he has committed treachery against his friend," saying this, I related the entire account exactly as it was, through the grace of Sarasvatī.
Then, having been released from that curse, I was praised by the prince; the king asked me, "How did you come to know this?"
Then, O King, I said: "By means of inference from his physical marks, and by intuition, the intellects of the wise perceive everything."
"Just as the mole was known, so too is all this known by me"; at these words of mine, the king became filled with shame and remorse.
Then, disregarding honor and receiving gain through my very purity, I went to my own home; for indeed, moral conduct is the wealth of the wise.
And as soon as I had arrived there, the local people wept before me; then Upavarṣa, approaching me in great agitation, spoke.
Having heard that you were slain, King Upakośā, her body consumed by fire, then caused her mother’s heart to burst from grief.
Hearing that, my consciousness overwhelmed by the sudden onset of a surge of grief, I immediately fell to the ground like a tree broken by the wind.
In an instant, I became a connoisseur of lamentations; for whom does the fire of grief arising from the loss of a dear kinsman not cause torment?
Throughout this cycle of existence, impermanence alone is indeed eternal; knowing this to be the sovereign power of Māyā, why do you still remain deluded?
Having approached me with these words for a year, I was awakened to the truth as it is, and then I somehow regained my composure.
Then, with a heart free from passion and having abandoned all attachments, I, with tranquility as my sole companion, took refuge in a forest of asceticism.
Then, as the days passed, once while I was present, a certain Brahmin arrived from Ayodhyā at that penance grove.
I questioned Yogananda regarding matters of state; having recognized me, he then spoke these words with sorrow.
Listen to what happened to Nanda after you had departed from his presence; having finally gained an opportunity, that Śakaṭāla was there for a long time.
While he was reflecting on a stratagem for the destruction of Yogananda through skillful means, he saw on the road a brahmin named Cāṇakya who was digging the earth.
When he was asked, "Why are you digging the earth? the brahmin then replied: "I am pulling up a blade of darbha grass here, for my foot has been wounded by it."
Having heard that, the minister immediately perceived that the irascible Brahmin, who was firm in his cruel resolve, intended a means for the murder of Yogananda.
Having asked his name, he said to him, "O Brahmin, I shall cause [the offering] to be given to you; I am performing the Trayodaśī Śrāddha at the house of King Nanda."
"A hundred thousand gold pieces shall be yours as a reward; you shall enjoy the foremost position among others. Come now to my house."
Having said this, Śakaṭāla led Cāṇakya to his house; on the day of the *śrāddha* ceremony, he presented him to the king, and the king placed his trust in him.
Then, having gone there, Cāṇakya sat down at the head of the funeral feast (śrāddha), and a brahmin named Subandhu desired that head position for himself.
Having gone there, Śakaṭāla petitioned King Nanda, who said: "No one else is more suitable; let Subandhu stand at the head of the procession."
Having arrived, Śakaṭāla, bowing low out of fear, reported this royal command to Cāṇakya, saying, "I have committed no offense."
Then Cāṇakya, as if blazing with anger on all sides, loosened his topknot and made this vow there:
"Alas, I must certainly destroy this Nanda within seven days; therefore, his topknot must be bound so that he is rendered powerless."
When Yogananda had spoken thus in anger, Śakaṭāla settled him unobserved in his own home as he fled.
When those provisions had been secretly delivered by that very minister, the brahmin Cāṇakya went somewhere and performed a ritual of black magic (kṛtyā).
Then, under its influence, Yogananda contracted a fever with a burning sensation, and when the seventh day arrived, he met his death.
Having slain Hiraṇyagupta and his son Śakaṭāla, he established the fortune of the former Nanda dynasty upon Candragupta.
Having requested Cāṇakya, who was equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, to the office of minister, and having appointed him, that minister attained a sense of fulfillment.
Considering that he had avenged his enmity against Yogananda, and being despondent due to grief for his son, he entered the great forest.
Having heard this from the mouth of that brahmin, and having observed everything as flickering, I became all the more despondent, O Kāṇabhūti.
Out of weariness, I came here to see Vindhyavāsinī; by her grace, having seen you, my former birth has been remembered by me, my friend.
Divine knowledge has been attained by me, and the great narrative has been told to you; now that my curse is exhausted, I shall strive to cast off this body.
And you, meanwhile, remain here until that twice-born man named Guṇāḍhya—accompanied by his disciples and having mastered the three languages—comes into your presence.
For that best of the Gaṇas, named Mālyavat, who was devoted to my side, was likewise cursed by the Goddess out of anger and has come to the state of a mortal, just like me.
This great narrative, spoken by Maheśvara, should be told to him; thereby he shall be liberated from the curse, and he too shall be freed.
Having thus informed Kāṇabhūti there, Vararuci set out for the holy hermitage of Badarikāśrama in order to relinquish his body.
As he was walking along, he then saw a sage eating vegetables by the Ganges; and in the very presence of that ṛṣi, his hand was injured by a blade of kusha grass.
Then, out of curiosity and by his own power, he turned the blood flowing from him into vegetable juice for the purpose of testing [the king's] sense of self-identity.
Seeing that, the sage became filled with pride, thinking, "Aha! I have succeeded. Then Vararuci, as if smiling slightly, said to him:
O Sage, because you were intent on inquiry, I have turned you into one who subsists on vegetables; for as yet, you have not abandoned your egoism.
For on the path of knowledge, egoism is an impassable barrier; and without knowledge, there is no liberation even through hundreds of vows.
But heaven, which is subject to decay, should not distract the minds of those seeking liberation; therefore, O sage, exert yourself in knowledge through the renunciation of the ego.
Having thus instructed the sage, who bowed down and offered him praise, Vararuci departed for that peaceful region of the Badarikā hermitage.

Then, having sought refuge with intense devotion in that Goddess who grants protection, he desired to be released from his mortal state; she too, manifesting her own form, personally taught him the concentration arising from fire for the sake of liberation from the body.

Then, having consumed his body by means of that meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*), Vararuci attained his own divine state; meanwhile, Kāṇabhūti remained in the Vindhya forest, longing for reunion with him who was enriched by all desired virtues.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Kathāpīṭha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave. Then Mālyavat, wandering in the forest in human form under the name Guṇāḍhya, attended upon King Sātavāhana.
After those [languages] beginning with Sanskrit, he vowed three further languages; then, abandoning them with a weary mind, he went to see the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhya mountains.
Having gone there at his command, he beheld Kāṇabhūti; then, suddenly remembering his own former birth, he became awakened.
Resorting to the Paiśācī language, which is distinct from the other three languages, and having caused his own name and that of Kāṇabhūti to be heard, he spoke.
"O friend, quickly tell me the divine story that you heard from Puṣpadanta, by which both you and I may together cross over this curse."
Having heard that, Kāṇabhūti bowed down and, filled with joy, said to him: "I shall tell you the story; however, O Lord, my curiosity is great."
"Please show me your favor by first recounting my life from birth," he requested; thereupon Guṇāḍhya began to speak.
In Pratiṣṭhāna there was a city named Supratiṣṭhita; there lived a certain most excellent Brahmin named Somaśarman.
O friend, he had two sons, Vatsa and Gulmaka, and a third child was born, a daughter named Śrutārthā.
Then, in due course, that Brahmin passed away along with his wife; his two sons remained there, looking after their sister.
Seeing that she had suddenly become pregnant, a suspicion arose between Vatsa and Gulma, as there was no other man present there.
Then she, who had heard the matter and understood their thoughts, spoke to those two brothers: "No suspicion of evil should be entertained; listen, for I shall tell you."
There is a prince named Kīrtisena, the son of the Naga king Vāsuki’s brother; by him I was seen while I had gone to bathe.
Then, overcome by passion, he announced his lineage and name and made me his wife according to the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
Hearing from her sister, "This child of mine is born of a Brahmin," Vatsa and Gulma asked, "What proof is there for this?"
Then, in private, she called to mind that Naga prince; as soon as he was remembered, he arrived and spoke to Vatsagulma.
"This excellent Apsaras, fallen by a curse, was made my wife by me alone; she is your sister, and both of you were likewise cast down to earth by that very curse."
"A son will be born here to your sister-in-law without a doubt; through him, her release from the curse and yours as well shall come to pass."
Having spoken thus, he vanished; then, after a few days, a son was born to Śrutārthā—know me, my friend, to be that very son.
"This Brahmin named Guṇāḍhya has been born as an incarnation of Gaṇeśa"—thus did the voice of Sarasvatī resound from the sky at that moment.
Then, their curse having been exhausted, my mother and maternal uncle passed away in the course of time; and I, for my part, fell into a state of despondency.
Then, casting aside my grief, though I was but a child, I set out for the Deccan on my own initiative to acquire the sciences.
Having attained all branches of knowledge there in due time and having achieved renown, I returned to my own country to demonstrate my own virtues.
And as I entered that city of Supratiṣṭhita after a long time, accompanied by my disciples, I then beheld an indescribable splendor.

In some places, the chanters of the Sāman hymns sang the melodies according to the prescribed rules; in other places, there arose disputes among the Brahmins regarding the determination of Vedic matters.
"He who knows the art of gambling here has the treasure in his hand"—in such deceptive ways did gamblers sometimes praise gambling.
And once, in the midst of some merchants who were each boasting of their own skill in the art of trade, one merchant said this:
How wonderful it is that one who possesses self-restraint attains wealth through riches! Yet, in the past, I attained fortune even without any wealth at all.
Furthermore, while I was still in the womb, my father passed away; and at that time, all of my mother's property was seized by her kinsmen through their wicked deeds.
Then, out of fear of him, she went and remained in the house of Kumāradatta, a friend of her father, protecting her own fetus.
There, I was born as the support for that virtuous woman's livelihood; thereafter, she raised me while performing arduous labors.
Then, having honored my preceptor with that [offering] so humble and destitute, I was gradually instructed in writing and arithmetic as well.
"You are a merchant's son; therefore, my son, engage now in trade. In this country there is a very wealthy merchant named Viśākhila."
"He gives the price for the goods to those who are poor but of noble birth; go and ask him for the price," my mother said to me.
Then I went into his presence, and at that very moment, Viśākhila spoke thus in anger to a certain merchant’s son:
This mouse that is seen here on the ground, its life having departed—even with this as merchandise, a skillful man may acquire wealth.
"Furthermore, O sinner, many dinars were given to you by me; let alone their increase, even those were not protected by you."
Having heard that, I immediately said to Viśākhila: "I have accepted this mouse from you as payment for the goods."
Having said this, I took the mouse in my hand, drew its likeness upon a panel, and departed; that merchant, too, laughed.
For the price of two handfuls of chickpeas, I gave that mouse to a certain merchant for the sake of his cat.
Having roasted those chickpeas and taken a water jar, I went to the crossroads outside the city and stood there in the shade.
There, to the group of wood-carriers who had arrived exhausted, I respectfully offered cool water and those chickpeas.
Each wood-seller joyfully gave me two pieces of wood; I took those logs and sold them at the market.
Then, having purchased those chickpeas for a small price, I likewise brought wood from the wood-sellers on the following day.
Having done this every day and obtained payment in the prescribed order, she purchased all the wood from the woodcutters over the course of three days.
Then, when the cutting of the wood was unexpectedly brought to completion by heavy rains, I sold that timber for many hundreds of paṇas.
Using that very wealth as capital for trade and engaging in commerce through my own skill, I have gradually become a man of great fortune.
Having fashioned a golden mouse, I presented it to Viśākhila; he, in turn, gave his own daughter to me.
