For this very reason, she is well-known in this world by the name "Mouse"; thus has this Lakṣmī been obtained by me, though I am destitute of wealth.
Having heard that, the other merchants there were filled with wonder: "Why does the intellect not marvel at this, as if it were a painting executed on a wall?"
Once, a certain twice-born man who had received eight gold māṣas as a gift was addressed by someone who was mostly a Vaiśya: "Who is this Chāndoga?"
"Since you have food due to your status as a Brahmin, that much is yours; however, for the sake of worldly affairs, let this cleverness be learned by you through gold."
When that simpleton asked, "Who will teach me? he replied, "Go to the house of this courtesan named Caturikā."
When the Brahmin asked, "What shall I do there? the rogue replied: "Having given gold, you should employ some conciliation to win her over."
Having heard this, the singer of the Sāmaveda went quickly to Caturikā’s house; having entered there, he sat down after being welcomed by her.
"Teach me now this very day the ways of the world," he said, and as he spoke thus, the brahmin handed over the gold to her.
Then, while the people standing there were laughing, he reflected for a moment and, having joined his palms together with the fingers extended like cow-ears, formed the *sāraṇa* seal.
The dull-witted man sang the *sāman* chant in such a loud voice that rogues, eager to see a spectacle of mockery, gathered there.
And they said, "This is a jackal; how else could he have entered here? Therefore, let a crescent-shaped mark be quickly placed upon his neck."
Thinking the arrow to be a crescent moon and fearing the severing of his head, he departed from there, roaring, "I am well-trained in the ways of the world!"
He then went into his presence, by which he had been sent; he related the news to him, and he in turn spoke to him.
I have spoken these words of conciliation to you; what occasion is there here for the Veda? For indeed, what a profound dullness has taken hold in a person who is benumbed by the Veda!
Having laughed and gone there, he said to that wanton woman: "Give up those golden grasses for this two-footed beast."
Having obtained the gold that had been dropped by her as she laughed, that twice-born man returned home, considering himself as if born again.
Beholding such wonders at every step, I reached the royal palace, which resembled the abode of Mahendra.
Then, having entered within, I was announced by my disciples; I beheld King Sātavāhana seated in his assembly hall.
Surrounded by his ministers, headed by Śarvavarman, he sat upon a jeweled lion-throne like Vāsava among the immortals.
Then, as I sat upon the seat having performed the svastika gesture and was being shown honor by the king, Śarvavarman and the others offered their praises.
"O King, this man is renowned on earth as one proficient in all branches of knowledge; for this reason, his name is truly 'Guṇāḍhya' (Abundant in Virtues)."
Having seen such praise of him, Sātavāhana was delighted; immediately honoring me, he appointed me to the office of minister by his counselors.
Then, having taken a wife, I lived there happily, reflecting on matters of state and instructing my disciples.
Once, while wandering at my leisure on the bank of the Godāvarī out of curiosity, I beheld a garden renowned as Devīkṛti.
Beholding that exceedingly beautiful place, which was like the Nandana grove descended to earth, I then questioned the garden-keeper regarding its origin.
And he said to me, "Master, it is heard from the elders that in former times a certain silent Brahmin arrived here while fasting."
He created this divine garden together with the celestial abodes; then all the brahmins gathered there, filled with curiosity.
Being questioned by them with persistence, that twice-born man told his own story: "There is here a district called Bharukaccha on the bank of the Narmadā."
I was born as a brahmin in that [place], and formerly, because I was poor and lazy, no one gave me even almsfood.
Then, out of weariness, having abandoned my home and become disenchanted with life, I wandered through sacred fords and went to see the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhyas.
Then, having seen that goddess, I thought to myself: "The world propitiates this granter of boons with the sacrifice of animals."
"Having resolved, 'I myself shall slay this foolish beast here,' I took up a weapon to cut off its head."
At that moment, the goddess herself, being pleased, spoke to me: "Son, you have attained success; do not kill yourself, stay by my side."
Thus, having obtained the boon from the Goddess, I attained divinity; from that time forth, both my hunger and thirst have vanished.
Then, on one occasion, the Goddess herself commanded me as I stood there: "Go, my son, and construct an excellent garden in Pratiṣṭhāna."
Having said this, she herself gave me a divine seed; then, by her power, I came here and created this beautiful garden.
"And this must be protected by you," he said, and then he vanished; thus, O Lord, was this garden created by the Goddess in the past.
Having heard of the goddess's grace in that region from Udānapāla, I returned home filled with wonder.
When Guṇāḍhya had spoken thus, Kāṇabhūti said: "O Lord, why was his name Sātavāhana?"
Then Guṇāḍhya said: "Listen, I shall tell you this: there was a king renowned as Dīpakarṇi, possessed of great prowess."
He had a wife named Śaktimatī, who was dearer to him than his own life; once, while she was sleeping in a garden at the end of lovemaking, a serpent bit her.
When she had passed away, the king, whose mind was fixed upon her, took up the vow of celibacy, even though he was childless.
Then, on one occasion, the Blessed One whose crest is the moon appeared to him in a dream while he was grieving over the absence of a son worthy of the kingdom, and commanded him as follows:
While wandering in the forest, you will see a young boy mounted upon a lion; taking him, go home, for he shall become your son.
Then, having awakened from that dream, the king rejoiced; and once, out of a passion for the hunt, he went to a distant forest.
There at midday, that king beheld upon the shore of a lotus lake a boy mounted on a lion, possessing the splendor of the sun.
Then the king, remembering his dream, struck with a single arrow that lion which had set down the boy and was longing for water.
Having cast off that lion's body, he immediately assumed a human form; and when asked by the king, "Alas! Tell me, what is this?", he replied:
"O King, I am a Yakṣa named Sāta, a friend of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). Previously, while bathing in the Gaṅgā, I beheld a daughter of the Ṛṣis."
She too, upon seeing me, became filled with passion, as did I; then, by the Gāndharva rite, she was made my wife by me.
And his kinsmen, having learned of that, cursed both her and me in their wrath, saying: "O wicked ones, you two shall become lions who act according to your own will."
The sages fixed the end of her curse at the birth of a son; for me, however, it shall end immediately thereafter with the strike of your arrow.
Then we were born as a pair of lions; in the course of time she became pregnant, and when this son was born, she passed away.
And this one was raised by me on the milk of other lionesses; today, struck by your arrow, I am liberated from my curse.
Therefore, accept this son given by me, O Great Being; for this purpose was ordained long ago by those very sages.
When that Guhyaka named Sātana had vanished after saying this, the king took the boy and returned home.
Because he was carried [in his arms] by Sāta, he therefore gave him the name Sātavāhana; and in due course, he established him in the kingdom.
Then, when that lord of the earth had departed for the forest, this King Sātavāhana became a sovereign ruler of the whole world.
Having spoken thus in the midst of the conversation at the request of Kāṇabhūti, the wise Guṇāḍhya, recollecting the original subject matter, spoke again.
Then, on one occasion during the festival of the spring season, King Sātavāhana visited that garden which had been prepared by the Goddess.
Having dwelt there for a very long time like Mahendra in the Nandana grove, he descended into the water of a lotus pond to sport, accompanied by his beloved.
There his beloveds playfully sprinkled him with handfuls of water, and he was sprinkled by them in turn, like an elephant by female elephants.
The women greeted him with faces whose eyes were copper-red from washed kohl and moistened by the waters of the Jahnu, and with limbs where the contours were revealed by clinging garments.
He made those beloved creepers dwelling in the midst of the forest—whose leaf-marks were blossoming and whose ornaments had fallen away—as if they were women with flowers for their jewelry.
Then one of that king’s queens, languid from the weight of her breasts, her limbs as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, became exhausted while playing.
Unable to endure the king sprinkling her with water, she said, "O Lord, strike me instead with sweetmeats!"
Having heard that, the king quickly had many sweetmeats brought; then, laughing, the queen spoke thus once more.
"O King, what occasion is there here for sweets within the water? 'Do not sprinkle me with water,' indeed, this is what was said by me to you."
"You do not understand the mere connection between the word 'mā' and the word 'udaka', nor do you grasp the context; how can you be such a fool?"
Thus addressed by her, the king, who was learned in the science of grammar, was instantly overcome with internal shame as his attendants laughed.
Having abandoned his water-sports and being instantly stripped of pride, he entered his own palace feeling humiliated and devoid of all distinction.
Thereupon, lost in thought and bewildered, he turned his back on eating and other such activities; like one depicted in a painting, he did not say anything at all, even when questioned.
Reflecting, "Shall I take refuge in scholarship, or shall it be death?", he became filled with anguish, having abandoned his bedchamber.
Then, seeing the king in such a state all of a sudden, the entire retinue became bewildered, wondering, "What is this?"
Then Śarvavarman and I gradually came to know her; meanwhile, the day was almost coming to an end.
Reflecting at that moment that the king was not in good health, we summoned the royal servant named Rājahaṃsa.
Being thus questioned, he spoke these words regarding the king's condition: "O King, never before has Your Majesty been seen so dejected."
"The other queens, filled with intense anger, said, 'He has been rendered utterly embarrassed by that daughter of Viṣṇuśakti, who is a false scholar.'"
Having heard this from the mouth of that royal servant, I became dejected and, with Śarvavarman as my companion, thought thus out of doubt: "Alas!"
If there were a disease of the king, physicians would enter; or if there were an internal anxiety for him, no other cause would be found therein.
For in his kingdom, which has been cleared of all thorns, there is indeed no adversary; these subjects are devoted, and no decline is observed.
"Why does such distress come suddenly upon the Lord?"—when this was thus reflected upon, the wise Śarvavarman spoke as follows.
I know that this king’s anger arises from the remorse of his own folly; for he always desires wisdom, thinking, "I am a fool."
"I had already perceived this intention of his long ago; I have now heard that he has been insulted by the queen for that very reason."
Having thus deliberated with one another and passed that night, we two went in the morning to the palace of the lord of the earth.
There, although entry was blocked for everyone, I somehow managed to enter; and after me, Śarvavarman followed with quick steps.
Then, having sat down near him, I addressed the king: "O Lord, why do you remain despondent without cause?"
Even after hearing that, Sātavāhana remained silent just as before; then Śarvavarman spoke these wonderful words:
"O King, you previously told me that I might hear something from someone; therefore, today at night, I created the dream-brahmin."
Then, in a dream, I saw a lotus fallen from the sky, and it was opened by some divine youth.
Then a divine woman, clad in white garments, emerged from that [lotus]; and immediately thereafter, O King, she entered your mouth.
Having seen this much, I have awakened; I believe that Sarasvatī herself has undoubtedly entered directly into the mouth of the Lord.
When Śarvavarman had thus reported his dream, Sātavāhana, breaking his silence at that very moment, spoke to me with significant intent:
"Tell me this: through what duration of time and with what effort does a man, while training, attain proficiency?"
Indeed, without him, this splendor does not appear beautiful to me; for what use are riches to a fool, like ornaments upon a piece of wood?
Then I said, "O King, grammar is always known by men as the gateway to all branches of knowledge within twelve years."
"But I shall teach you that, O Lord, in six years. Upon hearing this, Śarvavarman is said to have suddenly replied with envy:
"How could a person accustomed to comfort endure such hardship for so long? Therefore, O King, I shall instruct you in that within six months."
Upon hearing this incredible thing, I said to him in anger: "If the god has been trained by you in six months, then he shall be trained by me."
Likewise, Sanskrit, Prākṛta, and the regional dialects—these three languages that exist among human beings are always abandoned [by him].
Then Śarvavarman said: "If I do not do this, then for twelve years I shall carry your sandals upon my head."
When he had spoken thus and departed, I too went home; and the king, considering that success was achieved on both fronts, became reassured.
And Śarvavarman, rendered helpless and filled with remorse as he beheld that difficult vow, related everything to his wife.
She too, being distressed, said to him: "O Lord, in this calamity, no other way of escape is seen for you except through the young master."
Having made this resolve, saying "So be it," Śarvavarman, abstaining from food, set out for that very place during the final watch of the night.
Having learned this from the mouth of a spy, I reported it to the king in the morning; and he, having heard it, reflected, "What could this be?"
Then the prince named Siṃhagupta said to him affectionately: "O King, when you were distressed, I then felt great despondency."
Then, for the sake of attaining spiritual welfare, I went outside this city and began to cut off my own head before the goddess Caṇḍikā.
"Do not do this; the king's wish will surely be fulfilled"—thus a voice from the sky then restrained me, and I think that therefore you shall have success.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, Siṃhagupta then quickly dispatched two spies after Śarvavarman.
Subsisting solely on air, maintaining silence, and firm in his resolve, he eventually reached the presence of Śarvavarman, the prince’s own preceptor.
Pleased there by his asceticism that was indifferent to the body, Kārttikeya granted him his heart's desire.
Then, having arrived before the king, Udaya was reported by the two spies dispatched by Siṃhagupta as being Śarvavarman.
Upon hearing that, both dejection and joy arose within me and the king, like those of a cloud-watching swan and a cātaka bird respectively.
Then Śarvavarman, having arrived and possessing the supreme accomplishment of Kumāra, bestowed all the sciences upon the king, which appeared as soon as they were thought of.
And they appeared before King Śātavāhana at that very moment; for what indeed might the grace of the Supreme Lord not accomplish?

Then, upon hearing of the king's acquisition of all branches of knowledge, a great festival took place throughout the delighted kingdom; even the banners fluttering in the wind and dancing at that moment seemed to perform a fixed dance within every dwelling.

Then King Śarvavarman was honored with heaps of jewels worthy of a monarch by that king who had prostrated himself, calling him his "guru"; and he was made the lord of the territory named Marukaccha, situated on the banks of the Narmadā.

The king, who had previously heard of Siṃhagupta’s attainment of the boon of the Six-faced One through the practice of *cāramukha*, was delighted and made him equal to himself in splendor; likewise, he personally and affectionately consecrated that queen, the daughter of Viṣṇuśakti, as the cause for the acquisition of the sciences (*vidyā*) over the other queens.

Thus ends the sixth wave in the Kathāpīṭha-lambaka of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Seventh Wave. Then, having observed a vow of silence, I approached the presence of the king. There, a certain Brahmin recited a verse he had composed himself:
And the king himself explained it in perfectly refined speech; and the people standing there, having seen it, became filled with joy.
Then King Śarvavarman spoke with humility to him: "Tell me yourself, O Lord, how you have bestowed your favor upon me."
Having heard that favor from the king, Śarvavarman spoke: "O King, I then departed from here, abstaining from food and observing silence."
Then, when only a short distance remained on the path, emaciated by intense asceticism and exhausted, I fell unconscious upon the surface of the earth.
"Arise, my son! Everything shall be accomplished for you"—thus did a man with a spear in his hand clearly approach me and speak those words at that time.
At that moment, as if sprinkled by a shower of nectar, I awoke and became free from hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions, feeling as if restored to health.
Then, having reached the presence of the deity, overwhelmed by the weight of devotion, I bathed and entered his inner sanctum with an agitated mind.
Then, by that Lord Skanda, an audience with me was granted within; thereupon, Sarasvatī herself entered my mouth in embodied form.
Then the Blessed One, manifesting with his six lotus-like faces, uttered the aphorism: "The collection of phonemes is established."
Upon hearing that, alas, out of the fickleness natural to human beings, I myself inferred the subsequent Sūtra and spoke it.
Then that god said to me: "If you had not spoken yourself, this treatise would have been a subverter of Pāṇini's work."
Now, because it will be a very concise treatise, it shall be known as the Kātantra; likewise, it shall be called the Kālāpaka after the name of my mount, Kalāpa.
Having spoken thus and having revealed that new and concise science of grammar, the Lord himself addressed me once more in this way.
That king of yours was also a sage in a previous birth; he was a disciple of the sage Bharadvāja, known by the name Kṛṣṇa, and possessed of great ascetic power.
Beholding a certain hermit maiden whose longing was equal to his own, he suddenly experienced the sensation of being struck by the arrows of the flower-bowed god.
Therefore, having been cursed by the sages, he has now descended here; and that daughter of the sage has likewise descended into the state of being his queen.
Thus, this King Sātavāhana is an incarnation of a ṛṣi; once you have been seen by him, he will surely attain all branches of knowledge through your grace.
For the supreme goals of great-souled beings are obtained without affliction; they are accomplishments projected by vast formative forces acquired in other lifetimes.
When the deity had vanished after saying this, I went outside; there, rice was given to me by those who subsist upon the deity.
Then I returned, O King; and those rice grains remained exactly as many on my path even as they were being consumed day after day.
When Śarvavarman had thus related his own story and ceased speaking, King Sātavāhana rose up, filled with joy, to bathe.
Then, because I had observed a vow of silence and was thus excluded from ordinary discourse, I addressed the king—who was unwilling to do so—with a mere salutation.
Having departed from that city accompanied by his two disciples, he set his mind on asceticism and came to see the goddess Vindhyavāsinī.
Then, dispatched by that very goddess according to her command in a dream, I entered this terrifying Vindhya forest in order to see you.
Having somehow reached a caravan by chance on account of the words of a Pulinda, I arrived here and beheld these very many Piśācas.
Having overheard their conversation from afar, I learned this language of the Piśācas, which is the means for breaking my vow of silence.
Having approached her after hearing that you had gone to Ujjayinī, I waited for her until your arrival.
"Having seen you and offered a welcome in the fourth language of spirits, I remembered my past birth; such is the account of my life in this present existence."
When Guṇāḍhya had spoken thus, Kāṇabhūti said to him: "Listen now to how your arrival was known by me this very night."
"I have a friend named Bhūtivarma, a Rākṣasa with divine vision; I went to Ujjayinī, which was his abode, to visit him in his garden."
There, when questioned by me regarding the end of his own curse, he said: "He has no power by day; stay here, and I shall tell you at night."
Saying "So be it," I remained there; and when night had fallen, I asked those leaping spirits about the cause of their joy in the course of conversation.
"Listen; I shall tell you that which was spoken by Śaṅkara in a former dialogue with Viriñca. Having said this to me, Bhūtivarmā then spoke.
During the day, these yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas have no power, being overwhelmed by the brilliance of the sun; therefore, they rejoice at night.
Where the gods are not worshipped, nor the Brahmins as is their due, and where food is consumed even against the rules—it is there that these [spirits] prevail.
Whether they are abstainers from meat or virtuous women, these beings do not go here or there; they are never overcome by those who are pure, brave, and awakened.
Having said this, Bhūtivarmā spoke to me again at that time: "Go; Guṇāḍhya has arrived, and he is the cause of your release from the curse."
Having heard this, O Lord, I have come here and you have been seen by me; I shall now relate to you that story told by Puṣpadanta.
However, I have one curiosity; let it be told for what reason he is renowned as Puṣpadanta and you as Mālyavān.
Having heard this from Kāṇabhūti, Guṇāḍhya said to him: "On the banks of the Gaṅgā there is a royal grant (agrahāra) named Bahusuvarṇaka."
There lived a learned Brahmin named Govindadatta; his wife was Agnidattā, who held her husband as a deity.
In time, that twice-born man begot five sons upon her; they were handsome and full of pride, yet they were fools.
Then a guest arrived at the house of Govindadatta, a Brahmin named Vaiśvānara, who was like another Vaiśvānara (Fire).
At that moment, while Govindadatta was standing even outside his house, he approached his sons and offered them his salutation.
They offered him a greeting with nothing more than a laugh; thereupon, the twice-born man began to depart from that house in anger.
Then, when Govindadatta had arrived, that best of brahmins, though thus enraged and entreated, spoke as follows when questioned.
"Your sons are fallen fools; because of association with them, you too have become so. Therefore, I will not eat in your house, for otherwise I would require an expiation."
Then Govindadatta spoke to him after taking an oath: "I shall never even touch these wicked sons."
His wife, who was fond of guests, likewise approached him and spoke; then, with some difficulty, Vaiśvānara accepted hospitality there.
Having seen that, Devadatta, the only son of Roviṃdadatta, then became filled with remorse due to his cruelty.
Then, perceiving his life to be useless and defiled by his parents, he became filled with world-weariness and, desiring to propitiate Umāpati, set out for asceticism.
Then, first subsisting on leaves and subsequently subsisting on smoke, he remained for a long time in asceticism, seeking to gratify the Lord of Umā.
And Śambhu, won over by his intense austerity, granted him a vision; he, in turn, chose as a boon from the Lord the status of being his very attendant.
"Obtain the sciences and enjoy pleasures upon this earth; thereafter, everything desired by you shall come to pass"—thus Śambhu commanded him.
Then, having gone to the city of Pāṭaliputra as a seeker of knowledge, he attended upon a teacher named Vedakumbha according to the prescribed rites.
Once, while he was staying there, the teacher’s wife, afflicted by passion, spoke to him impetuously—alas, how fickle are the mental states of women!
Having abandoned that region, Devadatta, his agitation caused by the god of love subsided, set out for Pratiṣṭhāna without delay.
There, having requested the aged preceptor named Mantrasvāmin, who was accompanied by his aged wife, he thoroughly studied the sciences.
And there the king’s daughter beheld that fortunate youth named Suśarman, who had completed his studies, just as the goddess Śrī beholds Acyuta.
He too beheld that maiden standing above the window, moving in her celestial chariot like the presiding deity of the moon.
As if bound together by her gaze, which was like the fetters of Māra, both of them became unable to move away.
Then, with one finger as if it were the personified command of the God of Love, the princess signaled to him, "Come near here."
Then he went from the inner apartments into her presence, and she, taking a flower, threw it at him with her teeth.
Not understanding this secret designation devised by the princess, he went to the house of his preceptor, bewildered as to what ought to be done.
He rolled there upon the ground, unable to say anything, burning within with anguish, mute like one who has been scolded by his master.
Having reflected upon the signs born of desire, the wise preceptor questioned him by some means or other with logical reasoning, and he related everything exactly as it had occurred.
Having understood that, the teacher Vidagdha spoke these words to him: "By her letting fall a flower with her tooth, she has given you a sign."
"Having come to that divine abode called Puṣpadanta, which is rich with flowers, you should wait there; now, you may depart."
Having heard this, that youth, whose purpose was now understood through his knowledge, abandoned his grief; then, having gone inside the temple, he remained there.
On the eighth day as well, the princess went there alone to see the deity, and then she entered the inner sanctum.
Then, behind the door-panel, her beloved was seen by her; and having seized him, he suddenly rose up and embraced her around the neck.
When she asked, "Citra, how did you know that she was Saṃjñā? he replied, "She was recognized by my teacher, not by me."
Saying, "Release me! You are unrefined," the princess then departed from that spot in an instant, out of anger and fear that her secret counsel had been betrayed.
He too, having gone to a secluded place and remembering his beloved who had vanished from sight, Devadatta lived on only by the threads of life that were slipping away due to the fire of separation.
Having seen him in such a state, Śambhu, who was already well-disposed, commanded the Gaṇa named Pañcaśikha for the sake of accomplishing his desired goal.
Having arrived and comforted him, that leader of the Gaṇas caused him to assume the dress of a woman, while he himself took on the form of an elderly Brahmin.
Then, having gone with him to King Suśarman, the father of that Sudṛś, the leader of the Gaṇas spoke to him.
"My son has gone away somewhere; I am going to search for him. Therefore, O King, let this daughter-in-law of mine be protected by you now as my entrusted deposit."
Having heard that, Suśarman, fearing a curse, took the youth and established him as a woman in his own secret inner apartments for women.
Then, after Pañcaśikha had departed, that brahmin, dwelling within his beloved’s inner apartments in female attire, became an object of her complete trust.
And once, being eager, she revealed herself to him at night, and he married that daughter of the king by the secret Gāndharva rite.
And while she was carrying the fetus, that best of attendants, having arrived at night as soon as he was thought of, carried the brahmin away unobserved.
Then, having quickly removed that female attire from the youth, Pañcaśikha in the morning became once more a Brahmin in form, just as before.
Having gone along with him, he addressed King Suśarman: "O King, my son has arrived today; therefore, give me your daughter-in-law."
Then that king, having learned that she had fled somewhere during the night, was agitated by the fear of her curse and said this to his ministers:
"This is not a Brahmin; he is some deity who has come to deceive me, for such occurrences happen constantly in this world."
And likewise, in former times there was a king named Śibi, an ascetic devoted to compassion, a donor, steadfast, and one who granted fearlessness to all sentient beings.
Then Indra, in order to deceive him, himself assuming the form of a hawk, swiftly swooped down upon Dharma, who had taken the illusory form of a pigeon.
And the pigeon, having fled out of fear, took refuge in the lap of Śibi; then the hawk, speaking in human speech, addressed that king.
"O King, release this pigeon, my food, for I am hungry; otherwise, know me to be dead, and what dharma would accrue to you from that?"
Then Śibi said to him, "This one has come to me for refuge; he must not be abandoned. Therefore, I shall give you other meat equal to this."
The hawk said, "If it is so, give me your own flesh. Then, being greatly delighted, the king consented, saying, "So be it."
And as the king continued to cut off his own flesh and place it upon the scale, the pigeon grew increasingly heavier on the balance.
Then the king placed his entire body upon the scale; "Excellent! Excellent!"—then this divine voice arose: "But this [body] is lighter."
Then Indra and Dharma, having abandoned their forms as the hawk and the pigeon, praised King Śibi whose body remained uninjured and restored him to his original state.
Having granted him other boons as well, those two vanished; likewise, this must be some god who has come here desiring to test me.
Having thus spoken privately to his ministers, King Suśarman, bowing low in fear, addressed that foremost of the Gaṇas who was in the form of a Brahmin.
"Grant me safety this very day; your daughter-in-law has been lost in the night. Though guarded day and night, she has gone away somewhere by means of illusion."
Then, with great difficulty and as if out of compassion, the attendant in the form of a brahmin said: "In that case, O King, give your own daughter to me as a son."
Having heard that, the king, fearing a curse, gave his own daughter to Devadatta; thereafter, Pañcaśikha departed.
Devadatta, having once again obtained that beloved wife in public, flourished amidst the splendors of his father-in-law, who had no other son.
In due time, having consecrated his son named Mahīdhara and his grandson in the kingdom, Suśarman retired to the forest.
Then, having seen the sovereignty of his son and feeling his purpose fulfilled, Devadatta retired to the penance grove together with that princess.
There, having propitiated Śambhu and cast off his mortal body, he attained the status of a Gaṇa through His very grace.
Because he did not recognize the name [of his wife] from the flower dropped from her teeth, he consequently became known as Puṣpadanta in the assembly of the Gaṇas.
And his wife became the queen's female door-keeper, named Jayā; thus was he known as Puṣpadanta—now hear my own story.
I was formerly the son named Somadatta of that very brahmin who was known as Govindadatta, the father of Devadatta.
Driven by that very same indignation, I went to the Himalayas and performed austerities, constantly gladdening Śaṅkara with many garlands.
In that very manner, when the moon-crested Lord had manifested himself in his gracious form, I, desiring no other enjoyment, chose to become one of his attendants.
"Since I have been honored by you with a garland gathered from the ground of a difficult forest, you shall become my attendant named Mālyavān"—thus did the Lord, the husband of Girijā, instruct me.
"Then, having suddenly cast off my mortal body, I attained that meritorious state of being his attendant. Thus, by the grace of Dhūrjaṭi, was this name "Mālyavat" bestowed upon me.

Thus, O Kāṇabhūti, alas, I have returned here today to human form by the curse of the Daughter of the Mountain; therefore, tell me now the story told by Hara, by which the affliction of our curse may be pacified.

Thus ends the seventh wave in the Kathāpīṭha book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Eighth Wave. In this manner, according to the words of Guṇāḍhya, that divine story consisting of seven tales was then narrated by Kāṇabhūti in his own language.
And in that very same way, Guṇāḍhya composed it in seven years, consisting of seven hundred thousand verses, in that Paiśācī language.
Thinking that the Vidyādharas had stolen this [poem], that great poet wrote it out with his own blood in the forest, because of the lack of ink.
And likewise, with the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others who had come to listen, the sky there became so densely crowded that it was as if covered by a canopy.
Upon seeing that great tale composed by Guṇāḍhya, Kāṇabhūti was released from his curse and returned to his own state.
Even the piśācas who were there, and others who were his companions, they all reached heaven after hearing that divine tale.
"This *Bṛhatkathā* of mine must find a firm footing on earth; this purpose was also declared by the Goddess when she spoke of the end of my curse."
"Therefore, how can I bring her here? To whom, first of all, shall I entrust her? Thus did the great poet Guṇāḍhya reflect there.
Then two disciples, one named Guṇadeva and the other named Nandideva, both following after him, spoke to that preceptor.
The sole recipient for the offering of that poem is the illustrious Sātavāhana; for a connoisseur carries poetry just as the wind carries the fragrance of flowers.
"So be it," said Guṇāḍhya; and giving the book to those two virtuous disciples, he sent them into the presence of that king.
And having gone there himself, outside the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, he stayed in a garden prepared by the Goddess, where he had made an appointment.
And having gone with the two disciples, they showed that manuscript of the poem to King Sātavāhana, saying, "This is the work of Guṇāḍhya."
Having heard that speech of the Piśāca and having seen those two of such appearance, the king, out of pride in his own learning and with feelings of envy, spoke as follows.
The Paiśāca language consists of seven hundred thousand measures; its speech is sapless. The arrangement of syllables is done with blood—fie on this story of the Piśācas!
Then, taking the book and returning by the same way they had come, they related everything that had occurred to their two disciples, who were rich in virtue.
Even Guṇāḍhya, upon hearing that, immediately fell under the sway of grief; for who indeed, when treated with contempt by one who knows the truth, does not suffer within?
Then, having gone not very far from there with his disciples to a mountain peak, he prepared a fire-pit in front of him on a secluded and delightful stretch of ground.
There, having caused each leaf to be read aloud by the two disciples while being gazed upon with tears, he cast it into the fire, making the beasts and birds hear it.
The life story of Naravāhanadatta was [composed] for the sake of his two disciples, excluding one desired tale of his that consisted of a hundred thousand verses.
And while he was reciting that divine discourse, even as it was being read and even as it was being burned, those who had abandoned their diet of grass listened with eyes full of tears.
Having approached that very spot, all the deer, boars, buffaloes, and other animals stood motionless, forming a circle.
In the meantime, King Sātavāhana fell ill, and the physicians declared his malady to have been caused by the consumption of dried meat.
Provoked by that cause, the cooks said, "The hunters are giving us meat such as this."
When questioned, the hunters said: "Not far from here on the mountain, some Brahmin is reading one leaf at a time and casting each into the fire."
Having gathered there, all living beings listen while abstaining from food; they do not go elsewhere, and for that reason, this flesh of theirs has become parched with hunger.
Having heard these words of the hunter and placing those very men before him, the king himself went out of curiosity into the presence of Guṇāḍhya.
He saw him covered with matted locks from his dwelling in the forest, as if surrounded on all sides by the smoke of the fire of his remaining curse that had now been extinguished.
Then, having recognized him as he stood in the midst of the deer, the lord of the earth bowed down and, with tears in his eyes, questioned him regarding his circumstances.
That wise man also related to King Puṣpadanta his own experience regarding the curse and other events, recounting that introduction to the story in the Bhūta language.
Then, recognizing him as the one who had introduced the Gaṇas, the king prostrated at his feet and requested from him that divine narrative which had issued from the mouth of Hara.
Then Guṇāḍhya said to King Sātavāhana: "O King, six hundred thousand verses of the six stories have been consumed by me."
This collection consists of one hundred thousand [verses]; let this single narrative alone be taken up. These two disciples of mine shall become its commentators here for you.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, Guṇāḍhya, freed from the curse, abandoned that body through yoga and attained his own divine station.
Then, taking that story composed by Guṇāḍhya and named the *Bṛhatkathā*, which consisted of the life-story of Naravāhanadatta, the king returned to his own city.
And there, he shared with Guṇadeva and Nandideva—the two disciples of that poet of his stories—land, gold, garments, vehicles, houses, and wealth.

Having comforted her with that conversation in the company of those two, Sātavāhana proceeded to relate the introduction of that [language] by means of its own tongue, and thus established the "Foundation of Narratives" (Kathāpīṭha).

And that story, filled with diverse flavors, having caused the stories of the gods to be forgotten through its own curiosity, attained uninterrupted fame here in the city and throughout the three worlds.
Thus ends the eighth wave in the Kathāpīṭha book of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And here concludes this first book, the Kathāpīṭha. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Book, named "The Opening of the Story. It is said that long ago, this nectar of stories emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the daughter of the King of Mountains (Pārvatī). Those who forcibly taste it, having attained their desires through the removal of obstacles, shall, by the grace of Bhava, establish a city of the gods upon this earth.
First Wave: May the sweat-water of the Lord upon his first embrace of Gaurī protect you—water placed there by Kāma, as if it were a Vāruṇa weapon, out of fear of the fire of his eye.
On Mount Kailāsa, [the teaching] passed from the mouth of Dhūrjaṭi to Puṣpadanta, the best of the Gaṇas; from him, having become Vararuci, it reached Kāṇabhūti on the surface of the earth.
Listen now to this wonderful tale of the Vidyādharas, which was obtained from Guṇāḍhya by Kāṇabhūti, and from Guṇāḍhya by Sātavāhana.
There is a land known as Vatsa, created by the Creator for the quelling of pride, like a rival to heaven upon the earth.
There, in its center, lies the great city named Kauśāmbī, the abode of the play of Fortune and like the pericarp of the earth.
In that city lived King Śatānīka, born of the lineage of the Pāṇḍavas; he was the son of Janamejaya and the grandson of King Parīkṣit.
And his great-grandson was Abhimanyu, whose first ancestor was Arjuna, whose prowess of arm was witnessed by the pillar-like arms of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
The earth became his wife, as did Queen Viṣṇumatī; one gave birth to jewels, while the other did not yet give birth to a son.
Once, as that king was wandering in the forest due to his addiction to hunting, he formed a friendship with the sage Śāṇḍilya.
Having arrived at Kauśāmbī for the sake of that king who desired a son, the best of sages caused the queen to eat the sacrificial porridge (caru) consecrated by mantras.
Then a son was born to him, named Sahasrānīka; he shone with that [son] as virtue shines through discipline.
Then, having gradually made his son Śatānīka the crown prince, the king devoted himself solely to enjoyments and no longer to the concerns of the burden of sovereignty.
Then, when war with the asuras had begun, Śakra, desiring assistance for him, dispatched Mātali as an envoy to that king.
Then he [entrusted it] into the hands of the chief minister named Yugandhara, who was the lead driver, and into the hands of the principal commander-in-chief named Supratīka.
Having entrusted his son and the kingdom to him in order to slay the asuras in battle, Śatānīka went into the presence of Śakra along with Mātali.
In Vāsava’s realm, he saw many Asuras, such as Yamadaṃṣṭra and others; having slain them in that very battle, the king met his death.
The queen followed that king whose body had been brought by Mātali, and the royal fortune (Rājalakṣmī) took refuge with his son, Sahasrānīka.
When that king had ascended his father’s variegated lion-throne, the heads of all the kings bowed down on every side under its weight.
Then Śakra, having dispatched Mātali, led his friend’s son Sahasrānīka to heaven on the occasion of his victory over his enemies.
There in the Nandana grove, seeing the gods sporting with their beloved consorts, the king, longing for a wife worthy of himself, was as if overcome by grief.
Having understood this intention, Vāsava then said to him: "O King, enough with despondency; that which you desire shall be accomplished."
For this wife who has been born upon the earth is equal to one previously ordained for you; listen now to this account, which I shall describe to you here.
Formerly, I went to the assembly hall of the Grandfather (Brahmā) to see him; subsequently, a Vasu named Vidhūma came to me alone.
While we were still standing right there, an Apsaras named Alambuṣā arrived to see Viriñca, her garment blown away by the wind.
Upon seeing her, Vasu fell under the sway of desire; and that apsaras, too, was instantly drawn toward him by her form.
Having observed that, the Lotus-born One looked at my face; and perceiving his intention, I cursed him in anger.
"May there be an incarnation of you two ill-behaved ones in the world of mortals; and there, you two shall become husband and wife."
O King Sahasrānīka, you have been born as that very Vasu, the son of Śatānīka and the ornament of the lunar dynasty.
That very Apsaras has been born in Ayodhyā as the daughter of King Kṛtavarman, named Mṛgāvatī; she shall become your wife.
Thus, fanned by the winds of Indra’s words, the fire of passion suddenly blazed up within the heart of that affectionate king.
Then, having been honored by Śakra and sent off in his chariot, the king set out toward his own city together with Mātali.
And as he was departing, Tilottamā, out of affection, said to him: "O King, I shall tell you something; wait but a moment."
Without even hearing that, he departed while meditating on Mṛgāvatī; then Tilottamā, feeling ashamed and enraged, cursed him.
O King, because your mind has been captivated by her, you do not hear my words; for fourteen years, you shall endure separation from her.
Mātali heard that, and the king, longing for his beloved, traveled by chariot to Kauśāmbī, while in his mind he returned once more to Ayodhyā.
Then, with an anxious mind, he related everything concerning Mṛgāvatī that he had heard from Vāsava and the other ministers, such as Yugandhara.
Unable to endure any further delay, the king dispatched a messenger to Ayodhyā to request that maiden from her father, Kṛtavarman.
And Kṛtavarman, having heard that message from the messenger, spoke [it] to Queen Kalāvatī with joy; then she too spoke to him.
"O King, Mṛgāvatī must certainly be given to Sahasrānīka; for I perceived this matter in a dream, and some brahmin told it to me."
Then, filled with joy, the king showed to that messenger Mṛgāvatī’s skill in dancing, singing, and other arts, as well as her incomparable beauty.
And Kṛtavarman gave that daughter, the sole abode of all lovely arts, to that king like the very personified form of the moon.
For the sake of attaining each other's virtues, the union of Sahasrānīka and Mṛgāvatī was like that of sacred learning and wisdom.
Then, before long, sons were born to the king's ministers; and to Yaugandharāyaṇa, the son of Yugandhara, a son was likewise born.
And from Supratīka was born Rumaṇvat, who became his intimate companion; and from him was born Vasantaka as a son.
Then, after some days, Queen Mṛgāvatī, her face turning pale, conceived a child by King Sahasrānīka.
Then she requested of her husband, whose eyes were never sated by gazing upon her, a pregnancy-longing for immersion in a pleasure-pool filled with blood.
Fulfilling the queen's desire, that righteous king had a pond constructed, saturated with lac and other red dyes until it appeared as if covered in blood.
And while she was bathing there, a bird born of the lineage of Garuḍa suddenly swooped down upon her, who was smeared with lac, and carried her off, suspecting her to be raw meat.
At that moment, as if to search for her who had been carried away somewhere by a bird, Sahasrānīka’s fortitude fled from his agitated heart.
Surely even the heart of that king, which was devoted to his beloved, was carried away by that bird, whereby the monarch fell to the ground unconscious.
In an instant, when the king had regained consciousness through that power, Mātali descended by way of the celestial path and arrived there.
Having comforted the king according to what he had previously heard regarding the time limit, and having told him the curse of Tilottamā, he then departed.
"Alas, my beloved! That wicked Tilottamā has attained her desire! Thus did the lord of the earth lament, afflicted by grief.
Having learned the details of the curse and being consoled by his ministers, he somehow sustained his life with the longing for a future reunion.
And that lord of birds, having carried Queen Mṛgāvatī away in an instant, released her alive upon Mount Udaya by the power of fate.
When he had departed after abandoning her, the queen, overwhelmed by grief and fear, saw herself left without a protector on a difficult mountain slope.
Then, in that forest, a great python rose up and set out to swallow her as she was alone, clad in a single garment, and weeping.
And having slain that serpent, she—whose future was auspicious—was likewise released by a certain divine man who vanished from sight as soon as he was seen.
Then, seeking death herself, she threw herself before the wild elephant; yet he, as if out of compassion, protected her.
It is remarkable that even a beast of prey did not kill her, even though she had fallen within its range; for what indeed might not happen by the will of the Lord?
Then the young woman, facing the precipice and languid from the weight of her womb, remembered her husband and wept aloud with a free throat.
Having heard that, the son of a sage then came there alone, having arrived for the sake of fruits and roots, appearing like sorrow personified.
Having questioned her about what had occurred and somehow comforted her, he, his mind moistened with compassion, led the queen to the hermitage of Jamadagni.
There she beheld Jamadagni, who was like confidence incarnate, making the mountain of sunrise appear as if it possessed the steady rays of the sun.
The Sage, compassionate toward those who seek his protection and possessing divine vision, spoke to the queen as she lay prostrate at his feet, afflicted by the sorrow of separation.
"O daughter, here your father has begotten for you a son who shall uphold his lineage; moreover, he will become your husband. Your reunion is certain, so do not grieve."
Thus addressed by the sage, the virtuous Mṛgāvatī accepted residence in that hermitage and the hope of being reunited with her beloved.
Then, in the course of days, that blameless woman gave birth to a jewel of a son whose conduct was praiseworthy, just as association with the virtuous produces excellent character.
A king named Udayana, illustrious and of great fame, will be born; and he shall have a son who will become the sovereign lord of all the Vidyādharas.
At that time, Sarasvatī emerged from the intermediate space, restoring to Mṛgāvatī the festival that had been forgotten from her heart.
Then, in that forest of asceticism, that boy Udayana gradually grew up along with his own virtues, as if with companions.
Having performed all the purificatory rites appropriate for a Kṣatriya by Jamadagni, that heroic youth was instructed in the sciences and in the science of archery.
And having drawn it from his own hand out of affection, his mother Mṛgāvatī placed upon his wrist a bracelet engraved with the name "Sahasrānīka."
Then, while wandering once during a hunt for deer, that Udayana saw a snake forcibly seized by a Śabara in the forest.
Feeling compassion for that beautiful serpent and for the Śabara as well, he said to him, "Let this serpent be released at my word."
Then that Śabara said: "O Lord, this is my livelihood; for I am a wretched man who lives by constantly playing with snakes."
When the serpent had previously perished, this man was seized by me through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs; search this great forest for him as he is found.
Having heard this, Udayana gave that bracelet given by his mother to the Śabara and released the serpent for him.
When the Śabara had departed with the bracelet he had taken, that serpent, having cleared a path before him, spoke joyfully to Udayana at that time.
"I am known as Vasunemi, the elder brother of Vāsuki; take this lute from me, which has been well-preserved by you."
And [he saw] lutes, delightful with their resonant sounds and divided into distinct musical intervals, as well as betel-leaf plants accompanied by unfading garlands and decorative forehead marks.

Accompanied by him, Jamadagni’s son [Rāma] led Udayana, who had been lifted up by the elephant, back to the hermitage; he arrived within his mother’s sight, raining down as it were the nectar of immortality.
In the meantime, that Śabara, having reached the forest and wandering about, by the power of fate, took up the bracelet obtained from Udayana.
And while selling that [ring] there in the marketplace, he was seized by the king’s men because it bore the king’s name, and he was taken to the royal palace.
"From where did you obtain this bracelet? King Sahasrānīka himself asked him there out of grief.
Then, from the moment he was seized by the serpent on the mountain of sunrise, that Śabara related to him his own account of how he had attained the royal diadem.
Having learned that from the Śabara and having seen that bracelet of his beloved, King Sahasrānīka ascended the swing of reflection.
"O King, that curse of yours has been exhausted; and there, on the Mountain of Sunrise, in the hermitage of Jamadagni, your wife Mṛgāvatī stands together with your son."
Thus, that divine voice then gladdened the king, who was tormented by the heat of separation, just as a shower of rain delights a peacock.

Then, when this day had finally come to an end after being drawn out by longing, on the following day that king, placing the Śabara at his head, set out with his army and a thousand attendants toward the hermitage on Mount Udaya, impetuously hastening to reach his beloved.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Kathāmukha* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The second wave begins: Then, having traveled a long distance, the king took up residence on the bank of a certain forest lake on that day.
Exhausted and reclining upon his bed, the king spoke in the evening to a storyteller named Saṅgatika, who had arrived there out of a love for service.
Tell me some story that gladdens the heart, for I long for the festival of beholding the lotus-face of Mṛgāvatī.
Then Saṅgataka said: "O King, why do you grieve in vain? Your reunion with the queen is imminent; her curse has been exhausted."
Many unions and separations occur for human beings; likewise, I shall tell you a certain story in this regard—listen, O Lord.
In the past, there was a certain twice-born man named Yajñasoma in Mālava; and two sons were born to that virtuous man, who were beloved by the people.
Of those two, one was known by the name Kālanemi, and the second was called Vigatabhaya.
When their father had passed away and they two brothers had emerged from childhood, they set out for the city of Pāṭaliputra in order to acquire knowledge.
Thereupon, Devaśarman gave his own two sons to those two who had mastered the sciences, as if they were two other personified forms of knowledge.
Then, seeing those other wealthy householders, Kālanemi, having undertaken his vows, sought to acquire such prosperity through burnt offerings out of envy.
And Śrī herself, being pleased, spoke thus to him: "You shall obtain abundant wealth, as well as a son who will be a lord of the earth."
However, at the end, your death will be like that of a thief, because you offered oblations into the fire with a soul defiled by resentment.
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmī vanished; and Kālanemi, in due course, became very wealthy, and moreover, a son was born to him within a few days.
Thinking, "This son has been obtained from Śrīvara," that father, his desires fulfilled, gave him the name Śrīdatta.
Gradually attaining maturity, Śrīdatta, though being a Brāhmaṇa, became peerless on earth in the use of missiles and in hand-to-hand combat.
Then Kālanemi’s brother, seeking a sacred ford, set out for another land without fear on account of his wife who had been devoured by a serpent.
Śrīdatta, too, was made a friend there by King Vallabhaśakti, who knew his virtues, to his own son Vikramaśakti.
In his childhood, that proud prince lived together with him, just as the swift Duryodhana lived with Bhīma.
Then two Kṣatriyas born in the land of Avanti, Bāhuśālī and Vajramuṣṭi, became friends with this Brahmin.

Others, southerners who were fond of virtue, having been conquered by him in hand-to-hand combat, sought refuge with him as friends through their alliance in the *svayaṃvara*. So too did the sons of ministers.
Mahābala, Vyāghra, Bhaṭa, Upendrabala, and likewise one named Niṣṭhuraka, formed a bond of friendship with him.
Then once, during the rainy season, that Prince Śrīdatta went with those friends to the bank of the Ganges to enjoy himself.
There, his own servants made that prince their king; and at that time, Śrīdatta was also recognized as king by his friends.
Then, his anger aroused by that much, the prince, intoxicated with pride, quickly challenged that heroic brahmin to battle.
Then, defeated by Śrīdatta in that wrestling match, he harbored a desire to kill the now-defiled Vardhamāna in his heart.
And having understood that intention of the prince, Śrīdatta became apprehensive and withdrew from his presence along with those friends.
As he approached, he saw a woman situated in the middle of the Ganges, being carried away by the flood of water like the goddess Śrī dwelling in the ocean.
Then, having stationed his friends—headed by Ṣaḍbāhuśālin—on the bank, he descended into the water to lift her out.
And even as that woman reached his hair and was submerged deep in the water, that hero too plunged right there in pursuit of her.
And having plunged in, Śrīdatta beheld there a divine temple of Śiva, but neither water nor a woman.
Having witnessed that great marvel and being weary, he bowed to the bull-bannered god and spent that night there in that beautiful garden.
And having arrived, she came to worship the god Īśāna; she was seen by him like the embodied splendor of beauty, endowed with all feminine virtues.
After worshipping the Lord, that moon-faced woman then went to her own palace, and Śrīdatta followed after her.
She beheld that palace of hers, which resembled the city of the gods, and entered it with agitation, like a proud woman feeling slighted.
Without speaking to him at all, that slender woman sat upon a couch in her inner chamber, attended by thousands of women.
Śrīdatta also sat down right there beside him; then, suddenly, that virtuous woman began to weep.
Scalding teardrops fell upon her breasts, and at that moment, compassion took hold in Śrīdatta’s heart.
Then he asked her: "Who are you, and what is your sorrow? Speak, O beautiful one, for I am able to dispel it."
Then, with some difficulty, she said: "In the army of the Lord of the Daityas, we are one thousand granddaughters; among them, I am the eldest, named Vidyutprabhā."
That grandfather of ours was led into long imprisonment by Viṣṇu, and our father was slain by that very Śauri in a wrestling match.
Having killed him, we were banished from our own city by him, and a lion was stationed there in the middle to block our entrance.
That state is obscured by that suffering, and our hearts are likewise; moreover, that yakṣa has attained the state of a lion due to the curse of Kubera.
In ancient times, it was declared that his defeat by mortals would be the end of the curse; when Viṣṇu was petitioned for a means of entering the city, he gave his command.
Therefore, let that lion, our enemy, be conquered by you; it was for this very purpose, O hero, that you were brought here by me.
And from him, once he has been conquered, you shall obtain a sword named Mṛgāṅkaka; by its power, having conquered the earth, you will become a king.
Having heard that, Śrīdatta said, "So be it," and after that day had passed, on another day he went to that city, placing those daughters of the Daityas before him.
There he conquered that arrogant lion in a wrestling match; and he too, being freed from his curse, assumed human form.
And having given his own sword to him who had brought an end to the curse, he, being satisfied, vanished from sight along with the burden of the sorrow of the asura women.
Then Śrīdatta, together with his younger brother and the daughter of the Daitya, entered that supreme city, which was as if infinite and extending beyond its gates.
The daughter of the Daitya gave him a poison-neutralizing ring; then that youth remained there, filled with longing for her.
Then, employing a stratagem, she said to him: "Take a bath here in the pond; and taking with you this sword which wards off the fear of crocodiles, you must dive in."
Saying "So be it," Śrīdatta, having submerged himself in the pond, rose up from that very spot on the bank of the Ganges from which he had previously descended.
Then, seeing the sword and the ring, he rose up from Pātāla; he was both despondent and amazed, deceived by the Asura maiden.
Then he set out toward his own home to search for those friends; and as he was going, he saw on the road a friend named Niṣṭhura.
Having approached and prostrated, Niṣṭhuraka then quickly led him aside; when asked for news of his kinsmen, he spoke as follows:
Having searched for you for many days while you were submerged at the end of the Gaṅgā, we then became prepared to sever our own heads out of grief.
"Sons, you must not act rashly; your friend will return while still alive. Thus, a voice from the sky restrained them from that exertion.
Then, as we were returning to your father’s side, a certain man approached us quickly on the road and spoke these words.
"You must not enter the city here at this time, because that beloved king, Vallabhaśakti, has perished there."
Datta and Vikramaśakti, having joined together with the ministers, were installed in the kingdom; and on another day, once he had obtained the throne, he went to the house of Kālanemi.
Filled with indignation, he asked him, "Where is that son of yours, Śrīdatta? And he replied to him, "I do not know."
Thinking, "My son has been hidden by him," the king, in a fit of rage, had that Kālanemi impaled upon a stake on the charge of being a thief.
Upon seeing that, the heart of his wife burst asunder of its own accord; for the evil deed of the cruel is indeed cruel enough to provoke further evil.
And he, Vikramaśakti, is searching for Śrīdatta and his companions in order to kill them; therefore, you must depart from here.
Thus addressed by that man, Bāhuśālī and the other four, afflicted with grief, consulted together and went to Ujjayinī, their own land.
"O friend, I have been stationed here by them in concealment for your sake; therefore come, let us go right there to the presence of our friend."
Having heard this from Niṣṭhura and mourned for his parents, he repeatedly cast his gaze upon his sword as if fixing his hope for retaliation upon it.
Then the hero, accompanied by Niṣṭhuraka and awaiting the proper time, set out for that city of Ujjayinī in order to reach his friends.
Describing the entire account of his friend up until their immersion in the water, Śrīdatta saw a certain woman crying out on the road.
To her who said, "I am a weak woman who have lost my way and am setting out for Mālava," he then, out of compassion, made her his traveling companion.
And out of consideration for that woman's compassion, he stayed that day in a certain deserted city together with Niṣṭhuraka.
There, having suddenly woken from his sleep during the night, he saw that woman devouring Niṣṭhuraka’s flesh with joy after she had killed him.
Then, drawing forth his sword Mṛgāṅkaka, he rose up; and that woman also resumed her own terrible form as a Rākṣasī.
And he seized that night-stalker by her hair in order to kill her; at that very moment, she attained a divine form and said to him:
"Do not kill me, O illustrious one! Release me; I am certainly not a rākṣasī. This curse of such a nature befell me from the sage Kauśika."
Indeed, when he was previously performing austerities with the desire to attain that station, I was sent by this Lord of Wealth to create obstacles for him.
Then, unable to disturb him with my lovely form and feeling ashamed, I assumed a terrifying body to frighten her.
Seeing that, the sage then pronounced upon me a fitting curse: "O sinful woman, become a Rākṣasī who slays human beings!"
"When my hair was seized by you, he brought about the end of my curse; thus I have fallen into this miserable state of a rākṣasī."
"This city was swallowed by me alone today after a long time, and you have brought its end to the curse; therefore, now accept a boon."
Having heard these words of hers, Śrīdatta respectfully replied: "O noble lady, what need is there for any other boon? Let this friend of mine live."
"So be it," she said, and having granted him the boon, she vanished; and Niṣṭhuraka rose up again, alive with his limbs uninjured.
Then, together with him, Śrīdatta set out in the morning, joyful and filled with wonder, and reached Ujjayinī in due course.
There he greeted those friends who were looking out for his path, appearing to them like a dark cloud approaching a flock of peacocks.
And having performed the rites of hospitality, that man was led to his own home by the mighty-armed one, while he related the entire wonder of his own adventures.
There, being cared for by his parents, Śrīdatta lived together with his friends, who were possessed of great strength, just as if he were in his own home.
Once, when the great festival of the month of Madhu had arrived, he went with his friends to see the procession in the grove.
There he saw a maiden, the daughter of King Śrībimbaka, who had arrived with perfect form, appearing like the very goddess of spring in person.
At that moment, she named Mṛgāṅkavatī entered his heart as if given passage by his blossoming gaze.
Her gaze, too, repeatedly moist with affection and proclaiming her first love, went back and forth toward him like a messenger sent to him.
Then, not seeing her who had entered the thicket of trees even for a moment, Śrīdatta became empty-hearted and could no longer perceive even the directions.
"Friend, I have understood your heart; do not deny it. Come, let us go to that place where the princess has gone."
Thus addressed by his strong-armed friend, who was skilled in reading gestures, he agreed, saying "So be it," and went into her presence accompanied by his friend.
"Alas, what a tragedy! The princess has been bitten by a snake!"—at that moment, such a cry arose there, causing a fever of grief in Śrīdatta's heart.
"My friend has a poison-neutralizing ring and a spell," said the chamberlain to Bāhuśālin after he had gone and told him this.
And at that very moment, the chamberlain approached, bowed at her feet, and quickly led Śrīdatta into the presence of the princess.
He, too, placed the ring upon her finger; then he recited a spell, and by that means she was restored to life.
Then, while all the people were delighted and intent on praising Śrīdatta, King Bimbaki arrived at that very spot, having learned of the events.
Thus, having left his ring behind, Śrīdatta returned with his friends to the palace of Bāhuśālin.
There, whatever gold and other gifts the king, being pleased, sent to him, he delivered in its entirety to his father, Bāhuśālin.
Then, as he brooded over that beloved woman, he was so consumed by anguish that his friends became bewildered as to what ought to be done.
Then a dear female friend of the princess named Bhāvanikā approached her under the pretext of delivering a finger-ring.
And he said to him, "O fortunate one, for that friend of mine, you are now either the giver of life as her husband, or death—this is the certainty."
When this had been said by Bhāvanikā, Śrīdatta, she herself, Bāhuśālī, and the others, having come together, performed a consultation.
"Let us carry away this princess secretly and by means of a stratagem; for the sake of a dwelling, let us go from here to Mathurā in concealment."
When they had thus deliberated and established a mutual agreement for the perfect accomplishment of their purpose, Bhāvanikā departed from there.
On another day, Bāhuśālī, accompanied by his three companions, set out toward Mathurā under the pretext of trade.
As he went along, he stationed his mounts at every step—clever and well-concealed—for the princess's secret rendezvous.
Then Śrīdatta, having had the woman together with her daughter drink wine at the residence of the princess in the evening, placed them there.
Then, under the pretext of providing lamps, she secretly gave fire into the chamber of Vāsava and had the princess carried outside by a group of women.
Having reached her at that very moment, Śrīdatta, who was standing outside, sent word to Bāhuśālin, who had previously set out.
He gave her two female companions, as well as Bhāvanikā; and in that house, that drunken woman was burned along with her daughter.
The world, however, believed that the princess had been burned along with her companions; and in the morning, Śrīdatta was seen there by the people just as before.
Then, on the second night, Śrīdatta, holding the deer-marked moon [the sword], set out toward his beloved who had departed earlier.
Having passed that night and traveled a long distance, he, full of eagerness, reached the Vindhya forest at dawn when the first watch had elapsed.
There, first on the road, he saw those omens; afterwards, he saw all his companions from the caravan, who had been struck by blows.
And seeing him approach in agitation, they said to him: "We have been plundered today by an army that has descended upon us with many horsemen."
And by a single horseman, the princess, overwhelmed with fear, was mounted upon a horse and carried off while we were in such a state.
Before she has been led far away, go by this direction; do not remain near us, for she is in every way superior.
Thus urged by those friends, Śrīdatta turned back again and again, looking repeatedly, and pursued that princess with great speed.
Having traveled a great distance, he found that cavalry force, and among them he beheld a certain young Kṣatriya.
There he saw that princess held up above the stage, and he gradually approached the presence of that young Kṣatriya.
When that prince would not let go of the princess from his feet despite gentle persuasion, Śrīdatta threw him from the horse onto a stone and crushed him to pieces.
Having slain him, he mounted that very horse and struck down those many other enraged cavalrymen who were charging forward.
Then those who remained after the slaughter, having seen such superhuman prowess of that hero, fled in terror.
And Śrīdatta, mounted upon his horse together with that princess Mṛgāṅkavatī, set out toward those friends.
Having gone but a short distance, his horse, severely wounded in battle, fell as he and his wife dismounted, and it died.
And at that very moment, right there, his beloved Mṛgāṅkavatī became exhausted by fear and fatigue, and afflicted by thirst.
Having left her there, he went far away in this direction and that, searching for water, and as he was doing so, the sun set.
Then, although he had obtained water, wandering due to the loss of his path and crying out like a cakravāka bird, he passed that night in the forest.
In the morning, he reached that place, which was marked by the fallen horse; yet, he did not see his beloved princess there at all.
Then, out of delusion, having laid his sword Mṛgāṅka upon the ground, he climbed to the top of a tree to look for her here and there.
At that very moment, a certain lord of the Śabaras came along that path; having arrived, he seized Mṛgāṅkaka from the foot of the tree.
Upon seeing him, Śrīdatta, overcome with intense grief, descended from the top of the tree and questioned the lord of the Śabaras regarding news of his beloved.
"Go from here to my village; I know she has gone there. I shall come to that very place myself and give this sword to you."
Having spoken thus, Śrīdatta, eager and sent by that Śabara, went to that village together with the man's men.
"First, cast off your fatigue," he was told there by those men; and having reached the house of the village chief, the exhausted man fell asleep in an instant.
And upon waking, he saw his own feet bound by shackles, as if they were two efforts toward the means of attaining his beloved, rendered motionless because that goal had not been reached.
Then, grieving for his beloved there, he stood watching her—she who grants happiness for a moment and destroys it in the next, like the course of destiny itself.
Once, a maidservant named Mocanikā approached him and said: "O illustrious one, where have you come here, alas, to meet your death?"
For that certain lord of the Śabaras has gone forth to accomplish his purpose; having returned, he will offer you as a sacrifice to Caṇḍikā.
For this very purpose, having reached you here from the slopes of the Vindhya forest by a clever stratagem and having released you, he has now brought you into captivity.
Since you were conceived as an offering to the Blessed One, for that very reason you are always served with garments and food.
If you think that there exists a single means for your liberation, there is such a one: the daughter of this Śabara chief, named Sundarī.
And upon seeing you, she will become exceedingly afflicted by love; therefore, enjoy her as my companion, and then you shall attain well-being.
Having been told "So be it" by her, Śrīdatta, seeking liberation, replied "Yes" and secretly made that beautiful woman his wife according to the Gāndharva rite.
And night after night, she untied his bonds; and before long, that Sundarī became pregnant.
Then, having learned all of that from the mouth of Mocanikā, his mother went of her own accord out of affection for her son-in-law and spoke to Śrīdatta.
"My son, this man named Śrīcaṇḍa, the father of Sundarī, is prone to anger; he will not forgive you. Therefore, depart; Sundarī must be forgotten."
Having spoken thus, Śrīdatta was released by his mother-in-law; he handed the sword that had been in Śrīcaṇḍa’s hand over to Sundarī and departed from there.
Overcome with anxiety, he entered that very same forest once more, desiring to seek out the path of Mṛgāṅkavatī.
Having seen an auspicious omen, he went to that very place where his horse had died and where that bride had been lost.
And there he saw a hunter approaching from the opposite direction; having seen him, he asked for news of that fawn-eyed woman.
When asked by the hunter there, "Are you Śrīdatta?", he sighed and replied, "I am that very same unfortunate man."
Then that hunter said, "In that case, friend, listen; I have seen your wife weeping here and there for you."
Then, having inquired into her story and comforted her, I, overcome with pity, led that wretched woman from this forest to my own settlement.
And there, having observed some young Pulindas, she was led by me in fear to the village of Nāgasthala, near Mathurā.
And there, having respectfully entrusted them as a deposit, she placed them in the house of an elderly brahmin named Viśvadatta.
Therefore, having learned your name from his mouth, I have come here; go now quickly toward Nāgasthala to search for her.
Having been addressed thus by the hunter, Śrīdatta departed from there immediately and reached that city of Nāgasthala on the following day at the close of the day.
Then, having entered the residence of Viśvadatta and beheld him, he begged, "Give me back my wife, who was placed with the hunter."
Having heard that, Viśvadatta said to Śrīdatta: "In Mathurā, I have a friend who is a Brāhmaṇa beloved by the virtuous."
Both the preceptor and the minister of King Śūrasena have been entrusted by me with your wife, who has been placed in their hands.
For a village devoid of people is indeed a place of fear and cannot provide protection; therefore, go there tomorrow morning, and rest here today.
Having been addressed thus by Viśvadatta, he spent that night right there and set out in the morning, reaching Mathurā on the following day.
Exhausted from his long journey and stained with dust, he performed his ablutions in the pure water of a large pond just outside that city.
Then, from the midst of the water itself, he unexpectedly recovered the garment placed there by the thief, along with a necklace tied in a knot at its edge.
Then, taking that garment and not noticing the necklace, Śrīdatta, desiring to see his beloved, entered the city of Mathurā.
There, having recognized him and recovered both the garment and the necklace, the city guards seized him as a thief and led him away.
And they showed him in that state to the lord of the city; he, in turn, informed the king, and the king ordered his execution.
Then Mṛgāṅkavatī saw him from afar being led to the place of execution to be slain, with the drum beating behind him.
"This husband of mine is being led away for execution! Thinking thus, she went in great agitation to the chief minister and told him what had happened in her house.
Then the minister, having restrained the executioners and petitioned the king, had Śrīdatta released from execution and brought to his own home.
How is it that this uncle of mine, who previously went to another land, has now by fate returned here and attained the position of minister, free from fear?
Then Śrīdatta, having arrived at that house, recognized the minister after questioning him, and fell at his feet.
He too, recognizing him as his brother's son, embraced him around the neck with wonder and inquired about the entire account of what had happened.
Then Śrīdatta related his entire history to his paternal uncle, beginning from the murder of his father.
Wiping away his tears in that secluded place, he said to his brother's son: "Do not despair, my son; for the Yakṣiṇī has indeed been won by me."
She gave me five thousand horses and seven crores of gold coins, for I was childless; all that wealth is yours alone.
Having spoken thus, the paternal uncle handed over his beloved to Śrīdatta; and Śrīdatta, having acquired his fortune, married her there.
And then he remained right there, united with his beloved Mṛgāṅgavatī, full of joy like a bed of night-lotuses with the night.
But for him, whose prosperity was complete, thoughts of possessing many arms and the like became a source of stain upon his heart, like a streak of the moon's dark spot.
Once, that paternal uncle spoke to Śrīdatta in private: "Son, the king has a daughter, the maiden of Śūrasena."
"And by his command, she is to be led by me to the land of Avanti to be given [in marriage]. Under that very pretext, I shall take her away and give her to you."
"Therefore, when his followers have arrived and my own forces are present, you shall before long regain that kingdom which was ordained for you by Śrī."
Having thus decided, Śrīdatta and his paternal uncle set out from there, taking that maiden with them, accompanied by their armies and retinues.
Then, as soon as these two had unexpectedly reached the Vindhya forest, a vast army of bandits, raining down arrows, hemmed them in.
Having bound Śrīdatta—who was unconscious from the blows and whose army had been broken—the thieves took all his wealth and led him to their own village.
And they brought him to the terrifying abode of Caṇḍikā, which, with the sounds of its bells, seemed to summon Death itself for the sake of an offering.
There, his wife—the daughter of the village chief—saw him; Sundarī had come to visit the goddess, accompanied by her young son.
Then Śrīdatta entered her palace together with Niṣiddhavatī, who was full of joy, while the robbers remained indifferent.
At that very moment, he obtained that Pallī kingdom which had been entrusted to him by his father, who, having no other son, had already departed for heaven long before.
And he obtained that thief along with his paternal uncle and retinue, together with his wife, as well as that sword named Mṛgāṅkaka.
And having married that very daughter of Śūrasena, the great king Śrīdatta also established himself in the city.
Then he dispatched messengers to those two fathers-in-law, to Bimbaka, and also to that king Śūrasena.
Accompanied by their assembled armies, the two of them approached him; having recognized that kinship, they were filled with joy, for they were both deeply affectionate toward their daughter.
Those companions of his, Bāhuśālin and the others, having recovered from their wounds and being restored to health, learned of this and approached him.
Then, accompanied by his father-in-law, that hero went to that patricide and made Vikramaśakti an offering into the fire of his wrath.
Then Śrīdatta, having regained the earth girt by the ocean, rejoiced like the moon that has emerged from an eclipse, accompanied by Mṛgāṅkavatī.
In this way, O Lord of Men, those of steadfast mind cross over the ocean of calamity caused by long separation and attain what is auspicious.
Having heard this story from Saṅgataka, King Sahasrānīka, longing for his beloved, passed that night on the road.
