Then, mounted upon his desire, with his mind sent forward, Sahasrānīka set out in the morning toward his beloved.
After a few days, he reached that hermitage of Jamadagni, where even the deer had abandoned their restlessness due to the peace.
There he beheld Jamadagni, who had prepared hospitality for him, bowing before that man of purifying gaze, who was like the very personification of ascetic penances.
And that sage restored Queen Mṛgāvatī, along with her son, to the king—she who was like joy itself, though long lost, now returned in the form of liberation.
At the end of the curse, that mutual beholding of the couple rained down, as it were, nectar upon their eyes, which were filled with tears of joy.
Upon seeing his son for the first time, the king embraced that Udayana and released him from his distress, as if he were pinned down by his own bristling hair.
Then, taking Queen Mṛgāvatī along with Udāyana, he proceeded toward the penance grove, followed even by the deer as they wept.
Having taken leave of Jamadagni, King Sahasrānīka set out toward his own city from that tranquil hermitage.
Listening to accounts of his beloved’s separation and describing them himself, he gradually reached Kauśāmbī, which was adorned with triumphal arches and banners.
Together with his wife and son, he entered that city, as if being drunk in by the eyes of the citizens, whose lashes were raised in reverence.
And there, impelled by his virtues, the great king immediately consecrated his son Udayana in the position of crown prince.
For the sake of that counsel, he entrusted his own ministers' sons to him: Vasantaka, Rumaṇvat, and likewise Yaugandharāyaṇa.
"With these excellent ministers, he shall obtain the entire earth"—such was the divine voice that then arose along with a rain of flowers.
Then, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his son, that king enjoyed with Mṛgāvatī the happiness of the world of the living which he had long desired.
Then, suddenly perceiving that old age had arrived at the monarch's ear as a messenger of peace, his longing for sense-objects, alas, vanished far away.

Then, having installed that auspicious son Udayana—whose subjects were devoted to him—in his own kingdom for the sake of the world’s welfare, King Sahasrānīka, accompanied by his ministers, his beloved wife, and [Udayana], departed for the Himalayas on the Great Departure.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Kathāmukha* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave: Then, having obtained the kingdom of Vatsa bestowed upon him by his father, Udayana, residing in Kauśāmbī, ruled his subjects with perfect justice.
Having entrusted the burden of governance to his ministers, beginning with Yaugandharāyaṇa, that king gradually became solely devoted to pleasures.
He constantly pursued the hunt and that lute Ghoṣavatī; he played it day and night, for it had been given to him long ago by Vāsuki.
And he brought under control, having bound them, the wild elephants that were always intoxicated and enchanted by the delusive spells of the sound produced by the tuning of their respective lutes.
The King of Vatsa drank the wine, which was adorned by the moon-like faces of the women of Vārāṇasī, and he drank at the same time as the reflected splendor of the ministers' faces.
"A wife suitable to my family and appearance is not to be found anywhere; however, it is heard that there is a maiden named Vāsavadattā."
"And how might she be obtained?"—this was the single thought that occupied Caṇḍamahāsena as he reflected while in Ujjayinī.
There is no husband for my daughter equal to him in this world; however, there is one named Udayana who is always my rival.
How, then, can he truly become a submissive son-in-law? There is only one means: that he must wander in the forest.
"The king, addicted to hunting, will be alone while binding elephants; through that opportunity, I shall skillfully seize him and bring him here."
"I shall make this daughter of his a pupil under that master of the Gandharva arts; then, through her, his eye will undoubtedly become attached to him."
"In this way, that son-in-law of mine will certainly become submissive; there is no other means whatsoever by which he might be brought under control."
Having reflected thus, he went to the temple of Caṇḍikā for its accomplishment; having worshipped Caṇḍī, he praised her and made a vow to her.
"O King, this which you desire shall be accomplished before long"—thus did he hear an incorporeal voice there.
Then, having arrived satisfied, Caṇḍamahāsena, together with the minister Buddhadatta, reflected upon that very matter.

Arrogant with pride, free from greed, devoted to his servants, and possessed of great strength—even though he is incurable by means such as conciliation, let him first be approached with gentle persuasion.
Having deliberated thus, the king commanded a messenger: "Go and speak these words to the King of Vatsa in my name."
"My daughter wishes to become your pupil in the art of music; if you have affection for us, then come here yourself and instruct her."
Having spoken thus, the messenger was sent by him; having gone, he delivered that message exactly as it was to the King of Vatsa in Kauśāmbī.
Vatsarāja, having heard those improper words from the messenger, spoke thus in private to his minister Yaugandharāyaṇa.
"What is this that has been sent by that arrogant king to me? What is the intention of that evil-minded one in sending such a message?"
Thus addressed by the King of Vatsa, the great minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, who was devoted to his master’s welfare, spoke to him with harshness.
O Great King, this is the bitter fruit of that passion for vices which has grown like a creeper upon you on this earth.
For Caṇḍamahāsena, thinking you to be full of passion and seeking to entice you with that jewel of a maiden, has taken you away, bound you, and desires to possess you as his own.
Therefore, abandon those vices, for kings who sink into them through their own ease are seized by their enemies, like wild elephants in pits.
Having been addressed thus by his minister, the steadfast Vatsarāja dispatched a return envoy toward King Caṇḍamahāsena.
And he gave this command: "If there is a desire for your daughter to be my disciple, then let her be sent here at once."
Having done this, Vatsarāja said to his ministers: "I shall go and bring back here that Caṇḍamahāsena, having bound him."
Having heard that, the preeminent minister Yaugandharāyaṇa said to him: "O King, this cannot be done, nor indeed is it even proper."
For that king is powerful and worthy of being won over by you, O Lord; therefore, listen as I tell you everything concerning him.
There is here a city named Ujjayinī, an ornament of the earth, which seems to mock Amarāvatī with its palaces washed white with plaster.
In that city dwells Viśveśa himself in the form of Mahākāla—Hara, who has set aside his attachment to residing on Kailāsa.
In that city there was a king named Mahendravarman, the best among rulers; he had a worthy son named Jayasena.
Then, a son named Mahāsena was born to that Jayasena, a prince among kings who possessed incomparable strength of arm.
Then that king, while protecting his own kingdom, reflected: "I have no sword worthy of me, nor a wife of noble birth."
Having reflected thus, the king went to the temple of Caṇḍikā; staying there without food, he propitiated the Goddess for a long time.
Then, having cut off his own flesh, he performed the rite of oblation; thereupon, the goddess Caṇḍī, being pleased, appeared before him in person and spoke to him.
"I am pleased with you; take this, my son, my supreme sword. By its power, you shall become invincible to your enemies."
Furthermore, you shall soon obtain as your wife a maiden named Aṅgāravatī, the daughter of the Asura Aṅgāraka, who is the most beautiful woman in the three worlds.
"Because this exceedingly fierce deed has been performed here by you, therefore your name shall be Caṇḍamahāsena."
Having spoken thus and given him the sword, the goddess vanished; then there appeared again the joy of the king’s fulfillment of his resolve.
O Lord, that sword and the lordly elephant Naḍāgiri were his two jewels, just as the thunderbolt and Airāvaṇa are the two jewels of Śakra.
Then, at times made happy by the power of those two, King Caṇḍamahāsena once went to the great forest for the sake of hunting.
There he beheld a single, immense, and terrifying boar, like nocturnal darkness that had suddenly assumed a solid form even in broad daylight.
That boar, though pierced by his sharp arrows, remained unwounded; having struck the king’s chariot, it fled and entered a cave.
The king also, abandoning his chariot and pursuing him in fury with his bow as his only companion, entered that very same cave.
Having entered far within, he beheld a great and lovely city; filled with wonder, he sat down on the bank of a long pond therein.
Standing there, he beheld a maiden accompanied by a hundred women, moving about like the arrow of the God of Love that pierces through fortitude.
She too, as if bathing the king repeatedly with her eyes that rained down a shower of the essence of love, slowly approached him.
"Who are you, O fortunate one, and for what reason have you entered here now?"—being thus addressed by her, the king described the matter exactly as it was.
Hearing that, the maiden simultaneously shed a stream of tears from her impassioned pair of eyes and also cast away her fortitude from her heart.
"Who are you, and why do you weep?"—when asked this by the king, she, who was obedient to his great command, replied to him thus:
O King, that boar who entered here was the Daitya named Aṅgāraka; and I am his daughter, O monarch, known by the name Aṅgāravatī.
And he, whose nature is as firm as diamond, having snatched away these hundred princesses from the palaces of various kings, made them my retinue.
Moreover, this great asura, having become a rākṣasa due to the fault of a curse, has abandoned you today even though he found you, being afflicted by thirst and fatigue.
And now, having assumed the form of a boar, he himself rests; and once he has arisen from sleep, he will surely commit some evil against you.
Thus, as I behold no good fortune for you, these teardrops of mine fall like my very life-breaths, which have been boiled away by the heat of my anguish.
Having heard these words of Aṅgāravatī, the king said to her: "If you have affection for me, then do this which I say."
Once he has awakened, go and weep before your father; then he will certainly ask you the cause of your distress.
"If someone were to strike you down, what would become of my state? 'This is my suffering'—you should then say this to him."
"When this is done, there will be welfare for both you and me. Having been addressed thus by the king, she agreed to him, saying, "So be it."
Having left him there concealed, she, fearing some evil might befall the king, went to her father, the Asura, while he was fast asleep.
The father-in-law also woke up, and she began to weep; then he said to her, "Daughter, why do you weep?"
"O father, if someone were to kill you, what would become of my fate?"—with such distress she spoke to him, and he, smiling, then replied:
"Who could kill me, my daughter? For I am entirely made of diamond; yet there is a hole in my left hand, and that is protected by my bow."
In this manner, that Daitya consoled his own daughter; and all of this was heard by the king, who remained concealed.
Then, as if rising in an instant, that Dānava performed his ablutions, observed silence, and proceeded to worship the god Hara.
Manifesting at that very moment, that king, having drawn his bow, approached the Daitya and challenged him violently to battle.
Raising his left hand while remaining in silence, he then gave this signal to the king: "Wait for a moment."
The king, too, being light-handed, at that very moment struck that Daitya in that same vital spot with an arrow right there on his hand.
And that great asura, struck in a vital spot, let out a terrible cry; falling to the ground with his life ebbing away, he spoke:
"May he by whom I was struck while thirsty not satisfy me with water; if it be so, may five of his ministers perish every year."
Having spoken thus, that Daitya met his death; and the king, taking his daughter Aṅgāravatī, departed for Ujjayinī.
After he had married that daughter of the Daitya there, two sons were born to King Caṇḍamahāsena.
One was named Gopālaka and the second Pālaka; when they were born, the king held an Indra-festival for them both.
Then Vāsava, being pleased, spoke to that king in a dream: "By my grace, you shall obtain a son who has no equal."
Then, in the course of time, a slender daughter was born to this king, fashioned by the Creator as an unprecedented being, like a second body of the Moon.
At that moment, a voice arose from the heavens, saying: "Her son shall be an incarnation of Kāmadeva and a sovereign of the Vidyādharas."
"This was given to me by Vāsava, who was pleased," said that king; he then gave his daughter the name Vāsavadattā.
And she, who was to be given in marriage by her father, now resides within him, like Lakṣmī within the hollow of the ocean's belly before its churning.
"O King, that monarch Caṇḍamahāsena, possessing such power and stationed in an inaccessible region, cannot be conquered by any means whatsoever."
Moreover, O King, he always desires to give that daughter to you; yet that proud king seeks the great advancement of his own side.
And I believe that Vāsavadattā must certainly be wedded by you alone; thus, the King of Vatsa immediately became one whose heart was captivated by Vāsavadattā.

Thus ends the third wave in the Kathāmukha book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave. In the meantime, that envoy from the Lord of Vatsa spoke thus to Caṇḍamahāsena, the king, having returned with his reply.
And upon hearing that, Caṇḍamahāsena thought: "That proud Lord of Vatsa certainly will not come here."
For a maiden should certainly not be sent there, as that would indeed be a sign of disrespect; therefore, having bound him by some stratagem, I shall bring the king here.
Having reflected thus and deliberated together with his ministers, the king had constructed a great mechanical elephant that was equal to himself.
And having stationed it within the Vindhya forest, guarded by hidden heroic men, the king placed that mechanical elephant there.
There, the scouts saw from a distance those dependents of the King of Vatsa who were intent on capturing elephants.
And they, having arrived in haste, informed the King of Vatsa: "O Lord, we have seen a single elephant wandering in the Vindhya forest."
In this world of mortals, there is none to be seen elsewhere who, like the Vindhya mountain, has filled the sky with his body as he moves along.
Then, having heard the words of the spies, the King of Vatsa rejoiced and gave them a hundred thousand gold pieces as a reward.
If I obtain that lordly elephant, the rival of Naḍāgiri, then Caṇḍamahāsena will certainly come under my control.
"Then he himself will give Vāsavadattā to me"—thinking thus, the king passed that night.
And in the morning, disregarding the words of his minister due to his thirst for elephants, he set out toward the Vindhya forest, placing those very spies at the head of his procession.
Regarding the result of the auspicious moment for his departure—the acquisition of a maiden along with her kinsmen—which the astrologers had predicted, he did not consider that at all.
Having reached the Vindhya forest, the King of Vatsa, fearing the agitation of that elephant, halted his armies from afar.
Accompanied by only his servant and carrying his resonant lute, Vīṇāvatsa entered that great forest which was as vast as his own misfortune.
On the southern slope of the Vindhya mountains, that king beheld an elephant appearing like a real elephant, pointed out from afar by those who followed his tracks.
Playing the lute alone, reflecting upon his bonds, and singing with a sweet voice, he slowly approached him.
Because his mind was captivated by Gāndharvadattā and due to the influence of the twilight darkness, the king did not perceive that forest elephant as being an illusory elephant.
That elephant too, with its ears and trunk erect as if drawn by the melody of the song, approached and approached, and while swaying, drew the king far away.
Then, suddenly emerging from that mechanical elephant, armed men surrounded the Lord of Vatsa.
Seeing them, the king, drawing his dagger in anger, began fighting those standing before him with others, but was subsequently seized from behind.
Together with other warriors who had assembled by appointment, those soldiers led the Lord of Vatsa into the presence of Caṇḍamahāsena.
And Caṇḍamahāsena, having gone out to meet him with great respect, entered the city of Ujjayinī together with that Lord of Vatsa.
There, the King of Vatsa, having arrived anew, was like the moon—a delight to the eyes—yet stained by the disgrace of being insulted by the citizens.
Then, fearing that he would be killed because of his passion for those virtues, all those citizens gathered together and made a firm resolve to die.
Saying to them, "The Lord of Vatsa is not to be slain by me; he is to be made peace with," Caṇḍamahāsena then restrained the citizens from their agitation.
Then the king, right there, entrusted his daughter Vāsavadattā to the King of Vatsa for the purpose of her instruction in music.
And he said to him, "O Lord, teach this Gandharva art to her; then you shall attain prosperity, so do not despair."
Upon seeing that maiden, the mind of the King of Vatsa became so saturated with affection that he did not even perceive his own resentment.
Both her eye and her mind went toward him together; however, out of shame, her eye turned back, but her mind did not turn back at all.
Then, having Vāsavadattā sing while his eyes were fixed upon her, that King of Vatsa dwelt there in the music hall.
Ghoṣavatī stood on his lap, Gītaśruti at his neck, and Vāsavadattā before him, delighting his mind.
And Vāsavadattā became intent on his service; like Lakṣmī herself, she remained inseparable from him, even though he was bound [in chains], with her mind fixed solely upon him.
In the meantime, when the people following the King of Vatsa returned to Kauśāmbī and learned that their lord had been imprisoned, the entire kingdom was thrown into turmoil.
Then, incensed by their devotion to the Lord of Vatsa, the subjects desired to launch a simultaneous assault upon Ujjayinī from all sides.
Caṇḍamahāsena cannot be overcome by force, for he is great; nor would it be well for the body of the King of Vatsa in this manner.
Therefore, it was not appropriate to launch a sudden assault; however, Rumaṇvat did not restrain the subjects from their agitation, thinking, "This matter must be accomplished through intelligence."
Then, observing that the kingdom was thus devoted and unwavering, the steadfast Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke to Rumaṇvat and the others.
Right here you must all remain, ever-vigilant; this kingdom must be protected, and valor must be exercised at the proper time.
And accompanied by Vasantaka, I shall go and, by means of my own wisdom, release that Lord of Vatsa and bring him back; of this there is no doubt.
He whose wisdom flashes forth even more intensely in times of adversity, like the brilliance of a lightning fire struck by water—he alone is truly steadfast.
I know the applications that shatter walls, those that break fetters, and the applications for invisibility that are effective.
Having spoken thus and having placed the ministers' hands in Rumaṇvat's, Yaugandharāyaṇa departed from Kauśāmbī together with Vasantaka.
And he entered the great Vindhya forest along with him, which was rich in living beings like his own wisdom, and difficult to traverse like his own policy.
There, he went to the house of the lord of the Pulindas named Pulindakā, a friend of the King of Vatsa who dwelt on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains.
Having placed him there in readiness, he sent forth a vast army accompanied by Prahlāda to protect Vatsarāja as he approached.
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa, accompanied by his friend Vasantaka, traveled on and eventually reached the Mahākāla cremation ground in Ujjayinī.
And he entered that place, which was filled with vetālas smelling of raw flesh, who were like other funeral pyre-smokes, dark with soot, drifting here and there.
There, a Brahmarākṣasa named Yogeśvara, delighted by the sight of him, approached at that very moment and chose him as a friend.
Then, by means of the method instructed by him, Yaugandharāyaṇa did not immediately effect a transformation of his own appearance.
By that [act], he instantly became deformed, hunchbacked, and old; dressed like a madman, bald, and exceedingly laughable.
By that same method, he then transformed even Vasantaka’s form into one with a large belly bound by veins and a jagged, hideous face.
Then, having first sent Vasantaka to the gate of the royal palace, that Yaugandharāyaṇa entered Ujjayinī in such a manner.
Dancing and singing there, surrounded by young students, he was watched with curiosity by everyone as he proceeded toward Rājagṛha.
There, having had the marriage-thread ceremony performed for him by the king's harem women, he gradually came within the range of Vāsavadattā’s hearing.
She quickly sent a maidservant to summon him; for youth, indeed, is solely devoted to the hall of music and the pleasures of jest.
And having gone there, Yaugandharāyaṇa, dressed in the garb of a madman with tears streaming down his face, beheld the aged Vatsarāja.
He gave a name to that King of Vatsa, and the king, for his part, recognized him who had arrived disguised in a different dress.
Then, by the power of his yogic skill, Yaugandharāyaṇa rendered himself invisible to Vāsavadattā and her maidservants.
The king alone beheld him, and they all looked on with astonishment; they said, "That madman has suddenly gone away somewhere."
Having heard that and seeing him before his eyes, the King of Vatsa realized through the power of yoga that it was indeed Vāsavadattā, and spoke this to her with skillful artifice.
"Go, girl, and having performed worship to Sarasvatī, return. Having heard that, she said "So be it" and went out together with her companions.
Then, having approached the King of Vatsa as was appropriate, Yaugandharāyaṇa gave him the yogic formulas for breaking the fetters.
Furthermore, he presented to this king other enchanting spells, along with strings of lutes, which had been employed by Vāsavadattā.
And he informed him, "O King, Vasantaka has arrived here; standing at the gate in another form, you should bring that brahmin into your presence."
"When this Vāsavadattā gains confidence in you, then I will tell you what I have to say; for now, remain here."
Having spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa departed quickly from there, and Vāsavadattā went at that very moment, taking with her the offerings of worship.
Then the king said to her: "A brahmin is standing at the outer gate; let him be admitted for the sake of a sacrificial fee for my worship of Sarasvatī."
Saying "So be it," Vāsavadattā had Vasantaka, who was assuming a deformed appearance, brought there from the vicinity of the door.
Upon seeing him brought there, the Lord of Vatsa cried out in grief; then, so that no one else might overhear, the king spoke to him.
"O Brahmin, I shall ward off all this—your disease and disfigurement. Do not weep; remain right here in my presence."
"O King, there is great favor," Vasantaka said; then, seeing that deformed being, the king’s face broke into a smile.
And having observed that and understood his intention, Vasantaka too laughed, his face distorted by an even greater degree of deformity.
Seeing him laughing in that manner, appearing like a mere plaything, Vāsavadattā there also laughed and was delighted.
Then, in jest, that young woman asked Vasantaka: "O Brahmin, what science do you know? Tell me."
"O Queen, I know how to tell stories," he said; "then tell me one story," she replied to him.
Then Vasantaka, seeking to delight the princess, told her this story, which was full of various kinds of humor and charm.
There is here a city named Mathurā, the birthplace of the enemy of Kaṃsa; in it there was a famous courtesan named Rūpaṇikā.
Her mother was an old procuress named Makaradaṃṣṭrā; she was a spray of poison for the eyes of young men who were drawn toward her by her charms.
Once, at the time of worship, Rūpaṇikā went to her own quarters; from afar, she beheld a certain man.
Upon seeing that handsome man, he entered her heart so completely that the instructions given to her by her mother departed from it.
Then she said to the maidservant: "Go and, in my name, tell that man: 'You must come to my house today.'"
"So be it," said the maidservant, and having gone, she told him that; then that man, reflecting for a moment, spoke to her.
"I am a brahmin named Lohajaṅgha, and I have no wealth; for what am I in the house of Rūpaṇikā, which can only be obtained by wealthy people?"
When she said, "O Master, I do not desire wealth from you," Lohajaṅgha accepted her words, saying, "So be it."
Then, having learned of that from the mouth of her maidservant, Rūpaṇikā went to that house in eager anticipation and remained there, fixing her eyes upon his path.
In a moment, Lohajaṅgha then arrived at her residence; he was seen by the procuress Makaradaṃṣṭrā, who wondered, "Whence has this man come?"
Rūpaṇikā, too, seeing him, rose up of her own accord with respect; delighted, she led him into the inner chamber of the bedchamber while clinging to his neck.
There, having been won over by the excellence of that Lohajaṅgha’s good fortune, she, being devoted, considered no other fruit to exist in her life.
Then, having desisted from association with other men, that young man remained right there in her palace with her at his ease.
Seeing that, Makaradaṃṣṭrā, her mother, who had instructed all the women in their attire, spoke in private to the distressed Rūpaṇikā.
"O daughter, why do you serve this man who is destitute? Noble people touch a corpse, but courtesans do not serve one who is penniless."
"How have you forgotten how affection differs from the state of being a courtesan? Like the twilight, a passionate courtesan does not shine for long, my daughter."
Like an actress, she displays feigned affection for the sake of wealth; therefore, release this man who is penniless, lest you bring about your own ruin.
Having heard these words of her mother, Rūpaṇikā said in anger: "Do not speak thus; for he is dearer to me than even my own life."
"I possess abundant wealth; what else shall I do with anything more? Therefore, mother, you must never speak to me in this manner again."
Having heard that regarding the decree for Lohajaṅgha’s banishment, Makaradaṃṣṭrā stood there in anger, devising a means to counter it.
Then she saw a certain prince who had come along the road, his treasury exhausted, surrounded by men with weapons in their hands.
Having approached him quickly and led him to a secluded spot, she said: "My house has been occupied by a certain penniless suitor."
"Come to the truth today and act accordingly, so that he may turn away from my house and accept my daughter."
"So be it," the prince replied, and he entered that house; at that very moment, Rūpaṇikā remained in the temple.
And at that time, Lohajaṅgha was standing somewhere outside; after a short while, he returned to that very spot without any apprehension.
At that very moment, the prince's servants ran forward and struck him firmly on all his limbs with kicks and other blows.
Then, having been thrown by them into a pit filled with impurities, Lohajaṅgha somehow managed to escape from there.
Then Rūpaṇikā, having learned of this, arrived overwhelmed with grief; but upon seeing him, she became composed, and the prince departed as he had come.
Lohajaṅgha, having been forcibly humiliated by the courtesan, set out for a sacred bathing place to abandon his life, being overcome by the pain of separation.
As he traveled through the forest, tormented in his heart by resentment toward the procuress and on his skin by the heat of summer, he longed for shade.
Then, failing to reach the tree, they obtained the carcass of an elephant; having entered inside through the hindquarters, it had been made fleshless by jackals.
When only the skin remained there, Lohajaṅgha, having entered and become thoroughly exhausted within, fell asleep in that place cooled by the entering breeze.
Then, rising up suddenly, a cloud began in that very instant to rain down in torrents from all sides.
By that means, the elephant hide contracted until it was without any gap; and in an instant, a great flood of water came surging along that path.
Having snatched it away, he threw that elephant-hide into the Ganges; and having been carried by the current of its waters, it was deposited within the ocean.
Seeing that hide there, a bird born of the lineage of Garuḍa swooped down, mistaking it for meat, and having carried it off, flew to the far shore of the ocean.
Thereupon, having torn open this elephant-hide with his beak and looked within, the bird saw a human being and fled from that place.
Then, alerted by the agitation of the birds, Lohajaṅgha emerged from that skin, having made an opening with his beak.
Seeing himself standing on the far shore of the ocean, he was filled with wonder and regarded that entire event as if it were a dream from which he had not awakened.
Then he saw two terrible rākṣasas there, and they too, alarmed, saw him from a distance.
Remembering their defeat at the hands of Rāma and seeing that very same man having once again crossed the ocean, they felt fear within their hearts.
After deliberating, one of them went at that very moment and reported to their lord, Vibhīṣaṇa, exactly what he had seen.
Having witnessed Rāma’s power, King Vibhīṣaṇa, fearing the arrival of humans, spoke to that Rākṣasa.
"Go, my good man, and at my request speak with affection to that mortal: 'Please come to our home; let favor be shown to us.'"
Saying "So be it," that Rākṣasa returned and, filled with wonder, related those words of his master's request to Lohajaṅgha.
Having accepted that, the brahmin Lohajaṅgha, with a tranquil mind, then went to Laṅkā together with him as his companion.
And having entered the royal palace, he—astonished by the various golden palaces he beheld there—saw Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having offered him hospitality and received his blessing, the king also asked him: "O Brahmin, how have you come to this land?"
Then that rogue Lohajaṅgha said to Vibhīṣaṇa: "I am a Brahmin named Lohajaṅgha, residing in Mathurā."
Thus, tormented by poverty, I went to that temple of Nārāyaṇa and, having gone there, I performed austerities while remaining without food.
Then, in a dream, the Blessed Lord Hari commanded me: "Go to Vibhīṣaṇa; for he is my devotee and will grant you wealth."
When I asked, "Where am I? Where is Vibhīṣaṇa?", that Lord replied once more: "Go this very day; you shall see Vibhīṣaṇa."
Thus addressed by the Lord, I immediately awoke and saw myself standing here on the far shore of the ocean; I know nothing else.
Having been addressed thus by Lohajaṅgha, and beholding Laṅkā so difficult to access, Vibhīṣaṇa thought, "Truly, this is one of divine power."
Having said to that brahmin, "Stay, and I shall give you wealth," and having considered him as one who could not be sent into the hands of the Rākṣasas, those slayers of men—
Having observed the Rākṣasas from that mountain called Svarṇamūla where he was stationed, he summoned the young bird born of the lineage of Garuḍa.
And at that very moment, he gave him a vehicle for the purpose of subjugation, so that Lohajaṅgha might travel to Mathurā.
Lohajaṅgha, too, having mounted it and driven it through Laṅkā, rested for some time, being honored by Vibhīṣaṇa.
Once, filled with curiosity, he questioned that lord of the rākṣasas: "How is it that this entire city of Laṅkā is made of wood?"
Having heard that account, Vibhīṣaṇa said to him: "O Brahmin, if you have curiosity, then listen; I shall tell it to you."
Long ago, Garuḍa, the son of Kaśyapa, desiring to release his mother from her state of servitude to the nāgas, who had been brought there by a previous vow.
Intent on seizing the nectar from the gods as its price, and desiring food for the sake of Bala, he went into the presence of his father.
And when he was entreated, he said to him: "My son, there are two great beings, an elephant and a tortoise, in the ocean; go and eat them once they have fallen from their curse."
Then Garuḍa, having gone there and taken both of them as food, perched upon a branch of a great kalpa-tree.
And he immediately held that branch, which had been broken by his own weight, with his beak out of consideration for the Vālakhilyas who were engaged in ascetic penance beneath him.
Then, out of fear of oppressing the world, he brought her by his father's command and abandoned her here on this branch in a secluded place by means of Garuḍa.
"Upon its back, Laṅkā was built; thus this ground here is made of wood. Having heard this from Vibhīṣaṇa, Lohajaṅgha was greatly pleased.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa gave him very many highly precious jewels to him who desired to go to Mathurā.
And out of devotion to the god Hari who resides in Mathurā, he placed golden lotuses, maces, conchs, and discs into his hand.
Having taken all of that which was offered by Vibhīṣaṇa, he ascended the bird capable of traveling a hundred thousand yojanas.
Having leaped into the path of the sky and crossed the ocean from Laṅkā, that Lohajaṅgha arrived at Mathurā without any difficulty.
Descending from the sky outside that empty monastery, he deposited that heap of jewels and tied up the bird.
Then, having gone to the marketplace, he sold one jewel; subsequently, he purchased clothing, cosmetics, and the like, as well as food.
And having eaten right there in that monastery and having given [food] to the bird, he adorned himself with those clothes, body-unguents, flowers, and other ornaments.
And at twilight, having mounted that very bird, he went there to the house of Rūpaṇikā, carrying the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Then, standing there above and moving through the sky, he who knew his place made a deep sound, so that his beloved, staying in private, might hear it.
And as soon as she heard that, Rūpaṇikā went out at night and saw him in the sky, adorned with jewels and resembling Nārāyaṇa.
"I, Hari, have come here for your sake"; having been told this by him, she bowed and said, "May the Lord show mercy."
Then, having descended and tethered the bird, Lohajaṅgha entered his dwelling together with that lovely woman.
Having there obtained his enjoyment, he emerged in another moment and, mounted upon the bird just as before, departed from there through the sky.
"I am a goddess, the wife of Viṣṇu; I do not converse with mortals. Having said this, Rūpaṇikā stood in silence at dawn.
"Daughter, why do you behave in such a manner? Tell me," thus Makaradaṃṣṭrā questioned her by her mother.
When pressed with persistence, she explained the reason for her silence to her mother by recounting the events of the night, having first caused a curtain to be drawn between them.
Having heard that, the procuress was filled with doubt; she herself then beheld Lohajaṅgha for a moment at night, mounted upon a bird.
And at dawn, having approached Rūpaṇikā—who was inside the cloth—in private, that procuress Makaradaṃṣṭrā bowed low and addressed her thus.
"O daughter, by the grace of the God, you have attained the state of a goddess here; and I am your mother in this place—therefore, grant me the fruit of being a mother."
"Grant me your favor; act as my petition to the Lord so that I may go to heaven with this very same aged body."
"So be it," said Rūpaṇikā, and she made that very matter known to Lohajaṅgha when he approached her at night in the guise of Viṣṇu.
Then Lohajaṅgha, appearing in the guise of a god, said to his beloved wife: "Your mother is wicked; it is clearly not fitting for her to lead you to heaven."
Furthermore, on the eleventh day, the gate in the sky is opened at dawn; and there, many hosts of Śambhu's attendants enter first.
In the midst of that [assembly], your mother, having assumed that very disguise, shall be brought forward; therefore, you must shave her head, leaving only five tufts of hair.
Make her neck rich with a garland of skulls, one side smeared with black pigment, and the other side anointed with vermilion, as she stands divested of clothing.
"Thus indeed shall I lead this woman, who has become a member of my retinue, to a happy heaven," having said this, Lohajaṅgha paused for a moment and then departed.
In the morning, Rūpaṇikā had him assume that appearance as described; then she too, dressed as her mother, stood facing toward heaven alone.
And at nightfall, Lohajaṅgha returned there once more; and Rūpaṇikā delivered that mother to him.
Then, mounted upon the bird and taking that procuress with him, he flew swiftly into the sky along with the women who were dressed in disfigured attire.
And standing there in the sky, he beheld a tall stone pillar in front of the temple, marked at its summit with a discus.
Upon its back, he placed that courtesan—who was like a banner for the counteraction of her detractors—resting solely upon the wheel.
"Stay here for a moment while I go and perform the favor of my presence upon the earth," he said, and then he departed from her sight.
Then, having seen the people gathered for the night vigil during the festival procession right there before the deity, he spoke thus from the sky:
"O people, today a plague that will destroy everyone shall fall upon you from above; therefore, seek refuge in Hari."
Having heard this voice from the sky, all those people of Mathurā became terrified; they took refuge in the Lord and remained there, intent on performing rites for their well-being.
Lohajaṅgha also, having descended from the sky and observing them, stood there unseen in their midst after he had discarded that divine guise.
"Even now the prince has not arrived, nor have I gone to heaven," thought the procuress as she stood upon the back of a pillar.
Unable to remain above any longer, making herself heard by the people below, she cried out in terror, "Alas! Alas! I am falling!"
Hearing that, they fell into a state of agitation, suspecting, "This is Mārī. Then those people standing before the goddess cried out, "O Goddess, do not fall! Do not fall!"
Then those people of Mathurā, including both children and the elderly, passed that night with great difficulty, distracted by the fear of Mārīca’s attack.
And in the morning, upon seeing that bawd standing there in such a state upon the pillar, the entire populace, including the king, recognized her.
When all the people there had overcome their fear and were bursting with laughter, Rūpaṇikā then arrived, having heard the news of what had occurred.
And she, seeing her own mother at the top of the pillar, immediately caused her to descend along with the people standing there, feeling both bashful and joyful.
Then that procuress was questioned there by all of them with curiosity as to what had happened, and she related it to them.
Then, having reflected upon that wondrous account of the Siddhas and others, those people—the king, the brahmins, the merchants, and the common folk—spoke these words.
"Let him who has thus deceived and cheated this woman of many suitors have the royal turban bound upon his head here in public."
Having heard that, Lohajaṅgha revealed himself there; and being questioned, he described the entire account from the very beginning.
And there he presented to the God offerings such as the conch and the discus, sent by Vibhīṣaṇa, which caused wonder among the people.
Then, having immediately bound the turban upon him, all the Mathurans, being well-pleased, made Rūpaṇikā subject to his will by royal decree.

Then, with his treasury overflowing with vast accumulations of jewels, Lohajaṅgha dwelt there at his ease together with his beloved, having avenged the humiliation and resentment inflicted by the procuress.

Having heard this story from the mouth of Vasantaka, who had assumed another form, Vāsavadattā felt supreme satisfaction within herself regarding her husband, the Lord of Vatsa, who was nearby in captivity.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the Kathāpīṭha book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave. Then Vāsavadattā, turning her back upon her father’s side, gradually established a deep bond of true affection toward the Lord of Vatsa.
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa entered once more into the presence of the Lord of Vatsa, having made himself invisible to all other people.
And in private, in the presence of Vasantaka, he informed him: "O King, you have been bound by Caṇḍamahāsena through his magical power."
Having given his daughter and honored you, he now wishes to release you; therefore, let us take this daughter of his ourselves and depart.
For in this way, a remedy for this arrogant one would have been ordained; moreover, there would be no reproach for you in the world on account of this lack of human effort.
And there is, O King, an elephant named Bhadravatī, which was given by this king to his daughter Vāsavadattā as a gift for her hand.
And she could not be followed with speed by any other elephant except Naḍāgiri; even he, upon merely seeing her, would not fight.
There is a certain elephant-driver here named Āṣāḍhaka; having given him abundant wealth, I took possession of him and established him [in this office].
Having mounted that female elephant together with Vāsavadattā, you must depart from here at night, well-armed and in secret.
And let a high official here, who understands the gestures of elephants, bring him to a state of intoxication with liquor so that he does not perceive this [plot].
Having said, "I shall go to Pulindaka's side and ahead of you for the purpose of guarding the path," Yaugandharāyaṇa departed.
Vatsarāja also took all that which was to be done to heart; then Vāsavadattā approached his presence.
Then, while engaged in various confidential conversations with her, the king related to her what had been told by Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Having understood that and being certain about her departure, she summoned Āṣāḍhaka and made him ready as an elephant-keeper.
Under the pretext of worshipping the gods, she gave him wine filled with intoxication; and by means of all the magical incantations, she brought about the Great Māra.
Then, at twilight, amidst the tumultuous roar of shimmering clouds, Āṣāḍhaka prepared that female elephant and brought her there.
As she was being harnessed, that female elephant let out a cry; and then the mahout, who was skilled in understanding the cries of elephants, heard it.
"Today I shall go sixty-three yojanas," said the female elephant; and he replied with words faltering from unrestrained intoxication.
Furthermore, the mind of that intoxicated elephant was not inclined toward reflection; and the drunken mahouts did not hear his words at all.
Then King Vatsa, having taken up his own lute there, had his bonds loosened by means of the stratagems obtained from Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Having been provided with weapons by Vāsavadattā, he mounted the female elephant at his own will, accompanied by Vasantaka.
Then Vāsavadattā also, together with her friend Kāñcanamālā, who shared her secrets, mounted that very same [palanquin].
Then, at night, the Lord of Vatsa departed from Ujjayinī with the elephant-driver as his fifth companion, by a path through which a rutting elephant had broken down the city wall.
The king then easily slew both those heroic guardians of that place, as well as both princes, Vīrabāhu and Tālabhaṭa.
Then that king, accompanied by his beloved wife, set out with speed; joyful and mounted upon a female elephant, he held the goad in his hand during the month of Āṣāḍha.
And having seen those two in Ujjayinī, the city guards, agitated at night, reported to the king that the rampart defenders had been slain.
Having searched for him in due course, Caṇḍamahāsena discovered that the King of Vatsa had fled and carried off Vāsavadattā.
Then his son, named Pālaka, when a clamor had arisen in the city, pursued the Lord of Vatsa after mounting Naḍāgiri.
The Lord of Vatsa also fought him as he approached with arrows, and Naḍāgiri, seeing that female elephant, did not strike her.
Then that Pālaka, skilled in speech, was turned back by his brother Gopālaka, who followed after him and was intent on performing his father’s funeral rites.
Then Vatsarāja also set out to proceed with confidence; as he went along slowly, the night gradually drew to a close.
Then, having reached the Vindhya forest at midday, the female elephant, who had come from sixty-three yojanas away, became thirsty for that king.
And when that king had descended along with his wife, that female elephant drank the water and, due to its defect, met her death in an instant.
Then the Lord of Vatsa, despondent along with Vāsavadattā, heard this voice rising up from the sky.
"O King, I am a Vidyadhara woman named Māyāvatī; for so long a time, I have been an elephant due to the fault of a curse."
"O Lord of Vatsa, I shall indeed repay your kindness today, and I shall do so once again for the son who is yet to be born to you."
"And this Vāsavadattā, your wife, is not at all human; she is a goddess who has descended to earth for a specific purpose."
Then, filled with joy, the king dispatched Vasantaka down the slope of the Vindhya mountains to inform his friend Pulindaka of his arrival.
And he himself, traveling on foot slowly accompanied by his beloved, was surrounded by bandits as he was rising up while proceeding right there.
With his bow as his only companion, that King of Vatsa slew one hundred and five of those bandits before Vāsavadattā.
At that very moment, Pulindaka, a friend of this king and a companion of Yaugandharāyaṇa, arrived there preceded by Vasantaka.
Having warded off those other dasyus, the king of the Bhillas prostrated before the Lord of Vatsa and led him, along with his beloved, to his own forest settlement.
There, that night, the Lord of Vatsa rested together with Vāsavadattā, while his feet were lacerated by the darbha grass of the forest.
In the morning, his commander-in-chief Rumaṇvat arrived in his presence, having been alerted by Yaugandharāyaṇa, who had previously dispatched a messenger.
And the entire camp, filling the very quarters of the sky, reached the Vindhya forest in such a way that it became indistinguishable from its own congestion.
Then, having entered that camp in that very forest region, the Lord of Vatsa remained there to learn news of Ujjayinī.
Then a merchant from Ujjayinī, a friend of Yaugandharāyaṇa, arrived there where he was staying and, having approached him, spoke as follows:
"O King, Caṇḍamahāsena is pleased with you, his son-in-law; he has therefore dispatched this door-keeper here to your presence."
As he was approaching and standing behind, I remained right in front, having come quickly in concealment to inform the Lord.
Having heard this, the Lord of Vatsa rejoiced and recounted everything to Vāsavadattā; she too attained the highest joy.
Having abandoned her kinsmen and being in haste for the marriage rites, Vāsavadattā was then both bashful and full of longing.
Then, for her own diversion, she said to Vasantaka, who was standing nearby, "Tell me some story."
And then the wise Vasantaka told this story to that lovely-eyed woman, which increased her devotion to her husband.
There is a city in this world renowned as Tāmraliptī; and in it there lived a merchant named Dhanadatta, who possessed great wealth.
Being childless, he assembled many Brahmins and, bowing down, said: "Act in such a way that I may have a son without delay."
Then those brahmins said to him: "This is not at all difficult; for here, O twice-born ones, everything is accomplished through Vedic rites."
And likewise, O King, there was once a certain king who was childless; he had one hundred and five women in his inner apartments.
And by means of the Putrīyeṣṭi sacrifice, a son named Janturna was born to him; he was like the rising of the new moon to the eyes of all his wives.
Once, as the boy was crawling about on his knees, an ant bit him on the thigh, causing him to let out a terrified shriek.
At that moment, a tumultuous cry of lamentation arose within the inner apartments; even the king wailed, "O son! O son! like an ordinary man.
When the boy had recovered in an instant and the ants had been removed, the king lamented his state of having only one son, which was the sole cause of his sorrow.
"Is there some means by which I might have many sons?"—with this anxiety, he questioned the brahmins.
They replied to him, "O King, you have this means here: offer this son of yours into the fire; thus, his entire flesh will be consumed."
"By smelling that fragrance, all the queens shall obtain sons from you. Having heard this, the king caused all of that to be done accordingly.
That king obtained as many sons as there were wives; therefore, we shall also accomplish the birth of a son for you through the fire-oblation.
Having spoken thus to Dhanadatta and having provided him with the prescribed sacrificial fee, those brahmins performed the fire-oblation for that merchant; thereafter, a son was born to him.
And that boy named Guhasena grew up gradually; meanwhile, his father Dhanadatta began searching for a wife for him.
Then that father went together with his son to another island on the pretext of trade, for the sake of his daughter-in-law.
There, for the sake of his own son Guhasena, he requested the maiden named Devasmitā from the eminent merchant Dharmagupta.
But Dharmagupta, out of affection for his daughter, did not accept that proposal, considering Tāmraliptī to be difficult to reach.
But as soon as Devasmitā saw Guhasena, her heart was drawn away by his virtues, and she became single-mindedly resolved to abandon her kinsmen.
And having made an appointment with her beloved—who was accompanied by his father—through the mouth of a female friend, she departed from that island at night.
Then, having reached Tāmraliptī after the two had performed their marriage, the minds of the husband and wife became bound to one another by the bond of mutual love.
Then, when his father had passed away, Guhasena was urged by his kinsmen to travel to the island of Kaṭāha, as it happened by chance.
But his wife Devasmitā then did not consent to that departure; she was full of jealousy, fearing the attachment of her husband to another woman out of desire.
Then, while his wife was unwilling and his kinsmen were urging him on, Guhasena became bewildered, remaining paralyzed as to what ought to be done.
Then, having gone there, he observed a vow at the temple without food, thinking: "May the god here point out a means to me."
Devasmitā likewise undertook that vow together with him; then Śiva granted a vision of himself to the couple in a dream.
Having presented two red lotuses, that god spoke to those two: "Both of you, each take one of these lotuses in your hand."
And even though they are situated at a distance, if one should commit a breach of moral conduct, the lotus in the hand of the other will wither; it cannot be otherwise.
Having heard this and awakened, the couple saw what seemed like each other's heart—a red lotus held in their hands.
Then Guhasena, holding a lotus, set out; but she remained there with Devasmitā, her eyes fixed upon the lotus.
Guhasena also quickly reached that island of Kaṭāha, and there he proceeded to engage in the buying and selling of jewels.
And seeing that lotus, which was never withered, always in his hand, four sons of merchants there were filled with wonder.
Having led him to that house by a clever stratagem and made him drink copious amounts of wine, they questioned him regarding the story of the lotus; and he, being intoxicated, related it to them.
Then those four merchant's sons, having reflected upon Guhasena’s long-standing business of buying and selling jewels and other goods, [acted accordingly].
Having consulted together out of curiosity, those wicked men, desiring to bring about the ruin of her wife's virtue, went quickly and unobserved to Tāmraliptī.
Seeking a means there, they approached a female renunciant named Yogakaraṇḍikā, who resided at the Sugata-āyatana.
And with affection, they said to her, "O Blessed One, if that which we desire can be accomplished by you, then we shall give you many riches."
She also said: "Surely some woman is desired here by you youths; therefore, go and accomplish it, for I have no desire for wealth."
"I have a disciple named Siddhikarī who is endowed with great intelligence; indeed, it was through her favor that I acquired immeasurable wealth."
"How was such great wealth obtained by you through the lack of faith among your disciples?"—thus questioned by those merchant's sons, the female ascetic replied.
If you have curiosity, O sons, listen as I describe it to you: once upon a time, a certain merchant arrived here from the North Country.
While he was staying here, my disciple went to his house and, having altered her appearance, resorted to the status of a servant there by means of a stratagem.
Having gained the merchant's trust and secretly stolen the entire hoard of gold from his house, she then departed at dawn.
Seeing her depart from the city with a hurried gait as if out of fear, a certain *ḍomba* named Mṛdaṅgahasta quickly followed after her for the purpose of plundering her.
Having reached the foot of a banyan tree and seeing that the Domba had approached, the deceitful Siddhikarī spoke these words with feigned distress:
"Having quarreled with my husband today, I have come out from my home; therefore, O good sir, please tie this noose for me so that I may die."
"Let her die by the noose; why should I kill this woman? Thinking thus, that Domba fastened the noose upon that tree.
Then Siddhikarī, appearing as if bewildered, said to that Domba: "How can this hanging be performed by you? Let it be shown to me."
Then that Domba, having placed that mṛdaṅga drum beneath his feet and saying, "Let it be done thus," fastened the noose around his own neck.
That Siddhikarī also immediately crushed that mṛdaṅga with a kick of her foot; then that Ḍomba too perished in the noose.
Arriving at that time to search for her, the merchant saw from a distance at the foot of the tree that Siddhikarī had been robbed of her entire treasury.
She too, seeing him approaching, climbed that tree unobserved and remained upon a branch, her form concealed by a mass of leaves.
And when he arrived with his merchant followers, they saw only that Domba bound by the noose; they did not see Siddhikarī anywhere at all.
Thinking, "Perhaps she has climbed that tree," at that very moment, one of the merchant's servants climbed up that tree.
My love has always been for you alone, and you have likewise ascended upon my affection; therefore, O handsome one, this wealth is yours—come, enjoy me.
Having spoken thus, she embraced and kissed his face; while bestowing success upon him, she bit off the tongue of that foolish-minded merchant’s servant with her teeth.
Overcome by agony and vomiting blood from his mouth, he fell from that tree, uttering some indistinct sound like "lalala."
Seeing that, the merchant was terrified; realizing he had been seized by a spirit, he fled from there with his servants and went to his own home.
Then, having descended from the treetop, the female ascetic, likewise terrified, went home taking with her that wealth which brought about success.
For such is my disciple, endowed with great wisdom; and thus, by her grace, sons and wealth have been obtained by me.
Having spoken thus to those sons of merchants, the female ascetic then showed them her own disciple who had arrived at that very moment.
And he said to them, "O sons, tell me now your true intention; what woman do you desire? I shall quickly procure her for you."
Having heard that, they said to her, "This woman named Devasmitā is the wife of the merchant Guhasena; unite us with her."
Having heard this, that female ascetic then promised to perform that task and gave her own house for these sons of merchants to stay in.
Then, having delighted the people there with gifts of food and other provisions, she entered the house of Guhasena together with her disciple.
Then, as she approached the door of Devasmitā’s dwelling, the dog, which had never before obstructed her, barred her way while bound by a chain.
Then Devasmitā, having seen her, sent a maidservant out, thinking, "What could she have come for? and then admitted her herself.
Having entered and offered her blessings, the wicked female ascetic, feigning great respect, spoke to that virtuous Devasmītā.
I have always had a desire to see you, and today, moreover, I saw you in a dream; therefore, being eager, I have come to see you.
Seeing you deprived of your husband, my heart is pained; for beauty and youth are indeed fruitless and barren when devoid of the enjoyment of a beloved.
Having comforted that virtuous woman for a long time with these and other words, the female ascetic took her leave and returned to her own home.
And on the second day, having taken a piece of meat filled with powdered black pepper, she went once more to the house of Devasmitā.
There he gave that piece of meat to the dog at the door; and the bitch immediately devoured it along with the pepper.
Then, due to the defect caused by the pepper, unobstructed tears flowed from her eyes, and her nose began to run.
At that very moment, that deceitful female ascetic entered into the presence of Devasmitā; having been offered hospitality by her, she began to weep.
And when questioned by Devasmitā, she spoke thus with great difficulty: "Daughter, look now at this bitch weeping outside."
For today, having recognized me as one who was her companion in a previous birth, she has begun to weep; therefore, tears have risen from my compassion.
Having heard that and looking outside at the bitch who seemed as if she were weeping, Devasmitā reflected for a moment, "What is this strange thing?"
Then that female ascetic said: "Daughter, in a previous birth, this woman and I were both the two wives of a certain Brahmin."
And that husband of ours, by the king's command, went repeatedly from here and there to distant lands on various missions.
And while he was away on his travels, by freely engaging in sexual union with men, I did not deceive the collection of elements and senses through worldly enjoyments.
For non-injury toward living beings and the senses is considered the supreme dharma; therefore, O daughter, I have become one who remembers her past births in this life.
At that time, however, she protected only her virtue due to a lack of knowledge; because of that, she fell into the womb of a dog, yet she remembers her former birth.
"What dharma is this? Surely this is a clever ruse devised by her. Having reflected thus, Suprajñā said to that Devasmītā:
"O Blessed One, for so long this Dharma has not been known by me; therefore, bring about my union with some beloved man who possesses the truth."
Then she said to the female ascetic, "Some sons of merchants who have come from another island are staying here; I shall bring them to you."
Having spoken thus, the female ascetic departed for her home filled with joy; and Devaśmitā, at her own leisure, addressed her maidservants as follows.
Surely, having seen that unfading lotus in my husband's hand and having questioned him about what had happened, he once asked me out of curiosity why I drink wine.
"These certain deceitful sons of merchants have come here from that island for my destruction; it was by them that this wicked female ascetic was employed."
"Go quickly and bring wine mixed with that dhattūra; then, having gone, have an iron foot made for the dog."
Thus addressed by Devasmitā, those maidservants did exactly as she said; and one maid, at her word, then assumed that very form.
That female ascetic also, having taken one from among those four merchant sons who had been designated by turns starting with the first, then departed.
Having brought him—who was disguised as his own disciple—into Devasmitā’s house that evening, he departed secretly.
Then, there, that maidservant disguised as Devasmitā respectfully made the merchant's son drink that honey infused with dhattūra.
His consciousness stolen by that intoxication which is like wine, he had his clothes and other belongings taken away by the maidservants and was made naked there.
Having marked his forehead with the paw of a dog, they led him away at night and threw him into a pit filled with filth.
Then, having regained consciousness during the final watch of the night, he saw himself as if plunged into a pit of Avīci hell brought about by his own evil deeds.
Then, having risen and bathed, that merchant's son, still naked, went to the house of the female ascetic while touching the mark upon his forehead.
"Lest I alone become an object of ridicule," he said to his other friends there, "I have been robbed as I was coming here."
Having excused his headache by claiming it was caused by staying awake and excessive drinking, he stood in the morning with his head wrapped in a cloth.
And in the same way, that second merchant's son also came to Devasmitā’s house in the evening and met with the same humiliation.
He too, having arrived there naked, said: "Even though I had set my ornaments right there, I went out and was robbed by thieves."
In the morning, he too, under the pretext of a headache, wrapped his head in a cloth and concealed the mark upon the surface of his forehead.
Thus, all those sons of merchants, filled with shame, were successively subjected to public humiliation, disgrace, and the loss of their wealth as they each denied their involvement.
Thinking, "Let it be so for her as well," they humiliated that female ascetic and departed from there without revealing her identity.
Then one day, the female ascetic Devaśmitā, joyful at the thought, "I have accomplished my purpose," went to the house of [the king] together with her disciple.
There, Devasmitā, having shown her respect, made her drink wine mixed with dhattūra, as if it had been brought forth out of sheer joy.
Then that virtuous woman had Mātā, along with her disciples, their ears and noses cut off, and threw them into a mire of impurity.
"Lest these merchant's sons go and kill their husband at any time," she said, and being thus distressed, she related that entire account to her mother-in-law.
Then her mother-in-law said to her, "Daughter, you have done well; however, some harm might perhaps come to that son of mine."
Then Devasmitā said, "Just as Śaktimatī protected her husband in the past through her wisdom, so shall I protect him."
"How did you, O capable daughter, protect your husband? Let it be told! Thus questioned by her mother-in-law, Devasmitā then spoke.
In our country, within the city, there is a powerful great yakṣa known as Maṇibhadra, whose installation was performed by our ancestors.
The people living there come before him and perform various offerings for the sake of accomplishing their respective desires.
Whatever man is caught there at night with another's wife is placed by her together with her in the inner chamber of this yakṣa.
In the same manner at dawn, having brought him along with his wife to the royal assembly and having made that conduct manifest, he is to be punished; such is the established rule.
Once, at night, a merchant named Samudradatta, who had met with his wife there, was apprehended by the city guard.
And having led him there, the merchant was cast by him into that temple of the Yakṣa along with the other woman, its door secured with a firm bolt.
At that very moment, the merchant's wife, named Śaktimatī, who was possessed of great wisdom and devoted to her husband, learned of this event.
Then, at night, she went confidently to that abode of the Yakṣa with her circle of friends, taking offerings in the guise of a woman of noble character.
Having gone there out of greed for the sacrificial fee, he became the worshiper of that very deity; opening the door and announcing the city governor, he granted him entrance.
Having entered and seeing her husband with his wife, he looked embarrassed; she then had her own attire put on him and told the woman, "Go out."
And having gone out at night, that woman departed from there in that very disguise; Śaktimatī, however, remained there together with that husband.
And when the king’s officials arrived in the morning and began their investigation, they saw that merchant accompanied by his own wife, to the astonishment of everyone.
Having learned of this, the king, as if from the mouth of Death itself, punished the city magistrate and released that merchant from the abode of the yakṣas.
Thus, in the past, Śaktimatī protected her husband through her wisdom; in the same way, I shall go and protect my husband by means of skillful stratagems.
Having spoken thus in private to her mother-in-law, the ascetic Devasmitā, accompanied by her own maidservants, assumed the guise of a merchant.
And having boarded a ship under the pretext of trade, he then went to the island of Kaṭāha, where her husband resided.
Having gone there, she saw her husband Guhasena among the merchants, appearing like consolation itself embodied in external form.
He too, seeing that figure in human form from afar as if drinking it in, thought: "Who could this be who resembles my beloved? Could he be a merchant?"
And that Devasmitā, having gone there to the king, made this request: "I have a petition; therefore, let all the subjects be assembled."
Then, having summoned all the citizens with curiosity, the king spoke to her while she was disguised as a merchant, saying, "What request do you have?"
Then Devasmitā said: "The four servants who were standing here in my midst have fled; let the King restore them to me."
Then the king said to her: "All these citizens are standing here; having recognized them all as your own servants, take them."
Then, she took those four merchant’s sons into her own house—men who had previously been humiliated and whose heads were now bound with cloths.
"How can these sons of the caravan leader become your slaves? the merchants standing there then said to her, filled with anger.
Then she replied to them: "If you have no conviction, let the foreheads of these dogs be examined; they were marked with my footprints."
Saying "So be it," he untied the head-cloths of those four, and they all beheld there the dog's paw imprinted upon their foreheads.
Then, while the merchant community was ashamed, the king, filled with wonder, asked Devasmitā himself, "What is this?"
She related everything exactly as it had happened, and all the people laughed; the king then said to her, "Those men are your slaves."
Then other merchants gave abundant wealth to that virtuous woman for the sake of liberating those four from slavery, as well as a fine to the king.

Having taken that wealth and recovered her own husband, Devasmitā—honored by all virtuous people—returned to her own city of Tāmraliptī; and from then on, she never again experienced separation from her beloved.

Thus, O Goddess, women born of noble families worship their husbands with pure and steadfast conduct, their minds never turning elsewhere; for the husband is indeed the supreme deity of virtuous wives.

Having heard this noble tale from the mouth of Vasantaka while on the road—she who had recently been abandoned by Vāsavadattā at her father’s house—the mind of the King of Vatsa, though previously bound by mature affection for her as his wife, became solely intent upon devotion to him, thereby making her a vessel of shame.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Kathāmukha* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave. Now, while the King of Vatsa was staying there in the midst of the Vindhya mountains, the doorkeeper of Caṇḍamahāsena arrived at his side.
Having arrived and paid his respects, he said this to the king: "King Caṇḍamahāsena has sent this message to you."
It was right that Vāsavadattā was carried off by you yourself; for it was for that very purpose that I brought you here.
And this [gift] was not given by me personally to you here while you were self-restrained, because I was apprehensive that such might not be your affection toward us.
Therefore, O King, you should wait a little while so that the marriage of this daughter of mine may not take place now in an improper manner.
For my son Gopālaka will indeed come here before long; he shall perform his sister's marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites.
Having thus delivered this message to the King of Vatsa, the doorkeeper reported each point to Vāsavadattā.
Then, together with the joyful Vāsavadattā, the delighted Lord of Vatsa set his mind upon going to Kauśāmbī.
"You two should wait here for the arrival of Gopālaka; afterwards, you shall come to Kauśāmbī together with him."
Having spoken thus, the lord of the earth stationed that doorkeeper, his father-in-law, and his own friend Pulindaka right there.
He was followed by the lords of the nāgas, who were shedding streams of rut like mobile slopes of the Vindhya mountains that had come out of affection.
The earth, as if offering praise with the sound of the hoofbeats from the massed cavalry of horses—a sound surpassing the compositions of bards—seemed to celebrate him.
With the uplifted masses of dust from his army that leaped into the sky, he caused Indra to suspect the appearance of winged mountains.
Then, on the very next morning, that king of kings set out for his own city together with Queen Vāsavadattā.
Then, having reached that territory after two or three days, the king rested for one night in the palace of Rumaṇvat.

And on the following day, accompanied by his beloved, he entered Kauśāmbī, where a great festival had finally arrived after a long time, and where the people looked up with eager faces, longing for him on the road.
And then, with auspicious baths and ornaments commenced by the women, that city shone like a woman when her husband has returned after a long absence.
And there the citizens, their grief now stilled, beheld the King of Vatsa accompanied by his bride, like a rain-cloud charged with lightning seen by peacocks.
And the women of the city, standing upon the tops of the palaces, covered the sky with their faces, which possessed the splendor of blooming golden lotuses on the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā.
Then the King of Vatsa entered his own royal palace together with Vāsavadattā, who was like a second royal splendor.
Crowded with kings who had come for audience and filled with the auspicious songs of the Magadhas, that city of Rājagṛha then shone as if it had just awakened from sleep.
Then Vāsavadattā’s brother, Gopālaka, arrived shortly thereafter, bringing with him both the warder and Pulindaka.
Vāsavadattā, her eyes wide with joy, approached him as he was being welcomed by the king like another Ānanda.
"Lest there be shame for her as she beholds this brother of hers"—with this very thought, he restrained the tears in her eyes at that moment.
Then, encouraged by those words of her father’s message, she considered herself to have achieved her purpose, as if reunited with her own kin.
Then, on the following day, Gopālaka busied himself there with the great festival of the wedding between her and the Lord of Vatsa, proceeding exactly according to tradition.
Then the Lord of Vatsa took the hand of Vāsavadattā, which was as radiant as a fresh sprout newly blossomed upon the creeper of love.
She too, with her eyes closed from the intense bliss of the touch of her beloved's hand, her limbs drenched in trembling and perspiration, was covered in a dense horripilation.
At that moment, he appeared as if pierced by the flower-bowed god of love with a continuous stream of the Susaṃmohana, Vāyavya, and Vāruṇa weapons.
As she circumambulated the fire, her gaze, copper-red with smoke, cast forth, as it were, the first thread of the sweetness of intoxication.
With his treasury filled by the jewels offered by the cowherds and the presents from other kings, the Lord of Vatsa then truly embodied the sovereignty of a king of kings.
Having completed their marriage ceremony, the bride and groom first appeared before the eyes of the world, and afterwards entered their own dwelling.
Then, on his own festival, King Vatsarāja personally honored Gopālaka and Pulindaka with the binding of turbans and other marks of distinction.
For the purpose of honoring the kings and the citizens as was appropriate, Yaugandharāyaṇa and Rumaṇvat were appointed by him.
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke thus to Rumaṇvat: "We have been appointed by the king to a difficult task, for the minds of people are indeed hard to grasp."
Even a fool, when provoked, will certainly give rise to anger; therefore, my friend, listen to this story of a ruined fool.
In ancient times, there was a certain Brahmin named Rudraśarman; and that householder had two wives.
One woman, having given birth to a son, passed away; he was then placed by him into the hands of his stepmother.
And when he had grown somewhat, she gave him coarse food; by that, the boy became one with dusty limbs and a large belly.
"How was this infant of mine, who is deprived of his mother, neglected by you? Thus Rudraśarman then spoke to that other wife.
"Even though he is served with affections, he remains just like this; what can I do for him? she said to her husband in this manner.
And that twice-born man thought, "Surely this is her true nature"; for who would believe the false and artless words of women to be anything but a lie?
Thinking, "This one has perished while still a child," he became known by the name Bālavinaṣṭaka; thus that boy came to be called by that name in his father's house.
"This stepmother of mine torments me constantly; it would be better if I were to perform some kind of counter-action against her."
Thus did that Bālavinaṣṭaka reflect, for although he was only five years of age, alas, he was possessed of great intelligence.
Then, having arrived from the royal palace, he spoke to his father in private with indistinct words: "Father, I have two fathers."
Thus that boy spoke every day, and his father, suspecting his wife was with another man, avoided even touching her.
She too reflected: "Why is my husband angry with me when there is no fault? Could something have been done by some misdeed of the child?"
Having respectfully bathed him and given him wholesome food, she took the boy Vinaṣṭaka onto her lap and questioned him.
"Son, has my father Rudraśarman been angered by you on my account? Upon hearing this, the boy spoke to his stepmother.
If you do not desist even now, I shall do even more than this to you; why do you, who are nourishing your own son, constantly afflict me?
Having heard that, she bowed to him and spoke these words following her oath: "I shall never do such a thing again; therefore, grant my husband his life through your favor."
Then the boy said to her, "In that case, let one maidservant show a mirror to my father when he has arrived; I shall know for certain."
Having said, "So be it," she appointed a maidservant to show a mirror to Rudraśarman when he arrived a moment later.
There, showing him at that very moment his own reflection, the boy said, "This is my second father; he is my father."
Having heard that, Rudraśarman’s doubts vanished; he immediately became gracious toward his wife, who had been unjustly defamed.
Thus even a fool, having fallen into a state of transformation, would produce such a fault; therefore, this entire retinue of ours is worthy of being properly delighted.
Having spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa, together with Rumaṇvat, then honored all the people gathered for the festival of the King of Vatsa.
And they so delighted the circle of kings that everyone thought, "These two are devoted to me alone."
And the king honored those two ministers, along with Vasantaka, by bestowing upon them garments, unguents, ornaments, and villages from his own hand.
Then, having celebrated the wedding festival, the Lord of Vatsa, united with her, Vāsavadattā, considered himself to have attained the very fruits of his heart's desires.

After a long time, there arose between the two of them, out of affection, a certain sequence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that was ever-present, heart-stealing, and delightful like the movement of a pair of ruddy geese weary from their nightly wanderings.
And just as the intimacy between the husband and wife reached maturity, so too did their love attain, as it were, a state of ever-newness.
Then Gopālaka, having been requested by the King of Vatsa to return quickly, set out at once upon his father’s command to arrange the marriage.
Once, that King of Vatsa, being fickle, secretly consorted with a female attendant of the harem named Viracitā, who had been his companion in a former life.
Having stumbled over her name, he clung to the queen's feet to propitiate her; consecrated by her tears, he obtained the empire of good fortune.
Furthermore, there was a princess named Bandhumatī, won by the strength of his own arm; sent by Gopālaka as a gift for the Queen.
She was concealed under the very name Mañjulika, like another Goddess of Fortune risen from the ocean of loveliness.
Accompanied by Vasantaka, that king, having seen her in a bower of creepers in the garden, married her secretly according to the Gāndharva rite.
Vāsavadattā, standing there in concealment, saw this; she became enraged and, having bound Vasantaka, led him away.
Then the king sought refuge with her female ascetic friend, Sāṅkṛtyāyanī by name, who had come from his father’s family.
Having propitiated that queen, she, acting upon her command, gave Bandhumatī to the king; for the mind of a virtuous woman is indeed gentle.
Then the queen released Vasantaka from his bonds; and he, approaching the queen, spoke to her with a smile as follows:
"O Queen Bandhumatī, what offense have I committed against you? You, who are angry with the snakes, are striking at the mandalaka-snakes."
When he was thus questioned by the queen out of curiosity, saying, "Explain this simile to me," Vasantaka then spoke again.
Long ago, a certain son of a sage named Ruru, while wandering at will, beheld a maiden of wondrous appearance.
Born from a Vidyadhara upon the celestial nymph Menaka, she was raised by the sage Sthulakesa in his own hermitage.
And upon seeing her, who was named Pramadvarā, the mind of that Ruru was captivated; he then went and requested her from Sthūlakeśa.
Sthūlakeśa also promised that maiden to him; and when the wedding was near, she was suddenly bitten by a snake.
Then, with a despondent heart, he heard this voice in the sky: "O Brahmin, restore this woman, whose life has reached its end, by giving her half of your own lifespan."
Having heard that, he gave her half of his own life right then; by means of that, she was restored to life, and he married her.
Then Ruru, constantly enraged, killed every snake he saw, thinking, "My wife might have been bitten by one of these."
