Then one of them, a *ḍuṇḍubha*, spoke to him who was seeking to kill him in human speech: "O Brahmin, you are angry with snakes; why do you kill *ḍuṇḍubhas*?"
"Your beloved has been bitten by a snake, and both a snake and a *duṇḍubha* have been torn apart; all snakes are venomous, but *duṇḍubhas* are without venom."
Having heard that, he replied to him, "Friend, who indeed are you? The Dundubha also said, "O Brahmin, I am a sage fallen [from my state] due to a curse."
"This curse of mine has reached its limit with your conversation"; having said this, when he had vanished, the Guru did not strike them again.
O Queen, this has been spoken by me as a comparison for you: "Strike at the Dundubhas, you who are enraged at the buffaloes!"
When Vasantaka had finished speaking these words with a playful laugh, Vāsavadattā, standing by her husband’s side, was pleased with him.
Thus the amorous Udayana, the King of Vatsa, at the feet of the queen, constantly performed various springtime arts—sweet as honey—to appease her anger.

The tongue of that happy king was ever devoted solely to the taste of wine, his sense of hearing was enamored with the sound of the sweet lute, and his gaze remained fixed upon the face of his beloved.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the Kathāmukha book of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And this second book, the Kathāmukha, is completed. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Book, named Lāvāṇaka. This nectar of stories, it is said, emerged long ago from the ocean of Hara’s mouth when it was churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Mountain King (Pārvatī). Those who taste this forcibly, having attained the state of the gods through the grace of Bhava (Śiva), bear the burden of divinity upon the earth, free from obstacles.
The First Wave.
Salutations to that Conqueror of Obstacles, whose grace even the Creator sought for the sake of achieving the unimpeded manifestation of the universe.
Even Śaṅkara, though being embraced by his beloved, trembles at his command; victorious is he of the peerless arrow who thus conquers the world.
Thus, having obtained Vāsavadattā, that King of Vatsa gradually became even more intensely devoted to her alone, his mind entirely absorbed in the joy of that union.
And his great minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, along with the general Rumaṇvat, bore the burden of the kingdom day and night.
Once, having brought Rumaṇvat home at night, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, filled with anxiety, spoke to him.
This Lord of Vatsa was born into the lineage of the Pāṇḍavas; the entire earth and the city named Gajasāhvaya have come to him by hereditary succession.
All that has been renounced by this king without any desire for conquest; yet here, in this very single province, his sovereignty has been established.
Addicted to women, wine, and hunting, he remains indeed free from care; all responsibility for the kingdom has been entrusted by him to us.
Therefore, we ourselves must act with our own intelligence in such a way that he indeed obtains that hereditary sovereignty over the entire earth.
For when this is done, both devotion and the practice of mantra will have been accomplished; everything is achieved through intelligence—listen, therefore, to this account.
In former times, there was a king named Mahāsena; he was once attacked by another king who was exceedingly powerful.
Then, having assembled with his ministers who were intent on preventing the failure of their own interests, Mahāsena was indeed made to pay a fine to that enemy.
And having inflicted the punishment, that proud king was deeply tormented, thinking: "Why have I performed a prostration before the enemy?"
And by that very [act], a tumor arose within him due to his grief; and overcome by both the tumor and his sorrow, the king became one on the verge of death.
Then, considering her incurable by medicine, a certain wise physician falsely said to that king, "O Lord, your queen is dead."
Upon hearing that, as the king suddenly fell to the ground, his abdominal tumor burst of its own accord due to the powerful force of his grief.
Recovered from his illness, the king enjoyed his desired pleasures for a long time together with that very queen, and he conquered his enemies once again.
Just as that physician, through his wisdom, acted for the benefit of the king, so do we act for the benefit of the king; we shall bring his realm to fulfillment.
And there is one obstacle there: Pradyota, the lord of Magadha; for he is always our rear-enemy and raises up a rebellion from behind.
He possesses a jewel of a daughter named Padmāvatī; we shall request her for the sake of this King of Vatsa.
Having concealed Vāsavadattā by means of our own ingenuity and having set fire to the bedchamber, let us announce everywhere that the queen has been burnt.
The Lord of Magadha will not give that daughter to any other king; for this very reason, when he was previously entreated by me, he spoke thus.
"I will not give this daughter, who is dearer to me than my own self, to the King of Vatsa; for his affection for Vāsavadattā is indeed very great."
As long as Queen Satyavatī lives, the King of Vatsa will never marry another; however, once the report spreads that the queen has been consumed by fire, everything will be accomplished.
Once Padmāvatī has been obtained, the Lord of Magadha, as a relative by marriage, will no longer harbor resentment and will instead become an ally.
"Therefore, let us go to conquer the eastern quarter and the others in succession; in this way, we shall bring the entire earth under the Vatsa king's control."
Moreover, while we have exerted ourselves, this king shall surely obtain the earth; for previously, a divine voice spoke thus.
Having heard these words from Yaugandharāyaṇa, the bull among ministers, Rumaṇvat spoke to him, suspecting that this was a rash act.
If a pretext were ever made for the sake of Padmāvatī, it would lead only to our own ruin; therefore, listen to a story on this matter.
There is a city named Mākandikā on the banks of the Jāhnavī; in that city there once lived a certain wandering mendicant who observed a vow of silence.
And he, subsisting on alms and surrounded by many wandering mendicants, took up residence in a small cell within a temple.
Once, having entered the house of a certain merchant for the sake of alms, he saw a beautiful maiden coming out, carrying the alms.
Upon seeing her of such wondrous form, that rogue, fallen under the power of desire, cried out "Alas! Alas! What misery! while the merchant listened.
Having accepted the alms, he then went to his own home; thereupon, that merchant, having approached him in private, questioned him out of wonder.
"Why have you suddenly abandoned your silence and spoken just now? Having heard that, the wandering mendicant spoke thus to the merchant:
This daughter of yours possesses ill-omened marks; when her marriage takes place, the destruction of you, along with your sons and wife, will certainly occur.
"Seeing this, sorrow has arisen within me, for you are my devotee; it was for your sake that I broke my silence and spoke thus."
"Therefore, let this maiden be placed by you tonight in a chest with a lamp set upon it, and cast into the Ganges."
Having agreed, saying "So be it," that merchant then went there and performed everything accordingly at night out of fear; for the fearful are indeed devoid of reflection.
At that time, the wandering mendicant also said to his own followers: "Go to the Ganges; go there and look for whatever river flows within it."
"Bring here that chest which has a lamp on its back, keeping it hidden; and it must not be opened even when the sound is heard within."
Saying "So be it," they set out, but before they reached the Ganges, one of the princes descended into it.
There, seeing that casket which had been cast in by the merchant, he had it brought by his servants by means of a lamp and suddenly opened it out of curiosity.
And inside he beheld that maiden who maddened his heart, and at that very moment he united with her by the Gāndharva rite.
Having placed that casket and likewise the lamp fixed upright within it, he cast them into the Ganges, having set a fierce monkey inside.
Then, when that prince had departed with the jewel of a maiden, those disciples of the wandering mendicant arrived, searching for him.
They saw that basket and, taking it, brought it to the presence of the wandering mendicant; then he, being delighted, said to them:
"I alone shall accomplish the mantra here above; you must lie silently below for this night."
Having said this, that wandering mendicant, desiring the merchant’s daughter, placed her in that chest and opened it upon the roof of his hut.
Then, emerging from her, a monkey of terrifying form rushed toward him, like his own misconduct incarnate.
At that moment, with his teeth he tore out the nose of that wicked one, and with his claws his ears, like an expert in subduing enemies acting in fury.
Then, having descended from there in that state, the wandering mendicant was seen by his disciples, who had restrained their laughter with great effort.
Having awakened in the morning and learned all of that, every person laughed; and that merchant and his daughter rejoiced, having now attained their goal.
Just as that wandering mendicant fell into ridicule, so too might we at some time fall [into ridicule] if our employment of a stratagem were not successful.
"Separation from Queen Vāsavadattā is indeed fraught with many evils"; having been addressed thus by Rumaṇvat, Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:

Success in one's endeavors cannot come otherwise than through exertion, and it is certain that in the absence of exertion, even what is already established would perish if the king were to fall into calamity.
Even if we have attained the reputation of being ministers, it would turn out otherwise for us; and we would become violators of our master's trust.
For a king whose success depends on his own efforts, wisdom is considered the primary instrument; what need is there for ministers, whether they act or do not act?
But for one whose success depends upon ministers, their wisdom alone is the means of achieving one's goals; if they themselves lack energy, a final farewell has been offered to prosperity.
Now, if you have any doubt regarding Caṇḍamahāsena, the father of the Goddess, both he and his son, along with the Goddess herself, will surely do my bidding.
To Yaugandharāyaṇa, the leader of the wise, who had spoken thus, Rumaṇvat, his heart apprehensive of negligence, spoke again.
"Even one possessed of discernment is afflicted by the pain of separation from a beloved woman; how much more so this King Vatsa? In this regard, hear this story."
In former times there was a king named Devasena, the best among the wise; Śrāvastī was his capital city.
And in that city there was a certain merchant of great wealth; it is said that to him was born a daughter who had no equal.
That maiden also became renowned by the name Unmādinī; for upon seeing her form, every person who encountered her would go mad.
"The daughter must not be given by me anywhere without first informing the king; for he might become angry," thought her father, the merchant.
Then, having gone there, he addressed King Devasena: "O King, I have a jewel of a daughter; if she is of use to you, let her be accepted."
Having heard that, the king then dispatched trusted brahmins, saying, "Go and investigate whether she possesses the auspicious marks or not."
"So be it," said those twice-born ones; having gone and seen that merchant's daughter Unmādinī, they were immediately overcome by agitation as passion arose within them.
Once she is married, the king will abandon everything with his mind fixed solely upon her; the affairs of state will perish, and thus, what is the use of her?
Having thus returned to their natural state and consulted together, those twice-born ones went away and falsely told the king, "That maiden possesses the marks of a low lineage."
Then that merchant gave Unmādinī, who had been abandoned by the king, to his general, even though she felt deep humiliation within herself.
Then, once while she was staying in the palace in her husband's house, she perceived that the king had arrived by that path and showed herself to him.
And as soon as the king beheld her, that medicine for the enchantment of the world, he became like one possessed by madness, as if Love himself had cast a spell upon him.
Having returned to his own abode and realized that she had previously been treated with contempt, he became despondent and fell into a state of intense suffering from the fever of burning anguish.
"She is a maidservant, not the wife of another; let her be taken, or else I shall abandon her at a temple, and then let my lord accept her."
Thus, being earnestly entreated by that husband of his, his own general, the king spoke as follows.
"I shall not take another's wife, nor will you abandon her; otherwise, your dharma will perish and you shall be punished by me."
Having heard that, the other ministers and the rest remained silent, and the king, by that very fever of love, gradually met his death.
In this way, even that steadfast king became lost without Unmādinī; how much more so must the King of Vatsa be without Vāsavadattā?
Having heard this from Rumaṇvat, Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke again: "Suffering is endured by kings who keep their objectives in view."
Did Rāma not endure the agony of separation from Queen Sītā, even though he was separated from her by the gods through a stratagem devised for the destruction of Rāvaṇa?
Having heard this, Rumaṇvat spoke once more: "For those such as Rāma and the others are gods; their minds endure all things."
But it is unbearable for humans; therefore, let this story be heard: there is here a great city called Mathurā, rich in many jewels.
In that city there was a certain merchant’s son named Yaïllaka, and he had a beloved wife whose mind was bound exclusively to him.
Then, while living with her, the merchant's son once resolved to go to another island due to the weight of his business affairs.
His wife also desired to go with him; for the hearts of women, devoted out of affection, cannot endure separation.
Then that merchant’s son set out after performing the auspicious rites; however, he did not take his wife, who was already fully adorned, along with him.
Then, watching him as he departed, she stood with tearful eyes, leaning against the edge of the door-panel at the entrance of the courtyard.
When he had passed from the range of her vision, she, unable to endure that separation, was so bewildered that she could not emerge; her life-breaths departed.
Having understood that, the merchant's son returned at that very moment and beheld his beloved wife in a state of distress, her life having departed.
With its beautiful, pale luster and its mark of dangling curls, she was like the lunar splendor upon the earth, as if fallen from heaven while sleeping.
And as he immediately took her onto his lap and wailed, the vital breaths fled swiftly from his body, which was ablaze with the fire of grief, as if terrified.
Thus, through their mutual separation, that couple perished; therefore, the king and the queen must protect themselves from being parted from one another.
When Rumaṇvat had finished speaking and ceased, his mind filled with apprehension, the wise Yaugandharāyaṇa, an ocean of fortitude, spoke.
I have determined all this: the affairs of kings invariably turn out exactly like this; listen now to a story regarding this matter.
Formerly, there was a king named Puṇyasena in Ujjayinī; once, he was attacked by another powerful king who came against him.
Then his wise ministers, seeing that the enemy was invincible, spread a false report everywhere that the king had died.
They secretly established King Puṇyasena [in his place], and they cremated some other corpse according to the rites befitting a king.
"Be you now our king, for we are without a ruler!"—thus they spoke to that enemy through the mouth of a messenger.
When the enemy, being pleased, had said "So be it," they then gathered together with their armies and gradually broke through his camp.
When the army was broken, those powerful ministers revealed King Puṇyasena and struck down that enemy.
Royal affairs are of such a nature; therefore, we shall carry out this task with fortitude under the pretext that the Queen has been consumed by fire.
Having heard this from Yaugandharāyaṇa, whose mind was thus resolved, Rumaṇvat spoke as follows: "In that case, if this is the firm decision..."
"Bring that cowherd, the respected brother of the queen; having consulted with him, let everything be properly arranged."
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa said, "So be it," and because of his confidence, Rumaṇvat also made a firm resolve to carry out the task.
On another day, those two chief ministers dispatched their own messenger, Gopālaka, under the pretext of longing to see him, in order to bring him back.
Having previously departed on account of his business, that cowherd returned there upon hearing the words of the messenger, appearing like the festival itself incarnate.
When that day had arrived, Yaugandharāyaṇa took Gopālaka, along with Rumaṇvat, to his own house at night at his own leisure.
And there he recounted to him his enthusiasm for that which he intended to do—everything that had previously been deliberated upon by him together with Rumaṇvat.
And Gopālaka, desiring the welfare of the king, consented even to that which brought sorrow to his sister; for the word of the virtuous must indeed be carried out.
"All this has been well arranged; however, considering that the Queen has been burned, reflect on how the Lord of Vatsa is to be protected while he gives up his life."
Indeed, even when the collection of conditions such as the correct means is present, the primary limb of the mantra is the counteraction of misfortune.
When Rumaṇvat had thus spoken once more at that time, Yaugandharāyaṇa, who had deliberated upon every course of action, replied:
There is no need for concern here that the princess is Gopālaka’s younger sister, for she is a queen dearer to him than even his own life.
And seeing his grief to be slight at that time, the Lord of Vatsa will regain his composure, thinking, "Perhaps the Queen is still alive."
Moreover, this supreme being will be married off quickly; therefore, Queen Padmāvatī shall be presented before him shortly thereafter.
Having thus reached this decision, Yaugandharāyaṇa, Gopālaka, and Rumaṇvat then held this consultation.
"By means of this stratagem, let us go to Lāvāṇaka together with the Queen and the King; for that is a frontier district situated near Magadha."
Because it is a land of easy prey and because the king is absent, if one sets fire to the inner apartments there, whatever was intended will be accomplished.
And the queen shall be taken by a stratagem and established in the house of Padmāvatī, so that she, remaining there in concealment, may serve as her witness of virtuous conduct.
Having thus conferred with one another during the night, Yaugandharāyaṇa and all the others entered the royal palace on the following day.
Then, having been thus addressed by Rumaṇvat, Vatsarāja said: "Your Majesty, all is well with us who have gone to Lāvāṇaka."
Moreover, O King, that region is exceedingly delightful, and there are excellent hunting grounds there, with abundant grass and easy access.
Moreover, that lord of Magadha oppresses everyone because of his proximity; therefore, you should go there for the sake of protection and for diversion.
Having heard this, the Lord of Vatsa, together with Vāsavadattā, who was solely intent on pleasure, resolved to go to Lāvāṇaka.
When the departure had been decided upon and the auspicious moment for the next day had been determined, the sage Nārada suddenly appeared, illuminating the quarters of the sky with his splendor.
Descending from the midst of the sky, he provided a festival for the eyes; out of affection for his own family, he approached that Lord of Vatsa like the moon.
Having accepted the hospitality and honors, that sage, being pleased, gave a garland made of *pārijāta* flowers to the king who stood before him with bowed head.
"You shall obtain a son who is a lord of the Vidyādharas and an incarnation of Kāmadeva"; thus he greeted Vāsavadattā with great respect.
Then, while Yaugandharāyaṇa stood by, he said to the Lord of Vatsa: "O King, having seen Vāsavadattā, alas, I have been reminded [of her]."
In former times, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others were your great-grandfathers; Draupadī was the sole wife of those five.
And she was peerless in beauty, like Vāsavadattā herself; then, apprehensive of that very defect, I spoke to them thus:
"One must guard against enmity with women, for that is indeed the seed of calamities in this world; therefore, listen as I relate this story to you."
There were two brothers named Sunda and Upasunda, Asuras who were difficult to conquer and who had overwhelmed the three worlds with their prowess.
And desiring their destruction, Brahmā, having given his command to Viśvakarman, caused the divine woman Tilottamā to be fashioned.
It is said that even Śarva, though possessing four faces, had to circumambulate her as he gazed at her form from all four directions.
At the command of the Lotus-born One, she went to the side of Sunda and Upasunda, who were residing in the gardens of Kailāsa, in order to seduce them.
As soon as they saw Sundarī approaching nearby, both those two demons, infatuated by desire, seized her by both her arms.
Seizing her at that very moment in mutual opposition, both of them met their destruction because they had engaged in combat.
Thus, for whom is the object known as "woman" not the cause of calamities? And yet, Draupadī alone is the beloved of many of you here.
"Indeed, you must protect yourselves from mutual strife caused by various motives; by my word, let this agreement always abide among you."
The mother who stays near the eldest son should be regarded as such by the younger; and she who stays near the youngest should be known as a daughter-in-law by the eldest.
O King, having heard these words of mine, your great-grandfathers, whose minds were intent on performing what is auspicious, agreed, saying, "So be it."
They were my friends, and out of affection for them I have come here, O Lord of Vatsa, to see you; therefore, listen as I speak this to you.
Just as you have carried out these words of mine, so should you act toward the ministers; in a short time, you shall attain great prosperity.
For a short time you will experience suffering, but you must not give way to excessive delusion therein; for that shall end in happiness.

Having spoken thus correctly, the sage Nārada, who was skilled in the art of indicating future events through indirect hints, vanished at that very moment from the sight of the King of Vatsa as he was about to rise.

And then, at the word of that bull among sages, all those ministers, headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa, perceiving the imminent success of their own intended undertaking, exerted themselves with even greater effort to bring it to completion.

Thus ends the first wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave: Then, by the aforementioned stratagem, Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others led the King of Vatsa together with his beloved toward Lāvāṇaka.
The king reached that region, where the swelling roar of his army seemed to announce to his ministers the successful accomplishment of their desired goal.
Thereupon, having learned that the King of Vatsa had arrived with his retinue, the Lord of Magadha trembled, fearing an attack by surprise.
Sad-buddhi dispatched a messenger to the presence of Yaugandharāyaṇa; that excellent minister, who understood the nature of affairs, welcomed him with joy.
The Lord of Vatsa, while residing in that country, wandered day after day through the most distant forests for the sake of hunting.
One day, when that king had gone out for a hunt, he made an agreement regarding his duties and set out accompanied by Gopālaka.
The wise Yaugandharāyaṇa, together with Rumaṇvat and Vasantaka, went into the presence of Queen Vāsavadattā in a secluded place.
There, with various words, he entreated her—who had already been persuaded by her brother—to provide assistance in this royal matter, as she bowed humbly before him.
And she consented to that which caused her heart such pain of separation; for what indeed do virtuous women devoted to their husbands not endure?
Then the skillful Yaugandharāyaṇa, having bestowed upon her a transformative magic (*yoga*), turned that goddess into the form of a Brahmin woman.
And he made Vasantaka one-eyed and disguised him in the form of a young brahmin student; he himself likewise assumed the appearance of an elderly brahmin.
Then, having taken that queen who was of such a form, the high-minded one set out at his own will toward Magadha, accompanied by Vasantaka.
Likewise, having departed from her own home, Vāsavadattā went with her mind to her husband, but with her body along the road.
Then, having set that palace ablaze with fire, Rumaṇvat proclaimed aloud, "Alas, alas! The Queen, together with Vasantaka, has been consumed by the flames!"
And so, both the fire and the cries arose there simultaneously; the fire gradually subsided, but not the sound of weeping.
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa, together with Vāsavadattā and Vasantaka, reached the city of the lord of Magadha.
Seeing Padmāvatī, the princess, there in the garden, he approached her together with those two, even though he was being restrained by the guards.
As soon as Padmāvatī saw Queen Vāsavadattā assuming the form of a Brahmin woman, love arose in her eyes.
Having dismissed the guards, the princess then had Yaugandharāyaṇa, who was in the guise of a Brahmin, summoned into her presence.
And he asked, "O Great Brahmā, who is this young girl of yours? For what purpose have you come? and he, in turn, replied to her.
"Thus, this daughter of mine is a princess named Āmāvantikā; her husband, being addicted to vice, has abandoned her and gone away somewhere."
Therefore, O illustrious lady, I entrust her to your care today, so that I may go and bring back her husband after searching for him without delay.
"And let this brother Kāṇabaṭu remain right here near her, so that she does not experience the sorrow of being alone."
Having spoken thus, and having had his words accepted by her, that excellent minister took leave of the princess and went quickly to Lāvāṇaka.
Then he saw Vāsavadattā standing there under the name of Āvantikā, and Vasantaka following her in the form of a one-eyed boy.
Taking him with her and having offered him noble hospitality, the affectionate Padmāvatī entered her own palace, filled with many wonders.
There, Vāsavadattā entered and, beholding Sītā in the course of Rāma’s life depicted on the painted walls, she endured her own anguish.
By her form, her delicacy, the elegance of her posture while reclining or sitting, and even by the fragrance of her body, which was as sweet-smelling as a blue lotus;
Having determined her to be the most excellent, Padmāvatī attended upon her according to her desire with costly honors equal to her own.
And he thought: "Surely this is some woman staying here in disguise; was Draupadī not hidden while we dwelt in Virāṭa's kingdom?"
Then Vāsavadattā, on the occasion of the queen’s arrival, prepared for her an unfading garland and a forehead mark (tilaka), which she had previously learned from the Lord of Vatsa.
And seeing Padmāvatī adorned with those ornaments, her mother asked her in private, "By whom were these two—the garland and the tilaka—created?"
Padmāvatī said to her, "A certain woman named Āvantikā, staying here in my palace, did this for me."
Having heard that, her mother said to her: "Daughter, she is not some mere human; she is surely a goddess, for she possesses such supernatural knowledge."
Deities and sages likewise remain in the homes of the virtuous for the sake of testing them; therefore, my daughter, listen to this story.
There was a king named Kuntibhoja; into his very palace came and stayed the sage Durvāsas, whose sole delight was in deception.
For the sake of serving him, King Kuntibhoja commanded his own daughter Kuntī; she, too, attended upon the sage with great diligence.
Once, that sage, desiring to test Kuntī, said to her: "Cook some excellent rice-pudding quickly, so that I may return as soon as I have bathed."
Having spoken thus, that seer quickly bathed and came to eat; Kuntī then presented to him a vessel filled with that food.
And with food that was exceedingly hot, the sage cast his gaze upon Kuntī’s back—she who was as if blazing and unfit for him to touch by the hand.
Having discerned the sage's intention, she also placed that vessel upon her back; then he ate as he pleased, while Kuntī’s back was scorched.
Although she was being intensely burned, because she remained unchanging, the sage was pleased; having eaten, he then granted her a boon.
Thus was that sage there; and this Avantikā of yours is likewise some such being remaining in that very state. Therefore, you should propitiate her for the sake of the ultimate truth.
Having heard this from her mother’s mouth, Padmāvatī esteemed that Vāsavadattā—who was there in another form—all the more highly.
Vāsavadattā too, separated here from her own lord, remained dejected and lusterless like a lotus-bed at midnight.
And those various compositions of Vasantaka, suited for children, repeatedly provided occasions for a smile upon the face of that woman separated from her lover.
In the meantime, after wandering through hunting grounds at a great distance, the King of Vatsa finally returned to Lāvāṇaka again in the evening.
And he saw that the inner apartments had been reduced to ashes by the fire there; moreover, from his ministers, he heard that the queen, along with Vasantaka, had been burnt.
As soon as he heard this, his consciousness was stolen away by delusion and he fell to the ground, as if wishing to cast off the affliction of experiencing that sorrow.
In an instant, having regained consciousness, he blazed with grief in his heart, as if possessed by the fire of the sight of the Goddess burning there.
Then, lamenting and afflicted by grief, intent solely on abandoning his body, the king in a moment recollected this and reflected:
"The son of that goddess shall become the lord of the Vidyādharas; the sage Nārada told this to me, and it is not false."
For some time, suffering was proclaimed to me by that very sage; yet the grief of this cowherd appears to be quite small.
Furthermore, no extreme suffering is seen among Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others; therefore, I know that the queen must somehow still be alive.
This must be some kind of policy devised by the ministers; therefore, O Queen, I might eventually come into contact with her.
Thinking, "I shall see the end of this matter here," that king, though being exhorted by his ministers, fixed his heart in fortitude.
And Gopālaka, having instructed him regarding the matter exactly as it was, immediately dispatched a scout there unobserved for the sake of reassurance.
When his own account had thus been related, those who were in Lāvāṇaka then went to the King of Magadha and reported everything to him through their spies.
Having learned of this, the king, who knew the proper time, desired to give his daughter Padmāvatī—who had previously been sought by the minister—to the King of Vatsa.
Then, through the mouth of a messenger, he communicated this matter as he desired to the Lord of Vatsa and also to Yaugandharāyaṇa.
And at the word of Yaugandharāyaṇa, the Lord of Vatsa consented to that, thinking, "Perhaps the Queen might at some time discover this purpose."
Then, having determined an auspicious moment, Yaugandharāyaṇa quickly dispatched a counter-messenger to that King of Magadha.
We have accepted your wish; therefore, on the seventh day from now, the King of Vatsa will come here for the marriage of Padmāvatī.
"Quickly arrange for Vāsavadattā in such a way that he will forget her," the great minister thus instructed the king.
Having gone there as a counter-messenger, he delivered the message exactly as instructed; and the King of Magadha also welcomed him with joy.
Then the Lord of Magadha prepared the wedding festivities and their necessary materials, according to his affection for his daughter, his own desire, and his wealth.
Upon hearing the news of her desired boon, Padmāvatī attained joy, while Vāsavadattā fell into grief upon hearing that report.
That news, reaching Karna's ears and causing him great distress, seemed to provide assistance to Indra by concealing his own deformity.
"In this way, even an enemy can be made a friend, and not otherwise, O Mistress"—thus did Vasantaka’s words provide her with comfort, like a true friend.
Then, for Padmāvatī, whose wedding was imminent, that wise woman once again fashioned two divine garlands and forehead marks that would never fade.
Then, on the arrival of the seventh day, the Lord of Vatsa, accompanied by his army and ministers, reportedly came there to take her in marriage.
How could that man separated from his beloved even mentally touch the effort toward her, were it not for the hope: "May I obtain that goddess in this way"?
And the Lord of Magadha immediately went out to meet him with joy, as the ocean meets the moon that has risen, a festival for the eyes of his subjects.
Then that Lord of Vatsa entered the city of the King of Magadha; and a great festival entered the hearts of the citizens on every side.
There the women beheld him, his body emaciated by separation and causing confusion to the mind, like the god of love deprived of Rati.
Then the Lord of Vatsa, having entered the palace of the Lord of Magadha, went to the bridal chamber, which was filled with women whose husbands were living.
There the king beheld Padmāvatī within the inner chamber, adorned with wedding ornaments, her full moon-like face surpassing the orb of the full moon itself.
And beholding those two divine garland and tilaka of his own, the king reflected: "From where do these belong to her?"
Then, having ascended the altar, he took her hand; that very act constituted the commencement of his taking the hand of the entire earth.
As if thinking, "This man, whose beloved is Vāsavadattā, cannot bear to see this," the smoke from the sacrificial altar covered his eyes with tears.
As the fire was circumambulated, the copper [mirror] then reflected Padmāvatī’s face; having perceived her husband’s intention, it appeared as if agitated with anger.
Having completed the marriage, the Lord of Vatsa released his bride from his hand; yet he did not abandon that Vāsavadattā from his heart for even a moment.
Then the lord of Magadha bestowed such jewels upon him that the earth seemed to realize it had been milked dry and was now empty of its treasures.
And having made fire his witness at that moment, Yaugandharāyaṇa caused the King of Magadha to give a pledge of non-hostility toward the king.
With garments and ornaments being bestowed, with excellent bards singing, and with noble women dancing, the great festival spread forth.
At that time, Vāsavadattā remained unnoticed, as if asleep, awaiting the rising of her husband; she was like the lunar splendor during the day.
Then, when the King, the Lord of Vatsa, had entered the inner apartments, the skillful Yaugandharāyaṇa became apprehensive regarding a meeting with the Queen.
Out of fear that his secret counsel might be leaked, he spoke thus to the Lord of Magadha: "O King, the Lord of Vatsa will not depart from your palace this very day."
Having agreed with "So be it," he explained that very matter to the King of Vatsa at that very moment; and he, in turn, believed it to be so.
Then the Lord of Vatsa set out, having eaten and drunk, taking with him his retinue and his ministers, and leading his bride Padmāvatī.
And having mounted the comfortable vehicle sent by Padmāvatī, he set out together with those high officials whom she herself had commanded.
Vāsavadattā also arrived secretly behind the army, placing Vasantaka—who had assumed a disguised form—in front of her.
In due course, having reached Lāvāṇaka, the Lord of Vatsa entered his own residence together with his bride; however, he remained solely intent upon the Queen's thoughts.
Having arrived at Gopālaka’s palace, Vāsavadattā then entered it at midnight, after having stationed the high officials outside.
There, seeing her brother Gopālaka showing such great affection, she embraced him around the neck while weeping, her eyes clouded with tears.
At that very moment, Yaugandharāyaṇa, who was present there with his knowledge of the situation, arrived accompanied by Rumaṇvat, having been received with honor by the queen.
While he was dispelling her sorrow caused by the separation from her beloved, those high officials arrived at the side of Padmāvatī.
"O Queen of Avanti, you have arrived; yet, having somehow left us, you have entered the house of the prince Gopālaka."
Thus addressed by her own chief ministers, Padmāvatī, filled with apprehension, spoke thus to the King of Vatsa in their presence.
"Go to Avantikā and say: 'Indeed, you remain as my deposit; therefore, what is it to you here? Come to that very place where I am.'"
When they had departed after hearing that, the king asked Padmāvatī in private, "By whom were these two, the garland and the forehead mark, made for you?"
She then said: "This woman named Āvantikā was deposited in my house by a certain brahmin; this is her great craft."
Upon hearing that, the Lord of Avanti went to the cowherd's house, thinking, "Surely she must be Vāsavadattā here."
And having gone there, he entered that place where the chief minister stood at the door, while the queen, the cowherd, the two ministers, and Vasantaka were within.
There he beheld Vāsavadattā, who had returned from her exile, like the lunar orb released from an eclipse.
Then, overwhelmed by the poison of grief, he fell upon the surface of the earth; meanwhile, a tremor arose within the heart of Vāsavadattā.
Then she too fell to the ground with limbs pale from separation, and she lamented, reproaching her own conduct.
Then that couple, wretched with grief, wept in such a manner that even Yaugandharāyaṇa had his face washed with tears.
And hearing such a clamor at that time, Padmāvatī also approached that very spot in great agitation.
Gradually coming to understand the situation of both the King and Vāsavadattā, she too became in exactly the same state; for virtuous women are indeed tender and guileless.
"What use have I for life that brings such suffering upon my husband? Vāsavadattā said, weeping repeatedly.
"O Lord, desiring for you the imperial sovereignty obtained through the birth of the son of the King of Magadha, I have done this; there is no fault whatsoever on the part of the Queen."
"But this very woman is her rival's witness to her virtue during her absence," said the steadfast Yaugandharāyaṇa to the Lord of Vatsa.
"I shall enter this fire for the sake of demonstrating her purity," Padmāvatī said there, her heart free from malice.
"I alone am at fault, for whose sake this great suffering has been endured even by the Queen," the king also said.
"I must enter the fire for the sake of proving the purity of the king's heart," Vāsavadattā declared with firm resolve.
Then that wise Yaugandharāyaṇa, the foremost among the accomplished, having sipped water for purification and facing the east, uttered these words: "I am pure."
"If I am a benefactor to the king, and if the queen Śuddhimatī is pure, then speak, O World-Guardians; otherwise, I shall cast off this body."
When he had finished speaking, this divine voice arose: "O King, you are blessed, for you have Yaugandharāyaṇa as your minister."
"Since Vāsavadattā is his wife and was his deity in a previous birth, there is no fault whatsoever in her"—having said this, the voice ceased.

Having heard that sound which filled all quarters of space with the splendor of the deep thundering of fresh rain-clouds, they all—with necks outstretched and long-standing distress dispelled—became like clear imitations of the peacock (Nīlakaṇṭha).
And even together with Gopālaka, the King of Vatsa praised the conduct of Yaugandharāyaṇa, and he considered the earth as already within his grasp.
Then the king, beholding his two beloved wives standing near him like the personified forms of Rati and Nirvṛti, experienced the supreme joy of their constant companionship and mutual affection.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Lāvāṇaka* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. Then, on another day, the Lord of Vatsa, having retired to a private place with Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī, engaged in the sport of drinking wine.
Having brought together Yaugandharāyaṇa along with the cowherd Gopālaka, Rumaṇvat, and Vasantaka, he engaged them in confidential conversations.
There, on the occasion of his own departure, while all of them were listening, the lord of the earth related this story.
There was a king named Purūravas, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, whose movement was unimpeded both upon the earth and even in heaven.
Once, as he was wandering in the Nandana grove, an Apsaras named Urvaśī—like another bewildering weapon of Kāma—beheld him.
Merely upon seeing him, she became so captivated in heart that she caused the minds of her friends—Rambhā and the others—to tremble with fear.
When the king beheld her—a veritable torrential stream of the essence of loveliness—he fainted from being overcome by thirst, for he did not obtain her embrace.
Then Hari, the omniscient one dwelling in the ocean of milk, gave instructions to the eminent sage named Nārada, who had approached him for a vision.
O divine sage, King Purūravas, dwelling in the Nandana grove, remained with his heart stolen by Urvaśī, unable to endure the pangs of separation.
O Sage, having gone there and informed Śatakratu with my words, cause that Urvaśī to be given quickly to that king.
Having been thus commanded by Hari, Nārada replied, "So be it," and returning, he awakened Purūravas in that state and spoke to him.
Arise, O King; I have been sent here for your sake by Viṣṇu. For He indeed never neglects the calamities of those who are devoted to Him with sincere devotion.
Having spoken thus, the sage Nārada, together with Purūravas who had been comforted, went into the presence of the king of the gods.
Having reported Hari’s command to Indra, who was bowed down before him, he then caused Urvaśī to be given to Purūravas.
To him, the gift of Urvaśī was like a life-restoring elixir for heaven; but to Urvaśī, it was as a medicine that restores the dead to life.
Then Purūravas returned to the world of mortals, taking her with him, thereby providing a wondrous sight of a celestial bride for the eyes of mortal men.
Then those two, Urvaśī and the king, remained there inseparable, as if bound by the mutual noose of their glances.
Once, when the wielder of the thunderbolt had entered into battle with the Dānavas, Purūravas went to heaven, summoned for the sake of providing assistance.
When that lord of the asuras named Māyādhara had been slain, there was a festival for Śakra, in which the throngs of celestial nymphs danced.
Then, while the teacher Tumburu stood by, Purūravas saw Rambhā dancing with her gestures faltering and laughed.
"Do you know this divine dance, or do you know it as a human, O Rambhā? she said to him at that time with indignation.
Then Purūravas said to her, "I know that which even Tumburu does not know, and your preceptor as well, through my union with Urvaśī."
Having heard that, Tumburu, out of anger, then pronounced a curse upon him: "May you suffer separation from Urvaśī until you have propitiated Kṛṣṇa."
Having gone to Urvaśī, Purūravas reported his own story, which was as terrible as an untimely stroke of lightning, and informed her of the curse he had heard.
Then, it is said, Urvaśī was suddenly snatched away and carried off to some unknown place by Gandharvas who remained invisible to that king.
Having understood that fault of the curse, Purūravas then went and performed the propitiation of Hari at the hermitage of Badarikāśrama.
But Urvaśī, afflicted by the pain of separation while staying in the realm of the Gandharvas, was as if dead, as if asleep, as if painted, and devoid of consciousness.
It is a marvel that she, clinging to the hope for an end to the curse, did not lose her life during those nights made long by separation, like a female cakravāka bird.
And Purūravas, through that austerity, gratified Acyuta; by his grace, the Gandharvas released Urvaśī to him.
Reunited with that Apsaras, who had obtained the end of her curse, the king enjoyed divine pleasures even while remaining on the surface of the earth.
When the king had spoken thus and ceased, Vāsavadattā, who had heard of Urvaśī’s passion for him, felt shame because she herself had endured separation from him.
Seeing the queen thus rebuked by the king with skillful reasoning and looking abashed, Yaugandharāyaṇa then spoke in order to comfort the monarch.
If you have not heard it, O King, then let this story be heard by you: there is here a city named Timira, the abode of Fortune.
In that city there was a famous king named Vihitasena; he had a wife named Tejovatī, who was like an apsarā upon the surface of the earth.
Intent on grasping her neck and greedy for her touch, the king could not endure even his body being quickly brushed by her bodice.
Once, that king was afflicted with chronic fever; the physicians forbade him from having union with that queen.
In the heart of that king, who was deprived of the company of a queen, there arose a disease that could not be cured by the application of medicines.
"Due to fear or the onset of grief, the king’s illness may at any time burst forth," the physicians thus said to the minister in private.
He who formerly felt no fear when a great serpent fell upon his back, nor was he agitated even when a hostile army entered his inner apartments.
"How could fear arise for this courageous king? We have no idea how to deal with him; what can we ministers do?"
Having reflected thus and consulted together with the queen, those ministers concealed her and told the king, "The queen is dead."
As that king was being tormented by the excessive weight of his grief, his heart-disease burst forth while he was overwhelmed with distress.
Then, once that king had been delivered from the calamity of disease, the ministers presented to him that great queen as if she were another perfection of happiness.
And that king, though wise, highly valued her as the savior of his life; yet he did not give way to anger toward her, for she had concealed her true nature.
For that which constitutes a husband's desire for his wife's welfare is the cause of her being called "Queen" (devī); the title "Queen" is not obtained merely by doing what is pleasing to him.

And that which consists solely in deliberating upon the burden of state affairs is "counsel"; whereas that which consists in merely following the whims of the mind is the characteristic of a "parasite."
Therefore, this effort has been made by us for the sake of your conquest of the earth, so that you may form an alliance with the King of Magadha, who stands as an obstacle to it.
Therefore, O King, the Queen has committed no offense against you; rather, she has performed a complete service for you, having endured an unbearable separation through her devotion to your majesty.
Upon hearing these words of the prime minister, which were both true and to the point, the King of Vatsa considered himself at fault and was filled with satisfaction.
And he said this: "I know that the earth has already been given to me by the Goddess through Ākāravatī, who was employed by you as if she were Policy (Nīti) personified."
However, out of excessive affection, I have spoken this which is improper; for how can those whose minds are blinded by passion possess the capacity for discernment?
With such words of consolation, the King of Vatsa removed on that very day both his own and the Queen’s stain of shame at once.
On another day, a messenger sent by the Lord of Magadha with a gift of precious objects approached the King of Vatsa and announced his message.
"We have already been deceived by these ministers; therefore, act now in such a way that this world of living beings shall no longer be filled with sorrow for us."
Having heard this and honored him, the Lord of Vatsa then dispatched that messenger to the side of Padmāvatī in order to receive a reply.
She too, bowing solely before Vāsavadattā, presented herself to the messenger in her presence; for modesty is indeed the vow of a virtuous woman.
"O daughter, you were led away by a ruse and your husband has become attached to another; thus, out of grief, I have obtained the fruit of being the father of a daughter."
When the messenger had thus delivered his father's message, Padmāvatī then said to him, "O good man, let my father and mother be informed of this by my word."
What is the use of grieving? For my noble husband is supremely compassionate toward me, and Queen Vāsavadattā is affectionate toward me like a sister.
Therefore, my dear father, you must not act with such fickleness toward my noble son, if my own life is as dear to you as your own innate truth.
When Padmāvatī had thus delivered her appropriate reply, Vāsavadattā then honored that messenger and dispatched him.
When the messenger had departed, Padmāvatī, remembering her father’s house, remained there for a while as if her mind were clouded by longing.

Then, at Vāsavadattā’s request for diversion, Vasantaka, who had arrived nearby, related this story: Vāsavadattā said to him: "Friend, tell me some tale that will divert my mind. He replied: "Queen, listen; I shall tell you a story that will delight you. There was once a king named Mahendravarman in the city of Mahendrapura. He had a son named Mahābala, who was brave, handsome, and skilled in all the arts. That prince, having grown up, went out one day to hunt with his friends in a forest near the city. While he was wandering there, he saw a certain maiden of celestial beauty, who had come from somewhere or other to gather lotuses. She was so lovely that she seemed like a second Lakṣmī, the goddess of fortune. As soon as the prince saw her, he was pierced by the arrows of the god of love. And she too, upon seeing him, felt her heart captivated by his excellence. Then, after gathering the lotuses, she went to a temple of the Goddess situated on the bank of a lake within that forest. The prince also followed her, concealing himself behind a tree, thinking: 'I must find out who she is. While she was worshipping the Goddess there, she spoke these words aloud: 'O Goddess, if I am truly devoted to Mahābala, may I become his wife in another birth. Hearing this, the prince stepped forward and said to her: 'Fair lady, I am that very Mahābala; why do you trouble yourself with penance? When she heard this, she recognized him by his voice and fell at his feet. Then, having revealed themselves to one another, they both returned to their respective homes, their hearts bound together by a bond of love. But the prince, being separated from her, became so utterly distraught by the pangs of love that he abandoned his kingdom and wandered through various lands. Eventually, he reached a great city called Vardhamāna, where he entered the service of a certain merchant as a servant. There, while he was living in disguise, he happened to see that same maiden, now married to another man, entering the house of a courtesan to perform a dance. When the prince saw her, he was once again struck by the arrows of the god of love. She too, recognizing him by his appearance, was overcome with longing. Then, having arranged a meeting, she went to her own home and sent a message to him through a female messenger: 'If you wish to see me, come here tonight at midnight. The prince, having accepted her invitation, went there at the appointed time and found her waiting for him. They spent the night together in union, and in the morning, the prince departed from that place. After some time, he reached a city named Pāṭaliputra, where he entered the service of a certain king as a courtier. There, while he was living in the guise of a minister's son, he saw that same woman, now a courtesan, performing a dance in the palace. Recognizing her, he approached her and said: 'Fair lady, I am that very Mahābala; why do you not welcome me? When she heard this, she remembered him and was filled with joy. Then, having made arrangements, she went to her own quarters and sent word to him: 'Come here tonight at midnight; I shall reveal myself to you. The prince, having agreed, went there at the appointed hour and found her waiting. They spent the night in union, and in the morning, the prince departed. After some time, he reached a city named Kāñcī, where he entered the service of a certain king as a courtier. There, while he was living in disguise, he saw that same woman, now a courtesan, dancing in the palace. Recognizing her, he approached her and said: 'Fair lady, I am that very Mahābala; why do you not welcome me? When she heard this, she remembered him and was filled with joy. Then, having made arrangements, she went to her own quarters and sent word to him: 'Come here tonight at midnight; I shall reveal myself to you. The prince, having agreed, went there at the appointed hour and found her waiting. They spent the night in union, and in the morning, the prince departed. After some time, he reached a city named Ujjayinī, where he entered the service of a certain king as a courtier. There, while he was living in disguise, he saw that same woman, now a courtesan, dancing in the palace. Recognizing her, he approached her and said: 'Fair lady, I am that very Mahābala; why do you not welcome me? When she heard this, she
There is a city named Pāṭaliputra, an ornament of the earth; and in it there lived a certain great merchant named Dharmagupta.
He had a wife named Candraprabhā, and she once became pregnant; she then gave birth to a daughter who was beautiful in every limb.
As soon as she was born, that girl, illuminating her chamber with her radiance, spoke clearly and sat up.
Then, seeing the women in the birth-chamber struck with wonder and terror, Dharmagupta himself came there filled with fear.
Bowing down at that very moment in private, he asked the maiden: "O Blessed One, who are you that have descended into my house?"
She also said, "I must not be given by you to anyone at all; I am auspicious while staying in your house. Why do you ask me this, father?"
Thus addressed by her, Dharmagupta, filled with fear, kept her hidden in his own palace, while proclaiming abroad that she was dead.
Then that maiden, named Somaprabhā, gradually grew up with a human body, yet possessed of divine beauty and luster.
Once, however, a merchant’s son named Guhacandra beheld her as she stood upon the palace roof, joyfully watching the spring festival.
As if struck by the arrow of love that had suddenly lodged in his heart, he then fainted and returned home with great difficulty.
There, tormented by the pain of love, he was questioned persistently regarding the cause of his parents' ill health, and he spoke through the mouth of his friend.
Then his father, named Guhasena, went out of affection to the house of the merchant Dharmagupta to ask for his daughter.
There, Dharmagupta rejected Guhasena, who had made his request seeking a daughter-in-law, saying, "O fool, where am I to get a daughter?"
Thinking that his daughter had been hidden by him, Guhasena went home; seeing his son overcome by the fever of love, he reflected:
I shall urge the king in this matter, for he was formerly served by me; he will even grant that maiden to my son, though he is on the verge of death.
Having thus resolved and gone there, that merchant gave him an excellent jewel and made his own request known to the king.
The king, being well-pleased, granted him the assistance of the city governor; together with him, he went to the house of Dharmagupta.
And he besieged the house of that Dharmagupta with his forces, while [Dharmagupta], fearing total destruction, blocked his own throat with his vital breaths.
Then Somaprabhā said to that Dharmagupta: "Give me up, father; let there be no calamity for you on my account."
"I must never be placed upon the bed by my husband; you must ensure that such a restriction is observed by your kinsmen through their words."
Thus addressed by his daughter, Dharmagupta then agreed to give her away, having spoken with her regarding the avoidance of being placed upon a bed.
And Guhasena, with a suppressed smile, consented to it exactly as requested, thinking, "Let my son's marriage take place for now."
Then Guhacandra, the son of Guhasena, having taken that bride Somaprabhā after her marriage was performed, set out for his own home.
In the evening, his father said to him: "Son, place this bride upon this bed; for whose bed indeed shall she, your own wife, ever lie?"
Hearing that, the bride Somaprabhā looked at her father-in-law in anger and brandished her forefinger like the command of Yama.
Upon seeing that finger of his daughter-in-law at that very moment, the merchant's life departed, and fear came upon the others.
When his father had met his death, Guhacandra thought, "My wife Mārī has entered my house."
Then, not enjoying the company of his wife who remained in the house, Guhacandra observed a vow as perilous as the edge of a sword.
Burning within with that sorrow and becoming dispassionate toward the abundance of enjoyments, he, firm in his vows, fed the Brahmins every day.
And his wife as well, maintaining silence, constantly gave sacrificial fees to those brahmins after they had eaten, she who possessed a divine form.
Once, an elderly brahmin arrived alone for a meal and beheld her, who, by the perfection of her beauty, was a source of wonder to the world.
Then, filled with curiosity, the twice-born one asked Guhacandra in private: "Whose daughter is this? Tell it to me."
Being questioned persistently, Guhacandra, with a heavy heart, related to that brahmin the entire account concerning her.
Having understood that, the best of the twice-born, moved by compassion, then gave him the mantra for the propitiation of Agni in order to achieve his desired goal.
Then, as Guhacandra was performing the recitation of that mantra in secret, a man emerged from the midst of a fire.
And that fire, in the form of a twice-born, said to him as he bowed at his feet: "Today I shall eat in your house, and I shall stay there for the night."
"Having shown you the truth, I shall accomplish your desire," said that Brahmin to Guhacandra, and then he went to his house.
There, after eating as the others had done, he attended to his bed for about one watch of the night in the presence of Guhacandra, remaining unwearied.
And at that moment, Somaprabhā, the wife of Guhacandra, departed from that palace where the people were fast asleep during the night.
At that time, the Brahmin there awakened Guhacandra and said to him, "Come, let us see the account of your wife's conduct."
Having assumed the form of a bee through his yogic power, he likewise transformed himself and, emerging from it, showed her his wife as she had stepped out of the house.
That beautiful woman went a great distance outside the city together with Guhacandra, and the brahmin followed after her as well.
Then, there he beheld a single nyagrodha tree, possessing great boughs and beautiful with its shady trunk, named Guhacandra.
And beneath that, he heard the sound of divine music, accompanied by the resonance of lutes and flutes, sweet with the melody of a shimmering song.
And at the place where the trunk had been, he saw a divine maiden seated upon a great throne, her form resembling that of his own wife.
She surpassed the moonlight with her own radiance and was fanned by white chowries; she was like the presiding deity of the moon’s treasury of all its loveliness.
Then, having climbed that very tree, Guhacandra saw his wife seated upon half of her seat.
At that moment, as he gazed upon those two celestial maidens of equal beauty standing together, that night shone for him as if it possessed three moons.
Then, overcome with curiosity, he reflected for a moment: "Is this a dream, or a delusion? Or perhaps both are to be cursed?"
This association with the wise is the cluster of blossoms upon the tree of the true path; this emergence of flowers is for me the precursor to its appropriate fruit.
While he was thus reflecting at his ease, those two celestial maidens, having eaten food suitable for themselves, drank divine wine.
"Today some brahmin of great splendor has arrived at our home; therefore, sister, my mind is filled with apprehension, and I shall depart."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of that second divine maiden, she, the wife of Guhacandra, descended from the tree.
Having seen that, Guha, Candra, and that brahmin, who were in the form of bees, returned to the house and stood before it at night just as they had been before.
Then that divine maiden, the wife of Guhacandra, arrived and entered her own residence right there, unobserved.
Then that Brahmin spoke freely to Guhacandra: "You have seen that this wife of yours is divine, not human."
Moreover, that second sister of hers was seen by you today; how could a celestial woman desire union with a human?
To accomplish this, I give you a mantra to be inscribed upon the door; I also instruct you in the external reasoning that serves as its reinforcement.

Even a completely pure fire blazes; what need is there to mention it when joined with a gale? In the same way, a mantra alone bestows its purpose, so what need to speak of it when combined with the correct method?
Having spoken thus and having bestowed the mantra upon Guhacandra, that best of the twice-born instructed him in that stratagem and vanished at dawn.
Guhacandra, having inscribed that mantra on the door of his wife's house, again devised an enticing stratagem for the evening.
Having gone there while she was looking on, he, having adorned himself with magnificent ornaments, engaged in conversation with a certain excellent woman.
As soon as she saw him, that divine maiden, filled with jealousy, summoned him with a voice released by mantra and asked, "Who are you?"
"That beautiful woman is deeply in love with me, and today I am going to her house," he replied to her falsely.
Then, with her face turned sideways and her brows arched, she looked at him and, warding him off with her left hand, spoke to him.
"Hūṃ! This purpose is understood; this is merely a disguise, so do not go there. What have you to do with her? Leave her alone, for I am your wife."
Thus addressed by her, who was agitated by the trembling of her hair standing on end, as if possessed by the evil spirit of the messenger of his mantra;
Having entered the dwelling immediately with her, even though he was a mortal, he experienced a divine enjoyment that had never been touched by the desires of the mind.
Having thus obtained her, who was full of love and perfected through the power of mantras, Guhacandra abandoned his celestial state and remained there at his ease.
Thus, by means of meritorious deeds such as the performance of sacrifices and other good works, women who have fallen from their divine state due to a curse remain in the position of householders.

For the service of the gods and the twice-born is considered by the wise to be the wish-fulfilling cow; what indeed cannot be obtained from her, whose remnants are described as the Sāman and other Vedic chants?
In you, however, there is a misdeed toward those born in the exceedingly high station of the gods; it is the sole cause for their downfall, like a gale for flowers.
Having spoken thus, Vasantaka said again to the princess: "Moreover, listen to this account of what happened concerning Ahalyā."
In former times there was a great sage named Gautama, who knew the three periods of time; and his wife was Ahalyā, who surpassed the Apsarases in beauty.
Once, Indra, lusting after her beauty, solicited her in private; for the minds of masters, blinded by power, run toward what is improper.
And that foolish woman, seeking sexual pleasure, consented to the lord of Śacī; but the sage Gautama, having perceived this through his supernatural power, arrived there.
And at that very moment, even Indra assumed the form of a cat out of fear; then Gautama asked Ahalyā, "Who is standing there?"
"Look, the cat is standing right here," she replied to her husband with words that were both Apabhraṃśa and crooked, yet consistent with the truth.
Saying, "It is true, this is indeed your cat," the sage laughed and then cast a curse upon her, which was destined to reach its conclusion in accordance with the truth.
"O you of evil character, may you attain the state of being stone for a long time, until the sight of Rāghava wandering through the forest."
For you, who are greedy for the finest limb, that thousand-fold merit shall reside in your body; [you shall behold] Tilottamā, that celestial woman whom Viśvakarman shall fashion.
"Upon seeing her, your eyes shall become a thousand at that very moment"—thus did Gautama curse Indra even then.
Having pronounced the curse as he desired, that sage departed for his ascetic penance; Ahalyā, too, underwent the terrible state of being turned into stone.
Then Indra, his entire body covered by those excellent limbs, thought: "His name would not be 'Aśīla' (Ill-behaved) if it were not a cause for humiliation."
Thus, the evil deed of everyone always bears fruit within oneself; for whatever seed one sows, that is the fruit one receives.
Therefore, noble-minded persons do not venture to oppose others; for this is the established rule and the virtuous vow of those of supreme character.
And you two are both goddesses who were elder sisters, fallen due to a curse; likewise, your hearts are indeed free from conflict, acting for each other's benefit.
Having heard this from Vasantaka, both Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī completely abandoned even the slightest trace of jealousy toward one another.
And Queen Vāsavadattā, having made her husband common to both, looked toward Padmāvatī’s welfare and treated her as dearly as herself.
Having learned from the messengers sent by Padmāvatī that her majesty was indeed such as he had perceived, the Lord of Magadha was filled with joy.
Then on another day, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa approached the Lord of Vatsa in the presence of the Queen, while the others stood by, and spoke to him.
O Lord, let us now exert ourselves; why is Kauśāmbī not being gone to? There is no longer any fear even from the King of Magadha, for he has been deceived.
For how could he, having been properly restrained by the Sāman chant named *Kanyā-saṃbandha*, abandon his daughter—who is dearer to him than life—after having seized her?
Truth must be upheld by him and by you as well, and he was not deceived; for this was done by me myself, and it brought no suffering to him.
I have learned from my spies that he does not employ such transformations; it was for that very purpose that we remained here for these days.
While Yaugandharāyaṇa was speaking thus, having accomplished his task, a messenger related to the Lord of Magadha arrived there.
At that moment, having been announced by the doorkeeper, he entered; and sitting down after his salutation, he addressed the King of Vatsa.
"Delighted by the message sent by Queen Padmāvatī, the Lord of Magadha has now sent this communication to Your Majesty."
What is the use of much from me? I am pleased with you and wish to know everything. Therefore, do that for which this undertaking was begun; we are bowed before you.
The King of Vatsa joyfully welcomed these words of the messenger at his own pleasure, like a flower upon the tree of policy produced by Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Then, having summoned Padmāvatī together with the queen, he honored the envoy who had presented the gifts and dismissed him.
Then the messenger of Caṇḍamahāsena also arrived there; having entered, he bowed to the king and spoke as was appropriate.
"O King, King Caṇḍamahāsena, who understands the true nature of affairs, having learned of your situation, has joyfully sent this message."
Your excellence has already been sufficiently described by this much alone: that Yaugandharāyaṇa is your minister; what need is there for further words?
Blessed indeed is Vāsavadattā; by her devotion to you, she has performed such an act that we have held our heads high for a long time among the virtuous.
Padmāvatī is not different from Vāsavadattā for me; indeed, the two share one heart, so exert yourselves quickly.

Upon hearing these words of his own father-in-law’s messenger, joy instantly arose in the heart of the Lord of Vatsa; moreover, an indescribable intensity of affection for the queen increased, as did a profound bond of friendship toward the preeminent minister.

Then, having joyfully dispatched that messenger—who had been received with the appropriate rites of hospitality by the two queens—with an impetuous mind, the king, intending to make haste in his preparations, consulted with his ministers and resolved to go toward Kauśāmbī.

Thus ends the third wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave: Then, on the following day, the King of Vatsa set out from that city of Lāvāṇaka for Kauśāmbī, accompanied by his ministers and his beloved wife.
And he advanced with his forces, which filled the earth with resounding shouts, like the waters of the ocean overflowing its bounds out of season.
An analogy for that king as he proceeded, seated upon his lordly elephant, would be the sun traveling through the sky together with the mountain of sunrise.
Provided shade by a white parasol, the king shone as if being attended by the moon, which had been won over by his splendor that surpassed the brilliance of the sun.
The neighboring vassals hovered all around him—who was radiant with his own splendor and stood above them all—just as the hosts of planets revolve around the Pole Star.
Behind him, two goddesses mounted on female elephants shone as if they had followed him in person out of devotion to Śrī and Bhuvā.
The ground along his path was marked by the tips of the hooves and the scratches of the nails of the throngs of galloping horses; it was as if the earth itself had been enjoyed by that lord of men.
Thus the Lord of Vatsa proceeded, being praised by bards, and in a few days reached Kauśāmbī, where great festivities were spread abroad.
Covered by crimson silk banners, her eyes blossoming like those in the lattice windows, she displayed a pair of full, lofty jars upon her breasts at the gateway.
At that moment, as her husband returned from his journey, the city shone forth, laughing with its palaces amidst the joyful chatter and clamor of the people.
Followed by the two queens, the king entered that city; and there was an indescribable festival of joy for the women of the citizens upon seeing him.
The sky was filled by the hundreds of faces of the women situated in the golden palaces, as if by the armies of the moon—who had been surpassed by the queens' countenances—come to pay their respects.
And others, standing at the windows with unblinking eyes, watched him and created the illusion that he was a celestial being seated in a vimāna who had arrived out of curiosity.
Some women, with their eyelashes clinging to the edges of the lattice windows, seemed to create cages of arrows for the god of love.
The gaze of one woman, eager and blossoming at the sight of the king, turned toward her ear as if to tell it what she had seen, for she could not see its side.
The breasts of a certain woman who had arrived in haste heaved repeatedly, as if they wished to emerge from her bodice out of a desire to see him.
The pearls from the necklace of another woman, broken by her agitation, shone like droplets of tears of joy falling from her heart.
If one were to commit a sin against this [scripture], then Agni, though he is the illuminator, would cast blinding darkness upon the world, just as he did at Lāvāṇaka.
Thus, having seen Vāsavadattā and remembering those events as they had occurred, some women spoke with longing regarding the rumor of her cremation.
"By good fortune, the queen was not put to shame by her co-wife, who is like a friend," said one female companion to Padmāvatī upon seeing her.
Surely this beauty of these two has never been seen by Hara and Murāri; otherwise, why would Umā and Śrī bestow such great honor upon them?
Thus spoke others, seeing those two goddesses together, casting garlands of blue-lotus eyes wide with joy at one another.
Thus the Lord of Vatsa, performing a festival for the eyes of the people, entered his own palace together with the Queen, having performed the auspicious rites.
At that moment, the splendor of the royal palace was like that of a lotus pond at dawn or of the ocean at the rising of the moon.
In an instant, that place was filled with auspicious gifts from the neighboring vassals, as if signaling the arrival of tributes from all the kings of the earth.
Having honored the assembly of kings and celebrated the festival, the King of Vatsa then entered the inner apartments, just as he had entered the hearts of all the people.
Standing there between his two queens like the God of Love between Rati and Prīti, the king spent the remainder of the day in the pleasures of drinking and other diversions.
And on the following day, while that king was seated in his assembly hall in the presence of his ministers, a certain brahmin cried out at the gate.
"O Lord, in this forest, an act of unrighteousness has been committed against me by sinful cowherds; my son's feet have been cut off without cause."
Having heard that, the king immediately arrested two or three cowherds, brought them before him, and questioned them; they then spoke as follows.
"O King, let us become cowherds and play together in a secluded place. Among us, O King, there shall be one named Devasena who stands as the leader of the cowherds."
And having sat down upon a stone seat in a certain part of the forest, he says, "I am your king," and instructs us.
"And among us, no one transgresses his command; thus, O Lord, does Gopālaka exercise sovereignty in the forest."
And today, as the son of this brahmin was going along that same path, he did not offer his salutation to that Gopālarāja.
"Do not go without bowing," said the king as he spoke; but that young brahmin student, even though thus commanded, shook us off and departed with a laugh.
Therefore, O boy, we have been commanded by the King of the Cowherds to inflict punishment upon that ill-behaved fellow by cutting off his feet.
And having run from there, O Lord, his foot was severed by us; for who like us is capable of transgressing the command of the Lord?
When the cowherds had thus addressed the king, the wise Yaugandharāyaṇa reflected upon it and spoke to the king in private.
"Surely that place is endowed with hidden treasures and the like, by the power of which even a cowherd becomes so influential; therefore, let us go there."
Thus addressed by the minister, the king placed cowherds at his front and proceeded to that forest region with his army and retinue.
As the ground was being excavated there by the workmen after it had been inspected, a yakṣa with a form made of stone rose up from beneath.
And he said, "O King, take possession of this treasure which has been guarded by me for a long time—the one buried by your grandfather."
Having spoken thus to the Lord of Vatsa and accepted his worship, the Yakṣa vanished, and a great treasure appeared in the pit.
Then a highly precious lion-throne made of jewels was obtained; for indeed, at the time of one's rise, a succession of auspicious events occurs.
Then, having taken possession of the entire treasure and celebrated a festival, the Lord of Vatsa, after instructing those cowherds, departed for his own city.
There, with the spreading rays of its rubies and emeralds, the mountain seemed to display the future military conquests of the Lord across the quarters of the world.
Jagged with rows of pearls threaded through the openings of silver sprouts, it seemed to gaze repeatedly at his minister’s astonishment as if laughing.
The people beheld that golden throne brought by the king, and they rejoiced, made beautiful by the sound of drums that had struck away their sorrow.

The ministers also celebrated a festival, having determined the victory of the king; for indeed, an auspicious omen appearing at the very outset portends the successful accomplishment of one's purpose.
Then, amidst the expanse of the sky filled with banners like flashes of lightning, that royal cloud rained down gold upon his followers.
When that day had been spent in celebration, Yaugandharāyaṇa, wishing to test the mind of the Lord of Vatsa on another day, spoke to him.
"Having ascended this great lion-throne, which has come down through the lineage of your family and which you have now obtained, may Your Majesty be consecrated."
Where my great-grandfathers ascended after conquering the earth, what fame shall be mine if I ascend there without having conquered all the directions?
Having conquered this earth, bounded by the oceans and adorned with vast treasures, I shall grace the great jeweled lion-throne of my ancestors.
Having spoken thus, the king did not mount at that moment; for among those of noble birth, pride is indeed natural and uncontrived.
Then, being pleased, Yaugandharāyaṇa said to the king: "Excellent, O King! Then first make an effort for victory in the eastern direction."
Upon hearing that, the king, in the course of conversation, asked his minister: "Even though the northern and other directions exist, why do kings travel toward the east?"
Having heard this, Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke to him again: "O King, although the northern region of Kubera is prosperous, it is censured due to its association with barbarians."

The western direction is not worshipped because it is the cause for the setting of the sun and other luminaries; the southern direction is avoided because it is inhabited by wicked Rākṣasas; and the northern direction is not relied upon.
The sun rises in the east, Indra presides over the east, and the Ganges flows toward the east; for these reasons, the east is praised.
And among all regions situated between the Vindhya and Himālaya mountains, that which is purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā is considered the most praiseworthy.
Therefore, kings seeking auspiciousness first set out toward the east, and they also dwell in the land situated along the celestial river.
For even by their ancestors, the quarters were conquered by proceeding toward the east, and a residence was established at Hastināpura on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
But Śatānīka took refuge in Kauśāmbī out of a sense of its loveliness, seeing that sovereignty depends upon human effort and that the country itself is not the cause [of success].
When Yaugandharāyaṇa had spoken thus and ceased, the king, out of his singular high regard for human effort, spoke.
