Truly, there is no restriction of place that is the cause of sovereignty here; for in times of prosperity, one's own manly effort is the sole cause for those of noble character.
Even one who is alone and deprived of support, if he possesses courage, attains prosperity; have you not heard here the story of that courageous man?
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Vatsa, at the request of his ministers, related this auspicious and wonderful tale in the presence of the two queens.
There is this city of Ujjayinī, renowned throughout the world; in it there formerly lived a king named Ādityasena.
Like that of the sun, his chariot—being the abode of majesty through his status as a sole universal monarch—never indeed stumbled anywhere in this world.
When that lofty umbrella, white as the moon, illuminated the sky, the parasols of other kings—whose heat had already subsided—were set aside.
He became the receptacle for all the jewels produced throughout the entire expanse of the earth, just as the ocean is the receptacle for all waters.
Once, for some reason, that king, having set out on a journey with his army, reached the bank of the Ganges and took up residence there.
There, a certain wealthy man named Guṇavarman, born in that very region, approached the king bringing a jewel of a maiden as a gift.
"This maiden, a jewel born even in the three worlds, has been produced in my own house; she cannot be given to anyone else, for such a god is indeed her master."
Having thus informed him through the mouth of the doorkeeper, Guṇavarman then entered and presented his own daughter to that king.
He beheld her, named Tejasvatī, who illuminated the quarters of the sky with her brilliance, like the flame of a jewel-lamp that serves as a sacred abode for the God of Love.
Beholding him, the king, composed of affection, embraced by the splendor of his beauty as if scorched by the fire of desire, perspired and began to melt away.
And having at that moment accepted her, who was worthy of the rank of Great Queen, Guṇavarman, being highly pleased, treated her as his own equal.
Then, having married that beloved Tejasvatī, the king, considering his purpose fulfilled by her, went with her to Ujjayinī.
There, with his gaze fixed solely upon her face, the king became so absorbed that he did not even notice the most important affairs of state.
His ear, as if pinned down by the sweet speech of Tejasvatī, could not be drawn away by the cries of his distressed subjects.
The king, having entered long ago, did not emerge from the inner apartments; yet the fever of pain emerged from the hearts of his enemies.
In due time, there was born to that king by Queen Tejasvatī a daughter who was beloved by all, as well as a desire for conquest in his intellect.
Exceedingly wonderful in form, that maiden—treating the three worlds as mere straw—produced joy in him, as well as pride and a desire for conquest.
Then one day, King Ādityasena set out from Ujjayinī against a certain neighboring vassal who was arrogant enough to challenge him.
And he made Queen Tejasvatī, mounted upon her female elephant, his companion on the journey, like the presiding deity of the army.

And he mounted an excellent horse, which was like a moving mountain—tall, girdled by its saddle-cloth, and with its mane rising like a spring of righteousness from its pride—and adorned with the auspicious *śrīvṛkṣa* mark.
[Regarding the mountain interpretation, "śrīvṛkṣa" refers to the *bilva* tree;
however, regarding the horse interpretation, Mallinātha states in his commentary on the *Śiśupālavadha* (5.56) that "śrīvṛkṣa" is a particular kind of whorl of hair.]
With his feet raised as high as his ears, he was practicing in the sky the flight of Garuḍa, which he had previously seen, as if he were a fellow-student of its speed.
Lifting his neck, he seemed to measure the earth with a steady gaze, wondering, "Would my speed perhaps be sufficient?"
Having traveled a short distance and reached level ground, that king urged on his horse, showing it to Tejasvatī.
Then, propelled by the horse's kick like an arrow released from a machine, he went somewhere with such extreme speed that he became invisible to the eyes of the world.
Seeing that, while the army was in a state of agitation, horsemen by the thousands pursued him, yet they did not catch the king who had been carried away by his horse.
Then, fearing an undesirable outcome, the ministers, along with their army, took the weeping queen and returned to Ujjayinī out of fear.
There, having closed their gates and secured their defenses with ramparts, they remained, comforting the subjects while seeking news of the king.
In the meantime, that king was also carried by that horse in an instant to the difficult Vindhya forest, where fierce lions roam.
There, by fate, that horse having come to a halt, the king suddenly became bewildered and distressed, his sense of direction lost within the vast forest.
Seeing no other course and descending from his chariot, the king—who was skilled in discerning the breeds of horses—bowed down and spoke to that excellent steed.
"O Lord, one such as you ought not to commit treachery against his master; therefore, you alone are my refuge—lead me by an auspicious path."
Having heard that, the horse, remembering his former birth, felt remorse; then, that best of steeds mentally accepted it as "so be it," for he was indeed a divine being.
Then, once the queen had mounted, that horse set forth along a path lined with lakes of clear, cool water, which dispelled the fatigue of the journey.
And at evening, that best of horses brought the king, who was a hundred yojanas away, into the vicinity of Ujjayinī.
Seeing that even his own seven horses had been surpassed by their speed, the sun, as it sank into the cave of the western mountain, seemed to hide itself in shame.
When darkness had spread, he saw that the gates of Ujjayinī were closed, and that the cemetery outside was terrifying at that hour.
The intelligent horse led the king to his dwelling, a secluded Brahmin monastery situated in a remote spot outside the city, hidden there during the night.
And seeing that monastery suitable for passing the night, King Ādityasena, whose horses were exhausted, began to enter it.
The Brahmins living there blocked his entrance, saying, "Who is this? Is he a cemetery-keeper or perhaps a thief?"
And they departed, engaged in quarrels, fickle and harsh; for Vedic scholars are indeed the abode of fear, cruelty, and anger.
While they were thus shouting, a certain virtuous Brahmin named Vidūṣaka, the foremost among the courageous, emerged from that monastery.
A youth, powerful-armed, having propitiated the Fire-god through asceticism, obtained from him an excellent sword that appeared as soon as it was thought of.
Seeing that king of noble appearance who had arrived at night, the wise Vidūṣaka thought, "This must be some god in disguise."
Having dismissed those Brahmins and all the others, he, whose disposition was now appropriate, bowed with humility and led the king into the interior of the monastery.
And when the king had rested and the dust of the journey had been brushed away by female attendants, they prepared for him in an instant a meal suited to his own rank.
And he removed the saddle from that excellent horse of his and relieved its fatigue by providing it with fodder and other necessities.
"I shall protect your body; therefore, sleep in peace, O Lord," she said to the king, who was weary and lying upon his prepared bed.
While he was asleep, that brahmin remained awake at the door for the entire night, with a sword of fire appearing in his hand as soon as it was thought of.
And in the morning, as soon as that king had awakened, Vidūṣaka himself, even without being told, readied the horse.
The king also, having taken leave of him and mounted his horse, entered Ujjayinī, seen from afar by the people who were overwhelmed with joy.
As soon as he had entered, all the subjects approached him in an instant, their confused clamor faltering with the joy born of his arrival.
Accompanied by his ministers, the king returned to the royal palace, and the great fever departed from the heart of Queen Tejasvatī.
At that moment, the sorrows of the city seemed to be driven away by the rows of silken banners on the festive poles, which were tossed about by the wind.
And the queen held that great festival until the end of day, until the people of the city, along with the sun, became as tawny as vermilion.
On another day, King Ādityasena had Vidūṣaka summoned from that monastery along with all the brahmins.
Having related the events of the night, he immediately bestowed upon his benefactor, Vidūṣaka, a thousand villages.
And the grateful king appointed that brahmin to the office of domestic chaplain, providing him with a royal umbrella and a vehicle, while he was gazed upon with curiosity by the people.
Thus, at that very moment, Vidūṣaka became equal to his peers; for how could service rendered to the great ever be in vain?
And all those villages which he received from the king, that noble-minded man made them common property, shared equally with the brahmins residing in his monastery.
And having taken refuge with him, he remained serving that king, enjoying along with those other brahmins the abundance of the village.
As time passed, all those others who desired preeminence—those twice-born ones, arrogant with the intoxication of wealth—did not take him into account at all.
Divided into seven groups yet residing in a single place, those [princes] oppressed the villages through mutual strife, like wicked planets.
Vidūṣaka remained indifferent toward those who were unrestrained; for among the wise, disdain alone is fitting when dealing with those of little character.
Once, seeing them engaged in a quarrel, a certain brahmin named Cakradhara, who was by nature harsh, approached them.
In the debates on the doctrines of others, though he was one-eyed, his vision remained undimmed; though he was hunchbacked, he was very clear in speech; and the Brahmin addressed them thus.
"O deceitful ones, this prosperity was obtained by you while you were acting as mendicants; why then do you destroy the villages, being intolerant of one another?"
This is the fault of the Vidūṣaka by whom you were neglected; therefore, without doubt, you shall soon again wander for alms.
Indeed, it is better to have a single leader whose prosperity depends on fate than to have many divided leaders through whom all purposes are ruined.
Therefore, if you have a need for stable prosperity protected by a leader, then follow my word and appoint one wise man as your sole guide.
Having heard that, when they all desired leadership for themselves, the Wielder of the Discus reflected upon those fools and spoke to them again:
"In that case, I shall grant you an opportunity for your contest: three thieves have been executed on a stake in the cremation ground from here."
"Whosoever among you, being a noble being, should cut off their noses at night and bring them here, he shall be the chief among you; for a hero indeed deserves to be a master."
Standing nearby, Vidūṣaka said to those Brahmins whom Cakradhara had thus addressed, "Do this; what is the harm?"
Then those brahmins said to him, "We are not capable of doing this; let whoever is able do it, for we remain bound by our agreement."
Then the Vidūṣaka said, "O sir, I shall do this: I will go at night and cut off their noses from the cemetery."
Then, considering that task to be difficult, those fools also said to him: "If you do this for us, you shall be our master; this is our agreement."
Having thus explained the agreement, when night had arrived, Vidūṣaka took leave of those brahmins and set out for the cremation ground.
And that hero entered his own terrifying abode, which was as formidable as his own past deeds, carrying only a flaming sword that had appeared the moment he thought of it.

In a place where it resounds with the cries of ḍākinīs and is howled at by vultures and crows, where the fire of the funeral pyre is fanned by the flames of meteors from the mouths of those with flaming faces;
And there in their midst, he saw those men impaled upon stakes, their faces turned upward as if out of fear of having their noses cut off.
And as soon as he reached their vicinity, all three of them, possessed by the Vetālas, began to strike him with their fists.
Remaining utterly unshaken, he struck back at them with his sword; for in the hearts of the steadfast, effort is never taught by fear.
Once they were freed from the transformations of the vetālas, that skillful man cut off their noses, bound them, and seized them by their garments.
And as he was coming, Vidūṣaka saw a wandering mendicant seated upon a corpse in that cremation ground, muttering prayers.
Out of curiosity to observe his actions and play, he approached that wandering mendicant and stood hidden behind him.
In an instant, the corpse beneath the wandering mendicant let out a shriek; flames issued from its mouth, and mustard seeds emerged from its navel.
Then, taking those mustard seeds, the wandering mendicant rose up and struck that corpse with the palm of his hand.
Then that corpse, possessed by a restless vetāla, rose up; and thereupon the mendicant ascended onto its very shoulder.
Having mounted it, he then suddenly set out to go; Vidūṣaka also followed him silently, unobserved.
Having traveled not very far, Vidūṣaka beheld an empty temple, presided over by an image of Kātyāyanī.
[This story imitates the plot of the fifth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*, involving Aghoraghaṇṭa, Kapālakuṇḍalā, Mādhava, Mālatī, and others.
Having descended from the shoulder of the vetāla, the mendicant then entered the inner sanctum, while the vetāla fell to the ground.
And Vidūṣaka was there, observing by means of a stratagem while remaining unobserved; and the mendicant, having worshipped the goddess there, made this request:
"If you are pleased, O Goddess, then grant me my desired boon; otherwise, I shall gratify you with the sacrifice of my own self."
To that wandering mendicant who had spoken thus, proud of his intense practice of mantras, a voice issued from within the inner sanctum and spoke these words:
"Bring here the maiden daughter of King Ādityasena and offer her as a sacrifice; then you shall obtain what you desire."
Having heard this, the mendicant went out, struck him again with his hand, and raised up that Vetāla, who was emitting hissing cries.
And having climbed onto his shoulder, whose mouth emitted flames of fire, he flew up into the sky and went to fetch that princess.
The Vidūṣaka, having seen all that, thought to himself: "How can the princess be killed by him while I am still alive?"
"I shall remain right here until that rogue arrives," having reflected thus, Vidūṣaka remained concealed in that very place.
And that wandering mendicant, having gone there, entered the inner apartments by way of the window-lattice and found the princess sleeping at night.
And Rāhu, consisting of darkness, arrived through the sky having seized her, just as he seizes a digit of the moon that illuminates the quarters with its radiance.
Crying out "Alas, father! Alas, mother! as the maiden wailed, he descended from the sky right there into the temple of the goddess.
And at that moment, having released the vetāla and taking that jewel of a maiden with him, he entered the inner sanctum of the queen's chamber.
Just as he sought to slay that princess, Vidūṣaka entered there with his sword drawn.
O wretch! You seek to strike down a *mālatī* flower with a stone; you desire to employ a weapon against one of such a form.
Having spoken thus, Vidūṣaka seized the wandering mendicant by the hair as he writhed, and cut off his head with his sword.
And he comforted that princess, who was overwhelmed by fear and whose limbs seemed to shrink within her as she began to recognize him slightly.
"How might I lead this princess from here into the king's inner apartments?"—thus did that wise man reflect at that time.
"O Vidūṣaka, listen to this: as for this ascetic who was killed by you, he had mastered a great Vetāla as well as mustard seeds."
Then, a desire for the sovereignty of the earth and for the king's daughters arose within him; because of that, he has now been thus deceived as a fool.
"O hero, take these mustard seeds belonging to him, by which you shall have the power to travel through the sky for this one night tonight."
Thus a voice from the sky spoke to him as his joy arose; for even the gods generally bestow their favor upon such a person.
Then, from the hem of that wandering mendicant’s garment, he took those mustard seeds in his hand and placed the princess on his lap.
And as he was departing from that palace of the queen, another voice suddenly resounded in the sky once more.
O great hero, you must come back here to the abode of the goddess at the end of the month; this must not be forgotten by you.
Having heard that, Vidūṣaka said, "So be it," and immediately, by the grace of the Goddess, he flew up into the sky carrying the princess.
Having traveled swiftly through the sky, he brought the princess into the interior of the harem while she was still comforted, and spoke to her.
"In the morning, I shall have no way to travel through the sky; therefore, everyone will see me departing. Thus, I must go right now."
Thus addressed by him, the young woman, trembling with fear, said to him: "Once you have gone, these life-breaths of mine, overcome by terror, will depart."
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, do not go; give me back my life. For the fulfillment of a promise undertaken is indeed the innate vow of the virtuous.
Having heard that, the noble-minded Vidūṣaka reflected: "Whatever may happen to me, I will not go; lest she release her life out of fear."
Then, reflecting, "What devotion can I possibly offer to the king? he remained right there in the inner apartments during the night.
Exhausted from physical exertion and staying awake, he gradually fell asleep; the princess, however, remained sleepless and passed that night in fear.
"Let him rest for a moment," she thought, her mind moist with love; thus, even at dawn, she did not awaken him who was sleeping.
Then, having entered, the attendants of the inner apartments saw him; they went in haste and informed the king of what had occurred.
The king also dispatched a warder to investigate the truth; and the warder, having gone inside, saw Vidūṣaka there.
And he heard from the mouth of that princess exactly what had occurred; having gone there, he reported it all in full to the king.
Having heard that from Vidūṣaka, the king, who knew his character, quickly became as if bewildered, wondering, "What could this be?"
And he had Vidūṣaka summoned from his daughter’s palace, accompanied by a retinue provided at her request, as her affection followed him in her mind.
And when he had approached, the king questioned him about everything that had occurred; and that Brahmin also related the entire account to him from the very beginning.
And he showed him those mustard seeds tied within the hem of his garment—seeds related to the wandering mendicant that pierce through the earth, with the noses of thieves attached to them.
Then, having considered that to be true, he summoned those brahmins of the monastery, including Cakradhara, and questioned them all regarding the root cause of the matter.
Having gone to the cremation ground himself and seen those men with their noses cut off, as well as that lowest of mendicants with his throat slit;
The noble-minded king, his confidence restored, was filled with joy for the skillful Vidūṣaka, who had returned his daughter's life.
And at that very moment, he gave his own daughter to him; for what is there that cannot be given by the noble when they are pleased with those who have rendered them assistance?
Surely it was through her love for the lotus that Śrī took hold of the hand of the princess’s son, by which Vidūṣaka obtained fortune from her.
Then, with that beloved wife, he of praiseworthy fame dwelt in the palace of King Ādityasena, treated with royal honors.
Then, after some days had passed, one night, impelled by fate, that princess spoke to Vidūṣaka.
"O Lord, do you remember what was said there in the goddess's house at night by a divine voice: 'At the end of the month, you shall come here'?"
"An entire month has passed since you went there, yet you have forgotten that," said his beloved; and upon hearing this, Vidūṣaka remembered and rejoiced.
"Excellent, you have remembered it, O slender one; I, however, had forgotten it. Having said this, he gave her an embrace as a reward.
Then, while she was asleep, he went out from the inner apartments at night; taking up his sword, composed and self-possessed, he proceeded to the temple of that goddess.
Saying aloud from outside, "O sir, here I am, Vidūṣaka," he heard a voice uttered by someone within saying, "Enter."
Having entered there, he beheld a celestial dwelling within it, and inside that, a maiden of divine form, adorned with celestial attire.
With the darkness dispelled by her own radiance, she was like a night ablaze; she was the life-restoring herb for Smara, who had been consumed by the fire of Hara’s wrath.
Filled with wonder, asking "What is this?", he was greeted by her, who was herself delighted, with a welcome full of affection and great respect.
When he was seated and had become confident through the manifestation of her affection, she spoke to him as he was eager to learn the truth of her own nature.
"I am a maiden of the Vidyādharas named Bhadrā, born of a noble lineage; because I travel at will, I beheld you here at that time."
And at that moment, my heart drawn by your virtues, I myself uttered an invisible voice to her, so that she would return to you.
Today, the application of my spells, having bewildered her, has been set in motion by me; thus, that very princess has brought this matter to your memory.
"I have remained here for your sake; therefore, O handsome one, I offer this body of mine to you—take my hand in marriage."
Thus addressed by Bhadrā, the Vidyādharī, the fortunate Vidūṣaka said, "So be it," and then married her according to the Gāndharva rite.
Then, having obtained divine enjoyments right there, he remained united with that beloved woman, as if by the power of the fruit of his own manly effort.
In the meantime, at the end of the night, that princess woke up; not seeing her husband, she suddenly fell into despair.
Rising up, she went toward her mother with faltering steps, overwhelmed and with eyes rippling with trickling tears.
And, fearing her own transgression and filled with remorse, she said to her mother: "My husband has gone somewhere during the night."
Then, as his mother became agitated out of affection for him, he gradually learned of it; the king also arrived there and fell into a state of extreme distress.
When the princess said, "I know he went outside to the cemetery; he has gone to that temple," the king himself went there.
There, by the power of the Vidyādharī’s spell, he was rendered invisible; even though the lord of the earth searched for him, he could not find that Vidūṣaka.
Then, when the queen had departed, a certain wise man approached that princess—who was now hopeless and intent on abandoning her body—and spoke these words.
"You should not entertain any fear of misfortune, for he is indeed your husband; endowed with divine enjoyments, he will come to you before long."
Having heard that, the princess sustained her life; it was held within her heart, blocked by the longing for his return.
Then, while the Vidūṣaka remained there, a certain female friend named Yogeśvarī approached his beloved Bhadrā.
Approaching her in secret, she then said this to Bhadrā: "Friend, the Vidyādharas are angry with you because of your association with mortals."
They wish to do you harm; therefore, you must depart from here. On the far shore of the eastern ocean, there is a city named Kārkoṭaka.
Having passed beyond that, there is the purifying river named Śītodā; having crossed it, one reaches the great mountain called Udaya, a field of spiritual attainment.
Go there now, for you cannot be overcome by the Vidyādharas; and do not harbor anxiety on account of this dear mortal.
Having told him all this, you shall depart, so that this courageous one may subsequently return to that very place.
Having been addressed thus by her friend, Bhadrā, though she was devoted to Vidūṣaka, consented to it, saying "So be it," as she was overcome by fear.
Having spoken thus to him with that stratagem and having given her own ring to Vidūṣaka, she vanished at the end of the night.
In an instant, Vidūṣaka found himself standing in that same empty temple as before, yet he saw neither Bhadrā nor the palace.
Remembering that expansion of magic and beholding the ring, Vidūṣaka fell under the sway of a mixture of despondency and wonder.
And he reflected on her words, remembering them as if they were a dream: "She has already departed, having announced me to Mount Udaya."
Therefore, I too must go there quickly to obtain it; yet, having found me visible to the world, the king would not abandon me.
"Therefore, I shall employ a stratagem here so that my purpose may be accomplished. Having reflected thus, the wise one assumed another form.
Then, wearing tattered clothes and covered in dust, he emerged from the temple of the goddess, crying out, "Alas, O blessed lady! Alas, O blessed lady!"
And at that moment, seeing him, the people living in that region raised a great clamor, crying out, "This is Vidūṣaka who has arrived!"
Having learned of this, the king went out in person, saw him in such a state, and having restrained that man of mad behavior, he was led back to his own palace.
There, whatever was said to him by his servants and kinsmen who were overwhelmed with affection, he gave that very same reply: "Alas, my dear lady!"
Although he had been anointed with ointments prescribed by physicians, at that very moment he smeared his limbs profusely with the dust of ashes.
The food, which had been served by the princess with her own hands out of affection, was suddenly struck with his foot by him and cast aside.
Thus Vidūṣaka remained there for some days, free from desire, tearing his own clothes and feigning madness.
This [suffering] is impossible to remedy; why then is it being made so wretched? One might even lose one's life, and from that would follow the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thinking, "In time, good fortune may come to this one who wanders according to his own will," King Ādityasena released him.
Then, moving about at his own will, the hero Vidūṣaka set out freely the next day toward Bhadrā, carrying the ring with him.
Traveling day after day toward the eastern direction, he eventually reached, by degrees, the city of Pauṇḍravardhana, which lay along his path.
Having said, "Mother, I shall stay here for one night," he entered the house of a certain elderly Brahmin woman there.
Having accepted the hospitality and settled upon her seat, that Brahmin woman, harboring inner grief, approached him in a moment and spoke thus:
"O son, this entire house has been given by me to you alone; therefore, accept it, for my life can no longer be sustained."
"Why do you speak thus? she was asked by him, who was filled with wonder; having said, "Listen, I shall tell you this," she spoke again.
"O son, there is a king named Devasena here in this city; to him was born a daughter who is an ornament of the earth."
"This daughter was obtained by me with great hardship"—thinking thus, the king, who was exceedingly fond of his child, gave her the name Duḥkhalabdhikā.
When she had reached her youth, that king brought her to his own palace and gave her to the King of Kacchapa.
That lord of tortoises entered the bedchamber of his wife at night, but as soon as he had first entered, he met his death at that very moment.
Then, with a dejected mind, the king gave that daughter once more to another monarch; yet he too met his end in the same manner.
And when other kings also, out of fear of him, no longer desired her, the king then commanded his own general in this manner:
From this region, you must bring one person at a time, day by day, from each individual house—a Brahmin or a Kshatriya—on behalf of my sons.
And having brought him here, he should be introduced at night into my daughter’s house; let us see how many perish here and for how long.
And whoever shall cross over here will become her husband; for the course of destiny, which ordains wonders, cannot be determined.
Thus commanded by the king, the general day after day takes men from their homes here in turn according to the sequence of their watches.
And thus, hundreds of men have perished there, yet here remains but one son for me, who have performed no meritorious deeds.
Today his turn has arrived to go there to his destruction; in his absence, I must enter the fire this morning.
While still alive, I give my entire house with my own hand to you, a man of virtue, so that I may never again be a partaker of suffering.
When she had spoken thus, the steadfast Vidūṣaka said to her: "If this is so, mother, then you must not give way to despondency."
"I shall go there today so that your only son may live; do not harbor such thoughts as 'Why should I kill him? and let there be no lack of compassion for me."
"Indeed, through the power of this perfected yoga, there is no fear at all for me who has gone there. When Vidūṣaka had spoken thus, that Brahmin woman said to him:
Therefore, O son, you must be some god who has come here by virtue of my merits; grant us our lives and likewise ensure our own welfare.
Thus followed by her, he went in the evening to the princess's palace together with a servant appointed by the commander-in-chief.
There he beheld the princess, exultant with the pride of youth, like a creeper bent down by the weight of its full, ungathered blossoms.
Then, when that princess had retired to her bed at night, he held in his hand the fiery sword that had appeared as soon as he meditated upon it.
In that residence of Vāsava, Vidūṣaka remained awake, thinking, "I shall see who it is that slays men here."
And while the people were fast asleep, he beheld a terrible Rākṣasa approaching from the gateway, having quickly flung open the door-panels.
And that Rākṣasa, standing there at the door within his dwelling, thrust forth an arm like the staff of Yama, which instantly struck down hundreds of men.
And Vidūṣaka, rushing forward in a rage, instantly severed that arm of the Rākṣasa with a single stroke of his sword.
With his arm severed, that night-stalker fled quickly, never to return again out of fear of that man’s excellence of character.
Having awakened and seen the fallen arm of the Rākṣasa, the princess became afraid, yet filled with joy, and was struck with wonder.
And in the morning, King Devasena saw him there at the door of his daughter’s inner apartments, standing with an arm severed and fallen away.
"From this moment on, no other men shall enter here"—thus was a very long bolt-bar placed across the door by Vidūṣaka.
Then, pleased with that man of divine power, the king gave his daughter to Vidūṣaka along with magnificent wealth.
Then Vidūṣaka remained there for some days with that beloved, as if with the very personification of prosperity in the form of Rūpavatī.
And one day, leaving the princess while she was asleep, he departed from there in haste toward Bhadrā during the night.
And that princess, distressed at not seeing him in the morning, was comforted by her father with the hope of his return.
Vidūṣaka, traveling day after day, eventually reached in due course the city of Tāmraliptikā, situated not far from the eastern ocean.
There, on that ship, he formed an alliance with a certain merchant named Skandadāsa, who was desirous of crossing to the other side of the ocean.
Together with him, he embarked upon a ship laden with no small amount of that man's wealth and set out by way of the ocean.
Then, as that ship reached the middle of the ocean, it was suddenly obstructed, as if held fast by something.
When that [ship] did not move even though the ocean was filled with jewels, then the merchant Skandadasa, distressed, spoke this:
"To whoever releases this carriage of mine that is stuck, I shall give half of my own wealth and my daughter."
Upon hearing that, the resolute-minded Vidūṣaka spoke thus: "I shall descend here and search within the waters of the ocean."
"In an instant, I shall release this ship of yours that has been bound; you too must hang on to me, securing yourselves with ropes made of grass."
And as soon as the ship is freed from the water, I must be pulled up by you using supporting ropes.
When that merchant had welcomed his words with "So be it," the helmsmen secured him between their armpits by binding him with ropes.
Bound by that, Vidūṣaka descended right into the ocean; for a person of courage never desponds when the opportune moment has arrived.
Having meditated upon and taken into his hand a fiery sword that appeared through his contemplation, the hero entered beneath the ship into the midst of the waters.
And there he beheld a man of massive body sleeping, and he saw his ship fastened to that man's leg.
At that very moment, he cut off his shank with a sword, and the ship, released from its obstruction, began to move immediately.
Upon seeing that, the wicked merchant, out of greed for the promised wealth, cut those ropes of Vidūṣaka.
And by means of that swift ship, which was both well-constructed and liberated [from obstacles], he quickly reached the far shore of the ocean, as if crossing over his own great greed.
The Vidūṣaka as well, his support of the rope severed and situated in the midst of the water, emerged and, seeing it thus, the steadfast man reflected for a moment:
What is this that has been done by that merchant? Or rather, what can be said? Those blinded by greed for wealth are ungrateful and incapable of even looking upon a favor received.
Therefore, this is precisely the time for supreme composure; for even a slight calamity is not overcome by a loss of fortitude.
Having reflected thus, he at that moment climbed onto that same shank which had been cut off from the man who was sleeping underwater.
With her, he crossed the ocean as if with a boat that scattered water with its hands; for destiny itself provides assistance to those endowed with courage.
To that powerful one, who had come for the sake of Rāma like Mārutī to the far shore of the ocean, a voice from the sky spoke thus:
"Excellent, excellent! O Vidūṣaka, what other virtuous being is there like you? I am pleased by this fortitude of yours; therefore, listen to this."
"You have now reached this realm of the Nagnas; furthermore, from here you will reach the city named Kārkoṭaka in seven days."
Then, having regained your fortitude, you shall go and quickly attain what you desire; for I was formerly your sovereign lord, the consumer of your sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors.
"And by my boon, hunger and thirst shall no longer afflict you from this time forth; therefore, go with confidence toward your success. Having said this, the voice ceased.
And Vidūṣaka, having heard that, was delighted by the fire of his affection; he set out and on the seventh day reached the city of Kārkoṭaka.
And there he entered a certain monastery presided over by noble men—by various twice-born guests from many lands who were fond of welcoming visitors.
It was built by the illustrious King Āryavarman, a local ruler; it is prosperous and endowed with delightful temples made entirely of gold.
There, after everyone had offered him hospitality, a certain brahmin took that guest to his home and attended to him with baths, meals, and garments.
And in the evening, while staying in that monastery, Vidūṣaka heard this proclamation being made in the city accompanied by the beating of drums:
Whether he be a Brahmin or even a Kshatriya, whoever desires to marry the king's daughter shall stay in her house tonight, having been invited there this morning.
Having heard that with its accompanying signs, and suspecting it at that very moment, he, who was fond of daring deeds, desired to go to the residence of the princess.
Those brahmins of the monastery said to him, "O Brahmin, do not act rashly! That is not the prince's palace; it is the wide-open mouth of Death."
For whoever enters there at night does not survive; indeed, very many rash men have met their destruction here in this manner.
Although addressed thus by those brahmins, Vidūṣaka did not accept their words and went to the royal palace along with their servants.
There, having been personally seen and welcomed by King Āryavarman, he entered his son’s residence at night like the sun entering fire.
And he beheld that princess, who was enamored with him because of his appearance, looking at him with tearful eyes, distressed by the sorrow of her despair.
And there he remained awake throughout the night, watching, while holding in his hand a sword of fire that appeared as soon as it was thought of.
And suddenly he saw at the door a most terrible Rākṣasa, who, because his right arm had been severed, was stretching out his remaining arm.
Seeing him, he thought: "Alas, this is that very night-stalker whose arm was severed by me in the city of Pauṇḍravardhana!"
Therefore, I shall not strike him on the arm again today; for he might flee as before, so I shall surely slay him now.
Having reflected thus, Vidūṣaka ran forward, seized the Rākṣasa by the hair, and began to cut off his head.
At that moment, the Rākṣasa, trembling with fear, said to him: "Do not kill me! You are a man of great virtue; therefore, show me mercy."
"What is your name, who is she, and what is this activity of yours?"—thus questioned by that hero, the rākṣasa released him and spoke again.
"These two daughters of mine, Yamadaṃṣṭrā by name, are as follows: this one here, and another who resides in Pauṇḍravardhana."
Since the king’s son must be protected from association with unheroic men, such was the favor granted by the command of Śaṅkara to me.
"In that regard, first my arm was severed by one at Pauṇḍravardhana; and today I have been conquered here by you. Thus, this [conflict] of mine has come to an end."
Having heard that, Vidūṣaka laughed and replied to him: "That arm was indeed cut off by me there in Pauṇḍravardhana."
The Rākṣasa also said: "In that case, you are a portion of a god, not a mere human; I believe it was for your sake alone that Śiva’s command of grace was bestowed upon me."
Therefore, you are now my friend; whenever you remember me, I shall be present for your success, even in times of distress.
Thus that Rākṣasa, having won over Vidūṣaka with his friendliness, vanished while Yamadaṃṣṭra’s words were still being welcomed by him.
The Vidūṣaka also, his valor joyfully celebrated by that princess, spent that night there in great delight.
In the morning, having learned the news, the king was pleased and gave his daughter to him along with great wealth, as if she were the very banner of valor.
Vidūṣaka remained there with her for some nights, as she did not leave even a single step behind him, bound to him by his virtues like the Goddess of Fortune herself.
And once, at night, he departed from there at his own will, longing for his beloved; for who, having tasted divine nectar, would take pleasure in any other flavor?
Having departed from the city, he called that rākṣasa to mind; and as soon as he was remembered, the rākṣasa arrived, and he spoke to him as he stood with joined palms.
"Friend, I must go to the mountain of sunrise, a field of spiritual accomplishment, for the sake of the Vidyādharī Bhadrā; therefore, lead me there."
When he had spoken thus, he mounted upon the shoulder of the Rākṣasa and traveled sixty yojanas through that difficult night by means of her.
And at dawn, having crossed the Śītodā river, which is difficult for humans to traverse, he then effortlessly reached the vicinity of the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayādri).
"This is that glorious mountain named Udaya situated before you; and above this, in the abode of the Siddhas, there is no further passage for me."
Having spoken thus, when that Rākṣasa had received permission and vanished, Vidūṣaka beheld there a single beautiful oblong pond.
And he sat down upon its bank, which possessed the beauty of a blooming lotus for its face, as if it were greeting him with the humming of wandering bees.
And there he saw a very extensive trail of footprints, as if belonging to women, which seemed to say, "This is the path for the arrival of your beloved."
"This mountain is impassable for mortals; therefore, it is better that I remain right here for a moment and see whose trail of footprints this is."
While he was reflecting thus, many beautiful women arrived there for the sake of water, carrying golden jars.
And he asked those women, who were carrying jars filled with water, in words tender with affection: "To whom is this water being carried?"
"O auspicious one, a Cid-yādharī named Bhadrā dwells here on this mountain; this is her bathing water," they said to him.
How wonderful! It is as if the Creator himself, pleased with those wise ones who have undertaken such magnificent deeds, provides them with the necessary collection of conditions for their success.
Then, one woman among them suddenly spoke to him: "O fortunate one, let the jar be lifted onto my shoulder."
Saying "So be it," when that jar had been lifted by her onto his shoulder, that wise man placed the jeweled ring previously given by Bhadrā inside it.
And he sat down right there once more on the bank of the pond; those women, taking that water, went to the house of Bhadrā.
There, while they were giving bathing water to Bhadrā, the ring fell into her lap.
Seeing that and recognizing it, Bhadrā asked her friends: "Have any of you seen here any man previously unknown?"
"We saw a certain young man on the bank of the pond; by him this jar was lifted," they replied.
Then Bhadrā said, "Go quickly and bring him here who has prepared his bath and ornaments; for he, my husband, has arrived."
When Bhadrā had spoken thus, she went and reported the matter exactly as it was; then Vidūṣaka, having bathed, was brought there by his companions.
And having arrived there, he saw Bhadrā after a long time, standing at the entrance of the path like the manifest glory of the ripe fruit of the tree of her own virtuous character.
She too, seeing him, rose up and, as if offering him the guest-water with the spray of her tears of joy, bound the garland of her vine-like arms around his neck.
As the two of them embraced one another, their long-accumulated affection seemed to flow forth like sweat due to the intensity of their pressing embrace.
Then, having sat down, both of them, never satiated with gazing at one another, bore an intensity of longing that seemed as if it had been multiplied a hundredfold.
When Bhadrā asked him, "How have you come to this place?", Vidūṣaka spoke these words at that time.
Having taken hold of you as my object of focus, I have developed affection for you, even at the risk of my life; having endured many hardships, I have come here—what more can I say, O beautiful one?
Having heard that and seeing his disregard for his own life, Bhadrā, her affection reaching its peak, spoke to him:
"Noble son, I have no need for friends nor for supernatural powers; you are my life, purchased by your virtues, and I am your slave, O Lord."
Then the Vidūṣaka said: "In that case, come with me, my dear; leaving behind this divine enjoyment, let us dwell in Ujjayinī."
"So be it," Bhadrā immediately assented to those words; and, deprived by his resolve, she cast away her magical sciences as if they were blades of grass.
Then Vidūṣaka rested there for that night with her, his hospitality being arranged by her friend Yogeśvarī.
And in the morning, having descended from the Mountain of Sunrise together with Bhadrā, that virtuous man again called to mind the Rākṣasa Yamadaṃṣṭra.
Having spoken of his own route to be traveled once she had arrived as soon as he thought of her, he placed Bhadrā before him and mounted upon her back.
She too endured that mounting upon the shoulder of an exceedingly fierce rākṣasa; for what will women not do when they are subject to passion?
Then, mounted upon the rākṣasa and accompanied by his beloved, Vidūṣaka set forth and once again reached that city of Kārkoṭaka.
Having been seen there by the people amidst the terror caused by the sight of the Rākṣasa, he beheld King Āryavarmā and sought out his own wife.
Having accepted that daughter given by him and won by the strength of his arm, he set out from that city mounted upon the same rākṣasa as before.
Having gone to the shore of the ocean, he encountered that wicked merchant by whom his ropes had previously been cut when he was cast into the sea.
And he carried off the daughter of that merchant, along with his wealth, which she had previously won as a prize for releasing the ship at sea.
He considered the mere seizure of that wicked man's wealth to be his execution; for in the cities of misers, life generally consists of accumulated riches.
Then, having mounted the chariot of the Rākṣasa and brought that merchant’s daughter, he flew up into the sky together with the two princesses, Bhadrā and Rājaputrī.
Displaying his own splendor to his beloveds, he crossed the ocean by way of the sky, as if crossing the sea of his own prowess with its surging mass of living beings.
And he reached that city of Pauṇḍravardhana once again, beheld with astonishment by everyone as he had made a rākṣasa his mount.
There he took as his wife the daughter of King Devasena, whom she had long yearned for, and who had been won by his conquest of the Rākṣasa.
Although his father tried to restrain him, he, longing for his own country, took her as well and set out from there toward Ujjayinī.
And before long, through the power of the Rākṣasa, he reached that city, which was like a state of bliss from beholding his own land, though it lay outside.
Then he stood upon the shoulder of that giant-bodied Rākṣasa, whose own presence was made manifest by the radiance of the circle of his wife’s jewelry resting thereon.
There, upon the mountain peak where the medicinal herbs were glowing, Vidūṣaka was seen by the people like the moon rising over the eastern mountain.
Then, perceiving that the people were struck with wonder and terror, his father-in-law King Ādityasena emerged from the city.
But Vidūṣaka, seeing him, quickly descended from the Rākṣasa, bowed to the king, and approached him; the king also greeted him with joy.
Having lowered all those wives of his from his shoulder, Vidūṣaka then released the Rākṣasa so that he might go wherever he pleased.
When that Rākṣasa had departed, he, together with his wife and his father-in-law the king, entered the royal palace.
There, having approached his first wife—the daughter of that king, who was overcome by long-standing longing—he gladdened her.
"How were these wives obtained by you, and who is this Rākṣasa?"—when asked thus by the king, he related all of that to him there.
Then, pleased by his power and knowing what ought to be done, that king gave half of his own kingdom to his son-in-law.
And at that very moment, having become a brahmin, he became Vidūṣaka, with a white parasol raised high and two chowries being waved on either side.
And then, filled with the resounding noise of auspicious musical instruments and echoing with the shouts of those released from joy, the city of Ujjayinī shone forth.

Thus, having attained the splendor of sovereignty and having gradually conquered the entire earth, his feet worshipped by all kings, he—accompanied by Bhadrā—long enjoyed himself with his own beloved wives, who were free from envy and filled with joy.
Thus, when destiny is favorable, for the wise, their very own nature becomes like a mantra that has achieved great joy through the forceful attraction of prosperity.
Having thus heard this wonderful tale of marvelous import from the mouth of the King of Vatsa, all his ministers seated at his side, as well as his two queens, attained the highest joy.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The fifth wave begins: Then, there, Yaugandharāyaṇa said to the Lord of Vatsa, "O King, you possess both the favor of destiny and human effort."
We too have exerted some effort here on the path of policy; therefore, quickly achieve victory over the quarters as you have intended.
When the chief minister had spoken thus, the King, the Lord of Vatsa, said: "Let it be so; however, the accomplishment of auspicious goals is always beset by many obstacles."
Therefore, for that purpose, I propitiate Śambhu through austerity; for without his grace, how can there be the accomplishment of one's desires?
Having heard that, the ministers also approved of his asceticism, just as the lords of the monkeys did when Rāma was intent on building a bridge across the ocean.
Then Śiva appeared to the king in a dream as he remained engaged in asceticism with his two queens and ministers, having fasted for three nights.
"I am pleased with you; therefore, arise, for you shall attain victory without obstacle and, before long, a son who is the sovereign lord of all Vidyādharas."
Then the king, his fatigue dispelled by her grace, awoke like the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, its nourishment restored by the rays of the sun.
In the morning, he delighted his ministers with that dream, as well as his two queens, who were tender as flowers and exhausted from their vows and fasts.

For those two, who were already satiated by the description of that dream—which was as worthy of being drunk by the ears as nectar—a course of sweet medicine arose solely for the sake of their recovery.
Through his ascetic power, that king attained an influence equal to that of his ancestors; and his two wives acquired the holy fame of devoted wives.
When the citizens were preoccupied with the festival and the breaking of the vow had been performed, Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke thus to the king on another day:
Blessed are you, for the Lord Hara is thus pleased with you; therefore, having now conquered your enemies, enjoy the prosperity earned by your own arms.
For she was born of her own dharma and established in the lineage of kings; indeed, there is no destruction of wealth acquired through one's own dharma.
And likewise, a treasure long buried in the earth, accumulated by your ancestors, has been lost to you but has now been found; furthermore, hear this story regarding it.
Long ago, in the city of Pāṭaliputra, there lived a certain merchant’s son named Devadāsa, born into a family of great wealth.
And his wife was the daughter of a certain wealthy merchant from the city of Pauṇḍravardhana, whom he had married.
When his father had passed away, Devadāsa, gradually overcome by misfortune, lost all his wealth at dice.
Then his wife, distressed by grief and poverty, was brought by her own father to his home in Pauṇḍravardhana.
Then Devadāsa, distressed by his misfortune yet wishing to remain in his own occupation and seeking wages, went to ask that father-in-law for [permission].
Having reached that city of Pauṇḍravardhana at the time of twilight, he beheld it covered in dust and its people without clothes, and reflected upon himself.
"How can I enter my father-in-law's house in such a state? For a person of honor, death is better than wretchedness before one's own kin."
Having reflected thus, he went to the marketplace and remained somewhere outside the shop at night, contracted like a lotus for that time.
And in an instant, she beheld a certain young merchant entering that shop, having thrown open its door.
And in another moment, he saw a certain woman approaching that very spot with silent steps and quickly entering within.
And as long as he cast his gaze within that space where the lamp was burning, he recognized her at once as his very own wife.
Then, seeing his wife—who had gone to another man—standing before a bolted door, Devadāsa, struck by the thunderbolt of grief, reflected:
By one devoid of wealth, even the body is lost; what then to say of women? For their fickleness is as natural as that of lightning flashes.
This, then, is the calamity for men who fall into the ocean of misfortune; this is the fate of an independent woman residing in her father's house.
Thinking thus, he remained outside and heard, as it were, the conversation of his wife as she enjoyed the confidence of the end of their dalliance.
Having approached, she placed Karṇa at the door; at that very moment, that wicked woman spoke thus to her paramour, the merchant, in private:
Listen, for today I shall tell you this secret, O devoted one: in former times, my husband’s great-grandfather was named Vīravarman.
In the courtyard of his own house, he buried four jars filled with gold, hidden in the ground at the four corners.
Then he made that known to his own wife alone; and at the time of her death, that wife spoke it to her daughter-in-law.
She told it to her daughter-in-law, she to my mother-in-law, and she to me; such is the oral tradition regarding the succession of mothers-in-law in my husband's family.
And I did not describe that to my husband, even though he was poor; for he was addicted to gambling and detestable, whereas you are most dear to me.
Therefore, go there and purchase that house from my husband with wealth; having obtained it and acquired the gold, come here and enjoy me happily.
Thus addressed by that crafty woman, the merchant, her paramour, was delighted with her, imagining he had obtained a treasure without any effort.
Devadāsa, too, having gone outside, felt at that moment as if his hope for wealth were pinned within his heart by those word-thorns of his wicked wife.
And from there he went immediately to the city of Pāṭaliputra; having reached his own home and obtained the treasure, he took possession of it.
Then that merchant, whose secret lover was his wife, arrived at that very place under the pretext of trade, greedy for the treasure.
And he purchased that house from Devadāsa; Devadāsa, for his part, gave it to him for a higher price.
Then, having established a household by means of a stratagem at his father-in-law's house, that Devadāsa quickly brought back his wife.
When this had been done, that deceitful merchant, who was enamored of his wife and had failed to obtain the treasure, approached Devadāsa and said to him:
"This house of yours is dilapidated; it does not please me at all. Therefore, give me its proper price and take back your own house."
Thus the merchant spoke, and Devadāsa replied; both, intent on their dispute, went before the king.
There, Devadāsa recounted before the king the entire account of his own wife, which was as unbearable as poison lodged in his chest.
Then the king, having summoned the merchant's wife and investigated the truth of the matter, punished that adulterer by confiscating all his property.
Devadāsa, having made that woman with the severed nose his wife, married another and remained there happily, having found the treasure.
Thus, wealth acquired through righteousness remains constant and does not perish; but other wealth is as transient as a drop of frost falling upon water.
Therefore, a man should strive to acquire wealth through righteous means; but a king especially so, since wealth is the very root of the tree of sovereignty.
Therefore, O Lord, having duly honored the circle of ministers for the sake of success, undertake the conquest of the quarters to obtain sovereignty that is preeminent in righteousness.
Through the successive involvement of their fathers-in-law and kinsmen, many kings do not act perversely, and they meet together.
But this lord of the earth in Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta is your constant enemy; therefore, conquer him first.
When that [eastern quarter] is conquered, you shall achieve victory over all directions by proceeding from east to east; indeed, raise high the fame of Pāṇḍu, radiant as a white water-lily.
Thus addressed by the chief minister, the King of Vatsa, intent on victory, replied, "So be it," and ordered the commencement of the march among his subjects.
And out of respect for his sister’s husband who was following him, that king bestowed the kingdom of the Vaideha country upon Gopālaka.
Furthermore, having honored him as he arrived together with his armies, he bestowed the region of Cedi upon Siṃhavarman, the brother of Padmāvatī.
And that lord summoned Pulindaka, the king of the Bhillas, his friend whose armies filled the quarters like clouds during the rainy season.
And there arose a great mobilization for the expedition in the kingdom of that mighty lord, while a strange agitation took birth in the hearts of his enemies.
And Yaugandharāyaṇa dispatched spies ahead toward Vārāṇasī to ascertain the activities of King Brahmadatta.
Then, on an auspicious day, the Lord of Vatsa, pleased by omens foretelling victory, set out first toward the east against Brahmadatta.
Mounted upon his lofty elephant of victory, beneath a raised parasol, he was like a rutting lion ascending a mountain with its solitary tree in full bloom.

Receiving great joy from the autumn season—which was like a messenger of accomplishment that had arrived—the king beheld a path that was exceedingly easy to traverse, with its shallow streams of water.
Filling the surface of the earth with armies accompanied by many sounds, he created the confusion of an unseasonable rain during a cloudless sky.
And then, the quarters of the sky, filled with the echoes of the army's roar, seemed to announce to one another the fear of its arrival.
And his horses, adorned with golden trappings and possessing the brilliance of the sun, moved along as if followed by the fire pleased by the lustration ceremony.
And his elephants shone on the road, their white ears adorned with chowries and their temples red with ichor mixed with vermilion as it flowed down.
Marked by autumn clouds as white as ash and possessing waterfalls of liquid minerals, they were sent forth on their journey like sons dispatched by the mountains out of fear.
"This king cannot endure the spreading splendor of others"—as if for this reason, the dust of his army concealed the brilliance of the sun.
And two goddesses followed him on the path, step for step: Fame and the Fortune of Victory, as if drawn by the king's quality of statesmanship.
"Bow down or flee!"—thus it seemed as if he were commanding his enemies by means of the silken banners of his army, tossed and scattered by the wind.
Thus he traveled through the various directions, beholding the blossoming white lotuses that appeared like the upturned hoods of Śeṣa, who had been startled by the fear of the Earth being crushed.
In the meantime, those spies, who had undertaken the vow of Kāpālikas and were dispatched by Yaugandharāyaṇa, reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Among them, one who was skilled in deception displayed his own knowledge and assumed the role of the teacher, while the others became his disciples.
Those disciples proclaimed him here and there as their teacher, saying, "This master knows the three times," while he was merely a false guru who lived on alms.
Whatever that wise man spoke regarding future events, such as fires and other calamities, to those who questioned him, his disciples kept it secret; by that means, he became renowned.
And he won over a certain lay disciple, a prince who was beloved by the king and delighted in minor supernatural attainments.
Through that very person, he became a knower of the secrets of King Brahmadatta as the latter was making inquiries, when the conflict with the Lord of Vatsa had arrived.
Then Brahmadatta’s minister, Yogakaraṇḍaka, devised various stratagems on the road for the King of Vatsa as he was approaching.
He defiled the road at every turn with mixtures of poisonous substances, and he corrupted the trees, flowering creepers, waters, and grasses.
He stationed poison-maidens among his troops disguised as courtesans, and he dispatched men during the nights to kill by means of treachery.
Having learned of that, the spy, bearing the marks of a wise man, then quickly reported it to Yaugandharāyaṇa through the mouths of his own companions.
Yaugandharāyaṇa, having learned of this, purified along the entire path at every step the grass, water, and other provisions by providing counter-measures against them.
He prohibited any union with an unprecedented woman within the camp, and together with Rumaṇvat, he put those assassins to death once they were captured.
Having understood that, his illusions destroyed, Brahmadatta considered the Lord of Vatsa—whose quarters were filled with his army—to be truly invincible.
Having consulted together and dispatched a messenger, he then approached the King of Vatsa in person as the latter drew near, with his hands joined in reverence upon his head.
Vatsarāja, for his part, honored with affection the king who had arrived bringing gifts; for the brave are fond of those who bow before them.
Thus, once that [western quarter] was conquered, he pacified the eastern kings by subduing the mild and uprooting the harsh, just as the wind treats the trees.
And the powerful one reached the eastern ocean, which was tossed by surging waves and seemed to tremble with fear at the conquest of Vaṅga.
And on the edge of that shore, he erected a pillar of victory, which rose up like the King of the Nāgas emerging to beg for protection from the underworld.
Then, as the Kalingas advanced and offered their hands in salutation, he bowed down and ascended Mount Mahendra; thus did the glory of that illustrious hero ascend.

Having conquered the forest of rival kings with elephants that seemed as if they had come from the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, terrified by the overwhelming power of Mahendra, he proceeded toward the southern direction.
There, on that wheel, he [slew] his mountain-dwelling enemies—who were pale and devoid of essence and who had ceased their roaring—just as autumn clouds are dispersed.
As the Kāverī was being overstepped by that cause of such commotion, both she and the fame of the Lord of Cola simultaneously fell into turbidity.
He could not endure the lack of elevation on the heads of the Murala women alone; he could not endure it even when their breasts were being struck by his hands.
The elephants, having drunk the waters of the Godāvarī divided into seven streams, seemed as if they were releasing them again in seven ways under the pretext of rut.
Then, having crossed the Revā, the Lord of Vatsa went to Ujjayinī, and he entered the city preceded by Caṇḍamahāsena.

And right there, he became the target of the side-long glances of the Mālava women, which were characterized by a lack of restraint due to the beauty of their loosened flower-garlands and disheveled braids.
And there he remained, contented and honored by his father-in-law, forgetting even his desired pleasures born of his own country.
And Vāsavadattā remained by her father’s side, remembering her childhood, appearing as if despondent even in the midst of happiness.
And King Caṇḍamahāsena rejoiced upon his reunion with Padmāvatī just as much as he did with his own daughter.
After resting for some nights, the King of Vatsa, being well-pleased, set out toward the western direction accompanied by his father-in-law's armies.
Surely his sword-blade was the smoke from the fire of his majesty, since it caused the eyes of the Lāṭa women to become clouded with tears.
"May he not uproot me while churning the ocean!"—as if thinking thus, Mount Mandara trembled when its forests were shaken by those elephants.

Truly, he was some extraordinary being of splendor, distinct from the sun and other luminaries; though he had already attained his zenith in the west, he achieved a supreme rising once more as a conqueror.
Then he set out toward that quarter which was marked by Kubera, which betokened union with Alakā, and which was as beautiful as the smile of Kailāsa.
Having brought the King of Sindhu under his control, Rāghava, pursued by the monkey forces, destroyed the Mlecchas as Rāma had destroyed the Rākṣasas.
The throngs of Turuṣka horses, like the waves of an agitated ocean, were shattered into fragments upon the forested shores by the herds of his lordly elephants.
The illustrious Pāpasya, the best of men, having seized his sword, severed the head of the King of the Persians as if it were that of Rāhu.
[In this context, Puruṣottama is Viṣṇu;
in his case, "the circle of enemies" refers to one who has taken a discus in his hand— this is the meaning.]
The fame of that king, who brought about the destruction of the Hūṇas, spread across the Himalayas like a second Gaṅgā, filling the quarters of the sky with its sound.
While his armies were roaring, the enemies stood paralyzed with fear; their own cries were heard only within the mountain caves, turned back in opposition.
That even the Lord of Kāmarūpa, bowing with his head uncovered, then attained a state of lusterlessness—that was no wonder at all.
Then that emperor set out, accompanied by the elephants given by him, as if by moving mountains offered to him like gifts.
Having thus conquered the earth, the Lord of Vatsa, together with his retinue, reached the city of the King of Magadha, the father of Padmāvatī.
And when he had arrived there accompanied by his two queens, the Lord of Magadha became filled with joy, like the God of Love under a moonlit night.
And he regarded Vāsavadattā—who had previously remained unrecognized and had now become manifest again—as a vessel of even greater humility.

Then, honored by that King of Magadha along with his city, and followed by the hearts of all the people who had come out of affection, that victorious Vatsarāja—having swallowed the surface of the earth with the weight of his army—departed for his own domain, Lāvāṇaka.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave. Then, while staying there at Lāvāṇaka for the sake of resting his army, King Vatsarāja spoke in secret to Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"By means of your wisdom, all the kings on earth have been conquered by me; they have been won over through strategic means and do not at all deviate from my will."
"This Brahmadatta, the lord of Vārāṇasī, is evil-minded; I know he is unfaithful alone—what trust can there be in the crooked?"
When the Lord of Vatsa had spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa said: "O King, Brahmadatta shall not transgress against you again."
But he, having been subdued and yet greatly honored by you—what conscious person indeed would do evil to one of such virtuous conduct?
Or rather, let him do that which would result in misfortune for himself; in this regard, listen as I relate a story to you.
In ancient times, in the land of Padma, there was a certain eminent brahmin named Agnidatta, who was renowned and enjoyed the revenue from a royal grant of land.
To him was born an eldest son named Somadatta, and a second son was born known by the name Vaiśvānaradatta.
Of those two, the first was a fool, handsome in appearance but ill-mannered; the other was learned, well-behaved, and fond of study.
After both of them had taken wives and their father had passed away, they then divided his agrahāras and other property equally, each receiving half.
Among them, the youngest was honored by the king, while the eldest, Somadatta, was fickle and performed the duties of a Kshatriya.
Once, seeing Somadatta engaged in conversation with some Śūdras, a certain Brahmin who was a friend of his father spoke to him thus:
Having become the son of Agnidatta, you act like a fool, O Śūdra; seeing your own younger brother honored by the king, you feel no shame.
Hearing that, Somadatta then became enraged; casting aside all decorum, he rushed at the Brahmin and struck him with a kick.
Thereupon, that Brahmin, having immediately summoned other twice-born men as witnesses, went in a rage caused by the blow to the king's feet and made this representation to him:
The king also dispatched soldiers to arrest Somadatta; but having gone out, they were struck down by his friends, who held weapons in their hands.
Then the king, blinded by rage, dispatched even more troops and ordered the impalement on a stake of Somadatta, who had been thus subdued.
Then, as he was being mounted upon the stake, that brahmin suddenly fell to the earth as if thrown down by someone.
His future welfare was protected by his very fortunes, since his executioners became blind as they prepared to hang him.
At that moment, having heard the news, the king was pleased; at the request of his younger brother, he released him from execution.
Then, having escaped death along with his household, King Somadatta desired to go to another land due to that royal humiliation.
And when his assembled kinsmen did not wish for him to depart, he then adopted a state of life in which he relinquished half of the royal lands and grants.
Then, because there was no other means of livelihood, he desired to practice agriculture; on an auspicious day, he went to the forest to look for land suitable for that purpose.
There he obtained an auspicious site, anticipating the perfection of its fruit; and in the midst of it, he beheld a great, prosperous *aśvattha* tree.
Beholding him, who cooled the rays of the sun like the rainy season with the shade of his auspicious cloud-like form, that seeker of the fruits of agriculture attained great satisfaction.
Having declared, "I am a devotee of him who is the presiding deity here," he circumambulated that Aśvattha tree and bowed down to it.
Then, having yoked a pair of oxen and performed auspicious rites, he made an offering at that tree and began his cultivation there.
He remained day and night beneath that very tree, and his wife always brought him food right there.
And when his crops had ripened there in due season, that land was unexpectedly plundered by a foreign kingdom, which arrived there by the turn of fate.
Then, when the enemy force had departed and the grain was lost, that courageous man comforted his weeping wife and took what little remained.

Then, having performed the ritual offering as before, he remained right there beneath the tree; for it is the natural disposition of the steadfast that they become even more firm in times of adversity.
Then, as he stood alone at night, sleepless with anxiety, a voice issued forth from that aśvattha tree.
"O Somadatta, I am pleased with you; therefore, go to the kingdom of the king named Ādityaprabha, located in the region of Śrīkaṇṭha."
There, at the gate of that monarch, you should recite this speech after having chanted the mantras for the twilight fire-sacrifice (sandhyāgnihotra) without interruption.
I am a brahmin named Phalabhūti; listen to what I say: one who performs good deeds shall obtain good fortune, and one who performs evil deeds shall obtain misfortune.
And by speaking thus there, you shall attain great supernatural power; now, recite from me alone the mantras for the twilight fire-sacrifice.
Having said, "I am a Yakṣa," and having instantly instructed him in those mantras by means of his own power, the voice vanished from the banyan tree.
In the morning, that virtuous Somadatta set out with his wife, having received the name Phalabhūti bestowed upon him by the Yakṣa.
Having traversed those various rugged and winding forests, which were like difficult circumstances, he reached the realm of Śrīkaṇṭha.
There, having performed the twilight rites, the fire-oblation, and so forth, he duly announced his own name as "Phalabhūti" at the gate of the king.
He spoke these words, which arouse curiosity in the world: "May the doer of good obtain good, and may the doer of evil obtain evil."
And while he was speaking thus, King Ādityaprabha, having learned of Phalabhūti's presence there, being filled with curiosity, had him ushered in.
He too, having entered, repeated those very same words before him again and again; at that, the king laughed along with those standing by his side.
And having given him garments and ornaments, the king, along with his vassals, granted him villages; for the satisfaction of the great is never in vain.
And thus, at that very moment, Phalabhūti—having become emaciated through the favor of the Guhyaka—attained the splendor bestowed by the king.
Constantly repeating what he had previously said, he attained the favor of the king; for the minds of lords indeed delight in diversion.
Gradually, in this city of Rājagṛha, throughout the kingdoms and the inner apartments, he attained the affection and great esteem of one beloved by the king.
Then once, having returned from hunting in the forest, King Ādityaprabha suddenly went to his inner apartments.
Entering with anxious haste and apprehension, he beheld the queen named Kuvalayāvalī, intent upon the worship of the gods.
[The practitioner should visualize her] naked, with hair standing on end and eyes closed, bearing a large tilaka mark of vermilion, and her lips quivering with the recitation of mantras.
She stands in the center of a great maṇḍala laid out with powders of various colors, performing a fierce bali-offering prepared with blood, wine, and human flesh.
When the king had entered, she too, her garment disarrayed by her agitation, was questioned by him; having been granted safety, she spoke thus after a moment.
At that very time, I performed worship for the sake of attaining my rise; O Lord, hear from me now the account of its arrival and its success.
Long ago, while I was a maiden staying in my father’s house during the great festival of spring, I was thus addressed by my female companions as we gathered together in a garden.
Here, in the pleasure garden, situated in the midst of a circle of trees, dwells the god of gods, Vināyaka, who has manifested his power and bestows boons.
Approaching him with devotion, worship that granter of requests, by which you shall swiftly obtain a husband worthy of yourself without any obstacle.
Having heard that, out of my naivety, I asked those friends: "Do maidens obtain a husband by worshipping Vināyaka?"
Then they replied to me: "Why do you say such a thing? If he is not honored, no success whatsoever belongs to anyone here."
"And so, listen as we describe its power to you. Having said this, my friends told me this story.
Long ago, when Śakra was oppressed by Tāraka and the flower-weaponed god (Kāma) had been consumed, [the gods] desired to obtain a commander-in-chief who was the son of Purāri.

Having performed austerities, Gaurī sought out and obtained as her husband Tryambaka, who is one whose vital energy is drawn upward, who is exceedingly fierce, and who is established in very long-term asceticism.
She longed for the birth of a son and for the life of Madana, yet she did not remember to worship Vighneśvara for the sake of her success.
And Śiva spoke thus to his beloved, who was entreating him for her desired object: "O dear one, in former times, Smara was born from the mind of Prajāpati."
And as soon as he was born, he spoke out of pride, saying, "Whom shall I cause to tremble? Therefore, the Four-faced One gave him the name Kandarpa.
If you are so excessively arrogant, my son, then do not disregard the Three-eyed One; otherwise, you will surely meet death at his hands.
And thus, although he was commanded by Brahmā, that rogue has come to cause agitation; having been consumed by me, there shall be no further rebirth for him while his body still exists.
I shall produce a son for you by my own power alone; for my progeny is not caused by the impulse of passion, as is the case with worldly beings.
Even as the bull-bannered god was speaking thus to Pārvatī, Brahmā appeared before him, accompanied by Indra, the lord of a hundred sacrifices.
Having been praised by him and requested for the pacification of the demon Tāraka, Śiva consented to procreate a legitimate son through the Goddess.

And he consented to the birth of desire within the minds of embodied beings, for the sake of the creation, maintenance, and protection [of the world], even though that desire is formless, by means of his word.
And he gave even his own heart room for the god of love; pleased by this, the Creator departed, and Pārvatī attained great joy.
Then, after some days had passed, Śaṅkara, remaining in private one day, enjoyed the sport of amorous dalliance with Umā.
When there was no end to his dalliance even after hundreds of years had passed, the three worlds trembled at the pressure of it.
Then, out of fear for the destruction of the world and for the sake of obstructing the trident-bearer’s pleasure, the gods, at the command of the Grandfather, called upon Agni.
That fire, as soon as it was remembered, considering Madanāntaka to be unassailable, fled from the gods and entered the depths of the water.
And the frogs there, being scorched by that heat, informed the gods who were searching for him about that fire situated within the water.
Then, having instantly turned them into frogs whose voices were unexpressed by means of a curse, Agni vanished and went back to Mount Mandara.
There, the gods reached him who was staying within the hollow in the form of a snail, as described by Gaja and Śuka; and he granted them his sight.
Having caused the reversal of the tongues of Śuka and Dantī by means of a curse, he accomplished the purpose of the gods once they had offered him praise.
Having gone there, that fire, having checked Śiva from his amorous dalliance with its own heat, bowed to him out of fear of a curse and informed him of the task of the gods.
Śarva, having mounted his impetuous speed, deposited his seed into that fire; for neither the Fire nor Ambikā was able to sustain it.
Then Hara spoke thus to the Goddess, who was agitated by grief and anger as she said, "I have not obtained a son from you."
"This obstacle has arisen for you here because of the failure to worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa). Therefore, worship him so that a son may quickly be born to us from the fire."
Thus addressed by Śambhu, the Goddess performed the worship of Vighneśvara; and by that seed of Dhūrjaṭi, Anala also became pregnant.
Bearing that Śambhu-derived splendor, he then shone even during the days as if the seven-rayed sun had entered within him.
He then discharged that unbearable energy into the Gaṅgā; by the command of Hara, Gaṅgā abandoned it on Mount Meru into a sacrificial fire-pit.
While being protected there by the hosts of Śambhu, that embryo emerged after a thousand years and became the six-faced Kumāra.
Then, having drunk from the breasts of the six Kṛttikās who were commissioned by Gaurī with his six mouths, he grew in a very few days.
In the meantime, the king of the gods, defeated by the demon Tāraka and having abandoned the field of battle, took refuge on the inaccessible peaks of Mount Meru.
The gods, together with the sages, went for refuge to the six-faced one; and the six-faced one, surrounded by them, remained protecting the deities.
Having understood that and considering his kingdom lost, Indra then became agitated; filled with envy, he went forth and fought against Kumāra.
From the limb of Ṣaṇmukha struck by that vajra, there were born two sons named Śākha and Viśākha, both possessed of incomparable splendor.
Approaching his son, who had surpassed the prowess of Indra, Śarva himself restrained him from the fight.
