"You have been born to slay Tāraka and to protect the kingdom of Indra; therefore, perform your own duty," he thus instructed him.
Then, having bowed down with a joyful heart at that very moment, the enemy of Vṛtra began the consecration of Kumāra as the commander-in-chief.
When his arm became paralyzed because he had lifted the jar himself, Śakra fell into grief; then Śiva spoke to him.
Because you did not worship the elephant-faced one while desiring a commander-in-chief, this obstacle has arisen for you; therefore, perform his worship.
Having heard that and having done accordingly, the Lord of Śacī, with his arms released, duly performed the consecration festival for the commander-in-chief.
Then, before long, the commander-in-chief slew the demon Tāraka; the gods rejoiced at having accomplished their purpose, and Gaurī became a mother of a son.
Thus, O Goddess, even for the gods there are no accomplishments when Heramba is not worshipped; therefore, as one who desires boons, worship him.
Having been told this by my friends, I went previously to a secluded spot in the garden and worshipped Vighnarāja, O noble son.
And at the conclusion of the worship, I suddenly beheld those female companions of mine soaring up and moving through the courtyard of the sky by means of their own supernatural power.
Having seen that, out of curiosity, I summoned them from the sky and brought them down; when I questioned them regarding the nature of their supernatural power, they immediately said this:
These are the mantra-attainments of the Ḍākinīs born from the consumption of human flesh; she is known as Kālarātri, a Brāhmaṇī who is our guru in this matter.
Thus addressed by my friends, I was filled with longing for the power of flight, yet fearing the consumption of human flesh, I remained for a moment in doubt.
Then, out of greed for that success, I said to those friends: "This very instruction must be given to me by you as well."
Then, at my request, they went at that very moment and brought back Kālarātrī, who was there in her hideous form.
With meeting eyebrows and timid eyes, with a downward-turned flat nose, thick cheeks, protruding lips, bumpy teeth, and a long neck.
With pendulous breasts, a protruding belly, and feet so cracked that they seemed to be splitting open, she appeared like the Creator’s demonstration of his mastery in fashioning deformity.
Having bathed and performed worship of Vighneśvara, she prostrated at my feet; then, while naked within the mandala, she caused me to perform the terrifying worship of Bhairava.
And having consecrated me, she gave me those various mantras of her own, as well as human flesh that had been prepared as an offering for the worship of the gods, for me to eat.
Having recited the assembly of mantras and consumed the great flesh at that very moment, I flew up into the sky with my companions, entirely naked.
Then, O Lord, having finished my play and descended from the sky with my guru’s permission, I went to my own inner apartments among the maidens.
Thus, even when born in childhood, I became a sovereign of the circle of ḍākinīs; and there, having gathered together, we devoured many men.
In this interval of the story, O Great King, hear this tale: there was a twice-born man named Viṣṇusvāmin who was the husband of that Kālarātri.
And in that region, that preceptor, who was an expert in the knowledge of the Vedas, taught his disciples who had come from various directions.
And among his disciples there was one youth named Sundaraka, a disciple whose body and virtues were resplendent with moral conduct.
Once, when her husband had gone out somewhere, that preceptor’s wife—Kālarātri—being afflicted by desire, chose him in secret.
Surely Smara sports with excessive laughter through hideous forms, since, disregarding his own beauty, he conceived a longing for Sundaraka.
But he did not desire ruin with his whole soul, even though it was being sought; for however women may behave, the mind of the virtuous remains unshakable.
Then, after he had withdrawn, Kālarātri, filled with rage, tore her own body with the wounds of her own teeth and nails.
With her garments and hair disheveled, she remained weeping until the preceptor Viṣṇusvāmī entered the house.
When he had entered, she said to him, "Look, my lord, what a state Sundaraka has brought me to by his forceful desire."
Upon hearing that, the preceptor flared up with anger at that very moment; for trust in women robs even the wise of their discernment.
And in the evening, when Sundaraka had reached his house, he rushed out with his disciples and struck him with fists, feet, and clubs.
Moreover, having instructed his disciples to leave him outside while he lay motionless from the blows, he had him cast out onto the street at night with utter indifference.
Then, fanned by the night breeze, Sundaraka slowly reflected thus upon seeing himself so utterly overwhelmed:
Ah! The instigation of women indeed causes agitation in the hearts of men whose souls are overcome by passion, just as a whirlwind stirs the depths of lakes filled with water.
Because of which, though he was aged and learned, my preceptor acted improperly toward me out of excessive anger, without having reflected upon it.
Or rather, even for the wise, desire and anger—both of which are established by fate since the beginning of creation—are indeed the bolts on the door to liberation for brahmins.
For instance, why did the sages not formerly become enraged with Śarva in the Devadāru forest, fearing the loss of their own wives?
And they did not recognize this god, who had assumed the form of a mendicant, as he intended to show Umā the lack of tranquility even among the sages.
Having immediately realized that they had incurred a curse which would cause the agitation of the three worlds, they sought refuge in that very Lord Īśāna, the God.
Thus, even sages who are deceived by the sixfold group of enemies beginning with desire and anger become deluded; what then need be said of those who are merely learned in the Vedas?
Thus, meditating there at night out of fear of bandits, Sundaraka climbed onto the roof of a nearby empty cow-pen and remained there.
While he remained unobserved in that one spot for a moment, Kālarātri arrived at that very palace.
Brandishing a drawn hero’s dagger, terrifying with the hissing breath she emits, vomiting flames from her eyes and mouth, she is joined by a circle of ḍākinīs.
Seeing that night of doom approaching there in such a manner, Sundaraka, filled with fear, then called to mind mantras that destroy demons.
Then, deluded by his mantra, she did not see him as he stood hidden in a secluded spot, his limbs drawn together in fear.
Then, having recited the mantra for flight, Kālarātrī, together with her circle of friends, rose into the sky along with the cow-pen and the palace.
Having heard that mantra at that time, Sundaraka took it up; and she, along with her palace, quickly departed through the air for Ujjayinī.
Having brought her there into the palace by means of mantras, she went to the vegetable garden and, having entered the cremation ground, sported in the midst of the circle of dākinīs.
And at that moment, overcome by hunger, Sundaraka descended into a vegetable garden and there sustained himself with uprooted radishes.
When he had thus satisfied his hunger and returned to the cow-pen as before, Kālarātri emerged from her dwelling in the middle of the night.
Then, having mounted the cow-pen by means of the accomplishment of the mantra as before, she, together with her disciples, returned to her own home through the sky during the night.
Having placed that cow-pen carriage in its proper place and dismissed those female attendants, she entered her bedchamber.
Sundaraka, having spent that night astonished by the obstacles, left the cow-pen at dawn and went into the presence of his friends.
There, having related his own story and being intent on departing for a foreign land, he was consoled by those friends and took up residence among them.
Leaving the house of his preceptor and eating at a public almshouse, he dwelt there, wandering at will with his friends.
Once, having gone out to purchase household goods, that Kālarātri beheld Sundaraka in the marketplace.
Approaching him once more, she, afflicted by love, said to him: "O Sundaraka, even now favor me, whose life is dependent upon you."
Thus addressed by her, the virtuous Sundaraka then said: "Do not speak thus; this is not right, for you are my mother and the wife of my guru."
Then Kālarātri said: "If you know what is dharma, then give it to me; for what dharma could be greater than the gift of life by giving me my life?"
Then Sundaraka said, "Mother, do not harbor such a thought in your heart; where will there be righteousness in approaching the bed of one's guru?"
Thus repulsed by him, she, threatening him in her rage, tore her own upper garment with her own hand and went home.
"Look! Sundaraka has run here and torn this [garment] of mine," she said to her husband there, showing him her upper garment.
And her husband, having gone there in anger and proclaimed her as one deserving of death, immediately forbade Sundaraka's food at the sacrificial feast.
Then Sundaraka, out of weariness, prepared to abandon that place, knowing the mantra for flying through the air that he had learned from Govāṭa.
Then, having learned another lesson while descending—which had been heard but forgotten—he went again at night to that very same empty cow-pen and palace.
While he remained there, as before, Kālarātri approached; having likewise leapt up from her palace, she went through the air to Ujjayinī.
Having caused the cow-pen to be brought there by means of a mantra into the vegetable garden, she went once again to the cemetery for her nocturnal wanderings.
And although Sundaraka heard that mantra once more, he did not grasp it; for how can complete accomplishments be attained without the instruction of a guru?
Then, having eaten some radishes and other roots there, he threw them into the cow-pen to take away and remained there as before.
Then, having mounted her carriage drawn by oxen and traveled through the sky at night, Kālarātri entered her own abode after unyoking her vehicle.
Then Sundaraka, having emerged from the cow-pen in the morning, went to the marketplace with some radishes he had taken, seeking money for his meal.
While he was selling it there, the Mālava royal servants, seeing that it was produced in their own country, seized the radishes without paying any price.
Then, while making a commotion, he was bound by his friends who pursued him, and they led him before the king, crying out, "He is a thrower of stone-blowing clubs!"
"Why have you brought radishes here from Mālava to sell in Kānyakubja?"—when questioned by us thus, he did not speak.
"Rather, he strikes back with stones," said those rogues to the king; then the king asked about that marvel, and his friends replied:
"O King, if he is raised up to the palace together with us, then this curiosity will speak its whole secret; it cannot be otherwise."
"So be it," said the king; and while Sundaraka looked on, the palace, by means of a mantra, immediately flew up into the sky along with him.
Accompanied by his friend, he went there and reached Prayāga in due course; being exhausted, he saw a certain king bathing there.
Having stabilized the palace there and leaped down into the Ganges, he was gazed upon with wonder by everyone as he approached that king.
"Who are you, and for what purpose have you descended from the sky? Tell us. Thus questioned by the king who bowed before him, Sundaraka spoke as follows.
"I am a Gaṇa named Murajaka belonging to the god Dhūrjaṭi; by his command, I have come into your presence seeking human enjoyment."
Having heard that and suspecting it to be true, the king gave him a city abounding in crops, filled with jewels, together with its women and all its appurtenances.
Then, having entered that city and flown up into the sky with his followers, Sundaraka wandered there for a long time at his own will, free from all want.
Lying upon a golden couch, fanned with yak-tail whisks, and attended by excellent women, he experienced the bliss of Indra.
Then once, a certain perfected being (siddha) who traveled through the sky, having become his friend, gave him a mantra for descending from the heavens.
Having thus obtained the mantra for descent, Sundaraka then went and descended from the path of the sky into his own country, Kānyakubja.
Having learned that the city, filled with abundant splendor, had descended from the sky, the king himself went there out of curiosity.
Then, having been fully questioned by the king who was himself aware of the proper time, he, knowing the right moment, related his entire history as it had been brought about by Kālarātri.
Then the lord of the earth summoned Kālarātri and questioned her; she, being fearless, confessed her entire misconduct.
When the king was enraged and prepared to cut off her ears, she vanished even while everyone was looking on, despite having been seized.
Then his residence in his own kingdom was forbidden by the king; honored by him, Sundaraka once again took to the sky.
Having spoken thus to her husband, King Ādityaprabha, Queen Kuvalayāvalī addressed him once more.
"O King, such are the accomplishments of the *ḍākinī* mantras; and this event, which occurred in my father's country, is renowned everywhere."
"I am a disciple of Kālarātri," and so forth was described by me; however, because of my devotion to my husband, my spiritual attainment is even greater than that.
And today you saw me, having performed worship for the sake of your welfare; I was prepared to draw forth a man by means of a mantra as an offering.
Therefore, enter now into this system of ours as well, and place your foot upon the heads of those kings who have been conquered through the yoga of supernatural powers.
Having heard that, the king said, "Where is the eating of human flesh in the way of the ḍākinīs, and where is kingship? and thus he forbade it.
When the queen was prepared to give up her life, he consented to that; for how can those who are dragged away by sense-objects remain upon the path of the righteous?
Then, having led him into the mandala previously worshipped, she spoke these words to the king, who had now taken his vow:
"This Brahmin named Phalabhūti who stands here near you was intended by me to be drawn here for the purpose of being offered as a sacrifice."
And since attracting [him] would be laborious, it would be better to appoint some cook here who, while managing him, might himself kill and even cook him.

And one should not feel aversion, because by consuming the meat and the sacrificial offering (*bali*) from that [victim], once the worship is completed, full accomplishment (*siddhi*) shall be attained; for he is indeed the most excellent.
Thus addressed by his beloved, the king, though fearful of sin, accepted that once again; alas, fie upon the wretched subservience to women!
Then, having summoned the cook named Sāhasika, they gained his trust, initiated him, and the husband and wife spoke together.
"Today the king, accompanied by the queen, shall eat; therefore, act with haste! If anyone approaches you to say something regarding the meal, you must strike him down."
"And with their flesh, you should prepare a delicious meal for the two of us in private this morning. Having been thus instructed by the cook, he replied, "So be it," and went home.
In the morning, when Phalabhūti had arrived, the king said to him: "Go and speak to the daring cook in the kitchen."
"Today the king, accompanied by the queen, will eat delicious food; therefore, prepare the finest meal with all haste."
When Phalabhūti had thus departed and gone outside, a prince named Candraprabha approached him and spoke these words.
"By means of this gold, have earrings made for me this very day, exactly as those you previously had made for my noble father."
Thus addressed by the prince, Phalabhūti, having complied with his request, was dispatched at that very moment and departed for the sake of the two earrings.
The prince also went at his own will to the kitchen alone, having taken that royal command as told by Phalabhūti.
There, that cook, firm in his resolve and acting with reckless courage, immediately slew the prince with a knife, carrying out the royal command as it had been spoken.
Having performed their worship, the queen and the king ate the meal prepared with his flesh, unaware of the true reality of the matter.
Having passed that night with remorse, the king saw Phalabhūti approaching him in the morning with the earrings in his hand.
Bewildered by the sight of the earrings, he questioned him at that very moment; having had his own story related by him, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Crying out "Alas, my son! he lamented, blaming both his wife and himself; and when questioned by his ministers, he described everything exactly as it had happened.
And Phalabhūti replied: "It has been said that he who performs good deeds shall obtain good fortune, and he who performs evil deeds shall obtain misfortune."
Like a ball struck against a wall, repeatedly bouncing back, a fault intended for another usually falls upon oneself.
Because we, following evil conduct and desiring to commit the murder of a Brahmin, have committed the slaughter of our own sons and obtained the eating of their flesh.
Having spoken thus and having enlightened his own ministers who were hanging their heads in shame, he consecrated that very Phalabhūti in his own kingdom.
Having bestowed his gifts, the king, being childless, entered the fire along with his wife for the purification of his sins, even though he was already consumed by the fire of remorse.
And Phalabhūti, having obtained that kingdom, ruled the earth; thus, whether good or evil, what one has done is attributed to oneself.
Having thus related this story in the presence of the Lord of Vatsa, Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke again to that king.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, even though you practice virtue, that Brahmadatta might act perversely toward you once he has conquered you; if that should happen, you alone must slay him.
Having been addressed thus by his chief minister, the Lord of Vatsa welcomed those words, rose up, and performed his daily duties.
And on another day, having successfully completed his conquest of all directions, that accomplished king set out from Lāvāṇaka toward his own city, Kauśāmbī.
In due course, the lord of the earth, accompanied by his retinue, reached the city, which seemed to be dancing with its arms of banners uplifted as if out of festive joy.
And he entered that forest of blue-lotus eyes of the city women, creating at every step the agitation of a rising gale.
Being sung of by wandering bards, being praised by panegyrists, and being saluted by kings, the monarch returned to his palace.

Then, having established his command over all the kings of the lands who had bowed in submission, that King Vatsa forcibly ascended that ancestral lion-throne which he had previously recovered from its hidden store.

At that moment, the sky was filled with the echoes of loud and steady musical instruments struck for the auspicious occasion, as if by shouts of "Well done! from the world-protectors, who had been gratified by his chief minister, coming from every direction.

Then, having distributed in various ways the wealth acquired from his conquest of the earth among the twice-born, he who was free from greed held a great festival and fulfilled the purpose of the circle of kings and his own ministers.

When that king rained down upon the fields in accordance with their needs, the city resounded with the thundering of clouds and the beating of drums; anticipating the future harvest of abundant grain, the people likewise held festivals in every house within that city.

Having thus conquered the world, that virtuous King of Vatsa, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to Rumaṇvat and Augandharāyaṇa, remained there as he pleased with Vāsavadattā together with Padmāvatī.

Standing between those two queens as if between Fame and Fortune, he was praised by excellent bards; he enjoyed the rising of the moon, white with his own glory, and constantly drank the *sīdhu* liquor, which was like the majesty of his enemies.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the Kathāsaritsāgara, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa; and here concludes this third book, the Lāvāṇaka. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa; the fourth book, named "The Birth of Naravāhanadatta. This nectar of stories, it is said, formerly emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth when churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Mountain King. Those who forcibly swallow it, having attained prosperity through the removal of obstacles, bear upon this earth the status of gods by the grace of Bhava.

The first wave: Victorious is the Conqueror of Obstacles, who, by the forceful stroke of his ear-flaps, split asunder the principal mountain ranges, as if pointing out the path to the supernatural powers (siddhis).
Then King Udayana, the lord of Vatsa, residing in Kauśāmbī, enjoyed the conquered earth under his single umbrella.
Having entrusted the burden of governance to Yaugandharāyaṇa along with Rumaṇvat, he became happy, finding his sole delight in pleasure and accompanied by Vasantaka.
Playing the lute himself, accompanied by Queen Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī, he enjoyed a musical performance.
While there was no distinction between the goddess’s sweet, low-pitched song and the sound of her lute, the trembling of her thumb during playing indicated the difference.
And on the roof of his palace, white with moonlight as if with his own fame, he drank wine dripping from a stream, as if it were the intoxication of his enemies.
In private, beautiful women brought him honey, glowing with passion, from golden jars as if it were the water for his consecration to the kingdom of Love.
He offered the liquor, which was slightly reddish, delicious, and clear, with his face shimmering within it, between the two of them like his own heart.
Even though envy and anger had vanished from their faces, those two queens, with their arching brows and passionate countenances, could not find satiety in gazing upon him.
His drinking hall, with its many chalices of honey and crystal, shone like a lotus pond filled with white lotuses reddened by the morning sun.
And in between, a hunter met him—dark as a *palāśa* leaf, clad in a tunic, and equipped with his bow and arrows—he entered the deer-forest which resembled himself.
With his arrows, he struck down the swarms of boars muddied by the mire, just as the sun strikes away masses of darkness with its dense rays.
As he rushed forth, the terrified black antelopes fled; they appeared like the sidelong glances of the quarters of the sky, which had previously been overcome by him.
The earth, reddened by the blood of the slain buffalo, appeared like a forest lotus-pond that had fled from the falling of his horns to seek refuge with him.
He rejoiced even at the lions, whose lives had departed with internal roars as they were impaled by spears falling from their gaping mouths.
In that forest, there were dogs in the pits and snares along his paths; such was the preparation for the passion of the hunt, perfected by his own weapons alone.
Once, while the king was thus engaged in the enjoyment of pleasures and had taken his seat in the assembly hall, the sage Nārada approached him.
Forming a halo with the radiance of his own body, he was an ornament of heaven, like the sun descended out of affection for the noble race of the luminous ones.
Having been offered hospitality by that king who bowed repeatedly before him, he stayed for a moment and, being pleased, addressed the monarch.
Listen, O Prince of Vatsa, as I tell you this in brief: there was once a king named Pāṇḍu, who was your great-grandfather.
He, of great majesty, had exactly two wives worthy of him: one was Kuntī and the second was named Mādrī.
Having conquered this earth girt by the oceans, that Pāṇḍu, being happy, once went to the forest, addicted to the vice of hunting.
There, having released his arrow, he struck the sage named Kindama together with his wife while they were engaged in sexual union, as he had assumed the form of a deer.
That sage, casting off his deer-form, cursed the dejected Pāṇḍu—who had dropped his bow—with his life-breaths still lingering in his throat.
"Since I have been struck down by you while standing at ease and without suspicion, therefore your death shall come like mine at the time of sexual union with your wife."

Thus, having received this curse from the seer and fearing its consequences, Pāṇḍu abandoned all desire for sensual enjoyments; accompanied by his two wives, he dwelt in a peaceful forest of asceticism.
Although staying there, he was once impelled by that curse and suddenly desired his beloved Mādrī, and he met his death.
Thus, O King, this so-called hunting is a source of negligence for rulers; for by it even those various other kings have been destroyed, like deer.
With a terrible roar, intent on flesh, harsh, with smoke-colored hair standing erect, and teeth like spears—how indeed could she, like a Rākṣasī, bring about auspiciousness?
Therefore, abandon this fruitless exertion and the passion for hunting; for those who kill wild animals and those who ride them, the danger to life is equal.
Out of affection for you and your ancestors, you are dear to me and a vessel of auspiciousness; now hear how your son shall become a portion of Kāma.
Having been honored with hymns of praise by Rati for the sake of restoring the limbs of the Ancient One who was without limbs, Śiva, being pleased, spoke these words in brief to her in private.
"Descending to earth with a portion of himself and worshipping me personally, this Gaurī, desiring a son, shall bring forth Kāma."
Therefore, O lord of men, this queen Vāsavadattā was born as the daughter of Caṇḍamahāsena and has become your consort.
Therefore, having propitiated Śambhu, she will give birth to a son who is a portion of Kāma, who shall become the universal monarch (cakravartin) of all the Vidyādharas.
When the king had spoken thus with words that were not honored, the seer Nārada returned the earth that had been offered to him and vanished from sight.
When he had departed, the King of Vatsa spent that day together with Vāsavadattā, who was filled with the desire for a son and preoccupied with thoughts concerning him.
On another day, the eminent doorkeeper named Nityodita approached the Lord of Vatsa as he sat in the assembly hall and addressed him.
O Great King, a certain destitute Brahmin woman accompanied by two young children stood at the gate, longing for a sight of Your Majesty.
As soon as she heard that, the king granted her permission to enter; thereupon, that Brahmin woman, emaciated, pale, and greyish, entered within.
Distressed as if by a tattered garment, she bore both her young sons in her arms, who resembled sorrow and wretchedness personified.
Having performed the appropriate salutation, she addressed the king: "I am a Brahmin woman born of noble family, yet I have fallen into such a miserable state."
"By fate, these two sons were born to me simultaneously; therefore, O Lord, I have no breast milk for them without food."
Therefore, O Protector who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, I, wretched as I am, have now arrived at the Lord as my refuge; he is my authority and my master.
Having heard this, the compassionate king commanded his doorkeeper: "Take her and present her to Queen Vāsavadattā."
And then, led by that very warder as if by her own auspicious karma acting as a precursor, she was brought into the presence of the queen.
Having learned from the doorkeeper that she had been sent by the king, Queen Vāsavadattā placed even greater trust in the Brahmin woman.
Seeing her wretched state with her offspring born as twins, she reflected: "Aha! This conduct of the Lord of Creatures is somehow singularly perverse."
"Alas, what stinginess regarding a real thing! Alas, what devotion to a non-existent thing! Even now not a single son has been born to me; yet in this birth, these twins have appeared."
Reflecting thus, the queen, desiring to bathe, gave instructions to the Brahmin woman’s maidservants regarding her bathing and other preparations.
Having been embraced, given garments, and fed delicious food by them, that Brahmin woman, like parched earth sprinkled with water, recovered her breath.
Once she was comforted by skillful conversation and inquiries, she was addressed after a short while by Queen Vāsavadattā.
"O Brahmin lady, let some story be told by you to us. Having heard that, she said, "So be it," and proceeded to tell a tale.
Long ago, there was a certain ordinary king named Jayadatta, and a son named Devadatta was born to him.
Then, desiring to arrange the marriage of his son who had reached the prime of youth, that wise king reflected as follows.
Royal fortune is exceedingly fickle, like a courtesan to be enjoyed by the powerful; but the prosperity of merchants is stable and exclusive, like a woman of good family.
Therefore, I shall arrange my son's marriage with the daughter of a merchant, so that in this kingdom which has many claimants, no misfortune shall befall him.
Having thus resolved, for the sake of his son, that king requested the hand of the daughter of the merchant Vasudatta from Pāṭaliputra.
Vasudatta, desiring a praiseworthy alliance, gave his daughter to that prince, even though he was in a distant foreign land.
And he likewise filled his son-in-law with jewels, such that his great respect for him surpassed even his respect for his own father's wealth.
Then King Jayadatta lived happily together with his son, who was accompanied by the daughter of the wealthy merchant whom he had obtained.
Once, having arrived there at his relative's house with longing, that merchant Vasudatta led his daughter back to his own home.
Then, suddenly, that King Jayadatta departed for heaven; his kinsmen rose up and took possession of his kingdom.
Out of fear of him, his son Devadatta was led away at night by his own mother to another country, unobserved.
Thereupon, her mind distressed with grief, she said to that prince: "Our lord is a Cakravartin king, the sovereign of the eastern quarter."
"Go to his side, my child; he will secure the kingdom for you. When she had spoken thus, the prince then replied to his mother:
"Who will think much of me when I have gone there without any retinue? Having heard that, his mother spoke to him once again in this way:
Having gone to your father-in-law's house and obtained wealth from there, go to the presence of the universal monarch after making preparations.
Thus urged by his mother, the prince, though filled with shame, set out in due course and reached his father-in-law’s house in the evening.
Deprived of his father and having lost his fortune, he was unable to enter there at an improper time during the night, both out of fear that his tears might be noticed and out of shame.
Then, standing nearby outside the sacrificial hall, he suddenly beheld a woman descending by means of a rope from her father-in-law's house at night.
And in an instant, recognizing his own wife—who was radiant with the luster of jewels—to be like a meteor fallen from the clouds, he was consumed by grief.
Seeing him pale and emaciated, she did not recognize him and asked, "Who are you? Hearing that, he replied, "I am a traveler."
Then that merchant’s daughter entered the interior of the sacrificial hall, and the prince followed her as well, watching her secretly.
There she approached a certain man, and that man, thinking "you have come after a long time," struck her with kicks of his feet.
Then that wicked woman, her passion redoubled, propitiated him and remained there at his side with him as she pleased.
Having seen that, the wise prince reflected: "This is not the time for my anger; indeed, another task remains to be accomplished."
And how could this treatise spread among these two wretched ones—this woman of mine, who is fit for a wife, or this beast of a king, who is fit for an enemy?
What business has this wicked woman with this? For it is the work of that ill-disposed one who rains down misery, skilled in the sport of observing my fortitude.
She belongs to an incomparable family; what offense has she committed? How could a female crow, having abandoned her mate, take pleasure in a cuckoo?

Reflecting thus, he disregarded his wife who was in love with another; for in the minds of the virtuous, when desiring to conquer a great teacher, how insignificant is a woman, even one as small as a blade of grass?
And at that moment, due to the force of her passion, a beautiful ornament rich with pearls reportedly fell from the ear of that merchant’s daughter.
And she did not see that at all; then, at the end of the amorous encounter, she quickly took leave of her lover and went back home the way she had come.
When that secret lover had also departed quickly for some place, the prince saw those jeweled ornaments and took them.
With its mass of crest-jewels quivering, it was like a hand-lamp bestowed by the Creator to dispel the darkness of delusion while searching for lost fortune.
Beholding that object of great value, the prince departed at that very moment; having accomplished his purpose, he then went from there to Kānyakubja.
Having given that ornament there as a ransom for his release, he purchased elephants and horses with a hundred thousand gold pieces and went into the presence of the universal monarch.
Having arrived together with the forces provided by him and having slain his enemies in battle, the virtuous prince regained his paternal kingdom and was joyfully welcomed by his mother.
Having released that ornament from its binding, she sent it unhesitatingly to her father-in-law to reveal that secret.
Her father-in-law, seeing that very earring which was his daughter’s ear-ornament, approached it as it had come and, being bewildered, showed it to her.
She too, seeing that [letter] as if it were her own conduct fallen away from its former state, and realizing it had been sent by her husband, remembered everything with great agitation.
"This fell before me that night inside the sacrificial hall, in which I stood and saw some traveler."
Therefore, he has surely come here as my husband, desiring to test my character; but I did not recognize him, and thus this ornament was obtained by me.
As she was thinking thus, the merchant’s daughter’s heart, distressed by the manifestation of her wicked resolve, broke in its terror.
Then, having skillfully questioned a maidservant who knew her secret, that merchant father understood the truth and abandoned his grief for her.
Then the prince, having attained the kingdom and having won as his wife the daughter of a universal monarch—acquired through his virtues—enjoyed another form of prosperity.
Thus, in such daring acts, the heart of women is as hard as a diamond; yet that very same heart becomes as delicate as a flower-petal when struck by the onset of fear and agitation.
But some among them, born of noble lineage like pearls, being women of virtuous conduct and pure hearts, attain the status of ornaments upon the earth.
And royal fortune, like a doe, is ever thus prone to flight; yet some wise men know how to bind her with the tether of fortitude.
Therefore, even in times of adversity, those who desire prosperity must not abandon their integrity; this very principle applies here, and my own experience serves as the illustration in this matter.
"O Queen, that my conduct was preserved even in this calamity has indeed borne fruit for me through the attainment of the auspicious sight of you."
Having heard this story from the mouth of that Brahmin woman at that very moment, Queen Vāsavadattā reflected with respect.
This Brāhmaṇī is surely of noble birth; for her graceful bearing and the maturity of her speech testify to her high character.
"Her proficiency in entering the royal assembly is for this very reason"; having reflected thus, the queen spoke again to that Brahmin woman:
"To whom do you belong as a wife, or what is your history? Tell me. Having heard that, the Brahmin woman then proceeded to speak further.
O Queen, there was once a certain Brahmin in Mālava named Agnidatta, who was the abode of both Śrī and Sarasvatī, and who personally bestowed his wealth upon those who sought it.
And to him were born in due course two sons suited to himself: the elder was named Śaṅkaradatta, and the other was called Śāntikara by name.
O illustrious lady, while those two were thus engaged, Śāntikara, seeking knowledge, suddenly departed from his father's house even as a boy and went away somewhere.
And his second brother, the elder, married me—the daughter of Yajñadatta, whose wealth was acquired for the purpose of performing sacrifices.
In time, that father of my husband, named Agnidatta, being old, departed for the other world, followed by his own wife.
And because my husband had set out for a sacred pilgrimage site, he abandoned me while I was pregnant; having gone to the bank of the Sarasvatī, blinded by grief, he cast off his body.
When this account had been told, my companions arrived; I was able to obtain leave from my own people to follow along with them, even while pregnant.
Then, while I was still reeling with fresh grief, bandits suddenly arrived and plundered our entire estate, that agrahāra where we lived.
At that very moment, out of fear of losing my virtue, I fled from there with three Brahmin women, clutching a small piece of cloth to our bodies.
Having gone to a distant land after the destruction of my country, I remained there for about a month with him, subsisting on difficult labor.
Having heard from the world that the Lord of Vatsa was a refuge for the helpless, I have therefore come here with my Brahmin wife, carrying virtue alone as our provision for the journey.
Having arrived, I have given birth to both sons simultaneously, even while these three Brahmin women, my friends, were standing by.
Sorrow, exile, poverty, and even this double birth—alas, the Creator has flung wide open the door to my calamities!
"Therefore, there is no way for these two children to grow up [without me]; having reflected thus, she cast aside shame, which is the ornament of women.
Having entered the assembly, I entreated the King of Vatsa: "Who is able to endure the sight of the suffering of a woman whose child has met with calamity?"
And by his command, I have reached the vicinity of your feet; my calamities have ceased, as if repelled at the very threshold.
Such is my story; I am also named Piṅgalikā, because from childhood my two eyes have been turned tawny by the smoke from the fire-rituals.
But that husband of mine, O Goddess, who brings peace, has gone abroad; even now it is not known in which country he dwells.
Having been thus addressed, the queen, perceiving that she was of noble birth from her account of herself, reflected with affection upon this Brahmin woman and spoke as follows.
"Here stands our family priest named Śāntikara; I know him to be a foreigner, and he shall become your husband."
Having spoken thus and passed that night with the eager Brāhmaṇī, the queen summoned Śāntikara in the morning and asked about his lineage.
And to him who had thus explained the connection, she, having reached a firm conviction, showed that Brahmin woman, saying, "This is your sister."
And once full comprehension had arisen, he, having understood the destruction of his kinsmen, then led that Brahmin woman, his brother’s wife, to his home.
Having there lamented for his parents and his brother as was appropriate, he comforted her as she sat with her two young children.
Queen Vāsavadattā also appointed those two young sons of hers as the future domestic priests for her own son.
Of those two, the elder was named Śāntisoma and the other Vaiśvānara; they were given by that very goddess, who bestowed upon them abundant prosperity.
For this world, which is like a blind man being led by his own past actions acting as guides toward the ground of its fruit, one's own human effort serves merely as the instrumental cause.
Having arrived there and attained their respective fortunes, they all gathered together: those two boys, their mother, and that Śāntikara.
Then, as the days passed, on one occasion he encountered a female potter who had arrived with her five sons carrying earthenware bowls.
Having seen a certain woman in her own palace, that Brahmin lady Piṅgalikā spoke to Vāsavadattā, the queen, who was standing by her side.
"O friend, let even one of her five sons be seen by me today; such a vessel of merit as he is, yet there is no one like me to behold him."
Then Piṅgalikā said: "O Queen, this progeny, being full of sin, arises for the sake of suffering; it is most prevalent among the poor."
Whoever is born among those such as you would surely be someone most excellent; therefore, enough with this haste—you shall obtain a son worthy of yourself before long.
Thus addressed by Piṅgalikā, Vāsavadattā, though eager for the birth of her son, became one whose mind was overcome with anxiety regarding him.
Nārada told you that a son is to be obtained through the propitiation of the Lord of the Mountains; therefore, O Goddess, that Śiva, the bestower of boons, must certainly be propitiated by us here.
Thus addressed by the King of Vatsa, who had arrived at that very moment, the queen—having discerned his intention—immediately made her resolve to undertake the vow.
When she had undertaken that vow, the king also, together with his ministers and his entire kingdom, performed the vow for the propitiation of Śaṅkara.
Then, after the couple had fasted for three nights, that Lord, manifesting his grace, personally commanded them in a dream.
Arise! That portion of your desire shall be born as your son, who, by my grace, will become the lord of the Vidyādharas.

Having uttered these words, as the moon-crested Lord suddenly vanished, the couple awoke; having swiftly obtained the boon, they, their purpose fulfilled, experienced a joy that was entirely unfeigned.

Then, having risen at dawn and attended to the affairs of state, the queen and the king—satisfied by the nectar-like essence of recounting that dream—along with their kinsmen and servants, celebrated with great festivity as they performed the breaking of their fast.
After the lapse of a few days, a certain man with matted hair appeared in Queen Vāsavadattā's dream and, approaching her, gave her a fruit.

Then the Lord of Vatsa, having been delighted by her who had clearly related such a dream and being congratulated by his ministers, reflected and considered that the wish-granting son, bestowed by the moon-crested Lord Śiva, was no longer far off.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Naravāhanadatta-janana-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave. Now, a pregnancy that was a festival for the heart of the Lord of Vatsa arose for Vāsavadattā before long, radiant as the descent of a portion of Kāma himself.
With her face, which had trembling eyes and a slightly pale luster, she shone like the moon accompanied by the love of Kāma residing within its womb.
As she sat there, her two reflections shone on the sides of the jeweled couch, as if Rati and Prīti had arrived out of love for their husband.
Her friends, who grant all desires, attended upon her like personified sciences come to serve the womb of the future lord of the Vidyādharas.
Then she bore two breasts, dark-faced with their tips like fresh blue sprouts, which were like two jars for the consecration of her son in the womb.
In the center of the palace, she shone as she lay upon a comfortable bed, graced by a jeweled floor that was clear, sparkling, and possessed of a true luster.
It was as if it were being attended from all sides by heaps of jewels that had approached, their waters trembling with the fear of being trodden upon by the sons of Bhavitatman.
In the center of her celestial palace, an image formed of jewels shone like the splendor of the Vidyādharas come through the sky to offer salutation.
And she became pregnant during conversations concerning the foremost practitioners who were intent on the accomplishment of mantras, which arose as incidental topics.
In a dream, excellent Vidyādhara women, engaged in melodious song, attended upon her as she had ascended into the lap of the sky.
Having awakened, she longed to experience that very thing directly: the playful sport of roaming through the sky and the wonder of beholding the surface of the earth.
And Yaugandharāyaṇa fulfilled that pregnancy-longing of the queen by means of the employment of mechanical devices, spells, magic illusions, and other such arts.
And she remained there in the sky, employing various magical feats that inspired wonder in the women of the city with their long-lashed eyes.
Once, while she was staying at her dwelling, there arose in her heart a curiosity to hear the noble tales of the Vidyādharas.
Then, requested by the queen, Yaugandharāyaṇa related this story there while everyone was listening.
There is the Himavat, the king of mountains, who is the father of Ambikā; he is not only the preceptor of all mountains, but also of the Lord of Gaurī.
And on that great mountain, the abode of the Vidyādharas, the king named Jīmūtaketu, the lord of the Vidyādharas, dwelt.
In his house there was a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) descended through his paternal lineage, renowned by its appropriate name as the "Bestower of Desires."
And once, that King Jīmūtaketu approached him and requested of that celestial being, the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), in the garden.
"From you, we always obtain everything we desire; therefore, O Lord, grant me, who am childless, a son endowed with all virtues."
Then the wish-fulfilling tree said, "O King, a son shall be born to you who remembers his past lives, a hero among givers, and a benefactor to all beings."
Having heard that, the king was filled with joy; he bowed to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, went [to his palace], and by reporting that [news], he gladdened his queen.
Then, not long after that, a son was born to the king, and his father gave him the name Jīmūtavāhana.
Then, together with his innate compassion for all living beings, that Great Being Jīmūtavāhana grew in stature.
In due course, while established in the position of crown prince, he who was compassionate toward the world addressed his father in private, having propitiated him with his service.

I know, dear father, that all things in this world are momentary and subject to destruction; yet the one thing that remains constant for the great is their stainless fame, enduring until the end of the kalpa.
If that very thing arising from the act of helping others is indeed so, alas! what else could be the wealth of the noble, which is dearer to them than their own lives?
And prosperity, like lightning, causes distress to the eyes of the world; being fickle, it vanishes somewhere or other, providing no benefit to others.
If this wish-fulfilling tree that we possess were to be employed for the sake of others, then its fruit would truly be attained.
Therefore, I shall act here in such a way that, through his prosperities, this entire assembly of seekers may no longer remain destitute.
Having thus informed his father and obtained his permission, Jīmūtavāhana went to that wish-fulfilling tree and spoke to it.
O Lord, you are the constant bestower of our desired fruits; therefore, fulfill this one wish of mine today.
"O friend, make this entire earth free from poverty; may it be well with you, for you have been bestowed upon the world that seeks wealth."
Thus addressed by that steadfast one, the wish-fulfilling tree rained down abundant gold upon the earth, and all the subjects rejoiced.
Who else but Jīmūtavāhana—a compassionate portion of a Bodhisattva—could, being so skillful, even turn the wish-fulfilling tree itself over to the service of supplicants?
Thus, as affection arose toward him even in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, the pure fame of Jīmūtavāhana spread far and wide.
Then, seeing that the kingdom of Jīmūtaketu had become firmly rooted in the fame of his son, his kinsmen, filled with envy, underwent a transformation of character.
And they considered that abode, which possessed excellent wish-fulfilling trees suited for giving, as indeed easy to conquer because of its lack of splendor.

Then, while they had assembled and resolved upon battle, the steadfast Jīmūtavāhana spoke thus to his father: [-yuktāspadaṃ em. for -muktāspadaṃ] Then, while they had assembled and resolved upon battle, the steadfast Jīmūtavāhana spoke thus to his father:
Just as this very body is like a bubble on the water, so too are riches as flickering as a lamp in a gale; for whose sake are they?
Who that is wise would desire those [pleasures] which involve the crushing of others? Therefore, I must certainly not fight with my kinsmen.
"Having abandoned the kingdom, I must go from here to some forest; let these wretched ones remain, lest there be the destruction of my own lineage."
When Jīmūtavāhana had spoken thus, his father Jīmūtaketu, having likewise made up his mind, replied to him in this way.
I too must go, my son; for what longing can I, an old man, have for a kingdom that has been cast aside by you, a youth, out of compassion as if it were a blade of grass?
When his father had spoken thus, Jīmūtavāhana, together with his wife, said "So be it" and went to Mount Malaya.
There, in that hermitage where perfected beings dwell and where mountain streams flow covered with sandalwood trees, he remained devoted to the service of his father.
Then, the self-controlled son of Viśvāvasu, the king of the Siddhas, named Mittrāvasu, became his friend there.
And once, in a secluded place, the wise Jīmūtavāhana beheld his sister as a young maiden, his beloved from a former birth.
And at that moment, the mutual sight of those two youths was like a binding snare for the deer of their minds.
Then, on one occasion, Mitrāvasu, having approached Jīmūtavāhana—who is honored by the three worlds—suddenly and joyfully spoke to him.
"I have a younger sister named Malayavatī; I shall give her to you. Do not act contrary to my wish."
Upon hearing that, Jīmūtavāhana also said to him: "O Prince, she was my wife even in a previous birth."
And you were born right there as my second heart and dear friend; I am one who remembers former births, and I recollect all of that previous life.
When he had spoken thus, Mitrāvasu said to him at that time: "Tell me first this story of another birth, for I am indeed curious."
Having heard this from Mitrāvasu, the virtuous Jīmūtavāhana related this story of his previous birth to him.
Formerly, I was a Vidyādhara who traveled through the sky; once, I went along the path of the Himalayan peaks.
Then Hara, standing below there and playing with Gaurī, cursed me, saying, "Fall into a mortal womb," being enraged by my leaping over him.
Having obtained a Vidyādharī as your wife and having installed your son in your own position, you shall regain your memory of your former birth and again enter a Vidyādhara womb.
Having thus heard the end of the curse and spoken these words, Śarva vanished; and before long, I was born upon the earth into a family of merchants.
In the city named Valabhī, I grew up as the son of a very wealthy merchant, known by the name Vasudatta.
In due time, having reached my youth and being provided with a retinue by my father, I went to another island for the sake of trade by his command.
Then, as I was coming from the forest, bandits fell upon me; having bound me and stripped me of my wealth, they led me to their own village, to the temple of Caṇḍikā.
With its terrible, long, and flickering banner of red cloth, it was like the tongue of Death as he sought to devour the lives of living beings.
There, I was brought by them as an offering into the presence of their own lord, named Pulindakā, who was worshipping the Goddess.
Upon seeing me, even that Śabara became soft-hearted; his mind felt affection without cause, as if remembering a love from a previous birth.
Then, having released me from execution, that lord of the Śabaras desired to complete his ritual worship by means of the sacrifice of himself.
"Do not do so; I am pleased with you, ask me for a boon. Being thus addressed by a divine voice, he, filled with joy, spoke.
Since you are pleased, what other boon could there be? Nevertheless, I request this much: may I maintain friendship with this merchant even in another birth.
When Śāntā had spoken thus, "So be it," that Śabara then sent me to his own home, having provided me with special provisions.
When I had returned from exile and from the jaws of death, my father, having learned the news of what had transpired, held a great festival for me.
In due course, I saw that very lord of the Śabaras there, having been captured for plundering a caravan and brought before the king.
At that moment, having informed my father and petitioned the king, I released him from the penalty of execution for a hundred thousand gold pieces.
Having thus performed this act of returning the favor for the gift of his life, and having brought him home with affection, he honored him fully for a long time.
Then, having been sent off with due honor and having placed his heart—tender with affection—upon me, that lord of the Śabaras departed for his own village.
There, reflecting on how to offer a gift to me in return for my favor, he considered even a small amount of pearls, musk, and other such items to be at his disposal.
Then, with me as his companion, he set out for the Himalayas to slay elephants in order to obtain for my sake pearls of the highest excellence.
Wandering there, he reached a great lake with a temple situated on its shore, where he found delight with its lotuses, which were like friends full of affection for him.
Suspecting that wild elephants might come there for the purpose of drinking water, he remained concealed in a secluded spot with his bow, desiring to slay them.
Meanwhile, there [he saw] a maiden of wondrous form, mounted upon a lion, who had arrived to worship Hara at the edge of that lake.
He beheld her, like another daughter of the King of Snowy Mountains, remaining in the state of maidenhood and devoted to the service of Śambhu.
And having seen her, the Śabara was overcome with wonder and thought: "Who might this be? If she is a mortal woman, then how can she have a lion for a mount?"
"Now, how could that divine being be visible to those like me? Therefore, this is certainly the personified fruition of my former merits for my two eyes."
If I were to unite him with this friend, then I would have performed a truly extraordinary act of service for him in return.
"Therefore, I shall approach her for a moment to inquire about the boon,"—having reflected thus, that Śabara of mine approached her.
Meanwhile, having descended from the lion who was seated in the shade, a maiden approached and began to gather lotuses from the lake.
And seeing that Śabara who had approached her and bowed down, she delighted him with a welcome out of unprecedented affection for a guest.
"Who are you, and why have you come to this region so utterly inaccessible?"—to her who had thus questioned him, that Śabara replied.
I am the lord of the Śabaras, whose sole refuge is the feet of Bhavānī; I have come to this forest for the sake of obtaining pearls from the Mātaṅgas.
And now, O Goddess, having seen you, I have remembered my own life-giving friend, the illustrious Vasudatta, the son of a merchant chief.
For you, O beautiful one, with your form and youth, are like him—without equal in this entire world, a cascading stream of nectar for the eyes.
Blessed is that maiden in this world whose hand is taken by him—the treasury of friendship, generosity, compassion, and fortitude—as her marriage bracelet.
If this form of yours is not united with one such as yourself, then my pain is that the God of Love carries his bow in vain.
Thus, by the words of the lord of hunters, the maiden’s mind was instantly captivated, as if by the syllables of a mantra for enchanting with the god of love.
And, impelled by the god of love, she said to that Śabara: "Where is that friend of yours? Bring him here and show him to me."
Having heard that and said "So be it," the Śabara took leave of her at that very moment; considering his purpose accomplished, he departed from there in high spirits.
Having reached his own village and taking with him pearls, musk, and other such things—vast quantities that could only be carried by hundreds of porters—he then arrived at our house.
Honored by all there, he entered and presented that gift, worth many hundreds of thousands of gold pieces, to my father.
When this day had passed in festivities, he related to me in private that night the entire account of his seeing the maiden, from the very beginning.
Saying, "Come, let us go right there," that lord of the Śabaras took me, who was eager to go, and set out at his own will during the night.
And in the morning, having learned that I had gone somewhere with the Śabara chief, my father remained there, maintaining his composure out of confidence in his affection for me.
And I was gradually led by that swift Śabara, who had prepared the way, to the Snowy Mountain.
Having reached that lake at evening and bathed, both he and I, eating sweet fruits, spent that single night there in the forest.
It was strewn with flowers from the creepers, made beautiful by the songs of female bees, carrying auspicious fragrances, enchanting, and illuminated by the lamps of glowing medicinal herbs.
As we drank the water of that lake at night, the mountain forest became for us like the chamber of Indra for the sake of rest.
Then, on the following day, my mind—bearing a longing for each step and racing along that path—seemed as if it were coming out to meet me.
With her right eye, which had indicated her arrival and was now throbbing as if out of a desire to see him, that maiden came here.
And I beheld her, with beautiful eyebrows, seated upon the back of a maned lion, like a digit of the moon resting upon the lap of an autumnal cloud.
And as I gazed upon her, filled with shimmering wonder, longing, and trepidation, I know not how my heart turned at that moment.
Then, having descended from the lion and gathered flowers, that maiden bathed in the lake and worshipped Hara who was situated on its bank.
And at the conclusion of the worship, that Śabara friend of mine approached, prostrated himself, announced his identity, and spoke to her who was full of respect.
"O Goddess, that worthy suitor who is a friend to me has been brought by me; if you so desire, I shall show him to you this very moment."
Having heard that and being told, "Show her," the Śabara then came near, led me there, and presented me to her.
She too, casting a sidelong glance at me with eyes overflowing with affection, fell under the sway of a passion-filled infatuation and addressed that lord of the Śabaras.
"This friend of yours is not human; some god has surely arrived here at his will. For how could a mortal today have this form, unless it be for the sake of deceiving me?"
Having heard that, I spoke to her myself in order to convince her: "It is true, O beautiful one, that I am a mortal; why use a pretext toward a person so honest?"
For I am the son of a caravan leader named Mahādhana, a resident of Valabhī, who acquired his wealth through the grace of Maheśvara.
For while he was performing austerities with the moon-crested Lord in view for the sake of a son, the God, being pleased, commanded him thus in a dream:
"Arise! A certain great-souled son shall be born to you. This is a supreme secret; enough with further elaboration on this matter."
Having heard this, as he was awakening, in the course of time a son was born to him, known by the name Vasudatta.
And this lord of the Śabaras, a friend from my own choosing, was previously encountered by me while traveling to another land; he is now my sole kinsman in this time of distress.
When I had finished speaking, saying, "This is the summary of reality for me," the maiden then addressed me, her face bowed down with modesty.
This is true: today in a dream, Hara perceived me as having worshipped him, and being pleased, he indeed commanded, "In the morning, you shall obtain a husband."
"Therefore, you alone are my husband, and this brother of yours is my friend. Having gladdened me with these words, which were like nectar, she became silent.
Then, having consulted with her regarding the marriage according to the prescribed rites, I made the decision to go to my own home accompanied by my friends.
Then that beautiful woman, having summoned her mount, the lion, by her own signal, spoke to me: "O noble son, please mount here."
Then, followed by that friend, the Śabara, I mounted the lion and took my beloved onto its lap.
Then, having accomplished my purpose, I set out for my own home with my beloved, seated upon a lion, while that friend preceded us.
Subsisting on the flesh of deer pierced by his arrows, we all eventually reached the city of Valabhī.
Seeing me arrive there, mounted upon a lion together with my beloved, the people were filled with wonder; they went quickly and told it to my father.
He too, having come forward with joy as I descended from the king of beasts, saw me bowing at his feet and greeted me with wonder.
Beholding her, who was peerless and had performed the salutation at his feet, he could not contain himself with joy as he gazed upon his worthy wife.
Having led us into the temple and inquired about our circumstances, he celebrated a festival, praising the friendship of the Śabara chief.
Then, according to the instruction of the astrologer, on the following day, that excellent maiden was married by me, having assembled all my kinsmen.
And upon seeing that, my son-in-law’s mount, the lion, suddenly assumed the form of a man while everyone was looking on.
While all the people standing there were bewildered, wondering "What is this?", he—adorned with divine garments and ornaments—bowed and spoke to me thus:
"I am a Vidyādhara named Citrāṅgada, and this is my daughter, a maiden named Manovatī, who is dearer to me than my own life."
Constantly wandering through the forest with her always held upon my lap, I once reached the Ganges, whose banks abound with ascetic groves.
As I was passing through her midst out of fear of disturbing the ascetic, my flower garland fell by chance into that water.
Then, rising suddenly from within the water, the sage Nārada, enraged by her falling upon his back, cursed me.
"O wicked one, by this arrogance you shall become a lion; having gone to the Himalayas, you shall carry this daughter on your back."
And when this daughter of yours is married by a human being, you shall be liberated from this curse simply by the sight of him.
Thus cursed by the sage, I became a lioness and remained on the Himalayas, carrying this daughter of mine who was devoted to the worship of Hara.
Immediately thereafter, how this entire auspicious event was accomplished through the efforts of the Śabara chief is already known to you.
"I shall accomplish that; may it be well with you; this curse has been crossed by me. Having said this, he immediately flew up into the sky as a Vidyādhara.
Then, overcome with wonder at that, my father—along with his kinsmen and relatives rejoicing, delighted by this praiseworthy alliance—celebrated a great festival.
For who indeed would contemplate the conduct of sincere friends—those who are never satiated with helping their well-wishers, even at the cost of their own lives?
And thus, no one there indeed spoke with wonder, as they reflected again and again upon that noble deed of the Śabara chief.
The king, having learned that to be so, was exceedingly pleased with the noble-minded Śabarādhipati for his affection toward us.
And being pleased, my father immediately caused the entire kingdom of the forest to be granted to him, who presented me with an offering of jewels.
Then, having achieved my purpose through that wife Manovatī and that friend, the lord of the Śabaras, I remained there in happiness.
And that lord of the Śabaras, his passion for dwelling in his own country having been slackened, continued to reside mostly in our very houses.
In their mutual assistance, never weary at any time, that period of time passed for both of us, my friend and his.
And not long after, a son was born to me by Manovatī; he was like a festival for the hearts of an entire lineage that had been cast out.
Named Hiraṇyadatta, he gradually grew up; having completed his education, he was then duly married.
Having seen that and considering the fruit of his life to be fulfilled, my father, though old, went with his wife to the Bhāgīrathī to cast off his body.
Then, afflicted by grief for my father, I was somehow made to take heart by my kinsmen, and I resolved to bear the burden of my own household.
Then, on one hand, the sight of Manovatī’s charming face, and on the other, my meeting with the lord of the Śabaras, brought me delight.
Then those days of mine passed away, joyful with a virtuous son, delightful with a good wife, and happy with the company of friends.
Then, in the course of time, old age seized me by the chin as I had grown up, as if out of affection saying for my own benefit, "Son, why are you still in the house?"
Therefore, with sudden detachment having arisen within me, I appointed my own son to bear the burden of the household, while I myself desired the forest.
Then, together with my wife, I went to Mount Kālañjara along with the Śabara king, who had renounced his kingdom out of affection for me.
Having arrived there, I suddenly remembered my own birth as a Vidyādharī and that curse of Śiva, which had reached its end.
And at that very moment, desiring to cast off my human body, I told this to my wife Manovatī and to my friend, the lord of the Śabaras.
"May these two alone be my wife and friend even in another birth as I remember them," having said this, he placed Śaṅkara in his heart.
Then, having violently hurled myself down from that mountain slope, I cast off my body along with those two, my wife and friend.
Thus, born from that [merit], I am now named Jīmūtavāhana, born into this family of Vidyādharas, possessing the memory of my former birth.
And you, that very lord of the Śabaras, have been born again as Mitrāvasu, the son of King Viśvāvasu of the Siddhas, by the grace of the Three-eyed One.
"And that Vidyādharī friend of mine, Manovatī, my wife, has been reborn as your sister, Valayavatī by name."
"Thus, this former wife of mine is your sister, and you were my friend in the past; therefore, it is fitting that she should be married by me."
However, go first from here and inform my parents; once they have given their consent, this desire of yours will be accomplished.
Having heard this from Jīmūtavāhana, Mitrāvasu, with a joyful heart, went and related everything to his parents.
His words welcomed by them, he was then filled with joy and, approaching his parents, informed them of that very matter.
When those two were satisfied by the fulfillment of their desire, the crown prince quickly made preparations for his sister's wedding.
Then Jīmūtavāhana, preceded by the King of the Siddhas, duly took the hand of Malayavatī in marriage.
And there a festival took place, with celestial *cāraṇas* moving about in excitement, throngs of *siddhas* gathering together, and *vidyādharas* leaping about exultantly.
Then, having performed the marriage ceremony, Jīmūtavāhana remained on that Malaya mountain together with his bride, in great splendor.
And once, he went together with his brother-in-law, Mitrāvasu, to behold the forested shores of the ocean.
There he saw a young man, distressed and newly arrived, turning back his mother who was crying out, "Alas, my son!"
Having been abandoned by another man, like a soldier by his follower, he reached a certain broad and lofty rocky surface.
"Who are you? What do you seek? And why does your mother grieve for you? he asked him; thereupon, he too related the account to him.
In ancient times, Kaśyapa had two wives, Kadrū and Vinatā; it is said that in the course of a conversation, they engaged in a dispute with one another.
One woman drove the dark horses of the Sun, while the other drove the white ones; they entered into a wager here, staking their mutual status as slaves upon it.
Then Kadrū, seeking victory, at her own will caused the horses of the Sun to be fouled by the venomous hissing of her own sons, the Nāgas.
Having displayed such [omens], he made Vinatā a slave by means of a deception; for the intolerance of women toward others is indeed a painful thing.
Having learned of this, Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, then approached and, through conciliatory words, begged Kadrū for his mother's release from slavery.
Then the Nāgas, the sons of Kadrū, having reflected thus, said to him: "O Vainateya, the ocean of milk has begun to be churned by the gods."
Therefore, having gathered the nectar, bestow it upon us for each object; then take back your mother, for you are the foremost among the strong.
Having heard these words of the Nāgas and having gone to the Ocean of Milk, Garuḍa displayed his great prowess for the sake of the nectar.
Then, pleased by his valor, the god Hari himself, being gratified, commanded him: "I am pleased with you; choose some boon."
"May the nāgas become my food," he said; then Vainateya, provoked by his mother's servitude, chose this boon from Hari.
"So be it," said Hari; and he, having obtained the nectar through his own prowess, was then addressed by Śakra, who had now understood the true state of affairs.
"O Lord of Birds, you must act in such a way that this nectar is not consumed by the deluded serpents, so that I may recover it from them."
Having heard this and said "So be it," Tārkṣya, empowered by the boon of Viṣṇu, took the jar of nectar and approached the Nāgas.
To those fools who were terrified by the power of the boon, he said from the king's presence: "This nectar has been brought; let it be taken, setting aside my mother."
"If you have fear, I shall set this down upon your bed of darbha grass; having released my mother, I will depart, so accept the nectar from here."
When those nāgas replied, "So be it," he placed the jar of nectar upon a pure bed of kuśa grass, and they brought his mother there.
When Garuḍa had departed after thus making his mother free from slavery, the nāgas, being now without fear, began to take that ambrosia.
Then, having suddenly prostrated himself and bewildered them by his own power, Śakra seized that jar of nectar from the bed of Kuśa grass.
Then those dejected nāgas licked that bed of darbha grass, thinking, "Perhaps there might be some smear of nectar on this."

Thus, with their tongues split open, they attained the state of being "double-tongued" (serpents) in vain; for what else could be the fruit of those possessed by excessive greed, other than becoming an object of ridicule?
Then, by the boon of Hari, the enemy Tārkṣya began to devour those nāgas who had not yet tasted the nectar, swooping down upon them again and again.
And at its onset, the underworld became devoid of life among its serpents due to terror, with the fetuses of pregnant women miscarried and the snakes themselves destroyed.
Seeing that every day, Vāsuki, the lord of the serpents, considered the entire world of the nāgas to have perished in a single instant.
Then, having reflected upon him whose valor was irresistible, he immediately made this agreement with Garuḍa, preceded by a formal request.
"O Lord of Birds, for the sake of food, I shall send you one nāga each day from the mountains on the shore of the ocean."
"You must not enter the underworld as one who causes oppression; for by the destruction of the world of the Nāgas, your own self-interest will surely perish."
Having been addressed thus by Vāsuki, Garuḍa said, "So be it," and began to eat one serpent sent by him here every day.
In that manner, countless hooded serpents have perished here; I am the nāga named Śaṅkhacūḍa, and today is my turn.
Therefore, for the sake of being food for the Garuḍa, I have come to this execution stone, having fallen into a state of lamentation for my mother due to the command of the Naga king.
Having heard these words of Śaṅkhacūḍa, Jīmūtavāhana, distressed and filled with inner sorrow, spoke to him.
Alas! What an utterly spiritless kingship is that of Vāsuki, since his own subjects are being delivered into the prey of his enemy by his very own hand!
Why was his very self not first given by him to Garuḍa? What is this witness-hood to the destruction of one's own family, sought by a coward?
Even Tārkṣya commits some evil after being born from Kaśyapa; what kind of delusion is this, even among the great, for the sake of a mere body?
Therefore, I shall protect you from Garuḍa today alone; by the sacrifice of my own body, do not despair, my friend.
Having heard that, Śaṅkhacūḍa also spoke this to him with composure: "Peace be with you, O Great Being; do not speak thus again."
It is never fitting for a pearl to suffer damage for the sake of glass; nor shall I enter into a conversation that brings disgrace upon my family.
Having spoken thus and restrained Jīmūtavāhana, that virtuous man, perceiving that the time for Garuḍa’s arrival was approaching within a mere moment, [acted accordingly].
Śaṅkhacūḍa went there to the shore of the ocean at the time of his end to pay homage to the Lord of Umā, known as Gokarṇa.
When he had departed, Jīmūtavāhana, that treasury of compassion, realized that the opportunity to save him through the gift of his own self had been obtained.
Then, having quickly made it as if forgotten through his own ingenuity, he sent his own friend Mitrāvasu home under the pretext of some business.
And at that very moment, struck by the wind from the wings of the nearby Tārkṣya, that earth seemed to reel as if from the wonder of beholding that being.
Therefore, perceiving that the enemy of snakes was approaching, Jīmūtavāhana, out of compassion for others, ascended that execution stone.
In an instant, Garuḍa, covering the sky with his shadow, swooped down right there and, striking him with his beak, carried off that Great Being.
Having brought him—who was streaming with blood from his wounds and whose crest-jewel had been torn out—to the peak of the mountain, she began to devour him.
At that moment, a rain of flowers fell from the sky; seeing this, Tārkṣya was struck with wonder, thinking, "What indeed could this be?"
Meanwhile, Śaṅkhacūḍa, having bowed there, arrived at Gokarṇa and beheld the surface of the execution stone drenched by a shower of blood.
"Alas! Fie! Surely that great-souled one has given himself for my sake; where has he been taken by Tārkṣya? What will become of him in this very moment?"
"I shall search quickly; perhaps I may find him. Thinking thus, that virtuous man proceeded, following the trail of blood.
In the meantime, seeing Jīmūtavāhana so joyful, Garuḍa abandoned his meal and reflected with astonishment:
Is this someone else entirely, who, even while being devoured by me, does not perish, but instead, being steadfast, actually rejoices?
While Tārkṣya was thus reflecting within himself, Jīmūtavāhana, despite being in such a state, spoke to him for the sake of accomplishing his own desired goal.
"O King of Birds, there is indeed flesh and blood in my body; why have you suddenly desisted from eating, even though you are not yet satiated?"
Hearing that, overcome with wonder, the king of birds asked him: "O virtuous one, you are certainly not a nāga; tell me, who are you?"
"I am indeed a nāga; eat, and complete what you have begun. For why would an undertaking that has been started but not finished be abandoned by the wise?"
Even as Jīmūtavāhana was thus replying to him, Śaṅkhacūḍa arrived there from afar and spoke.
"No, no, Garuḍa! This is not a serpent; indeed, I am a serpent for you. Therefore, release him! What is this sudden delusion that has come upon you?"
Upon hearing that, the lord of birds became utterly bewildered, and Jīmūtavāhana fell into a state of despondency at the failure of his desire.
Then, having learned from the cries of the Vidyādhara lords lamenting to one another that he had been devoured through delusion, Garuḍa was filled with remorse.
"Alas! A sinful deed has befallen me, a cruel man; for indeed, those who follow the wrong path find it easy to commit sin."

But praiseworthy is this one Great-Souled One, who, by giving up his life for the sake of another, has cast the entire world beneath him, having brought it under the sole power of the delusion that "this is mine."
Then Jīmūtavāhana spoke to Garuḍa, who was thus reflecting on how to purify his sin and was about to enter the fire:
"O Lord of Birds, why are you despondent? If it is true that you fear sin, then from now on these serpents shall no longer be your food."

Furthermore, you must exercise vigilance regarding those enjoyers who have previously partaken [of the offerings]; for this is the remedy in this matter, while any other concern you have entertained is in vain.
Thus addressed by him who was compassionate toward all beings, Tārkṣya was delighted and accepted his words, saying "So be it," as if they were the command of a guru.
And he went swiftly from the sky to fetch the nectar in order to restore to life him whose limbs were wounded there, as well as the other serpents who remained as mere skeletons.
Then Jīmūtavāhana was personally approached and sprinkled with nectar by the goddess Gaurī, who was pleased by his devotion to her wife.
By that [sound], his limbs became even more radiant, along with the joyful sounds of the celestial drums of the gods.
When he had risen up healthy, Garuḍa then brought that nectar from the sky and rained it down here upon the entire shore of the ocean.
By that [means], all those serpents there rose up alive; and then that place shone, crowded with a vast multitude of snakes.
Then Velāvana was freed from the fear of Vainateya, like Pātāla when it beholds Jīmūtavāhana.
Then, perceiving that Jīmūtavāhana was resplendent with a body free from decay and with glory, his kinsmen rejoiced in him.
His wife, his kinsmen, and likewise his parents, all rejoiced; for who would not be gladdened by sorrow that turns into happiness?
Dismissed by him, Śaṅkhacūḍa departed for the netherworld (rasātala), while his fame, not being dismissed, wandered at will even through the three worlds.

Then, having approached Garuḍa, the preeminent among the Vidyādharas, all his own kinsmen—headed by the one named Mataṅga—who for a long time had suffered his hostility due to the grace of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, bowed down to him with fear while the throngs of gods prostrated themselves in joyful devotion.
Then, being entreated by those very same people, the virtuous Jīmūtavāhana departed from the Malaya mountain for his own abode on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain.
There, together with his parents, Mitrāvasu, and Malayavatī, the steadfast one enjoyed the status of a universal emperor of the Vidyādharas for a long time.
