Thus, for those whose deeds cause wonder in the hearts of the entire three worlds, successions of auspicious events always follow in their footsteps of their own accord.
Having heard this story from the mouth of Yaugandharāyaṇa, Queen Vāsavadattā rejoiced, her womb heavy with the longing of pregnancy.

Thereafter, by means of the constant instructions received from the deities who were filled with joy due to their connection with him, she spent that day staying near her own husband, listening to the story of her future son, the lord of the Vidyādharas.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Naravāhanadattajanana* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. Then, on another day, Vāsavadattā spoke thus in private to the King of Vatsa, who was seated nearby with his ministers:
"O noble son, from the moment this embryo was conceived by me, from that time forth, the intense anxiety for its protection has tormented my heart."
Today, while I was sleeping at night due to my anxiety over that matter, I believe I saw a certain man who had come to me in a dream.
He was adorned by a form with ash smeared upon its limbs, white, with the moon as its crest, with tawny matted hair, and holding a trident in its hand.
And he, approaching me as if with compassion, said: "Daughter, you should not entertain any anxiety whatsoever on account of the pregnancy."
"I shall protect this for you, for it has indeed been given to you by me alone; furthermore, listen as I speak another word to provide you with proof."

Tomorrow, a certain woman will come to you for the purpose of making a request; she will be accompanied by her five sons and surrounded by many kinsmen, and she will be dragging along her own husband while holding him firmly and reproaching him.
And that unchaste woman, wishing to have her husband killed through the power of her kinsmen, spoke all of that falsely.
And you, daughter, should first inform the King of Vatsa in such a way that he may be released from the clutches of that wicked woman.
When that great-souled one had thus instructed me and vanished, I suddenly awoke, and the night was bright with dawn.
When the goddess had spoken thus, all those present, who spoke of Śarva’s grace, were struck with wonder, their minds intent on seeking confirmation.

At that very moment, the chief doorkeeper, having entered there, suddenly addressed the King of Vatsa, who was compassionate toward the distressed: "Enter! he said. "The king of the Kirātas has arrived at the gate. "Let him enter," the king replied; and the doorkeeper immediately ushered him in. He was a man of dark complexion, with a body like a mountain, his eyes red as if from drinking blood, and his face terrifying with its curved fangs. As soon as he had entered, he spoke these words to the King of Vatsa: "O King, you have been summoned by the Lord of the Gods. Rise quickly and go to the world of Indra. Hearing this, the king was filled with great wonder and thought: "How could the Lord of the Gods summon me to his own world? What must be the reason for this? While the king was thus reflecting, the doorkeeper announced: "The queen has arrived. Then the king, having dismissed the Kirāta, went out to meet her. When she saw him, she cried out in distress: "Alas, my husband! Alas, my lord! And the king, seeing her weeping, embraced her and asked: "What is this, O Queen? Why do you grieve so? She replied: "My husband, I have been summoned by the Lord of the Gods. Go quickly and save me from this calamity. Hearing this, the king was overcome with grief and thought: "This is surely some illusion created by the gods; how could the Lord of the Gods summon me? While the king was thus reflecting, the doorkeeper announced: "The minister Śukanāsa has arrived. The king then dismissed the queen and went out to meet the minister. When he saw him, he embraced him and asked: "What is this, O Minister? Why have you come here at such an hour? He replied: "O King, I have been summoned by the Lord of the Gods. "O King, a certain woman, surrounded by her kinsmen and having brought her five sons with her, has arrived to make a representation, having dragged her own husband along helplessly."
Having heard that, the king, amazed by the correspondence with the queen's dream, commanded the doorkeeper: "Let her be brought in right here."
Queen Vāsavadattā also attained supreme joy, having gained the certainty of obtaining a virtuous son born from the truth of her dream.
Then, watched with curiosity by everyone facing toward the doorway, that woman entered together with her husband at the command of the doorkeeper.
Having entered with an air of assumed dejection and having offered salutations in due order, she then addressed the king, who was seated in assembly together with his queen.
Although he is my husband, he does not provide food, clothing, and so forth to me, who am innocent and without protector.
When she had spoken thus, her husband informed him: "O King, this woman, along with her kinsmen, speaks falsely; she desires my death."
"For everything has been given by me to her until the end of the year; my other relatives here, standing as neutral witnesses, are my proof in this matter."
When he had thus petitioned him, the king himself spoke: "In this matter, the goddess Śūlin has herself provided testimony through the queen's dream."
When the king had said, "In that case, why should this very woman, along with her kinsmen, be punished by the witnesses? the wise Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
Nevertheless, O King, the case must be decided according to the testimony of witnesses as is appropriate; for the world, being ignorant of this, would not otherwise have any conviction at all.
Having heard that, the king immediately summoned the witnesses with the words "So be it," and when questioned, they identified that woman as a liar.
Then, because her treachery toward her noble husband was well known, the Lord of Vatsa banished her from his own country along with her kinsmen and her sons.
And with a mind moistened by compassion, he bestowed upon that virtuous man, his husband, abundant wealth sufficient for another marriage, and then dismissed him.
A cruel wife, like a female crow, tears apart even a living man who is distressed and fallen into the pit of misfortune, as if he were carrion.
Affectionate, of noble birth, great, and a remover of distress—a housewife such as this, like the shade of a tree for one on the road, is born to someone through their merits.
While the king was speaking thus in this context, Vasantaka, who stood by his side and was skilled in storytelling, said:
Moreover, O King, whether it be enmity or affection among embodied beings here, it generally arises through the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from previous births.
And so, let this story be heard as it is described by me: there was a lord of the earth in Vārāṇasī named Vikramacaṇḍa.
He had a beloved servant named Siṃhaparākrama, who was as matchless a victor in gambling as he was in all battles.
And she had a wife whose very disposition was as deformed as her body; she was known by the name Kalahakarī, a title that was entirely appropriate to her character.
Having repeatedly obtained vast wealth from her through gambling with the king, that steadfast man surrendered it all to her.
Although she had given birth to three sons by him, that deceitful woman did not remain without quarreling for even a single moment.
"You drink and eat outside, yet you give us nothing at all! Thus she, along with her son, constantly tormented him with such cries.
Even though she was being propitiated day and night with food, drink, and clothing, her insatiable thirst for enjoyment blazed up even more intensely within him.
Then, gradually distressed by that resentment, Siṃhaparākrama abandoned that very house and went to see the goddess Vindhyavāsinī.
In a dream, that goddess commanded him as he remained without food: "Arise, my son; go to that very city of Vārāṇasī."
There, from the root of that single, most massive banyan tree which stands there, you will obtain a treasure at your own ease once it has been excavated.
From among them, you shall obtain one vessel made of emerald and ruby, as stainless as a sword-blade, appearing like a fragment of the sky fallen down.
There, with your gaze fixed, you will see—as if reflected within—the former birth of every living being that you have desired to know.
Having understood through that very [means] the former births of your wife as well as your own, you shall dwell there, having attained your goal, happy, and free from weariness.
Thus addressed by the queen, Siṃhaparākrama woke up, broke his fast, and set out toward Vārāṇasī at dawn.
Having gone and reached that city, she obtained a treasure from the foot of that banyan tree; from within it, she found a great vessel made of jewels.
And there, desiring to know, he saw in that vessel his own wife from a previous birth as a fierce female bear, and himself as the lord of beasts.
Then, having realized that his own hatred toward his wife was as firm as the latent impressions of a great enmity from a previous birth as a bear, he cast off both grief and delusion.
Then, many girls of various castes from previous births were recognized there through the power of the bowl; having avoided them, [he chose] only maidens [of his own kind].
Having reflected upon this, Siṃhaparākrama married a second wife named Siṃhaśrī, who was his equal and had been a lioness in a previous birth.
Having made her, who had caused the quarrel, a sharer in the village's produce, he remained there in the company of his new bride, happy at having discovered the treasure.
In this world, O Lord of the Earth, wives and other such relations likewise become objects of hatred or affection for men due to the force of their prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Having heard this wonderful tale from Vasantaka, the King of Vatsa, together with Queen Vāsavadattā, was greatly delighted.
Thus, as the days passed, the king remained insatiable day and night in beholding the moon-like face of his queen, radiant with her pregnancy.
To all those ministers were born sons endowed with auspicious marks, who in due course indicated future prosperity.
First, a son was born to the chief minister, Yaugandharāyaṇa himself, who was known by the name Marubhūti.
From Rumaṇvat was born a son named Hariśikha; and then a son, Tapantaka, was born to Vasantaka.
Then, a son named Gomukha was born to the doorkeeper-in-chief known as Nityodita, who also had the other name Ityaka.
These shall become the ministers here of the future son of Vatsarāja, the destined universal monarch who will crush the lineages of his enemies.
While they had thus been born and a great festival was taking place, a bodiless voice issued forth from the sky.
Then, as those days passed, Queen Vāsavadattā, the consort of that King of Vatsa, reached the time when her delivery was near.
And she entered that wonderful chamber, adorned with women who had sons, which served as her birth-chamber and whose windows were protected by śamī trees.
It was surrounded by various weapons, radiant with the auspicious luster of jewels, as if blazing with a splendor capable of protecting the womb.
Guarded by ministers through various mantras, tantras, and other means, it became like the fortress of the host of Mātṛs—difficult to approach and invincible to misfortune.
And there, in due time, she gave birth to a prince of lovely appearance, like the sky giving birth to the moon with its emerging, pure, nectar-like luster.
By his birth, that supreme abode was not illuminated; indeed, even the heart of his mother was freed from the darkness of sorrow.
Then, while joy was spreading among those dwelling in the inner apartments, the King of Vatsa heard of this birth of his son from the people within.
To him who reported what was pleasing, he, being pleased, did not grant even the kingdom; that was out of fear of impropriety, and not out of greed.
Having entered the inner apartments with a heart suddenly filled with longing, the king, whose long-held aspiration had finally borne fruit, beheld his son.
He bears a face resembling a playful lotus of the Fortune of Sovereignty, with red, broad lower lips for its petals and a beautiful tuft of hair for its filaments.
Even before [the arrival of] the splendors of other kings, his soft feet were marked by the discarded umbrellas and chowries, as if by their own brand-marks used to strike fear.
Then, with eyes wide open from the pressure of being filled by a flood of joy and brimming with tears as if they were flowing, she poured out her maternal affection for her son upon the king.
And while the ministers, including Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others, were rejoicing, at that moment a voice from the sky spoke thus:
"O King, this son born to you is an incarnation of Kāmadeva; know him here by the name Naravāhanadatta."
And with this, one should remain unwearied for a divine eon, before long becoming a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all the lords of the vidyādharas.
Having spoken thus, he ceased his speech; at that very moment, showers of flowers fell from the sky in succession, spreading forth amidst the sounds of celestial drums.
Then, his respect further increased by the undertaking performed by the gods, the king, exceedingly delighted, celebrated a supreme festival.
The sounds of musical instruments, rising from the palace, resounded through the sky as if to proclaim the birth of a king to all the Vidyādharas.
On the tops of the palaces, the crimson-colored banners, tossed by the wind, seemed to scatter vermilion upon one another with their own splendors.
As if out of delight at the birth of Smara with all his limbs upon the earth, celestial nymphs and courtesans gathered at every step and danced.
And that entire city appeared uniform in its splendor, owing to the new garments and ornaments obtained by the king’s subjects who had celebrated their festival.
For then, while that king was raining wealth upon his supplicants and dependents, no one in that land experienced emptiness except for the royal treasury.

Preceded by auspicious rites, accompanied on the right by those skilled in proper conduct, followed by dancers, and provided with excellent gifts, they were escorted by various well-guarded attendants.
Then the women of the inner apartments of the vassal kings arrived from all sides, like the very quarters of the sky personified, accompanied by the resonant sounds of spreading musical instruments.
There, movement consists of dance; speech consists of full vessels; social conduct consists of great generosity; and sound consists of musical instruments.
In that entire city, which was composed of bliss, the people were made of fine silk-paste and the ground consisted entirely of precious gems.
Thus that great festival, which had been extended over many days, came to an end together with the fulfillment of the citizens' desires.

As the days passed, that infant prince grew like the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, having been given the name Naravāhanadatta as previously ordained by the divine voice announced by his father according to the prescribed rites.

Seeing those two or three footprints of his—marked by the shimmering, smooth, and lovely luster of his nails, and adorned with the emerging sprouts of his teeth—and hearing him faltering as he gave and spoke, the father was filled with joy.
Then the excellent ministers, having brought their own sons, presented those children—who were the delight of the king’s heart—to the infant prince.
Yaugandharāyaṇa first [married] Marubhūti, Rumaṇvat Hariśikha, Ityakanāman Gomukha, and Vasantaka his son named Tapantaka.
The domestic priest Śāntikara also entrusted his brother’s son Śāntisoma, as well as Vaiśvānara—the twin sons of Piṅgalikā—to him.

At that moment, a rain of celestial flowers, made beautiful by the sound of divine musical instruments, fell from the sky; and the king, together with his queen, rejoiced, having honored that circle of ministers' sons there.

Then, even in his childhood, that Prince Naravāhanadatta was always accompanied by those six sons of ministers whom he favored and who were devoted solely to him, just as great prosperity is joined with virtues that are the cause of its attainment.

And as he watched his son—whose lotus-like face was smiling, whose playful and charming laughter was indistinct with mirth, and who moved from lap to lap of the kings whose minds were inclined toward affection—the days of the King of Vatsa passed by in some indescribable way, bound up with joy.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Naravāhanadattajanana-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And here concludes this fourth *lambaka*, the *Naravāhanadattajanana-lambaka*. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The fifth book, named "The Four Maidens. This nectar of stories, it is said, formerly emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth when churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Mountain-King. Those who forcibly swallow it, having attained success through the removal of obstacles, bear upon this earth the divine burden [of the gods] by the grace of Bhava.

First Wave: May Heramba protect you from obstacles, scattering vermilion over the earth from his face as it tilts while reeling with intoxication, as if burning away impediments with his own splendor.
Thus the Lord of Vatsa remained at that time together with his queen, nurturing Naravāhanadatta as their only son.
And one day, seeing the king anxious about protecting him, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke to him while they were alone.
"O King, you must never again entertain any anxiety on account of Prince Naravāhanadatta."
For this future one has been created by the Blessed One Bharga in your house as the universal monarch, the sovereign lord of all Vidyādharas.
Having understood this through the power of their knowledge, the lords of the Vidyādharas—those who harbored evil desires and could not endure it in their hearts—fell into agitation.
And having understood this, the Moon-crested God, for the sake of protection, stationed his own attendant, the lord of the Gaṇas named Stambhaka, at this place.
And he remains there, invisible, protecting this son of yours; and Nārada, having approached quickly, informed me of this.
Even as the minister was speaking thus, a divine man, wearing a crown and earrings and armed with a sword, descended from the midst of the sky.
Then, as the prince bowed and offered him hospitality, the Lord of Vatsa immediately asked him with curiosity, "Who are you, and what business do you have here?"
He too said: "Having been a mortal, I have become a lord of the Vidyādharas named Śaktivega; moreover, my enemies are many."
Having recognized through my power that you will become our universal monarch, O lord of the earth, I have come to see your son.
When he had spoken thus—having seen the future universal monarch—the King of Vatsa, delighted and thrilled, questioned him again out of wonder.
"How is the state of a Vidyādhara attained, and of what nature is it? And how was it attained by you? Tell us this, my friend."
Having heard those words of the king, the Vidyādhara Śaktivega, bowing low with humility, then replied to him in this manner.
O King, in this very life or in a previous birth, the wise, having propitiated Śaṅkara, obtain the status of a Vidyādhara through his grace.
And that [attainment] is of many kinds, consisting of the means for achieving the sword of knowledge, the garland, and so forth; listen as I describe it exactly as I have received it.
Having spoken thus, Śaktivega related this story concerning himself in the presence of Queen Vāsavadattā.
In ancient times, there was a king named Paropakārī, a scorcher of his enemies, in the city called Vardhamāna, which was an ornament of the earth.
And that high-minded king had a queen named Kanakaprabhā; she was like a lightning-streak from a rain-cloud, yet entirely free from fickleness.
In time, a daughter was born to him by that queen, who was fashioned as if by the Creator himself for the purpose of quelling the pride of Lakṣmī’s own beauty.
And she, the moonlight for the eyes of the world, grew up gradually; her father gave his daughter the name Kanakarekhā, after the name of her mother.
Once, when she had reached her youth, the king, her father, spoke to Queen Kanakaprabhā as she stood in a secluded place.
"O Queen, as this Kanakarekhā grows up together with me, the anxiety over finding a suitable marriage for her torments my heart."
For a maiden of good family who has lost her proper station is like a discordant song; she causes distress even to others merely by being heard with the ears.
Like a maiden bestowed upon an unworthy recipient out of delusion, learning—when given thus—leads neither to fame nor to merit, but rather to regret.
"To whom, then, O Queen, is this daughter of mine to be given? Who might be her equal?"—this is my most weighty concern regarding the king.
Having heard that, Kanakaprabhā laughed and spoke thus: "You have spoken so, but the maiden herself does not desire marriage at all."
For today, in jest, she to whom I had given an artificial son was asked by me: "Child, when shall I see your marriage?"
Upon hearing that, she replied to me with reproach: "Mother, do not say such things; I must never be given away to anyone at all."
Separation from me was not ordained, and I am still a maiden, most beautiful; otherwise, know me to be dead—there must be some reason for this.
"O King, having been addressed thus by her, I have come to your side in distress; for one whose marriage has been forbidden, what consideration can there be for a suitor?"
Having heard this from the mouth of the queen, the king was utterly bewildered; he went to the maidens' quarters and then spoke to his daughter.
"Even the daughters of gods and asuras seek him through ascetic penance; how is it, my child, that you have reportedly rejected the prospect of obtaining such a husband?"
Having heard these words of her father, Princess Kanakarekhā then spoke, with her eyes fixed upon the ground.
"Father, marriage is not desired by me at this time; therefore, what need has my father for it, and what is your insistence on this matter?"
Having been addressed thus by his daughter, that king, the best among the wise and a benefactor of others, spoke to her once more as follows:
"O daughter, what other means than the giving away of a maiden could there be for the pacification of sin? Furthermore, a maiden is not dependent on her kinsmen; she deserves independence."
For a maiden is indeed protected for the sake of another from the moment of her birth; apart from childhood, what kind of home is there for her other than that of her husband?
For when a maiden reaches her menses, her kinsmen fall into a low state; she becomes a *vṛṣalī*, and her suitor is called the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
When her father had spoken thus, Princess Kanakarekhā immediately uttered the words that were in her mind.
"If that is so, dear father, then by whichever Brahmin or Kshatriya that skillful person has indeed seen the city named Kanakapurī,"
"You must give me to him; he shall be my husband. Not otherwise, father—do not subject me to such torment in vain."
When his daughter had spoken thus, the king reflected: "By good fortune, she has at least consented to the occasion of her marriage."
"Surely this lady in my house must have arisen from some specific cause; otherwise, how could she, being but a child, know so much?"
Having reflected thus and having said "So be it" to his daughter at that time, the lord of the earth rose and performed his daily duties.
On another day, having entered his assembly hall, he said to those standing at his side: "Has the city named Kanakapurī been seen by anyone among you?"
To whichever brahmin or kṣatriya she has been seen by, I shall give Kanakarekhā and the rank of crown prince.
"O King, we have not even heard of her; what talk can there be of seeing her?"—thus they all spoke, looking at one another's faces.
Then the king summoned his doorkeeper and commanded him: "Go and cause a proclamation by the beating of drums throughout this entire city."
"Find out whether that city has been seen by anyone or not. Thus instructed, the doorkeeper departed, saying, "So be it."
Having gone out and immediately commanded the king’s men, he caused a drum to be beaten, which aroused curiosity among those who heard it.
"Whosoever among you—a Brahmin or a young Kshatriya—has seen the city of Kanakapurī here, let him speak; to him the king shall give his daughter and the status of crown prince."
Thus, after the minds of those in that city were filled with wonder, this speech was proclaimed everywhere following the beating of drums.
"Who is this that is proclaimed here in the city by the name 'Golden City' (Kanakapurī), who has never been seen nor even heard of by us, even by the elders?"
And having heard that proclamation there, the citizens spoke thus: "Not even a single person has been seen by me."
At that moment, a certain Brahmin named Śaktideva, the son of Baladeva, who was a resident of that place, heard that proclamation there.
That young man, immediately reduced to poverty by gambling, became distracted in mind upon hearing of the princess's betrothal and began to reflect.
"Now that my entire fortune has been lost at dice, I have no entrance into my father's house, nor even into the house of a courtesan."
Therefore, since there is no other recourse, it is better that I speak falsely to those who proclaim the drumbeat, saying, "I have seen that city."
"Who would believe my ignorance? When indeed was she seen by whom? Yet, perhaps in this way, there might be a reunion for me with the princess."
Having reflected thus, Śaktideva then went to those royal officers and spoke falsely, saying, "I have seen that city."
"By good fortune! Come then to the side of the doorkeeper," they said at that moment, and together with them he approached the doorkeeper.
He reported to him exactly that false account of seeing his city; and having been honored by him, he was then led into the presence of the king.
Remaining free from hesitation even before the king, he spoke exactly as follows: "For what indeed is difficult for a gambler who is exhausted by the game?"
The king, too, in order to ascertain her resolve, then dispatched that brahmin into the presence of his daughter Kanakarekhā.
Having learned of this from the mouth of the doorkeeper, he approached her and was asked: "Have you seen that city of gold?"
"Certainly, while I was a student wandering the earth, that city was seen by me," he replied to her in this manner.
"By what path did you go there, and what was it like? Being asked this again by her, that Brahmin spoke as follows:
From here I went to the city named Harapura; from there, too, I reached the city of Vārāṇasī in due course.
From Vārāṇasī, in a few days, I reached the city of Pauṇḍravardhana; from there, I went to that city known as Kanakapurī.
And I beheld that land of enjoyment for those of well-performed deeds, its beauty to be savored by unblinking eyes, like the city of Śakra.
"Having acquired knowledge there, I returned here after some time; thus, by that same path, I reached this city which is also like that."
When that rogue twice-born man had spoken thus with such artifice, the princess laughed and said to Śaktideva:
"Oh, it is true, Great Brahmā! You have seen that city. Tell me, tell me again: by which path did you go?"
When Śaktideva again displayed such audacity upon hearing that, the princess had him expelled by her maidservants.
Once he had been sent away, she went at that very moment to her father's side; her father also asked, "Did that brahmin speak the truth?"
Then that princess said to Janaka: "Father, even though you are a king, you act without any deliberation."
O wicked women, do you not know that rogues deceive honest people? For this brahmin indeed seeks only to deceive me with falsehoods.
Furthermore, that city was not seen by him who speaks with such confidence; for on this earth, rogues employ deceptions of many different kinds.
"Listen then as I tell you the story of Śiva and Mādhava," having said this, the princess began to relate this tale.
There was an excellent city, truly named Ratnapura; and there lived two rogues known as Śiva and Mādhava.
Accompanied by many rogues as their retinue, those two for a long time made the city completely plundered by the employment of their magical deceptions, leaving the wealthy folk utterly stripped.
Once, those two alone deliberated thus with one another: "We have already plundered this entire city."
Therefore, let us go now to dwell in the city of Ujjayinī; for it is heard that there the king’s domestic priest is possessed of great wealth.
And we, through the wealth taken from him by stratagem, shall go there to become connoisseurs of the charms of Malava women, O Śaṅkarasvāmin.
He who seizes the southern half [of the sacrificial offering] with a frowning face is indeed sung of by the twice-born as the "Gatherer" (Kīnāśa), who possesses seven jars of treasure.
It has been heard that this brahmin possesses a single jewel of a daughter; surely she too will be obtained from him through this very occasion.
Having thus resolved and made a mutual agreement on their plan of action, Śiva and Mādhava, the two deceivers, then departed from the city.
Gradually reaching Ujjayinī with his retinue, Mādhava remained in a certain village outside the city, disguised as a prince.
But Śiva, being skilled in many forms of illusion, first entered that city alone, having assumed the complete attire of a religious student.
There he took up residence in a small hut on the edge of the bank of the Siprā river, where clay pots, darbha grass, alms-bowls, and deerskins were visible, set out for display.
And at the times of dawn, he smeared his body with thick clay, acting as if he were laying down the preliminary lines for a coating of the mud of Avīci hell.
And he remained submerged for a long time in the river water with his face turned downward, as if practicing the future state of downward descent born of his own evil deeds.
Having risen from his bath, he stood for a long time facing the sun, as if demonstrating his fitness for being impaled upon a stake.
Then, having gone before the gods, holding a bundle of *kuśa* grass and reciting prayers, he sat upon a lotus seat like a four-faced Brahmā, complete with his characteristic guile.
Having plucked pure flowers from within the hearts of the virtuous as if they were his own, he worshipped the Enemy of Tripura with deceit.
Having performed worship once more, he again became intent on false recitation; fixing his attention upon crooked paths, he extended his meditation.
And in the afternoon, seeking alms and clad in the skin of a black antelope, he wandered through the city like a deceptive glance of illusion intended to delude them.
Then, having silently received three portions of alms from the houses of the twice-born, he who carried a staff and a deerskin made them, as it were, into pieces like the Truth itself.
He gave a portion to the crows and a portion to the guest; with the remaining portion, which was the seed of his hypocrisy, he filled the bellows of his belly.
Again, as if counting all his own sins, he recited the mantra for a long time while turning a false rosary.
And at night, he remained alone within his small hut, reflecting upon even the most subtle points of vulnerability in the world.
Performing such painful and hypocritical penance every day, he captivated the hearts of the city's inhabitants.
And as all the people there bowed with devotion, a reputation arose everywhere for him: "Aho! This ascetic is truly peaceful."
And at that very moment, Mādhava’s second friend, having learned of this through a spy, also entered that city.
Having taken up residence there in a distant temple, he, disguised as a prince, went to the bank of the Siprā river to bathe.
Having bathed and seen him before the God, intent on recitation along with his followers, he prostrated himself deeply and fell at Śiva’s feet.
And he said before the people: "There is no other ascetic like him; for I have seen him many times wandering through the sacred fords."
But Śiva, even upon seeing him, kept his neck stiffened with hypocrisy and remained just as he was; then Mādhava also went to his dwelling.
Having met together at night and having eaten and drunk, the two of them deliberated on what remained to be done thereafter.
And in the last watch of the night, Śiva returned at his leisure to his own small hut; Mādhava, too, at dawn, commanded one of his rogues.
"Taking this pair of garments as a gift, go to the presence of Śaṅkarasvāmin, the royal chaplain here."
A prince named Mādhava, having been defeated by his kinsmen, came from the Deccan after taking with him much of his paternal wealth.
Followed by several other princes of equal status, he shall here perform service for your majesty, the king.
"Therefore, O treasury of glory, I have been sent by him to see you"; thus should that priest be addressed by you with humility.
Having been addressed thus by Mādhava, that rogue was then dispatched; carrying a gift, he went to the house of that priest.
Approaching him at the proper time and presenting a gift in private, she delivered Mādhava’s message to him as was appropriate.
He too, imagining a future gain, believed that out of greed for presents; for the offering of bribes is indeed the one medicine for attracting those who desire wealth.
Then, on another day, when that rogue had returned, Mādhava, having found an opportunity, went in person to see the domestic priest.
He was surrounded by attendants disguised as wandering mendicants, posing as princes, who carried pieces of wood as their identifying marks.
Announced by the attendants, he approached the family priest; he too greeted him with a joyful welcome and words of greeting.
Then, after staying with him for a moment in conversation, Mādhava returned to his own dwelling with his permission.
On the second day, having again sent a gift of a pair of garments, he approached the priest once more and said to him:
"Indeed, we are seekers of service out of deference to our followers; therefore, you have been resorted to by us, for we have need of nothing else."
Having heard that and fearing its attainment from him, the family priest then promised that desired object to Mādhava.
Having gone to the king in an instant, he informed him of this matter; out of respect for him, the king also agreed to it accordingly.
And on the following day, having led that Mādhava along with his retinue, the priest respectfully presented him to the king.
The king, too, seeing Mādhava whose appearance was like that of a prince, received him with respect and assigned him a livelihood.
Then Mādhava remained there serving that king, and night after night he met with Śiva for counsel.
"Stay right here in my house," he was thus entreated by that domestic priest, who lived off courtly formalities out of greed.
Then, together with his companions, he took up residence in that very house, like a water-crow seeking a perch on the branch of a tree as a cause for its destruction.

Having filled a chest with artificial ornaments made of rubies, he placed it in his treasury. [Alternative reading for cd: Or rather, this was the cause of his destruction, like a rat in the trunk of a tree.]
And in the meantime, having opened it, she captivated his mind with various ornaments half-revealed under pretexts, as one might entice a beast with young grass.
And when that priest had gained his confidence, he then feigned illness, his body emaciated by eating very little food.
After a few days had passed, that king of rogues spoke in a low voice to the domestic priest who was sitting near his bed.
"O best of brahmins, a dire state currently prevails within this body of mine; therefore, O most excellent of brahmins, bring some other distinguished brahmin here."

To whom shall I give my entire wealth for the sake of happiness both here and hereafter? For what reliance can there be on riches when life itself is so unstable, especially for one possessed of wisdom?
Thus addressed by him, that priest, who lived on gifts, said, "I shall do so," and he fell at his feet.
Then, whichever Brāhmaṇa that domestic priest brought forward, Mādhava did not place his trust in him, under the pretext of desiring further distinctions.
Seeing that, a certain rogue standing by his side said this: "Generally speaking, an ordinary Brahmin does not please him."
Therefore, let it be investigated whether or not that one named Śiva, who is currently established on the bank of the Śiprā performing great austerities, is shining with splendor.
Having heard that, Mādhava, overcome with distress, spoke to the domestic priest: "Alas! Be gracious and bring him; for there is no other brahmin such as he."
Having been addressed thus by him, he then went into the presence of Śiva; there the priest saw him motionless, absorbed in meditation.
And having circumambulated him, he sat down before him; at that very moment, that rogue also slowly opened his eyes.
Then, bowing low before him, the family priest said: "O Lord, if you will not be angry, I have something to request of you."
Having heard that, and being thus permitted by Śiva with a gesture of raising his lips, the family priest spoke to him as follows.
"Staying here is a wealthy prince from the south named Mādhava; he is unwell and is prepared to give away his entire fortune."
If you so desire it, he will grant all of that to you—resplendent with various ornaments made of priceless great jewels.
Having heard that, Śiva, it is said, slowly broke his silence and spoke: "O Brahmin, what use have I, a celibate student who subsists on alms, for wealth?"
Then the family priest also spoke to him again in this way: "Do not speak thus, O Great Brahmin; do you not know the sequence of the stages of life?"

Having taken a wife and performing the rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests at home, the householder attains the three goals of life through his wealth; indeed, he is the best among those in the stages of life.
Then Śiva also said: "How could there be a taking of a wife for me? For I will not marry from any family whatsoever."
Having heard that and considering his wealth to be so easily enjoyed, the greedy priest, seeing his opportunity, spoke to him:
"I have, however, a daughter, a maiden named Vinayasvāminī; she is exceedingly beautiful, and I shall give her to you."
Whatever wealth you obtain from Mādhava through the acceptance of gifts, that I shall protect for you; therefore, devote yourself to the householder's life.
Having heard this, Śiva, his desired purpose accomplished, said: "O Brahmin, if this [boon] is your wish, then I shall do as you say."
"I am indeed a simple ascetic regarding the true nature of gold and jewels; I shall proceed solely according to your word—do as you see fit."
Having heard these words of Śiva, the foolish priest was highly pleased and, saying "So be it," led him home just as he had been told.
Having stationed that inauspicious one there under the name of Śiva, he then reported all that had been done to Mādhava and congratulated him.
And at that very moment, he gave his daughter—who had been raised amidst great hardship—to Śiva, like one's own prosperity lost through folly.
On the third day after the marriage had been performed, she led him, for the sake of receiving a gift, into the presence of Mādhava, who was feigning illness.
Saying, "I bow to you whose ascetic power is beyond conception," Mādhava also rose and fell at the feet of that Śiva, speaking words that were not false.
And he then gave him, according to the prescribed rite, a vessel of ornaments made of many artificial rubies, which had been brought from the treasury.
Śiva, having accepted this from the hand of the priest, handed it back to him, saying, "I do not know this; you alone know it."
"I have already agreed to this; what cause for anxiety is there for you in this matter? Having said this, the priest immediately accepted it.
Then, after Śiva had pronounced his blessing and departed for the quarters of his own bride, he took that [jewel] and deposited it in his own treasury-chamber.
On the following day, Mādhava also gradually relinquished his pretext of illness and declared that his disease had been cured through the power of his great gifts.
"With you as my companion in dharma, I have crossed over these calamities," he said, praising his domestic priest as he approached him.
Proclaiming, "This is due to his power; this is my body," he openly established a friendship with Śiva.
When those days had passed, Śiva also said to that domestic priest: "In this very manner, how much more shall I eat in your house?"
"In that case, why do you not take this ornament yourself for a price? If you say it is of great value, then give me whatever price is appropriate."
Having heard that and considering it priceless, the priest gave all his possessions to Śiva as its purchase price, saying, "So be it."
And for that purpose, having realized that the wealth was greater than his own, he had a living portrait painted by his own hand, and he himself also had it done.
Taking the document written by each other in his hand, that priest sat apart; and Śiva also remained apart, maintaining his status as a householder.
And thereafter, both Śiva and Mādhava remained there together, enjoying the provisions provided by the domestic priest according to their desire.
When time had passed, that priest, seeking money, went to the marketplace to sell a single bracelet from among his ornaments.
Thereupon, those merchants who knew the true nature of jewels examined it and said: "Aha! Whose is this skill by which this artificial [jewel] was made?"
For these are pieces of glass and crystal, colored by various dyes and set in bronze; they are neither jewels nor gold.
Hearing that, the priest became distraught; he went at once to his house, brought all those ornaments, and showed them to them.
Seeing that everything was likewise entirely artificial, they said so; and having heard that, he became as if struck by a thunderbolt.
Then, having gone there at that time, that fool said to Śiva: "Take your own ornaments and give me my own wealth."
"From where could I have such wealth even now? For all that was in my house has been consumed by time," Śiva replied to him.
Then, disputing with one another, both Śiva and the priest approached the king, who stood nearby with Mādhava.
O Lord, having given away this great deceptive ornament fashioned from pieces of glass and crystal set in brass and brilliantly colored.
"Having given away my entire fortune, it was consumed by Śiva while I was unaware," thus did that domestic priest inform the king.
Then Śiva said, "O King, from my childhood I have been an ascetic; having been entreated by him, I was made to accept this very [gift]."
At that very moment, even though I was still a fool, I said to him: "Since I am ignorant of jewels and such things, you are my authority."
And he acknowledged that, "I am standing here by you," and having accepted all of it, it was delivered by me into his very hand.
Therefore, O Lord, he took that from me at his own will and according to its price; moreover, we both have a mutual document here written in our own hands.
"And now the Lord knows that you are supremely capable of providing assistance"; thus it was said regarding Śiva, and then Mādhava spoke.
"Do not speak thus; you are worthy of honor. What fault of mine is there in this? I have accepted nothing from you or from Śiva."
My paternal wealth had long remained deposited elsewhere; at that time, I brought it back and gave it to the twice-born man.
If that is not truly gold, nor are those truly jewels, then let there be for me the fruit of having given brass, crystal, and glass.

Because of his sincere heart, I have confidence in his generosity; indeed, he has manifested right before my eyes, since he has descended [into this world] for the sake of a disease that is exceedingly difficult to overcome.
When Mādhava had spoken thus, his facial expression unchanged, the king, together with his ministers, laughed and was well pleased with him.
"Nothing of this sort has ever been done unjustly by Mādhava or Śiva," the members of the assembly remarked there with suppressed laughter.
Then the family priest departed, his purpose frustrated and filled with shame; for to whom is a mind blinded by excessive greed not a cause of calamities?
And those two rogues, Śiva and Mādhava, remained there for a long time, happy by virtue of the favor obtained from the gratified king.
In this way, by means of various hundreds of sutras, those rogues who live by their nets spread out webs of words, like fishermen on the riverbank.
Therefore, father, this Brahmin too wishes to obtain me by deceiving you, speaking falsely as if he had seen the City of Gold.
Therefore, let there be no haste on your part now regarding my marriage; I remain as a maiden for the time being, and let us see what will come of this.
Having been addressed thus by his daughter Kanakarekhā, that king, who was ever intent on helping others, then replied to her in this manner.
"O daughter, it is not fitting for you to remain in the state of maidenhood for so long during your youth; for wicked people, envious of virtue, falsely attribute faults to others."
A person who especially brings disgrace upon an excellent man—listen here to this story of Harasvāmin which I shall relate to you.
In the vicinity of the Ganges there is a city named Kusumapura; there lived a certain ascetic named Harasvāmin who was seeking the goal of sacred pilgrimage sites.
That Brahmin, subsisting on alms and having constructed a hut there on the bank of the Gaṅgā, attained a position of great esteem among the people due to the excellence of his asceticism.
And once, having seen him from afar as he was coming out after his alms-round, a certain wicked man who could not endure his virtues spoke thus in the midst of the people:
"Do you know what kind of hypocritical ascetic this man is? By him alone were all the children in that city devoured."
Having heard that, another person there, being of a similar disposition, said: "It is true; I too have heard this being spoken by people."
"So it is," said the third as well, in agreement; for the chain of association with the wicked binds one to the censure of the noble.
And in that very same sequence, the rumor reached the ears of others by word of mouth and spread throughout this entire city.
And all the citizens, out of their homes, could not by force restrain their children, saying, "Harasvāmī is carrying off and devouring all the infants!"
Then the brahmins there, fearing the extinction of their lineage, assembled and deliberated upon his banishment from the city.
When they were unable to speak to him directly out of fear that "he, being enraged, might seize us," they then dispatched messengers.
Then those messengers, having gone there, spoke to him from a distance: "The twice-born say to you, 'Depart from this city!'"
When he asked, "What is the cause? being filled with wonder, they replied to him again, "You eat here at every appearance of a child."
Having heard that, Harasvāmin himself, desiring to convince those brahmins, went into their presence while his people fled out of fear.
Upon seeing him atop the pavilion, the Brahmins climbed down in terror; for a person deluded by popular rumor is generally incapable of critical inquiry.
Then Harasvāmī, standing below, called those twice-born men one by one by their names and spoke to them as they stood above.
O Brahmins, what is this delusion of yours today that you do not look at one another? How many children were there, whose were they, by whom were they eaten, and where?
Having heard that, while the brahmins were still deliberating among themselves, all the children were found to be standing there, alive.
In that same manner, other citizens appointed in succession likewise accepted it; all of them, including the Brahmins and merchants, spoke thus.
"Alas! By us, who are utterly deluded, this virtuous man has been falsely defamed. All children live; so whose children have been devoured by him?"
When they had all spoken thus, Harasvāmin, having attained purity at that very moment, set out from the city to depart.
What delight can there be for a wise person in a wicked place where the mind is made averse by the faults produced by evil men, and which lacks discernment?
Then, entreated by the merchants and brahmins who bowed at his feet, that Harasvāmin somehow consented to dwell there.

Thus, wicked people, made eloquent by their hatred for the brilliance of observing the virtuous conduct [of the good], generally offer such false accusations against the righteous. What more need be said? For if they find even a slight opening to see a flaw there, it is like a torrent of abundant clarified butter falling into a blazing fire.

Therefore, my child, if you wish to extract the arrowhead from me while this fresh youthfulness of yours is still blooming, you ought not to indulge for long in a maidenhood that is easily subject to the malicious rumors of wicked people.
Having been addressed thus by her father, the lord of men, that princess Kanakarekhā, whose resolve was already fixed, spoke to him once more.
"O Kṣatriya, if that city of gold has been seen by any Brahmin or by you, then search for him immediately and give me to him; for this is what I have declared."

Having heard that, and considering his daughter—who possessed the memory of her past lives—to be firm in her resolve, and seeing no other means for bringing about her desired husband, the king from that time forward ordered a daily proclamation by the constant sounding of drums throughout the land to question every newcomer.

"Let that brahmin or kshatriya who has indeed seen the City of Gold speak; the king shall surely bestow his own daughter upon him along with the status of crown prince. Thus it was proclaimed everywhere, and after the drum had been beaten repeatedly, not a single person was found who could claim to have seen the City of Gold.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Caturdārikā-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave. In the meantime, the young Brahmin Śaktideva, dejected and humiliated by the princess who had rejected him, thought to himself:
Because of my false claim here that I had seen the City of Gold, I suffered the greatest humiliation; yet she was not that princess.
Therefore, I must wander the earth until that city is seen, or even until my life has departed.
For if, having returned and seen that city, I do not obtain this princess won by that wager, what is the use of life then?
Having thus made his vow, that twice-born man then set out from Vardhamānapura, taking his course toward the southern direction.
Proceeding by degrees, he then reached the great Vindhya forest and entered that vast expanse, which was as deep and dense as his own desire.
And there, as if fanning herself, she was being cooled by the soft sprouts of trees shaken by the wind, which had been scorched by the mass of the sun's rays.
Day and night, as if crying out from the sorrow of being repeatedly plundered by many thieves, the forest resounded with the roars of deer being struck down by fierce lions and other predators.
With her own unrestrained, shimmering, and wild rays of desert mirage, she seemed as if she wished to conquer even the most fierce splendors of the sun.
Alas, even though the earth is devoid of any mass of water, calamity is easily found; and although it is being constantly trampled upon, it remains far away.
Having traversed a long distance over many days, he beheld in a secluded spot a vast lake with cool and clear water.
With its lofty white lotus as a parasol and its shimmering swans as fly-whisks, it seemed to exercise sovereign rule over all the lakes.
Having performed his ablutions and other rites there, he then beheld, to the north of that place, a hermitage with trees that were lush and laden with fruit.
There, at the foot of an aśvattha tree, he beheld an elderly sage named Sūryatapasa, seated and surrounded by ascetics.
He was resplendent with a rosary of beads whose number equaled the knots of his own hundred years, which rested upon the tips of his ears turned white by old age.
Having first offered his salutation, he approached that sage; and he was greeted by the sage with the hospitable rites due to a guest.
And he was questioned by that very person after being offered a share of fruits and other provisions: "From where have you come? Where will you go? O blessed one, please tell me."
"O Blessed One, I have come from Vardhamānapura; I have set out with the resolve to go to Kanakapurī."
"I do not know where she might be; if the Blessed One knows, please tell me. Thus Śaktideva spoke to the sage, bowing low before him.
"My child, eight hundred years have passed here in my hermitage, yet I have not even heard of that city."
Thus addressed by that sage, he, filled with despondency, spoke once more: "In that case, I am as good as dead, wandering here upon this earth."
Then, having gradually understood the matter, that sage said to him: "If this is your resolve, then do what I tell you."
There is a region called Kāmpilya three hundred yojanas from here; there is a mountain named Uttara there, and on that mountain as well is a hermitage.
"There is a noble elder brother of mine there named Dīrghatapas; go to his side, for that old man might perhaps know that city."
Having heard this and saying "So be it," Śaktideva felt inspired; after spending that night there, he set out from that place quickly the following morning.
Having finally reached that land of Kāmpilya after crossing hundreds of wildernesses of afflictions, he ascended the northern mountain there.
There, having seen that sage of long asceticism dwelling in the hermitage, he bowed down to him and, being pleased, approached him after the rites of hospitality had been performed.
And he informed him: "O Blessed One, I have set out for the city of Kanakapurī mentioned by the princess, but I do not know where that city is located."
"And she must certainly be visited by me; therefore, in order to find her, I have been sent to your presence by the seer Sūryatapas."
When Śaktideva had spoken thus, the sage replied to him: "My son, it is only at this age that I have today heard of such a city."
With whom among those who have come from other lands have I become acquainted? I have not even heard of them, let alone seen them at a distance.
And I know for certain, my child, that she must be somewhere very far away, perhaps on another island; therefore, I shall tell you the means to reach her.
In the midst of the ocean there is an island named Utsthala; there dwells a wealthy lord of the Niṣādas known as Satyavrata.
He has traveled back and forth to all the other continents; therefore, that city must have been seen or at least heard of by him.
Therefore, first proceed to the city named Viṭaṅkapura, situated on the shore of the ocean.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing his desired goal, go with some merchant on a ship to that island, the dwelling place of the Niṣāda.
Having been addressed thus by that sage, Śaktideva said "So be it," took his leave of him, and departed from that hermitage at that very moment.
Reaching it in due time and traversing many leagues and regions, he arrived at that supreme city of Viṭaṅkapura, the ornament upon the shore of the ocean.
Having sought out a merchant named Samudradatta who was traveling to the island of Utsthala, he formed a friendship with him.
And having boarded his ship along with him, he set out by way of the ocean, his provisions consisting entirely of that man's affection.
Then, when only a short distance remained to be traveled, there suddenly arose the demon of a rain-cloud, roaring and with lightning-tendrils for a tongue.
A fierce wind blew, lifting up light objects and casting down even heavy ones, like the onset of destiny.
And great waves rose from the ocean, struck by the wind, like winged mountains rising out of anger at the assault upon their refuge.
And that carriage moved upward for a moment and downward for a moment, displaying a succession of rises and falls like those of wealthy men.
And in another moment, filled with the intense cries of the merchants, that ship, as if from the weight, suddenly sprang up and was shattered.
When that ship was wrecked, its owner, the merchant, fell into the ocean; but having mounted a plank, he crossed over and after a long time reached another vessel.
But as Śaktideva was falling, a great fish with a cavernous mouth wide open swallowed him, his entire body remaining unhurt.
And that fish, moving at will through the midst of the ocean at that time, reached the vicinity of the island of Utsthala by the force of destiny.
There, by chance, that [jewel] was found and seized by the servants of that very fisherman Satyavrata, who were catching śaphara fish.
And out of curiosity, those fishermen dragged that very large body and brought it at once into the presence of their own master.
Having seen it in such a state, Satyavrata, filled with curiosity, had that pāṭhīna fish cut open by his own servants.
Then, from that split belly, Śaktideva emerged alive, having experienced another wondrous dwelling in a womb.
Then, seeing that youth who had emerged and performed the auspicious svastika-gesture, the fisherman Satyavrata asked him with astonishment:
"Who are you, how, and from where did you come by this state of lying within the belly of a fish? O Brahmin, what is this story of yours that is so utterly marvelous?"
Having heard that, Śaktideva replied to the chief of fishermen: "I am a Brahmin named Śaktideva from the city of Vardhamāna."
The city of Kanakapurī must necessarily be reached by me; yet, being ignorant of its location, I have wandered over the earth for a very long time.
Then, having honored her as one who had traveled across the ocean based on Dīrghatapas’s words, he sent messengers to the lord of fishermen residing in Utsthala Island to inform him of this matter.
While traveling to the side of Satyavrata, I was submerged in the ocean due to the breaking of my ship; swallowed by a fish, I have now been brought here.
To Śaktideva, who had spoken thus, Satyavrata said: "I am indeed Satyavrata; this very island is yours."
However, although I have seen many islands, that city desired by you has not been seen by me; it has only been heard of at the edges of the islands.
Having spoken thus and seeing Śaktideva despondent at that moment, Satyavrata, out of affection for his guest's return, addressed him once more:
"O Brahmin, do not fall into despair; stay right here for this night. Tomorrow morning, I shall devise some means for you to achieve your desired goal."
Having been thus consoled by that fisherman and dispatched from there, the brahmin went to a monastery for brahmins where hospitality toward guests was easily obtained.
There, having taken his meal with a twice-born man named Viṣṇudatta who resided there, he engaged in a series of conversations with him.
And in the course of that conversation, having been questioned by him, he briefly related to him his own country, his family, and his entire life story.
Having understood that, Viṣṇudatta embraced him at that very moment and spoke, his voice faltering with syllables choked by the water of tears of joy.
"By good fortune, you are the son of my maternal uncle and a fellow-countryman of mine; as for me, I came here from that country while still a child."
Therefore, stay right here; before long, you will achieve your desire through a succession of reports from merchants arriving from other islands.
Having spoken thus and made his lineage known, Viṣṇudatta then attended upon Śaktideva with appropriate marks of hospitality.
Śaktideva, too, having forgotten the fatigue of the journey, attained great joy; for in a foreign land, the acquisition of a kinsman is indeed a fountain of nectar in the desert.

And he considered the attainment of his own desired goal to be already within reach; for an auspicious omen occurring in the interim is indeed an indicator of the successful completion of an undertaking.
Then, as he sat upon his bed at night unable to sleep, his mind intent upon the attainment of his desired goal, he—
Standing by the side of Śaktideva, Viṣṇudatta, providing consolations in a playful manner, told this story.
In former times, there was a very great brahmin named Govindasvāmin, who resided in a large village situated on the banks of the Kālindī.
And two sons, similar to him and endowed with virtues, were born to him in succession: Aśokadatta and Vijayadatta.
As they were living there for some time, a terrible famine arose; because of that, Govindasvāmin said to his wife:
This country has already been devastated by the calamity of famine; therefore, I am unable to witness the misfortune of my friends and kinsmen.
"How much can be given to whom? Therefore, having given whatever food we have to our friends and kinsmen, let us depart from this realm."
"We shall go to Vārāṇasī with our families to take up residence there. When she had spoken thus, he was permitted by his wife and gave her his own food.
Accompanied by his wife, son, and servants, he then departed from that country; for the noble do not venture to witness the calamity of their own kin.
And as he was traveling on the road, he beheld a great ascetic with matted hair, white with ashes, carrying a skull-bowl, who resembled the Lord Śiva with his crescent moon.
Having approached that wise man and bowed with affection for his two sons, he inquired about their welfare, both auspicious and inauspicious; then that yogi spoke to him.
"Your two sons are destined for prosperity; however, O Brahmin, you shall suffer separation from this younger one, Vijayadatta."
Then, by the power of this second one, Aśokadatta, there will be a reunion for you all with him once again.
Having been addressed thus by that wise man at that time, Govindasvāmin, overcome by a mixture of joy, sorrow, and wonder, took leave of him and departed.
Having reached Vārāṇasī, he spent that day outside the city in the temple of Caṇḍikā, occupied with rites such as the worship of the Goddess.
And in the evening, he stayed right there outside at the foot of a tree with his family, together with other travelers who had come from foreign lands.
And there at night, when everyone had completed their journey and was asleep—exhausted and reclining upon traveler’s beds of strewn leaves and the like—
Suddenly, a great fever of cold arose in his younger son, Vijayadatta, who had just woken up.
Because of that sudden cause for separation from his beloved kinsman, he stood with his hair bristling and trembling, as if from fear or fever.
Afflicted by the cold, he woke his father and said to him: "Father, a severe fever of cold now oppresses me here."
Therefore, bring me fuel and kindle a fire that wards off the cold; otherwise, I shall find no peace, nor shall I pass this night.
Hearing that, Govindasvāmin, distressed by the thought of his son's suffering, exclaimed: "But where is the fire now, my child?"
"Father, surely this fire is seen blazing nearby; since it is most abundant right here, why should I not go and warm my limbs?"
"Therefore, take me by the hand while trembling and carry me quickly. Having been addressed thus by his son, that brahmin spoke again:
"This is a cremation ground, and this funeral pyre is burning; how can you go there, which is terrifying with its ghosts and spirits, for you are but a child?"
Having heard these words of his affectionate father, the hero Vijayadatta laughed and addressed him with firm resolve.
"Father, what can those wretched beings such as piśācas do to me? Am I someone of little strength? Therefore, lead me there without hesitation."
As he spoke thus with such persistence, his father led him there; and the boy, scorching his own limbs, approached that funeral pyre.
Blazing with flames of fire, her hair disheveled by smoke, she was like the very presiding deity of the Rākṣasas, visibly intent on devouring human flesh.
Having recovered there in an instant, that boy saw his father within the funeral pyre and asked, "What is this that has happened?"
"This is the skull of a human being; it is being burned on the funeral pyre, my son," his father, who was standing nearby, replied to him.
Then, as if by his own audacity, that boy struck him with a single piece of wood whose tip was blazing, and split open his skull.
Therefore, the fat that had flowed out from him fell into his mouth, like the accomplishment of a night-stalking sorceress bestowed by the fire of the cremation ground.
Through the relish of that [taste], that Rākṣasa became possessed of a child's form; his hair stood erect, he brandished a sword from its sheath like a flame, and he was formidable with his fangs.
And having pulled out that skull, he drank the fat and licked it with his own tongue, which flickered like the flames of fire clinging to the bone.
Then, having discarded the skull-bowl, he drew his sword and desired to kill his own father, Govindasvāmin.
"O Lord Kapālasphoṭa, your father must not be killed!"—at that moment, these words "Come here! arose from the cremation ground.
Having heard that and received the name "Kapālasphoṭa," the boy abandoned his father and, having become a Rākṣasa, vanished from sight.
His father, Govindasvāmin, also went away from there, crying out: "O son! O virtuous one! Alas, alas, Vijayadatta!"
Having arrived at that temple of Caṇḍī, he related everything that had happened to his wife and his eldest son, Aśokadatta, in the morning.
Then, together with those two, that ascetic experienced an onset of the fire of grief as terrible as the sudden flash of lightning from a cloudless sky.
Likewise, while staying in Vārāṇasī, another person who had come to see the goddess approached him there and shared in his sorrow.
Just then, a certain great merchant, having come there for the purpose of worshipping the goddess, beheld Govindasvāmin in that state.
The virtuous man named Samudradatta approached, comforted that brahmin, and immediately led him along with his attendants to his own home.
There he attended upon him with services such as bathing and the like; for it is the very nature of the great to show compassion toward those in distress.
Having heard the words of the great ascetic, Govindasvāmin, who had conceived hope for a reunion with his son, also took up fortitude along with his wife.
From that time forth, he dwelt in this Vārāṇasī, at the invitation of that very same wealthy merchant, in his house.
There, his second son, named Aśokadatta, having completed his studies and reached the prime of youth, learned the art of wrestling.
And he gradually attained such excellence there that he was not defeated by any rival wrestler on the face of the earth.
Once, during a festival of the gods, at that gathering of wrestlers, a certain famous great wrestler arrived there from the Deccan.
Therefore, all the wrestlers there were defeated before the king of Vārāṇasī, named Pratāpamukuṭa, by others.
Then that king, having summoned Aśokadatta from that excellent merchant whom he had heard of, commanded him to fight with that wrestler.
That wrestler also, having seized a limb with his hand, began the combat; but Aśokadatta, having seized the wrestler's limb, threw him down.
Then, even the battlefield, as if satisfied by the sound arising from the fall of the great wrestler, uttered a cry of "Well done! as it were.
The king, being pleased, filled Aśokadatta with jewels and made him his own attendant, having witnessed his valor.
Having become dear to the king, he too attained supreme prosperity in a few days; for the lord of the people was a treasury of valor and learning, and a connoisseur of excellence.
Then, on the fourteenth day, the king once went outside the city to worship the well-established god Śiva, who was situated at a distance.
Having performed his evening worship, as he was returning by way of the vicinity of the cremation ground at night, he heard this voice rising from within it.
O Lord, because I was falsely accused here by the chief magistrate, I have been pierced upon the stake out of malice for three days now.
Even now, the life-breaths of me, a doer of no evil deeds, have not departed; therefore, O Lord, I am exceedingly thirsty—grant me water.
Having heard that, the king, out of compassion, said to Aśokadatta who was standing by his side: "May you send water for him."
"Who would travel there at night, O Lord? Therefore, I myself shall go. Having said this, Aśokadatta took some water and departed from that place.
And when the queen had departed for her own city, that hero [remained] within the depths of the forest, which was enveloped on all sides by a most intense darkness.
In some places, great evening offerings of scattered flesh were presented to the jackals; in other places, the scene was illuminated by the blazing light of lamps from funeral pyres.
Accompanied by the loud-sounding cymbals of the *tāla* and *vetāla* spirits, he entered that cremation ground, which resembled the dwelling place of the dark night.
As he cried out loudly there, "By whom was water requested from the king?", he heard a voice from one direction saying, "It was requested by me."
Having gone there and followed it, he saw a certain man nearby at a funeral pyre, pierced upon the point of a stake.
And below him, he beheld a weeping woman, adorned with all her ornaments, never seen before, and beautiful in every limb.
When the moon, lord of the night, had set as the dark fortnight waned, she arrived like a night made beautiful by its rays for the purpose of ascending the funeral pyre.
"Who are you, mother, and why are you standing here weeping in such a state? When she was thus questioned by him, that woman spoke to him as follows:
I am the wife of this man pierced by the stake, devoid of good fortune; with my hopes certain, I stand here to ascend the funeral pyre along with him.
I shall wait for some time for the departure of his life-breaths; for even though the third day has passed, his vital breaths do not leave him today.
He repeatedly asks for water, and I have brought it here; however, my friend, I cannot reach his mouth while he is on this elevated spear.
Having heard her words, that great hero also said to her: "But this water was sent by the king himself into my hand."
"Therefore, placing your foot upon my back, give this [foot] to his mouth; for among women in times of distress, it is not merely physical contact that constitutes a defilement."
Having heard this, she said, "So be it," and taking up water, she stepped two paces and climbed onto the back of him who was bent low at the base of the stake.
In an instant, as drops of blood fell fearlessly upon the ground and his own back, that hero raised his face and looked.
Then he saw a woman who, having repeatedly cut with a knife the flesh of that man impaled on the tip of a stake, was devouring it.
Then, perceiving her to be a transformation, he seized her by the foot—where the anklets were tinkling—in his rage, intending to dash her against the ground.
She too, having swiftly kicked that foot with her own illusory power, quickly leapt into the sky and went somewhere out of sight.
And from his feet, that jeweled anklet, having slipped off due to that pulling, came to rest within the hand of Aśokadatta.
Then he [regarded] her as an association with wicked people—charming at first, harmful in the middle, and terrifying through transformation at the end.
Reflecting on what was lost, yet seeing the divine anklet in his hand, he became filled with wonder, distress, and joy all at once.
Then, having removed his anklets, he departed from that cemetery and went to his own home; and having bathed at dawn, he proceeded to the royal palace.
When the king asked, "Was water given to him who was pierced by the stake? he replied, "So it was," and presented the anklet to him.
When asked by that king, "How is this so?", he freely related to him the wondrous and terrifying account of his own night.
Then, having ascertained that his character was without equal, the king, though already pleased by the excellence of his other qualities, rejoiced all the more.
Taking that anklet, he went and gave it to the queen himself; delighted, he then related to her the account of how he had obtained it.
Having understood that and having seen that divine jeweled anklet, she rejoiced in secret, being solely intent on praising Aśokadatta.
Then the king said to her: "O Queen, by birth as well as by learning, by truthfulness as well as by beauty, he is great even among the great."
If Aśokadatta should become the husband of my worthy daughter Madanalekhā, then it would be well; this is my opinion.
In a bridegroom, these virtues are to be observed, not wealth which is subject to momentary destruction; therefore, I give this daughter to this preeminent hero.
Having heard these words of her husband, the queen spoke with respect: "This is fitting, for he is indeed a young husband suitable for her."
And her mind having been stolen by that sight of the honey-grove, she, with a vacant heart during these days, neither hears nor sees.
Having learned of that from her friend, I lay down at the end of the night with anxious thoughts; then I remember being addressed in a dream by some divine woman.
"My child Madanalekhā, this girl is not to be given to anyone else; for she is the wife of Aśokadatta, won by him in a previous birth."
Having heard that and awakened at once, I went there at the very break of dawn; through my own conviction of the truth, I comforted the daughter.
And now it has been said by the noble son himself; therefore, let him unite with her, as a seasonal creeper clings to its tree.
Thus addressed by his beloved, the king was delighted; having celebrated a festival, he summoned Aśokadatta and gave that daughter to him.
And the union of those two—the daughter of the lord of kings and the son of the lord of brahmins—was for the mutual enhancement of each, like that of Fortune and Modesty.
Then, on one occasion, the queen spoke to the king concerning that jeweled anklet brought by Aśokadatta.
"Noble son, this single anklet does not shine; therefore, let a second one be fashioned that is suitable for it."
Having heard that, the king commanded the goldsmiths and others: "Let a second anklet, identical to this one, be made."
Having examined it, they said: "O King, another such [work] cannot be made; for this is divine craftsmanship, not human."
Such jewels as these do not exist in great abundance upon the surface of the earth; therefore, let another be sought in that very place from which this one was obtained.
Having heard this, while the king and the queen were instantly despondent, Aśokadatta, standing there, saw it and suddenly said:
"I myself shall bring back for you the second anklet of this one," he said, having thus made his promise to the king who was apprehensive of rashness.
Although he was dissuaded by those endearments, he did not waver from his resolve; taking that anklet, he went back once more to the cremation ground.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at the very place where he had found him, he entered and [beheld him] with [limbs] blackened by the smoke of a blazing funeral pyre.
In that cremation ground, which was crowded with rākṣasas who resembled trees—with human beings hanging from their necks and shoulders, bound by nooses—it was like a forest of trees.
[Before the verse beginning with "pādapairiva," there is an additional half-verse in another manuscript: "With hollows and mouths blazing like internal firebrands and embers.
Not seeing that woman whom he had seen before, he conceived a single means for obtaining her anklet: the sale of his own human flesh.
Then, having taken the corpse from the tree-branch, he wandered about there, crying out, "Take it! Buy this great flesh! while offering it for sale.
"O Mahāsattva, take this and come with me for now," so was he addressed from afar by a certain woman in an instant.
Having heard that, he approached and followed that woman exactly as she had instructed, and from afar beneath a tree, he beheld a woman of divine form.
She was surrounded by women and seated upon her throne, radiant with jewel-encrusted ornaments, appearing there like a lotus plant in a desert where its presence is otherwise inconceivable.
And having been brought by that woman, he approached her as she stood there and said, "I am selling human flesh; let it be taken."
"O Great Being, for what price is this being given by you? thus spoke that woman of divine form.
Then that hero, with the corpse of a *preta* upon his shoulders and back, showed her that single jeweled anklet held in his hand and said to her:
"To whoever gives me a second anklet like this one of mine, I shall give him this flesh; if such a person exists, let him take it."
Having heard that, she also said to him: "I have another anklet; for this one anklet of mine alone was indeed stolen by you."
I am that very same person whom you saw at the side of the one pierced by the stake; having assumed another form by your own doing, I have not been recognized by you now.
"What is the use of that meat? If you do what I tell you, then I shall give you a second anklet equal to this one."
Thus addressed, that hero then agreed and said: "I shall indeed do everything you say in an instant."
Then she told him her desire from the very beginning: "My dear, there is a city named Trighaṇṭā on a peak of the Himalayas."
There dwelt a preeminent lord of the Rākṣasas named Lambajihva; I am his wife, named Vidyucchikhā, capable of assuming any form at will.
And when my only daughter was born, that husband of mine was slain in battle before the lord Kapālasphoṭa by the power of fate.
Then that lord, being pleased, gave me back my own city; and by his grace, I now dwell there happily with my son.
And now my daughter has entered the bloom of youth; therefore, my mind is occupied with thoughts of how she might obtain an excellent and heroic husband.
Therefore, seeing you traveling along this path with the king at night on the fourteenth day, I, staying here, thought to myself:
"This young hero is worthy and a suitable husband for my daughter; why then should I not devise some means to obtain him?"
Having thus resolved and made a request, you were brought by me into the middle of the cremation ground under the pretext of being pierced by a trident; all this was done by me falsely.
I am one who speaks of the falsity of the manifold world of forms and so forth displayed by illusion; and having deceived you there for even a mere moment, I remain.
In order to attract you further, I skillfully left behind one of my anklets like a noose of chains, and from there I departed.
Since you have been found by me here today in this manner, come to our home and accept my daughter; moreover, take this other anklet.
Thus addressed by the night-stalker woman, the hero said "So be it," and together with her, through her supernatural power, he traveled by way of the sky to that city.
