And he beheld that golden city upon a peak of the Himalayas, like the orb of the sun resting on a mountain, having ceased its toil from the journey through the sky.
There he obtained that daughter of the lord of the Rākṣasas, named Vidyutprabhā, who was like the great accomplishment of his own daring incarnate.
And there, together with that beloved wife, Aśokadatta dwelt for some time, finding contentment in the opulence of his mother-in-law.
Then she said to her mother-in-law, "Give me that anklet, for I must now go to the city of Vārāṇasī."
For there, in the presence of the king himself, he had made this vow: "I shall bring back a second [woman] who rivals the singularity of my anklet."
Having been addressed thus by him, his mother-in-law gave him her second anklet and further presented him with a golden lotus.
Having obtained the lotus and the anklet, Aśokadatta then departed from that city, having restrained his return by word.
By that very mother-in-law, through the path of the sky and by the power of her own supernatural accomplishment, he was once again brought back to that cemetery.
And remaining right there at the foot of that tree, she then said to him: "I always come here at night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight."
And whenever you come again on that night, then and there you shall obtain me from the root of this banyan tree.
Having heard this from her, and having said "So be it" and taken leave of that night-stalking demoness, Aśokadatta then departed for his father's house.
His parents there were distressed by such a separation from him; their grief was doubled by his departure, which brought the pain of being parted from their youngest son.
Just as he brought joy at that moment by arriving unexpectedly, his father-in-law, the king, learned of this and arrived right there.
Embracing him with limbs that seemed to bristle with thorns as if afraid of such a rash touch, the king, bowing low, rejoiced for a long time.
Then Aśokadatta entered the king’s palace together with that monarch, appearing like joy itself incarnate.
He gave that divine pair of anklets to the king, which seemed to offer praise for his heroism with their jingling sounds.
And he presented to him that lovely golden lotus, which was like a play-lotus plucked from the hand of the Fortune of the Rākṣasa’s treasury.
Then, questioned out of curiosity by that king together with his queen, he described exactly what had occurred, which brought delight to their ears.
Can one attain pure fame, which delights the mind with the description of its diverse deeds, without undertaking acts of daring?
When he spoke thus, the king and the queen—having recovered the pair of anklets—considered themselves to have accomplished their purpose through that son-in-law.
At that time, Rājagṛha, resounding with the music of festive instruments, shone as if it were singing aloud the virtues of Aśokadatta.
And on another day, that king placed that golden lotus, made for himself, upon a fine silver pitcher in his temple.
Both the white and red lotuses on the jars shone forth like the fame and majesty of the two kings, Aśoka and Datta.
Beholding them in such a state, the king, a devotee of Maheśvara, his eyes blossoming with joy, spoke out from the intensity of the aesthetic flavor of devotion:
Ah! This lofty pinnacle shines with this lotus, like the matted-haired Śiva, white with his ashes, with his tawny mass of matted locks.
If there had been a second such golden lotus, he would have placed it in that second pitcher as well.
Having heard these words of the king, Aśokadatta then said: "O King, I shall bring a second lotus for you as well."
Having heard that, the king replied to him, "I have no need for any other lotus; enough of this rashness of yours."
Then, as the days passed while he was intent on recovering the golden lotus, that fourteenth day of the dark fortnight arrived once more for Aśokadatta.

And while she was there, the sun, perceiving his desire for the golden lotuses, went to the peak of the setting mountain as if out of fear, having departed from the golden lotuses of the celestial lake.
As the night-demons, smoky-grey in hue, rushed everywhere for a moment as if out of pride at having swallowed the flesh of the twilight’s crimson clouds.
In the mouth of the Great Fierce Night-Walker, yawning wide and terrifyingly radiant with rows of teeth like flickering garlands of lamps.
Having departed at will from the palace where the princess was fast asleep, Aśokadatta went once again to that very cemetery.
There, at the foot of that banyan tree, he saw his mother-in-law, the rākṣasī, who had returned once more and offered him a respectful welcome.
And together with her, that youth went once more to that dwelling on a peak of the Himalayas, where the womenfolk were looking out expectantly for his return.
Having stayed there for some time together with his wife, he said to her: "Mother-in-law, give me a second golden lotus from somewhere."
Having heard that, she also said to him: "Where else could there be a lotus for me? This lake belongs to our lord Kapālasphoṭa."
In this place, such golden lotuses arise on all sides; therefore, out of affection, he gave that one lotus to my husband.
When she had spoken thus, he said: "In that case, lead me to that lake, so that I myself may take the golden lotus from it."
"For that place is guarded by fierce rākṣasas; it cannot be reached by them. Though thus forbidden by her, he did not abandon his persistence.
Then, having been led there with some difficulty by his mother-in-law, he beheld from afar that divine lake situated upon the ridge of a lofty mountain.
It was covered with dense, upright, and blazing golden lotuses, which seemed as if they had absorbed the radiance of the sun due to their constant upward-facing orientation.
As soon as he had gone there and began gathering the lotuses, the terrible night-stalkers who guarded them blocked his way.
Armed with weapons, he slew them; others, having fled, went to their master Kapālasphoṭa and reported that matter to him.
Having learned of this, the lord of the rākṣasas himself arrived there in a rage and beheld Aśokadatta with his lotuses plundered.
"How has this very brother of mine, Aśokadatta, come here? he recognized him at that moment with astonishment.
Then, casting aside his weapon, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy, he ran forward, immediately fell at his feet, and spoke to him:
"I am named Vijayadatta; I am that uterine brother of yours, your younger sibling. We two are both the sons of the eminent Brahmin Govindasvāmin."
I have been born as such a night-stalker for so long through fate; from splitting the skull of a funeral pyre, I am named Kapālasphoṭa.
And now, from the sight of you, that Brahminhood has been remembered by me; my state as a Rākṣasa, whose mind was shrouded by delusion, has departed.
While Vijayadatta was speaking thus, he embraced him and, as it were, washed his body which had been defiled by the state of being a Rākṣasa.
Then Aśokadatta descended from the sky in a flood of tears, accompanied by the preceptor of the Vidyādharas named Prajñaptikauśika.
The teacher approached both those brothers and said, "You are all Vidyādharas who have fallen into this state due to a curse."
And now that curse has come to rest for all of you; therefore, take back these sciences of yours, which are to be shared with your kinsmen.
"Go now to your own abode, you two who have accepted your kinsmen"; having spoken thus and bestowed the sciences upon them, the Guru ascended to heaven.
And having become Vidyādharīs, they woke up and departed from there through the sky, carrying the golden lotuses, toward that peak of the Himalayas.
And there Aśokadatta approached his beloved, the daughter of the lord of the Rākṣasas; she too, her curse having now expired, became a Vidyādharī.
Together with that beautiful woman, both those brothers traveled through the sky and reached Vārāṇasī in an instant.
And having approached their parents there, who were tormented by the fire of separation, they immediately brought them relief by raining down the nectar of their sight.
Even though their physical bodies were different, those two had entered into various other births; they became a cause for celebration not only for their parents but for the whole world as well.
And after a long time, Vijayadatta filled his father’s heart even more completely than he had filled the space between his arms when they embraced him tightly.
Then, having learned of that very matter, King Pratāpamukuṭa, the father-in-law of Aśokadatta, also arrived there in great joy.
Honored by him, Aśokadatta, together with his kinsmen, went to that royal capital, where his beloved awaited him with longing and where great festivities had been prepared.
And he gave many golden lotuses to that king; and the king, delighted by obtaining more than he had requested, was filled with joy.
Then, while everyone remained there, his father Govindasvāmin, filled with wonder and curiosity, questioned Vijayadatta.
"Then, my child, when you had become a rākṣasa in the cremation ground during the night, what kind of events occurred? Let them be described."
Then Vijayadatta said to him, "Father, through my own recklessness, I struck a skull blazing from a funeral pyre, and by the power of fate—"
Then, by that sudden spray of fat which entered your mouth, you were seen for a moment as a demon, deluded by magic.
For the rākṣasas gave me the name Kapālasphoṭa; then I was summoned by others and joined their midst.
And they gradually led me to the presence of their own lord of the Rākṣasas; he too, upon seeing me, was pleased and appointed me to the office of commander-in-chief.
Then, on one occasion, that lord of the rākṣasas went forth in his pride to attack the gandharvas; there, in battle, he was slain by his enemies.
At that very moment, my command was accepted by his servants; consequently, remaining in that city, I ruled over the kingdom of the Rākṣasas.
Then, because of the sudden sight of the noble Aśokadatta, who had arrived for the sake of the golden lotus, that state of mine was completely pacified.
Immediately thereafter, our noble brother will inform you all of how we regained our own magical sciences through the power of the release from the curse.
When Vijayadatta had thus reported there, Aśokadatta then described it from the very beginning.
Formerly, while we were two Vidyādharas, we beheld from the sky the daughters of sages bathing in the Gaṅgā at the hermitage of Gālava.
Having suddenly perceived that they both desired those women of equal longing in secret, their kinsmen, who possessed divine vision, rebuked them out of anger.
"Because of your evil conduct, both of you shall be born in a mortal womb; even there, a manifold separation shall befall you both."
When one of you has arrived even in a remote region beyond the reach of humans, and the second shall likewise attain wisdom upon seeing him.
Then, having obtained the lore from the preceptor of the Vidyādharas, you two shall once again become Vidyādharas, joined with your kinsmen and liberated from the curse.
Thus cursed by those sages, we two were both born here; how our separation occurred is all known to you.
Now, by means of the lotus and through the power of my mother-in-law’s accomplishment, I have gone to the city of the lord of the rākṣasas and this younger brother of mine has been recovered by me.
And having received the sciences from that very teacher, Prajñaptikauśika, we immediately became holders of the sciences (vidyādharas) and have swiftly come here.

Having spoken thus to his parents and to that most beloved daughter of the king, Aśokadatta—whose conduct was wondrous and who was then gladdened by the release from the darkness of the curse—immediately divided his own various special sciences among them, whereby they all instantly became Vidyādharas with awakened minds.

Then, having taken leave of that king along with his parents and his two beloved wives, the fortunate and swift one flew up and departed through the path of the sky toward the abode of his own universal emperor.
There, having seen him and received that command from him, he took the name Aśokavega; and his brother likewise took the name Vijayavega.
The two brothers, the most excellent young Vidyādharas, accompanied by their own kinsmen, went to their own abode, the best of mountains known as Govindakūṭa.

Pratāpamukuṭa, the king of Vārāṇasī, was likewise overcome with wonder; having placed a single golden lotus upon the second water-jar in his own temple and worshipped Tryambaka with other golden lotuses given by him, he was delighted by the greatness of that connection and considered his lineage to have achieved its purpose.

Thus, divine beings descend by reason of a specific cause and are born into this world of living creatures; maintaining the courage and vigor appropriate to them, they attain the fulfillment of their goals, even those that are difficult to achieve.

Therefore, O ocean of being, I know that you too must be some portion of a divinity, for your success is as you desire; generally, enthusiasm for even difficult tasks speaks of the excellence of one's nature, even among the great.
Moreover, that divine princess Kanakarekhā, who is desired by you, is surely a young girl; for how else could she wish for a husband who has beheld the City of Gold?
Having thus heard this collection of charming stories from Viṣṇudatta in private, Śaktideva, longing in his heart to behold the City of Gold, maintained his fortitude and passed the night.

Thus ends the second wave in the Caturdārikā-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. Then, at dawn on that island of Utsthala, Satyavrata, the lord of the fishermen, approached Śaktideva as he was staying in the monastery.
Having already set out, he approached him and said: "O Brahmin, for the sake of accomplishing your desired goal, a means has been devised by me."
In the midst of the ocean there is a preeminent island called Ratnakūṭa; there the Blessed Lord Hari resides, established by the ocean.
During the festival held there on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, people always come from all the continents with great effort to offer worship.
Perhaps that city of Kanakapurī might be found there; therefore come, let us go there, for that auspicious day is drawing near.
Having been addressed thus by Satyavrata, Śaktideva said, "So be it," and joyfully accepted the provisions for the journey prepared by Viṣṇudatta.
Then, having boarded the vessel offered by Satyavrata, he set out swiftly along the path of the ocean together with him.
And as he was traveling there, in that wondrous abode where crocodiles resembled islands, he questioned Satyavrata, who stood as the helmsman.
"What is this that appears in the ocean far from here, possessing great splendor, with the appearance of lofty winged mountains rising up at will?"
Then Satyavrata said: "That deity is the banyan tree; they say that beneath it lies the very great whirlpool called Vaḍavāmukha."
Having avoided this very place, one proceeds here; for those who have entered this whirlpool, there is no returning again.
While Satyavrata was speaking thus, that vessel began to move in that very direction, driven by the force of the water.
Seeing that, Satyavrata spoke again to Śaktideva: "O Brahmin, this time of our destruction has surely arrived."
Since this carriage has suddenly sped away right here, it cannot by any means be stopped by me now.
Thus we have been cast into this deep whirlpool, as if into the very mouth of Death, drawn by the water as if by a powerful force of karma.
This is not at all a source of sorrow for me, for whose body is indeed stable? But it is a sorrow that your heart's desire has not been accomplished, even through great hardship.
Therefore, while I hold back this carriage for just a moment, you must quickly grasp a branch of the banyan tree.
Perhaps some means of survival might exist for you, who possess such auspicious form; for who indeed can fathom the playful whims of Fate or the waves of the ocean?
While this Satyavrata, of firm resolve, was thus speaking, the ship then came near that tree.
At that moment, Śaktideva, having leaped up and being free from fear, seized a broad branch of that banyan tree by the sea.
But Satyavrata, with his body and his vehicle still carrying on, entered the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha) there, having dedicated himself to the welfare of others.
And Śaktideva, though he had taken hold of a branch of that tree whose quarters were filled with branches, became despondent and reflected:
I have not yet seen that city of Kanakapurī; while perishing in a place where there is no footing, even this lord of fishermen has been destroyed.
Or rather, since its foot is ever placed upon the head of all, by whom can the divine Destiny be subverted?
As that young man thus reflected upon his situation, appropriate to his current state, that day passed away while he remained on the trunk of the tree.
And in the evening, he saw many great birds from all directions entering that banyan tree, filling the quarters of the horizon with their cries.
He saw vultures being greeted, as it were, out of affection for their long acquaintance by the waves of the ocean tossed by the wind from their broad wings.
Then, concealed by a mass of leaves, he overheard the conversation among those birds perched on the branches, which they held between themselves in human speech.
One described another island, another a mountain, and another a distant region; each one recounted that place where they had set foot during the day.
And one aged bird among them spoke: "Today I went to the City of Gold to wander about."
And tomorrow morning I shall go back to that very place to wander at my ease; for what purpose is a long journey that brings only fatigue?
Thus, his distress being allayed by the bird’s words, which were like an unexpected shower of nectar, Śaktideva reflected:
By good fortune, that city truly exists, and this very means for reaching it is at my disposal: this bird of immense body who has been made into my vehicle.
Having reflected thus, Śaktideva then approached slowly and hid himself between the back and the wings of that sleeping bird.
In the morning, after those other birds had departed, that bird displayed a wondrous partiality, like the workings of fate itself.
Carrying Śaktideva unobserved upon his back, Dattāskanda returned in an instant to that City of Gold to roam about once more.
While that bird was seated there within the garden, Śaktideva quietly descended from its back.
Having moved away from his side, as he was wandering there, he beheld two women intent on gathering flowers.
Approaching slowly, while they stood amazed at the sight of him, he asked: "What region is this, and who are you two, ladies?"
"Friend, this city named Kanakapurī is the abode of the Vidyādharas; and in it dwells a Vidyādharī named Candraprabhā."
"And know us, O garden-keeper, to be her attendants here in this grove; this collection of flowers is for her sake," they both said to him.
Then that Brahmin also said: "Do for me likewise, so that I too may see your mistress here."
Having heard this and said "So be it," those two women led the young man from within the city to the royal palace.
Having arrived there, he beheld that mansion of Saṃketa, radiant with pillars of rubies and walls of gold, as if it were the very abode of all prosperity.
And seeing him arrived there, all the attendants went and reported that marvel of a human's arrival to Candraprabhā.
Having thus instructed the doorkeeper, she then had that Brahmin ushered without delay into her presence within the inner apartments.
Having entered, he too beheld her there, a feast for the eyes, as if she were the personified perfection of the Creator’s wondrous craftsmanship.
And she, rising from her couch of fine jewels even from afar, honored him herself with a welcome, captivated by the sight of him.
And when he had sat down, he asked him: "O auspicious one, who are you, being such as this? And how have you come to this earth, which is inaccessible to humans?"
Thus addressed by Candraprabhā, Śaktideva, with curiosity, announced his own country, his birth, and his name.
He described how he had come to obtain that princess named Kanakarekhā by wagering the sight of her city.
Having understood that and reflected for a moment, Candraprabhā then sighed deeply and spoke to Śaktideva in private.
Listen, O fortunate one, for I shall now tell you something: there is on this earth a lord of the Vidyādharas named Śaśikhaṇḍa.
We four were born to him as his daughters in succession; I am the eldest, Candraprabhā, and another is Candrarekhā.
Śaśirekhā was the third, and Śaśiprabhā the fourth; we have all grown up here in our father's house in that order.
And once, while I was observing the vow of maidenhood, all three of my sisters went together to the bank of the Mandākinī to bathe.
There, having begun their water-sports, they drenched with water a sage named Agryatapas who was standing in the water, out of pride in their youth.
Being excessively persistent, the sage became enraged and cursed them all, saying: "May you all be born as wicked daughters in the world of mortals."
Having learned of that, my father went and propitiated him; he then declared the end of the curse for each of them individually, according to their respective circumstances.
The great sage, endowed with divine knowledge, bestowed upon all of them the recollection of their past births while they were still in mortal form.
Then, after they had abandoned their bodies and departed for the mortal world, my father, having given this city to me, went to the forest out of weariness.
While I was dwelling here, the goddess Ambika appeared to me in a dream and commanded: "O daughter, a human shall become your husband."
Because I resisted my father as he pointed out various excellent suitors from among those Vidyādharas, I remain even today a mere maiden.
And now, having captivated you by this wondrous arrival and by my very form, I have been surrendered to you alone.
Therefore, on the coming fourteenth day, I shall go for your sake to the great mountain named Ṛṣabha to present my petition to my father.
On that lunar day, every year, the best of the Vidyādharas gather from all directions to worship the god Hara.
My father will come to that very place; having obtained his permission, I shall return here quickly, and then you may marry me.
Having said, "Therefore, stay here for now," Candraprabhā attended to Śaktideva with various enjoyments befitting a Vidyādhara.
And as he stood there saying "So be it," he experienced at that moment a bliss such as one feels upon plunging into a pool of nectar after being scorched by a forest fire.
When the fourteenth day arrived, Candraprabhā said to him: "Today I shall go to petition my father on your behalf."
This entire retinue shall go along with me; you must not remain in sorrow alone for these two days.
Furthermore, even while staying in this temple, you must by no means ascend to the middle level.
Having spoken thus to that youth, Candraprabhā, having surrendered her heart to him and following his mind, departed from there.
Remaining there alone, Śaktideva wandered from place to place of great splendor, diverting his mind.
"What indeed was forbidden to me by her there?"—thus he wondered, filled with curiosity as to why the daughter of a Vidyādhara had prohibited him from mounting upon her back.
He ascended that middle floor of the palace; for the inclination of the minds of men generally turns away from what is forbidden.
Having ascended there, he saw three jeweled pavilions guarded within; one of them had its door open, and he entered into its midst.
Having entered within, he beheld someone lying on a couch made of excellent jewels, upon which a mattress was placed, with his body covered by a cloth.
As soon as he lifted the cloth and looked, he saw that the excellent maiden, the daughter of King Paropakārin, was likewise dead.
Having seen this, he then thought: "What is this great marvel? Is she asleep in a state of unconsciousness, or is this some uncontradicted illusion?"
She for whose sake I am in this exile remains right here; she has departed from life, while I continue to live in that land.
"And her beauty remains unfading; therefore, it is certain to me that some creator is spreading this magic illusion for a certain purpose."
Having reflected thus, he went out and entered those other two pavilions in succession; inside, he beheld likewise other maidens.
Having emerged from that temple as well, he, filled with wonder, sat down and beheld an exceedingly excellent pond below.
On its bank he saw a horse with a jeweled saddle; having dismounted right there, he then approached its side out of curiosity.
Seeing that it was empty, he desired to mount it; but the horse, striking him with its hoof, cast him down into that pond.
Immersed therein, he quickly emerged in great agitation from the middle of a garden pond in his own city of Vardhamānapura.
And in his birthplace, he immediately beheld himself standing in the water of a pond, resembling a white water-lily, yet miserable in the absence of the moon's light.
Where is this city of Vardhamānapura, and where is that city of the Vidyādharas? Oh, what is this unfolding display of the grandeur of a magical illusion?
"What a tragedy! I, unfortunate as I am, have been deceived by someone. Or rather, who here knows what the course of destiny will be?"
Reflecting thus and other such thoughts, Śaktideva then emerged from the middle of the pool and, filled with wonder, went to his own father's house.
There, having feigned a circumambulation of the drum as instructed, he remained with his father’s approval and his own kinsmen amidst a festive celebration.
On the second day, having gone outside his house, he again heard these words being proclaimed with the beating of drums throughout that city:
The king bestows his daughter, along with the status of crown prince, upon him who has truly seen the City of Gold from among the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Upon hearing that, the skillful Śaktideva went to those criers of the proclamation and spoke again: "I have seen that city."
He was quickly led before the king; and the king, recognizing him as one who had spoken falsely once again, regarded him just as he had before.
"If I speak falsely, or if that city was not seen by me, then let my wager now be the punishment of this body."
When he had said, "Let that princess question me today," the king went with his attendants and had his daughter brought to that very spot.
Having seen that brahmin whom she had seen before, she said to the king: "Father, he will surely speak something false once again."
Then Śaktideva said: "O Princess, I shall tell you whether it is true or false; but first, speak thus to me, for I am curious."
In Kanakapurī, I saw you there on the couch as one whose life had departed; how is it that I see you here alive?
Having been addressed thus by Śaktideva with the token of recognition, that princess Kanakarekhā immediately spoke in this manner before her father.
"Father, that great-souled one has truly seen that city; and before long, he will become my husband while I remain there."
There he will marry my three sisters and others, and he will exercise sovereignty over the Vidyādharas in that city.
But today I must enter both my own body and that city; for by the sage’s curse, I was born here in your house.
When a mortal man, while bearing his human condition, beholds your body in the city of Kanakapura, he will effect the penetration of the ultimate reality.
"Then there shall be your release from the curse, and he shall become your human husband"—thus did that sage further prescribe the end of my curse.
Even in this human state, I am thus possessed of memory of my past births and endowed with wisdom; therefore, I shall now go to my own Vidyādhara realm for the sake of attaining perfection.
Having spoken thus, the princess abandoned her body and vanished; and a tumultuous cry of lamentation arose in that royal palace.
Śaktideva, too, having fallen from both [worlds] and being afflicted by various insurmountable sufferings, brooded upon those two beloved ones whom he had failed to reach even after reaching them.
Though he reproached himself and was distressed by his unfulfilled desire, he departed from the royal palace and reflected thus for a moment:
"What has been spoken by Kanakarekhā will surely come to pass for me; why then do I despair? For spiritual accomplishments depend upon one's own inner strength."
"I shall go once more to that City of Gold by that very same path; surely fate will again provide me with a means to reach it."
Having reflected thus, Śaktideva departed from that city; for the wise, having undertaken an effort, do not turn back until their purpose is accomplished.
And after traveling for a long time, he once again reached that city named Viṭaṅkapura, situated on the shore of the ocean.
There he saw that merchant approaching him face-to-face, with whom he had previously set out upon the ocean when his ship was wrecked.
Could this be Samudradatta? And how did he fall into the ocean and then emerge from it? This is no wonder; I myself am the proof.
Having reflected thus, as soon as the twice-born approached that merchant, the merchant recognized him and, filled with joy, embraced him around the neck.
He brought him to his own home, and having offered him hospitality, he asked: "When the ship was wrecked, how did you emerge from the ocean?"
Śaktideva also related that entire account exactly as it happened, beginning with how he had previously been swallowed by a fish and reached the island of Utsthala.
And immediately thereafter, he questioned that best of merchants as well: "Tell me, how did you yourself cross the ocean at that time?"
Then that merchant also said: "At that time, I fell into the ocean; wandering for three days, I took refuge upon a single plank."
Then, unexpectedly, a ship arrived along that path; seeing me crying out, those on board took me up onto it.
And having ascended it, I then saw my father there, who had previously gone to another island and had returned at that time after a long interval.
Upon seeing me and recognizing me, my father embraced my neck and, weeping, asked for news of me; and I spoke to him in this way.
"O father, although you had been away for a long time and had not yet returned, I myself engaged in trade, thinking it to be my own duty."
Then, while traveling to another island, I was submerged today in the ocean due to the wrecking of my vessel, and having been found there, I have been rescued by you.
When I had spoken thus, my father addressed me reproachfully: "For what purpose do you expose yourself to such risks to your life?"
"Indeed, my son, I possess wealth, and I am established in its acquisition; behold this ship brought by me for you, filled with gold."
Having spoken thus and comforted me, he brought me by that very same vessel to his own home in Viṭaṅkapura; from there, I was brought here by him.
Having heard this from that merchant, Śaktideva rested for that night of three watches and spoke to him on the following day:
"O caravan leader, I must go once again to the island of Utsthala; therefore, tell me now, how shall I go there?"
"My merchants have set out there today; you should board their ship and travel along with them."
Having been addressed thus by that merchant, Śaktideva then went to that island of Utsthala together with those traders.
"That great-souled kinsman of mine, Viṣṇudatta, who stays here—I wish to dwell near him in that very monastery as before."
Having thus reached the island and reflected upon that moment, the brahmin set out to travel along the middle of the marketplace path.
And at that moment, by chance, the sons of the fisherman chief saw him there; having recognized Satyavrata from nearby, they spoke as follows:
O Brahmin, you went from here at that time with my father to search for Kanakapurī; how is it that you have returned alone today?
Then Śaktideva said, "Your father fell into the ocean; his ship was dragged away by the waters, and he was cast into the mouth of the submarine fire."
Hearing this, the sons of the fisherman became enraged and said to their servants: "Bind this evil-minded man! By him our father has been killed."
Otherwise, how could it be that when there is but one ship, one person falls into the submarine fire while the second emerges from it?
Therefore, this slayer of his father must be offered as a sacrificial animal by us before the goddess Caṇḍikā tomorrow at dawn.
Having spoken thus, those sons of the fisherman then bound their servant and led Śaktideva from there to the temple of Caṇḍikā, which inspires fear.
With its vast belly perpetually devouring many living beings, and with rows of tinkling bells for its set of teeth, it was like the gaping mouth of Death.
There, bound and staying through the night, doubting his own life, that Śaktideva addressed the goddess Caṇḍī in this way:

O Blessed One, the world has been saved by you through your form, which resembles the orb of the rising sun, as if it were saturated with the blood flowing from the throats of the Dānavas as they were being greedily drunk.

Therefore, O Giver of Boons, protect me—who am constantly prostrate before you, who have fallen into the hands of a group of causeless enemies, and who have come from afar—with the thirst for attaining my beloved ones.
Having thus addressed the goddess and somehow obtained sleep, he saw in a dream a woman emerging from that inner chamber.
Approaching him with a divine form, she spoke to him as if out of compassion: "O Śaktideva, do not fear; no misfortune shall befall you."
Among these ten sons of the fisherman, there is a sister named Bindumatī; seeing you as a maiden in the morning, she will request you for the sake of being her husband.
You should accept that [instruction], for it alone will liberate you; she is not a fisherwoman, but a divine woman fallen from her state due to a curse.
Having heard this, as he awoke, that fisher-maiden arrived at the temple of the goddess at dawn like a shower of nectar for his eyes.
Approaching him and announcing her identity, she spoke to him with eager longing: "I shall release you from here; therefore, do what I desire."
"These suitors were indeed approved by my brothers, but they were rejected by me; however, upon seeing you, affection has arisen within me, so please accept me."
Thus addressed by Bindumatī, the daughter of the chief of fishermen, Śaktideva recalled his dream and, filled with joy, accepted her proposal.
He was liberated by her very self and married that beautiful-faced woman, whose union was desired and arranged by his brothers through the instructions of Ambikā obtained in a dream.
And he remained there together with that divine woman, who had assumed another form and was obtained solely through his merit, as if she were the very accomplishment of his happiness.
Once, while standing on the roof of his palace, he saw a Caṇḍāla coming along the road carrying a load of beef, and he said to his beloved:
O slender-waisted one, these cows are to be revered even by the three worlds; behold, how this evildoer eats their flesh!
Having heard that, Bindumatī then said to her husband: "Noble son, this is inconceivable; what can be said regarding the sin in this matter?"
By the power of the cows, though for even a very slight offense, I have been born into this family of fishermen; what atonement can there be for this?
Even as she was speaking thus, Śaktideva said to her: "It is strange; speak, my dear, who are you, and how did you come to be born as a fisherman's daughter?"
To him who was thus questioning her with such persistence, she said: "I shall tell you this, even though it is a secret, if you will do as I say."
When he replied with an oath, "Certainly, my dear, I shall do so," she then spoke to him thus regarding her initial desire:
"In this island, a second wife shall now also be yours; and she, noble son, will soon become pregnant."
And in the eighth month of her pregnancy, you must slit open her belly and extract that fetus; you must not feel any compassion in this matter.
When she had spoken thus, while he was wondering "What is this? and filled with rising compassion, that daughter of the lord of fishermen spoke further.
"O compassionate one, you must act upon these words of mine for some reason; now hear who I am and how my birth as a fisherman came about."
"In a former birth, I was once a certain Vidyādharī; now, however, I have fallen from that state into the world of mortals due to a curse."
And when, in my state as a Vidyādharī, I cut the strings of lutes with my teeth and rejoined them, it was because of that that I was born here in the house of a fisherman.
Thus, when the mouths of cows are touched by even a single dry sinew, such is their downward rebirth; what then can be said of those who eat their flesh?
While she was speaking thus, her brother approached in great haste and addressed Śaktideva.
"Arise! This great boar has emerged from somewhere and, having slain many people out of arrogance, has come here toward us."
Having heard that, Śaktideva descended from his own palace and, mounting his horse with his spear in hand, galloped toward the boar.
And as soon as he saw that hero rushing toward him, the wounded boar fled and entered a cave.
Śaktideva also, searching for him, entered that very place and in an instant beheld a great, secluded garden grove containing dwellings.
And standing there, he beheld a maiden of most wonderful form, approaching with agitation as if she were a forest deity come out of affection.
And he asked her, "O auspicious one, who are you, and what is this agitation of yours? Hearing that, the fair-faced woman replied to him in this way:
There is a king named Caṇḍavikrama, the lord of the southern quarter; O fortunate one, I am his daughter, a maiden named Bindurekhā.
And here, this wicked Daitya, with blazing eyes, having seized me by a ruse, has today brought me from my father's house.
Seeking meat, he assumed the form of a boar and went outside; today, while afflicted by hunger, he was pierced by a certain hero with a spear.
As soon as he was pierced, he entered [the fire] and met his death; and I, my maidenhood remaining untainted, fled and escaped.
Having heard that, Śaktideva said to her: "Why then this agitation? For it was I myself who killed that boar with my spear, O princess."
Then she also said, "In that case, tell me who you are," and he replied, "I am a Brahmin named Śaktideva."
Then, having been addressed by her, "In that case, you alone shall be my husband," the hero said, "So be it," took her, and emerged through the opening of the cave.
Having gone home and informed his wife Bindumatī of that, she trusted him and he married the maiden Bindurekhā.
Then, while that Śaktideva, who had two wives, was living there, one of those wives, Bindurekhā, became pregnant.
And in the eighth month of her pregnancy, her first wife Bindumatī approached him privately and said to Śaktideva:
O hero, remember that which was promised by you to me; this is now the eighth month of pregnancy for your second wife.
Go there, tear open her womb, and take out the fetus; for your own word of truth must not be transgressed.
Thus addressed by her, Śaktideva—overwhelmed by affection and compassion, yet constrained by his vow—was for a moment at a loss for what to do.
Filled with agitation, he went out and approached Bindurekhā; she too, seeing him approaching dejected, spoke to him thus:
"Noble son, why are you despondent today? Do I not know that you have been commissioned by Bindumatī to extract my fetus?"
And that task must necessarily be performed by you, for there is indeed something to be done; moreover, there is no cruelty whatsoever in this, so do not feel compassion.
Listen, O Lord, to this story of Devadatta: formerly, there was a brahmin named Haridatta in the city called Kambuka.
And that illustrious man had a son named Devadatta, who, though he had acquired his education in childhood, became a youth addicted solely to the vice of gambling.
Having lost his clothes and other possessions at dice, he was unable to go to his father's house; and once, he entered a certain empty temple.
And there he saw, all alone, a solitary practitioner of great vows named Jālapāda, who had accomplished many magical feats and was engaged in silent recitation.
And having approached him, he slowly offered his salutation; he, too, having cast off his silence, greeted him with a welcome.
Having stood there for a moment, he was asked by him the cause of his distress, and he explained to him his own misfortune arising from the depletion of his wealth due to calamity.
Then that observer of great vows spoke thus to Devadatta: "My son, for those who are addicted to vice, there is no wealth on earth sufficient to satisfy them."
If you desire to avoid calamity, then do as I say; for I have already made the preparations necessary to attain the state of a Vidyādhara.
O Sulakṣaṇa, you too must accomplish this together with me in order to attain that; you must observe my command, and may all your misfortunes perish.
Having been addressed thus by that ascetic, and having promised "So be it," Devadatta immediately took up residence at his side.
And on another day, having gone to the edge of the cremation ground beneath a banyan tree at night, he performed worship and offered milk-rice.
Having scattered offerings in all directions and thus completed that worship, the observer of the great vow spoke to the Brahmin standing at his side.
"In this very way, you must perform the daily worship here; O Vidyutprabhā, accept this offering," said he as he spoke.
"Beyond this, I know that our success will likewise be certain. Having said this, the practitioner went with him to his own dwelling.
Devadatta also went daily to the foot of that tree and performed worship in that very same manner, according to that same ritual procedure.
And once, at the conclusion of his worship, as he was looking on, a divine woman suddenly emerged from that tree which had split in two.

Having entered, he saw there a divine palace made of jewels, and within it, a single excellent woman seated upon a couch.
Thinking, "May this accomplishment (siddhi) of ours become embodied," as soon as he meditated, that beautiful woman provided him with hospitality.

And she said, "O illustrious one, I am the daughter of the lord of the Yakṣas; for I am the daughter of Ratnavarṣa, renowned by the name Vidyutprabhā."

"Therefore, accept my hand in marriage, for I am enamored of you at first sight. Thus addressed by her, Devadatta agreed, saying, "So be it."
After remaining there for some time while she bore that burden of pregnancy, he departed with the intention of returning once more to that observer of the great vow.

Having spoken thus and reminded him of their former agreement, Devadatta was sent by him once more and went to his beloved.

Therefore, tear open my belly and extract this fetus; for if I do not do this myself, there is indeed some matter here that must be accomplished.

Then, as soon as that twice-born man arrived and looked after having offered the oblation, he saw that all of that meat had been eaten by the ascetic.

When he had leapt up, his sword dark as the sky and adorned with necklaces and armlets, Devadatta then reflected:

At that moment, the Vetāla said to that great-souled being: "I am pleased with this courage of yours; do not act recklessly."
When the Vetāla had said, "Therefore, my good sir, what is your intention that I may accomplish for you?", the hero replied to him.

"No one else shall defeat you because of your supreme power; however, a universal monarch (cakravartin) shall arise again from the Lord of Vatsa. Among you, he who is destined to be the sovereign named Naravāhanadatta—unto him you should pay homage."

Dwelling in that city of shimmering golden palaces, where the concentrated rays of the sun seemed to fall with greater intensity due to its extreme height, he found even greater delight in the company of his four beloved wives—each with beautiful eyes—in the delightful gardens, jeweled stairways, and ponds.
Having thus related his own wondrous adventure at that time, the eloquent Śaktivega spoke further to the Lord of Vatsa.

O Śaktivega, ornament of the Lunar dynasty, know me to have arrived before you, O King of Vatsa; I am one who has become destined to be your new universal emperor, and I am filled with longing for the sight of the pair of feet of your daughter.

Thus, though I am but a human being here, I have obtained the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas through the grace of the Conqueror of Cities. And now, O King, I depart for my own abode; having beheld my Lord, may unbroken prosperity attend you.

Having said, "He has been seen," and speaking with palms joined in reverence, Śaktivega—whose splendor was like that of the moon—having received permission, ascended to heaven in an instant. Then the Lord of Vatsa, together with his two queens, his young son, and his ministers, attained an indescribable state of joy there.
Thus ends the third wave in the *Caturdārikālambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. This fifth book, the *Caturdārikālambaka*, is completed. Śrī!

"I was a merchant's servant; I myself am that very Devadāsa. Indeed, this very former birth has been remembered by me today."
Having spoken thus and recounted his own tokens of recognition, the king—both despondent and joyful—immediately departed for heaven along with that queen.
Thus, when both my parents had passed away to the other world, my mother’s sister took me to her own home to raise me.
While I was still a maiden, a certain sage arrived there as a guest; my mother’s sister then assigned me to him for the purpose of service.
And it was Kuntī herself whom Durvāsas was propitiated by me with great effort; and by her boon, O Lord, you were obtained by me as my righteous husband.
Thus do auspicious things come to pass solely through dharma, when, out of reverence, one has attained the kingdom together with one's parents; even one's lineage is thereby remembered.
Having heard these words of Queen Tārādattā, King Kaliṅgadatta, who was solely devoted to righteousness, spoke to her.
Truly, even a small dharma well-performed becomes of great fruit; likewise, O Goddess, hear the ancient story of the seven twice-born ones.
Formerly, in a city named Kuṇḍina, there were seven young Brahmin sons who were the disciples of a certain Brahmin preceptor.
Then, due to the hardships of a famine, that teacher sent those disciples to ask his father-in-law, who possessed many cows, for a single cow.
And those disciples, their bellies emaciated by famine, went to that father-in-law of theirs who was staying in another land and requested a cow from him with those words.
He also offered them a single milch cow for their livelihood; yet, though he was miserly, he did not give food to them even when they were hungry.
Then, having taken that cow and returning, they fell upon the surface of the earth midway on the path, exhausted and intensely tormented by hunger.
The preceptor’s house is far away, and we have fallen into calamity; food is difficult to obtain from any quarter, so our lives are as good as gone.
And so, even this cow has perished in this forest devoid of water, groves, and humans; what small matter for my teacher could possibly remain after that?
Therefore, by sustaining even these heavy vital breaths of yours quickly with her flesh, you should honor them with what remains after; for a time of calamity has indeed arrived.
Having thus deliberated, all seven of them, having turned that cow into a sacrificial animal there according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, slew their fellow student.
Having sacrificed to the gods and the ancestors, and having eaten that meat according to the prescribed rite, they took the remains and went into the presence of their preceptor.
Having bowed down to him, they related everything to him exactly as it had been done; he was pleased with them, even though they were at fault, because of their truthful speech.
Within seven days, they perished due to the calamity of famine; yet, by that very truth, they were born once again with the memory of their former lives.
In this way, even a very small seed of merit, when watered with the pure water of intention, bears fruit for men, just like that of farmers.
O Goddess, that very [mind], when corrupted by the waters of evil intention, bears undesirable fruit in this world; listen as I tell you something else regarding this.
In ancient times, two people—a Brahmin and a Caṇḍāla—stayed together at the Gaṅgā for an equal duration, practicing asceticism and fasting.
Overcome by hunger, the brahmin saw the Niṣādas there eating fish they had caught, and being thus deluded, he thought:
"Oh, blessed are these fishermen, the sons of a slave-girl, who in this world eat the flesh of fish every day according to their desire!"
But that second Caṇḍāla, seeing those very fishermen, thought: "Fie on these flesh-eaters who kill living beings!"
"What will happen to me if I remain here while these faces look upon me? Thinking thus, he closed his eyes and remained there, established in his own self.
In due course, both of them perished through fasting; there, the twice-born was devoured by dogs, while the outcaste was dissolved in the waters of the Gaṅgā.

Then that twice-born man, having failed to cultivate his self, was reborn right there in a family of fishermen; yet, by virtue of the power of the sacred ford, he possessed the memory of his former birth.
Even that Caṇḍāla was born right there on the bank of the Gaṅgā in the house of the king, as one who remembered his former births, steadfast and with an unimpaired soul.
Thus, of those two who were born having remembered their previous lives, one grieved while being a slave, whereas the other rejoiced while being a king.
Thus, for one whose mind is impure, the root of the tree of Dharma is impure; and for one whose mind is pure, its fruit is likewise pure—of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus to Queen Tārādattā, King Kaliṅgadatta addressed her once more on that occasion.
Moreover, O Goddess, whatever kind of action is characterized by a predominance of *sattva*, it leads to its corresponding fruit; for prosperity follows after *sattva*.
And so I shall relate here; listen to this wonderful tale: there is here a city named Ujjayinī, renowned throughout the world, among the lands of Avanti.
That abode of Mahākāla shines with its white palaces, as if they were the peaks of Mount Kailāsa attained through the joy of serving him.
Entering with hundreds of flowing streams, its expanse as deep as the ocean, it rests upon winged mountains.
In that city there was a king named Vikramasiṃha, whose name was truly significant, for wild beasts in the form of his enemies never once appeared before him face-to-face.
And he, having no rival, found no occasion for the festival of battle; thus, disregarded in both weaponry and the prowess of his arms, he burned within.
Then, on another occasion during the course of conversation, the minister Amara-gupta, who understood his master's intentions, spoke to the king.
O King, even among those rulers who merely boast of their enemies out of pride in their own staff-like arms and intoxication with the science of weapons, faults are not difficult to find.
And so, in the past, Hara, having been propitiated by Bāṇa out of pride in his thousand arms, was requested by him for an enemy worthy of battle.
Just as he had obtained such excellent boons, he was rendered by his enemy, the divine Murāri, one whose forest of arms was severed in battle.
Therefore, you too must not harbor dissatisfaction without engaging in battle, nor should you ever desire an undesirable adversary.
If you wish to display your training in weapons and your own prowess here, then demonstrate it in the forest on the grounds suitable for hunting and during the hunt itself.
Even hunting is considered appropriate for kings for the sake of exercise and the like; indeed, kings who have not undergone such exertion are not praised on the path of battle.
Wild beasts of prey desire the earth to be empty; therefore, they are to be slain by the king, and for this reason hunting is also permitted.
Yet they are not excessively indulged in, for by the addiction to such indulgence, even former kings such as the Pāṇḍavas have gone to their destruction.
Thus addressed by the wise minister Amaragupta, King Vikramasiṃha agreed to it, saying, "So be it."
On another day, the earth was filled with horses, foot-soldiers, and dogs, and all the directions were filled with the height of various snares.
Making the sky filled with the joyful sounds of the hunters' village, that king went forth from the city for the sake of the hunt.
As he was departing, seated upon the back of an elephant, he saw two men standing together in a secluded place outside in the empty abode of the gods.
And as those two were conversing privately with one another about something at their ease, the king, observing them from afar, proceeded to the hunting forest.
There, amidst the old tigers with their claws extended and the lions' roars, he found delight in the regions of the earth and upon the mountains.
He covered that earth with pearls fallen from the claws of slain elephants—slayers of lions—who were struck down by those whose seeds were valor.
The animals, leaping sideways like deer, fell obliquely before him; having quickly pierced them first, he who moved straight on attained great joy.
Having hunted for a very long time, that king, whose attendants were exhausted, returned again to Ujjayinī with his bowstring slackened.
While he was staying in that temple for that length of time, he saw those two men as they were departing, exactly as he had seen them before.
Who are these two that converse, and why for so long? Surely these two spies are engaged in a long, secret discussion.
Having reflected thus, the king dismissed his doorkeeper, summoned those two men, and having them seized, he had them bound.
On the second day, having summoned those two to his presence, he asked them: "Who are you two, who have been here so long, and what was that extensive counsel of yours?"
Then, when the two of them had been questioned there by the king himself and had requested his protection from fear, one of them, a young man, began to speak.
Listen, O Lord; I shall now describe this to you exactly as it happened. There was a Brahmin named Karabhaka in this very city of yours.

O Great King, I am that very son born from the propitiation of the sacrificial fire performed by that preeminent hero out of a desire for a son, and I am the offspring of one who was learned in the knowledge of the Vedas.
And when my father had passed away, followed by his wife, I—though having completed my studies—abandoned my own path due to being without a protector.
I became engaged in gambling and the practice of the science of weapons; for whose childhood is not unrestrained when it is devoid of the teacher’s instruction?
When my childhood had passed away in that sequence, and the intoxication of youth had arisen within me, I once went to the forest to discharge my arrows.
Just then, a bride emerged from the city along that same path; she had arrived mounted upon a palanquin, accompanied by a large retinue of kinsmen.
And at that very moment, a wild elephant, its chains suddenly snapped, arrived from somewhere and rushed toward that very bride in a state of rut.
Out of fear of that, all his followers abandoned her and fled from there along with her husband, being as cowardly as they were.
Seeing that, I suddenly thought with agitation: "Alas! How can these cowards have abandoned this poor woman?"
Therefore, I shall protect this defenseless woman from this elephant; for what is the use of life or manliness if it is devoid of the power to save those who have fallen into distress?
Thus, having uttered a roar, I rushed toward that lordly elephant; the elephant, too, abandoning that woman, charged straight at me.
Then, while being watched by that terrified woman, I roared and, fleeing away, drew that elephant far off.
Gradually reaching a thick branch of a great tree that had been broken off, I covered myself with it and went into the middle of the tree.
Having placed that branch across the front there with great agility, I fled; and that elephant crushed the branch to pieces.
Then I quickly went near that woman and asked about the well-being of her body, for she was terrified here.
Seeing me, she too, both pained by grief and filled with joy, then said: "What good fortune is mine that I have been given to such a base man?"
O Lord, he who has gone away somewhere, abandoning me in such a crisis—this alone is fortunate, that you have been seen again unharmed.
Who was that husband of mine? You are now my husband, by whom I was rescued from the jaws of death without regard for his own life.
"And here is my husband seen coming along with his servants; therefore, you must now follow behind us at your own pace."
"For once we have found an opportunity and met together, we shall go wherever we please. When she had spoken thus, I agreed, saying, "So be it."
"Though she be beautiful and though my soul be surrendered to her, what is the use of this woman who belongs to another?"—this is the path of fortitude, not of one possessed by youth.
Having arrived in an instant, that young woman was honored by her husband, and she gradually began to depart with him and his servants.
And I, having received provisions from him, went secretly by another path and traveled a long distance behind him without being noticed.
And she, falsely claiming on the road a pain produced by the broken limbs resulting from falling in fear of the elephant, avoided even the touch of her husband.
Whose heart would a woman—intent on passion, deeply rooted within, unbearable like internal poison, and distorted like a venomous serpent—not afflict by her very presence?
And in due course, we reached that city of Lohanagara, where the house of our master and his wife was located, and where they lived by means of trade.
We all remained there that day outside the abode of the gods, and it was there that this second Brahmin friend joined us.
Even on the ship, we both gained mutual confidence; for the mind knows the affection of living beings acquired in previous births.
Then I revealed my entire secret to him; having understood it, he spoke to me freely at that time as follows.
Be silent; there is a means here for the sake of which you have come, for there exists here the sister of this merchant's wife, who is her husband.
Having understood my purpose, she is now prepared to go from here with me; therefore, with her assistance, I shall accomplish what you desire.
Having said this to me, that Brahmin went then into private with the merchant’s wife, his sister-in-law, and informed her of the matter exactly as it was.
On another day, having made an agreement, that sister-in-law approached her brother's wife and led her into the interior of a temple there.
Then, while we were staying on the boat in the middle of it, she immediately made my friend assume the dress of that brother's wife.
Having dressed him in that same attire and taken him with him, he entered another house along with his brother, having made an agreement regarding our business.
And having departed from there, I arrived in due course at this city of Ujjayinī together with that merchant's wife who was dressed in male attire.
Then, that sister-in-law departed from that house with him during the night, while the people were intoxicated and asleep following the festivities of that day.
Then, taking her with him, he arrived at this city by means of secret journeys; thus we two have met here.
Thus, we two obtained both wives in the full bloom of youth—those sisters-in-law and brothers' wives, who had offered themselves out of their own affection.
Therefore, O King, we suspect that in every dwelling there is danger; for whose mind would feel secure when it has been subjected to arbitrary violence?
And while we two were consulting in secret for a long time—for the sake of maintaining our status and for the sake of wealth—the King saw us from afar.
Having seen them, they were brought here and detained under suspicion of being spies; today they were questioned regarding their history, and that is what has been told by me.
When the god had thus spoken, saying "He has power now," King Vikramasiṃha then addressed both those brahmins.
"I am pleased with you both; let there be no fear. Stay right here in this city, and I myself shall provide you with sufficient wealth."
Having said this, the king granted them their livelihood as they desired; and the two of them, accompanied by their wives, remained happily in his presence.

Thus, even though men dwell in such activities which are devoid of strong moral courage, kings nevertheless find satisfaction in those who possess the wealth of daring and are endowed with intelligence, becoming devoted to the act of giving.

Thus, by the power of their own karma—whether auspicious or inauspicious—both manifest in this life and previously performed, every being in this creation, including gods and asuras, shall eternally experience various enjoyments corresponding to that very karma.

O Goddess, that flame which you saw here entering your belly—resembling a dream-scene as it fell from the sky—is surely some kind of divine being who has entered your womb due to the power of karma from somewhere unknown.
Having heard this from the mouth of her husband, King Kaliṅgadatta, Queen Tārādattā, now pregnant, attained supreme joy.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave: Then, in Takṣaśilā, Queen Tārādattā, languid from the weight of her pregnancy, gradually became [heavy with child] for King Kaliṅgadatta.
With her face pale and her pupils trembling, she, whose delivery was near, resembled the eastern quarter that follows the rising crescent moon.
And before long, a daughter was born to her, peerless and like a brush for painting the creation of all beauty by the Creator himself.
As if thinking, "Why was no son like this not born? the protective lamps, filled with affection, became lusterless, surpassed by the radiance of his splendor.
And her father, Kaliṅgadatta, seeing that she had been born in such a state, became despondent at the futility of his hopes for a son with her beauty.
Even considering her to be divine, he, desiring a son, was tormented; for where is the root of sorrow—a daughter—and where is the joy of a living son?
Then, weary and seeking diversion for his mind, that lord of the earth departed from the palace and went to a monastery containing various images of the Jina.
There, in one part of that place, he heard these words being spoken by a monk who was a reciter of the Dharma, seated in the midst of the people.
They say that the giving of wealth alone is the greatest austerity in saṃsāra; the giver of wealth is declared to be the giver of life, for lives are pinned to wealth.
By the Buddha, whose mind was agitated by compassion for the sake of others, even his own self was given away like a blade of grass; what need is there to mention wretched wealth?
And by such steadfast austerity, having become free from longing and having attained divine insight, he became a Buddha and reached the state of Buddhahood.
Therefore, until death, a wise person should act for the benefit of sentient beings by turning back from all desired objects, in order to attain perfect enlightenment.
And so, formerly, to a certain king named Kṛtanāman, there were born in succession seven exceedingly beautiful daughters.
And those very girls, out of detachment, abandoned their father's house and resorted to the cremation ground; when questioned, they spoke thus to their attendants.
This entire universe is indeed devoid of essence, and within it, this body is likewise; even therein, the pleasure of union with the beloved and so forth is but a delusion like a dream.
In this cycle of existence, one thing alone is said to be essential; therefore, even with this very body, we shall work for the welfare of sentient beings.
"O Jīvadeva, let us cast this body into the cemetery for the use of the hosts of flesh-eaters; for what is the use of even such a beautiful one?"
And likewise, in former times, there was a certain prince here who became dispassionate; though he was young and very handsome, he took up the life of a wandering mendicant.
Once, that monk entered the house of a certain merchant and was seen by his young wife, whose eyes were as long as lotus petals.
Her heart captivated by the beauty of his eyes, she said to him: "How is it that such a painful vow as this has been undertaken by you?"
"Blessed is that woman who is gazed upon by this eye of yours. Having been thus addressed by her, the monk plucked out one eye.
And he said, taking it in his hand: "Mother, look at such a loathsome thing—blood and flesh; take it, if it pleases you."
"Tell me, what is so beautiful about these two that they are just like that? When she was addressed thus by him, the merchant's wife looked at them and despaired.
And she said: "Alas! A sin has been committed by me, an unfortunate woman, in that I became the cause for the plucking out of your eyes."
Having heard that, the monk said: "O mother, let there be no distress for you; for you have indeed rendered me a great service, so listen to an illustration."
Long ago, O beloved, there was a certain ascetic in a certain grove by the Ganges, who desired to test the very limit of dispassion.
And while he was performing austerities, a certain king happened by fate to arrive at that very place to enjoy himself together with the women of his harem.
Having stayed there, while the king was fast asleep from drinking, those queens rose from his side and, out of restlessness, wandered about in his garden.
And seeing that sage established in meditative absorption in one part of that place, they stood surrounding him out of curiosity, wondering, "What is this?"
After they had remained there for a long time, the king then woke up; not seeing his beloveds by his side, he wandered everywhere.
And there he saw those queens standing surrounding the sage; enraged by jealousy toward him, he struck the sage with his sword.
What could sovereignty, envy, cruelty, intoxication, and lack of discernment not accomplish individually? What need is there to mention their combined power when they possess all five limbs?
Then, after that king had departed, a certain deity appeared there and spoke to the sage, whose limbs were cut off, who remained free from anger.
O Great-souled One, if you agree to that, I shall slay with my own power that wicked person through whose anger this was done to you.
Having heard that, the sage said: "O Queen, do not speak thus; for he is my companion in dharma, not one who would cause me displeasure."

O Goddess, by his grace I have obtained from the Blessed One the dharma of forbearance, which has patience as its vehicle; whom would I not forgive, and for what reason, if he were not to act in such a way?
What anger can there be for a wise person on account of this perishable body? For equanimity toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, and patience, are indeed the state of Brahman.
Having been addressed thus by the sage, she, gratified by his asceticism, made her limbs free from wounds and vanished.
Just as that king was considered a benefactor to that seer because he caused the plucking out of his eyes, so too, O Mother, are you a benefactor to me through your increase of ascetic merit.
Having spoken thus to the humble merchant’s wife, that self-controlled monk, remaining indifferent even toward his own beautiful body, departed for the sake of spiritual perfection.
Therefore, what attachment can there be for this body, which is both foolish and beautiful yet subject to decay? For the wise, only service to sentient beings is praised as arising from it.
Therefore, let us cast off this little body here in this cemetery, this natural abode of happiness, for the sake of living beings.
Having spoken thus to her retinue, the seven princesses did exactly so, and thereafter they attained supreme perfection.
Thus, the wise have no sense of "mine" even toward their own bodies; how much less, then, toward the heap of grass that is the possession of children, wives, and the like?
Having heard these and other such words from the reciter of the Dharma in the monastery, King Kaliṅgadatta spent the day and departed for his own palace.
While the king was there, tormented once again by the impurity resulting from the birth of a daughter, he was addressed by a certain twice-born man who had grown old in his household:
O King, why do you grieve over the birth of this jewel of a daughter? Daughters are even superior to sons; they are auspicious both in this world and the next.
What reliance can kings place on those sons who are greedy for the kingdom—alas, they who devour their own father like young monkeys?
But the kings [were surpassed] by Kuntibhoja, who—through the virtues of his daughter Kuntī and the others—overcame the humiliation inflicted by Duḥsaha, Durvāsas, and others.
And as for that fruit which comes from giving away one's daughter, how could it come from a son in the next world? Listen, therefore, as I tell you here the story of Sulocanā.
There was once a young king named Suṣeṇa on Mount Citrakūṭa, who was like a second Kāma created by the Creator out of envy for the Three-eyed God.
At the foot of that great mountain, he created a divine grove, which brought weariness to the dwellers of the Nandana garden of the gods.
And in its center, he constructed a pond filled with blossoming lotuses, which was like a fresh field of nine-fold wealth for the play-lotuses of Lakṣmī.
And he remained forever on the bank of that river, which possessed stairs made of excellent jewels, without a wife because of the absence of any consort worthy of him.
Once, by chance, the celestial beauty Rambhā came through the sky along that path from the abode of Indra.
There she beheld the king sporting in that garden, like the god Madhu himself in the midst of a forest of blossoming trees.
Is this the moon fallen from heaven after the splendor had fallen into the lotus of a pond? Or rather, it is not so; for his splendor is indeed unfailing.
Surely this is that flower-arrowed god, desiring flowers, who has come to the garden; but where has his companion Rati gone?
Thus, having descended from the midst of the sky with a display born of longing, Rambhā approached that king in human form.
And seeing her suddenly approaching, the king was filled with wonder and thought: "Aha! Who might this be, possessed of such an inconceivable form?"
She cannot be human, since her feet do not touch the dust and her eyes do not blink; therefore, she must be some kind of divine being.
However, she must not be questioned by me, for she might otherwise flee; generally, divine beings are unable to endure the breaking of their pleasure when it occurs through some cause.
Meditating thus, the king, having conversed with her, at that very moment attained an embrace of her neck in that same sequence.
And he sported there for a long time together with that apsarā; she too did not remember heaven, for lovely love is not a matter of one's birthplace.
That ground of the king was filled with heaps of gold rained down by the Yakṣiṇīs who were his friends, as if the sky were filled with the peaks of Mount Meru.
And in due time, that excellent Apsaras, having conceived, gave birth to a daughter for King Suṣeṇa who was unlike any other.
And as soon as she had given birth, she said to that lord of the earth: "O King, this curse of mine has been such that it has now come to an end."
"I am indeed Rambhā, a celestial nymph; having fallen in love with you upon seeing you, we shall depart at that very moment once the child has been conceived."
Such is our agreement; therefore, you must protect this maiden. Through this marriage, our reunion shall take place again in heaven.
Having spoken thus, the Apsaras Rambhā vanished, rendered helpless; and because of that grief, the king then became intent on giving up his life.
Did Viśvāmitra, though free from worldly attachment, not even give up his life when Menakā had departed immediately after giving birth to Śakuntalā?
Having been addressed in this manner by his ministers, the king, who understood their meaning, slowly regained his composure and once again took up the maiden as the cause for their reunion.
And her father, his mind fixed solely upon that girl who was beautiful in every limb, gave her the name Sulocanā because of the exquisite beauty of her eyes.
In due time, a young sage named Vatsakāśyapa, wandering at will, beheld her standing in a garden, having reached the bloom of youth.
Although he was a mass of ascetic power, upon merely seeing this princess, he became acquainted with the essence of passion and thought to himself:
"Oh, how truly marvelous is the beauty of this maiden! If she does not become my wife, what other fruit is there for my asceticism?"
While the young sage was thus meditating, he was beheld by that beautiful-eyed woman, blazing with splendor like a smokeless fire.
Beholding him, who held a rosary and a water-pot, she too, filled with affection, thought: "Who might this be—he is both tranquil and so handsome?"
Approaching as if to choose him, she cast a garland of blue lotuses upon the sage’s body and offered her salutation.
"Obtain a husband"—this was the blessing bestowed upon her by him, whose mind was subject to the command of the god of love, difficult for even gods and demons to overcome.
Then, her modesty plundered by the greed for that extraordinary form, she too spoke to that bull among sages with her face bowed down.
"If this desire of yours is not without reproach, then, O Lord, let my father, the king, be entreated as the donor."
Then, having learned of her lineage from her attendants, the sage went to her father, King Suṣeṇa, and requested her hand.
Having honored him with hospitality, the king, seeing that young son of a sage who had reached the highest excellence through his asceticism and physical form, spoke to him.
"O Blessed One, this maiden was born to me from the Apsaras Rambhā; through her marriage, my union with her shall take place in heaven."
As she was thus ascending to heaven like Rambhā, she spoke to me: "O illustrious one, let it be investigated how this might come to pass."
Having heard that, the son of the sage reflected thus for a moment: "Was not Pramadvarā, born of Menakā, formerly bitten by a serpent?"
Having given half of his life, did the sage Ruru not take a wife? And was the hunter Triśaṅku not led to heaven by Viśvāmitra?
"By expending a portion of my own ascetic merit, why should I not do this? Having reflected thus, the sage said, "This is no burden," and spoke.
"O deities, by means of my own portion of ascetic merit, let this king go to heaven in his physical body for the sake of attaining union with Rambhā."
When that sage had spoken thus while the royal assembly was listening, a clear divine voice then arose from there, saying, "So be it."
Then, having given his daughter Sulocanā to that sage Kāśyapa as a bride for his son, the king ascended to heaven.
Having attained divinity there, he took delight once more with Rambhā, who was appointed by Śakra and possessed divine power.
"O King, thus Suṣeṇa attained his life's purpose through the maiden; for maidens such as she descend into the homes of those like you."
Therefore, this certain divine maiden born in your house has surely fallen from her station due to a curse; hence, O Lord, do not grieve over her birth.
Having heard this story from the twice-born man who had grown old in his service, King Kaliṅgadatta abandoned his anxiety and was filled with joy.
And he gave that young daughter of his, who brought joy to the eyes and resembled a digit of the moon, the name Kaliṅgasenā.
Then, in her father’s house, that princess Kaliṅgasenā gradually grew up, surrounded by her playmates.
And she dwelt in palaces, in houses, and in forests, like a wave of the ocean of childhood consisting of the essence of play.
Then once, as she was traveling through the sky, the daughter of the Asura Māya, named Somaprabhā, beheld her standing on the palace roof, absorbed in play.
Beholding her, who was enchanting the minds of sages with her beauty, Somaprabhā, while still stationed in the sky, felt affection arise and thought:
Who is she? Is this the form of the moon, for how could her radiance exist by day? Or is she Rati? If so, where is Kāma? As for that maiden, I understand her to be none other than this.
"Someone here in Rājagṛha must be a divine being fallen by a curse; I know that surely there was friendship between her and me in a previous birth."
For this very reason my mind, agitated by excessive affection for her, speaks thus to me; therefore, it is right that I myself should once again make her my own chosen companion.
Reflecting thus, and fearing that the young woman might be terrified, Somaprabhā descended unobserved from the sky.
Resorting to the guise of a human maiden as a means of consolation, she gradually drew near to this Kaliṅgasenā.
"By good fortune, some princess of most wonderful form has come of her own accord to my side; she is a fitting companion for me."
Thus, upon seeing her, Kaliṅgasenā reflected for a moment, then rose with respect and embraced that Somaprabhā.
Having seated her, he asked after a moment for her lineage and name; and Somaprabhā said to him, "I will tell you everything; stay."
Then, through the very course of their conversation, friendship was established by those two with words, preceded by the grasping of each other's hands.
Then Somaprabhā said, "Friend, you are a princess; even with great difficulty can friendship with princes be maintained."
For they become excessively angry even at a slight offense; in this regard, I shall relate to you the story of the prince and the merchant's son.
In the city of Puṣkarāvatī, there was a king named Gūḍhasena, and it is said that he had only one son born to him.
Proud because he was an only son, that prince endured whatever his father did, whether it were auspicious or even inauspicious.
Once, while wandering in the grove, he saw the only son of the merchant Brahmadatta, whose wealth and appearance were equal to his own.
And upon seeing him, he immediately made him his own friend for the svayaṃvara; and at that very moment, the prince and the merchant's son became identical in appearance.
The two were unable to remain for long out of each other's sight; for affection quickly binds those who have been acquainted in a previous birth.
The prince never enjoyed that luxury which had been prepared for him at the very outset by the merchant's son.
Once, having first decided upon his marriage with his friends, that prince set out for Ahicchatra for the sake of the wedding.
