Mounted upon an elephant together with that friend and his army, he proceeded and, having reached the bank of the Ikṣumatī, took up residence there in the evening.
There, having indulged in drink at the rising of the moon and retired to his bed, he began to tell a story when requested by his own nurse.
Having begun their conversation, the nurse and the intoxicated man were overcome by sleep from fatigue; the merchant’s son, however, remained awake out of affection for her.
Then, while the others were asleep, that merchant’s son, remaining awake, heard a conversation in the sky like the private talk of women.
"This man has fallen asleep without finishing his story; therefore, I shall curse him. If he sees the necklace in the morning and takes it," [he thought].
"By this [man] clinging to his throat, he will meet death at that very moment. Having said this, one woman fell silent, and then the second spoke:
Therefore, if he has crossed over, he will see the mango tree; he will partake of its fruits and thereafter be deprived of his life.
Having said this, she too ceased speaking; then the third one spoke: "If he has even crossed over this [obstacle], then let him go home for the sake of marriage."
"If he enters, that very thing will fall upon his back to kill him. Having said this, she too turned back; then the fourth spoke.
Therefore, even if he has crossed over, once he has entered the residence of Vāsava at night, he will immediately sneeze a hundred times.
If no one here were to say "Live! even a hundred times, then he would fall under the power of death.
"If he who heard this should speak of it for the sake of protecting him, his death too will come," she said, and then she turned back.
And the merchant’s son, having heard all that, as terrible as a thunderclap, was agitated by affection for the prince and reflected:
Fie on this story that has begun but remains untold, if the deities, having arrived unobserved to listen, should instead curse us out of curiosity!
"Therefore, now that this prince is dead, what purpose is there for me in my own life? Thus, saying 'He must be protected by me,' [the king] made his friend as dear to him as his own life."
"Even this account must not be told to him, lest I too incur blame because of it. Having reflected thus, the merchant's son passed the night with great difficulty.
The prince also set out in the morning accompanied by his friend; on the road, he saw that necklace ahead and desired to take it.
Then the merchant’s son said, "Friend, do not take the necklace; this is an illusion, for otherwise how could these soldiers not see it?"
Having heard that, the prince left him and, proceeding forward, saw a mango tree; he then desired to eat its fruits.
And as before, he was dissuaded from that course by the merchant's son; feeling inner distress, he proceeded slowly and reached his father-in-law’s house.
There, as he was entering the house made for the wedding, he was turned back at the door by that very friend; and in that very moment, the house collapsed.
Then, having somehow emerged from that with some confidence, the prince, accompanied by his bride, entered another dwelling at night.
Then, while that merchant's son had entered and remained there unobserved, he lay upon his bed and sneezed a hundred times.
Having uttered "Live long! to her here even a hundred times, the merchant's son, his purpose accomplished, went out joyfully at his own will.
And as he was departing, the prince, accompanied by his bride, saw him; with his affection for him forgotten due to jealousy, he spoke angrily to the gatekeepers:
"This evil-souled man has entered my inner apartments while I was in private; therefore, let him be bound and kept until he is apprehended at dawn."
Having learned of that, the merchant's son was bound by the guards and taken through the night; and as he was being led by them to the place of execution in the morning, he spoke to them.
"First, lead me for a moment into the presence of the prince, so that I may state a certain reason; thereafter, you may carry out my execution."
When he had spoken thus, those ministers went and informed the prince; and having been further enlightened by other counselors, the prince ordered her to be brought.
Having been brought there, he related the entire account to the prince; and he too, through that proof, believed it to be true, considering it as the falling down and rising again of his own house.
Then, being gratified by that friend who had been released from death, the prince returned to his own city, having taken a wife.
There, that friend of his, the merchant's son who had taken a wife, remained at ease while his virtues were being praised by all the people.
Thus having become unrestrained and crushing their own controllers, princes do not heed what is beneficial, like elephants in rut.
What friendship can there be with those Vetālas who snatch away one's life while laughing? Therefore, O Princess, never let our friendship falter.
Having heard this story from the mouth of Somaprabhā in the palace, Kaliṅgasenā affectionately replied to her friend.
"These are piśācas, O friend; they are not considered to be princes. Listen, for I shall tell you the story of the evil possession by a piśāca."
Long ago, in a brahminical settlement named Yajñasthala, there lived a certain twice-born man who was once impoverished; he went to the forest to gather wood.
There, a piece of wood being split by an axe fell by the force of fate; having struck his shank, it pierced through and entered inside.
Then, seeing him with blood flowing from his wounds and having fainted, he was lifted up by a certain man who recognized him and carried away to his home.
There, his agitated wife washed away his blood, comforted him, and bound a bandage upon his calf.
Then, even as he was being treated, his wound not only failed to heal day by day, but moreover turned into a sinus tract.
Then, distressed by that ulcerous sore, the poor man, intent on death, approached a certain Brahmin friend who spoke to him in private:
My friend, named Yajñadatta, having long been extremely destitute, performed a rite to propitiate a Piśāca, obtained wealth, and has remained happy ever since.
And since that means of accomplishment has been explained by him to me, you too, my friend, should therefore propitiate a Piśāca; he will heal your wound.
Having spoken thus, he who had received the mantra said to him: "Rising in the final watch of the night, with hair disheveled and naked as the sky, perform this rite."
Without having sipped water, and taking two handfuls of rice according to his capacity with both hands, he should go to a crossroads while reciting the mantra.
"O friend, having set aside two handfuls of rice from there, you should proceed in silence and must not look back."
Act thus always until the piśāca becomes manifest; he will say to you himself, "I shall indeed destroy your disease."
"Then he will welcome you, and he will take away your disease. Having been told this by that friend, the brahmin did exactly as instructed.
Then that Siddha Piśāca, having brought great medicinal herbs from the lord of mountains, the Himalayas, healed the wound of that suffering man.
Then, with the auspicious moment having arrived, he joyfully said to that brahmin: "Give me a second wound, so that I may heal it."
"If I do not cause you harm, I shall withdraw this body. Hearing that, the brahmin was terrified and immediately spoke to him for the sake of liberation.
"I shall inflict a second wound upon you in seven days," he said; thereupon, abandoned by him, that twice-born man became hopeless of his life.
Having spoken thus, Kaliṅgasenā ceased from the midst of her speech out of shame for having uttered such indecent words; then she spoke this again to Somaprabhā:
Then, seeing and questioning that distressed Brahmin, his daughter—who was clever and whose husband had died—spoke to him because she found an opening between his wounds.
"I shall deceive that Piśāca; go and say to him again: 'Let a sinus ulcer be inflicted upon my daughter by you.'"
Having heard that, the brahmin went away delighted; and having spoken exactly as he had been told, he then brought that piśāca into the presence of his daughter.
And she showed her own private parts to that piśāca, saying in secret, "O noble one, heal this wound of mine."
And that foolish piśāca constantly applied medicinal pastes and ointments to her noble limb, yet he was not able to heal it.
And after several days, becoming weary, he placed her two calves upon his own shoulders and examined that exquisite limb, wondering, "Is it not growing?"
When he saw a second wound beneath that one, the piśāca was immediately alarmed and thought to himself:
Before one wound has even healed, this other wound has arisen; the popular saying is true: "In times of vulnerability, misfortunes multiply."
From whom the worlds arise and by whom they go to their dissolution—who is capable of closing that path of saṃsāra which has been laid open?
Reflecting thus, and fearing imprisonment due to the realization that his purpose was thwarted, that foolish piśāca fled from there and vanished from sight.
And having thus deceived that piśāca, the Brahmin was released by his daughter; he remained at ease, as one who has emerged from a disease.
In this way, those fools and princes who are like piśācas bring about misfortune even when they have attained success; therefore, O friend, they must be guarded by means of wisdom.
"Princesses of noble lineage have never been heard of anywhere as being like this; therefore, my friend, you must not think otherwise regarding our union."
Having thus heard from the mouth of Kaliṅgasenā this account, which was full of laughter, wonder, and sweetness, Somaprabhā attained satisfaction in due order.
"My home is sixty yojanas from here, and the day is drawing to a close; I have stayed long enough, O slender one, so I must go," she said to her.

Then, as the lord of the day was slowly approaching the peak of the western mountain, Somaprabhā took leave of her affectionate friend and, having caused a momentary wonder by leaping into the path of the sky, she went straight to her own dwelling.

Having beheld that most wonderful and marvelous sight, which provoked many reflections, Kaliṅgasenā entered and thought to herself: "I do not know what this might be; could it be that my friend is indeed a Siddha woman, or perhaps an Apsaras, or even a Vidyādharī?"

Indeed, this divine power is unfailing, moving at will through the heights of the sky; and divine beings go into union with human women, drawn by their peerless affection. Did not Arundhatī share friendship with the daughter of King Pṛthu? And out of love for her, did not Pṛthu bring Surabhi from heaven down to the surface of the earth?

"By drinking her milk, did he not go to heaven even though he had fallen from his state? And have not flawless cows appeared on the earth ever since then? Therefore, I am fortunate that through the rise of my merit this divine friend has come to me; tomorrow morning, when she has arrived, I shall ask her very skillfully about her lineage and her name."
Thinking such things as these in her heart, Kaliṅgasenā passed that night there; and Somaprabhā, her mind once more eager for a sight of him, spent the night in her own dwelling.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. Then, in the morning, Somaprabhā [brought] a mechanical iron doll made of wood, which was designed to provide him with diversion.
Taking up the karaṇḍas, she, moving through the expanse of the sky, returned once more to the presence of Kaliṅgasenā.
Kaliṅgasenā, too, beholding her, was filled with tears of joy; rising up, she embraced her by the neck as she sat at her side and said:
O friend, without the sight of the full moon of your face, this night of three watches has passed for me as if it were a hundred watches, consisting entirely of darkness.
"What kind of connection must have existed between you and me in another birth, O Goddess, of which this is the result today? If you know, please tell me."
Having heard that, Somaprabhā spoke thus to the princess: "I possess no such supernatural knowledge; indeed, I do not remember my former birth."
And there are no sages here who possess supernormal knowledge; yet if some do know, it is because they previously performed such [practices], and they are knowers of the supreme reality.
When she had spoken thus, Kaliṅgasenā, filled with curiosity, again questioned her in that secluded place with words tender with love and confidence.
Tell me, friend, of which divine lineage is your father, by whose birth this family has been adorned as if by a well-rounded pearl?
O lady of auspicious marks, what is your name, which is like nectar to the ears of the world? For what purpose is this basket, and what object is contained within it?
Having thus heard these affectionate words from Kaliṅgasenā, Somaprabhā proceeded to relate everything in due order.
There is a great asura renowned throughout the three worlds named Maya; having abandoned his demonic nature, he has taken refuge in Śauri.
He granted him protection from fear, and he entered the assembly hall of the wielder of the thunderbolt; and the Daityas grew enraged toward him, thinking, "This one belongs to the side of the gods."
Out of fear of him, he constructed on the Vindhya mountain a palace within a cave of illusion, filled with many wonders and inaccessible even to the lords of the asuras.
"We have two daughters of that Maya who are practicing celibacy; the elder is a maiden named Svayaṃprabhā, who remains in his house."
"I am Somaprabhā by name, the youngest; such am I, my friend, given in marriage to the one named Nalakūbara, the son of Dhanada."
"I have been instructed here by my father in many kinds of magical contrivances; out of affection for you, this full casket has been brought by me."
Having said this, Somaprabhā, full of many wonders, opened up for her wooden mechanical dolls created by her own magic power.
Having traveled through the air with a mere stroke of her magic pin, she quickly returned, taking a garland of flowers by his command.
One brought water in that very manner by chance; another danced, and yet another engaged in conversation.
Having entertained her for some time with such great wonders as these, and having placed that mechanical casket under strict guard, he departed.
Then Somaprabhā, having taken leave of the longing Kaliṅgasenā, went through the air to her own palace, remaining devoted to her husband.
Kaliṅgasenā too, her hunger dispelled by the sight of that wonder, remained that day exceedingly joyful, turning away from all food.
Having seen that, her mother, suspecting illness, was examined by a physician named Ānanda and told without hesitation:
For some reason, her hunger has vanished through joy rather than from illness; her face, with its wide-open eyes, speaks thus as if it were smiling.
Having been addressed thus by the physician, her mother asked her the cause of her joy; she too related to her exactly what had occurred.
Then, perceiving her to be delighted by the company of her praiseworthy friends and congratulating her, her mother had her take food as was appropriate.
Then, on another day, having arrived and understood the matter in due order, Somaprabhā spoke in private to that very Kaliṅgasenā.
Having informed my friend of my intention to come to your side every day, I obtained permission from my husband, who is wise and understands the matter.
Therefore, you too should now obtain the permission of your parents, so that you may sport with me freely and without hesitation.
When she had spoken thus, Kaliṅgasenā took her by the hand at that very moment and went into the presence of her father and mother.
There, having first introduced her by name and lineage, she presented her friend Somaprabhā to her father, King Kaliṅgadatta.
And he showed her to his mother, Tārādattā, in the same manner; and having seen her just as described, they both rejoiced in her.
Then, both that husband and wife, delighted by her form, honored that beautiful great asura woman out of affection for their daughter and spoke to her.
"O child, this Kaliṅgasenā is now entrusted to your care; therefore, let both of you now enjoy yourselves as you desire."
Having welcomed these words of theirs, both Kaliṅgasenā and Somaprabhā then departed together from that place.
And they went to the monastery built by the king for their residence, and there they brought that basket containing the mechanical illusions.
Then, by means of her own magical power, Somaprabhā took a mechanical yakṣa and dispatched it to bring back the image of the Buddha.
That yakṣa, having traveled through the sky over a long distance, returned bringing with him a collection of pearls, excellent jewels, gold, and lotuses.
Having thus honored the Sugatas, Somaprabhā, together with her retinue, caused them to blaze there by means of that which bestows all wonders.
Having learned of this, King Kaliṅgadatta arrived with his queen; and having seen it, he was filled with wonder and asked her about the workings of the mechanical device.
Then, by the power of Soma, he said: "O King, these various arts, such as the mechanical contrivances of illusion and the like, were created for me by my father in the past."
Just as this machine of the world consists of the five elements, so too do all these machines; hear of them individually.
That machine which is primarily made of earth, such as a door and so forth, when it is closed, another person is unable to open it by means of that [machine].
The form produced by a water-engine appears as if it were alive; however, whatever engine consists of fire, that emits flames.
And it produces a wind-mechanism that performs movements such as coming and going, and it makes manifest speech arising from space.
"I have obtained these from my father; but as for that protective wheel-mechanism of Truth, my father alone knows it, and no one else."
As she was speaking these words, there arose the sound of conch shells being filled at midday, as if they were listening with faith to her speech.
Then, having requested the king to provide food suitable for her, and having obtained his permission, she placed him and her attendants in a mechanical celestial chariot.
Taking Kaliṅgasenā with her, Somaprabhā set out through the sky toward her father’s house, to the presence of her elder sister.
And in an instant, having reached her father’s palace situated on the Vindhya mountains, he led her to the side of his sister Svayaṃprabhā.
There Kaliṅgasenā beheld that self-luminous female ascetic, adorned with a mass of matted locks and wearing a long rosary of beads.
Clad in white garments, she was like the smiling Pārvatī, yet she had undertaken fierce ascetic practices despite being possessed of great enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
And Svayamprabhā, having herself performed the rites of hospitality for that princess named Somaprabhā who stood before her bowed in salutation, shared with her a meal of fruits.
"Friend, by eating these fruits, old age shall not come upon you; it will be like the frost's assault upon a lotus, destroying this perishable form."
"It was for this reason that I brought you here out of affection," Somaprabhā said to the princess.
Then Kaliṅgasenā ate those fruits there, and her limbs immediately became as if sprinkled by a shower of the essence of nectar.
And as she wandered there out of curiosity, she beheld a city garden containing ponds with golden lotuses and trees bearing fruits as sweet as nectar.

It was filled with various birds bright as gold, possessing the splendor of jeweled pillars; it produced the perception of walls in what is empty, and caused the cognition of emptiness within the wall.
Causing the perception of land upon water and the perception of water upon land, it was like an unprecedented other world fashioned by the magic of Maya.
This place had been entered previously by the monkeys while they were searching for Sītā; through the grace of Svayaṃprabhā, they had finally emerged after a long time.
Then, having taken leave of that Svayamprabhā—who had become a vessel for agelessness and was astonished by the extensive sight of that wonderful city—[he departed].
Having placed Kaliṅgasenā upon the mechanical device, Somaprabhā once again brought her through the air to her own residence in Takṣaśilā.
There, Kaliṅgasenā related everything to her parents exactly as it had happened, and they both attained the highest satisfaction.
Thus, as those two friends were passing their days, Somaprabhā once spoke to Kaliṅgasenā in this manner.
"As long as you are not yet married, let there be friendship between us; for once you have gone to your husband's house, how could I ever come there again?"
For the husband of one's friend is not to be seen, nor should he ever be accepted; like a she-wolf devouring the flesh of a lamb, the mother-in-law devours the daughter-in-law.

And so listen, for I shall tell you this story of Kīrtisenā. Long ago, in the city named Pāṭaliputra, there was a merchant who was the foremost among the wealthy; he was known by the truly appropriate name Dhanapālita.
And a daughter named Kīrtisenā was born to him, who was peerless in beauty and dearer to him than his own life.
And she, being of equal status with him, was given by him as a daughter to a merchant named Devasena, who possessed great prosperity in Magadha.
And that wicked woman, the mistress of the household, was the mother of that most virtuous Devasena, whose father had passed away.
Beholding her daughter-in-law Kīrtisenā, who was so highly esteemed by her husband, she burned with rage and, while her son was absent, tormented her.
And Kīrtisenā was not at all able to say that to her husband; for the condition of a wife who is dependent on a cruel and deceitful mother-in-law is indeed miserable.
Once, urged by her kinsmen, that husband of hers, Devasena, set out for the city of Valabhī on a trading expedition.
Then Kīrtisenā spoke thus to her husband: "O noble son, I have not told you this for so long."
"This mother of yours treats me with contempt even while you are present; I do not know what she might do to me when you have departed."
Having heard that, Devasena became greatly agitated; out of affection for her and filled with fear, he went slowly and, bowing down, spoke to his mother.
"O Mother, now that I am departing, you must not show any lack of affection toward Kīrtisenā in your hands; for she is indeed the daughter of a noble family."
Having heard that, her mother, with wide-open eyes, summoned Kīrtisenā and spoke at that moment to Devasena.
"What have I done? Ask him this; it is he who thus impels you, O son. You are a destroyer of the household, yet to me, both of you are equal."
Upon hearing this, that excellent merchant became peaceful in mind regarding her; for he was not one who could be deceived by his mother’s words of feigned affection.
But Kīrtisenā remained silent, her smile tinged with anxiety; meanwhile, on another day, that merchant Devasena set out for Valabhī.
Then, as she gradually succumbed to the suffering of separation from him, Kīrtisenā’s mother removed her maidservants from her side.
Having made an agreement with her own maidservant, who lived in the house, she had her brought into a secret inner room and stripped her of her clothes.
Having said, "You are taking my son away, you wicked woman! he seized her by the hair and, together with the maidservant, tore her apart with his feet, teeth, and claws.
And he cast her into an underground chamber that was provided with a lid and strong bolts, wherein the entire accumulation of wealth inherited from previous generations had been extracted.
And every day at the close of the day, that wicked woman placed half a bowl of rice for her husband inside it while he was in such a state.
And she thought, while her husband was still far away, "I shall say, 'She died of her own accord; lift her up and go,' after a few days."
Thus cast into an underground chamber by her wicked mother-in-law, Kīrtisenā, who deserved only happiness, reflected there while weeping:
Wealth, a husband, birth in a noble family, good fortune, and virtuous conduct—all these, alas, have turned into such a calamity for me through the grace of my mother-in-law!
And for this reason, relatives disparage the birth of daughters, fearing the terror caused by mothers-in-law and sisters-in-law, and the taints of misfortune and the like.
While she was thus lamenting, Kīrtisenā suddenly found a small spade in that underground chamber, as if the Creator had extracted a thorn from her mind.
With that iron [rod], she dug a tunnel there until, by fate, she emerged from her own dwelling.
And then, by means of that former lamp which had not been exhausted, she beheld that house illuminated by her own very dharma.
Having taken the garments and his own caste-mark at the end of the night, he departed secretly from there and went outside the city.
"It is not proper for me to go to my father's house in such a state; what shall I say there, and how will the people believe me?"
Therefore, by my own means, I must go to my husband's side; for in this world and the next, the husband alone is the sole refuge for virtuous women.
Reflecting thus, Kīrtisenā, having bathed in the waters of the lake there, assumed the full and magnificent attire of a prince.
Then, having gone to the market and purchased some gold for a small price, she stayed that day in the house of a certain merchant.
One day, a merchant named Samudrasena, who desired to go to Valabhī, formed a friendship there with her.
Together with him and his attendants, she set out toward Valabhī, having first departed to reach her husband who had already set out before her, while wearing the fine attire of a prince.
And he said to that merchant, "I am being harassed by my kinsmen; therefore, I shall go with you to Valabhī to be near my own people."
Having heard that, the merchant's son followed her on the road out of respect, thinking, "This must surely be some noble prince."
And that merchant caravan set out, following the forest path which had been abandoned by other people due to the fear of heavy tolls.
After several days, having reached the entrance of the forest and halted with the caravan at evening, a jackal let out a terrifying cry like a messenger of Death.
In that merchant community, which was skilled in such matters and apprehensive of the sudden onset of thieves and the like, every eye became an enemy with a weapon grasped in its hand on all sides.
Seeing that darkness, which resembled the vanguard and the troops of fleeing bandits, Kīrtisenā, dressed in male attire, reflected:
Alas! The karma of evildoers increases through its very continuity; behold, the calamity brought about by my mother-in-law has borne fruit even here for me.
First, as if by Death itself, I was devoured by my mother-in-law’s anger; thereafter, I entered an underground cellar, as if into another dwelling in a womb.
By fate, I emerged from there once more as if newly born; having returned here today, I have again fallen into a state where my life is in peril.
If I am killed here by thieves, my mother-in-law, who is my enemy, will tell your husband: "She has gone off somewhere else, attached to another man."
If I am recognized by anyone as a woman whose inner garments have been stolen, then death is better for me than the violation of my virtue.
Therefore, I must protect myself alone; this merchant friend need not be considered. For the duty of virtuous women is what must be guarded, not friends and the like.
Having thus resolved, she reached a pit shaped like a house situated among the trees, which seemed as if the earth had opened a passage out of compassion for her.
Having entered there and covered her body with grass, leaves, and other such things, she remained, sustaining herself through the longing for union with her husband.
Then, at midnight, a vast army of thieves suddenly descended with uplifted weapons and surrounded that caravan.
Then there arose a stormy day of battle, where the dark clouds were the shouting barbarians, the long flashes of lightning were the flames of weapons, and the showers of rain were blood.
Having slain Samudrasena, that lord of merchants, along with his followers, the powerful thieves then departed, taking away the accumulated wealth.
And at that time, Kīrtisenā heard the clamor; that she did not forcibly give up her life-breaths was due solely to fate.
Then, when the night had passed and the sun of fierce brilliance had risen, she emerged from that pit from within the midst of the branches.
Granted, for virtuous women who are devoted solely to their husbands and whose splendor is unswerving, even the gods themselves provide protection in times of distress.
That even when a lion saw her there in that desolate forest, he left her; moreover, no ascetic came from anywhere to approach her.
Having comforted her after she had asked for news and having given her water to drink from his water-pot, he pointed out the path to her and vanished somewhere.
Then, as if satiated by nectar and freed from hunger and thirst, that devoted wife set out upon the path described by the ascetic.
Then, seeing the sun mounted upon the peak of the setting mountain with its rays extended, as if saying, "Endure this one night," she—
He entered a hollow at the root of a great forest tree that resembled a house, and he closed its entrance with another piece of wood.
And at nightfall, she saw through a crack in the door that a terrible ogress had arrived there, accompanied by her sons, the young children.
"I have now crossed over misfortune; I have been devoured by her," thinking thus, the terrified rākṣasī climbed up that very tree.
And his sons, having climbed up after her, spoke to that Rākṣasī there at that very moment: "O Mother, give us some food."
Then that rākṣasī said to those children: "O little sons, even though I went to the great cemetery today, no food was obtained by me."
Although the host of ḍākinīs was entreated, they did not grant me a share therein; then, out of weariness with that, I petitioned Bhairava after making my request known.
And after asking me my name and lineage, the Lord commanded me thus: "O Bhayaṅkarī, you are of noble birth, born of the lineage of Khara and Dūṣaṇa."
Therefore, go from here to the city of Vasudatta, which is not very far away; there dwells a great king named Vasudatta who is devoted to righteousness.
He who, stationed at the border, protects this entire forest, himself collects the toll and suppresses the thieves.
And while that king was sleeping in the forest from the fatigue of hunting, a centipede unknowingly and swiftly entered his ear.
And she gave birth many times over the course of time within his head; because of that disease, this king now exists as nothing but sinews.
If his physicians do not recognize that disease, and if no one else should know it either, then he will perish in a few days.
When he has been destroyed by his own magic power, you should eat his flesh; by consuming it, you will remain fully satisfied for six months.
Thus, even by Bhairava, a distribution involving uncertainty and subject to time has been ordained for me today; O sons, what am I to do?
Thus addressed by that Rākṣasī, her sons then said to her: "Mother, now that this disease has been recognized and removed, does that king still live?"
"And tell me, how is such a disease as that to be removed? To those sons who had spoken thus, the Rākṣasī replied:
Once this disease has been identified and removed, that king will indeed live; hear now how this great malady of his is to be eliminated.
Having first anointed his head with ghee and applied warm clarified butter to it, he should place it for a long time in the midday sun when the heat is intense.
Having inserted a hollow bamboo tube into the cavity of his ear, which was connected to a hole in a shallow bowl placed upon the back of a jar filled with cold water;
Exhausted by sweat and heat, he emerged from within his head, entered that very bamboo tube through that same ear-cavity, and reached it.
Just as centipedes fall into a jar out of a desire for coolness, so shall that king be liberated from that great disease.
Having spoken thus to the Rākṣasī regarding her sons who were perched on the tree, she fell silent; and Kīrtisenā, staying within a hollow, heard all of that.
And having heard this, he reflected: "If I am to escape from this, then I shall go and restore that king to life by means of this very stratagem."
He protects this very forest with little toll while stationed at the border; and because of that convenience, all the merchants travel by this path.
The merchant Samudrasena, who had departed for heaven, said this: "Therefore, my husband will come back by this very same path."
Therefore, having gone to the edge of the forest to the city of Vasudattapura, I shall deliver the king from his illness and, remaining there, await my husband's arrival.
Reflecting thus, she passed that night with great difficulty; when the Rākṣasas had vanished in the morning, she emerged from the hollow of the tree.
Then, proceeding gradually through the middle of the forest while wearing male attire, she saw a virtuous cowherd as the afternoon arrived.
Approaching him, who was already distressed by his journey over such a long distance due to his extreme delicacy, she asked, "Tell me, what region is this?"
That cowherd also said: "This city standing before you is named Vasudattapura, belonging to King Vasudatta."
The king, that great-souled one, remained there afflicted by disease and on the verge of death; having heard this, Kīrtisenā spoke to that cowherd.
If someone leads me into the presence of that king, then I know how to cure him of his malady.
Upon hearing this, the cowherd said: "I am going to this very city; therefore, come with me while I make an effort on your behalf."
When Kīrtisenā had said, "So be it," the cowherd Vasudatta led her away at that very moment, disguised as a man, to the city of Vasudatta.
Having thus presented that object there at that very moment, he entrusted her, who possessed auspicious marks, to the doorkeeper.
The doorkeeper, having informed the king, ushered that blameless woman into his presence by the king's command.
And King Vasudatta, though afflicted by disease there, became comforted the moment he beheld her of such wondrous form; for one knows for oneself what is beneficial and what is harmful.
And he said to her while she was in male attire: "O one of auspicious marks, if you remove this affliction from me, I shall grant you half of my kingdom."
I know that in a dream a woman took away from my back a black woolen blanket; therefore, it is certain that you will remove this disease of mine.
Having heard that, Kīrtisenā said to him: "O King, today's day has passed; tomorrow I shall remove your illness. Do not speak thus in distress."
Having said this, he had cow’s ghee applied to the head of the king; by that means, sleep came upon him and that intense pain departed.
"This is some god who has come to us through our merits in the form of a physician"—thus did they all then praise Kīrtisenā there.
And the queen-mother attended upon her with various services; she also provided her with a separate residence at night, complete with female attendants.
Then, on the following day at midday, while the ministers and the women of the inner apartments were looking on, Kīrtisenā dragged that king away.
A hundred centipedes emerged from the path of her ear through her head, by means of that most wonderful stratagem previously devised by the Rākṣasī.
Having placed those centipedes into a small jar, she then satisfied the king by sprinkling him with ghee, milk, and other liquids.
When the king had gradually recovered his composure and was freed from illness, who among those present was not struck with wonder upon seeing those living beings inside the jar?
And the king, beholding those worms emerged from his head, was terrified, reflected, rejoiced, and considered his own birth to be renewed.
Having celebrated the festival and performed his ritual ablutions, he honored Kīrtisenā—who had shown no regard for half the kingdom—with villages, elephants, horses, and gold.
The queen and the ministers filled him with gold and garments, saying, "This physician, who has restored the life of our lord, is worthy of honor."
And she placed those objects in the hands of that very king, saying, "I am observing a vow for some time," while looking toward her husband.
Then, while being honored there by everyone, she remained for some days in the guise of a man, as Kīrtisenā.
Then, from that very place, she heard from the people that her own husband, the caravan leader Devasena, had arrived at Valabhī by way of that same road.
Then, having learned that the caravan had arrived in the city, she went out to meet him; and she beheld her husband as a peahen beholds a fresh rain-cloud.
With his very mind, which dissolved the long-standing fever of longing and offered a libation of tears of joy, he fell at his feet.
And he too recognized her upon observing her, though she was disguised in dress, as her husband did, for she possessed a splendor as formidable as the sun's rays—like the lunar form appearing by day.
As Devasena gazed upon that moon-like face of the moonstone, it was a marvel that his heart did not melt away.
Then, while Kīrtisenā stood there with her true nature thus revealed, and her husband remained filled with wonder, wondering "What is this?", [the following occurred].
When the merchant community was astonished upon learning of that, King Vasudatta himself, filled with wonder, reportedly came there in person.
Questioned by him, Kīrtisenā related her entire story before her husband, beginning with the misconduct of her mother-in-law.
And Devasena, her husband, having heard that, turned his face away from his own mother, filled with anger, forbearance, astonishment, and joy.

Victorious are the virtuous wives, whose devotion to their husbands is firmly established, who are protected by the armor of moral conduct, who have dharma as their charioteer, and for whom wisdom is their weapon.
Thus, having heard that wondrous account of Kīrtisenā’s life, all the people standing there spoke with joy.
The king also said: "By this Queen Sītā, who has endured suffering for the sake of her husband, even Rāma—who brought her such hardship—has been surpassed."
Then Kīrtisenā said to the king, who had spoken thus: "This sister of mine is the one who gave me my life."
"O King, that gift of your favor which has remained in my hands—the village, the elephants, the horses, the jewels, and so forth—let it be bestowed upon my husband."
Having been addressed thus by her, the king, being pleased, gave those villages and other gifts to him, and he bound the turban of honor upon his husband, Devasena.

Then, with his treasury forcibly filled by those riches bestowed by the king and those earned through trade, Devasena—having left his mother behind and dwelling in that very city—remained there, praising Kīrtisenā with floods of wealth.

Kīrtisenā, whose fame was won by her peerless conduct, having reached that place which was free from the wicked mother-in-law and where she enjoyed all pleasures and sovereignty, dwelt there like the very abundance of the fruits of merit embodied in a physical form beside her husband.

Thus, having endured the decree of adverse fate, virtuous women who have protected the wealth of their conduct in times of calamity—being guarded by the greatness of their own inner strength—bring about the welfare of both their husbands and themselves.

"O Princess, such are the many faults inflicted upon brides by mothers-in-law and sisters-in-law. Therefore, I entreat you for a husband's house where there is no mother-in-law and no treacherous sister-in-law."
Having heard this wonderful and delightful tale from the mouth of Somaprabhā, the daughter of the Asura king, Kaliṅgasenā, the princess, was filled with joy.
Then, seeing that the discourse on various matters had come to an end, and as they were about to depart, Somaprabhā embraced the longing Kaliṅgasenā and went to her own abode.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave. Then, out of affection for Somaprabhā—who had gone to her own home—[Vijayā] remained on the roof of the palace road to watch after her path.
From the sky, a young lord of the Vidyādharas named Madanavega happened by chance to see Kaliṅgasenā nearby.
As soon as he saw her, who could enchant the three worlds with her beauty, he fell into agitation, like a magician at the sight of his own wand.
Enough with the women of the Vidyādharas; what need is there even to mention the Apsarases? For such is this wondrous beauty of this mortal woman.
Therefore, if she were not my wife, what would life be worth to me? And how could I, even as a Vidyādhara, consort with a mere mortal woman?
Having reflected thus, he meditated upon the vidyā named Prajñapti; and she, appearing visibly before him, then spoke to him in this way.
In truth, she is not a human being; she is an Apsaras fallen by a curse, born in the house of King Kaliṅgadatta, O fortunate one.
When this was said by Vidyā, the Vidyādhara, delighted, went to his own abode; turning away from all else and tormented by love, he reflected:
If I carry her off by force, that would not be right for me; for there is a death-dealing curse upon me regarding the forcible enjoyment of women.
To attain this, Śambhu must be propitiated by me through austerity; for spiritual perfections depend upon austerity, and no other means is known to exist.
Having thus resolved, he went to Mount Ṛṣabha on another day and, standing on one foot without food, performed austerities.
Then, soon after, the Lord of Ambikā, pleased by his intense austerities, granted him an audience and thus commanded Madanavega:
This girl named Kaliṅgasenā is renowned on earth for her beauty; yet there is no husband even equal to her in the perfection of her form.
There is, however, a King Vatsa who desires her; yet, out of fear of Vāsavadattā, he does not openly ask for her.
This princess too, being fond of beauty, having heard this from the mouth of Somaprabhā, desires the King of Vatsa for herself as her husband by choice.
In that interval, before her marriage could take place, he assumed the form of the Lord of Vatsa, who was as if unable to endure the delay.
"Having gone there, you should take this woman as your wife according to the Gāndharva rite; in this way, the beautiful Kaliṅgasenā will become yours."
Having been thus commanded by Śarva, Madanavega prostrated before him and then departed for his own home on the slope of Mount Kālakūṭa.
In the meantime, she traveled by night to her own palace and returned every dawn by means of a machine that moves through the air.
Once, while Kaliṅgasenā was sporting with Somaprabhā in the city of Takṣaśilā, she spoke to her in private.
"O friend, you must not tell this to anyone: listen, for I know that my marriage has arrived."
"Many kings have sent messengers here to ask for me; they were turned away by my father and sent back from here in that very same manner."
As for the king named Prasenajit who resides in Śrāvastī, he was merely his messenger, yet he was honored by him with great respect.
Since even Ambā has consecrated him with mantras, I consider that king to be my chosen husband; he is likewise esteemed by my father and mother as one of noble lineage.
For he was born into that family where Ambā, Ambālikā, and the others—the grandmothers of both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas—were born.
"O friend, it is now settled that my father has given me to King Prasenajit in the city of Śrāvastī."
Having heard this from Kaliṅgasenā, Somaprabhā wept immediately with a torrent of tears, as if creating another necklace out of her grief.
Having beheld the entire world of mortals, that daughter of the Asura Maya spoke to her friend who was asking the cause of her tears.
"O friend, regarding the qualities sought in a bridegroom—namely age, appearance, lineage, character, and wealth—the first is age; after that come lineage and the rest."
And King Prasenajit was seen by me to be advanced in years; what is the use of the lineage of one who is as decayed as a jasmine flower?
O Hemantā, by that [season] white as snow, you will become pitiable, like a lotus pond whose lotus-faces have withered, joined with such a one.
Therefore, despondency has arisen in me; yet, O auspicious lady, joy would come to me if that Udayana, the King of Vatsa, were to become your husband.
For there is indeed no other king on earth equal to him in beauty, charm, lineage, valor, and sovereign power.
If you are united with such a husband, O slender-waisted one, then the Creator’s craftsmanship of beauty bears fruit in you.
Thus, impelled by the words fashioned by Somaprabhā as if by mechanical devices, Kaliṅgasenā’s heart went toward the Lord of Vatsa.
Then she asked that princess, the daughter of Maya: "Friend, who is this man called the King of Vatsa, and from what lineage is he descended?"
"And how was he named Udayana? Tell me that," [she said]. Then Somaprabhā replied, "Listen, friend, I shall tell you."
There is a famous land known as Vatsa, an ornament of the earth; there lies the city of Kauśāmbī, like a second Amarāvatī.
He rules his kingdom there; therefore, O blessed lady, listen as I recount the lineage of that Lord of Vatsa.
It is said that Abhimanyu was the son of the Pāṇḍava Arjuna; by him, through his breaking of the wheel-array, the Kuru army was brought to destruction.
From him was born Parīkṣit, the sustainer of the Bharata lineage and king; from him also came Janamejaya, the one who instituted the snake sacrifice.
From him was born Śatānīka, who dwelt in Kauśāmbī; he was the one who perished after slaying the Daityas in the host of gods and asuras.
Therefore, that king became celebrated throughout the world as Sahasrānīka, he who, having been sent a chariot by Śakra, traveled back and forth between heaven and earth.
To him, by his queen Mṛgāvatī, was born this King Udayana, an ornament to the lunar dynasty and a festival for the eyes of the world.
Hear also the cause of his name: for she was Mṛgāvatī, the pregnant mother of this noble-born king.
Having developed a pregnancy craving for a bath in blood, she was made to bathe in a pool of lac juice and other substances prepared by her husband, who was afraid of sin.
A bird of the Tārkṣya lineage, swooping down with the suspicion that it was meat, carried her off; by the power of destiny, she was released alive upon the Udaya mountain.
There she was seen by the sage Jamadagni staying in that hermitage; he comforted her further, speaking of her reunion with her husband.
For a certain period of time, indeed, such a curse arose from Tilottamā toward her husband, born of his contemptuous jealousy, which resulted in separation from her.
And after some days, she gave birth to a son right there in the hermitage of Jamadagni, just as the sky gives birth to the newborn moon upon the mountain of sunrise.
This Udayana has been born as a sovereign lord of the earth, and a son shall be born to him who will be the ruler of all the Vidyādharas.
Then, after this bodiless voice had been uttered from the sky, the gods gave him the name Nāgodayana because of his birth from Udaya.
Bound by hope for the end of his curse and informed by Mātali, Sahasrānīka passed the time with great difficulty without that Mṛgāvatī.
When the end of the curse arrived, by the power of fate, he obtained his own token of recognition from a Śabara who had come from the Mountain of Sunrise.
At that moment, having been informed by a voice arisen from the sky, he proceeded toward the Mountain of Sunrise, placing that Śabara at his head.
There, having obtained Mṛgāvatī as his wife—like the fulfillment of a long-cherished desire—and that son Udayana, who was like a kingdom of the mind, he rejoiced.
Then, taking them both and arriving at Kauśāmbī, he—satisfied by the excellence of that son's virtues—consecrated him in the position of crown prince.
And he gave him the sons of his ministers, beginning with Yaugandharāyaṇa; with that burden taken up by them, he enjoyed pleasures for a long time in the company of his wives.
In due time, having installed his son Udayana upon the throne, the aged king, together with his wife and ministers, departed upon the Great Path.
Thus, having obtained that ancestral kingdom and conquered the entire earth, Udayana, with Yaugandharāyaṇa as his companion, rules over the world.
Having quickly related this story in private, Somaprabhā spoke again in this manner to her friend Kaliṅgasenā.
O fair-limbed one, he is called the King of Vatsa because of his sovereignty over the Vatsas; likewise, he surpasses the Pāṇḍavas in age, prosperity, and as a scion of the Lunar dynasty.
He was called Udayana by the gods because of his birth at sunrise; even Kandarpa himself is not his equal in beauty within this world.
O most beautiful woman in the three worlds, he alone is your equal as a husband; and he, greedy for your beauty, will surely desire you when you are sought after.
But, my friend, there is a chief queen named Vāsavadattā, born from the loins of King Caṇḍamahāsena.
Likewise, having abandoned his kinsmen out of excessive passion, he was chosen by Uṣā, Śakuntalā, and other maidens who had cast aside their modesty.
In her was born his son named Naravāhanadatta, who was indeed ordained by the gods as the future sovereign of the Vidyādharas.
Therefore, that Lord of Vatsa, fearing her, does not ask you for her here; moreover, she has been seen by me, and she does not rival you in the perfection of her beauty.
When her friend Somaprabhā had spoken thus, Kaliṅgasenā, full of longing for the Lord of Vatsa, replied to her.
"I know this to be the will of my parents; but what can I do? Since she is omniscient and possesses great power, she alone is my refuge in this matter."
"This matter depends on destiny; therefore, hear a story regarding this. Having said this to Somaprabhā, he related this tale to her.
In ancient times, there was a king named Vikramasena in Ujjayinī; he had a daughter named Tejasvatī, who was peerless in beauty.
And for her, there was generally no king who was a desirable suitor; then one day, while staying in her palace, she saw a certain man.
By chance, she desired union with that man of handsome form; and having communicated her intention to him, she sent her own female friend to him.
Having gone there, that friend of his, despite the man's apprehension regarding such audacity and even though he was unwilling, requested him with effort and thus established a secret rendezvous.
"O noble one, behold this secluded temple here; you should wait for the arrival of the princess there during the night."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him, she went and told this to Tejasvatī; thereafter, she too remained gazing at the sun.
And that man, though having been inferred [by the frog], fled elsewhere out of fear; for a frog is not one who knows how to savor the filaments of a red lotus.
In the meantime, a certain prince of noble birth, having come upon his father's death, arrived to see that king who was his friend.
And there, at evening, arrived a young man named Somadatta, whose kingdom and other possessions had been seized by his kinsmen; he was handsome to behold and traveling alone.
By chance, she entered that very temple to spend the night, where the princess’s friend had previously directed a man to meet her.
Approaching him while he was staying there at night, the princess, blinded by passion and failing to recognize him, chose him as her husband in a self-choice marriage.
He too, being wise, silently welcomed that proposal offered by fate, which indicated the future union with royal fortune.
Then, in an instant, upon seeing him in that very way, the princess considered herself to have been truly favored by the Creator as one who possesses the most desirable of men.
After they had conversed with one another according to their mutual understanding, one went to her own home, while the other spent that night there.
Having gone there in the morning and announced his name through the mouth of the doorkeeper, the prince, once recognized, entered the presence of the king.
There, having shown great respect for the suffering caused by the aforementioned seizure of his kingdom and other misfortunes, the king accepted the role of an ally in crushing that enemy.
And he resolved to give him that daughter whom he had previously intended to bestow; at that very moment, he also disclosed this intention to his ministers.
And she related that account of her son to the king, for the queen had previously been informed of it by that very friend through the mouths of trusted confidantes.
Then, while the king was astonished there at the unproven success of his desired goal—which had occurred by mere chance—a certain minister spoke to him.

For destiny alone remains awake in bringing about the accomplishment of the goals of those destined for success, even while they themselves remain unconscious of it, just as a loyal servant serves his masters.
And so I shall tell this story; O King, listen to it here. There was once a certain Brahmin named Hariśarman in a particular village.
Poor and foolish, he was in a state of distress due to a lack of livelihood; born with many children, it was for the sake of experiencing the results of his past misdeeds.
Wandering for alms with his family, he eventually reached a certain city and took refuge with a very wealthy householder named Sthūladatta.
Having placed his sons, who were cowherds and the like, his wife, and his own servant near that man's house, he lived there performing menial service for him.
Once, there occurred for Sthūladatta a wedding festival for his daughter, crowded with people from various regions who had come for the bridegroom's procession.
And at that time, Hariśarman, together with his family, took up residence in that house, forming a habit of eating ghee, meat, and other delicacies until he was full.
Then, looking for that time [of day], he was not recognized by anyone there; consequently, distressed by his lack of food, he spoke thus to his wife at night:
"Because of my poverty and my folly in this world, I have met with such disrespect; therefore, I shall here employ a fabricated knowledge through skillful means."
"By this means, I shall become an object of respect for this Sthūladatta; and when the opportunity arises, you must inform him that I am a man of knowledge."
Having spoken thus and reflected upon her with his intellect while the people were asleep, he carried off the groom’s horse from Sthūladatta’s house.
Although the bridegroom’s party searched here and there in the morning, they did not find the horse that had been placed by him in a hidden spot at a distance.
Then, approaching Sthūladatta—who was terrified by ill omens and searching for the thief of his horse—Hariśarman’s wife said to him:
"My husband is learned and an expert in astrology and other sciences; why is he not asked why he is giving this horse to you?"
Having heard that, Sthūladatta summoned Hariśarman, who was saying, "Yesterday I forgot it, but today, now that my horses have been stolen, I remember."
Having requested the Brahmin, "Forgive us for our forgetfulness," he asked him, "Tell me, by whom has our horse been carried away?"
Then Hariśarman, drawing false lines, said: "At the southern boundary from here, a horse has been stationed by thieves."
"While he remains hidden until the end of the day and is led far away, go quickly and bring back that horse."
Having heard that, many men ran and reached him in an instant; praising Hariśarman’s discernment, they brought back the horse.
Then, honored by all the people as a man of wisdom and venerated by Sthūladatta, Hariśarman lived there in happiness.
Then, as the days passed, a great deal of gold, jewels, and other wealth was carried away from within Rājagṛha by some thief.
When it was not known who the thief was, the king then quickly had Hariśarman brought before him by virtue of his renown as a man of wisdom.

Having been brought there, passing the time by saying "I shall speak in the morning," he was placed in a dwelling by the king and guarded with great care, being distressed in mind despite his knowledge.
In that royal household there was a maidservant named Jihvā, by whom that wealth had been taken from the interior along with her brother.
Having gone there at night to Hariśarman’s dwelling, she pressed her ear against the door out of a desire to know, being suspicious of his supernatural knowledge.
And at that moment, Hariśarman, standing alone within, thus censured his own tongue, which speaks with false knowledge.
O tongue, greedy for enjoyments, what is this that you have done? O you of wicked conduct, now endure your punishment here.
Having heard that, the maidservant named Jihvā, fearing that she had been discovered by this wise man, skillfully entered his presence.
Falling at his feet, she spoke in the guise of a wise woman: "O Brahmin, I am that very tongue of yours who carries away the meaning you have understood."
And having taken that wealth, I buried it here in the ground beneath a pomegranate tree in the garden behind this very temple.
"Therefore, protect me; take this gold that is in my hand. Having heard this, Hariśarman spoke to her with pride:
"Go; I know all that has been, that is to be, and that is currently happening. But I will not expose you, for you are a wretched woman who has come to me for refuge."
"And whatever you have in your possession, you shall give that back to me. Having been addressed thus by him, the maidservant said, "So be it," and quickly departed from there.
And then Hariśarman, out of astonishment, thought to himself: "When fate is favorable, it accomplishes even an impossible task with ease."
Since this misfortune has occurred, my purpose here is accomplished beyond doubt; for as I reproached my own tongue, that thief of a tongue has fallen before me.
"Alas! These are secret sinners who reveal themselves only through their very suspicion"—reflecting thus and other such thoughts, he spent that night there in great joy.
And for the most part, having led that king there by means of false knowledge and artifice, he caused him to obtain that wealth which was buried in that garden.
He reported that the thief had been captured, his share confiscated, and had fled; thereupon the king, being pleased, proceeded to grant him villages.
"How could there be such knowledge regarding what is inaccessible to humans without a scripture? Surely this is a livelihood of rogues, devised as a secret code for thieves."
"Therefore, let him be tested once more by another method. "Your Majesty, he is a man of knowledge," the minister whispered into the king's ear.
Then King Hariśarman, having quietly summoned a new jar with its lid on that contained a frog inside, spoke to him:
O Brahmin, if you know what is contained within this jar, then today I shall perform a very great worship for you.
Having heard that, and realizing it was not the time for his destruction, he then remembered the name "Maṇḍūka" which his father had given him in childhood as a plaything.
Driven by the Ordainer and acting accordingly, the Brahmin Hariśarman suddenly uttered this lamentation here: "By him [the Ordainer], even here, this lamentation was made."
O frog, this jar has now suddenly and forcibly appeared here for the destruction of you, a virtuous being, against your will.
Hearing that, the people there rejoiced, exclaiming, "Oh! Even this frog is known by this man of great wisdom," as they connected it to the matter at hand.
Then, considering that to be intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*), the king, being pleased, gave villages along with golden parasols and vehicles to Hariśarman.
And in an instant, Hariśarman became like a feudal lord; thus are the noble goals of those who perform auspicious deeds accomplished by destiny.
O King, your daughter Tejasvatī, having been impelled by destiny itself toward a worthy match, has rejected Somadatta as an unsuitable suitor.
Having heard this from the mouth of his minister, King Vikramasena then gave his daughter to that prince, as if she were the goddess Lakṣmī herself.
Then, having gone with his father-in-law’s army and conquered his enemies, Somadatta remained happily in his own kingdom, accompanied by his wife.

Such is the way of fate; who here would be capable of fashioning you in such a manner by their own particular power? O friend Kaliṅgasenā, what could I do in this matter without destiny, were it not for the Lord of Vatsa, who is your equal?

Having heard this story thus in private from the mouth of Somaprabhā, Kaliṅgasenā, desiring him and with her fear of her kinsmen and her shame relaxed, became eager in her heart for union with the Lord of Vatsa.

Then, as the sun—the sole lamp of the three worlds—was about to set, Somaprabhā took leave of her friend, whose mind was fixed on her desired undertaking, until the arrival of dawn; and by way of the sky, that daughter of the Asura Maya departed for her own home.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave. Then, on the following day, Kaliṅgasenā spoke in confidence to her friend Somaprabhā, who had approached her in the morning, as she was making her comfortable.
"My father will certainly give me to King Prasenajit; I heard this from my mother, and you have seen that old man yourself."
Just as you yourself described the King of Vatsa’s form, so too was his heart captivated by him once he had entered the path of her hearing.
"First show me Prasenajit, and lead me there where the Lord of Vatsa dwells; what use have I for my father or my mother?"
When she had spoken thus, Somaprabhā said to her, who was full of longing: "If you must go, then let us depart by means of the sky-traveling machine."
"But take all your own retinue with you, for once you have seen the Lord of Vatsa, you will not be able to return here again."
You shall not see your parents again, nor will you remember them; having obtained your beloved who stands afar off, you will forget even me.
"For I shall not go thus to your husband's house, my friend. Hearing that, the princess spoke to her while weeping.
"In that case, my friend, bring that Lord of Vatsa here to me; for I cannot bear to remain there for even a single moment without you."
And why was Aniruddha not brought by Citralekhā through some stratagem? Even though you know this, listen to that story from me.
The daughter of Bāṇāsura was known as Uṣā; having propitiated Gaurī for the sake of obtaining a husband, Gaurī granted her a boon.

Out of greed for wealth, that female ascetic also spoke thus to her who was distressed: "O lady, what object is this? I shall procure it for you."
"I indeed know many various and very numerous applications [of spells]. Having thus comforted the queen, that female ascetic then departed.
Having reached his own hermitage, he thought thus as if terrified: "Alas! To what indeed would the hope for enjoyments not subject one to mockery?"
That I have rashly made a promise before the Goddess, and that I possess no such correct understanding in this matter—[I confess this].
Moreover, it is not possible to practice deception in Rājagṛha; for once the powerful lords have learned of it, they will surely inflict punishment.
There would be one expedient in this matter: that I have a barber who is my friend, and if he, being so skilled in such knowledge, were to make an effort here.
Having reflected thus, she went into the presence of that barber and told him her entire desire, which was to bring about the accomplishment of her purpose.
Then that old barber, who was also a rogue, thought to himself: "By good fortune, this opportunity for profit has now presented itself to me."
Therefore, she should not be harmed; rather, she must be protected, for her father possesses divine vision and would reveal all of this.
"Now that we have separated this queen from the king, let us enjoy her; for when a master has a servant who assists in his secrets, he behaves toward him like a mere hireling."
Having united them at the proper time, I shall speak thus to the king, so that the king and that daughter of the ṛṣi may both become my means of livelihood.
"Thus there would be no great sin, and my livelihood would be long-lasting. Having reflected thus, the barber said to that false ascetic woman:
"Mother, I will do all this; however, if by the power of yoga this new wife of the king were to be killed, that would not be proper."
"For if the king were ever to find out, he might destroy us all; furthermore, there would be the sin of killing a woman, and her father, being a sage, would curse us."
Therefore, by the power of our intellect, this queen must be separated from the king in such a way that the lady may remain in comfort and we may achieve our objective.
And how small is this [task] for me; indeed, what could I not accomplish through my intellect? Listen as I describe my own wisdom to you.
This King Dṛḍhavarman had a father who was ill-behaved, and I am here a servant of that king, performing the duties appropriate to my station.
Once, while wandering here, he beheld my wife; his mind became captivated by her, for she was beautiful and young.
Having questioned his attendants about her, he realized she was a barber’s wife; "What does a barber do? he thought, and entered my house at once.
Having enjoyed my wife at his own will, that wicked king departed; and by chance, on that very day, I was somewhere outside the house.
And on another day, having entered [the house], I saw her looking quite different; when I questioned my wife about what had happened, she spoke to me as if with pride.
In that very sequence, while she was unable to prevent him, that king constantly enjoyed my wife and thus insulted me.

How can there be any distinction between what is approachable and what is unapproachable for a master who is immoral and insane? To a forest fire fanned by the wind, what is a blade of grass and what is a vast woodland?
Then, as long as I had no means whatsoever to prevent that [suffering], I, emaciated by eating very little, resorted to the pretext of illness.
And so, sighing, emaciated and pale, I went into the presence of that king for the purpose of attending to my own duties.
Observing me there as if I were faint, that king, with a specific intent, asked me: "Hey! Tell me, why have you become like this?"
When I was questioned persistently and granted immunity upon my request in that secluded place, I replied to the king: "O Lord, I have a wife who is a ḍākinī."
And while I was asleep, she would pull out my intestines through my anus and suck them; likewise, she would thrust them back inside, and by that means I have become emaciated.
"And from where shall I always obtain nourishing food for my sustenance? Thus addressed by me, the king, filled with apprehension, reflected.
"Is it true that she is a ḍākinī? Was I carried off by her in such a manner? Or could she have even sucked out the entrails of me, who am nourished by food?"
"Thinking, 'Therefore, I myself shall test her tonight by some stratagem,' that king had food brought here for me."
Then, having gone to her house, I shed tears in the presence of his wife; and when questioned by her, I spoke to her thus:
"My dear, you must not tell this to anyone; listen, I shall tell you: teeth resembling the points of a diamond have grown in the anus of this king."
"And even though my razor is of high quality, it has broken today while I was working; thus, here now, my razor would break at every step."
"From where shall I obtain that ever-new razor? Therefore I weep, for this livelihood of mine at home has been destroyed."
Having been addressed thus by me, my wife resolved that she would go at night to this sleeping king while he was in the wonder of his anal-toothed gaze.
That which has not been seen since beginningless saṃsāra is unreal, yet it is not that she lacked awakening; for even women are deceived by the descriptions of a lover.
Then, having come to her at night and enjoyed my wife at his pleasure, that king, remembering my words, feigned sleep as if from exhaustion.
Then my wife, thinking he was asleep, slowly extended her hand toward his anus in order to find a tooth.
And as soon as that hand was reached into his anus, the king suddenly stood up; crying out "A ḍākinī! A ḍākinī!", he fled from there in terror.
From that time forth, having been abandoned by the king out of fear of him, my wife accepted her lot and became entirely dependent on me alone.
"First, one wife was released by me from the king through my ingenuity"; having said this to the female ascetic, the barber spoke again.
O noble lady, this which you have intended is indeed worthy of your wisdom; O mother, listen as I tell you how it shall be carried out.
Some elderly man of the harem should be employed here who would say to the king in private: "O King, your wife Kadalīgarbhā is a ḍākinī."
For this forest-dwelling woman has no personal attendants; everyone else is a stranger susceptible to division, and what would they not do out of greed?
Then, while the king was filled with apprehension, his hands, feet, and other limbs were diligently placed within the hollow of a plantain tree at night by the ear.
Having observed this at dawn and realized that what the old man had said was true, the king, being terrified, will himself abandon Kadalīgarbhā.
In this way, the queen would find happiness through separation from her rival wife; she would hold you in high regard, and some gain would accrue to us as well.
Having been addressed thus by that barber, the female ascetic said, "So be it," and having gone, she reported the matter exactly as it was to the king's chief queen.
The queen did exactly as she was told; and the king, having witnessed it with his own eyes through that stratagem, abandoned her, Kadalīgarbhā, thinking her to be wicked.
Then, being pleased, that goddess gave her a secret gift which the female ascetic, together with the barber, enjoyed as she desired.
And having been abandoned by King Dṛḍhavarman, Kadalīgarbhā, tormented by his curse, departed from the royal palace.
She set out for her father’s hermitage by the very same path by which she had come, using as a token of recognition the siddhārtha flowers that had previously grown there.
Seeing her arrive there unexpectedly, her father, the sage Maṅkaṇaka, stood still for a moment, suspecting some misconduct on her part.
Having understood that entire account through his supernatural insight, and having comforted her out of affection, he took her with him and departed from there.
Having approached that king who was himself bowing low, he related to him the drama of deceit performed by the queen out of malice toward her co-wife.
At that moment, the barber himself approached the king, related everything exactly as it had happened, and spoke further as follows:
"O Lord, having thus separated Queen Kadalīgarbhā from me by means of sorcery, I satisfied the Goddess with a clever stratagem and protected her."
Having heard that and having perceived the certainty of the words of the lord of sages, the king, his conviction fully aroused, accepted Kadalīgarbhā.
Having followed that sage, he provided for the barber with gifts, thinking, "He is devoted to me"; alas, wealthy men are easily deceived by rogues!
Then King Dṛḍhavarman, turning his back on his own queen, remained with Kadalīgarbhā alone, perfectly contented.

O Kaliṅgasenā of faultless limbs, such rival wives would fabricate many false accusations against you; yet you are but a young maiden whose marriage is still far off, and even the gods, whose ways are inconceivable, desire you.
Therefore, at this moment, you yourself must protect yourself alone—the sole jewel of the world—here, entrusted solely to the Lord of Vatsa; for this enmity is your own natural excellence.

"O friend, I shall indeed lead you now to your husband's house, for virtuous women do not go to the home of a friend's husband, O fair-limbed one; moreover, I have been forbidden by my husband today."

Nor was it possible for me to come here secretly, due to the power of my great affection for you; for my husband possesses divine vision and would somehow have discovered it. Having obtained his permission, I have indeed come today.
"Friend, there is indeed no business of mine here now; I am going to her house. And if my husband gives me his permission, then I shall come back here again, casting aside all shame."

Having spoken thus with tears to Kaliṅgasenā, the daughter of the lord of men, her face washed with weeping, the daughter of the lord of the Asuras, Somaprabhā, comforted her and departed through the sky to her own abode as the day was fading away.

Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Seventh Wave: Then Kaliṅgasenā, having abandoned her own country and kinsmen, remained there, constantly remembering that dear friend Somaprabhā who had departed.
With the great festival of her marriage to the Lord of Vatsa delayed, that princess remained in Kauśāmbī like a doe strayed from the forest.
And the King of Vatsa, as if filled with indignation toward the astrologers who were skillfully delaying the marriage of Kaliṅgasenā, said:
On that day, his mind distracted by longing, he went to the dwelling of Queen Vāsavadattā to divert his thoughts.
There, that queen, remaining especially free from any sign of emotion, attended upon her husband with her own customary services, as she had previously been instructed by the excellent minister.
Thinking, "How is it that this queen remains unchanged even though the story of Kaliṅgasenā has become known? the king, desiring to know the truth, said to her:
"O Queen, have you yourself learned why this princess named Kaliṅgasenā has come for the sake of my svayaṃvara?"
Upon hearing that, with a facial expression that remained unchanged, she said: "I have understood; my joy is immense, for indeed that Goddess Lakṣmī has come here to us."
For when the great king is under your control, and by his acquisition [of power] his father Kaliṅgadatta as well, the earth will be even more completely subject to you.
And I am happy solely through your majesty and through your happiness; O Noble Son, this has been known to you even before it was established.
Therefore, am I not fortunate, I who have such a husband as you—one whom princesses desire, even while being sought after by other kings?
Thus addressed by Queen Vāsavadattā, the Lord of Vatsa was inwardly gratified by the instruction imparted by Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Having enjoyed the drink with her that very night in her dwelling, he slept; and waking up in the middle of the night, he reflected:
What great power must she possess that this queen follows my will, even so much as to permit me to have Kaliṅgasenā as a co-wife?
Or how could this poor woman endure it, she who, even at her marriage to Padmāvatī, did not abandon her life due to fate?
If this were undesirable for him, then total destruction would follow; for my son, my brother-in-law, and my father-in-law all have him as their support.
"Between Padmāvatī and the kingdom, which is said to be more significant? Therefore, how can this Kaliṅgasenā be married by me?"
Having reflected thus, the Lord of Vatsa departed from there at the end of the night and went to the palace of Queen Padmāvatī in the afternoon.
She too, having been instructed by Vāsavadattā, attended upon him when he arrived in that same manner; and when questioned, she spoke in exactly the same way.
Then, on another day, the king, reflecting upon it, related that single thought and those words of the two queens to Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Seeing that king fallen into such deliberation, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, who knew the proper time, spoke slowly as follows.
"I know this is not merely that; the intention here is cruel. For it was said by the two queens exactly so, because of their firm resolve to give up their lives."

When their husbands are attached to others or have gone to heaven, virtuous women—free from wretchedness and profound in character—become resolved upon death, remaining entirely free from desire for anything whatsoever.
For the severing of deep love is indeed unbearable for women; and so, O King, hear in this regard the story of Śrutaśravas.
In the past, on the southern continent, there was a king in the city named Gokarṇa known as Śrutasena, who was an ornament to his lineage and endowed with sacred learning.
And a single thought arose in that king, whose prosperity was complete: that he had not yet obtained a wife who was a match for himself.
And once, while the king was engaged in that reflection during the course of conversation, he was addressed by a brahmin named Agniśarman.
"O King, two wonders have been seen by me; listen as I describe them. Having set out on a pilgrimage, I reached that Pañcatīrthī."
In that lake, Arjuna, having arrived on a pilgrimage, rescued five celestial nymphs who had been turned into crocodiles due to a sage’s curse.
Having bathed there at that excellent sacred ford, for those men who fast for five nights and bathe, it bestows the status of being an attendant of Nārāyaṇa.
Just as I was going along, I saw a certain farmer standing in the middle of a field, singing, with the earth furrowed by his plow.
When questioned about the way by a certain traveler who had come along the road, that farmer did not hear the excellent words, being intent on singing.
Then that wandering mendicant became angry with him and spoke harshly; thereupon the farmer, having ceased his singing, addressed him.
"Aha! You are a wandering mendicant, yet you do not know the hope for the Dharma; even by me, a fool, the essence of the Dharma has been understood once again."
Having heard that, when questioned out of curiosity by the wandering mendicant, "What did you understand from this?", the farmer spoke to him.
Sit here in the shade and listen while I tell you: in this region there are three brahmin brothers.
Brahmadatta, Somadatta, and Viśvadatta were performers of meritorious deeds; among them, the two eldest had wives, while the youngest remained without a wife.
Carrying out the command of those two elders like a servant, he lived with me without anger; for I was their agricultural laborer.
And those two elder brothers recognized him as being mild, devoid of worldly intellect, virtuous, not having abandoned the true path, upright, and free from deceit.
Once, when his two younger sisters-in-law solicited him in secret with lustful intent, the youngest brother, Viśvadatta, rejected them as he would his own mother.
Then they went to their two husbands and spoke falsely to them both: "This younger brother of yours desires us in secret."
Because of that, the two elder brothers became inwardly angry toward him; deluded by the words of a wicked woman, they could not distinguish between what was right and what was wrong.
