Then, on one occasion, those two brothers said to Viśvadatta: "Go and level that anthill situated in the middle of the field."
Saying "So be it," he came and began to dig that anthill with a spade; but I cried out to him, "Do not do this! A black cobra dwells here!"
Even after hearing that, he dug into the anthill, thinking "let it be so," for he did not disregard the command of his two elder brothers, even though they were seekers of evil.
As he was digging there, he obtained a jar filled with gold instead of a black cobra; for Dharma indeed provides his presence to the virtuous.
Having taken that jar, he offered it all to his two brothers, for despite my attempts to dissuade him, he was firm in his devotion to his elder siblings.
Then those two, having given a portion from that very place and incited the assassins, had his hands and feet cut off out of a desire to seize his wealth.
Nevertheless, he did not become angry nor did he feel resentment toward his two brothers; by that truth, his hands and feet were restored here.
From that time forward, having seen that, I have abandoned all anger; yet even you, though an ascetic, do not relinquish your anger even today.
"By freedom from anger, heaven has been won; behold this very moment, O sir! Having said this, that farmer cast off his body and went to the celestial realm.
"O King, this second marvel has been seen by me; now hear it," having said this to King Śrutasena, the brahmin spoke again.
Wandering even further along the shore of the ocean for the sake of visiting holy places, I reached the kingdom of King Vasantasena.
There, as I entered the royal sacrificial feast to eat, the twice-born said to me: "O Brahmin, do not go by this path, for the king’s daughter is staying here."
If even a sage were to behold her named Vidyuddyotā, he would be pierced by the arrows of desire and, falling into madness, would not survive.
Then I replied to them: "This is not surprising, for I constantly behold King Śrutasena as none other than Kandarpa himself."
When he has set out on a journey or the like, noble women are driven out of the range of sight by guards, out of fear that his presence might cause them to violate their virtuous conduct.
Having understood that you had spoken thus, the master of the almshouse and the royal priest led me into the presence of the king for the sake of a meal.
There, I beheld that princess Vidyudyotā, like the embodied magical spell of Kāma for deluding the world.
Restraining the agitation caused by seeing her after so long, I thought: "If she were to become the wife of our lord, he would forget his kingdom."
Nevertheless, I must relate this news to my master; for otherwise, the story of Unmādinī and Devasena might turn out differently.
Long ago, in the kingdom of King Devasena, there was a merchant’s daughter named Unmādinī, who caused madness to the world.
Although she was offered by her father, she was not accepted by that king, for the Brahmins who guarded him against calamities had declared her to be one with inauspicious marks for his lineage.
Then, having been married by his chief minister, she once showed herself to this king from the edge of a window.
Struck from afar by the gaze-poison of that female serpent, the lord of kings repeatedly fainted; he found no pleasure and took no food.
Although entreated by his ministers, headed by his father-in-law, that righteous man did not accept her; yet, being devoted to her, he gave up his life.
Thinking, "If such negligence as this occurs, an offense would have been committed," I came to you today and spoke these strange words.
Having heard these words from that Brahmin, which were like the commands of Madana, King Śrutasena became one whose mind was captivated by Vidyuddyotā.
And at that very moment, having dismissed that Brahmin right there, he did exactly as instructed; having quickly brought her back, he married her.
Then that king’s daughter, Vidyuddyotā, was inseparable from the body of that monarch, just as radiance is inseparable from the sun.
Then, a maiden named Mātṛdattā, the daughter of a very wealthy merchant, proud of her beauty, came to that king for the svayaṃvara.
Out of fear of unrighteousness, the king took that merchant’s daughter; then Vidyuddyotā, learning of this, died from a broken heart.
The king also arrived and, seeing his beloved in such a state, took her onto his lap; while lamenting, he was instantly deprived of his life.
Then that merchant’s daughter, Mātṛdattā, entered the fire; thus everything was lost, including that entire kingdom with its king.
Therefore, O King, the breaking of intense love is exceedingly difficult to endure, especially that of the high-minded Queen Vāsavadattā.
Therefore, if you were to marry this Kaliṅgasenā, Queen Vāsavadattā would undoubtedly give up her life.
O Queen Padmāvatī, for they two share but one life; how then could Naravāhanadatta become your son?
And I know that Your Majesty’s heart would not be able to endure it; thus, O Lord of the Earth, all this would perish in a single moment.
The very depth of the two goddesses' speech sufficiently reveals their hearts, which are devoid of desire and firmly resolved upon the renunciation of life.
Therefore, you must protect your own interests, for even animals know how to protect themselves; O King, how much more so should wise men like yourself?
Having heard this at his own leisure from the excellent minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, the Lord of Vatsa attained the path of perfect discernment and spoke.
"It is thus; there is no doubt that all this of mine will perish. Therefore, what purpose would there be for me in marrying Kaliṅgasenā?"

It has been said that the auspicious moment was far off, and therefore what the astrologers did was appropriate; or else, how much unrighteousness could there be from abandoning those who have come to the svayaṃvara?
Thus addressed by the King of Vatsa, the delighted Yaugandharāyaṇa reflected: "Our task is as good as accomplished, exactly as we desired."
Sprinkled with the essence of skillful means and nourished by the proper place and time, how could this great creeper of political science not bear fruit?
Having reflected thus and meditated upon the proper time and place, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa paid homage to the king and departed for his home.
The king also, having approached her in secret after arranging for hospitality, spoke thus to Queen Vāsavadattā while consoling her:
Why do I speak? You yourself know, O fawn-eyed one, that your love is my very life, just as water is to the lotus.
For how could I venture to take even the name of another? Yet Kaliṅgasenā has come to my house by force.
And it is well known in this regard that Rambhā, having approached Pārtha while he was established in asceticism, was rejected by him and consequently pronounced a curse of impotence upon her.
While remaining there, he spent that year in the house of Virāṭa under a curse, disguised as a woman of most wonderful form.
Therefore, I did not forbid this Kaliṅgasenā at that time; indeed, without your consent, I do not venture to say anything at all.
Having thus consoled her and perceived her cruel intention with his heart—as if with wine, full of passion, applied to his face—he realized the truth of her intent.
Together with Queen Vāsavadattā, the Lord of Vatsa spent that night in the company of his chief minister, gratified by the latter's great sagacity.
In the meantime, that which Yaugandharāyaṇa had previously employed day and night for the purpose of ascertaining the news concerning Kaliṅgasenā—
That Brahmarākṣasa, named Yogeśvara, having approached him as a friend, spoke freely to that excellent minister on that very same night.
I have always remained both inside and outside Kaliṅgasenā’s residence, yet I do not see the arrival of any beings, whether divine or human.
Even now, an indistinct sound was heard by me unexpectedly in the sky at the onset of night, while I was hidden here near the top of the palace.
Although I applied my magic science to discern his power, it was not effective; therefore, reflecting upon this, I thought:
"This is certainly the sound of someone possessing divine power, wandering in the sky, lusting after the beauty of Kaliṅgasenā."
I observe some slight interval by which knowledge does not proceed; for a clever person who is awake, another's vulnerability is not difficult to find.
"This is the desire of the divine ones," so it was said by the excellent minister; and I have heard this being spoken by her friend Somaprabhā as well.
Having thus resolved, I have come here to tell this to you; I ask about it in this context, so please explain it to me first.
For even animals protect themselves; that which you said to King Rajas, O Sage, I heard through my yogic power while remaining unobserved.
"If there is an illustration for this, tell it to me, O wise one," said Yogeśvara; thus addressed, Yaugandharāyaṇa replied.
There is a friend; likewise, I shall relate a story to you here—listen. Formerly, there was a great banyan tree outside the city of Vidiśā.
Four creatures lived there in that great tree: a mongoose, an owl, a cat, and a mouse, each having its own separate dwelling.
The mongoose and the mouse each dwelt in separate holes at the root of a great tree, while the cat stayed in a hollow in its middle.
The owl, however, is in the head region in a bower of creepers inaccessible to others; here the mouse is to be killed by the three [others], while the other three are to be killed by the cat.
The mouse, out of fear of the cat; the mongoose, likewise, out of hunger; and the owl, by its very nature—all three wandered about at night.
And that cat wandered about fearlessly day and night nearby a barley field, always with the desire to catch mice.
Others also, at that time, went there by means of their reasoning due to a lack of desire for food; once, a certain Caṇḍāla hunter arrived there.
Having seen the trail of cat's footprints leading toward that field, he set snares all around the field for the purpose of killing it and then departed.
There, during the night, a cat, having approached with the intent to kill a mouse, entered that field and was caught in its snares.
Then the mouse, seeking food, arrived there in secret; seeing the cat bound, he rejoiced and danced.
Meanwhile, as he was entering that field from afar by a single path, both the owl and the mongoose also arrived there.
And seeing the cat and the mongoose, they both desired to catch the mouse; and the mouse, having seen them from afar, was distressed and reflected:
If I take refuge with a cat that brings fear to both the mongoose and the owl, this enemy, though already bound, might kill me with a single blow.
"The owl and the mongoose will kill me from afar, while the cat will kill me from close by. Thus fallen into a crisis of enemies, where shall I go, and what shall I do?"
"Alas! I shall take refuge with this very cat here, for he is in distress; he might protect me for his own preservation when I am useful to him for cutting his snares."
Having reflected thus, the mouse went slowly and said to the cat: "I am in great distress because you are bound; therefore, I shall cut your snare."
Affection arises even toward enemies through living together among the upright; however, I have no confidence in you, as I do not know your mind.
Having heard that, the cat said: "My good sir, you may trust me; from this day forward, you are my friend and the giver of my life."
Having heard this from the cat, he immediately took refuge on his lap; seeing that, the mongoose and the owl departed from there, their hopes dashed.
Then the cat, tormented by the snare, said to the mouse: "Friend, the night is nearly spent; therefore, cut these snares of mine quickly."
The mouse, too, while cutting slowly and looking toward the arrival of the hunter, made a prolonged sound of "kaṭakaṭa" with his teeth as if they were gnashing in falsehood.
In an instant, when night had turned to dawn and the hunter was drawing near, while the cat was still pleading for mercy, the mouse suddenly snapped the snares.
Then, when the cat’s leash was severed and it had fled in terror of the hunter, the mouse, having escaped from the jaws of death, ran away and entered its burrow.
Not trusting when called back by the cat, he said: "For an enemy becomes a friend through the exigency of time, and not at all times."
Thus, when one's self is protected by wisdom from many enemies—even by a mouse, which is a mere animal—how much more so should it be guarded among human beings?

O Queen, that which was said by me to the king at that time—what you have heard—is that one should protect one's own duty with intelligence, for it is through protection [of oneself] that [duty] is preserved.
And in all matters, intellect is the primary friend, not physical prowess; O Lord of Yoga, listen now to a story regarding this as well.
There is a city named Śrāvastī; in it, King Prasenajit formerly reigned, and once a certain unprecedented brahmin arrived there in that city.
While he was eating the food of a Śūdra, a certain merchant, thinking him to be virtuous, placed that twice-born man in the house of a particular Brāhmaṇa.
There, he daily replenished it with dry food, sacrificial fees, and other gifts; then, having gradually learned of it, other excellent merchants also contributed to its filling.
Having gradually accumulated a thousand gold dīnāras, that miser went to the forest, buried them there, and departed.
Going there alone every day, he inspected that place; one day, he saw that pit empty of gold and its mouth wide open.
As he gazed at that empty pit with his mind destroyed, not only did emptiness enter his heart, but it was truly wondrous that emptiness pervaded even the quarters of space.
Then, lamenting, he approached that brahmin in whose house he had stayed; and when questioned, he reported his entire story to him.
Having gone to the sacred bathing place, he desired to give up his life while fasting; and the merchant who was his provider of food, having learned of this, arrived there along with others.
He said to him, "O Brahmin, why do you wish to die for the sake of wealth? Wealth comes and goes unexpectedly, like an unseasonable cloud."
Although addressed with these and other such words by him, he did not abandon his grip on death; for to a miser, even a mere trifle is dearer than life itself.
Then, as that twice-born man was going to the sacred ford to die, King Prasenajit himself, having learned of this, came into his presence.
And he asked him: "O Brahmin, is there any identifying mark on that ground where those dinars were buried by you?"
Having heard that, the brahmin said: "O King, there is a small tree here in the forest; at its root my wealth is buried."
Having heard this, the king said: "I shall give you that wealth after searching for it from my own treasury; otherwise, O twice-born one, do not abandon your life."
Having spoken thus, the king dissuaded him from his efforts toward death, placed that brahmin in the hands of a merchant, and entered the inner apartments.
There, having instructed the doorkeeper under the pretext of a headache, he summoned all the physicians by the proclamation of a drum.
"How many patients are there here? Whose are you? What medicine did you give? he asked, having brought them forward one by one while remaining in private.
Then each of them also told the king everything at that time; subsequently, one physician among them, being questioned in turn, spoke as follows.
"O King, today is the second day that the medicinal herb nāgabalā has been administered by me to the merchant Mātṛdatta while he was unwell."
Having heard that, the king summoned the merchant and said to him, "Tell me, by whom was the nāgabalā brought for you?"
When the merchant had thus spoken, "O King, by a laborer," the king had that laborer summoned quickly and said to him:
"Since you were digging at the base of the tree for the sake of *nāgabalā*, you obtained a quantity of silver coins; restore that property belonging to a Brahmin."
Thus addressed by the king, the terrified laborer immediately agreed; he brought those dinars and abandoned them there on the spot.
The king, having summoned him, gave those dinars—won back after being lost—to that brahmin who had fasted, as if they were his own life-breaths moving outside his body.
Thus, by means of his intellect, the king discovered that medicinal herb growing from the base of the tree, knowing it was the very one brought down for the sake of the brahmin.
Thus, in every case, it is intelligence that holds primacy, having surpassed human effort; and in such matters as these, what could mere physical prowess accomplish?
Therefore, O Lord of Yoga, you too should act with such wisdom that some fault may be discovered in Kaliṅgasenā.
And this is so: just as the gods and asuras here are infatuated with her, so too was a certain sound heard by you in the sky one night.
If a fault were found in her after she was obtained, it would not be unwholesome for us; the king would not have taken her in marriage, and no unrighteousness would have been committed.
Having heard all this from Yaugandharāyaṇa, the noble-minded Brahmarākṣasa Yogeśvara was highly pleased and spoke to him.
Who else besides the god Bṛhaspati is equal to you in statesmanship? You are the sprinkling of nectar for him; your counsel is the root of this tree of sovereignty.
"Thus, I shall always investigate the course of Kaliṅgasenā through both my intellect and my power," having said this, Yogeśvara then departed.
At that time, Kaliṅgasenā, staying in her own palace, grew faint with longing as she watched the King of Vatsa wandering about on the palace rooftops and other areas.
With her mind fixed on him, tormented by love, wearing bracelets of lotus stalks and anointed with sandalwood paste, she found no peace anywhere.
In the meantime, that lord of the Vidyādharas named Madanavega, having seen her before, stood there afflicted by the sharp arrows of intense passion.
Although she performed austerities to attain him and obtained a boon from Śaṅkara, she remained attached to another and stayed in a different land; thus, she was not easily accessible to him.
For that reason, in order to find an opportunity, that lord of the Vidyādharas was wandering through the sky at night above his palace.
But remembering that command of Dhūrjaṭi, who was pleased by his asceticism, he assumed the form of the King of Vatsa during one night by means of his own magic science.
And assuming that very form, he entered his palace, saluted by the doorkeepers, like the God of Death himself who had arrived in secret with his ministers, impatient for the passing of time.
Seeing him, Kaliṅgasenā also rose up, trembling with agitation; she seemed to be restrained by the cries of her ornaments, as if saying, "This is not he!"
Then, having gradually gained her confidence by assuming the form of the Lord of Vatsa, Madanavega made her his wife according to the Gāndharva rite.
And at that moment, the Lord of Yoga entered there unobserved through his yogic power; seeing that, he became despondent, mistaking it for the sight of the King of Vatsa.
Having gone and told this to Yaugandharāyaṇa, and by his direction, he skillfully observed the King of Vatsa standing near Vāsavadattā.
Delighted by the words of the excellent minister, he went once more to ascertain the appearance of the lover of Kaliṅgasenā while she was asleep.
Having gone to the bed of the sleeping Kaliṅgasenā, she beheld Madanavega lying there, restored to his own natural form.

His lotus-feet, marked by the parasol and banner, are free from dust; he possesses both divine and human [qualities], and his physical manifestation has ceased through the disappearance of those very vidyās within his sleep.
Having gone there and reported what he had seen with satisfaction, that master of yoga, filled with joy, spoke to Yaugandharāyaṇa.
One such as I knows nothing at all, whereas you know everything through the eye of political wisdom; by your counsel, this task of our lord—which was difficult to accomplish—has been achieved.
What is the sky without the sun? What is a lake without water? What is a kingdom without counsel? What is speech without truth?
Having addressed the Lord of Yoga who had spoken thus, the delighted Yaugandharāyaṇa then went in the morning to see the King of Vatsa.
Approaching him in the proper manner, he spoke to the king during the course of conversation, having been asked for his decision regarding what was to be done for the sake of Kaliṅgasenā.
"O King, she is independent; she does not deserve the touch of your hand here. For she has come of her own free will to see Prasenajit."
Having seen that you were old, she became detached; yet, out of greed for your beauty, she has now even freely engaged with other men of her own accord.
Having heard that, [he thought]: "How could this daughter of a noble family act in such a way? Who has the power to enter within my inner apartments?"
When the king had spoken thus, the wise Yaugandharāyaṇa replied: "O King, this very night I shall show this to you directly before your eyes."
The gods, the Siddhas, and others desire her; what mortal could possibly do so? And who here, O King, is able to obstruct the course of the divine?
When the minister said, "Therefore, come and see it for yourself," the king resolved to go there with him that very night.
"O Queen, as for what was said—that no other woman is to be married except Padmāvatī—that vow has been fulfilled by me today."
Then, having approached that queen and spoken to her, Yaugandharāyaṇa related the entire account of Kaliṅgasenā to her.
"This is the fruit of your instruction for me," said Queen Vāsavadattā; bowing, she too congratulated him.
Then, at midnight, while the people were fast asleep, the Lord of Vatsa departed for the house of Kaliṅgasenā, accompanied by Yaugandharāyaṇa.
And having entered there unobserved, he saw Madanavega lying asleep near her as she enjoyed her slumber, restored to his own natural form.
And just as the king was about to strike that reckless man, he was awakened by his magic science and became a Vidyādhara.
Having awakened, he emerged and instantly flew up into the sky; at that moment, Kaliṅgasenā also woke up.
Seeing the bed empty, she said, "How is it that the Lord of Vatsa, having previously awakened me, now departs leaving me while I am still asleep?"
Having heard that, Yaugandharāyaṇa said to the Lord of Vatsa: "Listen, she has been ruined by this man who assumed your form."
Having known him through the power of yoga, he has been shown to you by me in person; however, because of his divine majesty, he cannot be slain.
Having said this, both he and the king approached her; and Kaliṅgasenā, seeing them, stood there showing them respect.
"O King, where did you go just now, and how have you returned with your ministers? To her who was speaking thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
"Kaliṅgasenā, you have been deluded and married by someone using the illusory form of the Lord of Vatsa; you have not been married by this husband of mine."
Hearing that, Kaliṅgasenā was greatly agitated, as if pierced in her heart by an arrow; with eyes full of tears, she spoke to the Lord of Vatsa.
"Even though I was married to you by the Gāndharva rite, I have been forgotten; is it not just as when, O King, Śakuntalā was [forgotten] by Duṣyanta in the past?"
Thus addressed by her, the king, with his face bowed down, said to her: "It is true that you have not been married by me; for I have only just now arrived."
When the Lord of Vatsa had spoken thus, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa said, "Come," and then led him privately to the royal palace.
Then, when the queen had departed along with her ministers, she remained there in a foreign land like a doe strayed from the herd, abandoned by her own kinsmen.
With her lotus-face blooming through the enjoyment [of love], she was like a lotus pond pressed by an elephant, its rows of bees being the mass of her braided hair.
Having lost her status as a maiden and finding no means of escape, Kaliṅgasenā, gazing at the sky, spoke these words:
"By whomsoever I have been married while he was in the form of the Lord of Vatsa, let him be revealed; for he alone is my husband."
When she had spoken thus, that lord of the Vidyādharas, possessing a divine form and adorned with necklaces and armlets, descended there from the sky.
And when asked by her, "Who are you?", he replied to her thus: "O slender one, I am a lord of the Vidyādharas named Madanavega."
And previously, having seen you while you were staying in your father’s house, I performed austerities and obtained a boon from Maheśvara that would grant me the attainment of you.
And because you were so devoted to the Lord of Vatsa, I quickly married you through a stratagem, even though his marriage had not yet taken place, by means of your own likeness.
Thus, as that nectar of his speech entered the path of her hearing, Kaliṅgasenā’s lotus-heart was somewhat revived.

Then Madanavega, having comforted his beloved and restored her courage by bestowing upon her a heap of gold, and being deemed worthy by her whose inner devotion to her noble husband was firmly bound, flew back up into the sky at that very moment to return once more.

Observing that her husband’s home was a divine abode inaccessible to mortals, and considering that her father’s palace had been abandoned out of passion, Kaliṅgasenā then resolved to dwell right there, having received permission from Madanavega.

Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Eighth Wave: Then one night, the King of Vatsa, remembering the incomparable beauty of Kaliṅgasenā, became possessed by the god of love.
Rising with sword in hand, he went and entered her palace alone, where he was received with the honor of hospitality by her.
Thereupon, as that lord of the earth was seeking her for the sake of a wife, he was rejected by her with the words, "I am the wife of another," and he replied:
Since you have reached a third man, you are an unchaste woman; therefore, the fault of approaching another's wife does not apply to me in approaching you.
Thus addressed by the king, Kaliṅgasenā replied to him: "O King, it was indeed for your sake that I came here by means of a Vidyādhara."
I was approached at will by that very same husband of mine, who, assuming your form, was driven by the force of passion; so why am I a wanton woman?
What indeed can be said of these calamities that befall women who have overstepped their kin and whose souls are ruined by self-willed conduct; as for unmarried maidens, what even need be said?
Although I was forbidden by my friend, who perceived ill omens, I nevertheless dispatched a messenger to your side; this, then, is the fruit of that action for me.
If you touch me by force, I shall then give up my life; for what woman of noble birth would ever commit treachery against her husband?
And so, O King, I shall tell you a story here; listen. In former times, there was a lord of the Cedi country named Indradatta.
Desiring a body of fame and perceiving the fragility of his own body, he built a great temple for the sake of renown at the holy ford of Pāpaśodhana.
And that king went there constantly to behold him through the aesthetic relish of devotion (bhakti-rasa), and all the people always came there for the sake of bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
And once, that king saw there a merchant’s wife who had come for the purpose of bathing at a sacred ford, her husband being away on a journey.
Sprinkled with the nectar of her own pure luster, adorned with ornaments of wondrous form, she was as delightful as the moving capital city of the God of Love.
I was embraced by you at my feet as if out of affection, saying "I am the entire universe for your victory," while the two quivers of the five-arrowed god graced both sides.
As soon as he saw her, she so captivated the mind of that king that, searching for her house, he went there at night, utterly helpless.
And as he was making advances toward her, the king was addressed by her: "You are a protector; it is not fitting for you to violate another's wife."
If you touch me by force, a great unrighteousness would be yours; I shall die instantly, and I will not endure such defilement.
Even though she spoke thus, as that king desired to use force against her, her heart suddenly burst from the fear of losing her virtue.
Seeing that, he was immediately overcome with shame; having returned just as he had come, the king met his death within those days due to that remorse.
Having related this tale, Kaliṅgasenā, bowing with fear and humility, spoke again to the Lord of Vatsa.
Therefore, do not set your mind on unrighteousness that would take my life; grant me a place to dwell here as one who has sought refuge, otherwise I shall go elsewhere.
Having heard this from Kaliṅgasenā, the King of Vatsa, who was a knower of dharma, reflected upon it, desisted from his intent, and spoke to her.
"O princess, dwell here now with your husband as you please; I shall say nothing more to you now, so do not be afraid."
When the king had spoken thus and departed at his own leisure for his palace, Madanavega heard of this and descended from the sky.
"O dear one, you have done well; had you not acted thus, O auspicious one, no good would have come of it, for I could not have endured that."
Having spoken thus and comforted her, that Vidyādhara spent the night with her, and thereafter continued to come and go to that very place.
And Kalingasena also, while her husband was the lord of the Vidyādharas, remained there, even though she was in mortal form, endowed with the happiness of divine enjoyments.
Vatsarāja, too, casting aside that anxiety and remembering the words of his minister, rejoiced, considering himself to have regained the queen, the kingdom, and likewise his son.
And Queen Vāsavadattā and the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa became filled with joy when the fruit of the "Kalpalatā of Policy" was accomplished.
Then, as the days passed, Kaliṅgasenā, whose lotus-like face had become somewhat pale, conceived a child and experienced the longings of pregnancy.
Her two breasts, lofty and with dark nipples, shone like two treasure-pots of Love, marked as if with the seal of intoxication.
Then her husband Madanavega approached her and said, "O Kaliṅgasenā, we possess this custom among the divine beings."
Having abandoned a human child as soon as it was born, we are departing to a great distance; why did Menakā not leave Śakuntalā at Kaṇva’s hermitage?
O Goddess, although you were formerly an apsaras, you have now attained human birth due to your own lack of discipline and the curse of Śakra.
"Because of that very act, even though you are a virtuous woman, the title 'unchaste woman' has been born for you here. Therefore, you must protect your offspring; I shall go to my own place."
"When you remember me, I shall then appear before you. Having spoken thus to Kaliṅgasenā, whose eyes were filled with tears, [he departed].
Then, having comforted her and given her that collection of jewels, the lord of the Vidyādharas, his mind fixed on her and drawn by their agreement, departed.
Kaliṅgasenā also remained there, leaning upon the hope for offspring as if it were a friend, and taking refuge in the protective shade of the Vatsarāja’s arm.
In the meantime, the Lord of Ambikā commanded Rati, the wife of Ananga, who had performed austerities for the sake of obtaining her husband along with his limbs.
Born in the house of the King of Vatsa, that husband of yours named Naravāhanadatta was previously consumed by fire; he was not born from a womb because of my transgression.
But through my propitiation, you shall be born in the world of mortals without being born from a womb; thereafter, you shall be united with that husband in his entirety.
Having spoken thus to Rati, Śambhu then commanded Prajāpati: "Kaliṅgasenā shall give birth to a son of divine origin."
Having carried her away by means of illusion, you should create this Rati as a human maiden in her place and cast off her divine body.
Thus, having received the command of the Lord upon his head, when the Creator had departed, Kaliṅgasenā gave birth when the time for delivery arrived.
As soon as he was born, the Creator, having taken that son of hers by means of his own power of illusion and having transformed him into that girl Rati, placed her there unobserved.
And everyone there perceived that very maiden as if she were the crescent of the new moon risen unexpectedly even during the day.
She illuminated her dwelling with her splendor, making the rows of jewel-lamp flames appear lusterless as if they were ashamed, having been surpassed by her.
Seeing that she had given birth to such an extraordinary daughter, Kaliṅgasenā, out of joy exceeding even the birth of a son, held a great festival.
Then the King, the Lord of Vatsa, together with his queen and his ministers, heard that such a daughter had been born to Kaliṅgasenā.
And having heard this, the king, impelled by the Lord, suddenly spoke to Queen Vāsavadattā while Yaugandharāyaṇa stood nearby.
"I know that this Kaliṅgasenā is a divine woman fallen due to a curse; and thus, the daughter born of her is likewise divine, possessing a wondrous form."
Therefore, this maiden, who is equal to my son Naravāhanadatta in beauty, deserves to become his chief queen.
Having heard that, King Vāsavadattā said to him: "O Great King, why do you speak thus so suddenly today?"
This son of yours is pure on both sides of his family; where indeed is that Kaliṅgasenā, from whose womb this child was born as the offspring of a harlot?
Having heard this, the king reflected and said: "Indeed, I do not say this of my own accord; it seems as though someone has entered within me and is making me speak."
And I seem to hear a voice from heaven saying, "This maiden was ordained of old to be the wife of Naravāhanadatta."
Furthermore, Kaliṅgasenā was a woman of noble birth who had been devoted to a single husband; however, due to the power of her past karma, she has incurred the reputation of being an unchaste woman.
When the king had spoken thus, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa said: "O Lord, it is heard that when Smara was consumed by fire, Rati performed austerities."
Having descended to the world of mortals in bodily form, you shall be reunited with your own husband once he has attained mortal existence.
Thus Śarva granted a boon for the sake of pleasure to her who desired him as her husband; and previously, your son was described by a divine voice as an incarnation of Kāma.
And by the command of Hara, she was to descend into the state of a mortal through Rati; thus has she been described to me in secret today by Garbhagrāhikā.
Previously, I saw Kaliṅgasenā’s fetus joined with the bed of the womb; at that very moment, I saw it again, devoid of that.
"Having seen that wonder, I have come here to tell you," said that woman to me; "this intuition has also arisen within you."
Knowing this, the gods created through illusion this very Rati, not born from a womb, as the daughter of Kaliṅgasenā by means of stealing her embryo.
O King, she was the wife of your son, who is an incarnation of Kāma; furthermore, listen to this story concerning a yakṣa.
There was indeed a servant of Vaiśravaṇa known as Virūpākṣa, a Yakṣa who had attained the position of chief superintendent over hundreds of thousands of treasures.
And he appointed a yakṣa to guard a treasure situated outside Mathurā, who was as immovable as a stone pillar.
There, a certain twice-born Pāśupata living in that city, a seeker of hidden treasures who practiced the science of mining, once arrived there in search of a hoard.
As he examined the place with a lamp made of human fat in his hand, the lamp fell from his hand right there at that spot.
Having recognized the treasure situated there by that characteristic mark, he began to open it together with his other brahmin friends.
Then that yakṣa who had been appointed to the task of guarding, having seen this, went and informed Virūpākṣa of the situation exactly as it was.
"Go and quickly slay those vile seekers of subterranean treasures! Thus did the wrathful Virūpākṣa command that yakṣa.
Then that Yakṣa, having gone there, by his own artifice slew those Brahmins who had been proclaiming the location of the treasure, before they could achieve their desire.
Having learned of that, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) became enraged and said to Virūpākṣa: "O sinful one, how was this murder of a Brahmin suddenly committed by you?"
What indeed would a person of low status, driven by greed, not do? He is restrained by being terrified with various obstacles; he is not killed.
Having said this, the Lord of Wealth then cursed Virūpākṣa, saying: "Be born in a mortal womb because of your practice of evil deeds."
Then, having received a curse from a certain Brahmin on earth, that Virūpākṣa was born as the son of a Brahmin who had seized a land-grant.
Then his wife, the Yakṣiṇī, addressed the Lord of Wealth: "O Lord, cast me into that very place where my husband has been thrown."
"Be gracious, for I am not able to live separated from him. When he had been thus entreated by that virtuous woman, Vaiśravaṇa replied:
O sinless one, he who was born in that Brahmin’s house shall be your husband; you, however, shall be born not from a womb in the house of that very man’s female slave.
There, you will be reunited with that husband of yours; and by your grace, having crossed over his curse, he shall come to my side.
Thus, at the command of Vaiśravaṇa, that virtuous woman fell from there and became a human girl at the door of that maidservant's house.
And suddenly, that maidservant saw a girl of wondrous appearance; taking her, she showed her to her master, the twice-born man.
"This is some divine maiden, undoubtedly not born from a womb"—thus my inner self speaks here; bring her without hesitation.
"Indeed, I believe this woman deserves to be the wife of my son. Thus the brahmin spoke to that maidservant and rejoiced.
Gradually growing up there, that maiden and the son of the Brahmin became bound by intense mutual affection upon seeing one another.
Then, having performed their marriage with that brahmin, the couple remained as if they had emerged from a state of separation, even though they had not yet regained the memory of their past lives.
Then, in the course of time, at the end of her body, that husband followed her; his sins destroyed by that asceticism, he properly attained his own station as a yakṣa.
Thus, being free from sin and not born from a womb, these divine beings created by fate descend here upon the earth due to the power of their past causes.
"O King, what is her lineage? Therefore, this daughter of Kaliṅgasenā is ordained by fate to be the wife of your son, just as was foretold."
When Yaugandharāyaṇa had spoken thus, both the Lord of Vatsa and Queen Vāsavadattā accepted it in their hearts, saying, "So be it."
Then, after that chief minister had gone home, the king, together with his wife, spent that day happily in drinking and other diversions.
Then, as the days passed, that daughter of Kaliṅgasenā, though endowed with perfect beauty, had her own memory lost through delusion.
In due course, she grew up, and was given the name Madanamañcukā by her mother and the people because she was the daughter of Madanavega.
Surely she must have assumed the form of all other excellent women; otherwise, how could they have appeared deformed in her presence?
And having heard of that Rūpavatī, Queen Vāsavadattā once, out of curiosity, had her brought into her own presence.
There, King Vatsa saw her clinging to the nurse’s face, and Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others saw her as well, like the flame of a lamp within its wick.
And having beheld that body, never seen before, which was nectar to her eyes, who there did not think, "This must be Rati herself descended here"?
Then Queen Vāsavadattā had her son Naravāhanadatta, a festival for the eyes of the world, brought there.
There, upon her lotus-face in full bloom, he beheld that radiant Madanamañcukā, just as a bed of lotuses beholds the fresh splendor of the sun.
Beholding him, the delight of her eyes, with her face blossoming, that young woman found no satiety, just as a female cakora bird never tires of the moonlight.
From that time forward, even though they were but children, those two were unable to remain apart for even a moment, as if bound together by the snares of their glances.
Having determined over several days that their relationship was indeed ordained by the gods, the Lord of Vatsa set his mind upon the performance of their marriage ceremony.
Having learned that, Kaliṅgasenā rejoiced and, out of affection for her son-in-law, Naravāhanadatta, she fixed her heart’s resolve upon him.
After consulting with his ministers, the King of Vatsa then had a separate palace constructed for his son, as if it were his own.
Then, having gathered the necessary materials, that king, who knew the proper time, consecrated his son—who had been observed to possess praiseworthy qualities—as the crown prince.
First, there fell upon his head the water born of the tears of joy from his parents; thereafter, the water from sacred bathing places, purified by Vedic mantras.
When his lotus-face was washed with the waters of consecration, it is a marvel that even the faces of the quarters attained stainless purity.
When auspicious garlands and flowers were thrown for him by his mothers, even the heavens at that moment released a rain of celestial floral showers.
As if competing with the resonance of the drums of the gods, the echoes of the sound of the musical instruments of bliss expanded across the vault of the sky.
Who there did not bow down to that consecrated crown prince? For at that time, he alone rose up by his own power.
Then the Lord of Vatsa summoned the seventy sons of his own ministers, who had been the childhood friends of his son, and appointed them to the office of minister.
Then he appointed Marubhūtika, the son of Yaugandharāyaṇa, to the office of minister, and Hariśikha, the son of Rumaṇvat, to the command of the army.
He appointed Tapantaka, the son of Vasantaka, as his playmate, and Gomukha, the son of Ityaka, to the office of chamberlain.
And for the office of domestic priest, both sons of Piṅgalikā mentioned previously—Vaiśvānara and Śāntisoma, the two sons of his brother the priest—were appointed.
When the king had thus commanded them to assist his son, a voice arose from the sky, preceded by a rain of flowers.
These shall accomplish all the aims of this practitioner; Gomukha, moreover, shall be inseparable from his very body.
Having been thus addressed by the divine voice, the delighted Lord of Vatsa honored them all with garments and ornaments.
And while that king was raining down wealth upon his dependents, the word "poor" had no application there for even a single person.
The city was filled with dancers and wandering minstrels who seemed as if summoned by the rows of banner-cloths fluttering and tossed by the wind.
Then the daughter of a Vidyadhara, the future Lakṣmī herself, arrived for the upcoming festival of Kaliṅgasenā’s daughter-in-law.
Then Vāsavadattā, Padmāvatī, and she likewise—these three—danced with joy, like the three powers (śakti) united together.
With their creepers swaying in the wind, the trees here seem to be dancing everywhere; what need is there even to mention the sentient beings?
Then, having performed his ablutions and mounted the elephant Jayakuñjara, the crown prince Naravāhanadatta set forth.
And he was showered by the women of the city with upturned eyes—blue, white, and reddish—in hue like handfuls of blue lotuses, parched grain, and red lotuses.
And having seen that, while being praised by bards and panegyrists, he entered his own palace together with his ministers, accompanied by the tutelary deities of the city.
There, Kaliṅgasenā first presented him with divine foods and drinks that surpassed her own royal splendor.
Overcome with affection for her son-in-law, she gave him fine garments and divine ornaments, along with his ministers, friends, and servants.
Thus, with such great festivities, that day passed for all these people, including the King of Vatsa and the others, as beautiful as the taste of nectar.
Then, when night had arrived, Kaliṅgasenā, reflecting upon her daughter’s marriage, remembered her friend Somaprabhā.
As soon as she was remembered by her, the great sage Nalakūbara spoke to that auspicious daughter of the Asura Maya.
"O beloved, Kaliṅgasenā remembers you today with longing; therefore, go to the divine garden and do this for the sake of your daughter."
Having spoken thus and related both what was past and what was yet to come concerning that matter, the husband then and there sent his wife Somaprabhā away.
Having arrived, Somaprabhā embraced her friend Kaliṅgasenā, who had long yearned for her embrace, and after inquiring after her welfare, she spoke.
First, you were married by a Vidyadhara of great supernatural power; and by the grace of Śiva, Rati and your daughter were brought down [to earth].
And she was fashioned as the former wife of Naravāhanadatta, who was born to the King of Vatsa through his descent into the realm of desire.
He shall exercise divine sovereignty over the Vidyādharas for an eon, and she will be honored at the head of all his other wives.
And you, O Apsaras fallen to the world of mortals by the curse of Śakra, shall have fulfilled the remainder of your task and will obtain release from the curse.
"O friend, my wise husband has told me all of this; therefore, you need have no anxiety on his account, for everything will turn out well for you."
And here I am creating this divine garden for the sake of your daughter; there is nothing that does not exist in Pātāla, on earth, or in heaven that I do not provide.
Having spoken thus, Somaprabhā took leave of the longing Kaliṅgasenā and, by her own supernatural power, departed for her celestial garden.
Then, when night had turned to dawn, the world suddenly beheld that garden there, as if it were Nandana fallen from heaven to the earth.
Having learned of this, King Vatsarāja, together with his wife and ministers, and Naravāhanadatta with his followers, arrived there.
They beheld that garden, which was always filled with trees bearing flowers and fruit, and possessed pillars, walls, grounds, and ponds made of various kinds of jewels.
With its golden-colored birds and its wind of divine fragrance, that place had descended by the command of the gods like another heaven upon the earth.
Having seen that wonder, the King of Vatsa then asked Kaliṅgasenā, who was busy with her hospitality, "What is this?"
She replied to that king, while everyone was listening: "There is a great asura named Maya, who is an incarnation of Viśvakarman."
She who built the beautiful city for Yudhiṣṭhira and for the wielder of the thunderbolt—she has a daughter named Somaprabhā, who is my friend.
Having come to my presence during that night by means of her own illusory power, she created this divine garden out of affection for the sake of my daughter.
Having said this, and declaring that everything which had been spoken by her friend regarding the past and the future was indeed spoken by her, she then related it all.
Then, observing that Kaliṅgasenā’s statement was consistent with the facts, everyone there cast off their doubts and attained incomparable satisfaction.
And the Lord of Vatsa spent that day in this very garden with his wife, sons, and others, receiving the hospitality of Kaliṅgasenā.
On another day, having gone out to visit the deity at the temple, the king saw many women there, beautifully dressed and adorned with ornaments.
When asked by him, "Who are you?", they replied to him: "We are these sciences and arts; we have come here for the sake of your son."
Having said, "Let us go and enter through the sky," they vanished; and the King of Vatsa, the lord of the realm, also went inside, filled with wonder.
There, he related that to Queen Vāsavadattā and to the assembly of ministers; they both rejoiced and recognized it as a divine favor.
Then, by the king's command, as Naravāhanadatta entered there, Vāsavadattā instantly took up her lute.
Then, as his mother was playing it, the prince said to her with humility, "This lute has slipped from its place."
When his father said, "Take this and play it," he then played the lute, causing even the Gandharvas to be filled with wonder.
Thus examined by his father in all branches of knowledge and arts, he himself came to know everything that they had tested him upon.
Seeing that his son was endowed with such qualities, the King of Vatsa instructed Madanamañcukā, the daughter of Kaliṅgasenā, in the art of dance.
Just as Pūrṇakalā became like the moon with its full digits, so too did that ocean of Naravāhanadatta become agitated.
And he took delight in watching her as she sang and danced, appearing as if she were reciting the commands of Love through the expressive gestures of her limbs.
Not seeing her nectar-like beloved for even a moment, she too sat at dawn with tears in her eyes, like a night-lily wet with water.
Unable to remain constantly without beholding her face, that Naravāhanadatta went to various gardens.
There, having brought his daughter Madanamañcukā to her side, he remained with Kaliṅgasenā, who was filled with affection for him.
And Gomukha, who understood his master's mind and desired that he remain there for a long time, told various stories to Kaliṅgasenā.
The prince was pleased with her by that seizing of his heart; for entering the heart is the supreme means of enchantment for a lord.
There, in that garden-like music hall, he himself made Madanamañcukā fit for dancing and other arts.
While his beloved was dancing, Naravāhanadatta played all the musical instruments, putting even the most excellent bards to shame.
And he likewise defeated various learned men who had arrived from all directions—experts in elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, missiles, painting, literature, and other arts.
Thus passed the days of Naravāhanadatta’s childhood as he lived in this manner, chosen by the Science through his own free will.
And once, during a festival, that prince went to a garden named Nāgavana, accompanied by his beloved and his ministers.
There, a certain merchant’s wife, who had been rejected by him despite her longing, desired to kill Gomukha by bringing him a drink mixed with poison.
And Gomukha learned of this from the mouth of his friend; he did not take that drink and thus censured women.
Aha! First the Creator fashioned recklessness, and thereafter women; for there is nothing in this world that is difficult for them to accomplish by their very nature.
Surely this creation called "woman" was fashioned from both nectar and poison; for when she is attached, she is indeed nectar, but when she is detached, she is truly poison.
By whom can a woman of beautiful face whose sins are concealed be known? A wicked woman is like a lotus pond in full bloom that hides crocodiles within.
But one woman falls from heaven, impelled by the wheel of her virtues—a virtuous wife unable to endure the praise of her husband—pure as the radiance of the sun.
Once she has been taken hold of, that wicked woman—addicted to another, devoid of desire, and bearing the poison of passionlessness—swiftly destroys her husband, just like a female serpent.
For instance, in a certain village there was a man named Śatrughna, and his wife was unchaste.
One evening, he saw his wife united with her lover; standing within the inner chamber, he struck down that lover of hers with his sword.
Restraining his wife, he remained at the door awaiting the night; and at that very time, a traveler seeking lodging arrived there.
Having provided him with shelter by means of a stratagem, he took that adulterer, who had been killed along with him, and went to the forest there at night.
While he was throwing that corpse into the blind well, his wife arrived from behind and threw him in there as well.
"What kind of reckless deed does a wicked woman not commit? Thus did Gomukha, though but a boy, there censure the conduct of women.
Then, having personally worshipped the Nāgas there in that Nāga-grove, Naravāhanadatta went to his own residence together with his retinue.
Thereupon, on another day, although he already knew them, he questioned his ministers, Gomukha and the others, regarding the compendium of royal policy.
"You are omniscient; nevertheless, we speak thus because we have been questioned by you. Having said this and having determined the essential point among themselves, they spoke as follows.
Having first mounted the horses of the senses which he had brought under control, and having conquered those internal enemies such as desire, anger, and the rest, the king [proceeded].
One should first conquer one's own self for the sake of conquering other enemies; for how can one who has not conquered himself and is powerless bring another under his control?

Then he should appoint as ministers those endowed with qualities such as being natives of the realm, and as domestic priest one who is skilled, possessed of ascetic merit, and learned in the Atharva Veda.

Having examined them for their integrity regarding fear, greed, duty, and desire through various tests, the king, who knows the inner thoughts of others best, should appoint those ministers as suitable for specific tasks.

One should examine their speech when they converse with one another regarding mutual affairs—whether it be truthful, motivated by hatred, spoken out of affection, or consistent with their own interests.
One should be satisfied with the truth, but regarding untruth, one should inflict punishment as deserved; and one should always investigate their conduct separately through spies.
Thus, seeing with unobstructed vision, having uprooted the thorns and acquired treasury, army, and so forth, he should achieve firm rootedness.
Then, endowed with the three powers of energy, sovereignty, and counsel, he should desire to conquer foreign lands after having deliberated upon the differences between himself and his enemy.

One should conduct counsel without haste with those who are trustworthy, learned in the scriptures, and wise; having had it determined by them, one should then refine every aspect of it with one's own intellect.

One who knows the means such as conciliation and bribery should secure the acquisition and preservation of well-being; thereafter, one should employ the six political measures, beginning with peace and war.
Thus, remaining free from sloth and applying his thoughts to both his own country and that of his enemy, a king surely conquers and is never again defeated.
But the ignorant man, blinded by desire and greed, is led astray by those who falsely show him the way; having been cast into chasms, he is robbed by the servants of rogues.
No other person finds any opportunity in the presence of that king, just as farmers find no room for other crops when a field has been fenced off by rogues.
For once he has entered into their secrets, he is indeed brought under their control; thereafter, distressed by that knower of the glorious Raviśeṣa, she flees from him.
Therefore, a king should be self-controlled, one who applies punishment appropriately and discerns distinctions; for by being thus devoted to his subjects, he shall become a vessel of prosperity.
Formerly, a king named Śūrasena, who placed his sole trust in his servants, was brought under control by his ministers, who formed a clique and consumed his wealth.
When the king wished to give even a blade of grass to that servant of his, those ministers there were not willing to grant it to him.
But whoever among them was a servant there, they themselves gave it to him; and having petitioned the king, they caused it to be given even to those who were unworthy.
Having seen that and understood it, the king gradually caused those ministers—who were a band of rogues—to be divided from one another through wisdom and skillful means.
When they had been divided and ruined by engaging in mutual slander, that king ruled his kingdom properly, uncheated by others.

And Harisiṃha became king, together with his ministers who were knowers of the principles of policy; he honored devoted and wise counselors, maintained strong fortresses, and accumulated great wealth.
Having made his subjects devoted, he acted in whatever manner was appropriate; even when attacked by a universal monarch, he did not suffer defeat.

"Thus, deliberation and reflection are the essence; what indeed is more important than these in a kingdom? Having said this and other such things, Gomukha and the others ceased speaking, each according to his own turn.
And Naravāhanadatta, placing faith in their words, declared that while human effort is indeed to be considered, destiny is inconceivable.
Then, rising up, he went with them to see his beloved Madanamañcukā, who was filled with longing due to his delay.
When he had reached that palace and was seated upon his throne, Kaliṅgasenā, having shown him due respect, spoke for a moment to Gomukha with wonder:
While Naravāhanadatta, the prince, had not yet returned there, Madanamañcukā grew anxious to see his path.
While I was on the upper floor of the palace accompanied by Gomukha, a certain man descended there from the sky.
Wearing a crown and carrying a sword, he of divine appearance said to me: "I am the king named Mānasavega, the lord of the Vidyādharas."
The celestial woman named Surabhidattā and you yourself have fallen to earth due to a curse; that this daughter of yours is divine is indeed known to me.
"Therefore, give this daughter of yours to me, for this alliance is indeed a worthy one. When he had spoken thus, I suddenly laughed and said to him:
"Naravāhanadatta has been ordained by the gods as her husband; he shall become the sovereign emperor (cakravartin) over all of you here."
Having been addressed thus by me, that Vidyādhara flew up into the sky and departed, like a sudden flash of lightning that causes distress to the eyes of my daughter.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "O Mistress, when this prince was born here, we learned from a voice in the sky that he would be our future lord."
For those Vidyādharas immediately desired to inflict harm upon him; indeed, who would wish for a powerful master to be unrestrained?
Then, having been personally instructed by Śambhu, this Rakṣita was appointed over the Gaṇas; and these words of Nārada, as they were being spoken by my father, were heard by me.
"Therefore, these Vidyādharas are now our enemies. Upon hearing this, Kaliṅgasenā spoke out of fear for her own safety.
In that case, why is Madanamañcukā not married by the prince through an artifice, before she is deceived by him as I have been?
Having heard this from Kaliṅgasenā, Gomukha and the others said to her, "Let the Lord of Vatsa himself be urged to undertake this task."
Then, his mind fixed upon her, Naravāhanadatta spent the day in that garden, gazing at Madanamañcukā.
Her face was like a full-blown lotus, her eyes were like opening blue water-lilies, her lips were as lovely as the bandhūka flower, and her breasts were like clusters of mandāra blossoms.
Her limbs as delicate as the śirīṣa flower, appearing as if composed of five blossoms, she alone was fashioned by Smara as an arrow capable of conquering the world.
On another day, Kaliṅgasenā herself went to the Lord of Vatsa and, for the sake of her daughter’s marriage, made her request as she desired.
The Lord of Vatsa, having dismissed her and summoned his own ministers, spoke to them while Queen Vāsavadattā remained present.
Kaliṅgasenā is hastening toward her son’s marriage; how then can we act, since the world calls this most excellent woman an unchaste woman?
The world must always be protected; why was it not so in the past? By his mere reputation, Rāmabhadra abandoned Queen Jānakī, even though she was pure.
Even though Ambā was abducted by Bhīṣma with great effort for the sake of his brother, why did he not abandon her when she acted contrary to his will, having previously chosen another husband?
Thus, since this Kaliṅgasenā was married by Madanavega after I had already chosen her in a svayaṃvara, people despise her for it.
Therefore, let this Naravāhanadatta himself marry her, his own worthy daughter, according to the Gāndharva rite.
When the King of Vatsa had spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa said: "O Lord, how could Kaliṅgasenā desire such impropriety?"
"For she is divine and not ordinary, along with her son"—this has been understood by me repeatedly, and it was told to me by my friend, the wise Brahmarākṣasa.
While they were thus deliberating with one another, there suddenly emerged from the sky a voice belonging to Maheśvara.
This [story] was composed by me for Naravāhanadatta, who was created from the mind-born god [Kāma] after he had been consumed by the fire of Manasā’s eye.
Pleased by his asceticism, his wife Ratimadanamañcukā was granted to him; and he was accompanied by her, the foremost of all the women in the harem.
"By my grace, having conquered his enemies, he shall exercise divine sovereignty over the Vidyādharas for an eon (kalpa)," she said, and then her voice ceased.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, the King of Vatsa, together with his retinue, bowed to him and, filled with joy, made a firm resolve regarding the marriage.

Then the king, having greeted and summoned his chief minister—who already knew the truth of the matter—as well as the astrologers, asked them for an auspicious moment that would yield favorable results; and they, having received honors, told him that it would occur within a few days.
"Your son will experience some slight separation here from this wife of yours; we know this, O Lord of Vatsa, through the insight of our own science," so the astrologers declared to you once again.

Then the king made preparations for his son’s wedding in a manner befitting his own majesty, such that not only his own city, but the entire earth, was thrown into a state of agitation by those efforts.

Then, on the day of the wedding, Kaliṅgasenā’s father provided her with his own divine ornaments; and Somaprabhā, having come under the influence of her husband’s command, performed the rite of adorning his daughter.
Then, having had the divine marriage-thread fastened upon her, Madanamañcukā shone forth exceedingly; indeed, it was just like the lovely moonlight when it follows the month of Kārtika.
And by the command of Hara, divine women, their songs being heard, performed auspicious rites for her; though eclipsed by her beauty, they acted as if they were ashamed.

"O Daughter of the Mountain, compassionate toward your devotees, you have today come in person and made the penance of Rati successful!"—with such words, accompanied by the music of divine and excellent celestial bards, the Goddess Gaurī joins her dance here, even though she is only inferable from the sounds.

Then Naravāhanadatta entered the wedding chamber, which was occupied by Madanamañcukā and adorned with the splendor of the auspicious marriage-thread, while he himself bore various great musical instruments.

Having there completed the auspicious marriage rites with great zeal and without negligence, the bride and groom ascended the altar where the fire blazed brightly, which was like the crown of kings adorned with lamps of pure jewels.

If, at some point, the moon and the sun were to revolve simultaneously around the Golden Mountain here, then only would there be a resemblance to the circumambulation of the bride and bridegroom around the fire in this world.

Just as the drums in the sky drowned out the sounds of the wedding festival trumpets, so too did the showers of flowers released by the gods here overwhelm the parched grain scattered for the bride during the oblation.

Then the noble-minded Kaliṅgasenā indeed honored her son-in-law with heaps of gold and jewels made of gems, such that even the Lord of Alakā himself was perceived by the people there as utterly destitute in her presence; what then need be said of other wretched kings?

And when the ceremony for the marriage rite—which had been long desired and was now accomplished in such a manner corresponding to their wishes—was completed, the bride and groom entered the inner apartments, which were filled with joy, like the mind of the world filled with pure and variegated devotion.

O one honored by the whole world, that city was quickly filled with kings who, though surrounded by excellent armies and filled with valor, had been conquered and humbled; they arrived with noble gifts and jewels in their hands, like so many oceans.
During this great festival, that king also showered gold upon his subjects; indeed, there was no one in his kingdom who was not born of gold while still in their mother's womb.

Then, with throngs of excellent wandering minstrels and dancers gathered there from various quarters, the world of living beings was perceived as consisting entirely of that [festivity], surrounded by hymns, dances, songs, and instrumental music.
And in this festival, Kauśāmbī, with its creeper-like arms of banners tossed by the wind, seemed to dance itself, the city adorned with the ornaments fashioned by the women of the citizens.

And so, as he grew day by day, that great festival was celebrated here for a very long time; and all his friends, kinsmen, and the people were always joyful, and thus their desires were somewhat fulfilled.
And that Crown Prince Naravāhanadatta, together with Madanamañcukā, pursued the long-desired pleasures of the world of the living, seeking their fulfillment.
Thus ends the eighth wave in the Madanamañcukā book of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And this sixth book, the Madanamañcukā book, is completed. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Seventh Book, named Ratnaprabhā. It is said that long ago this nectar of stories emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Lord of Mountains. Those who forcibly swallow it, having attained prosperity through the removal of obstacles, bear upon this earth the divine status of the gods by the grace of Bhava.
May the head of Śarva be for your welfare—a head covered by the fingernails of Gaurī as she busily seizes his hair in play, appearing as if enriched by many moons. The First Wave.
May that Elephant-faced One protect you, who, extending his trunk with its tip curled and moistened by the water of his gift, appears as if bestowing spiritual perfection.
Thus, having married there in Kauśāmbī that Madanamañcukā, who was as dear to him as his own life, the young son of the Lord of Vatsa—
Naravāhanadatta remained together with his own ministers, Gomukha and the others, as he pleased, his heart's desires completely fulfilled.
Once, in a place resplendent with the warbling of intoxicated cuckoos and filled with the Malaya breeze, which was dancing and swaying the creepers;
When the spring festival had arrived, made beautiful by the singing of bees, the prince went to the garden to enjoy himself, accompanied by his ministers.
Having wandered there, his friend Tapantaka suddenly approached him and, with eyes wide open in great joy, spoke to him.
"O Prince, I have seen a certain maiden not far from here; having descended from the sky, she stands beneath an Ashoka tree."
And having been sent by that very maiden, who was accompanied by her friends and illuminated the quarters with her own radiance, I approached you to summon you.
Having heard that, Naravāhanadatta, eager to see him, went quickly to the foot of that tree along with his own ministers.
There he beheld his beloved, whose flickering eyes were like bees, whose sprout-like lips were crimson, and who was adorned with the clusters of her full breasts.
Her limbs were as white as a mass of pollen, she dispelled heat with her shadow, and having assumed a form worthy of her station, she appeared like the presiding deity of the grove in person.
And as she approached bowing before him, the prince, whose eyes were captivated by her beauty, greeted that celestial maiden with joy.
Then, when everyone had sat down, Gomukha, his minister, asked her: "O auspicious lady, who are you, and for what purpose have you come here?"
Having heard that, she—casting aside her shame due to the command of Love (Kāma), which is difficult to transgress—repeatedly [gazed] at the lotus-face of Naravāhanadatta.
Glancing sideways with her eyes, she spoke at length of her own life story in this manner, her voice flowing unevenly with sobs.
In the three worlds there is a famous lord of mountains known as Himavat; of that mountain with its many peaks, one peak is the mountain of the Lord of Gaurī.
Garlanded with the radiance of brilliant jewels and shimmering with the brilliance of snow, he cannot be measured, just like the vast expanse of the sky.
Whose ridges are the repository of both supernatural powers and medicinal herbs—powers obtainable through the grace of Śiva and which sever the fear of old age and death.
By its peaks, which are tawny with the radiance from the bodies of throngs of vidyādharas, the splendor of the summit of the king of the gods' mountain is surpassed.
Therein lies a golden city named Kāñcanaśṛṅga, which shines brilliantly as if it were the abode of the Sun-god with its radiant splendors.
In that realm, which extends for many yojanas, there dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Hemaprabha, who possesses firm devotion to Umāpati.
And among his many wives, he has a beloved chief queen named Alaṃkāraprabhā, who is like Rohiṇī to the moon.
Having risen with her at dawn, that righteous king bathed and duly worshipped Maheśvara, who is joined by Gaurī.
Having come to the world of men, he bestows a hundred thousand pieces of gold, mixed with jewels, day after day upon brahmins who are poor.
Then, having returned and attended to his royal duties in accordance with dharma, he partakes of food, drink, and so forth like a sage, being firm in his vows.
As the days passed in this manner, it is said that due to his lack of offspring, a concern regarding the king’s sonlessness eventually arose within him.
Seeing him so deeply distressed, his beloved queen Alaṅkāraprabhā asked him the cause of his dejection.
Then the king said to her: "O Queen, I possess every kind of prosperity; however, the single sorrow that I have no son afflicts me."
This thought has arisen in me because of the recollection of that discourse on a virtuous man who was previously childless, which I once heard.
When asked by the goddess, "O Lord, what kind of story is that?", the king described that very story to her in brief as follows.
In the city named Citrakūṭa, there was an excellent king, devoted to the worship of Brahmins, whose name was truly significant: Brāhmaṇavara.
He had a victorious servant named Sattvaśīla, who was devoted solely to battle; and month after month, he received a hundred gold pieces from that king.
And that gold did not suffice for his needs, because he was childless and his mind was solely intent on the joy of giving.
The Creator has granted me this son as a cause for diversion; yet he has also bestowed upon me a passion for giving, which is now rendered fruitless by the lack of wealth.
Better is the birth of a withered, decayed tree or even of a stone than that of a person in saṃsāra who is impoverished and whose sole passion is renunciation.
Constantly reflecting thus, that man of virtuous character, while once wandering through a garden, by chance discovered a treasure-trove.
And taking him along with his servants, he brought him by force to his home, which was radiant with abundant gold and beautiful with highly precious jewels.
Then, while enjoying pleasures and bestowing wealth upon the Brahmins, his servants, and his friends, he remained there in a state of sattvic purity.
Having seen that, his kinsmen inferred it was a discovery of treasure; they went to the royal court and reported it freely to the king.
Then, summoned by the king at the command of the chamberlain, Sattvaśīla stood for a moment in a secluded corner of the royal courtyard.
There, digging the earth with a playful fist-clenched vajra held in his hand, he obtained another great treasure contained within a copper jar.
Having given this heart of his own to the king as a pleasing gift, it was revealed by the Creator, who was pleased with his virtuous nature, as if it were something manifest.
In that very manner, he covered it with clay and entered it; then, announced by the doorkeeper, he approached the presence of the king.
"I have learned that you have found a treasure; surrender it to us. Thus was he addressed by the king himself, who had bowed before him.
"What should I offer to the god today? What should be said for this day? To him, Sattvaśīla spoke there to the king: "That too [should be offered]."
Thus addressed by the king, "Deliver this which you have newly obtained," he went to a secluded spot in the royal courtyard and handed over the treasure to him.
Then, dismissed by the king who was pleased with his treasure, Sattvaśīla went home with the words, "Enjoy the first treasure as you wish."
There he lived, making his name true to its meaning through both giving and enjoyment, and somehow dispelling the mental distress and sorrow caused by childlessness.
Thus, having previously heard this account of Sattvaśīla’s conduct, I remain in sorrow as I reflect upon the thought that my son does not exist.
When the lord of the Vidyādharas, Hemaprabha, had spoken thus to his queen Alaṅkāraprabhā, she replied to him:
It is true that destiny assists those of noble character; for what other treasure could have been found by one of virtuous nature in the midst of such peril?
By the power of your own merit, you too shall attain what you desire; hear now the story of Vikramatuṅga as an illustration of this.
There is a city named Pāṭaliputra, an ornament of the earth, inlaid with various excellent jewels that possess a perfect array of colors.
In that place, there was formerly a courageous king named Vikramatuṅga, who never turned his back on suppliants in matters of charity, nor on his enemies in battle.
Once, having entered the forest for the sake of hunting, the king beheld there a brahmin performing a fire sacrifice with *bilva* fruits.
Having seen him, although he wished to question him, he departed from his presence and went far away with his army, out of a passion for hunting.
Having played for a long time with lions and deer as if with balls—some leaping up, some falling down, and some being struck by their own paws.
Having returned and seeing that twice-born man there still intent on his fire-oblation, he approached him, bowed, and inquired after his name and the fruit of his oblation.
Then that brahmin, having offered a blessing to the king, addressed him: "I am a brahmin named Nāgaśarman; hear from me the result of my sacrificial rite."
When the fire becomes propitious through this oblation of bilva fruits, then golden bilvas emerge from the sacrificial pit.
Then Agni, having manifested himself, granted him a boon directly: "A great deal of time has passed for me while you have been offering *bilva* fruits."
"Yet that fire is not satisfied even now with one of such meager merit. When he said this, the king, being of firm resolve, addressed him:
"In that case, O Brahmin, give me a single *bilva* fruit so that I may offer it; I shall propitiate your fire this very moment."
How can you seek to propitiate that fire while remaining undisciplined and impure—a fire which is not satisfied even with me, who am thus established in my vows and purified?
Having been addressed thus by that brahmin, the king spoke to him again: "Do not give me the wood-apple in this manner; wait a moment so that you may see a marvel."
Then that brahmin, filled with curiosity, gave a bilva fruit to the king; and the king, at that moment, received it there with a mind of firm resolve.
"If he is not satisfied by this offering of a bilva fruit, then I shall sacrifice my own head upon you, O Fire," he thought, and meditating thus, he offered it into him.
And the seven-flamed fire emerged from the sacrificial pit, itself taking up a golden bilva fruit, like the fruit of the tree of being.
And Jātavedas himself spoke to that lord of the earth: "I am pleased with this courage of yours; therefore, O King, choose a boon."
Having heard that, the Great Being, bowing before the king, said: "What other boon do I have? Grant this twice-born man whatever he desires."
Having heard these words of the king, Agni, being well-pleased, said to him: "O King, this man shall become a Brāhmaṇa, a lord of wealth through the Maghā constellation."
"By my grace, you too shall possess the glory of an inexhaustible treasury. When the Fire-god had thus granted the boon, that Brahmin addressed him:
"You have suddenly appeared before the king who wanders according to his own will; but what is this to me, who am under religious observances? O Blessed One, why is this so?"
Then Agni, the giver of boons, said: "If I had not granted him my sight, this king of intense devotion would surely have offered his own head to me."
For those of intense resolve, the accomplishments indeed come without delay; but for those of dull resolve, such as yourself, O Brahmin, they come only after a long time.
Having spoken thus, when the Fire-god had vanished, that brahmin Nāgaśarman took leave of the king and departed; thereafter, he gradually became a man of great wealth.
King Vikramatuṅga, having witnessed that marvel and being praised by his followers, departed for his own city, Pāṭaliputra.
Once, while the lord was staying there, a doorkeeper named Śatruñjaya entered unexpectedly and addressed him in private:
"O King, a young Brahmin named Dattaśarman stands at the gate, desiring to make a representation in this secluded place."
When the king commanded, "Let him enter," he was ushered in; having offered a blessing and prostrated before the king, the young brahmin sat down.
And he informed [the king]: "O Lord, I know how to produce excellent gold immediately from copper by means of a certain formulation of powder."
For that method was indeed taught to me by my guru, and by means of that method, I myself directly perceived his gold as it was fully accomplished.
When the young student had spoken thus, the king had copper brought; once that had been melted, the student threw the powder into it.
And as that powder was being scattered, some invisible being carried it away; a certain Yakṣa saw him, while the king’s fire was satisfied.
The copper, not having reached the powder, did not turn into gold; thus, as the young brahmin performed this three times, his labor became fruitless.
Then, taking the powder from that despondent boy himself, the king—the best among the radiant—cast it into the molten copper.
The Yakṣa smiled and departed with that powder; through its combination with that powder, the copper attained the state of gold.
Then, to that astonished young brahmin who questioned him, the king related the account of the yakṣa exactly as it had been witnessed.
Having learned the art of preparing medicinal powders from that boy at that very time, the king made him successful by providing him with a wife.
