And Pūrṇakoṣaśrī, having made the twice-born free from poverty, sent them away with gold produced from that [mercury] along with their wives, providing them with incomparable enjoyments.
Thus, whether as if afraid or as if delighted, it is indeed the Lord himself who grants what is desired to those of intense resolve.
And who else, O Lord, possesses such steadfast courage as you? Furthermore, Śambhu, when propitiated, will grant you a son; do not grieve.
Having heard these words from the mouth of Queen Udāramalaṃkāraprabhā, King Hemaprabha believed them and was filled with joy.
And he believed that the attainment of a son would certainly result from the propitiation of Gaurī’s Lord, as indicated by his own heart, which was filled with enthusiasm.
Then, on another day, having bathed together with his queen and worshipped Śaṅkara, he bestowed ninety million pieces of gold upon the brahmins.
For the sake of a son, he performed austerities without food before Hara, having resolved: "Either my body shall be cast away, or Śarva shall be gratified."
And while engaged in austerity, he praised the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, the bestower of boons, who had effortlessly bestowed the Ocean of Milk upon Upamanyu when he sought refuge in him.
Salutations to you, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world; O Lord of Gaurī, whose eightfold forms are distinguished by the various elements such as space and the rest.
Salutations to you, Śambhu, who reclines upon the ever-blossomed lotus of the heart, the swan dwelling within the pure mind.
Homage to you, O Soma, of divine radiance, stainless, whose essence is water; who are visible to those whose defects have been extinguished, and who are most wonderful.

Salutations to You, who are identical with the universe, who hold Your beloved within half of Your body, who remain solely a celibate student, and who have fashioned the entire world by Your mere will.
When the king had thus offered praise and had fasted for three nights, the Lord of Girijā appeared to him in person in a dream and spoke as follows.
Arise, O King! A heroic son shall be born to you who will uphold your lineage; and by the grace of Gaurī, an excellent daughter shall also be born to you.
She shall become the queen of Naravāhanadatta, your future universal emperor and treasury of splendors.
When Śarva had vanished after saying this, Hemaprabha, the lord of the Vidyādharas, awoke delighted at the end of the night.
Having related his dream, he greatly delighted Alaṅkāraprabhā, whose wife had likewise been told of it by Gaurī in a dream, confirming their conversation.
Then, having risen from there and bathed, that king, having worshipped Dhūrjaṭi (Śiva), gave gifts and, having broken his fast, celebrated a festival.
Then, after some days had passed, Queen Alaṃkāraprabhā became pregnant with the king's child.
And she gladdened her beloved with her honey-scented mouth, which had eyes like restless bees, as if with a pale lotus.
Then, in due time, she gave birth to a son whose noble birth was proclaimed by her magnificent pregnancy longings, just as the sky gives birth to the sun.
By him, as soon as he was born, his innate splendors illuminated even the dwelling where he was born, turning it the color of vermilion.
And the king, his father, gave that infant—who brought fear to the lineages of his enemies—the name Vajraprabha, as instructed by a divine voice.
Then that boy grew gradually like the moon on the day of the full moon, being filled with its digits for the sake of the increase of the ocean of his lineage.
Then, before long, Queen Alaṃkāraprabhā became pregnant once again by that King Hemaprabha.
Pregnant, with a special luster arising from her physical form, she truly became the jewel of the inner apartments, seated upon a golden throne.
And she, whose pregnancy longings were thus manifesting, wandered through the sky in a celestial chariot fashioned from a lotus created by her magic power.
And when the time arrived, a daughter was born to that queen; it would be superfluous to describe her birth, which resulted from the grace of Gaurī.
Then, a voice from heaven was heard, which accorded with the words of Śiva’s command: "She shall be the future wife of Naravāhanadatta."
Then King Hemaprabha, having celebrated a festival for her birth that was no different from one for a son, gave his daughter the name Ratnaprabhā.
And that Ratnaprabhā, refined by her own learning, grew up in her father’s house, while her radiance spread throughout the quarters of the world.
Then that king, having performed the marriage rites for his son Vajraprabha, the wearer of armor, consecrated him as the crown prince.
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to him, he was not at ease; for at that time, the single concern of his heart was the thought of his son’s marriage.
Once, seeing that daughter of his who was seated nearby, the king spoke to Queen Alaṅkāraprabhā, who was sitting close at hand.
Behold, O Queen, how even a maiden who has become an ornament to her family is a source of great suffering in the three worlds; fie, alas, even upon the great!
Although she is disciplined, though she has acquired knowledge, and though she possesses beauty and youth, this Ratnaprabhā distresses me because she lacks the attainment of a boon.
"This woman has been declared as the wife of Naravāhanadatta by the gods; why then is she not given to him, who is destined to be our emperor?"
When he had been addressed thus by the goddess, the king spoke again: "Certainly, that maiden is blessed who shall obtain him as her husband."
For he has indeed descended here out of desire; however, he has not yet attained divinity, and therefore I await his acquisition of the vidyā.
As his father was speaking thus, those words—which were like the syllables of a mantra for the delusion of Kandarpa—immediately entered his ears.
Her heart stolen by that excellent man, Ratnaprabhā became as if possessed by delusion, as if her mind were entranced, as if she had fallen asleep, and as if she were licked away.
Then, having somehow paid homage to her parents and gone to her own inner apartments, she became overcome with anxiety and only after a long time did she finally fall asleep.
"Daughter, this morning is an auspicious day; you must go to the city of Kauśāmbī and see that chosen husband of yours, the son of the Lord of Vatsa."
And then, O auspicious lady, your father himself will bring him to this city of his and arrange the marriage between you and him.
Thus Gaurī, filled with compassion, instructed him in his dream; and having awakened from that dream, she reported it to her mother in the morning.
Then, having received his permission and perceiving through the power of her magic science that he was staying in a garden, she set out from her own city to see the bridegroom.
"Noble son, you know me as this Ratnaprabhā; you now know that I have arrived today, eager [to see you], and nothing more than this."
Having heard these words of hers, which surpassed nectar in sweetness, and having beheld that body of the Vidyādharī, which was nectar to the eyes;
Naravāhanadatta inwardly reproached the Creator, thinking: "Why did he not make me entirely composed of ears and eyes?"
And he said to her: "I am blessed; today my birth has become fruitful, O slender one, since I have been thus approached by you yourself out of affection."
While the two of them were thus engaged in conversation born of mutual and fresh affection, suddenly the army of the Vidyādharas was seen there in the sky.
When Ratnaprabhā immediately exclaimed, "Father has come here," King Hemaprabha descended from the sky with his son.
And he approached Naravāhanadatta together with his son Vajraprabha, who received him with the respect due to a welcome guest.
While they remained for a moment engaged in mutual conversation, the King of Vatsa, having learned of this, arrived there accompanied by his ministers.
Then Hemaprabha informed that king, who had offered him hospitality, of the entire account exactly as Ratnaprabha had told it.
And he said, "I have learned through the power of my magic science that this daughter has come here; I know the entire account of what has occurred in this matter."
For such a celestial palace of a universal monarch will indeed be his to enjoy in the future.
Give your consent; you shall soon behold this son of yours, the crown prince, returned here accompanied by his wife Ratnaprabhā.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Vatsa and having had his desire granted by him, he, together with his son, fashioned that celestial chariot by means of his own magic science.
There he placed Naravāhanadatta, whose face was bowed with shame, together with Ratnaprabhā and accompanied by Gomukha and the others.
And Hemaprabha, sent by his father who was accompanied by Yaugandharāyaṇa, was led to his own city, Kāñcanaśṛṅgaka.
And Naravāhanadatta, having reached that city of his father-in-law, beheld it made of gold, resplendent with golden ramparts.
It appeared as if adorned on all sides by spreading rays of light, with many arms extended out of the excitement of affection for his son-in-law.
There, the king Hemaprabha, undertaking a great effort, gave Ratnaprabhā to him according to the prescribed rites, just as the ocean gave Śrī to Hari.
Then he presented to him heaps of radiant jewels, which possessed the splendor of many blazing wedding fires.
In that king’s city, which was full of festivity as he showered wealth like rain, even the houses, adorned with banners, appeared as if they were clothed in garments.
And Naravāhanadatta, having completed the auspicious ceremonies of his marriage, remained there together with Ratnaprabhā, enjoying celestial pleasures.
And he took delight in divine gardens, ponds, and temples, as he traveled through the sky by means of that magical science, accompanied by her.

And having thus stayed for some days in that city of the lord of the Vidyādharas, the son of the King of Vatsa, accompanied by his bride, resolved, according to the counsel of Yaugandharāyaṇa, to return to his own city.

Then, having had the auspicious rites performed for him by his mother-in-law, and being honored once more by his father-in-law along with his ministers, he set out together with that very man and his son; accompanied by his beloved wife, he ascended the celestial chariot once again.

Having quickly reached that city, which was filled with joy and where the King of Vatsa had held a great festival, he—who was like a flood of nectar to his mother’s eyes—entered his own capital together with Ratnaprabhā, his son Hemaprabha, and his followers.

The Lord of Vatsa, possessed of mighty glory, together with Vāsavadattā, greeted the son and daughter-in-law who had prostrated at his feet; he then honored his new relative Hemaprabha and his son in a manner befitting his wealth.
Then, after taking leave of the King of Vatsa and the others, that king of the Vidyādharas, Hemaprabha, flew up into the sky with his son and departed for his own city.
Accompanied by his own friends, Naravāhanadatta spent that day in happiness together with Ratnaprabhā and Madanamañcukā.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave: On another day, while he was in her house together with his beautiful and new Vidyādhara wife Ratnaprabhā, who had been obtained by him...
In the morning, while Naravāhanadatta was staying there, his ministers, Gomukha and the others, arrived at the gate to see him.
Then, when they had been stopped for a moment by the female doorkeeper and subsequently announced, and had entered with due respect, Ratnaprabhā addressed that doorkeeper.
The door must not be barred against these friends of our noble son as they enter here again; for they are indeed our own bodies.
"Such protection as this within the inner apartments is not at all my opinion," she said, addressing the female door-keeper, and then spoke to her husband.
"Noble son, I speak to you at length; listen to that. I consider the guarding and restraining of women to be merely a matter of worldly policy."
Or perhaps this delusion was caused by jealousy; it serves no purpose whatsoever. For women of noble family are protected by their own virtue alone, which is a greater safeguard than anything else.
Even the Creator is generally not the master in the protection of the fickle; for by whom can a rutting river and a woman be restrained?
And so, listen; I shall tell you a story on this matter: there is here, in the middle of the great ocean, an island named Ratnakūṭa.
In that place, there was formerly a king named Mahotsāha, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, who was known by the meaningful title Ratnādhipati.
That king performed great penance as an act of worship to Viṣṇu in order to obtain victory over the earth, as well as all the daughters of kings as his wives.
Pleased by his asceticism, the Lord appeared in person and commanded him: "Arise, O King! I am gratified; therefore, listen as I speak these words to you."
In the kingdom of Kaliṅga, a certain Gandharva, having been born as an elephant due to a sage’s curse, became known as Śvetaraśmi, the white one.

Due to the power of penance in a previous birth, through the yoga of spiritual attainment, and likewise by virtue of devotion to me, that elephant became a man of knowledge, capable of traveling through the sky, and possessed of the memory of his former lives.
"I have given my command in a dream that this great elephant of yours shall come of its own accord through the path of the sky and become your vehicle."
Mounting that white elephant, like the wielder of the thunderbolt upon Airāvata, you shall proceed by way of the sky toward whichever king you intend to attack.
Terrified by your divine power, he will offer you his hand under the pretext of giving his daughter, having been given the command by me in a dream.
In this way, you shall conquer the entire earth and the inner apartments; you shall obtain eighty thousand princesses.
When Viṣṇu had spoken thus and vanished, the king, having broken his fast, beheld on another day that auspicious elephant arrived through the sky.
Having mounted that [chariot] which had been brought to him as directed by Viṣṇu, he conquered the earth accordingly and brought back the daughters of kings.
Then, together with those eighty thousand women, the king dwelt there on Ratnakūṭa, sporting as he pleased.
For the sake of pacifying that divine elephant, Śītaraśmi, he fed five hundred brahmins every day.
And once, having ascended that [ship] and wandered through other islands, that king, Ratnādhipati, returned to his own island.
As he was descending from the sky toward that excellent elephant, a bird born of Tārkṣya by chance struck him on the head with its beak.
Struck by the king with a sharp goad, that bird fled; but the elephant, fainting from the blow of the beak, fell to the ground.
When the king had descended, that elephant, though still conscious, was unable to rise; even when being lifted up, it remained prostrate, refusing to take a morsel of food.
In that same manner, as he remained fallen upon this elephant, the king, distressed and without food, spoke thus for five days.
"O World-Protectors, tell me a remedy for this my crisis; otherwise, I shall offer you my own head today after cutting it off."
As soon as he had spoken thus and raised his sword to cut off his own head, an unembodied voice from the sky spoke these words at that very moment:
"Do not act rashly, O King! If some virtuous woman touches this elephant with her hand, he will rise; it cannot be otherwise."
Upon hearing that, the king was delighted and summoned his own principal queen, Surakṣitā, by name Amṛtalatā.
When the elephant did not rise even though touched by her hand, the king then summoned all his other queens.
Having clearly felt the touch of their hands by all of them together, the king, seeing this in the presence of the people, was truly overcome with shame.
Seeing her even at eighty years of age, thousands of women from the inner apartments were clearly overcome with shame in the presence of the people; so too was that king.
Embarrassed, he summoned all the women from that city and, one by one, had them touch the trunk of that elephant.
Nevertheless, because that lord of elephants did not rise, the king felt ashamed, thinking, "Alas! Not even a single virtuous woman remains in my city."
Just then, a merchant named Harṣagupta arrived there from Tāmraliptī, having learned of that event and coming with great curiosity.
Afterwards, his female servant, a devoted wife named Śīlavatī who was alone, arrived; having seen that, she spoke to him.
"I touch this elephant with my hand; if it has not been meditated upon by anyone else even in their mind as belonging to another husband of mine, then let this elephant rise up."
Having said this, she approached and touched him with her hand; he rose up healthy, and then he took a morsel of food.
These are those rare virtuous women who are like lords themselves, capable of the creation, preservation, and destruction of this world.
Thus, seeing Śvetaraśmi rise up there, the people raised a great clamor and praised the virtuous woman.
King Ratnādhipati, being thoroughly pleased and rejoicing, filled the virtuous and faithful Śīlavatī with innumerable jewels.
And he likewise honored Harṣagupta, the merchant who was its owner, and gave him a house near Rājagṛha.
Having thus abandoned all physical contact with his own wives, he thereafter made them recipients only of food and clothing.
Then, having summoned her and finished his meal, the king spoke to that virtuous and well-conducted woman in private, in the presence of Harṣagupta.
"O virtuous lady, do you have any maiden from your father's family? Let her be given to me; for I know that she too will surely be like you."
Having been addressed thus by the king, Śīlavatī then said: "In Tāmraliptī there is a sister of mine named Rājadattā."
"O King, if you so desire, marry her of such praiseworthy form. Thus addressed by the queen, he agreed, saying, "So be it."
Having decided upon this, on the following day, he, along with Śīlavatī and Harṣagupta, mounted that vehicle which traveled through the air.
Having gone in person to Tāmraliptī with Śvetaraśmi, that king entered the palace of the merchant Harṣagupta.
There, on that day, he asked the astrologers for an auspicious moment for the marriage of his sister Śīlavatī and also for that of Rājadattā.
And the astrologers, having inquired about the lunar mansions for both, spoke thus: "O King, an auspicious moment for you both exists within three months from now."
O Lord, if Rājadattā is married today with such a man as exists [now], she will inevitably become unchaste.
Although addressed thus by the astrologers, the king, longing for his lovely bride, remained alone for a long time and reflected:
"Enough with deliberation; marry Rājadattā this very day, for she is the sister of Śīlavatī; being free from pride, she cannot be unchaste."
In that uninhabited island-fragment in the midst of the ocean, where there is a single empty four-winged building, I shall establish her there.
"In this inaccessible place, I shall provide her with a retinue consisting only of women; for if she does not see any men, how could she possibly become unchaste?"
Having thus resolved, on that very day the king suddenly married Rājadattā, who had been entrusted to him by Śīlavatī.
Having performed the marriage rites and fulfilled the customary ceremonies, he took that bride along with Harṣagupta and Śīlavatī.
Mounting that white-rayed steed, he then reached in an instant his own island, Ratnakūṭa, by way of the sky, where the people were looking out for him on the path.
And she shared with Śīlavatī so much more that the latter attained the fruit of her vow as a virtuous wife and became fulfilled.
Then, having mounted his new bride Rājadattā upon that very elephant Śvetaraśmi, who was capable of traveling through the sky, he [departed] as soon as it was thought of.
Having led her there to an island in the middle of the ocean inaccessible to humans, he established her in a four-winged palace with a retinue consisting entirely of women.
Whatever object was used by her, he, distrusting it, caused it to reach that place by means of that elephant as if through the sky itself.
He himself, being devoted to her, remained there constantly at night; however, for the sake of the royal business, he would return to Ratnakūṭa during the day.
Once, at dawn, the king, wishing to ward off an evil dream, enjoyed an auspicious drink together with Rājadattā.
Having released her even though she did not let go of him out of intoxication, he departed for Ratnakūṭa for the sake of his own purpose; for royal power is ever-fickle.
There he remained with apprehension, performing his duties with a mind that seemed to say, "Why have you released her alone while she is intoxicated?"
Meanwhile, Rājadattā remained all alone in that most inaccessible place, while her maidservants were occupied with the kitchen and other tasks.
At the gate, he saw a certain man who inspired wonder, appearing like another ritual officiant who had arrived with the desire to conquer those various guardians.
"Who are you, and how have you come to this place which is inaccessible? Thus, it is said, that intoxicated woman questioned him as he approached her.
Then, having observed her many afflictions, that man said to her: "O charming girl, I am a merchant's son from Mathurā named Pavana-sena."
My property having been seized by my kinsmen, I became protectorless upon the death of my father; having gone to a foreign land, I resorted to the miserable service of others.
Then, having with great difficulty acquired a small amount of wealth through trade, I was robbed by bandits while traveling to another country on the road.
Then, wandering for alms with others like myself, I went to a place known as Kanakakṣetra, a source of precious gems.
There, having agreed to pay the king's share for a period of one year, I dug the earth in a pit but did not obtain even a single jewel.
While those like me and others rejoiced at having obtained the jewels, I went to the shore of the ocean and, afflicted by grief, gathered pieces of wood.
Just as I was preparing a funeral pyre there for the purpose of entering the fire with them, a certain merchant named Jīvadatta arrived at that place.
Having saved me from death and provided me with a livelihood, that compassionate man took me onto his ship, desiring to go to Suvarṇadvīpa.
Then, while they were traveling through the middle of the ocean by ship, after five days had passed, a cloud suddenly appeared.
When this cloud rained down in thick torrents driven by the wind, that carriage reeled about like the head of an intoxicated elephant.
When this vessel had broken and I was submerged for a moment by the power of fate, I, while sinking, at that time obtained a single plank.
Having ascended it, when the mass of clouds had subsided by the power of destiny, I reached this region and have now emerged in the forest.
Having beheld this four-winged mansion and entered its interior, O auspicious one, I saw you—the rain of nectar for my eyes that soothes all my distress.
Having spoken thus, Rājadattā, deluded by both intoxication and passion, settled him upon her couch and embraced him.
Womanhood, intoxication, solitude, the acquisition of a man, and lack of restraint—where these five fires are present, what news can there be for the straw of moral conduct?
But this woman, deluded by Māra, did not consider that it was improper for her to desire the king, who was undesirable and fallen into calamity.
And at that very moment, King Ratnādhipati, mounted on a celestial elephant as his vehicle, arrived in haste from Ratnakūṭa, filled with anxiety.
And as he entered there, he saw his wife Rājadattā engaged in amorous dalliance with that very same man, even though he was of such a kind.
Seeing that man fallen at his feet and uttering piteous words, the king did not kill him, even though he had intended to do so.
Seeing his wife both terrified and intoxicated, he thought thus: "How can a woman remain faithful when she is addicted to wine, the sole friend of Māra?"
A fickle woman cannot be restrained even by guarding; for how could a whirlwind of calamity ever be bound by one's arms?
That which was not done as the astrologer said—this is its fruit for me; bitter is its ripening: the disregard of the words of a trustworthy person.
Alas, while I thought this woman was virtuous, I have forgotten that she is my own sister; that innate spray of *kālakūṭa* poison has been mixed with my nectar!
Or rather, who would be capable of overcoming through human effort the inconceivable workings of Fate, whose deeds are so wondrous?
Reflecting thus, the king did not become angry with anyone; instead, he released that merchant’s son, who had been his secret lover, after having inquired about his welfare.
Having been released from there, that merchant’s son, seeing no way forward, went out and beheld from afar a ship approaching upon the ocean.
Then, having once again mounted that very plank, he wandered upon the ocean and cried out with a loud wail, "O, save me!"
Therefore, a merchant named Krodhavarman, who was on that same ship, rescued that merchant's son and made him his own attendant.
Whatever action has been ordained by the Creator for one's destruction follows that person, pursuing them wherever they may run, even along the path.
While he remained there in a state of delusion, having met with his wife in secret, he was spotted by that merchant, cast into the ocean, and perished.
And then that king Ratnādhipati, free from anger, placed Rājadattā along with her attendants upon the white rayed elephant.
Having brought him to Ratnakūṭa and handed him over to Śīlavatī, he related that entire account to her and to his ministers.
And he said: "Alas, how much suffering have I experienced with my mind attached to these essence-less and tasteless enjoyments!"
Therefore, having now gone to the forest, I shall take refuge in Hari, so that I may never again be a vessel for such sorrows as these.
Having spoken thus, although he was being restrained by his ministers and by Śīlavatī, he remained sorrowful and, due to his world-weariness, did not abandon that resolve at all.
Then, having first offered half from his own treasury to a virtuous woman of good character, and having given the other half to the twice-born, he remained free from desire for enjoyments.
That king, according to the prescribed ritual, gave his own kingdom to the Brahmin Pāpabhañjana, who was most eminent in virtue.
Having bestowed the kingdom and intending to depart through the sky for the forest of asceticism, he caused Śvetaraśmi to be brought back while the citizens looked on with tears.
As soon as that elephant was brought there, it cast off its body and became a man of divine form, resplendent with necklaces and armlets.
When asked by the king, "Who are you? What is this? he replied, "We are two Gandharva brothers, both inhabitants of the Malaya mountains."
I am named Somaprabha, and he is Devaprabha, my elder brother; he has but one wife, and she is exceedingly dear to him.
Having placed that girl named Rājavatī on his lap, he wandered about, and once, together with me, he went to a place called Siddhavāsa.
There, in the temple of Keśava, having worshipped Acyuta, we all began to sing before the Blessed One.
Just then, a certain Siddha arrived there and stood gazing at Rājavatī with unblinking eyes, as she sang in a voice so melodious it was fit to be heard.
"Even though you are a perfected one (siddha), why do you gaze longingly at another's wife? Thus my brother, filled with jealousy and provoked to anger, spoke to that perfected one.
Then that Siddha, becoming enraged, spoke thus to him in order to curse him: "O fool, this woman was observed by me because of the wonder of her song, not out of lust."
Therefore, O jealous one, fall into a mortal womb along with her; there you shall see this very wife of yours in person, united with another.
When he had spoken thus, I then, out of childishness and due to the anger of that curse, struck him with a toy clay white elephant held in my hand.
Then he cursed me, saying: "Since I have been struck by you, may you be born on earth as a white elephant exactly like me."
Then, having been entreated by my brother Devaprabha, that compassionate Siddha spoke thus regarding the end of our curse:
By the grace of Hari, though you were once a mortal, you have become the lord of the island; you shall obtain this younger brother of yours, who has become an elephant, as a divine mount.
"You shall obtain eighty thousand women for your harem; you will discover the misconduct of them all in the presence of the people."
Furthermore, when you marry this wife of yours who has become human, you will see her with your own eyes united with another man.
Then, O Devaprabha, when your heart is dispassionate and you have given the kingdom to a twice-born man, you shall go to the forest in peace.
Then, when this younger brother of yours has first been released from his state as an elephant, you too shall be liberated from the curse along with this wife.

Thus, having reached the end of the curse as declared by the Siddha, we have been born in this manner due to the diversity of our past actions; through this separate union, that very end of the curse has come to us today.
When Somaprabha had spoken thus, King Ratnādhipati, remembering his former birth, said: "Ah! I am indeed that very Devaprabha."
"This Rājadattā was also my wife Rājavatī," he said, and together with that wife, he abandoned that body.
In an instant, all the Gandharvas, while the world looked on, flew up into the sky and went to their own abode, Mount Malaya.
Though she was virtuous, by virtue of the greatness of her moral conduct, she attained prosperity; having gone to the city of Tāmraliptī, she remained there devoted to the practice of Dharma.

Thus, in this world, no one anywhere is capable of forcibly protecting a woman; rather, it is the pure man alone who, bound by the tether of his own integrity, constantly protects a lady of noble family.

Thus, this vice called envy is the sole cause of suffering for men and brings hatred upon others; it is that which, far from preventing excessive longing for the protection of women, actually causes it to arise.
Having heard this meaningful tale told by his wife Ratnaprabhā, Naravāhanadatta rejoiced greatly together with his ministers.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. Now begins the third wave: Then, following the sequence of the story told by Ratnaprabhā, the minister Gomukha spoke to Naravāhanadatta.
It is true that virtuous women are rare, whereas women are always fickle; likewise, they are untrustworthy—O King, hear this story as well.
Here, there was a city named Ujjayinī, renowned throughout the world; in it, long ago, there lived a merchant's son named Niścayadatta.
That gambler, having won wealth through gambling day after day, would bathe in the waters of the Siprā and worship Mahākāla with a noble mind.
Having given gifts to the twice-born as well as to the poor and the helpless, he provided them with ointments, food, betel, and other such things without distinction.
Always, at the conclusion of his bathing, worship, and other rites, he would go near the abode of Mahākāla and smear himself with sandalwood paste and other substances in the cremation ground.
And having applied an ointment to that stone pillar standing there, the youth, alone every day, would rub his back against it as he smeared it.
In time, that pillar became very smooth on one side; then a painter came along that path together with a sculptor.
Seeing that very smooth pillar, he painted Gaurī upon it; even the sculptor carved her there as if in mere play with his tool.
Then, after those two had departed, a certain daughter of a Vidyādhara arrived there at Mahākāla and beheld that goddess within the pillar.
Perceiving his presence there because of her auspicious marks, she performed worship; then, becoming invisible for the sake of rest, she entered that stone pillar.
Just then, Niścayadatta, the son of a merchant, arrived there and, filled with wonder, beheld that Umā depicted within the middle of the pillar.
Having smeared his limbs, he applied an ointment to another part of that pillar; then, rubbing it, he began to scratch his back until it was completely covered.
Beholding him, that Vidyādhara maiden with tremulous eyes, standing behind a pillar with her heart captivated by his beauty, reflected:
"Even for one such as this, there is no one at all to anoint his back; therefore, I shall first anoint his back today."
Having reflected thus, that Vidyādharī then stretched out her hand from within the pillar and, out of affection, anointed his back.
At that very moment, having felt her touch and heard the sound of her anklets, that merchant’s son grasped her hand with his own.
"O highly fortunate one, what offense have I committed against you? Release my hand! Thus spoke that Vidyādharī to him from the pillar, remaining invisible.
"Appear before my eyes and tell me who you are; then I shall release your hand," Niścayadatta replied to her then.
After she had sworn an oath, saying, "I shall tell you everything that can be seen with my own eyes," the Vidyādharī spoke, and he then released her hand.
Then, emerging from the pillar, she who was beautiful in every limb sat down and, with her eyes fixed upon his face, spoke to him.
On the peak of the snowy mountain lies the city of Puṣkarāvatī; there dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Vindhyaka.
I am her daughter, a maiden named Anurāgaparā; having come here to worship Mahākāla, I have now taken my rest.
And at that very moment, having arrived here and applying ointment to my back, you were seen by me upon this pillar, resembling the weapon of Māra for the delusion of women.
First, my heart was colored by passion for me; afterwards, your hand was stained with the cosmetic ointment smeared upon your back.
"From now on, you know the abode of your father; I am departing," she said, and then the merchant's son replied:
O fierce one, that was accepted by me, but your heart was not taken; how then can you go away like this, having not relinquished the heart you accepted?
Thus addressed by him, she, overcome by the power of sudden passion, said: "I shall indeed unite with you, provided that you come to our city."
O Lord, that path is difficult to traverse, yet your desired goal shall be accomplished; for there is nothing in this world that is difficult for those who are resolute.
Having spoken thus, she flew up into the sky and departed with her passion for him; Niścayadatta also went home, his mind fixed entirely upon her.
Remembering her sprout-like hand as it emerged from her pillar-like body like a tree, alas, what a tragedy! Though I have grasped it, I have not obtained the taking of her hand in marriage.
Therefore, I shall go to her presence in that city of Puṣkarāvatī; I will either give up my life or fate will grant me assistance.
Reflecting thus, he spent that day there, afflicted by love; then, in the morning, he set out, taking the northern direction as his guide.
Then, as he was setting out, three other merchant’s sons traveling toward the Northern Region met him as companions.
Crossing cities, villages, forests, and rivers together with them, he gradually reached the northern region, which was largely inhabited by barbarians.
There, while on the road together with those very Tājikas, he was captured by other Tājikas and, having been led away, was handed over for a price to yet another Tājika.
He, moreover, dispatched it into the hands of his servants as a gift for the Turk named Muravāra.
Led there by those servants along with three others, he learned that Muravāra was dead and reported it to his son.
"This is indeed my father's gift sent to me by a friend; therefore, these must be thrown into a hole by me in his very presence tomorrow morning."
Thus, along with himself as the fourth, that Turuṣka bound him and his son firmly in fetters and kept them there for that night.
Then, in that prison at night, Niścayadatta spoke to those merchant's sons, his friends who were terrified by the fear of death.
What accomplishment is there for you through despondency? Remain firm, having taken hold of fortitude; for calamities, like those who are afraid, flee far away from the steadfast.
"Remember the one Blessed Goddess Durgā, who delivers one from calamity! Thus encouraging them with devotion, he then praised that Goddess.
Salutations to you, O Great Goddess! I bow to your feet, which are marked by red lac as if they were smeared with the mud of blood clinging from the crushed Asuras.
By your power, which establishes universal sovereignty even for Śiva, victory has been won; and this triple world, animated by you, moves.
O slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, you have been the protector of the worlds; protect me, who have come to you for refuge, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Having thus properly praised that goddess together with his companions, Niścayadatta then, being exhausted, quickly fell asleep there.
"Arise, my sons, go forth; for your bondage has indeed vanished," thus did the goddess command him and those others in a dream.
Having awakened that night and seeing their bonds fallen away of their own accord, they told each other their dream and departed from there in great joy.
Then, after traveling a long distance, when the night had faded, those other sons of merchants, having seen a cause for terror, said to Niścayadatta:
"Let this region be, for it is full of many barbarians; we shall go to the Deccan, my friend, while you may do as you please."
Having been addressed thus by them, and having granted them leave to go wherever they pleased, he once again set out, taking his course toward that very northern direction.
Then Niścayadatta set out forcefully on the road alone, his mind cast aside as he was dragged by the snares of Anurāgaparā’s love.
Proceeding by stages, he met with four practitioners of the Great Vow (Mahāvratika), and having reached the river Vitastā, he crossed it.
Having crossed over and taken his meal, when the sun was kissing the western mountain, he entered the forest that lay along his path together with those very companions.
Then some wood-carriers who had arrived at the front there said to him: "Where are you going now that the day has passed? There is no village whatsoever ahead."
In this forest, however, there is a solitary, deserted temple of Śiva; whoever stays there at night, whether inside or outside, [is seized].
The yakṣiṇī named Śṛṅgotpādinī first causes horns to grow upon him, then, having deluded him and turned him into a sacrificial animal, she devours him.
Even after hearing this, those four companions, who were great ascetics, spoke with contempt to Niścayadatta at that time.
"Come! What can that wretched yakṣiṇī do to us here? For we remain throughout the nights in various cremation grounds."
Having spoken thus, Niścayadatta went with them, reached the temple of Śiva, and entered it—which was empty—to pass that night there.
There, having quickly fashioned a great mandala with ashes upon the courtyard, and having entered within it, he kindled a fire with fuel.
The steadfast Niścayadatta and all those great ascetics likewise remained there, muttering mantras for the sake of protection.
Then, in the night, that Yakṣiṇī Śṛṅgotpādinī arrived there from afar, playing her lute, dancing, and accompanied by a Kiṃnarī skeleton.
Having approached them, she fixed her gaze upon one among those four who was observing the great vow, and outside the circle, she recited a mantra while performing a dance.
By that mantra, his horns grew back and he rose up deluded; dancing as that fire blazed, the practitioner of the great vow fell into it.
Having dragged him from the midst of the fire while he was fallen and half-burnt, that Yakṣiṇī Śṛṅgotpādinī joyfully devoured him.
Then, fixing her gaze upon the second initiate in the same manner, she recited that mantra for producing horns and danced.
The second one also, his horn grown from that mantra, was made to dance; having been dragged by her, he fell into the fire and was devoured while the others looked on.
Thus, having gradually deluded those observers of the great vow during the night, that yakṣiṇī devoured all four of them, including Śṛṅgaka.
And as she was eating the fourth [portion], intoxicated by the flesh and blood, she herself accidentally laid down her kinnarī lute upon the ground.
Then, rising quickly and taking that very [vīṇā], the resolute Niścayadatta played it, dancing, laughing, and whirling about.
With his eyes fixed upon the face of that yakṣiṇī, he repeatedly recited that mantra for producing horns, which he had learned by hearing it many times.
By the power of that practice, the Yakṣiṇī Śṛṅgī, helpless and fearing death, wishing to rise up, spoke humbly to him.
"Do not kill me, O Great Being; do not slay this wretched woman. Now you are my refuge; withdraw your recitation of mantras and other such acts."
"Protect me; I know everything, and I shall accomplish whatever you desire. Wherever your passion lies, there I shall lead you."

Having been thus addressed with confidence by her, the resolute Niścayadatta said, "So be it," and there he performed the recitation of mantras and other preliminary rites for the concentration of his purpose.
Then, having mounted the shoulder of that yakṣiṇī, being carried through the sky by her voice, he set out toward his beloved.
And when the night had turned to dawn, having reached a mountain forest, that guhyakī bowed down and addressed Niścayadatta.
"Now that the sun has risen, you have no power over me; therefore, O Lord, spend this day in this lovely forest."
"Eat the sweet fruits and drink the auspicious water from the mountain stream; I am going to my own abode and shall return at the arrival of night."
And at that very moment, I shall lead you to the presence of Anurāga, to the city of Puṣkarāvatī on the crown-garland of the Snowy Mountain.
Having spoken thus and being permitted by him, that yakṣiṇī, true to her promise, set him down from her shoulder and departed to return once more.
Then, after she had departed, Niścayadatta beheld there a lake that was deep within, poisonous, yet clear and cool on the surface.
"The mind of a passionate woman is like this"—thus the Sun, as if with his rays extended, revealed and displayed this illustration.

Perceiving by its scent that it was smeared with poison and realizing it was the work of a human, he—being thirsty and seeking water—abandoned it and wandered there on the mountain in search of divine water.
Wandering over that elevated region, he saw two objects shimmering like rubies and dug them out from the earth.
And as that monkey was still alive, he saw its head stripped of skin, and its two eyes, which were like rubies.
Then, while he was filled with wonder and reflecting, "What could this be?", that monkey addressed him in human speech.
"I am a human who has become a monkey; I am a Brahmin, so deliver me! O virtuous one, I shall then tell you my entire life story."
Upon hearing this, Niścayadatta was filled with wonder; he removed the earth and then lifted that monkey out of the ground.
Having been pulled up while prostrate at his feet, that monkey spoke to him once more: "My life has been restored by you, who rescued me from this peril."
Therefore come, since you are weary, partake of the fruits and water; through your favor, I too shall finally break my fast after a long time.

Having said this, the monkey led him a long distance away to the bank of a mountain river, where there were trees providing excellent shade and abundant, delicious fruit that required no effort to obtain.
Having bathed there and consumed water and fruit, Niścayadatta returned after he had completed his meal and spoke to that monkey.
"How is it that you, though having become a monkey, are still called a human? Then that monkey replied, "Listen now; I shall tell you this."
"O friend, there was a most excellent brahmin in Vārāṇasī named Candrasvāmin; I am this son born to him from his virtuous wife."
Named Somaśvāmin by my father, I gradually mounted the elephant of passion, which is unrestrained by the goad of love.
Once, as I was standing at the top of a window, the daughter of a merchant named Śrīgarbha, a resident of that city, saw me from afar.
A young woman named Bandhudattā, the wife of Varāhadatta, the merchant lord of Mathurā, was staying in her father’s house.
Having conceived love upon seeing me, she, desiring union with me, sought out my name and dispatched a trusted female friend to me.
That friend of hers, having approached me while I was blinded by passion, whispered my intention in my ear and led me to her own home.
Having left me there and departed, she immediately went secretly and, disregarding shame out of her eagerness, brought Bandhudattā back.
And as soon as she was brought here, she came to embrace my neck; for in women, the god of love becomes a peerless hero when he has reached his highest pitch.
Thus, coming at her own leisure from her father’s house day after day, Bandhudattā took her pleasure with me in the house of our friend.
Once, after she had stayed there for a long time, her husband, a great merchant, arrived from Mathurā to take her back to his own home.
Then, permitted by her father and desiring to be led away by that husband, she spoke to her second friend, Bandhudattā, who was privy to her secret.
"O friend, it is certain that I must be taken by my husband to the city of Mathurā; yet I cannot live there, deprived of Somasvāmin."
When she had been asked by her, "Tell me, what means is there for this?", the friend named Sukhaśayā, who was a yoginī, spoke to her.
I have two mantra-applications, by one of which, if tied around the neck upon a thread, a human being would instantly become a monkey.
And when this second thread is released, this human being shall again become a monkey, yet his wisdom shall not be lost.
Therefore, O fair-hipped one, if you desire that Somasvāmin be dear to you, then I shall turn this young monkey into him this very moment.
Therefore, taking him under the pretext of play, go to Mathurā; furthermore, I shall instruct you in these two methods involving counsel and stratagem.
"You shall arrange it so that this man, who has the form of a monkey when at his side, will become a beloved husband for you in private."
Having been thus addressed by that friend, Bandhudattā likewise brought me into her secret and, out of affection, informed me of her purpose.
And having granted me permission, that friend of hers, while I was bound by a mantra-thread around my neck, instantly made me into a young monkey, lying there at ease.
In that form, Bandhudattā brought me to her husband and showed him, saying, "This one was given to my friend for his amusement."
And he was delighted upon seeing me, his plaything, resting on his lap; and though I was a monkey, I was wise and possessed distinct speech.
"Ah, how strange is the conduct of women!"—thus laughing inwardly, I remained there; for who indeed is not mocked by desire?
Then, on another day, having been taught those mantras by her friend, Bandhudattā set out from her father's house toward Mathurā together with her husband.
And then that husband of Bandhudattā, desiring to do what was pleasing to her, placed me upon the shoulder of a single servant on the road.
Then we all, traveling along, reached after two or three days a forest situated on the middle of the path, terrifying with its many monkeys.
Then, seeing me, the monkeys rushed toward me from all sides in great numbers, shouting "kila-kila" cries and calling out to one another.
And those monkeys, difficult to restrain, arrived and began to devour that merchant’s servant upon whose shoulder I was seated.
Agitated by that, he abandoned me from his shoulder and fled on the ground out of fear; then those monkeys seized me there.
Out of affection for him, Bandhudattā, her husband, and his followers, though striking with stones and clubs, were unable to defeat those monkeys.
Then those monkeys, as if enraged by his wicked deed, tore out hair by hair from every limb of the fool with their claws and teeth.
Then, through the power of the neck-thread and by the recollection of Śambhu, I regained my strength; having loosened my bonds from them, I fled.
Having entered their dense thicket and passed beyond the range of their vision, I have traveled from forest to forest in succession and have now reached this grove.
How did this union with another's wife, which resulted in your birth as a monkey, come to pass for you in this very life after you had fallen [from your former state] through Bandhudattā?
Thus, while I was wandering here in the rainy season, blinded by the darkness of suffering, the dissatisfied Creator has bestowed yet another sorrow upon me.
When a female elephant, having suddenly approached me, seized me with her trunk and thrust me into the mud within an anthill drenched by rainwater from the clouds.
"I know that she must be some divinity appointed by destiny; for otherwise, how could I have been able to move even from this mire with such effortless ease?"
While he was being thus consoled, not only did I not die, but as I meditated incessantly upon Hara, knowledge arose within me.
And for that length of time, O friend, neither hunger nor thirst ever afflicted me, until today when I was pulled out by you from the mound of dry mud.
Even though knowledge has been attained, I do not possess such power by which I might liberate myself from this state of being a monkey.
When someone releases this neck-thread by means of that very mantra, then I shall once again become a human yoginī here in this world.
Such is my story; but tell me now, my friend, why and how have you come to this forest which is inaccessible?
Thus addressed by the brahmin Somasvāmin in the form of a monkey, Niścayadatta told him his own story.
Just as he had come from Ujjayinī for the sake of the Vidyādharī, he was brought back at night by that Yakṣiṇī, who had conquered him with her steadfastness.
Then, having heard that wondrous account, the wise Somasvāmin, who had assumed the form of a monkey, spoke to Niścayadatta.
Great suffering was experienced by you on my account because of a woman; yet in this world, neither prosperity nor women are ever stable for anyone.
Women are like the twilight, possessing a fleeting passion; they are like rivers, crooked in their disposition; they are like female serpents, untrustworthy; and they are like lightning, fickle.
Therefore, even though that Vidyādharī is passionate, she will in an instant become intent on love for some member of her own kind and turn away from you, a mere mortal.
Therefore, enough now with this effort on your behalf for the sake of a woman, which is like the fruit of the *kiṃpāka* tree—sweet at first but bitter in its final consequence.
"Friend, do not go to that city of the Vidyādharas, Puṣkarāvatī; instead, mount the shoulder of the Yakṣiṇī and go to this very Ujjayinī."
"Friend, act according to my words; for previously, out of passion, I did not follow the advice of my friend, and because of that, I am now filled with remorse."
Then my very affectionate friend, the Brahmin named Bhavaśarman, who was devoted to Bandhudattā, restrained me and spoke as follows.
"O friend, do not fall under the power of a woman, for a woman's heart is exceedingly difficult to fathom. Listen, as I tell you this account of what happened to me."
In this very city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a young woman of great beauty named Somadā, a Brahmin woman who was fickle and a secret practitioner of yoga.
By fate, I had a secret union with her; through the course of that union, my love for her increased.
Once, out of jealousy and anger, I struck her at my leisure; that cruel woman endured it, concealing her wrath for that moment.
On another day, under the pretext of a playful act of affection, he tied a string around my neck; at that very moment, I became as tame as an elephant.
Then, having become strong, I was sold by her to a certain man who lived by taming camels, after she had accepted the desired price.
There, a yoginī named Badhamocanikā, filled with compassion, beheld me suffering under the burden she had placed upon me.

Having recognized through her supernatural knowledge that I had been turned into a sacrificial animal by Soma and others, she released the string from my neck while my mistress, Madgosvāminī, was not looking.
Then, having become human, as he looked about quickly, my master—thinking that I had fled—wandered in all directions.
And as I was departing from there with her, who grants liberation from bondage, I was seen from afar by Somadā, who had arrived there by chance.
Blazing with anger, she said to that wise woman who liberates from bondage: "Why has this sinner been released by you from his state as an animal?"
"Shame on you, O woman of wicked conduct! You shall reap the fruit of this evil deed; tomorrow morning I will slay you along with that sinner."
When she had departed after saying this, that Siddha-yoginī Bandhamocinī spoke to me for the purpose of counteracting her [the other's] power.
"She will approach to slay me in the form of a black mare, and I shall assume the form of a red mare here."
Then, when the battle has commenced, you must strike Somadā from behind with a sword in hand, remaining vigilant toward her.
"In this way we shall kill her; therefore, you must come to my house tomorrow morning," she said, and then she showed me her own home.
When she had entered there, I went to my own home, having experienced many wonders even in this very life.
In the morning, sword in hand, I went to her house; then Somadā arrived there, assuming the form of a dark mare.
She too, the liberator from bondage, assumed the form of a red horse; then a battle ensued between the two by means of blows with hooves and teeth.
Then that wretched Śākinī, who had dealt me a blow with a sword, was slain by Bandhamocinī; by her, Somadā was subsequently killed.
Then, having become fearless and having crossed over the miserable rebirths of animal existence, I no longer even mentally contemplated union with a wicked woman.
Fickleness, recklessness, and [the influence of] *śākini* and *śambara*—these three faults in women generally bring fear to the three worlds.
"Why do you run after Bandhudattā, the friend of that Śākinī? How can she have any affection for you when she has none for her own husband?"
Although I was thus addressed by that friend Bhavaśarman, I did not follow his advice; consequently, I have reached this state.
Therefore I tell you: do not undergo suffering for the sake of Anurāgaparā; for when one of her own kind arrives, she will certainly abandon you.
Just as a bee desires flower after flower, so does a woman desire man after man; therefore, O friend, remorse will come to me alone, and likewise to you.
Thus, these words of Somasvāmin, who was in the form of a monkey, did not enter the heart of Niścayadatta, which was overflowing with passion.
He said to that monkey: "Indeed, she would never be unfaithful to me, for she was born into the pure lineage of the lords of the Vidyādharas."
While the two of them were thus conversing, the sun, red with the twilight, went to the mountain of setting as if desiring to please Niścayadatta.
Then, when night had arrived like a harbinger of the end, that Yakṣiṇī Śṛṅgotpādinī came into his presence there.
Mounted upon the shoulder of that monkey, Niścayadatta set out toward his beloved, after taking leave of the ape as he said, "I should be remembered."
And at midnight on the Himalayas, he reached his father's city, Puṣkarāvatī, belonging to the lord of the Vidyādharas, where she was devoted to him with love.
Having learned of his power from that report, she, devoted to him with love, went out from the city to meet him.
"Your beloved approaches at night, bestowing a festival for the eyes; she is like a second form of the moon. Therefore, I shall now depart."
Having spoken thus and shown him that [jewel] which she had taken down from the tip of her shoulder, the Yakṣiṇī bowed to Niścayadatta and then departed.
Then she too, devoted to him with passion, approached her beloved and greeted him with embraces and other gestures, fueled by long-standing longing and excitement.
He too, having embraced her and experiencing the festival of union obtained after many afflictions, no longer remaining in his own body, entered as it were into her body.
Having thus become his wife according to the Gandharva rite, she, devoted to him with passion, immediately created a city by means of her magic power.
There, Niścayadatta remained outside with her, unobserved by his parents, whose vision was obscured by her magic spell.
When questioned, he described to her those hardships of the journey; because of that, she held him in high esteem and attended to him with desired luxuries.
Then Niścayadatta related this wonderful story of Sīmasvāmin, who had become a monkey, to that Vidyādharī.
And he said to this friend of mine: "If, through some effort of yours, he were to be released from his animal state, that would be a great service rendered to my beloved."
Having been addressed thus by him, she, though overcome with passion, said to him: "Furthermore, this path of mantra belongs to the Yoginīs; it is not within our domain."
Nevertheless, I shall accomplish this dear wish of yours by entreating my friend named Bhadrarūpā, a perfected yoginī.
Having heard that, the merchant's son was delighted and said to his beloved: "In that case, come with me; let us go into the presence of my friend so that you may see him."
When she said "So be it," on the following day Niścayadatta, seated upon her lap, went through the air to the forest that was the dwelling place of his friend.
There, seeing his friend in the form of a monkey, he approached him together with his beloved; bowing down, he then inquired after his welfare.
"Today I have attained well-being because you, filled with affection, have been seen by me"—so indeed spoke that monkey Somasvāmin.
He greeted him and bestowed a blessing upon his beloved; then they all sat down there upon a delightful stone slab.
And they engaged in conversation concerning this and that for the sake of that monkey; meanwhile, Niścayadatta first deliberated with his beloved.
Then, having taken leave of that monkey and of her beloved’s dwelling, Niścayadatta went through the air, held in her embrace as she flew up into the sky.
And on another day, he spoke again to her who was devoted to him: "Come for a moment to the presence of that monkey friend."
Then she said to him: "Go yourself this very day; receive from me the science of flying up as well as that of descending."
Having been addressed thus, Niścayadatta then took those two spells and went through the air to the presence of that friend, the monkey.
There, while he engaged in long conversations with her, she, being deeply enamored, eventually departed from her house for the garden.
Then, while she was seated there, a certain young Vidyādhara arrived through the sky, wandering about by chance.
As soon as he saw her, he became helpless under the influence of passion and approached that Vidyādharī, having realized through his supernatural knowledge that she was destined for a mortal husband.
Seeing that handsome man approaching, she too, with her face bent down, asked him slowly out of curiosity: "Who are you, and for what purpose have you come?"
Then he replied to her: "O charming girl, know me to be a Vidyādhara named Rājabhañjana, endowed with the knowledge of my own sciences."
O fawn-eyed one, at the mere sight of you, I have been suddenly brought under the sway of the god of love and surrendered to you alone.
Therefore, O Goddess, enough of serving a mortal who dwells upon the earth; as long as your father does not know of you, so long remain with me as my equal.
While he was speaking thus, she, casting sidelong glances, thought with a fickle mind, "This man is suitable for me."
Then, having perceived his intention, she became his wife right there; for when two hearts are one, what need is there for Cupid in secret?
Then, when that Vidyādhara had departed from there, Niścayadatta arrived in the presence of Somasvāmin.
Though he had arrived, she—intent on her passion for him—did not offer him a long embrace or other courtesies, making the pretext of a headache.
But he, being straightforward and deluded by affection, unaware of that pretext, considered her illness itself to be her sorrow and passed that day with her.
And in the morning, being again dejected regarding that monkey friend, he went through the air by the power of his two sciences to Somasvāmin.
When he had departed, that lustful Vidyādhara returned once more to her, who was devoted to him; for, deprived of her, he had remained awake throughout the night.
And embracing her by the neck—she who was longing for him due to their separation during the night—he, exhausted from the end of their lovemaking, became overcome by sleep.
She too, by the power of her magic knowledge, concealed her beloved who was sleeping in her lap; and because she had stayed awake all night, she fell into a sleep overcome by passion.
Meanwhile, Niścayadatta also reached the presence of that monkey; and his friend the monkey, having offered him a welcome, questioned him.
"Why do I see you looking so dejected today? Tell me. Then Niścayadatta spoke to that monkey:
"O friend, she remains exceedingly ill due to her intense passion; because of that, I am in distress, for she is dearer to me than my own life."
Thus addressed by him, that wise monkey spoke to him: "Go now, and having placed her upon your body, make her sleep."
"Bring her to my presence through the sky by means of the spell granted by him, so that I may show you this great marvel right now."
Having heard that, Niścayadatta went through the air and, seeing Anurāgaparā there asleep, quickly took her into his arms.
But he did not see that Vidyādhara clinging to her body, for he had been rendered invisible at the outset by her through the power of his magic science.
And leaping into the air, he brought that Anurāgaparā in an instant into the presence of that monkey, Somasvāmin.
Then that monkey, possessing divine vision, instructed him in a yoga by which he beheld the Vidyādhara clinging to her throat.
And having seen him speaking thus—"Alas! Shame on this! What is this?"—the monkey, who was himself a seer of reality, informed him of exactly what had occurred.
Then, while Niścayadatta was thus enraged, that Vidyādhara, desiring his beloved, woke up and, leaping into the air, vanished from sight.
She too, having awakened at that time and seeing that disclosure of the secret by him whose soul was intent on passion, stood with her face cast down in shame.
Then Niścayadatta, his eyes filled with tears, said to her: "Alas, how have I, who trusted you, been thus deceived by you, O sinful woman?"
While a method for binding the fickle mercury in this world is well known, there is no such method whatsoever for the mind of a woman.
While he was speaking thus, she, weeping softly and overcome with passion, ascended and went to her own abode in heaven.
Then his friend, the monkey, said to Niścayadatta: "Since you pursued this beloved woman even though you were forbidden by me."
This is the fruit of that fierce fire of passion that you now regret: for what confidence can there be in fleeting prosperity or in women?
Therefore, enough with this grief; now find peace. For even by the Creator himself, that which is destined to be cannot be avoided.
Having heard this from the monkey, Niścayadatta abandoned that grief and delusion; detached from the world, he went there for refuge to Śiva.
Then, while he was staying in that forest with his friend the monkey, a female ascetic named Mokṣadā arrived by chance near him.
Having seen him bowing down in due course, she asked him, "Since you are a human being, it is strange that this monkey is your friend."

Then he related his own story and, following that, the piteous account of his friend's conduct to her; and then he spoke to her thus: "If your ladyship knows any ritual application or incantation, then please release this good friend and companion of mine from his monkey-state now."

Having heard that, she agreed to the monkey's request and, by means of a mantra, released that thread from his neck. Thereupon, Somaśvāmin cast off that monkey form and became a human being as before.

Then, when she—who possessed divine power—had vanished like a flash of lightning after he had performed abundant austerities, Niścayadatta and the brahmin Somasvāmin eventually attained the supreme goal there, it is said.

Thus, women are by nature fickle, their many series of wicked deeds bestowing neither discernment nor dispassion; yet among them, there may be some virtuous woman who adorns her vast family like a fresh crescent moon adorning the sky.
Having heard this wonderful tale from the mouth of his minister Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta, together with Ratnaprabhā, was filled with joy.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave. Seeing Naravāhanadatta pleased with the story of Gomukha, Marubhūti, as if out of rivalry with him, then said to him:
Generally, women are indeed fickle, yet not invariably so; even courtesans are seen to be rich in virtuous character, how much more so others?
And so, O King, hear this famous story here: there was once a king named Vikramāditya in Pāṭaliputra.
He had two intended friends, both kings: Hayapati and Gajapati, each possessing a vast force of horses and elephants.
His enemy was the powerful king named Narasiṃha, the lord of Pratiṣṭhāna, who possessed a vast army of infantry and was full of pride.
Filled with indignation toward that enemy and proud of his own forces, Vikramāditya impetuously made this vow:
I shall conquer that king, the lord of men, in such a way that he is announced at my gate by bards and panegyrists as my servant.
Having thus made his vow, he summoned his two friends, the lords of horses and elephants; together with them, he caused the earth to tremble with the movement of elephants and horses.
To attack that lion among men, the king, by force, King Vikramāditya set forth accompanied by his entire army.
When he arrived, King Narasiṃha, having learned that he was near Pratiṣṭhāna, armed himself and went out to meet him.
Then a battle occurred between those two kings that inspired great wonder, wherein even the foot soldiers fought on equal terms with elephants and horses.
And gradually, by the forces of King Narasiṃha, numbering ten million foot-soldiers, that army of King Vikramāditya was broken.
Defeated, Vikramāditya fled to the city of Pāṭaliputra, and his two friends each departed for their own respective countries.
The lion among men, the king who had conquered his enemies, entered his own city of Pratiṣṭhāna while his prowess was being extolled by bards.
Then Vikramāditya, his purpose unaccomplished, reflected: "It is better that I conquer that enemy, who is invincible by weapons, through wisdom."
Thinking, "Let some people censure me as they wish, but let my vow not be otherwise," he entrusted the kingdom to capable ministers.
Having departed secretly from the city together with one chief minister named Buddhivara and with excellent princes, he [set out].
Accompanied by five brave men born of noble families, he, assuming the guise of a pilgrim, set out for that city of his enemy, Pratiṣṭhāna.
There, he went to the excellent palace of the courtesan known as Madanamālā, which was like the residence of a sovereign.
It was as if calling out with its banners—whose silken cloths were raised upon the peaks of its lofty walls and tossed to and fro by the gentle breeze like fluttering sprouts.
At the main eastern gate, it was guarded day and night by twenty thousand foot soldiers equipped with various weapons.
In the other three directions, at every gate, it was protected by ten thousand brave warriors, arrogant with pride.
Announced by the doorkeepers, he entered in that state and beheld a place adorned in one spot with rows of many excellent horses spread out in array.
In some places, the passage was crowded by the jostling of herds of bound elephants; in other places, it was filled with the profound appearance of an array of weapons.
In some places it was radiant with many treasury-houses shining with the luster of jewels; in other places it was filled with circles formed by throngs of attendants.
In some places it was filled with the tumultuous clamor of crowds of bards reciting aloud; in others, it resounded with the sound of drums accompanied by fixed musical performances.
Beholding that [palace] divided into seven courtyards, he, together with his retinue, reached the lofty residential palace of Madanamālā.
Having heard from her attendants that he had been gazing with intent upon the horses and other things in the inner courtyards, she concluded that he was some distinguished person in disguise.
Then, having gone out to meet him and bowed down with longing and curiosity, she led him inside the palace worthy of a king and seated him upon a throne.
The king, his heart captivated by her beauty, grace, and modesty, greeted her while remaining entirely unrecognizable.
Then Madanamālā honored that king with baths, flowers, ointments, garments, and highly precious ornaments.
Having provided daily sustenance for them and their followers, he attended upon him along with his ministers with various kinds of food.
And she spent that day with him in the pleasures of drinking and other diversions; captivated by the sight of him, she surrendered herself to him.
Thus being propitiated by her day after day, even while remaining concealed, Vikramāditya continued to abide according to the conduct befitting a universal monarch.
He constantly gave whatever wealth he possessed to beggars; when Madanamālā saw this, she brought her own property to him.
And as that body and wealth were being enjoyed by him, she considered them to have fulfilled their purpose; she turned her back on any other man or any other object of desire.
Out of affection for him, he indeed restrained that lion among men—the devoted local ruler who was approaching—with skillful arguments.
While he was being served by her in this manner, the king once spoke in private to his minister, his companion there, Buddhivara.
A courtesan seeking wealth does not even take pleasure in sexual union without it; for greed has been bestowed upon them by fate through the creation of supplicants.
While this Madanamālā was enjoying my wealth, she did not become disenchanted; rather, due to her excessive affection, she was instead delighted with me.
How can I now repay her for this, so that my own vow may also be fulfilled in due course?
Having heard that, the minister Buddhi-vara said to the king: "If this is so, then as for those priceless jewels which he brought as tribute—"
"O monk, give some of these to that Prapañcabuddhi," the king was thus addressed by the minister, and he replied to him.
Even if all those things were given, nothing would have been done for him; however, what other atonement is there for him besides this account?
Having heard that, the minister said: "O King, what has that mendicant done? Let this account of how he performed service for you be told by you."
Having been addressed thus by that minister Buddhivara, the king said: "Listen; I shall relate that story to you."
Formerly, in Pāṭaliputra, after I had entered the assembly hall every day, a monk named Prapañcabuddhi would present me with a casket.
In that very same manner, I continuously entrusted it for one year into the hands of the treasurer, leaving it there without being opened.
Once, that casket was presented by the monk; by chance, as it fell from my hand, it broke in two upon the ground.
And from that [chest] emerged a great jewel, blazing with fire; it was as if his own heart, previously unknown to me, had been revealed by him.
Having seen that, I took it and brought back others; then, having opened all the caskets and distributed them, I obtained the jewels from everyone.
Then, out of wonder, I asked that man of elaborate intellect: "Aha! Why do you serve me with such jewels as these?"
Then, having cleared the place of people, that monk said to me: "On this coming fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at the arrival of night..."
"There is a certain vidyā that must be accomplished by me outside the cremation ground; O hero, I request your arrival there to assist me."
"For successes that are free from obstacles through the assistance of heroes are indeed easily obtained. Having been told this by that monk, I then undertook it.
Then, after he had departed delighted, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight arrived; on that day, I remembered the words of that ascetic.
Then, having performed my daily rites and awaiting the onset of evening, I completed the twilight rituals and, by fate, quickly fell asleep.
At that very moment, the Lord Hari, who is compassionate toward his devotees, mounted upon Garuḍa and with his lap marked by a lotus, commanded me thus in a dream:
"O son, this man named Prapañcabuddhi, whose name is true to his nature, will take you to the cremation ground during the worship of the mandala and offer you as a sacrifice."
Therefore, he will say: "Do not do that which he intends to kill you for; first train yourself, and then you shall do it"—thus you should speak to him.
Then, while he is acting in that manner, you should strike him at that very moment through that very vulnerability; thus, the success desired by him will become yours.
When Viṣṇu had vanished after saying this, I woke up and thought: "By the grace of Hari, that master of illusion has been identified by me today as one who must be slain."
Having reflected thus, when the first watch of the night had passed, I went alone to that cemetery with a sword in hand.
Having seen him there, I approached that monk who was honored by a circle of worshippers; he too, looking at me, greeted me and then spoke, being deceitful:
"With eyes closed, limbs outstretched, fall face-down upon the ground; O King, in this way the accomplishment of both of us shall be achieved."
Then I replied to him: "First do this yourself; show it to me, and having learned it, I shall perform it in that very same way."
Hearing that, the deluded ascetic fell upon the ground in such a manner that I severed his head with a stroke of my sword.
Then a voice arose from the sky: "Excellent, O Lord of the Earth! For today you have indeed offered this wicked monk as a sacrifice."
"That power of yours which was to be accomplished has today been mastered by you; your movement is now in the sky. I am pleased with your fortitude; I am the Lord of Wealth, who moves at will."
"Therefore, choose from us another boon, whatever you desire. Having been addressed thus, I bowed to him as he appeared before me and spoke.
But when I shall request a boon from you that is required, then, O Blessed One, having been remembered, you will appear before me and grant it.
Having said to me, "So be it," that Lord of Wealth vanished; and having attained my siddhi, I went quickly to my own palace.
"Thus was my own history told to me by Kubera’s boon; therefore, I must now perform a service in return for Madanamālā."
Therefore, O excellent intellect, go for now to Pāṭaliputra, taking with you the retinue of the prince, disguised in their attire.
And having performed this fresh service for my beloved, I shall now return to that very place in order to come back here once again.
Having spoken thus to his minister, King Vikramāditya, after performing his daily duties, dismissed him along with his retinue.
When he had departed saying "So be it," the king spent that night together with Madanamālā, longing for the impending separation.
She too, as if with her inner soul foretelling his departure, embraced him repeatedly with longing; she found no sleep that night.
Then in the morning, that king, having performed his necessary duties, entered the temple of the eternal deity alone under the pretext of reciting prayers.
There, having called to mind the god Vaiśravaṇa, who appeared before him as he had previously promised a boon, he bowed to him and made this request.
"O Lord, grant me today, by virtue of that boon you have accepted for me, those five great golden men who are inexhaustible."
Those very limbs which are incessantly cut off for their desired enjoyment grow back again and again in that same manner.
"May those men become such as you desire," having said this, the Lord of Wealth vanished in an instant.
At that very moment, the king also saw there in the temple those five great golden figures standing there suddenly.
Then, having entered, he emerged, not forgetting his own vow; and having ascended to the sky, he went to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
There, welcomed by his ministers, the citizens, and the women of the inner apartments, he remained performing his duties with a mind fixed on Pratiṣṭhāna.
Meanwhile, his beloved entered that city of Pratiṣṭhāna to see her husband, who had been away in that temple for so long.
Having entered there, she did not see her beloved king anywhere; however, she saw five men of great stature made of gold.
Seeing them but not finding him, she became sorrowful and reflected: "Surely that beloved of mine is some Vidyādhara or a Gandharva."
"He who, having shared me with these men, flew up into the sky—what shall I do now that I am separated from him, [left] with these [men] who are equal to straw?"
Having reflected thus, she repeatedly questioned her own attendants; then, having gone out, she wandered everywhere in search of news of him.
She found no pleasure anywhere—in palaces, gardens, houses, or elsewhere—lamenting, afflicted by separation, and intent on abandoning her body.
"Do not despair, O Queen; for he is a wanderer at will. That god will, by his own free will, approach you once more, O blessed lady."
Consoled with some difficulty by her attendants through such words as these, offered with steadfast resolve, she made this vow:
"If he does not grant me an audience within six months, then I must enter the fire after I have surrendered all my possessions."
Having thus steadied herself with this resolve, she thereafter remained daily bestowing gifts while meditating upon her beloved.
Once, being solely intent on the practice of giving, she cut off the two arms of one of those golden men and gave them to the twice-born.
And on the second day, having become filled with wonder, she beheld those two arms of his, exactly as they were, produced in the middle of the night.
Then, in succession, she cut off the arms of the others for the sake of giving; and for all of them, those arms grew back again exactly as they were before.
Then, seeing that those arms were inexhaustible, she cut them off day after day and gave them to the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, according to the number of Vedic branches they knew.
