Having heard from various directions that she had departed with only a few attendants, a Brahmin named Saṅgrāmadatta came there from Pāṭaliputra.
That poor man, though learned in the four Vedas and endowed with virtues, approached him seeking a gift; having been announced by the gatekeeper, he then entered his presence.
With her limbs emaciated by vows and pale from separation, she gave to him, who had been honored by her, golden arms equal in number to the Vedas.
Then that brahmin, surrounded by his followers, heard from the one afflicted by grief the entire account of that most terrible vow.
Both joyful and dejected, having mounted these two golden camels upon his arms, he returned to his own residence in Pāṭaliputra.
"There can be no security for me in this city of Kāñcanapura if it is not protected by a king," he reflected there, and having entered, he approached the one who was presiding over the assembly.
That Brahmin addressed King Vikramāditya: "O Great King, I am a twice-born man residing right here in this city."
Thus, being poor and seeking wealth, I set out for the southern region and reached Pratiṣṭhāna, the capital of King Narasiṃha.
There, seeking a gift, I went to the house of the courtesan Madanamālā, who was renowned for her fame.
Indeed, a certain divine man, having lived for a long time in her presence, departed for some unknown place after giving her five inexhaustible golden men.
Then, pained by separation from him, she regarded life as the agony of poison, her body as fruitless exertion, and food as the torment of a thief.
Thinking thus, her fortitude gone, that high-minded woman was somehow consoled by her attendants and made this vow.
If he does not honor me within six months, then I, my soul stricken by misfortune, must enter the fire.
Thus, having made this firm vow and resolved upon death, she, desiring the fruits of great merit, gives very large gifts every day.
And she was seen by me, O Lord, standing with her feet free from fetters, appearing exceedingly beautiful despite a body emaciated by lack of food.
With hands moistened by the water of charity and crowded with swarms of bees-like supplicants, she was like the personified state of rutting in an elephant of passion that has become ill-behaved.
I consider that lover both blameworthy and worthy of praise, by whom she—who is so beloved that without him this beautiful woman gives up her life—is abandoned.
There, she duly presented to me four golden human arms, corresponding in number to the Vedas, for the sake of the four Vedas.
Having made that a house for an excellent sacrificial session, I wish to practice my own dharma here; may Your Majesty grant me assistance in that matter.
Having heard this pleasant news of his beloved from the mouth of that twice-born man, King Vikramāditya’s mind was instantly captivated by it.
Having instructed the doorkeeper for the sake of accomplishing the Brahmin's desire, and having reflected upon her firm passion and her disregard for her own life;
Eagerly anticipating assistance in the fulfillment of his vow, he counted down the days until the end of his beloved’s life, which was now but a short time away.
Having swiftly departed through the air after entrusting the kingdom to his minister, that king entered the palace of his beloved in Pratiṣṭhāna.
There he beheld that beloved woman, emaciated yet radiant as moonlight, her splendor bestowed by the gods, like a digit of the moon on a full-moon night.
And Madanamālā, seeing him unexpectedly arrived—the very essence of nectar for her eyes—was for a moment as if bewildered.
Then, as if out of fear of fleeing, she embraced him even more closely and cast the noose of her vine-like arms around his neck.
"O pitiless one, why have you departed, abandoning me who am innocent? Thus she spoke to him with a voice whose syllables were choked with tears.
Having said, "Come, I shall speak to you in private," the king, accompanied by his retinue and cheered by them, went with her into the inner private quarters.
There, having revealed himself, he described his own history, explaining how he had come there to conquer King Narasiṃha through strategic means.
Just as he attained the power of moving through the sky by destroying the intellect of conceptual proliferation, so too did he receive a boon from the Lord of Wealth and distribute it among them.
And just as he had previously come there after hearing news from a Brahmin, so now, having related everything up to the point of his vow's fulfillment, he spoke to her once again.
This Narasimha, who is dear to him, is invincible and exceedingly powerful with his forces; he shall now engage in a duel with me in hand-to-hand combat.
Having been a dweller of the heavens, I became a wanderer upon the earth, yet I did not slay him; for what man, being a kshatriya, would desire victory through unrighteous combat?
That which must be accomplished by my vow is this: that the bards stationed at the gate announce [my presence] to this king; provide assistance in that matter.
Upon hearing this, the courtesan said, "I am blessed," and after consulting with the king, she summoned her own bards and spoke to them.
"When King Narasiṃha comes to my house, you must remain stationed at the door, keeping your eyes fixed upon him."
"O King, King Narasiṃha is devoted to you and remains loyal," this should be said by you repeatedly as he enters.
And if, having looked around at that moment, someone should ask, "Who stands here?", he must simply be told, "Vikramāditya stands here."
Having spoken thus and dismissed them, she then said to the female door-keeper: "King Narasiṃha must not be prevented from entering here."
Having done this, Madanamālā, having regained her lord of life, remained at her ease, bestowing immeasurable wealth.
Then, having heard of that extraordinary gift arising from the golden man, King Narasiṃha abandoned his affairs and went to see that house.
And as he entered there, unforbidden by the doorkeeper, all the bards cried out loudly from as far as the outer gate:
"O Lord, King Narasiṃha has bowed down with devotion"—hearing this, the king became filled with indignation and apprehension.
Having asked, "Who stands here? and having recognized that it was King Vikramāditya standing there, he reflected for a moment as follows:
This very thing which I previously promised—the announcement of my arrival at the gate—has been fulfilled by this king, who has forcibly entered within for me.
"Aha! This king is full of vigor, for by him I have been defeated this very day; yet he must not be slain by force, as he is alone and has come to my home."
Thinking, "I shall enter there for now," King Narasiṃha, announced by a multitude of bards, entered the interior.
As soon as he saw that the king had entered, Vikramāditya, with a smiling face, rose up and embraced the monarch around the neck.
Then, once those two kings were both seated, they inquired after each other's welfare while Madanamālā stood by their side.
And in the course of their conversation, Narasiṃha asked Vikramāditya, "From where did these golden men here come?"
Then, there, Vikramāditya—having slain that lowest of ascetics and having accomplished the power of traveling through the sky with the aid of the excellent Lord of Wealth—[remained].
Having attained the five marks of a Great Man made of inexhaustible gold, he related to him his entire wondrous life story.
Then Narasiṃha, perceiving that king Mahāśakti to be a sky-farer of pure intent, chose him as his ally.
Having then conducted him through the rites of hospitality and established his friendship, he led him to his own capital and attended upon him with his personal services.
Having been honored and dispatched by that king, King Vikramāditya returned once more to the home of Madanamālā.
Then Vikramāditya, having fulfilled the purpose of his difficult vow through the power of his own prowess, set his heart on returning to his own city.
Desiring to go with him, Madanamālā too, unable to endure separation and intending to abandon that region where she had made her dwelling for the sake of the Brahmin, was likewise unable to bear it.
Then, followed by her elephant, horses, and foot-soldiers, that moon among kings, Vikramāditya, went with her—whose mind was fixed on no other—to his own city, Pāṭaliputra.
There, having formed a bond of friendship with that lion-like king, he dwelt happily, accompanied by Madanamālā, who had abandoned her own country out of love for him.

Thus, O King, even the women of pleasure, being of noble character and firm in their devotion, become like the ladies of the inner apartments for monarchs; how much more so, then, other women of good family?
Having thus heard this noble tale from the mouth of Marubhūti, King Naravāhanadatta and his new bride Ratnaprabhā, born of a lineage of the highest Vidyādharas, were filled with joy.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave. When Marubhūti had spoken thus, Hariśikha, the commander of the army, spoke in the presence of Naravāhanadatta.
For virtuous women, there is truly no other ultimate refuge than their husband; and in this regard, let this even more wonderful story be heard.
There is a city on earth named Vardhamānapura; there lived a king named Vīrabhuja, the best among the upholders of dharma.
Although hundreds of women were present in his inner apartments, the lord had a single queen named Guṇavarā, who was dearer to him than his own life.
And despite his union with a hundred wives, no son was born to him from any one of them, due to the power of fate.
He questioned a physician named Śrutavardhana, asking: "Is there perhaps such a medicine by which the birth of a son might occur?"
Having heard that, the physician said: "O King, I shall accomplish this; however, let a wild goat be brought to me by Your Majesty."
Having heard these words of the physician, the king gave orders to his doorkeeper and had a goat brought for him from the forest.
Having handed over that goat to the royal cooks, the physician then prepared an excellent broth from its meat for the sake of the king.
When the king had departed to worship the deity after commanding the queens to assemble in one place, those queens gathered together there.
But one woman had not joined them; she was Guṇavarā, the king’s favorite, who at that moment stood near the king as he was engaged in the worship of the gods.
And when they had come together, the physician gave them the medicinal extract mixed with powder for the purpose of drinking it, without their even perceiving it, until it was entirely consumed.
Having performed his worship there in an instant, the king returned accompanied by his beloved; seeing that all the materials had been consumed, he spoke to that physician:
"Alas! Nothing has been established by you for the sake of the one who possesses excellent qualities; that which is the primary motive for this undertaking has been forgotten by you."
Having spoken thus, the king said to the embarrassed physician, "Is there any meat remaining from that goat here?"
When the cooks said, "The two horns are there," the physician then replied, "Excellent! For the *rasaka* produced from within the horn would indeed be the most superior."
Having said this and having had that prepared from the horn and the flesh, the physician gave it mixed with powder to Guṇavarā.
Then, ninety-nine queens of that king became pregnant, and in due time, they all gave birth to sons.
And that great queen, having conceived the fetus not long ago, subsequently gave birth to a son of supreme marks and excellent qualities.
King Vīrabhuja, having celebrated a great festival, named him Śṛṅgabhuja because he was born from the essence of the flesh of a horn, and raised him.
Though he grew up with those other brothers and was the youngest by age, he became the eldest among them by virtue of his qualities.
In due course, that prince became equal to Kāma in beauty, equal to Arjuna in the science of archery, and equal to Bhīmasena in strength.
Then, seeing that beloved queen Guṇavarā of King Vīrabhuja together with her son, the other queens became exceedingly envious.
Then, among them, a queen named Ayaśolekhā, who was ill-intentioned, consulted with those other women and made a secret agreement with them.
When the king had returned home and was questioning her while all his co-wives were present, she spoke with great difficulty, feigning a dejection on her face.
Noble son, how can you endure the defilement of your own home? You who protect the faults of another, how is it that you do not protect yourself?
This youth named Surakṣita is the master of the inner apartments; indeed, it is said that this Queen Guṇavarā of yours is devoted to him.
Since no other man can gain access here in the inner apartments, which are guarded by eunuchs, she has therefore united with him.
"This is well known throughout the entire harem and is sung here," having been told this by her, the king reflected and deliberated.
And having gone there, he questioned the other queens one by one in succession; and they all, having devised a pretense, spoke to him in the same manner.
Then that wise king, having conquered his anger, reflected: "This cannot be possible for those two, yet such is this rumor."
Therefore, without reaching a final decision, I must not disclose this to anyone; rather, those two must be avoided through skillful means while I observe the ultimate outcome.
Having thus resolved, on the following day, he summoned his well-guarded superintendent of the inner apartments to the assembly hall and, feigning anger, addressed him.
"O sinner, it has been understood by me that you have committed the murder of a Brahmin; therefore, I cannot bear to look upon you unless you have completed a pilgrimage to sacred fords."
Having heard that, as he was bewildered and crying out, "O God, how could I have committed the murder of a Brahmin?", the king spoke to him again.
Do not act with such audacity; go instead to Kashmir, which destroys all sins, where lies that field of victory and the purifying field of Nandi.
Where there is the sacred field of Vārāha, where those purified by the wielder of the discus dwell, and where the Jāhnavī flows under the name Vitastā;
Purified by a pilgrimage to that Maṇḍavakṣetra where it is, and to Uttaramānasa, you shall see me again; not otherwise.
Having spoken thus, King Vīrabhuja sent him away under a pretext of a pilgrimage to distant holy sites, keeping him well-guarded and against his will.
Then the king, filled with affection, anger, and reflection, went first to Queen Guṇavarā.
There, seeing him with a distressed mind, she asked him in agitation: "Noble son, why are you suddenly so dejected today?"
Having heard that, the king spoke these feigned words: "Today, some great sage came and addressed me thus, O Queen."

Do those who possess authority rebuke the ill-behaved with their own words? Rather, those standing near him must necessarily speak to him as is appropriate.
"It is true that I am the son of a cowherd, but you, moreover, are a bull among ministers; this speech of yours reveals nothing but stupidity—your horns are indeed present, yet they are not yours."
Thus addressed by Gomukha, Marubhūti spoke here: "Indeed, it is Gomukha who truly deserves the title of 'bull' (vṛṣabha)."
"Nevertheless, that you are so untamed is due to this confusion of your birth. Having heard this, while everyone there was laughing, Gomukha said:
This Marubhūti is like a jewel; for who indeed could introduce a flaw into this diamond, which cannot be pierced even by hundreds of efforts?
That which is pierced without effort is another jewel among men; hear now the illustration of this in the story of the sand-dam.
In Pratiṣṭhāna there was a certain twice-born man named Tapodatta; though he was exhorted by his father, he did not study the sciences during his childhood.
Thereafter, being censured by all and filled with resentment, he went to the bank of the Gaṅgā to perform austerities for the sake of attaining the power of vidyā.
There, having seen him engaged in fierce austerities, Śakra, filled with wonder and wishing to dissuade him, approached his presence disguised as a brahmin.
And having arrived, he repeatedly scooped up grains of sand and threw them into the surging waters of the Ganges, even as that man looked on.
Having seen that, Tapodatta broke his silence and asked him with curiosity: "O Brahmin, what is this that you are doing without rest?"
When questioned with persistence, Śakra, assuming the form of a brahmin, said to him: "I am building a bridge across the Gaṅgā for the crossing of living beings."
Then Tapodatta said: "O fool, why is this bridge ever being built with sands that are swept away by the current of the Ganges?"
Having heard that, Śakra, assuming the form of a brahmin, then said to him: "If you know it thus, then [know] this knowledge without study and without hearing."
Why are you striving to accomplish this through vows, fasts, and the like? This is like the desire for a rabbit's horn, or a painting in the sky.
If the arrangement of letters were without syllables, or if there were study of knowledge without [the letters], then no one at all would ever study.
Thus addressed by Śakra in the form of a brahmin, Tapodatta reflected upon those words, agreed with them as they were, abandoned his asceticism, and went home.
Thus, one who is wise is easily enlightened, but one who has become like a desert-dweller is dull-witted; he cannot be enlightened, and when being instructed, he becomes angry.
When this had been said by Gomukha, Hariśikha spoke there in their midst: "It is true, O King, that those of noble intellect are easily awakened to happiness."
And likewise, in the past, there was a certain excellent brahmin in Vārāṇasī named Virūpaśarman, who was both deformed and destitute.
Disgusted with his ugliness and misfortune, he went to that penance grove and performed intense austerities out of a desire for beauty and wealth.
Then the Lord of the Gods, having assumed the lowly form of a jackal with a deformed and diseased appearance, approached and stood before him.
Beholding him, whose limbs were covered with flies and who was devoid of auspicious marks, Virūpaśarman reflected slowly within his mind.
"Even such as these are born in saṃsāra due to their past actions; therefore, this little that has been done for me by the Creator is insufficient, in that I have not been made like them."
Realizing that "Who can transgress the enjoyment written by fate? Virūpaśarman slowly departed from his place of asceticism and went home.
In this way, O King, a person of keen intellect is awakened with little effort; however, one whose mind lacks discernment cannot be awakened even with great difficulty.
When Hariśikha had spoken thus, and Gomukha was full of faith, Marubhūti—who lacked self-knowledge, was intoxicated, and exceedingly angry—said:
"O Gomukha, the strength of those like you resides only in speech, not in arms; for a quarrel with talkative eunuchs brings shame to those who possess true might."
To Marubhūti, who was speaking thus and desiring battle, the lord Naravāhanadatta, with a smiling face, then personally consoled him.
Having sent him back to his own home, he, who was affectionate toward his childhood friends, spent that day happily performing his daily duties.
And in the morning, when all these ministers had arrived, his beloved Ratnaprabhā spoke thus to Marubhūti, who stood bowed with shame.
You are a man of merit, O Noble Son, you whose ministers, pure of heart, have been bound to you by the fetters of affection since childhood.
And blessed are these people for whom you, O Lord, are so devoted with such affection; you have undoubtedly been acquired by one another through the merit of past karma.
When she, the queen, had spoken thus, Tapantaka, the son of Vasantaka and the jester-friend of Naravāhanadatta, replied.
"It is true that this master of ours was acquired by us in a previous life; for everything exists solely through the power of past karma. Listen, therefore, to a story concerning this."
In the city named Vilāsapura, the abode of Śrīkaṇṭha, there was a king known by the name Vinayaśīla, a name truly significant of his character.
He had a queen named Kamalaprabhā, who was as dear to him as his own life; and devoted solely to sensual enjoyment with her, he remained there for a long time.
Then, in the course of time, old age—which robs one of beauty—manifested itself for that king; seeing it, he became exceedingly distressed.
How can I show my face to the Queen—faded by grey hair like a lotus struck by frost? Alas! Fie upon me; death would be better.
Reflecting thus, the king then summoned the members of the assembly and, showing them great respect, spoke to the physician named Taruṇacandra.
"O noble one, you are devoted to us and skilled; therefore, you are asked: is there perhaps some means by which this old age might be warded off?"
Upon hearing that, Vakracandra—whose essence was merely a single digit yet who desired fullness, whose inner name was truly "Crescent Moon"—reflected within himself:
"This king is a fool; I shall eat him, and I will do so gradually. Having reflected thus, that physician spoke to the king as follows.
"O Lord, since you have been taking this medicine alone in an underground chamber for eight months, I shall therefore remove your old age."
Upon hearing this, the king had that underground chamber constructed; for fools who are greedy for sensual objects do not tolerate reason.
O King, by means of the virtuous nature of their ancestors, through austerity, self-restraint, and the power of the age, elixirs were perfected.
And in the present age, O King, these very tastes, though prescribed in the scriptures, produce the opposite effect due to the absence of the necessary ingredients.
That is not right; for rogues indeed play with fools. O King, once youth has passed away, does it ever return?
These and other words of the ministers found no entrance into him, for the king’s heart was shrouded by an intense thirst for sensual enjoyment.
And at the physician's word, he entered that underground chamber alone, having set aside all the retinue befitting a king.
A certain physician, together with a single attendant of his own, became his personal caregiver there during the administration of medicines and other treatments.
And that king remained there within the womb of the earth, enveloped in darkness, like ignorance itself when it has spread extensively beyond the heart due to its abundance.
And when those six months had passed, that deceitful physician, observing that the old age of this king had become even more advanced, [acted accordingly].
He brought a certain young man of similar appearance with whom he had made an agreement, saying, "I shall make you the king."

Then, having constructed a tunnel from afar into the subterranean chamber, he killed the king while he was asleep there, carried him away through that passage, and threw him into a blind well at night.
Having led that man, who was young, into the underground chamber there, she placed him inside and closed up the tunnel.
Having found an unobstructed opportunity among those of deluded intellect, what act of rashness would an ordinary person of unrestrained mind not commit?
Then, on another day, the physician addressed all the subjects: "In six months, I have rendered this king free from old age."
"In two months his appearance will become different; therefore, show yourself to him now from a distance."
Having said this, he brought them all to the door of the underground chamber and, showing them to the youth, announced their names and deeds to him.
Thus, for two months, every day, he skillfully awakened that young man within the underground chamber, reaching even unto the inner apartments.
And when the time had come, he, remaining undecaying, drew that man nourished by enjoyments out from the underground chamber, declaring, "This one has become a king."
Then, because of his success with the medicinal herbs, that young man was surrounded there by the joyful subjects who cried out, "He is the king!"
Then, having bathed and thus obtained the kingdom, that young man, together with his ministers, performed the royal rites amidst great celebration.
From that time forward, having acquired the name Ajara, he remained ruling his kingdom with ease, sporting together with the women of the inner apartments.
And everyone, free from suspicion regarding this physician whose conduct was inconceivable, considered their lord to have his very form transformed by an elixir of immortality.
Having won over the subjects and Queen Kamalaprabhā with affection, King Ajara then enjoyed royal splendor together with his friends.
He appointed his friend named Bheṣajacandra and another named Padmadarśana as his two generals, equal to himself, with their armies filled with elephants, horses, and villages.
He brought the physician Taruṇacandra for the sake of medical treatment, yet he placed no trust in him, whose soul had fallen away from truth and righteousness.
And once, that physician spoke privately to the king: "Why do you act according to your own will, as if disregarding me entirely?"
"When I became king here, that was forgotten by me. As soon as he heard this, King Ajara addressed that physician:
"Oh, you are a fool! What man is the doer or even the giver for anyone? For it is one's own past karma, my friend, that acts and gives."
Therefore, do not be arrogant, for this power of mine is perfected through asceticism; and I shall demonstrate this very thing to you directly before long.
Having been addressed thus by him, the physician, as if terrified, reflected: "Aha! This man speaks with some degree of audacity; he is resolute and speaks like one possessed of knowledge."
Even that supreme secret intimacy which serves to win over one's master does not prevail in this case; therefore, he must be followed by me.
"Let me see first what he will show me directly. Having reflected thus, the physician agreed, saying "So be it," and remained silent.
On another day, King Ajara went forth to wander about, sporting with his friends and companions, such as Taruṇacandra and others who attended upon him.
Wandering about, he reached the bank of a river, in the middle of which he saw five golden lotuses being carried along by the current.
Having had it brought by his servants, taken hold of it, and examined it, he spoke to the physician Taruṇacandra who was standing nearby.
"Go from here along the riverbank upward; search for the place of origin of these lotuses."
And having seen that, you should come back, for my curiosity regarding these wonderful lotuses is very great; and you are skillful and a friend to me.
Having spoken thus, that physician was sent away by the king; saying "So be it," he departed from there, powerless and following the path as directed.
The king also departed for his own city, and as the physician traveled along, he eventually reached a Śiva temple situated on the bank of that river.
At the edge of that river-tirtha before him, he saw a great banyan tree, and hanging from it was a human skeleton.
Then, exhausted, having bathed and worshipped the deity there, while he was standing, a cloud arrived and rained down.
And from that human skeleton hanging from the branch of the banyan tree, which had been drenched by the rainclouds, drops of water fell down.
In the water of that river’s bathing-place, the physician saw those golden lotuses being born from them in an instant.
"Aha! What is this marvel? Whom shall I ask in this uninhabited forest? Or rather, who knows the creation of the Ordainer, which is filled with so many wonders?"
"I have indeed seen this very lake of golden lotuses; therefore, I shall cast this corpse of Naraka here into this sacred bathing place."
"Let there be dharma, or else let lotuses spring up upon its back"—having reflected thus, he then cast the skeleton from the top of the tree.
Having spent that day there and accomplished his task, the physician returned from that place toward his own country on the following day.
In a few days, he, emaciated and dusty from the journey, reached that city of Vilāsa and approached King Ajaras.
Announced by the doorkeeper, the physician entered, bowed at his feet, and when asked about his welfare by the king, he related the news to him.
Then, having cleared the place of people, the king himself said to him: "Friend, you have seen that source from which the golden lotuses arise."
That field is indeed supreme, and there you beheld that skeleton upon the banyan tree; know it to be my former body.
In former times, hanging there with my feet upwards and having dried up my body, I performed ascetic penance.
Then, by the power of that ascetic’s majesty, golden lotuses are produced there from the waters of the clouds falling upon his skeletal remains.
And as for that skeleton which was thrown by you into that sacred bathing place, you have acted rightly; for you were my friend in a previous birth.
This Bheṣajacandra and that Padmadarśana—these two were also my friends, associated with me since birth.
O friend, by the power of that former austerity, memory of my past lives, spiritual knowledge, and sovereignty have been bestowed upon me.
This very point has been demonstrated to you by me through reasoning and direct perception; I have described how the heap of bones cast away by you was accompanied by a token of recognition.
Therefore, you should not harbor the conceit that "the kingdom was given to you by me," nor should you allow your mind to remain in a state of instability.
For without prior karma, no one is a giver to anyone; from the womb onward, a living being enjoys the fruit of the tree of its former karma.
Having been addressed thus by the king, the physician saw that it was exactly so; he did not again experience dissatisfaction, for he remained happy in his service to him.
Then that noble-minded king, who was free from old age and possessed the memory of his former births, honored the physician with gifts of wealth as was appropriate.
Together with his harem and his friends, may he dwell in happiness, enjoying the earth won through policy, attained by his own merit, and free from thorns.
Thus it is in this world, O Lord, for everyone at all times: everything, whether auspicious or inauspicious, belongs to a living being as that which was acquired through their prior karma.
Therefore, I consider you to be our master from a previous birth; for if there were others [to serve us], how could you be so well-disposed toward us otherwise?
Having heard from the mouth of Tapantaka this story, so unprecedented, charming, and wonderful, Naravāhanadatta rose up there with his beloved to bathe.

Having bathed, he went into the presence of his father, the King of Vatsa; repeatedly shedding a rain of nectar from his eyes upon his mother, he took his meal with them, and accompanied by his beloved and his ministers, he spent that day and night in pleasures such as drinking parties.

Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Seventh Wave. Then, on another day, he remained in that dwelling together with Ratnaprabhā, conversing with his ministers about various tales.
There, in the courtyard outside the palace, Naravāhanadatta suddenly heard the sound of a man's lamentation.
When someone asked, "What is this?", the maidservants arrived and said, "O Lord, this Kañcukī Dharmagiri is weeping."
For having come here, that foolish friend has just now informed me that his brother, who had gone on a pilgrimage, has died in another land.
Thinking "I am in the royal palace," he was bewildered by grief; now, crying out, he has been led outside by the people to his home.
Hearing this, as grief arose in the crown prince, Queen Ratnaprabhā spoke there dejectedly out of compassion:
Alas, the suffering arising from separation from beloved kin is difficult to endure; why was this person not made by the Creator free from old age and death?
Having heard these words of the queen, Marubhūti said to her: "O Queen, how could this be among mortals? Listen, therefore, to this story."
In the city named Cirāyu, there was formerly a king named Cirāyu, who was indeed long-lived and the abode of all prosperity.
He had a minister named Nāgārjuna, born from a portion of a Bodhisattva, who was compassionate, generous, virtuous, and possessed of great wisdom.
He who knew the application of all medicinal herbs prepared an elixir of perfection, making both himself and that king free from old age and long-lived.
Once, the young son of that minister, who was the beloved child among all the sons of Nāgārjuna, passed away.
Having perceived through that [vision] the suffering of mortals, he prepared the nectar for the pacification of death by means of substances, through the power of his asceticism and generosity.
While he was waiting for the proper time to combine that one remaining medicinal herb, Indra became aware of it.
Indra, having consulted with the gods, thus commanded the two Aśvins: "Go to Nāgārjuna on earth and speak these words to him in my name."
What kind of injustice has been undertaken here by you, even though you are a minister? Alas, are you now prepared to conquer Prajāpati himself?
Mortals are by nature subject to death; therefore, those who were indeed created by you, you now desire to make immortal by accomplishing the nectar of immortality.

If this were done, what indeed would be the distinction between gods and humans? Furthermore, due to the absence of those to be sacrificed for and those who sacrifice, the very order of the world would collapse.
"Therefore, at our word, withdraw this means of obtaining nectar; otherwise, the gods, being enraged, will certainly bestow a curse upon you."
"Since this effort of yours is due to grief for him, your son remains in heaven"—having thus instructed them, Śakra dispatched both the Aśvins.
Having arrived and accepted the guest-offering, the two of them then delivered that message from Śakra to Nāgārjuna, who was pleased by their arrival.
And they told him of his son, who dwelt in heaven together with the gods; then Nāgārjuna, becoming despondent there, reflected:
"If I do not carry out Indra's command, let the other gods be; why would these two Aśvins themselves not bestow a curse upon me?"
Let this matter rest; my nectar has not been attained, and my desire remains unfulfilled; yet my son, through his past merits, has gone to a state beyond grief.
Having reflected thus, Nāgārjuna spoke there to the two Aśvin deities: "The command of Indra has been carried out by me; I shall now withdraw the process of the nectar."
If you two had not come, this earth would have been made free from old age and death by me within five days once the nectar was accomplished.
Having spoken thus in his presence, Nāgārjuna then buried that nectar, which was almost perfected, in the earth according to those various instructions.
Then the two Aśvins, having taken leave of him and gone to heaven, reported to Śakra that their task was accomplished; thereupon the King of the Gods rejoiced.
Meanwhile, that long-lived king, the lord Nāgārjuna, consecrated his son named Jīvahara as the crown prince.
And when he had been consecrated and approached his mother for the sake of a blessing, Queen Dhanaparā, seeing her son joyful, spoke to him:
"O son, why do you rejoice in vain upon obtaining this position of crown prince? For there is no way to attain the kingdom through this, nor indeed by means of asceticism."
For many of your father's sons have indeed gone forth as crown princes; no one has obtained the kingdom, but all have obtained only mockery.
For Nāgārjuna indeed gave this elixir to this king, by which he has attained this eighth century of his life.
Who knows how many other sons this short-lived king will also obtain in succession, acting as crown princes?
Having heard this, she spoke again to her despondent son: "If you have need of the kingdom, then employ this means."
This minister Nāgārjuna, having performed his daily rites every day, makes this proclamation at the time of giving food:
"Who is the petitioner? What does he seek? And what should be given to him?"—at that moment, go and say to him, "Give me your own head."
Then, when that Satyavāc had died with his head severed, the king would either succumb to death from grief for him or indeed take refuge in the forest.
"Then you shall obtain the kingdom; there is no other means for you in this matter. Hearing these words of his mother, the prince was delighted.
"So be it," he said, and made a firm resolve to carry that out; for the greed for sovereignty overcomes even the painful affection for one's kin.
Then, on another day, the prince Jīvahara went at his own will to the house of Nāgārjuna at the time of his meal.
At that time, upon hearing the minister there saying, "Who asks for what? and so forth, he entered right then and asked for his head.
"It is a marvel, my child! What will you do with this head of mine? For what use to you is this mass of flesh, bone, and hair?"
"Nevertheless, if you have need of this, cut it off and take it. Having said this, the minister presented his own neck to him.
And as the prince struck at her for a long time—she who was made firm by the elixir of immortality—his many swords were shattered into pieces.
Then, having learned that the long-lived king was approaching and attempting to prevent him from giving away his head, Nāgārjuna spoke there.
O King, I remember ninety-nine births; in each and every birth, my own head was given by me as a gift.
"O Lord, this is my hundredth birth for the sake of giving away my head; therefore, do not say anything to me, for a petitioner does not depart from me with his hopes frustrated."
"Therefore, I now give my own head to this son of yours; let him take the sword from you for the purpose of beholding your face. Thus he spoke to him.
Having spoken thus and embraced the king, he summoned some powder from his treasury and anointed the sword of the prince with it. Then, with that [powder], he [anointed] the blade for him.
Then, by that stroke of his sword, the prince severed the head of Nāgārjuna like a lotus from its stalk.
Then, while the great wailing had arisen and the king was intent on giving up his life, an incorporeal voice issued from the sky: "Thus!"
"Do not commit an improper act, O King, for this friend of yours is beyond mourning; Nāgārjuna, no longer subject to rebirth, has attained the state equal to that of a Buddha."
Having heard this, King Cirāyus desisted from death; having given gifts and abandoned his kingdom out of grief, he retired to the forest.
There, through timely asceticism, he attained the supreme goal; his son likewise took over that kingdom, for he was the one who had taken Jīva’s life.
And not long after he had obtained the kingdom, having caused a division within the realm, he was slain by the sons of Nāgārjuna, who remembered the murder of their father.
Then, from that grief, her mother’s heart burst; for how can there be well-being for those engaged in a path practiced by the ignoble?
And a son named Śatāyu was born to that long-lived king by another queen; he was then installed on the throne by those chief ministers.
Thus, even the gods were unable to endure this destruction of death for mortals initiated by Nāgārjuna, until he too fell under the power of death.

Therefore, this world of living beings, ordained by the Creator, is indeed impermanent and filled with unavoidable suffering; for nothing can be done here even by hundreds of efforts, since the Creator does not will anything that he does not intend.
When Marubhūti had finished telling this story and ceased speaking, Naravāhanadatta rose together with his ministers and performed his daily duties.

Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Eighth Wave: Then, on the following day, having comforted his beloved Ratnaprabhā—who was longing for him—by saying, "I shall return quickly," he departed for the hunt.
Accompanied by his father, the Lord of Vatsa, and his friends, Naravāhanadatta went to the forest, surrounded by horses and elephants.
There, with the pearls fallen from the claws and bellies of lions that had slain and then slept upon the split temples of elephants, it was as if seeds had been sown.
It was as if covered with sprouts by the fangs of tigers and bhallūka bears, and as if possessed of young leaves by the flowing blood of deer.
It seemed as if it were covered in clusters by the chests of śarabhas, marked with the impressions of sunken heron-feather arrows, and as if it were laden with fruit by their fallen bodies.
The sport of hunting, with its forest beautified by falling arrows that made a sound like crashing wealth, became a source of delight for him.
Exhausted, he rested for a while and then slowly entered the interior of the forest, mounted on his horse along with a single horseman named Gomukha.
And there, at that very moment, he began a certain game with small pellets; just then, it is said, a certain female ascetic arrived along that path.
From her hand, a pill slipped and fell upon his head; then, laughing slightly, that female ascetic spoke to him.
In the same way, if you ever obtain Karpūrikā as your wife, what will become of this pride of yours?
Having heard this, Naravāhanadatta immediately dismounted from his horse and, bowing at her feet, spoke to that female ascetic.
"I did not see you; by fate, my pill has gone down here. O Blessed One, it has blazed up; forgive this lapse of mine."
Having heard that, and saying, "My son, I have no anger," that female ascetic, who had conquered her wrath, consoled him with blessings.
Then, considering her to be self-controlled, awakened, and a true ascetic, Naravāhanadatta questioned her with humility.
"O Blessed One, who is this one named Karpūrikā whom you have mentioned? If you are pleased with me, please instruct me on this, for I am indeed curious."
To him who had spoken thus and bowed down, the female ascetic said: "Beyond the ocean there is a supreme city named Karpūrasambhava."
There dwells a king whose name is truly meaningful, known as Karpūraka; he has a daughter, an excellent maiden named Karpūrikā.
Having observed that one Kamalā had been carried away by the gods after being churned, the ocean deposited a second one as it were there and concealed her.
She is averse to men and does not desire marriage; only if you approach her will she become desirous of it.
Therefore, go there, my son, and you shall obtain that beautiful woman; however, as you travel through the forest, you will encounter great hardship.
"You should not feel any delusion in this matter, for all of that will indeed have a happy end. Having said this, the female ascetic flew up into the sky and vanished.
Then Naravāhanadatta, drawn by the command of that voice and by the god of love, spoke to Gomukha, who was standing at his side.
"Come, let us go to the city of Karpūrasambhava to the side of Karpūrikā; for without seeing her, I cannot bear to remain even for a moment."
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "O King, enough of this rashness! Where are you, and where is the ocean? Where is that city, where is that road, and where is that maiden?"
When merely his name was heard, why did you, alone and having abandoned your celestial consorts, run toward a mortal woman with such aimless and doubtful intent?
Thus addressed by Gomukha, the son of the King of Vatsa then said, "The word of that perfected female ascetic is not false."
"Therefore, I must certainly go to obtain that princess," he said, and mounting his horse, he set out from there at that very moment.
And Gomukha followed him in silence, even though he was unwilling; for a master, though his word be not obeyed, must still be followed by his servants.
Meanwhile, the Lord of Vatsa also returned to his own city after finishing his hunt, thinking that his son had arrived in the midst of his own army.
And his own army, together with Marubhūti and the others, returned to that very city, perceiving their lord to be stationed in the midst of the host.
Having arrived there and searched, the King of Vatsa and all the others, realizing that he had not yet returned, went to Ratnaprabhā.
And she, first distressed by hearing that news, and then by her own meditated spell, related the tidings of her beloved and spoke to her grieving father-in-law.
"The noble son has gone to the city of Karpūrasambhava to find Karpūrikā, the king's daughter, who was described to him by the female ascetic in the forest."
And having accomplished his task, he will return here quickly along with Gomukha; therefore, enough of worrying about this, for I have acquired this through my magical sciences.
Having spoken thus, she comforted the Lord of Vatsa along with his retinue; and he, for his part, employed the science named Ratnaprabhā for his husband.
For noble women, desiring the welfare of their husbands, take no account of the journey, thinking only of how to alleviate Naravāhanadatta’s hardships on the road.
And for such a long distance did Naravāhanadatta travel on the back of his horse through this forest, accompanied by Gomukha.
Then, suddenly approaching him on the road, a young maiden said to him: "I am named Māyāvatī, a magic science sent by Ratnaprabha."
"I shall protect you invisibly on the way; go now without anxiety. Having said this, the personified Vidyā vanished from his sight even as he looked on.
By its power, as he traveled along the road with his hunger and thirst stilled, Naravāhanadatta praised his beloved Ratnaprabhā.
Having reached a clear lake in the forest in the evening, he and Gomukha bathed and performed their eating, drinking, and other needs with very sweet fruits and water.
And there at night, having restrained the two horses and given them fodder, he climbed a great tree with his minister for the sake of lodging.
Resting upon its branch, he was awakened by the neighing of terrified horses; looking down from within, he saw a lion that had arrived below.
Seeing that he wished to descend for the sake of the horse, Gomukha said to him: "Aha! Disregarding your own body, you act without even consulting your ministers."
For kings have their foundation in the body, and sovereignty has its foundation in counsel; how then do you wish to fight with beasts of prey whose weapons are claws and fangs?
"It was for the sake of protecting him that we two have indeed just now ascended here. Thus restrained by Gomukha's words, the crown prince at that very moment—
Seeing that lion swiftly killing the horse, he quickly struck it from the back of a tree with a thrown dagger that sank deep into its body.
Although thus pierced by him, that powerful one killed the horse and then slew the second steed as well, just as a lion would slay its prey.
Then the son of the Lord of Vatsa, taking a sword from Gomukha, split that lion in two with it as he hurled it into the midst of him.
Having descended and seized a sword from the body of the lion, he mounted his own sword and spent that night right there in the tree.
Then, having descended in the morning, Naravāhanadatta set out accompanied by Gomukha toward that Karpūrikā.
Then, seeing him traveling on foot after his mount had been killed by a lion, Gomukha spoke these words on the road to console him:
"O King, listen as I relate to you this incidental story. There is here a city named Irāvatī, which surpasses Alakā."
In that city there was a lord of the earth named Parityāgasena, and he had two queens who were as dear to him as his own life.
One was his own minister’s daughter, named Adhikasamgamā; the second, Kāvyālaṅkārā by name, was born of a royal lineage.
Together with those two, that sonless king, seeking a son, performed austerities while fasting and sleeping on darbha grass, propitiating Ambikā.
Then Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, being pleased by his asceticism, appeared to him in person in a dream and, having given him two divine fruits, commanded him:
"Arise and give these two fruits as food for your wife; from them, O King, two heroic sons shall be born to you."
Having spoken thus, Gaurī vanished; and that king, having awakened, rose in the morning and rejoiced upon seeing both fruits in his hand.
Having delighted his wife with that description of the dream, he bathed, worshipped Mṛḍānī, and performed the concluding rite of his vow.
Having approached that queen, who was exceedingly passionate, at night as before, she gave her a single fruit, and she then ate it.
Then, out of respect for his own chief minister—who was that woman’s father—the king stayed that night in her palace.
And he placed that fruit right here, near the head of his own bed, for the sake of the second queen; it was the second fruit prepared for her.
Then, while the king was asleep there, the queen, having had excessive sexual union, rose up and desired two sons for herself who were like her.
She ate that second fruit as well, down to its core; for envy toward co-wives is indeed innate to women.
And rising in the morning, she said to that lord of the earth as he was gathering those fruits: "I myself have already eaten a second portion of those fruits."
Then that king, dejected in mind, departed and, having passed the day, went at night to the bedchamber of that second queen.
There, as she was begging for that very fruit, he said to her: "While I was asleep, your co-wife ate it by means of a trick."
Then, having failed to obtain the fruit that was the cause for the birth of a son, Queen Kāvyālaṅkārā remained silent and deeply distressed.
As those days passed while she remained there, the queen, having had excessive sexual union, became pregnant; and then, in due time, she gave birth to two sons simultaneously.
King Parityāgasena also rejoiced, his own desire having borne fruit through that event, after he had celebrated a great festival.
And of those two sons, the king gave the name Indīvarasena to the elder, who had eyes like blue lotuses and a wondrous form.
And he gave his younger brother the name Anicchasena, because his mother had enjoyed the fruit of her actions without her own desire.
Then, seeing that [work] of the king, which was adorned with poetic figures, his second queen became indignant and reflected:
"Alas! I have been deceived by this co-wife regarding the acquisition of a son; therefore, I must certainly take revenge for her offense."
Thinking, "These two sons of his must be destroyed by my own ingenuity," she remained there, searching for a means to that end.
And just as those two princes grew up there, so too did the tree of enmity grow within her heart.
In due course, having reached the prime of youth, those two princes, endowed with mighty arms and desiring victory, made their request to their father.
We have both been trained in the arts of weaponry and have reached the prime of youth; how can we endure bearing these arms of ours now rendered fruitless?
"Shame on the arms of a Kṣatriya who does not desire victory, and shame on his youth! Therefore, father, give us now your permission for our world-conquest."
Having heard these words of his two sons, King Parityāgasena was delighted; with their approval, he made preparations for their departure.
If at any time you should encounter distress here, then the goddess Ambikā, the remover of suffering, must be remembered; for it was by her that you two were granted to me.
Having spoken thus, the king dispatched his two sons on their expedition, accompanied by armies and vassals, and having had the auspicious rites performed for them by their mother.
And afterwards, I dispatched their maternal grandfather, my own chief minister, named Prathamasaṃgama, who was accompanied by Prajñā as his assistant.
Then those two princes, brothers endowed with great prowess, having gone together with their army toward the eastern direction, first conquered it in due course.
Then those two heroes, unimpeded, having met with many kings, and possessing proven majesty, set out toward the southern direction to conquer.
Upon hearing that news from the two of them, their parents rejoiced; however, the stepmother burned with the fire of internal hatred.
"Having conquered the earth by the pride of their arms and having slain me, these two sons of mine have intended to seize my kingdom for themselves."
Therefore, if you have devotion toward me, then these two sons of mine must both be slain by you here without any hesitation.
Then, at that time during the night, that deceitful woman, having written out the king’s command in the very name of that [minister] to the vassal chiefs residing in his camp, [sent it].
The secretaries of peace and war, having brought together stores of wealth, dispatched a messenger with poetic compositions and ornaments in private.
And that messenger, having gone secretly to the camp of those two princes, delivered those letters to the vassal chiefs from them.
Having made them recite it, they all reflected upon that exceedingly harsh royal policy and recognized it as the command of their lord, which must not be transgressed.
Having met together at night and deliberated on how to kill those two princes, they made a resolution to do so, even though they were captivated by their virtues and lacked any independent will.
Having learned of this from the mouth of one friend among them, the minister, who was the maternal grandfather and was staying together with those two princes, [acted].
Having awakened them according to the truth and having mounted the two excellent horses, he then secretly removed them from that camp at that very moment.
Dismissed by him, those two princes traveled through the night illuminated by its light, and, not knowing the way, entered the Vindhya forest.
There, as night had passed and the two were proceeding by stages, at midday, overcome by intense thirst, the two horses met their death.
And that aged maternal grandfather, his palate parched by hunger and thirst and exhausted by the heat, passed away while the two of them looked on in their weariness.
How have we two, who are innocent, been brought to this state by our father, who fulfilled the desire of that wicked stepmother of ours?
Thus, while those two brothers were grieving and suffering there, they meditated upon that Goddess Ambikā, who had previously been pointed out to them by their father.
By the power of that refuge-providing woman's meditation, at that very moment, those two became free from hunger, fatigue, and thirst, and were restored to strength.
Then, comforted by that assurance and their fatigue from the road forgotten, they went to see her who dwells in the Vindhya forest.
There, at her abode and before her, both those brothers began a fast and commenced austerities in order to propitiate her.
In the meantime, those neighboring chieftains stationed at the camp gathered together and approached, desiring to do harm to the two of them.
Searching everywhere, they did not see those two princes, the son and his maternal grandfather, who had fled somewhere, even though they continued their search.
Then, fearing that their secret counsel had been divulged, they all, out of dread of King Parityāgasena, went into his presence.
Having shown him the letters, they told him exactly what had occurred; then, having understood that, he became bewildered and, filled with rage, spoke to them as follows.
"These letters were not sent by me; this is some kind of sorcery. Do you fools not even know such a thing?"
"How can I kill my two sons, who were obtained through no small amount of austerity? They have already been killed by you, though they were protected by their own merits."
"And by my maternal grandfather, the fruit of counsel was shown to them. Having said this to those vassals, he [dismissed] the scribe, the forger of documents.
Although he had fled, the king quickly summoned him by his own power, questioned him thoroughly regarding what had occurred, and punished him appropriately.
And he cast that wicked wife, who had killed their son and was skilled in the ornaments of poetry and capable of performing such deeds, into an underground chamber.
But how could a sin committed impulsively with a mind blinded by excessive hatred, without having examined the consequences, not lead to misfortune?
And having restrained those neighboring vassals who had gone with the two princes and returned, the king appointed others in their place.
And he remained there, constantly seeking news of those two sons, afflicted with grief along with their mother, devoted to dharma, and remembering Ambikā.
And at that time, the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas became pleased with Prince Indīvarasena and his younger brother because of their ascetic penance.
And having given him the sword, she appeared to him in person in a dream and commanded him thus: "By the power of this sword, you shall conquer enemies who are otherwise invincible."
Whatever you shall think of, that shall be accomplished for you; and by this means, both of you shall attain the fulfillment of your desires.
When the goddess had spoken thus and vanished, Indīvarasena woke up and saw that sword still in his hand.
Then, having comforted his younger brother with the sword and by describing that dream, he, joined by him, broke his fast in the morning with forest fare.
Then, having bowed to that goddess, his fatigue dispelled by her grace, he departed from there with his brother, joyful and with that sword in hand.
And having traveled a great distance, he reached a certain great and excellent city, which, with its golden houses, created the illusion of being the peak of Mount Meru.
There, at the gate of the main street, he beheld a certain fierce Rākṣasa; and the hero asked him the name of that city and who its lord was.
This city named Śailapura is inhabited by our lord and master, the subduer of enemies, known as Yamadaṃṣṭra, the sovereign of the rākṣasas.
When this was said by that Rākṣasa, who desired to kill Yamadaṃṣṭra, Indīvarasena then proceeded to enter there.
And that mighty-armed one, having severed the head of the gatekeeper Rākṣasa who was blocking him with a single stroke of his sword, cast him down.
Having slain him, the hero entered the royal palace and beheld within that night-stalker Yamadaṃṣṭra seated upon his throne.
His face was terrible with fangs, a beautiful woman stood at his left side, and he was embraced by another maiden of divine form on his other side.
And having seen him, with the sword given by Ambikā in his hand, he challenged him to battle; and that Rākṣasa rose up, drawing his sword.
And as their battle proceeded, the head of that Rākṣasa was repeatedly cut off by Indīvarasena, yet it grew back again and again.
Having observed that illusion of his, he was signaled by Kūrmāyā, who stood at his side and was enamored with the sight of him.
Having severed that head of the Rākṣasa, the prince, being light-handed, once again split it in two with a stroke of his sword.
By means of that counter-illusion, the head of that Rākṣasa—whose own illusion had been destroyed—did not grow back; thus, that Rākṣasa was slain.
When he had spoken, those excellent women and young girls were delighted; then the prince, together with his younger brother, sat down and asked them:
"Was this Rākṣasa in such a city as this ever guarded by only a single doorkeeper? Who are you two, and why do you rejoice now that he has been slain?"
Having heard this, the maiden from between the two of them said to him: "In this city of Śailapura, there was a king named Vīrabhuja."
"This is his wife, Madanadaṃṣṭrā; and he was approached and devoured by this Rākṣasa Yamadaṃṣṭra through the power of illusion."
His retinue was already devoured; she alone was not eaten because she was beautiful. This Madanadaṃṣṭrā became the wife of that self-made man.
Then, having constructed golden houses in this secluded and delightful city, he remained there sporting with her, having cast aside all his royal retinue.
And I, named Khaḍgadaṃṣṭrā, am the younger sister of this Rākṣasa; upon seeing you, I have instantly become filled with love.
Therefore, now that he has been slain, she and I are filled with joy; O noble son, accept me, who am surrendered to you in love.
When she had spoken thus, Indīvarasena then married Khaḍgadaṃṣṭrā according to the Gāndharva rite.

And he remained right there in that city, by the power of the goddess’s sword, enjoying pleasures that appeared as soon as they were thought of, having taken a wife and being accompanied by his younger brother.
And once, by means of the power of his own sword-thought-jewel, he created through meditation a vehicle for traveling through the sky for his younger brother.
Having placed Vīra in a celestial chariot, he sent Anicchasena without fatigue to his parents to inform them of his own news.
He too, having traveled swiftly through the sky by means of that celestial chariot, reached his father's city, Irāvatī, where Anicchasena resided.
There he gladdened his parents with his sight, as the moon refreshes two cakora birds exhausted by the heat of intense sorrow.
Having approached and fallen at their feet, he was embraced by them in turn; as they questioned him, he dispelled their anxiety with news of his brother’s welfare.
And he related that entire account before them—concerning both his brother and himself—of how it had begun in sorrow but would end in happiness.
And there he heard of the kind of deceitful scheme that had been devised by that wicked woman, the stepmother, out of hatred and for her own destruction.
Then Anicchasena remained there, honored by the people, accompanied by his father who was celebrating a festival, and comforted by his mother.
After a few days had passed, apprehensive due to a bad dream he had seen and longing for his brother, he made a request to his father.
"I am going; having expressed my longing for you, I shall bring back that noble Indīvarasena. Father, grant me your permission."
Having heard that, and being permitted by his father who was eager for his son's welfare, as well as by his mother, he quickly ascended that very same celestial chariot.
Anicchasena departed through the air for the city of Śailapura, and in the morning, he entered the palace of his brother there.
There he saw his elder brother lying unconscious, with Khadgadamstra and Madanadamstra weeping at his side.
To him who asked in bewilderment, "What is this?", Khaḍgadaṃṣṭrā, with her face cast down, spoke while being censured by that other woman.
Once, while you were away and I had gone to bathe, this brother of yours secretly dallied with her, Madanadaṃṣṭrā.
Having bathed, I returned in an instant and saw him standing there in that very state, joined with her; and I rebuked them with my voice.
Then, although I was thus entreated by him, I was utterly deluded by envy—which, like destiny itself, cannot be transgressed—and I thought as follows:
"Aha! Disregarding me entirely, he is pursuing another woman; I know that this pride of his is caused by the greatness of his sword."
Thinking, "I shall hide this from him," that foolish woman cast this sword into the fire while he was asleep at night.
This sword has been stained with blemish, and it has come to this state; moreover, I am tormented and reviled by the fangs of passion.
And now you have arrived here at this very moment, while both she and I—our minds blinded by grief and resolved upon death—are in this state.
Therefore, you yourself take this sword, which performs cruel deeds; strike me down with it, for I have not abandoned my innate nature.
Having been addressed thus by his brother’s wife, Anicchasena, considering her to be beyond reproach due to her distress, desired to cut off his own head.
"Do not do this! This prince who has died is not your elder brother; he was deluded by the Queen out of anger over the negligence regarding the sword."
And in this matter of Khaḍgadaṃṣṭrā, no offense should be imputed [to her], because this was merely the manifestation of the power of those who have descended due to a curse.
Both of these were formerly the wives of your brother; therefore, propitiate that very goddess for the attainment of your desire.
Having heard this voice from the sky that had arisen at that moment, Anicchasena desisted from his attempt at suicide.
Having mounted that celestial chariot and taken up that sword stained with fire, he went to the foot of the goddess Vindhyavāsinī.
There, having fasted and intending to gratify her with the offering of his head, he heard this goddess Udgatā speaking from the sky:
"Do not act rashly, my son; go, let your elder brother live. Let the stainless sword be born [again], for I am pleased with your devotion."
Having heard these divine words and seeing that he had instantly attained freedom from blemish, he took the sword in his hand and performed a circumambulation of her.
Mounting a swift, perfected celestial chariot as if it were his own desire, Anicchasena arrived eagerly at that city of Śailapura.
There, as soon as his elder brother had regained consciousness after rising from his swoon, he seized him by the feet with tears; and he too embraced him around the neck.
Then both wives of his brother, falling at his feet and saying, "Our husband has been saved by you," spoke thus to that Anicchasena.
Then, when his elder brother Indīvarasena questioned him about that, he did not become angry with Khaḍgadaṃṣṭrā, and he was pleased with that brother.
And from his mouth he heard that his parents were longing for a sight of him, and that Māyā had been created by Paramātrā to cause their separation from him.
Then, having taken the sword offered by his brother, he ascended a magnificent celestial chariot that appeared as soon as it was thought of, through the power of that weapon.
Accompanied by his two wives and his younger brother, Indīvarasena, whose palace was adorned with gold, returned to his own city, Irāvatī.
Having descended there from the sky while being gazed upon with wonder by the people, he entered his father’s royal palace in the presence of his father, accompanied by his retinue.
And having seen his father and mother in such a state, he fell at their feet, his face washed by streams of tears.
And the two of them, suddenly beholding their son along with his younger brother, embraced him; their limbs as if sprinkled with nectar, they attained the cooling of their distress.
Beholding those two daughters-in-law of divine form, who had performed obeisance at his feet, he and [his wife] were thrilled and greeted them with joy.
Having learned from the course of their conversation that his two wives were previously ordained for him and had been described by a divine voice, they both attained supreme joy.
They rejoiced with wonder at the power of this son, manifested through such things as traveling by celestial chariot and bringing back golden palaces.
Then Indīvarasena, accompanied by those two parents and his retinue, remained there, providing a festival of joy for the people.
And once, having made a request to his father, King Parityāgasena, he set out once more for the conquest of the quarters, accompanied by his younger brother.
And having conquered the entire earth by the power of his sword, the mighty-armed one returned after seizing gold, elephants, horses, and jewels from the kings.
And he reached his own city, which seemed as if pursued by the earth, which had risen up like the dust from his own army out of fear of his victory.
Having entered the capital, he was then met by his father; together with his younger brother, he brought great joy to his mother, Adhikasamgamā.
Having honored the assembly of kings, Indīvarasena, accompanied by his wives and kinsmen, spent that day there in great joy.
On another day, having offered the earth to his father through that same hand, the prince suddenly remembered his own former birth.
Then, appearing like one who has awakened from sleep, he said to his father: "O father, I have remembered my birth; listen now as I tell you this."
On a ridge of the Himalayas there is a city named Muktāpura; there dwells a king called Muktāsena, a lord of the Vidyādharas.
To the queen named Kambuvatī, two sons were born to him in succession: Padmasena and Rūpasena, both endowed with excellent virtues.
Out of love for those two, the maiden named Ādityaprabhā, the daughter of an eminent Vidyādhara, chose Padmasena herself as her husband.
Having learned of this, a Vidyādhara maiden named Candravatī, his own childhood friend, came in person and, afflicted by love, chose him as her husband.
At that time, Padmasena, having two wives, was constantly distressed by his wife Ādityaprabhā out of jealousy toward her co-wife.
I am unable to endure daily the quarrels with my wife, who is blinded by jealousy; I shall go to the forest of asceticism to pacify this despondency.
"O father, grant me your permission," Padmasena said repeatedly and persistently to his own father, Muktāsena.
Enraged by that seizure, the father cursed him along with his wife: "Go to the forest of asceticism and return to the world of mortals!"
In that regard, this wife of yours, Ādityaprabhā, who is addicted to quarreling, will enter the womb of a Rākṣasī and become your very own wife once again.
This second one, Candravatī, who is devoted to you and very dear to you, will become a Rākṣasī and, as a royal woman, will find you, her beloved, on the earth.
Since I observed that Rūpasena was longing to follow you, his elder brother, he too shall become your brother in that place.
"You shall also experience some suffering there caused by having two wives. Having spoken thus and paused, he then established this end to our curse:
"When you, as a prince, have conquered the earth and offer it to your parents, then, together with these [beings], you will remember your birth and attain liberation."
Thus addressed by his father, Padmasena at that moment descended to the world of mortals along with those others.
"O father, that Padmasena has been born as your son here; he shall be named Indīvarasena, and everything that was to be done by me has been accomplished."
And that other youth, Rūpasena, the son of a Vidyādhara, was born as my very younger brother, named Anicchāsena.
Know that these two of yours, Khaḍgadaṃṣṭrā and Madanadaṃṣṭrikā, are those who were formerly my wives, Sādityaprabhā and Candrāvatī.
"Now this limit of the curse has been reached for us; therefore, father, let us go to our own Vidyādhara realm."
Having spoken thus, together with his wife and brothers who had remembered their former births, he cast off his human form and assumed the appearance of a Vidyādhara.
Having bowed at his parents' feet and placed his two beloved wives on his lap, he departed through the sky with his younger brother to his own Vidyādhara city.
There, Sanmati was welcomed by his father Muktāsena; he, who was a festival for his mother’s eyes, was reunited with his brother Rūpasena.
That Padmasena dwelt there again, free from manifest jealousy, living in happiness together with Ādityaprabhā and Candravatī.
Having told this delightful story on the road, the minister Gomukha spoke again to that Naravāhanadatta.
Thus, for the great alone does there arise such great affliction and such a rise; but for others, O Lord, how much affliction or even rise could there possibly be?
But you, protected by the power of the knowledge-mantra of Queen Ratnaprabhā, shall obtain that princess Karpūrikā without any difficulty.
Having heard this from the mouth of Gomukha, who was of pleasant countenance, Naravāhanadatta set out upon that path together with him, unaware of any fatigue.

And as I was traveling there, I reached at evening a lake whose king was the warbling of waterfowl; its abundant waters were cool and as sweet as nectar, its banks were lovely with rows of mango trees and pomegranates, and its lotuses were in full bloom.

Having bathed there, worshipped the beloved of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain with devotion, and taken his meal of those fruits which were pleasing due to their fragrant and sweet taste, the son of the Lord of Vatsa spent that night on its bank, sleeping upon a bed strewn with soft sprouts together with his friend.

Thus ends the eighth wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Ninth Wave. Then, having risen from the shore of that lake at dawn, Naravāhanadatta, as he set out, spoke to his minister Gomukha:
"Friend, I know that today at the end of the night, a certain maiden of divine form, clad in white garments, approached me in a dream and spoke this."
Be free from anxiety, my son; you will soon reach from here a great and wondrous city situated within a forest on the shore of the ocean.
Having rested there without distress, you will reach the city of Karpūrasambhava, and there you shall obtain that princess, Karpūrikā.
Having spoken thus to me, she vanished; and at that very moment, I awoke. To him who had spoken in this manner, Gomukha, being pleased, replied:
O Lord, you are favored by the gods; what is difficult for you? That which you desire shall certainly be accomplished by you without effort.
Having spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta then proceeded quickly along that path together with Gomukha.
And in due course, he reached that [city] situated on the shore of the ocean, which was endowed with watchtowers, gateways, and city-gates resembling mountain peaks.
The city, resplendent with royal palaces made entirely of gold like Mount Meru, possessed vast expanses and was like another terrestrial sphere.
Having entered there by way of the market street, he saw everything made of wooden machinery moving about as if it were alive.
The merchants, courtesans, and citizens were filled with wonder, perceiving him as being devoid of life solely because of his silence.
And in due course, accompanied by Gomukha, he reached the vicinity of the royal palace, observing there the same abundance of elephants, horses, and other such things.
And accompanied by his ministers, he entered with wonder the interior of that royal palace, which was adorned with golden turrets.
There, surrounded by mechanical porters and women, it was the single conscious principle that served as the cause for the movement of those inert things.
He beheld a noble man seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, standing as the presiding lord over his own senses.
That man, seeing him of such excellent appearance, rose up, offered a welcome, and seated him upon his own seat.
And having sat down before him, he asked: "Who are you? How did you come to this superhuman earth, being accompanied only by yourself?"
Then Naravāhanadatta, having had that man—who was bowing before him—report his own story in its entirety, questioned him.
"Who are you, and what is this marvel of a city? O good sir, tell me. Having heard that, the man began to relate his own story.
There is a city named Kāñcī, woven with most weighty virtues; it has attained the state of being a true ornament for the bride that is the earth, like the girdle of a woman.
In that city of Kāñcī, there was a famous lord of the earth named Bāhubala, by whom the goddess Śrī, though fickle, was won through his own arms and bound within his treasury.
In the kingdom of that king, we two brothers are both carpenters, experts in the construction of mechanical devices made of wood and other materials through the magic taught by Maya.
"O Lord, my elder brother is named Prāṇadhara, who is ruined by his addiction to courtesans; I am the younger one, devoted to him, and my name is Rājyadhara."
Having consumed his paternal wealth, my husband also enjoyed some of his own property and even that which I had earned, for it was offered to him by me with a heart softened by affection.
Even more addicted than before, out of a desire to steal wealth for the sake of the courtesan, he fashioned a pair of wooden swans that moved by means of a string mechanism.
Then, at night, that pair of geese, impelled by the pulling of a string through the application of a mechanism from the treasury of King Bāhubala, [flew] there.
Having entered through the window, he took the jewelry lying in the basket with his beak and went to my brother's house.
Having sold that [treasure], he lived with a courtesan as his elder brother; and in that same manner, day and night, he drained the treasury of the king.
And even though he was being restrained by me, he did not desist from that improper act; for who, blinded by calamity, can discern between the path and the non-path?
And so, for several days, out of fear, the royal treasury remained unrobbed, its bolts unshifted during the nights and free from mice.
Searching daily in silence, becoming increasingly distressed, that storekeeper went and clearly reported the matter to the king.
The king also stationed him and other guards, who were awake through the night, within the treasury in order to investigate the truth of the matter.
At midnight, the guards saw those two mechanical swans, my brothers, entering through the window and moving there as they were pulled by strings.
As the mechanical contrivances whirled about, they seized their ornaments with their beaks; and when the ropes were cut, they took them up to show to the king in the morning.
At that moment, my elder brother spoke with agitation: "Brother, two of my swans have been seized by the guards of the treasury."
For the rope has become slack and the pin in the machine has slipped; therefore, both of us must depart from here this very moment.
"Indeed, having learned of us at dawn, the king will arrest us both as thieves; for we alone are renowned as the two experts in the art of mechanical illusions."
And I possess here a wind-powered chariot that travels eight hundred yojanas in a single go as soon as its pin is struck.
Therefore, let us go far away today, even to a foreign land that may bring suffering; for where can there be happiness for one who persists in sinful deeds and disregards beneficial advice?
This ripening has now come forth upon you, though you are sinless, for those words which were not heeded by me due to my wicked mind.
Having spoken thus, my brother Prāṇadhara, together with his family, immediately ascended that celestial chariot which travels through the sky.
But although I was told this by him, I did not mount it while it was crowded with many people; then, having flown up into the sky, he departed for some distant place.
When that Prāṇadhara, whose name was truly significant, had departed, I, anticipating danger from the king at dawn, remained all alone.
Having ascended a wind-powered chariot that I had constructed myself, I then traveled swiftly for two hundred yojanas from there.
Then, urged by him, I traveled another two hundred yojanas further on that sky-faring celestial chariot.
Then, having abandoned his celestial chariot out of fear that he was near the ocean, he proceeded here on foot and reached this empty city in due course.
And out of curiosity, O King, I entered this royal palace, which was furnished with garments, ornaments, beds, and other royal requisites.
In the evening, having bathed in the waters of the garden pond and eaten fruits, I lay upon the royal bed at night and reflected alone.
