"What shall I do here in this desolate place? Tomorrow morning I shall go from here to wherever it may be; for my fear of the king has vanished due to the strength of my arms."
Having reflected thus, at the end of the night, a man of divine form mounted upon a peacock approached me while I was fast asleep and spoke to me in a dream as follows.
"O auspicious one, you must dwell right here; you must not go elsewhere. At the time of eating, you should mount [the chariot] and remain in the middle city."
When he had spoken thus and vanished, I awoke and reflected: "This divine place is certainly a creation of the Kumāra."
And he has bestowed a favor upon me through his past merits in a dream; for I have surely arisen here, and there is certainly welfare for me in dwelling here.
Having thus resolved and risen, I performed my daily rites and remained there; then, at the time for food, I ascended to this middle city.
Then, as golden vessels were presented before me, food consisting of ghee, milk, rice, and other delicacies fell from the sky into them.
And whatever else I thought of as food, it was brought to me; having eaten that, O God, I became exceedingly happy here.
Therefore, O Lord, I have indeed taken up residence in this city; day after day, I enjoy royal pleasures that appear as soon as they are thought of.
"A wife or attendants, though thought of by me, do not remain; therefore, I have created all these people here out of mechanical devices."
Thus, having come here, I, the carpenter, alone and by the power of destiny, am performing the play of the king under the name Rājyadhara.
Therefore, O sirs, today in this city created by the gods, please take rest as much as you are able while I am intent upon serving you.
Having said this, Naravāhanadatta was led by that Rājyadhara to his city garden along with Gomukha.
There, having bathed in the water of the pond and worshipped Dhūrjaṭi with lotuses, he was led to that middle enclosure, the ground for the meal.
And there, together with his ministers, he partook of auspicious foods that had been presented through meditation by Rājyadhara, who stood before him.
Then, having had his meal cleared away by some unseen person, he remained at ease after enjoying betel and drinking wine.
Then, filled with wonder at the greatness of that city which resembled the wish-fulfilling gem, he retired to his excellent bed at night after Rājyadhara had eaten.
Then, as he lay upon his bed, Rājyadhara spoke to him who was asking about the story of Karpūrikā, which had awakened his curiosity with its novelty.
"Why do you not sleep, O auspicious one? You shall surely obtain your desired beloved; for Fortune herself chooses a man of noble character, just as a woman chooses her own husband."
This is something seen directly before our eyes; listen as I tell you how it is so: that king of Kāñcī, Bāhubala, of whom I spoke.
His doorkeeper, named Arthalobha, was truly worthy of his name and possessed great wealth; he had a wife named Mānaparā, who was endowed with great beauty.
Driven by greed for wealth according to the custom of merchants, and distrusting his servants because of that greed, he appointed his wife to oversee their commercial dealings.
Though she was unwilling, she was compelled by them to engage in business with merchants; she captivated people with her sweet appearance and her speech.
Whatever sale of elephants, horses, jewels, garments, and other goods she made, he, out of greed for wealth, saw each one and approved it with increasing enthusiasm.
Once, a certain great merchant named Sukhadhana arrived there from a distant foreign land, carrying a vast quantity of goods such as horses and other merchandise.
As soon as he realized his wife had arrived, that merchant named Sukhadhana, driven by greed for wealth, said to her: "A man has arrived here from another land."
"O beloved, twenty thousand horses were brought by him, as well as countless pairs of fine garments produced in the land of China."
Therefore, go and bring from there five thousand horses, as well as ten thousand pairs of fine garments, having purchased them.
"With as many as ten thousand of my own horses, as well as those five thousand, I shall present myself before the king and carry out trade."
Having spoken thus, she was sent by that wicked man out of greed for wealth; devoted to pride, she went to the side of Sukhadhana.
And he sought to purchase those horses along with their trappings from him, who had offered a welcome and whose eyes were captivated by their beauty.
Overcome by passion, the merchant took her to a secluded place and said: "I will not give you even a single garment or a horse for a price."
"If you spend a single night with me, I shall give you five thousand horses and a hundred thousand garments."
Having said this, he sought Sundarī even more intensely; for who does not feel desire when women display unrestrained gestures?
Then she replied to him: "I shall ask my husband this very thing; for even in this matter, I know he would urge me on out of excessive greed."
Having said this, she went to her own home and told that husband what she had been told in private by that merchant Sukhadhana.
Then that wicked husband, greedy for wealth, said to her: "My dear, here are five thousand garments and five hundred horses."
If they are obtained in a single night, what fault is there in this? Therefore, go to his side today; you shall return quickly in the morning.
Having heard these words of her husband, that coward, Mānaparā felt doubt arise in her heart and reflected:
Fie on this wicked seller of wood, a man of base character! Alas, through constant cultivation of greed, he has truly become one with it.
That noble-minded man alone is my true husband who would purchase me for a single night with hundreds of horses and thousands of Chinese silk cloths.
Having reflected thus and having obtained his permission with the words "there is no fault on my part," she then went from there to the house of that wicked husband, Sukhadhana.
And he, seeing her arrived, questioning her, and understanding the matter to be so, was filled with wonder and considered himself blessed by the attainment of her.
Out of greed for wealth, she quickly sent to her husband those horses and garments that had been stipulated as the bride-price, exactly as described.
And with his desires fulfilled, he spent that night together with her, as if with the very embodiment of the glorious fruit of his long-attained personal prosperity.
Then, in the morning, Mānaparā spoke to the messengers whom that impotent man had sent, who were shamelessly incited by their greed for wealth.
"Having been sold and having become united with another, how can I, shameless as he is, become his wife again? Or am I likewise so?"
"You yourselves tell me if this is fitting now; go, for he by whom I was purchased is indeed my husband."
Having been addressed thus by her, those servants went and, with downcast faces, spoke those very words to him for the sake of their own gain.
Having heard that, that lowest of men desired to take her away by force; then a friend of his named Harabala spoke to him.
She cannot be brought back by you from that treasury of happiness; I do not see any fortitude in you before that great hero.
For he has been made a hero by that woman who is devoted to renunciation; and being powerful himself, he has arrived accompanied by allies who are also powerful.
But you, having sold yourself through wretchedness, abandoned by those who cherish solitude, devoid of energy due to humiliation, censured, and fallen into impotence—[how can you hope for success?]
He is neither strong by his own power nor endowed with the strength of allies; how then could you be capable of conquering that adversary?
If the king were to learn of this wicked deed of selling his wife, he would be enraged; therefore, remain silent and do not again engage in such playful jesting.
Thus, although forbidden by his friend, he—driven by greed for wealth and overcome by anger—went with his army and besieged the house of Sukhadhana.
At that moment, the army of Sukhadhana, together with his friends, rushed out and in an instant completely shattered that entire force.
Then, having fled, that Arthalobha went into the presence of the king and said, "O King, my wife has been carried off by the merchant named Sukhadhana."
Thus he informed the king, concealing his own misconduct; and the king, in his wrath, desired to seize that Sukhadhana.
Then the minister named Saṃdhāna said to the king: "O Lord, that merchant cannot be restrained by any means whatsoever."
O Lord, for him who is joined by those eleven friends who have come as allies, there exist more than a hundred thousand excellent horses.
The truth of the matter has not been ascertained here, for this cannot be without a cause; therefore, having dispatched a messenger, he must be asked what it is that he says in this regard.
Having heard these words of the minister, King Bāhubala then dispatched a messenger to that Sukhadhana in order to question him.
When that messenger, having gone there by his command, asked him, Mānaparā then related her own story to him.
Upon hearing of that marvel, King Sārthalobha went to the house of Sukhadhana to behold her form.
There he beheld her, devoted to pride, bowing before Sukhadhana, and inspiring wonder even in the Creator by the splendor of her beauty.
He heard from her own mouth, as she bowed at his feet and was questioned by him, the account of what had occurred exactly as it happened, while Arthalobha listened.
Having heard and reflected upon that truth, and being unable to resist his greed for its wealth, he asked that beautiful-faced woman, "What should be done now?"
Then she spoke with firm resolve: "O King, how can I approach that heartless and greedy man by whom I was sold to another when I was not in distress?"
When the king had heard this and was saying, "Well said," Arthalobha, agitated by lust, anger, and shame, spoke there:
"O King, let this Sukhadhana and I, though lacking reinforcements, fight with our own respective troops; let the strength or weakness of our forces be observed."
Having heard these words of Arthalobha, Sukhadhana replied: "In that case, let the two of us fight alone; what is the use of soldiers?"
"Whoever shall achieve victory, she will be devoted to him. Having heard this, the king also said, "Very well; let it be so."
Then, while King Mānapara and [his queen] were looking on, those two, mounted upon their horses, descended onto the field of battle.
When the battle had commenced there, Sukhadhana cast Arthalobha to the surface of the earth as his horse leaped up from the blow of a spear.

In that same manner, for three other times, as the horse was slain and he fell to the ground, that warrior who fought according to dharma, being firm and possessing the wealth of happiness, did not kill him.
On the fifth day, however, having fallen upon him while mounted on a horse, he struck him; that Arthalobha, rendered motionless, was then led away by his servants.
Then King Bāhubala honored Sukhadhana, who was being lauded with cries of "Well done! by everyone, according to his merit.
He then presented the gift that had been brought to him and surrendered it; he took away the entire wealth acquired through evil means by that man who was greedy for riches.
Having placed another in that position, he departed for his own home satisfied; for the virtuous, having ceased association with evil, attain ultimate peace.
Living there with ease, he too dwelt in happiness, possessing the wealth of bliss, together with his devoted wife who was intent on honoring him.
In this way, wives and wealth flee from one of inferior character; yet they come of their own accord from here and there to attend upon one of excellent character.
Therefore, enough with anxiety; go to sleep, for before long, O Lord, you shall obtain that Princess Karpūrikā.
Having heard these meaningful words from Rājyadhara there at night, Naravāhanadatta fell asleep along with Gomukha.
And there, having taken his meal in the morning, while he was standing for a moment, the wise Gomukha addressed that Rājyadhara.
"Construct a mechanical aerial chariot for this lord of mine, so that having reached the city of Karpūrasambhava, he may attain his beloved."
Having heard this, the carpenter presented to Naravāhanadatta a wind-mechanism aerial chariot that he had previously prepared.
Having ascended that sky-faring vehicle, swift as thought, together with Gomukha, he beheld its waves surging upward as if in joyful exultation at the sight of his courage.
Having crossed the ocean, Naravāhanadatta reached that city of Karpūrasambhava situated upon its shore.
Having descended from the celestial chariot that had entered the sky, he, together with Gomukha, wandered about within the city out of curiosity.
Having learned from the people he questioned that very city he desired had been reached, he went joyfully toward the vicinity of the royal palace, free from all doubt.
There, he entered a beautiful house presided over by an elderly woman for the sake of lodging, having been permitted by her as she bowed respectfully.
Seeking to ascertain the truth, he questioned that woman in an instant: "Noble lady, what is the name of the king here, and what is his offspring?"
"Tell us of his appearance, for we are foreigners," she was thus addressed by him; and having looked at him, that old woman beheld his excellent form.
The illustrious one replied, "Listen, O fortunate one, I shall tell you everything: here, in Karpūrasambhava, there was a king named Karpūraka."
Being childless, he performed austerities without food for the sake of progeny, directed toward Śaṅkara together with the Goddess through the exercise of his intellect.
Having fasted for three nights, the god Hara commanded him in a dream: "Arise, my son; a daughter shall be born to you who will be even more distinguished than yourself."
"The husband of this girl shall obtain the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas"—having been thus instructed by Hara, the king woke up at dawn.
Having reported that dream to the Goddess and to those engaged in intellectual pursuits, he arose; then, filled with joy, he performed the breaking of his fast together with her.
Then, not long after that, the queen of the king conceived a child; and when the time was complete, she gave birth to a daughter beautiful in all her limbs.
By her radiance, the lamps in that birth-chamber were so utterly surpassed that they seemed to exhale sighs under the guise of emitting soot.
Then her father, having celebrated a festival, bestowed upon her the name Karpūrikā, and he himself became King Karpūrika.
Gradually attaining growth, that Princess Karpūrikā, who is like moonlight to the eyes of the world, now stands in the full bloom of youth.
Her father here, the king, desires her marriage; but that high-minded woman, being a hater of men, does not desire him.
"Why do you not wish for marriage, friend, when the fruit of a daughter's birth [is such]? Thus was she questioned by my daughter and her friend, and she replied as follows:
"O friend, listen to the cause of my past life, as I am one who remembers her former births. On the shore of the great ocean, there stands a massive sandalwood tree."
Nearby that place was a lake adorned with blooming lotuses; there, by virtue of my past karma, I was born as a female swan in a previous life.
Once, on that sandalwood tree by the shore of the ocean, I made my home together with my own husband, a royal swan.
While I was dwelling there in that abode, a powerful wave of the ocean suddenly approached and carried away my newborn sons and calves.
When my children had been swept away by the flood, I remained weeping and fasting, standing in grief before a Śiva-liṅga situated on the shore of the ocean.
Then that royal swan, my husband, approached me and said: "Arise! Why do you grieve for children who are already gone?"
"Other [wives] shall be ours; everything is obtained by those who live"—pierced in my heart by these arrow-like words of his, I reflected thus.
Fie! Alas! Wretched are these men, so childish even toward their own offspring; they are devoid of affection and utterly merciless, even toward women who are full of devotion.
"What use have I for this husband, or for this suffering body?"—having reflected thus, she bowed to Hara and placed him within her heart with devotion.
Right there, in the presence of her husband as he watched, the princess, remembering her former birth, said: "May I become so again in another life."
Having thus resolved, I cast that body into the ocean; therefore, O friend, I have been born here today in this life in such a state.
And as she recalled that cruelty of her husband in their previous birth, her mind did not take pleasure in any suitor whatsoever.
"Therefore, I do not desire marriage; beyond this, everything depends on fate. Thus did the princess speak to my daughter in private.
My daughter also came and described this to me; thus, my son, I have related to you exactly what you asked.
Surely this princess is destined to be your wife alone; for she is the future universal sovereign of all the Vidyādharas.
"This woman was previously designated as my queen by Lord Śambhu; I see that you are endowed with those very characteristics, such as the *tilaka* and other marks."
"Could it be that you have been brought here by the Creator for some specific purpose? Rise first to my house; we shall see what will happen."
Having said this, Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by Gomukha, spent that night there with the old woman who had brought him food.
In the morning, having deliberated in private with Gomukha regarding his task, the son of the Lord of Vatsa assumed the garb of a Mahāvratin ascetic.
Then his companion, repeatedly crying out, "Alas! You have been killed! Alas! You have been killed!", went to the gate of the royal palace and wandered about, watched by the people.
And seeing him in such a state, the maidservants went there at once and spoke with wonder to Karpūrikā, the king’s daughter:
O Goddess, at the main gate we saw a youth of great vows who, though accompanied by a companion, possessed a peerless beauty.
She utters day and night this wondrous mantra that causes great delusion among women: "Alas, O swan! Alas, O female swan!"
Having heard that, the princess, who had previously been a female swan, was filled with curiosity and had him brought by those women into her presence so that she might see his true form.
And he beheld him, whose ground was adorned with unrestrained splendor, who had undertaken vows for the propitiation of Śaṅkara, appearing like a fresh god of love.
And looking at him with eyes wide open in wonder, she said: "What is this? Alas, O swan! Alas, O swan! Why is it that you speak thus?"
Even when she had spoken thus, he then cried out, "Alas! A swan! Thereupon, Gomukha, who was standing with him, replied to him:
I shall tell you this; listen, O Goddess, in brief: in a previous birth, through the power of his karma, he was a swan.
There, having made his dwelling upon the shore of the great ocean at the edge of a vast lake, he stayed together with his female swan beneath a sandalwood tree.
When her offspring had been swept away by the waves of the ocean through the power of fate, that female swan, afflicted with grief, threw herself into that very same place.
Then, afflicted by the pain of separation from her and feeling detachment toward the bird species, he desired to abandon that body and formed this resolution in his heart:
"May I be one who remembers his past lives as a prince in another birth, and may this virtuous woman, remembering her own past lives, become my wife there."
Having thus resolved and then called that body to mind, Śaṅkara, tormented by the fire of separation, cast it into the waters of the ocean.
Then, O auspicious lady, this son of the King of Vatsa was now born in Kauśāmbī, named Naravāhanadatta, who remembered his former birth.
"He shall become a universal monarch of the Vidyādhara lords"—such was the divine voice that clearly resounded at the moment of his birth.
In due course, having been established as the crown prince, he was married by his father to the divine Queen Madanamañcukā, who had arisen from a sacred cause.
Then a maiden named Ratnaprabhā, the daughter of the Vidyādhara lord Hemaprabha, came in person and chose him as her husband.
Nevertheless, remembering that female swan, he finds no peace; and this has been described by him to me, his young servant.
Then, while he was out hunting in the forest accompanied by me, he happened by fate to encounter a certain perfected female ascetic.
In the course of conversation, she, full of kindness, said this to him: "Long ago, my son, through the power of karma, Kama attained the state of a swan."
And he, who dwelt among the sandalwood trees on the shore of the ocean, had a beloved wife who was a celestial woman fallen due to a curse.
And when she threw herself into the ocean out of grief for her offspring carried away by the tide, that swan also cast himself into that very same place.
Thus, O child, by the grace of Śambhu, you have today become the son of the Lord of Vatsa; for you are one who remembers his former births, and you know that previous life.
That very same Hamsī has likewise now been born as a princess named Karpūrikā in the city called Karpūrasambhava on the far shore of the ocean.
"Therefore go there, my son, and you shall regain your beloved wife. Having said this, the perfected female ascetic flew up into the sky and vanished from sight.
And at that moment, our lord, having learned of these events, set out from there toward this place together with me.
Drawn by his affection for you and having staked his own life as the wager, he crossed hundreds of wildernesses and reached the shore of the ocean.
There, a carpenter named Rājyadhara, residing in Hemapura, joined me and my companion and gave us a mechanical aerial chariot.
Having ascended that terrifying vessel, which was like personified rashness itself, we have crossed the ocean wilderness and reached this city.
For this reason, O Goddess, my master arrived here in your presence while wandering and crying out, "Alas, alas! The swan! in such a manner.
But now, by beholding the noble full moon of your face, it enjoys the dispelling of the darkness brought about by the proximity of countless sufferings.
Worship this great guest with a garland of blue lotuses, which are his very gaze.
Having heard these words composed by Gomukha, Karpūrikā then believed them to be true, owing to the corroboration of their consistency.
"Oh! How great is the noble son's affection for me! My own detachment toward him was in vain," she reflected within herself, her heart moistened with love.
And she said, "I am that very swan; I am indeed blessed, for it is on my account that the noble son has experienced such suffering in two successive births."
Saying, "Therefore, I am now your slave, purchased by love," she honored Naravāhanadatta with baths and other services.
Then, through the mouth of his attendants, he informed his father of all this; and the father, having understood it, approached him in that very place.
There, he [beheld] his daughter, who had long desired marriage, and likewise her suitable bridegroom, Naravāhanadatta, who had finally arrived after a long time.
Seeing him marked with the characteristics of a great universal monarch of the Vidyādharas, the king then considered himself to have achieved his purpose.
Then, with due ceremony and respect, he gave that daughter of his, Karpūrikā, to Naravāhanadatta.
And at each circumambulation of the fire, he gave to his son-in-law thirty million pieces of gold and an equal amount of camphor.
The mountain peaks of Meru and Kailāsa, which had witnessed the marriage of the Daughter of the Mountain, seemed to have come there as if to behold the splendor of those who were present.
Furthermore, the virtuous King Karpūraka gave him ten million garments and three hundred well-adorned maidservants.
Then Naravāhanadatta remained there, having performed his marriage with that Karpūrikā, as if with Love incarnate.
To whose mind was that union of the bride and groom not a source of delight, like the meeting of a mādhavī creeper and the spring festival?
And on another day, the successful Naravāhanadatta said to his beloved Karpūrikā, "Come, let us go to Kauśāmbī."
Then she replied to him: "If it is so, why do we not go quickly by that very aerial chariot of yours which travels through the sky?"
If that is too small, I shall present another, more extensive one; for here there is a carpenter named Prāṇadhara, who constructs mechanical aerial chariots.
"Someone has arrived from another land; I shall have this done quickly. Having said this, she summoned the doorkeeper and gave instructions to the chamberlain.
"Go to that great carpenter of mechanical devices, Prāṇadhara, and say: 'Prepare for us a celestial chariot capable of traveling through the sky for our departure.'"
Having thus dismissed the chamberlain, Karpūrikā then informed her father, the king, through the mouth of a maidservant of her desire to depart.
As soon as he realized this, King Naravāhanadatta thought thus within himself while the monarch was still approaching that very spot:
"This woodcutter is certainly Prāṇadhara, the brother of Rājyadhara; he has been described by him as having fled from his own country out of fear of the king."
While the king was still thinking thus, Prāṇadhara, the carpenter, arrived there quickly accompanied by a doorkeeper.
And he informed him: "I have constructed a very great celestial chariot, which can carry thousands of men with ease."
When the carpenter had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta, having honored him and said "Excellent!", then questioned him with respect.
"Are you indeed the elder brother of Rājyadhara, Prāṇadhara by name, and a knower of the application of various great mechanical devices?"
"That very person is my brother; only the god knows the truth of how it is between us two. Thus spoke Prāṇadhara, bowing down to him in reply.
Then Naravāhanadatta related to him exactly how he had been seen and what had been said by Rājyadhara.
Then, when that great celestial chariot had been brought forth by Prāṇadhara with joy, he was given permission for it by his father-in-law, the king.
Having taken leave of him and loaded his female slave, camphor, and gold, he set out together with Prāṇadhara, who had been dismissed by the king.
And by that chief chamberlain, who had performed the auspicious rites for his mother-in-law, he took that bride, the young princess Karpūrikā.
Having bestowed gifts upon the twice-born along with heaps of fine garments, Naravāhanadatta, together with Gomukha, mounted [the elephant].
"First, let us go to the shore of the ocean to the presence of Rājyadhara; after that, we shall go home," he said to Prāṇadhara.
Then, struck by that [weapon], he quickly flew up into the sky with his retinue in the celestial chariot, as if in a fulfilled desire.
Crossing the ocean in an instant, he reached once more that city of gold situated on its shore, the abode of Rājyadhara.
There, he who held the kingdom bowed down, overjoyed at the sight of his brother; and he, along with festive celebrations, shared it with female slaves, though he himself was without a slave.
And having taken leave of him with tears in his eyes, he somehow parted from his elder brother and departed at that very moment for Kauśāmbī by means of that same celestial chariot.
There, the people were filled with wonder upon seeing him descend unexpectedly from the sky, borne by a magnificent celestial chariot, accompanied by his followers and joined by his new bride.

Having learned from the public proclamations of his son's prowess, the King of Vatsa, his father, went forth joyfully to meet him, accompanied by the Queen, the ministers, his daughter-in-law, and others.
Seeing his son, accompanied by his bride, bowing at his feet, the king rejoiced, for the celestial chariot signaled that he was destined for an empire over the sky-farers.
His mother Vāsavadattā, together with Padmāvatī, embraced him and shed tears as if to release the knot of grief caused by no longer seeing him.
Then his wife Ratnaprabhā and Madanamañcukā, filled with joy, simultaneously grasped his feet and his heart, their jealousy overcome by love.

Then that prince, having performed appropriate honors, delighted his paternal ministers headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa, as well as his own friends beginning with Marubhūti, who stood before him bowing in reverence.
And all of them were adorned by the noble family of the Sudarśanas; having crossed the ocean, they were clearly brought forth by their own lord as if they were personified forms of nectar.
The King of Vatsa and the others welcomed the new bride Karpūrikā, who had arrived accompanied by a hundred aged women, like the goddess Śrī herself, as she bowed down in accordance with propriety.
And the Lord of Vatsa honored that paternal warder of hers by bestowing upon him a heap of crores of gold, camphor, and garments, which had been carried away from his celestial chariot.
Then, having been informed by Naravāhanadatta, that king honored Prāṇadhara as well, who was the builder of the celestial chariot and a benefactor.
"How did this princess arrive, and how have we come here? the king asked with joy, honoring Gomukha.
Then [he related] how, from the time of going to the hunting forest, he had seen the ascetic woman; and how, by means of the celestial chariot obtained through Rājyadhara, he had crossed the ocean.
And how Karpūrikā, though averse to marriage, was made favorable; and how her arrival previously occurred by means of a celestial chariot, obtained through the acquisition of Prāṇadhara.
Then, in private, Gomukha related the entire event exactly as it had occurred to the King of Vatsa and his wife and ministers by means of logical reasoning.

Where is the hunt, and where is this female ascetic? Where is the carpenter Rājyadhara, skilled in machinery, on the shore of the ocean; and where was his crossing of the sea by means of her vehicle? And how could there have been a prior journey for him, the maker of celestial chariots, to the other side? Fate ordains such reflection upon the arrangement of auspicious means for the accomplishment of the welfare of the virtuous.
Thus, with their eyes trembling with wonder and joy, all of them spoke there with reverence, and they offered a hymn of praise for the lord’s devotion toward Gomukha.
And they praised Queen Ratnaprabhā, whose satisfaction was born from the dharma of devotion to her husband, and who protected the path prepared by her own supernatural knowledge for her lord.
Then Naravāhanadatta, his fatigue from traveling through the expanse of the sky dispelled, entered the capital together with his fathers, his wives, and the others.
There, having honored his kinsmen and friends who had come to him, Prāṇadhara filled both his father-in-law and the warder with wealth, as if his treasury were filled with heaps of gold.
And immediately after they had finished eating, Prāṇadhara, bowing low, informed him: "Your Majesty, King Karpūraka has indeed commanded us as follows:"
"You must come quickly once my daughter has reached her husband's home, so that I may know she has arrived here swiftly."
Therefore, O King, it is certain that we two must depart immediately; please cause Karpūrikā to give us a letter for the King written in her own hand.
For the heart of that king, tender with affection for his son, would not have consoled him otherwise; indeed, having ascended to a celestial palace, he would never fear a fall from it.
Now, having first granted him this principal edict together with me, permit this chief warder who is intent on setting out for his celestial chariot.
O Prince, I shall return here once more with my family; indeed, I shall not be able to abandon your two immortal lotus-feet.
When Prāṇadhara had spoken thus with great firmness, the son of Vatsarāja then and there appointed his bride Karpūrikā to write that letter.

"Father, you should not worry about me, for I dwell in the abode of happiness with a virtuous husband; for is Lakṣmī ever a cause for concern when she has taken refuge in the Supreme Person, the great ocean?"
And having honored Kṣattri and Prāṇadhara with those two letters written in her own hand and presented by Karpūrikā, the son of the Lord of Vatsa dismissed them.
Having ascended that celestial chariot, they traveled through the sky; watched with wonder by everyone, they crossed the ocean and went to the city of Karpūrasambhava.
Thereupon, having informed King Karpūraka that his daughter had reached her husband’s home by delivering the two letters, those two brought great joy to the lord of men.
On another day, having taken leave of that king along with his family, Prāṇadhara went to the side of Naravāhanadatta, who had been entrusted with the kingdom.
When he had arrived there and immediately accomplished his purpose, Naravāhanadatta granted him a dwelling near his own palace and a generous livelihood.
And wandering in celestial chariots provided for him, accompanied by his harem, he sported as if practicing for the future flight through the sky of a Vidyadhara universal emperor.
Thus, with his friends, kinsmen, and wives delighted, the son of the Lord of Vatsa spent those days in happiness, having obtained Ratnaprabhā, Madanamañcukā, and Karpūrikā as his third wife.
Thus ends the ninth wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And here concludes this *Ratnaprabhā* book. // Śrī //

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa; the eighth book, named Sūryaprabha. This nectar of stories, it is said, was churned from the ocean of Hara’s mouth by the Mandara mountain of the love for the Daughter of the Mountain-King (Pārvatī). Those who forcibly swallow it, having attained prosperity through the removal of obstacles, bear upon this earth the divine status of the gods by the grace of Bhava.

First Wave: Victorious is the elephant-faced god, who—even though it is not the proper time—creates a twilight as if with the sky reddened by the vermilion stirred up by the wind from his flapping ears.
Thus Naravāhanadatta, the son of the Lord of Vatsa, lived happily in Kauśāmbī at his father’s house, having obtained those wives.
Once, while he was seated in his father’s assembly hall, he saw a man of divine form who had descended from heaven and arrived there.
Having honored him as he bowed down along with his father, [the king] asked after a moment, "Who are you, and why have you come? whereupon he replied:
On the back of the Himalayas, there is here a city named Vajrakūṭa; because it is composed of the essence of diamond (vajrasāra), its name is known as being true to its meaning.
There, I was the lord of the Vidyādharas named Vajraprabha; because my body was fashioned from vajra, my name was likewise meaningful.
When you have been consecrated as a universal monarch at the proper time, you shall, through my grace, become invincible to your adversaries.
And when I was thus commanded by Śambhu, who was pleased with my ascetic penance, I have now come here for the purpose of paying homage to the Lord.
Naravāhanadatta, the son of Vatsarāja, born from a portion of Kāma, was created for us by the Moon-crested Lord for a divine kalpa.
"Even though he is a mortal, he will become a universal monarch over half of both Vidyādhara realms; this has indeed now been known by me through the power of my knowledge."
And it was said that in a former divine aeon, even though we were mortals, by the grace of Śarva, there was here a universal monarch named Sūryaprabha.
Nevertheless, he became the lord over one southern realm to be conquered, while at that time, the one named Śrutaśarman became the universal monarch over the northern realm.
Of those two, however, one will be a wheel-turning monarch among the sky-dwellers, remaining for a kalpa, a god indeed of exceeding merit.
When he had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta, together with the Lord of Vatsa, spoke again out of curiosity to that Vidyādhara.
"How was the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas obtained in former times by Sūryaprabha while he was still a human being? Let this be told to us by you."
Then, in a secluded place in the presence of the queens and ministers, King Vajraprabha began to relate that story.
In ancient times, there was a city named Śākala among the Madras; there lived a king named Candraprabha, the son of Aṅgāraprabha.

Though he was named Jvalanaprabha, which is meaningful as it signifies "one whose splendor blazes," he became one who brought delight to the entire world, yet he became a source of torment to his enemies.
To that king, by his queen named Kīrtimatī, was born a son whose future greatness was indicated by most auspicious marks.
This king named Sūryaprabha has been born, created by the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) as the future sovereign emperor of the Vidyādharas.
As he was born, these words resounded clearly from the sky—a rain of nectar for the ears of King Candraprabha.
Then, that prince Sūryaprabha grew up in his father’s house, abounding in the festive joy of the favor bestowed by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
And while still a child, that wise youth, having served his teachers, reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge and arts in due order.
Then his father, Candraprabha, consecrated him as the crown prince when he had reached his sixteenth year and had won over the subjects with his virtues.
He himself entrusted to him many of his own ministers' sons, such as Bhāsa, Prabhāsa, Siddhārtha, Prahasta, and others.
While he was bearing the burden of the office of crown prince together with them, a great asura named Maya once arrived there.
And when Sūryaprabha was seated, Maya approached King Candraprabha, who stood there, and having offered him hospitality, spoke thus to the monarch:
"O King, this Sūryaprabha, who is to be your son, has been created by the wielder of the trident as the future emperor of the Vidyādhara lords."
Why then does he not accomplish those rites that grant the attainment of that state? It is for this purpose that I have been dispatched here by Lord Śambhu.
"Grant me leave so that I may take him and teach him the ritual for accomplishing the vidyā, which is the cause for attaining the status of a Lord of the Vidyādharas."
For the lord of the sky-goers named Śrutaśarman exists as an obstacle to this undertaking; he too was created by Śakra.
But through the power of his perfected vidyā, he shall conquer him along with us and attain the status of a universal emperor over the lords of the Vidyādharas.
When Maya had spoken thus, King Candraprabha said, "We are blessed; this man is meritorious. Let him be led away as he desires."
Then, having taken leave of that king and quickly receiving his permission, Maya led Sūryaprabha along with his ministers down to Pātāla.
There he instructed him in such ascetic practices that the prince, together with his ministers, quickly mastered the sciences.
He likewise instructed him in the means for attaining a celestial chariot; by that, he acquired a celestial chariot named Bhūtāsana.
Maya brought Sūryaprabha, who had mastered the sciences and was accompanied by his wife, from Pātāla to his own city, having mounted him upon that celestial chariot.
Having brought him to his parents' side, he said to him: "I am departing; you should enjoy the fruits of your accomplishments here until I return again."
Having spoken thus, that Asura Maya departed after receiving honor; and King Candraprabha rejoiced at the successful attainment of the magic science by his son.
Then Sūryaprabha, by the power of his magic science, wandered at his pleasure with his ministers through various lands in a celestial chariot.
And wherever and whomever the princess saw, there and then she herself chose him, being infatuated by desire.
There was a daughter of the king of Tāmraliptī named Madanasenā, the son of one called Vīrabhaṭa, a maiden who was the most beautiful woman in the world.
The second was Candrikāvatī, the daughter of the king of Aparānta named Subhaṭa; she had been carried off by Siddhas from there and abandoned elsewhere.
The third daughter of the king named Kumbhīra, residing in the city of Kāñcī, was known as Varuṇasenā; she was renowned and possessed of great beauty.
The daughter of the king named Paurava, the sovereign of Lāvāṇaka, was Sulocanā by name, a fourth [princess] with beautiful eyes.
The fifth daughter, named Vidyunmālā, was born to King Suroha, the lord of the land of Cīna; her limbs were as radiant as gold and the color of a lion.
The daughter of King Kāntisena, the lord of the Śrīkaṇṭha region, named Kāntimatī, was the sixth [princess], who surpassed the celestial nymphs in beauty.
The seventh daughter of King Janamejaya, the lord of the city of Kauśāmbī, was named Parapuṣṭā, who possessed a charming voice.
And when their kinsmen learned that those women had been carried off without their knowledge, they behaved like reeds before him, who was arrogant due to the power of his magic science.
There, Sūryaprabha, having assumed multiple bodies created by his magic sciences, took pleasure simultaneously with those women who had likewise acquired their sciences.
Thus, together with those women and his ministers such as Prahasta, he sported in the sky through singing, drinking, social gatherings, and other diversions.
Skilled in the divine art of painting, he drew the wives of the Vidyādharas and, by uttering playful and sarcastic remarks, provoked his beloveds to anger.
And he took delight in their faces with their arched brows and reddened eyes, and in their words with syllables faltering from trembling lips.
Accompanied by his wife, that prince traveled to Tāmraliptī and, as a wanderer through the air, sported in the gardens together with Madanasenā.
Having left his beloved ones there, he traveled in a celestial chariot drawn by living beings to the city named Vajrasāra, accompanied solely by Prahasta as his friend.
There, while King Rambha looked on, he took the daughter of that king, named Tārāvalī, who was enamored with him and burning with the fire of love.
And he went again to Tāmraliptī, and there too he brought another princess, a maiden named Vilāsinī.
For that purpose, he paralyzed with his magic power the arrogant brother of that woman, named Sahasrāyudha, who had arrived in a state of rage.
Having subdued his maternal uncle, who had arrived as an ally along with his followers and was seeking to abduct her beloved, he caused him to have his head shaved.
Although he was angry, he did not speak ill of either his wife or his kinsmen; instead, laughing at them as they stood there embarrassed by the shattering of their pride, he replied:
Then Sūryaprabha, accompanied by his nine beloved wives and summoned by his father, departed for his own city of Śākala by means of a celestial chariot.
Then King Vīrabhaṭa dispatched a messenger from Tāmraliptī to his father, King Candraprabha.

And he sent this message: "Since my daughter has been carried off by your son, let it be so; for he is indeed a praiseworthy husband for those two, being one who has attained mastery over the sciences."
And if you have affection for us, then come here now, so that we may perform the wedding rites, the hospitality, and the friendship.
Having heard this, King Candraprabha then honored the messenger and quickly resolved to depart for that place the very next day.
Desiring to ascertain the certainty of the truth regarding King Vīrabhaṭa, he dispatched Prahasta, considering that the coming and going of messengers would take a long time.
Having gone swiftly, Prahasta saw Vīrabhaṭa and, upon seeing the king, was trusted and highly honored for that service.
Having told that man, who was filled with wonder, about the arrival of his masters in the morning, he returned through the air to the side of Candraprabha within a moment.
And he reported to the king that Vīrabhaṭa was standing ready; the king, being pleased with his minister for his son's sake, honored him in return.
Then the lord Candraprabha was with Queen Kīrtimatī, while Sūryaprabha was with Vilāsinī and likewise with Madanasenā.
Having ascended that celestial chariot made of living beings, the two of them, together with their retinue and ministers, departed from there the following morning.
In just one watch of the day, they reached Tāmraliptī, visible in the sky to the people who had raised their eyes in wonder.
Having descended from the surface of the sky, the two of them entered the city together with King Vīrabhaṭa, who had come out to meet them.
With its beautiful streets sprinkled at every step with sandalwood water, the city appeared as if strewn with blue lotuses by the side-long glances of the women of the citizens.
There, having performed the worship for the relatives and the son-in-law according to tradition, Vīrabhaṭa carried out the proceedings for his daughter’s marriage.
For Viśuddha carried a thousand loads of gold and a hundred camels laden with burdens of jeweled ornaments.
Five hundred camels laden with various loads of garments, seven thousand horses, and five elephants.
King Vīrabhaṭa bestowed upon his two daughters a thousand courtesans adorned with ornaments of gold and jewels at the sacrificial altar.
Furthermore, he honored both the son-in-law Sūryaprabha and his father with excellent jewels as well as with territories.
And his minister duly summoned Prahasta and the others; he then held a festival that caused all the people of the city to rejoice.
And Sūryaprabha was there with his father and accompanied by his beloved, enjoying at that time various pleasures such as food, drink, and song.
Just then, a messenger arrived there from Rambha’s presence via Vajrarātra, and he spoke his master’s words in the assembly hall.
"Our defeat, arising from the abduction of our daughter, was inflicted upon us by Prince Sūryaprabha, who is arrogant due to the power of his magic sciences."
And today we have learned that you have entered into an alliance with King Vīrabhaṭa, who shares our common calamity.
If you likewise agree to a treaty with us quickly, then come here; otherwise, there shall be no escape for us from death.
Having heard that and having honored the messenger, King Candraprabha, who was esteemed by Vīrabhaṭa, spoke again to Prahasta.
Go yourself to that Rambha and say these words on our behalf: "Why do you grieve in vain? For you have been ordained to become a universal monarch."
"Śiva has now declared to the Vidyādharas that this Sūryaprabha, as well as your daughter and the others, are his wives; so too have the Siddhas proclaimed."
Your son has reached that place; you, however, were not requested [to come]. Therefore, be pleased; you are our friend, and we shall all come there as well.
Having been thus given his message by the king, Prahasta traveled through the sky and reached Vajrarātra in just one watch.
Having delivered the message there to Rambha and being granted his approval by him, he returned and spoke it exactly as it was to King Candraprabha.
Then Candraprabha, having dispatched his minister Prabhāsa from Śākala, had Tārāvalī, the daughter of Rambha, brought to his side.
Then he departed by means of the celestial chariot, accompanied by King Sūryaprabha, as well as by Vīrabhaṭa and all the others who attended him with great devotion.
He reached Vajrarātra, which was crowded with people looking out for travelers on the road; welcomed by Rambha, he entered the royal capital.
There, Rambha also, having prepared the festival for the marriage ceremony, gave his daughter countless gold, elephants, horses, jewels, and other riches.
And he attended upon his son-in-law, Sūryaprabha, in such a manner that all of the latter's own enjoyments were forgotten.
And while they remained there happily, rejoicing in the festival, a messenger from the city of Kāñcī arrived at the presence of Rambhā.
Having received that message, Rambha said to King Candraprabha: "The King of Kāñcī has an elder brother named Kumbhīra."
Therefore, a trusted messenger has been sent by him today to deliver these words to me: "First my daughter was taken by Sūryaprabha, and then yours."
I have heard that you have already established friendship with them today; therefore, you should likewise establish friendship with them for me as well.
"May they come to my house until the light of the sun reaches it; here, with my own hand, I shall bestow my daughter Varuṇasenikā."
When Rambha spoke these words, "Let this request of his be granted," King Candraprabha then placed his trust in his speech.
And having quickly looked toward Prahasta, he had Varuṇasena brought from the city of Śākala into the presence of his father, Kumbhīra.
And on another day, Rambha, Sūryaprabha, Vīrabhaṭa, and all of them with their followers went to Kāñcī by means of a celestial chariot.
Emerging from the crocodiles, they entered that city of Kāñcī, which was inlaid with various jewels and, like a girdle, was strung together with virtues as it encircled the earth.
Having given his daughter to Sūryaprabha there according to the prescribed rites, Kumbhīra bestowed abundant wealth upon the bridegroom and the bride.
When the wedding had been completed and Candraprabha was seated in the pleasure that follows a meal, Prahasta spoke thus to him in the presence of everyone:
"O King, while wandering through the realm of Śrīkaṇṭha, I arrived there; having seen me by chance, King Kāntisena spoke to me."
"Let Sūryaprabha come to my house taking with him my abducted daughter Kāntimatī; I shall perform for him the rites of hospitality according to tradition."
"If I do not cast off my body, being deluded by affection for my daughter," he said; and at that point in the conversation, I spoke to him.
When Prahasta had spoken thus, King Candraprabha replied: "Go then, and bring Kāntimatī into his presence."
Then, having been told by that king, "Therefore, let us go there," Prahasta traveled through the sky at that very moment and did exactly as he was instructed.
And at dawn, all of them—Candraprabha and the others, together with Kumbhīra—went to the realm of Śrīkaṇṭha by means of a celestial chariot that travels through the sky.
Thereupon, King Kāntisena, having escorted his daughter to his own palace as the foremost of all, performed the auspicious marriage ceremony for her.
Then he gave to Kāntimatī and Sūryaprabha an immeasurable collection of jewels that caused wonder even among kings.
Then, while they were all standing there enjoying various pleasures, a messenger arrived from Kauśāmbī and spoke as follows.
King Janamejaya says this to you: "My daughter Parapuṣṭā has been carried off by someone not long ago."
It has been understood here that since she has come into the hand of Sūryaprabha, let him come to our house with her without any hesitation.
I shall send him off with due honor and according to the prescribed rites, together with his wife; otherwise, you are my enemies, and I am yours as well.
Having spoken these words of his master, the messenger became silent; then King Candraprabha spoke to them all in private.
"How is it understood that [the treasure] is in his house from such a statement made with pride? Having heard this, the minister named Siddhārtha spoke as follows:
"O King, you should not think otherwise; for he is indeed worthy to speak thus. For that king is a great donor, wise, and born of a noble lineage."
He was a hero, a performer of the horse sacrifice, and always unconquered by others; what indeed could he have said that was contradictory, since he spoke according to the facts?
Whether it was Śatrughna who spoke those words, or Vāsava himself, now you must go to his house; for that king is true to his promise.
"Let someone else also be sent to perceive his mind"—thus did they all place their trust in the words of Siddhārtha.
Then, wishing to investigate that Janamejaya, Candraprabha dispatched Prahasta and brought him back as a messenger.
And Prahasta, having gone there and made an agreement with that lord of Kauśāmbī, brought back his letter and satisfied Candraprabha.
That king also, having quickly dispatched Prahasta from Śākala, had that female cuckoo brought to the presence of Janamejaya.
Then those kings, Candraprabha and the others, led by Sūryaprabha and accompanied by Kāntisena, arrived at Kauśāmbī by means of a celestial chariot.
There, King Janamejaya honored his kinsmen and sons-in-law, who had come forward with humble prostrations and other marks of respect, by receiving them with a formal welcome and similar courtesies.
And having performed the auspicious rites for his daughter's marriage ceremony, he gave five thousand elephants and a hundred thousand choice horses.
He also gave five thousand camels laden with loads filled with jewels, gold, fine cloths, camphor, and agallochum.
And he held a great festival for the world, consisting entirely of music and dance, in which the most excellent brahmins were honored and all the kings were respected.
Meanwhile, the sky there unexpectedly turned a golden-brown, as if announcing its own imminent transformation into a deep crimson.
And suddenly the quarters of the sky became filled with tumultuous and confused noises, as if terrified upon seeing the enemy army approaching through the air.
And at that very moment, a great wind began to blow, as if lifting up the earth-dwellers to do battle with the sky-goers.
And in an instant, a great host of Vidyādharas was seen in the sky, illuminating the circle of the quarters with their brilliance, raising a loud roar, and possessing immense speed.
In the midst of them, Sūryaprabha and the others, filled with great wonder, beheld a single, exceedingly handsome young Vidyādhara.
Victorious is this Crown Prince Dāmodara, the son of Āṣāḍheśvara! O mortal who dwells upon the earth, Sūryaprabha, fall at his feet!
"O Janamejaya, bow down! Why have you given away your daughter in such an improper place? Propitiate this very god; he will not tolerate anything otherwise."
At that moment, from the sky, a Vidyādhara bard then spoke these words in a loud voice before that Dāmodara:
Having heard that and having seen his army, Sūryaprabha took up his sword and shield and flew into the sky with his own magic power out of anger.
And all his ministers followed him, bearing their weapons: Prahasta, Prabhāsa, Bhāsa, and Siddhārtha as well.
A great battle ensued between them and the Vidyādharas, involving Prajñāḍhya, Sarvadamana, Vītabhīti, and Śubhaṃkara.
And Sūryaprabha ran toward where Dāmodara was, striking down his enemies with his sword and parrying their weapons with his shield.
As for the number of those sky-dwellers, they were in the hundreds of thousands; fighting with one another, they met their end in equal measure.
And here the sword-blades, red with blood and falling upon the bodies of the heroes, appeared like the agitated glances of Kṛtānta.
And the Vidyādharas, as if seeking refuge out of fear upon the earth, fell before Candraprabha with their heads and their bodies.
Sūryaprabha shone with the splendor of a sky-dweller as seen by the world; the sky became as red as blood, as if strewn with vermilion.
And Sūryaprabha, having reached him, fought face-to-face with that Dāmodara, who was likewise equipped with sword and shield.
And fighting by means of the application of his skillful technique, he entered [the fray] and struck down the enemy to the ground, having shattered his shield with his sword.
And just as he desired to cut off his quivering head, Viṣṇu arrived through the sky and uttered the syllable "Huṃ."
Having heard that and beheld Hari, Sūryaprabha bowed with reverence for Him and then released Dāmodara from execution.
Taking that devotee who had been released from execution, Hari went somewhere; for the Blessed One protects his true devotee both in this world and the next.
And all those followers of Dāmodara departed here and there; Sūryaprabha also descended from the sky to his father’s side.
His father welcomed Candraprabha upon his safe return with his ministers, and other kings praised him, having witnessed his valor.
Then, while they all remained there delighted by that story, another messenger belonging to Subhaṭa arrived from that place.
And he presented the letter first to Candraprabha himself; having opened it, Siddhārtha read it aloud in the midst of the assembly as follows:

The illustrious King Candraprabha, a pearl-jewel upon his lofty lineage, was respectfully informed by Śrī Subhaṭa from Śrī Koṅkaṇa: "My daughter was carried away by some being during the night; it has now been understood that she has been recovered by your son, and for this we are well-pleased."

Therefore, you should make an effort here without hesitation to bring that Sūryaprabha, along with his son who is endowed with those qualities, to our house; so that we may behold our daughter as if she had returned from the other world, and we may now perform her marriage ceremony.
When the letter had been read thus, King Candraprabha honored the messenger with the words "So be it," and he rejoiced.
And having swiftly dispatched Prahasta to Aparānta, he had Candrikāvatī, the daughter of Subhaṭa, brought into the presence of Subhaṭa.
And in the morning, having placed Sūryaprabha at their head, they all departed by means of the celestial chariot toward the western region, accompanied by Janamejaya.
Thereupon King Subhaṭa, delighted by the birth of his daughter, honored them most highly and celebrated the festival of his daughter's marriage.
And he gave Candrikāvatī such jewels and other gifts that Vīrabhaṭa and the others were put to shame by what had been given to her.
Then, while Sūryaprabha remained there in his father-in-law’s house, a messenger related to the Paurava king arrived from Lāvāṇaka as well.
He too spoke these words of his master to Candraprabha: "My daughter Sulocanā has been carried off by the illustrious Sūryaprabha."
Therefore, I feel no distress at all regarding that; rather, let him be brought to my house by you, so that we may perform the customary rites.
Upon hearing this, King Candraprabha, having honored the messenger with joy, had Sulocanā brought by Prahasta to his father’s presence.
Then all of them, together with their warriors and accompanied by Sūryaprabha, went to Lāvāṇaka by means of a celestial chariot that arrives as soon as it is thought of.
There, having performed the marriage festival for Sūryaprabha and Sulocanā, that Paurava king, who had honored the assembly of monarchs, filled them with jewels.
While they were being thus attended to and remained in comfort there, Suroha, the lord of the Cīna people, dispatched a messenger.
That king also, like the others, made a request through the mouth of a messenger for their arrival at his palace along with the maiden who had been taken away.
Then King Candraprabha, being delighted, had his daughter Vidyunmālā brought to that palace by Prahasta.
And on another day, Candraprabha and all the others, together with Sūryaprabha and the citizens, departed by means of a celestial chariot for the land of Cīna.
Thereupon the king went out first, led them into his own fortress, and that King Surūha performed the marriage ceremony for his daughter.
And from him, he took for Vidyunmālā and for Sūryaprabha countless numbers of gold, elephants, horses, jewels, fine Chinese silks, and other such riches.
And there Candraprabha and all the others remained for some days, honored by Suroha with various enjoyments.
And there was Sūryaprabha, radiant with the full bloom of youth, who shone like the rainy season graced by a garland of lightning.
In this manner, Sūryaprabha enjoyed various pleasures here and there in his father-in-law’s house, accompanied by his beloveds and his kinsmen.
Then, having deliberated together with his ministers headed by Siddhārtha, he [prepared] those kings, Vīrabhaṭa and the others, along with their cavalry, in due order.
Having dismissed that King Suroha to his own lands, and having taken leave of him, he departed together with his father and mother, accompanied by his son and his followers.
Then, having ascended that celestial chariot which served as his seat, the virtuous Sūryaprabha traveled by way of the sky to his own city, Śālaka.

In that city, there was joy born of his arrival: in one place an attachment to dancing, in another a passion for music, in some places the sport of drinking, in others the act of adorning beautiful women, and in yet other places the sound of bards made resonant by the praise they had received as desired.

There, having summoned other women who were residing in their fathers' houses, he arrived together with them and the multitudes of elephants and horses given by their fathers; and displaying the wealth arising from his conquest of the quarters as a mere sport, with countless camels bowed down under loads filled with various jewels, he aroused the wonder of the subjects.
Inhabited by that man of great wealth, who possessed abundant riches and vast treasures, that city of Śākala shone as if it were fashioned from the cities of the gods, Kubera, and the serpents.

Then Sūryaprabha dwelt there together with Madanasenā, enjoying all desired pleasures and happy in the fullness of every prosperity; accompanied by his father, his ministers, and his other wives, he awaited day by day Maya, who had promised him a visit.

Thus ends the first wave in the Sūryaprabha-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave. Now, once while King Candraprabha was seated in his assembly hall and Sūryaprabha was present there accompanied by all his ministers—
While I was recollecting the story related by Siddhārtha, the earth suddenly split open right here in the midst of the assembly.
Then, from the opening in the earth, first a fragrant wind accompanied by sound appeared; after that, the demon Maya emerged.
With his dark, lofty head and his hair like blazing medicinal herbs, he was like a mountain at night with its red garments appearing as surging minerals.
And having been honored by King Candraprabha as was fitting, the lord of the Dānavas, seated upon a jeweled throne, spoke.
These earthly enjoyments have now been experienced by you; it is time for others, so apply your minds now to that endeavor.
"Send forth messengers and bring here our own kings, as well as our kinsmen and relatives; then we shall meet with Sumeru, the lord of the Vidyādharas."
"We shall conquer Śrutaśarman and attain the sovereignty of the sky-goers; and Sumeru stands here with us as an ally, regarding us as kinsmen."
"Protect Sūryaprabha and give your own daughter to him"—thus was he commanded at the very outset by the god who wields the Pināka bow.
When the asura Maya had spoken thus, Candraprabha dispatched Prahasta and the other sky-dwellers as messengers to all the kings.
And by the command of Maya, Sūryaprabha shared his magical sciences with all his wives and ministers—those who had not previously been so endowed.
While they were still standing there, the sage Nārada arrived, descending from the vault of the sky and illuminating the quarters of the horizon with his radiance.
Having accepted the guest-offering and sat down, he said to Candraprabha: "I have been sent here by Indra, and this was said to you by him:"
I have understood how you, the friends of the asura Maya, deluded by ignorance, acted against Sūryaprabha at the command of Maheśvara.
For this mortal body, it is desired to accomplish the great state of a universal monarch over all the lords of the Vidyādharas.
That which was given by us to Śrutaśarman is improper; for that [kingdom] belongs to him by hereditary succession, as he is the moon of the ocean of the Vidyādhara race.
Whatever you do in opposition to us and by obstructing the Dharma will certainly lead to your own destruction.
Previously, while you were performing a sacrifice to Rudra, I told you, "First perform the horse sacrifice," yet you did not do so.
Therefore, that which you have practiced out of arrogance, disregarding the gods and relying solely on the hope of Rudra, will not lead to your welfare.
When Śakra’s message had been thus spoken by Nārada, Maya laughed and said to him, "O great sage, what has been said by the Lord of the Gods is not well-spoken."
That which says Sūryaprabha is mortal is meaningless; for what did he not know of him during the battle with Dāmodara?
For mortals alone, being rich in spiritual essence, are entitled to all accomplishments; was not the position of Indra previously achieved by Nahuṣa and others?
And as for what he said—that the empire we gave to Śrutaśarman belongs to him by right of succession—that too is inconsistent.
Where Maheśvara is the giver [of authority], who has any authority over what? And how was the sovereignty of Indra, which had passed to Jyeṣṭha, taken away from Hiraṇyākṣa?
And whatever else he calls an adversary or unrighteousness is false; for it is he himself who forcibly makes us his adversary for his own sake.
And what unrighteousness could there be in our desire for victory? For we do not carry off the wife of a sage, nor do we commit the murder of a Brahmin.

As for his prattling about the non-performance of the horse sacrifice and his contempt for the gods—that is false; for once the sacrifice to Rudra has been established by others, what is the use of other rituals?
When Śambhu, the god of gods, is worshipped, what deity is not thereby worshipped? Furthermore, the claim that Rudra alone is the object of devotion and not Śiva—that too is false.
What need is there for other hosts of gods where Hara is prepared? When the sun has risen, do other lights shine forth?
O Sage, all of this must be told by you to the King of the Gods; as for us, we shall do what is required, and let him do whatever he knows to be right.
Thus addressed by the Asura Maya, the sage Nārada said, "So be it," and taking that message back, he went toward the Lord of the Gods.
When that sage had departed, the Asura Maya spoke thus to King Candraprabha there, who was filled with apprehension regarding Śakra’s message:
"You need have no fear of Śakra; he, along with the hosts of gods, will be on the side of Śrutaśarman in this battle out of hatred for us."
Therefore, O Great King, we are innumerable, presided over by Prahlāda; we stand firmly on your side, joined together with the Daityas and Dānavas.
When the Destroyer of Tripura has shown us favor and is exerting himself on our behalf, what other wretched being in the three worlds has any power?
When Maya had said, "Therefore, O heroes, exert yourselves in this task," they were all delighted and agreed, saying, "So be it."
Then, following the message delivered by the messenger, all those kings led by Vīrabhaṭa, as well as other friends and kinsmen, arrived there in succession.
When these kings, together with their armies, had performed the appropriate rites of hospitality, the Asura Maya spoke thus again to King Candraprabha:
"O King, perform today at night a great sacrifice to Rudra; then you shall carry out everything exactly as I shall instruct."
Having heard these words of Māyā, King Candraprabha then immediately had the preparations for Bali made for Rudra.
Then, having gone to the forest at night with me as his ritual instructor, Candraprabha himself performed an offering to Rudra with devotion.
And while that king was engaged in the sacrificial rite, Nandi, the lord of the hosts of spirits, appeared there visibly and without hesitation.
Having been honored according to the prescribed rites by the delighted king, he spoke this: "This was commanded by Lord Śambhu himself through my mouth."
"By my grace, let there be no fear for you even from hundreds of Śakras; Sūryaprabha shall surely become the universal monarch of the sky-dwellers."
Having received such instructions from Śaṅkara and having accepted his portion of the sacrificial offering, Nandīśvara vanished there along with the hosts of spirits.
Then Candraprabha, having gained confidence regarding the birth of his son, completed the sacrificial offering at the conclusion of the *homa* and, observing the proper time, entered the city.
And in the morning, when King Candraprabha was alone with the queen, his son, the kings, and his ministers, Maya addressed him.
Listen, O King, I shall tell you today a secret long preserved: you are the mighty Dānava named Sunītha, my own son.
Sūryaprabha and your younger brother, known as Sumuṇḍīka, were both slain in the battle of the gods; now you two have been born here as father and son.
Having preserved that body of the Dānava, I have kept it by skillfully anointing it with divine herbs and clarified butter.
Therefore, having entered the opening and reached the netherworld (pātāla), enter your own body by means of the method I have instructed you.
And having entered that body, you shall become superior in splendor, heroism, and strength, such that you will conquer the sky-dwellers in battle.
But Sūryaprabha, with this very same beautiful body, shall before long become this Sumuṇḍīka, the lord of the sky-goers.
Having heard this from the asura Maya, King Candraprabha joyfully accepted it, saying "So be it," while Siddhārtha, his purpose accomplished, spoke as follows:
"O best of Dānavas, when we were deluded, thinking, 'Has he entered another body, or has he met his death?', what stability could there have been for us?"
Furthermore, when he has entered another body and gone to the next world, he forgets us; just as that is so for him, then who is he and who are we?
Having heard this from Siddhārtha, the asura Maya said: "By means of yogic power, enter this [being] into that body."
Come of your own accord and behold it there directly; he does not forget you in this way—listen to the reason why.
One who dies without independence is not born elsewhere in a womb; being obscured by those afflictions such as death and so forth, he does not remember anything.
But by means of yoga, one who enters another body independently, having entered the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), may also enter the sense organs.
With his mind and intellect undisturbed, that wise master of yoga suddenly remembers everything, just as one moves from one house to another.
Therefore, let there be no doubt in you; on the contrary, this king shall attain a great divine body, free from old age and disease.
And all you Dānavas, having entered Rasātala, shall become possessed of healthy, divine bodies through the drinking of the nectar.
Having heard these words of Maya the Asura, they all said, "So be it," and with their doubts abandoned through that conviction, they accepted his proposal.
And on the following day, at his word, Candraprabha—having assembled the entire circle of kings—went to the confluence of the Candrabhāgā and the Airāvatī.
Having stationed the kings there and cast them outside among those [guards], Sūryaprabha approached the harem shown to him by Maya.
Candraprabha entered the opening in the water together with Sūryaprabha, along with the queen and his ministers, Siddhārtha and the others.
Having entered and traveled a long distance along that path, he beheld a divine temple and entered it together with all of them.
And at that moment, the kings who were stationed there outside the opening were attacked from the sky by the Vidyādharas together with their armies.
Having paralyzed them with their magical powers, they carried off those wives of Sūryaprabha; and at that very moment, a voice arose from the sky:
"O wicked Śrutaśarman! If you touch these wives of the universal monarchs, then immediately, along with your army, you shall meet your death."
Therefore, looking upon them with reverence as you would your own mother, you must protect them; for it was precisely because I did not kill you this very moment that they were released by me.
"There is a certain reason for this; let that matter rest for now. When this was said by a divine voice, those sky-dwellers vanished from sight.
Having seen those queens led away, Vīrabhaṭa and the others drew near, making an effort to give up their lives through mutual combat.
There is no destruction for these women; you shall regain these daughters again. Therefore, you must not commit such a rash act. May it be well with you.
Thus a celestial voice restrained them from that undertaking; thereafter, those kings remained right there, waiting.
In the meantime, Maya spoke thus to Candraprabha, who was staying in that temple in Pātāla surrounded by all those [beings]:
O King, becoming single-minded, listen now to this unsurpassed [teaching]; I shall instruct you in the yoga that grants entry into another body.
Having spoken thus and having explained both Sāṃkhya and Yoga along with their secret doctrines, he taught him the method for entering another body.
And that lord of yogis said: "This is that very perfection, and this is that knowledge—the sovereignty of absolute freedom, the abode of the powers such as *aṇimā*."
Established in this sovereignty, the lords of the gods do not desire liberation; for this very purpose, others as well undergo the hardships of recitation and austerity.
Noble-minded men do not desire even the enjoyment of heaven when it has been attained; and in this regard, listen as I tell you a story.
In a former age, there was a certain great brahmin named Kāla; having gone to the sacred site of Puṣkara, he performed silent recitation day and night.
As he was reciting, two hundred divine years passed there; then, a great, unbroken flame appeared from his head.
By him, as he rose into the sky like ten thousand suns, the movement of the *siddhas* and others was obstructed, and the three worlds blazed forth.
"O Brahmin, choose whatever boon you desire; these worlds are blazing with your radiance," said Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, approaching him.
"May I have no delight in anything other than japa; this alone is my boon, and I choose nothing else"—thus he replied to them.
While they persisted in their pursuit, that practitioner of recitation went even further away and remained on the northern side of the Himalayas, engaged in silent prayer.
When that splendor of his became increasingly unbearable even there, Indra then dispatched celestial nymphs to create obstacles for him.
That steadfast one did not regard those seductive women as even a blade of grass; thereupon, the gods dispatched Death to him with full authority.
Approaching him, he said: "O Brahmin, mortals do not live for such a long time; therefore, abandon yourself and do not transgress the established order."
Hearing that, the brahmin said: "If my limit for life is full, then why do you not lead me away? Why do you wait?"
And I myself, O wielder of the noose, would not abandon my own self; for by casting off this body out of desire, I would become a suicide.
When death was unable to lead him away despite his power because he had spoken thus, death turned its face away and departed as it had come.

Then, at that very moment when he had been defeated, Indra seized the twice-born man—who was still possessed of latent defilements—by his two arms with force and carried him off to the abode of the gods.
There, turning away from those enjoyments and never ceasing his recitation, he was brought down by the god and returned once more to that very Himālaya.
While Indra and the other gods were there, repeatedly awakening him for the sake of a boon, King Ikṣvāku arrived by that same path.
Having understood that according to the facts, he spoke to that reciter: "O sir, if you do not accept a boon from the gods, then receive one from me."
Having heard that, the reciter laughed and addressed the king: "You are capable of granting me a boon, even if it were taken from the gods themselves."
To that brahmin who had spoken thus, Ikṣvāku replied: "I am not capable of giving to you; you are capable of giving to me. Therefore, grant me this boon."
Then that reciter said, "Choose whatever you desire; I shall surely grant it. Hearing this, the king reflected within himself.
"It is the proper rule that 'I give' and 'this Brahmin receives'; yet this is the reverse, since I am receiving while he gives."
While the king was thus delaying in doubt, two Brahmins arrived there, engaged in a dispute.
Seeing the king, they spoke before him for the sake of justice; one said, "A cow was given to me by this man, along with a sacrificial fee."
"Does he not take that from my hand as I am giving it back? Then another replied, "I have not previously accepted it."
"And yet I have no desire for it; why then does he force it upon me? Having heard this, the king said, "This accuser is not cleared."
To that king who had said, "Having accepted [the cow], how can I give it back by force to the donor?", Śakra, having found an opportunity, replied:
O King, if you know this to be right, why do you not accept from that twice-born reciter the excellent gift he has obtained by making his request?
Then King Niruttara said to that reciter: "O Blessed One, grant me as a boon half of the fruit of your own recitation."
"Very well; let half of the fruit of my recitation belong to you. Thus did that reciter then grant a boon to the king.
By that [merit], both the king and the reciter attained the state of all the worlds; and he who was called Śiva reached the world of the gods.
Having remained there for many eons, he returned once more to the surface of the earth; having attained independence through yoga, he obtained eternal perfection.
Thus, by the wise who are averse to heaven and such things, only spiritual perfection is sought; that has been attained by you, O King, as one who is independent—therefore, enter your own body.
Having been addressed thus with these words of counsel by Maya, King Candraprabha, together with his wife, son, and ministers, then rejoiced greatly.
Then, having led him to the second underworld, that Māyā caused the king, together with his sons and others, to enter a celestial palace.
And there, in the midst of it, they all beheld a single great man lying fallen upon an excellent bed, as if asleep.
Anointed with great medicinal ghee, terrifying with his deformed appearance, and surrounded by the daughters of the Daitya king whose lotus-faces were downcast.
"Therefore, this very body of yours stands here occupied by your former wife; enter it," Maya then said to Candraprabha.
Then, having undertaken that yoga taught by him, the king entered within that human body, casting off his own physical form.
Then, having yawned and slowly opened his eyes, that man rose from his bed like one whose sleep had departed.
"By good fortune, our lord Sunītha has today been restored to life!"—thus arose a cry there, uttered by the joyful wives of the asuras.
But Sūryaprabha and all the others suddenly became despondent upon seeing the body of Candraprabha fallen and lifeless.
And Candraprabhasunītha, as if rising from a pleasant sleep, saw Maya and prostrated at his father's feet in salutation.
The father also embraced him and asked in the presence of everyone: "My son, do you now remember both of your births?"
Having said, "I too remember," he related what had occurred during his birth as Candraprabha and during his birth as Sunītha.
Calling them by name, he comforted each one individually—the goddesses headed by Sūryaprabhā, as well as his former wives who were daughters of the Dānavas.
