Thinking that his body, produced during his birth as Candraprabha, might one day prove useful through the strategy of a dual kingship, he preserved it and established it in safety.
Then Sūryaprabha and the others, having bowed down and feeling reassured by their newly born confidence, joyfully praised that noble Candraprabha.
Then the asura Maya, having led all those delighted ones out from that city, caused them to enter another city adorned with gold and jewels.
Having entered there, they beheld a pool of lapis lazuli filled with the essence of nectar, and they all sat down upon its bank.
And there, they drank that nectar-like beverage, which surpassed even the ambrosia of the gods, from various jeweled vessels presented by the wife of Sunītha.
Then, having arisen from their intoxicated sleep due to that drink, they all attained divine bodies endowed with great strength and prowess.
Then the asura Maya spoke to Candraprabha, the son of Sunīthā: "Come, my son, let us go and see your mother after a very long time."
Then, saying "So be it," Sunītha prepared himself and, with Maya leading the way, went to the fourth underworld along with Sūryaprabha and the others.
Beholding there various cities composed of many different elements, they all reached a single city that was entirely made of gold.
There, in that palace made of jewels and the abode of every prosperity, they beheld the wife of Maya, the mother of Sunītha.
Named Līlāvatī, she surpassed the celestial nymphs in beauty; she was surrounded by the daughters of the asuras and adorned with every ornament.
Upon seeing Sunītha, she rose up in great agitation; Sunītha, for his part, fell at her feet in salutation.
Then, having embraced her son—who had not been touched for so long—she wept; and she praised her husband Maya as the cause of that reunion.
Then Mayā said, "O Queen, Sumuṇḍika was another son of yours; this Sūryaprabha has been born as the son of that very son."
"O Goddess, this one has been ordained by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) to become the universal emperor of the Vidyādhara lords, even in this very body."
Upon hearing this, as she gazed at him with eyes full of longing, Sūryaprabha approached and fell at her feet along with his ministers.
"What is the use of this shaven-headed body, my child? You shine with this very [appearance]," Līlāvatī said to him after bestowing her blessing.
Then, on this occasion of his son’s triumph, Maya called to mind his daughter Mandodarī and Vibhīṣaṇa; and as soon as they were remembered, the two of them arrived.
Having accepted the festive honors, Vibhīṣaṇa said to him: "O Lord of Dānavas, if you will follow my word, then I shall speak it."
Among the Dānavas, you alone are a doer of good deeds and one whose life is auspicious; therefore, you should not harbor causeless enmity toward the gods.
For when there is opposition between them, no advantage exists for you except through destruction; indeed, in battles, the Asuras were slain by the gods, and the gods were not slain by the Asuras.
Having heard that, Maya said to him: "We do not act by force; but tell me, how can we endure it if Śakra acts by compulsion?"
Those asuras who were slain by the gods were negligent; but why were Bali and the others not slain, since they were vigilant?
Having been addressed with these and other words by Maya, the lord of the rākṣasas then took leave of him and, together with Mandodarī, went to his own abode.
Then Sunītha, accompanied by Sūryaprabha and the others, was led by Maya to the third underworld to see King Bali.
There, they all beheld Bali, who was even superior to heaven itself, wearing a necklace and a crown, and surrounded by the sons of Diti and the Dānavas.
Sunītha and the others fell at his feet one after another; he too honored them with hospitality as was appropriate.
Delighted by the account related by me, Bali then quickly summoned Prahlāda and the other Dānavas to that place.
There, Sunītha and the others also bowed at his feet; and he, filled with joy, greeted them as they stood humbly before him.
Then Bali said: "Having become Candraprabha on earth, this Sunītha has been restored to life for us by the recovery of his own body."
Sumuṇḍīkāvatāra has been attained by this Sūryaprabha as well, and he has been commanded by Śarva that he shall become the lord of the Vidyādharas.
And by the power of this sacrifice, I have been born with my bonds loosened; therefore, since these two have been obtained, our prosperity is certain.
Having heard these words of Bali, his preceptor Śukra said: "For those who act according to dharma and abide in truth, there is no lack of prosperity anywhere."
"Therefore, conduct yourselves according to righteousness and follow my word even now. Having heard that, the Dānavas there established a rule, saying, "So be it."
Then the lords of the seven netherworlds who had assembled there, as well as Bali, celebrated a festival out of joy at the recovery of Sunītha.
In the meantime, the sage Nārada arrived there once more; having accepted the guest-offering and sat down, he spoke to those Dānavas.
"I have been sent here by Indra, and he says this to you: 'My supreme satisfaction comes from the recovery of Sunītha's life.'"
Therefore, we must no longer engage in this groundless enmity; nor should Śrutaśarman, who is on our side, be opposed by us.
When Indra had spoken these words, Prahlāda said to the sage: "What else could it be but that Indra finds satisfaction in the life of Sunītha?"
Furthermore, we do not engage in causeless hostility; for this very day, a rule was established by all of us in the presence of our teacher.
If Śrutaśarman, relying on his allies, acts in opposition to us by force, what blame can we incur for that?
Indeed, this was previously commanded by Śambhu, the God of gods, acting on the side of Sūryaprabha, because he had been worshipped by him in the past.
Therefore, what can we do regarding this task ordained by the Lord? Śakra speaks this without cause and improperly.
Thus addressed by Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, the sage Nārada said, "So be it," and while censuring Vāsava, he vanished from sight.
When he had departed, Uśanas addressed those lords of the Dānavas: "In this matter, a persistent enmity toward Indra is clearly observed."
But while Maheśvara has bound his girdle solely to show favor toward us, what power does he have, or what could his Vaiṣṇava resolve accomplish?
Having heard these words of Śukra and having given their assent, those Dānavas took leave of Bali along with Prahlāda and departed for their own abodes.
Then, after Prahlāda had returned to his own abode in the fourth underworld, King Bali rose from the assembly hall and entered the inner apartments.
Maya, Sunītha, and all the others, including Sūryaprabha and his companions, bowed to Bali and returned to their own respective abodes.
Then, after they had partaken of food and drink as was fitting, Līlāvatī’s own mother approached Sunītha and said to him:
"Son, you know that these wives of yours are the daughters of great beings: Tejasvatī is the daughter of Dhaneśa, and Maṅgalāvatī is the daughter of Tumburu."
And she who was married by you with the body of Candraprabha— the daughter of Prabhāsa Vasu, Kīrtimatī— do you recognize her?
"O son, these three must be regarded by you with an equal eye"; having said this, she handed those three principal wives over to him.
Then, on that night, Sunītha entered the bedchamber together with his elder wife, Tejasvatī.
There he enjoyed with her, who had long been filled with longing, various pleasures of amorous play—pleasures that, though experienced before, seemed ever new.
But Sūryaprabha, together with his ministers, sat that night on a bed in another chamber, without his wife.
"Of what use is this [man] who is devoid of affection and abandons his own beloveds? Thinking thus, as it were, sleep—the woman—did not come even to him, though he was alone and constant.
And Prahasta, who was solely intent on considering his duties as if out of envy [for their ease], while the others around Sūryaprabha fell into a pleasant sleep.
Meanwhile, Sūryaprabha and Prahasta beheld there that peerless maiden, the daughter of a noble family, as she was entering accompanied by her female companions.
"Lest the creation of celestial nymphs appear lusterless before her," so saying, the Creator, as if having produced her, established her in the netherworld.
And while Sūryaprabha was reflecting, "Who might this woman be?", she approached his sleeping companions and gazed at each one of them individually.
Leaving those who lacked the marks of a universal monarch, she saw Sūryaprabha, endowed with those very characteristics, lying in their midst, and approached him.
And he said to his friend: "Friend, touch his feet; awaken him with these two hands, cool with water."
Having heard this, her friend did exactly as she was told; and Sūryaprabha, leaving his feigned sleep, opened his eyes.
Having observed them, he said, "O maidens, who are you two, and why have you come here? Hearing this from him, her friend spoke to him.
Listen, O God: in the second Pātāla there is a victorious sovereign, the powerful lord of Daityas named Amīla, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa.
"This daughter of his, Kalāvatī, is dearer to him than even his own life-breaths; her father has come here today from the presence of Bali and said this:"
"By good fortune, Sunītha has regained his life today and is seen again; and the youth Sūryaprabha, the incarnation of Sumuṇḍīka, has been beheld."
"He who was created by Hara as the future sovereign of the circle of sky-dwellers—therefore, I shall here bestow honor and joy upon Sunītha."
"I shall give this daughter Kalāvatī to Sūryaprabha; however, because she belongs to the same lineage as Sunītha, it is not proper for me to give her to him."
And Sūryaprabha is his son born as a king rather than an Asura; by honoring his son, honor has been shown to him.
Having heard these words of her father, this friend of mine, her mind drawn by your virtues, has come here out of curiosity to behold you.
When she had spoken thus, Sūryaprabha then feigned sleep, while his friend pretended to sleep as well, in order to ascertain the intent behind her words.
Then that maiden, having gone quietly to the side of the sleepless Prahasta and spoken everything to him through the mouth of her friend, went outside.
And Prahasta, having approached, said to Sūryaprabha, "O Lord, are you awake or not? and he, opening his eyes, replied to him:
"Friend, I am awake; for how could there be sleep for me today while I am alone? I shall indeed tell you the specific reason; listen, for what is there to hide from you?"
Just now, upon entering here, I saw a certain maiden accompanied by her friends, whose equal is not to be seen even in the three worlds.
In an instant she has gone somewhere, having truly stolen my heart; therefore, search for her immediately, as she must be staying somewhere right here.
Having been addressed thus by Sūryaprabha, Prahasta then went outside; seeing the maiden standing there with her friend, he spoke to her.
At your request, I have awakened this master of mine; therefore, at my request, grant him your audience once again.
Behold his form once more, which brings fulfillment to the eyes; let him too behold you, for he is captivated by the mere sight of you.
"For once he has awakened, he said to me, 'After telling your story, bring her to me from wherever she may be; otherwise, I shall not live.'"
"Therefore I have come to you; so come, look for yourself. Thus addressed by Prahasta, she, with the modesty natural to a maiden, [replied].
When she was unable to go on by force and began to reflect, he then took her by the hand and led her into the presence of Sūryaprabha.
And Sūryaprabha, seeing Kalāvatī approaching his side, said: "O fierce lady, what is this that you have done here today against me?"
"Having entered by stealth while you were asleep, you have stolen my heart; therefore, O thief, I shall not release you here until you have been caught."
Having heard this, that clever friend said to him: "Her father already knew of this beforehand, and he has sent her as a thief for the purpose of capturing you."
Since you have resolved to hand her over, who then is your restrainer? Why do you not simply inflict upon her the punishment appropriate for a thief?
Hearing that, as Sūryaprabha desired to embrace her, Kalāvatī, feeling ashamed, said, "O noble son, do not! I am a maiden."
Then Prahasta said to her: "O Queen, let there be no hesitation on your part; for this Gāndharva rite is indeed the best among all forms of marriage here."
As soon as he had spoken thus, Prahasta went outside along with all of them; at that very moment, Sūryaprabha took Kalāvatī as his wife.
And together with that daughter of Pātāla, he enjoyed the delights of sexual union, difficult for mortals to attain, a meeting so new as to be inconceivable.
And at the end of the night, when Kalāvatī had gone to her own dwelling, Sūryaprabha went to the side of Sunītha and Maya.
Then they all gathered together and went into the presence of Prahlāda; having honored them according to their rank while seated in his assembly hall, he spoke to Maya.
"At this festival of Sunītha, we must certainly do what is pleasing to him; therefore, let us all eat together in one place for as long as today lasts."
When Maya said, "We shall do so; what fault is there in this?", Prahlāda then invited the lords of the asuras there through messengers.
And they all arrived there from all the netherworlds in succession; first came King Bali, accompanied by countless great asuras.
Anantaramāmila, Durāroha, the valiant Vīryavān, Sumāya, Tantukaccha, Vikaṭākṣa, and Prakampana.
Dhūmaketu, the great illusionist, and those other lords of the asuras each arrived surrounded by a thousand of their own vassals.
The assembly was filled by them as they exchanged mutual salutations; and once they were seated in due order, Prahlāda honored them.
And when the time for food arrived, they all, together with Maya and the others, having bathed in the Ganges, came to the great assembly hall for their meal.
It was a hundred yojanas in extent, with floors inlaid with gold and jewels, adorned with pillars of precious gems, and set with various vessels of wonderful jewels.
There, those asuras, together with Prahlāda, Sunītha, and Maya, were accompanied by Sūryaprabha and his ministers.
Together with the asuras,
they enjoyed various kinds of divine food— consisting of edibles, masticables, linctuses, and so forth, possessing the six flavors— and they drank the most excellent drink.
Having eaten and drunk, they all went to another assembly hall made of jewels and beheld the exquisite dance of the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas.
In that context, Sūryaprabha saw there the daughter of Prahlāda, named Mahallikā, who was dancing by her father's command.
Illuminating the quarters with her splendor and raining nectar into the eyes, she was like the very form of the moon descended to the underworld out of curiosity.
Adorned with a tilaka on her forehead and beautiful anklets upon her feet, she possessed a smiling gaze, appearing as if created by the Creator himself as the very embodiment of dance.
With her curling locks and pointed teeth, and bearing breasts that formed circles upon her chest, she seemed to be performing a brand-new dance.
And as soon as Caṇḍī saw Sūryaprabha, she forcibly stole his heart, even though it had already been claimed by others.
Then she too, from afar in the midst of the lords of the Asuras, beheld him like another Smara created by the Creator after the original Smara had been consumed by Hara.
Upon seeing him, her mind became fixed upon him so that she remained motionless; even her physical gestures were like those of one who, having seen his immodesty, stands still in anger.
Those present in the assembly perceived that state of mind belonging to both of them; and they concluded their gazing, saying, "The prince is weary."
Then, casting a sidelong glance at Sūryaprabha, Mahallikā, having been dismissed by her father, paid homage to the lords of the Dānavas and went home.
And all those lords of the Dānavas went to their respective homes; Sūryaprabha also returned to his own residence at the close of day.
And at nightfall, having slept secretly within with Kalāvatī who had returned, he remained outside while all his followers slept.
Meanwhile, that old woman, eager to see him, arrived there accompanied by two confident female companions.
A minister of Sūryaprabha named Prajñāḍhya, who had at that moment been abandoned by sleep, saw her as she was wishing to enter within.
"O Queen, stay for a moment until I have entered within and come back out"; having recognized her, he rose and said:
When she asked him with apprehension, "We are besieged; why are you outside, and who are you?", Prajñāḍhya spoke to her once again.
"Why have you entered so suddenly into the presence of one who is sleeping at his own ease? Moreover, this master of ours is alone because of his vow."
Then, having been told by that daughter of the Daitya Prahlāda, who was filled with bashfulness, "Enter through her," Prajñāḍhya entered within.
Seeing Kalāvatī asleep, he woke Sūryaprabha and told him privately that Mahallikā had arrived.
And Sūryaprabha, having understood this, rose slowly and went out; seeing Mahallikā and his two companions, he spoke to them as well.
This guest has already been brought to the fulfillment of his purpose; let him also be led to his place, and let this seat be accepted.
Having heard that, Mahallikā then sat down together with the other two; Sūryaprabha also sat down there, accompanied by Prajñāḍhya.
Having sat down, he said: "O slender one, even though you showed me contempt while I was in the assembly, seeing me later, you have grown [in beauty]."
Nevertheless, O fickle-eyed one, by the mere sight of you, my two eyes have been made fruitful by your dance, as it were, through your beauty.
Thus addressed by Sūryaprabha, that daughter of Prahlāda replied: "O noble son, this is not my fault; he is the one who is at fault here."
"By whom I was made to feel humiliated in the assembly, with my dramatic performance shattered"—hearing this, Sūryaprabha laughed and said, "I am conquered."
Then that prince took her hand with his own, as if she were trembling and perspiring from the fear of being seized by force.
To her, who was saying, "O noble son, release me; I am a maiden under the power of my father," that Prajñāḍhya then spoke to the daughter of the lord of the asuras.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the Gāndharva form of marriage exists for maidens; and your father, having perceived your intention, will not give you to anyone else.
And he will certainly show him honor here; therefore, enough with this anxiety—let such a meeting not be in vain.
While Mahallikā and all the others, up to Prajñāḍhya, were speaking with her in this manner, Kalāvatī woke up inside there.
Not seeing Sūryaprabha on his bed, she waited for a moment, and then, becoming anxious and apprehensive, she went outside.
Seeing her own beloved there accompanied by the old woman, she became filled with anger, shame, and fear.
Upon merely seeing her, the old woman was struck with fear and shame, while Sūryaprabha stood motionless as if he were a painted figure.
"How can I flee once I have been seen? If I were to feel shame or envy," she thought; and so Kalāvatī then went right up to her side.
"Good fortune, my friend! Where have you come from here at such a late hour of the night? she said to that elderly woman with a touch of jealousy.
Then the old woman said: "This house is mine; you have arrived here today as a guest from another subterranean dwelling."
Having heard that, Kalāvatī laughed and said this to her: "This is indeed seen to be true, that you [are the object] of everyone."
"You perform the hospitable reception for a guest who has just arrived. When Kalāvatī had spoken thus, Mahallikā replied:
If you were addressed by me with affection, why then do you speak such hateful and harsh words, O shameless one? Am I like you?
Was I not given away by my kinsmen, yet having come from afar to another land, I lay alone at night upon the bed of a stranger in secret?
"I have come to my father's quarters to see him as a guest; she has just now arrived with her two friends to offer me hospitality."
When that minister first entered after deceiving us, it was at that very moment that I understood this, which you have now made clear by yourself.
Thus addressed by Mahallikā, Kalāvatī departed from there, glancing askance at her beloved with eyes clouded by anger.
Then that old woman, who had many lovers, said to Sūryaprabha in anger, "I am going now," and departed from there.
And Sūryaprabha was despondent; for it was only natural that his mind had become so attached at that time, being occupied entirely with his two beloveds.
Then, in order to learn of Kalāvatī’s conduct during their quarrel, he quickly raised up his minister Prabhāsa and dispatched him.
In the same manner as for Mahallikā, he dispatched Prahasta; and he himself remained there, joined by Prajñāḍhya, awaiting him.
Then, having investigated Kalāvatī’s actions, Prabhāsa returned to his presence; when questioned, he spoke to him thus.
From here, concealing my true form by means of my own magic power, I went to the dwelling of Kalāvatī, which is situated in the second underworld.
There outside, I also heard the conversation of two female servants; one said, "Friend, why is Kalāvatī so distressed today?"
Then the second one also said: "Friend, hear the reason for this: today, in the fourth underworld, there is indeed the descent of Sumuṇḍīka."
There was one named Sūryaprabha, who surpassed the god of love in beauty; it is said that she went to him in secret and gave herself to him.
When she had gone today to his presence at the arrival of night, Mahallikā, the daughter of Prahlāda, also came there in person.
Having engaged in a quarrel with her out of jealousy, she was about to commit suicide when she was seen and protected by her sister, who was intent on [sending her] to Sukhāvatī.
Then, having entered within and fallen upon the bed, she remained there with her sister, who was distressed by the account of what had occurred.
Having heard this conversation of the two maidservants, I entered there and likewise beheld Kalāvatī and Sukhāvatī, who were identical in appearance.
While Prabhāsa was thus speaking to Sūryaprabha in private, Prahasta also arrived there; being questioned, he too spoke as follows.
By the time I had gone as far as the old woman’s dwelling, she had entered there with her two female companions, looking dejected.
And there, having entered invisibly by means of the power of my magic science, I saw her twelve companions, who were equal to her in every respect.
Having surrounded that Mahallikā, who was seated upon a couch of excellent jewels, they sat down near her, and then one among them spoke to her.
"Friend, why do you appear so suddenly distressed today? Even though the wedding is at hand, alas, what is this despondency of yours?"
Hearing that, she, filled with reflection, said to that daughter of Prahlāda: "What is this marriage of mine? To whom have I been given? By whom was this told to you?"
When she had spoken thus, they all said with certainty: "Friend, your marriage is settled; tomorrow morning you shall be given to Sūryaprabha."
And today, in your absence, this was said by your mother, the Queen, as she appointed us to the task of preparing your festive decorations.
Therefore, you are truly blessed, for Sūryaprabha shall be your husband; it is because he is captivated by your beauty that the women here do not sleep at night.
But for us there is this despair: "Where are you now, and where are we? For when that husband has arrived, you will forget us."
Having heard this from their mouths, Mahallikā said: "Have you seen him? And has your mind gone out toward him?"
Having heard that, they said to her: "He was seen by us from the palace; who is that woman whose mind he would not captivate even when not seen?"
Then she also said, "In that case, father, I shall speak to him in such a way that I will cause him to give all these things to you as well."
"In this way, there shall be no mutual separation for us through our living together"—as they spoke thus, those maidens replied in agitation.
"Friend, do not do this; it is not proper, for this would bring us shame. To those who had spoken thus, the daughter of the Asura lord replied:
What is improper? For he alone shall not marry me; indeed, all the Daityas and Dānavas will give their daughters to him.
Furthermore, other princesses already married by him remain on earth, and he will also marry many daughters of the Vidyādharas.
Among you who have been married, what loss is there for me? On the contrary, we shall dwell happily together as friends with one another.
But what intimacy can I have with those others who are opposed? What shame is there for you in this? I shall do all of this myself.
While their conversation, in which their souls were entirely fixed upon you, was thus proceeding, I departed from there and came to your side of my own accord.
Having heard this from the mouth of Prahasta, Sūryaprabha spent that night with joy on his bed, without even falling asleep.
In the morning, together with Sunītha, Maya, and his ministers, he went to the assembly hall of Prahlāda, the lord of the Asuras, to see him.
There Prahlāda, showing great respect, said to Sunītha: "I give my daughter Mahallikā to this Sūryaprabha."
"For this guest-hospitality must be performed by me, which will be pleasing to both you and him. Sunītha rejoiced at these words of Prahlāda.
Then, having ascended the altar where the fire blazed in its center, which was illuminated by lofty jeweled pillars shining with its radiance;
Prahlāda gave that daughter Mahallikā to Sūryaprabha with splendors equal to those of the sovereignty of the asuras.
He gave heaps of excellent jewels to his daughter and her husband—jewels brought back from the conquest of the thirty-three gods, resembling the peaks of Mount Sumeru.
"Father, give those twelve dear friends of mine to him as well"; thus did Mahallikā then speak freely to Prahlāda.
"Daughter, since they are under the control of my brother and have been taken captive by him, it is not proper for me to give them away," he also said to her.
When that day had passed, Sūryaprabha, having celebrated the festival of his marriage, entered his bedchamber at night together with Mahallikā.
And there he experienced that festival of love, enriched by the enjoyment of all desires, together with her, in a state of mental joy and happiness.
When Prahlāda had departed for the assembly hall with his followers in the morning, Amīla, the lord of the Dānavas, addressed Prahlāda and the others.
"Today you must all come to my house; for there I shall offer hospitality to this Sūryaprabha."
"If it is for your benefit, I shall give my daughter Kalāvatī to him"; all of them accepted those words, saying, "So be it."
Then, at that very moment, they all went together with Sūryaprabha and his companions to the second underworld.
There, Āmīla gave that daughter Kalāvatī to Sūryaprabha according to the prescribed rites, even though he had already offered himself to him of his own accord.
Having performed the wedding and having eaten at the house of Prahlāda together with the Asuras, Sūryaprabha spent that day there amidst the refinements of pleasure.
On the second day, the lord of the asuras, Durāroha, having likewise invited them all, led them to the fifth subterranean realm, Svarasātala.
There, for the sake of hospitality, he gave his daughter Kumudāvatī to Sūryaprabha according to the prescribed rites, by her own name, as one would give a bride to another.
Then, having spent that day with all those gathered together in various enjoyments, Sūryaprabha enjoyed the company of Kumudāvatī in her bedchamber during the night.
There, he spent that night together with her, Trilokasundarī, who was eager for their first union and possessed a tender, innocent charm.
And in the morning, escorted by Tantukaccha and led by Prahlāda, he invited him and led him to his own palace in the seventh underworld.
There, the lord of the asuras gave him his daughter named Manovatī, who was adorned with jeweled ornaments and possessed the luster of refined gold.
Then Sūryaprabha, having spent that day there in exceeding happiness, passed the night in the joy of his first embrace with Manovatī.
And on the following day, having extended an invitation, Sumāya, the lord of the asuras, led that sixth [son], who was fully prepared, to his own Pātāla.
There, he too gave him his daughter named Subhadrā, whose limbs were dark like a blade of dūrvā grass, appearing like the very personification of the god of love.
On that day, Sūryaprabha remained there together with that dark-complexioned Śyāmā, whose face was like the full moon and who was fit for the enjoyment of amorous dalliance.
And on another day, King Bali, accompanied by the Asuras, led Sūryaprabha in that very same manner to his own third underworld.
He too gave him his daughter there, named Sundarī, who was like a cluster of blossoms on a mādhavī creeper, possessing the luster of young sprouts.
There, Sūryaprabha took his pleasure with that jewel among women; that day was made delightful by him, adorned as it was with divine enjoyments.
On another day, Maya likewise brought that prince, who had gone to the fourth underworld, back once more to his own palace.
A palace of variegated jewels, created by his own *māyā*, appearing as if ever-new at every moment through its splendor.
There, he too gave him his own daughter named Sumāyā, whose beauty was a marvel to the world, as if she were his own power incarnate.
And because she was human, he did not consider her to be fit to be taken by him; yet the virtuous Sūryaprabha took his pleasure with her there.
Then, having divided his body through his supernatural power, the prince took pleasure simultaneously with all those Asura maidens together.
But with his true body, he repeatedly enjoyed the company of Mahallikā, the beloved daughter of the asura Prahlāda.
And once at night, while they were sitting at their ease, Sūryaprabha asked that noble Mahallikā during the course of conversation:
"My dear, as for those two friends who came with you at night, where are they from? I do not see them; and what has become of them?"
Then the old woman said, "I have been well reminded by you; there are not only two of them, for I have twelve companions here."
And by my paternal uncle, having carried them away from heaven, they were brought here—one named Amṛtaprabhā and the second Keśinī.
These two daughters of the sage Parvata, endowed with auspicious marks, were Kālindī as the third and Bhadrikā as the fourth.
Likewise, Darpakamālā was the fifth, and Cārulocanā; these three, O great sage, were born from the self of Devala.
The sixth was named Saudāmanī and the seventh was called Ujjvalā; these two were both daughters of the Gandharva named Hāhā.
The eighth was named Pīvarā, the daughter of the Gandharva Huha; the ninth was named Añjanikā, the daughter of the powerful Kāla.
From the Gaṇa Piṅgala was born Daśamī Kesarāvalī; the eleventh was named Mālinī, also known as Kambalanandinī.
Named Mandāramālā, she was the twelfth of the eight daughters; all of them were born among the Apsarases and were indeed celestial women.
"Once they have been brought to the first underworld and my marriage has been performed, they must be given by me to you, so that I may always remain united with them."
"I have indeed made this promise, for I have affection for them; even my father was told by me, and so he did not give them away out of regard for his brother."
Hearing this, Sūryaprabha, filled with embarrassment, said to her: "My dear, you are a woman of great noble character; how could I do such a thing?"
Thus addressed by Sūryaprabha, Mahallikā spoke with anger: "In my very presence you carry another woman, yet you do not wish for my companions!"
"Separated from which I would not take even a single moment's pleasure"—when addressed thus by Tuṣṭi, Sūryaprabha consented to that.
Then, having first led him to that very Pātāla, she, the daughter of Prahlāda, bestowed all twelve of them upon him.
Then, having married them in due order, Sūryaprabha enjoyed those divine women, headed by Amṛtaprabhā, during that night.
And in the morning, Prabhāsa, having led them to the fourth subterranean realm (rasātala), established them there in concealment after questioning Mahallikā.
And he himself, unobserved, went there together with her; and as before, he proceeded to Prahlāda’s assembly hall to pay his respects.
Thereupon the lord of the asuras said to Sunītha and Maya, "Go, all of you, to see both the goddesses Diti and Danu."

"So be it. Then, having emerged instantly from the netherworld (rasātala), Mayasunītha and Sūryaprabha, together with the asuras, each according to his own station, mounted that celestial chariot (vimāna) called Bhūtāsana which they had merely thought of, and proceeded to the hermitage of Kaśyapa on a ridge of Mount Sumeru.
There, Diti and Danu, who were staying together, were announced by the respectful sages; having approached, they beheld him in due order and bowed their heads at his feet.

And those two mothers of the Asuras, beholding them both along with their followers with great affection, kissed them on the head with tears and, out of joy, spoke blessings immediately following Māyā.
O dear son, seeing this Sunītha, your son, restored to life, our eyes have today attained their fruitfulness; we consider you alone to be a doer of meritorious deeds.

Beholding this Sumuṇḍika here, who has been reborn as Sūryaprabha, possessing a divine form and extraordinary qualities, and whose body is marked by a multitude of auspicious signs that portend his future welfare—you should clearly manifest within your own bodies a joy born from seeing him.

Therefore, rise quickly, my children, and go to see the Noble Son, the Lord of Creatures, here; from seeing him, the accomplishment of your purpose will come to you, and his word shall be for your welfare.
Thus instructed by those two goddesses, Maya and others went accordingly and beheld the sage Kaśyapa there in that divine hermitage.
In the hermitage of the gods, he was resplendent with a brilliance like molten, pure gold; his matted locks were tawny with flames, and he was as unassailable as fire itself.

Having approached, they and their followers prostrated themselves at his feet in succession; then he too, having repeatedly offered appropriate blessings, seated them out of great satisfaction, and spoke to them.

"This is my supreme joy, that all of you sons have been seen by me. You are praiseworthy, O Sunītha, who have not wavered from the path of truth and are the repository of all sciences. You are blessed, O Sūryaprabha, by whom life—even though it had departed—has been regained, and who shall become the lord of the sky-dwellers through your merit."

Therefore, you must now proceed upon the path of Dharma; you must understand my words, so that by attaining supreme glory, you shall enjoy constant happiness. Let there never again be such humiliation from others as occurred before, for those Asuras who transgressed the Dharma here fell under the power of the discus of the conqueror of Mura.
And those asuras who were slain by the gods, O Sunītha—these very ones have descended here as mortal heroes; he who was Sumuṇḍika, your younger brother here, is indeed this Sūryaprabha born today.
These other asuras here are indeed his companions, born from the same source, and truly his kinsmen; and he who was the great asura named Śambara has today been born as this minister Prahasta.
He who was the asura Triśiras was born as the minister of Maya named Siddhārtha; and the dānava who was Vātāpi became his very same minister named Prajñāḍhya.
The demon who was named Ulūka is this friend of his called Śubhaṅkara; and he who is his friend Vītabhīti was also a foe of the gods named Kāla.
And this minister Bhāṣa is that very Daitya who has descended here named Vṛṣaparvan; and this Prabhāsa is that very Daitya who has descended as Vatsa, known by the name Prabala.
By that great-souled one, who was composed of jewels and who, even when entreated by the gods—even his adversaries—cut his body into pieces and descended, from which all these jewels were born.

And because she was pleased with him, the goddess Caṇḍikā granted him a boon that followed him into another body, by which he has now become this Prabhāsa—possessed of great strength and difficult for enemies to withstand.
Those two Dānavas who formerly existed by the names of Sunda and Upasunda have now been born as his two ministers, Sarvadamana and Bhayaṅkara.
And those two who were Asuras named Hayagrīva and Vikaṭākṣa have been born as his two ministers, Sthirabuddhi and Mahābuddhi.
Furthermore, those others who are his fathers-in-law, ministers, and other kinsmen—they too have descended as asuras, by whom Indra and the other gods were defeated many times in the past.
Thus, your side has once again gradually attained growth; be steadfast, and you shall attain supreme prosperity without falling away from the Dharma.
While Kaśyapa was speaking thus, it is said that all his wives, the daughters of Dakṣa, headed by Aditi, arrived there at the time of the midday libation.

After they had offered blessings to Maya and the others who were bowing down, and after their lord had given the command for their daily duties, Śakra then arrived there with the world-protectors to see that sage.
Having paid homage to the feet of the Sage Śāradvatīputra-Kāśyapa, who was himself honored by Maya and others today, Śakra then looked at Sūryaprabha with anger and spoke to Maya.
I know this boy desires the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas; why then is he satisfied with so little, and why does he not request the status of Indra?
Upon hearing that, Maya said to him: "O Lord of Gods, that sovereignty of yours was ordained by the Supreme Lord; furthermore, he has commanded that you shall be the lord of the sky-dwellers."
At these words of Maya, Maghavan then spoke with a smile and with indignation: "For that is indeed too little for such a form endowed with such auspicious marks."
Then Maya also said to him: "Śrutaśarman is certainly fit for the sovereignty over the sky-dwellers; his form is worthy even of the lordship of Indra."
To him who had spoken thus, Maghavan rose up in anger, raising his thunderbolt; meanwhile, the sage Kaśyapa uttered a roar of wrath.
Diti and the others fell into a rage, their faces copper-red and vocal with cries of "Shame! Thereupon Indra, out of fear of their curse, withdrew his weapons and sat down with his head bowed.
Then, having prostrated at the feet of Kaśyapa Muni—the progenitor of gods and asuras—and having propitiated him, Śakra, with palms joined in reverence, made this request.
"O Blessed One, Sūryaprabha is now striving to seize from Śrutaśarman that sovereignty over the Vidyādharas which was granted to him by me."
And I, who consist of all forms, am here making an effort to accomplish this for him. Having heard that, Prajāpati, together with Diti and Danu, spoke to Indra.
"O Maghavan, Śrutaśarman and Sūryaprabha are dear to you as they are to Śarva; yet I do not desire him [Sūryaprabha] for myself, and Maya was previously commanded by him in this matter."
Why indeed do you speak thus of Maya? Tell me, what fault is there in him? For he stands upon the path of Dharma; he is wise, possessed of discernment, and deeply devoted to his teacher.
If you had committed this evil, the fire of our wrath would have reduced you to ashes; yet you were not capable against him—do you not know his power?
When the Sage had thus spoken here to Indra, who was bowed down with shame and fear along with his wife, Aditi said: "What is that Śrutaśarman like? Let him be brought here and shown to us."
Having heard this, Śakra immediately commanded Mātali to bring there Śrutaśarman, the sovereign of the sky-dwellers.
Seeing him bowing in prostration and looking toward Sūryaprabha, the wives of the sage Kaśyapa asked: "Which of these two is more endowed with beauty and auspicious marks?"
Then that Lord of Sages said: "This [power] does not belong even to Śrutaśarman, nor to Prabhāsa; how much less could it belong to this peerless minister?"
This is Sūryaprabha, for he is endowed with those divine marks of physical beauty by which, were he to apply his resolve toward it, even the status of Indra would not be difficult to attain.
Thus all believed the words of the sage Kaśyapa, saying, "So be it"; then, while Mahendra listened, the sage granted him this boon.
O son, because you remained unshaken even when Indra raised his weapon, by that merit you shall be free from old age and death, and with limbs as firm as adamant, you shall remain invulnerable.
These two great beings of yours, Sunītha and Sūryaprabha, who are so like you, will also forever remain invincible to the entire host of enemies.
This Prince Suvāsakumāra, whose splendor is like the autumnal moon, will come to my aid when thought of during nights of distress; he is my own son.
When the sage had spoken thus, his wife, the seers, and the world-protectors likewise granted boons to Maya and all the others in that assembly.
Then Aditi said to Śakra, "O Indra, appease Vira for his lack of discipline! For today you have seen the fruit of discipline, in that he has obtained excellent boons."
Having heard that, Indra took Maya by the hand and gratified him; and Śrutaśarman, overwhelmed by the splendor of Sūryaprabha, became like the moon by day.

Then, having prostrated before that preceptor Kaśyapa for a moment, the Lord of the Gods departed as he had come, accompanied by all the guardians of the world; and Maya and the others, by the command of that best of sages, likewise departed from that hermitage to accomplish their intended purpose.

Thus ends the second wave in the Sūryaprabha-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. Now begins the third wave. Then Mayasunītha and Sūryaprabha, along with all of them, departed from that hermitage of Kaśyapa and arrived at their destination.
There, at the confluence of the Candrabhāgā and the Airāvatī, those kings—his friends and kinsmen—stood for the sake of Sūryaprabha.
And seeing Sūryaprabha arrived there, those kings standing before him rose up weeping, despondent and facing death.
Suspecting that they were distressed by the sight of Candraprabha’s absence, Sūryaprabha related the entire matter to them exactly as it had happened.
Nevertheless, being questioned by him, they described with great difficulty how the abduction of his wife had been carried out by Śrutaśarman.
And she likewise informed him that her own attempt to cast off her body, born of the sorrow of his defeat, had been prevented by a divine voice.
Then Sūryaprabha, filled with rage, made a vow there: "Even if all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, should protect him,"
Nevertheless, that Śrutaśarman must certainly be uprooted by me—he who is a rogue, bold in his deceit, and a stealer of another's wife.
Having thus made his vow, he determined, with the astrologers' approval, that the auspicious moment for setting out on that conquest would be on the seventh day.
Then, knowing him to be resolute and having grasped his resolve for victory, Maya spoke again to Sūryaprabha, strengthening him with these words:
"If you have truly made such an effort, then I shall tell you: at that time, having displayed an illusion, I led your beloveds away and established them in Pātāla."
Thus you exert yourself for victory with such impetuosity; it is not simply thus, for fire blazes forth when fanned by the wind.
"So come, let us go to Pātāla; I shall show those beloved women to you. Having heard these words of Maya, they all rejoiced.
And by that very same opening as before, they, preceded by the Asura Maya, entered and went to the fourth underworld.
There, Maya brought those wives, Madanasenā and the others, from their quarters and presented them to Sūryaprabha.
Having taken those and other wives, the daughters of the asuras, Sūryaprabha went to see Prahlāda at the word of Maya.
Then that Asura, having heard from me that he had obtained the boon, and wishing to test him as he stood bowed down, took up his weapon and spoke with feigned anger.
"O Durācāra, I have heard that you have abducted twelve maidens who were acquired by my brother; therefore, I shall kill you—behold me!"
Having heard that, Sūryaprabha, remaining unperturbed, looked at him and said: "My body is at your disposal; discipline me, for I am ill-behaved."
To him who had spoken thus, Prahlāda replied with a smile: "I have observed you, and not even a trace of pride remains in you."
"Choose a boon; I am pleased," he was told by him; "So be it," replied Sūryaprabha, and chose as his boon devotion toward his gurus and toward Śambhu.
Then, when everyone was satisfied, Prahlāda gave his second daughter, named Yāminī, to that Sūryaprabha.
And that lord of the Asuras gave him two sons as companions; then Sūryaprabha went to the side of Āmīla together with all of them.
He too, delighted by the attainment of the boon he had heard, gave him his second daughter, Sukhāvatī, and two sons to assist him.
Then, during those days, Sūryaprabha remained there with his beloved, honoring other lords of the Asuras for their assistance.
Mayā and the others heard that all three wives of Sunītha and the princesses who were his own wives had become pregnant.
When questioned about their longings, they all likewise expressed a desire to behold the great battle; then the asura Maya rejoiced.
"By good fortune, those Asuras who were slain of old have been born among these; for that reason, this desire has arisen for them," he said.
In this manner six days passed; on the seventh day, Sūryaprabha and all the others emerged from the netherworld accompanied by their wives and attendants.
The magical illusions created as obstacles by their enemies were destroyed by Suvāsakumāra, who had arrived while remaining mindful.
Then, having consecrated the infant Ratnaprabha as the crown prince over the realm of Cāndraprabha, they ascended celestial chariots that had become their seats.
At the word of Maya, they all went from Mount Sumeru—the abode of the lord of the Vidyādharas—to the ascetic grove on the bank of the eastern Gaṅgā.
There, Sumeru, remembering the prior command of Śambhu and having related the entire account as told by me, honored those who had approached him with friendship.
And those [princes], Sūryaprabha and the others, remaining in their respective regions, caused their own armies to be brought there in their entirety, as well as their kinsmen and friends.
First, the sons of Sūryaprabha’s father-in-law arrived—those princes headed by Maya, who had been commanded by me and were diligent in having mastered the sciences.
The force following each one of those sixteen, beginning with Haribhaṭa, consisted of ten thousand chariots and twenty thousand foot soldiers.
Thereafter, the Daityas and Dānavas who had established their alliance arrived, along with his brothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, friends, and other kinsmen.
Hṛṣṭaroman, Mahāmāya, Siṃhadaṃṣṭra, Prakampana, Tantukaccha, Durāroha, Sumāya, and Vajrapañjara.
Dhūmaketu, Pramathana, and the Dānava Vikaṭākṣa, as well as many others, arrived from as far as the seventh netherworld.
One [came] with seventy thousand chariots, another with eighty thousand; one with sixty thousand, another with thirty thousand, and he who was the very least came with ten thousand.
One [army] had three hundred thousand foot soldiers, another two hundred thousand, another one hundred thousand, while the lowest had fifty thousand.
For each one, elephants and horses arrived in accordance with that number; and another innumerable army belonging to Maya and Sunītha also came.
And the immeasurable native army of Sūryaprabha arrived, as did that of King Vasudatta and the others, and likewise that of Sumeru.
Then the asura, together with Sūryaprabha and the others, questioned that sage named Suvāsakumāra, who had appeared before them by his mere thought.
"O Blessed One, this army is scattered; it is not perceived here. Therefore, tell us where it is spread out so that it may be seen all at once."
Just one yojana from here there is a region known as the village of Kalāpa; go there and, once you have reached that vast place, let this be observed.
When that sage had spoken thus, all those [gods], together with their own forces and including Sumeru, went to that village of Kalāpa.
There, standing upon the elevated ground, they beheld separately the armies of the Asuras and of the kings, each drawn up in its respective position.
Then Sumeru said: "Śrutaśarman is superior in strength; for he has one hundred and one lords of the Vidyādharas."
And each one of those thirty-two kings has his own separate sovereign; let it be so, for I shall break some of them apart and bring them together for you.
Therefore, we shall go tomorrow morning to that place known as Valmīka; for tomorrow morning is the great lunar day, the eighth of the dark fortnight of Phālguna.
And when that [mark] arises there, it is the sign of a universal monarch; for his sake, the Vidyādharas quickly come to that very lunar day.
When Sumeru had spoken thus, they spent the day according to the military regulations; then, at dawn, they proceeded with their forces toward that anthill in their chariots.
There, on the southern slope of the Himalayas, those troops with their forces shouting were encamped when they beheld many lords of the Vidyādharas who had arrived.
And those Vidyādharas there, having kindled fires in the sacrificial pits, became engaged in the performance of oblations, while some were intent on the recitation of mantras.
Then Sūryaprabha also prepared a great fire-pit there; by the power of his magic science, the fire blazed up within it spontaneously.
Upon seeing that, joy arose in Sumeru, but envy arose again; among the Vidyādharas, one then spoke to him.
Having abandoned the sovereignty of the Lord of Vidyādharas, fie upon you, O Sumeru! Why do you follow this one named Sūryaprabha, who is merely a dweller of the earth?
Having heard that, Sumeru rebuked him angrily and spoke these words to Sūryaprabha, who was asking for his name:
There was a Vidyādhara named Bhīma, and Brahmā lustfully desired his wife; from that [union], he (Vatsa) was born.
That which is secret regarding Brahman, when born from it, is called "Brahma-gupta" (the secret of Brahman); for this very reason, these words of his are consistent with his own birth.
Having said this, Sumeru also prepared a fire-pit; then Sūryaprabha offered oblations into the sacrificial fire along with him.
And in an instant, from the fissure in the earth, there emerged an exceedingly terrifying great python. "Why [has this happened]? [he asked].
Then that lord of the Vidyādharas, named Brahmagupta—by whom Sumeru had been reviled—ran forward in pride to seize him.
There, that serpent, having drawn him in with the wind from the breath of its mouth, flung him a hundred cubits away, and he fell like a withered leaf.
Then a lord of the Vidyādharas named Tejaḥprabha approached, desiring to seize him; he too was likewise hurled away by that [serpent].
Then a lord of the Vidyādharas named Duṣṭadamana approached him, but he too was cast away by that same breath as the others.
Then the lord of the Khecaras named Virūpaśakti approached him; he too was struck down by him with that very same breath, as easily as a blade of grass.
Then, as the two kings Aṅgāraka and Vijṛmbhaka likewise rushed toward him simultaneously, he sent them both to a distance with a single breath.
In this manner, all those lords of the Vidyādharas were likewise hurled by him one after another; somehow they rose up again with their limbs covered in pulverized stone.
Then, out of pride, Śrutaśarman approached that serpent; desiring to seize it, he was in turn cast away by the serpent with its breath-winds.
Then, having fallen short of his mark, he rose again and ran; but having been led even further away by him, he was cast to the ground by his breath.
When Śrutaśarman had risen up, his limbs crushed and his pride shattered, Sūryaprabha was dispatched by Sumeru to seize the serpent.
"Look! Even he has risen to seize this python. Oh, these humans are as thoughtless as monkeys!"
"Whatever is being done by another, they see and imitate that"—thus the Vidyādharas then laughed at Sūryaprabha.
While they were still laughing, Sūryaprabha went there, seized that python by the mouth, and dragged it out from its hole.
At that very moment, the serpent attained the state of being a jewel for the quiver; moreover, a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon the head of Sūryaprabha.
"O Sūryaprabha, this inexhaustible jewel-quiver has been perfected for you; therefore, take it!"—thus a divine voice resounded loudly at that time.
Then the Vidyādharas fell into despondency, while Sūryaprabha took up his quiver; and Maya, Sunītha, and Sumeru experienced great joy.
Then, after Śrutaśarman had departed accompanied by the forces of the Vidyādharas, his messenger approached Sūryaprabha and spoke as follows:
"The illustrious Lord Śrutaśarman commands you: deliver this quiver to me, if you have any regard for your own life."
Then Sūryaprabha replied, "Go, messenger, and say this to him: 'The quiver, filled with my arrows, shall remain within your own body.'"
Having heard this reply and seeing the messenger turn away and depart, all those followers of Śrutaśarman laughed at that impetuous speech.
Then Sūryaprabha, joyfully embraced by Sumeru, said: "By good fortune, the word of Śambhu has today undoubtedly borne fruit."
For when this jewel of a quiver is mastered, your status as a universal monarch is secured; therefore, come now and, free from distraction, master the jewel of the bow.
Having heard this concerning Sumeru, Sūryaprabha and the others then proceeded toward Mount Hemakūṭa, with that very leader at their head.
And on its northern side, they reached the lake named Mānasa, which was like a palette of colors for the Creator in the fashioning of the ocean.
The faces of divine women sporting within the water were concealed by golden lotuses in full bloom, tossed there by the winds.
And while they were beholding the splendor of that lake, Śrutaśarman and all the others also arrived there.
Then Sūryaprabha and his companions performed a fire sacrifice with ghee and lotuses; and in an instant, a terrible cloud rose up from that lake.
Having pervaded the sky, that cloud released a great rain; and from within it, a single black serpent fell from the cloud.
And when he rose up from the words of Sumeru, although he was being pierced, that nāga who had been firmly seized by Sūryaprabha became a bow.
When he had become that bow, a second serpent fell from the sky, terrifying all the denizens of the air with the fire of his venom as he fled.
Sūryaprabha seized him there as well, and by that act, he became a bowstring as before, and that cloud quickly vanished.
"This bow of yours, Sūryaprabha, has been empowered by the power of Amitabala; its string is likewise indestructible. Take these two jewels as well."
Thus a divine voice was heard, preceded by a rain of flowers, and Sūryaprabha took up that excellent bow along with its string.
Śrutaśarman also went, distressed, to the ascetic grove with his followers; then Sūryaprabha and all those led by Maya were filled with joy.
Then, questioned by them regarding the origin of the bow, Sumeru said: "In this place there is a great, divine forest of kīcaka bamboos."
Then, those kīcaka reeds which are cut and thrown into this lake become these great, divine bows.
And those very [arts] were accomplished by those various gods of old, as well as by the asuras, the gandharvas, and the highest vidyādharas.
The names of those bows of the universal monarchs are distinct; they are called Amitabala, having been deposited here in ancient times by the gods.
And those [relics] of those who have performed virtuous deeds are accomplished through these afflictions; for some future universal monarchs, they come into being by the will of Īśvara.
And this great bow, which has now been mastered by Sūryaprabha, is worthy of him; therefore, let these friends of his prepare those [other weapons] for him.
For those heroes who have mastered the vidyās and possess the requisite capacity, those [mantras] indeed still succeed even today for those who are worthy, according to their respective fitness.
Having heard these words of Sumeru, those companions of Sūryaprabha, headed by Prabhāsa, went to that Kīcaka forest.
Having conquered the king who protected it and whose punishments were fierce, they brought the kīcakas there and placed them within the lake.
And for those endowed with fortitude who fasted on its banks while reciting mantras and offering oblations, their bows were perfected within seven days.
Then, together with those who had arrived and reported their adventures, as well as Maya and the others, Sūryaprabha went to that ascetic grove on Mount Sumeru.
There Sumeru said to him: "It is a marvel that Caṇḍadaṇḍa, though invincible, has been conquered by your friends in the forest of Veṇu."
He possesses a lore named Mohinī; for that reason he is difficult to conquer. Surely it was established by him for the sake of his chief enemy.
Therefore, these [mantras] have not been employed against your friends at this time; for that [mantra] yields fruit for him only once, and not again and again.
For she had been employed by him solely for the purpose of observing the guru's power; therefore, he pronounced such a curse upon her.
This is indeed a matter for reflection, for the power of these sciences is difficult to overcome; therefore, you should ask the venerable Maya about its cause.
"What can I say in his presence? What lamp is there before the sun? When Sumeru had spoken thus to Sūryaprabha, Maya replied:
What Sumeru has spoken to you is true; listen briefly as I speak this: from the Unmanifest arise here those various powers and subordinate powers.

Therein, the resonance (nāda) arising from the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), resting upon the path of the point (bindu), attains the state of a mantra beginning with Vidyā, endowed with the digit of the supreme reality (paratattva).
And by means of knowledge of those mantra-sciences, or even through asceticism, or by the command of the perfected ones who have attained success, their power is difficult to overcome.
Therefore, my son, all the sciences have been mastered by you, yet you lack two; the two sciences of Mohinī and Parivartinī have not been accomplished by you.
"And Yājñavalkya knows it; go and entreat him. Having been told this by me, Sūryaprabha went into the presence of that ṛṣi.
That sage, having caused him to dwell for seven days in the serpent-lake, made him perform ascetic penance for three days in the midst of fire.
Within seven days, he bestowed upon him the "Enchanting" spell, which withstands the bite of snakes; and within three days, he gave him the "Reversing" spell, which withstands fire.
The sage commanded him—who had already attained the vidyā—to enter the fire-pit once more; and he did exactly as he was told.
And at that very moment, the great lotus-palace of Sūryaprabha, which could travel according to his will and move through the sky, appeared before him.
It was adorned with one hundred and eight petals and one hundred ancient [ornaments], fashioned from various forms of great jewels.
This celestial palace of a universal monarch has been accomplished for you; you shall establish the harems of that king within all these cities.
"By this means they shall become invincible to your enemies," Sarasvatī then spoke thus to that wise man from the intermediate space.
Then, bowing low before his teacher Yājñavalkya, he requested: "Please command me; what kind of sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall I bestow?"
"Remember me at the time of your own consecration; this indeed shall be your sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Go now to your own army," the sage said to him.
Then, having bowed to that sage and ascended his celestial chariot, Sūryaprabha went to his army stationed on Mount Sumeru.
There, Mayapura and the others—including Sunītha and Sumeru—joyfully greeted him as he related his own adventures, now possessing a perfected vidyā-vimāna.
Then Sunītha remembered that boy Suvāsakumāra; and he, having arrived, spoke thus to Maya and the others, together with the king.
The celestial chariot is accomplished, as are all the vidyās of Sūryaprabha; why do you remain indifferent even now regarding the conquest of the enemy?
Having heard that, Maya replied: "What Your Reverence has said is appropriate; however, let a messenger be sent first, and let diplomatic policy be employed for now."
When the asura had spoken thus, that son of a sage said: "Let it be so; what harm is there? Let this Prahasta then be dispatched."
He is quick-witted, eloquent, and knows the proper course of action for both the task and the time; he is firm yet patient, endowed with all the qualities of an envoy.
Having thus placed full faith in his words, they all then dispatched Prahasta, who had been given his instructions, on a mission as an envoy to Śrutaśarman.
When he had departed, Sūryaprabha said to all his own people: "Listen to this unprecedented and wondrous dream that was seen by me."
"I see today, as the night wanes, that we shall all be carried away by a great flood of water."
And as we were being carried away, we danced and did not sink at all; then that flood turned back due to a contrary wind.
Then, having been approached by a certain man of blazing splendor, we were lifted up and thrown into fire, yet we are not consumed by the flames.
Then a cloud arrived and rained down a torrent of blood; by that blood the quarters were pervaded, and consequently my sleep vanished along with the night.
To him who had spoken thus, that Suvāsakumāra replied: "Prosperity preceded by hardship has been indicated by this dream."
That flood of water was the battle; that non-sinking was fortitude; and for those being carried away by the waters while dancing, it was the turning back.
Whoever among you is Marut, he too is some refuge and protector; and that man of blazing splendor who is the deliverer is Śaṅkara himself in person.
Because you were cast into the fire, you have been stationed in this great battle; and because the cloud arose thereafter, there has come once again the onset of fear.
That which rains down a torrent of blood is the destruction of fear; that the quarters of the sky are filled with blood is a great prosperity for you.
A dream has many purposes: it may be true to its object, or entirely without purpose; that which indicates an event immediately is called "true to its object."
A dream that takes the form of an instruction from a propitious deity is true to reality; they say that [a dream] produced by intense experience, reflection, and so forth, is without purpose.
For when the mind is deluded by passion and turned away from external objects, a living being, under the sway of sleep, perceives various dreams through those respective causes.
The slowness or swiftness of its fruition depends on the specific time; however, a dream seen at the end of the night yields swift results.
Having heard this from that young sage, Sūryaprabha and the others were thoroughly relieved; rising up, they performed their daily duties.
Then Prahasta returned from the presence of Śrutaśarman; questioned by Maya and the others, he described everything exactly as it had happened.
From here, I went swiftly to that city named Trikūṭapatākā, situated on Mount Trikūṭa and fashioned of gold.
Having entered it, announced by the doorkeeper, I beheld that Śrutaśarman surrounded by those various lords of the Vidyādharas.
By his father Trikūṭasena, as well as by Vikramaśakti, Dhuraṃdhara, and other heroes such as Dāmodara and the rest.
Then, having sat down upon Dhara, I said to that Śrutaśarman: "I have been sent into your presence by the illustrious Sūryaprabha."
And he sent this message to you: "By the grace of Dhūrjaṭi, I have mastered spells, jewels, wives, and even companions."
Therefore, come and join my army along with these lords of the sky-dwellers; I shall be the slayer of those who oppose us and the protector of those who bow before me.
And that maiden whom you have abducted in secret while she was unapproachable—the daughter of Sunītha and crest-jewel of passion—release her, for that act is indeed inauspicious.
When I had spoken thus, they all became enraged and said this right there: "Who indeed is he who, out of arrogance, issues such commands to us?"
"Let him thus issue commands among mortals; but who is he among the Vidyādharas? Being a mere wretched human, though so arrogant, he shall perish."
Having heard that, I said: "What? What? Let it be heard who he is! He has been appointed by Hara here as your universal sovereign."
Even if a mortal, together with other mortals, has achieved divinity, the prowess of that mortal has been witnessed by the Vidyādharas as well.
"For if he should ever come here, your destruction would surely be seen. When I had spoken thus, that assembly became enraged and fell into agitation.
And as Śrutaśarman and Dhuraṃdhara rushed forward to kill me, I said to them both, "In this way I perceive your valor."
Then Dāmodara rose up and restrained them both, saying, "Peace! Neither the messenger nor the brahmin is to be slain."
Then Vikramaśakti said to me, "Go, O messenger! For we all have been created by the Lord just like your master."
"Therefore, let him come; we shall see if we are capable of receiving him as a guest. When he had spoken thus with pride, I said, laughing:
The swans remain happily established, making their cries in the lotus grove, only so long as they do not see a cloud approaching that covers the sky.
Having spoken thus, he rose and departed with contempt; having come here, I heard this from Prahasta, and satisfaction was attained by me and the others.
Having resolved upon their exertion for battle, Sūryaprabha and all the others then appointed Prabhāsa, who was fierce in combat, as their general.
And on that day, having received instructions from Suvāsakumāra regarding the initiation for battle, they all entered [the fray] with their vows firmly restrained.
And there at night, Sūryaprabha, remaining awake, beheld an extraordinary and beautiful maiden who had entered the interior of his vow-chamber.
Approaching him at her leisure while he was feigning sleep and his ministers were fast asleep, she spoke to a female companion standing nearby.
If even while asleep, his splendor of form remains such as this—exhausted though his play may be—then, my friend, what must it be like when he is awake?
Let it be; he is not to be awakened, for the curiosity of my eyes has been satisfied. For what further use have I for this heart fixed upon him?
For he shall have a battle with Śrutaśarman; who there indeed knows what will happen to whom?
For heroes, the festival of battle indeed arises for the sake of sacrificing their very lives; let there be well-being for him in that regard for now, and thereafter we shall know again.
Moreover, what woman like me could possibly delight the heart of this man, who is the crest-jewel of those with desire and who wanders through the sky?
When she had spoken thus, her friend said to her: "What are you saying this? O fierce one, why is your heart's attachment dependent upon him?"
If he, by whose mere sight the heart of the crest-jewel of Love was stolen, were not to steal the heart of another woman—even if she were Arundhatī herself in person—then who indeed would?
And by the power of your knowledge, do you not know his welfare in battle? For the Siddhas have declared that you are the wives of this true universal monarch.
"You are Kāmacūḍāmaṇi, and Suprabhā is born of the same lineage; indeed, during these very days, Suprabhā was married by him."
So why would there be any misfortune for him in battle? For the word of a perfected being is never false. Moreover, what can happen to one whose heart has been captivated by Suprabhā?
O sinless lady, you should not take [him], for you are superior in beauty; or, if you have a hesitation out of regard for your kinsmen, that is not right.
"For indeed, apart from their husband, there is no other kinsman for virtuous women. Having heard these words of her friend, that excellent maiden said:
"Truly, my friend, you have spoken; I have no need for other kinsmen. And by means of my own magic power, I know that victory will belong to this noble son in battle."
His jewels and his spells have been mastered even to this day; how much more so, then, his medicinal herbs? Since those herbs have not yet been mastered by him, my mind is deeply pained.
And all those [goddesses] reside within the caves on Mount Candrapāda; they grant success to those who possess merit, and they belong exclusively to universal monarchs (cakravartin).
Therefore, if he were to go there and procure all those medicinal herbs, it would be well; for his great battle is close at hand tomorrow morning.
Having heard all this, Sūryaprabha abandoned his feigned sleep, rose up, and spoke with humility to that maiden there.
"O girl with most charming eyes, you have shown me great partiality; therefore, I shall go there—tell me, who are you?"
Having heard this, the maiden became bowed with shame, thinking, "He has heard everything," and remained silent; but her friend spoke to him.
This maiden named Vilāsinī, the younger sister of Sumeru, the lord of the Vidyādharas, is filled with curiosity at the sight of you.
Even as her friend had spoken thus, that playful woman said to her, "Come, let us go now," and departed from there.
Then, having awakened Prabhāsa and the others, Sūryaprabha explained to his ministers that method for acquiring the medicinal herbs as it had been described.
And he dispatched Prahasta, who was capable of accomplishing that task, to inform Sunītha, Sumeru, and Maya.
Accompanied by those who had arrived with faith and by his ministers, Sūryaprabha set out at night toward the Moonbeam Mountain.
And as they proceeded, there arose in succession obstacles blocking their path—yakṣas, guhyakas, and kūṣmāṇḍas—with various weapons raised aloft.
Having bewildered some of them with weapons and paralyzed others with magic spells, Sūryaprabha and his companions reached that Candrapādagiri mountain.
There, as they reached the entrance of that cave, the hosts of Śiva approached and blocked their entry, possessing faces of various distorted shapes.
One must not fight with these, for the Lord Hara might become angry; therefore, let us praise that very giver of boons with his eight-thousand-name hymn.
"By that very means those hosts will be propitiated," said Suvāsakumāra to Sūryaprabha and the others.
Then, saying "So be it," they all praised Hara in that very manner; and those attendants, pleased by the praise of their master, spoke to them.
"This cave has been opened for you by us; take the great medicinal herbs within it. However, Sūryaprabha himself must not enter it."
"Let Prabhāsa enter this [city], for it is easy for him to traverse; all those members of the assembly agreed, saying, 'So be it.'"
Then, as soon as Prabhāsa entered, that cave, though shrouded in dense darkness, became somehow brilliantly illuminated.
And having risen, even those four *kiṃkara* rākṣasas of most terrible form, bowing down, said to him, "Enter."
Then, having entered and gathered those seven divine medicinal herbs, Prabhāsa emerged and gave them all to Sūryaprabha.
"O Sūryaprabha and the others, these seven herbs of great power have been accomplished,"—at that moment, such a voice arose from the sky.
Having heard that, Sūryaprabha and all the others were delighted; they quickly returned to their own army, which was stationed at the abode of Mount Sumeru.
Then Sunītha asked that youth Suvāsaka: "O Sage, why was Prabhāsa admitted while leaving Sūryaprabha behind?"
"Why is he honored by hosts in the cave, and even by the *kiṃkaras*? Having heard this, while everyone listened, the sage replied:
Listen with your assemblies; I shall tell this: Prabhāsa is the supreme benefactor. He is the very self of Sūryaprabha; there is no difference between these two.
Moreover, there is no other equal to Prabhāsa in terms of valor and power; due to his merits in previous births, he possesses this very cave.
I shall relate to you exactly who he was and what he was like in former times: there once lived a preeminent Dānava named Namuci.
For that great hero who was devoted to giving, there was nothing whatsoever that he would not give—even if it were harmful—to anyone who requested it.
Having performed ascetic penance as a smoke-drinker for ten thousand years, he obtained from Viriñca the boon of being incapable of being slain by iron, stone, or wood.
Then, having conquered Indra once and for all, he made him flee in all directions; thereupon, the sage Kaśyapa, being entreated by the gods, brought about a peace treaty with him.
Then, their hostilities having ceased, those gods and asuras, having deliberated together, approached the Ocean of Milk and churned it with Mount Mandara.
Just as Acyuta and the others obtained their shares, beginning with Kamala, so too did Namuci obtain the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
Other gods and asuras received various portions assigned separately by Brahmā, which arose from the ocean while it was being churned.
When the nectar had been obtained from the churning and taken away by the gods, enmity arose once again between those Asuras and them.
Then, in the battle between the gods and the asuras, whichever asura was slain by the gods, Uccaiḥśravas would smell him and restore him to life at that very moment.
By that [means], the Daityas and Dānavas became invincible to the gods; thereupon, Bṛhaspati spoke in private to the despondent Śakra.
There is one means for you in this matter; perform it without delay. Go yourself and beg that supreme horse from Namuci.
Even though you are an adversary, he will not fail to give you that horse; nor will he let his reputation for generosity, accumulated over lifetimes, be shattered.
Thus addressed by the preceptor of the gods, Mahendra, together with the thirty deities, went and begged Namuci for that horse Uccaiḥśravas.
"Even Indra himself does not depart from me with his face turned away when he comes as a petitioner; therefore, having become Namuci, how could I not give him the horse?"
If that fame for generosity which I have long cultivated throughout the worlds has now withered away, then what is the use to me of prosperity or even life itself?
Having reflected thus, the noble-minded Namuci gave that Uccaiḥśravas to Śakra, even though he was being restrained by Śukra.

Then, having gained the confidence of Namuci by giving him a horse, he struck him with the foam of the Gaṅgā; just as the slayer of Vṛtra killed him who was otherwise invulnerable to weapons and other means by hurling the thunderbolt in the form of foam.
Alas! The thirst for enjoyment in saṃsāra has such a miserable end that even the gods do not fear impropriety or ill repute because they are carried away by it.
Having learned of that, Namuci’s mother Danu, tormented by grief, made a resolve through the power of her asceticism for the sake of pacifying her sorrow.
"May that same powerful Namuci be born again in my womb, so that he may be invincible by all the gods in battles."
Then, having been conceived in her womb, he was born again as an Asura, composed of all kinds of jewels, named Prabala because of his possession of great strength.
That powerful lord of the Dānavas, a man of merit who performed intense austerities and delighted even his suppliants with his very life-breaths, conquered Indra a hundred times.
Then, having consulted together, the gods approached him and made this request: "By all means, give us your body for the sake of the human sacrifice."
Having heard that, he gave his own body even to those enemies; for the noble do not turn their backs on those who come as supplicants, but rather relinquish their very lives.
Then that powerful Dānava was cut into pieces by the gods; today he has been born again in the world of men with the body of Prabhāsa.
Thus, in the beginning he was Namuci, and then he became Prabala; this very person is now Prabhāsa, who, through the power of that merit, is invincible to his enemies.
And that powerful medicinal cave belonging to him was connected to Prabhāsa; therefore, it was under his control along with its attendants.
And below that, in Pātāla, is the palace of Prabala, where he has twelve principal wives, all beautifully adorned.
Various jewels and diverse weapons, wish-fulfilling gems and a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], as well as warriors and horses.
All that belongs to Prabhāsa was acquired by him in former lives; such is this Prabhāsa, so nothing about him is at all wonderful.

Having thus heard this from the young sage, Sūryaprabha and the others, who were radiant with their vows, set out at that very moment to reach the powerful palace located in the subterranean realm, entering through its cavernous openings.

Having entered there and seized his former wives, the wish-fulfilling gem, the horses, and the Asura warriors, Prabhāsa emerged alone with all their wealth taken; he then greatly gratified Sūryaprabha.

Then Samayasunītha, accompanied by King Sumeru and others, as well as by kings and ministers, quickly attained his desired success; and that Sūryaprabha returned once more to his own military encampment.

There, among those lords of asuras, humans, and others who had each returned to their own dwellings, he spent the remainder of the night on a bed of kusha grass, restraining himself once more, consecrated for battle.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave: Then, in the morning, Sūryaprabha set out from that grove of ascetics on Mount Sumeru together with his armies, desiring to conquer Śrutaśarman.
Having reached the vicinity of Mount Trikūṭa, which was his residence, he encamped there after driving back that army with his own force.
And when he had settled there, together with Sumeru, Maya, and the others, while they were seated in the assembly hall, an envoy belonging to the Lord of Trikūṭa arrived.
And having arrived, he spoke thus to Sumeru, the lord of the sky-goers: "The king, the father of Śrutaśarman, has sent this message to you."
"While you were far away, we never once performed the customary rites of hospitality for you; yet today you have arrived within our domain together with your guests."
"Therefore, we shall now provide you with hospitality as is fitting. Having heard this message from his enemy, Sumeru replied to him.
"Excellent! You shall not find another guest who is a worthy recipient equal to us; the fruit of hospitality will be realized in this very world, not in the next."
Thus, when Sumeru replied, "Let hospitality be prepared," that messenger returned to his own master exactly as he had come.
