Then Sūryaprabha and the others, situated on an elevated place, beheld their own armies encamped separately.
Then Sunītha said to his father, Māyāsura: "Tell us here the distribution of the chariots and other equipment within our army."
Having said, "I shall do so; listen," and pointing with his finger, that omniscient lord of the Dānavas proceeded to speak as follows.
There were Subāhu, Nirghāta, Muṣṭika, Gohara, as well as Pralamba, Pramātha, Kaṅkaṭa, and Piṅgala.
And these kings, Vasudatta and the others, are but half-charioteers; as are Aṅkurin, Suviśāla, Daṇḍin, Bhūṣaṇa, and Somila.
Unmattaka, Devaśarman, the youth Pitṛśarman, and these others beginning with Haridatta—all of them are considered to be Pūrṇaratha.
Prakampana, Darpita, Kumbhīra, Mātṛpālita, Mahābhaṭa, Sograbhaṭa, Vīrasvāmī, and Surādhara.
Bhaṇḍīra, Siṃhadatta, Guṇavarman along with Kīṭaka, Bhīma, and Bhayaṃkara—all these are chariot-warriors of double strength.
Virocana, Vīrasena, Yajñasena, and then Khujjara; Indravarman, Śabaraka, Krūrakarman, and Nirāsaka.
O son, these three chariot-warriors—the princes Suśarman, Bāhuśālin, and this Viśākha Krodhana—would each be possessed of triple strength.
And Pracaṇḍa—these princes each possessed four times the strength of a chariot; they were Juñjarī, Vīravarman, and Pravīravara.
Then there were Supratijña, Amarārāma, and Caṇḍadatta the fowler; and also Siṃhabhaṭa, Vyāghrabhaṭa, and Śatrubhaṭa—these three.
These kings and princes are chariots possessing five qualities; however, this prince Ugravarman would be a chariot possessing six qualities.
Rājaputra, Viśākha, Sutantu, Sugama, and Narendraśarman—these are considered chariot-warriors endowed with sevenfold qualities.
Furthermore, this son of King Sahasrāyu is a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*); indeed, Śatānīka is the leader of a host of great chariot-warriors.
Subhāsa, Harṣa, and Vimala were the companions of Sūryaprabha; and there were also those named Mahābuddhi and Acala, as well as Priyaṃkara and Śubhaṃkara.
These are the great chariot-warriors: Yajñaruci, Dharmaruci, as well as Viśvaruci, Bhāsa, and Siddhārtha—these three.
The ministers of Sūryaprabha shall be leaders of hosts of great chariot-warriors; Prahasta and Mahārtha shall be his leaders of hosts of atiratha warriors.
The two leaders of the chariot-hosts were Prajñāḍhya and Sthirabuddhi; likewise, there were the Dānavas Sarvadamana and Pramathana.
Dhūmaketu, Pravahaṇa, Vajrapañjara, Kālacakra, and Marudvega—these are the chariot-warriors and great chariot-warriors.
Prakampana, Siṃhanāda, Rathayūthapa, Atirathayūthapa, Mahāmāya, Kāmbalika, and this Kālakampanaka as well.
Rathāti, Prahṛṣṭaroman, and Ceti—these four are the lords of the asuras; they are the sovereigns over the sons who are commanders of the hosts of atirathas.
And this general of the army, Prabhāsa, is equal to Sūryaprabha; and this Śrīkuñjarakumāra is the son of Sumeru.
"These two are the leaders of the hosts of great chariot-warriors. Thus, these and other heroes in our army are surrounded by their respective forces.
Although they are superior in number in the enemy army, they will not be sufficient against our forces once Maheśvara is pleased.
While the Asura Maya was thus speaking to Sunītha, another messenger arrived from the presence of Śrutaśarman’s father.
And he said, "The lord of Trikūṭa speaks thus to you: 'This so-called battle is indeed a great festival for heroes.'"
This is his perilous territory; therefore, let us depart from here and go to a region of vast extent called the village of Kalāpa.
Having heard this, Sunītha and the others, saying "So be it," all went with their armies and accompanied by Sūryaprabha to that village of Kalāpa.
Śrutaśarman and the others likewise, intent on battle, arrived at that very place surrounded by their Vidyādhara forces.
Seeing the elephants in Śrutaśarman’s army, Sūryaprabha and the others brought forth their own elephant force, mounted upon their celestial chariots.
Then Dāmodara, the best of the Vidyādharas, formed for Śrutaśarman’s army within the host a great needle-shaped array.
There, Śrutaśarman himself stood at the side with his ministers; Dāmodara was in front, and the other great chariot-warriors were elsewhere.
In the army of Sūryaprabha as well, Prabhāsa, the commander of the host, formed an "arrow-head" (ardhacandra) array, and he himself took his place in its center.
Sakuñjarakumāra and Prahasta stood at his two flanks, while Sūryaprabha, Sunītha, and all the others remained behind him.
On Mount Sumeru and in its vicinity, where the prince Suvasa was present, the musical instruments of war were sounded by both armies alike.
And meanwhile, the sky was filled with gods who had come to witness the battle, together with Indra, the world-protectors, and the celestial nymphs.
And there Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Universe, accompanied by Pārvatī and followed by the gods, the Gaṇas, the Bhūtas, and the Mothers, arrived.
And the Blessed Lord Brahmā arrived, accompanied by Sāvitrī and the others, as well as the Vedas in embodied form, the Śāstras, and all the great ṛṣis.
And Lord Hari arrived, borne on the chariot of the king of birds, holding his discus weapon, accompanied by goddesses such as Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and others.
Kaśyapa also arrived with his wife, as did the Ādityas and the Vasus; the lords of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas, as well as the Asuras headed by Prahlāda.
When the expanse of the sky was covered by them, a great battle ensued between those two armies, terrible with the clashing of weapons and filled with a mighty roar.
Then, when the circle of the quarters was completely covered by a dense web of arrows, flashes of fire and lightning were produced from the mutual friction of the shafts.
Rivers of blood issued forth, filled with streams of gore from the multitudes of elephants and horses wounded by weapons, wherein the bodies of heroes were carried away like crocodiles.
For the sake of the festival, that battle took place between the heroes, the jackals, and the spirits, as they danced, leaped in the blood, and howled.
When the tumultuous battle had subsided and countless soldiers had been slain, the distinction between one's own army and the enemy's forces could gradually be discerned.
And as the names of the heroic adversaries who have engaged in battle with Sumeru—beginning with Sūryaprabha and the others—are heard in succession, [the earth trembles].
Formerly, there occurred a duel between King Subāhu and the lord of the Vidyādharas named Aṭṭahāsa.
As he was fighting for a very long time and pierced by arrows, Aṭṭahāsa severed Subāhu’s head with a crescent-headed shaft.
Seeing Subāhu slain, Muṣṭika rushed forward in a rage; he too fell, struck in the heart by an arrow from that very Aṭṭahāsa.
When Muṣṭika was slain, the enraged king named Pralamba rushed forward with a loud roar and fought him with showers of arrows.
Aṭṭahāsa, too, repeatedly striking that army and piercing them in their vital organs, cast the hero Pralamba down upon the back of his chariot.
Seeing Pralamba slain, the king named Mohana rushed forward and struck Aṭṭahāsa with his arrows.
Then Aṭṭahāsa struck down Mohana, whose bow was severed, whose charioteer was slain, and who had been overwhelmed by a powerful blow.
Seeing those four slain by the clever Aṭṭahāsa, Śrutaśarman’s army, intent on victory, roared with joy.
Seeing that, Harṣa, the companion of Sūryaprabha, became enraged and, together with his army, rushed toward Aṭṭahāsa and his troops.
Having warded off his arrows with his own shafts and having struck down his army, he slew the charioteer and, after cutting through the bow along with its banner two or three times, [proceeded].
When Harṣa shattered Aṭṭahāsa’s head with his arrows, the latter, vomiting blood, fell from his chariot to the ground.
When Aṭṭahāsa was slain, such a commotion arose in that battle that in an instant those two armies were reduced to half their original strength.
Slain there, the horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers fell indeed; yet at the front of the battle, only headless trunks (kabandhas) rose up.
Then the lord of the Vidyādharas named Vikṛtadaṃṣṭra, enraged by the death of Aṭṭahāsa, approached and overwhelmed him with arrows.
Harṣa also, having shaken off his arrows, slew him along with his banner and charioteer, and after killing his chariot-horses, severed his head adorned with beautiful earrings.
When Vikṛtadaṃṣṭra was slain, the Vidyādhara king known as Cakravāla, filled with indignation, rushed toward Harṣa.
Cakravāla slew Harṣa in battle, who was repeatedly deprived of his bow, exhausted in combat, and whose other weapons were shattered.
Out of anger at that, King Pramātha approached and fought him; he too was then slain by Cakravāla in the battle.
In the same manner, he also struck down four other leading kings one by one in succession as they rushed forward there, encircled by his retinue.
Kaṅkaṭa, Viśāla, Pracaṇḍa, and likewise Aṅkurī—seeing that, the king named Nirghāta rushed toward him in fury.
Those two, Cakravāla and Nirghāta, fighting for a long time in succession, eventually became foot-soldiers after their chariots had been pulverized by one another.
Both of them, wielding swords and discs and meeting in a state of fury, fell to the ground with their heads split in two by sword-strokes.
Seeing those two heroes fallen and both armies despondent, Kālakampana, the lord of the Vidyādharas, came to the front of the battle.
And a prince named Prakampana rushed toward him; there, in an instant, he was struck down by that Kālakampana.
When he had fallen, five other charioteers rushed toward him: Jālika, Caṇḍadatta, Gopaka, and Somila as well.
And Pitṛśarman and all of them loosed their arrows at him; but Kālakampana rendered even those five, who were deprived of their chariots, powerless.
Piercing him simultaneously in the heart with five iron arrows, he struck him down; at that, the sky-dwellers raised a shout, while the humans and asuras were despondent.
Then four other chariots rushed forward at the same time: Unmattaka, Praśasta, Vilamba, and Dhuraṃdhara.
Kālakampana slew all of them with ease; likewise, he struck down six other chariot-warriors who had likewise rushed forward.
Tejika, Geyika, Vegila, and likewise Śākhila, Bhadraṅkara, and Daṇḍin—these great car-warriors possessed vast armies.
Furthermore, in battle, he slew another five combined avadhis: Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Kumbhīra, Vikaṭa, and Savilocana.
Seeing that slaughter wrought in battle by Kālakampana, a prince named Sugaṇa rushed forward to face him.
He engaged in battle with him for as long as both remained equal, until they both became deprived of their chariots, their horses and charioteers having been slain.
Then Kālakampana, remaining on foot, struck Sugana—who was also on foot—with a sword-fight upon the ground.
And at that moment, as if distressed by witnessing such an inconceivable battle between humans and Vidyādharas, the sun went to its setting.
Not only was the battlefield filled with a flood of blood, but even the sky turned crimson as it took on the hue of twilight.
Then, while the spirits together with the headless trunks were intent on the twilight dance, those two armies withdrew from the battle and went to their respective camps.
On that day, three heroes were slain in Śrutaśarman’s army, while thirty-three preeminent warriors were killed in the army of Sauryaprabha.
Deeply distressed by that death of his kinsmen, friends, and others, Sūryaprabha spent that night without the women of the inner apartments.
Remaining sleepless, he spent that night conversing with his ministers about various accounts of battle, once again intent upon war.
And his wives, grieving for their slain kinsmen, met together on that night, having come to one another for mutual consolation.
Even on this occasion for weeping, they engaged in various kinds of conversation; for there is no moment for women in which their talk does not take recourse in something other than themselves.
In the course of that conversation, a certain princess there said this: "It is a marvel! How is it that my noble husband has slept today without his consort?"
Having heard that, another spoke: "How can my noble husband, who is today so distressed by the slaughter of his own kin in battle, find pleasure among women?"
Then another said: "If he were to obtain a beautiful young maiden, he would forget that very sorrow this very moment."
Then the other said: "Do not say so; even though he was a libertine among women, nevertheless, he would not have been such as this in this kind of suffering."
While they were speaking thus, one among them said with astonishment: "Tell me, why is my noble husband so devoted to women that he is like this?"
Even though he had taken many wives, he was never satisfied as he continually took ever-new princesses.
Having heard this, one among them, clever and named Manovatī, said: "Listen to how kings come to have many favorites."
Due to differences in country, form, age, gestures, knowledge, and so forth, the qualities of excellent women are diverse; no single woman is endowed with all qualities.
Women born in regions such as Karṇāṭa, Lāṭa, Saurāṣṭra, and Madhyadeśa delight [their lovers] with their respective local customs.
Some of these beautiful women bear [the fruit] with faces resembling the autumnal moon; others do so with breasts that are high, firm, and like golden jars.
Others with their hips resembling the throne of Smara, and still others with their various limbs, each enchanting with its own beauty.
One had limbs as fair as gold, another was dark like the priyaṅgu plant, and yet another was bright red; at the mere sight of them, they captivated the eyes.
One was fresh and lovely; another was in the full bloom of youth; another was radiant with the mature delight of passion and the spreading splendor of her amorous charms.
One woman shines while laughing; another is charming even in anger; one moves like an elephant, while another is radiant like a swan.
One woman speaks as if sprinkling the ear with nectar; another shines by her very nature as she gazes with the playful movement of her eyebrows.
One woman is pleasing through her dancing; another shines with her singing; yet another beloved woman is radiant through her knowledge of playing the lute and other instruments.
One was skilled in external pleasures, another was fond of internal ones; one was radiant with ornaments, while another was adorned by her cleverness.
Another, skilled in capturing her husband's heart, enjoys good fortune; how much more could I say? For many other women possess various distinct virtues as well.
Thus, in this world, some excellent woman may possess some particular virtue, but there are none in the three worlds who possess every virtue.
Therefore, those lords who have attained their rank through the enjoyment of various flavors indeed always take new wives, even after having already taken others.
But superior men never desire another's wife under any circumstances; therefore, this fault would belong to our noble lord, and not to us, for we are capable of enduring jealousy.
Thus were the wives of Sūryaprabha, beginning with Manovatī, described; and others, such as Madanasenā and the rest, likewise related their stories in succession.

Then, beyond hundreds, those women—free from restraint and unimpeded—taught one another even the technical methods for the acts of sexual pleasure. Meeting in the course of conversation, their minds intent on the flow of talk, they said to each other: "Oh, there is nothing here that these women do not utter!"

Then, somehow that long conversation of theirs came to an end, and that night gradually reached its close; meanwhile, Sūryaprabha, desiring only to observe the moment when the darkness vanished, remained intent on conquering the enemy forces.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the Sūryaprabha-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The fifth wave begins.
Then at dawn, Sūryaprabha and his companions went to the battlefield, and Śrutaśarman and his followers likewise returned, fully armed and accompanied by their armies.
Furthermore, the gods along with Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, together with the asuras, yakṣas, uragas, and gandharvas, came to witness the battle.
Dāmodara formed a wheel-array (*cakravyūha*) against the army of Śrutaśarman, while Prabhāsa created a thunderbolt-array (*vajravyūha*) against the army of Sūryaprabha.
Then the battle between those two armies commenced, deafening the horizons with the sounds of trumpets and the shouts of great warriors.
"Brave warriors struck down by sharp weapons pierce my mandala"—as if out of fear of this, the sun became shrouded within a net of arrows.
Then, by the command of Sūryaprabha, Prabhāsa broke through the wheel-array formed by Dāmodara, which was difficult for anyone else to pierce, and entered.
And Dāmodara himself, having reached that breach in the formation, blocked it; and Prabhāsa fought him there, alone upon a single chariot.
Then, seeing that he had entered alone, Sūryaprabha subsequently dispatched fifteen great chariot-warriors after him.
Prakampana, Dhūmaketu, Kālakampanaka, Mahāmāya, Marudvega, Prahasta, and Vajrapañjara.
Kālacakra, Pramathana, Siṃhanāda, Sakambala, Vikaṭākṣa, Pravahaṇa, and that Kuñjarakumāraka.
And all those great chariot-warriors, having rushed forward, went to the gate of the formation toward that best of Asura lords, whose hair stood on end with joy.
In that regard, Dāmodara first displayed his own prowess, in that he alone fought against those fifteen together.
Seeing the sage Nārada standing by his side, Vāsava said to Sūryaprabha and all the others who were incarnations of the Asuras:
Śrutaśarman is a portion of me, and all these Vidyādharas are portions of the gods; therefore, O Sage, this is in truth a battle between the gods and the asuras through a strategic artifice.
And in that matter, Hari, the companion of the gods, is always present; this Dāmodara is a portion of him, and thus he fights here.
While Śakra was speaking thus, fourteen great chariot-warriors arrived to assist this Dāmodara, the commander of the army.
Brahmagupta, Vāyubala, Yamadaṃṣṭra, Suroṣaṇa, Roṣāvaroha, Atibala, Tejaḥprabha, and Dhuraṃdhara.
Kuberadatta, Varuṇaśarman, Kambalika, as well as Vīra, Duṣṭamadanaka, and both Dohana and Ārohaṇa.
Those fifteen heroes, accompanied by Dāmodara, also checked those heroes belonging to Sūryaprabha who were fighting at the front of the battle array.
Then, hand-to-hand combat took place among them there one with another; Prakampana engaged in a battle of missiles with Dāmodara.
Dhūmaketu fought with Brahmadatta, while Mahāmāya fought together with Atibala.
The Dānava Kālakampana fought with Tejaḥprabha, and the great Asura Marudvega fought with Vāyubala.
Vajrapañjara fought together with Yamadaṃṣṭra, and Kālacakra, the best of asuras, fought together with Suroṣaṇa.
Pramathana waged war with Kuberadatta, and the Daitya lord Siṃhanāda fought alongside Varuṇaśarman.
The Dānava Pravahaṇa engaged in battle with Duṣṭadamana, his hair standing on end with joy and his face clouded by a descent of rage.
Vikaṭākṣa engaged in combat with Dhuraṃdhara, and Kambalika fought with Kambalika.
And that young elephant, Prahasta, was accompanied by Ārohaṇa, who was also known as Mahotpāta, and by Dohana.
While these duels between great chariot-warriors were thus taking place there at the front of the battle array, Sunītha spoke to Maya.
Alas! These heroic chariot-warriors of ours, though skilled in various modes of combat, have been hemmed in by these rival chariot-fighters; behold them as they enter the formation.
And Prabhāsa alone entered here first without hesitation; therefore we do not know whose [victory] it will be, nor what indeed will happen here.
Having heard this, the youth Suvāsaka said to him: "Even all those in the three worlds, including gods, asuras, and humans, would not be sufficient."
How much more so for these sky-dwellers regarding this single radiance? Therefore, how can such groundless doubt arise in you, even though you possess knowledge?
While this young sage was speaking thus, the Vidyādhara Kālakampana advanced to face Prabhāsa in battle.
Then Prabhāsa said to him: "Ho there! You have indeed done us a great wrong; today we shall see your prowess right here."
Having said this, Prabhāsa loosed a series of arrows at him; Kālakampana, for his part, covered him with sharp shafts.
Then those two, the Vidyādhara and the human, fought each other with a battle of missiles and counter-missiles, providing a marvel to the world.
Then Prabhāsa brought down the banner with one shaft and slew Kālakampana’s charioteer with a second.
With four [arrows] he cut down the four horses, with one the bow, with two the hands, with two the two arms, and with two each the two ears.
And Prabhāsa, displaying marvelous agility, severed the head of his enemy with a single sharp-edged arrow.
Thus, with the fury arising from the many heroes previously slain, Prabhāsa seemed to effect the subjugation of Kālakampana.
And seeing that lord of the Vidyādharas slain by humans and Asuras, the sky-dwellers immediately raised a cry and fell into despair.
Then the lord of Mount Kālañjara, named Vidyutprabha, the sovereign of the Vidyādharas, rushed toward Prabhāsa in a fit of rage.
As he was fighting, Prabhāsa cut down his great banner and repeatedly severed his bow each time it was taken up again.
Then, having flown up through his illusory power and remaining concealed in the sky like a flash of lightning, that ashamed Vidyutprabha rained down swords, maces, and other weapons upon Prabhāsa.
Prabhāsa, too, having warded off that succession of weapons with his own missiles, made that sky-dweller visible by employing the Prakāśana weapon.
Having discharged the great Āgneya weapon, he caused it to fall from the sky onto the surface of the earth, its brilliance burning and its life extinguished like a flash of lightning.
Seeing that, Śrutaśarman spoke to those great chariot-warriors: "Behold, by this man two leaders of hosts of great chariot-warriors have been slain."
"Therefore, do you endure this? Let him be slain by all of you acting together! Hearing that, eight chariot-warriors, filled with rage, surrounded Prabhāsa.
There was a certain lord of the Vidyādharas, a leader of chariot-divisions who dwelt on the great mountain Kaṅkaṭaka, renowned by the name Ūrdhvaroman.
The lord of mountains, Dharaṇīdhara, was named Vikrośana; and the second was Mahāratha, the sovereign of the Vidyādharas.
And the third was Indumālin, whose banner bore the emblem of a pleasure-mountain; he was a hero, a lord of a host of great chariot-warriors, and a sovereign of the Vidyādharas.
And the fourth king, an inhabitant of the Malaya mountains known as Kākāṇḍaka, was a leader of chariot-divisions and the best among the sky-dwellers.
The lord of mountains named Niketa was the fifth, and the sixth was Darpavāha; the seventh was named Dhūrtavahana, the lord of Añjanagiri.
These two are Vidyādharas, both commanders of great chariot-divisions; the seventh is King Gardabharatha on Mount Kumuda.
He who is named Varāhasvāmī, a leader of a host of great chariot-warriors—he, in that form, is the eighth [son], Dundubhi, the lord of the earth, a chariot-warrior of excellent intellect.
Having arrived with these eight, Prabhāsa shook off the released arrows and simultaneously pierced all of them with his own shafts.
He struck down the horses of one, and likewise the charioteer of another; he cut down the banner of one, and severed the bow of another.
Having pierced Medhāvara squarely in the heart with four arrows, they struck him down upon the surface of the earth, instantly depriving him of his life.
Then, while fighting others with his hair tied up in a knot, he cut off the head of Ūrdhvaroman from nearby with an añjalika arrow.
Having severed the necks of the remaining six with individual arrows, Prabhāsa struck them down, leaving their horses and charioteers slain.
Then a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon his head, while the gods and kings were emboldened and the celestial beings were cast into shadow.
Then four other great chariot-warriors, skilled archers, were dispatched there by Śrutaśarman; they besieged that Prabhāsa.
One was named Kācaraka, the lord of Mount Kuraṇḍaka; the second was Diṇḍimālin, who took refuge on the Five Mountains.
Vibhāvasu was the third king on the Jayapura mountain, and the fourth was named Dhavala, the ruler of Bhūmituṇḍaka.
Those supreme sky-dwellers, lords of hosts of great chariot-warriors, simultaneously discharged five hundred arrows each at Prabhāsa.
And Prabhāsa, in turn, with effortless ease, struck down one by one their banner, their bow, and their charioteer.
With four arrows he struck down the horses, and with one he felled his head; having thus finished each one with eight shafts, he let out a roar.
Then, once again at the command of Śrutaśarman, four other Vidyādharas arrived for him in the battle at Prabhāsa.
One was named Bhadraṃkara, dark as a blue lotus, born in the field of Viśvāvasu from Budha; and the second was Niyantraka.
The third, known as Kālakopa, was born in the field of Jambhaka from Bhauma, possessing a radiance like fire, and in the field of Dāmodara as well.
Born from Śanaiścara, he was exceedingly black with tawny hair; he was born in the field of the Moon from the planet who is the minister of Mahendra.
The fourth was named Vikramaśakti, possessing a golden luster; among these, three were leaders of hosts, commanders of throngs of great chariot-warriors.
But the fourth was Mahāvīra, whose prowess exceeded that of the others; and those arrogant ones fought Prabhāsa with divine weapons.
Prabhāsa warded off those weapons with the Nārāyaṇa-weapon; and with effortless ease, he severed the bow of each one of them eight times over.
Then, having parried the darts, maces, and other weapons hurled by them, he deprived them all of their horses and charioteers and rendered them carless.
Having seen that, Śrutaśarman quickly dispatched ten other lords of the Vidyādharas, who were commanders of hosts of chariot-warriors.
In the field of Ketumāleśvara, two sons of the Aśvins were born, known as Dama and Niyama, whose forms resembled their own essential nature.
Vikrama, Saṃkrama, Parākrama, and then Ākrama; Sammardana, Mardana, Pramardana, and Vimardana.
They were equal to the eight sons of the Vasus, who were born from Makaranda as his field-born sons; when they arrived, those first ones also mounted other chariots.
Amidst those fourteen complete hosts, all united and raining down arrows, Prabhāsa fought alone, truly unshakable—how marvelous!
Then, at the command of Sūryaprabha, Kuñjarakumāra and Prahasta, having abandoned the battle and grasped their weapons, departed from the front of the array.
Leaping up into the path of the sky, those two of white and dark forms approached his side like another Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Those two foot-soldiers, with their bows broken and their charioteers slain, threw both Dama and Niyama—who were standing in their chariots—into utter confusion.
Out of fear, as those two ascended into the sky, Kuñjarakumāra and Prahasta also climbed up after them, both bearing their weapons.
Seeing that, Sūryaprabha immediately dispatched his two ministers, Mahābuddhi and Acalabuddhi, to serve as charioteers for the two of them.
Then Prahasta, together with Kuñjarakumāra, saw those two, even though they were invisible through the application of the magic ointment of the siddhas.
He pierced them likewise with floods of arrows, so that both those sons of Vidyādharas, Dama and Niyama, fled away.
And Prabhāsa, fighting along with the remaining twelve, repeatedly cut down their bows even as they were being drawn.
Prahasta approached and simultaneously slew the charioteers of all of them; that Kuñjarakumāra, too, struck down their horses.
Then all twelve of them, being without chariots, gathered together there; being struck by the three heroes, they fled from the battle.
Then Śrutaśarman, agitated by grief, anger, and shame, dispatched two other Vidyādharas, both leaders of hosts of chariot-warriors and great chariot-warriors.
From the Moon, born in the field of the Lord of the Moon-mountain (the Himalayas), there arose one named Candragupta, as lovely as another moon.
He brought forth his second minister, named Nagaraṅga, who was born in the field of Dhuraṃdhara, the lord of mountains, and possessed great luster.
Those two, having discharged floods of arrows, were rendered chariotless in an instant; abandoned by Prabhāsa and the others, they both fled from the battle.
Then, while the men and the asuras were shouting, Śrutaśarman himself arrived, accompanied by four great chariot-warriors.
They were born from the self of Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhaga, Aryaman, and Pūṣan, and were known respectively as Mahāugha, Ārohaṇa, Utpāta, and Vetravat.
By the sons born of the womb of four kings of the Vidyādharas—beginning with Citrapāda—who were lords of mountains such as Malaya and possessed abundant valor;
Then, blinded by extreme indignation, those three—Prabhāsa and the others—fought there against Śrutaśarman with him as their fifth.
Then the mass of arrows released by them against one another shone in the sky like a canopy spread out by the Fortune of Battle while the sun blazed.
Then those Vidyādharas also returned to that battle; they who had previously fled from the conflict after being deprived of their chariots now came back once more.
Then, having seen those many others of his own, such as Śrutaśarman and the rest, assembled for battle, Sūryaprabha [beheld] Prabhāsa and the others engaged in fasting.
Then he dispatched his great chariot-warriors, his friends headed by Prajñāḍhya, as well as the princes led by Vīrasena and Śatānīka.
As they traveled there through the sky, Sūryaprabha dispatched their chariots along the celestial path by means of his Bhūtāsana aerial vehicle.
Then, when all those archers had mounted their chariots, the remaining lords of the Vidyādharas also arrived from Śrutaśarman’s side.
A battle ensued between those lords of the Vidyādharas and Prabhāsa and his companions, bringing about the destruction of great armies.
And there, in those head-to-head battles between the two armies, various great chariot-warriors—humans, asuras, and sky-dwellers—were slain by one another.
Dhūmralocana, along with his followers, was slain by Vīrasena; and Vīrasena, too, having been deprived of his chariot, was killed by Hariśarman.
The heroic Vidyādhara Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by Abhimanyu; likewise, Abhimanyu was slain by Sunetra, and Haribhaṭa as well.
Sunetra was struck down by Prabhāsa after his head was severed; both Mahāyu and Jvālāmālī were also killed by one another.
Kumbhīraka, though sapless, struck with his very teeth; and Suśarman, of fierce prowess, was rendered short by the severing of his arms.
These three—Śatrubhaṭa, Vyāghrabhaṭa, and Siṃhabhaṭa—were also slain by that Vidyādhara king using a magical vehicle.
Pravahaṇa was killed by both Suroha and Viroha, and those two were killed by Siṃhabala, who dwells in the cremation ground.
Then there were Pretavāhana, Siṃhabala, Kapilaka, Citrāpīḍa, and thereafter the lord of the Vidyādharas, Jagajjvara.
Then there were the heroic Kāntāpati, Suvarṇa of great strength, and the two lords of the Vidyādharas, Kāmaghana and Krodhapati.
Then King Baladeva and Vicitrāpīḍa—these ten were struck down by the prince Śatānīka.
When those heroes had thus been slain and he beheld the destruction of the Vidyādharas, Śrutaśarman himself rushed toward Śatānīka in a rage.
Then, until the end of the day, there occurred between those two a great battle that caused the destruction of their armies—an event that was a marvel even to the gods.
Hundreds of headless trunks rose up on all sides and provided a support for the spirits at the onset of the twilight dance festival.

Then, at the close of day, the Vidyādharas—distressed by the destruction of their vast army and grieving for their slain kinsmen—and the mortals and Asuras, having achieved victory by force, both withdrew from the battle and returned to their respective abodes.

At that moment, two Vidyādharas who had been announced by Sumeru as the lords of the chariot-leaders arrived there; having approached Sūryaprabha—leaving Śrutaśarman’s faction behind—and having performed their salutations, they spoke to him.

We two possess the excellent illusory perception of the Mahāyāna, and this Siṃhabala is the third; having attained the siddhi of lordship over the great cremation grounds, we are unassailable by other lords of the Vidyādharas.
Once, while we were dwelling happily within that cremation ground, there approached our presence a yoginī named Śarabhānanā, who was ever-gracious and possessed of divine, great power.

"Tell us, where were you staying, and what unprecedented thing did you see there, O Blessed One? Thus questioned by us after we had prostrated ourselves before her, she spoke of the events as follows, "O King."
I went with the yoginīs to see my own lord, the god Mahākāla; and there, a certain master of vetālas approached me and spoke to him in my presence.

"O Lord, O Tejaprabha, behold how the daughter of Agnikākṣa—the great commander of our army, who was slain by the lords of the Vidyādharas—is being carried off unseasonably, she of most precious form."

"O Lord, she has been declared by the Siddhas to be destined to become the wife of the universal emperor of the Vidyādharas; therefore, release her and show us favor before she is carried away by force to a distant place."
Having heard these words of the Vetāla from the corpse, he commanded us, "Go and release her! Then, having traveled through the air, we recovered that maiden.
And while he was saying, "I am carrying her away for the sake of Saccakravartin Śrutaśarman," we, having paralyzed Tejaḥprabha by our own power, brought him here and presented her to the Lord.

"And a maiden of such radiance was offered by him to his own kinsman; I have seen this truly unprecedented thing. Having stayed there for some days and having paid homage to that deity, I have come here."
When she had spoken these words, that Śarabhānanā yoginī was then questioned by us in this way: "Tell us, who will become the sovereign of the Vidyādharas? For you surely know everything."
When she had said, "Alas, Sūryaprabha shall indeed become [king]," Siṃhabala said to us: "This is surely untrue; for the gods, including Indra, have girded their loins on the side of Śrutaśarman."
Having heard this, the noble lady said to us: "If you do not believe me, listen as I speak; a battle between Sūryaprabha and Śrutaśarman will take place before long."
"When this Siṃhabala is slain in battle by a human being in your very presence, you two, upon seeing this token, will recognize that these words of mine are true."
Having said this much, that yoginī indeed departed, and those days passed away; and now this has been seen here by a mortal with his own eyes: that Siṃhabala has been slain.
Having ascertained that you alone are the sovereign lord of all sky-dwellers, we have taken refuge at your pair of lotus feet and abide by your command.

When they had spoken thus, Sūryaprabha, together with Maya and the others, having placed his faith in those two lords of the sky-goers who were joyful and well-versed in the Mahāyāna, honored them as was fitting.

Having heard that, Indra, sending Viśvāvasu as a messenger, provided consolation to Śrutaśarman, who was there exceedingly distressed; for out of affection for him, he sent this message to grant him courage: "Be steadfast; accompanied by all the gods, I shall provide you assistance at the head of the battle tomorrow morning."

And he, his joy arising from witnessing the destruction of the enemy forces and having seen the ruin of the opposing side at the head of the battle, once again abandoned his own beloveds and, accompanied by his ministers, entered his quarters that night, Sūryaprabha.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave: Then, at night, while lying on his bed without his weapons and eager for battle, Sūryaprabha spoke to his minister Vītabhīti.
"I have no sleep; therefore, my friend, tell me some unprecedented story centered on a heroic being that will provide diversion during this night."
Having heard these words of Sūryaprabha, he, free from fear, said, "As you command," and related this story.
There is on this earth a city named Ujjayinī, which is the ornament of this world, filled with every kind of jewel and adorned with most pure virtues.
In that city there was a king named Mahāsena, who was beloved by the virtuous, the sole repository of all arts, and who bore the appearance of both the sun and the moon.
He had a queen named Aśokavatī who was as dear to him as his own life; in beauty, there was no other woman like her in the three worlds.
While that king was ruling his kingdom together with that queen, there was a brahmin named Guṇaśarman who was both honored and beloved by him.

And that brave, exceedingly handsome young Brahmin, who had mastered the Vedas and sciences and was skilled in the arts as well as in hand-to-hand and missile weapons, constantly attended upon that king.
Once, during a discussion on dancing in the inner apartments, the king and the queen said to Guṇaśarman, who was standing by their side:
"You are omniscient; there is no doubt for you in this matter, yet we have a curiosity. If you know how to dance, then please show us today."
Having heard this, Guṇaśarman, with a smiling face, said to the two of them: "I know; however, it is not proper for dancing to take place in an assembly."
Laughter and the dancing of fools are generally condemned by the scriptures; yet even in that regard, to do so before the king and queen—alas, what shamelessness!
When Guṇaśarman had spoken thus, King Guṇavarman, being urged by that queen out of curiosity, replied to him.
This is not a dance on a stage or the like that would cause shame to a man; rather, it is a private gathering of friends, wherein one displays one's own cleverness.
"I am not your king, for you are my friend beyond all constraint; therefore, I shall not eat today without having seen your performance of the dance."
When the king was thus firmly intent upon his resolve, that brahmin agreed to it; for how can the word of a master who is possessed by a spirit be transgressed by his servants?
Then that youth Guṇaśarman danced there with his limbs in such a manner that both the king and the queen danced with their hearts.
And at the conclusion of that, the king gave him a lute to play; while tuning its strings, he spoke to the monarch.
"O God, this lute is ill-favored; let another one be given to me, for within the strings of this one there is dog hair."
"Indeed, I recognize this by the characteristics of the resonance of its strings," said Guṇaśarman, and he released that lute from his lap.
Then, as soon as the king had moistened that lute-string and unwound it to examine it, a puppy emerged from its interior.
Then, praising his omniscience and filled with great wonder, King Mahāsena had another lute brought.
Singing, Guṇaśarman played that lute, which was as beautiful as the triple-pathed Gaṅgā with its surging currents, and whose sound was purifying to the ear.
Then, to that king and his kinsmen who were filled with wonder, he demonstrated the sciences of hand-to-hand combat and weaponry in their proper sequence.
Then that king said to him: "If you know that wrestling, then show me one feat of binding with empty hands."
"O Lord, take up your weapons and strike me in succession, so that I may show them to you," the Brahmin replied to him.
Then, whatever weapon he took up, such as a sword or the like, Guṇaśarman effortlessly parried each one as the king struck with it.
Using that very same binding device, he repeatedly snatched it away and bound the king's hand and body again and again, yet remained unhurt himself.
Then, considering that best of the twice-born capable of assisting him in the governance of the kingdom, the king praised him and held him in high esteem as one who surpassed all others.
But Queen Aśokavatī, having seen again and again that brahmin’s form and those virtues of his, immediately became one whose mind was fixed upon him.
"If I do not attain this, what is the fruit of my life? Having reflected thus, she spoke these words to the king with reason.
"Noble son, be gracious and give this Guṇaśarman an order, O Lord, so that he may teach me how to play the lute."
Indeed, having witnessed this skill in playing the lute today, a certain feeling has arisen in me toward him that is dearer to me than my own life.
Having heard that, the king said to Guṇaśarman: "By all means, teach this queen how to play the lute."
"We shall begin this undertaking on an auspicious day, just as you have instructed. Having said this and taken leave of the king, Guṇaśarman went to his home.
But for many days he made the lute-playing his sole occupation, having become apprehensive about the queen's altered gaze.
And one day, while standing near the king as he was eating, he stopped a certain cook who was giving him side dishes, saying, "Do not!"
When asked by the king, "What is this?", that wise man replied: "I have recognized through its characteristics that this dish contains poison."
Indeed, as this cook was serving me the side-dish, his face was trembling with fear and his eyes were startled with apprehension.
"And this is being seen even now; let this food and its condiments be given to someone to whom I shall remove the poison."
When he had spoken thus, the king had that very cook serve him that same side-dish; and having eaten it, he fell into a swoon.
Then, his poison having been neutralized by that mantra, the cook was questioned by King Guṇaśarman and spoke exactly as it had happened.
"O gods, I have been sent here by King Vikramaśakti, the lord of Gauḍa and your enemy, to administer poison to you."
Thus, having become a foreigner skilled in the art of cooking, I presented myself as a servant to the king and entered the great kitchen.
"And even as I was giving that poison, which had been mixed into the sauce, today, I was noticed by this wise man; therefore, let the Lord know what follows."
Having restrained that cook who had spoken thus, the king, being pleased, gave a thousand villages to Guṇaśarman as a reward for saving his life.
And on another day, as the queen persisted, the king with great effort had Guṇaśarman begin his instruction in the lute.
Then, while Guṇaśarman was teaching him the lute, Queen Aśokavatī constantly displayed her playful smiles and other such charms.
Once, in a secluded place, she, afflicted by the arrows of Love, repeatedly pricked that steadfast man as he tried to restrain her with her fingernails and spoke to him.
"O handsome one, under the pretext of the lute's music, you were entreated by me; for a deep passion has arisen in me for you, so please accept me."
When the queen had spoken thus, Guṇaśarman said to her: "Do not speak so; for you are my master's wife, and such [behavior] is not fitting."
"One such as we should not commit treason against his lord; desist from this rashness!"—to him who had spoken thus, Queen Guṇaśarman said:
What is this fruitless beauty and skill of yours in the arts? Why do you treat me, such as I am, with cold indifference?
Having heard that, Guṇaśarman spoke to her with derision: "Well said! What is the fruit of that beauty and cleverness?"
That which is not stained by infamy through the abduction of another's wife, and that which would not lead to a fall into the ocean of hell in this world and the next.
When he had spoken thus, the queen, as if filled with anger, said to him: "My death is certain if you do not carry out my word."
"Therefore, having killed you, I shall die, insulted as I am. Guṇaśarman then replied, "Let that indeed be so."
Better indeed is life for even a single moment bound by the fetters of Dharma, than a hundred million eons lived in violation of Dharma.
For me, who have committed no sin, death is praiseworthy and blameless; but for one who has committed sin, the king’s command is censurable.
Having heard this, the queen spoke to him once more: "Do not commit an act of treachery against yourself and me; listen, for I shall tell you."
"This king does not transgress even my word, however impossible it may be; therefore, having made a request to him, I shall cause the territories to be granted to you."
And I shall cause all your neighboring vassals to follow you; by that means, you alone, radiant with virtue, shall become the king here.
Therefore, what fear do you have? Who will overcome you, and how? So, serve me without hesitation; otherwise, you shall cease to exist.
Perceiving that the queen was speaking thus with her followers, Guṇaśarman immediately spoke to her with a clever artifice in order to dispel her [intentions].
If you are so insistent, O Goddess, I shall do as you say; however, it is not appropriate to do so suddenly, for fear of causing a rift.
Endure for some days; know my words to be true. What purpose do I have in opposing you, which would result in total ruin?
Having thus satisfied her with this intention, and having been granted her word by her, Guṇaśarman departed from there and went forth, breathing a sigh of relief.
Then, as the days passed, King Mahāsena went and besieged Somakeśvara, who was stationed within the fortress.
Having learned that he had arrived there, that king Gauḍanātha, Vikramaśakti, came and surrounded Mahāsena.
Then King Mahāsena said to Guṇaśarman: "While we were standing there having blocked one [enemy], we have now been blocked by another foe."
Therefore, O hero, being insufficient for now, how shall we fight against two? And if we do not fight while being besieged, O brave one, how long shall we remain here?
When the king asked him, "In this crisis, what should we do?", Guṇaśarman, who was standing nearby, replied.
"Be steadfast; I shall devise such a divine means by which we may escape from this peril, even if it requires action."
Having thus comforted the king and applied the ointment of invisibility to his eyes, he went at night to the camp of Vikramaśakti, remaining unseen.
Having entered into his presence and awakened him from sleep, he said: "Know me, O King, to be a messenger of the gods who has arrived."
Having made a treaty with King Mahāsena, depart quickly; otherwise, your destruction along with your army will certainly occur here.
"And once you have dispatched a messenger, he will agree to a peace treaty with you; it is for this purpose that I have been sent to you by the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu."
"You are devoted, and he looks after the welfare and security of his devotees. Having heard that, King Vikramaśakti reflected upon it.
This is certainly the truth; otherwise, how could anyone enter this place so difficult to penetrate? This is no deed worthy of a mortal.
Reflecting thus, he said to him: "I am blessed, O King, that Your Majesty commands me in this way; I shall do exactly as you have instructed."
While the king was speaking thus, Guṇaśarman, inspiring confidence in him, vanished by means of an ointment and departed from that place.
Having gone there, he reported everything as it had been done to Mahāsena; and he, embracing him around the neck, congratulated him for bestowing both his life and his kingdom.
In the morning, King Vikramaśakti dispatched a messenger, and having concluded a treaty with Mahāsena, he set out from there with his army.
Mahāsena, too, having conquered that Somaka and obtained elephants and horses, returned to Ujjayinī through the power of Guṇaśarman.
And while the king was staying there, Guṇaśarman protected him from a crocodile during a river bath, and from the venom of a snake-bite in the grove.
Then, as the days passed, King Mahāsena, having gathered his forces, marched against his enemy Vikramaśakti to attack him.
Having learned of this, the king also set out before him for battle; then a truly great conflict ensued there between the two of them.
And in due course, having encountered one another in a duel, both those kings suddenly deprived each other of their chariots.
Then, as those two rushed forward in a fury with swords in hand, King Mahāsena stumbled upon the ground due to his agitation.
When he stumbled, Guṇaśarman struck him with his discus and severed the arm of King Vikramaśakti, along with the sword still held in it.
Striking him again in the heart with an iron club, he felled him; and when Mahāsena rose up and saw this, the king was filled with joy.
"What shall I say? This is the fifth time these very life-breaths of mine have been given away by you, O heroic Brahmin," she said to him repeatedly.
Then Mahāsena attacked that army of Vikramaśakti, along with his entire kingdom, now that he had been slain by Guṇaśarman.
Having subdued other kings with Guṇaśarman as his ally, the king returned to Ujjayinī and remained there in happiness.
But Queen Aśokavatī, full of longing for Guṇaśarman, did not desist from her persistent entreaties day and night.
But he did not by any means accept that improper act; for the virtuous would rather desire the falling away of the body than immodesty.
Then Aśokavatī, having understood his resolve born of enmity, once feigned distress and remained there with a weeping face.
Then Mahāsena entered; seeing her standing there in such a state, the king asked, "What is this, my dear? By whom have you been provoked to anger?"
"Tell me, and I shall effect his restraint by means of my wealth and even my life"—to the king who was speaking thus, the queen spoke as if with great difficulty.
"You are not capable of punishing him who has done me wrong; he is not such a person, so what is the use of this false accusation?"
Having spoken thus, when the king persisted, she spoke falsely: "Noble son, if you are so insistent, listen as I tell you."
In order to obtain wealth from the Lord of Gauḍa, Guṇaśarman established an alliance with him; therefore, he desired to commit treachery against you through deceit.
And that lowest of brahmins dispatched his own trusted and secret messenger to the king, in order to have him compose the *Kośanibandha* and other works in the Gauḍī style.
Seeing him there, the trusted cook addressed the king: "I shall accomplish this task for you; do not let your wealth perish."
Having said this and having bound that messenger of Guṇaśarman, the cook, guarding against the disclosure of the secret counsel, returned here as the deliverer of the poison.
And having fled from among them and escaped from that captivity, that messenger of his arrived in the presence of Guṇaśarman.
Having related all that he had learned, he pointed out to Guṇaśarman the cook who had entered our kitchen.
Then, having discovered this, that cook was reported by that rogue of a Brahmin to you, and he was put to death by him, intent on administering poison.
Today, that wise Guṇaśarman came here to seek news of that cook’s mother, wife, and younger sister.
Having discovered this, he killed his wife and mother; however, by chance, his brother escaped and entered my palace.
While he was describing all of that to me as I sought refuge, Guṇaśarman entered my dwelling.
Upon seeing him and hearing his name, that brother of the cook fled from my side out of fear; I do not know where he has run away.
Guṇaśarman, too, seeing him whom his own servants had previously pointed out, was instantly filled with embarrassment, as if reflecting upon something.
Then, desiring to know the cause, I asked him in private: "Guṇaśarman, why do you appear so different today?"
Then, desiring to accept me and fearing exposure, he said: "O Queen, I am consumed by the fire of my passion for you; therefore, accept me."
"Otherwise I shall not live; grant me the gift of my life. Having said this, he fell at my feet in the empty dwelling.
Then, as soon as I had thrown down my foot and risen up in agitation, he too rose up and forcibly embraced me, who was powerless.
At that very moment, my maidservant Pallavikā entered; as soon as he saw her, Guṇaśarman came out and fled in fear.
"If Pallavikā had not entered here today, that wicked man would certainly have destroyed me; such was my situation this day."
Having spoken thus falsely, the queen ceased speaking and wept; for women first utter untruthful words and subsequently become wicked wives.
And having heard that, the king suddenly blazed with anger; for reliance on the words of women destroys the discernment even of the great.
And he said to his beloved wife, "Take heart, O beautiful one; I shall certainly carry out the execution of that traitor."
However, he must be slain through a stratagem; otherwise, there will be infamy. For it is well known that my life was saved by him five times when it was given to me.
"And it is not fitting to speak of the fault of having assaulted you in this world. Having been addressed thus by the king, the queen replied to him.
If this fault is considered unspeakable, then why is that other effort—the attempt to harm the Lord through friendship with the King of Gauḍa—not also spoken of?
When she had spoken thus, King Mahāsena said, "What you have said is right," and departed for his own assembly hall.
There, all the kings, princes, vassals, and ministers likewise assembled to see that monarch.
And at that moment, Guṇaśarman also came from his house toward the royal palace, and on the way he observed many ill omens.
From that, his left side became like a crow; from the left, it moved toward the right; the right side became like a horse, while his left arm, together with its shoulder, throbbed.
"These omens certainly portend something inauspicious for me; therefore, let whatever occurs befall me alone, but let nothing happen to my lord, the king."
Thinking thus within himself, he then entered the king’s assembly hall out of devotion, lest anything unfavorable should occur in the royal family.
When he had bowed and sat down there, the king did not greet him as before; instead, he looked at him askance with a gaze kindled by anger.
When Guṇaśarman was thus suspected of what this might be, the king rose from his seat and sat upon his shoulder.
He said to the astonished members of the assembly, "Listen to my case against Guṇaśarman," and then Guṇaśarman made his representation.
"I am the servant and you are the master; how can our legal proceeding be equal? Sit upon the seat first, and then give your command as you wish."
Thus addressed by that steadfast one and exhorted by his ministers, the king sat upon his throne once more and spoke again to the members of the assembly.
O ministers, you already know that, setting aside those who have served in succession, this Guṇaśarman has been made equal to myself.
Listen to me: by means of these repeated missions of envoys, this [minister] has conspired with the Lord of Gauḍa to commit treachery against me.
Having said this, the lord of the earth described to them that which Aśokavatī had told him, having fabricated it falsely.
That objection he raised regarding the destruction of the self was also declared by that king to be a false statement, having expelled him from the company of the learned.
Then Guṇaśarman said to him: "O King, by whom was such an untruth reported to you? By whom was this wonderful sky-painting created?"
Upon hearing this, the king said: "O sinner, if this is not true, how did you know that the poison was inside the vessel of sacrificial porridge?"
When Guṇaśarman said, "Everything is known through wisdom," the other ministers, out of hatred for him, replied, "This is impossible."
O King, it is not even fitting for you to speak without having investigated the truth; a ruler who acts without deliberation is not praised by those who know statecraft.
As Guṇaśarman was speaking thus, the king rushed forward and, shouting "You are a bold one!", struck him with a blow from his dagger.
When that [hero] was thus deceived by him through the application of a weapon in that blow, the king’s followers struck at that hero from another side.
And Guṇaśarman, having deceived them with feats of combat, snatched away the small swords from all of them at once.
And he bound them together, entwining their massed hair with one another, having performed this by means of manual skill alone, with a dexterity learned through marvelous training.
And then he emerged forcibly from that royal assembly and struck down about a hundred warriors who were pursuing him.
Then, having applied that invisibility ointment from the corner of his garment to his eyes, he became invisible and departed from that place at that very moment.
As he was traveling toward the southern region, he thought on the road: "Surely that foolish king has been incited by that Aśokavatī."
Alas! Women who are rejected after being loved are even worse than poison; alas! Kings who perceive the truth are unfit to be served by the virtuous.
Reflecting thus and so forth, Guṇaśarman somehow reached a village, where he saw an excellent brahmin beneath a banyan tree.
Approaching him as he was teaching his disciples, he saluted him; and that Brahmin, having offered him hospitality, questioned him after a moment.
"O Brahmin, which branch of the Veda do you study? Please tell me. Thereupon, Guṇaśarman replied to that Brahmin.
O Brahmin, I study twelve branches: two from the Sāmaveda, two from the Ṛgveda, seven from the Yajurveda, and one from the Atharvaveda.
Having heard that, and being told "Then you are a god," the brahmin, his excellence already indicated by his appearance, bowed low and questioned him again.
"Tell me, what country and what lineage have been adorned by your birth? What is your name, how have you studied so much, and where [did you do so]? Speak!"
Having heard that, Guṇaśarman said to him: "In the city of Ujjayinī, there was a certain son of a Brahmin named Ādityaśarman."
While that boy was still a child, his father passed away; and his mother entered the fire along with her husband.
Then Ādityaśarman grew up in that city, in the house of his maternal uncle, studying the Vedas, the sciences, and the arts.
When he had acquired that knowledge and was devoted here to the practice of recitation and vows, friendship arose between him and a certain wandering mendicant.
That wandering mendicant, together with his friend Ādityaśarman, went to the cemetery and performed a fire sacrifice for the sake of attaining mastery over a yakṣiṇī.
Then, there appeared before him a celestial maiden, beautifully adorned and surrounded by excellent maidens, seated within a golden celestial chariot.
With sweet words she spoke to him: "O Maskarin, I am a yakṣī named Vidyunmālā, and these other women here are also yakṣiṇīs."
Therefore, take one [woman] from among my retinue here according to your pleasure; by this very means, the accomplishment of your mantra-practice is already achieved for you.
For you have not understood my mantra-attainment in its entirety; therefore, I am not yet accomplished for you. Do not undergo further hardship in vain.
Having been addressed thus by that yakṣī, the wandering mendicant, after giving his consent, took one yakṣiṇī from her retinue.
Then that Yakṣiṇī Vidyunmālā vanished; and Ādityaśarman questioned her, she who had been perfected by the wandering mendicant.
"Is there some yakṣiṇī superior even to Vidyunmālā? Having heard that, the yakṣiṇī replied to him, "There is, O handsome one."
Vidyunmālā, Candralekhā, and the third, Sulocanā—these are the most excellent among the Yakṣiṇīs, and among these, Sulocanā is the best.
Having spoken thus, the yakṣiṇī departed to return at the appointed time; and the mendicant went to her house together with Ādityaśarman.
There, every day, that Yakṣiṇī Kālopagā, being pleased with that renunciant, bestowed upon him the enjoyments he desired at the appropriate time.
Once, Ādityaśarman asked through the mouth of a wandering mendicant: "Who knows the ritual procedure for the mantra of Sulocanā?"
She too, at his very face, spoke thus to him: "There is indeed a place named Tumbavana in the southern region."
There dwells a wandering mendicant named Viṣṇugupta, who has made his home on the bank of the Veṇā; he is the foremost among venerable monks and knows that matter in full detail.
Having understood this from the words of the Yakṣiṇī, Ādityaśarman went eagerly to that place, followed with affection by the wandering mendicant.
Having searched for him there and approached that venerable one accordingly, he attended upon him with devotion, intent on service, for three years.
And that wandering mendicant was attended by that accomplished yakṣiṇī with superhuman services provided according to his needs.
Then that venerable one, being pleased, bestowed upon that Ādityaśarman the requested mantra of Sulocanā, together with its ritual procedure.
Then Ādityaśarman, having obtained and mastered that mantra, went to a secluded place and performed the fire-oblation in its entirety according to the prescribed rules.
Then, from within that celestial chariot, the Yakṣiṇī Sulocanā appeared, her form bestowing wonder upon the world.
And she said to him, "Come, come! I am accomplished for you; however, for six months my state as a maiden must not be removed by you."
If you desire to obtain from me a son who is a great hero, possessed of auspicious marks, a vessel of supernatural power, nearly equal to the Omniscient One, and unconquered;
Having spoken thus, the Yakṣiṇī took Ādityaśarman, who had replied "So be it," and departed for Alakā by means of a celestial chariot.
And there Ādityaśarman remained, constantly beholding her standing nearby, as he observed the "sword-edge" vow for six months.
Then the Lord of Wealth, being pleased, personally bestowed that beautiful-eyed woman upon Ādityaśarman according to a divine rite.
In that [city], this son was born to that twice-born man; and my father gave me the name Guṇaśarman on account of my virtuous qualities.
Then, right there, from the lord of the Yakṣas named Maṇidhara, I gradually acquired the Vedas, the sciences, and the arts.
Then once, Śakra came there to the presence of the Giver of Wealth; and seeing him arrive, those who were sitting there stood up.
But my father, Ādityaśarman, at that moment, due to the turn of fate and because his mind was elsewhere, did not rise up in agitation.
Then Śakra, enraged, cursed him: "Fie upon you, fool! Go back to that very world of mortals; you are not fit to remain here."
Then, having been entreated by that Sulocanā after she had prostrated herself, Śakra said: "In that case, let him not go to the world of mortals himself."
"Let this son go; for a son is said to be one's very own self. Let my word not be in vain," having said this, Indra attained tranquility.
Then my father brought me and placed me in the house of his own maternal uncle in Ujjayinī; for whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass.
There, by fate, friendship arose between me and the king who was there; now hear from me everything that happened to me there as I tell it to you.
Having said this, he described the entire account from the beginning—what Aśokavatī had done and what the king had done, ending with the battle.
And he spoke to him again, "O Brahmin, having fled in this manner, while traveling to another land, I have seen you here on the way."
Having heard this, that Brahmin said to Guṇaśarman: "In that case, O Lord, I have become blessed by your arrival."
Therefore, come with me to my home; know me as Agnidatta by name, and let this village, which is my royal grant, be your place of rest.
Having said this, Agnidatta led Guṇaśarman into his own prosperous home, which abounded in cattle, buffaloes, and horses.
There, he honored that guest with baths, unguents, garments, and ornaments, as well as with various kinds of food.
And he showed him his own daughter, named Sundarī, who could assume any form at will even for the gods, and who was so beautiful that even the gods desired to behold her marks of excellence.
Guṇaśarman, too, having beheld her whose beauty was unequaled by any other, said to Agnidatta, "She will have rivals among wives."
She has a mole on her nose, and because of its connection with that, I say: there is also a second one on her breast; the wise know this to be the fruit of those two.
When he had spoken thus, her brother, with his father’s permission, opened her chest; as soon as he did so, he beheld a sesame seed.
Then Agnidatta, filled with wonder, said to Guṇaśarman: "You are omniscient; these two tilaka marks of hers do not portend anything inauspicious."

For in this world, when a husband is prosperous, women generally become co-wives; but how could a poor man support even one, let alone many? How much more difficult would it be for him to support many?
Having heard that, Guṇaśarman replied to him: "O sir, as you say; for how could there be misfortune for one of such auspicious appearance as Sulakṣaṇā?"
Having spoken thus, when questioned in the course of conversation, he explained to him the specific results for men and women regarding moles and other marks on each individual limb.
And then, as soon as Sundarī saw Guṇaśarman, she became eager to drink him in with her very eyes, like a cakorī bird longing for the moon.
Then Agnidatta said to Guṇaśarman in a secluded place: "O noble one, I shall give this daughter Sundarī to you."
"Do not go abroad; stay here in my house as you please. Having heard these words of his, Guṇaśarman also spoke to him:
"Truly, if this were done, what happiness would not be mine? However, that [happiness] does not at all please me, for I am scorched by the fire of the king's insult caused by falsehood."
A beloved woman, the rising of the moon, and the fifth note of the lute—these things which delight those who are happy, cause pain to those who are suffering.
And his wife shall be naturally devoted and faithful; though she may be under the control of her father, she shall remain like Aśokavatī.
Moreover, that city of Ujjayinī is near to this region; having learned of this, that king might at some point cause me trouble.
Having wandered through those sacred fords and washed away the sins of my birth, I shall cast off this body and then become liberated.
To him who had spoken thus, Agnidatta replied with a laugh: "When even you are under such delusion, what can be said of anyone else?"
Tell me, what loss can there be for you, whose intention is pure, from being disregarded by the ignorant? For mud thrown into the sky falls upon the head of the thrower.
That king alone shall soon reap the fruit of his lack of discernment; for Prosperity does not long serve one who is blinded by delusion and devoid of discrimination.
Furthermore, if you have developed a distaste for women upon seeing Aśokavatī, why do you not feel confidence in them upon seeing a virtuous woman? You also know the signs [of virtue].
Or, if Ujjayinī is near, I will provide for you in such a way that no one at all will know you are staying here.

If pilgrimage is desired by you, then that [pilgrimage] is prescribed for him by the wise; for one in whom prosperity does not arise according to rule during Vedic ritual, [then pilgrimage is the remedy].

Otherwise, how could there be the same accumulation of merit at home through rites for the gods, ancestors, and fire, as well as vows, recitations, and so forth, as that which belongs to one wandering on the true path?
Using his arm as a pillow, sleeping on the ground, subsisting on alms, solitary and without wealth—even having attained equanimity like a sage, the traveler is not yet freed from the afflictions.
That you desire happiness from the abandonment of the body is an illusion; for those who commit suicide, there is indeed suffering even more painful than this in the hereafter.
Therefore, this delusion is unbecoming of you, who are both young and wise; reflect upon it yourself, for my word must certainly be carried out by you.
"I shall have a large and beautiful underground chamber built for you here in secret; for after marrying Sundarī, there will indeed be suffering in the next world for those who commit suicide."
Thus enlightened by Agnidatta, Guṇaśarman diligently agreed, saying "So be it," and spoke to him.
I have done as you commanded; for who would abandon a beautiful wife? However, being a man of no merit, I shall not marry your daughter.
"I shall first propitiate some deity with great self-restraint, so that I may perform a service in return for that ungrateful king."
Delighted by these words, Agnidatta gave his consent; and Guṇaśarman also rested there comfortably for that night.
And on another day, Agnidatta had a secret underground chamber constructed there for his son's comfort, resembling a dwelling in the underworld.
Remaining there, Guṇaśarman spoke to Agnidatta in private: "Tell me here within, which deity should I worship with devotion, and by what mantra?"
"I shall first propitiate that giver of boons through the practice of a vow. To him, who had spoken thus, the steadfast Agnidatta replied:
"I have a mantra belonging to Svāmikumāra that was taught to me by my preceptor; with it, propitiate that god, the commander-in-chief who is the destroyer of Tāraka."
He for whose sake Kāma—though born of a mere thought and once burnt by Śarva—was sent by the gods, oppressed by their enemies, seeking his birth.
They proclaim his wondrous birth from Maheśvara, from the sacrificial fire-pit, from the fire itself, from the forest of reeds, and from the Kṛttikās.
By him, as soon as he was born, the entire world was gladdened with his invincible splendor, and the invincible demon Tāraka was slain.
Having said, "Receive this mantra from me," Agnidatta gave that mantra to Guṇaśarman.
Thereupon, Guṇaśarman, firm in his vows and being attended by Sundarī, propitiated Skanda while staying in an underground chamber.
Then, having become manifest before his very eyes, that six-faced god said to him: "I am pleased with you; choose a boon, my son."
Having become one whose treasury is inexhaustible and having conquered Mahāsena, you, my son, shall go forth unimpeded and rule over the sovereignty of the earth.
Having thus granted him this further boon, Skanda vanished; and Guṇaśarman, too, became one who possessed an inexhaustible treasury.

Then, by means of his supernatural power suited to his own greatness, that virtuous man married Sundarī according to the prescribed rites—she who was the daughter of the Brahmin Agnidatta, whose love for him increased day by day, and who appeared like the personified attainment of a destined purpose endowed with beauty.

Due to the power arising from his inexhaustible treasury and stores, he assembled a vast army of elephants, horses, and foot soldiers; obstructing the earth with his forces, he marched toward Ujjayinī, where all the kings had gathered through their devotion to his generosity.
Having proclaimed that lack of virtue among the subjects of Aśokavatī and having defeated King Mahāsena in battle, he stripped him of his kingdom and attained the sovereignty of the earth himself.

And having married other maidens as well, that sovereign Guṇaśarman, his eyes never turning away even from the shores of the ocean of kings, enjoyed his desired pleasures for a long time together with Sundarī.

Thus, due to ignorance regarding the specific nature of persons, King Mahāsena suddenly met with calamity through his deluded intellect; yet Guṇaśarman, being wise, relied solely upon fortitude as his companion and attained the highest prosperity.

Having thus heard this noble discourse from the mouth of his own minister Vītabhīti during the night, the heroic Sūryaprabha, desiring to cross the great ocean of battle, attained even greater enthusiasm and gradually fell asleep.

Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Seventh Wave: Then, having risen in the morning, Sūryaprabha went to the battlefield accompanied by his ministers and all the forces of the Dānavas and others.
And Śrutaśarman departed, surrounded by the forces of the Vidyādharas; meanwhile, all the gods, asuras, and others returned once more to witness the spectacle.
Both those armies formed two crescent-shaped battle arrays, and then the battle between those two forces commenced.
Even the arrows, as they sped along their feathered courses, fought one another with great velocity, clashing with a roar as they cut each other apart.
Emerging from their scabbards, long and dripping with blood, the flickering sword-blades shone like the tongues of Death.
Then that great lake of battle became a place for the destruction of royal swans, where the multitudes of wheel-weapons fell upon the lotus-faces of blooming heroes.
With the heads of heroes being severed, leaping up, and falling down, the battlefield shone like the ball-play of Death.
On the battlefield, where the darkness of dust was washed away by the sprinkling of blood, duels took place between the indignant great chariot-warriors.
There, Sūryaprabha had a battle with Śrutaśarman, and Prabhāsa had a combat with Dāmodara.
Then Siddhārtha fought with Mahotpāta; Prahasta fought with Brahmagupta, and Vītabhī with Saṃgama.
Prajñāḍhya fought with Candragupta, Priyaṅkara with Akrama, and Sarvadamana with Atibala.
That prince Kuñjaraka fought with Dhuraṃdhara, while other great chariot-warriors fought separately with their respective opponents.
There, Pūrva first repelled Siddhārtha’s arrows with his own; having severed Siddhārtha’s bow, he struck down his horses along with their charioteer.
Deprived of his chariot, Siddhārtha also rushed forward in fury and crushed that man’s chariot, along with its horses, using a great iron staff.
Then Siddhārtha, moving on foot, cast that other foot-soldier down upon the earth with a wrestling hold during their hand-to-hand combat, like a great portent.
And for as long as he desired to crush him, that sky-goer, protected by his father Bhaga, rose up and departed from the battle.
Prahasta and Brahmagupta, having deprived each other of their chariots, fought one another with various weapons and sword-combats of diverse kinds.
And Prahasta, by means of a sequence of instruments, skillfully caused that Brahmagupta—whose skin had been sliced away by his sword—to fall to the surface of the earth.
Just as he desired to cut off the head of that fallen man, he was restrained from afar by his own father, Brahmā himself.
"You have come to protect your sons, not to witness the battle," saying this, all the Dānavas then mocked the gods.
Then Vītabhaya, having pierced Saṃkrama in the heart with the Pradyumna-weapon, slew him whose bow was broken and whose charioteer was killed.
And Prajñāḍhya, being on foot due to the destruction of his two chariots, slew Candragupta—who was also on foot—with a sword-fight, having severed both his arms.
Then Candramas, enraged by the slaughter of his son, came in person and fought with Rajādhyaya; and the battle between the two was equal.
And Priyaṅkara, being himself deprived of his chariot due to the destruction of his vehicle, split his opponent in two with a single stroke of his sword as he advanced.
When the bow was severed, Sarvadamana struck the exceedingly powerful [opponent] in the chest with a hurled goad, slaying him effortlessly in battle.
Then that young elephant prince repeatedly deprived his opponent, the leader of the host, of his chariot through a battle of missiles countered by missiles.
And Vikramaśakti repeatedly presented him with a chariot; moreover, he protected him in the midst of danger, warding off his weapons with his own weapons.
Then that young elephant, having rushed forward in a rage, suddenly hurled a massive rock upon Vikramaśakti’s chariot.
When his prowess and power had departed and his chariot was crushed, he then pulverized that leader of the host with that very same rock.
Although Sūryaprabha was engaged in battle there with Śrutaśarman, out of rage for the slaying of Virocana, he struck Dama with a single arrow.
Out of anger at that, the two divine Aśvins rushed toward him with arrows for battle; Sunītha received them, and a great battle ensued between them.
And Sthirabuddhi, having displayed his prowess by slaying Śakti in battle, fought with the eight Vasus who were enraged by that slaughter.
And seeing Bhāsa deprived of his chariot by Mardana, Prabhāsa, though engaged in combat with Dāmodara, struck him down with a single arrow.
Having slain Tejaḥprabha in battle through a duel of missiles, the Dānava Prakampana fought with Agni, who was enraged by that slaughter.
And when Dhūmaketu struck Yamadaṃṣṭra in battle, a most terrible fight ensued with the enraged Yama.
Having ground together *siṃhadraṣṭa* and *suroṣaṇa* with a stone, he [prepared it] for battle against Nirṛti, who was filled with indignation at his slaughter.
Kālacakra also, with his discus, split the power of Vāyu in two; and out of anger, he fought against that blazing wind.
Assuming the forms of elephants, mountains, and trees, Mahāmāya, who brings about utter delusion, destroyed the [palace] given by Kubera by assuming the forms of Tārkṣya, the thunderbolt, and fire.
Then Kubera, enraged, fought there with him; likewise, the other gods also fought out of anger that their own portions were being destroyed.
And there, other various lords of the Vidyādharas were also struck down by those various men and Dānavas who sprang up at every step.
Meanwhile, there occurred between Prabhāsa and Dāmodara a battle terrifying with the mutual exchange of missiles and counter-missiles.
Then Dāmodara, his bow broken and his charioteer slain, took up another bow and, seizing the reins himself, continued to fight.
And Indra asked the lotus-seated one, who was offering him words of praise: "O Blessed One, why are you pleased with one who is declining?"
Then Brahmā said to him: "How is it that he is not satisfied with this man, who has been fighting with Prabhāsa for so long?"
Indeed, who other than Dāmodara, an expansion of Hari, could have performed this? For all the gods together were insignificant in battle against that single Prabhāsa.
He who was the asura named Namuci, the crusher of the gods, was then born as the one called Prabala, who was composed of all kinds of jewels.
This very Prabhāsa has today become the invincible son of Bhāsa; formerly, Bhāsa himself was the great Asura Kālanemi.
Furthermore, having previously been Hiraṇyakaśipu, he then became Kapiñjala; and he who was the asura Sumuṇḍīka is now this Sūryaprabha.
And he who was formerly Hiraṇyākṣa is this very asura Sunītha; and those who were Prahasta and the others—all these are Daityas and Dānavas.
Those whom you slew have been born again as these Asuras, beginning with Maya; for this very reason, they have taken refuge in their side.
Behold Bali, whose bonds have been loosened through the power of the sacrifice to Rudra performed by Sūryaprabha and others; he has come here to see you.
Protecting his own word of truth, he remains in the netherworlds until the end of the period of your reign; after that, he will become a *rājarṣi*.
These have now been taken under the protection of Tripurāri; therefore, this is not the time for your victory—make peace, what is the use of these hostilities?
While the lotus-seated Brahmā was thus speaking to the lord of the gods, Prabhāsa discharged the great Pāśupata weapon.
