Seeing that all-devouring, fierce weapon had been unleashed, Hari, out of affection for his son, released the Sudarśana discus.
Then there occurred a battle between those two, who were equal in form and possessed of divine weapons, causing the three worlds to tremble with the fear of an untimely universal dissolution.
"Withdraw this weapon of yours until I withdraw mine. Having been addressed thus by Hari, Prabhāsa then replied to him.
"Let this discharged weapon not be in vain; let Dāmodara turn his back and flee from the battle, so that I may withdraw the weapon."
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said: "In that case, honor it; let there be no fruitlessness for either of us regarding the wheel."
Having heard these words of Śauri, Prabhāsa, who knew the proper time, said: "So be it; let this wheel of mine destroy your chariot."
When Hari had thus withdrawn Dāmodara from the battle, Prabhāsa withdrew his weapon; the discus then fell upon his chariot.
Then, having mounted another chariot, he went into the presence of Sūryaprabha; Dāmodara also then proceeded into the presence of Śrutaśarman.
And meanwhile, the duel between Śrutaśarman, who was arrogant because he was a portion of Vāsava, and Sūryaprabha reached its highest pitch.
Whatever weapon Śrutaśarman employed with great effort, Sūryaprabha countered each one in an instant with his own counter-weapons.
Whatever illusions were employed here by Śrutaśarman against Sūryaprabha, each one was neutralized by the latter's counter-illusion.
Then, out of extreme rage, Śrutaśarman discharged the Brahmā weapon; the skillful Sūryaprabha also released the Pāśupata weapon.
Having neutralized that Brahmā-weapon with that fierce great weapon, Śrutaśarman was then overcome by Duṣpradharman.
Meanwhile, the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, being filled with indignation, discharged supreme weapons such as the thunderbolt from all sides.
But that Pāśupata weapon, having overcome all those other weapons as well, blazed forth even more intensely with the intent to slay Śrutaśarman.
Then Sūryaprabha, having offered praise, made this request to that great weapon: "Do not slay Śrutaśarman; instead, bind him and hand him over."
Then, driven by the desire to conquer him, all the gods donned their armor and prepared for battle, while the other Asuras also joined as spectators out of a similar ambition.
At that very moment, the attendant named Vīrabhadra, dispatched by Śambhu, arrived and delivered this command of his to Indra and the other gods.
"You have come here to look on; what business of yours is it to fight? Furthermore, by transgressing the bounds of propriety, other improprieties may also arise."
Having heard this, the gods said: "We are being slain and have been slain; all our sons are here. Therefore, how can we not fight?"

For the affection for a son is difficult to abandon; therefore, a remedy must certainly be applied. Since this [affection] must be directed toward those who destroy it, what impropriety is there in doing so here to the best of one's ability?
When the gods had spoken thus and Vīrabhadra had departed, a great battle then ensued between the gods and the asuras.
Sunītha was equal to the Aśvins; Prajñāḍhya was equal to Indu; Sthirabuddhi was equal to the Vasus; and Kālacakra was equal to Vāyu.
Prakampana was [conquered] by Agni, Siṃhadaṃṣṭra likewise by Nirṛti, Prathamana by Varuṇa, and Dhūmaketu by Yama.
Then Mahāmāya fought with the Lord of Wealth using missiles and counter-missiles, as well as against the other gods.
At the end, whatever supreme weapon each deity discharged, Hara destroyed each one of them with a "hum" sound.
But Dhanada, with his mace raised, was restrained by Śarva with gentle words; and those various gods, their weapons shattered, abandoned the battle and departed.
Then Śakra himself, out of anger, fought against Sūryaprabha; he loosed a torrent of arrows upon him as well as various other weapons.
And Sūryaprabha, having effortlessly shaken off those weapons, struck Indra with a hundred iron arrows drawn back to his ear.
Then the enraged Lord of the Gods seized his thunderbolt, but Rudra uttered the sound "hum," and that thunderbolt was destroyed.
Then, when Śakra had turned his back and departed, Nārāyaṇa himself, out of anger, fought Prabhāsa with millions of arrows having many points.
Unshaken, he fought equally with his own weapons against the other weapons; even when his horses were slain and he was deprived of his chariot, he mounted another chariot.
He fought without distinction against that enemy of the Daityas; then the enraged god released his flaming discus.
Prabhāsa also, having consecrated it with mantras, released a divine sword; and as those two weapons were clashing in combat, he beheld the discus.
As his sword was gradually failing him, Hara uttered the syllable "huṃ"; by that, both his sword and discus vanished from sight.
Then the Asuras rejoiced and the gods despaired, since Sūryaprabha had achieved victory and Śrutaśarman was bound.
Having offered praise, the gods then propitiated the bull-bannered Lord; thereupon, the Lord of Ambikā, being pleased, commanded the gods as follows.
"Sūryaprabha, set aside what has been promised and choose another boon; O Lord, who is able to make otherwise that which you have already vowed?"
"But, O Lord, let that which was promised by us regarding this Śrutaśarman also come true; let there be no destruction of our lineage."
Having spoken thus to the gods who had ceased [speaking], the Blessed One commanded them: "This shall come to pass once a treaty is made; and let there be a treaty between you here."
Let Śrutaśarman, together with his followers, pay homage to Sūryaprabha; then we shall speak in such a way that it may be for the benefit of both sides.
Having thus received the word of the Lord, saying "So be it," the gods made Śrutaśarman bow down before Sūryaprabha.
Then, as those two had mutually abandoned their enmity and were locked in an embrace, the gods and asuras, their own hostilities pacified, established peace between them.
Then, while all the asuras and suras were listening, the Blessed Lord Śambhu spoke these words to Sūryaprabha:
Bestow upon yourself the status of a universal monarch for the sake of the southern altar; but for the sake of the northern altar, grant that [kingdom] to Śrutaśarman.
"O son, you shall before long obtain a fourfold sovereignty over all the Kinnaras and other beings who roam the heavens."
And when he has arrived, you should give even half of the sacrificial fee as a gift to Kuñjarakumāra, for he stands in a position of special distinction.
And those heroes who have been slain here in battle on both sides—let them all rise up alive, with their limbs uninjured.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished, and all those who had been slain in battle rose up unhurt, as if awakened from sleep.
Then Sūryaprabha, the subduer of enemies, having received the command of Śambhu upon his head, went to a secluded and spacious plot of ground.
Seated in his great hall, he himself seated Śrutaśarman upon half of his own lion-throne as the latter arrived.
Their companions, Prabhāsa and others, as well as the companions of Śrutaśarman, Dāmodara and others, sat down on both sides of the two of them.
Sunītha, Maya, and the other Dānavas sat down on seats according to their rank, as did the lords of the Vidyādharas.
Then all the lords of the seven netherworlds, the chiefs of the Daityas and Dānavas led by Prahlāda, arrived there in great joy.
And Śakra, accompanied by the world-protectors and others, with his preceptor at the head, as well as the Vidyādhara Sumeru and that prince Suvāsakumāra.
All the wives of Kaśyapa, beginning with Danu, as well as the wives of Sūryaprabha, arrived in the aerial chariot Bhūtāsana.
When they had all sat down, having established a mutual bond of affection and proper conduct, a friend named Siddhi, having offered [greeting], spoke these words:
"O gods and asuras, this goddess Danu speaks to you: 'Whatever joy and happiness we have in this assembly of affection,'"
Therefore, tell me if this has ever been experienced by you; then let no mutual hostility, which is as terrible as suffering, be committed.

Those by whom he was formerly chosen for the sovereignty of heaven by his elder brothers, such as Hiraṇyākṣa and others, have now gone to Śakra himself; since he alone is the eldest today, what cause is there for opposition?
Therefore, dwell in mutual happiness free from enmity, so that we may have contentment and there may be welfare for all worlds.
Having thus heard the words of Danu from the mouth of Siddhimukha, Bṛhaspati, looking toward Śakra, spoke to her.
There is no lingering enmity on the part of the gods toward the asuras, provided that these asuras do not act falsely toward the gods.
When this had been said by the preceptor of the gods, Maya, the lord of the Dānavas, replied: "If there were to be any transformation among the Asuras, how could Namuci not have given it?"
And how could Prabala offer his own body to the gods, along with the horse Uccaiḥśravas, who restores the dead to life, for Indra?
Having given the three worlds to Hari, how could Bali enter prison? And how could he, whose body was made of iron, give his body to Viśvakarman?
Or how much more need I say? Since the asuras are ever-present, if they are not thwarted by deceit, they undergo no change at all.
When the Asura Maya had spoken thus, Siddhi replied accordingly; and so the gods and Asuras felt mutual joy, following it with embraces around each other's necks.
Just then, a female doorkeeper named Jayā, sent by Bhavānī, arrived there; she was honored by everyone and spoke as follows regarding Sumeru.
"I have been sent to you by the Queen, and she has given this message to you: 'You have a daughter, a maiden named Kāmacūḍāmaṇi.'"
"Give her to Sūryaprabha at once, for she is devoted to me. Thus addressed by Jayā, Sumeru bowed and replied to her.
That the Goddess commands me is indeed a supreme favor; for this very purpose was previously commanded to me by the Lord as well.
Thus addressed by Sumeru, Jayā said to Sūryaprabha: "You must make her the presiding lady over all your wives."
"From all those [goddesses] desired by others, this one shall also belong to you"—thus has it been commanded to you today by the gracious Goddess Gaurī.
Having spoken thus, Jayā, who had been worshipped by Sūryaprabha, vanished; and on that very day, Sumeru quickly decided upon the auspicious moment for the marriage.
There he had an altar constructed with pillars and a floor made of excellent jewels, which appeared as if covered by fire concealed by the mass of their radiance.
And he caused his daughter Kāmacūḍāmaṇi to be brought forth—she whose loveliness was being drunk in by the restless eyes of gods and asuras.
"Umā was born from Himavat, and she too was born from Sumeru"—as if supported by such a resemblance in beauty.
Then, having placed upon the altar that which was adorned with the auspicious marriage-thread and beautifully decorated, he gave that Sumeru to Sūryaprabha.
And then Sūryaprabha took the lotus-hand of Kāmacūḍāmaṇi, upon which bracelets had been fastened by Danu and the others.
And at the first scattering of parched grain, Jayā, who had arrived at that very moment sent by Bhavānī, gave her a divine, imperishable garland.
Then Sumeru also gave him priceless jewels and a divine, excellent elephant born from Airāvaṇa.
And at the second scattering of parched grain, Jayā gave her a jeweled necklace, by wearing which around her neck neither death, nor hunger, nor thirst causes affliction.
And Sumeru gave him a double store of jewels, as well as an unsurpassed jewel among horses born from Uccaiḥśravas.
At the third release of the parched grain, Jayā gave her a single-string necklace, by which, when fastened around the neck, youth never fades away.
Having distributed a heap of jewels three times the size of Mount Sumeru, he gave him a divine pill that is effective for all accomplishments.
Then, when the wedding was concluded, Sumeru addressed all the gods, asuras, vidyādharas, and divine mothers in this way:
"All of you must eat today in my house; please grant me your favor, for I join my palms in supplication upon my head."
While all of them were thus making this request to Sumeru and had not yet desisted, Nandī arrived there.
He said to them as they bowed: "The Trident-bearer has commanded that you must eat at the house of Sumeru; for this is our domain."
"Once this food has been eaten, may there be eternal satisfaction for you all. Having heard this from Nandimukha, they all accepted it as true.
Then, immeasurable hosts dispatched by Śaṅkara arrived there, presided over by Vināyaka, Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, and others.
And having prepared that altar for the meal, they seated those gods, celestial beings, asuras, and humans in due order.
And they offered them foods prepared by magic, as well as those produced from the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu at the command of Śaṅkara, all brought forth by Mount Sumeru.
And Vīrabhadra, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, and the other gods stood before each [of them] individually, according to their merit, carrying out their will.
And at every step, there occurred a celestial concert, beautiful with the dancing of divine women, while the *cāraṇa* bards sang praises mingled with expressions of contentment.
And at the conclusion of the meal, Nandīśvara and the others gave to them all divine garlands, garments, and ornaments.
Having thus honored the gods and others, all the lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin, departed with all their attendants just as they had come.
Then all the gods and asuras, as well as those mothers of theirs, and Śrutaśarman and the others, departed for their respective abodes after taking their leave.
Accompanied by his wife and his friends along with their wives, Sūryaprabha traveled by means of a celestial chariot to that first grove of asceticism on Mount Sumeru.
And he dispatched his friend Harṣa to the kings to announce his own rise to power, as well as to his brother Ratnaprabha.
And at the end of the day, he entered that bedchamber of Kāmacūḍāmaṇi’s bride, which contained a couch made of excellent jewels and was well-constructed.
There, by means of firm embraces and the biting of her lips, he gradually caused her to abandon the modesty so easily found in a newlywed bride.
Together with her, he enjoyed a fresh, indescribable love-making, charming, clever, and sweet—a pleasure never tasted before by any other woman.
"Now let the dwelling of others be outside, but in my heart let there be room for you alone"—with these words, he won her over.
Then, for him who had fallen asleep at the end of their lovemaking, the night—and his sleep—gradually came to an end, bringing with it the pleasure of his beloved's embrace.
And at dawn, having risen and gone there, Sūryaprabha then gratified those first wives of his who were staying with him.
And while those women were mocking him, who was infatuated with his new bride, with a series of words that were playful, indirect, sweet, affectionate, and charming;
Then, announced by the doorkeeper, a Vidyādhara named Suṣeṇa arrived, prostrated himself, and addressed that skillful man:
"O Lord, I have been sent here by all the lords of the Vidyādharas, headed by Trikūṭanātha; they thus address Your Majesty."
On the third day from the full moon of the month of Ṛṣabha, your auspicious consecration shall take place; let it be announced to all, and let preparations be made for this occasion.
Having heard that, Sūryaprabha then replied to the messenger: "Go and speak to the lord of Trikūṭa and the others in my name."
"May you yourselves undertake the preparations and speak; as for us, we stand here already fully prepared."
"We shall provide a formal greeting for all of them, each according to their rank. Having received this message, Suṣeṇa then departed.
And Sūryaprabha also [consoled] each of his friends, beginning with Prabhāsa, as well as the gods, the sages beginning with Yājñavalkya, and the kings.
And he dispatched messengers separately to all the Vidyādharas and Asuras to invite them to his own great festival of consecration.
And he went alone by himself to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, making an effort to invite both Hara and Ambikā.
And as he ascended, he beheld that mountain, white with bright ashes, frequented by celestial sages and perfected beings, like a second Śaṅkara.
Having ascended more than half of that which was difficult to climb beyond that point, he saw there a single door made of coral.
When he did not obtain entry there even though he was a perfected one, he then praised the Moon-crested Lord with a one-pointed mind.
Then, having opened that door, a man with the face of an elephant said: "Come, enter; the blessed Lord Heramba is pleased with you."
Then Sūryaprabha, having entered there into the interior with wonder, sat down upon a great and comfortable slab of jyotīrasa stone.
Resembling twelve suns, with a single tusk and the face of an elephant, he has a protruding belly and three eyes, and wields a flaming axe and mallet.
Then he saw Vināyaka surrounded by hosts with the faces of various creatures; having prostrated himself at his feet, he paid him homage.
He too, delighted by the conqueror of obstacles, asked the reason for his arrival and spoke with affectionate words: "Ascend by this path."
Having mounted another five-yojana vehicle, Sūryaprabha saw yet another great gate made of ruby.
And not having obtained entry even there, he, with a single-minded heart, praised the god who wields the Pināka bow with a thousand names.
Then, having personally opened the door himself, he was ushered inside by that son of a prince named Viśākha, who had been told [to do so] by his own self.
Having entered, he beheld there Skanda, possessing the splendor of a blazing fire, accompanied by his five sons who resembled him, such as Śākha, Viśākha, and the others.
He was surrounded by millions of Gaṇeśas, who had prostrated at his feet as soon as they were born, and who were like mischievous planetary spirits or young children.
When he too was satisfied and had inquired about the reason for his arrival, Śarajanman pointed out to him the path by which he might ascend there.
In this manner, he [constructed] the other five jewel-gates in succession, together with Bhairava, Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, and Nandin.
Having passed through the successive gates guarded by Bhṛṅgin and his followers, he reached the excellent crystal gate on the back of the mountain.
Then, praising the God of gods with devotion among the Rudras, he was ushered in by one of them and beheld that abode of Śambhu, which surpassed even heaven.
It possessed winds carrying divine fragrances, trees always laden with flowers and fruit, the music commenced by Gandharvas, and the festive dances of Apsarases.
There, seated upon a crystal lion-throne in one part, was the three-eyed one, holding a trident in his hand, resembling clear crystal.
He has his tawny matted locks bound up and wears the beautiful crescent moon as a crest; he is attended by the Blessed Lady Girijā standing at his side.
Filled with joy, Sūryaprabha beheld Maheśvara; approaching him, he fell at the feet of the Lord together with his consort.
Then, placing his hand on [his] back, the Blessed Lord Hara raised him up, seated him, and asked, "For what purpose have you come?"
"My consecration is near; therefore, I request your presence there, O Lord. To him, Sūryaprabha replied:
Then Śambhu said to him: "In that case, why have you been so distressed? Why, my son, was I not remembered for the sake of my presence right here?"
Having said, "So be it; I shall remain present," he, who is affectionate toward his devotees, summoned a certain Gaṇa standing nearby and commanded him.
Go; lead this [child] to Mount Ṛṣabha for the sake of his consecration, for that is the site of the great consecration for these universal monarchs.
Having been thus instructed by the Blessed One, that Gaṇa circumambulated Īśāna and, bowing down, took Sūryaprabha onto his lap.
Having led him there, she established him on that Ṛṣabha mountain; then, by her own supernatural power, she vanished from that spot in that very instant.
And while Sūryaprabha remained there, his companions arrived—Kāmacūḍāmaṇi and the others, along with their wives, the lords of the Vidyādharas.
The gods together with Indra, the Asuras, the great sages beginning with Samaya, Śrutaśarman, Sumeru, and that prince Suvāsakumāra.
And Sūryaprabha honored them all as was appropriate; and they too welcomed him, having been told the account of Rudra and the others.
Then Prabhāsa and the others personally brought water from rivers, streams, oceans, and sacred fords, mixed with various medicinal herbs, in jars made of jewels and gold.
At that moment, the Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, arrived there accompanied by Gaurī, his feet being saluted by gods, asuras, vidyādharas, kings, and great sages.

While all those gods, dānavas, and sky-dwellers resounded with the proclamation of an auspicious day, the ṛṣis consecrated Sūryaprabha with all the waters upon his throne in the sovereignty over the sky-goers.

The Asura Maya, composed of pure knowledge, being greatly delighted, bound upon him the turban and the crown; and amidst the sounding of musical instruments and the celestial drums, preceded by the dances of excellent Apsarases, he roared in the heavens.
And that assembly of great seers, having consecrated her as the crest-jewel of all desires, appointed her as the appropriate Great Queen for Sūryaprabha.
Then, after the gods and asuras had departed, Sūryaprabha, the sovereign of the Vidyādharas, together with his kinsmen, friends, and companions, held a great consecration festival there.

And after some days, having given the northern half of the earth to Śrutaśarman as commanded by Hara, he obtained other beloved wives along with his companions and enjoyed for a long time the royal fortune of the sky-dwellers.
Thus, by the power of Hara’s grace, Sūryaprabha, though a mere human, formerly attained the status of a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
Having thus related this tale before the King of Vatsa, Vajraprabha, the foremost of the Vidyādharas, bowed to Naravāhanadatta and ascended into the sky.

And when he had departed, the hero Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by his queen Madanamañcukā, remained in the palace of his father, the King of Vatsa, awaiting the attainment of the rank of Lord of the Vidyādharas.
Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And this eighth *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* is completed. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa; the ninth book, named Alaṃkāravatī. This nectar of stories, it is said, was formerly churned from the ocean of Hara’s mouth by the churning-stick of the love for the Daughter of the Mountain King; those who forcibly taste it, having attained prosperity through the removal of obstacles, bear upon this earth the dignity of the gods by the grace of Bhava.
First Wave: We pay homage to that Vināyaka, who, as he dances, even the mountains—dwarfed by the earth bent under the weight of Niśumbha—seem to bow down before him.
Thus the son of the Lord of Vatsa, while dwelling in his father’s palace in Kauśāmbī, was at the very outset saluted by the lords of the Vidyādharas.
Once, having gone out hunting, that Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by Gomukha and having dismissed his army, entered a vast forest.
There, his right eye throbbing as a sign that auspicious news had arrived, he heard the sound of wailing intermingled with the resonance of celestial lutes.
Having gone not very far along that path, he saw a temple of Śiva built by himself; having restrained his horse, he entered it.
There he saw a celestial maiden playing the lute for the Lord of Gods, surrounded by many excellent young women.
As soon as she was seen, with her cascading streams of radiance spreading across his heart, she agitated him instantly, like the form of the moon upon the ocean.
She too, having beheld him with an eye that was fresh, tender, and charming, became entirely focused on him, forgetting her own natural grace and melody.
Then Gomukha, who knew the mind of Naravāhanadatta, asked her companions: "Who is this woman, and whose daughter is she?"
And at that moment, a mature Vidyādharī woman, possessing a luster like gold and dawn, descended from the sky, appearing exactly like her.
Having descended, she sat down beside the maiden; then the maiden also rose and fell at her feet.
"May you obtain as your husband, without obstacle, the sovereign lord of all Vidyādharas"—thus did she, though mature, bestow this blessing upon the maiden.
Then Naravāhanadatta, having approached and bowed to that gentle Vidyādharī who had bestowed her blessing upon him, questioned her slowly.
"Mother, who is this maiden? Who is she to you? Tell me. Then that Vidyādharī said to him, "Listen, I shall tell you this."
On the mountain of Gaurī’s father, there is a city named Śrīsundarapura; there dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas known as Alaṃkāraśīla.
That king of noble qualities had a queen named Kāñcanaprabhā; and in due time, a son was born to him by her.
When Umā had prophesied in a dream that he would be devoted to the Dharma, his father gave him the name Dharmashila.
When his son had gradually reached youth and was established in the nature of righteousness, the king, having equipped him with the sciences, consecrated him as the crown prince.
Then, established as the crown prince, self-controlled and devoted solely to righteousness, he—being of virtuous character—endearred the subjects even more than his father had done.
Then, Queen Kāñcanaprabhā, being pregnant with King Alaṃkāraśīla, gave birth to a daughter.
At that time, a divine voice proclaimed: "This girl shall become the wife of Naravāhanadatta, the universal emperor."
Then, having been given the name Alaṃkāravatī by her father, that girl grew up in due course like the crescent of the moon.
In due time, having reached youth and acquired learning from her own father, she prepared to wander with devotion to those various shrines of Śambhu.
Meanwhile, his brother Dharmaśīla, though young and tranquil, privately informed his father that he was inclined toward wearing ornaments.
"Father, these pleasures, which perish in an instant, do not delight me; for what is there in saṃsāra that is not ultimately bitter?"
And have you not likewise heard these words of the sage Vyāsa: "All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall"?
Unions end in separation, for life ends in death; therefore, my dear, what delight can wise men find in these transitory things?
In the next world, neither enjoyments nor accumulated wealth accompany one; dharma alone is a kinsman that does not abandon one even for a single step.
Therefore, having gone to the forest, I shall practice supreme austerity, so that I may attain that eternal, highest state.
When his son, who was virtuous by nature, had spoken thus, King Alaṃkāraśīla, deeply distressed and with eyes full of tears, then addressed him.
O son, what is this sudden delusion of mind in you, who are still a child? For it is held by the virtuous that tranquility should be sought once youth has been fully enjoyed.
For you, who have taken a wife and are righteously protecting the kingdom, this is the time to enjoy pleasures; it is not yet the time for dispassion.
Having heard these words of his father, Dharmaśīla replied once more: "In this matter, there is no restriction based on age regarding whether one is capable of tranquility or its absence."
For even a child, if favored by the Lord, attains tranquility; yet some base person, though old, does not reach peace.
I have no delight in sovereignty, nor in the acquisition of a wife; this ascetic practice of propitiating Śiva is the very fruit of my life.
Seeing him speaking thus, who could not be turned back even with effort, his father, Alaṅkāraśīla, shed tears and spoke.
If even you, my son, though young, possess such dispassion as this, then I, who am old, have no [other recourse]; shall I too take refuge in the forest?
Having spoken thus, he went to the world of mortals and gave ten thousand loads of jewels and gold to poor Brahmins.
Having returned to his own city, he said to his wife Kāñcanaprabhā: "By my command, you must remain right here in your own city."
"O Rākṣasī Alaṃkāravatī, this maiden’s year is now complete; there is an auspicious moment for her marriage on this very lunar day."
"Then I shall give her to Naravāhanadatta; he, as our son-in-law and a universal emperor, shall protect both this city and us."
Having spoken thus and made his wife take an oath, the king turned her back along with her weeping daughter; and accompanied by his son, he retired to the forest.
That virtuous wife, Kāñcanaprabhā, dwelt in her own city together with her daughter; for who indeed would transgress the command of her husband?
Then her daughter, Alaṃkāravatī, wandered through many shrines together with that mother who followed her out of affection.
On one occasion, the vidyā known as Prajñapti said to her: "Go yourself to the self-arisen sacred sites in Kaśmīra and worship them."
For you shall then obtain as your husband that Naravāhanadatta, the unimpeded sole universal emperor of all the Vidyādhara lords.
Having been told this by Vidyā, Alaṃkāravatī went to Kaśmīra with her mother and worshipped Śambhu in those holy places.
In the field of Nandi, on Mount Mahādeva, on the Immortal Mountain (Amaraparvata), on the mountains of Sureśvarī, as well as in Vijaya and Kapaṭeśvara.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the Mountain-Daughter in these and other sacred fields, that daughter of the Vidyādhara king and her mother returned home.
"Know this maiden to be Alaṅkāravatī, O fortunate one; and know me to be her mother, Kāñcanaprabhā."
And today she came to this temple of Śiva without even telling me; therefore, having learned of it through the Prajñapti-vidyā, I have come here.
"I learned from his very lips that you too have come here; therefore, accept this daughter of mine, who has been bestowed upon you by the deity."
In the morning, he was told by her father: "The day for the wedding has arrived; therefore, my son, go today to Kauśāmbī, your own city."
And from here we two shall go; returning in the morning from the penance grove, that King Alaṃkāraśīla will himself give this daughter to you.
When she had spoken thus, a certain indescribable state came over both Alaṅkāravatī and Naravāhanadatta.
At the approach of evening, the two of them, whose eyes were filled with tears because they could not endure even a single night's separation from one another, were like a pair of ruddy geese.
Seeing them both in such a state, Kāñcanaprabhā said: "Why is there this lack of fortitude in you two at a separation of but a single night?"
The steadfast endure separation for a long time, even when its end is uncertain; hear now the story of the noble Rāma and Queen Sītā.
King Daśaratha, the sovereign of Ayodhyā, had a son named Rāma, who was the eldest among Bharata, Śatrughna, and Lakṣmaṇa.
An emanation of Viṣṇu descended for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa; Sītā, the daughter of Janaka and mistress of his life, became his wife.
By the decree of fate, he was sent to the forest by his father, who had entrusted the kingdom to Bharata, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
There, Rāvaṇa carried off his beloved Sītā by means of illusion and, having slain Jaṭāyu on the way, took her to the city of Laṅkā.
Then that Rama, separated from her, having won over Sugriva through the slaying of Vali and having dispatched Hanuman, learned news of her whereabouts.
Having gone to the ocean and built a bridge, and having slain Rāvaṇa, he established Vibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā and recovered Sītā.
Then, while he was ruling the kingdom of Ayodhyā—which had been entrusted to Bharata and was free from disturbances—Sītā conceived a child.
Meanwhile, wandering at his own will with few attendants in order to observe the activities of the people there, the lord saw a certain man.
He seized his wife and cast her out from his own home, proclaiming the fault: "She has gone to the house of another."
Sītā, though she dwelt in the house of a Rākṣasa, was not abandoned by Lord Rāma; yet this man, who has gone to the home of his own kinsmen, abandons me—this is what makes him superior.
Thus King Rāma heard his wife speaking in that manner to her own husband; distressed, he went into the inner apartments.
Fearing public censure, he abandoned Sītā in the forest; for a man of renown endures the suffering of separation rather than infamy.
And she, languid from pregnancy, by chance reached the hermitage of Vālmīki; consoled by that sage, she was made to take up residence right there.
Surely this Sītā must be guilty; otherwise, how could she have been abandoned by her husband? For it is from seeing her that sin constantly transfers to us here.
Out of compassion, Vālmīki banishes her from the hermitage; he thus dispels the sin born of seeing her by means of his ascetic power.
"Therefore, let us go now to some other hermitage," so the other sages there deliberated at that time.
Having understood that, Vālmīki said to them, "O twice-born ones, there is no doubt in this matter; she has been seen by me through pure concentration to be innocent."
Nevertheless, when they remained unconvinced, he then said: "O Blessed Ones, purify me here in whatever manner you know."
"Let the punishment of decapitation be carried out upon me for my impurity. Hearing that, those sages there were moved with compassion and said:

In this great forest, there is a sacred bathing place named Ṭīṭibhasaras; for in ancient times, a certain female Ṭīṭibha was [abandoned] by her husband, who suspected her of being attached to another.
The virtuous woman, falsely defiled and without refuge, cried out to the earth and to the world-protectors; and for the sake of her purification, they were dispatched by them.
"Let this wife of Rāghava perform a purification for us there. Having spoken thus, Jānakī went to that lake together with them.
"O Mother Earth, if my mind has not turned toward anyone other than the noble son even in my dreams, then let me cross to the far shore of this lake."
Having spoken thus, that virtuous woman entered that lake and was carried to the further shore by the Earth, who had appeared and taken her upon her lap.
Then all those sages bowed down to that great virtuous woman, and out of anger at her abandonment, they desired to curse Rāghava.
"You must not think ill of my noble son; you may curse me alone, O wicked ones—here is my salutation to you."
Because that devoted wife Sītā thus restrained them, those sages were pleased and bestowed upon her the blessing of sons.
Then, while staying there, she gave birth to a son in due time; and that sage Vālmīki gave the infant the name Lava.
Once, when she had gone to bathe taking the boy with her, that sage saw the hermitage empty and thought:
"Having left the child behind, she has gone to bathe; where can that child be? He has surely been carried off here by a wild beast; therefore, I shall create another."
Thinking, "If Sītā returns after bathing and does not find them, she will not sustain her life here," he fashioned a sacred thread from *kuśa* grass and created a young boy.
The sage established him there in a manner similar to Lava; and when Sītā arrived and saw the sage, she made this request:
"This child standing here is my own; how could he be anyone else, O Sage? Having heard that, the Sage related what had occurred and said to her:
"O sinless one, you must accept this second son named Kuśa, since he was created by me from blades of kuśa grass through my own power."
Having been addressed thus by that sage, Sītā raised her two sons, Lava and Kuśa, performing for them all the sacramental rites right there.
And even as children, those two kṣatriya princes obtained the entire collection of divine weapons and all the sciences from the sage Vālmīki.
Once, having killed a deer from the hermitage, they took its meat and fashioned a plaything out of a termite-mound linga of Vālmīki.
Then that sage, distressed by this, being entreated by Queen Sītā, prescribed such an expiation for those two princes.
"Having gone to the lake of Kubera, let this Lava quickly bring golden lotuses from there, and let him also fetch Mandāra flowers from that garden."
"Let both these brothers worship this liṅga with those [flowers]; by that, this sin of theirs will come to rest."
Upon hearing this, even though he was but a child, Lava went to Kailāsa; he leapt upon the lake and the grove belonging to Kubera.
Having slain the yakṣas and taken the lotuses and flowers, he returned; exhausted on the way, he rested at the foot of a tree.
In the meantime, Lakṣmaṇa came by that path, searching for a man endowed with auspicious marks for Rāma’s human sacrifice.
Having challenged Lava to battle and bewildered him with the mohana-weapon, he bound him according to the duty of a kshatriya and led him to the city of Ayodhya.
Meanwhile, the wise Vālmīki, having consoled Sītā who was distressed by the departure of Lava, spoke to Kuśa there in his own hermitage.
Lakṣmaṇa has taken Lava, my son, and held him captive in Ayodhyā; go and release him from that place, which he has conquered by means of these weapons.
Having spoken thus and been granted divine weapons by him, Kuśa then went and besieged the sacrificial ground at Ayodhyā while it was being guarded.
There he defeated Lakṣmaṇa, who had rushed forward for that purpose; then Rāma approached him in battle with those great divine weapons.
Even he, despite his own power, was unable to overcome Kuśa with his weapons due to the influence of Vālmīki; therefore, he earnestly asked him, "What is your purpose? Who are you?"
Kuśa then said: "My elder brother was bound by Lakṣmaṇa and brought here; I have come here for the purpose of releasing him."
Having said, "We two, Lava and Kuśa, are the sons of Rāma," and "Our mother Jānakī says so," he related that entire account to him.
Then Rāma, with tears in his eyes, having summoned both of them, Lavas and Lavaṅga, embraced them around their necks, saying, "I am that very same sinful Rāma."
Then, while the two heroes were praising Sītā and those two children were watching, and as the citizens gathered there, Rāma took hold of his two sons.
Then, having had Queen Sītā brought from Vālmīki’s hermitage, he dwelt happily with her, having entrusted the burden of his responsibilities to his sons.
Thus do the steadfast endure such separation even for a long time; why then, my two sons, can you two not endure it for even a single night?
Having thus spoken to Naravāhanadatta, who was eager to marry her daughter Alaṅkāravatī, Kāñcanaprabhā said:
Taking his daughter, Naravāhanadatta also departed through the air in the morning and went to Kauśāmbī with a heavy heart.
There, as he lay sleepless at night, Gomukha said to him to divert his mind: "O King, listen; I shall relate to you this story of Pṛthvīrūpa."
There is a city named Pratiṣṭhāna in the southern region; there lived a king of exceeding beauty, known by the name Pṛthvīrūpa.
Two ascetics, possessed of full knowledge, once approached him; beholding his wondrous form, they spoke thus to the king.
"O Lord, we two have wandered over the earth, yet we have never anywhere seen another man or woman who is equal to you in beauty."
However, on the island-city of Muktipura, there is a daughter named Rūpalatā, born to King Rūpadhara by Queen Hemalatā.
This maiden is a match for you, and you alone are her match; if a union were to take place between you two, it would be a great merit.
Thus, along with the words of the ascetic, the arrows of Love entered through the path of his ears and lodged in the heart of that king.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa, filled with eagerness, commanded his own preeminent painter, named Kumāridatta.
Taking my form as it has been duly painted upon the cloth, go with these two monks to the island-city of Muktipura.
In that regard, by means of a stratagem, you must manifest my form to Rūpalatā, the daughter of the king named Rūpadhara.
See whether that king will give his daughter to me or not; and having painted her, who is like a creeper of beauty, in a picture, bring her here.
Having spoken thus, the king sent that painter, along with a monk, to that island, having had his own form depicted upon a painted canvas.
Then those painters and mendicants set out in succession from there and reached a city named Patrapura on the shore of the ocean.
Then, having boarded a ship and traveled by way of the ocean, they reached that island-city of Muktipura in five days.
Thereupon, the painter went and hung his notice at the king's gate, declaring: "There is no other painter equal to me."
As soon as he learned of this, he was summoned by King Rūpadhara; having entered the royal palace and bowed before him, he made his request.
"O Lord, having wandered the earth, I have not seen anyone equal to a painter. Therefore, O God, whom among the gods, asuras, or mortals shall I paint? Please command me."
Having heard that, the king summoned Rūpalatā before him and commanded him: "Paint this daughter of mine and show her [to him]."
Then that painter, Kumāridatta, having painted the princess on a canvas, showed her to her in an image exactly like her own form.
Then King Rūpadhara, considering him to be wise and being pleased, questioned that painter with the desire to obtain him as a son-in-law.
"O noble one, you have wandered over the earth; therefore, tell me if anywhere you have seen a woman, or even a man, equal in beauty to my daughter."
Thus addressed by the king, that painter replied to him: "I have never seen any woman or even any man equal to her."
"But there is a lord of the earth named Pṛthvīrūpa in Pratiṣṭhāna; he was seen to be her equal, so if she were united with him, that would be excellent."
When he did not find a princess of equal form, he remained without a wife, even though he was in the bloom of youth.
And as soon as I saw that king, O Lord, who is so dear to the eyes, I painted him correctly upon a cloth and took him with me out of curiosity for his form.
Having heard that, when the king asked, "Does that painting exist?", the painter said, "It exists," and showed him the cloth-painting.
There, having seen that form of King Pṛthvīrūpa, King Rūpadhara shook his head in wonder.
And he said: "We are blessed, for even we have seen this king here though only in a painting; salutations to those who behold him in person!"
Having heard these words of her father and having seen that king in the painting, Rūpalatā became filled with longing; she heard nothing else and saw nothing else.
Seeing his daughter thus deluded by Māra, King Rūpadhara then spoke to that painter Kumāridatta.
There is no discrepancy between the painting and your daughter, my child; that King Pṛthvīrūpa is a husband who is her very image.
Therefore, taking this painted cloth of my daughter, go today with haste to King Pṛthvīrūpa and show her to him.
And having related to him exactly what had occurred, if it pleases him, then let him come here quickly to marry my daughter.
Having spoken thus and honored him with wealth, the king dismissed that painter, along with the monk who had been staying with him, and his own messenger.
Having traveled and crossed the ocean, those painters, messengers, and mendicants all reached Pratiṣṭhāna, into the presence of King Pṛthvīrūpa.
Having presented a gift there, they reported to that king the message from Sarūpadhara, explaining how their business had been accomplished.
And that painter then showed her to the king—his beloved Rūpalatā standing within the painting, whom Kumāridatta had given to him.
As the king gazed upon that beautiful woman, who was like a lake of loveliness, his sight became so submerged in her that it was unable to lift itself up again.
For that king, chewing upon her who was composed of the flowing nectar of loveliness, did not reach satiety, his longing increasing ever more, just as a cakora bird never tires of the moonlight.
The venerable Creator spoke to that painter: "O friend, both the hand of yours by which this form was fashioned and the hand of mine by which it was painted are worthy of praise."
I accepted the word of that king who had assumed that form: "I shall go to the island-city of Muktipura and marry his daughter."
Having spoken thus and honored those painter-messengers with wealth, King Pṛthvīrūpa remained there gazing at the painted canvas.
Having spent that day in gardens and other such places, the king, distressed by separation, determined an auspicious moment and set out on his journey the following day.
He was accompanied by various elephants and horses, by vassal kings and princes, by those envoys who bore his likeness, and by painters and ascetics.
The king, having mounted the lordly elephant Maṅgalaghaṭa, traveled for several days and, reaching the entrance of the Vindhya forest, stayed there in the evening.
On the second day, having mounted the elephant named Śatrumardana, King Pṛthvīrūpa entered that forest.
Just as he was proceeding forward, he suddenly beheld his own vanguard army fleeing and then turning back.
Approaching him at that very moment as he stood bewildered, wondering "What is this?", the prince named Nirbhaya, mounted upon an elephant, addressed him thus:
A very large army of Bhillas charged from the front of the gods; by them, about fifty of our elephants were slain in battle.
A thousand foot soldiers and three hundred horses, along with two thousand of our own Bhilla warriors, were struck down.
For one Kabandha was seen in our army, and two in his army; consequently, our soldiers were broken, oppressed by his thunderbolt-like arrows.
Hearing that, King Pṛthvīrūpa became enraged and, rushing forward, struck down the army of the Bhillas just as Arjuna did the Kauravas.
Then, while the other bandits were being slain by Nirbhaya and the others, he severed the head of the Bhilla army commander with a single broad-headed arrow.
With blood flowing from wounds inflicted by arrows, that elephant, the crusher of enemies, resembled a mountain of collyrium with streams of mineral ores gushing forth.
Then, when that entire army had returned after achieving victory and reassembled, those Bhillas who remained after the slaughter fled and scattered in the ten directions.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa, having ceased his battle, had his prowess praised by the messenger Rūpadhara.
For the rest of his wounded army, the victorious king stayed that day on the shore of a lake in that very same forest region.
Then, setting out in the morning and traveling by stages, the king reached that city of Patrapura situated on the shore of the ocean.
There I rested for one day, having been accorded appropriate hospitality by the local ruler named Udāracarita.
Having crossed the ocean in ships provided by him, he reached that island, Muktipura, in eight days.
Having understood that, the king, assuming his true form, approached him with joy; and the two monarchs met, embracing one another around the neck.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa entered that city together with him, as if being drunk in by the eyes of the city's women.
There, Queen Hemalatā and King Rūpadhara, seeing that he was a suitable husband for their daughter, rejoiced.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa remained there, honored by King Rūpadhara with courtesies appropriate for his own high status.
And on another day, at an auspicious moment long desired, he joyfully took the hand of Rūpalatā after she had ascended the altar.
As they gazed upon each other’s forms, their eyes blossomed wide as if to say to their ears, "Have you not heard this before?"
During the scattering of parched grain, the two of them, assuming human forms, bestowed jewels in such a manner that he was regarded by the people as a veritable mine of gems.
When the marriage of his son was completed, he honored those ascetics who had performed the painting with garments and ornaments, and he honored all the others as well.
Then, remaining in that city, King Pṛthvīrūpa, together with his followers, partook of food and drink suitable for that island.
When the day had passed in dancing, singing, and other diversions, that king, filled with longing, entered at night the dwelling-chamber of Rūpalatā.
It was furnished with couches spread with jewels, adorned with jeweled floors, its expanse supported by jeweled pillars, and illuminated by jeweled lamps.
There, that youth enjoyed with her, who was like a creeper of beauty, a festival of love-play as he desired, multiplied by his long-cherished longing.
Having fallen asleep from the exhaustion of lovemaking, he was awakened in the morning by bards and panegyrists chanting; rising, he stood there like Indra in heaven.
In this manner, King Pṛthvīrūpa dwelt there for ten days, sporting with ever-new enjoyments provided by his father-in-law.
Then, on the eleventh day, joined by Rūpalatā and having performed the auspicious rites, the king set forth with the approval of the astrologers.
Accompanied by his father-in-law as far as the seashore, he, together with his bride and his followers, boarded the ships.
Having crossed the ocean in eight days, when his forces had assembled on the shore and Udāracarita had reached the front, he went to Patrapura.
Having been thus entertained by that king and having rested there for some days, Pṛthvīrūpa, the lord of men, then departed from that place.
Having placed his beloved Rūpalatā upon the female elephant Jayamaṅgalā, and having himself mounted the elephant named Kalyāṇagiri, he set forth.
Then, traveling by successive marches without ceasing, the king reached his own city of Pratiṣṭhāna, which was adorned with raised banners and flags.
There, upon seeing the creeper of beauty, the women of the city instantly cast aside their pride in their own forms, their eyes wide with wonder and unblinking.
Then, having entered the capital and celebrated a great festival, King Pṛthvīrūpa bestowed villages and wealth upon that painter.
Having honored the two ascetics with wealth as was appropriate, he likewise treated the neighboring vassals, ministers, and princes with equal respect.
Then that virtuous lord of the earth, accompanied by his beloved Rūpalatā, enjoyed the pleasures of the world of the living there.
Having thus told this story, the minister Gomukha, eager for his master's pleasure, spoke again to the anxious Naravāhanadatta.
Thus do the steadfast endure both affliction and long separation; but how is it, O King, that you cannot endure even a single night?
"Tomorrow morning you shall indeed marry Alaṅkāravatī. When Gomukha had spoken thus, someone arrived there at that very moment.
Marubhūti, the son of Yaugandharāyaṇa, said: "Why do you not speak while remaining composed, as if you have never experienced the torment of love?"
A man possesses fortitude, discernment, and even virtuous conduct only so long as he does not fall within the range of the arrows of desire.
Blessed are Sarasvatī, Skanda, and the Jina—these three in the world—who, having shaken off Smara like a blade of grass caught at the edge of a cloth, cast him away.
Seeing Gomukha speaking thus in agitation, Naravāhanadatta spoke in order to support him: "Marubhūti, speak! he said, looking at Gomukha with concern.
Gomukha has spoken this appropriately to me for the sake of diversion; for does one who is affectionate offer words of praise during the distress of separation?
Afflicted by separation, he was consoled by his kinsmen according to their ability; beyond that, he knows only the god who possesses the peerless arrow.
Muttering such words and listening to various reports from his attendants, Naravāhanadatta passed that night.
Then, having risen in the morning and performed his necessary duties, he beheld a woman with a golden luster descending from the sky.
She was accompanied by her husband Alaṃkāraśīla, her son Dharmaśīla, and her own daughter Alaṃkāravatī.
Having descended, they all approached his presence; he greeted them, and they also greeted him, each as was appropriate.
And at that moment, thousands of other Vidyādharas, carrying loads of gold, jewels, and other treasures, descended there from heaven.
Having learned of this event, the King of Vatsa, together with his ministers and his wife, arrived there, delighted by the excellence of his son.
Then, when the King of Vatsa had extended hospitality to him as was fitting, that King Alaṅkāraśīla spoke to him, bowing with affection.
"O King, this maiden named Alaṅkāravatī is my daughter; as soon as she was born, she was thus foretold by a voice arisen from the sky."
She is the wife of Naravāhanadatta, your son, who shall become the future emperor over all the lords of the Vidyādharas.
"Therefore, I give this girl to him, for today is an auspicious moment for their union; it was for this purpose that I came here together with all these people."
Saying, "This is a great favor," the Lord of Vatsa welcomed these words of that King of the Vidyādharas with joy.
Then, by the power of his own vidyā-mantra, that lord of the Vidyādharas sprinkled the surface of the ground with water produced from the palm of his hand.
There arose an altar made of gold, covered with divine garments, and an unadorned chamber of wonders composed of various jewels.
Then that virtuous King Alaṅkāraśīla said to Naravāhanadatta, "Arise! The auspicious hour has arrived; bathe."
Having brought Alankāravatī, who was dressed as a bride, to the altar while she stood bathed and wearing the marriage-thread, he joyfully gave his daughter to him in spirit.
At the scattering of parched grain into the fire, he and his son gave thousands of loads of jewels, gold, garments, and ornaments, as well as celestial women, for his daughter.
When the wedding was completed, having honored everyone and then taken his leave, he departed with his wife and son, just as he had come, like a cloud through the sky.
Then, seeing his son being thus attended by the prostrate kings of the sky-dwellers, King Vatsarāja, like the sun about to rise, was filled with joy and extended that festival for a long time.

And Naravāhanadatta, having obtained Alaṅkāravatī—who was delightful through her virtuous conduct and possessed of noble qualities—remained there as a connoisseur of her charms, just as a skilled poet remains devoted to the Goddess of Speech (Vāṇī), who is charming through her excellent style and endowed with sublime virtues.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave: Then Naravāhanadatta, the son of the Lord of Vatsa, remained there in his father’s house together with his new bride, Alaṃkāravatī.
Delighted by the celestial dancing and singing of those female attendants, he remained there enjoying the drinking hall together with his ministers.
And once, having come to him after he had offered her hospitality, his mother-in-law Kāñcanaprabhā, the mother of Alaṅkāravatī, spoke to him.
"Come to our house and behold that city of Sundarapura; take your delight there in the groves together with Alaṅkāravatī."
Having heard this and saying "So be it," he informed his father; then, by his father's word, taking Vasantaka with him along with his wife and his minister, he departed.
Having ascended that excellent celestial chariot created by his mother-in-law through the power of her knowledge, he set out along the path of the sky.
And staying in his celestial chariot, looking down from the sky, he beheld the earth measured out like a mere plain, and the oceans as small as moats.
Together with his mother-in-law, his wife, and the others, he gradually reached the Himalayas, which resounded with the songs of *kiṃnarīs* and was as beautiful as a multitude of celestial nymphs.
Then, beholding there many great wonders, the youth Naravāhanadatta reached that city of Sundarapura.
It was adorned even on the Himalayas with palaces made of gold and studded with jewels, which created the illusion of being the peaks of Mount Sumeru.
Having descended from the celestial chariot, he entered that city, which seemed to dance with its fluttering silken banners at the sight of a protector.
And having had the auspicious rites performed for him by his mother-in-law, he entered the capital accompanied by Alaṃkāravatī and his friend Vasantaka.
There, on that day, the virtuous man dwelt in his father-in-law’s house like a resident of heaven, provided with divine enjoyments produced by the power of his mother-in-law.
And on another day, her mother-in-law Kāñcanaprabhā said to him: "In this city dwells the Lord Svayambhū, the husband of Umā."
When seen and worshipped, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; there, a great garden was established by the father of Alaṃkāravatī.
A sacred ford named Gaṅgāsaras has been established there with a name true to its meaning; go there today to worship that deity and to enjoy yourselves.
Thus addressed by his mother-in-law, Naravāhanadatta went with his followers to Śarva’s garden, accompanied by Alaṅkāravatī.
It was lovely with trees that had golden trunks, were enchanting with branches of jewels, possessed clusters of pearls as their pure blossoms, and featured coral for their sprouts.
Having bathed there in the lake of the Gaṅgā and worshipped the Lord of Umā, he wandered among the ponds with jeweled steps and golden lotuses.
On their delightful banks and in dwellings formed by wish-fulfilling creepers, he sported together with Alaṅkāravatī and his followers.
And there he took delight in divine drinking parties and music, in clever jests, and in the straightforwardness displayed by Marubhūti.
Thus Naravāhanadatta dwelt for a month, sporting in the garden grounds, aided by the magical powers of his mother-in-law.
Then, honored with garments and ornaments befitting a god, he, together with his bride, his ministers, and Kāñcanaprabhā, [departed].
Accompanied by his followers and his bride, he arrived in Kauśāmbī by that very same celestial chariot, providing a festival for the eyes of his father as he was presented.
There, before Vāsavadattā and the King of Vatsa, her mother Kāñcanaprabhā spoke to Alaṅkāravatī.
"You must never, out of jealousy or anger, cause suffering to your husband; for separation born of such sin, my daughter, brings about intense remorse."
Because of my former jealousy, I caused suffering for my husband; therefore, now that he has gone to the forest, I am consumed by remorse.
Having spoken thus and embraced her, Kāñcanaprabhā, her eyes choked with tears, flew up into the sky and departed for her own city.
Then, when that day had passed, Naravāhanadatta performed his customary morning rites and remained there accompanied by his ministers.
As soon as she had entered the presence of Alaṅkāravatī, one of the courtesans, trembling with fear, said: "O Queen, protect me! Protect me!"
"For this brahmin has come to kill me and is standing outside; out of fear of him, I have entered here, fleeing and seeking refuge."
"Do not fear; tell me what has happened—who is this, and who seeks to kill you? Thus questioned, she began to speak once more.
"O Lord, in this very city, I was born as the daughter of a kṣatriya named Balasena, and my name was Aśokamālā."
Formerly, while I was still a maiden, I was requested by my father from a wealthy Brahmin named Haṭhaśarman, who was enamored with my beauty.
"I do not desire this man of hideous form and terrible countenance as my husband; I told my father, 'I shall not be given to him.'"
Having heard that, Haṭhaśarman nevertheless did this in his father's house: he took a vow of fasting until I was given to him by that man who feared the act of killing.
Then that brahmin took me away to be married, even though I did not wish it; and I, having abandoned him, went to another son of a kṣatriya.
Thus overcome by Haṭhaśarman through his arrogance regarding wealth and other means, I, accompanied by that second Kṣatriya youth Dhanavat, took refuge [with him].
That man went there at night and set his house on fire with that fire; then, having been abandoned by him, I went to a third kṣatriya.
His house, too, was set on fire by that twice-born man at night; consequently, I was abandoned by him as well and have fallen into a state of utter desolation.
Then, fearing that Haṭhaśarman, the twice-born, who was intent on killing her, would not let go of even a single step from her, she fled like a doe afraid of a jackal.
Right here, I have taken refuge in the state of a maidservant to your servant, the powerful Prince Vīraśarman, who is a protector of those seeking shelter.
Having learned of that, Haṭhaśarman—despondent due to his lack of hope in me and afflicted by separation—became nothing but skin and bone; yet he was restrained.
And that prince Vīraśarman, O Queen, who had set out here for the sake of my protection and to bind him, was restrained by me.
"Today, by chance, seeing me gone out, that Haṭhaśarman, having drawn his sword, has rushed from here in order to kill me."
Therefore, having fled here, I was let in by the compassionate doorkeeper who opened the gate; I know that he remained outside.
When she had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta summoned that Brahmin Haṭhaśarman, who was his own equal.
He saw him wearing that garland of *aśoka* flowers, gazing with a blazing look, deformed, holding a dagger in his hand, and with the joints of his limbs trembling from rage.
And he said to him: "O base Brahmin, you kill and even burn women; for their sake, why do you commit such sinful deeds by entering the houses of others?"
Having heard that, the brahmin said: "This woman is my lawful wife; having abandoned me, she has gone elsewhere—how could I endure that?"
When this was said by him, Aśokamālā was distressed and then spoke: "O guardians of the world, tell me this: why [is this so] when you yourselves are witnesses?"
Though unwilling, I was forcibly led away and married here by him; why did I not say then, "I shall not live in your house"?
When she had spoken thus, a divine voice there proclaimed: "Just as this Aśokamālā speaks, so indeed is it true."
And she is not human; hear this truth concerning her: there is a heroic lord of the Vidyādharas named Aśokakara.
To that sonless man, by the grace of fate, a single daughter was born; she was named Aśokamālā, and she grew up in her father's house.
And she, being in the prime of youth, though offered by him who sought a kinsman for her, desired no husband at all due to her excessive pride in her own beauty.
Enraged by her persistence, her father gave her this curse: "Go to the human state; and there, your name shall be exactly your own."
And here, a deformed Brahmin will forcibly marry you; abandoning him out of fear of him, you will successively obtain three husbands.
Harassed even by him, you will take refuge as a slave with a powerful prince, and he certainly will not turn back.
When he saw her and ran toward her, desiring to kill her, she fled and entered the royal palace; "You shall be released from this curse."
Thus, that Vidyādharī Yaśokamālā, who was formerly cursed by her father, has now been born here as a human being under that very same name.
Now that he has been born, this end of the curse has arrived; go now to his Vidyādhara abode, and staying there, she shall enter her own body.
Then, accompanied by her husband, who was chosen by the Vidyādhara king named Abhirucita, she will enjoy herself, remembering her curse.
Having spoken thus in divine speech, Aśokamālā also, at that very moment, suddenly became lifeless and fell to the ground.
And having seen her, Alaṅkāravatī, her eyes filled with tears, stood there at Naravāhanadatta’s side.
But that brahmin Haṭhaśarman, though overcome by grief and blinded by passion, even as he lamented, suddenly became one whose face blossomed with joy.
When asked by everyone, "What is this?", that Brahmin said: "I have remembered my former birth; listen as I relate it."
On the Himālaya mountain there is an excellent city named Madanapura; there resides a lord of the Vidyādharas named Pralambabhuja.
O Lord, a son named Sthūlabhuja was born to him; and that noble prince gradually reached the prime of youth.
Then the lord of the Vidyādharas named Surabhivatsa himself came to his house with his daughter and spoke to that Pralambabhuja.
This daughter named Surabhidattā is given today by me to your grandson Sthūlabhuja; let that virtuous youth wed her.
Having heard that and immediately acting upon it, he, whose arms were long, summoned his own son and communicated this matter to him.
Then his son Sthūlabhuja said to him out of pride in his own beauty: "Father, I will not marry her; for she is merely mediocre in beauty."
"O son, what is the use of excessive beauty? For she is of noble lineage and must be honored; given by my father and accepted by me for your sake, do not treat her otherwise."
Although he was addressed thus again by his father, Sthūlabhuja did not do that which was commanded; therefore, his father, becoming enraged, cursed him.
Due to the fault of identifying with form, descend into the human realm by means of this [body]; and there you shall become deformed, with a hideous face.
Having forcibly obtained as your wife the woman named Aśokamālā, who had fallen [to earth] due to a curse, you experienced the suffering of separation after being abandoned by her against her will.
And for the sake of her, who is attached to another, you—emaciated by grief and deluded by passion—will commit sinful acts such as setting fires and the like.
Having been thus addressed with a curse, that virtuous Surabhidattā, weeping, then clung to the feet of that Pralambabhuja and entreated him.
"Grant me this same curse as well; let our destinies be equal. Let my husband not suffer affliction alone on account of my transgression."
When she had spoken thus, the long-armed king, being pleased, comforted that virtuous woman and declared this end to his son's curse:
As soon as the release from the curse of Aśokamālā occurs, he will likewise remember his former birth and be liberated from this curse.
Having regained his own body and remembering the curse, he will soon marry you here, free from egoism, and being united with you, he will be happy.
Having been addressed thus by him, that virtuous woman somehow regained her composure; and know me to be Sthūlabhuja, fallen here from my celestial state due to a curse.
I have seen that this great suffering of men arises from the fault of egoism; whether the [object of desire] is unseen or seen, how could there be any welfare for those possessed by egoism?
"Today that curse of mine has been exhausted," said Haṭhaśarman, and casting off that body, he became a young Vidyādhara prince.
And having taken the body of Aśokamālā, he cast it into the Gaṅgā while remaining invisible through the power of his magic knowledge, out of compassion.
And with those waters brought forth by the power of his knowledge, he instantly and thoroughly washed that bedchamber of Alaṅkāravatī on all sides, as if it were a mere ornament.
And having bowed to Naravāhanadatta, his future lord, he flew up from there into the sky and departed to accomplish his own purpose.
Then, while everyone was filled with wonder, Gomukha, taking the opportunity, told this story related to Anaṅgarati.
There is on earth a city named Śūrapura, which is true to its name; there lived a king named Mahāvarāha who was exceedingly haughty.
From the propitiation of Gaurī, a daughter named Anaṅgarati was born to that king—who had no other offspring—by his queen Padmarati.
In time, having reached the prime of youth and being proud of her beauty, she did not desire any husband, even though kings were entreating her.
"He who is a hero, handsome, and possesses a single, excellent discernment—to him I must give myself," she said with firm resolve.
Then four heroes arrived there from the Deccan, having heard news of him, desiring to find him, and possessing the very qualities he sought.
When they had been announced by the doorkeepers and had entered, King Mahāvarāha questioned them in the presence of Anaṅgarati.
"What is your name, whose are you, and what is your birth and your knowledge? Having heard these words of the king, one among them addressed him:
"I am a Śūdra named Pañcapaṭṭika; I possess knowledge, for I weave five pairs of cloths every day."
Of these, I bestow one upon them and give it to a Brāhmaṇa; the second I offer to the Supreme Lord, and the third I keep for myself.
"If she becomes my fourth wife, I shall give that [wealth] to her; as for my own bodily sustenance, I shall provide it by selling my fifth [organ]."
Then the second one also declared: "I am known as Bhāṣājña; I am a Vaiśya who understands the cries of all beasts and birds."
Then the third spoke: "I am named Khaḍgadhara; I am a Kṣatriya who can be defeated by sword-fighting alone, and not by any other means."
And the fourth said, "I am a preeminent brahmin named Jīvadatta; by means of the lore obtained through the grace of Gaurī, I restore dead women to life."
When they had spoken thus, the remaining three—the Śūdra, the Vaiśya, and the Kṣatriya—each praised their own form, heroism, and strength.
The Brahmin, however, praised his strength and valor, excluding his physical form; thereupon, King Mahāvarāha spoke to his own steward.
"Take all these men now to your own home and let them rest. Having heard that, the chamberlain said, "So be it," and led them to his house.
Then that king said to his daughter Anaṅgarati, "O daughter, which among these four heroes is your preference?"
Having heard this, Anaṅgarati then said to her father: "O father, not one of these four is pleasing to me."
If a Śūdra and a weaver are made into one, what is the use of their qualities? And if a Vaiśya and a bird are made into a second pair, what is the use of their cries being known?
Being a Kṣatriya woman, how could I give myself to those two? A third man, a virtuous Kṣatriya of equal caste, would be suitable for me.
But he is a servant for his livelihood, a poor man who sells his very life; how could I, being the daughter of a lord of the earth, become his wife?
Even the fourth Brahmin, Jīvadatta, is not approved by me; he is deformed, engaged in improper occupations, fallen, and devoid of the Vedas.
It is fitting that he should punish you; why indeed do you give me to him? O dear one, you are the king and the protector of the dharma of the social classes and stages of life.
A king who is a hero in righteousness is praised more than one who is a hero with the sword; a hero in righteousness would be the lord of thousands of heroes with the sword.
Having dismissed his daughter, who had spoken these and other words, the king rose from there to attend to his bath and other personal needs.
And on the second day, those four heroes, having departed from the house of the Kṣattṛ, wandered about that city with great curiosity.
And at that moment, a rogue elephant named Padmakavala, having broken its tethering post, emerged from the stable in a state of rut, crushing the people.
Seeing those heroes, that great elephant also rushed forward to slay them; and they too, with weapons raised, charged toward him.
Then, that Kṣatriya among them named Khaḍgadhara, having warded off those other three, alone rushed toward that elephant.
And with a single blow, as effortless as one would pluck a lotus stalk, he lopped off the trunk of that roaring elephant as it was extended forward.
Emerging from between the elephant's feet and displaying his agility, he delivered a second blow to the back of that tusker.
And with the third [arrow], he cut off both of his feet; then, letting out a cry, the elephant fell down and died.
Seeing that prowess of his, all the people were amazed; and King Mahāvarāha, having learned of it, was filled with wonder.
On another day, that king went out for the hunt mounted upon an elephant; those four heroes, Khaḍgadhara and the others, also followed him.
There, while the king was slaying tigers, deer, and boars along with his army, enraged lions rushed forward upon hearing the trumpeting of the elephants.
Then, as a single lion was charging at him, he, wielding a sword, cut it in two with one stroke of his sharp blade.
And seizing the second one with his left hand by the foot, he dashed it against the ground and rendered the lion lifeless.
Bhāṣājña, Jīvadatta, and Pañcapaṭṭika likewise each struck a lion upon the ground.
Thus, in due course, as the king looked on, many lions, tigers, and other beasts were slain with ease by those heroes moving on foot.
Then that king, filled with wonder and satisfied after his hunt, entered his own city; those heroes also went to the house of the chamberlain.
And the king, having entered the inner apartments, immediately summoned his daughter Anaṅgarati to that very spot, even though he himself was exhausted.
Having recounted the prowess of each one of those heroes as he had observed it during the hunt, he spoke to her, who was greatly amazed.
If both are of the same caste, possessing knowledge of the five scripts and speech, yet the Brahmin Jīvadatta is devoid of beauty and performs improper acts;
What fault can there be in that Kṣatriya, that wielder of the sword, who is perfectly proportioned, handsome, and endowed with strength and valor?
He who slew such an elephant and likewise crushed it upon the ground, and who, seizing lions by their feet, struck others down with his sword.
If it is argued that he is at fault because he is poor and a servant, I shall in an instant make him the lord to be served by others.
"Choose a husband from among them, daughter, if one pleases you," her father said; thus addressed by him, Anaṅgarati spoke to him.
Therefore, once all those heroes have been brought here by you, let the astrologer be questioned for now; let us see what he says.
Thus addressed by her, the king summoned those heroes there and, out of consideration for them, personally questioned the astrologer in their presence.
Behold, among these who delight in formless passion, with whom does she have mutual compatibility? And when will her auspicious moment for marriage occur?
Having heard that and being asked about the constellations, that best of astrologers calculated for a long time and then spoke to the king.
If you do not become angry with me, O Lord, I shall clearly explain this: there is not even a single quality among these that is favorable to your daughter.
Furthermore, there is no marriage for her here, because she has fallen here due to a curse; she is a Vidyādharī, and that curse of hers will terminate after three months.
Therefore, let these people wait here for three months; if she has not gone to her own world by then, this will come to pass.
All those heroes there placed their trust in these words of the astrologer and remained there for a period of three months.
When three months had passed, the king summoned those heroes, that astrologer, and Anaṅgarati to his own presence.
Seeing that his daughter had suddenly become even more beautiful, the king rejoiced, while the astrologer considered her to have reached the proper time [for marriage].
"Now tell me what is appropriate, for those three months have indeed passed," the king said as he questioned that astrologer.
Then, remembering her own birth, Sānaṅgarati covered her face with her upper garment and cast off that human body.
While the king himself was wondering, "How is she situated thus? and was about to lift her face, he beheld that she was dead.
With her bee-like eyes averted and her lotus-face discolored, she was like a lotus plant struck by frost, deprived of the sweet sound of its swans.
Then, immediately struck to the ground by that thunderbolt-fall of grief, the king fell motionless, as if swooning from the loss of his own wings.
Queen Padmarati also fell into a state of delusion and went [forth], her ornaments and flowers fallen away, like a cluster of blossoms on a tree broken down by an elephant.
While the attendants were crying out in lamentation and those heroes were in distress, the king regained consciousness in an instant and spoke to Jīvadatta.
They have no power here; now let it be your turn. You have promised, "I shall revive a dead woman."
If you possess the power of knowledge, then restore my daughter to life; once she has regained her life, O Brahmin, I shall give her to you alone.
Having heard these words of the king, Jīvadatta sprinkled the princess with consecrated waters and sang this noble verse:
O Cāmuṇḍā, who laughs with loud, piercing laughter, who is garlanded with skulls, who is difficult to behold, and who is most formidable—grant me your assistance quickly!
When, despite such efforts made by him, that young girl did not regain her life, Jīvadatta became despondent and said:
"Even though the lore was bestowed upon me by Vindhyavāsinī, it has gone forth fruitlessly; therefore, what is the use of this life of mine, which is now a source of ridicule?"
Having said this, just as Jīvadatta proceeded to cut off his own head with a great sword, a voice arose from the sky.
"O Jīvadatta, do not act rashly; listen now! This is a virtuous daughter of the Vidyādharas named Anaṅgaprabhā."
Having attained human form for this long a time due to the curse of her parents, she has now abandoned this body and gone to her own world, assuming her natural form.
Go once again to that very Vindhya-dweller and propitiate her; through her grace, you shall regain this virtuous Vidyādharī as well.
"And this place of divine enjoyment is not to be grieved for by the king, nor even by you. Having thus spoken according to the truth, that divine voice fell silent.
Then, having performed the consecration rites for his daughter, the king abandoned his grief; and those other three heroes, together with their wives, departed as they had come.
Jīvadatta, however, having conceived hope, went to that goddess dwelling in the Vindhya mountains and propitiated her with ascetic penance; she, too, commanded him in a dream.
"I am pleased with you; arise and listen, for I shall tell you this: there is a city named Vīrapura on the Snowy Mountain."
There lived a sovereign of the Vidyādharas named Samara; by his queen Anaṅgavatī, a daughter named Anaṅgaprabhā was born.
When she, arrogant with her beauty and youth, desired no husband at all, then her parents, enraged by her most obstinate persistence, cursed her.
Go to the human realm; even there you shall not obtain the happiness of a husband. Like a sixteen-year-old maiden, having abandoned that body here, you shall depart.

"Your husband shall become a mortal and deformed, yet he will be one perfected in the mastery of the sword; having fallen into the state of mortality due to a curse arising from his desire for the daughter of a sage."
And though you do not desire it, he will lead you back to the world of mortals; there, a separation from him will occur for you because you have been led elsewhere.
In a previous birth, he indeed abducted eight wives belonging to others; therefore, he will experience suffering worthy of being endured for eight lifetimes.
And in this single birth, you—though made a human being—will experience suffering through the loss of your sciences, as if they were sciences lost over many lifetimes.
