For association with any sinner indeed results in sharing his sin; however, for women, union with a sinful husband results in equal sin.
Having lost your memory, you shall obtain many human husbands here, because you harbored a stubborn attachment born of hatred toward the husband chosen by you.
"That celestial being Madanaprabha who entreated you, having become a mortal king, shall eventually become your husband."
Then, released from the curse, you shall return again to your own world and regain that very husband who is worthy of you, though he has become a wanderer of the sky.
Thus, having been cursed by her father and become Anaṅgarati on earth, she has today returned to her parents and become Anaṅgaprabhā once again.
Therefore, having gone to Vīrapura and defeated her father in battle—even though he is of noble lineage and well-protected—obtain her.
"Take this sword; with it held in your hand, you shall have the power to move through the sky and you shall become invincible."
Having spoken thus and surrendered her sword, the goddess vanished; he woke up and saw the divine sword lying in his hand.
Then, rising up with a joyful heart, Jīvadatta bowed to the Mother; his exhaustion from all his ascetic toil was stilled by being nourished with the nectar of her grace.
With sword in hand, he leaped into the sky and, after circling the Himalayas, reached that battle where the lord of the sky-dwellers stood in the city of Vīrapura.
Having married that Anaṅgaprabhā, who was bestowed upon him there by the one victorious in battle, he enjoyed divine excellence of sensual pleasure.
Having stayed there for some time, Jīvadatta spoke thus to his father-in-law Samara and to his beloved Anaṅgaprabhā.
"Let us go to the world of men; I am longing for it, for even the lowliest birthplace of living beings is most dear."
Having heard these words of his, the father-in-law gave his consent; but Anaṅgaprabhā, understanding the situation, reluctantly agreed.
Then Jīvadatta, together with that Anaṅgaprabhā whom he held in his arms, descended from the sky to the world of mortals.
Seeing a single beautiful mountain there, Anaṅgaprabhā said to him, "I am weary; let us rest here quickly."
Then, saying "So be it," he descended right there with her and, through the power of those various vidyās, partook of food, drink, and other necessities.
Then Jīvadatta, impelled by destiny, said to Anaṅgaprabhā, "My dear, please sing something sweet."
Having heard that, she began with devotion a hymn of praise to Dhūrjaṭi; then, by the sound of that singing, the brahmin fell asleep.
Meanwhile, a king named Harivara, exhausted from hunting and longing for the water of a mountain stream, arrived by that very path.
Drawn by that sound of singing which he heard, like a deer, he dismounted from his chariot and rushed there alone.
Having previously been foretold of her auspiciousness by omens, that king beheld Anaṅgaprabhā, who was truly like the radiance of the God of Love himself.
Then, by means of her song and form, she brought him to a state of agitation; and Madana pierced his heart at will with his arrows.
She too, seeing that fortunate man—the very arrow of the flower-bowed god—suddenly fell within his range of vision; and Anaṅgaprabhā reflected for a moment:
Who is this? What is this? Is it the Mind-born God who has released his flowery arrows? Or is it the personified grace of Śarva, pleased by my song, directed toward me?
Having reflected thus, she, infatuated by passion, asked him: "Who are you, and how have you come to this forest? Let it be told."
Then he related everything to her exactly as it had happened; the king then asked her, "Who are you, O beautiful one? Tell me."
And when he asked her, "O lotus-faced one, who is this man lying here asleep?", she replied to him briefly:
"I am a Vidyādharī, and this man here is my husband, who has attained mastery over the sword; as soon as I saw you, I have now become filled with passion for you."
Therefore, come now; let us go quickly to your city, before he awakens, so that I may explain it to you in detail there.
Having heard these words and assenting with "So be it," King Harivara experienced a joy equal to the attainment of sovereignty over the three worlds.
"Taking this king upon my lap, I shall fly up into the sky with speed," thought Anaṅgaprabhā within herself, full of haste.
At that moment, she lost her magic power through that betrayal of her husband, and remembering her father’s curse, she suddenly fell into despair.
Having seen that and asked the reason, the king said to her: "This is not the time for despondency; this husband of yours will wake up."
O beloved, you should not grieve over this matter which is dependent on fate; for who can overstep the shadow of their own head or the course of destiny?
Saying, "Come, let us go," that best of monkeys, the king of the Cakras, whose word was trusted, quickly took Anaṅgaprabhā onto his lap.
Then, as delighted as if he had discovered a hidden treasure, the king went swiftly from there and, cheered by his attendants, mounted his own chariot.
With that chariot, swift as thought and yoked with Ramanī, he reached his own city, providing a source of wonder for the people.
Then King Harivara dwelt in that city marked with his own name, together with Anaṅgaprabhā, enjoying celestial bliss.
Anaṅgaprabhā too remained right there, enamored of him; deluded by the curse, she had forgotten her entire innate power.
In the meantime, Jīvadatta, having awakened there on that mountain, did not see only Anaṅgaprabhā, but even his own sword.
"Where is that Anaṅgaprabhā? Alas! Where is that sword as well? Has she gone away having stolen it, or have both of them been carried off by someone?"
Thus, bewildered and making many such reflections for three days, he searched that mountain while being consumed by the fire of love.
Then, descending and searching through the forests for ten days, he wandered about, yet he did not see even a footprint of hers anywhere.
"Alas, O wicked Fate! Why was my beloved Anaṅgaprabhā, though given to me with great difficulty, snatched away by you along with the power of the sword?"
Lamenting thus and remaining without food, he wandered until he reached a certain village; there, he entered the wealthy house of a brahmin.
There, his fortunate wife, named Priyadattā, dressed in fine garments, seated him upon a throne and quickly commanded her maidservants.
"Quickly wash the feet of Jīvadatta, for today is the thirteenth day of his fasting due to separation."
Having heard that, Jīvadatta was struck with wonder and reflected within himself: "Has Anaṅgaprabhā been found here? Or is she perhaps a yoginī?"
Reflecting thus, having washed his feet and consumed the food she had given him, he bowed down and, with great distress, questioned Priyadattā.
"Tell me one thing, O blameless lady: how do you know my history? And tell me a second thing as well: where have my two beloved swords gone?"
Having heard that, the devoted wife Priyadattā said to him: "No one other than my husband makes a place in my heart, even in a dream."
I regard other men as equal to my own sons and brothers; moreover, no guest ever departs from my house without having been honored.
By its power, I know the past, the present, and the future; and that Anaṅgaprabhā has been taken away by your king Harivara.
While you were asleep, by the power of destiny, a resident of his own city approached him along that path, drawn by the sound of singing.
Moreover, you will not be able to obtain her by force, for that king is possessed of great might; furthermore, having abandoned him, that unchaste woman will go elsewhere.
And the Goddess gave him a sword; having performed the rites for its acquisition, when she was carried off, he went into the presence of the Goddess herself because of his divine nature.
Furthermore, O Queen, how have you forgotten that which was prophesied to you in a dream regarding the description of the curse of Anaṅgaprabhā?
Therefore, why do you harbor this futile delusion regarding what is destined to be? Abandon this pursuit of evil, which brings such intense suffering again and again.
Or what use have you now for that sinful woman who was once devoted to you, O brother, but who has become a mere mortal and lost her magic powers through her malice toward you?
Having been addressed thus by that virtuous woman, Jīvadatta—having abandoned his longing for Anaṅgaprabhā and having turned his soul away from her fickleness—spoke to her.
"O Mother, my delusion has been stilled by your truthful words. Indeed, for whom does association with those whose actions are for sale not lead to their own ruin?"
"This suffering has befallen me due to the power of my past sins; therefore, casting aside all envy, I shall go to sacred fords (tīrthas) to wash them away."
"What need have I for enmity with others on account of Anaṅgaprabhā? For by one who has conquered anger, this entire world is indeed conquered."
While he was saying this, the virtuous husband of Priyadattā, who was fond of guests, arrived at her house.
Having been granted hospitality by him as well, he was made to leave there with sorrow; after resting, he took his leave of both of them and set out on a pilgrimage.
Then, subsisting on roots and fruits, he wandered in due course through all the sacred fords (tīrthas) on earth, enduring the hardships of many wildernesses.
And that deluded seeker of truth went to that very goddess Vindhyavāsinī; there, abstaining from food, he performed severe penance upon a bed of kusha grass.
And Ambikā, pleased by his asceticism, spoke thus to him in person: "Arise, my son; for you four are indeed my own attendants."
The first has five roots and four faces, the second has a great belly and three mouths, and you are the fourth, known as Vikaṭavadana, the supreme sequence.
Once, you all went to the sandy bank of the Gaṅgā to sport; there, you saw a certain daughter of a sage bathing.
Cāpalekhā, the daughter of the sage known as Kapilajaṭa, was sought in marriage by all of you who were overcome by passion.
When she said, "I am a maiden; I am departing," those other three remained silent, but she was seized by the arm by force by you.
And she cried out, "O father! O father! Save me! Hearing that, the enraged sage who was nearby arrived there.
Seeing him, she was released by you; thereupon he cursed you all, saying, "O most wicked ones, go to a human womb! at that very moment.
Then, being entreated for an end to the curse, that sage spoke thus to you: "When the princess Anaṅgaprabhā is sought after by you."
"Then these three shall go to the world of the Vidyādharas and will be liberated; but you, having obtained her once she has become a Vidyādharī, will lose her."
Thereupon, O Vikaṭavadana, you shall encounter great misfortune; and only after propitiating the Goddess for a long time will you be released from this curse.
Since you have touched the hand of this woman, who is like a streak of fickleness, you possess great sin arising from the abduction of another's wife.
Thus, you who were my attendants and were cursed by that great seer have now been born as four preeminent heroes in the southern region.
Those two who hold the five-fold sword and the shield, and he who carries the scimitar—these three are your friends, and you, Jīvadattaka, are the fourth.
And those three, when Anaṅgarati had departed for her own abode, came here and were released from the curse by my grace.
I have been propitiated by you today, and the end of your curse has arrived; therefore, taking this Āgneyī dhāraṇā, cast off your body.
"Burn away that sin which would have been experienced over eight lifetimes by this single [act]! Having said this and bestowed the dhāraṇī, the Goddess vanished from his sight.
Having burned away his mortal body and its sin through that very concentration (*dhāraṇā*), Jīvadatta was finally released from the curse and became an excellent attendant (*gaṇa*).
Alas! By such evil as this, arising from union with another's wife, even the gods suffer such affliction; what then will be the fate of others?
And in that very time, Sānaṅgaprabhā attained the position of chief consort among the ladies of the inner apartments of King Harivara in the city of Harivara.
And that king remained day and night with his mind fixed one-pointedly upon him, having entrusted the great burden of the kingdom to his minister named Sumantra.
Once, a new master of dance named Labdhavara came from the Middle Country into the presence of that king.
Having observed his skill in instrumental music and dance, that king honored him and appointed him as the master of dance for the women of the inner apartments.
By him, Anaṅgaprabhā was brought to such excellence in dancing that even while she was dancing, she became an object of envy for her co-wives.
Furthermore, due to living together with him and her delight in the practice of dance, she became enamored of that master of dramatic arts.
And behold! Drawn by her beauty and her dancing, even that master of the dramatic art slowly began to dance something else entirely out of desire.
And once, in a secluded dance hall, that Anaṅgaprabhā, longing for sexual union, approached that master of dance by force.
And at the end of their union, she, filled with intense passion, said to him: "Without you, I shall not be able to endure remaining even for a moment."
"King Harivara, having learned of this, will certainly not tolerate it; therefore, come, let us go elsewhere, to a place where the king does not know us."
"You possess wealth such as gold, horses, and camels, which was given to you by the king out of satisfaction with your dance; and I too possess ornaments."
"Let us go there quickly; we shall stay where we are free from fear. Delighted, the dance master agreed to those words.
Then Anaṅgaprabhā, having assumed the dress of a man, went with a single very affectionate female servant to the house of a master of dramatic arts.
Then, together with that man who sought wealth and had placed it upon the back of a camel, she set out on horseback with that teacher of dance.
Having first abandoned the fortune of the Vidyādharas and then the royal splendor, she took refuge in the power of a Cāraṇa; fie on the fickle mind of women!
And having traveled with that master of dance, Anaṅgaprabhā reached a distant city named Viyogapura.
There she remained happily with him, and he too, the leader of the actors, considered his own attainment of the boon to be true because of her.
And when King Harivara learned that his beloved Anaṅgaprabhā had gone away somewhere, he became intent on abandoning his body out of grief.
Then the minister Sumantra spoke to the king, consoling him: "O Lord, what is there that you do not know? Reflect upon this yourself."
O Lord, having abandoned her husband Khaḍgavidyādhara as soon as she saw you, how could there be any constancy in her even toward you?
Taking up some small trifle, she departed, indifferent to things of value; like one who, out of a fondness for the sight of grass, mistakes a blade of grass for a precious gem.
"She has surely been taken by the dance master, for he is not to be seen; moreover, it was heard that the two of them were staying in the music hall this morning."
Therefore, O King, tell me: why do you persist in this pursuit even though you know her nature? For a wanton woman is like the twilight, momentarily passionate toward everyone.
Thus addressed by the minister, the king then fell into reflection and thought: "Ah! Truly has this been said to me by this wise man."
For a courtesan is indeed like the condition of worldly existence: ultimately devoid of flavor, miserable, changing at every moment, and characterized by impermanent associations.
A wise man does not fall into women or into rivers—both of which show their waves and cause those who have fallen into them to sink to the bottom.
Those who remain unperturbed in calamities, unarrogant even in prosperity, and undaunted in their duties—they are the steadfast; by them the world is conquered.
Having reflected thus and abandoned his grief at the word of his minister, King Harivara established contentment with his own wife alone.
That Anaṅgaprabhā also remained for some time in that city named Viyogapura, accompanied by her dance teacher.
Just then, by the power of fate, that teacher of dance also formed a connection there with a young gambler named Sudarśana.
Thereupon, Sudarśana, having lost his entire fortune at dice, was soon appointed by him as a master of dramatic performance in the presence of Anaṅgaprabhā.
Then Anaṅgaprabhā, as if deprived of her splendor by his anger, abandoned him and forcibly took Sudarśana alone as her husband.
Then that dance teacher, having lost his wife and wealth and being without shelter, went to the bank of the Gaṅgā with matted hair, bound for asceticism out of world-weariness.
That Anaṅgaprabhā, having united with that gambler Sudarśana, remained right there, ever-newly devoted to her beloved.
And once, while her husband Sudarśana was away at night, he was entered by thieves who plundered all his possessions.
Then, seeing Anaṅgaprabhā distressed by her lack of wealth and filled with remorse, Sudarśana spoke these words to her:
"I have a wealthy friend named Hiraṇyagupta; come today, let us seek some debt from him."
Having spoken thus, his mind struck by fate, he went with her and begged that preeminent merchant, Hiraṇyagupta, for a debt.
And when he saw Anaṅgaprabhā, and she too saw him at that time, they both became filled with mutual longing.
And that merchant spoke thus with respect to Sudarśana: "I shall give you gold tomorrow; for now, let it be eaten right here today."
Having heard that and perceiving a different disposition in those two, Sudarśana said: "I am not fit for food today."
Then the merchant leader said: "In that case, friend, let your wife eat first among us, for she has come to our home."
Having been addressed thus by him, even though he was a gambler, he remained silent; and the merchant, accompanied by Anaṅgaprabhā, went into his inner apartments.
There, in that circle, he enjoyed with her the fulfillment of food, drink, and other pleasures—she who had appeared unexpectedly and was radiant with the grace of intoxication.
Sudarśana, standing outside while waiting for her departure, was then addressed by her servants who had been incited by her.
Having eaten, she went home; as she was departing, you did not see her. Why do you still remain here? Go now.
Remaining inside, neither coming out nor saying "I will not go," he was driven away by those servants after they had struck him with kicks.
Then Sudarśana, having gone there, reflected in his distress: "How is it that my wife has been carried off by this merchant, even though he was my friend?"
"Has such a fruit of my own evil deed been brought upon me right here? That which was done by me to another has been done to me by another."
Why am I angry with another? That which deserves my anger is my own karma; therefore, I shall cut that [karma] so that there may be no further defeat for me.
Having reflected thus, the gambler abandoned his anger, went to Badarikāśrama, and there performed penance that cuts through worldly existence.
And having obtained that beloved merchant as her husband, who was superior even in beauty, Anaṅgaprabhā took her delight in him, like a female bee that has moved from flower to flower.
Gradually, she became the mistress—possessing both affection and authority over his life as well as his wealth—of that merchant of vast fortune who was devoted to her.
And King Vīrabāhu, although he learned that Ekasundarī was staying there, did not carry her off, as he maintained the boundaries of righteousness.
And as his wealth was exhausted day by day, he became a merchant whose riches were diminishing; for prosperity withers like a noblewoman in a house presided over by an unchaste woman.
Then, having gathered his wares, that merchant Hiraṇyagupta set out for trade toward the island known as Suvarṇabhūmi.
And out of fear of separation, taking Anaṅgaprabhā with him, he traveled along the road and eventually reached the city of Sāgarapura.
There, in that city near the ocean, he met a certain chief of fishermen named Sāgaravīra, who was a resident of that place.
Then, having gone to the shore of the ocean with that sea-farer, he, accompanied by his beloved, boarded the ship presented by him.
Then, as that merchant Sāgaravīra traveled upon the ocean in his ship for some days, his wealth was exhausted.
One day, a fierce dark cloud, resembling the time of universal destruction and terrifying with its eyes of lightning and thunder, arrived.
Struck by a powerful wind with thick, torrential rain, that ship then began to sink amidst the waves.
While his attendants raised cries of lamentation as if for their own lost desires, and while the ship was sinking, he fastened his upper garment around his waist.
The merchant Hiranyagupta, not seeing the face of Anaṅgaprabhā, cried out, "Alas, my beloved! Where are you? and threw himself into the ocean.
Having gone forth and casting his arms about, he by chance reached a certain merchant's ship; seizing it, he climbed aboard.
Then that Anaṅgaprabhā was instantly hoisted up by that Sāgaravīra onto a pile of planks bound together with ropes.
Having himself climbed right there, he comforted her as she was terrified; swimming across the ocean, he went along, splashing the water with his arms.
In an instant, when the ship was shattered, the sky became cloudless; the ocean became as still as the Sage whose anger had been pacified.
Having boarded the ship driven by the wind, the merchant Hiraṇyagupta then reached the shore of the ocean in five days by the power of fate.
Then, having descended to the shore, he, distressed by the pain of separation from his beloved, realized that the workings of destiny were impossible to remedy.
Having returned slowly to his own city, Hiraṇyagupta, firm in his resolve, maintained his steadfastness; and having acquired wealth once more, he lived in perfect contentment.
But that Anaṅgaprabhā, remaining on the plank for a single day, was brought by that Sāgaravīra to the shore of the ocean.
There, having been comforted by that lord of merchants, she was led by him to his own residence, the city named Sāgarapura.
There, he beheld a hero who possessed a splendor equal to that of Rājasena, who had bestowed his life upon him, who was in the prime of youth, handsome, and obedient to his commands.
Sānaṅgaprabhā chose that very fisherman as her husband; for a woman whose conduct is unshakable does not look toward the ups and downs of life.
Then she lived together with that fisherman chief in his house, enjoying the prosperity bestowed upon her by him.
Once, from the top of that palace, she saw by way of that street a handsome young son of a Kṣatriya named Vijayavarman passing along.
Overcome by desire for his beauty, she descended and approached him, saying, "Love me, your devoted lover, for my heart has been captivated by the sight of you."
And he, rejoicing and thrilled, took her—who was like one fallen from the sky—and went to his own home with that woman who was the most beautiful in the three worlds.
Then Sāgaravīra, having learned that his beloved had gone somewhere, abandoned everything and, intending to cast off his body through asceticism, went to the celestial river.
How could such suffering not have occurred when he went there? Where is the state of being a fisherman, and where is union with such a Vidyādharī?
And that Anaṅgaprabhā remained right there in that city with Vijayavarman, living at her ease and without restraint.
Then once, King Sāgaravarman, having mounted a female elephant, went out from that place to wander through the city.
Beholding that city he had built himself, which bore his own name, the king proceeded by that same path to the residence of Vijayavarman.
And perceiving that the king was approaching, Sānaṅgaprabhā then ascended to the roof of the palace out of curiosity to see him.
As soon as she saw the king, she fell under his power; thus overcome, she spoke impetuously to the elephant-driver seated upon the royal elephant.
"O elephant-rider, I have never mounted an elephant before; therefore, let me mount here and see how much pleasure there is."
Having heard that while the elephant-driver was looking at the king's face, the king beheld her, like the splendor of the moon fallen from the sky.
Drinking her in with eyes like a cakora bird never satiated, the king, his hopes fixed on regaining her, said to the elephant-driver:
Having brought the female elephant near, fulfill her desire; place this moon-faced woman upon it without delay.
When the king had spoken thus, that elephant-driver brought the female elephant down to the foot of the palace at that very moment.
Seeing that she had arrived near King Sāgaravarman, Anaṅgaprabhā threw herself into his lap.
Where did that hatred for her husband begin, and what is this insatiability toward husbands? Alas! Through her father’s curse, such a complete perversion has been revealed.
As if terrified of falling, she clasped the king by the neck; his limbs drenched by the nectar of her touch, he too attained supreme joy.
Taking her—who had offered herself through reasoning and was longing for a kiss—he, the king, departed quickly to his own palace.
Thereupon, having brought that celestial woman—who had related her story—into his inner apartments, the king made her his chief queen at that very moment.
Having learned that she had been carried off by the king, Vijayavarman then went there and, like a true Kshatriya, fought the king's servants outside.
And there in battle, he cast off his body without turning his back; for heroes do not endure defeat on account of a woman.
"What use have you for this wretched woman? Come and enjoy us, O Nandin!"—as if thus entreated by the celestial women, he was led back to the abode of the gods.
And that Anaṅgaprabhā, like a river entering the ocean, fixed her steadfastness upon King Sāgaravarman, never turning to anyone else.
By the power of destiny, he considered his purpose fulfilled through that wife; she too regarded her birth as having borne fruit by virtue of him as her husband.
And after some days, that Queen Anaṅgaprabhā conceived a child by King Sāgaravarman, and in due time she gave birth to a son.
Having performed the great festival for the birth of his noble son, the king, his father, gave that infant the name Samudravarman.
And when he had gradually grown up, possessed of virtues and attained youth, the king consecrated that son, who was endowed with powerful arms, as the crown prince.
Then, for the sake of his son Samaravarman’s marriage, he brought home the daughter of the king named Kamalavatī.
And that king, won over by his virtues, bestowed his own kingdom upon his son Samudravarman, who had already been married.
Having obtained that kingdom, the powerful Samudravarman, who knew the duty of a Kshatriya, bowed to his father and addressed him thus.
"Grant me leave, father; I am going forth to conquer the quarters. A lord of the earth who does not desire victory is as contemptible as a eunuch is to a woman."
For kings in this world, that prosperity which is acquired by conquering foreign kingdoms through the strength of one's own arms is both righteous and conducive to fame.
O father, what sovereignty can those base men possess who exist only to oppress others, devouring their own subjects like greedy cats?
When he had spoken thus, he was told by his father, Sāgaravarman: "Son, your kingdom is new; therefore, you must first bring it under your control."
For one who governs the subjects with righteousness, there is neither demerit nor ill repute; and for kings, conflict is not appropriate when they act with due regard for their own capacity.
My child, although you are a hero and your army is vast, nevertheless, there can be no reliance on the fortune of victory in battle, for it is fickle.
Although addressed with these and other words by his father, the resplendent Samudravarman took leave of him with great effort and departed, desiring to conquer the quarters of the world.
Having gradually conquered the quarters and brought the kings under his control, he returned to his own city, having acquired elephants, horses, gold, and other riches.
There, bowing down before his well-pleased parents, he honored their feet with great jewels produced in various lands.
And by his command, that highly illustrious one bestowed upon the brahmins great gifts consisting of elephants, horses, gold, and jewels.
Then he rained down wealth upon those who sought it and upon his servants; so that here, the single word "poor" remained devoid of its actual meaning.
Having seen that greatness of his son and his own state of having accomplished all that was to be done, King Sāgaravarman, united with Anaṅgaprabhā, considered his purpose fulfilled.
Having passed those days in celebration, King Samudravarman spoke to his son in the presence of his ministers.
"O son, that which was to be done by me has been accomplished in this birth; the happiness of sovereignty has been enjoyed, and no defeat at the hands of enemies has been seen."
"You have been seen with your empire secured; what else remains for me to attain? Therefore, while my body still endures, I shall resort to a sacred ford."
"Look, this old age whispers into my ear as if saying: 'While this body is perishable, why do you still remain in your home?'"
Having spoken thus, the virtuous King Sāgaravarman then departed for Prayāga with his beloved wife, even though his son was unwilling.
Having followed his father and returned to his own city, Samudravarman ruled that kingdom according to the prescribed law.
King Sāgaravarman, accompanied by Anaṅgaprabhā, gratified the bull-bannered god through ascetic penance at Prayāga.
At the end of the night, the Enemy of Tripura spoke thus to him in a dream: "I am pleased with you and your wife because of your ascetic penance; therefore, hear this."
"This is Anaṅgaprabhā and you; both of you are Vidyādharas. At dawn, my son, you shall both go to your own world upon the expiration of the curse."
Having heard that, the king and Aṅgaprabhā woke up; having seen such a dream, they then spoke to one another.
Then, filled with joy, Anaṅgaprabhā said to that king: "Noble son, my entire past life has now been remembered by me."
"I am the daughter of the lord of the Vidyādharas, Samara; my name is Anaṅgaprabhā, and I live in the city called Vīrapura."
Having come here due to my father’s curse, I became a human through the loss of my magic sciences; thus, I forgot my own nature as a Vidyādharī.
And just as she said, "Now I have awakened," her father, Samara, descended from heaven at that very moment.
Having been saluted there by King Sāgaravarman, he spoke to his daughter Anaṅgaprabhā, who had prostrated herself at his feet.
"Come, daughter, take these sciences; that curse of yours has passed away, for the suffering of eight births has indeed been experienced by you in a single birth."
Having said this, she took her onto her lap and bestowed the sciences upon her once more; then she addressed King Sāgaravarman.
"You are the sovereign of the Vidyādharas named Madanaprabha, and I am Samara by name; Anangaprabhā is my daughter."
Although she was to be given away, she was previously solicited by various suitors; yet, proud of her beauty, she did not desire any one of them as a husband.
Then she was requested by you with such intense longing and with equal merit; yet, due to the turn of fate, you were not accepted by her at that time.
Because of this, I, filled with passion, gave her a curse so that she might come to the world of mortals, thinking, "May she become my wife even in the mortal realm."
Having formed this resolve in your heart and meditated upon the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, the bestower of boons, you then abandoned your own body through yoga and became a Vidyādharī.
Then you were born as a human, and she too was born as your wife; now, joined together as a couple, both of you come to your own world.
Thus addressed by Samara, Sāgaravarman—having remembered his former birth—cast off that body in the waters of Prayāga and immediately became Madanaprabha.
Furthermore, having attained that science, she suddenly shone forth as another being entirely—a Vidyādharī—her body blazing with the radiance of the god of love.

Then Madanaprabha was filled with joy, as was Anaṅgaprabhā; both of them felt a deep passion kindled by gazing upon each other’s divine forms. That illustrious Samara, lord of the sky-dwellers, and all of them together—along with that physician—flew up into the air and went to Vīrapura, which is indeed the city of the Vidyādharas.

There, according to the prescribed rites, he gave his daughter Anaṅgaprabhā at that very moment to Madanaprabha, the king of the sky-dwellers; and then Madanaprabha departed for his own city together with her, who was now freed from her curse and filled with joy, and there he lived happily.

Thus, by the power of the ripening of their own misconduct, divine beings fall through a curse and descend into the world of men; having experienced the fruit appropriate to that state, they return again to their own destination by virtue of their previously acquired merit.
Having heard this story from his minister Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta, together with Alaṅkāravatī, was delighted; and then he performed his daily duties.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. Then, on another day, his friend Marubhūti addressed Naravāhanadatta, who was seated beside Alaṃkāravatī:
"Look, look, O King! This wretched traveler of yours is clothed in nothing but a piece of leather, with matted hair, emaciated and grey."
Day and night, whether in the cold or even in the heat, he never stirs from the lion-gate; why then do you not yet show him favor?
For a gift given at the right time, even if small, is excellent; what is the use of much given at the wrong time? Therefore, show him mercy for as long as he does not die.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "Marubhūti has spoken well; however, O King, there is no fault whatsoever on your part in this matter."
For as long as the destruction of the obstructing evil has not occurred, so long even one engaged in giving is unable to give; he is not the master.
But when evil has been completely exhausted, even though one is being restrained with effort, the Lord indeed bestows [favor]; for this world is said to be dependent upon karma.
And likewise, O King, I shall relate to you this story of King Lakṣadatta and the mendicant Labdhadatta; listen.
On the surface of the earth, there was a city named Lakṣapura; there lived a king called Lakṣadatta, the foremost among the generous.
It is said that he did not know how to give less than a hundred thousand to a petitioner; however, whatever he spoke of, he gave five hundred thousand of that to him.
He was pleased with him, yet he again inflicted upon him the poverty of sleep; for this very reason, his name became known as Lakṣadatta.
A certain traveler named Labdhadatta stood at his palace gate day and night, wearing only a piece of leather on his hips and a single rag as a garment.
With his matted hair bound up, he did not move from that spot quickly even in cold rain or the heat of summer; and the king beheld him.
Thus, as he remained there for a long time living in affliction, that king, although being both generous and compassionate, gave him nothing at all.
Then one day, that king went to the forest for hunting, and a certain beggar followed after him, carrying that very club.
There, as he stood upon his mount with his army, that archer struck down tigers, boars, and deer with a rain of arrows.
Walking on foot at the front, that solitary pilgrim struck many boars and deer with nothing but his staff.
Having witnessed his marvelous prowess, the king thought to himself, "What a hero this man is! yet he gave him nothing at all.
Having finished his hunt, the king entered the city for his own pleasure, while that traveler remained as before at the main gate.
Once, King Lakṣadatta went forth to conquer a kinsman living within his own borders, and a great battle ensued with him.
In that battle, standing before the king, that kārpaṭika slew many enemies with blows from the tips of his sturdy staffs made of khadira wood.
King Jitaśatru returned to his own city, and having witnessed his prowess, he did not grant him anything at all.
In this manner, five years passed for that pilgrim named Labdhadatta as he remained there, subsisting on wood.
Once, when the sixth year had begun, King Lakṣadatta saw him by the turn of fate; moved by compassion, he reflected:
"Even now, I have not given anything to him who has suffered for so long; therefore, by some stratagem, shall I not give him something and see what happens?"
Has the destruction of this wretched man's sins even occurred, or not? Does Fortune still withhold her very sight from him today, or not?
Having reflected thus, the king entered his treasury of his own accord and fashioned a citron filled with jewels, like a small casket.
Having arranged the entire assembly hall outside, he entered it, and all the citizens, vassals, and ministers followed him inside.
And as that kārpaṭika entered into their midst, the king himself said to him in an affectionate voice, "Come here close to me."
Then, having heard this, Labdhadatta, the attendant, filled with great joy, approached the presence of the king and sat down before him.
Then the king said to him, "Recite some well-spoken verse. Having heard that, the kārpaṭika then recited this āryā:
This collection of waves fills the ocean, which is already full; but for one who is destitute, prosperity does not even come within the range of his vision.
Having heard this and having had it recited again, the king was delighted and gave him that citron fruit filled with excellent jewels.
For whomever this king is pleased, he cuts away their poverty; yet pitiable is this mendicant who has summoned him with such respect.
"This citron has been given by this king who is pleased; for even the wish-fulfilling tree generally turns into a mere Palāśa for those who are unworthy."
Thus, having all seen that which was out of place, they became despondent; because they did not know the ultimate truth, they spoke among themselves at their own will.
Taking a citron, that kārpaṭika went forth; and as he was proceeding along, a certain monk appeared before him in a state of dejection.
That man named Rājabandin gave him the garment and took from that traveler a beautiful citron.
Having entered, that monk presented the fruit to the king; and the king, recognizing it, questioned the ascetic.
"Venerable sir, from where did you get this citron? Then he pointed out to him that traveler who had given it to him.
Then the king became both despondent and amazed, thinking: "Alas! Even today his sin has not yet been exhausted."
Having accepted that citron, King Lakṣadatta rose from his seat in an instant and performed his daily duties.
That traveler also went and remained at the palace gate; having sold his cloth, he stayed there, provided with food, drink, and other necessities.
On the second day, that king arranged that entire assembly hall in exactly the same manner, and all the citizens entered there once again.
Then, seeing that traveler who had entered, the king likewise called him again and seated him near him.
And having taught that same noble lady once more out of favor, he gave him that very citron, which was a hidden jewel.
"Aha! On the second day, this master is pleased with her for no reason at all!"—thus did they all reflect with wonder, asking, "What could this possibly mean?"
And that kārpaṭika, having laughed at that result with a sense of despondency, yet considering the king’s favor to have borne fruit, went outside.
Just then, a certain official in charge of the realm came before him, desiring to enter the assembly hall and behold the king.
Seeing that citron, he then requested it from the traveler; desiring a favorable omen, he took it after giving the man a pair of garments.
Having entered the king's assembly hall, he bowed at the king's feet and first presented that citron to him, and then his other own gift.
Having learned of that fruit from the king, the ruler of that realm was asked, "From where did you obtain this? and he replied, "From the kārpaṭika."
"Alas! Even now Lakṣmī gives him no sight of herself here. Thinking thus within himself, the king then became exceedingly despondent.
Taking that mātuluṅga fruit, he rose from his place; then that kārpaṭika, having obtained a pair of garments, went to the market.
Having sold one garment, he provided himself with food, drink, and the like; and having divided the second garment into two, he fashioned two pieces of clothing for himself.
Then, on the third day as well, that king held a general assembly in the same manner, and all the people entered once again.
And when he had entered, the king likewise called that noble lady once more, had her recite it, and gave him that very same citron.
Then, while everyone was filled with wonder, that kārpaṭika went outside and gave that citron to the king's mistress.
Like a moving creeper on the tree of royal honor, she gave him gold as if it were a flower indicating the fruit to come.
Having sold that, the pilgrim remained there happily on that very day; meanwhile, that wanton woman also entered into the presence of the king.
And he presented him with that large and beautiful citron; he too, recognizing it, then asked about its origin.
Then she said, "This was given to me by a pauper. Hearing that, the king reflected, "Even now he has not been looked upon by Fortune."
Alas, he of little merit who does not know that my grace is never fruitless; to him alone do these great jewels repeatedly come.
Having meditated thus, taken it, and placed it there for protection, the king rose and performed his daily rites.
And on the fourth day, the king held his court in that same manner, and it was filled with all the vassal kings, ministers, and others.
Then, when that pilgrim had arrived there once more, the king seated him before him as before and made him recite the Āryā verse.
And he gave him that citron, which was dropped by him in haste; having reached halfway toward his hand, it fell to the ground and split in two.
And from that [treasury], whose seams had been broken open by the lid, many highly precious jewels emerged, illuminating that assembly hall.
Seeing them, they all said: "For those of us who did not know the ultimate truth, there was a false delusion for three days; such, however, is the grace of the Lord."
Having heard this, the king said: "By this stratagem, I have tested whether or not Fortune grants him her vision."
The end of his evil was not reached for three days, but today it has been reached; by that very fact, Lakṣmī has now granted him her vision.
Having said this, and having given those jewels, villages, elephants, horses, and gold, the lord made that kārpaṭika his vassal.
Then, while the people were praising him, he rose from the assembly hall to bathe; and that traveler also, having achieved his purpose, went to his own dwelling.
In this way, as long as the end of one's misdeeds has not occurred, the favor of a master cannot be obtained by a servant, even through hundreds of hardships endured.
Having related this tale, that chief minister Gomukha spoke again to his lord, Naravāhanadatta.
Therefore, O King, I know for certain that the destruction of this mendicant's sins has not yet occurred, since you are not pleased with him even now.
Having heard these words of Gomukha and exclaiming, "Ah, well said!", he [the King] addressed that man known as Kārpaṭika, his own personal attendant.
The son of the Lord of Vatsa immediately bestowed a collection of villages, elephants, horses, ten million gold pieces, and excellent garments and ornaments.
At that very moment, that successful traveler became like a king; for when a master is grateful and has a virtuous retinue, how can service not bear fruit?
While he was staying there in this manner, a young Brahmin from the Deccan once came to serve Naravāhanadatta.
And that hero named Pralambabāhu addressed him: "O Lord, drawn by your fame, I have come here to take refuge at your feet."
I do not move even a single step from the footstep of the Lord; he travels upon the earth by means of elephants, horses, and chariots, but never again through the sky.
"Since it is heard that the lordship of the Vidyādharas will belong to my master in the future, let a hundred gold pieces be given to me every day for my livelihood."
When he had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta bestowed that means of livelihood upon that brahmin of incomparable splendor.
In connection with that, Gomukha said: "O King, the attendants of monarchs are indeed of such a nature; therefore, hear a story concerning this."
There is here a great and excellent city named Vikramapura; in that place, there was formerly a king known as Vikramatuṅga.
Sharpness resided in his sword, not in his rod of punishment; he was constantly devoted to dharma, but never to women, hunting, and the like.
And during that king's reign, there was a falling away from virtue among the dust of the households, a lack of discrimination regarding arrows, and a failure of cattle-herders in their pens.
Once, a brave Brahmin named Vīravara, a man of handsome form born in the land of Mālava, came to that king for the purpose of service.
He had a wife named Dharmavatī, a daughter named Vīravatī, and a son named Sattvavara; these three were his retinue at home.
Furthermore, there is another triad consisting of the equipment for service: a small sword at the waist, a shield in one hand, and a beautiful mirror in the other.
For his livelihood, he requested from that king five hundred dīnāras every day for this much retinue.
And the king granted that livelihood to him whose power had been observed, thinking, "I shall first observe his excellence."
And afterwards, the king gave him spies to investigate whether this two-armed man would do such things for so many dinars.
And that Vīravara gave a hundred of those dinars every day from his own hand for the sake of food and other needs for his wife.

With one hundred [pieces of gold], he used to purchase garments, garlands, and other offerings; furthermore, with another hundred, after bathing, he prepared them for the worship of Hari, Hara, and the other deities.
He gave another two hundred to the twice-born, the wretched, and others; in this manner, he constantly distributed even the five hundred.
He remained at the lion-gate of this king until midday; and having performed his daily rites and so forth, he returned and stayed there again for the night.
The spies constantly reported this daily conduct to that king; thereupon, being pleased, he dismissed those spies.
That Vīravara also remained day and night at the king's main gate, bearing his weapons, except for the time set aside for bathing and other such duties.
Then, as if wishing to conquer that Vīravara there, the arrival of the clouds came forth, fierce with thunder and unable to endure the prowess of heroes.
Then, while the cloud rained down a terrible shower of arrow-like torrents, that Vīravara did not stir from the lion-gate, remaining as immovable as a pillar.
And King Vikramatuṅga, having constantly observed him from the palace, climbed that very palace again at night, desiring to know his purpose.
Standing at the main gate, he called out from above, "Who is there? Hearing that, I replied, "I am standing here," and Vīravara said the same.
"Aha! This Great Being deserves a most exalted station, he who does not abandon the lion-gate while such a rain falls from the clouds."
While the king was thus reflecting after hearing this, he heard from afar the piteous weeping of a woman.
"There is no one suffering in my kingdom; who then is this that weeps? Having reflected thus, the king then spoke to Vīravara.
"O Vīravara, listen! Some woman is weeping there in the distance. Go there and investigate who she is and what her sorrow is."
Having heard that, Vīravara said, "So be it," and then set out from there to go, shaking his hand and with his dagger-belt fastened.
Seeing him set out while such a cloud, flashing with lightning, filled the space between heaven and earth with the falling of raindrops, he was filled with curiosity.
And that king, full of compassion, descended from the palace and set out behind him, unobserved, with sword in hand.
And as he was following the sound of weeping, Vīravara, accompanied by the king who had followed him in secret, went outside the city and reached a certain lake.
"Alas, my lord! Alas, compassionate one! Alas, hero! How shall I live, now that I have been abandoned by you? Thus she was seen weeping in their midst.
When she was asked by him, "Who are you that grieves, and who is your protector?", she replied, "O Vīravara, know me to be this Earth, your mother."
"King Vikramatuṅga is my righteous protector today; moreover, his death will certainly occur on the third day."
"O son, how could there ever be such a husband for me again? For this reason, being deeply distressed, I grieve for him and for myself."
For with divine vision, I behold the future, both auspicious and inauspicious, just as the son of a god Suprabha, while staying in the third heaven, was able to see.
For, possessing divine vision, he foresaw that his fall from heaven would soon occur due to the exhaustion of his merit, and that within seven days he would take birth in the womb of a sow.
Then, reflecting upon the suffering of dwelling within the womb of a sow, that son of the gods lamented for those divine enjoyments along with himself.
Alas, O heaven! Alas, O apsarases! Alas, O groves of creepers in the Nandana garden! Alas, how shall I dwell thereafter in the belly of a sow, amidst the mire?
Hearing him lamenting in this way and more, the Lord of the Gods approached and questioned him; he, for his part, described to him the cause of his own sorrow.
Then Śakra said to him: "There is a means for you in this matter; listen. Reciting the mantra 'Vrajaṃ namaḥ śivāya,' take refuge in the Lord."
Having gone to him for refuge and abandoned evil, you will attain merit; by means of which you shall not enter the womb of a boar, nor fall from the heavenly realms.
Having been thus addressed by the king of the gods, Suprabha then said, "So be it," and taking refuge in Śambhu, he uttered, "Obeisance to Śiva."
Absorbed in that [meditation], by the grace of it, in six days he not only was cast into the womb of a sow, but went even beyond heaven.
And on the seventh day, Śatakratu saw him there in heaven; as he looked further, that man had gone to another world.
Just as Suprabha grieved upon seeing the impending calamity, even so do I grieve upon seeing the impending death of the king.
When Bhūmi had spoken thus, Vīravara said to her: "Mother, just as there was a means for Suprabha by virtue of Śakra's words,"
When Vīravara had said, "In that case, if there is a means for this king's protection, let it be told," the Earth spoke to him.
"There is only one means here, and it is entirely within your own power. Upon hearing this, the brahmin Vīravara spoke joyfully.
Then speak quickly, O Goddess, if there may be welfare for my lord; whether by my life, or by my sons and wife, that birth shall be fruitful for me.
When Vīravara had spoken thus, the Earth said to him: "There is the goddess Caṇḍikā here, who resides near the royal palace."
If you offer that best of beings as a sacrifice to her, then this king will live; there is no other means whatsoever.
Having heard these words of the Earth, the steadfast Vīravara then said, "O Goddess, I am going; I shall do this right now."
"Who else is as devoted to his master's welfare as you? May it be well with you; go! Having said this, the Earth vanished; and the king, following after her, heard all of it.
Then, while King Vikramatuṅga followed her incognito, Vīravara quickly went to his own home that very night.
There, having awakened his wife Dharmavatī, he told her that, according to the word of the Earth, their own son must be offered for the sake of the king.
Having heard that, she said: "The welfare of my master must certainly be accomplished; therefore, let his sons be informed by you today and told [this]."
Then, having awakened that boy, Vīravara told him everything that had been said by the Earth for the sake of the king, ending with the matter of the sacrifice.
Hearing that, the boy Sattvavara, whose name was true to his nature, replied: "Father, am I not a man of merit, having offered my life for the sake of my lord's business?"
"I have eaten that food which must also be expiated by me; therefore, take me and offer me as a sacrifice for her sake."
To that best of beings, the heroic youth who had spoken thus, he replied without hesitation, "Truly, you are born from my very marrow."
Having heard this while standing outside, King Vikramatuṅga thought: "Oh, how all these people possess equal courage!"
Then Vīravara placed that excellent being, his son, upon his shoulder, and his wife Dharmavatī placed her daughter Vīravatī upon his back.
Taking it, the two of them went that night to the temple of Caṇḍikā, and King Vikramatuṅga followed behind them, remaining concealed.
Then, having been brought down from his father's shoulder, that best of beings, though but a child, being a mass of fortitude, bowed to the Goddess and made this request:
"O Goddess, let our lord King Vikramatuṅga live by means of the sacrifice of my head; may he rule the earth here free from all thorns."
When he had spoken thus, Vīravara exclaimed, "Excellent, my son! and drawing his sword from its scabbard, he severed his son's head with the palm of his hand.
And Caṇḍikā, the goddess, gave [the child] to the king, saying, "May there be well-being for you! Indeed, for those devoted to their master, there is no longing for a son or even for oneself."
"Excellent, O best of heroes! You have restored the life of your master, even at the cost of your own son's life"—such was the voice heard then from the sky.
And while the king, filled with great wonder, was seeing and hearing all of that, Bālā Vīravatī, the daughter of his brother Vīravara, [was there].
Approaching the head of the slain man, embracing it, and kissing it, she cried out, "Alas, brother! and perished from a broken heart.
Then, seeing even her daughter dead, his wife Dharmavatī, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Vīravara with dejection:
"I have already performed what was for the king's welfare; now grant me permission so that I may enter the fire, taking with me my two deceased children."
Since even this young girl, though ignorant, has died here from grief for her brother, what beauty is there in life for me now that both my children are lost?
To her who was speaking thus with certainty, Vīravara said: "Do exactly as you say; what more can I tell you now, O blameless one?"
"In this cycle of existence, which consists solely of grief for your offspring, is there any happiness for you? Wait until I have prepared a funeral pyre for you."

Having said this, those who remained there constructed a funeral pyre from the timber used for building the temple of the Goddess; upon it they placed the corpses of their children and set it ablaze with the fire of lamps.
Then his wife Dharmavatī, having bowed at his feet, said: "O noble prince, may you be my husband even in another birth."
Saying, "May it be well with the king," the virtuous woman threw herself into that funeral pyre, thick with masses of flames, as if into the sport of a cool lake.
And King Vikramatuṅga, having seen this while remaining in concealment, became bewildered by reflection, thinking, "By what means shall I be free from my debt to these?"
Then Vīravara, being firm of mind, thought to himself: "The task of my master has been accomplished; for I have heard a divine voice directly."
"Now that I have eaten this pure morsel from my lord, I shall spend all that is desired upon the family members who must be supported."
Life indeed shines forth only through the support of oneself; so why should I not honor this Mother Ambika even by the sacrifice of my own self?
Thus Vīravara, being firmly established in his resolve, first approached that goddess Caṇḍikā, the bestower of boons, with a hymn of praise after having made his vow.
O Maheśvarī, salutations to you, the bestower of fearlessness to those who bow before you; rescue me, who have come for refuge, from this deep mire of saṃsāra.
You are the vital energy of all beings; by you this world is set in motion. At the beginning of creation, having arisen from yourself, you were beheld by Śambhu himself.
Blazing and illuminating the entire universe with a brilliance difficult to behold, she appeared like a row of ten million fierce, untimely young suns that had suddenly risen.
With the circle of her arms covering the intermediate quarters of space, she bore swords, shields, bows, arrows, spears, and other weapons.
And you have been praised by that very god, the wielder of the trident, thus: "Homage to you, O Caṇḍī, Cāmuṇḍā, Maṅgalā, Tripurā, Jayā!"
O Ekānaṃśā, Śivā, Durgā, Nārāyaṇī, Sarasvatī, Bhadrakālī, Mahālakṣmī, Siddhā, and Ruruvighātinī!
You are Gāyatrī, the Great Queen, Revatī, and the dweller of the Vindhya; you are Umā, Kātyāyanī, and the dweller of the Śarva mountain.
O Goddess, having heard you being praised by Hara with these and other names, Skanda, Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā, and the others likewise offered hymns of praise to you.
And while praising you, O Blessed One, the immortals, sages, and men have obtained and continue to obtain their desired objects, exceeding even their expectations.
Therefore, be gracious to me, O Giver of Boons; accept even this worship consisting of the offering of my own body, so that there may be welfare for my lord, the king.
Having spoken thus, just as he desired to cut off his own head, an incorporeal voice arose from the expanse of the sky.
"Do not act rashly, my son; for I am well-pleased with this very courage of yours. Therefore, ask from me whatever boon you desire."
Having heard that, Vīravara said: "If you are pleased, O Goddess, then let King Vikramatuṅga live for another hundred years."
When he requested the boon, "May my wife and children live," a voice arose again from the sky, saying, "So be it."
At that very moment, all three of them—Dharmavatī, Sattvavara, and Vīravatī—arose alive with their bodies uninjured.
Then Vīravara, delighted by the awakening [of his sons] through the goddess's grace, led them all to his own home and returned once more to the king’s gate.
And King Vikramatuṅga, seeing that, was filled with joy and wonder; he went back and ascended that palace unobserved.
Standing at the main gate, he asked from above, "Who is there? Hearing that, Vīravara, who was stationed below, replied to him.
I remained there, having dismounted to look for that woman; but she, like a goddess, vanished from my sight as soon as she was seen.
Having heard this entire account and witnessed that most extraordinary marvel, King Vikramatuṅga reflected alone during the night:
Oh, what an unprecedented and extraordinary being this is! For he performs such praiseworthy deeds, yet does not speak of them.
Though deep, vast, and a great being, the ocean does not rival this mountain, even when it is buffeted by the touch of mighty winds.
What recompense can I possibly offer to him who, out of my sight in the night, has thus given up his own life for the sake of the loss of my son and wife?
Reflecting on these and other matters, the king descended from the palace, entered the inner apartments, and spent that night with a smile upon his face.
And in the morning, while that best of heroes stood in that great assembly hall, he related the wondrous account of his deeds during that night.
Then, while that best of heroes was being praised by all, the lord of men bound the turban upon him and his son as well.
He bestowed many territories, horses, jewels, and elephants, as well as ten crores of gold and a sixtyfold livelihood.
At that very moment, the brahmin Vīravara became like a king; with a raised parasol, he and his family were fulfilled.
Having thus told this story and bringing it to its conclusion, the minister Gomukha spoke again to Naravāhanadatta.

Thus, O King, by the power of merit, certain servants who are peerless heroes among kings meet; those beings of noble character, having cast aside regard for their own bodies and possessions for the sake of their master, conquer both worlds.
Therefore, O Lord, this foremost of the twice-born, your servant, is seen to be exactly such as that—just arrived, preeminent in the quality of courage, with long arms and a form of steady grace.
Having thus learned from his own minister Gomukha, who was possessed of noble character and vast intelligence, Prince Naravāhanadatta experienced unsurpassed satisfaction in his heart.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave: While he was thus dwelling there in the house of his father, the King of Vatsa, he was attended by his devoted ministers, Gomukha and the others.
And while he was dwelling there, Queen Alaṅkāravatī, who was devoted to him, had her jealousy stolen away by the intensity of that love which could not endure any obstacle to his honor.
Then, on one occasion, Naravāhanadatta mounted his chariot and went to a forest of deer, with Gomukha following behind him.
And while that heroic brahmin with long arms went ahead as their leader, he engaged in the sport of hunting there together with his followers.
Even as the chariots and horses were galloping with all their might, he, with his long arms, overcame their speed and went on ahead.
Standing in his chariot, he struck lions, tigers, and other beasts with arrows; but Pralambabāhu, moving on foot, slew them with his sword.
And Naravāhanadatta, seeing that brahmin again and again, was filled with wonder, thinking, "Oh, what heroism! Oh, what speed of leg!"
Having finished his hunt and being thoroughly exhausted, he, along with his charioteer Gomukha, [halted] while that great warrior Pralambabāhu was leading the way.
Mounted upon his chariot and overcome by thirst, the son of the Lord of Vatsa entered another great forest far away in his search for water.
There he reached a great, divine lake filled with blossoming golden lotuses, like a second sky descended to earth with its many solar discs.
There, having bathed and drunk water, and having performed his ablutions and other rites along with his followers, he beheld from afar four men in a certain part of that place.
They were of divine form, clad in divine garments, and adorned with divine ornaments; they were gathering golden lotuses, having plucked them from that lake.
Out of curiosity he approached them, and when questioned by them, "Who are you?", he related his lineage, his name, and his own history to them.
Delighted by this vision, they said to him as he questioned them: "In the midst of the great ocean, there is a vast and glorious, preeminent island."
There is a place renowned in the world as Nārikela-dvīpa, beautiful to behold; there are four mountains there, whose grounds are like the heavens.
Maināka, Vṛṣabha, Cakra, and Balāhaka are remembered as their names; we four dwell upon those four mountains.
One among us is named Rūpasiddhi, who assumes various forms; another is Pramāṇasiddhi, who perceives both large and subtle dimensions.
The third is Jñānasiddhi, who knows the past, present, and future; and the fourth is Devasiddhi, who possesses the accomplishments of all the deities.
Taking these golden lotuses, we shall now go to Śvetadvīpa to worship the Lord of Śrī, the God.
For we are all devoted to him, and by his grace, we possess sovereignty over those mountains of ours and are endowed with perfections and prosperity.
Therefore come, let us show you the Lord Hari in Śvetadvīpa; we shall carry you through the air, O friend, if it pleases you.
When those sons of the gods had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta agreed, saying "So be it," and there, where water, fruit, and other things were available at will, he remained with them.
Having established Gomukha and the others on Śvetadvīpa, he traveled through the air; there, he was seized by Devasiddhi from their midst and placed upon his own lap.
Having descended there from the sky and approached from a distance, he [beheld] the son of the Ocean standing at his side, with the Earth situated at his feet.
He was being served by the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in embodied forms, and was being praised with devotion in song by Gandharvas such as Nārada and others.
Hari, who was being prostrated to by gods, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas alike, with Garuḍa seated at his front, reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa.
He saw that he had been brought there by those four sons of gods; for to whom could the company of the virtuous not be a cause for prosperity?
Then Naravāhanadatta, with palms joined in reverence, praised that Lord who had been honored by the sons of the gods and extolled by Kaśyapa and the others.
Homage be to you, O Blessed One, the wish-fulfilling tree for those who offer devotion; you whose body is embraced by the wish-granting creeper of Fortune, the bestower of all desired things.
Salutations to you, the divine swan, who dwells in the lake of the heart, whose sound is ever-arising, and who roams in the supreme ether.
Homage to you, who transcend all, who abide within the heart of all, whose form surpasses all qualities, and whose embodiment is the perfection of the six sovereign attributes.
Brahmā, rising from his own meditation with a soft sound within the lotus of your navel, though he possesses many feet born of that [lotus], acts as if he has six feet.

With the earth as your feet and the heavens as your head, with the quarters as your ears and the sun and moon as your eyes, you are praised by the wise as a certain primordial Puruṣa whose belly contains the entire universe.
O Lord, from you, the storehouse of light, this multitude of beings unfolds, like a mass of sparks from a blazing fire.
And again, at the arrival of universal dissolution, he enters into you alone, like a multitude of embodied beings entering a great dwelling-tree at the end of the day.
Exulting, you emit these lords of the world as your own portions, just as the ocean, agitated by its endless tides, emits waves.
Though you possess all forms, you are formless; though you are the creator of all, you are actionless; though you are the support of all, you are without support—who truly understands your reality?

The gods have attained their respective supernatural powers by being gazed upon by your gracious eye; therefore, be gracious, look upon me who has sought refuge in you, and look with a compassionate glance.
Seeing Naravāhanadatta having thus offered praise, Hari addressed Nārada with a gracious eye.
Go to those excellent Apsarases who were born from the Ocean of Milk in ancient times; having been entrusted by me, they have been established by me as your own, O Śakra.
Therefore, O great sage, having searched for them at my word and placed them all upon that chariot, you must bring them here with haste.
Having been addressed thus by Hari, Nārada went and, saying "So be it," brought those Apsarases from Śakra on his chariot together with Mātali.
Then, when those apsarases had been presented by him with a prostration, the Blessed One gave instructions to that son of the King of Vatsa.
"O Naravāhanadatta, these Apsarases are given by me to you, the future emperor of the Vidyādhara lords."
"You are the worthy husband for these women, and they are the worthy wives for you; for you have been fashioned by the Enemy of Tripura as an incarnation of Kāmadeva."
Having heard that, while the son of the Lord of Vatsa lay prostrate at his feet, Hari, delighted by the favor he had received, commanded Mātali:
"Let this Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by you and the Apsarases, be conducted to his own home by whatever path he desires."
When the Blessed One had thus instructed him, Naravāhanadatta, together with the Apsaras, bowed to him and [mounted] that chariot which had Mātali as its charioteer.
Having ascended together with those sons of the gods who had extended invitations, he went to the island of Nārikela, while the gods themselves looked on with longing.
There, the successful one was honored by those four divine beings, beginning with Rūpasiddhi, together with Śakra’s charioteer.
On those mountains where he resided, beginning with Maināka and Vṛṣabha, he took delight in succession with those celestial nymphs in places rivaling heaven itself.
And full of curiosity, he wandered through the grounds of those garden groves, where various trees were in full bloom with the arrival of the spring month.
Behold these clusters of blossoms on the trees; with their wide-open eyes of full-blown flowers, they seem to gaze upon the approaching beloved Spring.
"May we not suffer here in this birthplace from the heat of the sun's rays"—as if thinking thus, behold the lake covered with blossoming lotuses.
Behold how bees, even upon approaching the radiant *karṇikāra* tree which lacks fragrance, abandon it as base, just as virtuous men leave behind a wealthy man who is devoid of merit.
Behold here how the concert of the king of seasons is being performed through the songs of the kinnarīs, the warbling of the cuckoos, and the humming of the bees.
Saying these and other words, those sons of the gods showed that series of their own pleasure gardens to Naravāhanadatta.
In those cities as well, the son of the Lord of Vatsa took his pleasure, beholding the songs and dances of the citizens who were dancing wildly during the spring festival.
Accompanied by the Apsarases, he enjoyed there the pleasures cherished by the immortals; for wherever those of meritorious deeds go, their supernatural powers precede them.
Having remained thus for three or four days, Naravāhanadatta spoke to those sons of the gods, his friends.
"I am going to my own city, eager for a sight of my father; therefore, having reached that city, you too should see it and fulfill your purpose."
Having heard that, they said: "Your Honor has seen the very essence of her city; what else remains? We, who have attained this knowledge, should simply be remembered by you."
Having spoken thus, he was released by them; and when Mātali had brought the chariot equal to that of Indra, Naravāhanadatta addressed him.
"Wherever Gomukha and the others are staying on the shore of the celestial lake, by that path lead me to the city of Kauśāmbī."
Then, having been told "So be it" by him, he ascended that chariot together with the Apsaras and reached that lake; there he saw Gomukha and the others.
"Return quickly by your own paths; I shall tell you everything at home. Having said this to them, he departed for Kauśāmbī in the chariot of Śakra.
Having descended there from the sky and sent Mātali back after he had been honored, he entered his own palace accompanied by those celestial nymphs.
Having left them there, he went to the King of Vatsa, who was delighted by his arrival, and paid homage at the feet of his father.
And they too, their eyes satiated with the sight of him, greeted both his mother Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī in the same manner.
And at that moment, Gomukha, mounted on his chariot along with his charioteer, arrived there together with that Brahmin Pralambabāhu.
Then, while the circle of ministers was present, Naravāhanadatta, being questioned by his father, related that most wonderful account of his own adventures.
The Lord grants that person union with a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), for he desires to bestow his grace upon one who has performed virtuous deeds.
While everyone was thus praising him, King Vatsarāja, being well-pleased, then held a festival for his son to celebrate the grace bestowed by Acyuta.
And together with his wife, he beheld those apsarases who had been brought by Gomukha to prostrate themselves at his feet—daughters-in-law obtained through the grace of Hari.
Devarūpā, Devarati, Devamālā, and likewise Devapriyā as the fourth; these were the names asked for by the maidservants.
Where am I, and where are these Apsarases? By good fortune, I have been made a city of heaven upon earth by Prince Naravāhanadatta!
Thus, as if scattering vermilion for an extensive festival, Kauśāmbī appeared at that time with its fluttering red banners.
And Naravāhanadatta, having brought a festival of joy to the eyes of his parents, honored his other wives who were looking out for him on the road.
And they, having emaciated him in four days as if in four years, delighted him by describing each various agony of separation.
And Gomukha described the heroic deed of Pralambabāhu in slaying lions and other beasts while protecting the chariot horses during their forest dwelling.
Thus, listening to unrestrained conversations that were pleasant to the ear, and gazing upon the lovely forms of beautiful women which were nectar to his eyes, he remained there.
And there, accompanied by his ministers, Naravāhanadatta spent that time happily, speaking endearments and drinking honeyed wines.
Once, while staying with his friends in a residence within the city of Laṅkāvatī, he heard from outside the tumultuous sound of musical instruments.
Then he said to his own general, Hariśikha: "From where does this great sound of trumpets come here so suddenly?"
Having heard this, Hariśikha immediately went out and re-entered, and in that moment he addressed his lord, the son of Vatsarāja.
"There is a merchant named Rudra here in this city; he went from here to Suvarṇadvīpa for the sake of trade."
Although his own accumulated wealth had been obtained, it was lost and went to destruction as it sank into the ocean due to the wrecking of his ship upon his arrival.
O Lord, having crossed the ocean by himself alone while still alive, he has reached here today on the sixth day and arrived at his own home.
While he remained there for some days in distress, by chance, a great treasure was discovered by him from his own pleasure-garden.
The Lord of Vatsa learned of this from the mouth of those born of his own lineage; then, having arrived today, that merchant made this representation to the sovereign.
"I have obtained four crores of gold together with a flood of jewels; if Your Majesty commands, I shall offer them."
Seeing you robbed by the reservoir and rendered wretched, who with a non-dull heart would rob you again, whom the Creator has already shared out of compassion?
"Go and enjoy at your pleasure the wealth obtained from your own land," thus was that merchant commanded by the Lord of Vatsa.
Having prostrated at the feet of the king, that merchant, overflowing with joy, went to his own home accompanied by his followers while sounding musical instruments.
Having thus heard Hariśikha describe the righteousness of his father, Naravāhanadatta, filled with wonder, spoke to his own ministers.
If he first takes away wealth, why does he give it back immediately after? Fate seems to be playing with men, as if through the alternation of rising and falling.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "Such indeed is the course of destiny; listen now to the story of Samudraśūra in this regard."
Formerly, there was a city belonging to King Harṣavarman, flourishing by the name of Harṣapura, where the subjects were made happy by excellent governance.
In that city, there was a great merchant named Samudraśūra, who was of noble birth, righteous, firm in character, and a lord of vast wealth.
Once, while traveling for the sake of trade to Suvarṇadvīpa, he reached the shore of the great ocean and boarded a ship.
As he was traveling on that path over the ocean when only a small portion remained, a terrible cloud arose and a wind stirred up the sea.
When the ship, tossed by the force of the wind and struck by sea-monsters, broke apart, that merchant fastened his belt and leaped into the ocean.
And for as long as the hero crosses over there for a moment by flailing his arms, so long he reaches a man who has been dead for a long time and is driven by the wind.
Mounted upon it, he was carried by a favorable wind to Suvarṇadvīpa, where the water was cast forth from his arms by fate itself.
Having stepped onto the shore from that [boat], he beheld upon the dead man a cloth garment tied at the waist with a knot.
As soon as he untied and looked at that cloth-bag from his waist, he found within it a divine necklace, rich with jewels.
Seeing that priceless object and taking it, he performed his ablutions and was satisfied, considering the wealth lost at sea to be as a blade of grass before him.
Then, having traveled by stages, he reached the city named Kalaśapura; with a ring held in his hand, he entered a certain temple.
There, seated in the shade and greatly exhausted from his exertion in the water, he, deluded by fate, gradually fell asleep.
While he was sleeping there, the city guards arrived unexpectedly and saw Kaṇṭhaka standing by his side, unheeded.
"This is that Kaṇṭhaka, who was stolen from the neck of the princess Cakrasenā here; surely this man is that very thief."
Having said this, those merchants woke him up and led the merchant to the royal palace; there, questioned by the king himself, he related everything exactly as it had happened.
"This man is a thief; look at this thorn!"—saying this, as the king stretched him out and spoke to the members of the assembly:
Seeing him so radiant, a vulture swooped down from the sky with great speed, seized Kaṇṭhaka by the neck, and departed somewhere out of sight.
Then, as the merchant cried out in extreme distress seeking refuge with Śiva, while the king had ordered his execution in a fit of rage, a voice was heard from the sky.
"O King, do not slay this man; he is a virtuous merchant named Samuraśūra from the city of Harṣapura, who has arrived here within your realm."
The thief by whom Kaṇṭhaka had been led away, overwhelmed with fear and fleeing, fell from his horse into the ocean at night and died.
But this merchant, having reached the body of that thief and climbed upon it, crossed the ocean with his ship wrecked and has now arrived here.
And at that time, Kaṇṭhaka was found by this merchant within the knot of the cloth tied around his waist; he had not brought him from his home.
"Therefore, O King, release this righteous merchant who is not a thief; honor him and send him on his way. Having said this, the voice fell silent.
Having heard this, the king was satisfied; he spared the merchant from execution, honored Samudraśūra with wealth, and sent him on his way.
And that merchant, having acquired wealth and purchased his merchandise, crossed the ocean once more by ship as he was returning to his own country, though it was filled with terrors.
Having crossed the ocean and traveled from there with a caravan, he reached a forest one day at the close of the day.
When that caravan had encamped there and while he was keeping watch during the night, an invincible army of thieves fell upon Samudraśūra.
While the caravan was being slaughtered by her, Samudraśūra abandoned his goods and fled; he climbed up a banyan tree and remained there unobserved.
