When the army of thieves had departed with all his wealth taken, he, overwhelmed by fear and afflicted by grief, spent that night right there under the tree.
In the morning, that fortunate man, casting his gaze upon the top of that tree, saw something shimmering amidst the leaves like the light of a lamp.
Having climbed there out of wonder, he beheld a vulture's nest containing a collection of brilliant and priceless jewel ornaments.
He took all of that from him, and among it he found the necklace—the very one which the vulture had carried off on the Island of Gold.
Then, having obtained immeasurable wealth, he descended from the banyan tree and, traveling joyfully, eventually reached his own city of Harṣapura.
Then the merchant Samudraśūra, having abandoned all desire for other wealth, remained there with his kinsmen, rejoicing according to his wish.
His falling into the ocean is the loss of that wealth; his crossing out from there is the finding of the thorn, and his subsequent departure is its disappearance.
That was the attainment of a state of being unjustly imprisoned; yet at that very moment, it became a gain from the gratified Lord of the Island, and furthermore, the crossing of the ocean.
Then there was the total loss of everything on the road due to an encounter with bandits, and at the end of that, for the merchant, the recovery of his wealth from the back of a tree.
Thus, O Lord, such is the wondrous activity of Fate: even one who has performed virtuous deeds experiences suffering before attaining happiness.
Having heard this from Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta, filled with faith, rose up and performed his daily rites, beginning with his bath.
On another day, a young attendant named Śūra, who was called Samaratuṅga, approached the prince while he was seated in the assembly hall and addressed him.
"O King, my kingdom has been destroyed by my own kinsman, who, joined by his four sons beginning with Vīrajit, rained down a shower of battle."
"Therefore, having gone there, I shall bind even those five and bring them here; let this be known to my lord. Having said this, he went to that place.
Perceiving that he had few troops while those others possessed vast armies, the son of the Lord of Vatsa ordered his own forces to follow him.
Without even seizing them, that proud man went forth, conquered all five enemies in battle with his own two arms, bound them, and brought them back together.
Then, having honored that victorious hero as he approached, the lord Naravāhanadatta praised his own servant.
Having conquered these five enemies—who have invaded their objects, who possess strength, and who are like the senses—he has accomplished the goals of human endeavor; this is truly marvelous.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "O King, if you have not heard such a story of King Camarabāla, then listen; I shall tell it."
There is a city named Hastināpura, and there lived a king named Cāmaravāla, who was endowed with wealth, fortresses, and military force.
His kinsmen, the kings beginning with Samarabāla, who were his immediate neighbors on earth, assembled together and reflected thus.
"This Chamara-tailed one constantly harasses each of us individually; therefore, let us all join together and bring about his defeat."
Having thus deliberated, these five kings, desiring to march forth for his conquest, asked the astrologer in private for an auspicious time of departure.
Not seeing an auspicious moment and observing ill omens, the astrologer said, "There is no favorable moment for you in this entire year."
In whatever manner you may go, victory shall not be yours; moreover, what is the use of your persistence here, when you behold his prosperity?
Enjoyment is indeed the fruit of prosperity; therefore, you possess more of it than he does. If you have not heard this, then let the story of two merchants be heard here.
In ancient times, there was here a city named Kautukapura; in that city lived a king named Bahusuvarṇaka, whose name was truly appropriate to his deeds.
He had a young Kṣatriya servant named Yaśovarman; although that king was a giver, he never gave anything to him at any time.
And whenever that king entreated him with such distress, he would show him the sun and speak to him thus at each instance.
"I wish to give to you; why then does this Blessed One not wish to give to you? What shall I do? Tell me."
Then, while he remained there in distress, waiting for an opportunity, the time of a solar eclipse arrived.
At that time, his constant servant Yaśovarman went to the king, who was engaged in extensive and great acts of charity, and addressed him thus.
"O Lord, this sun, who was not giving anything to you, has now been seized by his enemy; therefore, grant me whatever little I request."
Having heard that and having laughed, the lord of the earth, who had bestowed gifts, gave him garments, gold, and other riches consisting of much gold.
When that fuel had been consumed, Yaśovarman, distressed because his wife had died, offered himself to the Lord and went to the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas.
"What is the use of this useless body of mine, which is as good as dead though still living? I shall abandon it before the Goddess and obtain the boon I desire."
Thus, lying before the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhya mountains upon a bed of darbha grass, he, with his mind fixed on her and abstaining from food, performed great penance.
And that goddess commanded him in a dream: "I am pleased with you, my son; I shall grant you either the glory of wealth or the glory of enjoyments—tell me, which do you desire?"
Having heard that, Yaśovarman replied to the queen: "I do not perceive any distinction between these two forms of prosperity."
Then the queen said to him: "In that case, there are two merchants in your own country of yours, Bhogavarman and Arthavarman."
"Go and behold the splendor of those two; then, having returned, let that which is suitable for you and which pleases you be requested from them."
Having heard this and being awakened, Yaśovarman broke his fast in the morning and then departed for his own country, which was filled with curiosity.
There he first went to the house of Arthavarman, whose wealth had been acquired through trade in countless gold, jewels, and other treasures.
Beholding that prosperity of his, he approached him in the proper manner; and having been offered hospitality by him, he was invited to take a meal.
Then, by the side of that Arthavarman, he ate food suitable for a guest, consisting of rice with ghee, meat, and various condiments.
But Arthavarman ate groats mixed with half a *pala* of ghee, as well as a small amount of boiled rice and a little meat curry.
When Yaśovarman asked him with curiosity, "Caravan leader, why do you eat only this much?", the merchant spoke as follows.
Today, out of consideration for you, I have eaten a small amount of food with meat as a condiment; I have consumed half a pala of ghee and some barley meal.
I always eat only one karṣa of ghee and plain roasted barley flour; more than this, my weak digestive fire cannot digest in my stomach.
Having heard that, Yaśovarman, filled with doubt, inwardly censured the fortune of Arthavarman as being fruitless.
Then, at the arrival of night, the merchant Arthavarman again brought food and milk for the sake of that Yaśovarman.
And Yaśovarman enjoyed that further according to his desire; meanwhile, Atharvarman then drank one *pala* of Kīra.
And right there, in that same place, having spread out their beds, both Yaśovarman and Arthavarman gradually fell asleep.
And at midnight, Yaśovarman unexpectedly saw in a dream terrifying men with staffs in their hands entering there.
"Fie on you! Why have you consumed a karṣa of ghee exceeding the small measure, and today you have eaten meat with rice and drunk a pala of milk?"
Thus speaking in anger, those men dragged Arthavarman by his feet and beat him all over with clubs.
They drew out from his stomach all that he had eaten—ghee, a karṣa of milk, meat, and rice—as well as whatever else was in excess.
Having seen that, as Yaśovarman woke up and looked around, the spear of the awakened Arthavarman came toward him.
Then, while crying out and being massaged by his attendants, Arthavarman vomited up even more than what he had eaten.
When the pain had subsided, Yaśovarman then reflected: "Fie, fie upon this wealth and glory, for which such an experience as this must be endured!"
"May this [world] be rendered desolate by such a lack of fortune"—thinking thus within himself, he passed that night there.
In the morning, having taken leave of Arthavarman, Yaśovarman then went to the house of that merchant Bhogavarman.
He arrived there exactly as he had described, and having been received with honor by him, he was invited by the merchant to take a meal that very day.
And that merchant did not see any accumulation of wealth belonging to him; however, he did see a beautiful house, as well as garments and ornaments.
Then, while Yaśovarman remained there, that merchant Bhogavarman proceeded to conduct his own customary business.
Taking a vessel from one person, he gave it to another at that very moment; even without his own wealth, he produced dinars from the earth.
He quickly placed those dinars in the hand of his servant for the purpose of providing various foods and drinks for his wife.
And in a moment, a certain friend named Icchābharaṇa approached Bhogavarman with great haste and said to him:
"The meal is ready for us; arise, come, let us eat. For other friends have gathered and are standing here waiting for you."
"I will not come today, for this guest is staying with me"—to him who was speaking thus, his friend spoke again.
"Then let this guest also come along with you; is he not also our friend? Arise quickly!"
Thus, out of persistence, Bhogavarman was led by that friend; having gone together with Yaśovarman, he enjoyed excellent food.
And having drunk his wine and returned to his own home in the evening, that Yaśovarman again partook of various kinds of food and drink.
When night had arrived, he asked his own attendants: "Is there enough wine for us tonight, or not?"
"Master, there is none," he said; and so the merchant went to his bed, saying, "How shall we drink water this evening?"
Then Yaśovarman, having fallen asleep by his side, saw in a dream two or three men who had entered there, and others behind them.
"Why was the sake of the late-night drink for Bhogavarman not thought of by you today? Where have you been staying, you rogues?"
Thus, those men who entered later, staffs in hand, struck with blows from their staves in anger those who had entered earlier.
"Forgive this one offense of ours," said those men as they were struck by the staff, and they, along with others, departed from there.
Then Yaśovarman, having seen that, was awakened and reflected: "The inconceivable acquisition of wealth, the fame, and the glorious fortune of Bhogavarman are truly praiseworthy."
"Though she is prosperous, she is devoid of enjoyments; she is not the glorious wealth of Arthavarman. As he was thinking thus, the night passed away.
And in the morning, having taken leave of that excellent merchant, Yaśovarman went once more to the feet of the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhya mountains.
While established in austerity, he chose from those two previously mentioned forms of Śrī the one seen in his dream—the Śrī of enjoyment—and she granted it to him.
Then Yaśovarman, having returned home by the grace of the Goddess, lived happily with a wealth of enjoyments that came upon him unexpectedly.
Thus, it is better that even a very small fortune be endowed with enjoyments; for a vast fortune, though extensive, is useless if devoid of enjoyment.
So why do you burn with envy at King Camarabāla’s wealth of miserliness; do you not see that your own prosperity is rich in both giving and enjoyment?
Therefore, an attack against him is not auspicious for you; there is no favorable moment for an expedition, nor is victory even visible.
Although addressed thus by that astrologer, those five kings, unable to endure King Camaravāla, marched against him.
Having learned that they had reached the boundary, King Camaravāla, intending to go forth to battle, first bathed and worshipped Hara.
And he praised him appropriately with auspicious names that destroy sins, grant all desires, and are fixed upon sixty-eight supreme states.
"O King, fight without fear; you shall conquer your enemies in battle"—thus he then heard a voice arising from the sky.
Then, greatly rejoiced and having equipped himself with his own forces, King Camaravāla marched forth from the front to do battle with his enemies.
In the army of his enemies, there were thirty thousand elephants, three hundred thousand horses, and ten million foot soldiers.
In his own army, there were twenty lakhs of foot soldiers, ten thousand elephants, and also one lakh of horses.
When the great battle between those two armies had commenced, with the doorkeeper named Vīra—whose name was true to his character—leading the way;
King Camaravāla himself entered that field of battle, just as the Blessed One Mahāvarāha entered the great ocean.
And though his army was small, he crushed that great enemy force in such a way that there arose heaps of horses, elephants, and foot soldiers.
Having run toward that army-force which had come before him, he struck the king with a spear, dragged him with a noose, and bound him.
Then, having likewise dragged out the second king, Samarashura, who had been struck in the heart by an arrow, he bound him with that very same noose.
And there, his doorkeeper named Vīra bound a king named Samarajita and brought him before him.
The general Devabala brought and presented to him King Pratāpacandra by name, the fourth [prince], who had been struck by an arrow.
Then, having seen that, the fifth king named Pratāpasena rushed in battle toward King Camaravāla out of anger.
Having shaken off those arrows and pierced him with a shower of his own shafts, King Camaravāla struck him in the forehead with three swift arrows.
Then, like Time itself, he drew that man toward him with a noose cast around his neck, bringing him under his control as he reeled from the impact of the arrow.
Thus, when those five had been thoroughly bound by the king, the remaining armies of each fled toward their respective directions.
Immeasurable gold, jewels, and other riches, as well as numerous harem women, were obtained by King Camaravāla from those other monarchs.
And in their midst was the great queen, renowned as Yaśolekhā, that most excellent of women who had been obtained by King Pratāpasena.
Then, having entered the city, he bound the turbans of office upon Vīradeva and Balasena, the chamberlain and the commander-in-chief, and filled them with jewels.
That king made Yaśolekhā, the chief queen of Pratāpasena, his own wife from the inner apartments, because she had conquered him through the dharma of a Kṣatriya.
Thinking, "I was won by his arm," that fickle woman tolerated him; for the latent impression of dharma is mottled in those who act under the delusion of passion.
Then King Camarabāla was entreated by Queen Yaśolekhā to release those five bound monarchs.
Having received their due discipline, he released Pratāpasena and the others who were bowing before him; having honored them, he sent them forth to their own kingdoms.

Then that lord of the land of Camaravāla ruled for a long time his own prosperous kingdom, now free of thorns and with its enemies conquered; and he took delight with that Yaśolekhā, whose beauty and loveliness surpassed even the finest celestial nymphs, and who served as the banner of victory over his foes.

Thus, even alone, a steadfast man—whose prowess is unequaled by any other—conquers at the forefront of battle even many enemies who have rushed forward impetuously, who are agitated by hatred, and who disregard the distinction between self and others, having shattered their core pride and the fever of their arrogance.
Having heard this meaningful tale told by Gomukha and having offered praise, Naravāhanadatta then performed his daily duties, beginning with his bath.

Accompanied by his women, he spent that night in that manner, singing himself out of a passion for music; meanwhile, Sarasvatī, stationed in the sky, bestowed upon him the boon of long-lasting intimacy with his beloveds.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave. Then, on another day, while Naravāhanadatta was staying in his residence in Alaṃkāravatī in the presence of all his ministers, [the following occurred].
Then the servant of Marubhūtika, the uterine brother of the *sauvidalla* who guards that inner apartment, approached and made this representation.
"O Lord, I have performed service for Marubhūti for two years; food and clothing were provided by him to me along with my wife."
"Furthermore, fifty dīnāras were promised by him to me every year; he does not give those to me."
While he was searching for me, I was struck by this foot; consequently, I have been lying here at his gateway for some time.
"If the Lord does not grant me this here, I shall enter the fire; what more can I say? For he is my master."
When he had finished speaking, Marubhūti said: "I ought to give him dinars, but at present I have none."
When his minister Marubhūti had spoken thus while everyone was laughing, Naravāhanadatta addressed him.
"Why is there such foolishness on your part? This intellect of yours is not superior. Arise and give him one hundred dinars without delay!"
Having heard these words of his master, Marubhūti was overcome with shame; he immediately brought that hundred dīnāras and gave them to him.
Then Gomukha said to him: "O King, Marubhūtika should not be blamed, for the creation of the Lord of Creatures possesses such diverse mental dispositions."
Have you not heard here this story of the long-suffering king Prasaṅga and his servant?
In former times, there was a king named Ciradāta, the lord of Cirapura; although he himself was a virtuous man, his retinue was exceedingly wicked.
It is said that a servant named Prasaṅga, having arrived from another country, became an attendant to that king along with two friends.
As he performed service for five years, that king gave him nothing, even on occasions such as festivals and the like.
And he never found an opportunity to inform his lord, because of the wickedness of his attendants who were constantly inciting him against his two friends.
Once, the young son of that king passed away; and all the servants, being distressed, surrounded him.
And in the midst of that, out of sheer grief, that servant named Prasaṅga, even though being restrained by his two friends, made this petition to the king:
"O King, we have been your servants for a long time, yet nothing has been given to us by you; nevertheless, we remain here with the hope that you might grant it to your son."
If you do not give it, then your son will give it to us; but if he too is taken away by fate, what can we do in this matter now?
Having said, "Let us go," he fell at the king's feet; then, accompanied by his two friends, he departed from that presence.
"Aha! Even toward my son, these servants of mine remain steadfast; therefore, I must not abandon them. Having reflected thus at that very moment, [he acted].
The king, having summoned those who were involved in such circumstances, filled them with wealth in such a way that poverty never again touched them.
"O King, such diverse natures are seen among embodied beings; at that time the king did not give, yet he gave in such a manner at an improper time."
Having spoken thus, that Gomukha, skilled in the narration of stories, related this tale at the command of the daughter of the Lord of Vatsa.
Formerly, on the banks of the Gaṅgā, there was an excellent city named Kanakapura, whose citizens were purified by its waters and which was delightful due to its good governance.
Wherein the binding of the poets' words was seen as a break in the ears of grain, and the breaking of women's tresses was like the threshing floor during the harvest.
There, from Priyadarśana, the son of Vāsuki, the lord of nāgas, a highly illustrious son was born to the princess named Yaśodharā.
In ancient times, there was a king named Kanakavarṣa in that city; though he bore the entire burden of the earth, he was adorned with every virtue.
He was greedy for fame rather than for wealth, fearful of sin rather than of enemies, and a fool regarding the scandals of others rather than the sacred scriptures.
In that high-souled one of firm mind, there was meagerness in his anger but not in his favor; and his hand remained clenched upon the bowstring, but never upon gifts.
By him, who protects the entire world with his most wondrous form, even the host of women was made distressed by the pain of Māra merely upon being seen.
Once, during the autumn season, when the heat had subsided and the elephants were in rut, amidst a retinue of royal swans and with his subjects rejoicing in festive celebration;
To enjoy himself with one whose virtues were equal to his own, he entered a magnificent palace, cooled by breezes carrying the fragrance of drawn-out lotuses.
While he was there, gazing upon it and praising that painting, the doorkeeper entered and addressed the king.
"O Lord, an unprecedented painter has arrived here from Vidarbha, proclaiming himself to be peerless in the art of painting."
And by that man named Roladeva, having depicted this deity here at the lion-gate, a proclamation was indeed hung today.
Upon hearing this, the king respectfully ordered his delivery; the doorkeeper went and brought that painter there in an instant.
Having entered, he saw there in private that King Kanakavarṣa standing amidst the playful display of viewing the paintings.
His body’s weight was resting upon the bosoms of beautiful women, and with a playful hand raised, he held a betel-roll.
Having bowed and sat down before the king, who had shown him due respect, that painter Roladeva addressed him slowly.
"O King, this notice was hung by me out of a desire to see your lotus feet; it did not grant me knowledge [of your whereabouts]. Therefore, this of mine should be forgiven."
"O Lord, let it be commanded: what form shall I paint here on this canvas? May this effort of mine in training in the arts bear fruit."
When the painter had spoken thus, the king said to him: "Teacher, paint whatever you please as you wish."
"We delight your eyes; what wonder could there be in your skill?"—when the king had spoken thus, those standing by his side replied:
"Let the king himself be painted; what is the use of other ugly people? Hearing this, the painter was pleased and painted that king.
With a prominent bridge of the nose, long and reddish eyes, a broad forehead, and dark, curly locks of hair.
With a broad chest adorned by scars from arrows and other wounds, and with a pair of arms as beautiful as the trunks of the elephants of the quarters;
By their middles, which could be measured by a single fist, they were like young lion cubs who, having been defeated by his prowess, had been presented to him as tribute.
And by her pair of thighs, which resembled the girth-ropes of the elephant of youth, and by her beautiful pair of feet, which were like the tender sprouts of the Aśoka tree.
Upon seeing the king depicted in a form that perfectly corresponded to his own, everyone then offered words of praise to the painter.
And we do not wish to see that Lord alone, who has made the world his mouth, while these [beings] here are depicted upon this painted wall.
"O Preceptor, having carefully deliberated upon them, paint one from among these queens who is suitable for this place; may it be a full feast for our eyes."
Having heard that, she looked there, and the painter said: "Even among these many women, not one is at all like the king's [wife]."
And I know that on this very earth there exists no woman equal in beauty to her; there is one princess, and listen as I describe her to you.
In Vidarbha there is a glorious city named Kuṇḍina, and there dwells a lord of the earth renowned as Devaśakti.
He had a queen named Anantavatī, dearer to him than his own life; by her he had a daughter born, named Madanasundarī.
Who like me would dare to describe her form with this single tongue? Nevertheless, I shall say this much.

Having created her, I believe that even though the Creator’s desire was fulfilled by the taste of that creation, he would not know how to create another of such beauty even in the course of many aeons.
There was a princess on earth who was the equal of this king in beauty, grace, and modesty, as well as in age and lineage.
While staying there, I once sent a maidservant to summon her, and I went to the inner apartments of that princess.
There I saw her, anointed with fresh sandalwood paste, wearing a necklace of lotus stalks, and tossing about upon a bed of lotus leaves.
Fanned by her companions with plantain leaves, she was pale and emaciated, manifesting the symptoms of the fever of love.
"O friends, what is the use of these sandalwood ointments and breezes from plantain leaves? What have you achieved with this fruitless labor?"
For these, though cool, burn me who am of little merit, even as they thus restrain my friends who are anxious to comfort me.
Beholding her in that condition and agitated by thoughts concerning her, I offered my salutations and sat down before her.
"Preceptor, having painted such a form, give it to me as a fee," he said, holding the brush in a trembling hand.
Slowly drawing on the ground, the princess showed me that she had depicted a certain youth of exceeding beauty.
Having painted that beautiful man, O Lord, I thought: "This very Kāma himself has been depicted by me here in person."
But since these bow and arrows made of flowers have not been drawn by him, I know that this is not Kāma; he must be some youth of similar form.
Surely he has been seen by her somewhere, or perhaps even heard of; for this manifestation of passion in her must have this as its cause.
Therefore, I must depart from here, for this king wields a terrible rod of punishment; if his father, Devaśakti, were to learn of this, he would not tolerate it on my account.
Having reflected thus, I bowed to that Princess Madanasundarī and departed from there, honored by her.
And in this matter, O Great King, I have heard from my attendants as they were speaking privately among themselves how she was filled with passion upon hearing of you.
Then, taking that princess who had been secretly painted upon a canvas, I have come swiftly to the feet of your majesty.
Having seen Your Majesty’s appearance, my doubt has been dispelled; it was Your Majesty alone who was depicted by her on the canvas with my own hand.
Moreover, since it is impossible to depict her likeness even once, I shall not paint her—even though she is my equal—by the side of the God in this picture.
When Roladeva had spoken thus, the king said to him, "In that case, let her who is depicted on that painted cloth be shown by you."
Then, having pulled it out from the bag, he showed the painting to the king—the Madanasundarī depicted within that picture by the painter.
King Kanakavarṣa, too, upon beholding her of such wondrous form even in that painted image, immediately fell under the sway of Love.
And having rewarded that painter with much gold, the king, taking the portrait-cloth of his beloved, entered the inner apartments.
There, his eyes satiated by the sight of her form and beauty, he stood with all other activities abandoned, his mind entirely absorbed in her alone.
Finding an opening, he struck him with arrows, depriving him of his composure, just as the god of love, provoked by rivalry over beauty, strikes one who is intent on destroying him.
That very affliction of love which was bestowed by him upon women who were greedy for his beauty has now, as it were, borne fruit for that king in a hundred branches.
Then, after some days, having become thin and pale from separation, he disclosed his heart's intent to his trusted ministers when they questioned him about it.
And having consulted with them, he dispatched a messenger to King Devaśakti to request the hand of the maiden Madanasundarī.
He was a Brahmin named Saṃgamasvāmin, who knew the proper time, understood what ought to be done, was self-restrained, of noble birth, and spoke with sweet and dignified speech.
Having traveled there with a most magnificent retinue, that brahmin Saṅgamasvāmin entered the city of Kuṇḍina in the land of Vidarbha.
There he beheld King Devaśakti exactly as he was; for the sake of his master, he then requested the king's daughter from him.
"I must first give her to another, for he is a suitable match; King Kanakavarṣa, even one such as he, is requesting her."
Having deliberated, "I shall give this one to him," he too, through the power of the gods, placed his faith in the words of Saṃgamasvāmin.
And that lord of the earth showed him the wondrous dance of his daughter Madanasundarī, as if it were her very form.
Then the king, having accepted the gift of his daughter, honored Saṅgamasvāmin—who was delighted by that sight—and sent him on his way.
"Having determined an auspicious moment, please come here for the sake of the marriage"; having thus instructed him, he dispatched a counter-messenger along with him.
Then Saṅgamasvāmin, having arrived accompanied by his counter-messenger, reported to King Kanakavarṣa that the mission had been accomplished.
Then, having determined an auspicious moment and having honored that counter-messenger, he repeatedly ascertained that Madanasundarī was indeed enamored of him.
For the sake of that marriage, King Kanakavarṣa, whose valor was irresistible and whose mind was free from doubt, set out for that city of Kuṇḍina.
Mounted upon an Ashoka creeper, he struck down the lions and other beasts dwelling in the remote forests—creatures that snatch away the lives of living beings—just as he would strike down Shabaras.
Having reached the city of Vidarbha, he entered that city of Kuṇḍina together with King Devaśakti, who had come out to meet him.
There, providing a festival for the eyes of the city’s matrons, he entered the royal palace where the preparations for his wedding were being readied.
There, King Devaśakti, delighted by the noble hospitality shown to him, stayed for that day together with his retinue.
On another day, Devaśakti gave that daughter Madanasundarī to him, together with his entire fortune, leaving only the kingdom behind.
Having stayed there for seven days, King Kanakavarṣa then returned to his own city together with that new bride.
When he, who bestows joy upon the world, arrived united with his beloved, that city became filled with celebration, like the night of the full moon when the moon is joined with the moonlight.
And Madanasundarī was dearer than life to that king, even though he had a large harem, just as Rukmiṇī was to Acyuta.
With their eyes fixed upon each other's faces, those two, husband and wife, remained as if nailed down by the arrows of Love, which possessed beautiful lashes.
And once, there arrived the lion of spring, with its rows of blossoming filaments, shattering the elephant-like pride of haughty women.
The spring season prepared the flower-bow of the god of love, with its rows of bees as bowstrings and its blossoming mango creepers as the bow-staffs.
And the Malaya breeze blew, shaking the minds of the women of the travelers like groves of trees, inflaming their passion.
The floods of rivers, the blossoms of trees, and the digits of the moon return once they have waned; but the youth of embodied beings does not.
"O you who have abandoned pride and strife, rejoice together with your beloveds!"—thus, as it were, did the cuckoos address the people with their sweet songs.
And at that time, King Kanakavarṣa entered Madhudyāna to enjoy himself there together with all his women of the inner apartments.
He robbed the Ashoka trees of their splendor with the red garments of his attendants, and he silenced the songs of the beautiful women with the warbling of cuckoos and bees.
There, that king, together with Queen Madanasundarī and his harem, sported in activities such as gathering flowers.
Having stayed there for a very long time, the king descended into the Godāvarī to bathe and engaged in water-sports together with the people of his inner apartments.
With their faces they were lotuses, with their eyes blue water-lilies, with their breasts pairs of ruddy geese, and with their hips sandy banks.
Having conquered that river, her women agitated its depths, displaying the frown of indignation through their tossing waves.
At that time, his mind took delight in those women of Kanakavarṣa, whose graceful movements of their limbs were revealed by garments shifting as they moved through the water.
And he struck one queen on her pair of breasts, which resembled two golden jars, with water from his hand as her garment was loosened.
Seeing that, Madanasundarī became angry with her out of jealousy; as if agitated, she said, "How much can a river be disturbed? and so forth.
Having emerged from the water, she went to her own palace in anger, wearing another garment and recounting her beloved's offense to her friends.
Then, having understood her intention, King Kanakavarṣa abandoned his water-sports and went to her dwelling.
Though he was being forbidden by the parrots staying in their cages there, he entered in his rage and saw the queen within, tormented by grief.
With her lotus-like face resting dejectedly upon the palm of her left hand, she was drenched by falling teardrops resembling clear pearls.
If separation cannot be endured, then you must avoid pride; O heart, if separation can be endured, then you should increase your pride.
"If separation cannot be endured, then pride must be abandoned by you, even for the sake of happiness; O heart, if separation can be endured, then pride alone must be increased by you.
Having understood this skillfully, remain hanging on with only one foot dangling; with both feet placed upon a blade of grass, you will surely perish.
"Knowing this, stand skillfully, supporting yourself by one side; with your feet placed on both banks, you will surely perish if you fall into the middle"—
reciting this fragment of a *dvipadī* verse with a voice faltering with tears, charming in its Apabhraṃśa dialect and captivating with the luster of her emerging teeth.
And beholding her in such a state, beautiful even in her anger, that king approached her both with shame and with fear.
Then, embracing her as she turned her face away with words tender with affection, he began to appease her with humble entreaties.
And he fell at her feet, censuring himself as an offender, while his retinue was made to feel ashamed by the indirect speech [of the messenger].
Then, as if sprinkling him with the tears that had fallen from her own grief, she, clinging to the neck of the king, was reconciled to him.
Then, having spent that day with her—whose anger had been appeased by his devotion—the king, delighted, enjoyed amorous dalliance with her and fell asleep at night.
While asleep, he suddenly saw in a dream that a single-stringed necklace had been taken from his neck and a crest-jewel from his head by a woman of distorted appearance.
Then he saw a vetāla whose body was composed of the limbs of various creatures; as that vetāla engaged him in a wrestling match, he threw him down to the ground.
And sitting upon his back, like a bird taking flight through the air, the Vetāla carried the king away and cast him into the ocean.
Then, having somehow emerged from it, he saw that supreme single-string necklace around his neck and that crest-jewel upon his head, both remaining as they were before.
Having seen this, the king woke up and in the morning questioned the mendicant who had come from his previous acquaintance about the fruit of his dream.
One should not speak what is unpleasant; however, why should I not speak when asked?
"That single-string necklace and the crest-jewel which were seen and taken by you—this shall result in your separation from the queen and from your son."
And when the single-stringed pearl necklace is obtained by you after crossing the ocean, that reunion with the Queen’s son will also come to pass at the end of your suffering.
When the mendicant had spoken thus, the king reflected and said: "I do not yet have a son; let him first be born."
Then, upon his arrival, he heard from a reciter of the Rāmāyaṇa about King Daśaratha, who had undergone great hardships for the sake of obtaining a son.
When the Kṣapaṇaka had departed, King Kanakavarṣa, his mind preoccupied with the thought of obtaining a son born from him, spent that day in despondency.
One night, while lying alone in bed and suddenly awake, he saw a woman enter inside even though the door had not been opened.
Disciplined and gentle in appearance, she spoke to the lord of the earth, who had risen up in wonder and offered his salutation, after she had bestowed her blessing upon him.
"O son, know me to be the daughter of Vāsuki, the king of the Nāgas, and this elder sister of your father, named Ratnaprabhā."
For the sake of protecting you, I have always dwelt near you while remaining invisible; having seen you today filled with anxiety, I have revealed my true self to you.
"I cannot bear to see your distress; therefore, tell me the cause. Thus addressed by his paternal aunt, the king spoke to her.
"I am blessed, O Mother, that you show such favor to me; know also that my lack of peace is caused by the absence of a son."
O Mother, since even royal sages such as Daśaratha and others in former times desired that place for the sake of heaven, how could those like me not desire it?
Having heard these words of King Kanakavarṣa, the Nāga maiden Ratnaprabhā spoke to her brother’s son.
"In that case, my son, I shall tell you one means; perform it. Go and propitiate Svāmikumāra for this purpose."
"You shall endure that unbearable stream of Kumāra falling upon my head as an obstacle, once it has entered within my body through your power."
"Having overcome the host of obstacles, you shall obtain whatever else you desire. Having said this, the Naga maiden vanished; the king, filled with joy, passed the night.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers in the morning out of a desire for a son, that king went to the feet of Svāmikumāra.
There he performed intense austerities in order to propitiate that Lord, his strength being offered by the serpent who had entered within his body.
Then, like a thunderbolt, that stream of water from the prince began to fall incessantly upon the king's head.
But that novice, by the power of the nāginī within his body, [overcame] her; then Guha dispatched Heramba to create an obstacle for him.
And there, in the midst of the stream, Heramba created a most terrible great serpent; yet he was not shaken even by that.
Then Vināyaka himself, invincible even by the gods, approached and proceeded to strike him on the chest with his tusks.
Then, considering that god invincible, King Kanakavarṣa proceeded to worship him with hymns of praise, having first endured his power.
Homage to you, O Lord of Obstacles, Lambodara, who are adorned with serpents and whose self is like a treasure-pot for the accomplishment of all aims.
Victory to you, O Gajānana, who causes even Brahmā to tremble as his lotus-throne is shaken by the playful blows of your uplifted trunk!
Even for the lords of the gods, asuras, and sages, there are no spiritual accomplishments if you, the sole refuge of the world and beloved of Śaṅkara, are not satisfied.
Ghaṭodara, Śūrpakarṇa, the leader of the Gaṇas Madotkaṭa, Pāśahasta, Ambarīṣa, Jambaka, and Triśikhāyudha.
In this manner and others like it, the supreme gods praised you with sixty-eight names that destroy evil, each name being fixed to a corresponding number of places.
O Lord, for one who remembers and praises you, fear born of battle, royal families, gambling, thieves, fire, wild beasts, and the like, perishes.
With these words of praise and many others of various kinds, King Kanakavarṣa worshipped that Lord of Obstacles.
"I am pleased; I shall not create obstacles for you. Obtain a son," said that Vighnajit (Gaṇeśa) to the king there, and then he vanished.
Then Svāmikumāra said to that king, who was bearing that stream: "O steadfast one, I am pleased with you; ask for a boon."
Having heard that, the king was delighted and petitioned the god: "O Lord, by your grace, let a son be born to me."
"Let it be so; a son shall be born to you from a portion of my host, O lord of the earth, and he shall be named Hiraṇyavarṣa."
Having spoken thus, the one whose vehicle is peacocks (Kārttikeya), desiring to show special favor, summoned the king to enter the inner sanctum of the womb-chamber.
Therefore, that nāgī emerged invisibly from the body of the king; for women, fearing a curse, do not enter the prince’s quarters.
Then Kanakavarṣa, by means of his own human splendor, entered the inner chamber of that god of fire.
Seeing that king deprived of his former splendor due to the absence of the serpent's empowerment, the god also reflected: "What could this be?"
Having learned that the king had fulfilled his difficult vow under the pretext of the power of the Naga women, Guha became enraged and, because of a prior resolve, cursed that monarch.
"O Durdānta, because you have committed this deception, there shall be separation from your son as soon as he is born, and from the Great Queen as well."
Having heard this curse, as terrible as a thunderclap, that king, a great poet, cast off his delusion and praised the god with well-spoken hymns.
Then Ṣaṇmukha, pleased by his well-spoken words, addressed him: "O King, I am gratified by your eloquent verses; I shall tell you that end to your curse."
For one year you shall suffer separation from your wife and son; thereafter, being freed from the three types of untimely death, you shall regain them.
Having spoken thus, when the Six-faced One had ceased speaking, the king bowed to him and, satiated by the nectar of his grace, returned to his own city.
There, from that Queen Madanasundarī, a son was born in due course, like a flow of nectar from the moon amidst its moonlight.
Then, having beheld the face of their son, both the king and the queen were repeatedly overwhelmed by such intense joy that they could not contain it within themselves.
At that time, raining down wealth, the king held a festival, bringing his own name, "Golden Shower" (Kanakavarṣa), to its literal truth upon the earth.
When five nights had passed and on the sixth night, while the protective rites were being performed there in the birth-chamber, a cloud arrived unexpectedly.
As it gradually attained growth there, it covered the sky, just as a neglected enemy might seize the kingdom of a negligent king.
Then, like a rutting elephant intoxicated by wind, uprooting trees with its torrential spray, it began to charge forward.
At that very moment, having flung open the bolted door, a certain terrifying woman with a dagger in her hand entered that birth-chamber.
Having carried off her son—whose face was pressed against the breasts of Madanasundarī—she fled from the queen, having utterly deluded the attendants.
"Alas, alas! My son has been carried off by the ogress!"—thus crying out in distress, the queen pursued that woman even through the darkness.
And having gone there, that woman fell into the middle of the lake along with her child; the queen also followed after her, falling in that very place out of longing for her offspring.
In an instant the cloud withdrew and the night came to an end; and the wailing of the attendants was heard within the lying-in chamber.
Then King Kanakavarṣa, having heard that news, went to his son’s quarters; seeing it empty and devoid of his beloved son, he fell into a swoon.
Having regained his composure, he lamented, "O Queen! O little son! and then remembered that curse which had its term limited to one year.
O Blessed One, how was this boon given by you to me, one of such meager merit, when it is beset by a curse? O Skanda, it is like nectar mixed with poison.
Alas! How shall I pass this year, which seems like a thousand ages, without the goddess Madanasundarī, who was dearer to me than life itself?
Thus lamenting, the king, even though being consoled by his ministers who had learned the news, could not regain his composure regarding the queen who had departed.
And in due course, helpless under the impulse of passion, he departed from the city; wandering about with a distracted mind, he entered the Vindhya forest.
There, he [compared] the beauty of his beloved's eyes with the eyes of young does, and the splendor of the mass of her braided hair with the bushy tails of yaks.
As he recalled those elephants and female elephants whose gaits had become sluggish with passion, the fire of his love blazed up even more intensely.
Wandering on, exhausted by the heat of his thirst, he reached the foot of the Vindhya mountains; having drunk the water of a mountain stream, he sat down at the root of a tree.
Then, roaring like a loud laugh from the mouth of the Vindhya cave, a maned lion emerged and sprang forward to kill him.
At that very moment, a certain Vidyadhara descended from the sky and, swooping down with speed, split that lion in two with a blow from his sword.
Approaching the king, that sky-goer asked him: "O King Kanakavarṣa, how have you come to this land?"
Having heard that and regained his memory, the king replied to him: "How do you know me, who am consumed by the fire of separation?"
Then the Vidyādhara said: "Formerly, when I was a human being, I lived in your city as a renunciant named Bandhumitra."
"Since you have rendered assistance here at my request through your service, I have attained the state of a Vidyādhara by means of the accomplishment of the Vīravetāla."
Therefore, having recognized you so that I might perform a service for you in return, I slew this lion upon seeing it intent on killing you.
To him who was saying, "Today I have become Bandhuprabha by name," King Kanakavarṣa, filled with affection, spoke.
Ah, I remember that friendship which was cultivated by you here; therefore, tell me, when will the reunion with my wife and son take place?
Having heard these words of his and having understood them through the power of his magic science, that Vidyādhara Bandhuprabha spoke to the king.
"By the grace of Vindhyavāsinī, you shall obtain a wife and two sons; therefore, go there for the sake of your success, while I depart for my own world."
When he had spoken thus and departed into the sky, King Kanakavarṣa, having regained his composure, slowly set out to see that goddess who dwells in the Vindhya mountains.
As the king was proceeding along the road, a great wild elephant, intoxicated with rut, with its head shaking and its trunk extended, rushed toward him.
Seeing that, the king fled by way of the chasm; as he was pursuing him, the elephant perished from falling into the abyss.
Then, traveling by degrees, the king, exhausted by the fatigue and toil of the journey, reached a great lake abounding with tall white lotuses.
Having bathed there and drunk the water, and having eaten the lotus stalks, he rested at the foot of a tree and was for a moment overcome by sleep.
Just then, some Śabaras returning from a hunt came along that path and saw the king, endowed with auspicious marks, fast asleep.
And having bound him for the purpose of offering him as a sacrifice to the goddess, they led him at that very moment to the presence of their own Śabara king, named Muktāphala.
That lord of the Śabaras, having observed the king to be praiseworthy, led him to the sanctuary of the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas in order to make him a sacrificial victim.
Upon seeing the goddess and bowing before her, by her grace and through the favor of Skanda, the king's bonds were loosened.
Beholding that and considering it a divine favor bestowed upon him, the lord of the Śabaras released the king from execution.
Thus, for Kanakavarṣa, who had escaped from his third untimely death, that year of the curse came to an end.
And at that very moment, his paternal aunt, that Nāga woman, arrived there taking with her Queen Madanasundarī and her son.
And he said to him, "O King, having learned of the curse of Kumāra, I have taken these two and brought them to my own abode, protecting them with care."
Therefore, O Kanakavarṣa, accept these two, your own beloved son and daughter; enjoy this sovereignty over the earth, for your curse has now come to an end.
Having spoken thus to the king who bowed before her, the Nāga woman vanished; the king, for his part, regarded that arrival of his wife and son as if it were a dream.
Then, as the king and queen finally embraced one another after a long time, the suffering of their separation dissolved along with their tears of joy.
Then, realizing that his lord was the sovereign Kanakavarṣa, Śabarendra Muktāphala fell at his feet.
Having asked for his forgiveness and led him into his own village, he attended upon him and his wife and children with various services appropriate for himself.
Then, remaining there, the king had his father-in-law, King Devaśakti, and his own army summoned from their city by means of messengers.

Then King Kanakavarṣa, having placed his beloved wife Madanasundarī—who was mounted upon an elephant—and his son, named Hiraṇyavarṣa as ordained by the six-faced god (Kārttikeya), before him, set out from his residence in his father-in-law’s palace, accompanied by them.

And after a few days, he reached his father-in-law’s home situated in the Vidarbha region, the city named Kuṇḍina; and there, honored by his father-in-law, he dwelt for some days in that prosperous place, accompanied by his son, his wife, and his army.
Setting out from there, he gradually reached his own city, Kanakapura, as if being drunk in by the eyes of the city’s women, who had long been longing for him.
And that king, accompanied by his son and joined by Madanasundarī, entered the capital like a festival incarnate, endowed with the splendor of joy.
Having consecrated her and bound the ceremonial turban upon her head, he, who honors his subjects, made Madanasundarī the chief of all the women of the harem on that auspicious occasion.

Together with that queen and his son, King Kanakavarṣa held perpetual festivals; never again experiencing the sorrow of separation from those he loved, he then ruled this entire earth, bounded by its four oceans, free from all thorns.
Having heard this delightful story from his chief minister Gomukha, Prince Naravāhanadatta, together with Alaṅkāravatī, was filled with joy.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave: Then, accompanied by his beloved, he was delighted by the story told by Gomukha; yet, seeing Marubhūti’s display of anger born of jealousy toward him, [he spoke].
Naravāhanadatta addressed him, seeking to win him over: "Marubhūti, why do you not also tell us one story?"
Then, saying "Very well, I shall tell it," with a contented heart, Marubhūti proceeded to relate this story.
Long ago, O King, in the city named Kamalapura, there lived an excellent Brahmin named Candrasvāmin, in the service of King Kamalavarman.
To him was born a wife named Devamati, who was like Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī combined, radiant with modesty, and equal in virtue to Sumati.
In her, the wife of that Brahmin, was born a son endowed with auspicious marks; as soon as he was born, this voice arose from the heavens:
"You must give birth to a son named Candrasvāmī; for having become king, he shall protect the earth for a long time."
Having heard these divine words, he held a celebratory festival and gave that very protector of the earth the name Candrasvāmisuta.
And in due course, that protector of the earth, having grown up, was made to master the science of weapons and missiles, and was trained equally in all branches of knowledge.
And at that very time, Candrasvāmin’s wife, Devamati, gave birth again to a daughter who was beautiful in every limb.
And she, named Candravatī, and that protector of the earth—those two brothers gradually grew up together in the palace of their father.
Then, in that region, a calamity of famine caused by drought arose, once the crops had been scorched by the rays of the sun.
And due to that fault, the king here began to act like a thief; having abandoned the path of the righteous, he extracted wealth from his subjects through unrighteous means.
Then, sinking down deeply in that place, his wife Devamati spoke there to the Brahmin Candrasvāmin.
"Come, let us go from this city to my father's house; for these two children might perish here at any moment."
Having heard that, Candrasvāmin said to his wife: "Do not do this; it is a great sin to flee from one's home during a famine."
Therefore, I shall take these two children and place them in their father's house; you remain here, and I will return quickly.
Having spoken thus and established his wife—who had replied, "So be it"—in her home, Candrasvāmin took those two children of his own.
Then, taking both that protector of the earth and the maiden Candravatī, he set out from the city toward his wife’s father’s house.
Proceeding by degrees, after three or four days, he reached a vast forest where the sands were scorched by the rays of the sun and the trees were withered and sparse.
Having set those two children down there while they were overcome by thirst, Candrasvāmin went a long distance to search for water for their sake.
Just then, the lord of the Śabaras, named Siṃhadaṃṣṭra, arrived there at the head of his followers, having set out for some purpose or other.
Having seen him, and having understood that he was a hunter seeking water without even asking, he made a sign and said to his servants, "Take this man and let him obtain water."
Having heard that, two or three of his servants, who had discovered his intentions, led the upright Candrasvāmin to the village and bound him.
Realizing that he had bound himself to them for the purpose of being offered as a human sacrifice, Candrasvāmin grieved for his two children who had gone into the forest.
"Alas, O protector of the earth! Alas, dear Candravatī! How is it that I have abandoned you both in this desolate forest, leaving you as mere prey for lions and tigers?"
"My life has been destroyed by thieves and there is no refuge for me"—wailing thus, the Brahmin, out of distress, beheld the sun in the sky.
"Alas! Abandoning this delusion, I shall take refuge in my own Lord. Having reflected thus, the twice-born man began to praise the Sun.
Salutations to you, O All-pervading One, the Light who rests in the supreme ether beyond all, who dispels both internal and external darkness.
You are Viṣṇu, pervading the three worlds; you are Śiva, the treasure-house of all blessings; stirring the sleeping universe into motion, you are the supreme Lord of Creatures.
"May these two, fire and moon, shine forth; for the sake of these [women], you have deposited your own splendor within them. O Night, you depart as if out of compassion."
Even the rākṣasas flee and the bandits do not prevail; moreover, the virtuous rejoice when you have risen like the shining sun.
O sole lamp of the three worlds, protect me who have come to you for refuge; shatter this darkness of my suffering and show me compassion.
As the brahmin Candrasvāmin was thus praising the Sun with devotion through these and other verses, a voice issued forth from the sky.
"I am pleased with you, Candrasvāmin; you shall not suffer death. And by my grace, there shall be a reunion for you with your sons and others."
Having been thus addressed by a divine voice, Candrasvāmin remained there while staying in his birthplace, provided with baths and food brought by the Śabaras.
Meanwhile, that protector of the earth was traveling with his sister to the forest; as his father did not return, he was distressed by lamentation and apprehensive of some misfortune.
A great caravan leader named Sārthadhara, who had arrived by that same path, saw him and asked about his circumstances.
Having comforted him out of compassion and seeing that the child possessed auspicious marks, the caravan leader then led him to his own country along with his sister.
There that protector of the earth remained devoted to the fire-ritual even in his childhood, while the merchant looked on from his house out of affection for his son.
Once, the king’s minister came along that same path on business for a man named Tārādharmā who resided in Tārāpura.
A preeminent brahmin named Anantasvāmin, accompanied by elephants, horses, and foot soldiers, entered the house of that caravan leader as his friend.
Having rested there and seeing that protector of the earth of auspicious appearance, who was devoted to the recitation of mantras and fire-rituals, he inquired about his circumstances.
Realizing he was childless, the minister, desiring offspring, requested from the caravan leader Savarṇa both his daughter and that sister of his.
Then, having accepted the two children given by that merchant, Anantasvāmin departed for Tārāpura with the caravan leader.
There, that king, treated as a son by the minister, remained in his residence, which was filled with the abundant wealth of his magical sciences.
In the meantime, Siṃhadaṃṣṭra, the lord of the Bhillas, approached Candrasvāmin while he was bound and spoke to him in that village.
O Brahmin, I have been thus commanded by the god Bhānu in a dream: "Having honored him, you must release him; he is not to be slain by me."
Having said, "Therefore, rise and go as you please," he released him, having provided him with pearls and musk and arranged for his escort through the forest.
Then, having been released from there, Candrasvāmin, unable to find his son Mahīpāla in the forest, searched for him along with his younger brother.
Wandering along the shore of the ocean, he reached a city named Jalapura and, becoming a guest, entered the house of a certain Brahmin.
There, after they had finished eating, that brahmin householder addressed Candrasvāmin, who had related his own adventures in the course of conversation.
In days past, a merchant named Kanakavarman arrived here; by him was found in the forest a young Brahmin accompanied by his sister.
Taking those two most excellent boys with him, he departed from here; however, he did not mention their names on the great island of Nārikela.
Hearing that, and thinking, "Surely those two are my own sons," Candrasvāmin made up his mind to go to that excellent island.
Having spent the night and searched for him, he formed an alliance with the merchant Viṣṇuvarman, who was about to depart for the island of Nārikela.
And having embarked upon that very ship together with him, Candrasvāmin went by way of the ocean to that island out of affection for his son.
There, the merchants living there said to him as he questioned them: "A merchant named Kanakavarman certainly arrived here."
Having taken the two sons of the brahmin upon reaching the Surūpā forest, he has now departed from here for Kaṭāha Island accompanied by them.
Having heard that, the brahmin then went with the merchant Dānavarman, who was traveling by ship, to the island of Kaṭāha.
There too, that twice-born man heard that the merchant Kanakavarman had departed from that island for the island known as Karpūra.
Thus, traveling in succession to Karpūradvīpa, Suvarṇadvīpa, and Siṃhala along with merchants, he still did not find that merchant.
From the people of Siṃhala, however, he heard that his own merchant had gone to the country of Kanakavarman, to the city named Citrakūṭa.
Then, having crossed the ocean by means of that ship, Candrasvāmin went together with a merchant named Koṭīśvara to Citrakūṭa.
There he encountered that merchant Kanakavarman and, eager for news of his children, related his entire story to him.
Then Kanakavarman, having learned of his distress, showed him those two children whom he had found and brought from the forest.
And as long as Candrasvāmin gazed upon those two boys, they were not his at all; rather, they were simply two others.
Then, afflicted by grief and devoid of hope, he lamented with tears: "Alas! Even after wandering so far, neither a son nor a daughter has been found by me."
Like a wicked master, the Creator showed me hope but did not fulfill it; and by that evil-souled one, I have been led astray in vain, from afar to even further distance.
Lamenting in this manner, Candrasvāmin was gradually consoled by the merchant Kanakavarman; then, still grieving, he spoke:
If, while wandering the earth, I do not find those two sons of mine within a year, then I shall abandon this body through ascetic penance on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
To him who had spoken thus, a certain wise man standing there replied: "Go; by the grace of Nārāyaṇī, you shall surely regain those two sons."
Having heard that, his heart filled with joy as he recalled the favor of the Sun-god, Candrasvāmin departed from that city, honored by the merchants.
Then, searching for agrahāras, villages, and cities, he wandered and one evening reached a forest filled with many tall trees.
There, having made his sustenance from fruits and water, he climbed a tree and remained there for the night, out of fear of lions, tigers, and other predators.
And there, at midnight, while remaining sleepless, he saw gathered beneath a tree a great circle of Mothers, headed by Nārāyaṇī.
Having gathered various kinds of offerings suitable for himself, he was indeed awaiting the arrival of the god Bhairava.
And there the mothers asked Nārāyaṇī, "O Goddess, why does he delay today? but she laughed and did not speak.
And when she was questioned by them with great persistence, she replied to them: "Friends, although this brings me shame, I shall nevertheless speak."
In this city of Surapura, there is a king named Surenāka; he has a daughter named Vidyādharī, renowned for her beauty.
And by him, for her who was to be given in marriage, the king had heard of a son of King Vimala named Prabhākara, who was equal to Rūpa in beauty.
While he was wishing to give her to that king, it was heard by Vimala that this daughter of his was a worthy match for his own son.
Then Vimala requested that daughter of Surasena from him through the mouth of a messenger for the sake of his son.
Surasena, having fulfilled his expectations, gave that daughter to Prabhākara, his son, according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having reached her father-in-law’s city named Vimalapura, that Vidyādharī went with her husband to their bedchamber at night.
There, full of longing, she gazed at her husband Prabhākara as he slept without embracing her; yet, as she looked, she saw that he was not a man.
"Alas, I am ruined! How have I obtained a eunuch as a husband? Thus lamenting in her heart, the princess passed that night.
"How was I given to a eunuch by you without being investigated? Having written this letter, she then dispatched it to her father.

Thinking, "Knowing you to be established in the kingdom, how could she have forgotten me because of him? her son, having suffered for a very long time, might one day curse her in his anger.
One who has been cursed by his mother and father never enjoys happiness; listen, therefore, to this ancient tale concerning a merchant's son.

Then, having been lifted up by that man seated upon the lion-throne, the wheel, encircled by a noose, was carried a great distance to the assembly hall.
By his command, while he remained seated, that young merchant was led away by the same man holding the noose and cast into an iron house.
There he beheld a man being tormented within by a wheel—a wheel of heated iron revolving incessantly upon his head.

"O you of evil conduct, since you cause us pain with your head resembling a heated iron wheel, such shall indeed be your own suffering."
Having spoken thus, both of them ceased, and they said to me as I was weeping: "Do not weep; let such suffering be yours for only one month."
Having heard that, I spent that day in grief and remained reclined upon my bed; then at night, as if in a dream, I beheld a terrifying man who had arrived.
Therefore, having seized me by force, I was cast into this iron house, and this blazing wheel has been placed upon my head and set spinning.
"Thus was this curse from my father; because of it, my life-breaths do not depart. That month has now been completed, yet even so, I am not released."
To Khaḍga, who had spoken thus, Cakra replied with compassion: "Even by me, while traveling abroad for the sake of wealth, my parents' word was not heeded."
"Your acquired wealth shall perish," they both cursed me; because of that, my entire fortune, earned from another island, was lost in the ocean.
This is the very same situation elsewhere; what is the use of my life? Give this discus upon my head, and let your curse depart from you.
Even as he was speaking thus, a divine voice was heard there: "You have been released from the sword; place this discus upon the head of Cakra."
Having heard that, at the very moment he placed the discus upon the head of the wheel, that sword was carried by some invisible being from there to his father's house.

Devotion to Him is indeed the wish-fulfilling cow; even in that regard, hear this story. Formerly, there was a certain sage who lived in the forest and performed great austerities.

"And by my boon, you shall enter his presence unobserved by others. Then Nala accepted this command of the god, saying, "So be it."

Having heard that, the virtuous woman said: "May those gods be such as you describe; nevertheless, Nala alone shall be my husband, for I have no need for the deities."

"We are now under your control, coming to you as soon as we are remembered; O speaker of truth! saying this, they were pleased with him and granted him boons.
Then, after Nala had departed for Vidarbha in high spirits, the lords of the gods and others, desiring to deceive him, assumed the form of Nala for Damayantī.

Seeing there the qualities of shadow, the blinking of eyes, and the six atoms, she became distressed and reflected while her brother was bewildered.
"Surely this illusion has been created for me by those five world-protectors; I consider Nala to be the sixth here, and I have no other recourse."
Having reflected thus, that virtuous woman, whose mind was solely intent on Nala, turned toward the sun and spoke these words to Damayantī:
O guardians of the world, if my mind has not turned toward anyone other than Nala even in a dream, by that truth, reveal your own forms to me!
Other men than the one previously chosen by her husband are strangers to the maiden, and she is the wife of another; so how can this delusion of yours exist?
Upon hearing this, the five beginning with Śakra returned to their own forms; the sixth, King Satyānala, remained in his own form as the sovereign.
Thereupon, Damayantī, filled with joy, cast her gaze—beautiful as a blooming blue lotus—and the garland of choice upon King Nala.

And having received the appropriate honors from that King of Vidarbha, the kings and those gods, headed by Śakra, departed as they had come.

"Therefore, we must certainly bring about the separation of those two. Having thus made their vow, the two of them turned back and departed from there.
