Meanwhile, Kali, intent on fulfilling his vow, continued for a long time searching for a flaw in Nala, who remained steadfastly following the scriptures.
Then one day, having performed his twilight devotions but without washing his feet, Nala fell asleep, his memory stolen by the intoxication of drink.
Having found this very opening, Kali cast his gaze upon him day and night, and he entered within the body of that Nala.
By that Kali who had entered his body, King Nala abandoned righteous conduct and acted according to his own whims.
He gambled with dice, took pleasure in female slaves, spoke untruths, and indulged in sleep by day; yet he remained awake throughout the nights.
He displayed anger without cause, seized wealth through unjust means, showed contempt for the virtuous, and bestowed honor upon the wicked.
Finding an opening, Dvāpara entered the body of his brother named Puṣkara—who had likewise strayed from the path of truth—and afflicted him.
Once, in the house of his younger brother named Puṣkara, Nala saw a beautiful, white bull known as Dānta.
Out of greed, Puṣkara, whose devotion to his elder brother was consumed by the Dvāpara age, did not give the bull to him who was seeking it.
And he said to him: "If you have a desire for this bull, then win it from me by gambling and take possession of it without delay."
Having heard that, Nala, out of delusion, agreed to it, saying "So be it. Thereupon, a game of dice began between those two brothers.
The bull named Puṣkara was the stake, as were Nala’s elephants and other possessions; Puṣkara won, and Nala was defeated again and again.
Even when his army and treasury had been lost at dice within two or three days, Nala, overwhelmed by Kali, did not desist, though he was being restrained.
Realizing that the kingdom had been lost, Damayantī placed her two children upon an excellent chariot and sent them to the house of her own father.
In the meantime, Nala had lost his entire kingdom; then he was addressed by the one named Puṣkara, who appeared radiant with victory.
"All else has indeed been staked by you; that bull was my stake. Now, stake Damayantī herself as the counter-stake in this game of dice."
Thus, as if blazing like fire at the gale of his words, Nala neither said anything untimely nor did he enter into the wager.
Then that man named Puṣkara said to him: "If you do not make your wife the stake, then depart from this country along with your friend."
Upon hearing that, Nala was immediately banished from the country by the king's men; he departed from there together with Damayantī as far as the border.
Alas! Since even Nala has been reduced to such a state by Kali, what more need be said of other embodied beings, who are like mere worms?
"Fie, fie upon gambling—devoid of dharma and devoid of affection, the abode of calamities even for such royal sages, the very lifeblood of the Kali and Dvāpara ages!"
Then Nala, having lost his sovereignty to his brother, while traveling to a foreign land with Damayantī, reached the interior of a forest, exhausted by hunger.
There, having rested on the shore of the lake with her—whose delicate feet were pierced by darbha grass—he beheld two swans that had arrived.
And for the sake of food, he threw his upper garment to catch them; but having snatched that up as well, those two swans departed from him.
"Those two have approached in the form of swans, and having taken away both the dice and the garment, they have departed"—this was the voice that Nala heard from the sky.
Then, having sat down with only a single garment, the king, dejected, skillfully pointed out the path to Damayantī’s father’s house.
This path leads to Vidarbha, my dear, like one’s father’s house; this is the path to Aṅga, and this other one to Kośala.
Upon hearing that, Damayantī then became as if filled with apprehension, thinking: "Is he saying this because he intends to abandon my son and take him from the path?"
Then, having subsisted on fruits and roots, both husband and wife, exhausted at the arrival of night, lay down there in the forest upon a bed of kusha grass.
Exhausted by the journey, Damayantī gradually fell asleep; Nala, however, remained awake and intent on departing, deluded as he was by Kali.
Rising up, he released Damayantī, who was clad in but a single garment; then, covering himself with that half of her upper robe which had been torn from her, he departed.
And at the end of the night, Damayantī woke up; not seeing her husband in the forest, she lamented after reflecting that he had departed, having abandoned her.
O Prince, Great Being, compassionate even toward an enemy! Alas, you who are so affectionate toward me, by whom have you been made heartless toward me?
And how will you travel alone on foot through the forests? Who will attend to you to dispel your fatigue?
How can dust defile those two feet of yours, which have been colored by the pollen from the garlands upon the heads of kings?
Since even your body, though anointed with the powder of yellow sandalwood, cannot endure it, how will it endure the heat of the midday sun?
"What use have I for a foolish son, what use for a daughter, or even for myself? O gods, may you bring about my welfare alone, if I am indeed virtuous."
Thus lamenting for Nala alone at that time, Damayantī set out from there along the very same path she had previously seen.
In some way or another she traversed rivers, mountains, forests, and wildernesses; yet she never, under any circumstances, transcended her devotion to her husband.

And by the power of Satī’s splendor, the hunter was reduced to ashes on the path by the serpent-weapon as she, whose mind was fixed upon him, was being protected; for in that moment, his heart had departed from her.
Then, by chance, having met with a caravan of merchants along the way, she traveled with them and reached the city of a king named Subāhu.
There, the princess, having seen her from afar from the palace roof, was filled with delight at her beauty; she had her brought down and presented as a gift to her own mother.
She stood there respectfully by the side of the Great Queen; and when questioned as to why her husband had left her, she spoke only this: "He has gone, having abandoned me."
Meanwhile, Bhīma, the father of those two, having learned the news of Nala, dispatched trusted men in all directions to search for them.
And from among them, one minister named Suṣeṇa, wandering about while assuming the form of a Brahmin, reached that capital city of Subāhu.
There he saw Damayantī constantly searching for those who had arrived, and she too, in her distress, saw him, the minister of her father.
Having recognized one another and come together, the two of them wept in such a manner that Queen Subāhu’s wife perceived it there.
As soon as that queen had summoned them and questioned them about the facts as they were, she recognized Damayantī as her own sister’s daughter.
Then, having informed her husband and honored her, he placed her upon a chariot along with Suṣeṇa and the army, and sent her to her father’s house.
There, Damayantī remained with her two children; even while being watched by her father, she continued searching for news of her husband.
His father dispatched spies to search for him and his husband, who were distinguished by two divine skills: the art of driving chariots and the art of archery.

O cruel one, having abandoned the young girl who is as lovely as a night-blooming lily while she slept in the forest, where have you gone, becoming invisible even after reaching a fragment of the sky?
"In this manner you must speak wherever he might be suspected of staying," thus did King Bhīma instruct those spies.
In the meantime, that King Nala, having gone a long distance through that forest at night with his cloak half-drawn over him, beheld a forest fire.
"O Great Being, before I, being weak, am consumed by this fire, move me away from the vicinity of this forest conflagration."
Having heard these words, Nala cast his gaze and beheld there, near the forest fire, a serpent that had formed a circle.
His head was entangled in a mass of light from the jewels on his hoods, as if seized upon the crown of his head by that fire of the forest with its fierce flames in hand.
Having approached him out of compassion, placed him on his shoulder, and carried him a great distance, just as he was wishing to set him down, the nāga spoke to him:
"Count ten other steps and lead me from here. Then Alas set out, counting his steps in this manner.
"We hear one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten"—thus we addressed him by means of his own speech, as he was speaking.
Standing upon Nala's shoulder, that serpent bit him on the edge of his forehead; by that act, King Kṛṣṇa became short-armed and deformed.
Then, having taken him down from his shoulder, the king asked the serpent: "Who are you, and what is this service you have rendered me?"
Having heard these words of Nala, that serpent replied to him: "O King, know me to be the king of serpents named Kārkoṭaka."
I have given this gadfly to you for your own benefit, and you shall understand its purpose; for even great beings assume deformity when it serves the accomplishment of their goals.
"Take from me this pair of garments called 'purified by fire'; by wearing them alone, you shall regain your own form."
Having said this, once Kārkoṭaka had departed after giving him that pair of garments, Nala left that forest and reached Kośalā in due course.
There, in the house of King Ṛtuparṇa, the lord of Kośala, he, though known by the name Hrasvabāhu, took up the office of a cook.
And because he prepared meals of divine flavor for him, he attained fame here through his skill in chariot-making as well.
Once, while that Nala—known as Hrasvabāhu—was staying there, one of the spies of the King of Vidarbha arrived at that place.
"There is here a short-armed man who is an expert in his own science and the science of chariots; he is a new cook equal to Nala"—thus did the spy hear there.
Having reflected with his intellect that the king was situated in an improper place regarding Nala, he went there by a clever stratagem and recited this Āryā verse uttered by her.

O cruel one, having abandoned the young girl who was sleeping in the forest—she who is as lovely as the night-lotus—and having reached a fragment of the sky, where have you gone, O moon, becoming invisible?
Hearing that, which sounded like the speech of a madman, those present there treated it with contempt; but Nala, who was stationed there in the guise of a cook, replied to him.
When the moon, having waned, reaches a portion of the sky and enters another orb, it becomes invisible to the night-lily; what cruelty is there in that?
Having heard this reply and considering it to be true regarding that Nala, the spy then departed from there, his dejection born of misfortune having vanished.
Having reached Vidarbha, he related everything that had been seen and heard to King Bhīma and his wife, as well as to Damayantī.
Then Damayantī spoke privately to her father: "Without a doubt, that is my noble husband himself, having taken refuge in the guise of a cook."
In this matter, let my plan for bringing them here be carried out: let a messenger be dispatched to King Ṛtuparṇa.
As soon as he had reached that king, he spoke to him thus: "King Nala has gone somewhere; no news of him is known."
Therefore, Damayantī will hold her svayaṃvara once again tomorrow morning; for this reason, you must come quickly to Vidarbha this very day.
Then, having heard this news, that king, who is skilled in the management of chariots, will certainly come here within a single day together with his noble son.
Having thus deliberated with her father and given him instructions accordingly, Damayantī dispatched a messenger to the Kośalas as was appropriate.
Having gone there, Ṛtuparṇa was addressed in that same manner; filled with longing, he spoke out of affection to Nala, who was standing by his side in the guise of a cook.
"O short-armed one, you said, 'I possess knowledge of chariots'; if you are capable, lead me to Vidarbha this very day."
Upon hearing that, Nala said, "Certainly, I shall bring her," and having gone there, he harnessed excellent horses and made his supreme chariot ready.
I know that this rumor of a self-choice marriage was made by her for the sake of attaining me; yet Damayantī herself could not possibly be such a person even in a dream.
Thinking, "I shall go there first and see," he brought the ready chariot of that King Ṛtuparṇa.
And when that king had mounted, Nala proceeded to drive the chariot with a speed that surpassed even the swiftness of Tārkṣya.

Then Nala spoke to Ṛtuparṇa, who was speaking on the road as his garment, blown off by the speed of the chariot, had caught upon the pole of the vehicle: The king said: "O charioteer, what is this that has been caught upon the pole? It has fallen from the chariot due to its great speed. Nala replied: "O King, this is your garment which has been carried away by the wind. Take it; it is yours. The king said: "I shall take it when I have reached my own city. O charioteer, drive the horses with speed. Nala said: "O King, I shall take it when we have reached our own city. But first, please tell me: whose son are you? The king said: "I am the son of Śvaphalka, and my name is Ṛtuparṇa. And you, who are you, O handsome one? Nala said: "Know me to be Nala, the son of Viśvāvasu. I have come here for the sake of your service, O King. The king said: "I know you to be Nala, the son of Viśvāvasu. You are welcome; stay here as you desire. Nala said: "If you truly know me to be Nala, then let us go to the city where I may dwell at ease. The king said: "O Nala, I know you to be Nala. Come, let us go to my city, which is filled with many jewels. Nala said: "O King, I have come to your presence for the sake of your service. I wish to go to my own city, for I am weary. The king said: "O Nala, I shall go to my own city together with you. But first, tell me: what is the distance between here and your city? Nala said: "The distance from here to my city is fifty-two yojanas. The king said: "O Nala, I shall go to my own city together with you. But first, tell me: how long will it take to reach there? Nala said: "If the horses are yoked properly, it will take three days to reach there. The king said: "O Nala, I shall go to my own city together with you. But first, tell me: what is the speed of these horses? Nala said: "These horses can travel sixty yojanas in a single day. The king said: "O Nala, I shall go to my own city together with you. But first, tell me: how can we travel so far in such a short time? Nala said: "O King, if you desire to travel quickly, I shall yoke the horses with skill. I am an expert in the management of horses. Nala said: "O King, if you desire to travel quickly, I shall yoke the horses with skill. I am an expert in the management of horses. The king said: "O Nala, I shall go to my own city together with you. But first
"O King, where is that garment of yours? For in this very instant, your chariot has already traversed many yojanas."
Having heard this, Ṛtuparṇa said to him: "Come now, give me this knowledge of chariots; in exchange, I shall give you the knowledge of dice."
By which the dice become submissive and knowledge of numbers arises—see for yourself right now, and I shall provide you with proof here.
"This tree which is seen before you—now I shall tell you its number; having counted the fruits and leaves, observe it!"
Having said this, he stated exactly how many fruits and leaves there were; and when Nala counted them, they were found to be exactly that many on the tree.
Then Nala gave that knowledge of charioteering to Ṛtuparṇa, and Ṛtuparṇa also gave that knowledge of dice to Nala.
Nala went to another tree and examined that knowledge; there, he correctly understood that calculation regarding the leaves and other features.
Then, as he rejoiced, a black man emerged from his body; he asked him, "Who are you?"
"I am Kali; out of envy, I entered your body while you were occupied with Damayantī, and by that means, your fortunes were lost at dice."
Therefore, when you were bitten by that Kārkoṭaka in the forest at that time, you were not burned; but look, this one situated within you has been burned.
For a wrongful injury inflicted upon another would bring no happiness to anyone; therefore, my child, I shall go, for there is no other place for me.
Having spoken thus, that Kali vanished from his sight; and at that very moment, Nala became as he was before, having regained his splendor and attained a mind devoted to righteousness.
Having arrived and mounted the chariot, he swiftly brought King Ṛtuparṇa to Vidarbha on that very same day.
And being thus ridiculed by the people who asked him the reason for his arrival, Ṛtuparṇa took up residence near Rājagṛha.
Having learned that he had arrived there, Damayantī—having heard the wondrous sound of the chariot and anticipating Nala’s arrival—rejoiced within her heart.
Then she dispatched her own maidservant to investigate the truth; and that maidservant, having returned after her search, spoke to her who was longing for her beloved.
"O Queen, having gone there, I have investigated this man who is the Lord of Kośala; it seems he has come here after hearing a false report regarding your *svayaṃvara*."
He has been brought today by the chariot-driver Sūda, who possesses short arms and is skilled in the knowledge of chariots, in the space of a single day alone.
And having gone to that cook's kitchen, I beheld the cook; he was black in complexion and deformed, yet he possessed some extraordinary power.
The water that had risen up in his vessels was not even poured out; and the pieces of wood, though fire had not been applied to them, burst into flame of their own accord.
And in an instant, by means of various foods, it became truly divine; having seen this great marvel, I have therefore come here.
Having heard this from the mouth of the maidservant, Damayantī reflected: "The cook has mastery over Agni and Varuṇa, and he knows the secret of the science of charioteering."
This noble son has become disfigured; otherwise, he would not be so. I know him to be afflicted by separation from me, and I wish to test this very point regarding him.
Having thus resolved, she skillfully sent both her children with that very maidservant to show them to him.
Seeing his two children and holding them in his arms for a long time, Nala wept silently with a continuous stream of tears.
"My two children were just like this when they stayed at my maternal grandfather's house; from remembering that, sorrow has arisen within me," she said to the maidservant.
Having arrived with the two children, the maidservant related everything to Damayantī; thereupon, she too felt even greater hope.
And on another day, in the morning, she gave this command to her own maidservant: "Go and speak these words of mine to that cook of Ṛtuparṇa."
"I have heard that there is no other cook equal to you; therefore, come today and prepare a side dish for me."
Saying "So be it," Nala then went there and, having been entreated by that maidservant, took leave of Ṛtuparṇa and approached Damayantī.
"Tell the truth, O King Nala! If you are indeed the one assuming the form of a cook, lead me today to the further shore, for I am submerged in an ocean of anxiety," she said.
Having heard that, Nala—agitated by affection, joy, sorrow, and shame—with his face cast down, spoke to her at the appropriate time in a voice choked with tears.
I am indeed that very Nala; truly, I am a sinner as hard as a thunderbolt, by whom you were treated like fire through delusion while causing you such torment.
When Nala had spoken thus, he was questioned by Damayantī: "If this is so, then how did you come to lose your form?"
Then Nala described his entire history to her, beginning from his friendship with Kārkoṭaka and ending with the departure of Kali.
At that very moment, having put on the pair of garments given by Kārkoṭaka, he purified himself with fire and regained his own form.

Seeing Nala once again restored to his own natural beauty and form, Damayantī—her lotus-face instantly blossoming as if the forest fire of her sorrow had been extinguished by the waters of her tears—attained an incomparable joy beyond all measure.

Having learned of this from his attendants who were filled with joy, King Bhīma of Vidarbha arrived there suddenly; having greeted Nala and offered him appropriate honors, he turned his own city into a scene of great festivity.
While King Bhīma smiled and performed the formal courtesies of concealment in his heart, King Ṛtuparṇa, having honored Nala in return, departed for Kośalā.

Then Nala, the lord of the Niṣadhas, dwelling there with his dear friend who was as dear to him as life itself, lived happily while describing to his father-in-law the manifestation of Kali’s wickedness.

Having traveled for only a few days with his father-in-law’s armies, the righteous Nala reached the Niṣadhas; there he humbled that man named Puṣkara—who had previously defeated him at dice—by making him acknowledge his defeat. Having restored half the kingdom to his brother, who had departed from his body like the Dvāpara age itself, Nala, happy in the joy of having regained Damayantī, enjoyed his own kingdom in due order.
Having thus related this story in the city of Tārāpura, the noble-minded brahmin Sumanas spoke again to that princess Bandhumatī, whose husband was away on a journey.
Thus, O Queen, the great endure suffering to attain prosperity; indeed, having experienced their setting, the sun and other luminaries go forth again toward their rising.

Therefore, O sinless one, you too shall soon regain your husband who has returned from his journey; maintain your fortitude, cast off your despondency, and enjoy yourself through the attainment of your desire for your husband.
Having thus honored that twice-born man of virtuous qualities with abundant wealth for his well-spoken words, Bandhumatī took heart and remained there, awaiting her beloved husband.
And after only a few days, that lord of the earth, the king, arrived, bringing his mother who had been staying in another land, accompanied by his father.
And having arrived, the moon, like the full moon, bestowing a festival for the eyes of the people, gladdened Bandhumatī with the splendor of the waters of the ocean.
Then, accompanied by her and having been entrusted with the burden of the kingdom previously given by her father, that protector of the earth enjoyed his desired pleasures as a king.

Having heard from the mouth of his own minister Marubhūti this wonderful, incomparable, and passion-delighting tale, King Naravāhanadatta, the son of the Lord of Vatsa, was greatly delighted in the company of his wives.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And this ninth book, the *Alaṃkāravatī*, is completed. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Tenth Lambaka, named Śaktiyaśas. This nectar of old indeed emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, churned by the Mandara mountain of the love for the daughter of the Lord of Mountains; those who forcibly taste it, having obtained the two-fold power free from obstacles, shall bear upon this earth the burden of the gods through the grace of Bhava.
First Wave: We bow to the sword of Heramba, which cannot be obstructed by enemies yet obliterates them, which is smeared with vermilion, and which cuts away sins from afar.

May the third eye of Śambhu protect you—eye that throbbed with greater intensity than his two others as he fixed his arrow for the burning of Tripura while all his eyes were equally intent on the task.
May the blood-red, curved row of claws and the gaze of Nṛsiṃha, intent upon the slaying of his enemies, destroy your misfortunes.
Thus Naravāhanadatta, the son of the Lord of Vatsa, remained happily in Kauśāmbī with his ministers and his wives.
Once, while he was staying there, a merchant residing in that city came to make a petition to his father, the King of Vatsa, who was seated in the assembly hall.
Announced by the doorkeeper, the merchant named Ratnadatta entered, bowed to the king, and addressed him thus:
"O King, there is a poor porter here named Vasudhara; today he is seen suddenly giving, eating, and drinking."
Out of curiosity, he led me to his house, gave me food and drink as much as I desired, and having brought me to a state of intoxication, he was questioned by me and spoke this.
I obtained a jeweled bracelet from the gate of the royal palace; having extracted a single gem from it, I then sold it.
And that was given by me to the merchant Hiraṇyagupta for a price of one hundred thousand dīnāras; because of that, I am now living in comfort today.
Having said this, he showed me my bracelet, which was marked with the name of the king; therefore, O Lord, I have today made this representation to my master.
Having heard this, the Lord of Vatsa had both of them brought there: the porter with the bracelet, and that merchant with the jewel.
"Ah! I remember now; this slipped from my wrist during my wandering through the city. Having seen that bracelet, the king himself spoke thus.
"Having obtained this bracelet engraved with the king's name, what have you done with it?"—thus questioned by the courtiers, the porter then spoke in the presence of the king.
"How could I, who live by carrying loads, know the letters of the king's name? Having found this, I accepted it while burning with the pain of poverty."
When he had spoken thus, the merchant, being challenged regarding the jewel, said: "I purchased this jewel at its price in the marketplace by force."
And he possesses no royal insignia; thus it is said that he is composed of that [ordinary nature]. However, for a price of five thousand, he has brought away what remains beyond.
[In another manuscript, the reading is "tad ayam ucyate" (then this is said).
Having heard these words of Hiraṇyagupta, Yaugandharāyaṇa, remaining there, said: "There is no fault here attributable to anyone."
Tell me, what can be said of a poor man who is illiterate and a porter? Out of poverty he commits theft; but who has ever abandoned what he has obtained?
"Even a merchant who purchases jewels for their price is not to be blamed"; at that time, the Lord of Vatsa placed his trust in these words of the great minister.
Having given five thousand [coins] spent by the porter, he took from that merchant Hiraṇyagupta the jewel belonging to himself.
Having taken his own bracelet, which he had previously released but now found heavy, and having enjoyed five thousand [gold pieces], he too went home free from fear.
Thinking, "This man is a wicked betrayer of trust," and hating him inwardly, the king summoned that merchant Ratnadatta for the sake of his business.
When they had departed, Vasantaka, who was walking ahead of the king, said: "Alas! For those cursed by fate, even when wealth is attained, it flees away."
This is the story of Bhārika concerning the auspicious jar; for there was once a certain man in the city of Pāṭaliputra in the past.
Named Śubhadatta, he would daily bring a load of wood from the forest and, by selling it, supported his family.
Once, having come to a distant forest by chance, he beheld four yakṣas standing there, adorned with divine ornaments and garments.
Seeing him terrified, all those yakṣas questioned him with affection according to the facts; and having understood that he was poor, compassion arose within them, and they spoke.
"Stay here in our presence, O good man; be our laborer. We shall provide for your household maintenance without causing you any hardship."
Having been addressed thus by them, Śubhadatta replied, "So be it," and remained in their presence; he then performed for them the entire service of bathing and other attendances.
When the mealtime had arrived, those yakṣas said to him, "Give us food from this auspicious jar."
While he was lingering there, having seen that jar to be empty within, those Guhyakas spoke to him once more with smiling faces.
"Śubhadatta, you do not know; cast your hand into the interior of the jar, and you shall obtain everything as you desire, for this jar is indeed a granter of all wishes."
Having heard that, as soon as he thrust his hand inside the jar, he saw whatever food, drink, and other desired things he wished for.
Śubhadatta gave these to them, and then he himself ate.
Thus attending upon the yakṣas every day with devotion and fear, Śubhadatta remained in their presence, distressed by anxiety for his family.
And that family, afflicted by suffering, was consoled by the Guhyakas through a prophetic dream; by their grace, they found joy, and thereafter he [the king] did likewise.
Within just a month, those yakṣas said to Śubhadatta: "We are pleased with this devotion of yours; tell us something, and we shall give it to you."
Having heard that, he said to them, "If you are truly satisfied, then let this auspicious jar be given to me by you."
Then those Yakṣas said to him: "You will not be able to protect this; for he flees at the slightest setback. Therefore, choose another boon."
Although he was addressed thus by those yakṣas, when Śubhadatta did not desire another boon, they then gave him that auspicious jar.
Then, having bowed to them, the joyful Śubhadatta took that jar and, with his kinsmen rejoicing, quickly reached his own home.
Having obtained food and other provisions from that pot and placed them inside it, he ate together with his kinsmen, using other vessels for the sake of concealment.
Having been freed from his burden and enjoying pleasures, he was once asked by his relatives while intoxicated with drink: "From where does this splendor of yours come?"
Clearly speaking like a fool, he took the jar that granted all desires and, placing it upon his shoulder, began—alas!—to dance.
And as he was dancing, his gait faltering from the excess of rut, that auspicious jar fell from his shoulder and shattered into pieces upon the ground.
At that very moment, having become whole again, he departed as he had come; and Śubhadatta, filled with despondency, returned to his former state.
Thus, those whose intellects are struck by the influence of the faults of drinking and so forth are incapable of protecting even that which they have already fully attained.
Having heard this humorous tale of the auspicious jar from Vasantaka, the Lord of Vatsa rose and performed his customary duties, such as bathing and eating.
Naravāhanadatta also, having bathed and eaten in the presence of his father, went at the end of the day to his own palace together with his friends.
There, while his friends and these ministers were listening, Marubhūtika spoke to him as he lay upon his bed, sleepless during the night.
"O King, I know that you did not summon the inner apartments out of a desire for the company of a maidservant, nor was she summoned; therefore, you have no sleep today."
Why then do you still feel attachment for courtesans even though you know this? For they possess no true affection; listen to this story concerning them.
In this world, there is a great and prosperous city named Citrakūṭa; there lived a merchant named Ratnavarman, a lord of immense wealth.
From the propitiation of Īśvara, one son was born to him; therefore, he gave that son the name Īśvaravarman.
And seeing that he had completed his studies and was approaching youth, Ratnavarman, the chief merchant who had an only son, reflected:
In this world, the Creator fashioned the courtesan as a visible snare for the wealthy who are blinded by youth—a snare that seizes both their wealth and their lives.
Therefore, I entrust this son to a certain courtesan so that, through training in the guise of a prostitute, he may not be deceived by them.
Having reflected thus, he went with his son, Īśvaravarman, to the house of a procuress named Yamajihvā.
There he saw that procuress, who had a thick jaw, long teeth, and a crooked nose, as she was instructing her daughter.
"O daughter, everyone is honored by wealth, and a courtesan especially so; that wealth does not belong to one who is full of passion, therefore a courtesan should abandon passion."
For passion is the foremost messenger of the faults; like a well-trained actress, the courtesan displays it falsely during both the first and last twilights.

By that means she should first win his affection; then, once he is attached, she should milk him for wealth. Having extracted the wealth, she should eventually abandon him, but she should retrieve it again when the opportunity arises.

That courtesan who, like a sage, treats with equal regard the young, the infant, the old, the deformed, and the beautiful, and who seeks her own interest as prescribed by the supreme scripture; [she is a true courtesan].
While his daughter was speaking thus, Ratnavarman approached that procuress; having been offered hospitality by her, he sat down with her.
And she said to her, "Noble lady, let this son of mine be instructed by you in the arts of a courtesan, so that he may attain proficiency."
"And I shall give you a thousand dīnārs as your ransom. Having heard that, she accepted his proposal, saying, "So be it."
Then, having distributed the dinars and entrusted his son to her, Ratnavarman went home with that Īśvaravarman.
Then Īśvaravarman, having learned the arts in the house of Yamajihva within a single year, went to the house of his father.
And having reached his sixteenth year, he said to his father: "For from wealth come both dharma and pleasure; from wealth comes honor, and from wealth comes fame."
When he had spoken thus, his father, full of joy and placing his trust in him, replied, "So be it," and gave him the merchandise consisting of five crores of wealth.
Then, taking that [wealth], the merchant’s son Īśvaravarman set out on an auspicious day with his caravan, desiring to reach Suvarṇadvīpa.
Traveling by degrees on the road, he reached the city named Kāñcanapura, and there he stayed in a garden situated near the outskirts.
Having bathed, eaten, and anointed himself, that youth entered this city and went to a temple to see a performance.
There he saw a dancing girl named Sundarī, who was like a wave from the ocean of beauty tossed up by the wind of youth.
Upon seeing her, his mind became focused on her alone at that moment; it was as if the instructions from the angry procuress had vanished far away.
Having sent away his companion at the conclusion of the dance, he made his request to her; and she, bowing low and realizing "I am blessed," gave her consent.
Having stationed skillful guards over his own quarters to protect the goods, Īśvaravarman went to the residence of that Sundarī.
His mother, named Makarakaṭī, honored him as he arrived with various domestic rites appropriate for that occasion.
And at the arrival of night, he was led by her into a bedchamber with a canopy of shimmering jewels, wherein a couch had been prepared for him to lie upon.
There he took delight with Sundarī, who was skilled in the various arts of dance and amorous dalliance, and who had given her consent.
Seeing her displaying such intense passion and not departing from his side, he was unable to leave that place on the second day.
And on those two days, that young merchant gave twenty-five lakhs of gold, jewels, and other treasures to that Sundarī.
I have acquired abundant wealth, yet I have not found one such as you; if I have indeed found him, what shall I do with wealth?
When Sundarī would not accept him because of his attachment to falsehoods, her mother Makarakaṭī, who had only this one child, spoke to her thus:
"Now, whatever belongs to us is indeed his own wealth; having placed it among those [other riches], let it be taken, daughter—what harm is there in that?"
Thus addressed by her mother, Sundarī accepted it as if with great reluctance; and the foolish Īśvaravarman believed her to be truly devoted to him.
Then, as his heart was captivated by her beauty, dancing, and singing, two months passed for that merchant while he remained there.
And he gave two crores to that Sundarī one after the other; then a friend named Arthadatta approached him and spoke to him privately.
Friend, has that instruction from the procuress, though acquired by you with such effort, gone to waste at this critical moment—like the science of weapons to a coward?
That you perceive a state of genuine affection in this love for a courtesan—is water ever truly present in the mirages of the desert?
All that will be exhausted before your wealth here is gone; therefore, let us depart while there is still time, for once your father realizes this, he will not forgive it.
Having been addressed thus by that friend, the merchant’s son said: "It is true that there is no trust in courtesans, yet Sundarī was not like them."
For if she does not see me for even a moment, my friend, she will give up her life; therefore, go and awaken her, if you must depart by all means.
Having been addressed thus by him, Arthadatta then spoke to Sundarī in the very presence of his mother, Makarakaṭī.
Your affection for Īśvaravarman is indeed extraordinary; yet, you must now certainly go to Svarṇadvīpa for the sake of trade.
"Therefore, he shall obtain that fortune by which, having come into your presence, he will dwell happily for as long as time permits; grant your consent to this, my friend."
Hearing that, her eyes filled with tears and her face clouded with despondency, Sundarī looked at Īśvaravarman's face and said to him:
Know this: who, disregarding the end, would speak? Who would believe it? Therefore, enough; let Fate do with me as it will.
Having heard that, his mother said to her: "Do not grieve; let there be fortitude in you. This beloved Siddhārtha of yours will surely come back; he will not abandon you."
Having thus consoled him, the mother, acting in concert with her accomplice, had a net laid secretly over a well at the entrance of the road.
Then Īśvaravarman’s mind became fixed upon her like one on a swing, and Sundarī, as if out of grief, took only very little food and drink.
She took no pleasure in singing, instrumental music, or dancing; she was consoled by various expressions of affection from Īśvaravarman.
Then, on the day appointed by his friend, Īśvaravarman set out from the palace of Sundarī, having had auspicious rites performed for him by the procuress.
Weeping, Sundarī followed him along with her mother from the city as far as the well outside, which was enclosed by a net.
Then, as he was turning back and approaching Sundarī, she threw herself into a well upon the surface of a net.
Then, a great cry of "Alas, alas! O mistress! O daughter! was heard there from the maidservants, the circle of attendants, and her mother.
Having turned back with his friend, that merchant’s son realized that his beloved had cast her body into the well, and for a moment he fell into a swoon.
Then, lamenting with cries of distress, Makarakaṭī caused her affectionate servants, who were privy to her secret plan, to descend into that well.
"By good fortune he lives! By good fortune he lives! saying this, they drew Sundarī out from that well by means of ropes.
Having been cast out and made herself appear as if dead, she offered herself up; when the merchant's son returned, she slowly began to converse with him.
Having taken up his beloved, who was now comforted, Īśvaravarman returned to that very house, joyful and accompanied by his followers.

Having ascertained that the proof of Sundarī’s love was the very fruit of his birth, and considering her attainment alone to be his goal, he abandoned the intention of setting out on his journey once more.
Then, while he remained there bound, his friend Arthadatta spoke to him again: "Friend, why have you destroyed yourself through delusion?"
Let there be no cause for you to fall into the well out of affection for Sundarī; for the deceptive schemes of a procuress are indeed inconceivable, even to Fate itself.
And having squandered your father's wealth, what will you say, or where will you go? Therefore, depart from here this very day, if your mind is set on what is auspicious.
Disregarding these words of his friend, that young merchant spent those three crores there in other expenditures within a single month.
Then, his wealth having been seized and the half-moon brand bestowed upon him, Sundarī was expelled from her house by that procuress Makarakaṭī.
Then Arthadatta and the others went quickly to their own city and related everything exactly as it had happened to his father.
When his father Ratnavarman learned of that, he became deeply distressed; going to the procuress Yamajihvā, the merchant lord spoke to her.
"Having received such a price for him, you have taught my son this; Makarakaṭī has easily seized his entire fortune."
Having said this, he described the account of his son to her; then that old procuress spoke to Yamajihvā.
"Bring your son here; I shall act in such a way that he will seize all the property of that Makarakaṭī."
When she had thus made her promise, the procuress Yamajihvā immediately dispatched her with a message, preceded by a gift for her livelihood.
Then Ratnavarman dispatched his well-wishing friend Arthadatta in order to bring back that son.
Having gone to that city of Kāñcanapura, Arthadatta related that entire message to Īśvaravarman.
Then he said to that friend: "Indeed, you did not follow my words; therefore, today the true nature of courtesans has been seen by you with your own eyes."
Having given five crores, you have obtained but a half-moon; what wise man would desire affection from courtesans, any more than he would seek it from grains of sand?
Or what do you say? Is this simply the nature of things—that a man so clever and heroic is a partaker of fortune?
As long as he does not fall upon the grounds of Rāma’s amorous dalliances, come then to your father’s side and provide a remedy for his wrath.
Having said this, he was quickly led by Arthadatta; and after being consoled, Īśvaravarman approached his father’s side.
And his father, out of affection for their only son, consoled him and led him once again into the presence of the procuress Yamajihvā.
Being questioned on this matter by her, he related through Arthadatta’s mouth his own history, ending with his fall into Sundarī’s well and the loss of his wealth.
Then Yamajihvā said: "I alone am the offender, since, having forgotten it, I did not teach him this illusion."
For Makarakaṭī had indeed cast her net inside the well; Sundarī threw her body onto its back, yet she did not die.
Having said, "There is a remedy for this," that procuress also had her own monkey named Āla brought there by her female slaves.
Having first given him her own thousand dinars, she said to him, "Swallow it! Then he, being thus instructed, swallowed it.
"Give twenty sons to him; give twenty-five to him; sixty to him and a hundred to him"—thus [the forms are used] in various instances of expenditure.
Being made to pay, that monkey, having repeatedly disgorged those dinars which had been swallowed by her tongue of Yama, gave them back exactly as they were.
Having displayed this skillful artifice, Yamajihvā spoke again: "O Īśvaravarman, take this young monkey."
"Furthermore, going day by day to that house of Sundarī as before, search for those [jewels] which have thus been secretly swallowed from it for expenditure."
Having seen that monkey, who resembles a wish-fulfilling gem and is adorned with a garland of flowers, Sundarī will offer him her entire wealth and, having made her request, take him alone.
Having taken that wealth and given her the expenses for two days already consumed, you should then depart from her presence without delay.
Having said this, Yamajihvā gave that monkey as a gift to Īśvaravarman, and his father gave him two crores of gold pieces.
Taking that very [letter], he set out once more for that city of Kāñcanapura; having dispatched a messenger ahead, he entered Sundarī’s house.
Sundarī welcomed him, along with his friends, with embraces around the neck and other gestures of affection, as if he were the very essence of her means of success and her own persistent longing.
Then, in a moment, while they were in each other's presence, Viśvāsīśvaravarman said to Arthadatta, "Go and bring Āla."
Saying "So be it," he went and brought a monkey; when the monkey had swallowed the previous thousand dinars, he spoke to him.
"O son, give today three hundred dinars for the sake of food and drink, and one hundred for the expense of betel leaves and other such items."
Give one hundred to Makarakaṭī and one hundred to Ambā among the twice-born; of the remainder of the thousand, offer that which is left to Sundarī.
Thus addressed by Īśvaravarman, that monkey likewise vomited up those previously swallowed dinars one after another and gave them for his expenses.
In this manner, by this reasoning, Ālo was constantly made to pay dinars for as long as Īśvaravarman lived—specifically, for a period of only one fortnight.
Then Makarakaṭī and Sundarī thought thus: "Aha! This is a perfected wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) that has assumed the form of a monkey for him."
"He who gives a thousand dinars day after day—if he has given this to us, our desires are fulfilled."
Having reflected thus, she, together with her mother, entreated Sundarīśvaravarman in private while he was resting after his meal.
"If your favor toward me is sincere, grant me this [favor]. Hearing that, Īśvaravarman spoke to her as if laughing:
"That is my father's entire fortune, and it is not proper to give that away"—to him who had spoken thus, Sundarī replied once more.
"I shall give five crores; let this garment be given. Then Īśvaravarman, having made his decision, spoke to him.
Even if you were to give me all your possessions or this entire city, it would still not be appropriate to give him away; why then speak of millions?
Having heard this, Sundarī said: "I shall give you my all; give this monkey to me, even if my mother should be angry with me."
Having said this, Sundarī grasped the feet of Īśvaravarman; then Arthadatta and the others said, "Let that which shall be given be given."
Thereupon, Īśvaravarman agreed to give her away in that manner; and he spent that day with Sundarī, who was filled with joy.
In the morning, he gave that monkey to Sundarī, who had requested it, after she had swallowed two thousand hidden gold dinars within its belly.
Taking her entire household wealth—the price for that [slave girl]—at that very moment, he departed quickly from there and went to Suvarṇadvīpa for trade.
And for two days, that monkey Āloda, being entreated by the joyful-faced Sundarī, gave her a thousand dīnāras each day.
On the third day, when he did not give anything even though she repeatedly entreated him with affection, Sundarī struck him with her fist.
Struck thus, the monkey flew up in a rage and, with his teeth and claws, tore open the faces of both Sundarī and her mother as they were striking him.
Then his mother, her face dripping with blood, struck him in anger with clubs; by that, the boy died there.
Seeing him dead and perceiving that all her possessions were lost, Sundarī became sorrowful; together with her mother, she prepared to give up her life.
Having made a net of her jawbone, he by whom her wealth was taken has today, making it his snare, seized her entire fortune with great skill.
"By her, another's snare was perceived, but not her own. Thus spoke the people there, laughing, once they had learned the facts of the matter.
Then that Sundarī, her purpose frustrated and her face lacerated, was with great difficulty dissuaded from abandoning her body by her kinsmen together with her mother.
And having acquired great wealth from Suvarṇadvīpa, Īśvaravarman soon returned to his father’s house at Citrakūṭa.
Seeing his son returned with immeasurable wealth acquired, his father Ratnavarman honored the procuress Yamajihvā with riches and held a magnificent festival.
Having realized the incomparable nature of illusion and his mind being detached from the company of wanton women, that Īśvaravarman then took a wife and remained there in his own home.

Thus, O Lord of Men, not even a fragment of truthful speech ever dwells in the heart of a woman without deceit; therefore, one who desires prosperity should never take pleasure in them, for they are like desolate forests whose journey can only be accomplished by means of a caravan.
Having heard from the mouth of Marubhūti this story of the web of lies exactly as it happened, Naravāhanadatta, together with Gomukha and the others, believed it and laughed.

Thus ends the first wave in the Śaktiyaśas book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave. When Marubhūti had thus related the true nature of courtesans, the wise Gomukha told a story similar to that of Kumudikā.
There was a lord of the earth named Vikramasiṃha in Pratiṣṭhāna, who by his very name and deeds was ordained by Fate to be like a lion in valor.
The beloved of that lord was the auspicious river Nandinī, and his queen, whose body was adorned with ornaments, was named Śaśilekhā.
Once, while he was staying in his own city, five or six kinsmen gathered together, came to his house, and surrounded the king.
Mahābhaṭa, Vīrabāhu, Subāhu, Subhaṭa, and King Pratāpāditya—all of these were also possessed of great strength.
Having rejected conciliation and other means toward them by employing his own minister, King Vikramasiṃha went forth for battle against them.
When the clash of weapons had commenced between the two armies, that king, mounted upon an elephant out of pride in his heroism, personally entered the battle.
Seeing him with his bow as his companion, shattering the army of his enemies, the five kings, headed by Mahābhaṭa, rushed forward together.
And as that entire force rushed forward together with equal might, it was shattered by the incomparable strength of Vikramasiṃha.
Then the minister named Anantaguṇa, standing at his side, said to him: "Our army has been broken; for now, there is no victory here."
Having cast us aside, you have entered into this powerful conflict; therefore, for the sake of your welfare, now follow these words of mine.
"Descend from this elephant and mount a horse; come, let us go to another realm, so that you may live and conquer your enemies once again."
Thus, at the minister's word, he dismounted of his own accord from the elephant; mounted upon a horse, he went out again with him and his children.
And King Vikramasiṃha, disguised in this attire and accompanied by that minister, gradually proceeded to the city of Ujjayinī.
Accompanied by his minister, he entered the residence of that courtesan named Kumudikā, who was renowned for her abundant wealth.
Seeing him arrive at her house unexpectedly, she too thought: "This is some extraordinary man who has come to my home."
By his splendor and his marks, it is indicated that he is a great king; if such a one as this is accepted, then my desire shall be fulfilled.
Having reflected thus, Kumudikā rose up, greeted him with a welcome, and offered great hospitality to the king.
When the king had rested, she said to him after a moment: "I am blessed today; my past merit has borne fruit for me."
"Since my house has been sanctified by Your Majesty coming here in person, I have become your slave, purchased by this very favor."
The hundred elephants I possess, the twenty thousand horses, and the palace filled with jewels—all this is now at your disposal.
Having spoken thus, Kumudikā attended upon the king and his ministers with costly services such as bathing and other comforts.
Then, in that palace, King Vikramasiṃha remained at ease with her, having entrusted his own person to her care.
He enjoyed her wealth and gave it away to beggars; yet she showed no sign of resentment toward him, for she remained content.
Then, as the king was pleased, thinking, "Ah, she is devoted to me," that minister Anantaguṇa, who stood by him, spoke to him in private:
"O King, courtesans possess no true affection at all; yet Kumudikā shows you devotion—of that I know not the cause."
Having heard these words of his, the king said to him: "Do not speak thus; Kumudikā would even give up her life for my sake."
"If you do not believe me, I shall show you proof," having said this, the king devised this stratagem with his own minister.
Gradually emaciating his body, restricting his drink and eating little, he made himself appear as if dead, motionless with his limbs sprawled out.
Then, having placed him upon a palanquin, his attendants led him to the cremation ground while they grieved, feigning sorrow for one whose virtues were infinite.
And she, Śokākumudikā, though being restrained by her kinsmen, came and ascended the funeral pyre together with him.
As long as the fire had not yet blazed up, the king, perceiving that Kumudikā had arrived behind him, rose with a yawn.
Crying out, "By good fortune! By good fortune! He has been restored to life here! they all joyfully led him, together with Kumudikā, to their own home.
Then, when the festival had been concluded, the king approached his minister in private and said to him, "Has her affection been observed?"
Then the minister said to him, "Even though it is thus, I do not believe you; there must certainly be a reason for this, so let us investigate the matter to reach a certainty."
Let him reveal himself to her, by whom this strength and the other, the strength of our allies, have been bestowed; having obtained it, let us slay the enemies in battle.
Even as the minister was speaking thus, that spy sent by Gupta arrived there once more; and when questioned, he spoke as follows.
The kingdom was overrun by enemies, but Queen Śaśilekhā, hearing from the people that the king had perished, falsely, entered the fire.
Having heard these words of the spy, the king, struck then by the thunderbolt of grief, lamented, "Alas, my queen! Alas, the virtuous one! and so forth.
Then, having gradually come to understand the truth of the matter, Kumudikā approached King Vikramasiṃha, comforted him, and spoke.
Why was this not commanded by Your Majesty even earlier? Why now, as well, do you say: "Let the suppression of the enemy be carried out with my wealth and my forces"?
Having been addressed thus by her, the king, having augmented his forces with that wealth, went into the presence of his powerful ally, the other king.
Having gone there with both their own forces and those troops, he slew all five enemy kings in battle and obtained their kingdoms as well.
Then, being pleased, he said to Kumudikā who was standing with him: "I am gratified by you; tell me, what desired thing shall I do for you?"
Then Kumudikā said: "If you are truly pleased, O Lord, then please extract this one thorn from my heart that has remained there for a long time."
"In Ujjayinī, my dear friend named Śrīdhara, the son of a brahmin, has been imprisoned by the king for a minor offense; therefore, release him from that."
O Lord, having seen you endowed with the most excellent royal marks that portend future prosperity, I have served you with devotion, knowing you to be capable of accomplishing this task.
Despairing of attaining my desired goal, I even ascended your funeral pyre, considering life to be fruitless without that young son of a brahmin.
When she had spoken thus, the king said to that charming woman: "I shall accomplish that for you; be steadfast, O fair-faced one."
Having spoken thus, and recollecting the words of the minister, he thought: "It is true that the lack of integrity among courtesans was described to me by Anantaguṇa."
"Therefore, this desire for the maiden named Varā must be fulfilled by me"; having thus resolved, he went to Ujjayinī accompanied by his army.
Having released Śrīdhara and given him much wealth, he established Kumudikā there, well-settled in union with her beloved.
Having returned to his own city and not transgressing the counsel of his ministers, that Vikramasiṃha gradually enjoyed the entire earth.
"The heart of courtesans is thus unknowable and unfathomable. Having told this story, when Gomukha had finished speaking there before Naravāhanadatta, Tapantaka then spoke.
"O King, one should never place trust in women, for they are all fickle; even those who are mature are not to be relied upon, just like courtesans."
Listen as I relate a marvel that I witnessed right here: there was once a merchant named Balavarman in this very city.
Candraśrī was his wife, and she, from the front of a window, saw a certain merchant's son named Bhavyaśīlahara.
Having had him brought to her friend's house, she, overcome by passion, sported with him at that very moment, unobserved, through the agency of her friend's mouth alone.
And every day, as she enjoyed herself with him in that manner, she was recognized by all the servants and kinsmen as being attached to him.
But her husband Balavarman did not know her to be unchaste; for generally, a person blinded by affection does not perceive the wickedness of his wife.
Then a fever with burning sensations arose in that Valavarman; by means of it, the merchant gradually reached his final state.
Even while he was in that state, his wife went day after day to the house of her friend, into the presence of that paramour.
While she remained right there, her husband died on another day; having learned of this, she quickly took leave of that lover and departed.
Firm in her resolve, she ascended that funeral pyre together with her husband, even though she was being restrained by her kinsmen who were well-acquainted with her virtuous character.
Thus, indeed, the course of a woman's mind is difficult to comprehend; they form attachments to others and yet die without their husband.
When Tapantaka had spoken thus, Hariśikha replied in turn: "Have you not heard what happened in this very case regarding Devadāsa?"
In former times, there lived in that village a householder named Devadāsa; his wife was named Duḥśīlā, a name truly descriptive of her character.
The neighbors discovered that she was attached to another man; on one occasion, this Devadāsa went to the royal court on business.
And at that moment, his wife, desiring his death, brought that other man and placed him on the upper floor of the house.
Then, at midnight, she had her own husband Devadāsa—who had returned and was sleeping after having been enjoyed by that lover—put to death.
Having dismissed that paramour and remained silent until the end of the night, she went out at dawn and cried out, "My husband has been killed by thieves!"
Then his kinsmen, having arrived there and seen him, said: "Since he was killed by thieves, how is it that nothing at all has been taken from here by them?"
Having spoken thus, they questioned their son who remained there: "By whom was your father killed? Thereupon, he spoke clearly.
One day, a certain youth climbed onto the roof of my house; at night, having descended from it, he killed my father even as I looked on.
"But first my mother took me away from my father's side," the child said; and upon hearing this, the wife’s lover realized that he had been killed by him.
Her kinsmen searched for and killed that paramour of hers at that very moment; then, having taken charge of that child and that woman of ill-repute, they banished them both.
"Thus, a female serpent whose heart is colored by another kills without a doubt. When Hariśikha had spoken thus, Gomukha replied once more.
What need is there for anything else here? Listen now to this laughable account of what happened to Vajrasāra, who was once a servant of the King of Vatsa.
That hero, beloved and handsome, who was like adamant in his essence, had a wife born in Mālava who was beautiful and dearer to him than his own body.
Once, the father of that woman’s wife, accompanied by his sons, came in person from Mālava, full of longing, to extend an invitation.
Then Vajrasāra, having honored him and informed the king, went with his wife to Mālava, invited by the king to accompany him.
Having rested for just one month there in his father-in-law's house, he returned here for the purpose of serving the king, while his wife remained there.
Then, after some days had passed, a friend named Krodhana approached Vajrasāra and spoke to him thus:
Having abandoned your wife at her father's house, why did you destroy your home? For there, that sinful woman indeed committed adultery with another man.
"Since this was told to me today by a trustworthy person who has come from there, do not consider it to be false; therefore, restrain her and carry off the other woman."
Having spoken thus, Krodhana departed; Vajrasāra stood for a moment like one bewildered and thought, "I suspect this may indeed be true."
"Even though the messenger was sent, she did not come; how could this be? Therefore, I shall go myself to bring her back and see what will happen."
Having thus resolved and gone to Mālava, he took leave of his parents-in-law, and having taken his wife, set out from there.
Having traveled a long distance, he, having artfully deceived his followers, entered a dense forest by a wrong path, taking his wife with him.
Having seated her there in the middle of a secluded place, he said to her: "I have heard from trustworthy people that you are attached to another man."
"Since you did not come when you were summoned by me while I remained right here, tell the truth; otherwise, I shall inflict punishment upon you."
Having heard that, she said to him: "If this is your resolve, then why do you ask me? Do as you please with me."
Having heard her words with such contempt, Vajrasāra, filled with rage, bound her to a tree with creepers and beat her.
As she was taking away his garment, the lustful fool, seeing her naked, felt a desire for sexual pleasure arise within him.
Then, having settled her down and bound her, he embraced her to dally with her; but she did not desire it, and even when entreated by him, she spoke.
"Just as I was bound and struck with creepers by you, so too, if I were to strike you, I desire it no other way."
"So be it," he agreed, for he was deluded by his passion; it is a marvel how the mind-born god, though possessing the strength of a diamond, has been reduced to the essence of straw.
Then she bound him, along with his hands and feet, firmly to a tree; and while he was thus bound, she cut off his ears and nose with that very same weapon.
Having taken his weapons and garments and having assumed the dress of a man, that wicked woman then departed from there as she pleased.
Vajrasāra was there with his ears and nose cut off, his face bowed down by a flowing torrent of blood and by pride.
Then a certain physician, having come there into the forest for the sake of medicinal herbs, saw him, released him out of compassion, and that virtuous man led him to his own home.
There he was comforted by him, and slowly returned to his own home; yet Vajrasāra, not finding her, did not meet his wicked wife.
And he related that entire account to Krodhana, who in turn recounted it all before the King of Vatsa.
"This man has become a woman because he lacks manliness and indignation; surely his male attire was taken away by his wife, and she has inflicted upon him the punishment he deserved."
Thus, although he was mocked by everyone in the royal court, Vajrasāra remained right there with a mind as firm as adamant.
When Gomukha had thus said, "O King, who can place their trust in women?", Marubhūtika spoke once more.
"The minds of women are unstable; hear now a story regarding this as well. Formerly, there was a king named Siṃhabala in the Deccan."
And his wife was named Kalyāṇavatī, the daughter of a feudatory chief of Mālava, who was beloved by all the women of the inner apartments.
Once, while that king was ruling his own kingdom together with her, he was expelled from the country by powerful kinsmen who had banded together.
Accompanied by his queen, armed and with a small retinue, the king then set out in secret for Mālava, the residence of his father-in-law.
And as he was traveling on the road through the forest, he effortlessly split in two with a stroke of his sword a lion that had charged at him from the front.
And as a forest elephant approached, trumpeting and wheeling in circles, he struck it down so that its trunk and legs were severed by his sword and it ceased its cries.
Then, alone, he strode through the forest like an elephant crushing lotus-stalks, trampling the multitude of thieves like a herd of fresh lotuses.
Having thus traversed the road and reached Mālava, where he beheld his own queen of most wonderful prowess, that ocean of courage spoke to her.
"O Queen, you must not speak of this conduct of mine on the path while in my father's house; for what praise is there in the prowess of a Kshatriya? It would only bring shame."
Having said this, he entered his father's house together with her; and when questioned by him in great agitation, he related his own story.
Honored by that very father-in-law and provided with elephants and horses, he went into the presence of the exceedingly powerful king named Gajānīka.
But he, intent on conquering his enemies, kept his wife Kalyāṇavatī right there in her father’s house.
When he had departed and several days had passed, on one occasion that queen, standing at the window, beheld a certain man.
As soon as he was seen, his form captivated her heart; and being drawn by the god of love, she reflected at that very moment:
I know, O noble son, that there is another who is more handsome and possesses greater valor; nevertheless, alas, my heart runs toward this man alone.
Thinking then, "I shall resort to him this very day," she disclosed her intention to her friend, who kept her secret.
Having had him brought by that very woman at night through the path of a window, she caused him to enter that harsh inner apartment, having been hoisted up by ropes.
Having entered there, that man was unable to sit upon her couch by virtue of his own splendor; he sat down instead on a separate seat.
Seeing that, while he was despondent, thinking, "Alas, this man is base," the queen arrived there at that very moment, as a serpent was gliding above.
Beholding him, that man there suddenly rose up in fear, took up his bow, and struck the serpent with an arrow.
And he threw that fallen, ruined object out through the window; having escaped from that fear, the coward danced with joy.
Seeing him dancing, Kalyāṇavatī was deeply distressed and thought: "Fie, fie! What is the use of this cowardly and base wretch of mine?"
As soon as she saw that she was indifferent [to him], her friend, who could read her mind, went out quickly and, entering there in a state of agitation, said:
"O Queen, your father has arrived; therefore, let this youth now go quickly to his own home by the very same path by which he came."
When she had spoken thus, he went out through the window by means of a rope; overwhelmed by fear, he fell, yet by fate he did not meet his death.
When he had departed, Kalyāṇavatī said to her friend: "Friend, you have done well; it was right that this base man was turned away by you."
"You have understood my heart; for indeed my mind is distressed. Out of shame, my husband conceals his having struck down tigers, lions, and other beasts."
But this one, having killed a snake, dances like a man of little spirit; having abandoned such a person as that, how could I find delight in this common fellow?
Fie on me, whose mind is so unsteady! Or rather, fie on women, who, like flies abandoning camphor, run toward impurity.
Thus, having felt remorse, that queen spent the night and remained there in her father’s house, waiting for her husband.
Meanwhile, Siṃhabala, having been granted the strength of an army of elephants by the king, went and slew those five sinful kinsmen.

Then, having regained his own kingdom and brought back his wife from her father's house, and having gratified his father-in-law with floods of wealth, he ruled the earth for a very long time without any thorns.
"Thus, O King, even among noble women who possess discernment, the fickle mind runs hither and thither toward a brave, fortunate, and virtuous husband; yet women of pure character are rare indeed."
Having heard this story told by Marubhūti, Naravāhanadatta, the son of the King of Vatsa, passed that night sleeping happily.

Thus ends the second wave in the Śaktiyaśas book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. Then, in the morning, having performed his necessary duties, Naravāhanadatta went with his ministers to wander about his own garden.
Standing there, he first beheld a mass of light even beyond the sky, and then he saw many Vidyādharīs descending from it.
And in the midst of those radiant women, he beheld a certain maiden who captivated the eyes, like a digit of the cool-rayed moon among the stars.
Her face was like a blooming lotus, her tremulous eyes were like bees, her gait was like that of a graceful swan, and she possessed the fragrance of a flowing blue lily.
Her waist was adorned with the three folds of skin like charming waves, appearing as if she were the presiding deity of the beauty of a pond in the garden of the God of Love.
Upon seeing her, who was the reviver of his love and filled with longing, that prince was agitated like the ocean at the sight of the moon's form.
"Aha! What an indescribable variety of beautiful creation this is from the Creator!"—thus praising it, he approached her accompanied by his ministers.
And as she gazed at him with a sidelong glance moistened by love, he gradually asked her: "Who are you, O blessed lady, and what is the reason for your arrival here?"
Having heard that, the maiden said: "Listen, I shall tell you this: there is a golden city named Kāñcanaśṛṅga on the Himālaya."
There dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Sphaṭikayaśas, who is righteous and compassionate toward the wretched, the poor, and those who have come to him for refuge.
Know me to be this daughter of his, named Śaktiyaśas, born of Queen Hemaprabhā, produced by the grace of Gaurī.
I, who was my father’s beloved as his own life and the youngest of five brothers, then propitiated Pārvatī with vows and hymns at his command.
Satisfied, she granted me all the sciences and commanded me thus: "Daughter, the power of your science shall be tenfold that of your father."
And Naravāhanadatta, the son of the King of Vatsa and future emperor of the sky-dwellers, shall be your husband.
Having spoken thus, the wife of Śarva vanished from my sight; and by her grace, having acquired the power of knowledge, I have gradually attained youth.
And that goddess, having granted me her vision during the night, commanded me today: "Daughter, you must go in the morning and see your own husband."
"You must indeed come here this very month, for your father, with his mind fixed on this resolve, will arrange your marriage."
Having spoken thus, that goddess vanished; the night had passed, and then, O noble son, she came here to see you.
Having said, "Therefore, I shall depart now," Śaktiyaśas, together with her circle of female companions, flew up into the sky and went to her father's city.
And Naravāhanadatta, eager for that marriage, entered the inner apartments dejected, perceiving the month to be like an eon.
Seeing him despondent there, Gomukha then said to him: "Listen, O King, I shall tell you a story that will amuse you."
In ancient times there was a city known by the name Kāñcanapurī, and in it there lived a great lord of the earth named Sumanas.
By him, who traversed difficult fortresses and wildernesses, even such enemies were rendered strange and eclipsed by his resplendent glory.
Once, when he was seated in his assembly hall, the doorkeeper informed him: "Your Majesty, there is a daughter of the Niṣāda chief named Muktālatā."
Taking the parrot held in a cage, she stood outside at the gate, followed by her brother Vīraprabha, desiring to see the King.
When the king said, "Let her enter," that Bhilla maiden entered the courtyard of the royal assembly hall by the command of the doorkeeper.
"Is she not human? Surely she is some divine woman! thought everyone there upon seeing that wondrous form.
And she, having bowed to the king, then addressed him thus: "O Lord, this parrot named Śāstragañja is a master of the four Vedas."
This poet, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge and the arts, has been brought here today for the use of the Lord; let him be accepted.
Having been thus presented by her and taken by the doorkeeper out of curiosity, the parrot was led before the king and recited this verse.

O King, this is always fitting: that he, with a face darkened by smoke, is kindled by the gusts of breath from the wives of his enemies who are separated from their lords. But this is truly a marvel, that through the floods of tears from their humiliation, the great fire of his majesty blazes forth here in the ten directions.
Having thus recited and explained it, Śuka spoke again: "What is the object of knowledge? From which scripture shall I speak? Please instruct me."
Then, while the king was greatly amazed, the minister said this to him: "O Lord, I suspect that this is some ancient seer who has been turned into a parrot by a curse."
When the minister had said, "One who remembers his past lives recalls what was studied in former times through the power of dharma," the king then questioned that parrot.
"I am curious, my good sir; tell me your own story: where was your birth? From whence comes your knowledge of the scriptures while in the form of a parrot? And who indeed are you?"
Then, shedding tears, that parrot spoke slowly: "Though this is indeed unspeakable, listen; I shall speak by your command."
O King, near the Himavat there is a single rohiṇī tree, which, like the Veda, has birds perched upon its many branches that extend throughout the quarters.
In that place, a certain parrot lived together with a female parrot, having made his home there; from her, I was born through the force of my past misdeeds.
As soon as I was born, my mother, that female parrot, passed away; but my father, though old, placed me within his wings and raised me.
Then my father remained there, eating the remnants of fruits brought by nearby parrots and offering some to me.
Once, a terrifying army of Bhillas, making the cow-horns resound with the blast of musical instruments, arrived there for the purpose of hunting.
Her eyes like those of a terrified black antelope, her garment disarrayed by dust, and the mass of her braided hair loosened as the chowries were tossed about in her agitation.
Suddenly that great forest became as if agitated by flight, as the hosts of Pulindas ran about to slaughter various living beings.
Having spent the day sporting like Death himself on the hunting grounds, that army of Śabaras returned, carrying loads of raw flesh.
But there, an old Śabara who had not obtained any meat, being hungry at evening, saw that tree and approached it.
Having climbed there, he quickly seized other parrots and birds from their nests one by one, and having killed them, he threw them down upon the ground.
Seeing him approaching nearby, resembling a servant of Yama, I cowered in fear and slowly hid within my father's wing.
Meanwhile, that sinner reached our nest, dragged my father out by force, wrung his neck, killed him, and threw him down at the foot of the tree.
And I, having fallen along with my father from the edge of that wing, emerged and cautiously entered among the grass and leaves in fear.
Then, having descended, that Bhilla roasted and ate some parrots in the fire; taking others, the wicked man went to his own village.
Then, having spent that night which was long with suffering, my fear being stilled, at dawn when the sun—the eye of the world—had mostly risen;
My wings obstructing the earth, stumbling repeatedly and afflicted by thirst, I reached the shore of a lotus lake situated nearby.
There I saw the sage named Marīci, who had performed his ablutions and was seated upon that sandy bank, appearing like my own past merit incarnate.
Seeing me and comforting me with drops of water from his mouth, the sage compassionately placed me in a leaf-cup and carried me to the hermitage.
Having seen me there, the patriarch Pulastya reportedly laughed; questioned by the other sages regarding this, he, who possessed divine vision, spoke.
"Seeing this cursed parrot, I laughed out of sorrow; and having performed my daily rites, I shall relate to you this connected story."
"By hearing this, he will remember his birth and his former life"—having said this, the seer Pulastya rose for his daily rites.
And when he had performed his daily rites, being requested once more by the sages, that great sage related this story concerning me.
In the city of Ratnākara, there was a king named Jyotiṣprabha, who, with his powerful command, ruled the earth as far as the ocean.
To him was born a son by his queen named Harṣavatī, produced from the boon of Gaurī’s husband, who was pleased by his intense asceticism.
Because the queen had seen the Soma enter her mouth in a dream, the king gave his son the name Somaprabha.
And that prince Soma-prabha gradually grew, spreading nectar-like virtues that brought a festival for the eyes of all creatures.
Seeing that he was a hero capable of bearing the burden of sovereignty, young, and naturally beloved, his father Jyotiṣprabha joyfully consecrated him as the crown prince.
He appointed his own minister’s son, named Priyaṅkara, who possessed excellent qualities, to the office of prime minister. This son belonged to the one known as Prabhākara.
At that moment, Mātali, having taken a divine horse from the sky, descended and, approaching Somaprabha, spoke to him.
"You have descended here as a Vidyādhara, the friend of Śakra; and by him, the son of Uccaiḥśravas named Aśvaśravas was [bestowed]."
O King, out of former affection, this best of horses has been sent to you; mounted upon him here, you shall become invincible to your enemies.
Having spoken thus and given that jewel of a horse to Somaprabha, the charioteer of Vāsava, having received worship, flew up into the sky and departed.
Then, having spent that day—which was delightful with festivities—Somaprabha spoke on the following day to his father, the king:
"Father, this is not the duty of a Kṣatriya: that he should lack the desire for victory. Therefore, give me your command so that I may set out for the conquest of the quarters."
Having heard that, his father was pleased and replied, "So be it," and Jyotiṣprabha made the necessary arrangements for his journey.
Then, having bowed to his father, on an auspicious day under the moonlight, Somaprabha set out for the conquest of the quarters accompanied by his forces, mounted upon Indra’s horse.
With that jewel of a horse, he conquered the lords of the earth in all directions; and he of irresistible prowess took treasures from them.
By him, his own bow and the heads of his enemies were bent down simultaneously; yet while that bow attained loftiness, the heads of those enemies did not.
Then, having accomplished his purpose, as he was returning on the road near the Himalayas, he encamped his army and engaged in a hunt within the forest.
By chance, he saw there a Kinnara adorned with excellent jewels, and he rushed toward him on that horse given by Indra to capture him.
