That kiṃnara entered a mountain cave and vanished from sight, while Somaprabha was carried a great distance by that horse.
Having thus scattered [the offerings] in all directions while the sun of fierce radiance was shining, when it reached the western quarter, which brings about the union with twilight.
Exhausted, he somehow turned back and beheld a great lake; desiring to spend the night on its shore, he dismounted from his horse.
Having given grass and water to him, he himself returned with water and fruit; and while resting in one place, he suddenly heard the sound of singing.
Having gone a short distance along that path out of curiosity, he saw a divine maiden singing before a Śiva-liṅga.
Thinking, "How wonderful this form must be," she too, seeing him of noble appearance, offered him hospitality and spoke with wonder.
"Who are you, and how have you come alone to this inaccessible land? Having heard this, he told her his own story, and she in turn questioned him.
"Tell me, who are you? Who are you in this forest, and what is your dwelling? To him who had thus questioned her, that celestial maiden replied:
"If you have curiosity, O noble one, then I shall tell it; listen to my story. Having said this, she began to speak, her eyes overflowing with shimmering tears.
Here, on a ridge of the Himalayas, there is a city named Kāñcanābha; therein dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Padmakūṭa.
Know that I am this daughter of his, named Manorathaprabhā, who was dearer than a son to King Hemaprabha by virtue of Queen Hemaprabhā.
By the power of that knowledge, I [traveled] with my friends to hermitages, islands, principal mountains, forests, and groves.
Having thus played every day, I would return to my own abode at the time of my father's meal during the third watch of the day.
Once, having arrived here while dwelling on the shore of a lake, I beheld a son of a sage standing here together with his companions.
Drawn by the beauty of his form as if by a messenger, I approached him; he too welcomed me with a meaningful glance.
Then, as I sat there, a friend of mine, who perceived the intentions of both parties, asked her companion, "Tell me, O fortunate one, who are you?"
And her companion said: "Friend, not far from here, in a hermitage, dwells a radiant sage named Dīdhitimat."
Once, that religious student, having come there to bathe in the lake, beheld the goddess Śrī who had arrived at that very moment.
Since he was unattainable by body and utterly tranquil, she, filled with desire, loved him with her mind alone; through him, she obtained a son born of her thought.
"Since this son was born to me from seeing you, let him be accepted," saying this, she took that newborn son of Dīdhitimat.
Having entrusted the boy to that sage, Śrī vanished; and the sage, delighted, accepted the son who had been obtained without effort.
Having given him the name Raśmimān and having raised him in due course, he initiated him and affectionately taught him all the sciences.
Know this radiant young sage to be the son of Śrī, who has come here to sport together with me.
Having said this, my friend was questioned by his companion, and she told him everything exactly as I had described it, including her own name and lineage.
Then, through our mutual knowledge of one another's lineage, both that son of the sage and I remained there, filled with even greater affection.
Just then, a second friend came to me from her own home and said, "Arise, O charming girl; your father awaits you in the dining hall."
Having heard that, and having said, "I shall come quickly," and having left the sage's son there, I went into my father's presence out of fear.
There, while I had taken some food and was still inside, my first friend came to me and spoke privately:
That friend of the Sage’s son has arrived here; standing at the door of the courtyard, he quickly spoke to me.
"Now I have been sent by Raśmimant to the side of Manorathaprabhā, after he had given me his paternal knowledge for traveling through the sky."
For, deprived of her, the mistress of his life, he has been brought to such a cruel state by Love that he is unable to sustain his breath for even a moment.
As soon as I heard that, I went out and, accompanied by him as my leader and by my friend, the son of a sage, I have come here.
And having arrived here, I beheld that son of a sage dead—his life-breath departed at the very moment of the moon's rising—without me being present.
Then, pained by separation from him and censuring my own body, I desired to enter the fire, taking his corpse with me.
Then, descending from heaven in the form of a mass of radiance, a person took that body and, soaring up, departed into the sky.
Then, just as I was preparing to throw myself into the fire all alone, a voice arose here from the sky, speaking thus:
"Manorathaprabhā, do not act thus; in time, you shall have a reunion with this son of a sage."
Having heard this, I have turned away from death; awaiting that [reunion], I remain right here with my hopes fixed, intent upon the worship of Śaṅkara.
To that Vidyādharī who was speaking thus—"Even that friend of the sage’s son has vanished from my sight somewhere"—Somaprabha replied:
"If you are staying here all alone, then where is that friend of yours, and where are they? Hearing this, the Vidyādhara maiden said to him:
There is a lord of the Vidyādharas named Siṃhavikrama; he has a daughter, Makarandikā, who is without equal.
That maiden, my friend who is as dear to me as my own life, suffers in sympathy with my sorrow; she sent her friend here today to learn news of me.
Then, along with that friend of hers, I too sent my own friend to her side; therefore, I am now left here all alone.
Speaking thus, she immediately showed that female friend of hers, who had descended from the sky, to Somaprabha.
Having been told that news by her friend, she had a bed of leaves prepared for her, and she also caused fodder to be given to Somaprabha’s horse.
Having spent the night there, they all rose in the morning and saw a Vidyādhara who had descended from the sky and approached them.
And that Vidyādhara named Devajaya, having bowed down and sat beside Manorathaprabhā, spoke to her thus:
"O Manorathaprabhā, King Siṃhavikrama says to you: 'As long as your boon is not fulfilled, my daughter shall not [be given away]'"—
Out of affection, your friend Makarandikā desires marriage; therefore, come and inform her so that she may proceed with the wedding.
Having heard this, King Somaprabha then spoke to that Vidyādhara maiden as she was preparing to depart out of affection for her friend.
"O sinless one, I have a curiosity to see the world of the Vidyādharas; therefore, take me there, and let this horse remain here with its fodder provided."
Having heard that, she said, "So be it," and immediately, accompanied by her friend, she traveled through the sky together with him, who had been placed upon Devajaya’s lap.
Having arrived there and been offered hospitality by Makarandikā, she saw Somaprabha and was asked by her in private, "Who is this?"
And when Makarandikā had been told that news by her, her heart was immediately captivated by Somaprabha.
Having mentally attained her, as if she were the goddess Lakṣmī incarnate in bodily form, he thought: "What fortunate man is he who would be her husband?"
Then, during their private conversation, Manorathaprabhā said to Makarandikā, "O fierce one, why do you not desire marriage?"
Having heard that, she also said to her: "If you do not accept the proposal, how could I desire marriage? For you are dearer to me than my own body."
When Makarandikā had thus spoken with affection, he said, "O charming girl, by the power of my heart's desire, the boon has been chosen by me."
When she said, "I shall remain here indeed, awaiting union with him," Makarandikā replied, "In that case, I will do as you say."
Then Manorathaprabhā, having understood her thoughts, said to her: "Friend, Somaprabha has wandered the earth and has arrived as your guest."
"Therefore, O beautiful one, you must perform the rites of hospitality for this guest. As soon as she heard this, Makarandikā replied:
"Right now, everything here, even unto my own body, has been made into an offering-vessel for him by me; let him accept it as he desires, if he so wishes."
When she had spoken thus, Manorathaprabhā informed her father in due course of their affection and settled the matter of their marriage.
Then Somaprabha, having regained his fortitude and being satisfied, said to her: "I am going to your hermitage now; perhaps there, at last, [my purpose will be fulfilled]."
The army, searching for his tracks and led by a minister, might approach; but failing to find me and suspecting danger, it would turn back and retreat.
Having gone there and learned the news regarding the army, I shall return; then, having made my decision, I will marry Makarandikā on an auspicious day.
Having heard that, she said "So be it" and led him back to her own hermitage, where she once again placed Manorathaprabhā upon Devajaya's lap.
Meanwhile, his minister Priyaṅkara, searching for Somaprabha’s tracks, arrived at that very place with his army.
Then, as Somaprabha joyfully related his entire story to that minister who had joined him, he told it all.
Just then, a messenger arrived from his father’s presence, bringing a message written on a letter and saying, "Come quickly!"
Taking that army with the approval of his ministers, and not transgressing his father’s command, he went to his own city.
And as he departed, he said to Manorathaprabhā and Devajaya: "I shall come back before long once I have seen my father."
Then Devajaya went and informed Makarandikā of all that in the same manner; because of this, she became distressed by the pain of separation.
She found no delight in the garden, nor in song, nor in her circle of friends; she did not even listen to the playful words of the parrots.
She did not even partake of food, let alone engage in adornment and such; though exhorted with great effort by her parents, she did not maintain her composure.
Soon after leaving her bed of lotus leaves, she wandered about like one intoxicated, causing anxiety to her parents.
When she did not heed the words of those two as they sought to console her, they then became angry and cursed her.
"Deprived of splendor, you shall fall for some time into the midst of the Niṣādas, with this very same body and devoid of the memory of your own birth."
Having been thus cursed by her two parents, Makarandikā went to the abode of the Niṣādas and immediately became a Niṣāda maiden.
And his father, Siṃhavikrama, the lord of the Vidyādharas, having repented and out of grief for that, passed away along with his wife.
And he was formerly a lord of the Vidyādharas and a seer who knew all the scriptures; due to some remnant of past demerit, he became a parrot.
In the same way, his wife was born as a wild sow in the forest; and this parrot, by the power of his asceticism, knows exactly what he studied in the past.
Then, having seen the manifold course of karma, I laughed at him; and after he had told this story in the royal assembly, he will be liberated.
And Somaprabha shall indeed obtain her daughter Makarandikā, who, having been born as a sky-dweller, has come to the state of being a Niṣāda woman.
And Manorathaprabhā shall obtain as her husband that very son of the Sage, Raśmimat, who has now been born as a ruler of the earth.
Somaprabha, too, having seen his father and gone to that hermitage, was now staying there, propitiating Śarva for the sake of regaining his beloved.
Having related this story there, the sage Pulastya ceased; and I, overwhelmed by joy and sorrow, remembered my own birth.
Then, out of compassion, that sage Marīci took me to the hermitage where I had been brought and raised me there.
And once my wings had grown, out of the restlessness natural to a bird, I wandered here and there, displaying the marvel of my knowledge.
Having fallen from the Niṣādas, I have gradually reached your presence; now my evil karma born of the bird-womb has been exhausted.
When that learned parrot of wondrous speech had concluded this discourse in the assembly, King Sumanas was instantly moved by waves of joy, forgetting his inner self.
In the meantime, Śambhu, being well-pleased, commanded Somaprabha in a dream: "Arise, O King! Go to the presence of King Sumanas; there you shall obtain your beloved."

Indeed, having become a Niṣāda woman named Makarandikā due to her father’s curse, she who was formerly known as Muktālatā took him, her own father—who had attained the state of a parrot—and went into the presence of that king.
But upon seeing you, that Vidyādharī, her curse having been lifted, will remember her former birth; then your union shall take place, resplendent with joy increased by mutual recognition.
Having thus addressed the lord of the earth, the Blessed Lord Giriśa, compassionate toward his devotees, spoke likewise to the other woman, Manorathaprabhā, who was returning to her own hermitage.

He who was formerly known as Raśmimat, the esteemed and excellent son of the Sage, has now been born again under the name Sumanas. Therefore, go there and find him; by the sight of you, O auspicious one, he will immediately remember his own former birth.
Thus, having been separately instructed by the Lord in a dream, those two Vidyādhara maidens, Somaprabhā and Vidyunmālā, then entered the well-disposed assembly of that king.
And there, beholding Somaprabha and remembering her own birth, Makarandikā—freed from her long-standing curse—immediately assumed her own divine form and embraced him around the neck.

Having obtained that daughter of the Vidyādhara king through the grace of the Lord of the Mountain-born, Somaprabha, embracing her as if she were the very Fortune of divine enjoyment in embodied form, became fulfilled.

And as soon as he saw Manorathaprabhā, King Sumanas remembered his own former birth; having entered the body that had previously descended from the sky, he became the son of the Lord of Munis, Raśmimān.
Having united once more with his own beloved after longing for her so long, he departed for his own hermitage; and King Somaprabha also went to his own city, taking that dear wife of his with him.

The parrot too, having cast off that avian body, went to the abode earned by his own austerities; thus, even for embodied beings separated by vast distances, a destined reunion inevitably occurs in this world.
Having heard this tale, wonderful, diverse, and beautiful, from his own minister Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta then rejoiced with eager longing for Śaktiyaśas.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave. Then, having related the story of the pair of Vidyādharīs, Gomukha, the foremost of ministers, spoke to Naravāhanadatta:
O gods, some who desire the welfare of both worlds, being of refined intellect, endure even the agitation caused by sensual desires and the like, though they are common to all.
And so there was a son of good family named Śūravarma, a servant of the king named Kuladhara, renowned for his prowess.
Once, having returned from the village, he entered his house without suspicion and saw his wife engaged in a private liaison with her own friend.
Seeing this, he restrained his anger and reflected with fortitude: "What is the use of my killing this beast who has betrayed his friend?"
"Or even by this wicked woman, a woman of evil conduct who has been restrained—what can I do, for I too am a partaker in this sin?"
Having reflected thus and abandoning both of them, he said: "Whichever of you two I might see again and again, him I would slay."
"You must not come here again within the range of my sight," he said; having spoken thus, he released them, and they went away to some distant place.
But he, having married another, became Śūravarmā and was perfectly at ease; thus, O King, one who has conquered anger shall not become a vessel for suffering.
O King, one who has cultivated wisdom is never afflicted by calamity; for even among animals, wisdom leads to welfare, not mere physical prowess.
And so, listen to this story concerning a lion, a bull, and others: there was once a certain wealthy merchant's son in a particular city.
Once, as he was traveling to the city of Mathurā for the purpose of trade, his ox, while pulling the yoke, broke it due to the excessive weight.

Previously, a certain crane used to devour every offspring as soon as it was born; consequently, a serpent came and ate his young, and because of that, the crane was filled with grief.
Then, following the instruction of the fish, Baka climbed from the rat's burrow into a snake's hole, where he scattered the fish-flesh.
Having emerged and eating that [food], Nakula followed its trail; seeing a hole, he entered it and killed the serpent along with its offspring.
Thus it is done by means of a stratagem; hear another matter from me: formerly, there was a certain son of a merchant who had only his balance scale remaining from his paternal inheritance.
Having entrusted that balance, which was fashioned from a thousand palas of iron, into the hands of a certain merchant, he departed for another country.
When he arrived there, he searched for the scale; at that moment, the merchant said to him, "It has been eaten by mice."
"It is true that that iron was very sweet, and it was eaten by mice. Thus the merchant's son also spoke to him, laughing within his heart.
Then he requested food from that merchant; the merchant, being well-pleased, agreed to give it to him.
Then, having entrusted that merchant's young son to his care, the merchant’s son set out to bathe, taking with him only a single myrobalan fruit.
Having bathed and placed that infant secretly in the house of a friend, that wise man went alone to the house of the merchant.
To that merchant who was asking, "Where has that boy gone?", he replied, "That boy was carried off by a hawk, swooping down from the sky."
"O son, you have deceived me," said that merchant in anger; yet even when brought before the royal court, he spoke in that very same manner.
"How could a hawk possibly carry off this child? This is impossible! When the members of the assembly had spoken thus, the merchant's son said:
Where a great balance-scale is devoured by mice, there even a hawk could carry off an elephant, let alone a child.
Having heard that, the members of the assembly, out of curiosity, asked for his story and caused the balance to be brought; he too brought it, and the child was placed upon it.
Thus, those possessed of intelligence accomplish their desired ends through skillful means; by you, however, through sheer recklessness alone, the Lord has been brought into a state of peril.
Having heard this from Karaṭaka, Damanaka said with a laugh, "Do not say so; for what doubt can there be regarding the lion's victory in a fight with oxen?"
Where is the lion, adorned with deep scars from the blows of the tusks of rutting elephants; and where is the tamed elephant, its body wounded by the goad?
While those two jackals were thus conversing with one another, Piṅgalaka spoke to Sañjīvaka’s bull in the midst of the fray.

When he was slain, Damanaka remained for a long time by the side of that lord of beasts, Piṅgalaka, together with Karaṭaka; thereafter, having once again attained unimpeded ministership, he dwelt there filled with joy.
Having heard this wonderful tale from his excellent minister Gomukha, who was possessed of wisdom and the power of intellect, Naravāhanadatta rejoiced greatly.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave: Then the minister Gomukha, wishing to dispel the longing of Naravāhanadatta, spoke again to Śaktiyaśas.
"O King, you have heard the stories of the wise; now hear the story of the simpleton. There was once a certain son of a wealthy merchant who possessed a simple mind."
Once, he went to the island of Kaṭāha for the purpose of trade, and among his merchandise there was a great store of aloeswood.
That [incense] was not [the same] as that which is used for other goods sold there; no resident of that place took it up, nor did anyone there know of it.
Then, seeing people buying charcoal from the wood-sellers, that fool burned his black aloe-wood and turned it into charcoal.
Having sold it for the price of charcoal and returning home from there, he fell into the ridicule of the people by boasting of that very same skill.
This story concerning one who burned what was not heavy has been told; now hear the tale of the sesame-farmer. There was a certain villager, a farmer who was almost entirely possessed by spirits.
Once, having eaten roasted sesame seeds and found them delicious, he sowed only roasted seeds in abundance, desiring such a harvest.
When those seeds were parched and failed to sprout, the people laughed at him who had lost his wealth; he was called a "sesame farmer," so hear now of the one who threw fire into the water.
Once upon a time, there was a certain man of dull intellect who, one night at dawn, intending to perform worship to the deity in the morning, thought thus:
Water and fire have been utilized by me for bathing, incense, and other purposes; therefore, I shall place them together in one spot so that I may obtain them quickly.
Having reflected thus, he threw the fire into the water-jar and went to sleep; and when he looked in the morning, the fire was gone and the water had vanished.
When he saw water soiled with charcoal, his face became just like it; yet when the people laughed, he smiled once more.
You have heard the account of Agnikumbha; now hear of the implanting of a nose. Once, there was a certain man who was foolish and dull-witted.
Seeing his wife with a flat nose and his teacher with a prominent nose, he cut off the nose of the sleeping teacher and took it.
Having gone there and cut off his own nose, he placed it upon his wife; yet, although her nose was large, it did not fit into her mouth.
In this way, both his wife and his father-in-law were deprived of their noses by him; now, let the forest-dweller Paśupāla be heard of.
In a forest there was a certain very simple-minded but wealthy cattle-herder; many rogues, having relied upon him, met with him in friendship.
Those city-dwellers said to him, "She is the daughter of a wealthy man; we have requested her on your behalf, and she has been promised by her father."
Having heard that, he was pleased and gave them wealth; and when some days had passed, they said to him again, "Your marriage has been successfully completed."
Thereupon, being exceedingly pleased, he gave them abundant wealth; and after some days, they said to him, "A son has been born to you."
He rejoiced at that, and being deluded, he entrusted everything to them; then, on another day, he wept, saying, "I am longing for my son."
Weeping, he drew laughter from the world, for he had been deceived by rogues; like a cowherd, he had inherited their dullness.
O Lord, you have heard of Paśupāla; now listen to the story of Alaṃkāralambaka: a certain rustic man, while digging the earth, obtained a great treasure of ornaments.
At night, thieves carried him away from the royal palace and settled him there; having taken him, he adorned his wife right there with him.
He bound a girdle upon her head and a necklace upon her hips; he placed anklets on her hands and bracelets upon her ears.
Having learned that it had been pointed out by people laughing, the king seized it; however, he released him, who was like a mere beast, along with his own ornaments.
The Ornament has been told, O King; now listen as I speak of the Tuḷika. A certain foolish man went to the marketplace to sell cotton.
No one there accepted it as impure; meanwhile, he saw gold there in the fire, purified by being heated.
The goldsmith sold it and the customer took it; yet even after seeing that, the fool desired to purify that very cotton-wool.
He threw it into the fire, and when it was burnt, the people laughed at him. This Tūlika has been heard of; now hear of Devakharjūrī-chedaka.
Some foolish villagers were summoned by officials and appointed to fetch dates as commanded by the royal court.
Seeing there a single date-palm tree that was easy to grasp and naturally laden with dates, she cut down all the date-palms in her own village.
Having fallen, they gathered all the dates that had dropped; they tried to lift them up and place them back on the trees, but it did not succeed for them.
Then, having brought back the date palms and diligently planted them, they were punished by the king instead, as he realized they had cut down the date palms.
This "laughing date-palm" has been described; now the "beholding of treasure" is told. A certain king once brought forth a certain man who could see hidden treasures.
"Lest this man escape and flee elsewhere," the king's wicked minister had the eyes of the one who had revealed the location of the treasure gouged out.

Seeing that he did not perceive the characteristics of the elements and regarded both movement and non-movement as equal, the minister, observing him to be blind, laughed along with the people, saying, "He is a fool."
Having heard about the discovery of the treasure, listen now to the story of the salt-eater: there was once a certain dull-witted man who lived in a remote village.
Once, he was led home by a city-dwelling friend and fed savory foods and condiments seasoned with salt.
Then that Gahvara asked, "By what does this sweetness of food and other things arise? and he was told by his friend at that time, "Primarily, by salt."
Saying, "In that case, this very thing must be eaten," he took a handful of ground salt, threw it into his mouth, and ate it.
That powder smeared the lips and beard of that evil-minded man; meanwhile, the faces of the people there turned white with laughter.
"O Lord, you have heard of the one who eats salt; now hear about the cow-milker. There was a certain foolish villager, and he had a single cow."
And that cow of his gave him a hundred palas of milk every day; once, however, there was a festival approaching for him.
"I shall drink her abundant milk just once during the festival"—thinking thus, that fool did not even milk the cow for a single month.
And as soon as he, having reached the festival, milked her, all the milk was gone; it had been cut off for him, yet the laughter of the people remained uninterrupted.
The foolish cow-milker has been heard of; now hear these two others. There was a certain man with a bald head that resembled a copper pot.
A certain young man, hungry and carrying wood-apples, came along that path and saw him seated at the foot of a tree.
He struck his head with a wood-apple for sport; though he was bald, he endured it and said nothing to him.
Then he struck him on the head with all the other wood-apples one after another; yet he remained silent even as blood flowed from it.
And that foolish youth, exhausted by hunger, departed from there without the wood-apples that had been crushed during his fruitless youthful play.
Saying, "Why should I not endure blows for the sake of sweet wood-apples?", that bald-headed fool, with blood dripping from his head, went home.
Seeing his head encircled by that blood as if by a turban binding the empire of folly, who there did not laugh?
Thus, those of little intelligence become objects of ridicule for the gods in this world; they do not achieve their goals, whereas those of great intelligence are honored.
Having heard these stories of charming laughter from Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta rose and performed his daily duties.
Then, at the arrival of night, being urged by him who was full of longing, Gomukha told this story which culminates in wisdom.
In a certain region of the forest, there was a great silk-cotton tree; a crow named Laghupāti made his home there and lived upon it.
Once, while staying in his own nest, he saw a fierce man arrive there beneath the tree, carrying a net in his hand and holding a staff.
Then, as soon as the crow looked, that man spread out his net upon the ground, scattered rice there, and remained hidden.
Just then, the lord of pigeons named Citragrīva, wandering through the sky surrounded by hundreds of pigeons, arrived there.
Seeing that heap of rice, he fell into the net out of a desire for food; thus, along with his retinue, he became bound by the multitude of snares.
Seeing that, Citragrīva said to all his followers: "Seize the net with your beaks and fly up into the sky with speed!"
Then, saying "So be it," they all took up the net and, terrified, began to fly swiftly through the sky as pigeons.
The hunter, rising up with an upward gaze and filled with agitation, turned back; then Citragrīva, free from fear, spoke to those who were following him.
"Let us go quickly to our friend Hiraṇya the mouse; he will cut these snares and set us free."
Having said this, he went with his followers, those who were drawing in the net, and reaching the entrance of the mouse's burrow, he descended from the sky.
"O Hiraṇya, come out! I, Citragrīva, have arrived," thus did that king of pigeons call out to the mouse there.
Having heard this and seeing his friend approaching by way of the entrance, the mouse emerged from that hundred-mouthed hole.
Having approached and inquired about the situation, that mouse, his friend, also cut the snares of the lord of the pigeons and his followers out of great agitation.
Having addressed the mouse with these kind words, Citragrīva, his bonds severed, flew up into the sky and departed together with his followers.
Having observed that [the mongoose] had entered the hole, the swift-flying crow followed him there, came to the entrance, and spoke to the mouse:
"I am a crow named Laghupāti; having seen that you are affectionate toward friends, I choose you as a friend—one capable of rescuing me from such a calamity."
Having heard that and seen the crow from within, the mouse said to him, "Go away! What friendship can there be between the eater and the food?"
Then that crow said: "Peace! If you were eaten by me, my satisfaction would last but a moment; but in a friend, there is the constant protection of life."
Having spoken thus and made a solemn oath, the crow, having been reassured by him, formed a friendship with the mouse as he departed.
The mouse brought lumps of meat and grains of rice; eating together in one place, the two of them lived happily.
And once that crow said to his friend, the mouse: "Friend, not far from here, in the middle of the forest, there is a river."
In that place there is a friend of mine, a tortoise named Mantharaka; for his sake I am going to that location, where food consisting of meat is easily obtained.
When the crow had said, "I obtain food here only with great difficulty, and I am constantly in fear of hunters," the mouse spoke to him as well.
In that case, we shall dwell together; take me there as well. I too have grown weary of this world, and I shall explain that very matter to you right there.
Taking Hiraṇyaka while he was speaking thus with his beak, Laghupāti flew through the air and went to the bank of the forest river.
Having met there with his friend Mantharaka the tortoise, who had offered him hospitality, he remained there together with the mouse.
And in the course of their conversation, the crow related to that tortoise the reason for his own arrival, including the account of his friendship with Hiraṇya.
Then that tortoise, having made the mouse—praised by the crow—his friend, questioned him regarding the cause of his weariness with exile from his country.
Then Hiraṇya, while both the crow and the tortoise were listening, related this story of his own adventures.
Dwelling there in a great cave situated near the city, I brought the horse from the royal palace and tethered it at night.
Seeing me endowed with vigor by that visible necklace and capable of procuring food, the mice surrounded me.
In the meantime, there was a certain wandering mendicant who had built a small hermitage near our cave and subsisted on various kinds of alms-food.
At night, he would hang his alms-bowl upon a peg and set aside the remnants of the food for the sake of eating them in the morning out of hunger.
And while he was sleeping there, I entered inside through a hole, leaped up, and carried him off entirely, O night-walker.
Once, another mendicant friend of his arrived there; after they had eaten, he engaged in conversation with him during the night.
Just as I set out to carry the food, that mendicant, lending an ear, repeatedly struck his small gong.
"How did you tear it away? What are you doing with this?"—thus questioned by that visiting mendicant, the ascetic spoke to him.
"An enemy, this mouse, has arisen here for me; he who always, even from afar, leaps up and carries away my food from right here."
"I am frightening him by shaking this worn-out food bowl," said the other wandering mendicant to the monk who had spoken thus.
This greed of living beings leads to their ruin; hear a story regarding this matter. Once, while wandering among sacred fords, I reached a certain city.
And there, for the residence of a certain Brahmin, I entered a house; while I was staying there, that Brahmin spoke to his wife.
"Today, on this festival day, cook kṛsara for the sake of the Brahmins," she said to him; and he replied to her, "How can you expect this from one who is destitute?"
Then that Brahmin said to her, "My dear, even when there is a need for accumulation, one should not have a mind excessively intent on hoarding; hear in this regard this story."
In a certain forest, a hunter who had finished his hunt, with his arrow fixed in place, took some meat upon his bow and ran toward a boar.
Struck by that very arrow and wounded by the spear, he perished; and the jackal saw this from afar.
And he, having arrived, though afflicted by hunger, desiring to make a store, did not eat any of that abundant venison from the hunter's shoulder.
He went and proceeded to eat that which was placed upon the bow; at that very moment, pierced by an arrow from a springing mechanical device, he died.
"Therefore, one should not engage in excessive accumulation," said that brahmin; his wife agreed to this and cast the sesame seeds out in the sun.
Once she had entered the house, a dog defiled those grains by eating them; consequently, no one would take these kṛsarā-grains even for a price or otherwise.
"Thus, greed does not lead to enjoyment, but only to affliction. Having said this, that wandering mendicant who had arrived there spoke again:
"If you have a spade, give it to me; today I shall use a stratagem to ward off this calamity arising from the mouse."
Having heard that, the mendicant living there gave him a small spade; and I, remaining hidden, having seen this, entered the subterranean passage.
Then, having seen the hole where I was moving, that rogue wandering mendicant began to dig it with his spade.
And while I was intent on fleeing, he dug gradually until he reached that necklace of mine and another collection of jewels lying there.
"By this splendor, such strength as that arose in his serpent," he said to that resident ascetic while I was listening.
Having taken all that I possessed and placed the necklace upon his head, those two wandering mendicants, joyful at having arrived and being established there, went to sleep.
When those two were fast asleep, that mendicant Sthāyin woke up and struck me on the head with a staff as I returned to seize him.
Therefore, though wounded by fate, I did not die but entered a cave; furthermore, I no longer possessed the strength for the exertion of fetching that food.
For youth is indeed the wealth of men, and its absence is old age; by that [loss], one's vigor, strength, beauty, and even enthusiasm decline.
Then, seeing that I was intent on supporting myself alone, that entire retinue of mice departed, leaving me behind.
Even after dwelling there for a long time, servants abandon a master who provides no livelihood, bees a tree that bears no flowers, and swans a lake that has no water.
Thus, having long been distressed there, O best of tortoises, I have now reached your side after finding this swift-flying friend.
When Hiraṇyaka had spoken thus, the tortoise Mantharaka replied: "This is your own place; therefore, do not show lack of fortitude toward your friend."
For the virtuous there is no foreign land; for the contented there is no unhappiness; for the steadfast there is no calamity; and for the persevering there is nothing unattainable.
Even as he was speaking thus, a deer named Citrāṅga, terrified by a hunter, arrived at that forest from afar.
Having seen him, and seeing that the hunter had subsequently departed, the tortoise and the others formed a friendship with him, who was thus comforted.
Then the crow, the tortoise, the deer, and the mouse lived there together as friends, equally happy through their mutual service to one another.
Once, in a certain forest, Laghupāti climbed a tree to look for Citrāṅga, who had been away for a long time, and beheld him there.
And he saw Citrāṅga on the riverbank, bound by a tethering rope; descending from that [tree], he spoke these words to the mouse and the tortoise.
Then, having consulted together, Laghupāti seized that mouse, Hiraṇyaka, with his beak and carried him into the presence of Citrāṅga.
And Hiraṇyaka, the mouse, having comforted the deer who was distressed by his bonds, released him in an instant, having severed the snare with his teeth.
Then Mantharaka, the turtle, having approached by way of the middle of the river, climbed onto the bank near them, he who was dear to his friends.
At that very moment, a hunter who had set the snare arrived from somewhere; while the deer and other animals fled, he caught the tortoise.
And having thrown it inside the net, just as he was departing, distracted by the lost deer, that wicked one [the hunter] heard this from the words of the far-sighted mouse.
The deer then went a short distance away and lay down as if dead; meanwhile, the crow remained upon its head, as if pecking at its eyes.
Seeing that, the hunter, thinking the deer was dead because it had been caught, set the tortoise down on the bank of the river and proceeded to go away.
Seeing him gone, the mouse approached and cut the snare of the tortoise; released by that means, he fell into the river.
The deer, seeing the hunter draw near, abandoned the tortoise, rose up, and fled; the crow also climbed a tree.
Having arrived there, the hunter, failing to catch the tortoise which had escaped by severing its bonds and being deprived of both [the net and the water], went home grieving for his fate.
Then those tortoises and others gathered together there in joy; and the deer, being full of affection, spoke thus to the tortoises and the rest.
I am fortunate that you, my friends, have been found by me; for disregarding even their own lives, you have today rescued me from death.
Thus praised by that deer, the crow, the tortoise, and the mouse dwelt there together with him, happy in their mutual affection.
In this way, even animals accomplish their desired ends through wisdom; they likewise do not abandon a friend in times of distress, even at the cost of their own lives.
Thus, attachment to friends is superior to that toward women; because it is the basis for jealousy, they praise the former. Listen, therefore, to this story.
O Lord, in a certain city there lived a man who was full of envy; he had a beloved wife who was endowed with great beauty.
Lacking trust, he never left her alone; for he feared the loss of her virtue even from those depicted in paintings.
Then, on one occasion, that man set out for another region together with his wife, having been compelled by some necessary business.
Seeing a forest infested with snakes ahead on the road, he, out of fear of them, left her in the house of an elderly village Brahmin and departed.
While she was staying there, he saw her coming along the path with a certain bold young Bhilla; she then departed from that place with him.
Possessed by him, she wandered at will through that village, her jealousy toward her husband vanished like a river whose banks have been breached.
Meanwhile, that husband of hers, having finished his business, returned and requested that wife from the village-dwelling brahmin; and that brahmin spoke to him.
"I do not know where she has gone; I know only this much: the Bhillas had come here, and she must have been taken away by them."
Go quickly from here to that village nearby; there you will find your wife, so do not entertain any other thought.
Having been addressed thus by him, weeping and reproaching his own perverted intellect, he went to that Bhilla village and saw his wife there.
Seeing him, that wicked woman approached him and, being terrified, then said: "It is not my fault; I was brought here by force by a Bhilla."
"Come, let us go there before anyone sees us. To her husband, who spoke thus and was blinded by passion, she replied:
This is the time for the arrival of that Bhilla who has gone hunting; having pursued us, he will certainly kill both you and me.
"Having entered this cave, remain hidden for now; and having killed him while he sleeps at night, we two shall depart from here without fear."
Thus addressed by that deceitful woman, he entered that cave; for what room is there for discernment in the heart of one whose mind is blinded by passion?
Then that wicked woman showed him, who had been brought inside the house by her addiction, to the Bhilla when he arrived at the end of the day.
And having dragged him out, that powerful Bhilla of cruel deeds bound him very tightly to a tree in the morning for the purpose of an offering to the goddess.
And having eaten, while he was watching, that man enjoyed the pleasure of sexual union with his wife at night and fell asleep together with her.
Seeing him asleep, that jealous man, bound to the tree, worshipped Caṇḍī with hymns and, afflicted by distress, went for refuge.
She manifested herself and granted him that boon by which, with that very sword, he severed the head of the Bhilla, whose bonds had already slipped loose.
"Now come! This wicked man has been slain by me," he said, awakening his wife; she too rose up, deeply distressed.
Having taken the head of that Bhilla unnoticed during the night, that wicked woman then set out together with her husband.
And having reached the city in the morning, showing him that head there, she cried out, attacking her husband: "My husband has been killed by this man!"
Then, accompanied by him, he was led before the king by the city guards; questioned there regarding what had occurred, the envious man described it exactly as it had happened.
Then the king, having investigated the truth, had that wicked woman's ears and nose cut off; he released her husband and let him go.
Released and freed from the grip of affection for his wicked wife, he went to his own home; for such, O King, does a woman act when constrained by jealousy.
For jealousy alone teaches women an excessive attachment to men; therefore, a wise man should protect his wife by never revealing that jealousy.
A secret must not be disclosed to women in any way whatsoever by a man who desires his own welfare; in this regard, let this story be heard.
A certain nāga, out of fear of Vainateya, had fled somewhere to the house of a courtesan on earth, having assumed a human form.
The courtesan also received the fee of five hundred elephants; and by his own power, that Naga gave them to her every day.
"From where have you come every day with so many elephants? Tell me, who are you? Thus the playful woman questioned him persistently.
"Out of fear of Tārkṣya, do not say to anyone that you are standing here; I am a nāga," he said to her, being deluded by Māra.
Then that courtesan told her secret to a procuress; subsequently, Tārkṣya, searching the world, arrived there in human form.
Having approached that bawd, she said to her, "Noble lady, I am staying today in your daughter's house; let my lodging fee be taken."
"Here a nāga dwells eternally, providing five hundred elephants; why then hire him for a single day? Thus even the procuress spoke to him.
Then Garuḍa, perceiving that the Nāga was staying there, entered the house of the woman at the gate in the guise of a guest.
There, beholding that nāga situated upon the roof of the palace, he revealed himself, leaped up, struck him, and devoured him.
"Therefore, a wise man should not speak of secrets without restraint to women. Having said this, Gomukha began to relate another story concerning a simpleton.
Who was that bald man with a head resembling a copper pot? He was a fool, yet he possessed wealth in this world and felt ashamed of being without hair.
Then a certain rogue, a professional parasite, approached him and said: "There is a physician who knows a medicine that causes hair to grow."
Having heard this, he said to him: "If you command me, then I shall give wealth to you and to that physician."
When he had spoken thus, that rogue, having consumed the wealth of the simpleton, soon brought him a fraudulent physician.
Having lived off that bald-headed physician for a long time, he too removed his turban, bound his own head, and showed it to the foolish woman.
Even upon seeing that, being devoid of discernment, that dull-witted man requested medicine from the physician for the sake of his hair; thereupon, the physician said to him:
"How can a bald man himself produce hair for another?"—O fool, you who are hairless, it was for this reason that I showed you my own head.
"Nevertheless, you will certainly not know [the truth]," saying "Fie!", the physician departed. Thus, O King, rogues always sport with those of dull intellect.
Thus has been heard the story of the one deluded by hair; now let the story of the one deluded by oil be heard: there was a certain man who was the servant of a particular learned man.
Once, sent by that master to a merchant to fetch oil, he took some oil from him into his bowl.
Then, as he was coming along holding a vessel of oil, he was addressed by a certain friend: "Guard this vessel of oil; it is leaking below."
Having heard that, the fool turned the vessel over to look beneath it; consequently, all of that oil fell upon the ground.
Having learned of this, he was laughed at by the world and expelled from his master's house; therefore, for a fool, one’s own wit is better than instruction.
Listen now to the story of the fool who was infatuated with oil and the one who was infatuated with bones; there was once a certain foolish man whose wife was unchaste.
Once, when her husband had gone to another country on business, she [instructed] her own trusted maidservant in the house, having given her instructions regarding her duties.
Having appointed Ananyadāsī as her attendant and departed from there, she then went to the house of her paramour, desiring unrestrained pleasure.
Then, as her husband arrived, she stood with her training intact, her voice choked with tears, and said to him like a servant-woman: "That wife of yours has died and has been cremated."
Having said this, she led him to the cemetery and showed him the bones from another funeral pyre; taking them up, he wept.
Having performed the water libations at the sacred fords and having cast those bones into them, that fool proceeded with the funeral rites for his wife.
And by that very same female servant who had brought him, saying "O good Brahmin," he made that very man his wife's paramour a Brahmin invited to the śrāddha.
Having approached there together with that Upapati, she, dressed in magnificent attire, would eat choice food with him month after month.
O Lord, by the power of the dharma of a virtuous wife, your wife has come from the other world in person and now eats together with the brahmin.
Just as that female servant spoke to her husband, so did that crest-jewel of fools carry out everything exactly as instructed.
In this way, those of simple disposition are deceived with ease by wicked women; you have heard the story of Asthimugdha—now let the tale of the Caṇḍāla maiden be heard by you.
There was a certain beautiful and charming Caṇḍāla maiden who formed a resolution in her heart to obtain a universal monarch as her husband.
Once, seeing the king who had gone out for a stroll through the city—the most excellent of men—she proceeded to follow him with the thought that he was her husband.
Just then, a sage came along that path; having bowed at his feet while still mounted on the elephant, the king proceeded to his own palace.
Having seen that and having reflected upon this supreme sage even more than the king, the Caṇḍāla girl abandoned the king and followed the sage.
That sage, as he was proceeding, saw an empty temple of Śiva ahead; placing his knees upon the ground there and bowing to Śiva, he departed from that place.
Seeing that and considering Śiva to be even superior to the sage, that woman of the lowest caste abandoned the sage with the thought that he was her husband and took refuge right there in the God.
And in an instant, a dog having entered there and climbed onto the king's footstool, raised its leg and did what was appropriate for its kind.
Seeing that, the outcaste woman, perceiving that dog to be the supreme deity, followed him as he went, abandoning the god in her desire for a husband.
And the dog, having arrived at the Caṇḍāla’s house, rolled affectionately at the feet of a certain familiar young Caṇḍāla.
Then, beholding him and considering the son of a Caṇḍāla to be superior even to dogs, that low-born woman, satisfied with her own kind, chose him alone as her husband.
Thus, fools who have set foot upon the wrong path fall far from their own station; and having thus described the foolish king, hear now another in brief.
There was once a certain foolish king who, though possessing great wealth, was miserly; one day, his well-wishing ministers spoke to him as follows.
In this world and the next, generosity removes one from an unfortunate rebirth; therefore, give that gift, for both lifespans and wealth are fragile.
Having heard that, the king said: "I shall give a gift at that time, provided that after I have died, I may see myself fallen into a miserable rebirth."
Then those ministers sat silent, laughing inwardly: "In this way, the fool does not abandon his interests until he is abandoned by them."
O Lord, you have heard the story of the King and the Ghost; now listen to the account of two friends. There was once a sovereign named Candrāpīḍa in Kānyakubja.
He had a certain servant named Dhavalamukha, who would always enter the house after having eaten and drunk outside.
Once, when asked by his wife, "From where do you always come back having eaten and drunk?", that Dhavalamukha replied to her thus:
"O beautiful one, having constantly eaten and drunk at the side of my friend, I always return here, for I have two friends in this world."
One was named Kalyāṇavarman, who provided assistance with food and other necessities; the second was Vīrabāhu, who assisted even with his own life.
Having heard this from his wife, Dhavalamukha said, "Show me those two friends of mine."
Then he went, accompanied by him, to the house of that Kalyāṇavarman; and he too attended upon him with costly services.
On another day, he went into the presence of Vīrabāhu accompanied by his wife; and he, being occupied with dice, offered him a welcome and then dismissed him.
Then his wife, full of curiosity, said to Dhavalamukha: "Kalyāṇavarman performed a great act of hospitality for you."
Only a mere welcome was offered to you by Vīrabāhu; O noble son, how is it that you consider him to be a superior friend?
Having heard that, he said: "Go and tell both of them in turn a lie: 'The king is suddenly angry with us. Then you will find out for yourself."
Having been addressed thus by him, she went at once and said "So be it" to Kalyāṇavarman; and as soon as he heard her, he spoke to her.
"I am the son of a merchant; tell me, what shall I do for the king?"—having been addressed thus by him, she then went into the presence of Vīrabāhu.
She likewise informed him of the king's anger toward her husband; upon hearing this, he ran forth, taking up his sword and shield.
Dissuaded from his anger by his ministers, the king then sent Dhavalamukha to that Vīrabāhu's house with the command, "Go to him."
"In this way, O slender one, there will be an interval between these two friends of mine. Thus addressed by Dhavalamukha, his wife was then satisfied.
Thus, one is a friend by way of metaphorical designation, while another is so in reality; for even though the quality of oiliness is equal, sesame oil remains sesame oil and ghee remains ghee.
Having thus related this tale, the minister Gomukha again told a series of charming stories in succession to Naravāhanadatta.
A certain foolish traveler, having crossed a forest with great difficulty while tormented by thirst, reached a river but did not drink; he merely gazed at the water.
When someone asked him, "Though thirsty, do you not drink water?", the dull-witted man replied to him, "How could I drink so much?"
"Will the king punish you if you have not drunk it all?"—though mocked by him with these words, that simpleton did not drink the water.
Thus, those of little intelligence, who are unable here to perform anything in its entirety, do not perform even a fraction of it according to their capacity.
"O Lord, it has been heard that there was one named Jalabhīta; now hear this story of Putraghātī. There was once a certain man who had many sons, yet he was poor and foolish."
When one son had died, he himself killed the second, thinking, "How could this child travel alone on a distant road?"
Consequently, he was censured and ridiculed by the people and banished from the country; thus, the beast and the fool are equal, for both possess minds devoid of discernment.
"You have heard of the slayer of his son; now hear this tale concerning his brother. Once, in the midst of a crowd, there was a certain man of dull wit who was telling stories somewhere."
Seeing a worthy man from afar, the fool said this: "This man shall be my brother; I shall take his inheritance from him."
"But I am someone other than this [man], therefore this debt is not mine"—having said this, that fool made even the stones laugh there.
Thus, O King, you have heard of the folly of the fool and the extreme strangeness of one blinded by self-interest; now hear of the son of a religious student who was terrified by his brother.
A certain innocent youth, standing in the midst of his friends who had begun to recount the virtues of his father, described his father’s excellence in this manner.
"Because of his weakness, my father is a celibate student; there is no other equal to him. Hearing that, his friends asked him, "From whom were you born?"
Saying once again, "I am his mind-born son," that crest-jewel of fools was laughed at even more specifically by them.
Those of dull intellect speak such utterly irrational things; having heard about the son of a celibate student, listen now to this story of the astrologer as well.
There was a certain astrologer who was devoid of true knowledge; he, along with his wife and son, [set out] from his own country due to a lack of livelihood.
Having thus gone to another country, he displayed to himself an object of worship by means of a fabricated conviction, based on his own false perception.
Having embraced his young son in the presence of all the people, that wicked man wept when questioned by the folk, and spoke thus:
"I know the past, the present, and the future; therefore, I weep because this child will perish for me on the seventh day."
Having spoken thus and having caused the world there to marvel, when the seventh day arrived, he killed his son while he was still asleep at the very break of dawn.
Then, having seen that the boy was dead, he was honored by people who had gained conviction; and having acquired wealth, he returned to his own country at his own will.
Thus, out of greed for wealth and desiring to falsely proclaim their own knowledge, fools even kill their own sons; a wise person should not take pleasure in them.
And hear this, O Lord, concerning a certain foolish and wrathful man who was listening to someone else standing outside somewhere.
Someone praised his inner virtues before his own people; then one person there said, "Friend, he is truly virtuous."
"But he has two faults: he is impulsive and wrathful. Hearing this from the speaker as he stood outside, he [the king]—
The man, entering suddenly, wrapped his garment around [the other's] neck and said: "O wretch, why this rashness? What anger have I shown toward you?"
Thus he spoke with reproach, blazing with the fire of anger; then others there, laughing, said to him, "What is this that he says?"
"Even though you have displayed such anger and rashness before our very eyes, O Lord, thus your own fault, though manifest, is not perceived by the ignorant."
Now listen, O simple one: there was once a certain king who raised a daughter; he had a single daughter who was exceedingly beautiful.
Desiring to raise her up with great affection, the king quickly summoned physicians and spoke to them with joy.
"Perform some application of excellent medicine by which this daughter of mine may grow quickly and be given in marriage to a good husband."
Having heard that, those physicians said, "In order to treat this fool, there is a medicine; however, it must be obtained from a land far from here."
We shall bring her back as soon as that [time] arrives; meanwhile, this daughter of yours must be kept invisible, for such is the ritual requirement in this matter.
Having said this, they concealed the princess there for many years, proclaiming that she had obtained the medicinal herbs.
And when she had reached youth and been made to grow by means of the medicine, they showed their daughter to that king, saying: "Behold her!"
He too, being pleased, filled those physicians with heaps of wealth; thus, under such pretexts, foolish lords are exploited by rogues.
And let this be heard: there was a certain man living in a city who, having acquired his wisdom for the price of half a paṇa, was full of pride in his own intelligence.
And a certain villager who had been his servant for a year, having become dissatisfied with his livelihood, took leave of him and went to his own home.
When he had gone, she asked her husband, "O slender one, has he not gone away taking something from you? She replied, "Half a paṇa."
Then, having set aside ten paṇas for provisions on the journey, he went to that hired laborer on the riverbank and brought back half a paṇa from him.
By boasting of that skill in wealth, he became an object of public ridicule; thus, one whose intellect is blinded by riches squanders much for the sake of a trifle.
Now, O Lord, hear also of the one who performed the supernatural feat: as a certain fool was traveling upon the ocean by means of a ship...
A silver vessel fell from his hand into the midst of the water; there, that fool took it as a sign, such as a whirlpool or the like.
"I shall come and pull it out from this ocean water," he thought; yet, having reached the far shore and crossed over, he saw whirlpools and other dangers in the water.
Having repeatedly asked him with the thought that he was a supernormal power-holder in order to obtain my bowl, and having been told his true intention by others, he was mocked and reviled.
And so listen now: once, a certain foolish king beheld two men from his palace as they were bestowing meat.
Seeing that the meat had been taken by one of those two in the kitchen, he cut off five palas of flesh from his own body for the thief.
Seeing him fallen on the ground, his flesh torn away and crying out, the king was moved with compassion and commanded his doorkeeper:
"Even if five palas of flesh are cut from his body, that pain of his will not be stilled; therefore, let even more flesh than that be given to him."
"Does one whose head is severed live, even if hundreds of heads are given? Having said, "I shall give [the heads], O King," the Kṣattṛ went out and laughed.
Having consoled him with words of comfort, he handed over the excised flesh to the physicians; thus does a foolish lord understand neither punishment nor favor.
And let this be heard: there was a certain dull-witted woman with an only son who, desiring another son, longed for the child of another woman.
To her as she was questioning, a certain heretical and wretched female ascetic said: "This young son whom you have, having killed him, shall be an offering to the deity."
"If it is done, then another son will certainly be born to you. When she had been told this by her, she desired to act accordingly.

Having learned of this, another aged woman who was well-disposed toward her spoke to her in private: "O wicked woman, you are killing the son already born, while you desire to obtain one not yet born."
"If even he is not born for you, then what will you do? Thus was she restrained from that evil deed by that noble old woman.
In this way, women who associate with Śākinīs fall into improper acts; however, by the instruction of elders, they are protected when kept under restraint.
Now, O gods, listen to this story concerning these āmalaka fruits: there was once a certain simple-minded servant belonging to a particular householder.
The householder, who was fond of *āmalaka* fruits, commanded that servant: "Go from the grove and bring me some very sweet *āmalaka* fruits."
The fool tasted each one by biting it off and brought them back; let the Lord taste these sweet things that have been brought and look upon them.
Having looked upon those half-remnants with loathing, he too said, "I shall discard them," and the householder threw them out along with that witless servant.
Thus, one devoid of wisdom ruins both the master's interest and his own; in this regard, listen now to this story of two brothers.
In the city of Pāṭaliputra, there were two brahmin brothers; the elder was named Yajñasoma, and his younger brother was Kīrtisoma.
The two sons of the Brahmin possessed abundant ancestral wealth; Kīrtisoma increased his own share through business dealings.
But Yajñasoma, while consuming and giving away [his wealth], brought it to exhaustion; then, having become destitute, he spoke to his own wife:
"My dear, having once been wealthy, how can I now live among my kinsmen while being destitute? Therefore, let us seek refuge in a foreign land."
When she asked, "Where can one go without provisions for the journey? and he persisted, his wife then said to him:
"If you must certainly go, then having gone there, seek some wealth from Kīrtisoma as provisions for your journey, O younger brother."
Then, having gone after his younger brother while he was searching for provisions for the journey, that younger brother was addressed there by his own wife:
How and how much can we give to him who has squandered his own wealth? For only he who is truly poor will resort to us.
Having heard this, Kīrtisoma, although filled with brotherly affection, did not wish to give him anything; alas, how difficult is subjection to wicked women!
Then Yajñasoma, having gone silently and informed his wife of that matter, set out from there with her, taking refuge solely in destiny.
While traveling, he reached a forest and was by fate swallowed by a python; and his wife, seeing that, fell to the ground and wailed aloud.
"Why do you cry out, O blessed lady?"—when he had spoken thus in human speech, that Brahmin woman replied to the serpent.
Why do I not weep, since you, O Great Being, have today taken away my alms-bowl from me while I am suffering in a foreign land? Alas!
Having heard that, the serpent disgorged from its mouth a great golden vessel and gave it to her, saying, "Take this as your alms-bowl."
"O illustrious one, who will give alms to me, a woman, in this place?"—when he was thus addressed by that virtuous Brahmin lady, the python replied:
If anyone here, when requested, does not give you alms, his head shall split into a hundred pieces at that very moment; this word of mine is the truth.
Having heard that, the virtuous Brahmin woman said to the serpent: "Since it is so, then you yourself must grant me the alms of my husband."
As soon as these words were spoken by the truthful Brāhmaṇī, that serpent disgorged from its mouth the sacrificial Soma, unharmed and still very much alive.
Having instantly disgorged him, that divine python man, being thoroughly pleased, spoke to the joyful couple.
I am the sovereign of the Vidyādharas named Kāñcanavega; I have attained this state of a python due to the curse of Gautama.
"That curse of mine reached its conclusion with my conversation with that virtuous woman. Having said this, he immediately filled a golden vessel with jewels.
The lord of the Vidyādharas, filled with joy, flew up into the sky and departed; and that couple returned home, bringing with them a flood of jewels.
There, that Yajñasoma dwelt happily, having acquired inexhaustible wealth; for the Ordainer bestows everything upon everyone in accordance with their merit.
Listen: there is a certain foolish man here, a barber by trade, a native of Karṇāṭaka, who gratified his own king with his valor in battle.
The king, being pleased, granted him a desired boon; the soldier, appearing like a eunuch, chose that very barber for it.
Everyone, by the measure of their own mind, desires either existence or non-existence; yet this seeker of nothing at all is utterly deluded—listen now!
A certain fool traveling on the road was told by someone standing in a cart: "Make this cart of mine slightly level."
When he said, "If I make it equal for you, what will you give me? Śakaṭī replied to him, "I will give you nothing."
Then that fool, having leveled his cart, begged him for it, saying, "Give me nothing at all for that," and the other laughed.
Thus, O Lord, fools always become objects of ridicule, contempt, and reproach from people, as well as the locus of misfortune; whereas the virtuous in this world remain worthy of honor.

Thus, having heard this diversion of stories told from the mouth of Gomukha during the night, King Naravāhanadatta, together with his ministers, went to sleep for the sake of the rest of the entire three worlds.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the Śaktiyaśas book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave. Then, having risen in the morning, Naravāhanadatta went there into the presence of his father, the Lord of Vatsa, to see him.
Thereupon, when Prince Siṃhavarman, the son of the Lord of Magadha, had arrived from his own home at the house of his brother, Queen Padmāvatī—
When the day had passed in conversation, inquiries, and talk of welcome, Naravāhanadatta ate his meal and returned to his own palace.
Then, in order to dispel Śaktiyaśas’s longing during the night, the wise Gomukha told him this story.
Somewhere there stood a great banyan tree, providing cool shade, as if calling out to travelers with the songs of its birds to rest.
There lived a king of crows named Meghavarṇa who had made his home; his enemy was the lord of the owls, named Avamarda.
That king of owls, having come there at night to that king of crows, killed many crows and departed after inflicting humiliation upon them.
In the morning, that king of crows, having been honored there, spoke to his ministers—Uḍḍīvin, Ḍīvin, Saṃḍīvin, Praḍīvin, and Cirajīvin.
That powerful enemy, having humiliated us and found his mark, will surely attack again; therefore, let a remedy for that situation be devised.
Having heard that spoken by Abhāṣata, O Lord, [he said]: "When the enemy is powerful, one must either seek refuge in another country or else offer him conciliation."
Having heard this, Āḍīva said immediately: "There is no cause for fear even in this; having observed the intentions of our enemies and our own strength, we shall act according to our capability."
Then Saṇḍīvin said: "O King, death is better than bowing down to an enemy, or even living in a foreign land."
We must fight with that enemy who has made a pact with us; for a king who possesses allies, is brave, and is full of energy, conquers his foes.
Then Praḍīvī said: "That powerful one cannot be conquered in battle; rather, having made a treaty with him, he should be slain when the opportunity arises again."
Then Cirajīvin said: "Who is the mediator? Who indeed is the messenger? Since there has been enmity between crows and owls since the beginning of creation, who would go there?"
"This is to be accomplished by means of mantras; the mantra is said to be the very root of sovereignty. Having heard this, the king of crows spoke to that Cirajīvin.
"You are an elder; if you know, tell me for what reason there is enmity between the crow and the owl. After this, you shall speak the counsel."
Having heard that, Cirajīvin said to the king of crows: "Is this not a fault of speech? Have you not heard the story of the donkey?"
A certain washerman, having arrived, covered a lean donkey with a leopard skin and released it among the crops of others for the purpose of fattening it.
While he was eating them, he was not deterred by people out of fear that he was a leopard; however, he was once seen by a certain farmer who carried a bow.
Thinking that it was a leopard, he crouched down, bent low with fear, wrapped his body in a blanket, and then proceeded to move away from there.
Seeing him approaching in that manner and thinking, "This is a donkey," Kharu—who was nourished by grain—cried out to him loudly with his own voice: "Donkey!"
Having heard that, and thinking it was a donkey, the farmer approached him and killed him with a stroke of his arrow, for he had been made an enemy by his own voice.
Thus, due to a verbal fault, we have come into enmity with the owls; for previously, at one time, the birds were without a king.
Gathering together, they all began the consecration of the king of birds, the owl, bringing forth parasols and fly-whisks.
Just then, a crow arriving from the sky saw this and said: "O fools! Are there no birds such as swans and cuckoos among us?"
Why do you consecrate this wicked man of cruel gaze and unpleasant appearance in this kingdom? Fie upon this inauspicious owl!
A king of great power should be appointed, whose very name brings about success; and so, listen as I relate to you a story on this matter.
There is a great lake of abundant water named Candrasaras; on its bank lived a lordly hare named Śilīmukha.
Once, when another watering place had dried up due to drought, the leader of a herd of elephants named Caturdanta came there to drink water.
As his herd plunged into that place, many of Śilīmukha’s followers were crushed by the king of the hares.
Then, when that lord of elephants had departed, the arrow there, being distressed, spoke to a hare named Vijaya in the absence of others.
"Having tasted this, this lordly elephant will come here again and again; he will leave us nothing remaining, so let a remedy for this be devised."
"Go to him and see whether there is any means by which he might be persuaded; for you understand both the task and the expedient, and you are skilled in speaking with reason."
"Wherever you go, there indeed shall be prosperity. Thus dismissed by him, he went slowly to that place, filled with joy.
Following the path, he saw that lordly elephant which had been captured; and he thought, "Just as it is, a union with one who is powerful would be appropriate."
The wise hare, having ascended the mountain peak, spoke to that elephant: "I am the messenger of the god Candra, and he says this to you:"
I have a lake named Candrasaras, a cool abode which is my dwelling; there dwell the hares, and I am their king, and they are dear to me.
For this very reason, I have attained the fame of being the cool-rayed moon; that lake has been destroyed by you, and those rabbits of mine have been killed by you.
"If you do this again, you shall receive that same fruit from me. Having heard this from the messenger-ghost, the lordly elephant spoke out of fear:
"I shall never do so again; the Blessed One Śaśin is worthy of my respect. Therefore come, friend, let us show ourselves to him while you are still making your request."
Having spoken thus, the hare brought the lord of serpents into the middle of the lake and showed him there the reflection of the moon.
Seeing that from afar, trembling with fear and overwhelmed by agitation, that lordly elephant fled back into the forest and did not return there again.
Having seen that with his own eyes, Śilīmukha, the king of the hares, honored the hare-messenger and dwelt there free from fear.
Having spoken thus, the crow addressed those birds further: "In this way, a master is truly a master by his very name, he who does not cause harm to anyone."
This owl is blind by day; how can such a wretch deserve a kingdom? Moreover, a base person is untrustworthy—listen to this story regarding that point.
Once, I lived in a certain tree, and there below me dwelt a bird named Kapiñjala who had made his home.
Once, having gone somewhere for many days, he did not return; meanwhile, a hare approached that nest and stayed there.
After some days, Kapiñjala arrived there; then a dispute arose between him and the hare, each claiming, "The nest is mine, not yours."
Then, as both of them set out to seek a judge who could decide the matter, I followed them unobserved out of curiosity to see what would happen.
Having gone a short distance to the shore of the lake, they both saw a cat who had undertaken the vow of non-violence and truthfulness, with his eyes half-closed in meditation.
"Let us ask him this very thing: what is just and righteous in this matter? Having said this, the two approached the cat and spoke thus.
"Listen to our case, O Blessed One, for you are indeed an ascetic and righteous. Having heard this, the cat spoke to them in measured words:
"I do not hear you, though you have come from afar to my presence, emaciated by asceticism; for dharma wrongly determined destroys one in both worlds."
Having spoken thus and consoled them, that base cat brought the two foremost ones before him and killed both the hare and the partridge together.
Thus, there is no trust to be placed in a base person engaged in petty deeds; therefore, this king Ulūka must not be made a ruler, for he is exceedingly wicked.
Having been addressed thus by that crow, the birds said, "So be it," and having prevented the consecration of the owl, they departed here and there.
"From this day forward, you and we shall be mutual enemies; remember this! Having said this to the crow, the owl departed in a rage.
The crow, however, considering what had been said to be appropriate, became despondent; for who does not feel remorse when unbearable enmity is produced by mere words?
"Thus has this enmity with the owls arisen from a fault of speech. Having said this to the king of the crows, Cirajīvin spoke again:
Those many powerful ones cannot be conquered by the Kauśikas; for many indeed are victorious here—listen to an illustration of this.
A certain twice-born man, having purchased a goat and carrying it on his shoulder, was seen on the road by many rogues who desired to steal the goat.
And one among them came to him and said with agitation: "O Brahmin, why have you taken this dog upon your shoulder? Abandon it!"
Having heard that, when the brahmin disregarded him and proceeded on his way, two others approached him first and spoke to him in exactly the same manner.
Then, while he was walking along in doubt, examining the goat, three other rogues approached him and spoke to him thus:
"How is it that you carry both a sacred thread and a dog together? Surely you are a hunter, not a Brahmin; you intend to kill deer with this dog."
Having heard that, the brahmin reflected: "Surely I have been deluded by some being who has stolen my sight; do all people see falsely?"
Thus, having abandoned that goat and bathed, the Brahmin went home; and the rogues, taking the goat, ate it as they pleased.
Having said this, Cirajīvin spoke to that lord of the crows: "Therefore, O Lord, there are many who are powerful and difficult to conquer."
Therefore, in this conflict with Bali, do as I say: leave me here beneath this very tree with my feathers slightly plucked out.
"Go to this mountain while I am still successful. Having heard that, they said "So be it" to him, as if their petals were plucked off in anger.
Having accomplished his task, that king of crows went with his followers to the mountain; Cirajīvin, however, remained there, having alighted at the foot of his own tree.
Then, during the night, that king of owls, Avamarda, arrived there with his followers; yet he did not see even a single crow there.
Meanwhile, that Cirajīvin was crying very softly from below; and hearing him, the king of owls descended and beheld him.
Filled with wonder, he asked him, "Who are you, and why are you in such a state? Thereupon, that Cirajīvin replied to him in a low voice, as if pained by illness.
"I am Cirajīvin, the minister of that lord of crows; and he desired to launch an assault with the approval of his ministers."
Then, having rebuked those other ministers of his, I said to him: "If you ask me for counsel, and if I am approved by you,"
Therefore, one who is powerful should not engage in conflict with the Lord of the Kaushikas; rather, if you approve of statesmanship, conciliation should be practiced toward him.
Hearing this, [the crow] thought, "This man is on the side of my enemy," and out of anger he struck me; that foolish crow, together with his own friends, has brought me to this state.
"Having cast me down at the foot of some tree, he departed with his followers," said Cirajīvin, and then sat with his head bowed, sighing deeply.
Then the king of owls questioned his own ministers: "What should we do regarding this Cirajīvin?"
Having heard that, the minister named Dīptanayana said to him: "Even a thief who is not to be protected is protected by the virtuous if he is helpful."
For instance, in the past, there was a certain merchant who, although old, married a merchant’s daughter by means of his wealth.
She was constantly averse to his bed because of old age, like a female bee in a forest that has missed its flowering season and stays away from the tree.
Once, while the two were lying in bed at night, a thief entered; seeing him, she turned around and embraced her husband out of fear.
Thinking that such prosperity was wonderful, while the merchant looked about in all directions, he then saw that thief in a corner.
"You have been helpful to me; therefore, I shall not have you executed by my servants. Having said this, the merchant then protected that thief and sent him on his way.
"Thus must this long-lived one, who has been so helpful to us, be protected," said the minister, and with eyes blazing, he fell silent.
Then the Lord of Kauśika questioned another minister named Vakranāsa, saying, "What is the task? May you speak correctly."
Then Vakranāsa said: "This man, who knows the vital secrets of others, must be protected; for the enmity between these two—the master and the minister—is for our own benefit."
"O King, listen; I shall relate to you here an illustrative story. A certain eminent brahmin obtained two cows as a gift."
