Then, having seen him, those thieves thought of taking his two cows; at that very moment, a certain Rākṣasa desired to devour that Brahmin.
For that purpose, as they were traveling at night, those two—a thief and a rākṣasa—by chance met, explained their respective goals to one another, and proceeded together to that place.
"I shall take the cows first, for this brahmin has been seized by you; if he wakes up while asleep, how then could I take the pair of cattle?"
"Do not do so; I shall carry off the Brahmin first, otherwise my labor will be in vain once he has been awakened by the sound of the cows' hooves."
Having thus entered that Brahmin’s house, while the thief and the Rākṣasa were quarreling, the twice-born man woke up.
When that Brahmin had risen with sword in hand and was chanting the Rakshasa-slaying mantra, those two thieves and demons fled, having escaped.
Just as the separation of those two was for the benefit of the twice-born, so too has the separation of us, the king of crows and Cirajīvin, been for our benefit.
Having been addressed thus by Vakranāsa, the lord of the Kauśikas questioned his minister named Prākārakarṇa, and he spoke to him.
This long-lived one is worthy of compassion; he has fallen into distress and has come for refuge. For the sake of one who has sought refuge, Śibi previously gave away his own flesh.
Having heard this from Prākārakarṇa, the king of owls questioned his minister Krūralocana, and he too spoke in the same manner.
Then the Lord of Kauśika questioned his minister named Raktākṣa in the same manner; that wise man spoke as follows.
O King, you have been ruined by these ministers through their misconduct; for those who know policy do not show favor to an enemy who has shown them contempt.
Even when a fool has been seen committing an offense, he is satisfied by feigned conciliation; for instance, there was once a certain carpenter whose wife was dear to him.
Having learned from other people that she was attached to another man, the carpenter, desiring to know the truth of the matter, once spoke to his wife.
"My dear, by the king's command I am going far away on my own business; therefore, you must give me some parched grain and other provisions for the journey."
Saying "So be it," and having been given provisions for the journey by her, he departed from his home; accompanied by his disciples, he arrived secretly and entered right there.
But he remained unseen on the spot where his disciple stood by the bed; then his wife summoned that paramour of hers.
While sporting with him upon the couch, that wicked woman, having somehow touched her husband with her foot, thought he was still standing right there.
In an instant, the husband there, becoming agitated, asked her: "Speak, my dear; am I more beloved to you, or is it your husband?"
Hearing that, she, skilled in deceit, said to her paramour: "My husband is dear to me; for his sake, I would even give up my life."
But this fickleness of women is innate; what can be done about it? If they had no noses, then perhaps filth would not be something they would eat.
Having heard these deceitful words of that unchaste woman, the carpenter emerged from beneath the bed, satisfied, and addressed his pupil:
"You have seen her today; you are my witness that she is such a devotee of mine. Since she has taken refuge in this very beloved, I shall carry her upon my head."
Having said this, that fool, together with his disciples, suddenly lifted both the husband and wife as they remained on the bed and carried them on his head.
Thus, even when a fault is clearly perceived, a fool is satisfied by deceitful conciliation; alas, he becomes an object of ridicule and loses his sense of discernment.
Therefore, O King, this long-lived one who has taken a wife must be protected by you; for if neglected, he might quickly destroy you, like a disease.
Having heard this from Raktākṣa, the lord of the owls said to him: "This virtuous one, while performing what is beneficial for us, has reached this state."
"How could that be? He must be protected; what could he do to us alone?"—thus did the king of the owls reject those words of his ministers.
And he comforted that long-lived crow; then Cirajīvin addressed that lord of owls.
"What use have I for life in this state? Therefore, give me wood so that I may enter the fire."
And I pray for the boon of an owl-birth from the Fire-god, in order to cross over the enmity of that king of crows and take my revenge.
To him who had spoken thus, Raktākṣa replied with a laugh: "By the grace of our lord, you are already restored to health; what need is there for fire?"
And you, Kauśika, shall not become anything else as long as your state as a crow remains; for whatever one has been made by the Creator, such indeed one shall remain.
And likewise, in former times, a certain sage, having found a young mouse dropped from the talons of a hawk, compassionately turned it into a girl by the power of his asceticism.
Seeing that she had grown up in the hermitage and had reached the prime of youth, the sage, wishing to give her to a powerful man, summoned the Sun.
"Marry this daughter of mine, whom I wish to give to you," said that seer to him; then Ravi replied to him.
"Even more powerful than I is this cloud; it shrouds me in an instant. Hearing that, the sage released the sun and summoned the cloud.
And he spoke in that very same way; he was told by him: "The wind is even stronger than I, for it scatters me in all directions."
When he had spoken thus, that sage summoned Vāyu; and being addressed by him in that same manner, the Wind-god spoke to him as follows.
"Those mountains which cannot even be moved by me are truly powerful. Having heard this, the best of sages challenged a certain lord of mountains.
Just as he was saying this, the mountain spoke to him: "The mice are stronger than I, for they create holes in me."
Having been thus addressed in succession by those gods who possessed spiritual knowledge, the great seer summoned a single mouse born in the forest.
When he was told, "Tell this maiden," the mouse said to him: "Let her be seen how she shall enter my hole."
Then, saying, "It would be better if she were a mouse as before," the sage turned her into a mouse and gave her back to that hawk.
Even after traveling so very far, one remains exactly as they were; therefore, O Cirajīvin, you shall never become an owl.
Having been addressed thus by Raktākṣa, Cirajīvī reflected: "This king has not followed the advice of this man who is skilled in policy."
"All these others are fools; that task is already accomplished for me," thinking thus, he took Cirajīvin with him.
Without even reflecting on the words of Raktākṣa, that king of owls, arrogant in his own strength, went to his own abode, Avamarda.
And Cirajīvin, nourished by eating the meat and other food given by him, remained at his side and before long became like a peacock with beautiful plumage.
Once, he said to that king of owls, "O Lord, I am going; having comforted that king of crows, I shall bring him to my own abode."
"By whom he was struck down as he lay sleeping last night—him you shall slay today; and I shall accept this recompense for your favor."
Covering the entrance within the interior of the nest-house with grass and other materials, all of you remain protected during the day out of fear of their falling upon it.
Having said this, Cirajīvin went to the side of his own master, who was inside a cave whose entrance was covered with grass, leaves, and other debris, where he had made owls his companions.
Accompanied by them, he returned, carrying firebrands glowing with flames in his beak, together with crows each holding a single wooden stick dangling from their own bills.
Having arrived, he secretly ignited a fire with grass and other materials at the entrance of the cave of those owls, who were blind by day.
At that time, each of those wood-gatherers threw one [owl] after another; having kindled the fire, he burned those owls there along with their king.
Having destroyed his enemy, the king of crows was then filled with joy; accompanied by the flock of crows, he went to his own banyan tree.
There, having related the account of his own dwelling in the midst of enemies, Cirajīvin spoke thus to Meghavarṇa, the lord of crows.
O Lord, that very Raktākṣa was the excellent minister of your enemy; yet, because I was blinded by pride, I disregarded his words and neglected him.
Because that rogue did not act upon my words, thinking them to be groundless, he—a foolish and misguided man—was deceived by me after I had gained his confidence.
Just as frogs were gained over by a snake through feigned compliance, so too a certain old man, unable to achieve happiness on his own, sought refuge with a man.
A frog and a snake stood perfectly still on the bank of that lake; and as he remained thus, the frogs, staying at a distance, questioned him.
"Tell us, why is it that you do not eat us today as you did before?"—thus questioned by those frogs, the serpent then replied to them.
While I was chasing a frog, thinking it to be a young Brahmin, I bit my own thumb by mistake; alas, he passed away as a result.
"And by my father's curse, I have been made a vehicle for frogs; therefore, how can I eat you? On the contrary, I carry you."
Having heard that, the king of the frogs, eager for a ride, emerged from the water and, casting aside all fear, joyfully mounted his back.
Then, having won him over with the pleasures of riding and having made himself appear exhausted along with his ministers, that deceitful man said:
"O Lord, without food I do not venture to go; therefore, give me sustenance, for how can a servant exist without a livelihood?"
Having heard that, the king of frogs, who was fond of his mount, said to him: "In that case, eat some of my followers, however few they may be."
Then, in due course, that snake ate the frogs at his will; yet the lord of the frogs, blinded by pride in his vehicle, endured it.
"In this way, a fool is deceived by a wise man who has gained his confidence; likewise, O King, having gained your trust, I have likewise destroyed your enemies."
Therefore, a king should be one who knows the science of polity and has disciplined his own self; for the dull-witted man is enjoyed at will by his servants and is slain by his enemies.
And this prosperity, O Lord, is always like a fraudulent game of dice, as fickle as a ripple on water, and as intoxicating as wine.
Though she is full of energy, she remains as if bound by a snare before that wise and well-advised king, who is free from calamity and possessed of discernment.
Therefore, now, remaining attentive and abiding by the words of the wise, rule your kingdom free from thorns, having been made happy by the destruction of your enemies.
Having been addressed thus by his minister Cirajīvin, Meghavarṇa, the king of crows, honored him and ruled the kingdom in that very same manner.
Having said this, Gomukha spoke again to the son of the Lord of Vatsa: "Thus, even by animals, a kingdom is enjoyed through the power of their own intelligence."
But those devoid of wisdom sink into despair, constantly ridiculed by the world; for instance, there was once a certain wealthy man who had a servant of dull intellect.
Although he did not know it, out of the conceit that he knew it was on his body, he applied a broad [ointment] through the power of his folly and tore the skin of the Lord.
Then, abandoned by his master, he fell into ruin; for one who considers himself wise perishes when acting impulsively without understanding.
And hear this other story: in Mālava there were two brothers who were both Brahmins; their paternal wealth was held in common between them without division.
While this matter was being deliberated, the two disputants—one claiming too little and the other too much—appointed a teacher learned in the Vedas as their arbiter, and he spoke to them.
"Divide each object into two equal halves; let it be distributed by you two in such a way that no dispute arises over deficiency or excess."
Hearing that, those two fools divided everything—household goods, beds, and so forth, even down to the animals—cutting each single item into two parts.
They had a single maidservant, but she too was divided between the two; having learned of this, the king punished them both by confiscating all their property.
In this way, fools destroy both worlds through the instruction of fools; therefore, a wise person should not serve fools, but should serve the learned.
Lack of contentment is also a fault; listen to this illustration: there were certain mendicants who were robust from their contentment with alms.
Seeing them, some men who were friends said to one another: "Aha! Even though they subsist on alms, these mendicants are so stout!"
Then one among them said, "I shall show you a marvel: I will make these [servants] emaciated even as they eat, just as before."
Having spoken thus, he invited these wandering mendicants to his house and fed them for one day with excellent food of six flavors.
Then those fools, remembering the taste of that [food], no longer desired their alms-food in the same way; because of that, they fell into a state of weakness.
Then, having shown them to his friends and having seen those wandering mendicants in their presence, that man who provided them with food spoke:
At that time, they were content with alms and were joyful and well-nourished; now, due to the suffering of discontent with that, they have become weak.
Therefore, a wise person desiring happiness should fix the mind in contentment; for discontentment in both worlds brings unbearable and unceasing suffering.
Thus instructed by him, those friends abandoned their dissatisfaction, which was the abode of evil deeds; for to whom is association with the virtuous not auspicious?
And now, O King, hear this story of Suvarṇamugdha: a certain young man once went to a pond to drink water.
Standing upon the tree, that dull-witted man saw there in the water the golden-colored reflection of a bird whose crest was made of gold.
Thinking it was gold, he entered that pond to seize it, but he did not find it, as it had vanished from his sight in the shifting water.
And repeatedly climbing back up from the water while watching it, he entered the pool again and again, desiring to seize that lotus, yet he did not obtain anything at all.
Then, having been seen by his own father and questioned, the dull-witted man was led home; there, upon seeing that reflection in the water, he drove away the bird and was awakened to the truth.
Thus, those of little intelligence, lacking discernment, are deluded by false cognitions; they become objects of ridicule for others and objects of pity for their own kin.
Now, let this other story of a great fool be heard here: On a certain road, the camel of a merchant became exhausted under its burden.
He said to his servants, "Go and bring another camel, one that can carry half of this young camel's load."
Just as one would not let water touch leather items kept in these cloth chests at the onset of the rainy season, so must you act while remaining here.
Having thus stationed his servants at the side of the camel, as he had departed from there, the merchant suddenly raised his head and a cloud began to rain.
"Act in such a way that the water does not touch the leather of the boxes"—having reflected thus upon what was said by their master, those fools then [acted accordingly].
Having pulled out their garments from the chests, they wrapped themselves in those hides; thus their clothes were destroyed by that water.
"O wicked ones, why has the entire mass of clothing here been destroyed by the water? Then that merchant, having arrived, spoke angrily to his servants.
"By our very word, we commanded that the leather covering the chest be removed from the water; what fault of ours is there in that? they also said to him.
I have stated that clothes are ruined when hides are still wet; this was said by me for the sake of protecting the clothes, not the hides.
Having spoken thus, the merchant then shifted his burden onto another camel, went to his own home, and punished all those servants with the forfeiture of their entire property.
Thus, fools whose hearts are ignorant, having created a misconception, destroy their own interest as well as the interest of others, and they offer such a reply.
Now, let this story of the simple cake-seller be heard in brief: a certain traveler once purchased eight cakes for a single paṇa.
And as he ate up to six of them, he did not feel satisfaction; however, with the eating of the seventh, satiety arose within him.
Then that fool wailed, "I have been robbed! What have I not done? This very cake, by which I was satisfied, has been eaten by me from the very beginning!"
"Why were others destroyed by me in vain, and why were they not taken into my hand?"—grieving thus and finding no satisfaction in his gradual losses, he was laughed at by the people.
Once, a certain foolish servant was told by a merchant: "Guard the shop door for a moment; I am going inside the house."
When the merchant had spoken thus and departed, the servant took the door-leaf from the shop upon his shoulder and went to see the actor.
And as he was returning from there, he was seen and rebuked by that merchant; he replied, "This door has been guarded by me exactly as you instructed."
Thus, one who is devoted solely to the literal sound, ignorant of the intended meaning, acts to his own ruin; now hear this unprecedented example involving a simple-minded buffalo.
A certain buffalo was led by some villagers outside the village, to the foot of a banyan tree in a Bhilla settlement, where it was slaughtered and eaten.
Then, having gone there, Mahiṣasvāmin informed the king, who had those village buffalo-eaters summoned.
In the presence of the king, he spoke thus before the buffalo: "O King, having led me to the vicinity of the pond, beneath a banyan tree..."
"The buffalo was killed and eaten by these fools while I looked on. Hearing this, one among those others—an old fool—said this:
"There is not even a pond in this village, nor is there a banyan tree anywhere; this buffalo speaks falsely—where was he killed, or by whom was he eaten?"
Having heard this, Mahiṣasvāmin said: "Is there not a banyan tree and that pond to the east of your village?"
"And on the eighth day, that buffalo was eaten by you here; this is my proof. Being addressed thus by him, that old fool spoke as follows:
"In our village there is no such thing as an eastern direction, nor is there even an eighth lunar day. Hearing this, the king laughed and spoke to the fool, encouraging him:
"You are a speaker of truth; you do not say anything that is false. Therefore, tell me the truth: was that buffalo eaten by you all, or not?"
Having heard this, Jaḍa said: "I was born three years after my father died; by him alone have I been taught this skill in speech."
"That is untrue, O Great King; I never speak falsely. A buffalo was eaten by us; this other person is indeed speaking a lie."
Having heard this, the king, along with his followers, was unable to restrain his laughter; he handed over the buffalo to him and fined those villagers.
Thus, out of the pride of their own folly, fools conceal what is not secret and reveal what is secret, in order to gain confidence in themselves.
A certain foolish husband was addressed by his fierce wife: "Tomorrow morning I shall go to my father's house, for I have been invited to a festival."
"If you have not brought even a single lotus garland for me from anywhere, then I am not your wife, nor are you my husband."
Then, for that purpose, he went at night to the royal lake; and having entered it, he was seen and questioned by the guards: "Who are you?"
Saying, "I am called Cakrāhva," he was bound by them and led away at dawn; and when questioned before the king, he produced the cry of a cakravāka bird.
Then, having been questioned by the king himself and pressed for details, that fool related the account; moved by compassion, the king released him in his distress.
And once, a certain foolish-minded physician was told by a certain twice-born man: "Bring my son, who is hunchbacked, inside."
Having heard this, the physician said: "Give me ten coins as a wager; I shall give you ten times that amount if I do not accomplish this."
Having thus made a wager and taken those stakes from the twice-born man, the physician treated that hunchback solely with sweating and other such methods.
And he was unable to make it clear; he offered ten times the wager. For who here is able to straighten a human being who is hunchbacked?
Such boastful proclamation of an impossible thesis is for the sake of mere laughter; therefore, a wise person should not travel by such deluded paths.
Having heard this charming tale from his minister named Gomukha at night, the wise Prince Naravāhanadatta was pleased and rejoiced with a delighted heart.
And he, though eager for Śaktiyaśas, gradually succumbed to sleep after reaching his bed, accompanied by his own friends of his own age, as they amused themselves with talk of him.

Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Seventh Wave: Then, having woken up in the morning, Naravāhanadatta fell into a state of agitation as he brooded there upon his beloved Śaktiyaśas.
Considering the remainder of the month until the time of his marriage to be like an eon, he found no pleasure, his mind being filled with longing for his newly-wedded bride.
Having learned that from the mouth of Gomukha, the King of Vatsa, out of affection for him, dispatched his own ministers, including Vasantaka, to his presence.
Out of respect for him and out of consideration for his composure, the wise minister Gomukha spoke to Vasantaka in the presence of that son of the Lord of Vatsa.
"Noble Vasantaka, tell some new and wonderful tale that will delight the mind of the prince."
Then the wise Vasantaka began to tell a story: "In Mālava, there was a renowned and excellent brahmin named Śrīdhara."
To him were born two twin sons who resembled each other: the elder was named Yaśodhara, and his younger brother was Lakṣmīdhara.
And those two brothers, established in their youth, set out together for another land to acquire knowledge, accompanied by one who was known as their father.
Traveling along the path in succession, the two reached a vast forest that was devoid of water, lacking the shade of trees, and covered with scorching sand.
As they were traveling there, exhausted by the heat and parched with thirst, they reached a single tree in the evening that possessed both fruit and shade.
And at the foot of that tree, there was a separate pond situated apart, containing cool and clear water, perfumed with the fragrance of lotuses.
Having bathed in it and eaten their meal, they were refreshed by drinking cool water; then, seated upon a stone slab, the two of them rested for a moment.
When the sun had set, the two brothers, having performed their evening devotions, climbed that tree to spend the night out of fear for living beings.
And at the onset of night, while those two were watching, many men rose up from within the water of that pond below.
Among them, one cleared the ground, another smeared it [with plaster], and another scattered five-colored flowers there.
Someone brought a golden couch and placed him upon it; another spread a mattress over it, covered with a fine upper cloth.
Some, having brought flowers, unguents, and the like, as well as drinks and excellent food, set them down in one place at the foot of the tree.
Then, from that pond-bed, there emerged a man who surpassed the God of Love in beauty, armed with a sword and adorned with divine ornaments.
While he was seated there upon that throne, all his attendants, adorned with prepared garlands and unguents, plunged into that very pond.
Then, from his bliss, he brought forth a beloved woman of auspicious form, modestly attired and wearing auspicious garlands and ornaments.
And his second wife was exceedingly beautiful, radiant with fine garments and ornaments; of those two wives, the latter was again his favorite.
Then, having placed jeweled bowls there, the virtuous woman brought food and drink for both her husband and his co-wife, using two of those bowls.
When those two had finished eating, she too ate; then her husband retired to his couch to lie down together with that second woman.
Having experienced the pleasure of amorous play, he fell asleep; and his first wife massaged his feet.
Even on her bed, that beloved wife remained sleepless; seeing this, those two sons of a brahmin, perched upon the tree, spoke to one another.
"Who might this be who has descended here to massage his feet? Let us all ask him, for these people appear entirely composed."
Then, having descended, as the two of them were approaching that first one, the second one beheld Yaśodhara.
Rising from her bed with unrestrained impetuosity as her husband slept, she approached him who was handsome and said, "Love me."
When he said, "O sinful woman, you are another's wife to me, and I am another man to you; why then do you speak thus? she replied once more.
"What fear do you have even if you were joined by a hundred like you? If you do not believe me, look at these one hundred rings of mine."
"Indeed, I took one ring from each of you," he said, and showed him the rings from his own hem.
Then Yaśodhara said: "Whether you join with a hundred or even a hundred thousand [men], you are my mother, but I am not of such a nature."
Thus repulsed by him, that deceitful woman, having awakened her husband Yaśodhara and shown him [the child], spoke while weeping in anger.
"By this wicked one, while you were asleep, I was forcibly destroyed. Upon hearing that, her husband rose up, drawing his sword.
Then his other virtuous wife, having seized him by the feet, said: "Do not commit a falsehood; listen to my words."
Having seen him, this wicked woman rose from your side and implored him with persistence; yet that virtuous man did not comply with her words.
Having been told by him, "You are my mother," she rejected him; out of indignation, she incited you to slay him in her wrath.
"O Lord, by her, while staying here at this tree during the nights in my presence, hundreds of travelers have been consumed after their rings were stolen."
Out of fear that you might harbor resentment, I never spoke such words to you before; today, however, out of fear of your sin, I have spoken this which ought not to be said.
If you do not believe her, look at the rings on the hem of her garment; yet it is not my duty as a virtuous wife to speak a falsehood to my husband.
"O Lord, behold this power of mine as proof of my chastity! Having said this, she reduced that tree—which had been gazed upon with anger—into ashes.
And out of favor, he made her even more beautiful than before; seeing this, her husband was finally satisfied after a long time and embraced her.
Having abandoned that wicked wife, having cut off her nose, and having obtained rings from the hem of her garment, her husband departed.
Having seen Yaśodhara together with his brother engaged in the recitation of study, he indeed asked for forgiveness and spoke with a sense of world-weariness:
Keeping these two wives always in my heart, I protect them out of jealousy; yet even so, this one wicked woman could not be guarded by me.
Who could steady a flash of lightning? Who could protect a fickle woman? Only if she is virtuous is she protected by her own singular character alone.
Guarded by that [vow], she protects her husband in both worlds, just as I have been protected today by this vow which is capable of warding off curses.
"By his grace, my association with unchaste women has ceased, and the exceedingly terrible sin of killing a brahmin, which had come upon me, has also vanished."
Having spoken thus, he seated Yaśodhara and asked him: "From where have you two come, and where are you going? Let it be told."
Then Yaśodhara, having related his own life story to him, gained his confidence and, out of curiosity, questioned him in this same manner.
"It is no secret, O illustrious one; if so, tell me now: who are you, even amidst such luxury, and why do you dwell in the water?"
Having heard that, the man who dwelt in the water said, "Listen, I shall speak," and then proceeded to tell his own story in this way.
To the south of the Himavat lies the region called Kaśmīra, which the Creator fashioned as if to create a curiosity for mortals regarding heaven.
There, having forgotten their own blissful abodes on Kailāsa and Śvetadvīpa, the self-born Hara and Acyuta occupy hundreds of other stations.
Purified by the waters of the Vitastā, it was crowded with heroes and learned men, and remained invincible against enemies, even those who were powerful and skilled in deceit.
There, in a previous birth, I was indeed a village-dweller named Bhavaśarman, the son of an ordinary twice-born man with two wives.
Thus, at one time, having become familiar with them, I undertook together with the monks the observance known as the *upoṣadha*, as prescribed in their scriptures.
And when that observance was nearly completed, while I was lying on my bed, one wicked wife indeed approached me by force and feigned sleep.
But during the fourth watch of the night, having forgotten that vow and its observance, I engaged in sexual union with her due to the delusion of sleep.
When that vow was thus partially broken, I became a water-man here today, and two wives were born to me here as well.
"One was that wicked unchaste woman, and this second one is a devoted wife; such is the power of my vow, even though it was broken."
I remember my birth and whatever enjoyments were mine that night; had I not violated them, this present birth would not have been mine.
Having thus related his own history, he honored both those guests, the two brothers, with refined foods and divine garments.
Then his virtuous wife, having understood that former event, knelt upon the ground and, gazing at the moon, spoke:
"O guardians of the world, if I am truly virtuous and devoted to my husband, then let this husband of mine go to heaven today, freed from the water-dwelling."
As soon as she had spoken thus, a celestial chariot descended from the sky; having ascended it, the couple departed together for heaven.
"For what indeed is impossible for virtuous women in the three worlds? And seeing those two brahmins, they were struck with the utmost wonder."
Having passed that remainder of the night, at dawn those two Brahmin brothers, Yaśodhara and Lakṣmīdhara, set out from there.
In the evening, they reached the foot of a tree in a deserted forest; and as they were seeking water, they heard a voice from that tree.
"O Brahmins, wait here while I today provide you with hospitality—baths, food, and drink—for you have both come to my home."
Having spoken thus, she ceased; and there a water-tank appeared, and then a wonderful array of food and drink presented itself upon its bank.
Filled with wonder, asking "What is this?", those two sons of the twice-born bathed in the pond as they pleased and there partook of food and other refreshments according to their desire.
Then, while the two of them remained at the foot of the tree having performed their twilight devotions, a handsome man descended from that tree.
Having been saluted by them and offered a welcome in due order, he sat down with the two twice-born men and was asked, "Who are you?"
Then that man said: "Formerly I was a destitute brahmin; by chance, I came into contact with a śramaṇa."
While performing the vow of fasting as instructed by him, I was once again forcibly fed in the evening by some deceitful person.
Because of that, I have been born as a Guhyaka from that interrupted vow; had I completed it, I would have become a god in heaven.
Thus have I related my own account; now you two tell me: from where do you come, and why have you both entered this desert region?
Having heard that, Yaśodhara told him his own story; then those two brahmins and the yakṣa spoke thus once more.
"If that is so, then I shall give you both these sciences by my own power; having mastered the sciences, go home—what is the use of wandering through foreign lands?"
Having said this, he gave the sciences to them, and they grasped them at that very moment through his power; then the Yakṣa spoke to them.
Now I request one thing from you both as a teacher’s fee: for my sake, you two must perform this vow of fasting.
Speaking the truth, practicing celibacy, circumambulating the deities, eating at the time of the mendicants' meal, restraint of the mind, and patience.
Having performed this for one night, this fruit should be offered to me, so that by means of the fruit of the completed vow, I may attain divinity.
Having spoken thus, the Yakṣa said "So be it" to those two Brahmins who were bowed low; and having had his purpose accepted by them, he vanished right there in the tree.
Having spent the night, those two brothers, both delighted that their purpose was accomplished without effort, returned and came back to their own home.
There, having related his own story and gladdened his parents, he and they both undertook the vow of fasting for the sake of the Yakṣa’s merit.
Then that Yakṣa teacher, having approached while remaining in his celestial chariot, said to the two of them: "By your favor, I have attained divinity, having transcended my state as a Yakṣa."
"Therefore, this task must be performed by you both for your own sake, and that vow must be undertaken so that divinity shall be yours at the end of your bodies."
"And now, you two shall possess unexhausted wealth through my boons. Having said this, he departed for heaven by means of his celestial chariot, traveling at will.
Then both brothers, Yaśodhara and Lakṣmīdhara, having performed that vow and attained their desired goals and knowledge, lived happily as they pleased.
Thus, even the deities protect those who abide in the Dharma and do not forsake their ethical discipline even in times of hardship, accomplishing their desired aims.
Thus, entertained by the wonderful tale told by Vasantaka, the son of the King of Vatsa, desiring to win his beloved Śaktiyaśas, remained there.
Then, at the time for the meal, having been summoned by his father, Naravāhanadatta went into his presence along with his ministers.
Then, having eaten a suitable meal there, he returned to his own residence in the evening together with his own companions, Gomukha and the others.
Thereupon Gomukha spoke again in order to amuse him: "Listen; I shall tell you another sequence of stories, O King."
There was a bull among monkeys named Valīmukha, who had strayed from his own troop and lived in a forest of udumbara trees on the shore of the ocean.
As he was eating, a single udumbara fruit fell from his hand and was swallowed there by a crocodile dwelling in the waters of the ocean.
Delighted by the taste of that fruit, he let out a sweet cry, at the sound of which the monkey threw many more fruits to him.
In that very manner, he constantly threw fruits at him, and the crocodile likewise made its sound; thus, friendship arose between the two of them.
Thus, every day, that porpoise would stay near the monkey who remained on the bank while he was in the water, and having spent the day there, he would go to his own home in the evening.
His wife, who knew the truth of the matter, always felt the pain of separation during the day; unwilling to accept friendship with the monkey, she resorted to the pretext of illness.
"Tell me, my beloved, what is this unease of yours, and by what can it be pacified? Thus the distressed Śiśumāra repeatedly questioned his wife.
When she gave no answer even though questioned persistently, her friend, who knew her secret, then spoke to him.
Even if you do nothing and she does not desire it, nevertheless I speak: how can a wise man conceal the suffering of people?
Such a great malady has arisen in this wife of yours, which will not be pacified except by the decoction of a monkey's heart-lotus.
Having been addressed thus by his beloved’s friend, the porpoise reflected: "Alas! How could I ever obtain the lotus-heart of a monkey?"
If I were to commit treachery against my friend the monkey, what would that befit me? Is a friend more dear than a wife, or is a wife even dearer than one's own life?
Having reflected thus, the porpoise said to his wife: "In that case, I shall bring you an unbroken monkey; why do you grieve, my dear?"
Having said this, he went to the presence of that monkey friend; and having initiated a conversation, he spoke thus to the monkey:
"Even now, my friend, you have not seen my house or my wife; therefore come, let us go there for rest for even a single day."
Where people do not eat together freely by visiting one another's homes, and where wives are not seen, that is deceit and not friendship.
Having thus deceived him, the porpoise caused the monkey to descend into the ocean, took hold of him, and set out from that place to go away.
Seeing him as he went along, agitated and startled, the monkey asked, "Friend, I see you looking quite different today."
Then, perceiving that the monkey was persistently questioning him and was already within his grasp, the dull-witted porpoise spoke thus to the leaper.
My wife remains unwell, and she requests from me a lotus-heart of a monkey for her medicinal diet; for that reason, she stands today despondent.
Having heard these words of his, the wise monkey reflected: "Alas! I have been brought here for this very purpose by that wicked man."
"Alas! Overcome by passion for women, he is intent on betraying his friend; or rather, does one possessed by a spirit not devour his own flesh with his own teeth?"
Having reflected thus, that monkey said to the crocodile: "If this is so, my friend, why was this not told to me by you at the very beginning?"
"I was coming, having taken my own heart-lotus for the sake of your beloved; indeed, it now remains with me within the Udumbara tree where I am staying."
Having heard that, the foolish Śiśumāra, being distressed, said this to him: "In that case, bring one of these from the Udumbara tree."
The crocodile brought him back again to the shore of the ocean; there, he released that monkey onto the bank as if he were Death himself.
Flying up and perching upon the top of a tree, he said to that crocodile: "Go away, you fool! Can the heart exist separately from the body?"
"I have indeed liberated myself in this way, and I shall not return here again. Have you not heard, O fool, the story of the donkey?"
In a certain forest, there lived a lion who had a jackal as his minister. Once, having been struck by the weapons of a king who had come there for the hunt, he somehow entered his cave alive.
When the king had departed and remained there, unable to endure hunger, his minister, the jackal, who subsisted on the remains of that [meat], spoke to him.
"O Lord, having gone out, why do you not gather food according to your ability, since your body, along with your attendants, is surely wasting away?"
Thus addressed by that jackal, the lion said to him: "Friend, overcome as I am by wounds, I am unable to wander anywhere."
If I obtain the heart and ears of a swan as food, then my wounds will heal and I shall return to my natural state.
"Then, having gone from here to somewhere else, bring a donkey for me quickly. Being thus addressed by him, the jackal said, "So be it," and departed from there.
Wandering near the water and finding the washerman’s donkey, he approached it as if out of affection and said, "Why are you so weak?"
"I have become emaciated from constantly carrying this washerman's burden. To the donkey who had spoken thus, the jackal replied:
"Why do you carry this suffering here? Come, I shall lead you to the forest that possesses the bliss of heaven, where you may flourish together with female donkeys."
Having heard that, the donkey, greedy for enjoyment, said "So be it" and went to the lion's forest together with that jackal.
And as soon as he saw him, the lion, weakened by the distress of his failing life-breaths, approached from behind that donkey and struck it with a blow of his paw.
Gazed upon by him, the donkey was terrified and fled suddenly; as he came, the lion also fell down, overwhelmed and agitated.
But the lion, his purpose unaccomplished, quickly entered his own cave; then the jackal, his minister, addressed him with reproach:
O Lord, if even this wretched donkey was not killed by you, what account will you have regarding the slaughter of deer and other animals?
Having heard that, the lion said: "Bring that donkey back again as you know how; once he is ready, I shall slay him."
Thus dispatched by that lion, the jackal went back and, having approached the donkey, asked him: "Why have you fled?"
To him who was saying, "I have been struck here by some creature," that jackal laughed again and spoke harshly to the ass.
This delusion has been seen by you as utterly false; there is no such reality here, for even I dwell here in such a state of happiness.
"Therefore, come now with me to that forest of unimpeded happiness"; at these words of his, the foolish donkey went there once again.
As soon as he saw that [lion] had arrived, the enemy of deer emerged from the mouth of the cave, threw himself upon his back, and struck him with his claws until he was torn apart.
Having slaughtered that donkey and appointed the jackal as its guardian, the lion, being weary, went to bathe.
At that moment, that deceitful jackal devoured the heart and the ears of that donkey for his own satisfaction.
Having returned from his bath and seeing the donkey in such a state, Hari asked that jackal, "Where are its ears and its heart?"
That jackal also said to him, "O Lord, he was already devoid of ears and heart; otherwise, how could he have returned even after having gone?"
Having heard that, the lion, thinking it was exactly so, did not eat it; the jackal, however, ate that other meat which remained from it.
Having spoken thus, the monkey addressed the crocodile again: "I will not come here again; I shall act like a donkey."
Having heard this from the monkey, the crocodile went home; grieving that his wife had been lost through delusion and his friend had been abandoned.
And upon the departure of that friendship, his wife returned to her natural state; and that monkey also wandered at his pleasure along the shore of the ocean.
Thus, a wise person should never place trust in a wicked person; for how can there be happiness from trusting a wicked person, who is like a black cobra?
Having thus related these stories, the minister Gomukha spoke once more to Naravāhanadatta, seeking to amuse him.
Now listen in order to these other fools who are not to be ridiculed; among them, hear first of this fool who brought satisfaction to the Gandharvas.
A certain wealthy man, delighted by the singing and instrumental music of a musician, summoned his treasurer and spoke to him in that person's presence.
"Give two thousand coins to this musician," he said; and having replied, "I shall do so," the treasurer departed.
Then the musician went and asked for those stakes from him, but the treasurer, remaining firm in his resolve, did not give those stakes to him.
Then that wealthy man, being requested by the lute-player for his sake, said: "What have you given me, so that I may give it back to you?"
"Just as you quickly provided me with pleasure for the ears through the playing of the lute, so too have I quickly acted for you through these words of a gift."
Having heard that, the lute-player departed with his hopes shattered, yet he laughed; for does not laughter arise even from a stone at such a speech from a miser?
O King, listen now to this story of two disciples of an elemental being: once there were two disciples of a certain guru who were jealous of one another.
Of those two, one daily anointed the right foot of that teacher and washed it, while the other likewise did the same for the left foot.
Once, when the student who was massaging his right foot had been sent to the village, the teacher directed his second student to massage his left foot.
"Anointing your own right foot, you yourself must wash it for me today. Hearing this, that foolish disciple spoke freely to his teacher:
"This foot of mine, belonging to the antidote, is not to be anointed. When he had spoken thus, the teacher insisted upon it.
Then, out of hostility toward his rival and anger at his teacher, that disciple took hold of the teacher's foot and forcibly broke it with a stone.
While that teacher was crying out in distress, that bad disciple was seized by others and beaten; he was then released by that very teacher, who was overcome with grief.
On another day, that other disciple arrived from the village; seeing his teacher’s foot injury and having inquired about the circumstances, he blazed with rage.
"I will not break the foot belonging to that enemy," he said; having thus spoken, he pulled out the second foot of his teacher and broke it.
Then, while being beaten there by others as well, that wicked disciple was released even by that teacher out of compassion, though both his feet were broken.
Then those two disciples departed, despised and ridiculed by everyone; and the teacher, praiseworthy for his own forbearance, gradually became composed once more.
O Lord, when the retinue is thus mutually hostile and foolish, it surely destroys the master’s interests and does not attain its own welfare either.
And let this account of the two-headed serpent also be taken to heart: a certain snake had two heads, one at its front and one at its tail.
The tail became the head, and the blind one again became possessed of sight; between them there arose a stubborn insistence, each thinking, "I am the principal one! I am the principal one!"
That serpent moved along with its natural mouth, but once, on the path, its head and tail became entangled, causing it distress.
Having bound it firmly, he blocked the snake's progress at its mouth; then that powerful snake considered itself the victor, having won the first half of the contest.
Then, wandering with that very blind face, the serpent fell into a pit of fire and was consumed by the flames because he could not see the path.
Thus, those fools who do not perceive the vast difference between even a small virtue and its opposite, go to ruin through attachment to inferior qualities.
Now listen to this story of a foolish man who ate raw rice: once, a certain fool went for the first time to his father-in-law's house.
Seeing there the white rice grains set aside by his mother-in-law for cooking, he threw a handful of them into his mouth to eat them.
And as soon as his mother-in-law had arrived at that moment, the fool was unable to swallow the rice, nor could he spit it out due to shame.
Perceiving that his cheeks were swollen and protruding and that he was speechless, his mother-in-law, suspecting him of that disease, summoned her husband and brought him there.
Having seen him, he quickly brought a physician; and the physician, suspecting a swelling, seized the head of that fool and cut open his jaw.
The rice grains went out along with his public laughter; thus the ignorant man performs an improper act and does not know how to conceal it.
And some foolish boys, having seen the milking of cows and other animals, seized a donkey, tied it up, and began to milk it out of curiosity.
One person milked [the cow], while another held the vessel of milk; they vied with one another to be the first to drink the milk.
And they did not obtain milk despite their exertion with the horns; for a fool who undergoes hardship over a non-existent object becomes an object of ridicule.
O King, there was once a certain foolish son of a Brahmin, and his father said to him in the evening: "My son, you must go to the village tomorrow morning."
Having heard this, and without even asking his father about the matter, he went to that village in the very morning for no purpose at all, and returned in the evening, exhausted by his efforts.
Having gone to the village, he returned and said to his father, "I have come back. His father then asked him, "While you were away, was nothing accomplished?"
Thinking "it is so," the fool experiences suffering through purposeless activity and becomes an object of public ridicule; he does not, however, accomplish his task.

Having heard this instructive tale from Gomukha, the chief minister, and having announced himself with a longing to recover Śaktiyaśas, the son of the Lord of Vatsa—perceiving that the night had mostly passed—went to his bed with his companions, his eyes sealed by sleep.

Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Eighth Wave. Then, on another day, at night, Naravāhanadatta remained in his own dwelling, longing intensely for the recovery of his beloved.
At the king's command, his minister Gomukha, diverting the son of the Lord of Vatsa with stories, described things to him in this manner in due course.
In a certain city, there lived a brahmin named Devaśarman; he had a wife named Devadattā, who was of a similar lineage.
Having conceived a child by him, she gave birth to a son in due time; though he was poor, that twice-born man regarded him as if he had found a treasure.
At the end of the period of impurity, his wife went to the river to bathe, while Devaśarman remained at home guarding his infant son.
Just then, a maidservant who summoned him came quickly from the king's inner apartments to that Brahmin, whose livelihood depended on reciting benedictions.
Then, out of greed for the sacrificial fee, he stationed Nakula as the protector of his child and departed for his home, where the boy had been raised since early childhood.
When he had departed, the mongoose, seeing a snake that had suddenly approached the young boy, killed it out of devotion to his master.
Then, seeing Devaśarman approaching from afar, the mongoose, drenched in the serpent's venom, emerged joyfully before him.
Upon seeing him in that form, Devaśarman struck him with a stone out of agitation, thinking, "Surely this boy, my son, has been killed by him."
Having entered within and seen that snake struck by the mongoose—still alive and standing there—the Brahmin was consumed with inner remorse.
"Without even considering his service, why was that mongoose killed by you?"—thus reproached he even by his wife, who had arrived there and learned of the matter.
Therefore, O Lord, a wise person should not do anything impulsively; for one who acts with haste is destroyed in both worlds.
And by performing an action contrary to the prescribed rule, one reaps a contrary fruit; for instance, there was once a certain man whose body was overcome by wind.
Having administered the medicine for an enema, the physician once said to him, "Go to your own home and grind this, by the time I return."
Having spoken thus, the physician departed; while he was delayed for even a moment, that fool ground the medicine and drank it with water.
Then, having approached him whose malady had arisen, the physician administered an emetic and with great difficulty restored him to life when he was nearly dead.
"The enema medicine is administered in the anus, O fool, and not drunk; why do you not wait for me?"—thus was he rebuked by him.
Thus, even that which is desired turns into the undesired when performed contrary to the rule; therefore, a wise person should not do anything while abandoning the prescribed rule.
And one who acts without prior reflection is censured as a doer of blameworthy deeds from that very moment; likewise, there was once a certain man of dull intellect in a certain place.
Once, while he was traveling to another country, his son followed after him; when the caravan had encamped in the forest, the son entered the woods to wander about.
Torn by monkeys there, he approached his father while barely alive; being ignorant of bears, the dull-witted man spoke thus to his father who was questioning him.
"I was torn by some hairy fruit-eaters in the forest. Hearing this, his father, drawn by anger, went to that forest with his sword unsheathed.
Seeing those matted-haired ascetics there gathering fruits, he rushed toward them, crying, "They have wounded my son; they are the Lomaśas!"
"Your son has been torn apart by bears seen by me; do not kill the sages! Thus was he prevented from killing them by a certain traveler.
Then, by chance, he emerged from that sin and encountered a caravan; therefore, a wise person should never act without prior reflection.
What else should a person of cultivated intellect always contemplate? For those lacking wisdom, who are constantly ridiculed by the world, surely perish.
And so, a certain poor man, while traveling on the road, found a leather water-bag filled with gold that had fallen from the caravan of a certain merchant.
That fool, having taken it, did not go elsewhere; remaining right there, he began to count that gold.
Then, having remembered, the caravan leader quickly returned mounted on his horse and seized that gold bag from the delighted man.
Then, having seen his wealth vanish, he departed with his head bowed in grief; for even when wealth is acquired, it is snatched away in an instant by one of dull intellect.
Once, a certain dull-witted man, desiring to see the full moon, was told by another who had seen the new moon, "Look toward my finger!"
Having left the sky and looking at that very finger of his, he stood there; yet he did not see the moon, but saw people laughing.
"Even that which is impossible is accomplished through wisdom; listen, therefore, to this story. Once, a certain woman set out alone to go to another village."
And on the path, suddenly encountering a monkey who desired to seize her, she eluded him by repeatedly moving about while taking refuge in a tree.
The deluded monkey covered her with his two arms, and she, in turn, pressed his arms against the tree right there with her hands.
And at that moment, while the monkey remained motionless and filled with rage, a certain woman spoke to a cowherd who was passing along that path.
"O fortunate one, take this monkey for a moment in your arms, while I adjust my disheveled garment and braid."
"I shall do so, if you will accept me"—when she was thus addressed by him, she consented for the time being; he then seized that monkey.
Then, having drawn her knife and killed that monkey, the woman said to the Ābhīra, "Come with me to a secluded place," and led him a great distance away.
Then, while the merchants were still milling about, she abandoned them and went with those [others] to her desired village, having warded off all calamities through her wisdom.
Thus, in this world, wisdom alone is the primary means of worldly conduct; even one poor in wealth lives, but one poor in intellect does not truly live.
Now listen, O Queen, to this wonderful and marvelous tale: in a certain city, there were two thieves named Ghaṭa and Karpara.
Once at night, Karpara placed the jar outside those two, sealed the opening, and entered the princess's bedchamber.
There, as soon as the princess saw him lying in the hut, desire was instantly born within her, and she summoned him privately.
Having sported with him and given him wealth, she said to him: "I will give you even more if you come back again."
Then, having departed, related the news, and handed over the wealth, Karpara returned home with the jar containing the king's property and sent him away.
Then, drawn by desire and greed, he himself entered that inner apartment once again; for who perceives impending ruin?
There, exhausted from amorous play and intoxicated by drink, he slept together with that princess and did not perceive that the night had passed.
Having entered in the morning and captured him, he was bound by the guards of the inner apartments and reported to the king; the king, in his anger, ordered his execution.
While he was being led to the place of execution, his friend Ghaṭa arrived at night and followed his tracks to search for him.
Then, seeing that he had arrived, Karparaka spoke again to him in his own secret sign, saying: "Having seized the princess, you must protect her."
Then, having accepted the request through a sign, that Karpara was led away by the executioners; while hanging from a tree, he was quickly killed against his will.
Then, having gone home at nightfall, Ghaṭa, lamenting, broke through a tunnel and entered the palace of that king's daughter.
There, seeing one woman who was restrained, he approached her and said: "I am Ghaṭa, the friend of Karpara, who has been killed today on your account."
I have come here to take you away from this place because of my affection for you; therefore, come, before your father does you some harm.
When he had spoken thus, the princess was delighted and agreed to it, saying "So be it," and he released her bonds.
Then, having emerged together with her, who had immediately surrendered her body, that thief went to his own dwelling by way of the tunnel.
And in the morning, having learned that his own daughter had been carried off by someone through a subterranean tunnel that was difficult to detect, the king reflected:
Surely that wicked man who has been apprehended must have some audacious kinsman by whom my daughter was thus abducted.
Having reflected thus, the king had his servants station themselves to guard Karpara’s body and spoke to them as follows:
If anyone should come here grieving to perform the cremation and other rites for you, then I shall seize that wicked woman, the defiler of her family.
Thus commanded by the king, those guards said, "So be it," and remained there, guarding that body in the skull-bowl without ceasing.
Having searched for it and understood the situation, Ghaṭa said to that princess: "My dear, Karpara was my closest kinsman and friend."
"By whose grace I obtained you along with this collection of jewels and the sea—without having repaid his debt of affection, there is no peace in my heart."
Having gone to the cremation ground, I lament while observing [the body] according to my own reasoning; then, in due order, I perform the cremation in the fire and cast its bones into a sacred ford.
"Let there be no fear in you, for I am not as devoid of intellect as Karpara. Having said this to her, he then immediately assumed the dress of a great ascetic.
Taking curd-rice in a bowl near another pot, he approached like one who had come from the road; and there he stumbled.
Having knocked it from his hand and broken that bowl filled with curd-rice, he lamented various things, saying, "Alas, the bowl filled with the nectar of immortality! and so forth.
The guards reported that lamentation over broken vessels; and returning home in an instant, he told it to the princess.
And on another day, having placed one servant in front dressed in the attire of a bride, and another behind him carrying a vessel of food containing dhattūra, [he set out].
And having himself assumed the guise of a drunken villager, at the close of day, he approached those guardians of the pot, staggering along near them.
When he was asked there by them, "Who are you, brother, who is this woman, and where are you going?", that rogue spoke to them with faltering syllables as follows:
"I am a rustic man; this is my wife, whom I am taking from here to my father-in-law's house, and I have brought this store of provisions for her sake."
"Through our conversation, you have now become my friends; therefore, I shall take half of those provisions there, and let the other half be yours."
Having said this, he gave a single morsel of food to each of those guards; they all took them and ate them while laughing.
While those guards were thus stupefied by the dhattūra, he caused Karpara’s body to be consumed by fire at night, having brought wood from a potter’s kiln.
When he had departed, the king, having learned of it the next morning, dismissed those bewildered guards and stationed others, saying to them:
"Even these bones must now be guarded; whoever comes to take them away should be seized by you, and no food whatsoever should be obtained from elsewhere."
Thus addressed by the king, they remained there as guards day and night with vigilant attention, and Ghaṭa learned of that entire occurrence.
Then, understanding the power of the deluding mantra given by Caṇḍikā, he made a certain wandering mendicant his friend and a sign of reassurance.
Having gone there together with that mantra-reciter ascetic, he bewildered those guards and took the skull-bones.
Having thrown those [bones] into the Ganges and related everything as it had happened, he remained happily with the princess and his fellow mendicants.
The king, too, having learned of the removal of the bones and the bewilderment of his guards, considered everything from that point up to the abduction of his daughter to be the work of that yogin.
"To him by whom this was done for me—the abduction of my daughter and so forth—I shall give half the kingdom, provided that he reveals himself."
Thus the king caused a proclamation to be made in his own city; and having heard it, Ghaṭa then desired to reveal himself.
"Do not do so; you must not place your trust in this man who strikes with deceit. Thus was he restrained by that princess, who addressed him as "Your Majesty."
Then, out of fear of discovery, he set out for another country together with that mendicant and accompanied by that princess.
And on the road, that princess spoke privately to the renunciant: "By one I was ruined, and by this other I have been cast down from my station."
"That thief is dead; this jar is not mine, you are very dear to me," saying this, she united with him and killed Ghaṭa with poison.
Then, as she was traveling along with that wicked mendicant, she encountered on the road a merchant named Dhanadeva.
Saying, "Who is this skull-bearer? You are my beloved," she departed together with that merchant, leaving behind that wandering mendicant while he was fast asleep.
And that renunciant, having woken up in the morning, reflected: "There is neither affection nor courtesy in women; alas, there is nothing but fickleness."
"Even though she is wicked, she has taken my wealth and fled while I trusted her; yet this is actually a gain, or rather, it is a blessing that I was not killed by her like a water-jar."
Having reflected thus, that wandering mendicant then departed for his own country; and the princess also reached that country together with the merchant.
"Shall I suddenly bring this unchaste woman into my house? thus reflected Dhanadeva upon reaching his own country.
It is said that there a merchant entered the house of an elderly woman at the close of day, together with that princess.
There at night, he asked that old woman, who did not know him: "Mother, do you know anything here concerning the merchant Dhanadeva's household?"
Having heard that, the old woman said, "What news is there of her? Her wife always takes her pleasure with ever-new men."
For there, a leather bag is suspended by a rope through a window; whoever enters it at night is the very one who is made to go inside.
In the same way, she is driven out here at nightfall; intoxicated by drink, she does not perceive anything at all.
And this state of affairs became known throughout this entire city; much time has passed, yet that husband of hers still does not return.
Having heard these words of the old woman, Dhanadeva immediately departed by a clever ruse and went there, inwardly distressed and filled with doubt.
Seeing there a chest suspended by ropes by the female slaves, he entered it; then, having lifted him up, they carried him inside.
Having entered, he was embraced by her and led to the bed by his own wife, who was blinded by passion, unaware of him, and deluded by intoxication; she did so by force.
As long as he had no desire for pleasure because he perceived those faults, his wife fell asleep due to the fault of intoxication.
At the end of the night, he was quickly cast out through a window by the maidservants with a rope-basket; exhausted, the merchant reflected:
Enough for me with delusion regarding the home; women are the bond within the home. Such is their very nature; therefore, the forest is far superior.
Having thus resolved and even abandoning that princess, Dhanadeva set out to travel far into another forest.
And as he was traveling, he met on the road a Brāhmaṇa named Rudrasoma, who had returned from a long journey abroad, and they became friends.
Having been told his own story by him, the brahmin, fearing for his wife, reached his own village in the evening together with that very merchant.
There, near his own palace on the riverbank, he saw a cowherd who seemed to be singing while intoxicated; he questioned him with a jest.
O cowherd, is there some young woman who is in love with you, that you sing thus out of intoxication, regarding the entire world as mere straw?
Having heard that, the cowherd laughed and said, "How much of a secret is there for me [to reveal] regarding this twice-born Rudrasoma, who has been away from here for a long time?"
I always enjoy the company of the young wife of the village headman; his female servant introduces me into his house, disguised in woman's attire.
Having heard this from Gopāla and restraining his inner anger, Rudrasoma spoke to him, desiring to know the truth.
"If that is so, I am your guest here; give me this garment of yours, for I shall go there today just like you, as I have a great curiosity."
"Do this: take this black blanket of mine and stay here with the club until her maidservant arrives."
And under the impression that it was me, she summoned him and gave him her own woman's garment; "Go there at night, and I too shall rest for this night."
When the cowherd had spoken thus, Rudrasoma took the staff and the blanket from him and remained there in that very disguise.
And that cowherd, together with the merchant Dhanadeva, stood there for a short while at a distance; then that maidservant arrived from there.
Approaching him silently in the darkness while he was disguised in female attire, she said, "Come," and then led Rudrasoma away under the impression that he was a cowherd.
And having been led there, Rudrasoma saw his own wife; thinking her to be a cowherd woman, he rose up, embraced her, and reflected:
Even toward one who is base and close at hand, wicked women feel passion; for this woman is devoted to sin, even though the cowherd stands near her.
Meditating thus and feigning a sneeze, he immediately departed with indistinct speech; with a dispassionate soul, he went into the presence of Dhanadeva.
Having related the events concerning his own home, he said to that merchant: "I too shall go to the forest with you; let my house go to ruin."
Having spoken thus, Rudrasoma and that merchant Dhanadeva set out from there at that very moment, both together toward the forest.
And on the way, they met Śaśin, a friend of Dhanadeva; in the course of conversation, the two of them related their own adventures to him.
Having heard that, Śaśin—jealous and having returned from abroad after a long time—became suspicious of his own wife, even though she had been placed in an underground chamber.
Traveling together with them, Śaśin reached the vicinity of his own home in the evening; he then desired to offer them hospitality at his house.
And there he saw a man standing, emitting a foul odor, with hands and feet shattered by leprosy, yet full of passion and singing.
And out of wonder, he asked him, "Who are you, being such as this? He too replied to him, "I am Kāmadeva, though afflicted with leprosy."
"What delusion is this? You are Kāmadeva; your very beauty proclaims it to you. Thus addressed by Śaśin, he spoke again: "Listen, I shall tell you."
In this case, a rogue named Śaśin, having deposited his wife—who had been given to him as a sole attendant—in an underground chamber, departed for another country out of jealousy.
By her, whose heart was drawn away by passion, my very self was immediately offered as soon as she saw me here through the power of destiny.
And with her, I always take my pleasure night after night; that maidservant, having taken me on her back, used to lead me there.
Tell me then: am I not Kāma? Whose attainment am I, other than that of the wives of others—such as the beloved of the Moon, whose wife assumes various wonderful forms?
Having heard these words of the leper, which were as terrible as a thunderbolt, the Moon, concealing his sorrow and desiring to ascertain the truth, spoke to him with resolve.
"Truly you are Kāma; therefore I entreat you thus: curiosity has arisen in me regarding her, having heard of her from you."
Therefore, this very night, I shall enter there through your disguise; be gracious, for what loss is there to you in this matter that is easily obtained?
Thus addressed by Śaśin, the leper spoke to him: "So be it; take this garment of mine and give me your own."
"Stay here, wrapping your hands and feet with your garment as I am, until her maidservant arrives when the darkness has deepened."
And because of that [woman's] perception of me as her husband, go along as if you were being held by her on your back; for indeed, due to a deformity of my feet, I always move about in this manner.
Thus addressed by the leper, Śaśin then assumed his disguise and sat there; his two companions and the leper remained at a distance.
Then, having arrived, Śaśin saw him disguised as a leper; thinking him to be her husband, he said, "Come," and placed him upon the back of his wife's maidservant.
And then, at night, he was led by her into the interior of that underground chamber belonging to his own wife, who was waiting there for her leprous lover.
There, having certainly recognized her as his own wife by the touch of her limbs as she lamented in the darkness, the Moon attained a state of world-weariness.
Then, while she was fast asleep, he went out unobserved and approached Dhanadeva and Rudrasoma.
Having related his own story to them, he spoke in distress: "Alas! Fie upon those things that fall into low places, which are fickle, yet charming from afar!"

Women who are difficult to agitate cannot be restrained, like rivers flowing into a chasm; for even though she was staying in an underground chamber, this wife of mine has gone to one afflicted with leprosy.
Saying, "Therefore, even for me, the forest is better; fie on the household life," he spent that night together with the merchant who shared his sorrow.
In the morning, all three set out together toward the forest; at the end of the day, they reached a tree by the path whose base was surrounded by a pond.
Having eaten and drunk, they climbed that tree at night and remained there; they saw a traveler who had arrived and was sleeping beneath the tree.
And in an instant, they saw another man emerge from the middle of the pond, vomiting up a bed together with the woman.
Having enjoyed that woman, he fell asleep upon his bed; and as soon as she saw him, the woman rose and united with a traveler.
When asked by him at the end of their dalliance, "Who are you two?", she replied: "This is a Naga; I am his wife, a daughter of the Nagas."
And let there be no fear for you, because I have already consumed ninety-nine travelers; you shall complete the full hundred.
As she was speaking thus and the traveler was listening, the serpent woke up by chance; having bitten them both, he released flames from his mouth and reduced them to ashes.
Since women cannot be protected even when kept within the body, what can be said of them in a house? Fie, fie upon them!
When Nāga had thus departed for the pond, those three—Śaśin and his companions—having spent the night talking, went to the forest contented.

In that [place], those three, their minds stilled by the practice of the four meditations—loving-kindness and the rest—possessing perfectly disciplined intellects and being gentle toward all beings, attained accomplishment in the meditative absorption of incomparable supreme bliss; and with their darkness dispelled, they gradually reached liberation.
But their wives—wicked women who had fallen from both worlds and were experiencing a miserable state born from the ripening of their own sins—perished very soon thereafter.
Thus, passion born of delusion leads to suffering for whom, not among women? But for those who maintain detachment even toward them, dispassion indeed leads to liberation.
Thus, having listened for a long time to this diversion of stories from Gomukha, the son of the King of Vatsa—eager for reunion with Śaktiyaśas through his minister—gradually fell asleep once more.

Thus ends the eighth wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Ninth Wave. Then, on another day, once again entertaining Naravāhanadatta during this night as before, Gomukha told him a story.
In a certain city, there was the son of a wealthy merchant, born from a portion of a Bodhisattva, who was a reviver of the dead.
Driven by his father, who was infatuated with another's wife, he was expelled; thus, accompanied by his wife, he departed from his home to dwell in the forest.
But leaving behind his younger brother—who was coming along as a companion, had likewise been rejected by his father, and whose mind was not yet at peace—he proceeded by another path.

And as he proceeded, he eventually reached a vast desert wilderness, scorched by the fierce rays of the sun, which was devoid of water, grass, and trees, and where all provisions for the journey had been exhausted.
Traveling along it for seven days, he sustained his wife—who was exhausted by hunger and thirst—with his own flesh and blood; yet that wicked woman consumed them as well.
On the eighth day, he reached a mountain forest resonant with the sound of river waves, where the trees possessed excellent fruit and dense shade, and the ground was covered with lush green grass.
There, having comforted his weary wife with roots, fruits, and water, he descended to a mountain river garlanded with waves in order to bathe.
And there he saw a man whose four limbs—both hands and feet—had been severed, being carried away by the flood of water and longing for protection.
Then, although exhausted by many fasts, that compassionate Great Being plunged into the river and rescued that man.
"Brother, by whom was this done to you? Thus questioned by that compassionate man, who had brought him ashore, that mangled man replied:
"With my hands and feet cut off, I was cast into a river by my enemies who wished to subject me to a death of suffering; yet I was rescued from there by you."
When he had spoken thus, the Great Being, perceiving his state, applied a bandage to his wound, provided him with food, and performed his own bathing and other personal duties.
Then, subsisting on roots and fruits, that son of a merchant—an incarnation of a Bodhisattva—remained in that forest together with his wife, practicing austerities.
Once, while he had gone out for the sake of fruits and roots, his wife, afflicted by love, took pleasure with that Ruṇḍa whose wounds were still healing.
Having consulted with him, that wicked woman, desiring the death of her husband, feigned illness through a stratagem on another day.
Then, having shown him a medicinal herb situated in a pit difficult to descend and by a river difficult to cross, that wicked woman spoke to her husband.
"I live because this great medicinal herb has been brought by you; for a deity told me in a dream that she was here with me."
Having heard that, he said, "So be it," and descended into that chasm by means of a rope made of grass and tied to a tree, for the sake of obtaining the medicinal herb.
Once he had descended, they cast that rope away; it slipped from his grasp, and then he fell into the river and was carried off by its great current.
Having led him to a place far, far away, and having protected him well, she deposited him on the bank of a river near a certain city.
Then, having ascended to dry land and reflecting upon the behavior of women, he, exhausted from plunging into the water, rested at the foot of a tree.
At that time, the king in that city had died; and when the king has died, such is the situation in a land without a ruler.
Whomever the auspicious elephant, while being led through the streets by the citizens, places upon his back with his trunk, that person is consecrated here in this kingdom.
Pleased by his fortitude, the elephant, wandering like the Creator himself, approached the merchant’s son and, lifting him up, placed him upon its back.
Then, having been led to the city, that son of a merchant—who was born from a portion of a Bodhisattva—was consecrated in the kingdom by the subjects in an instant.
Having attained the kingdom, he took delight in compassion, sympathetic joy, and patience, but not in women of wicked character and fickle conduct.
His wife, too, being fearless and believing him to have been carried away by the river, wandered here and there with that maimed paramour mounted upon her back.
"This husband of mine has had his feet and hands cut off by an enemy; I am a devoted wife who sustains him by begging. Therefore, grant me alms."
Thus, begging from village to village and town to town, she reached that city of her husband, who was established in his kingdom.
In that very manner, as she wandered for alms there, the report of her devotion to her husband reached the ears of the citizens, who honored her in due course.
The king had her brought before him, with a vulture perched upon her back; having recognized from afar that she was a devoted wife, he questioned her: "Who is she, this woman of such fidelity?"
Not recognizing him, that sinful woman, though devoted to her husband, spoke thus to her lord, O King Śrī, who was endowed with majesty.
Then that king, who was a portion of a Bodhisattva, said to her with a smile: "Your devotion to your husband has been witnessed by me through this very fruit."
That human rakshasi, who was not even willing to accept her own blood and flesh when offered by her husband with his own uncut hand, [is now acting thus].
Alas, how is it that she, who is always taking away my blood and flesh, has now been accepted and made into a vehicle even by this mangled and mutilated man?
Who indeed was that blameless husband carried by you, who was cast into the river? By that deed, you carry this mangled man and now bear him upon yourself.
Then, having recognized her husband by his disclosed conduct, she became as if fainted from fear, like a painting, or as if dead.
"What is this? Tell us, O Lord!"—thus questioned by his ministers who were full of curiosity, the king then described everything to them exactly as it had happened.
Then, having learned that she was the wife of another, they cut off her ears and nose, branded her with a mark, and banished her from the country along with the minister.
Then Fate displayed a fitting union: a maimed man with a severed nose joined with the Bodhisattva, who was endowed with royal splendor.
Thus, the course of women's minds is indeed difficult to discern, like that of an unpredictable fate which is ever intent upon the base.

Thus, for those who have not abandoned ethical discipline, who possess compassion for sentient beings, and who have conquered anger, prosperity comes of its own accord and unexpectedly, as if out of satisfaction.
