Having thus told this story, the minister Gomukha once again related this tale to Naravāhanadatta.
In a certain forest, there lived a certain portion of a Bodhisattva who had constructed a hut; a Great Being whose heart was single-mindedly devoted to compassion, he was practicing austerities.
There, rescuing creatures in distress as well as Piśācas, he satisfied others with water and food through his own supernatural power.
Once, while wandering in this forest region for the sake of helping others, he saw a large well and cast his gaze into its depths.
And at that moment, a woman standing inside spoke loudly to him: "O Great-souled One, I am a woman; he is a lion; and this bird is Svarṇaśikha."
"And including the serpent, we four have fallen here into this well during the night; therefore, out of compassion, deliver us from this distress."
Having heard this, he said to that woman: "If you three have fallen here blinded by darkness, how did the bird fall here?"
"In the very same way, this one has also fallen and is bound by the net of hunters," thus that woman replied to the Great Being.
Then, as he desired to rescue them by the power of his asceticism, he was unable to rescue them; rather, his spiritual success began to diminish.
"This woman must certainly be evil, for my success has been destroyed simply by conversing with her; therefore, I shall now employ another stratagem."
Having reflected thus, the Great Being, while they offered him praise, drew them all out from the well using a rope made of grass.
Filled with wonder, he questioned the lion, the bird, and the serpent: "How is it that you possess articulate speech? Tell me, what is the story of this?"
Then the lion said, "We have clear speech and remember our former births; we are mutually antagonistic, so hear our history in due order."
Having said this, the lion began to relate his own story: "On the Snowy Mountain, there is a preeminent city named Vaidūryaśṛṅga."
There dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Padmavega, and a son named Vajravega was born to him.
Living in the world of the Vidyādharas, that Vajravega, arrogant and intoxicated by his own valor, engaged in conflict with whomever he encountered.
When he disregarded the words of his father who was forbidding him, his father then cursed him, saying, "Fall into the world of mortals!"
Then, his pride destroyed and his magic power lost, Vajravega, struck by the curse and weeping, begged his father for an end to that curse.
Then his father, Padmavega, having reflected for a moment, said: "Having become the son of a Brahmin on earth, you have once again displayed such pride."
Then, due to your father's curse, you shall become a lion and fall into a well; and some great being, out of compassion, will rescue you.
"By performing a service for him in times of distress, you shall be released from this curse," his father thus ordained the end of his curse.
Now, here in Mālava, this Vajravega was born as the son named Devaghoṣa to a brahmin named Haraghoṣa.
There too, out of pride in his valor, he created enmity with many; then his father said to him, "Do not create enmity with many."
His father, proud of his own valor, became enraged and cursed him for failing to obey his word: "O evil-minded one, become a lion this very moment!"
Thus, by his father's curse, that Devaghoṣa was once again born as a lion in this forest, having been an incarnation of a Vidyādhara.
"Know me to be that very lion; wandering by fate through the night, I have today fallen into this well and have been rescued by you, O Great Being."
Therefore, I shall depart for now; when you fall into some kind of calamity, you must remember me, and by performing a service for you, I shall release myself from my own curse.
When the lion had departed after speaking thus, that bird Suvarṇacūḍa was questioned by the Bodhisattva and then related his own story.
On the Himalayas there was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Vajradaṃṣṭra; five daughters were born to him in succession from his queen.
Then, having propitiated Hara through ascetic penance, that king obtained a son named Rajatadamshtra, who was dearer to him than life itself.
Although he was but a child, that Rajatadamshtra was made to acquire the sciences by his father out of affection; there he grew up, a festival for the eyes of his kinsmen.
Once, he beheld his elder sister, named Somaprabhā, playing the piñjaraka lute before the goddess Gaurī.
"Give me your lute; I too shall play it," he then requested her, out of childishness and persistence.
When she herself, out of fickleness, offered that [food] to him with a cry of "Tat," he seized it from her and flew up into the sky like a bird.
Then his sister cursed him: "Since you flew away after forcibly killing my Piñjaraka, you shall become a bird with golden crests."
Having heard that, Rajatadamṣṭra approached him as he lay prostrate at his feet and, being entreated by him, his sister told him the end of the curse.
When you, O fool, have become a bird and fall into a blind well, someone filled with compassion will then rescue you.
"By performing a service for him, you shall cross over this curse"; having been told this by her, his brother Svarṇacūla was born as a bird.
"I am that very bird with a golden crest who fell into this pit at night; having been rescued here by you, I shall now depart."
"Remember me when you are in distress, for having performed this service for you, I shall release you from the curse"; having said this, the bird also departed from there.
Then, questioned by that Bodhisattva, the serpent related his own story to that great-souled one.
In former times, I was a young ascetic in the hermitage of Kaśyapa; there I had a single friend, the son of a sage.
Once, while my friend had descended into this lake to bathe, I, standing on the bank, saw a three-hooded serpent approaching.
To frighten that friend of mine in jest, I bound that serpent at the edge of the bank by the power of a mantra in his very presence.
Having bathed in an instant, my friend reached the bank; seeing that great serpent unexpectedly, he was terrified and fell into a state of confusion.
Then, having perceived through meditation that my act of frightening him had finally brought him comfort, he, though my friend, rebuked me in anger.
"Go! Become a great serpent with three hoods, just like this! Then, being entreated for an end to the curse, that son of a seer spoke to me.
When you have fallen into the well and become like a serpent, he who rescues you will grant you release from the curse as an opportunity for his service.
As soon as he had spoken and departed, I became this serpent; and having been lifted out of the well by you today, I shall now depart.
"Once you have remembered me and performed a service for my shrine, I shall be released from my own curse. Having said this, the serpent departed, and the woman described her own history.
I am the wife of a son of the kṣatriya caste, an attendant of the king—brave, generous, youthful, handsome, and proud.
"Even though I, a sinful woman, had ceased my attachment to other men, my husband, having learned of that, set his mind upon punishing me."
Having learned of this from the mouth of my friend, I fled at once; I entered this forest at night and was rescued by you after falling into a well.
"By your grace, I shall now go somewhere and live; may that day come for me when I may perform a return service for you."
Having spoken thus to that Bodhisattva, the unchaste woman departed from his presence and went to the city of King Gotravardhana.
Having established a connection with her through her attendants, she remained with the king’s chief queen, adopting the status of a maidservant.
Because of that conversation with the woman, even for that bodhisattva, whose spiritual attainments had vanished, roots, fruits, and other such provisions no longer appeared in the forest.
Then, exhausted by hunger and thirst, he remembered that lion; and the lion, having arrived upon being remembered, provided for his sustenance with the flesh of deer.
After restoring him to his natural state with that meat for some time, the lion said, "My curse has been exhausted; I am now departing."
Having spoken thus, he abandoned his lion-form, became a Vidyādhara, and with the king’s permission, took leave of him and departed for his own abode.
Then that portion of the Bodhisattva, distressed for want of livelihood, again remembered Khaga; and he too, being thus remembered, approached him.
Having been informed of his distress, that bird went and returned in an instant, giving him a casket filled with jeweled ornaments.
And he said, "By this means, your livelihood shall be eternal; and for me, the end of the curse has come. May it be well with you; I shall now depart."
Having spoken thus, he too became a young Vidyādhara and, traveling through the sky to his own world, obtained the kingdom from his father.
Wandering about to sell those jewels, the Bodhisattva reached that city where the woman he had rescued from the well was staying.
There, having placed those ornaments in the secluded house of a certain elderly Brahmin woman, he went as far as the marketplace.
Just then, he saw that very woman being pulled up from the well in the forest as she approached him face-to-face; and that woman also beheld him.
When they had conversed with one another, that woman then, in the course of their talk, informed him that she was staying by the side of the king’s chief queen.
Questioned by her regarding his own adventures, the upright man related to her how he had obtained those jeweled ornaments from the bird Svarṇacūla.
Having taken the ornament, she showed it in the house of the old woman; that deceitful woman also went and reported it to her mistress, the queen.
And while that queen was looking on, a bird with a golden crest deceitfully carried off her jewelry box from within the palace.
And having learned from the mouth of that woman—who had known what was to be known—that he had reached her own city, the queen informed the king.
The king, having been shown that Bodhisattva by that wicked woman, had him brought from his house by his servants, bound along with his ornaments.
Having questioned him about his story and considering his words to be true, he nevertheless had him bound and took away even his ornaments.
While held there in captivity, the Bodhisattva remembered the serpent; and he, too, approached him, having manifested as the son of a seer.
Having seen him and being asked about his purpose, the serpent spoke kindly: "I shall go and coil myself around this king from head to foot."
"And I shall not release him until you have come and said to me here: 'I will free the king from the serpent.'"
"When you have arrived, I shall release the king from here at your word; and once he is released by me, this king will bestow half of his own kingdom upon you."
Having said this, that serpent went and coiled itself around the king, remaining there with its three hoods spread over his head.
Then, while the people were crying out, "Alas! Alas! The king has been bitten by a snake," the Bodhisattva said, "I shall protect the king from the serpent."
When his attendants, who were learned in the scriptures, informed him of those words, the king summoned the Bodhisattva and, seized by the serpent, spoke to him.
"If you release me from this serpent, I shall give half of my kingdom to you, as well as these ministers of mine who stand here between us."
Having heard that and being told "So be it" by the ministers, he said to the serpent: "O portion of a Bodhisattva, release the king at once!"
Then, released by that serpent, the king gave half his kingdom to the Bodhisattva; he too became healthy in an instant.
And the serpent, his curse having been exhausted, became a young son of a sage; after relating his story to the assembly, he departed for his own hermitage.
Thus, for those of virtuous nature, what is determined comes to pass as auspicious; likewise, transgression leads to suffering even for the great.
Even a service as great as the gift of life touches upon the destruction of women's trustworthiness; what more need be said of them?
Having thus told this story, Gomukha said to the son of the King of Vatsa: "I shall tell you more of these charming tales; listen."
There was once a certain dull-witted mendicant in a certain monastery; while wandering one day along a street, he was bitten on the knee by a dog.
Bitten by a dog, he returned to his own monastery and thought: "Each person here will ask me, 'What happened to your knee?'"
And how much, and for how long, shall I continue to convince them in this way? Therefore, I shall employ a means here to awaken everyone all at once.
Having reflected thus, that foolish monk quickly climbed atop the monastery, took up his staff with a sling, and struck it.
Hearing him say, "Why do you play the lute at this improper time and without cause? the monks then gathered together in amazement and questioned him.
"My knee has been bitten by a dog; ask each one of you individually how much of it was eaten. In this manner, I have brought you all together.
"Therefore, all of you understand this: behold my knee! he said to those monks, pointing out his knee that had been bitten by a dog.
Then all those monks laughed heartily at his side, saying, "How much of an effort has he made, and yet how great is this outburst!"
O fool, listen to this account of a Śramaṇa who was a fool among fools: there was once a certain miserly man somewhere who was a fool among fools yet possessed great wealth.
In the assembly hall, he always ate barley meal devoid of salt; he never once perceived the taste of any other food.
Once, impelled by the Creator, he said to his own wife: "Faith has arisen in me toward Kṣīriṇī; cook her for me today."
"So be it," she replied; then his wife cooked the milk-porridge, while that *ṭakka* remained hidden inside, having taken to his bed.
Seeing him, [the thief thought], "May no guest come here to me"; at that moment, a certain friend of his, a rogue named Ṭakka, arrived there.
"Where is your husband? he asked her, his wife; she, however, gave him no answer and entered the presence of her husband.
Having related the arrival of his friend, he said to that wife: "Sit here weeping and remain holding my feet."
And you should say to my friend, "My husband has died"; then, once he has departed, we two may enjoy the milk-tree in comfort.
When she had been addressed thus by him and began to weep, her friend entered and asked her, "What is this?"
"Look, my husband has died! she said; at this, he reflected: "Where have I ever seen her cooking so happily while possessing such milk?"
"How is it that this husband of theirs has just now perished without any illness? Surely, having seen me as a guest, they have fabricated this falsehood."
Thinking, "Therefore, I must certainly not go," that rogue sat down and remained there, crying out, "Alas, friend! Alas, friend!"
Hearing his cries, his kinsmen entered the cemetery and prepared to take that foolish Ṭakka away, as he lay there like one dead.
"Arise, before you are taken away by these kinsmen and cremated," his wife then said to him in a whisper at the root of his ear.
"Not so! This rogue Takka wishes to devour my milch cow. Therefore, I shall not rise; even if he comes, I will remain as if dead."
"For even a handful of food is weightier than one's own life for those such as I," that dull-witted man replied to his wife in private.
Then, led away by that evil friend and those kinsmen of his, though being burned, he remained motionless and did not utter a word until death.
Thus that fool gave up his life rather than [cut] the milky tree; yet he consumed its wealth, acquired through hardship, which others had taken with ease.
The miser has been heard of; now let these ghostly cats be heard of. In Ujjayinī, there was once a certain foolish teacher in a monastery.
There, he could not sleep at night due to the harassment of mice; distressed by this, he described it to a certain friend.
"Having brought a cat and established it here, he eats mice. Thus did that Brahmin friend speak to his preceptor.
"What kind of cat is it, and where does it stay? I have never seen one before," said the teacher; to him, his friend replied once more:
His eyes are made of glass, his complexion is tawny and grey, and he has a hairy skin upon his back; thus he wanders here in the streets.
"Search for him by these identifying marks and bring him here quickly. Having said, "Friend, [bring] Mārjāra," his friend departed for his home.
Then that dull-witted preceptor said to his own disciples: "The identifying marks have surely been heard by you while standing here."
"Therefore, search for that cat here somewhere in the streets. Saying "So be it," those disciples went and wandered here and there in that place.
Nevertheless, they did not see that cat at all; then, they beheld a certain young brahmin coming out from the mouth of the street.
He had glass beads upon his pair of eyes, was ash-brown in complexion, and wore a hairy deer-skin over his back.
"Having seen him, they said, 'This is indeed that cat who has been found by us just as we were told,' and having seized him, they led him into the presence of their teacher."
The preceptor, too, having observed that he possessed the characteristics of a cat as described by Maitra, placed him there inside the monastery at night.
Hearing the name "Mārjāra" given to himself by those foolish men, that dull-witted boy thought, "Surely there is a cat here."
And that foolish boy was the pupil of that brahmin, by whom that description of a cat had been told out of friendship to his preceptor.
In the morning, that brahmin arrived there and, seeing the boy inside, asked the servants, "By whom was he brought here?"
"This cat was recognized by us from its ears, and it has been brought here by you," said the foolish teacher and his disciples.
Then, laughing, that brahmin said: "O fools, where is a human being, and where is this cat—a beast with four legs and a tail?"
Having heard that, those dull-witted men released the boy and said, "In that case, let us search for and bring back another cat just like that one."
When they had spoken thus, the people there laughed at those fools; for to whom in this world does ignorance not become a cause for ridicule?
The story of the Cat-Bhūta has been told; now hear these others as well. Once, in a certain monastery, there was a foolish man who was the leader of many other fools.
Once, while being recited by someone, he heard from a treatise on dharma that there is very great fruit for the maker of a pond in the next world.
Then, having been filled with wealth, he had a large tank constructed, brimming with water, not far from his own monastery.
Once, that leader of fools went to see that pond and beheld its sandy banks torn up by someone.
Having arrived there once more on another day, he saw that the bank of that same pond had been excavated elsewhere, and filled with agitation, he reflected:
"Starting from dawn, I shall remain right here for the day; I will see who is doing this," he reflected, and set out in the morning.
On the following day, when he arrived and was there, he saw a bull descending from the sky and digging into the bank with its two horns.
"This bull is divine; why then should I not go to heaven with him? Thinking thus, he approached the bull and seized its tail with both hands.
Then, having swiftly lifted up that Bhūta who was clinging to the tip of his tail, the Blessed Lord Bull carried him in an instant to his own abode, Kailāsa.
There, having obtained divine foods such as sweetmeats and the like, that Bhauta dwelt happily for several days while enjoying them.
Seeing that great bull moving back and forth, he—the foremost of the ignorant, deluded by fate—reflected thus:
"I shall go, clinging to the tip of the bull's tail, and behold my kinsmen; having related this marvel to them, I will likewise return again."
Having reflected thus, he once approached the bull as it was walking along, and seizing its tail, that wondrous being descended to the surface of the earth.
Then, having arrived at the monastery, he was embraced by the other Bhūtas residing there; when they asked him, "Where have you been?", he related his own adventures to them.
Then all those who had heard the marvels were filled with wonder and entreated him: "Be gracious; take us there as well and feed us with sweetmeats."
Having heard that, he said, "So be it," and after uttering these words, on the following day he led them to the edge of the pond; and there the bull arrived.
The chief one seized his tail with both hands; another seized his feet, and yet another seized those as well.
As soon as those ghosts had formed a chain by clinging to one another's feet, that bull suddenly leapt into the sky with great speed.
And as that bull walked along with its tail held up by a ghost, another ghost, who was a deity, then questioned that chief ghost.
"Tell us now, Śraddhā, how it is that sweetmeats are so easily obtained in heaven according to one's desire; what quantity of sweetmeats have you eaten?"
Then, having lost his concentration and released that bull's tail, the leader of the Bhūtas joined his two hands together in the shape of a lotus.
As soon as he replied to them, "They are of such a size," they all—both he and the others—fell from the sky and perished.
The bull set out for Kailāsa, and the people laughed upon seeing him; thus, an action such as answering the questions of a fool leads only to fault when devoid of reflection.
You have heard of those fools who go to heaven; now hear of this other fool as well: a certain fool, while traveling along a different path, forgot his way.
And as he was asking people for the way, they said to him: "Go by the upper path over the tree standing on the riverbank."
Then that fool-minded man went to the back of that tree and climbed up, thinking, "The people pointed out the path to me by way of this tree's back."
As he crawled upon its back, the branch at the edge bent under his weight; with great effort, he grasped it and did not fall.
While he remained there, holding onto her, an elephant came along that path by way of the ascent, having drunk water from the river while standing on its bank.
Seeing him, that Bhauta, hanging from the tip of a tree branch, spoke in a piteous voice to the elephant-rider: "O Great-souled one, take me!"
And the elephant rider, letting go of the hook, seized that fool by both feet with his two hands in order to bring him down from the tree.
And as soon as the elephant had gone out and departed, that elephant-driver clung to the feet of that terrified man who was hanging from the top of a tree.
Then that fool, hurrying him along, said to the elephant rider: "If you know anything, sing something quickly."
One should never descend from here, lest people, having heard of us and come down, should carry us off as we fall below; this river [will] sweep us away.
Thus addressed, that elephant-riders sang so sweetly that even the fool himself attained the highest satisfaction therein.
Uttering cries of "Well done!", the fool forgot himself and, letting go of the tree, began to snap his fingers with both hands.
At that very moment, having fallen right along with his elephant rider, he perished in the river; for to whom can association with fools bring any happiness?
Having thus related this story once more to the son of the Lord of Vatsa, Gomukha told him this tale of Hiraṇyākṣa.
In this region within the lap of the Himalayas, there is a land that is the crest-jewel of the earth, known as Kaśmīra, the abode of sciences and of Dharma.
There, the capital city named Hiraṇyapura was established, and a king known as Kanakākṣa reigned there.
To that king, by his queen Ratnaprabhā, was born a son named Hiraṇyākṣa, produced through the propitiation of Śaṅkara.
Once, while playing with pellets, the prince deceitfully struck an ascetic woman who was coming along the path with one of his pellets.
That female ascetic, a mistress of yoga who had conquered her anger, laughed at the prince Hiraṇyākṣa and spoke to him with a distorted face.
If such pride as this arises in you because of your own youth and other qualities, then what would it be like if you were to obtain that Mṛgāṅkalekhā as your wife?
Having heard that and having asked her for forgiveness, the prince asked: "O Blessed One, please tell me, to whom does this name Mṛgāṅkalekhā belong?"
Then she said to him: "There is a highly illustrious lord of the Vidyādharas on Himavat, the king of mountains, known by the name Śaśitejas."
He has a daughter, an excellent maiden named Mṛgāṅkalekhā, who by her beauty causes the lords of the sky-dwellers to lose their sleep during the nights.
"She is a suitable wife for you, and you are a fitting husband for her. Having been addressed thus by the perfected female ascetic, Hiraṇyākṣa said to her:
"How then may I obtain her from the Blessed One? Please tell me that. Having heard this, the mistress of yoga spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having gone there, I shall learn his intention from your narration; then, having returned, I myself will lead you away from that place.
"There is a deity here named Amareśa; you shall reach his temple tomorrow morning, for I always go there to worship him."
Having spoken thus, that female ascetic departed through the sky by means of her own supernatural power toward the Snowy Mountain, to the presence of Mṛgāṅkalekhā.
There, she skillfully praised the virtues of Hiraṇyākṣa to her in such a way that the celestial maiden spoke to her with great longing.
O Blessed One, if I do not obtain such a husband, what is the use of this fruitless life of mine?
Thus, her passion having been aroused by that conversation, Mṛgāṅkalekhā spent the day with the female ascetic and dwelt with her through the night.
Meanwhile, Hiraṇyākṣa, having spent his day in those reflections, fell asleep; at the end of the night, Gaurī somehow addressed him in a dream.
Having been a Vidyādhara, you have attained the state of a mortal through the curse of a sage; from this, you shall be liberated by the touch of the hand of this female ascetic.
"And then you shall soon marry that Mṛgāṅkalekhā; you need have no anxiety about this, for she was indeed your wife in a former life."
Having thus instructed him, the goddess vanished from his sight; and he too, waking up and rising in the morning, performed the auspicious rites of bathing and so forth.
Then, having gone before the Lord of the West and bowed to him, she stood where the rendezvous with that female ascetic had been arranged by her.
In the meantime, Gaurī commanded Mṛgāṅkalekhā, who had somehow fallen asleep in her own palace, in a dream:
Hiraṇyākṣa, whose curse has been exhausted and who has become a Vidyādhara once again, will regain his wife through the touch of the ascetic’s hand; enough with your grief.
When the goddess had spoken thus and vanished, Mṛgāṅkalekhā woke up in the morning and related that dream to the female ascetic.
Having heard that, the perfected female ascetic came to the world of mortals and addressed Hiraṇyākṣa as he stood in the sacred field of Amareśa.
Saying, "Come, my son, to the world of the Vidyādharas," she took him by the hand as he bowed, and leaping up, they both flew into the sky.
Then, having become that lord of the Vidyādharas, Hiraṇyākṣa, remembering his birth as an ascetic woman due to the exhaustion of his curse, spoke to her.
Know me to be this king of the Vidyādharas, named Amṛtatejas, residing in the city called Vajrakūṭa on the Himālaya mountain.
Thus, having received a curse from the sage in the past due to my transgression and anger, I entered a mortal womb with the condition that it should end upon the touch of your hand.
"She who was my wife when I was cursed and who abandoned her body out of grief—she has now been born as Mṛgāṅkalekhā, my former beloved."
And now, having gone with you, I shall obtain her; for today that curse of mine has been pacified, as I have been purified by the touch of your hand.
Speaking thus, that lord of sky-dwellers, Amṛtatejas, went with that female ascetic through the air to the Himalaya mountain.
There he saw Mṛgāṅkalekhā staying in a garden, and she too saw him approaching as he was pointed out by the female ascetic.
Having first entered each other’s minds by way of the path of hearing, they both then entered again through the path of sight, without ever departing.
"In order to accomplish our marriage, you must tell this to your father," Mṛgāṅkalekhā was thus addressed there by that mature female ascetic.
Then, her face bowed with shame, she went to her father and immediately informed him of everything through the mouth of her friend.
His father, the lord of the sky-dwellers, who had been commanded by Ambikā in a dream, honored Amṛtatejas and brought him to his own abode.
And he gave Mṛgāṅkalekhā to him according to the prescribed rites; having performed the marriage, he returned to his own city, Vajrakūṭa.
There, having regained his own kingdom along with his wife, that Amṛtatejas brought back his own father, who had been brought there by the perfected female ascetic because of his mortal nature.
Having worshipped Kanakākṣa with offerings and brought him down to the earth, he enjoyed that prosperity for a long time together with Mṛgāṅkalekhā.
Thus, whatever is destined for a living being in this world by the decree of past karma, that he obtains without effort, even if it be unattainable, as it falls right before him.
Having thus heard at night on his couch the tale told by Gomukha concerning Śaktiyaśas, Naravāhanadatta, longing for her, fell asleep.

Thus ends the ninth wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Tenth Wave. Then, on another night, for the sake of diversion, that Gomukha related this story to Naravāhanadatta.
Long ago, a certain great sage dwelt in the Śaiva holy site named Dhāreśvara, being attended by many disciples.
He said to his disciples one day: "If any among you has seen or heard anything unprecedented, let it be reported."
When that sage had spoken thus, a certain disciple said to him: "I shall relate what I have heard, which has never been told before; let it be heard."
In Kaśmīra there is a great Śaiva sacred field called Vijaya; there lived a certain wandering mendicant who was conceited about his learning.
Having prostrated before Śambhu with the aspiration, "May I be victorious everywhere," that wandering mendicant set out for Pāṭaliputra to engage in debate.
And as he traveled along the road, passing through forests, rivers, and mountains, he reached a wilderness; exhausted, he rested at the foot of a tree.
And in an instant, in that pool-cool place, he saw a righteous man arrive, dusty from a long journey, with a staff and a water-pot in his hands.
When he was seated there, the religious mendicant asked him, "Where are you from? Where are you going? and the righteous man spoke to him thus:
"Friend, I have come from Pāṭaliputra, the field of learning; I am going to Kaśmīra to defeat the scholars there in debate."
Having heard these words of the righteous man, that wandering mendicant thought: "If this single inhabitant of Pāṭaliputra has not been conquered by me here,"
"Having gone there, how shall I defeat so many others?"—having reflected thus, that wandering mendicant insulted the righteous man and said:
Tell me, O righteous one, why is this conduct of yours so contrary? Where is the righteous seeker of liberation you claim to be, and where is this debater afflicted by calamity?
Bound by the pride of debate, you seek liberation from saṃsāra; you seek to extinguish the heat of fire with fire, and you seek to destroy cold with cold.
O fool, you wish to cross the great ocean with a boat made of stone; you seek to extinguish a fire blazing with wind.

Brahmin conduct is known as forbearance; kṣatriya conduct is the protection of those who have sought refuge; the conduct of one seeking liberation is tranquility; and quarreling is said to be the conduct of rākṣasas.
Therefore, one who desires liberation must be peaceful and self-controlled, having cast off the suffering of dualities and being fearful of the afflictions of saṃsāra.
Therefore, with the axe of tranquility, cut down this tree of existence; but do not provide it with the watering of the pride of causal theorizing.
Having been addressed thus by him, the righteous man was highly pleased; bowing to him and saying, "You are my guru," he departed as he had come.
Standing right there at the foot of the tree, the wandering mendicant heard from within it the conversation of a yakṣa sporting with his wife.
And as long as that mendicant was lending his ear, the yakṣa there struck his wife with a garland of flowers in jest.
Then that deceitful woman, having falsely made herself appear as if dead, remained there; and her retinue suddenly broke out into loud lamentation.
Opening her eyes as if she had returned from the dead after a long time, her husband, the Yakṣa, then asked her: "What have you seen?"
Then she spoke falsely: "When I was struck by you with a garland, I saw a dark man arrive."
Holding a noose in his hand, with blazing eyes, tall in stature, and with hair standing erect on his head, he was terrifying, darkening the horizons with the shadow of his own form.
Led by that wicked man, I went to the abode of Yama; however, I was released there by the officials who restrained him.
When the yakṣiṇī had spoken thus, the yakṣa laughed and said to her: "Aha! Without the power of illusion (indrajāla), there is no such thing as the conduct of women."
"What is death? A blow from a flower. What is returning from the abode of Yama? O fool, you have merely imitated the story of the women of Pāṭaliputra."
For in that city there was a king named Siṃhākṣa; his wives were the wives of the minister, the general, the chaplain, and the physician.
Once, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, he took her with him and went to see the Sarasvatī river, which had thereby been made to have a protector.
There, all the women headed by the king were entreated by those who had encountered that path—by the hunchbacked, the blind, the lame, and the diseased.
"Grant us medicine for those who are afflicted by disease and miserable, so that we may be freed from illness; show compassion toward those who are suffering."

This world of living beings is as restless as the waves of the ocean and as fleeting as a flash of lightning; though it appears beautiful for a moment like the occasion of a journey or a festival, it is ultimately fragile.
In this essence-less cycle of existence, the only essence is compassion for the wretched and generosity toward the destitute; where, then, does a man of virtue not live?

What is the use of giving for one who is wealthy? What is the use of food for one who is well-fed? What is the use of sandalwood for one who is cold? What is the use of wealth when winter has arrived?
"Therefore, rescue us, miserable ones, from this calamity!"—having been addressed thus by those who were afflicted with disease, the king's wives and others replied:
"These wretched, diseased men speak most appropriately; therefore, we must provide medical treatment for them even at the cost of our entire possessions."
Having conversed with one another in this way and having honored the queen, the women led those who were afflicted by disease back to their respective homes, each to her own.
Having urged their husbands, they had those great beings treated with potent medicines, yet they did not rise from their presence.
And through living together with those very beings whose passion had been aroused, they entered into such a state of worldly existence that they perceived everything as being composed of that alone.
"Where are these wretched, diseased husbands, and where are kings and the like?"—thus their minds, blinded by passion, did not reflect.
And then their husbands saw them marked with nail and tooth wounds, which could only have arisen from sexual union with an impossible lover.
And those [ministers], headed by the king’s counselors and generals, being alert and filled with doubt, then spoke to one another.
Then the king said to the others, "You all wait for a moment; today I shall first question my own wife with due deliberation."
Having spoken thus and dismissed them, the king went to his private chamber and, displaying both affection and fear, questioned his wife.
"By whom was this lower lip of yours bitten? By whom were your breasts wounded with nails? If you tell the truth, it will be well for you; otherwise, it shall not be so."
Having been addressed thus by that king, the queen spoke a fabrication: "I shall tell you something that ought not to be spoken; listen now to this marvel."
From this painted wall, a man bearing a discus and a mace emerges at night and enjoys me; in the morning, he dissolves right back into it.
"That limb which has never before been seen even by the sun and the moon—such a state is being brought upon it by him while you stand here."
Having heard these words of hers, which seemed as if she were in great distress, the foolish king believed them to be true, suspecting it to be a Vaiṣṇava illusion.
He reported this to his ministers and the others, and they too, being as dull-witted as he, considered those wives to have already been enjoyed by Acyuta and remained silent.
Thus, deceitful and wicked women, clever in the fabrication of a single falsehood, deceive those of dull intellect; but I am not such a fool.
Speaking thus to his wife, the yakṣa put her to shame; and the wandering mendicant, standing at the foot of the tree, heard all of it.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, that wandering mendicant addressed the yakṣa: "O Blessed One, having reached your hermitage, I have come to you for refuge."
"Forgive this offense of mine, that I have heard your words"—when he had spoken thus, the Yakṣa was pleased with him because of his truthful speech.
"I am the yakṣa named Sarvasthānagata, and I am pleased with you; accept a boon," said that yakṣa to the wandering mendicant.
"Do not harbor anger toward this woman, who is my own wife; let this alone be my boon," the wandering ascetic said to that Guhyaka.
Then that yakṣa said to him, "I am exceedingly pleased with you; therefore, this boon is granted to you by me—let another be requested."
Then the wandering mendicant said: "In that case, this is another boon for me: from this day forward, may you two, husband and wife, recognize me as your son."
Having heard this, the Yakṣa immediately appeared before him together with his wife and said to him: "Excellent! Son, you are the son of us both."
By my grace, no misfortune shall befall you anywhere; and in debate, in strife, and in gambling, you shall be victorious.
Having spoken thus, the Yakṣa vanished; and after bowing to him and passing the night there, the wandering mendicant arrived at that city of Pāṭaliputra.
There, through the mouth of the doorkeeper, he announced himself as a debater who had come from Kashmir to that King Siṃhākṣa.
Having been granted permission to enter by the king, he entered that place and, calling out to those who were standing there, challenged the scholars.
Having defeated all of them in debate by virtue of the greatness of that supreme dice, he then made this reproach against them in the presence of the king:
Emerging from the painted wall, a man bearing a mace and a discus appeared, his lower lip bitten by teeth and the surface of his breast wounded by nails.
Having made [me] his meal and consumed me at night, he dissolves right into that very wall; I ask you, "What is this?"—let an answer be given to me in this matter.
Having heard these words, the wise gave no reply there; not knowing the ultimate truth, they merely looked at one another's faces.
Then King Siṃhākṣa himself said to him: "Tell us yourself that which has been spoken by you."
Having heard this, the wandering mendicant related all of that to the king—the deceptive conduct of his wife which he had learned from the Yakṣa.
"One should never form such an attachment, for it is the sole cause for the confession of sin"—thus did that person speak to the king.

The king, being pleased, desired to give him his own kingdom; but when that mendicant, who delighted only in his own country, would not accept it, [the king said: "I shall give you whatever else you desire. When he replied, "I desire nothing," the king, having heard this, was struck with wonder. Then, having bestowed upon him a great honor, he dismissed him. And that mendicant went to his own hermitage. There he remained, practicing yoga and meditation, until he attained liberation. Thus ends the story of the mendicant. Now hear the story of King Śibi. Long ago, there was a king named Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, who was devoted to truth and righteousness. Once, a hawk pursued a pigeon, and the pigeon fell into the king's lap for protection. The hawk said to the king, "Give me this pigeon; it is my food. The king said, "This pigeon has sought refuge with me; I cannot give it to you. The hawk replied, "If you do not give it to me, I shall take it by force. The king, being compassionate, said, "I will give you an equal amount of flesh from my own body. Having said this, he cut off flesh from his own thigh to weigh against the pigeon. As he weighed the flesh, it was always less than the pigeon. Finally, the king placed his entire body on the scale. At that moment, Indra appeared in the form of a Brahmin and said, "O King, I am Indra; I tested you out of curiosity. You have proven yourself a hero of truth and righteousness. Having said this, he restored the king's body to its former state and departed. Thus ends the story of King Śibi. Now hear the story of King Trivikramasena. Long ago, there was a king named Trivikramasena, the son of Vikramāditya, who was wise, brave, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. Once, while wandering through the forest, he encountered a sage who had been cursed by a goddess. The sage said, "O King, I have been cursed by a goddess; release me from this curse. The king asked, "What must I do? The sage replied, "Go to the city of Pratisthāna and bring back the head of a man who has never told a lie. The king agreed and set out. After many days of wandering, he reached the city of Pratisthāna. There he searched for such a man, but could find none. Finally, he found an old woman who said, "I know of one man who has never told a lie. The king went to that man and asked for his head. The man said, "I have never told a lie; however, I have a condition. If you can answer three questions of mine correctly, I will give you my head. The king agreed. The first question was: "What is heavier than the earth? What is higher than the sky? What is swifter than the wind? What is more numerous than grass? The king answered: "Grief is heavier than the earth; the father is higher than the sky; thought is swifter than the wind; and worries are more numerous than grass. The second question was: "Who is the friend of the traveler? Who is the friend of the householder? Who is the friend of the sick? Who is the friend of the dying? The king answered: "The caravan is the friend of the traveler; the wife is the friend of the householder; the physician is the friend of the sick; and charity is the friend of the dying. The third question was: "What is the remedy for fire? What is the remedy for cold? What is the remedy for darkness? What is the remedy for death? The king answered: "Water is the remedy for fire; fire is the remedy for cold; light is the remedy for darkness; and there is no remedy for death. Having answered the questions correctly, the man gave him his head. The king took the head and returned to the sage. The sage was released from his curse and blessed the king. Thus ends the story of King Trivikramasena. Now hear the story of King Vikramāditya. Long ago, there was a king named Vikramāditya, the son of Gardabhilla, who was a great hero and a patron of the learned. Once, while wandering through the forest, he encountered a sage who was performing austerities. The sage said, "O King, I am hungry; give me some food. The king said, "I have nothing with me. The sage replied, "If you have no food, then give me your own body. The king agreed and prepared to sacrifice himself. At that moment, the goddess Lakṣmī appeared and said, "
Then the king honored him with a heap of jewels; having received those jewels, the mendicant returned to his own country, Kaśmīra.
"There, by the grace of the yakṣa, he lived happily, free from poverty. Having related this, the disciple spoke to that great sage.
"I heard this from that very renunciant. Thereupon, the sage, along with his other disciples, was struck with wonder for a long time.
Having spoken thus, Gomukha further addressed the son of the Lord of Vatsa: "Such indeed are these deeds of wicked women and of the Creator."
O God, the behaviors of the world are always diverse; hear now this other story of a woman who was a killer of eleven.
In Mālava, there lived a certain householder who was a village-dweller; to him was born a daughter, younger than two or three sons.
And as soon as she was born, his wife passed away; then, after a few days, his only son also died.
When he had perished, his brother was killed by a bull’s horn; then that householder gave his daughter the name Trimārikā.
"Three have been killed by this woman born with such characteristics," he said; therefore, in due time, [the king] asked his father for her when she had reached the prime of youth.
A certain wealthy son born in that village married Trimārikā; her father gave her to him after performing the wedding festivities according to tradition.
There she enjoyed herself with that husband for some time, but before long, her husband passed away.
In just a few days, that fickle woman took another husband; yet even he, her husband, met with misfortune in a very short time.
Then, intoxicated by her youth, she took a third husband; yet he too perished, for the husband of a woman who slays her husband meets his end like any other.
In this manner, her husbands died one after another in succession; consequently, she became widely known by the name Daśamārikā, "the Killer of Ten."
Then, having been rejected by her father because he had accepted another husband for her, and being shunned by the people, she remained in her father's house.
And once, a young traveler of handsome appearance, permitted by his father, entered there as a guest for the sake of staying one night.
Upon seeing him, the maiden who was to die on the tenth day became intent upon him; and the traveler, too, having seen the young woman, became filled with desire for her.
Then, having completely cast aside her shame, she said to her father: "Father, I choose this one traveler as my husband."
"If even this one should fail, then I shall take the vow myself"—as she was saying this, her father spoke to the traveler who was listening.
"Do not feel such great shame, my daughter; ten husbands of yours have died. Therefore, even if this one dies, people will laugh all the more."
Upon hearing that, the traveler too cast aside his shame and said: "I shall not die; for ten of my wives have already died in succession."
"We two are equal here through the touch of Dhūrjaṭi’s feet"—when this was said by that traveler, who there was not struck with wonder?
Having learned of this, the traveler was then taken as her husband by Daśamārikā, who had been granted permission by the assembled villagers.
And while she remained with him for some time, he too, overcome by a feverish chill, met his end along with her.
Then that laughing Eleven-Maiden, distressed even by the stones, went to the bank of the Ganges and took refuge in the religious life.
Having spoken thus and laughed, Gomukha said again to the son of the King of Vatsa: "Listen to this other story concerning those who live by taming elephants."
In a certain village there was a certain poor man who had a family; he possessed only one bull as his wealth in the house.
Devoid of livestock due to the lack of food, he even suffered along with his family; yet, though fasting himself, he did not sell that tamed horse out of greed.
Having gone before the Goddess dwelling on the Vindhya mountains, he prostrated himself upon a bed of darbha grass and performed austerities, abstaining from food out of a desire for his goal.
"Rise up! You have but one ox, yet you always possess wealth; therefore, by selling that very one, you shall live in constant happiness."
Having been thus instructed by the goddess in his dream, he woke up in the morning; rising and having performed some breaking of his fast, he returned to his own home.
Even having arrived, that undisciplined man was unable to sell the bull, thinking, "If this is sold, I shall be penniless and will never be able to subsist."
Then, on that occasion, a certain wise friend spoke to him, who was emaciated from fasting, regarding the instruction from the goddess he had received in his dream.
"There is only one tame animal for you; by selling it, you shall always have a livelihood. Thus was it said by the Goddess, yet, O fool, you did not understand that.
Sell this bull and provide for your family; then there will be another for you, and after that another, and then yet another.
Having been told this by that friend, the villager did exactly so; and by selling each bull one at a time, he lived constantly in happiness.
Thus, for everyone, the ritual procedure bears fruit according to the quality of the being; therefore, one should be a noble being, for prosperity does not choose one who is devoid of virtue.
Listen also to this other story of a rogue and a false minister: there was a king named Pṛthvīpati in a city in the Deccan.
In that kingdom there was a certain rogue who made his living by deceiving others; once, due to his great ambition, he became dissatisfied and thought to himself:
What is the use of such cunning for me, which achieves only food and the like? Why do I not practice that [cunning] by which such great prosperity is obtained?
Having reflected thus, he assumed the most magnificent attire of a merchant and approached the doorkeeper after going to the gate of the king.
Having entered inside through his mouth and presented the gift, he informed the king, saying, "I have a request to make in private."
The king, whose identity was concealed by his disguise and who was won over by the gift, agreed, saying "So be it," and having secured him in private, addressed him thus:

Thus did King Naravāhanadatta listen in succession to these stories told by Gomukha; and although he was eager for the upcoming marriage of Śaktiyaśas, who was standing nearby, he passed that night as if it were but a moment.
