When she had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta then married that maiden there according to the Gāndharva rite.
Having spent that night there with her in the proper manner, he spoke to his beloved in the morning, employing a stratagem to ascertain her family lineage.
"O beloved, listen; I shall tell you this unprecedented tale. Once, there was a sage named Brahmasiddhi in a certain penance grove."
And near the hermitage of that true sage who had attained perfection in yoga, there lived an old female jackal who had made her dwelling in a cave.
On a cloudy day, when she had gone out for food while fasting, a wild elephant—driven mad by the separation from his mate—came there to kill her.
Seeing that, the compassionate sage, possessed of knowledge, transformed that female jackal into a female elephant for the sake of bestowing grace upon both of them.
Then, seeing that female elephant, the elephant’s agitation subsided; he became devoted to her, and she too was released from death.
Then, while wandering with her, that elephant once entered an autumn lake choked with mud in order to fetch a lotus for her sake.
Today, stuck there in the mire, he was unable to move; he stood like a mountain whose wings have been shattered by the thunderbolt, having fallen from its place.
Seeing him thus dejected, that female jackal-elephant immediately sought refuge with another elephant and departed from there.
And at that very moment, his own female elephant, who had been separated from him earlier, arrived at that place by the power of fate while searching for her mate.
As soon as that noble-natured woman saw her husband swallowed by the mud, she then entered that very same lake-mud to follow after him.
At that time, the sage Brahmasiddhi, accompanied by his disciples, arrived along that very path; upon seeing him, he was filled with compassion.
And that great ascetic, by means of his disciples whose strength was produced through boons, raised up those two elephants under his control from within the mud of the lake.
Then, when that sage had departed, the couple—the female elephant and the bull elephant—having escaped both death and separation, wandered about as they pleased.
Thus, even animals of noble birth do not abandon their master or friend in times of calamity, O beloved; rather, they rescue them from that very distress.
But for those born of low birth, who are fickle-minded, neither affection nor even a sense of being a living being ever touches their hearts.
Having heard this from the daughter of the Lord of Vatsa, that divine maiden said to him, "It is exactly so; there is no doubt in this matter."
And my intention has been understood by you as you speak thus; therefore, O noble son, listen now to this story from me as well.
In Kānyakubja, there was a most excellent brahmin named Śūradatta, who was honored by King Bāhuśakti as the lord of a hundred villages.
He had a wife named Vasumatī, who regarded her husband as a deity; through her he begot an auspicious son named Vāmadatta.
Before long, Vāmadatta, who was beloved by his father, became proficient in all branches of knowledge and married a wife named Śaśiprabhā.
In time, when his father had gone to heaven followed by his wife, he entered into the life of a householder together with that same wife.
And she became his wife, acting according to her own will without his knowledge; by some stroke of fate, she had obtained the mastery of the *siddhi* of a *śākinī*.
Once, while he was staying in that royal camp for the purpose of serving the king, his own paternal uncle came from home and spoke to him in private.
"Our lineage is ruined, my son, since your wife was seen by me in the company of the buffalo-herder who belongs to you."
Having heard this from his paternal uncle and having settled him in the camp, Vāmadatta returned to his own home, accompanied only by his sword.
While he remained there in concealment, the buffalo-herder entered the flower garden at night and arrived at that very spot.
In an instant, his wife, eager for union with him there, approached that buffalo-herder, carrying various kinds of food in her hands.
Then, after he had finished eating, she departed with him toward Śasyana; seeing this, Vāmadatta ran after them with his weapon raised.
As he cried out, "O you two sinners, where are you going?", his wife saw him, stood up, and saying, "Shame on you, wretch!", she threw dust into his face.
Then that man Vāmadatta quickly became a buffalo; yet his memory was not lost even in that state.
Then that deceitful wife, having thrown him into the midst of the buffaloes, had him beaten with clubs by the buffalo-herder.
At that very moment, that cruel woman sold him, rendered helpless by his animal state, to a certain merchant who was seeking a buffalo.
Then, having been made to bear that burden and oppressed by the condition of being a buffalo, Vāmadatta was led to a village situated near the Gaṅgā.
In his house, his wife—though of very wicked conduct—was unexpectedly like a female serpent that has entered the interior of a thicket; for whose happiness could she be?
While he was thus reflecting there, weeping and deeply distressed, his body reduced to mere bones through the exhaustion of his burden, a certain yoginī beheld him.
Having understood that entire account through her supernatural knowledge, she, filled with compassion, sprinkled him with consecrated water and liberated him from his state as a buffalo.
Having brought him who had assumed human form to her own home, she gave him her daughter, a maiden named Kāntimatī.
"Having struck that first mare, Durbhāryā, with these, make her [your own]," he said, and gave him consecrated mustard seeds.
Then Vāmadatta, taking that beautiful new wife along with the mustard seeds, returned to his own home.
Having killed that buffalo-herder and having performed [the rite] there with mustard seeds, he turned his first wife, Vaḍavā, into a mare tied up in the stable.
And having given her seven blows with a club every day, he, bound by his vow, provided her with food for the sake of avenging his enmity.
While Vāmadatta was thus dwelling there together with his wife Kāntimatī, a certain guest arrived at their house.
And when he had begun to eat, Vāmadatta, remembering the blow from the club dealt by his wicked wife, quickly went out without having eaten.
And having given blows with a staff to her who was in the form of a mare, he entered there regularly and, his heart's desire fulfilled, enjoyed himself.
Then the guest, filled with wonder and curiosity, asked him: "Where did you go in such agitation, having abandoned your meal?"
Then Vāmadatta told that guest his own story there from the very beginning, and he too related his own to him.
"What is the use of this persistent obsession, by which your state as a beast has been taken from you? Propitiate that very mother-in-law of yours and bring about some improvement."
Having been addressed thus by that guest, Vāmadatta agreed, saying "So be it"; and having honored the guest with faith, he dismissed him in the morning.
Then, seeing that his mother-in-law, a perfected yoginī, had arrived home unexpectedly, he, desiring her favor, honored her and earnestly made this request.
Then Yogeśvarī, according to the prescribed rite, instructed him and his wife in the Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī mantra, preceded by initiation.
Then, having gone to Śrīparvata, he mastered that lore; and once it was perfected, she appeared in person and gave him an excellent sword.
And having obtained the sword, that accomplished Vāmadatta, the best of the Vidyādharas, became successful together with his wife Kāntimatī.
Then, by the power of his own supernatural attainments, he established that excellent city upon the peak of Mount Malaya known as Rajatakūṭa.
Then, in due course, a daughter named Lalitalocanā was born there to that lord of the Vidyādharas by his wife.
As soon as she was born, it was prophesied by a voice arising from the sky that she would become the wife of a noble universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
Know me, O Noble Son, to be one who has mastered her own science; I am devoted to you and have brought you here to this, my own Malaya mountain.
Having learned that she was a Vidyādharī of such a lineage, Naravāhanadatta then held his wife Lalitalocanā in high esteem, his heart filled with joy.
And he remained there with her; meanwhile, Vatsarāja and the others learned of his situation through the power of Ratnaprabhā’s magic science.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave: Then, having obtained that beautiful-eyed new wife, Naravāhanadatta remained on that Malaya mountain.
He sported with her in various forest regions, which were beautiful with trees in full bloom and delightful with the onset of spring.
And in a certain forest, while his beloved was wandering out of sight into the thicket in the course of gathering flowers for play, [he remained behind].
As he was wandering, he beheld a great lake of clear water, which, with the flowers fallen from the trees on its banks, resembled the sky filled with stars.
Until my beloved returns while gathering flowers, I shall bathe in this lake and sit for a moment on its shore.
Having reflected thus, he bathed, performed worship to the gods, and sat there upon a stone slab shaded by a sandalwood tree.
Staying there, he beheld the gait of the royal swans, which resembled her own, and heard the warbling of the female cuckoos among the mango vines, which was like her speech.
Beholding the eyes of the does, which resembled her own eyes, he remembered his beloved Madanamañcukā, who was far away.
As soon as he remembered her, he was tormented by the fire of desire and fainted; at that very moment, a certain eminent sage arrived there to bathe.
Seeing him in that state, the one named Piśaṅgajaṭa sprinkled him with sandalwood waters equal to the touch of his own beloved.
Then, seeing that he had awakened and was bowing down, the sage with divine vision said to him: "O son, you shall obtain whatever you desire; maintain your fortitude."
Therefore, everything will be attained; likewise, come to my hermitage and hear from me the story of Mṛgāṅkadatta, if it has not already been heard by you.
Having spoken thus, the sage bathed and led Naravāhanadatta to his own hermitage, and there he performed his daily rites with haste.
Having offered him hospitality with fruits and having himself eaten there, that Piṅgalajaṭa proceeded to tell him a story.
There is a city named Ayodhyā, renowned throughout the three worlds; in it, there was formerly a lord of the earth named Amaradatta.
To him, whose splendor was exceedingly radiant, there was a wife named Surataprabhā who was eternally devoted to him alone, just as Svāhā is to the fire.
To him was born a son named Mṛgāṅkadatta, who, like his own bow, was bent by a string that had reached its highest excellence.
And that prince had ten personal ministers: Pracaṇḍaśakti, Sthūlabāhu, and Vikramakesarī.
Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Meghabala, as well as Bhīmaparākrama, likewise Vimalabuddhi, Vyāghrasena, and Guṇākara.
And the tenth is named Vicitrakatha; they are all of noble lineage, young, heroic, wise, and seekers of their master's welfare.
While staying happily with them in his father’s house, Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta had not yet obtained a suitable wife.
And once, while they were alone, a minister named Bhīmaparākrama said to him: "Listen, O King, to what happened to me today during the night."
Today, while sleeping in my palace, I woke up unexpectedly in the night and saw a lion with sharp, adamantine claws rushing toward me.
When I rose with my knife raised, that lion then began to flee, and I pursued him with speed.
Having gone to the other side of the river, he extended his tongue toward me; I, however, cut that long tongue of his with my knife.
As soon as I had crossed that river by means of that very embankment-earth, that great lion was transformed into a deformed man.
And when asked by me, "Who are you?", that man replied: "I am a Vetāla, O hero; I have been gratified by your courage."
Having heard that, I asked him: "If this is so, then tell me: who will become the wife of my lord Mṛgāṅkadatta?"
Having heard these words of mine, the Vetāla then said: "In this city of Ujjayinī, there is a king known as Karmasena."
That king has a daughter who eclipses the Apsarases with her loveliness, appearing like a treasury of beauty deposited upon earth by the Creator himself.
She shall become his wife, named Śaśāṅkavatī; and by obtaining her, your master will rule over the kingdom of the earth.
Having said this, he vanished from my sight; "I am that very Vetāla, and I have come home"—this, O Lord, is what occurred to me during the night.
Having heard this from Bhīmaparākrama, Mṛgāṅkadatta summoned all his own ministers and had it recounted to them.
And he said to them, "Listen to what was seen by me in a dream: I know that we have all entered a certain great forest."
There, thirsty from traveling on the road and having with great difficulty reached water, we were surrounded by five men armed with weapons who rose up against us.
Having killed them, we wished to drink again as long as we were afflicted by thirst; yet there, we saw neither those men nor that water.
Then, having fallen into a state of distress, we beheld Maheśvara approaching unexpectedly, resplendent as the moon and mounted upon his bull.
As we bowed before him, he let fall a drop of tear from his right eye upon the ground; that became the ocean there.
Therefore, having fastened that auspicious pearl necklace which I had obtained around my neck, I drank that ocean from a human skull smeared with blood.
And at that very moment I awoke, and the night had passed; thus was the wondrous dream reported by Mṛgāṅkadatta.
While the others were rejoicing, the minister Vimalabuddhi said to him: "O King, you are blessed, for Hara has thus bestowed his grace upon you."
Because you obtained a string of pearls in a dream and drank the ocean, you will certainly enjoy the earth after winning Śaśāṅkavatī.
When Vimalabuddhi had said, "Others, however, lead somewhat to affliction," Mṛgāṅkadatta then spoke again to those ministers.
Just as the fruit of my dream, and just as Bhīmaparākrama has heard this from the Vetāla here, so too shall it come to pass.
Nevertheless, by the power of my wisdom, I shall obtain that daughter Śaśāṅkavatī from Karmasena, who relies on the strength of his army and his fortresses.
And the power of wisdom is the foremost means for accomplishing all tasks; therefore, listen to this story which I shall relate to you.
In Magadha there was a king named Bhadrabāhu; he had a minister called Mantragupta, the best among the wise.
Once, that king spoke privately to his own minister: "The daughter of the king who rules Vārāṇasī is named Anaṅgalīlā."
There is a woman who is the most beautiful in the three worlds, belonging to Dharmagopa; though I have requested her, that king does not grant her to me out of hatred.
And by the power of that elephant Bhadradanta, he is difficult to conquer; moreover, I have no desire to live without his daughter.
"Therefore, my friend, there is no remedy for this; tell me, what should be done? When the king had spoken thus, the minister replied to him.
"O King, is success achieved through valor alone and not through intelligence? Therefore, enough with this anxiety; by my own wit, I shall accomplish this for you."
Having spoken thus to the king, on the following day, that minister, accompanied by seven or five followers and wearing the garb of a Mahāvratika ascetic, went to Vārāṇasī.
There, those disciples in the guise of students proclaimed from all sides to the throng of people bowing in devotion, "This one is a perfected master."
And once, while wandering at night with his followers in order to discover the truth of the matter, he saw from a distance a woman who had come out of her house.
The wife of Hastipāla, her gait hurried by fear, was being led away somewhere by three or four men bearing weapons.
"Surely she has risen and departed; let us see where she goes. Having reflected thus, he followed her at his ease along with his attendants.
Having gone there, she entered that house; and having seen her own dwelling-place from afar, he returned to it at that very moment.
And in the morning, while Hastipāla was searching for his beloved who had gone there after her wealth was stolen, he skillfully dispatched his wandering attendants to her presence.
Seeing him, they then neutralized that poison—which had been consumed through the suffering of not attaining her—by means of their own spells, as if out of compassion.
"Come to our teacher's side; he is a man of knowledge and knows everything. Having said this, they brought him into the presence of that minister.
And that elephant-keeper, having seen him adorned with the ornaments of his vow, bowed at his feet and asked about the news concerning his wife.
That minister, having meditated falsely, declared with signs of recognition the place where she had been taken by other men during the night.
Then, having bowed to him and departed together with the city guards, that elephant-keeper reached that place and surrounded it.
He slew those wicked men who had abducted his wife, and he recovered his own woman along with her ornaments and her wealth.
On the second day, he arrived in the morning, bowed, and having taken his place, extended an invitation for a meal to that impostor ascetic.
And for him, who desired to enter a house and who professed to be an eater only at night, they prepared food in the elephant stable at twilight.
By the power of his mantra, the practitioner of spells took all that had been placed within the bamboo tube, carried it away in secret, and having arrived there, ate it along with his followers.
Then, when the elephant-keeper had departed and the others there were asleep, he inserted him into a bamboo tube of the elephant Bhadradanta.
Having spent that entire night there with a snake at his ear while he slept, he returned to his own country, Magadha; and by that [snake], the elephant was killed.
When that excellent minister had slain Dharmagopa’s elephant as if it were his own pride, King Bhadrabāhu rejoiced.
Then he dispatched Anaṅgalīlā, that maiden, as an envoy to Vārāṇasī to request [the hand] of Dharmagopa.
He too, weakened by the absence of that elephant, gave her to him; for kings who know the proper time adopt the conduct of a reed.
Thus, by means of that very wisdom, King Bhadrabāhu attained the amorous dalliance of that minister, Mantragupta.
To Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was saying, "Therefore, I too shall obtain that wife by means of my intellect," his minister Vicitrakatha replied:
Everything will be accomplished for you through the favor of the necklace seen in your dream; for what could the unfailing grace of the deities not achieve?
And so, listen here to a tale being related by me: there was once a king named Bhadrākṣa in the city of Takṣaśilā.
Desiring a son, he worshipped Lakṣmī on the sword day after day with one hundred and eight white lotuses.
Once, while that king was worshipping and maintaining his vow of silence, by chance one lotus was missing as he mentally counted them.
He then tore open his own heart-lotus and gave it to the goddess; and she, being pleased, granted him a boon that would bestow upon him a son who would rule the entire earth.
Having restored the king's body to its uninjured state, he departed from sight. Then, a son was born to that king by his chief queen.
Because he was born through the grace of the lotus of the heart, the king gave that son of auspicious marks the name Puṣkarākṣa.
And in due course, having consecrated that virtuous son who had reached youth upon the throne, King Bhadrākṣa retired to the forest.
Puṣkarākṣa, having obtained the kingdom, worshipped Hara every day; once, after performing his adoration, he made a request of him regarding his wife.
"O son, everything you desire shall be accomplished," he then heard that voice rising from the sky.
Then, filled with joy and having gained confidence, that king, while remaining in his palace, once went to a forest of deer for the diversion of hunting.
There, seeing a young camel engaged in devouring a pair of serpents that were intent on copulation, he, overcome with grief, struck it down.
As soon as he was struck down, having abandoned that body of a camel and become a Vidyādhara, he joyfully spoke to Puṣkarākṣa:
"You have done me a favor; therefore, listen to what I say to you: O King, there is a preeminent Vidyādhara named Raṅkumālin."
Seeing that youth, the daughter of an eminent Vidyadhara named Tārāvalī, being herself filled with passion and enamored of his beauty, chose him for herself.
And when they had performed their marriage according to her own wish, her father, out of anger, cast upon them a curse that would cause separation for a certain period of time.
Then Tārāvalī and Raṅkumālin, that couple whose love was ever-expanding, wandered through various regions of their own domain.
Once, by that curse, they both fell from each other's sight and were born separated from one another somewhere in the depths of a forest.
Then Tārāvalī, searching for her husband, eventually reached a forest frequented by perfected seers on the shore of the western ocean.
There she saw a single great rose-apple tree in full bloom, which seemed to comfort her with its sweet humming, as if out of affection.
And assuming the form of a female bee, she sat down upon a certain flower on that tree to rest as a drinker of nectar.
Seeing her husband returned there after a long time by a stroke of fate, she immediately shed a flower, moistened by the semen falling from her in a surge of joy.
Having abandoned her body as a female bee and departed, she was reunited with him, her husband Raṅkumālin, who was searching for her, just as moonlight is united with the moon.
Then, having gone with him to her own abode, she became impregnated by his seed; from that, a fruit arose from a jambu flower.
And from that fruit, in due course of time, a daughter was born; for indeed, the potency of divine beings never goes to waste.
Once, the sage named Vijitāśva came there for the sake of fruits and roots; and a ripe fruit from a jambu tree fell upon him.
Then, emerging from that fallen and shattered [object], a divine maiden appeared and, bowing low with humility, paid homage at the feet of that sage.
Having seen her with his divine vision and understood the truth of the matter, the sage, filled with wonder, led Vinayavatī to his own hermitage and gave her that name.
There, in the hermitage of that sage, she gradually attained maturity; and while traveling through the sky, I saw her, Vinayavatī, endowed with modesty.
Then, deluded by pride in my physical form and by intoxication, I approached her and proceeded to seize her by force, even though she was unwilling.
At that moment, O King, that sage—having been informed by her as she was crying out—became enraged; having approached, he who had conquered the Asuras pronounced a curse upon me.
"O you who are proud of your beauty, become a camel despised in all your limbs; when your death is brought about by King Puṣkarākṣa, you shall be released from the curse."
"He alone shall be the husband of Vinayavatī"—thus was I cursed by the sage, and so I was born as a young camel upon this earth for her sake.
And today, through you, the end of that curse has been brought about; therefore, go from here to that forest situated on the far shore of the western ocean, known by the name Surabhimāruta.
"Obtain that divine wife, who shall take away the pride of Śrī’s beauty," having said this to Puṣkarākṣa, the Vidyādhara went to heaven.
Puṣkarākṣa, too, having gone to his own city and entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, mounted a horse and set out alone during the night.
Proceeding by stages, he reached the shore of the western ocean once more and reflected there: "How shall I cross the sea?"
Then he saw there an empty temple of Caṇḍikā; having entered it, he bathed and bowed down before that goddess.
Taking a lute that had been placed there by someone, he respectfully began to play it for the queen with his own songs.
And being pleased by his lute-playing, she led him, while he slept there that night, across the ocean by means of her own host of spirits.
Then, having woken up in the morning, the king saw himself standing within the forest on the shore of the ocean, and not in that temple of Caṇḍikā.
Rising up in amazement, he wandered about and beheld the hermitage, which seemed to bow in greeting through its trees bent low with the weight of fruit as if out of hospitality.
Entering there, he saw the sage standing surrounded by his disciples, as if welcoming him with the warbling of the birds.
Having approached, the king paid homage at the feet of that ṛṣi; and the wise sage, having offered him hospitality, spoke to him.
"O lotus-eyed one, she for whose sake you have come has gone for a moment to gather firewood and such; therefore, wait here for now."
"O King, marry that former wife this very day!"—being thus addressed by the sage, Puṣkarākṣa reflected.
By good fortune, it is that very sage, Vijitāsu; and this is that same forest. Surely, O Queen, I have been delivered from the great ocean.
"This Citrā has been described by this sage as my former wife"—reflecting thus, the king was delighted and questioned that sage.
“Blessed One, please tell me how she was my wife in a former life. Then that sage said, “Listen, if you have curiosity.”
In former times, there was a merchant named Dharmasena in Tāmraliptī, and he had a beautiful wife whose name was Vidyullekhā.
That merchant, robbed by thieves by fate and struck by weapons, being on the verge of death, went out with his wife to enter the fire.
And suddenly, both the husband and wife beheld a pair of swans of beautiful form arriving through the sky.
Then, with their minds fixed upon one another, those two royal swans entered the fire and died; they were both reborn again as husband and wife.
Once, during the rainy season, while the two were staying in their nest in a date-palm tree at night, a whirlwind uprooted that tree and separated them.
In the morning, while the storm had subsided, that swan searched for his mate in the lakes and at the ends of the quarters, but he did not find her anywhere.
Then, afflicted by love and having conceived a longing for another female swan on the road, he went to Lake Mānasa, which is frequented by swans at that time of year.
Having found his own female swan there and having waited until the arrival of the rainy season, he went with her to a certain mountain peak to sport together.
There, having taken up his slain female swan and seeing that it was dead, he observed many armed men approaching from afar along the path.
The hunter, having taken up that slain female swan and seeing from afar several armed men approaching along the path, [reflected].
Quickly cutting [the stalks] with her knife, she covered her with grass on the ground and placed Haṃsī there, thinking, "Lest these people see her and carry her off."
When those men had departed, that female swan approached the hunter who desired to seize her; while he was looking on, she plucked out his grass.
Having regained life through the juice of the "life-restoring" herb (*mṛtasaṃjīvanauṣadhi*) that had been cut within that grass, he flew up into the sky and departed from there.
Meanwhile, that swan, her husband, having gone to the shore of a certain lake, fell down bewildered among a flock of swans, his mind fixed solely on her as he gazed at her.
At that very moment, a certain fisherman cast his net, captured all those swans, and indeed sat down for a meal within a moment.
Meanwhile, having arrived at that very spot, the female swan, searching for her mate, saw him caught in the net; distressed, she gazed toward the quarters of the sky.
Then, as someone who had come there to the edge of the lake to bathe was about to enter, he saw a jeweled necklace placed upon a garment.
Having gone there, while he looked on, she took that necklace and, showing it to the fisherman, departed slowly through the sky.
Seeing the female swan with the necklace held in her beak, the fisherman abandoned that net of birds and, taking up a cudgel, pursued her.
The female swan went to the top of the mountain and placed the necklace far away; out of greed for it, the fisherman also proceeded to climb up there.
Seeing that, the female swan went quickly to her husband, who was fastened to a tree, and struck with her beak the monkey who was sleeping beside him in the eye.
Struck by the monkey and terrified, he fell and tore through the net; consequently, all those swans emerged from it.
Then, having come together and related their respective adventures to one another, the two swans, husband and wife, rejoiced and sported as they pleased.
While searching there, that man found the fisherman who had arrived with the necklace, lured by his desire for the bird; he recovered the necklace that had been stolen from him.
Having taken the necklace from the hand of that fisherman, who was betrayed by his own fear, the man severed the fisherman's right hand with a knife.
And those two swans, having made a single lotus into a parasol, rose from the lake at midday and moved through the sky.
In an instant, those two birds reached the bank of a certain river, where a sage was seated, intent upon the worship of Dhūrjaṭi.
There, as the couple was passing by, they were struck simultaneously with a single arrow by a certain hunter and fell to the ground.
And then that lotus used as a parasol fell upon the top of the Śiva-liṅga while the sage was worshipping it.
Then that hunter, having seen them, took the male swan for himself and gave the female swan to the sage; he, in turn, worshipped Śiva with her.
O King Puṣkarākṣa, by the power of that very lotus which fell upon the summit of that Liṅga, you have now been born as a swan in this lineage.
And this very Haṃsī was born in the lineage of the Vidyādharas as Vinayavatī; for Hara was especially worshipped by her with her own flesh.
Having been told thus by the sage Vijitāsu that she was his former wife, King Puṣkarākṣa spoke to him again.
O Blessed One, how did that act of entering the fire—which destroys the flood of sins—result in our birth as birds? What was the fruit of it for us two?
To the king who had spoken thus, the sage replied: "Whatever state a living being has cultivated within itself, that very form he attains at death."
For instance, in the city of Ujjayinī, there was formerly a young Brahmin girl named Lāvaṇyamañjarī who was a lifelong celibate.
Upon seeing the young Brahmin named Kamalodaya, her heart suddenly went out to him, and she was consumed by the fire of love.
Without abandoning her own vow, and being absorbed in meditation on the enjoyment of that [union], she went to the bank of the Gandhavatī and gave up her life at the sacred ford.
Why did she not become attached to enjoyments through that very meditation? For in the city of Ekalavyā, she was born as a beautiful courtesan named Rūpavatī.
And by the power of her vows at sacred fords, she herself, being one who remembers her past lives, [bestowed herself] upon the twice-born Jāpaka, Coḍakarṇa, as an incidental consequence.
He related the secret account of his own previous births, along with the instruction for one who practices the rite of recitation with a one-pointed mind.
And previously, even that courtesan attained a blessed state because her resolve was pure; for in this world, a king—or indeed anyone—attains the very nature of that upon which his mind is fixed.
Having spoken thus, the sage dismissed the king to bathe, and he himself performed the midday ritual ablution.
That king Puṣkarākṣa also went to the bank of a river in the forest, and there he saw Vinayavatī gathering flowers.
Shining with her own form like the radiance of the sun, she had entered out of curiosity a dense forest never seen before.
While he was reflecting with eager curiosity, "Who might this be?", she, seated there, spoke confidently to her friend.
"Friend, that Vidyādhara who formerly desired to abduct me has today come to me, freed from his curse, and announced here my recovery of my husband."
Having heard that, her friend replied to the hermit maiden: "This is true; for this very morning, while I was listening, Muñjakeśa [spoke]..."
Thus addressed by the sage Vijitāsu, his own disciple said: "Go and bring Tārāvalī and Raṅkumālin here quickly."
"Indeed, today the marriage of their daughter Vinayavatī with King Puṣkarākṣa will take place here, my child."
Having been addressed thus by his preceptor, Muñjakeśa replied, "So be it," and departed. Therefore, come now, friend; let us go to the hermitage.
When she had spoken thus, Vinayavatī then departed from there; and Puṣkarākṣa heard that from afar, remaining unobserved.
As if to plunge into a river to escape the torment of the blazing fire of desire, that king returned once more to the hermitage of Vijitāsu.
There Tārāvalī and Aṅkumālin met him; they paid homage to him as he bowed down, and the ascetics surrounded him.
Then, upon the sacrificial altar illuminated by his own splendors, the great seer sat like a second embodied Fire who had conquered his vital breaths.
He bestowed Vinayavatī upon that king, and Raṅkumālin gave him a divine chariot that travels through the sky.
"Rule over the earth bounded by the four oceans together with her"—thus did the great sage, having conquered the Asuras, grant him this boon.

Then, with her permission, that king Puṣkarākṣa, taking his new bride and mounting that divine chariot which travels through the sky, crossed the ocean and immediately went from there to his own city, appearing like the rising of the moon to the eyes of his subjects.
And having conquered the earth there by the power of his chariot and attained universal sovereignty, he dwelt together with Vinayavatī, enjoying pleasures for a long time.

Thus, even a task that is extremely difficult to accomplish succeeds spontaneously when the deities are disposed to bestow grace; therefore, O Lord, by the favor of the beloved of the Mountain-Daughter seen in your dream, your own desired goal shall also be achieved before long.
Having heard this wondrous tale from his minister, Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta became eager to find Śaśāṅkavatī; together with his own ministers, he set his mind upon going to Ujjayinī.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave: In this manner, Mṛgāṅkadatta, desiring to obtain that Śaśāṅkavatī—the daughter of King Karmasena who had been described by the Vetāla—remained there.
He consulted with his ministers regarding a secret departure from his own city to go to Ujjayinī in the guise of a Mahāvratika ascetic.
And that prince privately commanded his minister Bhīmaparākrama to collect a skull-topped staff, a begging bowl, and other such items.
He brought that [gift] to his own house, where it was soon discovered by the chief minister of King Mṛgāṅkadatta’s father.
And at that moment, as he was suddenly walking along the roof of the palace, Mṛgāṅkadatta spat out the essence of his betel.
And by chance, it fell upon the head of his father’s minister, who was traveling along that path out of sight below.
Having realized that Mṛgāṅkadatta had spat at him, the minister, having performed his ablutions, suppressed his indignation and anger within his heart.
Then, by the power of fate, on another day, King Amaradatta, the father of Mṛgāṅkadatta, was afflicted with cholera.
Then, having found an opportunity, the minister, who had been granted immunity from fear, spoke suddenly to the king in private about him being afflicted by a sudden disease.
"O Lord, an act of black magic was commenced in the house of Bhīmaparākrama by Mṛgāṅkadatta; for that reason, you were afflicted."
I have learned this from the mouth of my spy, and it is now seen before my very eyes; therefore, expel him from the country, just as one drives a disease out of the body.
Having heard that, the king was greatly agitated and dispatched his own general to the house of Bhīmaparākrama to investigate the matter.
And having obtained that mass of hair and the other items, the commander-in-chief brought them back immediately and showed them directly to the king.
"Let that son of mine, greedy for the kingdom and treacherous, be exiled from this city this very day without delay by you, together with his ministers."
Then the king, having become enraged, commanded his general in this manner; for what master, once reassured, does not recognize the treachery of his own ministers?
Then that general, having gone and reported the king’s command to him, escorted Mṛgāṅkadatta along with his ministers out of the city.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, having obtained the desired success, was filled with joy; having worshipped Vināyaka and mentally prostrated before his parents, he then—
Having departed from Ayodhyā and traveled a great distance, he spoke to those ten ministers, headed by Pracaṇḍaśakti, who were his companions.
There is a great lord of the Kirātas named Śaktirakṣita; he is my fellow student in the sciences and has been my friend since childhood.
For previously, when his father was taken prisoner in battle, he offered himself here as a substitute for his father's sake, in order to secure his release through a vow.
When his father had died, he was installed in the paternal kingdom by my father, who had been urged by me, acting on his own authority as a kinsman born of the same lineage.
Therefore, friend, let us first go to his presence; from there, we shall proceed in due course to Ujjayinī for the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī.
Having spoken thus, accompanied by those ministers who replied, "So be it," he set out from there and reached a great forest in the evening.
In that place devoid of trees and water, he reached with great difficulty a single lake where a lone withered tree grew upon its bank.
Having performed the evening rites and drunk water there, he, being weary, slept with his ministers beneath that very same withered tree.
And at night, on a moon-bright night, he woke up and saw that withered tree gradually becoming filled with leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Seeing that its ripe fruits were falling at that very moment, he woke [the king] and showed that wonder to his ministers.
Then, together with those who were filled with wonder and hungry, he ate the fruits of that tree, which possessed a most delicious flavor.
And while they were all eating there and watching, that young Brahmin suddenly turned into a withered tree.
Then, questioned by the astonished Mṛgāṅkadatta, he said: "There was a certain excellent Brahmin named Damadhīra in Ayodhyā."
I am his son, named Śrutadhi; having lost his wife during a famine, he wandered with me and reached this land.
Having obtained five fruits given here by someone, he, emaciated by hunger, gave three to me and set two aside for himself.
Then, when he had gone to the lake waters to bathe, I ate all those fruits here and feigned sleep.
Then, having returned from his bath and perceiving me standing there like a log under a disguise, he cursed me: "Become a withered tree right here on the shore of this lake!"
"And at night, you shall have flowers and fruit on the Candravatī; by satisfying guests with those fruits, you will eventually be released from the curse."
Thus cursed by my father, I immediately became like a withered tree; and today, having had its fruit enjoyed by you, I am finally released from that curse after a long time.
When Śrutadhi had thus related his own story and questioned him in turn, Mṛgāṅkadatta then informed him of his own adventures.
Then that twice-born man, Śrutadhi, who was without kinsmen and well-versed in the science of polity, chose from Mṛgāṅkadatta the boon of becoming his follower.
Then, having passed the night, at dawn Mṛgāṅkadatta set out from there accompanied by his ministers and that Śrutadhi.
And as he was going, having reached the forest named Karimaṇḍita, he saw five men with abundant hair and hideous forms.
Approaching him with humility, they spoke to him, their wonder having been aroused: "We were born in the city of Kāśī as Brahmins who subsist on cows."
"Scorched by droughts from that region, we have come to this forest, which abounds in grass, along with our cows during a time of famine."
And here we have obtained a rejuvenating elixir from the water of the pond, which is constantly infused with the three myrobalans falling from the trees growing upon its banks.
"May they always drink that [water] of ours; for these five hundred years have passed while we, though living on milk, have remained in this uninhabited forest."
Therefore, O Lord, we are such as you are now—your guests; since we have been reached by you through destiny, please come to our hermitage.
Thus entreated by them, Mṛgāṅkadatta went with his followers to that hermitage and spent that day there, subsisting on milk and other such food.
Setting out from there in the morning, he beheld various other sights of curiosity and reached the territory of the Kirātas in due course.
And there he dispatched Śrutadhi to inform his master of this arrival, regarding that friend, the Kirāta lord Śaktirakṣita.
Having learned of this, the Lord of the Kirātas went out before him and, bowing low, led Mṛgāṅkadatta along with his ministers into his own city.
Then, having been thus attended to by him, Mṛgāṅkadatta remained there for several days, having declared the reason for his arrival.
Having stationed Śaktirakṣita there, ready to assist him whenever the time for his own task arrived, the prince took his leave.
Then, on an auspicious day, he set out again toward Ujjayinī; his mind was captivated by Śaśāṅkavatī, and he traveled with twelve companions.
And as he went along, having reached a forest, he saw a certain ascetic seated at the foot of a tree, covered in ashes, wearing a deerskin, and bearing matted locks.
"O Blessed One, why do you stay here alone in this forest where there is no hermitage? Thus he approached him and questioned him along with his followers.
Then that ascetic spoke to him: "I am a disciple of the great guru named Śuddhakīrti, who has attained mastery over a multitude of various mantras."
Once, on one occasion, I happened to enter into a state of self-possession after encountering a certain kṣatriya youth endowed with auspicious marks.
That prince, being possessed, was questioned by me regarding various kinds of perfected medicinal herbs and fields of elixirs; having described them, he then spoke as follows.
In this northern region, there stands a solitary śiṃśapā tree; and beneath it, in the Vindhya forest, lies a great palace of the lord of the nāgas.
And that water, though covered by moist dust, is clearly perceived at midday by pairs of swans sporting there along with water-fowl and cranes.
There dwells a powerful and excellent nāga named Pārāvata; he possesses an unsurpassed sword obtained from the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Whatever man obtains that sword named Vaidūryakānti becomes a lord of the Siddhas and wanders about unconquered.
When it was said, "And that sword is obtained by heroes with the aid of companions," I then performed its dismissal by means of that [mantra] infused [into me].
Turning away from everything else and seeking that sword, O Great Earth, I wandered about; failing to find my companions, I became exhausted and came here to die.
Having heard this from that ascetic, Mṛgāṅkadatta said to him, "I am your companion, along with my ministers."
And having welcomed him with joy, that ascetic went together with him and his followers to the abode of that nāga by means of a foot-ointment.
There, having established Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others at night within the quarters secured by spells and reached through supernatural power, he stationed them with consecrated [substances].
Having made it manifest with mustard seeds and having scattered them so that the water was covered with their dust, he proceeded to perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *nāgadamanī* mantras.
By the power of his mantra, he conquered obstacles such as portents and clouds; then, from that śiṃśapā tree, a divine woman emerged.
As if reciting a spell of delusion with the tinkling of her jeweled ornaments, she approached him in an instant and pierced his heart with a sidelong glance.
And she, whose firm breasts were pressed against him, deprived him of his composure; as he forgot the mantras, she caused the sacrificial vessel to fall from his hand.
And at that moment, having found an opportunity, that serpent named Pārāvata rose up from his abode like a rain-cloud at the end of an eon.
Seeing him, who was terrible with flames of fire from his eyes and fierce in his roar, that ascetic—bereft of his celestial nymph—met his death by the bursting of his heart.
When he had perished, the Naga, his transformation having subsided, cursed Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others who had assisted him there.
"Since you have done this without cause by breaking the community, you shall therefore remain separated from one another for some time."
When the Naga had vanished after saying this, they all at that moment found their vision obstructed by darkness and their power of hearing sounds destroyed.
Separated from one another by the power of the curse, Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others wandered here and there, crying out and searching for each other.
And then, when the confusion of night had passed, Mṛgāṅkadatta wandered here and there in that forest, remaining there without his ministers.
When two or three months had thus passed, the Brahmin Śrutadhi, while searching for him, suddenly arrived in his presence.
Falling at his feet with tears, Śrutadhi comforted him—who was full of respect and was asking for news of his own minister—and spoke to him thus:
"I have not seen them, my lord, but I know they will go; Ujjayinī is the city you must reach, for that indeed is your destination."
Having been thus urged by him who had spoken these words, Mṛgāṅkadatta then set out slowly for Ujjayinī accompanied by him.
After traveling for a few days along a path where his arrival was unexpected, he joyfully encountered his own minister, Vimalabuddhi.
Embracing him as he bowed down with eyes brimming with tears at the sight of him, and seating him, he asked after the welfare of his other ministers.
Then Vimalabuddhi said to that beloved servant: "I do not know, O King, which among them has gone where due to the curse of the Naga."
But listen as I explain how I know that you will attain them: at that time, being dragged far away by the serpent-noose, I was wandering about.
Exhausted in the eastern part of the forest, I was led by a certain holy man to the hermitage of the great seer Brahmadaṇḍin.
There, my fatigue dispelled by the fruits and water given by that seer, I wandered near the hermitage and beheld a vast cave.
Having entered that [city] out of curiosity and seen a jeweled palace within, I proceeded to look through the lattice windows there.
Meanwhile, a woman stood inside, spinning a wheel together with bees; then those bees settled upon it, while a bull and a donkey remained there in their separate places.
And having drunk the foam of milk and blood vomited by those two, they became white and black respectively according to their source; thus born, they became spider-like weavers of webs.
Then, with their own excrement and those two kinds of substances, various nets were fashioned, joined together with both beautiful flowers and poisonous flowers.
Stuck in those snares as they pleased like fishermen, they were bitten by a great serpent that approached with its white and black heads.
Then, having been thrown into various jars by that woman, they emerged once again, clinging to those very same nooses in exactly the same manner as before.
Then, due to the terror caused by the poison, as those trapped in that web began to shriek, others who were situated in other webs also started to cry out.
Then, by a certain compassionate ascetic staying there, whose meditation was broken by that sound, a flame was released from his forehead.
Their bonds having been burnt away by her, they entered the hollow coral staff and merged into the radiant light situated above it.
Meanwhile, that woman had gone somewhere together with the bull, the ram, and the donkey; seeing this, I remained there in wonder while wandering about.
There I saw a charming lotus pond, which seemed to be calling out to me with its lotuses resounding with the humming of bees, as if saying, "Come here too and look!"
Seated on its bank, as I gazed upon the great forest, I saw a certain hunter there within the forest through the opening of the net.
Having obtained ten arms and having grown up as a lion cub, he was exiled from that forest out of anger because he was no longer under control.
That lion, too, having heard the sound of lions within the forest, was going there when his arms were scattered by a great wind.
Then, having been approached by a man with a protruding belly who placed his arms around him, he was escorted and went to that forest for the sake of the lioness.
Having experienced suffering there in the depths of the forest for her sake, he recovered her who had previously been taken away; united with her, he returned to his own forest.
Upon seeing Karimardana arrived with his wife, the hunter handed over the forest to him and departed from there.
Having observed this as well, I then went to the hermitage and related both of those great wonders to Brahmadaṇḍin.
Then, out of affection, the sage who knows the three periods of time addressed me thus: "You are blessed; everything has been shown to you by the gracious Lord."
The woman whom you saw there is illusion (māyā), and that which was whirled by her is the wheel of saṃsāra; those who were bees are the living beings.
Dharma and Adharma take on the forms of a bull and a donkey respectively; good deeds and evil deeds rest upon them in the form of the milk and blood they have vomited.
Having served that which arises from their own respective substrates and becoming white with impurity, they are twofold, resembling spiderwebs, and are supported by their own inherent power.

Having fashioned two kinds of nets and snares, such as those consisting of children and so forth, which resemble flowers—both beautiful flowers and poisonous flowers—and which are attended by pleasure and pain;
Attached to those [objects] according to their respective natures, O son, they were struck down by Time in the form of a serpent through its auspicious and inauspicious mouths, each as was fitting.
Then, by means of her illusory power (*māyā*), she assumed the form of a woman and cast them into various wombs in the shape of jars; having been thus cast in, they rose up once again.
They fall into two kinds of forms, white and black, which are equal; they are caught in the snares of the net of sons and so forth, which are bound up with pleasure and pain.
Then Kṛṣṇā, bound by her own snares and afflicted by the poison of sorrow, began to cry out in distress, seeking refuge in the Supreme Lord.
Seeing that, those white creatures too became filled with world-weariness; remaining within their own web, they began to cry out to that very lord.
Then, having awakened, that god in the form of an ascetic caused all their bonds to be consumed by the blazing fire of his knowledge.
Having entered the solar orb, which has the form of a staff made of coral, they have taken refuge in that supreme abode situated above it.
And that illusion, together with cyclic existence in its wheel-like form, has perished, along with the phenomena of merit and demerit that take the forms of bulls and donkeys.
Thus do living beings wander in saṃsāra through their own white and black karmas; yet, it is only through the propitiation of Īśvara that they are liberated.
Thus, for the sake of pacifying your delusion, this has been shown to you by the Lord; now hear that which was seen by you in the water of the pond.
The Blessed One has created this for you, like a reflection appearing in water, to reveal the future destiny of Mṛgāṅkadatta.
For he, like a young lion cub, was nurtured by ten ministers who were like his own arms, growing from what resembled a forest.
Exiled out of anger by his father, who was like a hunter, he attained fame arising from the Avanti country, which is comparable to another forest.
Having heard [the news] from Śaśāṅkavatī as if from his own lioness, he rushed forward; however, by a serpent's curse, he was deprived of the arms of his ministers by a wind.
Then, by the Leader (Vināyaka) there, who had assumed the form of Lambodara, his arm was reattached and he was restored to his natural state.
Then, having gone there and endured extreme suffering, he returned here, bringing with him that lioness Śaśāṅkavatī whom he had found elsewhere.
Then, seeing that lion Mṛgāṅkadatta together with his wife, who had arrived nearby having slain the elephant of his enemy by means of magic power;
Having personally surrendered his entire forest in his own country to him, that father of his, who resembled a hunter, departed for the penance grove.
Thus has the Lord shown you what was already accomplished and what is yet to come: that your master shall regain his ministers, his wife, and his kingdom.
Thus enlightened by that best of sages, I regained my fortitude and departed from that hermitage; then, proceeding slowly, O Lord, I have today met with you.
Therefore, having obtained ministers headed by Pracaṇḍaśakti, you will surely attain your desired goal, for Vighneśvara has been propitiated by the worship performed at the time of your departure.

Having thus heard this wonderful account for a moment from his own minister Vimalabuddhi, Mṛgāṅkadatta was filled with satisfaction; yet, having deliberated further with him regarding the acquisition of another minister, he set out toward the city of Avanti in due course for the sake of his own mission.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave: Then, accompanied by Vimalabuddhi and Śrutadhi, he set out toward Ujjayinī for the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī.
On the way, Mṛgāṅkadatta reached the Narmadā river, whose vine-like arms were the undulating waves and which was white with shimmering foam.
Seeing him, she—whose mind was fickle—was as if dancing with joy and laughing, thinking, "By good fortune, this man has become one whose ministers are reunited."
And while he had descended into it to bathe, a certain Śabara king named Māyāvaṭu arrived there to bathe as well.
As he was bathing, three water-demons suddenly rose up there and simultaneously seized the Bhilla, whose attendants had fled in terror.
Seeing that, Mṛgāṅkadatta drew his sword, entered within, slew those water-demons, and liberated the lord of the Bhillas.
Freed from the fear of being seized by him, the Bhilla king rose up from the water and, falling at his feet, questioned the prince.
"Tell me, who are you that has been brought here by the Creator for the protection of my life? And whose virtuous father’s lineage has been adorned by you?"
"Or what region, blessed by its merits, will you visit? Having said this, he heard the entire account of Śrutadhi's life in full.
Bowing down even more deeply to him, that lord of the Śabaras spoke again: "In that case, I shall be your helper here in this desired undertaking, just as you have commanded."
"O Lord, together with my friend Durgapiśāca, the lord of the Mātaṅgas, show favor to me, your servant; come to my home."
Having thus entreated Mṛgāṅkadatta with various affectionate words, that lord of the Śabaras then led him to his own forest settlement.
And there, the entire village community honored the prince with all their respective riches, attending upon him in a fitting manner.
That king of the Mātaṅgas also approached him there and greeted him with joy; having become his servant, he bowed his head to the ground before the one who had given him his life and friendship.
Then, out of consideration for that Bhilla chief Māyāvaṭu, Mṛgāṅkadatta remained right there for some days.
And once, while he was staying there, that lord of the Śabaras began a game of dice together with his own chamberlain, Caṇḍaketu.
While the clouds were thundering in the sky, that king Māyāvaṭu rose up to see the domestic peacocks dancing.
Then that doorkeeper, who was fond of gambling, said to him: "O King, what is the use of watching these people whose dancing is so poorly trained?"
"I have a peacock in my house that does not exist anywhere else on earth; if you are a connoisseur of it, I shall show it to you tomorrow morning."
Having heard that, and having said to the doorkeeper, "He must by all means be shown to me," the king performed his daily duties.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, having heard all that there, rose up with his followers in the same manner and performed his daily duties, such as bathing and eating.
Then, when night had arrived and blinding darkness had spread, his limbs were smeared with musk and he was dressed in two blue garments.
That prince, for the sake of heroic conduct according to his own purpose, went out alone from his sleeping quarters with sword in hand, leaving behind his sleeping attendants.
And as he was wandering there, he was struck shoulder to shoulder by some man coming along the path who, due to the darkness, had not seen him.
Then, becoming enraged, he overcame him and challenged him to battle; and that mature man, being struck, spoke words appropriate for the occasion.
Why do you grieve without even investigating? If you are to investigate, then the Lord of Night should be questioned, by whom this night was not made manifest.
Or perhaps it was created by Dhātṛ himself, for whom there is no further authority here; he has fashioned such a cause in the darkness that enmities arise.
Having heard that and saying "It is true," Mṛgāṅkadatta was pleased by the words of the city-dweller, and he asked that man, "Who are you?"
"I am a thief," he said; but that man also spoke falsely, saying, "Bring me your hand; you are my student."
Having formed a friendship and desiring to test him, Mṛgāṅkadatta walked along with him and reached an overgrown old well covered with grass.
Having entered there with that man through the tunnel, he went and reached the inner apartments of King Māyāvaṭu.
There, having seen him by the light of a lamp, he recognized that man; meanwhile, it was the doorkeeper Caṇḍaketu, and not a thief.
But the doorkeeper, who was secretly in love with the king’s wife, did not recognize him as he stood in a corner of dim light, disguised in another's dress.
As soon as he arrived, he was embraced by the king's daughter, named Mañjumatī, who was deeply in love with him; she rose up and clasped him around the neck.
And having seated him upon the couch, she was then asked by her: "Who is this man who has been brought here by you this very day?"
Addressed by that doorkeeper with the words, "He is my friend; have confidence," Mañjumatī spoke thus, filled with agitation:
"How can there be trust for me, unfortunate as I am, that this king was protected by Mṛgāṅkadatta even though he had come within the very jaws of death?"
Hearing that, the doorkeeper said to her, "Enough with this grief, my dear; I shall slay both the king and Mṛgāṅkadatta before long."
When he had spoken thus, she said to him by chance: "Why do you boast? When that king was seized by crocodiles in the waters of the Narmadā..."
At that time, Mṛgāṅkadatta alone was intent on protecting him; why did you not kill him there? For you were terrified and fled.
Therefore, remain silent; let no one hear these words of yours, lest you incur misfortune from the heroic Mṛgāṅkadatta.
When she had spoken thus, her paramour, the chamberlain, could not tolerate it: "O sinful woman, you are now certainly fixed in your affection for Mṛgāṅkadatta!"
"Now let this insult of mine bear its fruit," he said, and drawing his sword, he rose up to kill her.
Then, a certain maidservant there who was a keeper of secrets ran forward and seized that dagger in her hand.
Meanwhile, Mañjumatī departed from there and went elsewhere; and the chamberlain [took] that [ring] from the hand of her maidservant, from which the finger had been cut off.
Having cast aside his knife, he returned to his own home just as he had come, accompanied by Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was both agitated and filled with wonder.
And there, remaining unobserved in the darkness, Mṛgāṅkadatta said to that chamberlain, "I am leaving; may you go home."
"Rest here quickly; for you are exceedingly exhausted," the doorkeeper said to that prince.
Then, when he had replied, "So be it," the Steward, desiring to observe his actions, summoned one of his own servants there and spoke to him.
"Lead this man to his dwelling wherever that peacock is staying, and provide him with a bed for rest."
Saying "So be it," that servant led Mṛgāṅkadatta into the house and, having brought him there, provided him with a bed and a lamp.
When he had gone out and closed the outer door with a chain, Mṛgāṅkadatta saw there that peacock standing within a cage.
Having been told this by that Kṣatriya, he reflected, "It is a peacock," and out of curiosity, he opened the cage of that peacock.
And that peacock, having emerged and carefully scrutinized the feet of Mṛgāṅkadatta, fell down again and again and rolled about them.
Seeing the cord tied around his neck as he was rolling about, the prince quickly loosened it, thinking that he had been strangled by it.
And while he was looking on, that peacock, its neck-string released, then became his minister Bhīmaparākrama.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, having embraced him as he bowed down in eager expectation, asked him out of wonder: "Friend, tell me, what indeed is this?"
Then, filled with joy, he of terrible prowess said to him: "Listen, O Lord; I shall tell you my own history from the very beginning."
Then, having been separated from your presence by a Naga's curse, I wandered through the forest and came upon a single Śālmalī tree.
Having seen a carved image of Gaṇeśa buried there, I bowed before it and sat down at its base, exhausted.

"O Lord, now that you have been brought here by fate and have released the necklace from my neck, I have regained my own human form once more."
Therefore, let us depart from here quickly; for that wicked warder always slays those who accompany him on his nocturnal rounds out of fear of being discovered.
And you, O Lord, were brought here today by this one who witnessed your night-vigil; having bound this thread, created by a yoginī, around your neck.
"Having become a peahen, go out through this window; then, with arms outstretched, [take] the string from your uplifted neck."
Just as he released it and tied it around his own neck, so shall I depart quickly; but when you have released my thread, we both shall remain in our natural state.
"There is no exit through the door, as it is barred from the outside," said that wise Bhīmaparākrama.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by him, saying "So be it," departed from there and went to his own dwelling, where his other two ministers were staying.
There, Mṛgāṅkadatta and all the others, filled with joy, passed that night recounting their respective adventures to one another.
In the morning, that Māyābaṭu, the Bhilla king and lord of that settlement, came into the presence of Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Having been asked about the comfort of his nights, Māyāvaṭu spoke to that prince in order to divert him, saying, "Come, let us play with dice."
Then, seeing that Bhillas had arrived along with his doorkeeper, Śrutadhi, the friend of Mṛgāṅkadatta, spoke.
"Have you forgotten because of the dice, or is there something visible today? For the dancing of the doorkeeper's peacock has indeed been announced by me."
Having heard this from Śrutadhi and remembering it with curiosity, the lord of the Śabaras dispatched that doorkeeper to bring Mayūra.
"How is it that through negligence I forgot and did not kill that thief, who was the witness to my secret at night, even though he had been cast into the fire-chamber?"
Thinking, "I shall go there quickly and accomplish both tasks," that doorkeeper also remembered [his duty] and went home in haste.
There, as soon as he had entered and looked about in the peacock's dwelling, he saw neither the thief nor that peacock there.
Then, terrified and despondent, he went to his own king and said, "O Lord, that peacock of mine has been carried off by a thief in the night."
"That great thief is well known, by whom that peacock of yours was stolen"—this was said there by Śrutadhi with a smiling face.
Seeing Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others laughing as they looked at one another, Māyāvaṭu asked them insistently, "What is this?"
Then, as had been arranged by that kṣatriya, the lustful man went to the house of the king's wife at night and engaged in a struggle with weapons.
Just as he reached the house of the steward, and just as Bhīmaparākrama was released from his state as a peacock here, and how he subsequently emerged from there.
In that manner, Mṛgāṅkadatta related the entire account to that lord of the Śabaras, including his own story and that of his relative, the kṣattṛ.

Having understood that and seeing a maidservant in the inner apartments with her hand wounded by a knife, and then observing that very thread fastened around her neck, the Lord of the Śabaras immediately slew that Māyābaṭu—the warder who had assumed the form of Bhīmaparākrama and was destroying the harem.
But that Mañjumatī, who was ill-behaved, he kept at a distance from King Mṛgāṅkadatta, protecting her from death and avoiding any physical contact with her.
Honored by them there in that Pulinda village, Mṛgāṅkadatta remained for those days, even though he was intent on attaining Śaśāṅkavatī, yet still awaiting reunion with his remaining friends.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave: While Mṛgāṅkadatta remained thus in the house of Māyābaṭu, the lord of the Bhills, accompanied by Vimalabuddhi and the others;
Meanwhile, his own army commander, having approached that lord of the Śabaras in his presence, once addressed him with great agitation:
"O Lord, while searching for such a person on your command for the sake of the Blessed Lady as an offering, we have found him."
By him, five hundred of our heroic warriors were shattered, and he was brought back, rendered helpless by a multitude of blows.
Having heard that, the lord of the Pulindas said to his commander-in-chief: "Let him be brought in here at once; let him be shown to us."
Then, as he was ushered in by him, he was beheld by everyone, stained by the dust of the battlefield and smeared with blood gushing from his sword wounds.
Muddy with the flowing ichor mixed with vermilion from his temples, reeling and intoxicated, he was like an elephant bound and encircled by nooses.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, having recognized his own minister Guṇākara, ran forward and, weeping, embraced him around the neck.
Then, having learned from his friends that Guṇākara had prostrated himself at the feet of his own lord, the Bhillendra comforted him.
Having brought him into the house, once he had bathed and his wounds were bound with bandages, they attended to him with wholesome food and drink as prescribed by physicians.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta asked his minister, who had been comforted: "Friend, tell me, what is your story?"
Then, while everyone was listening, Guṇākara said: "Listen, O King; I shall relate to you my own story."
Then, by the curse of the Naga, I was separated from you; wandering through that vast forest, I knew nothing due to my delusion.
Having finally attained my wits after a long time, I, being distressed, reflected: "Alas! This is some strange whim of the Creator toward one so ill-taught."
How could Mṛgāṅkadatta, who would feel distressed even while staying on the roof of a palace, endure this forest with its scorching sands?
Reflecting repeatedly within myself on how those companions of mine might be, I happened by chance, while wandering, to reach the goddess who dwells in the Vindhya mountains.
Day and night, with many various living beings brought there for her, I entered the palace of that queen, which resembled the abode of Yama.
There, having bowed to the goddess, I saw a man who was a corpse, holding a sword within his throat, offering himself as a sacrifice.
Upon seeing him again, however, because of my separation from you, a source of suffering for me, the thought arose in me to propitiate the Goddess by means of the sacrifice of my own self.
As soon as I ran toward that very sword and seized it, it seemed to ward me off from afar with a trembling caused by old age.
A certain compassionate female ascetic, having approached me with her head bowed and having extinguished my intent for death by inquiring into my circumstances, spoke to me.
"Do not act thus; for even the reunion of the dead has been seen, how much more so that of the living, my son? Listen therefore to this story."
There is a city on earth renowned by the name of Ahicchatrā; in that city, in former times, there was a preeminent king named Udayatuṅga.
He had a great steward named Kamalamati, and he too had an incomparable son named Vinītamati.
Even by a lotus stalk gathered for its qualities, which is both perforated and curved, the equality of that bow was not attained.
Once, while standing upon the fifth floor of a palace washed with white plaster at the onset of night, he beheld the moon rising.
It was fashioned from a sprout risen from the wish-fulfilling tree of love, like a brilliant ear-ornament for the eastern quarter by the night.
Gradually, seeing the world illuminated by those networks of rays, Vinītamati, with a heart full of joy, reflected:
"Aha! The paths are illuminated by the moonlight as if with nectar; since they are visible, why do I not go along one of them and enjoy myself?"
Having meditated thus, that archer went forth and wandered about; when he had traveled only a *krośa*, he suddenly heard the sound of weeping.
Having gone there and following her, he saw a certain maiden of divine beauty weeping, taking refuge at the foot of a tree.
And he asked, "O auspicious lady, who are you? And why is this man being led to the scales? Why has the moon of your face been made soiled with tears, as if by a stained moon?"
Having been addressed thus by him, she said: "I am the daughter of the great-souled Gandhamālin, the lord of the Nāgas, a maiden named Vijayavatī."
"My father, having fled from battle, was once cursed by Vāsuki: 'O wicked one, you shall go into servitude, conquered by your enemy!'"
And by that curse, he was defeated by his enemy, the Yakṣa Kālajihva, and made to follow the mind [of others], forever becoming a carrier of flower-burdens.
Out of sorrow for him and for his sake, I gratified Gaurī with ascetic penance; and she, the Blessed One, having appeared before me in person, spoke thus:
"O child, listen: within Lake Mānasa there is a great, divine crystal lotus, expanded with a thousand petals."
It shone with splendor scattered by the touch of the sun’s rays, like the head of Śeṣa, thick with hoods and tawny with the rays of jewels.
Once, Vaiśravaṇa, having seen that lotus there in Lake Mānasa and having bathed, conceived a sense of faith and began the worship of Hara toward that lotus.
At that time, his Yakṣa followers sported there within the lake in the forms of cakravāka ducks, swans, and other creatures suited for moving upon the water.
There, by fate, that enemy of yours, Kālajihva, had an elder brother, a yakṣa named Vidyujjihva, who was a dear friend.
Playing in the form of a ruddy goose, by the flapping of his wings, he caused the vessel of guest-offering held in the tip of Kubera’s hand to fall.
Then the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), enraged, transformed him right there in Lake Mānasa, along with his wife, into a cakravāka bird named Vidyujjihva by means of a curse.
And having done so out of affection, assuming the form of his beloved, he entertained his elder brother night after night while he was distressed by separation.
Today Kālajihva stays there during the day, assuming his own form, accompanied by your father Gandhamālin, whom he has made his servant.
Therefore, my daughter, you must urge there the son of the warder, the great hero Vinītamati of Ahicchatrā, who is diligent and resolute.
"Take this bow and this sword; having conquered that yakṣa with these two, for he is a great hero who will liberate your father."
Whatever man becomes the master of this sword-jewel, he shall conquer all enemies and become a king upon the earth.
Having spoken thus and given me a horse and a sword, the goddess vanished; then, at your instigation, I have come here today in due course.
Seeing you depart at night accompanied by the favor of the Goddess, I brought you back here by a stratagem, having made you hear the sound of weeping.
Requested by her with the words, "Therefore, accomplish this which is desired by me, O fortunate one," Vinītamati agreed to it, saying, "So be it."
Then, having gone there at that very moment, that Naga maiden [beheld] that swift white horse, which was like a mass of moonlight condensed into form.
A web of rays rushed forth to the ends of the quarters to destroy the darkness, like the glance cast by the Goddess Śrī as she looked upon the Hero.
Having brought forth the sword-jewel, which possesses the luster of the starry sky, bestow both of them upon that Vinītamati.
He too, having taken up his sword and mounted that horse, set out with her and reached Lake Mānasa at that very moment by the power of the horse.
With its lotus-hands tossed by the wind and the cries of distressed cakravāka birds, it seemed to say, "Do not, do not," out of compassion for the serpent-like tongue of Time.
Seeing there that Gandhamālin was under the control of the yakṣas, he drove away those lowly beings, wounding them with his sword, for the sake of his liberation.
Seeing that, Kālajihva, having cast off his form as a female cakravāka bird from the middle of the lake, rose up roaring like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
And when the battle had commenced, Vinītamati, leaping up with his horse, seized that Kālajihva by the hair as he sprang into the sky.
Even as he intended to cut off his head with a sword, the yakṣa, lamenting piteously, sought refuge with him.
Being liberated, he gave him his own ring which wards off calamity; bowing low, he also released that Naga Gandhamālin from servitude.
Then Gandhamālī, joyful and disciplined in mind, gave his daughter Vijayavatī to him and went home.
Then, at dawn, the skillful Vinītamati returned home, bringing with him the sword, the ring, the horse, and the jewel maiden.
There, welcomed by his father who was pleased by the account he had heard, and by his own king as well, he married that Naga maiden.
Then, on one occasion, his father Kamalabuddhi, augmented by those four jewels and his own virtues, spoke to him in private.
"O King, this daughter of yours, named Putrodayavatī, who is well-trained in all branches of knowledge, belongs to him who is rising here to greatness."
A wager was made by him regarding her: "Whichever Brahmin or even Kshatriya defeats her in debate, to him I shall give her."
And all other disputants were defeated in debate by her, who was like a celestial nymph in form that causes wonder throughout the world.
And you are a peerless hero in the science of your own kshatriya tradition; why then do you remain silent? Conquer him in debate and marry this girl.
Thus addressed by his father, he, with a humble mind, replied: "Father, what dispute can there be for those like me with women who are so charming?"
Nevertheless, when he replied, "I shall carry out this command of yours," his father went into the presence of the king along with that mature youth.
"O King, a debate with the princess will be held tomorrow morning," Vinītamati informed the monarch there.
Having accepted the matter from the king, he returned home and related it exactly as it was to his son, Vinītamati.
Then, having arrived himself, that eloquent Vinītamati approached the lotus-pond of the assembly of the learned, which was inhabited by that royal swan.
Resplendent, he illuminated [the assembly] as he was gazed upon from all sides by throngs of virtuous men who had taken refuge in him, with their flickering eyes like bees.
And in another moment, Udayavatī, the princess, drawn by his virtues, arrived there slowly like the bow-staff of the God of Love.
It was adorned by its own virtuous qualities and beautiful words as ornaments, which, from the very beginning, seemed to be setting forth the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
If a stainless crescent moon were to appear in a faultless sky, it would then bear a resemblance to her seated upon a throne of emerald.
Then she set forth her preliminary argument, as if weaving a garland composed of exquisite jewel-like words upon the threads of the rays from her gleaming teeth.
Having rendered Sumukhī speechless at every step, that Vinītamati established his own doctrine regarding the meaning of faults in a mere moment.
Then, when he was praised by the members of the assembly, the princess considered herself victorious even in defeat, because she had obtained a virtuous husband.
Then King Udayatuṅga, being delighted, gave that daughter—who had been won as the prize of the debate—to Vinītamati.
Then Vinītamati, his hands filled with the jewels given by him, remained there together with those two, the daughter of the Naga and the daughter of the king.
Once, while playing at dice and being defeated by others, his mind was deeply distressed; a Brahmin approached him with persistence and requested a meal.
Then, having whispered it into the ear of his servant, he, overcome with rage, covered a bowl of sand with a cloth and had him give it to him.
Taking that [bundle] along with the gold because of its weight, the upright brahmin thought it was a great treasure; out of joy, he went to a secluded spot and opened it.
Having seen it filled with sand, he cleared it away from the surface of the earth; thinking, "I have been deceived by him," he went to his own home dejected.
Vinītamati, having disregarded this and abandoned that gambling, remained at his own home as he pleased, in the company of his beloved.
As time passed, his joints and limbs became loosened by old age; there, King Udayatuṅga became incapable of bearing the burden of the kingdom.
Then, having consecrated that very Vinītamati as his son-in-law in the kingdom, he, being childless, went to the Ganges for the sake of liberating his body.
And not long after that, having obtained the kingdom, Vinītamati conquered even the ten directions through the power of his horse and sword.
By the power of this plague-quelling ring, the kingdom became free from disease and famine, just like that of King Raghu.
Once, a mendicant named Ratnacandramati, a lion among the elephants of disputants, arrived from another land before that king.
And that monk, having been treated as a guest, requested the king—who was fond of the virtuous—for the sake of a debate, and uttered such a wager:
