"O King of Kings, if you are victorious, you must accept the teaching of the Sugata; if I am victorious, I shall serve the brahmins and cast off my robe."
Having heard this and saying "So be it," King Vinītamati engaged in debate with that monk for seven days.
On the eighth day, that monk defeated the lord of the earth, by whom Udayavatī—the "shaven-headed mallet" against disputants—had been conquered.
Then, having conceived faith, the king accepted from that monk the teaching of the Sugata, which is rich in the merit of benefiting sentient beings.
Devoted to the worship of the Jina, he constructed monasteries, sacrificial halls, and dwellings for all, including monks, brahmins, and others.
And having been pacified by that practice, he then requested from the monk the instruction on the conduct of a Bodhisattva, which benefits sentient beings.
Then that monk said to him: "O King, the great conduct of a bodhisattva is to be practiced here by those who are free from defilement, and not by others."
Indeed, for one such as you, no gross offense is even to be perceived; rather, you should seek out and pacify any subtle fault by means of this method.
Having said this, that monk instructed him in the science of dream-omens; and the king, having seen such a dream because of it, related it to him in the morning.
"O Teacher, I know that today in a dream I went to the other world; there, men carrying staffs said to me, who was seeking food out of hunger: 'Give us food!'"
O King, eat these abundant burning sands that you have earned—the very ones which were formerly given by you to a hungry Brahmin who came as a petitioner.
"By giving ten crores of gold, you shall be liberated from this sin"—having been addressed thus by those men with staffs in their hands, I awoke at the end of the night.
Having spoken thus and related that account, and having given those ten crores of gold, the king once again performed the ritual for inducing dreams.
Having seen that dream again, he rose at dawn and described it: "Even now, they have given me food in my dream while I was hungry in the other world."
When they were asked by men for food, they replied to me: "Even if alms are given, how shall we eat these grains of sand?"
Then they did not weep for you, saying, "That gift of yours was fruitless, because among it there was one piece of gold belonging to a brahmin."
Having heard this and exclaiming, "I have awakened from a dream," the king bestowed ten more crores of gold upon those who requested it.
Then, later in the night, he again had an individual dream; having seen that dream once more, he rose at dawn and described it.
"Even now, alas! those men gave me that very same meal of sand in the next world; and when I questioned them in a dream, they said this to me:"
O King, even that gift of yours has become fruitless, because today in the forest region of your own country, a brahmin was robbed by bandits and killed.
And since your protection was not effective, that lack of protection has now become fruitless; therefore, give today a gift twice as great as that previous one.
Having heard this, the king declared to the mendicant, "I am awakened even here," and gave his teacher twice as much as the gift he had seen in the dream.
Then he said to that monk, "O Teacher, how can such a dharma, full of many flaws, be maintained in this world by those like me?"
Having heard that, the monk said: "O King, it is not on account of this alone that the minds of the wise lose their zeal for the duty of protecting the Dharma."
The deities protect those who are steadfast, endowed with perseverance, and who do not despise their own duty; they also nourish their desires.
Likewise, O King, this Jātaka of the Blessed One as a boar has not been heard by you; let it now be heard from me.
Long ago, in a cave on the Vindhya mountains, there lived a certain wise boar born from a portion of a Buddha, together with a monkey who was his friend.
Always accompanied by that friend who acts for the welfare of all beings, he passed his time honoring guests according to the traditional rites appropriate for himself.
And once there occurred a storm lasting five days, terrible because it prevented the movement of living beings with its unceasing torrents.
On the fifth day, at night, while the boar was asleep along with Kapinjala, a lion accompanied by his wife and son went to the entrance of his cave.
There, the lion said to his wife, "In this foul weather, we shall certainly perish today from hunger, having failed to catch any living creature in this long stretch of time."
Having heard that, the lioness said: "We are all hungry; we cannot survive. Therefore, eat me alone, and you two shall live."
For you are the master, and this son is our very life and all-in-all; let there be another woman like me for you, or let it be only through him—may there be auspiciousness for both of you.
Thus, at that time, the noble-souled boar, having awakened by chance, overheard the mutual conversation between that husband and wife.
Delighted, he thought: "By good fortune, where is this night, where is this foul weather, and where is the arrival of such a guest? Oh, what a rise in my merit today!"
Before an obstacle to that occurs, why should I not satisfy these guests with this body, which perishes in an instant?
Having risen and gone out, that boar spoke to the lion with a gentle voice: "O noble sir, do not fall into despair."
"I have come as food for you, along with my wife and children; therefore, eat me," said the boar to the lion. Thus addressed by him, the lion—
Delighted, he said to his wife, "Let this child eat first; after him I shall eat, and after that you shall eat."
When she had said "So be it," the lion then proceeded to eat the flesh of that boar which had previously been devoured by the lion cub.
While he was eating, that Great Being, the boar, said to him: "Drink this blood of mine quickly, before it sinks into the ground."
"Find satisfaction with my flesh, and let your beloved eat the remainder," he said, speaking thus as he was gradually reduced to nothing but bones by that lion.
Even though the boar was deprived of his life, he did not abandon his state of courage; he remained as if standing there to witness the very limit of that fortitude.
Meanwhile, that lioness, exhausted by hunger, died there; her son, the lion, went somewhere else, and the night came to an end.
In the meantime, that monkey woke up, went outside, and seeing the boar in such a state, asked him in great agitation:
"Tell me, friend, if you are able, by whom has this unwellness been inflicted upon you? Having heard that, the steadfast boar related to him exactly what had occurred.
Then, weeping and bowing at his feet, the monkey said: "You are a portion of a divinity, by whom I have been liberated from this state of being an animal."
"Tell me some desire of yours; I shall fulfill it for you. Being addressed thus by that monkey, the boar said to him:
That desire of mine for my friend which was difficult to accomplish even by fate—behold, while I looked on, this poor lioness has died of hunger.
"O friend, my heart desires that she, having regained her life, should now satisfy herself by eating once more, as she did when she previously attained my body."
Thus, appearing before that disputant Kroḍa, Dharma touched him with his hand and transformed him into a lord of sages with a divine form.
And he said: "This illusion in the form of a lion and so forth was created by me alone, desiring to test you who have girded your loins solely for the sake of others."
By you, whose being is unbroken and who have given up your life for the sake of others, having conquered me, this Dharma has been attained; today you have truly reached the state of a Lord of Sages.
Having heard that and perceiving Dharma standing before him, the sage said: "Now, while these two monkeys have not yet abandoned their animal state, O friend..."
"O Blessed One, even this attainment of the state of a Lord of Sages does not please me," he said. Having heard this, the Sage made that monkey his attendant for the sake of the Dharma.
"Association with the great certainly leads to great fruit. Then Dharma vanished, and Siṃhī disappeared, as if dead.

Thus, O King, for those who have not abandoned their enthusiasm for the Dharma through the power of their resolve and who receive assistance from the deities, the accomplishment of their desires is not difficult to attain.
Having heard these words of the monk, King Dānaśūra, who was humble-minded, again performed that dream-inducing spell at night.
Having seen it, he related the dream to that monk in the morning: "I know that today in a dream some divine sage spoke thus to me."
"O son, now practice the stainless conduct of a Bodhisattva. Upon hearing those words, I was awakened this day and attained peace.
Having thus informed his preceptor, the monk, that lord of the earth undertook that great practice on an auspicious day with his permission.
And he remained there, raining down desired objects upon those who sought them without ceasing; consequently, his wealth became inexhaustible, for prosperity indeed has its root in dharma.
Then once, a needy Brahmin approached him and petitioned: "O King, I am a Brahmin residing in the city of Pāṭaliputra."
There, having surrounded the fire-sanctuary, my son too has been seized by a Brahmarākṣasa; and no means of rescue succeeds for me in this matter.
Therefore, I have come here to you, who are a wish-fulfilling tree for those who seek, to make this request: grant me this ring, which destroys all evils, for my well-being.
Thus entreated by that Brahmin, the king, remaining unperturbed, gave him that very ring which he had obtained from Kālajihva.
When that brahmin had departed taking it, the fame of the king’s vow as a Bodhisattva spread even to the furthest quarters by her means.
Then once, another guest, a certain prince named Indukalaśa, arrived from the Northland before the lord.
Having been shown courtesy by that king, whose noble lineage he knew, and being asked what he desired, the wise prince spoke to him.
You are indeed renowned on earth as a wish-fulfilling gem for the multitude of supplicants; for even when he asks for your very life, no petitioner ever turns away from you empty-handed.
And I, having been seized by my brother named Kanakakalaśa, was banished from the kingdom; having come to you out of necessity, I have approached you.
"O hero, give me those two jewels, the horse and the sword, by whose power I may conquer my kinsman and obtain the kingdom."
Upon hearing that, King Vinītamati gave those two, Aśvakhadga and Rājyarakṣāmaṇi, to the prince.
And no doubt arose in that firm-minded one, even as the ministers, with downcast faces, were heaving sighs.
Then, having obtained the horse and the sword, the prince went there and, by its power, conquered that brother and regained the kingdom.
His brother, Kanakakalaśa, having been deposed from the kingdom, came to that city of King Vinītamati.
And there he began, with great sorrow, to enter the fire; having learned of this, King Vinītamati spoke to his ministers.
"This virtuous man has reached this state because of my transgression; therefore, by restoring his own kingdom to him, I shall now become free from my debt to him."
"What use have I for this kingdom which serves no purpose for others? Since I am childless, let him alone be my son and the sustainer of my kingdom."
Having spoken thus, the king summoned Kanakakalaśa and bestowed his own kingdom upon him, even though his ministers were unwilling.
Having bestowed the kingdom, he departed from that city at that very moment, accompanied by his two wives, with a mind free from doubt.
Alas, alas! Fie upon it! The full moon, the nectar-rayed one who nourishes the world, has been born and yet has been eclipsed by a cloud that falls out of season.
And by destiny, that king—who was like a wish-fulfilling tree for his subjects—was led away somewhere, even though he had been active in fulfilling all the hopes of every embodied being.
Seeing this, the citizens, overwhelmed with grief and vocal with such lamentations, followed after him, drenching the earth with their tears.
Having somehow turned them back, the unshakable Vinītamati then departed for the forest with his wife, driving the chariot in reverse.
In due course, he reached a desert land created by fate to test his fortitude—a place where the sands were scorched by the sun and devoid of water or trees.
Afflicted by thirst and exhausted by the fatigue of the long journey, he sat down for a moment in one part of it, and even with his wife, he was overcome by sleep.
As soon as he awoke and looked around, he beheld there a magnificent and wondrous garden, brought into existence by the excellence of his own spiritual merit.
It possessed ponds filled with cool, clear water and blooming lotuses; it was covered with dark green grass, and its trees were bent low under the weight of their fruit.
With its smooth, broad, and lofty rocky surface situated in deep shade, it was like the Nandana grove of heaven drawn down from the triple realm by the power of his generosity.
"Is this a dream, or a delusion, or perhaps a divine favor bestowed upon me?"—as the king gazed and gazed at that sight, he was filled with wonder.
Then he heard a voice uttered from the sky by a certain pair of perfected beings (siddhas) who were traveling through the air in the form of a pair of swans.
O King, what cause for excessive wonder is there here regarding the greatness of your own power? Therefore, dwell at your pleasure in this forest, which always bears flowers and fruit.
Having heard these words of the Siddha, Vinītamati remained there in that forest, contented, performing austerities together with his two wives.
And one day, while seated there upon a stone slab, he saw from a distance a certain man who was intent on taking his own life by means of hanging.
Having gone quickly, he consoled him with affectionate words and dissuaded him from death, and then questioned that man regarding the cause of his intent.
Then that man said, "Listen from the very beginning as I speak to you: I am Somaśūra, the son of Nāgaśūra, known by the name Somaka."
Thus, because I was designated as a thief in my birth horoscope by those learned in the treatises on that subject, my father diligently had me instructed in the Dharmaśāstra out of fear of that.
Even after studying that, I engaged in theft due to association with the wicked; by whom can one's past karma in this world be altered?
Then once, having been seized from the midst of thieves by the city guards, I was brought to the place of impalement on a stake for execution.
At that very moment, a great royal elephant, frantic with rut and having broken its tethering post, came to that same spot while trampling living beings.
Out of fear, those executioners abandoned me there and fled somewhere; I, too, having escaped from that tumultuous fray, departed from that place.
I heard from the world that my father had lost his life as soon as he heard that I was being led away for execution; thereafter, I heard that my mother had followed him.
Then, afflicted by grief, wandering about, exhausted, and intent on casting off my body, I gradually reached this great, desolate forest.
As soon as I had entered here, a certain divine woman appeared suddenly; approaching me and offering words of comfort, she spoke.
"O son of the royal sage Vinītamati, you have arrived at this hermitage; your sin has departed, and from him you shall obtain knowledge."
Having said this, she vanished; and as I wandered about, unable to find that royal sage and desiring to abandon my life out of grief, I was seen by you.
Having spoken thus, that royal sage led Somaśūra to his own hermitage, announced himself as a guest, and honored him.
And having finished his meal, that royal sage, wishing to restrain him from ignorance amidst various discourses on the Dharma, spoke to him as he stood bowed before him.

O child, ignorance must be abandoned, for it belongs to those of perverted intellect; it leads to harm in both worlds. Listen now to a scriptural tradition on this point: "From ignorance arises delusion; from delusion, attachment; from attachment, desire; from desire, anger; from anger, the loss of discernment; from the loss of discernment, the destruction of memory; and from the destruction of memory, one perishes."
Formerly, among the Pañcālas, there was a twice-born man named Devabhūti; he was a follower of the Vedas and possessed a virtuous wife named Bhogavatī.
When he had gone to bathe, she entered the vegetable garden for the sake of vegetables and saw a washerman's donkey eating the greens.
Taking up a club, she ran after him, and that donkey, while fleeing, fell into a pit and broke its hoof.
Having learned of this, the washerman, its owner, arrived there in a rage and beat that Brahmin woman with clubs and kicks.
Because of that, the pregnant woman suffered a miscarriage with a sudden convulsion; then the washerman, taking the donkey, went to his own home.
Then her husband, having returned from his bath and learned of this, saw his wife and, being greatly distressed, went to the city governor and made his request.
Having heard the dispute between those two, that fool summoned a washerman named Balāsura at that very moment and spoke this:
"Because of this breaking of the donkey's hoof, let this twice-born man carry the load of this washerman's donkey until the donkey returns to its natural state."
"Let this washerman also produce another embryo in the wife of that Brahmin by causing her to miscarry that [first] fetus."
When he had said, "This is the punishment for these two," that Brahmin, out of distress, consumed poison and gave up his life along with his wife.
Having learned of that, the king killed there the city superintendent, Duravadhāraka, who was a slayer of a Brahmin; he entered the womb of an animal for a long time.
Thus, those shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, who wander on the wrong path due to their own faults and do not hold the lamp of the true scriptures before them, will certainly fall.
Having spoken thus, that royal sage, Vinītamati, addressed Somaśūra again in order to further instruct him who was seeking spiritual guidance.
"My child, I shall tell you the meaning of the perfections; listen now to them in order. Formerly, there was a king named Malayaprabha in Kurukṣetra."
Once, when the king was giving wealth to his subjects during a famine, his son Induprabha spoke to him after he had been restrained by his ministers out of greed.
O dear one, how can you remain indifferent toward your subjects because of the words of evil counselors? For you are their wish-fulfilling tree, and they are your cows of plenty.
To his son who was thus prattling with persistence, the king, under the influence of his minister, said out of weariness: "My dear child, what inexhaustible wealth do I possess?"
If I am to become a wish-fulfilling tree for these subjects even without him, then why do you not yourself assume the state of a kalpa-tree for them?
Having heard this from his father, that prince made a vow: "I must either die or achieve the state of a wish-fulfilling tree through ascetic penance."
Having thus resolved, that Great Being set out for the forest of asceticism; and as soon as he had departed, that famine came to an end.
Then, having obtained his desired boon from Mahendra, who was pleased by his intense asceticism, that wish-fulfilling tree appeared right there in his own city.
With its branches extended in all directions and with the cries of birds, it seemed to draw near those standing at a distance and to call out to those seeking it.
And day after day he granted desires even to those who sought what was difficult to obtain; he made his subjects free from longing, as if they were dwelling in heaven.
And at that time, Mahendra approached him and spoke, tempting him, saying: "Your service to others is complete; come now for the sake of heaven."
Then, having become like a wish-fulfilling tree, that prince said to him: "In this place, even these other trees are delightful with their flowers and fruits."

Those who are constantly devoted to the welfare of others and are free from desire for their own self-interest—how could such people go to heaven for their own pleasure, having become wish-fulfilling trees for that purpose?
"Having shattered the hopes of these people, I am departing"—hearing those noble words of his, Śakra spoke again.
"In that case, let all your subjects also go to heaven," said that prince, who was himself like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
If you are pleased, lead my subjects to heaven; I have no need for that myself. I shall perform great austerities solely for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others.
Having praised him who had spoken thus, saying "So be it," that lord of the gods, the Sugata’s attendant, took the subjects with him and, being satisfied, departed for the third heaven.
Having abandoned that tree-form and resumed his own natural appearance, the prince Induprabha, dwelling in the forest, attained the state of a Bodhisattva through ascetic penance.
Thus has this highly exalted accomplishment of those devoted to giving been described by me; this is the perfection of generosity for you—now hear the perfection of ethical discipline.
Formerly, on the Vindhya mountain, there was a king of parrots born from a portion of the Sugata; rich in virtue practiced in previous births, he was self-controlled and named Hemaprabha.
Although he was one who remembered his former births and was a teacher of the Dharma, he had a gatekeeper named Śuka, who was passionate and foolish.
Once, grieving for his wife, a female parrot who had been killed by a fowler with a snare, he fell into a state of deep compassion, tormented by the pain of separation from her.
Then that wise king of the parrots, Hemaprabha, wishing to dispel his grief through skillful means and for his own benefit, spoke these words falsely.
That wife of yours is not dead; having escaped from the fowler's snare, she was indeed seen by me just now, still very much alive.
Saying, "Come, I shall show her to you," the king led Cārumati through the path of the sky to a certain lake.
Having shown him his own reflection there within the water, he said to him: "This is that wife of yours; look, she stands here."
Having heard that and seeing his own reflection there, that fool, filled with joy, entered the water and embraced and kissed her.
Not obtaining the touch of his beloved nor hearing her voice, he thought: "Why does my beloved not give me her touch and conversation?"
Then, fearing his anger, he went and brought an *āmalaka* fruit; out of a desire for conciliation and mistaking it for his beloved, he placed it upon the reflection.
Perceiving that it had fallen from his mouth after being swallowed and then spat out by his beloved, he went with sorrow to King Hemaprabha and addressed him.
"Your Majesty, that wife of yours does not grant me even a touch or a word; moreover, she rejected the āmalaka fruit that was offered by me."
Having heard this, the king spoke slowly to him as if with difficulty: "It is not proper for me to say this; nevertheless, I speak to you out of affection."
"For how could she, who is now devoted to another, feel affection for you? Come, I shall show her to you directly right here within this water."
Having said this, the king led him there and showed him both his own reflection and his own reflection in the water, joined together with his.
As soon as that fool saw his wife united with another man, he turned back in disgust and informed his own king.
"O Lord, because this instruction of yours was not heard by my foolish self, that is the ripening of that karma; now, command me as to what must be done by me in this matter."
When he had thus made his request, King Hemaprabha, having found the opportunity for instruction, spoke to the chamberlain.
It would be better to consume the Hālāhala poison or have a serpent bound around one's neck than to place trust in women, who are beyond the reach of jewels, mantras, and other such protections.
Like extremely fickle whirlwinds laden with much dust, women utterly defile those who tread the path of virtue and utterly humiliate them.

Those of steadfast character and wise intellect should not be attached to those [sensual pleasures]; rather, they should practice ethical discipline in order to attain the state of one free from passion.
Thus instructed by the king, Cārumati renounced women and gradually became one whose vital energy was drawn upward, equal to a Buddha.
Thus, because they cause others who are rich in virtue to cross over as well, I have described this to you as the perfection of ethical discipline; now hear the perfection of patience.
On Mount Kedāra there was a great sage named Śubhanaya, who constantly bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī, was self-controlled, and was emaciated by his austerities.
Once at night, some thieves came there to search for gold previously buried in the ground, but they did not find it anywhere.
Then, thinking that the place was secluded, those thieves entered his hut and spoke thus to that sage who had taken it: "It has been stolen by him."
"O Dambhamuni, release the gold we have brought from the earth! Alas, you have arrived as a thief even among thieves."
Thus challenged by those wicked men, the sage, his purpose unattained, spoke falsely: "I have not taken anything; nor have I seen anything."
Then, although he was beaten with those wicked clubs by the bandits, that best of sages, being truthful in speech, continued to say exactly the same thing.
Then those thieves, thinking "this man is cruel," cut him down; they gradually tore off his hands, his feet, and gouged out his eyes.

Nevertheless, perceiving him to be unchanging and having realized that his speech was not otherwise, and considering him to be like gold whose impurities have been removed, those thieves departed as they had come.
And a king named Śekharajyotis, who had arrived there to see that sage, beheld him in such a state as he was a disciple who had come for an audience.
Then that lord, afflicted by grief for his teacher, having seen him and understood what had happened, searched for and brought those thieves to that very place.
And when that king set about their slaughter, the sage said to him: "O King, if you kill these, then I shall kill myself."
If this was done by me with a weapon, then what is their fault? Or rather, since they are the instigators of that act, then my anger should be directed toward them as well.
For them as well, there was the destruction of their gold; that was my own past misdeed. For him too, it was his own ignorance; therefore, he did me no harm.
Therefore, that very [hostility] is what must be countered by me; moreover, if these people are to be slain because of their harm, why should they not be protected here because of their benefit?
"If these people do not grant me this forgiveness which has liberation as its fruit, for whom else should I act? Thus, they have already performed a complete service for me."
With these and many other such words, the sage, devoted to forbearance, awakened that king and released the thieves from their punishment.
By the greatness of his asceticism, his body instantly became uninjured as it was before, and at that moment, spiritual perfection (siddhi) manifested for him.
Thus has been described for you the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), by which those who are patient cross over saṃsāra; now hear the perfection of fortitude (dhairya-pāramitā).
Formerly, there was a young Brahmin named Mālādhara; once, he beheld a perfected youth traveling through the sky.
In emulation of that, having fastened wings made of grass to his sides, he practiced the art of movement by leaping again and again into the sky.
And as he was thus performing his daily labor in vain, he was one day observed by a prince traveling through the sky.
"Though devoid of fortitude and exhausted, this child still exerts himself even for an unattainable goal; he is to be pitied by me, for he is my own charge."
Having reflected thus, Skanda, being pleased, took that foremost of brahmins by his own power and made him his attendant.
Thus, even the deities are pleased by those who possess fortitude; I have thus explained the perfection of fortitude—now hear the perfection of meditation.
In ancient times, there was a merchant among the Karṇāṭas named Vijayamālin; he had a son, Maharddhi, who was named Malayamālin.
Once, accompanied by his father, he went to the royal court and there beheld the young daughter of King Indukeśarin.
As soon as that maiden named Induyaśas—enchanting like a creeper of Māra—saw the merchant’s son, she entered his heart.
Then, having returned home, that pale one remained sleepless at night and stayed contracted during the day, observing the vow of the night-lotus.
Meditating upon her alone every day, he turned his back on food and other necessities; even when questioned by his own kinsmen, he said nothing at all, like one who is mute.
Then, in a private place, a trusted royal painter named Mantharaka spoke to that friend who was so distressed by separation.
"Friend, why do you stand leaning against the wall like one who has been painted there? You whose sole essence is beauty, being without hope, you neither hear nor see."
Thus, when his friend persistently questioned him, that merchant’s son, Malayamālin, explained his intention to him.
"O son of a merchant, your longing for the princess is not fitting; let the swan indeed desire the delightful beauty of the lotuses in another lake."
"What more can be said of him than that he possesses the splendor of the serpent-king who enjoys the lotuses in the lake of Viṣṇu’s navel?"—though speaking thus, the painter was unable to depict him.
Then, in order to ward off that longing and to pass the time, he painted the princess on a canvas and gave it to him.
Having obtained her depicted in a painting, the merchant’s son Malayamālin remained gazing at her, consoling her, touching her, and adorning her.
Meditating thus, "This is indeed the princess Induyaśas," he gradually attained identity with her and performed his activities through that very disposition.
And as she spoke to him softly and engaged in kissing and other such acts, he—being permeated by the cultivation of that very thought—beheld her even though she was merely a painting.

Then, firmly established in the enjoyment of his beloved who was perfected through meditation, he remained content with the entire cycle of existence as it appeared upon the single canvas of the painting.
Then one day, taking that painted cloth at moonrise, he went out to the garden with his beloved to enjoy themselves.
There, having placed that painting at the foot of a certain tree, he went a short distance away to gather flowers for the sake of his beloved.
At that moment, the sage named Vinayajyotis, seeing him from the vault of the sky, descended out of compassion, intending to rescue him from delusion.
There, by his own power, he drew a black, living snake upon one part of that painted cloth and remained unobserved.
Meanwhile, Malayamālin, having gathered flowers there, arrived and, seeing that black serpent on the cloth, reflected:
Whence has this serpent come here now? Has it been created by Fate to protect this Sundarī, who is like a treasure-house of beauty?
Having reflected thus, he adorned his beloved with flowers upon a cloth; then, having embraced her as she was brought forth through meditative visualization, he asked this:
Then, through the power of that sage's illusion, he saw her there, bitten by that black serpent and deprived of life.
Then, having forgotten his cloth and crying out "Alas!", he fell unconscious to the ground like a Vidyādhara who had lost his perfected magic garment.
And in an instant, regaining consciousness and lamenting as death approached, he rose up, climbed to the top of a tall tree, and threw himself down.
As he was falling from that [tree], the Lord of Sages appeared, caught him with both hands, comforted him, and spoke.
"O fool, do you not know that she is the princess staying in her own palace, whereas this is a lifeless painted doll upon a canvas?"
Whom do you embrace then, or who has been bitten by the great serpent? What is this delusion of your own mental construction, O passionate one?
Why do you not seek the reality through such firmness of meditation, by which you would no longer become a vessel for such miseries as these?
Having been addressed thus by that sage, the night of his delusion having come to an end, the merchant’s son was awakened; he prostrated himself before him and said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace I have crossed over this calamity; now grant me your favor so that I may cross over saṃsāra."
Thus entreated by Malayamālin, the sage Bodhisattva taught him his own realization and then vanished from sight.

Then Malayamālin, having gone to the forest, through the power of his asceticism became one who knows the reality of what is to be abandoned along with its causes and what is to be adopted, and attained the state of an Arhat.
And having arrived, the compassionate one, through the instruction of knowledge, made that King Indukeśarin, along with his citizens, partakers of liberation.

Thus, even that which is unreal attains the status of reality for those possessed of the power of meditative concentration; this is called the perfection of meditation. Now listen to the perfection of wisdom.
Formerly, in the island of Siṃhala, there was a thief named Siṃhavikrama, whose body had been nourished from birth by the wealth of others taken from every quarter.
Having grown old in the course of time, he desisted and reflected thus: "What means do I have for the next world? To whom there shall I go for refuge?"
If I go for refuge here to either Śambhu or Śauri, who am I compared to those two, to whom even the gods, sages, and others are but servants?
Therefore, I serve Citragupta, who alone records the good and evil deeds of living beings; may he protect me through his own skillful means.
For the Scribe alone performs the activity of Brahmā and Rudra; in an instant, he writes and erases the universe held within his hand.
Having reflected thus, he began to practice devotion toward him alone; he worshipped him and daily fed brahmins for his pleasure.
While he was conducting himself in this manner, Citragupta once came to his house in the guise of a guest to observe the mind of that thief.
Then that thief, having honored him, fed him, and given him a sacrificial fee, said: "Tell Citragupta, 'May he be pleased with you.'"
Then Citragupta, appearing in the form of a Brahmin, said to him: "Setting aside Hari, Hara, and the others, tell me, what do you have with Citragupta?"
Having heard that, the thief Siṃhavikrama also said to him: "What use have you for this? I have no need for any other deities."
Then Citragupta, in the form of a brahmin, spoke to him again: "In that case, if you will indeed give me your own wife, then I shall say this."
Upon hearing this, Siṃhavikrama was delighted and said to him: "For the sake of pleasing my cherished deity, your wife has indeed been given by me to you."
Then Citragupta, having heard that, revealed himself and said: "This is I; I am pleased, so tell me, what may I do for you?"
Then, filled with joy, he whose prowess was like that of a lion addressed him: "O Blessed One, act in such a way that death may not come to me."
Then Citragupta said: "Death cannot be prevented; nevertheless, I shall employ a stratagem for you—listen to it from me."
From that time forward, Time was consumed by the wrathful Lord on account of Śveta; yet it was fashioned here once again for the sake of his purpose.
From that time forward, wherever Śveta dwelt, he did not harm even the smallest living creature, being restrained by the command of his lord.
And that Śvetamuni is now situated on the far shore of the eastern ocean, having crossed the river named Taraṅgiṇī in a grove of asceticism.
There, having led you to a place unassailable by death, I shall establish you; and you must not return to this other shore of the river.
If death should afflict you upon your arrival here through negligence, I shall provide the means for you once you have come to the next world.
Having spoken thus to Siṃhavikrama, Citragupta, being delighted, led him to that Śvetāśrama, placed him there, and vanished from sight.
Then, in the course of time, the time for that river arrived to lead Siṃhavikrama, who was staying there, to the other shore.
When, remaining there, he saw no other means, he then dispatched a divine woman to him, having created her through his illusory power.
Having gone there and approached him, that playful woman brought Siṃhavikrama under her control through skillful means, having enchanted him with the perfection of her own beauty.
When the days had passed, under the pretext of a desire to see her kinsmen, she entered that surging river to cross it.
While he, possessing the prowess of a lion, was watching and following her as she stood on the bank, she caused herself to stumble in the middle of the river.
As if being carried away by a flood, she cried out there for help: "O noble son, do you not protect me as I am dying?"
"Are you one who has the prowess of a jackal, and not rather one with the prowess of a lion? Upon hearing this, Siṃhavikrama immediately descended into the river.
That woman also, as if being carried away by the force of the water, led him to the opposite shore in an instant as he followed her there to rescue him.
There, Death, with a noose cast around his neck, said to him: "For those whose minds are devoured by sense-objects, ruin indeed stands upon their heads."
Then, having been led to the assembly hall of Yama by Kāla, Citragupta, who had previously been pleased with him, looked at this negligent man and spoke aside to his attendants:
If you are asked here, "Will you first experience hell or heaven?", you should first pray for residence in heaven.
While dwelling in heaven, you should perform meritorious deeds for the sake of attaining firmness [in that state]; thereafter, you should practice austerity there for the removal of all sins.
Thus addressed by Citragupta, that Siṃhavikrama, embarrassed, with his face cast down and terrified, assented to it, saying, "So be it."
And in an instant, Dharmarāja addressed Citragupta there: "Does this thief have even a fraction of merit here, or not?"
Then Citragupta said: "He is fond of guests; he even gave away his own wife to a petitioner for the sake of pleasing his chosen deity."
"Therefore, O Lord, he possesses a divine day and a destination in heaven. Having heard this, Dharmarāja beheld him, who possessed the prowess of a lion.
"O friend, tell me first which you shall enjoy—the auspicious or the inauspicious? Thereupon, Siṃhavikrama requested that he enjoy the auspicious first.
Therefore, by the command of the King of Dharma, he boarded that celestial chariot which had arrived and departed for the third heaven, remembering the words of Citragupta.
There, devoted to bathing in the celestial river, reciting prayers, and observing vows, he reached the second day, being entirely free from desire for heavenly enjoyments.
Thus, having reached heaven in due course through the power of intense asceticism, he propitiated Śaṅkara and attained knowledge, his sins being utterly consumed.
Then the hell-wardens were unable even to look upon his face; Citragupta wiped away [the record] from the birch-bark, and Yama remained silent.
Thus, even that thief attained perfection through the power of true wisdom; this is what is proclaimed as the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) known as Siṃhavikrama.
In this way, O child, the wise, having embarked upon the six perfections such as giving taught by the Buddha—which are like a ship—cross over the ocean of existence.
Thus, in that forest, while Somaśūra was instructing him—that king Vinītamati who stood in the station of a Bodhisattva—[the following occurred].
Having heard those teachings on the Dharma, Bhāskara became tranquil; with his saffron robes appearing as if dyed by the glow of twilight, he entered the cave of the western mountain.
Then, having performed the twilight worship according to the rules, King Vinītamati and Somaśūra spent that night there.
And on another day, Vinītamati gradually instructed Somaśūra in the Buddhist doctrine along with its secret mysteries.
Then that Somaśūra, having approached his teacher in the forest, remained there at the foot of a tree, having constructed a small hut and being devoted to meditative absorption.
And in due course, both of them—the teacher and the disciple—having attained the great siddhis of yoga, simultaneously reached supreme enlightenment there.
In the meantime, that king Kanakakalaśa, out of envy, approached Indukalaśa by means of the power of his sword and horse.
Exiled from that kingdom of Ahicchatra by his brother, Vinītamati gave it to him [the brother] who had overthrown him.
Deprived of his kingdom and wandering along with two or three ministers, he reached by chance the hermitage of Vinītamati.
There, as long as he, afflicted by irresistible hunger and thirst, desired fruits, roots, and water, so long did that forest remain a mere illusion created by Māyāvin, the lord of the Gandharvas.
Having previously burned the Mārūkṛta tree with the desire to deceive Vinītamati out of greed for such hospitality from a traveler;
Seeing that hermitage of his suddenly turned into a desert, Vinītamati wandered here and there for a moment, bewildered.
Then he saw that guest, who had arrived wandering with a golden water-pot, his life-breath at his throat from hunger, accompanied by his followers.
Having approached him and inquired about such matters, that Bodhisattva, hospitable and having asked his questions, spoke.
"In this forest, which is devoid of guests and has become like a desert, I tell you who are hungry and thirsty even this means for sustaining life."
"Having fallen into a pit here, only half a krośa from this spot, a deer lies dead; go and preserve your lives with its meat."
When the distressed guest and his followers were thus prepared to depart, that Bodhisattva Vinītamati went forth from there first.
Having reached that pit and assumed the form of a deer through his yogic power, he cast himself into it and gave up his life for the sake of the seeker.
Then, slowly, Kanakakalaśa and the others arrived; they beheld that pit and saw the deer lying there dead.
Having dragged him out and then kindled a fire with grass and thorns, they roasted his flesh and ate it entirely without remainder.
Meanwhile, the Bodhisattva’s two wives were distraught; they saw the destruction of the hermitage, yet they did not see their husband.
Having gone there, the daughter of the Naga king and the daughter of the king spoke this to Somaśūra, who had emerged from his intense meditative absorption.
Having understood the teacher's conduct through that very aspiration, he reported it to the teacher's two wives, even though it brought them suffering.
Together with those two, he went quickly and directly to that place where he had been excavated, where his teacher had likewise offered himself as a guest to him.
There, the two daughters of the Naga king and the princess, seeing their husband in the form of a deer with nothing remaining but his horns and bones, lamented for him.
Taking those horn-bones and gathering a heap of wood from their own hermitage, those two devoted wives entered the fire.
Then Kanakakalaśa, who was staying there, having learned the news and being pained by grief, entered the fire along with his followers.
Things having come to this pass, Somaśūra, unable to endure the heavy sorrow, sat down upon a bed of darbha grass with the intent of bringing about the departure of his life-breaths.
At that very moment, Indra himself approached him and said: "Do not do this; for it was I who tested your guru."
Although he remained as nothing but bones and ashes, he was indeed raised back to life by me along with his wife and his guest, after being sprinkled with a rain of nectar.
Having heard these words of Indra, he bowed to him and rose up with joy; having gone there, Somaśūra beheld his own preceptor.
Then the Bodhisattva, having been restored to life and with his mind disciplined, arose together with his two wives and those led by Kanakakalaśa.
Then he bowed his head to that teacher who had returned from the other world together with his wife; he honored him with the flowers of his speech and drank him in with his eyes.
Then, all the gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, arrived there at those golden jars and other vessels which were bowed down in devotion.
Satisfied with him because of his virtuous nature, they granted boons of divine power to that Vinītamati—powers dedicated to the welfare of others—and then vanished.
Accompanied by Somaśūra and the others who had related their adventures to him, Vinītamati set out for another divine grove of ascetics.
Thus they meet here again even after having been reduced to ashes; how much more so, dear father, for living men who move according to their own will?
Therefore, enough of casting off your body; my child, you are indeed a hero, so go! For you shall certainly have a reunion with Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Having heard this story from the mouth of that aged female ascetic, I conceived a firm resolve; with sword in hand, I bowed to her and set out from there.
Having gradually reached this forest, I was found by these Śabaras, who were searching for an offering for Caṇḍikā, through the power of fate.
Having been captured by these men, I was brought here, afflicted by wounds, into the presence of this lord of the Śabaras, Māyāvaṭu, for the sake of battle.
"O Lord, you have been found by me here, accompanied by two or three ministers; and through your grace, I have attained a sense of peace as if I were in my own home."
Having heard this account of his own circumstances related by his friend Guṇākara, Mṛgāṅkadatta, staying in the house of the Śabara chief, experienced supreme satisfaction.

And having observed that the wounded man required the proper regimen for his body during the conflict, as the day was turning, he rose with his other companions and performed his own daily religious duties.
And then, while he was restoring Guṇākara to health there during those remaining days, it occurred to him that he wished to go to Ujjayinī to obtain Śaśāṅkavatī and to find his other friends.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave: Now, when Guṇākara had recovered and his wound was healed, on an auspicious day, he took leave of that friend, the lord of the Śabaras.
He had followed from a great distance for the sake of his mission, accompanied by his friend, the lord of the Mātaṅgas, Durgapiśāca, with whom he had made an agreement.
For the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī, Mṛgāṅkadatta set out from that village toward Ujjayinī, taking Māyāvaṭu along with his followers.
And as he was traveling, he was accompanied by Śrutadhi, Vimalabuddhi, Guṇākara, and Bhīmaparākrama.
Once, while searching for her other friends in that Vindhya forest, he, along with his ministers, fell asleep on the road at night beneath the shade of a certain tree.
And having suddenly woken up, as soon as he rose and looked about, he saw there another man lying asleep.
As soon as he uncovered his face, he recognized his own minister, who had arrived, known by the name Vicitrakatha.
He too, having awakened and seeing his lord Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was engaged in various conversations, joyfully took hold of his feet, being a virtuous man.
He was embraced by him, whose eyes blossomed at the sight of him so unexpectedly, and he was greeted with joy by all those ministers who had likewise awakened.
Then, having been questioned in turn by all of them who had related their own respective adventures, Vicitrakatha proceeded to relate his own story.
Then, because of the curse of the one named Pārāvata, while you were scattered here and there, I wandered alone there for a long time out of delusion.
Having wandered far astray and lost my senses the following day, I suddenly reached, exhausted at the edge of a forest, a great celestial city.
There, a certain celestial man, accompanied by two celestial women, saw me and comforted me after I had been bathed with cool waters.
Having led me inside, he diligently offered me divine food; then he himself ate, and after him the two women ate, and after them those others.
And after he had finished eating, while I was resting there, I addressed him: "Who are you, and why have you rescued me when I was on the verge of death?"
"I must certainly abandon my body without my lord," he said; having spoken thus, I related my entire history to him.
Then that great-souled one, filled with affection, spoke thus to me: "I am a Yakṣa; these two are my wives, and you have arrived today as my guest."
"Hospitality according to one's ability is indeed the duty of householders; since you have been honored by me, why do you wish to abandon your life?"
Indeed, this separation of yours from us shall last only for a short time due to the curse of the Naga; for once your curse has been exhausted, your reunion is certain.
O noble one, who in this saṃsāra is born free from suffering? Listen as I describe the suffering that was witnessed even by me, though I am a yakṣa.
There is a city named Trigarta, which is like a garland adorning the crest of this bride, the Earth, and is woven with the virtues of flowers.
In that city, there was a certain young brahmin named Pavitradhara; he was poor in wealth but not poor in kinsmen, lineage, and other such qualities.
Living among those illustrious men, that proud brahmin reflected: "Though I abide by my station, I do not shine in the midst of these wealthy men."
Like a single word among the words of a great poem, I am one whose speech is meaningful; yet, being high-minded, I am unable to perform service nor accept gifts.
Therefore, having gone to some secluded place, I shall accomplish the siddhi of a yakṣiṇī; for I possess the instruction of the mantra there from the mouth of my guru.
Having thus resolved and having gone to the forest according to the prescribed rites, that twice-born man, the bearer of the sacred thread, sought to win the Yakṣiṇī as his wife.
And joined with that Siddhi named Saudāminī, he stood forth like a tree emerged from a harsh winter through the splendor of spring.
Once, seeing that Pavitradhara was distressed in mind due to the absence of a son's birth, his yakṣiṇī wife spoke to him.
"Noble son, do not worry, for a son shall indeed be born to us; listen to this account, which I shall relate to you here."
In the southern region, there is a grove of *tamāla* trees, dark as a dense cloud that obscures the sun, which is like the very birthplace of the rainy season.
In that city dwells a famous yakṣa named Pṛthūdara; I am his only daughter, Saudāminī by name.
Out of affection, I was led by that father to various noble mountains, where I constantly played in those very divine garden lands.
And once, while playing with my friend Kapiśabhrū, I saw on Mount Kailāsa a young Yakṣa named Aṭṭahāsa.
At that very moment, he too saw me standing in the midst of my friends; it is said that we both became captivated by each other's form and appearance.
Having seen that, and perceiving our equal union, my father summoned him there and immediately settled our marriage with Aṣṭahāsa.
When the day for the wedding had been fixed, my father led me to his home; and Aṭṭahāsa, also delighted, returned to his own abode together with his friends.
And on another day, my friend Kapiśabhrū, appearing dejected, came into my presence; when questioned, she spoke thus with great difficulty:
"O friend, although this is unspeakable and unpleasant, I shall tell it to you: today, as I was returning, I saw that Aṭṭahāsa, your chosen husband."
In the garden on the slopes of the Himalayas known as Citrasthala, the king of the Yakṣas, longing for you, was made to play by his friends who were diverting him with sport.
His brother was Dīptaśikha, and his son was Anaḍakūbara; they themselves prepared [the chariot] for him, and they also took up the office of his ministers.
Then, while traveling through the sky by chance, Naḍakūbara saw your beloved, who was thus amusing himself with his friends.
Enraged, the son of the Lord of Wealth summoned him and cursed him: "Since you, having become a servant, desire the playful sport of your master, therefore [this shall be so]."
"O evil-minded one, become a mortal; desiring the heights, you shall fall to the depths. Thus addressed by him, Aṭṭahāsa, being distressed, replied:
"O Lord, this was done by me, a fool, out of impatience; it was not out of pride regarding my office. Therefore, O Master, grant me forgiveness."
Having heard those piteous words and having understood them exactly as they were through his supernormal insight, Naḍakūbara spoke to him for the sake of ending the curse:
Having become a human being, you shall beget upon that very Yakṣiṇī for whom you yearn this son of yours, Dīptaśikha, as your younger brother.
"Released from the curse, you shall regain your own station together with that wife; meanwhile, your brother, having become your son on earth, shall rule the kingdom."
When the son of the Lord of Wealth had said, "The curse shall be released," that Aṭṭahāsa vanished somewhere due to the power of the curse.
"Having seen that, I have come here to your side, O friend, distressed. When I was told this by my friend, I fell into some indescribable state of suffering.
Then, having lamented for myself and gone to inform my parents of that, I spent this time with the desire for reunion once more.
Thus you were born as Aṭṭahāsa, and I am she; we two have now met, and in this way a son has been produced for us both here today before long.
When the wise Saudāminī had spoken thus, that twice-born Pavitradhara became filled with great joy, having conceived hope for the birth of a son.
In due time, a son was born to him by that yakṣiṇī; by that very birth, both his house and his mind were illuminated.
And having beheld the face of his son, that Pavitradhara instantly became the Yakṣa Aṭṭahāsa, possessing a divine form.
And he said to the Yakṣiṇī, "My dear, that curse upon us has passed; I have become this Aṭṭahāsa. Come, let us go to our own abode."
When he had spoken thus, his wife said to him: "Consider how your brother, who was but a child, might become a son again after having turned into a daughter due to a curse."
Having heard that and having observed through meditation, Aṭṭahāsa said to her: "My dear, there is a Brahmin named Devadarśana in this city."
For that man of five fires, two additional fires blazed up through hunger—the digestive fires of himself and his wife—just as the poor man’s fires blaze up due to the lack of offspring and wealth.
Once, while he was established in austerity, seeking wealth and a son, the blessed Fire-god instructed him in a dream.
"You have no biological son; however, there shall be one who is adopted. And by his power alone, O Brahmin, your poverty shall cease."
Thus, that Brahmin remains today awaiting him from the direction of Agni; this child must be given to him, for such was the destiny.
Having spoken thus to his beloved, he placed that child upon a golden pitcher filled with gold, and fastened a garland of divine jewels around the infant's neck.
Having cast [the corpse] into the house of that brahmin while he was asleep at night, Aṭṭahāsa, together with his wife, went to his own destination along with his wife.
Having awakened there, that brahmin Devadarśana, together with his wife, beheld the young moon with its shimmering jewel-like stars.
Wondering "What is this? and looking at that golden pitcher, he remembered the fiery instruction from his dream and rejoiced.
He took up that boy, his son bestowed by fate, as well as that wealth; and at dawn, he celebrated a great festival.
And on the eleventh day, she gave her young son his appropriate name, Śrīdarśana, right there.
Then, having become very wealthy, that brahmin Devadarśana remained performing rituals such as sacrifices and enjoying various pleasures.
Śrīdarśana also grew up there in his father’s house, and being full of vigor, he attained excellence in the sciences of the Vedas as well as in the knowledge of weapons.
In the course of time, while his son was still in his youth, his father Devadarśana, having arrived there on a pilgrimage to sacred sites, passed away at Prayāga.
Having learned of that, his mother also entered the fire; thereafter, Śrīdarśana performed for them the funeral rites prescribed by the scriptures while mourning.
Gradually, his grief diminished and he made no further acquisitions; though wise, he became addicted to gambling and, by fate, remained without kinsmen.
And before long, as his wealth was exhausted by that evil addiction, he experienced distress even regarding his food.
Once, while staying for three days without food in a gambling hall, he was unable to leave because of his shame over his inappropriate clothing.
A certain gambler friend named Mukharaka, seeing Śrīdarśana distressed because he was not eating what had been given to him by others, addressed him.
Why are you deluded? This very sight is the sin of the vice of gambling; have you not realized that the dice are nothing but the falling glances of unchaste women?
His arms are his cloak, the dust is his bed, the crossroads are his home, and his wife is ruin—indeed, the Creator has fashioned these for the gambler.
Why do you not enjoy it? Though you are wise, why do you neglect yourself? For what desired thing is there that a steadfast man, while living, cannot attain?
And so, listen to this wonderful story of Bhūnandana: there exists here, an ornament of the earth, the region known as Kaśmīra.
Having fashioned the first heaven for the enjoyment of those who have performed meritorious deeds, the Creator fashioned a second one, as it were, for the enjoyment of objects to be enjoyed.
That city was occupied by both Sarasvatī and Śrī, who had entered it as if out of mutual envy, each claiming, "I am the superior one here; I am not."
As if to prevent the entry of the Kali age, which is hostile to the Dharma, the Snowy Mountain protects itself with its own surrounding halo.
"Go far away from here, you defilement!"—thus do the waves, with hands adorned by the *vitasti* [measure], seem to push back the impurity from this sacred bathing place of the gods.
In which city, rows of lofty palaces washed with white lime produce the illusion of being the mountain ranges at the foot of the nearby Himalayas.

In that realm, there was a king named Bhūnandana, who was a preceptor to the castes and stages of life, a moon bringing joy to his subjects, and one learned in the sciences and the traditional scriptures.
His valor shone upon the pairs of breasts of amorous women, as well as upon the circles of his enemies' fingernails.
Though he was a man of policy, his subjects were constantly devoid of good governance; though his mind was solely attached to Kṛṣṇa, their minds were far from being devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Once, on the twelfth lunar day, having duly worshipped Acyuta, that king saw in a dream a certain daughter of the Daityas who had approached him.
Having attained union with her, he awoke and did not see her; however, filled with wonder, he clearly saw the marks of sexual enjoyment upon his own body.
"This is no dream, for it is vivid; I consider this to be a state of enjoyment. Surely I have been deceived by that woman, who must be some kind of celestial being."
Having understood this, his mind became so afflicted by the pain of separation that he gradually abandoned all his royal duties.
Not seeing any means to attain her, the king reflected: "By the grace of Hari, may that moment of union with her come to me."
In order to attain that [state], I shall go to a solitary place and propitiate Him alone; alas, I shall cast off this noose of kingship, which has become tasteless due to separation from Him.
Having thus resolved and informed his ministers, that delight of the earth gave the kingdom to his younger brother named Sunanda.
Having renounced his kingdom, he went to the sacred ford named Kramasaras, which arose from the footprint of Hari and was established in ancient times by Trivikrama.
It was occupied by the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—who, shaped like peaks, resided upon the summits of the nearby mountains.
By that same footprint of Viṣṇu, another river of the gods was created in Kaśmīra, named Viṣuvatī, which flows as the Vitastā as if out of envy.
There the king remained performing austerities, indifferent to other pleasures; weary and longing for a new flavor, he was like a *cātaka* bird in the heat of summer.
And when twelve years had passed while he remained there engaged in ascetic penance, a certain ascetic, the best among the wise, arrived by that same path.
With tawny matted hair and clad in bark garments, accompanied by a host of disciples, he was like Lord Śiva descended from the mountain peak of that sacred ford.
Upon seeing the king, he was filled with affection; approaching him and bowing low, he inquired after his welfare and, after reflecting for a moment as it were, spoke.
"O King, that Daitya maiden who dwells on Pātāla is your beloved; therefore, take heart, for I shall bring her into your presence."
For I am the son of a sacrificer named Yajñasamjña from the Deccan, a Brahmin named Bhūtivasu who is a teacher of yogins.
Thus, having had my knowledge transmitted by my father from the Pātālaśāstra, I was instructed in the sequence of rituals for the mantras and tantras of Haṭakeśāna.
Having gone to Śrīparvata, I performed austerities to propitiate Tryambaka; then, being pleased by that, Śiva appeared to me there in person and commanded me as follows.
Go, accompanied by the wives of the Daityas, and enjoy pleasures in Rasātala; you shall come to me, so hear from me the means for attaining that.
There are many openings to the netherworld here upon this earth, but there is one great opening made by Maya that provides light in Kaśmīra.
Having led him into the secret garden grounds of the Dānavas, Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, delighted Aniruddha, her beloved.
And then Pradyumna, in order to protect that son, made an effort by manifesting a door on one side using the mountain peak.
And for the sake of guarding that gateway, he worshipped Durgā—who bears the name Śārikā—by means of hundreds of hymns, and established her there.
That place there is even now designated by two names: Pradyumnaśikhara and Śārikākūṭa.
"Go, enter Pātāla through that opening at the head of the cave together with your followers; by my grace, you shall achieve success therein."
Having spoken thus, when the deity had vanished, by the power of his grace, all-encompassing wisdom arose within me, and I have come here to this land of Kaśmīra.
Therefore, O King, come with us to Śārikākūṭa; there I shall lead you to Pātāla, to the side of your beloved woman.
When the ascetic had spoken thus, the king, the delighter of the earth, agreed and went together with him to that heap of śārikā wood.
Having bathed there in the Vitastā and worshipped Vināyaka, one should fully honor the goddess Śārikā, preceded by the ritual binding of the directions and other preliminary rites.
When that great ascetic, graced by the favor of the Earth, had revealed the opening by casting mustard seeds according to the prescribed rite.
Having entered together with him and his disciples, that king traveled along the path to the underworld for five days, day and night.
On the sixth day, having all crossed the Ganges which flows to the underworld, they beheld upon the silver ground a divine forest.
It was perfumed by the fragrance of golden lotuses blooming upon the land, and it possessed trees of rising coral, camphor, sandalwood, and agallochum.
In its center was a vast expanse, beautiful with jeweled staircases, with golden walls and radiant with a multitude of ruby pillars.
And they joyfully beheld the lofty temple of Śiva, its vast and pure central core constructed of moonstone.
Then that ascetic, the best among the knowers of truth, addressed his own disciples and King Bhūnandana, who were filled with wonder.
"This is that god Hāṭakeśvara, whose abode is Pātāla; he is celebrated throughout the three worlds, therefore let him be worshipped."
Then all of them, drenched by those waters of the Gaṅgā, worshipped Śambhu there with various flowers produced in the netherworld.
Having rested for a moment at that place of worship, they departed from there and reached a single, divine, great jambu tree from which ripe fruits were falling.
Seeing them, that ascetic said to them: "These fruits are not to be eaten by you; for if they are consumed, they will surely cause an obstacle."
Even upon hearing that, one of his disciples, driven by hunger, ate that fruit; and having eaten it, he immediately became motionless, taking on the form of an immobile being.
Then, their desire for the fruit [of their penance] abandoned due to the terror of seeing that [creature], the ascetic, accompanied by those other disciples and Bhūnandana, [departed].
Having traversed a distance of one krośa, he beheld there a lofty golden wall with a gate constructed of excellent jewels standing before him.
On both sides of that gate, he saw two iron-bodied rams, striking with their horns, blocking the entrance on either side.
Having instantly struck them on the head with his staff empowered by the recited mantra, he drove them both away somewhere, as if they had been struck by a thunderbolt.
Then, having entered through that door, he, his disciples, and the king beheld divine dwellings made of gold and jewels.
And at every door they saw gatekeepers with iron clubs in hand, their lower lips fiercely bitten by their teeth.
Then they all sat down there at the foot of a single excellent tree; that ascetic, however, performed a yogic concentration (dhāraṇā) capable of destroying evil.
By the power of that dhāraṇī, all those fierce gatekeepers fled from every door and vanished from sight.
And in an instant, from those gates, courtesans adorned with divine ornaments and garments emerged, accompanied by retinues of Daitya maidens.
Approaching each of those ascetics individually, they requested entrance from them, each according to the words of her respective mistress.
"Once you have entered within, you must not disregard the words of your beloved"; having thus spoken to those others, that virtuous ascetic then departed.
And having entered the excellent palace together with some of those women, he obtained one preeminent Daitya maiden and all his desired enjoyments.
Others as well, one by one, were led by those other women into divine mansions and became vessels for the enjoyment of the Daitya daughters.
Then King Bhūnandana was also led by that single woman, who was bowed low with humility, to an outer palace made of jewels.
Because of the reflections of her excellent female attendants appearing on all sides upon the jeweled walls, it was as if they were the arrangement of a living painting.
It was constructed from an exceedingly smooth and vast expanse of sapphire, appearing as if it had ascended to the very surface of the sky out of a desire to rival celestial chariots.
It was like the banner of the Vṛṣṇis, rich with the power of Acyuta, where Rāma was radiant though agitated by intoxication, and Pradyumna displayed his charming amorous play.
Even a flower that withstands the morning sun cannot serve as a comparison for the delicate beauty of the women's bodies here.
Having entered there, which resounded with the music of celestial instruments, the king beheld that lovely asura maiden whom he had previously seen in his dream.

When this [city] was illuminated by its own luster, even though Pātāla was devoid of the sun and other celestial bodies, the Creator’s fashioning of the light of jewels and such things became a mere redundancy.
Beholding her, whose form was indescribable, the king, with tears of joy, seemed to have washed away the impurity of looking at others from his eyes.
And she too, having beheld that lord of kings as he was being proclaimed with songs of praise, experienced an indescribable joy, like a young night-lily at dawn.
Rising up and taking him by the hand, she said, "I have caused you distress," and with great respect, she seated him upon a throne.
When he had rested for a mere moment, bathed, and adorned himself with garments and ornaments, that Asura woman led him to a garden for a drinking feast.
There, on the bank of a pond filled with the blood, fat, and wine dripping from corpses hanging from trees growing on its edge, she sat down together with him.
She gave that vessel, filled with the essence of liquor, to the king for him to drink; however, he did not accept it, as it was loathsome.
"There would be no safety for you if you were to refuse this drink of ours. To her, as she spoke thus with persistence, the king replied:
"I have resolved that I shall certainly not drink this, whatever it may be. Then she threw the vessel at his head and departed elsewhere.
With his eyes and face contorted, that king was taken by the attendants of another woman and cast into a long pond within the water.
And at that very moment, as soon as he was cast down, he beheld himself arrived right there in that former penance grove, at the sacred ford of Kramasaras.
And seeing that mountain there, which was like snow and seemed to be laughing, he—dejected, astonished, bewildered, and deceived—reflected:
Where is that garden of the Daitya’s son, and where is this mountain Kramasaras? Oh, what is this marvel—is it an illusion, or is it a delusion of the mind?
What else could this be, other than the certain consequence of my having transgressed his word? Even after hearing the words of that ascetic, this [transgression] of mine has manifested itself.
And that drink is not to be despised; it was a test for me alone, since by its falling upon my head, a divine fragrance arises.
For in every way, even great effort made toward those who are incapable does not bear fruit; for the ritual procedure operates adversely toward them.
Thinking thus, Bhūnandana approached that place and was surrounded there by bees, drawn by the fragrance of his limbs which had been moistened by drinking the wine of the asura’s daughter.
"Alas! May this hardship not yield a desired fruit for me; rather, may it produce an undesired result, like the torment of a weak-minded person who raises a vetāla."
Thus being stung by those bees, the king, reflecting at that time and overcome with agitation, set his mind upon abandoning his body.
Just then, by chance, a certain son of a sage who happened to come along that path beheld the king in such a state.
Approaching quickly, his mind moistened with compassion, the seer warded off the bees; and having asked about the circumstances, he spoke thus to the king:

O King, as long as this body exists, how can there be an end to suffering? Therefore, the wise should always strive for the goals of human life through the absence of agitation regarding that [suffering].
As long as there is no realization of the oneness of Acyuta, Īśāna, and Viriñci, the accomplishments born from the worship of their distinctions will remain merely transitory.
Meditating upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara with the realization of their non-difference, perform penance here for another twelve years with fortitude.
Then you shall regain that beloved, and in the end, eternal perfection; meanwhile, your body has already been perfected—behold, it now possesses a divine fragrance.
And take this black antelope skin of mine as a symbol of equanimity, by which, when you have covered yourself with it, you will not be troubled by the bees.
Having spoken thus and given him the armor and the mantra, the sage departed; and the king, accepting them with the words "So be it," remained there at that sacred ford, his fortitude restored.
And after he had lived there for twelve years, having propitiated the Lord through asceticism, that Daitya maiden Kumudini approached the king herself.
Having gone to Pātāla with that beloved wife, King Bhūnandana enjoyed pleasures for a long time and attained perfection.
Thus, those who are by nature free from agitation, who are worthy, and who rely upon fortitude, regain their own ground even if they have fallen far away from it.
And you, Śrīdarśana, who possess auspicious marks and are destined for future prosperity—why do you neglect yourself out of distress without food?
Having been addressed thus by his friend Mukharaka within the gambling hall, Śrīdarśana, who had been fasting during the night, spoke to him.
"As you have said, though I am of noble birth, because I have been ruined by gambling, I am unable to go outside this city out of shame."
Therefore, O Miśra, if you do not forbid my departure for some foreign land on this very night, then I shall take food.
Upon hearing that, Mukharaka said, "So be it," and then, having brought food for him, he gave it to him; and he too then ate it.
And having eaten, Śrīdarśana then set out toward another country together with that very friend, who followed him out of affection.
And as he was traveling there on the road at night, his mother and father, who had arrived by chance through the sky, happened by fate to see him.
Those two, Saudāminī and Aṭṭahāsa, by whom that son of Devadarśana was placed here in the house of the Brahmin as soon as he was born;

Perceiving that he had fallen into such a state—deprived of his wealth by the vice of gambling and set out for a foreign land—the two of them, out of affection, spoke from the sky while remaining invisible.
"O Śrīdarśana, your mother-in-law Devadarśanā has placed her ornaments on the ground inside her own quarters."
Having gone there and taken those, proceed without anxiety to Mālava; for there resides a king named Śrīsena, possessed of exalted glory.
And because he had been greatly afflicted by the calamity of gambling during his youth, he established a large and flourishing monastery for gamblers.
Gamblers dwelling there obtain their desired food; in that same way, go there, and it will be well for you.
Having heard these words from heaven, Śrīdarśana went home; emerging from the pit in the earth, he took those ornaments along with Samiṣṭā.
Then, delighted and accompanied by his friend Mukharaka, he set out toward Mālava, considering it to be a favor from the gods.
Having traveled a very long distance during that night and day, he reached the village named Bahusasya with her at evening.
And being weary, he sat down with his friend on the bank of a lake of pure water, not far from that village.
At that moment, while he stood there with his feet washed in the water he had drunk, a certain maiden of incomparable beauty approached for the sake of water.
With limbs marked by lines the color of blue lotuses, she was like Rati alone, darkened by the smoke from Kāma when he was consumed by Hara.
Seeing Śrīdarśana, she approached him and his companion—who were delighted by the sight—and addressed them with eyes overflowing with love.
Where have you two, O illustrious ones, come here to this calamity? Have you fallen into the blazing fire out of ignorance, like moths?
Hearing this, Mukharaka was bewildered; he questioned the maiden there, "Who are you? And what is this that you have said? Tell me."
Then she said: "I shall speak this in brief; listen, you two. There is a very great agrahāra, renowned by the name Sughoṣa."
There lived a brahmin named Padmagarbha, the most eminent among those who know the Vedas; he had a wife of noble family named Śaśikalā.
And from her, two children were born to that noble man: a son named Mukharaka, and a daughter, who was myself, Padmiṣṭhā.
That brother of mine, Mukharaka, ruined by the vice of gambling, left home even in his childhood and went off somewhere to another land.
When my mother passed away due to that grief, my father, afflicted by the pain of both sorrows, abandoned his life as a householder.
And taking me alone, he wandered here and there to search for his son, and by the power of fate, he reached this village.
And here in this great village, there was a chief of a band of thieves known by the name of Vasubhūti, who was a Brāhmaṇa in name only.
Therefore, having arrived here with his attendants, that wicked man has taken away my father’s life and the gold contained within his body.
And having been led by him to his home, I was taken captive and intended to be given as a wife to his son named Subhūti.
And his son, having gone somewhere to plunder a caravan, has not yet returned; by my own merits, fate alone is now the authority.
Therefore, if this thief sees you two, he will certainly cause you great harm; devise a means by which you may both escape from him.
When she had spoken thus, Mukharaka, having recognized her at that very moment, embraced the maiden around the neck and said while weeping:
"Alas, Padmiṣṭhā! Here I am, your brother Mukharaka; a betrayer of kin, O sister, ill-fated as I am, I am destroyed—alas!"
Hearing that, Padmiṣṭhā was also distressed upon seeing her elder sister in such a state; she was as if instantly enveloped by all sorrows out of compassion.

And soon after Śrīdarśana had obtained those two as his wives, that Aṭṭahāsa approached him in the guise of a Brahmin and, by means of a stratagem, joined with him.
When you were reminded of your birth by means of a punning remark through the power of fate, and when he uttered your names, you abandoned that body and attained the state of a Yakṣiṇī.
"Know that those two are us, and this one is he with the many blazing crests. As soon as they had said this to him, Śrīdarśana remembered his former birth.
Then, having been instantly restored, that yakṣa with his blazing crest was again united with those two wives according to the prescribed rites.
"Know that I am this Yakṣa, O you of wonderful speech; likewise, O beloved, know these two to be Jyotirlekhā and Dhūmalekhā."
Thus, if even for those like me, born of the divine lineage, such pleasure and pain may occur at will, what need is there to mention the case of human beings?
"My child, before long you shall be reunited with your lord Mṛgāṅkadatta; therefore, do not give way to despondency."
"And for the sake of your hospitality here, I have established this earthly abode of mine; therefore, stay here, and I shall fulfill your desire."
Then, having told me his own story—"From here I shall go to Kailāsa, my own abode"—that Yakṣa attended upon me there for some time.
Having learned today that you had arrived here, that wise man brought me while you were sleeping at night and placed me in your midst.
"Then I was seen by you, and you were also seen by me; such, O King, is my account of our separation."

Having heard this from him—the one whose name, Vicitrakatha, was truly meaningful because of his wonderful tales—Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta experienced the utmost happiness that night together with his other ministers.
