Having spent the night there in the forest region, he set out for Ujjayinī with those companions, intent upon winning Śaśāṅkavatī; meanwhile, he searched for his remaining friends who had been separated by the curse of the Nāga.

Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Seventh Wave. Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by those ministers—with Śrutadhi as the fifth—proceeded through that region of the Vindhya forest.
He reached a certain forest, delightful with the shade of fruit-bearing, lush trees, and containing a reservoir of water that was perfectly clear, sweet, and cool.
Having bathed there with his ministers and having eaten various fruits, he heard what seemed like a conversation in a spot shaded by creepers.
Having gone there, as soon as she cast her gaze into that bower of creepers, she beheld within it a magnificent, great elephant.
He was comforting a man who was weary on the road and sightless, by means of water brought in his hand, fruits, and likewise by the breeze from his ears.
And he spoke to him repeatedly with clear speech, out of affection like a virtuous man, saying, "I hope you have recovered somewhat?"
Seeing him, the prince said to his friends in amazement: "Behold! Where is this wild elephant, and where is this conduct befitting a human?"
"Surely this man must stand here for some reason or another; he is a person who bears a striking resemblance to my friend Pracaṇḍaśakti."
"But this man is blind; let us see quickly," he said to those friends, and Mṛgāṅkadatta remained there, listening unobserved.
Then the elephant asked that blind man, who had now recovered his breath: "Who are you? How have you come here while being blind? Let it be told."
Then that blind man also said to that excellent elephant: "There is here a king named Amaradatta, the lord of the city of Ayodhyā."
He has a son named Mṛgāṅkadatta, possessed of excellent virtues; I am the servant of that noble-born youth, known as Pracaṇḍaśakti.
For some reason, that prince was banished from his own country by his father, accompanied by us as his ten companions.
Therefore, for the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī, we set out from there for Ujjayinī, but by the curse of a Nāga, we were all separated in the wilderness.
And I, having become blind by that curse, wandered about until I arrived here, subsisting on whatever fruits, roots, and water I could find.
Even death by falling into chasms and the like, or by starvation, is most desirable to me; yet alas, the Creator has not granted it to me while I am still experiencing such suffering.
I know that today, through your grace, the suffering of hunger has been pacified; likewise, may my blindness also be pacified, for you are indeed a deity.
When this was said by him, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having gained certainty and remaining poised between joy and sorrow, spoke to those ministers.
"This man is indeed Pracaṇḍaśakti; alas, he has fallen into such a state! It is not appropriate for us to reveal him to him now with such haste."
"Perhaps this elephant might do her a service to her eyes; however, upon seeing us, he would surely perish. Therefore, we must see what lies within him."
Having spoken thus, the prince stood there listening along with his followers; then Pracaṇḍaśakti questioned that elephant.
Now tell me, O high-souled one, what is your story? Who are you? And why is this elephantine form of yours, though belonging to one intoxicated with rut, devoid of pride?
Having heard that, the lordly elephant sighed and addressed him: "Listen; I shall tell you my own history from the very beginning."
Long ago, in the city of Ekalavyā, there was a king named Śrutadhara; he had two sons by his two wives.
When he had passed away, the younger brother named Satyadhara banished the elder brother, named Śīladhara, from the kingdom.
Then that Śīladhara, having gone there and propitiated Śaṅkara with ascetic penance out of that indignation, requested a boon from him once he was satisfied.
"O God, may I become a Gandharva who moves through the sky; then I shall slay that heir of Satyadhara with utter ease."
Having heard that, the Blessed One Śambhu himself commanded him thus: "This shall happen for you; however, today that enemy of yours has died of his own accord."
And he shall be born again in Rāḍhā as the son of King Ugrabhaṭa, named Samarabhaṭa, who will be dear to his father.
And you shall be born as his elder half-brother named Bhīmabhaṭa; having slain him, you will rule the kingdom.
"Because you performed this penance out of resentment, you shall, due to the sage's curse, fall from your station and become a wild elephant."
Remembering his past lives, he spoke: "Where will you console this weary guest when he tells you his own story?"
Then, released from the state of an elephant, you will become a gandharva; and at that time, there will also be a benefit for that guest.
When Bharga had vanished after giving these instructions, Śīladhara, seeing that his body was emaciated by long austerities, cast it into the Gaṅgā.
In the meantime, at this juncture of the narrative, there was a king previously mentioned named Ugrabhaṭa, who resided in the city of Rāḍhā.
While he was dwelling happily with the queen named Manoramā, a dancer named Lāsaka arrived at his side from another land.
And he demonstrated that dramatic performance to the king, in which the nectar had been carried off by Hari from the Daityas who were in the form of women.
And there, on that ground of immortality, the king beheld the dancing daughter of that dancer, named Lāsyavatī.
Upon merely seeing her form, which had utterly agitated the Dānavas, the king fell under the sway of desire as if he were truly immortal.
And at the conclusion of the dance, having bestowed abundant wealth upon her father, he then caused that maiden to enter his own inner apartments.
Then the king remained with that dancer Lāsyavatī, who had been given to him in marriage, his eyes fixed intently upon her face.
Once, he said to his priest named Yajuḥsvāmin: "I have no son here; therefore, perform for me a sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son."
Then, saying "So be it," that domestic priest duly performed that sacrifice for the king together with learned Brahmins.
And he, who had previously been propitiated by her, caused that most beautiful goddess to consume the foremost portion of the sacrificial porridge, purified by mantras.
And he gave the remainder to that second one, Lāsyavatī; and then Śīladhara and Satyadhara, both of them, [were given] to those two.
The two previously mentioned [beings] were conceived in the wombs of both queens; and when the time had arrived, the queen of that lord of the earth [gave birth].
Manoramā gave birth to a son endowed with auspicious marks; this king named Bhīmabhaṭa was born, one of renowned fame.
At that moment, a very clear voice resounded from the sky; then, on the following day, Lāsyavatī also gave birth to a son.
And the king gave that warrior the name Samarabhaṭa; then, having received the sacraments, the two children grew up gradually.
The elder, Bhīmabhaṭa, surpassed that younger brother in virtues; and through their rivalry, mutual enmity grew between them.
Once, during a playful wrestling match with his arms, the envious Samarabhaṭa forcibly struck Bhīmabhaṭa on the neck.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, out of rage, encircled Samarabhaṭa with both arms, lifted him up, and dashed him to the ground with a loud crash.
Struck severely by him, vomiting blood from all his orifices, he was raised up and led into the presence of his mother by his own servants.
Having seen him and learned the news, she, distressed by affection, placed her head upon his head and wept bitterly.
When the king had entered and seen this, his mind was agitated; he asked her, "What is this? and Lāsyavatī replied as follows.
"O King, this condition of my son was brought about by Bhīmabhaṭa; yet he constantly overcomes him, and I did not tell you."
Having seen this, I know how there could possibly be welfare for you alone; please consider this yourself regarding such a son.
When he was thus addressed by his beloved, King Ugrabhaṭa, becoming enraged, restrained Bhīmabhaṭa from his presence.
And having deprived him of his livelihood, he appointed a hundred princes along with their retinues for the protection of that Samarabhaṭa.
He placed the treasury under the control of his younger brother, while he completely excluded his elder brother Bhīmabhaṭa from every aspect of it.
Then his mother, Manoramā, called him and said to him: "Your father has already abandoned you because he is infatuated with the dancing girls."
Therefore, go to your maternal grandfather’s palace in Pāṭaliputra; there, being childless, he will give his own kingdom to you.
"However, here this powerful enemy Samarabhaṭa might kill you,"—hearing these words from his mother, Bhīmabhaṭa said to her:
Being a Kṣatriya, I shall not abandon my own country out of fear like a coward; be firm, O Mother, for what wretch is capable of oppressing me?
When he had spoken thus, his mother said to him: "In that case, procure many companions for the sake of protection with my wealth."
Then Bhīmabhaṭa said, "Mother, this does not befit you; for if it were so, it would constitute an act of hostility toward our father."
"By your blessing alone may that welfare be mine; be at peace," having thus consoled her, Bhīmabhaṭa departed from there.
And when the citizens there learned of this, they all reflected: "The King has committed a supreme impropriety toward Bhīmabhaṭa."
Samarabhaṭa does not dare to seize his kingdom; therefore, this is the time for us to perform service to Bhīmabhaṭa.
Having thus decided, those citizens secretly nourished Bhīmabhaṭa with wealth in such a way that he remained there happily together with his servants.
But he was the youngest of them, and he resolved upon the very execution of his father, having inferred that intention from the preparations made for the funeral attire.
At that moment, a brave, young, and wealthy Brahmin named Śaṅkhadatta, who was a friend of both [the king and Samarabhaṭa], approached Samarabhaṭa and said to him:
"Enmity toward a brother is not fitting for you; this is neither dharma, nor is it possible for you to oppress one who is your elder. It would only result in supreme infamy for you."
Speaking thus and reproaching him, he was reviled by him; for wholesome advice leads only to anger in a fool, not to peace.
Then, having gone there out of anger and desiring to conquer him, the resolute Śaṅkhadatta formed a friendship with Bhīmabhaṭa.
Now, a certain merchant named Maṇidatta, who had arrived from another land, brought with him a single, most excellent jewel among horses.
White as the moon, with the melodious sound of pure conchs and other instruments, it rose up like a mass of towering waves from the ocean of milk.
It was adorned with shining crest-jewels, armlets, and other ornaments, appearing as if perfected by those born from the lineage of the Gandharvas.
Having been informed by Śaṅkhadatta, Bhīmabhaṭa went there and purchased that excellent horse from that preeminent merchant for a great sum of wealth.
At that very moment, Samarabhaṭa, having learned of this, arrived there and sought that horse from the merchant for double its price.
When the merchant did not give him that horse which had been made dependent [upon him], he then proceeded out of envy to take the horse by force.
Consequently, as the servants of both those princes rushed forward with weapons in hand, a fierce battle ensued there.
There, his followers having been struck down by the fierce staff-like arms of Bhīmabhaṭa, Samarabhaṭa abandoned his horse and fled out of fear of him.
And as he was being broken, Śaṅkhadatta, overwhelmed by a weight of fury, ran up, seized him by the hair from behind, and struck him down.
Just then, Bhīmabhaṭa approached from behind and restrained him, saying, "Let it be; otherwise, my father will surely suffer grief at this moment."
Then, released by Śaṅkhadatta and vomiting blood from his wounds, the terrified Samarabhaṭa fled and went to the side of his father.
Then, a certain Brahmin approached the hero Bhīmabhaṭa, who had accepted the horse there, and taking him aside to a secluded spot, spoke to him in an instant.
Your mother, Queen Manoramā, the domestic priest Yajusvāmin, and your father’s minister Sumati now speak these words to you.
"My child, you know well what kind of man the king is toward you; now that this event has occurred, he has indeed turned into your enemy."
If you would protect yourself, the Dharma, and your reputation; if you have regard for the future; and if you consider us your well-wishers.
Therefore, before the sun sets from this point, depart unobserved and go now to your maternal grandfather’s house for the sake of attaining success.
"And having thus sent this message, they have dispatched this casket filled with excellent jewels and gold; please accept it through my hands."
Having heard this from the brahmin and having welcomed it with "So be it," the wise Bhīmabhaṭa took possession of that vessel of excellent gold and fine jewels.
Having given him a fitting reply and dismissed that twice-born man, he, sword in hand, mounted his horse.
Then, accompanied by Śaṅkhadatta, who had taken up gold and jewels and was mounted on a second horse, he set out from there.
Having traveled a long distance, that prince Bhīmabhaṭa reached a great forest of reeds on the road at midnight.
There, as he proceeded incessantly with his companions, [the army] was awakened by the sound of arrows crushed by the hooves of the galloping horses.
Rising up with its two lion cubs who were roaring, it tore at the horses below the bellies with its claws.
And at that very moment, that heroic lion, accompanied by his mate, rendered them all lifeless, their limbs severed by the blows of his sword.
Then Samitra also dismounted and looked; at that moment, both horses fell to the ground with their entrails spilled out.
Seeing that, he became despondent and said to Śaṅkhadatta: "Friend, we have fled with great effort from our own kinsmen who were hostile toward us."
Tell me, even with a hundred efforts, where can we flee from Fate, by whom we have been struck down here today, though he is unable to bear even the weight of his own vehicle?
Even that horse for whose sake the abandonment of our country was undertaken has died; therefore, how can we traverse this forest on foot in the night?
Thus addressed by him, his friend Śaṅkhadatta said to him: "It is no new thing that adverse fate should overcome human effort."
Such is his innate nature, yet it is overcome by fortitude; what can that wind do to a steadfast man who remains unshaken, any more than it can affect a mountain?
Then Bhīmabhaṭa set out from there together with Śaṅkhadatta, who said, "Come, let us go there now that we have mounted our horses with steadfast courage."
Then, as he gradually traversed that wilderness with his feet lacerated by arrows, the night passed away.
Then, when the sun—the lamp of the world that dispels the darkness of night—had risen, the lotuses of the path-lotus-beds hummed sweetly with swarms of bees.
"By good fortune, he has crossed this forest teeming with lions and other beasts, while they—looking at one another and gazing at him with mouths wide open as if speaking—seem to exclaim in wonder."
Proceeding by degrees, he reached the sandy bank of the daughter of Jahnu, which was strewn with the huts of ascetics, accompanied by his companions.
There, having bathed in those waters—sweet and cool as if they were the nectar of the moon clinging to the head of Śiva—he rested.
He maintained his bodily existence by means of roasted venison purchased from hunters encountered on the road, as well as that which was brought by Śaṅkhadatta.
And seeing the full river of Jahnu impossible to cross, which seemed to ward him off repeatedly with its uplifted hands of waves;
Then, having gone along its bank, he saw a young Brahmin son, intent on his Vedic recitation, in the courtyard of a two-storied hut.
Having approached him, he asked, "Who are you, and what are you doing here alone in this desolate place? Thereupon, he replied to him.
I am a resident of Vārāṇasī, the son of a twice-born man named Śrīkaṇṭha, known by the name Nīlakaṇṭha, whose sequence of sacraments was performed by my father.
Thus, having completed my studies at the teacher's house, as soon as I returned to my own home in my youth, all my kinsmen had perished.
Therefore, protectorless, destitute of wealth, and ill-situated due to the failure of my household life, I became despondent; having come here, I have resorted to severe austerity.
Then, in a dream, the goddess Gaṅgā said to him: "Having given these fruits to me, remain here eating them until you obtain what you desire."
Having heard this, I woke up immediately; at the end of the night, having gone and bathed, I obtained fruits that had arrived within the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Bringing those fruits, which were as delicious as nectar, I ate them in my hut; thus, eating them as they arrived day after day, I remained here.
When he had spoken thus, Bhīmabhaṭa said to Śaṅkhadatta: "I shall give this virtuous man wealth sufficient for the life of a householder."
Having heard that, the prince, his word trusted, then gave that wealth—which had been released by his mother—to that brahmin.
What indeed is the greatness of the great, whose treasury of courage is never depleted, if they do not instantly dispel the suffering of another once it has been heard?
Having thus fulfilled the purpose of that brahmin, he then went everywhere, searching for a means to cross the Ganges; but when he found none, he [proceeded].
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, with his sword fastened to his head and accompanied by Śaṅkhadatta, descended into it with his two arms to swim across.
And in the middle portion, having distanced his companions by means of the mass of water, he somehow reached the further shore while being carried away by the waves.
As he searched along the shore for his friend Śaṅkhadatta, who had reached the far bank but was nowhere to be seen, the sun went down.
Then, despairing and crying out "Alas, my friend! in extreme distress, he prepared to throw himself into the Ganges at the onset of night.
O Goddess, my life has been carried away by you along with Jāhnavī; therefore, take now even this body of mine, which is empty of it.
Having said this, just as he desired to throw himself therein, Gaṅgā herself appeared visibly from the midst of its waters.
At that moment, she, delighted by his intense agitation, said to him: "My son, do not act rashly; your friend remains alive."
Before long, you shall be united with him; meanwhile, receive from me this vidyā known as the *pratilomānulomā*.
A man reciting this in the direct order shall become invisible to others; reciting it in the reverse order, he may cause the manifestation of any desired form.
This is the power of this vidyā, which is adorned with seven syllables; by its power, you shall become the king upon this earth.
Having said this and bestowed the magic science upon him, Jāhnavī vanished from his sight; he too, having conceived hope for the recovery of his friend and so forth, desisted from death.
Having spent the night with difficulty like a lotus, Bhīmabhaṭa, eager to find his friend, set out from there in the morning while searching for him.
Then, wandering about in order to search for Śaṅkhadatta, he eventually reached the country of Lāṭa all alone.

Therein, even though its people possess unmixed castes, they abide in a state of variegated brilliance; and although it is the abode of all arts, it does not bear the name of the "mine of faults" (the moon).
There, wandering about and observing the temples and dwellings within the city, he reached a hall belonging to gamblers.
Having entered there, he saw gamblers playing with dice, who, though clothed in nothing but rags around their loins, were nonetheless elegant in appearance.
With well-proportioned and robust limbs indicative of enjoyment and physical exercise, he proclaimed his hidden sovereignty, which was currently dependent upon wealth for its sustenance.
Having conversed with them, he began a game of dice with those who had formed the intention: "He, along with his ornaments, is our prey."
Then, having defeated them at dice, he seized all their wealth—that which had been acquired by those rogues through deceiving others.
When the gamblers, having lost their wealth, were preparing to go to their own homes, Bhīmabhaṭa blocked them by placing his arms across the doorway and said to them:
"Where are you going? Take this wealth! What use have I for it? This must be given by me to those who are dear to me; and are you not dear to me?"
"From where shall I obtain dear friends such as yourselves?"—even as he was speaking thus, they did not accept [his offer] out of shame.
There, a certain gambler named Akṣakṣapaṇaka said: "This is the convention of gambling—that what has been lost is not returned."
Nevertheless, if he, having become our friend, offers us wealth—even though it was won by his own desire—why should we not accept it?
Having heard that, others said: "If he establishes such eternal friendship with us, then this will be appropriate."
When they had spoken thus, Bhīmabhaṭa, considering them to be heroes, said "So be it" to them, formed a friendship with them, and gave that wealth to them.
Requested by them, he went with them and their families to the garden and enjoyed himself with the food, drink, and other luxuries they had provided.
Then, questioned by Akṣakṣapaṇaka and the others, he told them his own account of his lineage and name, and likewise questioned them in turn.
Then Akṣakṣapaṇa related his own story to him: "There was a Brahmin named Śivadatta in Hastināpura."
I am his son, named Vasudatta, born of that man of great wealth; in my childhood, I was instructed in the science of weapons as well as the sciences of the Vedas.
Then my father arranged my marriage with a family of equal status; however, my mother was extremely fierce, difficult to propitiate, and exceedingly wrathful.
Although he was distressed by her, my father—upon seeing that I had acquired wealth along with a wife—abandoned his own home and departed for some unknown destination, unexpectedly.
Seeing that, I was filled with fear and diligently appointed my wife to the task of captivating my mother's heart; she too, being afraid, did accordingly.
But her mother, intent on quarreling, was not satisfied with her in any way; she met her with silence, contempt, dejected speech, and deceit.
Considering it to be a matter of conviction and dispute, those of evil intent [asked]: "For who is able to cause fire to abandon its own nature of burning?"
Then, because of those hostile actions of hers, my wife soon became distressed; she departed from the house, and I know not where she has gone.
Then, though agitated and intent on abandoning my home, I was forcibly made to undergo another marriage by my wicked kinsmen who had gathered together.
My wife, too, being thus tormented by her fear of her, hanged herself with a noose and brought about her own death.
Then, utterly despondent, I prepared to go to a foreign land; though my kinsmen sought to restrain me, I described to them the wickedness of my mother.

Regarding the exile of my father and other such matters, for those who asserted various alternative causes, that which they could not believe was demonstrated by means of logic through the wooden doll.
Having had her prepared for me in private, she was then married to me falsely; having been brought here, she was placed inside the house with its bolt fastened from the outside.
A single female guard was appointed for her, appearing like a servant; I have established this new wife in a separate house.
"You and I shall now remain right here in our own respective homes; you must not go there, nor must she come here."
"That immature girl does not yet know how to please you," I said to my mother, and she also agreed with that.
Then, as the days passed, she was unable to reach that deceitful daughter-in-law by any means whatsoever, for she remained inside the inner house with the door bolted shut.
Then, having struck her own head with a stone on one occasion, the mother, smeared with blood, cried out loudly in the courtyard of her own house.
Having heard the cry and entered, I and all my kinsmen saw her; when we asked, "Tell us, what is this?", she replied with indignation.
Such a state has been brought upon me by my daughter-in-law, who acted without cause; therefore, at this moment, only death can provide me with redress.
Upon hearing that, those kinsmen became enraged; taking her with them, they went along with me to the place where that wooden statuette was.
Having removed the bolt and opened the door, just as they were about to enter, they saw there nothing but a wooden woman.
Then, laughing at their own mockery and at their embarrassed mother, those kinsmen, having gained confidence, departed as they had come.
Having left that country and wandering about, I reached this region; and here, by chance, I entered a gambling hall.
There I saw these people playing with five dice: this one called Caṇḍabhujaṅga and this one Pāṃsupaṭa.
This Vetāla from the cremation ground, this Kālavarāṭaka, and this Śāri-prastara—these heroes are equal in prowess.
And there I played at dice with them, having mutually bound ourselves by a wager that the loser should become the slave of the winner.
"Then, having been defeated at dice, they entered my service; but I, conquered by their virtues, have myself come into their service."
Living together with these, I have forgotten my own suffering; know me here as Akṣakṣapaṇa, named according to my current condition.
Thus, having been born into noble families and concealing our true identities right here, we have remained together with these meritorious ones; and today you have joined us here.
Therefore, you are now our master; indeed, even before this, that wealth was already taken by us, who are devoted to your virtues, through this very understanding.
When Akṣakṣapaṇaka had thus related his own adventures in due order, all the others, including Bhīmabhaṭa, described their own adventures as well.
Then, concealing her true identity with various arts acquired for the sake of wealth, she engaged in diverse conversations, treating those heroes as mere companions.
Having spent the day in the monastery, he beheld the eastern quarter, its face adorned by the shining ornament of the cool-rayed moon.
Then that prince Bhīmabhaṭa departed from that garden together with those six companions, Akṣakṣapaṇaka and the others, for their dwelling place.
As he remained there together with them, the rainy season arrived, as if announcing his reunion with a friend through the thundering of the pouring clouds.
And then, the river named Vipāśā, which flows toward the ocean, became intoxicated; filled by the flood of the sea, it began to flow upstream.
Having filled the sandbank with a great flood of water, she proceeded toward the ocean as if the torrent had been stilled.
At that time, having been brought there and cast in by that torrential flood, the great fish, due to its heavy weight, became stranded on the riverbank.
And having seen him, the people there ran forward to kill him with various weapons and tore open the belly of that fish.
From that split [body], a young brahmin emerged alive; at that wondrous sight, the people there raised a great clamor.
Having heard that, Bhīmabhaṭa went there with those friends and saw his friend Śaṅkhadatta emerging from the fish.
And running toward him, he embraced him, drenching him with streams of tears as if washing away the stench of dwelling in the cave-like belly of a fish.
Having crossed over that calamity and having reached him, Śaṅkhadatta embraced his friend and then went from one festival to another.
Then, questioned there out of curiosity by that Bhīmabhaṭa, Śaṅkhadatta related his own adventures briefly as follows.
Then, carried away by the force of the Ganges' waves from the range of your vision, I was unexpectedly swallowed by an exceedingly large fish.
Having entered that great chamber which was his belly, I remained there for a long time, eating his flesh, which I cut with a knife, out of hunger.
"Today, this very fish was somehow brought here and cast up by the Creator; it has been killed by these people, and I have been pulled out from its belly."
"I have seen you and the sun, and the quarters of the sky have become bright for me. This, my friend, is my account; I know nothing beyond this."
When Śaṅkhadatta had spoken thus, Bhīmabhaṭa and all those present there said this out of sheer amazement:
Where is the swallowing by a fish in the Gaṅgā, and where is its movement in the ocean; and where, by that same path, is its settling in the Vipāśā?
Where is his slaughter, and where is his escape while still alive? Oh, how inconceivable is the course of Fate, whose actions are so wondrous!
Speaking in this manner with them—the Akṣakṣapaṇakas and the others—Bhīmabhaṭa led Śaṅkhadatta to his own abode.
And there, with great celebration, he attended upon him with baths, garments, and other offerings—[the king] who seemed as if born once again from the belly of a fish in that very same body.
Then, while Bhīmabhaṭa remained in that region with him, there arrived the festival procession of Vāsuki, the king of the Nāgas.
Surrounded by his friends, the prince set out to see that sight—the abode of that preeminent elephant, where great crowds of people were gathering.
There, having bowed down before that image in the temple—which was filled with garlands of flowers resembling hosts of serpents and which was like water in a deep well—[he worshipped].
Having gone to the south, he saw his great lake, filled with red lotuses that seemed like masses of light from the jewels on [serpents'] hoods.
It was filled with blue lotuses that resembled masses of smoke from poisoned fire, and it was surrounded by trees that seemed to be offering worship with flowers falling before them in the wind.
To me, this ocean appears very small before him who is without a seal (the Oceanless One), whose glory cannot be taken by another, yet whose glory has been taken away by Śauri.
Thus, while he was still reflecting in amazement upon seeing him, he beheld a maiden who had arrived there for the purpose of bathing.
There, the auspicious Haṃsāvalī was born as the daughter of King Candrāditya, the Lord of Lāṭa, by his wife Kuvalayāvalī.
Although her mortal nature was concealed by other limbs that imitated those of a divine being, it was revealed by her flickering eye through its blinking.
With her body as delicate as a flower, its tips endowed with shimmering virtues, she was like the bow-staff of the God of Love, whose middle can be grasped by a single fist.
Merely upon seeing him, even with side-long glances from her arrow-like eyes, she then deluded Bhīmabhaṭa, piercing him to the heart.
That thief of the world's beauty, having entered her very eyes, stole away her heart’s fortitude by means of his sidelong glances.
Then, through the mouth of a trusted, clever maidservant sent by her secret emissary, she sought out from his friends his name, residence, and other details.
Then she returned to her own palace, being led by her attendants; having bathed, she turned her face away, casting glances toward him again and again.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa also returned to his own dwelling with his friends, his gait faltering due to being bound by the noose of love for that beloved.
Thereupon, at that very moment, the princess Haṃsāvalī dispatched that maidservant as a messenger to him, having given her the desired message.
Approaching him in private, the maidservant said to Bhīmabhaṭa: "O Lord, Princess Haṃsāvalī entreats you."
Seeing a person you love being carried away by the flood of passion, it is not fitting for you to remain indifferent and stand on the sidelines, disregarding this one who is fleeing.
Having thus obtained from the messenger the nectar of his beloved’s words, Bhīmabhaṭa, thrilled at having regained his life, then spoke to her.
"My beloved does not know that I am standing in the flood and not on the bank; yet, having found this support, I shall surely do as she says."
"Having arrived here tonight, I shall honor her within the inner apartments; and as I enter, concealed by my magic sciences, no one at all will see me."
Having been addressed thus by him, the maidservant was pleased and went to report it; then Haṃsāvalī also remained there, longing for union with him.
At the time of dusk, he too, adorned with divine ornaments, [performed] the recitation in accordance with the sequence of the vidyā for crossing the Gaṅgā.
Having become invisible and gone there, Bhīmabhaṭa entered her excellent inner apartments, which had previously been cleared out by her.
In that place, which brings delight and joy, fragrant with black aloe-wood incense, and beautified by heaps of flowers arranged in five colors;
He beheld that beloved woman, who possessed a divine fragrance like a celestial garden of desire, resembling the blossoms of the creeper of the true knowledge of the Ganges.
Having recited that spell in reverse order, he suddenly became attractive to the princess.
Upon seeing him, she was instantly as if dancing, with her ornaments jingling like musical instruments, while her body trembled with joy and agitation.
And she, with her face bowed in the modesty of maidenhood, seemed to ask her own heart what ought to be done, as it was the source of that news.
O simple one, why do you now conceal with shame that very thing which has already been revealed? That object is not hidden; how then can it be concealed?
With words such as, "There is a thrill of horripilation upon your limbs," and "Why is this bodice bursting at its seams? and with other such expressions of affectionate advances, he addressed her.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, having made that beautiful-faced Haṃsāvalī cast off her shame, made her his wife according to the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
Having spent the night with her in the playful enjoyment of her lotus-like face, he took his leave, saying, "I shall come back tonight," and went to his own abode with great difficulty.
And in the morning, their own high officials, having entered there, saw Haṃsāvalī in the inner apartments, marked with the signs of sexual enjoyment.
Her hair and locks were disheveled, and she bore fresh wounds from teeth and nails; she appeared as if truly overwhelmed by the multitude of scars left by the arrows of the God of Love himself.
Having gone, the spies reported that very matter to his father, the king; he too stationed secret spies there to keep watch during the night.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, having spent the day happily with his friends, returned again at nightfall to the inner apartments of his beloved.
Seeing that he had entered there unobserved through the power of his magic science, and considering him to be a perfected master (siddha), those spies departed from that place.
Having gone, they told it to the king, and he likewise commanded them: "He who has entered here, though well-guarded, while remaining invisible, cannot be a human being."
"Bring him here at once so that I may see what this is; and speak to him on my behalf in words that are not harsh."
Why was my daughter not openly requested from me by you? What secret was kept? For where could there be a bridegroom possessed of such virtues as yours?
Having been thus addressed and dispatched by the king, those spies went and, while still standing at the gate, reported those words to Bhīmabhaṭa exactly as they were.
Realizing, "The king has discovered me," yet remaining composed within, the resolute prince boldly addressed them in return.
"Go to the king in the morning when he has entered his assembly hall and speak these words on my behalf: 'I shall inform you of the truth; for at present, the night is indeed blind.'"
Having heard that, when they had departed and spoken thus, the king remained silent; then, in the morning, Bhīmabhaṭa set out from there toward his friends.
And together with those seven heroes, having assumed a magnificent disguise, he went to the court of that king, Candrāditya.
When Bhīmabhaṭa, who had observed his splendor, heroism, and beauty, had honored him and was seated upon a seat befitting himself, the Brahmin—
His friend Śaṅkhadatta addressed that king: "O King, this is the son of King Ugrabhaṭa, the lord of Rāḍhā."
"By virtue of the greatness of his inconceivable knowledge, he possesses prowess that is difficult to overcome; named Bhīmabhaṭa, he has come here for the sake of your daughter."
Having heard that account of the night's events and considering him to be worthy, the king said, "Ah, we are truly blessed! and then placed his full trust in him.
Then, having arranged the elaborate ceremonies for the wedding, he gave his daughter Haṃsāvalī to Bhīmabhaṭa with magnificent wealth.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, having acquired many elephants, horses, and villages, lived there in contentment together with Haṃsāvalī and Lakṣmī.
And after some days, his father-in-law Candrāditya, being old and childless, handed over that Lāṭa kingdom to him and retired to the forest as a wandering ascetic.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, having attained that kingdom, ruled it successfully together with those seven heroes, Śaṅkhadatta and the others.
Then, as the days passed there, he one day heard from his spies that his father, King Ugrabhaṭa, had come to Prayāga and died.
And as he was about to die, he anointed his youngest son, Samarabhaṭa—the son of a dancing girl—as the king in his own kingdom of Rāḍhā.
Then, having mourned for his father and performed the funeral rites for him, the king dispatched a messenger to that Samarabhaṭa.
"O fool, son of a dancer, what fitness do you have for my lion-throne here in the kingdom of Lāṭa? he said.
Therefore, he sent a letter to that harmful heir, instructing him: "You must not ascend it."
And that messenger, having gone quickly, delivered the letter to him; having announced himself, he presented it to Samarabhaṭa, who was present at court.
Having read that very inscription, which bore the name Bhīmabhaṭa and was written in such a defiant manner, Samarabhaṭa spoke in anger:
"This false pride is fitting for that ill-behaved man, who was formerly banished from the country by his father on account of his unworthiness."
Even a jackal acts like a lion when staying within the shelter of its own cave; yet, once it has come into the sight of a lion, it is recognized for what it truly is.
Having roared thus and sent a letter with that very same message, he too dispatched his own counter-ambassador to Bhīmabhaṭa.
The returning messenger also went to the lord of the Lāṭa country and, having been announced by the chamberlain, delivered that letter to Bhīmabhaṭa.
Then, when that letter had been read there, Bhīmabhaṭa let out a loud, mocking laugh and addressed that counter-messenger from his kinsman.
"Go, O messenger, and speak to that son of a dancing-girl in my name: 'At that time, when the horse was being seized, you were protected by me from Śaṅkhadatta.'"
"You are a child and dear to your father; therefore, I shall forgive you no more and no more. I will certainly send you into the presence of your affectionate father."
"Be ready; know that I shall arrive here in just a few days. Having spoken thus and dispatched that messenger, Bhīmabhaṭa prepared for his expedition.
When that lord of kings, resplendent like the rising sun, had mounted his elephant-mountain, the great ocean of the army surged forward with a tumultuous roar.
And it was filled by countless neighboring princes who had arrived in great numbers, setting out from all directions with their armies.
Trembling and crowded with the great speed of many falling elephants and horses, the earth cried out as if in terror from being split apart by the arrows.
Thus Bhīmabhaṭa, having set out, reached the vicinity of Rāḍhā, making the sky obscure the radiance of the sun with the mass of dust raised by his army.
Meanwhile, King Samarabhaṭa, having learned of this and being unable to endure it, armed himself and went forth at the head of his army to fight him.
And those two oceans of armies, the eastern and the western, met together, and a great dissolution of heroes in battle ensued.
There, the fire born from the clashing of swords accompanied by loud sounds enveloped the sky, as if it were the fire arising from the crushing of teeth by the enraged God of Death.
And iron arrows flew forth, with sharp points and long, feathery shafts, possessing the grace of the glances cast by the women of heaven as they gazed upon the heroes.
Then that stage of the battlefield, covered with a canopy of dust, resounding with the noise of the army and the sound of musical instruments, and featuring dancing headless trunks, shone forth.
And here, the river of blood, carrying skeletons and garlands of skulls, flowed heedlessly like the Night of Doom, sweeping away the circle of living beings.
And in an instant, he was joined by Śaṅkhadatta, by that Akṣakṣapaṇaka, and by those such as Caṇḍabhujaṃga, who were experts in wrestling.
Like a rutting elephant among equally powerful and heroic warriors, that archer Bhīmabhaṭa shattered the enemy army.
When the army was broken, Samarabhaṭa then, standing upon his chariot, rushed forward in a rage and began to act like Mount Mandara in the ocean of battle.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, mounted upon his elephant, charging at him, cut his bow and slew all four horses of the chariot with his arrows.
Then, even though deprived of his chariot, that Samarabhaṭa rushed forward and struck Bhīmabhaṭa’s excellent elephant on the forehead with a lance.
And that elephant, struck by the *tomara* spear, fell to the earth; thereafter, both of them became foot-soldiers, deprived of their chariots.
Then those two impatient kings, having taken up their shields and swords, fought as foot soldiers in a duel.
Although he was capable of slaying him, Bhīmabhaṭa, out of regard for righteousness, did not kill that enemy in that manner, having rendered himself invisible through the power of a magic spell.
But he, an expert in sword-fighting, violently struck off the head of the dancer’s son with his sword as the latter was fighting him.
And while that warrior Samarabhaṭa was being completely slain along with his army, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas from the sky offered shouts of "Well done! (sādhuvāda).
When the battle had reached its conclusion, Bhīmabhaṭa, praised by bards and panegyrists, entered the city of Rāḍhā together with his friends.
Having returned from his long exile with his enemies slain, he gladdened his mother there—she who was longing for his sight—just as Rāma did for Kauśalyā.
Then, welcomed by the citizens, the virtuous prince sat upon his father’s throne, being honored by his ministers who were fond of his virtues.
Having honored all his subjects and celebrated a festival, he then, on an auspicious day, bestowed the kingdom of Lāṭa upon Śaṅkhadatta.
Having dispatched him to the Lāṭa region accompanied by troops from that country, he bestowed villages and wealth upon those [advisers], Akṣakṣapaṇaka and the others.
Then, joined by them, he remained there governing his ancestral domain together with that queen Haṃsāvalī, the daughter of the Lord of Lāṭa.
And having gradually conquered the earth and brought back princesses, King Bhīmabhaṭa then became solely devoted to their enjoyment.

Having entrusted the burden of affairs to his ministers, he remained within the inner apartments sporting with them; due to his addiction to drinking and other vices, he did not emerge from the interior.
Then once, the sage Uttaṅka came by chance to see him, as if the time for the ripening of the former command of Śarva had arrived.
When this sage had reached the gate and the doorkeepers announced his arrival, the king—blinded by the intoxication of passion and the pride of sovereignty—did not, it is said, even hear him.
Then, enraged, that sage pronounced this curse upon the king: "O you who are blinded by pride, fallen from your kingdom, you shall become a wild elephant."
Having heard that, the king, his pride shattered by fear, went forth and propitiated the sage with piteous words while bowing at his feet.
Then, his anger having subsided, that great seer spoke to him: "O King, you shall indeed become an elephant; it cannot be otherwise."
However, the minister of Mṛgāṅkadatta, named Pracaṇḍaśakti, has been struck down by a serpent's curse and has fallen into blindness.
When you have consoled him who has become your guest and shall recount your own history to him, then you will obtain release from this curse.
And you shall obtain that state of a Gandharva previously ordained by Giriśa; and then that guest of yours shall indeed become possessed of sight.
Having spoken thus, the sage Uttaṅka departed just as he had come; and that elephant Bhīmabhaṭa was restored to his former state, having been deprived of his kingdom.
"Know me, my friend, to be that very Bhīmabhaṭa who has become an elephant; and you are that Pracaṇḍaśakti. I know that this is the end of my curse."
Having spoken thus, Bhīmabhaṭa abandoned his elephant form and at that very moment became a Gandharva of divine splendor.
And Pracaṇḍaśakti, for whom the sight of that Gandharva present there became a festival for his eyes, experienced a surge of joy at that very moment as he beheld him.
Meanwhile, staying within the thicket of creepers and having heard their conversation, he, together with his other ministers, formed a very firm resolve.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, who knew the right moment, rushed forward with impetuous speed and seized his own minister, Pracaṇḍaśakti, by the throat.
Seeing him, Pracaṇḍaśakti, as if his limbs were sprinkled by a rain of nectar from a cloudless sky, suddenly seized the lord by the feet.
Then that Gandharva Bhīmabhaṭa consoled those two, who were weeping and deeply distressed after being reunited following their long separation.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, bowing before that Gandharva, said: "That this friend was obtained by us, and furthermore, that he was obtained by him..."
"Vision has been regained through your majesty; salutations be unto you! Having heard this, that Gandharva also spoke to the prince.
Before long, having recovered all your remaining ministers, you shall regain your wife Śaśāṅkavatī and sovereignty over the entire earth.
"Therefore, you must not act out of impatience, O auspicious one; I shall accomplish it for you, and I will remain present with you whenever you remember me."

Thus, freed from the curse and filled with the joy of attained auspiciousness, he revealed his state as a friend; having spoken to that prince, he—the peerless leader of the Gandharvas—suddenly flew up into the sky, making the quarters resound with the tinkling of his beautiful armlets and necklaces.
And having obtained Pracaṇḍaśakti in that forest, Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta spent that day with his ministers, his anxiety having subsided.

Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Eighth Wave: The Twenty-Fifth Story. Victory to the Conqueror of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), from whose dancing a rain of flowers falls from the sky like a shower of stars dislodged by the stroke of his trunk!
Then, having passed that night, at dawn he set out from that forest together with his ministers, headed by Pracaṇḍaśakti.
For the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī, Mṛgāṅkadatta set out once more toward Ujjayinī, searching for his remaining ministers.
As he was traveling, he saw on the road the minister Vikramakesarin being carried through the sky by an extremely hideous man.
And while he was showing it to the other ministers with great excitement, that minister descended from the sky into his presence.
Having quickly descended from the shoulder of that man and approached him, he seized Mṛgāṅkadatta by the feet with eyes full of tears.
Embraced by him in his joy, and likewise by his ministers in due order, he dismissed that man with the words, "Remember me, and you shall come back to me."
Then, having sat down out of curiosity, Vikramakeśarin was questioned by Mṛgāṅkadatta and related his own adventures in the forest.
Then, having fallen away from you due to the curse of the Naga and wandering about, I thought of you for many days while searching for you.
"I shall go to Ujjayinī, for they must certainly have gone there. Having thus resolved, I set out toward that city.
Gradually reaching a village named Brahmasthala in its vicinity, I sat down at the foot of a tree on the bank of a step-well.
Having come there, an old brahmin afflicted by a snakebite said to me: "Rise up from here, my son; you shall attain my own state."
For here there is a great serpent by whom I was bitten and afflicted with pain; I am now prepared to cast off this body into this great pond.
When he had spoken thus, I compassionately dissuaded him from abandoning his body and rendered that Brahmin free from poison by means of the science of poisons.
Then that brahmin, having respectfully asked me for the entire account with its underlying motive, spoke thus, being pleased once he had understood the matter.
"My life-breaths were restored by you; therefore, O great hero, accept from me this mantra for the propitiation of a vetāla, which I obtained from my father."
This [teaching], which brings about accomplishment, is suitable for those like you who possess courage; but as for people like me, what indeed can these cowards do?
Having been addressed thus by him, I replied to that best of the twice-born: "Separated from Mṛgāṅkadatta, what can I do with these Vetālas?"
Having heard that, the Brahmin laughed and spoke to me again: "Do you not know that everything desired can be obtained from a Vetāla?"
Furthermore, what sovereignty over the Vidyādharas was not previously attained by King Trivikramasena through the grace of the Vetāla?
And so I shall relate this story of his; listen to it. There is a region named Pratiṣṭhāna on the banks of the Godāvarī.
There, the son of Vikramasena was a king named Trivikramasena, who possessed the prowess of Śakra and was renowned for his celebrated fame.
Every day, as that king sat in his assembly hall, a monk named Kṣāntiśīla would approach him and present a fruit for the sake of service.
The king, having taken that fruit, gave it every day into the hand of the treasurer who was standing nearby.
When ten years had passed in this manner, it is said that once, after giving a fruit to the king, the mendicant departed from the assembly hall.
By chance, that king gave the fruit to a young pet monkey that had escaped from the hands of its keepers and entered there.
As that monkey was eating it, from within the fruit—its center having split open—there emerged an unsurpassed, priceless jewel.
Seeing that, the king took it and asked the treasurer: "Those fruits which were brought to me daily by the monk—"
"Where have those things given into your hand always been kept by you? Hearing that, the terrified treasurer replied to him:
"I cast them into the treasury through the window without opening them; if you command it, O King, I shall open that [treasury] and search for them."
Having spoken thus and being granted permission by the king, the treasurer departed; returning in a moment, he addressed his lord once more.
"I do not see those fruits here in the treasury, O Lord; instead, I see a heap of jewels, ablaze with rays of light."
Having heard that and being pleased with the treasurer for giving him those jewels, the king questioned the monk the following day when he had arrived as before.
"O monk, why do you serve me every day at such expense? I will not accept your fruit now until you speak."
To the king who had spoken thus, the monk said in private: "I have a means for accomplishing a mantra that requires the assistance of a hero."
"In that matter, O Lord of Heroes, I request your assistance. Having heard that, the king agreed to it, saying, "So be it."
Then that ascetic, being pleased, spoke again to the king: "In that case, on the coming fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at the arrival of night..."
"O Lord, you must come from here to my presence, as I wait beneath the banyan tree within this great cemetery."
When the king replied, "Certainly, I shall do so," that ascetic Kṣāntiśīla went to his own dwelling, filled with joy.
Then, having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, that Great Being, the king, remembered the request made by that monk.
At twilight, dressed in blue garments and with a crown made of *tāla* leaves, he went forth from the capital at night with sword in hand, unobserved.
And he went toward that place, blackened by a mass of terrible and dense darkness, its appearance made dreadful by the flames from the fierce eyes of the funeral pyre's fire.
It was crowded with the skeletons, skulls, and bones of innumerable dead men, and surrounded by joyful, nearby, and terrifying spirits and vetālas.
Like another form of Bhairava, deep and terrifying, that cremation ground resounded with the great howling of jackals; yet he remained undaunted.
Having searched for him there and found that monk beneath a banyan tree performing the ritual layout of a mandala, he approached and spoke to him.
"Here I am come, O monk; tell me, what shall I do for you? Having heard that and seeing the king, the monk spoke to him with joy.
"O King, if you have granted me this favor, then go from here alone toward the south for a great distance; there stands a śiṃśapā tree."
"There hangs a certain dead man suspended there; go and bring him here, O hero, and provide me with a protector."
Having heard that, the king, true to his promise, said "So be it," and then that great hero set out toward the southern direction.
Having traveled there along a path marked by blazing funeral pyres, he somehow reached that śiṃśapā tree in the darkness.
He saw him hanging from the shoulder of that tree—smelling of raw flesh and scorched by the smoke of the funeral pyre—like the corpse of a spirit.
Having climbed onto that ground, he caused the rope to fall away; and having fallen there, he suddenly cried out in distress as if in pain.
Then, having descended out of compassion and fearing for his life, he touched that limb of the king's corpse; by that act, the corpse let out a loud, mocking laugh.
Then that king, perceiving that he was possessed by a Vetāla, remained unshaken and said, "Why do you laugh? Come, let us go."
He spoke thus; he did not see the corpse with the vetāla upon the ground, but then he saw it again, hanging suspended right there in the tree.
Then, having climbed up again, he brought him down from there; for even more than a diamond, the jewel of the mind of heroes remains unbroken.
Then King Trivikramasena, having placed that corpse along with the vetāla upon his shoulder in silence, proceeded on his way.
And as he was traveling, the Vetāla seated within the corpse, perched upon his shoulder, said: "O King, listen; I shall tell you a story to divert you on your journey."
There is a city named Vārāṇasī, the dwelling place of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva), which, frequented by holy people, is like a plateau of Mount Kailāsa.
The celestial river, constantly abiding near her banks and laden with abundant waters, shines like a string of pearls upon her.
In ancient times, there was a king named Pratāpamukuṭa in that city, who consumed the forest of his enemies' clans with the fire of his majesty.
He had a son named Vajramukuṭa, who crushed the pride of both the God of Love and his enemies by means of his beauty and valor.
There, that prince had a high-minded minister’s son as a friend, named Buddhiśarīra, who was dearer to him than his own body.
Once, while playing with that friend, the prince traveled a long distance on account of his excessive addiction to hunting.
Like the chowries of the glory of valor, he severed the maned heads of lions with his arrows and entered a great forest.
There, while the cuckoos sang like bards, they recited at an improper time, as the trees offered their service with clusters of blossoms like waving chowries.
Accompanied by that minister’s son, he beheld a lake that was like another ocean, the abode where various lotuses were born.
At that very moment, a certain maiden of divine form arrived at that lake for the purpose of bathing, accompanied by her retinue; she was beheld by him.
As if filling the lake with a torrent of loveliness, she seemed to create a new forest of blue lotuses there with her glances.
With her face that surpassed the moon, she seemed to reject the lotuses; at that very moment, she captivated the mind of the prince.
The youth likewise captivated her eyes in such a way that the maiden could no longer perceive even her own modesty or her ornaments.
As he gazed upon that youth along with his followers, wondering "Who might this be?", she feigned a playful gesture in order to communicate her name and the location of her own country.
He took a blue lotus from his flower garland and placed it behind his ear; for a long time he fashioned his teeth, and having taken them up, he arranged them.
She placed a lotus with significant intent upon his head and then upon his heart; yet at that time, the prince did not understand her signal.
But his wise friend, the minister’s son, perceived this; and in an instant, that maiden was led away from there by her attendants.
Having reached her own home, she lay upon a couch with her body resting there, but she fixed her mind upon that prince for the sake of her own mental conception.
That prince too, having lost his learning like a Vidyādhara who has fallen from his magic power, went to his own city and fell into a state of great misery without her.
Then, questioned in private by that friend, the minister’s son, he—losing his composure as the boy described her as not difficult to attain—spoke.
How can she be found whose name, village, and lineage are not even known? Why do you deceive me with such falsehoods?
Thus addressed by the prince, the minister’s son replied to him: "Did you not see that which was indicated by her through a sign?"
Because an utpala lotus was placed upon your ear, she said this to you: "I dwell in the kingdom of King Karṇotpala."
Because she had arranged her teeth in such a way, she said this: "Know me there to be the daughter of a ivory-carver."
She who was adorned with lotuses gave her name as Padmāvatī; placing her hand upon his heart, she declared, "My life-breaths are in you."
In the country of Kaliṅga, there is indeed a famous king named Karṇotpala; he has a great ivory-carver who is well-known for his skill in craftsmanship.
That king named Saṅgrāmavardhana also has a daughter in the three worlds named Padmāvatī, a maiden dearer to him than his own life.
And this, O King, is known by me exactly as it is from common worldly experience; therefore, I have understood that name which indicates its location and so forth.
Having been addressed thus by that minister’s son, the prince was pleased with that wise youth and rejoiced, having found a means to achieve his purpose.
Having consulted with him, and being joined by him, he set out from his own palace once more toward that direction, seeking his beloved under the pretext of hunting.
And on the way, having outstripped his army with the speed of wind-swift horses, he went to the territory of Kaliṅga accompanied only by the minister’s son.
Having reached that city of King Karṇotpala, they searched for and found the palace of that ivory-carver.
Then, for the sake of lodging, both the minister’s son and the prince entered the house of a certain elderly woman, which was not far away.
Having provided water and fodder for the two horses and stationed them safely there while the prince remained, the minister’s son spoke to that old woman.
"Mother, do you know a tusk-carver named Saṅgrāmavardhana? Hearing this, that old woman spoke to him with faith.
"I am indeed her nurse; and by him, I have now been appointed as the senior attendant beside his own daughter, Padmāvatī."
However, I do not go there constantly because my garments are worn out; for a wicked son or a gambler, upon seeing my clothes, would surely steal them.
When she had spoken thus, the minister’s son, being pleased, gratified that old woman there with gifts such as his own upper garment and spoke to her again:
"You are our mother; therefore, we shall tell you what must be done in secret: go to this Padmāvatī, the daughter of Dantaghāṭa, and speak to her."
"The prince whom you saw at the lake has arrived here; he has sent me out of affection to inform you of this."
Having heard that, the old woman, subdued by the Dānava, said "So be it," and having gone to Padmāvatī's side, she returned a moment later.
Questioned by those two—the prince and the minister’s son—she said to them: "Having gone there, I secretly informed her of your arrival."
Having heard this, she rebuked me and struck my face on both cheeks with her two hands, which were smeared with camphor.
Then, distressed by that humiliation, I came here weeping; look at these finger-rings of theirs in my two sons' mouths.
When she had spoken thus, that highly wise minister’s son said aside to the prince, who was despondent with despair:
Do not fall into despair; for when she rebuked him while guarding the secret, she cast her ten fingers, white as camphor, into his mouth.
Thus it was said regarding this position: "Wait for these ten white nights, during which these [women] are as full of the moon as they are unaccustomed to union."
Having thus consoled the prince, the minister’s son then secretly sold some gold he had in his hand at the marketplace.
With that old woman, he prepared a costly meal; then the two of them ate it together with her.
Having thus spent ten days in this manner to test her, the minister’s son sent that old woman back once more to Padmāvatī.
She too, being greedy for fine food, drink, and other luxuries, went to that woman's bedchamber out of compliance with her wishes; returning once more, she spoke to the two of them.
Having gone from here today, even though I remained there in silence, she herself again uttered that offense against you in conversation.
Struck on this breast by her three finger-tips stained with lac, I have now come here from her presence.
Having heard that, the minister’s son spoke freely to the prince: "Do not entertain any other suspicion; for she has [placed] this very thing in her heart."
Having skillfully applied three finger-marks of lac-dye, she indicated by her presence that she had remained in her menses for three nights.
Having spoken thus to the prince, when three days had passed, the minister’s son sent that old woman back once more to Padmāvatī.
She went to her house, where she was honored and fed by her; with affectionate games of drinking and other diversions, she spent the day there in amusement.
And as that old woman was wishing to return home in the evening, a terrifying clamor arose outside at that moment.
"Alas, alas! This intoxicated elephant has broken free from its tethering post and is rushing about, trampling the people!"—such was the cry heard by the world there.
Then Padmāvatī spoke thus to that old woman: "It is not proper for you to travel by this path, which is clearly blocked by elephants."
Having placed you upon that platform with its firmly fastened ropes, we shall cast you down here through this large window.
Then, having climbed a tree in the house garden and leaped over that wall, descend by another tree and go to your own home.
Having said this, she then had that old woman cast down from the window into the garden by her maidservants using a rope-swing.
Having gone there, he related everything exactly as it had happened to that prince and to the minister’s son by the path previously described.
Then that minister’s son said to the prince: "Your desire is accomplished, for she has shown you the way through her skillful means."
Therefore, go this very day; when the king has departed at this twilight, enter the palace of that beloved by this very same path.
Thus addressed by him, the prince, accompanied by that old woman, went to that garden by the path along the wall as she had described.
There he saw that rope hanging down together with its seat, attended from above by maidservants who were looking out for the path.
As soon as he saw her mounted upon it, he was quickly hoisted up by those maidservants through the window and entered the presence of his beloved.
When he had entered, the minister’s son went to his own dwelling, while the prince beheld Padmāvatī there.
With a face like the full moon, her radiance was like a shimmering moon; she was like the night of the full moon itself, remaining hidden out of fear of the dark fortnight.
She too, seeing him, rose up and honored him with various services, such as embracing his neck, which were appropriate for her long-standing longing.
Then, having been married by her according to the Gāndharva rite, the prince remained there in secret with his beloved, his desires fulfilled.
After staying for some days, he spoke to his beloved at night: "My friend, who has come along as my companion, is actually the son of a minister."
And he remains here alone in the house of your elder sister; O slender one, having gone there and paid him my respects, I shall return once more to your side.
Having heard that, the crafty Padmāvatī said to her beloved: "Ah, noble son, I wish to ask you about those signs created by me."
"What did that friend, the minister's son, say to you?"—when she had spoken thus, the prince said to her:
Not even that little was known by me; but once I had learned it all, it was explained to me by that son of a minister, who is endowed with divine wisdom.
Having heard this and reflected upon it, that beautiful woman said to him: "In that case, you have acted improperly, since you spoke of him to me only after such a long time."
He who is your brother and friend is mine as well; therefore, I must always first offer him the customary hospitality of betel and other refreshments.
When she had spoken thus, he was permitted by her and went that night from there to the presence of his friend by the same path as before.
And in the midst of their conversation, he related to him that account concerning his beloved, which he had previously told in her presence regarding the description of her name and characteristics.
But that minister’s son did not believe him, thinking it improper; meanwhile, the night there turned into dawn for the two of them.
Then, when the ritual for these two at twilight had concluded and they were engaged in conversation, a friend of Padmāvatī arrived, carrying cooked food and betel in her hands.
Having inquired after the welfare of the minister’s son and provided him with hospitality, she skillfully contrived a means there to prevent the prince from eating.
In the course of conversation, having informed his mistress—who was waiting for his arrival at the time of the meal and other such occasions—he departed from there secretly in an instant.
Then that minister’s son said to the prince: "O King, behold a single marvel; I shall show it to you now."
Having said this, he then gave a single morsel of cooked food to the dog; and as soon as the dog had eaten it, it perished.
Seeing that, the prince asked the minister's son, "What is this wonder? and he replied to him.
Having recognized me as a rogue through her knowledge of signs, she—being devoted to you and desiring to kill me—sent me poisoned food.
"If he remains here, this prince will become single-mindedly devoted to me; otherwise, under my influence, he might abandon me and return to his own city."
Therefore, abandon your anger toward her; I shall consider and tell you a plan by which you may accomplish the abduction of that great-souled man, despite his abandonment of his kin.
When the minister’s son had spoken thus, the prince there praised him, saying, "It is true that you are the very embodiment of wisdom."
Unexpectedly, there arose outside a clamor of people distressed by grief; "Alas! Woe! The young son of the king has perished!"—thus was it heard.
Delighted upon hearing this, the minister’s son then said to the prince: "Come now, let us go tonight to the house of Padmāvatī."
There, one should make her drink it until, through the intoxication of the potion, she becomes unconscious, devoid of movement, and as if lifeless.
Then, while she was asleep, he marked her hip with a spear heated by fire and took away her collection of ornaments.
"You should come through the window, having gone out by hanging down from a rope; thereafter, I shall know how to ensure that all goes well."
Having said this and having had one fashioned with a point resembling the bristle of a boar's tail, the minister’s son gave that trident to the prince.
The prince took that hook, crooked and harsh, made of solid black iron, in his hand—like the hearts of his beloved and his friend.
"So be it," he said, and as before, he went to Padmāvatī’s house at night; for the word of a pure minister is not to be questioned by his lords.
There, having stripped her of her ornaments and marked her on the hips with a spike while she lay motionless from intoxication, she went into the presence of her friend.
Having shown him his ornaments, he related everything as it had been done; thereupon, the minister’s son also considered his desired goal accomplished.
Having gone to the cremation ground at dawn, he assumed the garb of an ascetic and freely made that prince his disciple.
And he said to him, "Go alone from here; taking this pearl necklace as if to sell it in the marketplace, depart from this place."
And he said, "I shall declare her to be of great value, so that no one at all will take her while she is being paraded about, and everyone who sees her [will be struck with wonder]."
If the city guards should seize you there, you must say without agitation, "My teacher gave this to me for sale."
Thus dispatched by him, the prince then went and stood in the marketplace, wandering about while clearly wearing a string of pearls.
And being such as he was, he was seized by the city guards—who were searching for a thief at the command of the ivory-carver’s daughter who had reported the theft—once they saw him.
And he was led by them at that very moment into the presence of the city magistrate; and seeing him in the guise of an ascetic, the magistrate questioned him kindly.
"O Blessed One, from where did you obtain this pearl necklace that was lost here? For the jewelry of the ivory-carver’s daughter was indeed stolen in the night."
Having heard that, the prince, who was in the guise of an ascetic, said to him: "This was given to me by my preceptor; let him be approached and questioned."
Then, having approached and bowed to him, the lord of the city asked: "Venerable sir, from where did you obtain this pearl necklace that has come into the hands of your disciple?"
Having heard this, that rogue made the place secluded and said to him: "I am an ascetic who wanders constantly here and there through the forests."
Thus, having arrived here by fate, I remained in this cemetery at night and saw a circle of yoginīs assembled here and there.
And in their midst, a prince whose heart-lotus was opened by a Yoginī belonging to the Single Vehicle was offered to Bhairava.
And she, intoxicated by drink, being unable to take the rosary from me as I was chanting, began to manifest great illusions, making contortions with her face.
And in my anger, I struck her excessively on the hip with a trident whose points were set ablaze by mantras.
"This pearl necklace was taken by me from her neck at that time; it is now unworthy of an ascetic and is for sale to me."
Having heard this, the city magistrate went and informed the king; the king, too, having heard it and learned of that pearl necklace, [acted].
And having heard from the mouth of a trusted elderly woman sent to observe her—that she truly possessed that very mark of the "dart" on her hips—he was struck with longing.
Having reached the firm conclusion that "my son has been seized by that ḍākinī," he went in person to the presence of the minister's son, the ascetic.
And having questioned her regarding the punishment for Padmāvatī, he, at her word, ordered her banishment from the city while she was being lamented by her parents.
Though she was distressed by being exiled and dwelling in the forest, she did not abandon her body, for she had anticipated that the minister’s son would employ such a stratagem and act accordingly.
At the end of the day, as she was grieving, the minister’s son and the king’s son—both having discarded their ascetic garb—approached her mounted on horses.
Having comforted her and placed her upon a horse, they led her back to their own kingdom; there the prince dwelt happily with her.
But Dantaghāṭa, believing his daughter had been devoured by carnivorous beasts in the forest, perished from grief, and his wife followed after him.
Having spoken thus, the Vetāla addressed the king once more: "Therefore, resolve this doubt of mine regarding the killing of this couple."
What sin was committed by the minister’s son, or perhaps by the prince, or even by Padmāvatī? For you are the foremost among the wise.
And if, O King, knowing this, you do not speak the truth to me, then this head of yours will certainly burst asunder into a hundred pieces.
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, King Trivikramasena, recognizing him and fearing the curse, replied to him in this manner:
"O Lord of Yoga, what is there not to be known? Indeed, this is no sin on the part of these three; rather, that evil belongs to King Karṇotpala."
The Vetāla also said: "O King, what indeed was done by those three? For what offense do the crows commit when the rice has been eaten by the swans?"
Then the king said to him: "None of those three are at fault; for that was the business of the master, and thus it is blameless for the minister's son."
For those two, Prince Padmāvatī and the prince, were scorched by the fire of the arrows of desire; they were beyond reproach, faultless, and intent upon their own purpose.
But King Karṇotpala, untrained in the treatises on political ethics, failed to investigate the true state of affairs among his subjects—even among his own—by means of spies.
Not knowing the conduct of rogues and being unskilled in interpreting gestures and other signs, he incurred sin by acting in such a thoughtless manner.

Having heard this, when the king had properly uttered his reply with his silence broken, the Vetāla—who was within that human corpse—immediately departed elsewhere, unobserved, by the power of illusion, in order to test the king's firmness; yet that king remained motionless and once again made the resolve to recover him.
The Ninth Wave. Then King Trivikramasena went once more to the vicinity of that śiṃśapā tree in order to bring back that vetāla.
Having arrived there at night, as he looked about by the light of the funeral pyre, he then beheld that corpse fallen upon the ground, groaning.
Then that lord of the earth, having placed the Vetāla residing in the corpse upon his shoulder, set out in silence with speed to bring him back.
Then, from his shoulder, the vetāla spoke again to the king: "O King, you have fallen into this great and unworthy hardship."
Therefore, for your amusement, I shall tell you a tale; listen. There is a land-grant village named Brahmasthala on the bank of the Kālindī.
There lived a Brahmin named Agnisvāmin who had mastered the Vedas; to him was born a daughter of exceeding beauty named Mandāravatī.
Having fashioned her of such fresh and priceless beauty, the Creator surely came to loathe his own previous creation of the celestial nymphs.
And while she was in the bloom of youth, three young sons of Brahmins, equal in all virtues, arrived there from Kānyakubja.
And for their own sake, each one of them asked her from her father; he, however, did not wish to give her to anyone else, even at the cost of his own life.
But her father did not give her to even one among them, fearing the death of the other two; consequently, she remained a maiden.
And all three of them, their gazes fixed solely upon the moon of her face, remained there day and night, adopting the vow of the cakora bird.
Then, it is said, due to the onset of a fever accompanied by a burning sensation that arose suddenly, the maiden Mandāravatī passed away.
Then those sons of the brahmin, overwhelmed with grief, took her—who had been adorned with ornaments—and having carried her to the cremation ground, they committed her to the fire.
And one among them, having constructed a small hut right there, remained with a bed made of their ashes, subsisting on unasked-for alms.
The second took her bones and went to the Bhāgīrathī; the third, having become an ascetic, went to wander through other lands.
Wandering on, that ascetic reached a village named Vakrolaka; there, as a guest, he entered the house of a certain Brahmin.
While he, having been honored by them, was about to begin eating there, a certain child began to cry out.
When he did not desist even though being pacified, his wife, out of anger, seized him by the arm and threw him into the blazing fire.
As soon as it was thrown, that creature of delicate limbs was reduced to ashes; seeing this, the ascetic guest, his hair standing on end with awe, said:
"Alas! Woe is me! I have entered the abode of a Brahmarākṣasa; therefore, I shall not eat this food here now, for it is indeed embodied sin."
To him who was speaking thus, that householder said: "Behold my power over this mantra, perfected through recitation, which restores the dead to life."
Having spoken thus, he took that manuscript of mantras, recited them, and scattered consecrated dust upon those ashes.
Then that boy rose up alive, appearing exactly as he had been; thereupon, the brahmin ascetic was comforted and partook of food.
Although he was a householder, he placed that manuscript on a wall-bracket, and having eaten, he retired to bed at night right there together with her.
While that master of the house was asleep, the ascetic, rising quietly and filled with apprehension yet desiring his beloved's life, took up that manuscript.
Having taken it and departed from there, traveling day and night, he eventually reached that cemetery where his beloved had been cremated.
And at that moment, he saw there a second person who had arrived—the one who had gone to cast those bones into the waters of the Ganges.
Then he spoke to both of them—both that man and the primordial one—who were lying there upon her ashes within their constructed hut.
"Let this hut be cleared away so that I may raise up my beloved from the ashes while she is still alive, by means of some power of mantras."
Having thus urged them with persistence and searched through the small hut, that brahmin ascetic opened it and read that little book.
Having consecrated the dust with a mantra, he scattered it upon the ashes; thereupon, Mandāravatī arose from it alive.
Having emerged from the fire, that maiden then bore a body of even greater luster than before, as if it were fashioned out of gold.
Upon seeing her born again in such a form, all three of them, afflicted by love and desiring to obtain her, engaged in a mutual quarrel.
