One said, "This wife is mine, won by the power of mantras," and another said, "This wife is mine, produced by the power of a sacred ford."
"Since I have preserved this woman here by means of my ascetic power and her ashes, she is my wife"—thus he spoke as the third in this matter.
O Lord of the Earth, regarding the resolution of their dispute, please tell me your own decision: to whom does this maiden rightfully belong as a wife?
"Your head shall split asunder if you know and do not speak," having heard this from the Vetāla, the king replied to him thus:
He who, even after experiencing affliction, restored her to life by means of a mantra—he was her father because he performed that act for her, but not her husband.
He who carried his remains to the Ganges is considered his son; but he who remained performing austerities while embracing that bed of ashes was [the other].
It is precisely in the cremation ground that her husband is said to take delight; for he, being deeply impassioned, has acted in a manner truly worthy of him.
Having heard this from King Trivikramasena, who had thus broken his silence, the Vetāla left his shoulder unexpectedly and returned to his own place.

Then the king, intent on the goal of the mendicant, again set his mind upon attaining it; for those of firm character do not abandon an undertaking they have once resolved upon, even at the cost of their lives, until it has been fully accomplished.
The Tenth Wave. Now, once again, that best of kings, Trivikramasena, went to that śiṃśapā tree in order to fetch the vetāla.
Having reached that [corpse] situated there, which was once within a dead body, he then proceeded silently to carry it away, taking it upon his shoulder.
And as he was departing, the Vetāla, seated upon his back, said to him: "It is strange, O King, that you are not agitated by making this journey back and forth in the night."
Therefore, so that you may not grow weary, I shall describe it further; listen to the story. There is a city renowned throughout the earth known by the name of Pāṭaliputra.
In that place, there formerly lived a king named Vikramakesarin, whom the Creator had fashioned as a repository for virtues, as if for jewels.
There, a parrot possessing divine knowledge descended by means of a curse; he was a knower of all scriptures, known by the name Vidagdhacūḍāmaṇi.
Thereupon, the prince married that princess of Magadha, a suitable bride named Candraprabhā, who had been recommended by him.
It is said that the princess also had a female parrot named Somikā, who was likewise endowed with all forms of wisdom.
And there were two, a parrot and a mynah bird, staying together in a single cage, serving their own master and mistress with their respective skills.
Once, filled with desire, that parrot said to the śārikā: "O beautiful one, share with me a single bed, seat, and meal."
"I do not desire association with men, because men are wicked and ungrateful," the sarika bird replied to him.
"Men are not wicked; it is women who are wicked and cruel-hearted. When Śuka had spoken thus once more, a dispute arose between the two of them.
Having made a mutual wager that one would become a slave and the other a wife, those two birds then approached the prince, who was presiding over the assembly, for a decision.
Having heard the subject of their dispute while seated in his father’s assembly hall, he said to Śārikā, "Tell me, how are men ungrateful?"
Then, saying "Listen," she told this story concerning the faults of men in order to establish her own position, through the parrot Śārikā.
There is a great city on earth named Kāmandikā; in it dwells a merchant of great wealth named Arthadatta.
And a son named Dhanadatta was born to him; when his father passed away, he too became unrestrained in his youth.
And when he was addicted to gambling and other such vices, rogues conspired together and cast him down; for association with the wicked is indeed the root of the tree of calamity.
Before long, his wealth exhausted by misfortune, he then abandoned his own country out of shame for his destitution and went wandering through other lands.
And as he was traveling, having reached a place named Candanapura, he entered the house of a certain merchant, seeking food.

Seeing that delicate youth and inquiring about his lineage and other details, the merchant, recognizing him to be of noble birth, honored him and took him into his own service through the turn of fate.
And he gave him his daughter, named Ratnāvalī, along with her dowry; thereafter, Dhanadatta remained there in the house of his father-in-law.
As the days passed, having forgotten his misfortune in his happiness, he desired to go to his own country; having achieved his goal, he was now facing a calamity.
Then, having somehow obtained the reluctant permission of his father-in-law, that rogue took his daughter—who was his sole offspring—and set out with her, beautifully adorned.
Accompanied by his wife Ratnāvalī and one elderly woman, he set out from there with himself as the third member of the party, according to the message.
Having gradually reached a distant forest and spoken of the danger arising from bandits, he took the jewelry of that wife and made it his own.
Behold, alas, the heart of those ungrateful men who cling to the miserable vices of gambling, harlots, and the like—a heart as cruel as a sword.
Then that wicked man, for the sake of wealth, threw his virtuous wife—accompanied by that old woman—into a pit in order to kill her.
As soon as he had thrown it and departed, that old woman died; however, his wife did not die, for she was protected by the thicket of creepers.
And then, because some of her life-force still remained, she slowly rose from the abyss, wailing piteously and clinging to grass, shrubs, and other vegetation.
With her limbs wounded and having asked the way at every step, she returned with great difficulty to her father’s house by the very same path by which she had come.
There, having suddenly arrived in such a state and being questioned with agitation by her mother and father, that virtuous woman, weeping, spoke as follows.
"We were robbed on the road by thieves; my husband was bound and led away. My aged mother fell and died in a pit, yet I, for my part, did not die."
Then, a certain compassionate traveler who had arrived there rescued me from that abyss, and by fate, I have reached this place.
Having been addressed thus by her mother and consoled by her father, the virtuous Ratnāvalī remained there, her mind fixed solely on her husband.
In the course of time, her husband Danadatta returned to his own country; having squandered all that wealth on gambling, he reflected:
"I shall go again and, having sought it out, bring wealth from my father-in-law; and there I shall say to him, 'Your daughter is staying in my house.'"
Having thus meditated in his heart, he set out for his father-in-law’s house; and when he arrived there, his wife saw him from afar.
She ran and fell at the feet of that wicked man; for even when their husband is evil, the minds of virtuous women do not change their conduct.
Then, being afraid, she reported to him in its entirety everything that she had previously described falsely to her parents regarding the fall of the thief and other matters.
Then, having entered the father-in-law's house with her, he remained there without fear; seeing him, the parents-in-law greeted him with joy.
"By good fortune, he has been released from the thieves and is alive!"—with these words, his father-in-law, having gathered his kinsmen, then held a great celebration.
Then Dhanadatta, enjoying the wealth of his father-in-law there together with his wife Ratnāvalī, lived happily as he pleased.
Once, during that night, that cruel man did something which, though peaceful and unspeakable, is told here for the sake of the narrative.
Having killed his wife as she slept in his lap and having stolen that collection of ornaments, he then departed for his own country unobserved.
When Śārikā had said, "Such men are wicked," the prince then said to Śuka, "Now you speak."
Then that parrot said: "O King, women are difficult to endure in their audacity, wicked in their conduct, and sinful; therefore, let this story be heard."
There was a city named Harṣavatī, and there lived a merchant named Dharmadatta, a leader among men and the owner of many millions.
And that merchant had a daughter named Vasudattā, peerless in beauty, who was dearer to him than his own life.
And she was given by him to that man of equal status, who was endowed with beauty and youth, and who was like a moonbeam of nectar to the eyes of excellent women.
To the virtuous son of a merchant named Samudradatta, who resided in the city of Tāmraliptī, which is frequented by noble ones.
Once, while her husband was in his own country and she was staying at her father's house, that merchant’s daughter saw a certain man from afar.
Fascinated by Māra, that fickle woman enjoyed his company—he who was young and handsome, brought secretly through the mouth of her friend, and a lover in hiding.
From that time forth, with her mind entirely devoted to him alone, she constantly took her pleasure there in secret with him night after night.
And once, her youthful husband returned there from his own country, like joy itself incarnate to his parents.
On that festive day, having adorned herself for the night, she was sent by her mother; yet, even though he was lying on the bed, she did not approach her husband.
Requested by him, she feigned sleep with her mind fixed elsewhere; and he too, intoxicated by drink and exhausted by the journey, was then overcome by slumber.
Then, while everyone who had eaten and drunk was fast asleep, the thief slowly broke into the wall and entered the interior of the bedchamber.
At that moment, not seeing him, the merchant’s daughter also rose up and, having made an appointment with her lover, departed from there secretly.
Seeing that, the thief, his purpose frustrated, thought: "She is adorned with those very ornaments for whose sake I entered here."
"She has gone out at midnight; therefore, I shall see where she is going. Having reflected thus, he went out and [saw] that merchant's daughter.

He followed Vasudattā, keeping his gaze fixed upon her while remaining unobserved; she, for her part, was accompanied by a single confidante carrying flowers and other offerings, and they shared a secret signal.
Having gone outside, she entered a garden not very far away; there she saw her own lover hanging from a tree.
Having found him at night at the place of appointment, the city guards, thinking him to be a thief, hanged him; he remained dead with a noose around his neck.
Then, overwhelmed and bewildered, crying out, "Alas, I am ruined!", she fell to the ground, lamenting piteously and weeping.
Then, having brought her lifeless lover down from the tree, she seated him and adorned him with unguents and flowers.
Embracing him while he was unconscious, her mind blinded by passion and grief, the distressed woman raised his face and kissed it.
Just then, that lifeless corpse of hers, suddenly possessed by a Vetāla, bit off the nose of that other man with its teeth.
Though she had retreated from there in agitation and with pain, alas, thinking "Could he perhaps still be alive?", she returned, overcome with grief, and looked at him once more.
And seeing him—freed from the vetāla, motionless, as if truly dead—she, terrified and humiliated, moved away slowly while weeping.
Then that thief remained hidden and observed everything; he thought, "What is this that has been done by this wicked woman?"
Alas! The disposition of women is terrifying and thick with darkness; like a bottomless blind well, it is profoundly deep and leads only to one's downfall.
Thinking, "What indeed will she do now? the thief followed her once more from a distance out of curiosity.
She too, having gone and entered that house where her husband was lying asleep, then began to weep loudly and spoke thus:
"Save me! By this wicked man, who is my enemy in the form of a husband, my nose has been cut off even though I am innocent."
Hearing her repeated cries, everyone there—the husband, the attendants, and the father—woke up and rose in great agitation.
Then her father arrived and, seeing that her nose had been cut off while still moist with blood, became enraged and had her husband bound, accusing him of being a traitor to his wife.
But he said nothing at all, remaining like a mute even while being bound, as his father-in-law and all the others looked on in bewilderment.
Then, having realized that the thief had quickly departed, and after the clamor had subsided, the night gradually passed away.
That merchant’s son was led by his father-in-law, the merchant, into the presence of the king together with that wife whose nose had been cut off.
And the king, having been informed that the man was an adulterer with his own wife, disregarded the merchant's son's words and ordered his execution.
Then, as he was being led to that execution ground accompanied by the beating of drums, the thief approached and spoke to the king's men:
"This man is not to be slain without cause; however, I know the facts as they occurred. Lead me before the king so that I may relate everything from beginning to end."
Having spoken thus, the thief was led by them into the presence of the king while granted immunity; there, the thief reported the entire course of events during the night from the very beginning.
And he said: "O King, if you have no confidence in my words, then let that nose on the mouth of that corpse be examined even now."
Having heard that, the king sent servants to investigate; once he had ascertained the truth, he released the merchant's son from the executioner's grasp.
Having cut off her ears as well, he banished that wicked woman from the country; he also punished her husband and his father-in-law, seizing all their property.
And the king, being pleased, made that city magistrate a thief; thus, women in this world are by nature treacherous and deceitful.
As soon as he had spoken thus, Śuka became the Gandharva named Citraratha; with his Indra-imposed curse exhausted, he departed for heaven in a divine form.
At that moment, Śārikā became Tilottamā, a celestial nymph; her curse having likewise expired, she suddenly departed for heaven.
"And thus their dispute remained undecided in the assembly. Having related this story, the Vetāla spoke again to the king:
Therefore, may you speak: are men sinful, or rather women? If you do not answer, while knowing the truth, your head shall shatter into pieces.
Having heard these words of the Vetāla resting upon his shoulder, the king said to him: "O Master of Yoga, women are sinful."
Indeed, some particular man might perhaps at some time or place be of such ill-conduct; however, women are generally always of that very same nature everywhere.
When the king had spoken thus, the Vetāla vanished from his shoulder as before; and the king once again undertook the effort of bringing him back.
The Eleventh Wave: Then King Trivikramasena went again near that śiṃśapā tree to the cremation ground there at night.
Having received that vetāla, who had burst into a loud laugh and was mounted upon the human corpse, he placed him on his shoulder and departed from there silently and without trembling.
And as he was walking, the Vetāla on his shoulder spoke to him again: "O King, why do you undergo this toil for the sake of this wretched mendicant?"
Alas, you lack discernment regarding this fruitless exertion; therefore, listen to me as I tell you a story to amuse you on the road.
There is on earth a city called Śobhāvatī, which is known as the "City of Truth"; and in it there was a king named Śūdraka, possessed of abundant valor.
The fire of whose majesty blazed incessantly for that victorious king, fanned by the winds from the chowries waved by the wives of his captive enemies.
While that king reigned, the earth was abundant with the practice of dharma unimpaired; he so eclipsed even kings such as Rāma that they were forgotten.
Once, a certain Brahmin named Vīravara came from Mālava to that protector of the earth, who was fond of heroes, for the purpose of service.
He had a wife named Dharmavatī, a son who was the best of beings, and a daughter named Vīravatī; these three were his household retinue.
There was another threefold retinue for service: a small sword at his waist, and in one hand a beautiful shield, while the other hand rested upon the palm.
Accompanied by only that many followers, he requested five hundred dinars daily from that king for his livelihood.
King Sūdraka, too, having beheld him whose noble manliness was revealed by his outward appearance, granted him that livelihood he desired.
"With such a small retinue, what is he doing with so many gold coins and silver pieces? Is he indulging in some vice, or perhaps making some virtuous expenditure?"
Thus, out of curiosity, that lord of the earth established secret spies behind her in order to investigate her conduct.
And that Vīravara, having presented himself to the king in the morning, remained at the main gate with his weapon grasped until midday.
Having gone home, he would indeed give a hundred dinars obtained from his own earnings into the hand of his wife every day for the purpose of food.
He purchased garments, body-unguents, and betel for a hundred [coins], and having bathed, he spent a hundred for the purpose of worshipping Viṣṇu and Śiva.
He gave two hundred gifts to the Brahmins and to the poor; in this manner, he constantly distributed those five hundred among them.
Then, having performed his fire-rituals and other duties, and having eaten, he went alone at night and stood again at the main gate, holding his palms together in reverence.
And having heard from the mouth of his spy this constant conduct of that most excellent hero, King Śūdraka rejoiced in his heart.
He halted those scouts who were following in his wake, for he considered him to be a superhuman being worthy of exceptional honor.
Then, after those days had passed, while the summer—with its fiercely blazing solar heat—was being boldly traversed by Vīravara, he arrived there.
Then, as if out of envy, the arrival of the clouds came forth, emitting flashes of lightning from its palms, striking with torrents of rain, and thundering aloud.
And then, while a terrible mass of clouds was raining day and night, that Vīravara remained there, motionless at the main gate.
Having seen that during the day, King Śūdraka then ascended the palace roof again at night, desiring to know his state.
And then he said: "Ho there! Who indeed stands here at the lion-gate? Hearing that, Vīravara replied: "I am standing here."
"Aha! This Vīravara is a devotee of mine with most firm resolve; therefore, he must certainly be led by me to the great state."
Having reflected thus, King Śūdraka descended from the palace, entered the inner apartments, and then retired to his bed.
And on another day, when a cloud was raining heavily with a downpour of torrents, at nightfall, in a secret chamber, as darkness spread abroad;
Again, that king, desiring to test him, ascended the palace and, standing alone at the main gate, spoke clearly to him: "Who is there?"
When Vīravara spoke again, "I am standing here," the king was filled with wonder at the sight of his fortitude.
Just then, from a distance, he suddenly heard a woman weeping—alone, overwhelmed by despair, uttering piteous cries of lamentation.
"In my kingdom there is no one defeated, nor any who is poor or suffering; so who is this woman that weeps alone in the night?"
Having heard this, the king was moved by compassion and thought thus; he then commanded Vīravara, who stood alone below him.
"O Vīravara, listen! Some woman is weeping there in the distance. Go and investigate who it is that is weeping and why."
Having heard that, Vīravara said, "So be it," and set out from there to go, with his sword-hilt fastened and his hand resting on the hilt.
Nor did he take account of that form of a Rākṣasa, which was a mass of clouds shrouded in darkness, with flashing lightning for eyes, raining down massive torrents like stones.
Seeing him thus alone on that night as he was setting out, the king, filled with compassion and curiosity, stood upon the roof of the palace.
Having descended and taken up his sword, Śūdraka also set out alone behind him, remaining unobserved right there.
And that Vīravara, having gone there and performed the rites of weeping and following [the corpse], reached a certain lake outside the city and beheld it.
"O hero! O compassionate one! O renunciant! How shall I live, now that you have left me all alone? Thus she wept, that woman standing in the midst of the water.
"Who are you that weeps, and why so? the king asked her as he approached from behind; filled with wonder, she then replied as follows.
"O Vīravara, know this, my child: I am this very earth; now King Śūdraka, the righteous one, is my husband."
"And on the third day, that king will die; and having obtained such a husband as him, from where else could I find another king?"
"Therefore, I grieve for him and for my own sorrowful self. Having heard this, Vīravara, as if terrified, said to her:
"O Goddess, is there perhaps some such means by which death might not befall this Lord, the jewel that protects the world?"
Having heard those words, the Earth spoke: "There is one remedy, and you alone are capable of performing it."
Then Vīravara said: "In that case, O Queen, speak quickly; I shall accomplish it at once, for what is the use of my life otherwise?"
Hearing that, the Earth said: "Who else is as devoted to his master as you? Therefore, listen to this means for his protection."
This supreme goddess Caṇḍikā, who has been established by the king near the royal palace and who possesses an excellence of presence, is here.
"If you offer that best of beings, your son, as a sacrifice to her, then this king will not die; he shall live for another hundred years."
If this were done by you this very day, it would be auspicious; otherwise, when the third day arrives, there will be no life at all for him.
Thus addressed by the Earth, that hero Vīravara then said, "I am going, O Goddess; I shall do this right now."
Then, having said, "May it be well with you," the Earth vanished; and the king, standing nearby in concealment, heard all of that.
Then, while the king followed him secretly out of a desire to know his intent, Vīravara went quickly to his home at night, accompanied by Śūdraka.
There, having awakened his wife Dharmavatī, he spoke to her exactly as he had been told by the Earth regarding the sacrifice of his son for the sake of the king.
Having heard that, she said to him: "O Lord, O Master, may you first awaken this infant son of ours and then speak what is for the welfare of our lord."
Then, having awakened his sleeping son, that best of beings, and having related that entire account to him, Vīravara spoke as follows:
Therefore, my son, since you have been offered as a sacrifice to the goddess Caṇḍikā, that king will live; otherwise, on the third day, he will perish.
Upon hearing this, that best of beings, though but a boy, revealed his name as it truly was and, with an undaunted mind, spoke to his father:
If the king lives, dear father, I shall have achieved my purpose with my very life; for I would then have provided atonement for that food I have consumed.
Why, then, is there delay? Take me now before the Blessed Lady and offer me as a sacrifice; let there be peace for my Lord through me.
When that best of beings had spoken thus, Vīravara said to him there: "Excellent! You have truly been born from me as a son."
Having heard all this, the king, who had been standing outside, followed after him and thought: "Ah, the inner nature of all these is indeed the same."
Then Vīravara, placing his excellent son Sattvavara upon his shoulder, as well as his wife Dharmavatī and their daughter Vīravatī, [set out].
Both of them went to that temple of Caṇḍikā during that night; King Śūdraka also followed behind them, traveling in disguise.
Then, having been lowered from his father's shoulders before the Goddess, that best of beings, a mass of fortitude, bowed to the Goddess and made this request:
"By the offering of my head, may King Śūdraka live; O Goddess, may he rule a kingdom free from thorns for another hundred years."
When he had spoken thus, [the father], exclaiming "Excellent! Excellent! to his son, the best of beings, then drew away the hand of the child from his palm.
Having severed his head, Vīravara offered it to the goddess Caṇḍikā, saying, "By this offering of my son, may the king live."
Excellent! Who else is as devoted to his master as you, O Vīravara, who have thus offered up the life of your only virtuous son?
"Life and the kingdom have been granted to this King Śūdraka,"—thus a voice arose from the sky at that very moment.
And while that king was listening and watching all of this from his concealment, there was that maiden Vīravatī, the young daughter of Vīravara.
Approaching and embracing the head of her slain brother, she, blinded by intense grief while lamenting, died from the bursting of her heart.
Then his wife Dharmavatī spoke thus to Vīravara: "The king has indeed performed what was beneficial; now I shall tell you this."
Where even this child, though lacking wisdom, has died from grief for her brother—now that these two children are lost, what is the use of my life?
How much more so, then, for the sake of the king's welfare, have I, in my folly, not offered my own head to the Goddess? Therefore, grant me permission now.
Then Vīravara said to her as she spoke with such persistence: "I shall enter the fire first, taking my children's bodies with me."
Do this; may prosperity be yours! For what delight can there be for you now, O wise woman, in a life consisting solely of the sorrow of losing your offspring?
Let there be no distress in you with the thought, "Why was my very self not given by me? For would I not have given myself if it had been something achievable by another?
Therefore, wait here until I prepare a funeral pyre for you with these logs gathered for the construction of the Goddess’s temple.
Having spoken thus, Vīravara constructed a funeral pyre with those logs and set it ablaze at the tip of a lamp, upon which he placed the two corpses of his children.
Then his virtuous wife, Dharmavatī, having fallen at his feet and bowed to the goddess Caṇḍī, that stainless lady made this request.
"May this noble son be my husband even in another birth; may there be well-being for this lord, the king, through this body of mine."
Having spoken thus, that virtuous woman cast herself with ease into the water and fell into the funeral pyre, which was matted with clusters of flames.
Then that hero Vīravara reflected: "The king's business has been accomplished by me, exactly as the divine voice had proclaimed."
I have become free from debt to my lord by consuming this morsel of food; therefore, why do I now harbor such greed for life when I am all alone?
Having squandered his entire beloved family who were to be supported, what man like me would look well while sustaining only himself?
"Shall I not gratify this Mother even by the sacrifice of my own self? Having reflected thus, he first approached that Goddess with a hymn of praise.

Victory to you, O slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, O destroyer of the Dānava Ruru, O wielder of the trident! Victory to you, O bringer of joy to the gods, O sustainer of the three worlds, O most excellent Mother!

Victory to You, whose feet are worshipped by the world, the refuge for devotees seeking the highest good! Victory to You, who have assumed the rays of the sun, the dispeller of the masses of darkness that are evil deeds!
Victory to Kālī! Victory to Kapālinī! Victory to Kaṅkālī, O Śivā! Homage be to you! Be gracious now to King Śūdraka by means of the offering of my head.
Having thus addressed the queen, Vīravara once again immediately severed his own head with a blow of his palm.
Having observed all of that from his concealed position, King Śūdraka, filled with agitation, sorrow, and wonder, reflected:
"Aha! What is this that has been done by this virtuous man, together with his family, for my sake—something never before seen or heard of elsewhere, and so difficult to perform?"
In this manifold cycle of existence, how could there be a steadfast person such as this, O Lord, who gives up his life for the sake of another without making it known?
And if I were not to perform a corresponding service for this benefactor, what sovereignty would I possess, and what life would it be, save that of a beast?
Having reflected thus, the heroic King Śūdraka drew his sword in anger, approached the queen, and addressed her.
O Blessed One, who are ever-attained by me, now be well-pleased by this offering of my head and grant me your favor.
"May this brahmin Vīravara, whose actions are worthy of his name, live on together with his family, having sacrificed his life for my sake."
Having spoken thus, just as King Śūdraka proceeded to cut off his head with a sword, a voice arose from the sky.
"Do not act rashly; for I am indeed pleased with this courage of yours. Let that brahmin Vīravara, along with his children and wife, return to life."
Having spoken thus, that voice ceased; and Vīravara rose up, alive and unhurt, together with his son, his daughter, and his wife.
Having beheld that wonder, the king concealed himself once more; yet, gazing upon her with eyes filled with tears of joy, he remained there, never satiated.
Vīravara too, seeing his wife and children as well as himself suddenly like one who has just awakened from sleep, became bewildered in mind.
And he questioned those wives and sons individually by name, asking: "How have you, who were reduced to ashes, risen up alive once more?"
"I too have cut off my own head, yet here he lives; what can this be? Is this a delusion, or is it the manifest grace of the Goddess?"
Speaking thus, he was addressed by them—his wife and children—who had not noticed him: "This is surely the grace of the Goddess, that we still live while these [others] do."
Then, having understood it to be so and having bowed to Ambikā, Vīravara took his wife and children and, his purpose accomplished, went home.
Having ushered his son, his wife, and that daughter into it, he went to the king's main gate during that night just as before.
King Śūdraka, too, having witnessed all this unobserved, went and then ascended his own palace residence once more.
And standing there, he called out from behind, "Who is stationed here at the lion-gate? Then Vīravara replied, "O Lord, it is I who stand here."
By the command of the god, I went toward that woman; but like a female demon, she vanished somewhere from my sight as soon as I saw her.
Having heard these words of Vīravara, the king, now seeing the truth of the matter, was filled with even greater astonishment and reflected:
Oh, how profound and steady is the mind of the wise, like the ocean! Though they have made an incomparable impression, they do not utter it.
Reflecting thus and other such thoughts, the king descended silently from the palace, entered the inner apartments, and passed the remainder of that night there.
And in the morning, at the time of the assembly, when Vīravara had arrived and stood before him for an audience, the king was delighted and likewise [bestowed] everything upon him.
He described that night's events to his ministers, so that they all became as if bewildered by wonder.
Then the king affectionately bestowed the kingdom of Lāṭa, together with Karṇāṭa, upon that Vīravara and his son.
Then, possessing equal power and assisting one another, Vīravara and King Śūdraka dwelt there in happiness.
Having thus told this most wonderful tale, the Vetāla then spoke again to King Trivikramasena.
Therefore, O King, tell me which one among all these heroes is the superior; that same curse previously mentioned shall be yours if you know and do not speak.
Having heard this, the king replied to the Vetāla: "Among all these, King Śūdraka is the preeminent hero."
Then the Vetāla said: "O King, why did Vīravara not say, 'He is superior, for his equal is not even born upon this earth'?"
Was his wife not superior, or was she a woman who had become so base that she disregarded her son, even while witnessing firsthand his state as a sacrificial victim?
Indeed, he was the best of beings; how could his son not be superior? Even though he was but a child, such was the excellence of his character.
"Why do you speak so highly of King Śūdraka compared to these others? To the Vetāla who had spoken thus, the king replied once more:
"Not so, Vīravara! That noble son was indeed such a man; his vow was the protection of his master, even at the cost of his own life, children, and wife."
His wife was likewise of noble birth, virtuous, and devoted to her husband as her sole deity; by following her husband's path, what other duty could she have?
But that best of beings, born from those two, was indeed of their very nature; for as the threads are, so indeed is the cloth produced.
But for those servants whose lives are protected by kings with their own selves, Śūdraka excels here by sacrificing his body for their sake.

Having heard these words of the king, the Vetāla suddenly departed from his shoulder to his own place by means of his magic power, unobserved; yet the king, firmly resolved, set out once more along that same path in that cemetery on that night to bring him back again.
The Twelfth Wave: Then, having gone again to the vicinity of that śiṃśapā tree, he saw him hanging there in the same manner, suspended from a human corpse.
Having set down the Vetāla and performed many acts of hospitality for him, that Trivikramasena immediately proceeded from there to depart.
And as he was approaching silently on the path at night in this great cemetery, the Vetāla, seated upon his shoulder as before, spoke to him.
"O King, you are intent upon what is painful, yet you are exceedingly dear to me; therefore, to dispel your mental distress, I shall relate a story—listen."
In Ujjayinī there lived a Brahmin named Harisvāmin, a virtuous and beloved minister who served as a loyal attendant to King Puṇyasena.
To that householder, from a wife worthy of himself, was born a virtuous and worthy son named Devasvāmin.
And likewise, a daughter named Somaprabhā was born to him, whose name was truly significant as she was renowned for her peerless beauty and grace.
That virtuous maiden, proud of her excellence of beauty, spoke through the mouth of her mother to her father and that brother.
I should be given to a hero, a man of knowledge, or even one of great discernment; I am not to be given to anyone else if my life is to serve a purpose.
Having heard such words from her, as her father Harisvāmin reflected upon choosing one of those suitors as the best, he was filled with intense anxiety.
Then King Puṇyasena dispatched him as an envoy to the presence of the southern king, who had come for war, in order to negotiate a peace treaty.
Having accomplished his purpose there, a preeminent brahmin, having heard of the excellence of her beauty, approached and requested that daughter from him.
"My daughter desires no husband other than one who is wise, learned, or heroic; tell me, among those [three], who are you?"
Having been addressed thus by Harisvāmin regarding the matter of his wife, that twice-born man replied to him: "I possess specialized knowledge."
When he was told again, "Then show that to me," the wise man, by his own power, fashioned a celestial chariot.
Having placed that master Harisvāmin upon a magical mechanical chariot there, he led him away in an instant and showed him the worlds of heaven and other realms.
And being pleased, he brought that army back once more to that very camp where the southern king had come for his own business.
Then Harisvāmin promised his daughter to him, and he decided that the marriage would take place on the seventh day for the sake of the one possessing such specialized knowledge.
At that time, in Ujjayinī as well, another brahmin came and asked Devaśvāmin for his daughter, who was that very same girl.
"She desires no husband other than those who are wise, learned, and heroic"; thus addressed by him, he too proclaimed himself to be a hero.
Then, to that hero who displayed the splendor of his weapons and missiles, the brahmin Devasvāmin agreed to give his younger sister in marriage.
And on the seventh day, having reached a firm decision, he announced that very marriage to him as well—though behind his mother's back—in accordance with the words of the astrologer.
At that very moment, his mother—the wife of Harisvāmin—was approached by a third person who separately requested her daughter's hand in marriage.
"A wise man, a hero, and one possessed of higher knowledge—such a man is fit to be the husband of my daughter," she said; and being thus addressed by her, O Mother, he replied, "I am wise."
Having inquired about his past and future, she promised to give her daughter to that wise man, and he likewise agreed on that very seventh day.
On the following day, Harisvāmin arrived there and related to his wives and son exactly what had been done regarding that decision to give away the girl in marriage.
And the two of them told him each of their respective deeds as they had been done; he, too, became bewildered by that invitation to three boons.
Then, on that day of the wedding, those three—the wise, the learned, and the brave—all arrived there at the house of Harisvāmin as the bridegrooms.
At that very moment, the wonderful maiden Somaprabhā, his bride, had unexpectedly gone away somewhere; though searched for, she was not found.
Then Harisvāmin, filled with agitation, said to that wise man: "O Knower, tell me quickly now: where has my daughter gone?"
Having heard that, the wise man said: "She was carried off by the Rākṣasa Dhūmaśikha and taken to his own dwelling in the Vindhya forest."
Thus addressed by the wise man, Harisvāmin was struck with fear and said: "Alas, what a pity! How can she be obtained, and how indeed can the marriage be accomplished?"
Having heard this, the wise and steadfast one said: "Be firm; I shall lead you right now to that place where this wise man says she stands."
Having said this, he immediately fashioned a chariot equipped with all kinds of weapons; mounting upon that sky-faring vehicle, he placed Harisvāmin, Jñānin, and Śūra within it.
In an instant, he brought them to the region of the Vindhya forest, to that dwelling of the Rākṣasa there which had been described by the wise man.
Then the hero, preceded by Harisvāmin, fought that enraged Rākṣasa who had come out after learning the news.
Then that wonderful battle took place between those two, the man and the rakshasa, who fought with diverse weapons for the sake of the woman, like Rama and Ravana.
And in an instant, that hero, with a crescent-headed arrow, severed the head of even that Rākṣasa who was intoxicated by battle.
When the rākṣasa was slain, they all then departed from that place, taking Somaprabhā with them on the chariot of Vijnaniratha.
Having reached Harisvāmin’s house, even as the auspicious moment for their departure arrived, a great dispute arose among those who were wise, learned, and heroic.
The wise man said: "If I did not know this, how could this girl—who is hidden away—be found? She must be given to me from here."
But the wise one replied, "If I do not construct a sky-going chariot, how could there be coming and going for you gods in an instant, as there is for yourselves?"
"How can there be a chariot duel between a warrior on a chariot and a Rākṣasa? Therefore, she must be given to me, for this auspicious moment has been fixed by me."
Śūra also said, "If I do not slay that Rākṣasa in battle, then even though you two have made an effort, who could bring back this maiden?"
While they were thus disputing, "This must be given to me," Harisvāmin remained silent for a moment, his mind bewildered.
"O King, tell me: to whom should she be given here? If you know and do not speak, your head shall split asunder."
Having heard this from that Vetāla and breaking his silence, King Trivikramasena spoke thus to him:
She must be given to that hero who, by exerting himself at the risk of his own life and through great valor, won her by slaying that Rākṣasa in battle.
The Creator has made the man of wisdom and the man of specialized knowledge his two servants; why then should they not always be like an accountant and a carpenter in serving others?

Having heard these words of the lord of men, the Vetāla instantly departed from the top of his shoulder back to his own place as before; and the king, remaining undaunted, set out once more toward him.
The Thirteenth Wave: Then, having gone back from there and reached that śiṃśapā tree once more, the king took the vetāla upon his shoulder as before, remaining silent.
While Trivikramasena was thus returning there in haste, the Vetāla spoke to him once more on the way:
"O King, you are wise and of noble character; therefore, you are dear to me. For this reason, I shall tell you an entertaining tale; listen now to my question."
There was a king renowned on the surface of the earth as Yaśaḥketu; his royal capital was a city named Śobhāvatī.
In that city there was a supreme temple of Gaurī, and to its south was a lake named Gaurītīrtha.
Every year on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, great crowds of people from various directions used to come there for the festival to bathe.
And once, on that lunar day, a young washerman named Dhavala came there from the village called Brahmasthala to bathe.
There, at that bathing-place, he saw the daughter of the washerman named Śuddhapaṭa, a maiden called Madanasundarī, who had come there to bathe.
His heart having been stolen by that moon-like woman who robbed him of his composure with her loveliness, he then went home, afflicted by love, after searching for her name and lineage.
Remaining there without food and unsettled in mind because of her absence, he was questioned by his mother, who was distressed for him, and he explained what was in his heart to her.
She went and reported that to her husband named Vimala; he too, having arrived and seen his son in such a state, spoke to him.
"Why do you despair thus, my son, even though the desired object is not difficult to obtain? For that Śuddhapada, when entreated by me, will give his daughter to you."
For we are not inferior to him in lineage, wealth, or action; I know him and he knows me, therefore this is not difficult for me.
Having thus consoled his son and set him to his meals and other duties, Vimala, accompanied by him, went on another day to the abode of Śuddhapaṭa.
And there he requested a maiden from him for the sake of his son Dhavala; and he, in turn, promised her to him with respect.
Having fixed the auspicious moment, on the following day, that Śuddhapaṭa gave his daughter Madanasundarī, who was a worthy match for him, to Dhavala.
And having performed the marriage ceremony with her, who was captivated by the sight of him, the virtuous Dhavala went to his father's house together with his wife.
Then, while he was dwelling in happiness, once the son of his father-in-law—the brother of that Madanasundarī—arrived there.
Having shown his respect to all, embraced by his sister, and greeted with joy, he—having been asked about his welfare by his relatives and having rested—spoke to them.
"I have been sent by my father to invite Madanasundarī and her son-in-law, because we have a festival for the worship of the Goddess."
Having faith in those words, all those relatives and others attended upon him that day with appropriate food and drink.
In the morning, Dhavala set out for his father-in-law’s house accompanied by Madanasundarī and that brother-in-law.
Having reached that city of Śobhāvatī with two others as his companions, he approached and beheld a great temple of Gaurī nearby.
Then, with faith, he spoke to his wife and brother-in-law: "Let us behold this divine goddess here."
Having heard that, the brother-in-law replied to him with this refusal: "How can we see the deity with so many empty-handed people?"
"I shall go alone for now; you two remain right here. Having said this, Dhavala then departed to see that goddess.
Having entered her abode, prostrated, and visualized her—who had crushed fierce dānavas with her eighteen staff-like arms—
He, whose mind was stirred by the impulse of fate, thought thus as he beheld her trampling the demon Mahiṣāsura with the soles of her lotus feet.
People worship this goddess with various offerings of living beings; why then do I not please her for the sake of my own success by offering myself as a sacrifice?
Having meditated thus, he took from that secluded inner sanctum the sword which had previously been presented as an offering to the Goddess by certain sea-faring merchants.
Having tied his own head to the chain of the bell with his hair, he cut it off with that sword; once severed, it fell to the ground.
While he was away for a long time, his brother-in-law went there to see him and entered that very temple of the goddess.
He too, seeing his sister’s husband with his head severed, was likewise bewildered and cut off his own head with that very sword.
Meanwhile, until he arrived, Madanasundarī too went to that queen’s palace with a bewildered mind.
Having entered and seen her husband and brother arrived in such a state, she cried out, "Alas! What is this? I am destroyed! and fell to the ground.
Rising in an instant and grieving for those two who had been struck down so unexpectedly, she thought: "What is the use of this life of mine now?"
And she, being intent on abandoning her body, addressed that queen: "O Queen, sole presiding deity of the ordinances for conjugal felicity and virtuous conduct!"
She who shared half the body of her husband, even the enemy of Māra; she who was the refuge for the entire world of women and the remover of their suffering.
"Why have you suddenly carried off both my husband and my brother? This is not right of you toward me, for I am eternally devoted to you."
Listen to this one piteous word from me, who has come to you for refuge: first, let me cast off this body here, which is stricken by misfortune.
O Goddess, in whatever birth I may be born hereafter, may these two alone be my husband and brother there as well.
Having thus praised and petitioned the goddess, and having bowed to her once more, he fashioned a noose from a creeper upon an *aśoka* tree.
And as she stretched out her neck and placed it within the noose, at that very moment, a voice issued forth from the expanse of the sky:
"Do not act rashly, my daughter; for even though you are but a child, I am pleased by this excellence of your character. Release this noose."
"Join your own heads to the trunks of your husband and your brother; by my grace, let both of them rise up alive."
Upon hearing this, Madanasundarī abandoned her noose and, approaching with joy, she became bewildered by her extreme impetuosity before being recognized.
By the decree of fate, the boy joined his brother’s head with his father’s body, and his father’s body with his brother’s head.
Then both of them rose up alive with their limbs uninjured, though a confusion had arisen between their bodies due to the exchange of heads.
Then, satisfied by each other’s accounts of their respective experiences as they had occurred, those three bowed to the goddess Śarvāṇī and departed as they pleased.
And as she was going along, seeing the exchange of heads they had performed, Madanasundarī became distressed, bewildered as to what should be done.
Therefore speak, O King: who is her husband between those two of mixed origin? He whom you previously mentioned shall be your curse if, knowing the answer, you do not speak.
Having heard this question regarding the story from the Vetāla, King Trivikramasena then replied to him in this manner:
That which is situated [there] is the head of its lord; he indeed is her husband, for among the limbs, the head is the primary part, and recognition resides therein.
When the king had spoken thus, the Vetāla unexpectedly departed from his shoulder; and the king went forth once more to bring him back.
The Fourteenth Wave. Then, having gone back and reached the Vetāla once more at the śiṃśapā tree, King Trivikramasena took him upon his shoulder.
As he set out having taken him up, the vetāla said to him on the way: "O King, listen; I shall tell you a story to dispel your fatigue."
There is here, on the shore of the eastern ocean, a city named Tāmraliptī; and in that city there was a king named Caṇḍasena.
He who turns his face away from the wives of others, but not from the fields of battle; he who seizes the fortune of his enemies, but not the wealth and property of others.
Once, a prince from the south named Sattvaśīla, who was beloved by the people, arrived here at the king's main gate.
Having introduced himself there out of poverty to that king, he tore through the deception along with the other princes.
Then, having become a kārpaṭika, he remained there for many years performing constant service, yet he never obtained any reward from the king.
If my birth is in a royal lineage, why such poverty? And even in the midst of poverty, why has the Creator endowed me with such great ambition?
For even though I am serving him in this way with such afflicted attendants, and have long been sinking from hunger, the king has not yet looked upon me.
While that traveler was thus meditating there, the king once went out on a hunting expedition.
While that kārpaṭika ran ahead carrying a staff, he then proceeded toward the deer-forest accompanied by horsemen and foot soldiers.
Having finished his hunt there, he pursued a large, intoxicated boar from afar and in an instant reached another forest region very far away.

There, on a path covered with leaves and grass in that great forest, the king—having lost his way and being exhausted from the hunt for the boar—then fell into a state of disorientation regarding the directions.
Then a certain pilgrim, afflicted by hunger and thirst, followed him on foot—disregarding even his own life—as he rode upon the back of a wind-swift horse.
And seeing him arrived in such a state, the king spoke affectionately: "Do you perhaps know the way by which you have come?"
Having heard that, the kārpaṭika joined his palms in reverence and said to him: "I know; however, let my lord rest here for a moment."
For now, this lord of the lotuses shines intensely, a central gem upon the girdle of the bride that is the day, with its mass of rays flickering like flames.
Having heard this, the king spoke to him with courtesy: "In that case, let some water be sought by you here somewhere."
Saying "So be it," that kārpaṭika then climbed a tall tree; seeing a river, he descended and led the king there.
Then I turned that horse back, reversed his course, gave him water and mouthfuls of grass, and rendered him free from fatigue.
And for the king who had finished his bath, he untied from the hem of his garment, washed, and brought to him some heart-pleasing *āmalaka* fruits.
To the king who asked him, "From where did these come?", he, kneeling with his palms joined in reverence, replied as follows.
Living by this conduct, I have constantly wandered for ten years past, propitiating the God while observing the vow of the Anekānta sages.

Having heard that, the king—overcome with compassion and filled with shame—thought to himself, "If you are truly named Satyanāman (Truth-named), why are you called Sattvaśīla (Virtuous-natured)? Thus he spoke.
Fie on those kings who do not recognize the suffering or the lack of suffering among their servants; and fie on that retinue which does not inform them accordingly.
Having reflected thus, the king took two *āmalaka* fruits from the hand of the mendicant, who was somehow persisting in clinging to him.
Having eaten that and drunk the water, he rested there for a moment, accompanied by the traveler who had likewise eaten the *āmalaka* fruits and drunk the water.
Then, having mounted the horse prepared by that traveler, he set out with him as his guide leading the way.
Although the horse was repeatedly entreated not to ascend its hindquarters, the king proceeded toward his own city, having regained his army along the way.
There, having made his devotion known, he gratified that pilgrim with wealth and objects of enjoyment, yet he did not consider this to be a sufficient recompense.
Then, having achieved his purpose, Sattvaśīla remained by the side of King Caṇḍasiṃha, having abandoned the conduct of a wandering petitioner.
Once, that king dispatched him to the island of Siṃhala for his own sake to request the daughter of the Lord of Siṃhala.
There, traveling by way of the ocean, having worshipped his chosen deity, he boarded the ship together with the twice-born men appointed by the king.
When that carriage had departed, a banner rose up unawares from the midst of that ocean, causing great wonder.
Its peak reached the clouds; it was vast and fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold, resplendent with multicolored, fluttering banners.
At that moment, a mass of clouds suddenly rose up there and began to rain heavily, and a fierce wind blew.
By those monsoon winds, as if by fierce goads, that elephant-like ship was forcibly dragged and fastened to that flagpole.
And at that moment, that banner, along with the ship, began to sink into that ocean agitated by waves.
Then those brahmins, remaining there and agitated by fear, proclaimed an outcry against their own king, Caṇḍasiṃha, as one who had acted contrary to the dharma of the twice-born.
Hearing that, Sattvaśīla, unable to endure it out of devotion to his master, took up his sword, wrapped his upper garment around him, and followed behind the banner.
Indifferent [to his own safety], the hero cast himself there into the great ocean, suspecting the cause to lie within the sea and desiring to counteract it.
When that [ship] was submerged, the vessel, tossed far away by wind and waves, was shattered; and those who were on it fell into the mouths of sea-monsters.
And having plunged into that ocean, Sattvaśīla looked about; then, he beheld there a divine city and no longer saw the sea.
In that radiant golden palace, adorned with pillars made of jewels and beautified by gardens and ponds featuring staircases set with excellent gems.
He beheld the temple of the goddess Kātyāyanī, towering as high as Mount Meru, with walls of various jeweled stones and uplifted banners variegated with gems.
There, having bowed to that goddess and worshipped her with hymns of praise before her, he sat down in wonder, thinking, "Could this be some kind of sorcery?"
And at that moment, a maiden suddenly emerged from within the circle of light situated before the queen, having opened the divine door-panel.
With eyes like blue lotuses, a face like a full-blown lotus, and a smile like a flower, her limbs as soft as a lotus stalk—she was like a moving lotus pond.
Surrounded by a retinue of thousands of women, she entered the inner chamber of the queen and, at that moment, simultaneously entered the heart of Sattvaśīla.
Then the goddess emerged from the inner sanctum after having performed her worship; she did not, however, depart at all from the heart of Sattvaśīla.
And she entered right there into the midst of that circle of light; Sattvaśīla also followed after her and entered there.
And having entered, he beheld within another most excellent city, which was like a pleasure garden for all the riches of enjoyment.
There, having observed that maiden seated upon a jeweled couch within, Sattvaśīla approached her side and sat down beside her.
And he remained with his eyes fixed upon her face, as if painted there, while his limbs—trembling and bristling with thrills—proclaimed his longing for an embrace.
And seeing him possessed by love, she looked at the faces of the maidservants there; and they, perceiving his intention at that moment, spoke to him.
"You have arrived here as a guest; therefore, accept the hospitality prepared by our mistress. Arise, bathe, and after that, eat."
Having heard that, he took hold of hope and rose up even from his exhaustion; he went to a certain garden pond shown to him by them.
And submerged in it, he rose up at that very moment from the middle of the garden pond in the city of Tāmraliptī, amidst the agitation caused by King Caṇḍasiṃha.
Having arrived there unexpectedly and beholding himself, he reflected: "Aha! What is this? Where is this divine garden, and where is that city?"
Where is that sight of hers, which was like a shower of nectar; and where is this immediate, great poison of separation from her?
This was no dream, for I experienced it with perfect clarity while awake; surely I, a fool, have been deceived by those maidens of Pātāla.
Meditating thus, deprived of that maiden, he wandered like one possessed in that garden; afflicted by love, he lamented.
And seeing him in that state, his limbs enveloped by tawny pollen from flowers stirred up by the wind, as if by the fires of separation.
The park-keepers went and informed King Caṇḍasiṃha; he, becoming agitated, came in person and beheld him.
Having consoled him, he asked: "Tell us, friend, what is this? Where were you going, where have you arrived, where were you standing, and where did the arrow fall?"
Having heard that, Sattvaśīla related his entire story to the king; and the king then reflected thus:
Ah! Even this hero has been mocked by desire through my merits; indeed, I have found the opportunity to discharge my debt to him.
Having thought thus within himself, the heroic king said to him: "Therefore, abandon this futile grief; I shall bring her to you."
Having led his beloved Asura maiden back by that very same path, the king comforted him with a bath and other such attentions.
On another day, having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, he embarked upon a ship and set out for the ocean with him, following the path shown by him.
Having reached the middle of it and seeing that banner with its flagstaff standing up as before, Sattvaśīla addressed the king:
This great banner, endowed with divine power, has now arisen here; since I have plunged into it, Your Majesty should follow this banner and plunge in as well.
Having said this, that Sattvaśīla first threw himself onto the path as the banner, which was sinking down, drew near to him.
Then the king likewise cast himself into that same place; and having both quickly sunk to the bottom, they reached that divine city.
Having seen her there, the king was filled with wonder; having bowed down to that goddess Pārvatī, he sat down together with her, endowed as she was with a virtuous character.
And at that moment, that maiden emerged there from the circle of light, accompanied by her circle of friends, like the personified splendor of radiance.
When it was said, "This is she, Sumukhī," King Sattvaśīla beheld her and considered his attachment to her to be entirely appropriate.
She too, beholding that king with his auspicious physical marks, thought: "Who might this be? He must be some unprecedented and extraordinary man."
She entered the abode of Ambikā for worship, while the king, taking Sattvaśīla with him, went to the garden with disdain.
In an instant, having performed her worship and requested from the goddess within the inner sanctum the attainment of a virtuous husband, that daughter of the Daityas emerged.
Having gone out, she said to one of her friends, "Friend, let him be sought; where does that great-souled man stand whom I saw here?"
"Please come and accept our hospitality; may you show us favor. Thus should this venerable person be entreated, for he is indeed some supreme being.
Thus addressed by her friend, she searched for him and, finding him in the garden, humbly reported that command of her mistress to him.
Hearing that, the heroic king said to her with indifference: "This alone shall be our hospitality; what else is required?"
Having heard this, her friend went and informed her; then that daughter of the Daityas considered him in every way a noble person worthy of honor.
Then, as if being drawn by the tether of his fortitude, she was led by that king—even though he was himself free from desire—to an act of hospitality unsuitable for a mere mortal.
Considering that garden to have been bestowed as the ripened fruit of her service to Pārvatī for the sake of obtaining a husband, the daughter of the Asura entered it herself.
She seemed to be greeted by the trees nearby with the various songs of birds, their creeper-arms swaying in the wind, and with flowers scattered about.
Having approached him there, she bowed with due humility and requested the king to accept her hospitality.
Then the king said to Sattvaśīla, referring to her: "I have come here to see the queen of whom he spoke."
Gaurī, whose most wonderful banner can be reached by the path of the flagstaff, was seen by her; and after that, you were seen—what guest-reception could we possibly request from you here?
Hearing that, the maiden said out of curiosity: "Then come to see my second city, which is a wonder of the three worlds."
When she had spoken thus, the king laughed and said to her: "That too was told to me by him, regarding where that bathing pool is located."
Then that maiden said: "O Lord, do not command me thus; I am not of a nature to mock, nor what mockery could there be toward one worthy of worship?"
For I have been made your servant by the excellence of your being; therefore, you ought not to act in such a way as to frustrate my request.
Having heard this and said "So be it," King Sattvaśīlasakha went with her to the edge of that circle of light.
And when the door was opened, he was likewise ushered inside, where he beheld that other divine city of hers.
It was ever-armored with trees that flowered and bore fruit in all seasons, appearing like the entirety of Mount Meru’s summit fashioned from jewels and gold.
Having seated the king upon a highly precious jewel-throne and having offered him the customary guest-offering (arghya), the daughter of the Daitya king spoke.
I was the daughter of the high-souled Kālanemi, the lord of the Asuras; and by him who wields the discus as a weapon, my father was sent to the heavenly realm.
And these two cities of my ancestors were built by Viśvakarman; here neither old age nor death afflicts anyone, and every desire is fulfilled.
"And now you are my father, and I, along with my city, am under your control. Having thus surrendered her entire self and all she possessed, the king spoke to her.
If this is so, then, O blameless one, you have indeed been given by me to him—this son of mine—who is a hero of virtuous character, a friend, and a kinsman.
Thus addressed by the king, who was like the grace of the Goddess incarnate, the humble Vinatā, recognizing his virtues, agreed, saying, "So be it."
Then the king spoke to Sattvaśīla, who had achieved his purpose by taking her hand in marriage and had been granted sovereignty over the city of the Asuras.
Of those two emblic myrobalans that were brought, one has been cleared by me from you; I am a debtor to you for the second, which remains uncleared.
Having spoken thus to him as he bowed, she said to that daughter of the Daitya: "Show me the path by which I may reach my own city."
Then that daughter of the Daitya gave him a sword named Aparājita and a fruit to be eaten; one of these two was capable of removing old age and death.
Endowed with those two [powers], that king, having plunged into the lake mentioned by them from his own country, rose up and gradually became one whose every desire was fully accomplished.
Although he was of a virtuous nature, that Daitya ruled over cities, women, and kingdoms; tell me, which of these two was superior in courage regarding their leap into the ocean?
Having heard this question from the Vetāla in such a manner, King Trivikramasena, out of fear of a curse, replied to him:
Between these two, I consider Sattvaśīla here to be superior in courage; for he, though ignorant of the true nature of reality and devoid of worldly hope, has fallen into the ocean.
But the king, having understood the truth, entered the ocean with resolve; he did not desire the Daitya maiden, thinking, "She is unattainable and should be desired [only] through hope."
Having heard these words of the king, who had now broken his silence, the Vetāla left his shoulder and returned to his own place, that śiṃśapā tree, just as before.
The king likewise pursued him with speed to bring him back once more; for do the wise ever slacken when a task has been begun but not yet completed?
The Fifteenth Wave: Having gone back to that śiṃśapā tree and once again reached the Vetāla, King Trivikramasena placed him upon his shoulder and set out from there.
As he was departing, the Vetāla spoke to him again from his shoulder: "O King, to relieve your fatigue, hear this question from me."
In the land of Aṅga, there was a great agrahāra named Vṛkṣaghaṭā; there lived a Brahmin named Viṣṇusvāmin, a performer of sacrifices and a man of great wealth.
And to him, by his wife who was a match for himself, were born in due course three sons who were young and possessed of divine cleverness.
Once, sent by their father who had begun a sacrifice for the sake of a tortoise, those three brothers went to the ocean.
Having obtained the tortoise, the elder brother then spoke to the two younger ones: "Let one of you two take the tortoise for the sake of our father's sacrifice."
"I am not able to grasp this, for it is slippery with slime"—when the elder brother had spoken thus, the two younger brothers said to him:
"If you have this doubt here, how could it not be ours as well? Having heard that, the elder brother said, "Take it; you two may go."
Otherwise, there would be a failure of your father’s sacrificial rites caused by you; consequently, both of you and he would certainly fall into hell.
When he had spoken thus, his two younger brothers laughed and said to him: "You will know the dharma of us two alone, but not your own."
Then the eldest said: "Do you not know my fastidiousness? I am fastidious about food; I am not fit to touch anything loathsome."
Having heard these words of his, the middle brother said to him: "In that case, I am even more skilled than you; I am an expert at charming women."
When the middle one had spoken thus, the elder spoke again: "Then let this younger one among us seize the tortoise."
Then, knitting his brows, even the youngest said to the two of them, "O fools! I am indeed more agile than Tūlikā and Caṅga, especially so."
Thus, those three brothers, addicted to their mutual quarrels and entirely consumed by pride, abandoned that tortoise in order to reach a decision.
They quickly went to the city named Viṭaṅkapura, which was near the territory of the king named Prasenajit.
There, having announced themselves through the mouth of the doorkeeper and entered within, they reported their own story to the king exactly as it had happened.
"Stay right here while I examine you one by one in due order. When addressed thus by the king, they remained there, saying, "So be it."
And at the time for his own meal, the king summoned them and caused them to be served the foremost seat and delicious food, fit for a king, endowed with the six flavors.
While everyone else was eating, that one brahmin—a glutton for food—did not eat there, his face contorted with disgust.
"Why does he not eat his food, O Brahmin, even though it is delicious and fragrant?"—when the king himself asked this, that Brahmin slowly replied.
"O Lord, there is here the foul odor of smoke from a corpse mixed with the rice; therefore, I do not venture to eat this, even though it is delicious."
When he had spoken thus, they all, having smelled it there by the king's command, said that the rice of the *kalama* variety was faultless and fragrant.
But he, being addicted to food, did not eat it while his nose was covered; then the king, having reflected, began to investigate in due order.
Then, from the officials, he learned that the rice was grown in a field near a village cremation ground.
Then, greatly amazed and pleased, the king said to him: "Truly, you are a master of eating; therefore, let something else be eaten."
And having finished his meal, the king dismissed those brahmins to their lodgings and summoned an excellent courtesan of his own.
And in the evening, she sent that woman, adorned with ornaments and beautiful in every limb, to that second Brahmin, Nāricangha.
And she, her face like the full moon of the night of the full moon, inflaming the god of love, went to his bedchamber accompanied by the king’s attendants.
And when she had entered, he—his chamber illuminated by her radiance—fainted and pressed his left hand against the tip of his nose to hold his breath.
Nārīcaṅga said to the king’s servants, "Let her be cast out; otherwise, I shall die, for the smell of a goat emanates from her."
Having been addressed thus by him, those royal officers led the dejected courtesan into the presence of the king and related that entire account to him.
The king, having summoned Nārīcaṅga at that very moment, said to him: "This [woman], who is [anointed] with the finest unguents of sandalwood, camphor, and black aloe-wood—"
For that courtesan, who has adorned herself and whose lovely fragrance spreads in all directions, how could there be the smell of a goat?
Although he was thus addressed by the king, since he did not then accept that woman's proposal, the king fell into reflection.
And by questioning her with logical reasoning, he understood that she had been reared on goat's milk, having been separated from her mother and nurse during her infancy.
Then, greatly amazed and praising the skill of that woman-dancer, the king [bestowed wealth] upon that third twice-born man.
Out of affection for him, she quickly had a bed prepared with seven cotton mattresses arranged one upon another on top of a couch.
And there, in a magnificent dwelling, he slept upon a couch provided with a pillow, covered with a bedspread of washed, very smooth cloth.
When only half a watch of the night had passed, he rose from his bed, clutching his side with his hand, crying out and tormented by agony.
And by the royal officers there, he was seen on his side, appearing like a curved, reddish mark left by a child who had been pressed tightly against him.
Having gone, they reported this to the king, and the king said to them: "Let it be examined whether there might be something beneath the mattresses."
And as they went along, looking at each individual layer of the mattress, they reached the hair on the surface of the couch from every single layer.
Having led him there, he showed him to the king; and the king, beholding that form of the one brought before him—his body as supple as a painting—was filled with wonder.
Thinking with wonder, "A hair from one of his seven beds has become stuck to his body," the king passed that night.
In the morning, thinking, "These three are possessed of wonderful wit and delicacy," he gave three hundred thousand gold pieces to those three excellent men.
Then, having forgotten the tortoise, they remained there in happiness, while their father incurred the sin resulting from obstructing the fruit of his intended sacrifice.
Having thus related this wonderful tale, the Vetāla, once more perched upon his shoulder, questioned King Trivikramasena with another riddle.
"O King, having reflected upon the curse previously mentioned, tell me among these—eating, women, and lying on a bed—which one is the most harmful?"
Upon hearing this, that wise king replied to the Vetāla: "I know more about these than they do—specifically, how to skillfully handle a paintbrush."
On whose body the reflected image of a hair was seen to have actually emerged, that [hair] must have previously been known by the other two [senses] from some other source.
When he had spoken thus, the Vetāla left the king’s shoulder as before; and the king likewise followed after him, undaunted.
The Sixteenth Wave: Then, having gone back from that śiṃśapā tree, King Trivikramasena again took the vetāla upon his shoulder.
And as he was setting out, the Vetāla said to him: "O King, where is your kingdom, and where is this wandering through a cremation ground at night?"
Why do you not behold this cremation ground, teeming with living beings and terrifying by night, where the darkness is as dense as the smoke from funeral pyres?
"What a painful obsession this is of yours, O monk, out of regard for that [person]. Therefore, listen now to this question of mine, which shall serve as a diversion on the road."
In the land of Avanti there is a city created by the gods at the beginning of the age, like the body of Śiva adorned with the splendor of a majestic serpent.
Padmāvatī, Bhogavatī, and Hiraṇyavatī—these names were renowned in the three ages beginning with Kṛta; in the Kali age, it is known as Ujjayinī.
And in that city there was a king named Vīradeva, the best among rulers; he had a chief queen named Padmarati.
Then the king, having gone with her to the bank of the Mandākinī, propitiated Hara through ascetic penance, desiring a son.
Having remained here for a long time in ascetic practice and having performed the rites of bathing and worship, he heard this voice from the sky uttered by the well-pleased Lord:
"O King, a son shall be born to you, a hero sprung from your lineage, and a daughter whose extraordinary beauty surpasses that of the Apsarases."
Having heard this celestial voice, King Vīradeva, his desires fulfilled by the Siddhas, returned to his own city accompanied by his queen.
There, when his first son named Śūradeva was born to him by that queen Padmarati, a daughter was subsequently born.
"Even though he is bodiless, she shall produce delight by means of his form"; thus was she named Anaṅgarati by her father.
And as she grew up, her father, desiring to find a suitable husband for her, had portraits of the kings on the earth brought to him.
Since not even one among them appeared to him as being her equal, the king, out of affection, addressed his daughter.
"For my part, daughter, I do not see a suitor who is your equal; therefore, assemble all the kings and hold a svayaṃvara."
Having heard these words of her father, the princess said: "Father, out of shame, I do not venture to hold a *svayaṃvara*."
However, you must give me to one who knows a unique, unprecedented science, who is handsome and young; I have no need for anyone else superior to him.
Thus, having heard those words of his daughter Anaṅgaratī, as that king was searching for such a bridegroom, [the following occurred].
Having learned of this from the world, four men—heroes, wise, capable, and from the southern region—approached him.
Honored by the king, they each individually declared their own specialized knowledge in his presence, while the princess, desiring that [knowledge], was there as well.
One said, "I am a Śūdra by name, Pañcapaṭṭika; I alone prepare five pairs of garments made of the finest cloth every day."
I give one of them to those [brahmins], one to the god, and I take one for myself from among the two garments.
I shall give one to my wife, provided she remains here with me; and by selling the other, I shall provide myself with food, drink, and other necessities.
When one man had thus said, "O wise one, let Anaṅgarati be given to me," the second man spoke.
"I am indeed a Vaiśya named Bhāṣājña; I understand the cries of all beasts and birds. Therefore, let this princess be given to me."
When this had been said, the second one then spoke to the third: "I am a king, a Kṣatriya named Khaḍgadhara, endowed with powerful arms."
"In the knowledge and mastery of the sword-skill, there is no rival to me on this earth; therefore, O King, let this daughter of yours be bestowed upon me."
When this had been said by the third, the fourth spoke as follows: "I am a Brahmin named Jīvadatta, and my knowledge is of this kind."
"Even by bringing back dead creatures, I quickly show them alive; let her take me as her husband, who am perfected through such heroic conduct."
Seeing those speakers, who possessed divine attire and forms, King Vīradeva, together with his daughter, became like one mounted upon a swing.
Having told this story, the Vetāla questioned King Trivikramasena, who had already been warned of the previously mentioned curse.
Therefore, O Lord of the People, please tell me first among those four whom that maiden Anaṅgarati should be given to.
Having heard this, the king replied to the vetāla: "You are likely making me break my silence merely for the sake of wasting time."
"Otherwise, O Lord of Yoga, tell me: how can this question be so profound? For how could a Kṣatriya woman be given to a Śūdra weaver?"
How could a Kṣatriya woman even be given to a Vaiśya? And as for that knowledge of the languages of deer and other animals which she possesses—where would such a thing be of use in practical affairs?
What is the use of that third brahmin here, who has fallen from his own duty, who is a mere conjurer, and who fancies himself a hero?
Therefore, she should be given to that fourth equal kṣatriya, who wields the sword and is endowed with the power of his own vidyā.

Having heard these words of the king, that Vetāla departed swiftly from the king's shoulder back to his own place by the power of yoga, just as before; yet the monarch likewise followed after him once more to bring him back, for in a hero’s heart, which is a solid mass of resolve, weariness finds no place.
The Seventeenth Wave: Then King Trivikramasena went to that śiṃśapā tree, took up the vetāla once more upon his shoulder, and set out.
And as he was departing, the Vetāla, seated upon the back of his shoulder, said to him: "O King, you are weary; therefore, listen to this story which shall dispel your fatigue."
There was a most excellent king, renowned by the name Vīrabāhu, whose commands were placed upon the heads of all monarchs.
He had an excellent city named Anaṅgapura; there lived a very wealthy caravan leader (sārthavāha) called Arthadatta.
That lord of merchants had a daughter named Madanasenā, a jewel among maidens, who was younger than his eldest son named Dhanadatta.
One day, a merchant's son named Dharmadatta, a friend of his brother, saw her playing in her own garden together with her circle of female companions.

Beholding her, who was like a cascading torrent overflowing with the essence of loveliness, he observed her whose pitcher-like breasts were prominent and whose body was rippled by the three folds of skin.
Like a pleasure-bathing pool for the elephant of youth, he suddenly became one whose consciousness was stolen away by the intense heat of the flood of Love’s arrows.
"Aha! This form, radiant with such an intensifying splendor, must have been fashioned by Māra as a crescent-headed arrow to pierce my heart."
Thus, as he meditated and gazed upon her for a long time, the day passed away for him like that of a cakravāka bird.
Then Madanasenā entered her own house, as did the pain of not seeing her into the heart of Dharmadatta.
And as if burning with the heat of the fire of grief from not seeing him, even the radiant sun, turning red, quickly fell into the western ocean.
