Having learned that the lovely-faced woman had gone inside at night, the moon slowly rose, though it was surpassed by the lotus of her face.
Having gone home, Dharmadatta remained there reflecting upon her, lying down upon his bed and tossing about as if struck by the rays of the moon.
Even when questioned with effort by his friends and kinsmen, he said nothing at all, being utterly deluded by the seizure of love.
Having obtained sleep with great difficulty during the night, he saw that same beloved woman in his dream; and being full of longing, what did he not do as he entreated her?
Having awakened in the morning and gone there, he saw her once again standing alone in that secluded garden, waiting for her friend.
Having approached her, longing for an embrace, he bowed at her feet and sought to persuade her with words tender with affection.
"I am a maiden and the wife of another; I do not belong to you here at present, since I have been given by my father to the merchant Samudradatta."
"In only a few days my marriage will take place; therefore, go away silently so that no one may see you, for trouble might arise from that."
Having been addressed thus by her, Dharmadatta spoke to her with great intensity: "Let whatever may be; for I cannot live without you."
Hearing this, the merchant’s daughter, agitated by the fear of being forced, said to him: "Let my marriage be performed here first."
"O father, may you obtain the long-desired fruit of giving away your daughter; thereafter, having won you through my affection, I shall certainly come to you."
Having heard this, he said: "Indeed, one who has belonged to another is not desired by me as a beloved; for when a lotus has been enjoyed by another, does pleasure arise from it?"
Thus addressed by him, she said: "In that case, I am already married; I shall first approach you, and thereafter I will go to that husband."
When the merchant’s son had spoken thus, she bound him—who was truthful in speech—with an oath, so that he would not abandon her without some proof.
Then, dismissed by him, she entered her own palace dejected; and when the appointed day arrived, the auspicious ceremony of marriage was completed.
Having gone to her husband's house and spent that day with great celebration, she entered the bedchamber with her husband at night.
There, even though she was lying on the bed, she did not respond to the embrace of her husband Samudradatta, as she was not facing him.
Although she was being entreated by him, the fact that she shed tears made him think in his heart: "Surely I am not beloved by her."
And he said: "O beautiful one, if I am not desired by you, then I have no need for you; go to him who is dear to you."
Having heard that, she, with her face cast down, slowly spoke thus to him: "You are dearer to me than my own life; nevertheless, hear my request."
Carry this out with joy and grant me safety; take an oath, O noble son, while I speak to you.
When she had spoken thus and he had done so with great difficulty, she spoke again, full of shame, despondency, and fear.
Once, seeing me alone in the house garden, a young man named Dharmadatta, my brother’s friend, who was afflicted by love, detained me.
In order to protect my father from the reproach that would follow from giving away his daughter, I restrained the speech of him who had acted with such impetuosity.
"Having first performed my marriage, I shall then approach you, my beloved; therefore, O Lord, grant me permission so that this word of truth may be preserved."
Once I have gone near him, I shall return to your presence in an instant; for I am unable to transgress the truth that I have practiced since childhood.
Thus, suddenly struck by the thunderbolt of her words, Samudradatta, bound by truth, reflected for a moment.
"Alas! Woe! She is in love with another; she will surely go to him. Shall I kill her for the sake of that truth? Let her go; what need has she for marriage?"
Having reflected thus, he consented to her departure as she desired; she too, rising from there, went out from her husband's house.
Meanwhile, the moon ascended the summit of the palace of the lordly eastern mountain, making the maiden of the eastern quarter laugh as she was touched by his rays.
Then, even as the darkness remained embracing the mountain caves like beloveds, and even as the bees frequented another bed of night-lotuses;
As Madanasenā was traveling alone at night, she was seen on the road by a certain thief who ran up and seized her by the hem of her garment.
"Tell me, who are you and where are you going? he asked her; and she, trembling with fear, replied: "What is this to you? Let me go; I have business here."
Then the thief said, "How can you be released from me, a thief? Hearing that, she said to him, "Take my ornaments."
Then the thief said, "O foolish woman, what use have I for these stones? [I desire her] whose face is like the moonstone and whose hair is black as the emerald."
With a vajra at my center, golden limbs, and enchanting feet of ruby-red hue, I shall never forsake you, the ornament of the world.
Having been addressed thus by that thief, the helpless merchant’s daughter related her own story and entreated him in this manner:
"Forgive me for a moment while I fulfill my commitment to truth; remaining right here, I shall come to your side with all speed."
"O good man, I shall not violate this word of truth. Having heard this and considering her to be one who is true to her word, that thief released her.
He remained right there, awaiting her arrival; and she, for her part, went into the presence of that merchant Dharmadatta.
And seeing her standing thus in a secluded place, though she was his beloved and had come to him, he questioned her about what had happened, reflected for a moment, and said:
"I am pleased with your truthfulness; what use have I for another's wife? Go back the way you came before anyone sees you."
Thus dismissed by him, she said, "So be it," and then went from there to the presence of that thief who was waiting for her on the road.
"To him who asked, 'Tell me, what is your story here since you departed? she related everything exactly as she had been released by that merchant."
Then that thief said to her: "If it is so, then you have been released by me as well, out of satisfaction with the truth; go home with your ornaments."
Thus she was abandoned by him, yet protected by her follower; with her virtue unimpaired, she returned joyfully to her husband's house.
Having entered there in secret, she approached him with great joy; seeing her husband, she described everything to him.

He too, perceiving that she—whose facial radiance was undimmed, whose appearance betrayed no sign of sexual union, whose conduct remained unbroken, and who was devoted to the attainment of truth—was indeed virtuous;
Then, having welcomed his wife Adṛṣṭamanas in a manner befitting their family, Samudradatta remained with her in comfort as he pleased.
Having thus told this story there in the cemetery grounds, the Vetāla then spoke again to that lord of the earth, Trivikramasena.
Therefore, O lord of men, tell us from among these thieves and merchants who is the generous one; if you know and do not speak, your head shall shatter into a hundred pieces.
Having heard that, the king broke his silence and said to the vetāla: "Among these, the thief is the one who abandoned them, and not both of those merchants."
For how could that man of noble birth, who abandoned her even though she was married to him and unfit to be forsaken, carry her as his wife once he knew she was attached to another?

Furthermore, that other husband of hers, whose sense of urgency had been worn away by time, abandoned her out of fear; having learned the facts, he would say to the king in the morning: "She is his wife."

But that thief, moving in secret, indifferent to consequences, and a doer of evil deeds, has now arrived; by not releasing this jewel of a woman along with her ornaments, he is a man of false renunciation.
Upon hearing this, the Vetāla departed from the king's shoulder as before and returned to his own place; yet the king, his lofty courage unbroken, set out once more to recover him.
The Eighteenth Wave: Then, having gone back and reached the śiṃśapā tree once more, King Trivikramasena took that vetāla upon his shoulder and set out.
And as he was approaching, the vetāla seated upon his shoulder said to the king: "O King, listen; I shall relate to you a single, wonderful tale."
Formerly, in Ujjayinī, there was a king named Dharmadhvaja; he had three wives, princesses who were exceedingly dear to him.
Among them, one was named Indulekhā, another Tārāvalī, and yet another Mṛgāṅkavatī; their physical beauty and virtues were beyond compare.
Sporting with those three queens, the king, having conquered all his enemies, sat there at ease, his purpose accomplished.
Once, when the festival of the spring season had arrived there, he went to the garden to sport with those beloved women.
There he saw creepers bent down with flowers, appearing like the bow-staffs of the Bodiless God (Kāmadeva), with rows of bees for their bowstrings, as if strung by the spring.
And he heard the song uttered by a cuckoo perched on the tip of that tree, which was like the command of the god of love, whose sole essence is sensual enjoyment.
That king, who was like Indra himself, indulged together with his inner apartments in the drinking of wine—the very life of intoxication and the life-force even of the god of love.
He took delight in drinking the honey-wines, which were fragrant with her breath, possessed the luster of her bimba-like lips, and remained as the remnants of what his beloved had already tasted.
There, as the king playfully seized Indulekhā by the hair, the blooming blue lotus fell from the tip of her ear onto his lap.
When a wound was suddenly inflicted upon the back of the lute by that blow, the noble queen, overcome with grief, cried out "Alas! Alas! and fell into a swoon.
Seeing this, the king and his attendants were overwhelmed with distress; the queen was then slowly revived by cool water and breezes.
Then, having led her back to his capital, the king attended to his beloved with divine medicines prepared by physicians, once she had been wrapped in bandages over her wounds.
And seeing her well-settled at night, the lordly king ascended the moon-palace together with his second wife, Tārāvalī.
There, as she slept in the king's lap, her rays fell through the lattice-work onto his body, where her garment had shifted.
Then, awakening in an instant, crying out, "Alas, I am burned!", she suddenly rose from her bed, feeling her limbs.
"What is this? he thought, bewildered; then, having awakened, the king rose up and beheld pustules that had burst forth upon her body.
And then Queen Tārāvalī said to him as he questioned her: "This was done to me by the rays of the moon falling upon my naked body."
When she had spoken thus, weeping and in pain, the king summoned her attendants, who ran about in a state of frantic agitation.
Therefore, he had a bed prepared for her with lotus leaves moistened with water, and he caused a fresh application of sandalwood paste to be laid upon her body.
Having learned this, his third beloved, Mṛgāṅkavatī, desiring to come to his side, departed from her own palace.
Having gone out, she heard somewhere in a house the distinct sound of a pestle striking grain, clearly audible in the silent night from a distance.
Upon hearing this, crying out, "Alas, I am dead! and shaking her hands, that fawn-eyed woman sat down on the path, overcome by agony.
Then, having turned back and been led by her attendants to her own inner apartments, the young woman, weeping, collapsed upon her bed.
There, searching through her belongings, he saw with tears his wife’s hands, marked by calluses like two lotuses with bees clinging to them.
Having gone there, he spoke to the king; the king also, having arrived in a state of agitation, asked, "What is this? Then Dharmadhvaja [spoke] to his beloved.
She too, showing her hands to him while afflicted by pain, spoke thus: "When the sound of the pestle was heard, these two [hands] of mine became marked with calluses."
Then the king, overcome with wonder and despondency, had sandalwood paste and other cooling remedies applied to her hands to alleviate the burning sensation.
One woman suffered a wound even from a falling blue lotus, while the limb of the second was scorched even by the rays of the moon.
Alas, even from hearing alone, such calluses have formed upon the hands of this third woman, as if they had been worn away by the sound of a pestle!
"Alas! Now, by fate, even this quality of extreme nobility has become a defect for me simultaneously with these beloved women."
As he wandered thus through the inner apartments with such thoughts, that night passed for the king with difficulty as if it were a hundred watches long.
And in the morning, that physician, together with surgeons, performed the operation in such a way that, before long, he became healthy and his inner apartments were filled with joy.
Having thus told this most wonderful tale, the Vetāla, remaining upon the shoulder of King Trivikramasena, then questioned him.
"O King, tell me which among these queens is the most noble-born; let that previously mentioned curse be yours if you know and do not speak."
Having heard that, the king said: "She is far more delicate; for her calluses have arisen by sound alone, even before a pestle was touched."
When the touch occurred with hands like blue lotuses and moons, sores and pustules arose on the other two; therefore, those [other two] were not equal to her.
When he had spoken thus, the Vetāla returned once more to his own place from the king's shoulder; and the king, remaining as firm in his resolve as before, followed after him.
The Nineteenth Wave: Then King Trivikramasena went back to that śiṃśapā tree, reached it, and once again placed the vetāla upon his shoulder.
And taking him, he set out silently just as before; then, from his position upon the king's shoulder, the Vetāla spoke to him once more.
"O King, since you are thus free from anxiety, you are sufficiently dear to me; therefore, listen to this heart-pleasing tale that I shall relate to you for your solace."
In ancient times, there was a king named Yaśaḥketu in the land of Aṅga; he rested upon the earth for the sake of protecting Aṅga like another Smara who had not been consumed by fire.
And he had a minister named Dīrghadarśin, who, like Bṛhaspati for Śakra, had conquered the entire host of his enemies through the prowess of his own arms.
Having entrusted the kingdom, from which all thorns had been removed, to that minister, the king gradually became devoted solely to pleasure due to the intoxication of his youth and beauty.

He remained constantly within the inner apartments, the pleasure-ground of women, rather than in a place of spiritual practice; he listened to impassioned songs, but not to the words of those who desired his welfare.
And he took delight, free from anxiety, in the latticed windows; he never again engaged in royal affairs, which are full of many pitfalls.
But the far-sighted great minister, bearing that burden of state affairs, remained day and night without weariness.
Having cast the king—who finds his stability in mere names—into calamity, the minister Dīrghadarśin now enjoys the royal fortune here.
When this great rumor had arisen among the people, Dīrghadarśin then spoke privately to his wife, named Medhāvinī.
"O dear Queen, while you were devoted to pleasure, although I bore that burden, the kingdom was devoured by him; thus an ill-repute has arisen among the people."
In this world, even false public rumor causes distress to the great; did not Rāma too abandon Jānakī because of public gossip?
When he had said, "Therefore, what must I do in this matter?", his wife Medhāvinī—wise, steadfast, and true to her name—addressed him.
"O high-minded one, it is proper for you to go abroad for some time; having taken leave of the king by means of the pretext of a pilgrimage to sacred sites."
Thus, this public rumor will cease for you who are free from desire; once you have departed, the king himself will take up the burden of the kingdom.
Then this misfortune of his will gradually come to an end, and once he has arrived here, your counsel shall be received without reproach.
Having been thus addressed by his wife, Dīrghadarśin replied, "So be it," and having gone there, he made a request to King Yaśaḥketu during the course of a conversation.
"Grant me leave, O King, for I shall go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords for some days; for that is the dharma I desire to pursue."
Having heard that, the king said: "Do not say such a thing; is there not another dharma, such as giving and so forth, which leads to heaven even at home without visiting sacred fords?"
Then that minister said to him: "O King, while purity of wealth and the like is sought after, the sacred fords (tīrthas) of giving and so forth are eternally pure."
O King, as long as youth lasts, so long should one who is wise pursue these [pleasures]; for since the body is inherently untrustworthy, how could there be union with them at any other time?
Even as he was speaking thus and the king was likewise forbidding him, the doorkeeper entered and addressed the king.
"O King, the sun is plunging into the midst of the celestial ocean; therefore arise, for this time for your bath is passing away."
Upon hearing this, the lord of the earth immediately rose to bathe; intent on his expedition, he and his minister bowed to him and departed for their homes.
Having settled his wife there—she who had forbidden him from following him—he set out from that place by a clever stratagem, unobserved even by his own servants.
Wandering alone through various regions and visiting sacred fords, the far-sighted and resolute Dīrghadarśin reached the territory of Puṇḍra.
There, having entered a certain city not far from the ocean, he sat down in the courtyard of a Śaiva temple.
There, a merchant named Nidhidatta, who had come to worship the deity, beheld him—exhausted by the heat of the sun's rays and dusted with the pollen of the long journey.
Seeing him in such a state, wearing the sacred thread and possessing auspicious marks, the hospitable man honored that most excellent brahmin and led him into his home.
There he honored him with the finest offerings, such as baths and meals; and once he had rested, he asked him, "Who are you? From where do you come? Where are you going?"
"I am a Brahmin named Dīrghadarśin, come here from the land of Aṅga for the purpose of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites"; with such depth of character, he spoke thus to him.
Then that great merchant Nidhidatta also said to him: "I am preparing to go to Suvarṇadvīpa for the purpose of trade."
Therefore, stay here in my house until I return from there; once you have rested from your exhaustion from the pilgrimage, you may then depart.
Having heard that, Dīrghadarśin said: "In that case, what is it to me here? O caravan leader, I shall go with you yourself as you please."
When the merchant replied, "So be it," the minister then spent that night in his house, finally obtaining a bed after a long time.
Then, on another day, having gone to the ocean together with that very merchant, he boarded a ship filled with those goods.
Traveling by that ship while beholding the ocean, which was wonderful and terrifying, he eventually reached that Golden Island.
Where is his status as chief minister, and where is his crossing of the ocean? Alas, what will virtuous men not do when they fear dishonor?
On that island, he lived for some time with that merchant Nidhidatta, who was engaged in buying and selling.
And as he was coming from there, suddenly standing upon his ship equipped for that journey, he saw a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) rising up from behind a wave in the ocean.
It was adorned with trunks as beautiful as coral branches, shining like refined gold, and with lovely fruits made of jewels and flowers.
And upon his shoulder, he beheld a maiden of most wonderful and lovely form, seated upon the lap of a couch made of the seven precious gems.
While he was reflecting for a moment, "Aha! What can this be?", that lute-playing maiden proceeded to sing as follows:
Whatever seed of karma was sown by someone in the past, that he surely experiences; for it is not possible, even by means of fate, to alter what was previously done.
Having thus sung, that divine maiden instantly sank right there into the ocean upon her couch of a bed made of a wish-fulfilling tree.
"Today I have seen something unprecedented and wonderful here: where is the ocean, and where is this tree that appears and vanishes from sight, with its celestial nymphs singing?"
Or rather, this ocean is indeed worthy of worship, for it is the eternal source of such things as Lakṣmī, the moon, and the pārijāta tree; have they not all emerged from it?
Seeing Dīrghadarśin thus reflecting at that moment and filled with wonder, the helmsman and the others said:
Thus this excellent maiden is always seen here; she sinks at that very moment, yet this vision of yours is new.
Thus addressed by them, the minister, accompanied by Nidhidatta, traveled by ship in due course and, filled with wonder, reached the shore of the ocean.
Then, together with that very merchant who had unloaded his wares and whose servants were joyful, he went to that house in high spirits amidst great celebration.
Having stayed there for no very long time, he said to Nidhidatta: "O caravan leader, I have rested for a long time in your house with great comfort."
"Now I wish to go to my own country; may it be well with you," having said this, he took leave of the merchant lord, even though the latter was unwilling.
That far-sighted one, with his son as his sole companion, set out from there; having gradually traversed the long distance, he reached his own realm of Aṅga.
There, the spies whom King Yaśaḥketu had previously dispatched to search for him saw him arrived outside the city.
Having gone there, the spies informed him, and the king approached him; having departed from the city himself, he was deeply distressed by the separation from him.
And having approached him, the king greeted him with an embrace and led him, who was emaciated and dust-covered from his long journey, into the interior of the palace.
Having abandoned us, alas, what have you taken away? Not only our hearts, but even this body has been reduced to a state of cold and harshness.
Or rather, who knows the course of what is destined for the Blessed One? For otherwise, how could this thought of yours to go to the sacred fords and other places have arisen so suddenly?
"Therefore, tell me: what countries have you wandered through, and what new thing have you seen? Thus the king spoke there to his minister.
Then, describing the road step by step as far as Suvarṇadvīpa, he told him about that divine maiden whom he had seen emerging from the ocean.
Dīrghadarśī related exactly as it happened to the king how she, who was the very essence of the three worlds, stood upon the Kalpa tree while singing.
As soon as the king heard this, he fell under the power of love in such a way that, without her, he considered both his kingdom and his life to be fruitless.
And then, having led his own minister aside to a private place, he said to him: "I must certainly see her; otherwise, there is no life for me."
I go by the path you have spoken, having bowed to destiny; I am neither to be dissuaded by you, nor am I to be followed in any way.
"I shall indeed depart alone in secret, but the kingdom must be protected by you. Do not act otherwise than my word; you are bound under oath by my very life."
Having spoken thus and rejecting his reply, the king dismissed the minister to his own home, longing for his kinsmen whom he had missed for a long time.
There, even amidst a great festival, Dīrghadarśin remained deeply dejected; for when a master is beset by an incurable calamity, how can there be happiness for his wise ministers?
And on another day, King Yaśaḥketu, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his hand, departed at night wearing the garb of an ascetic.
And as he was traveling, he saw on the road a sage named Kuśanābha; there, the sage instructed him, who was dressed in the garb of an ascetic and bowing before him.
"Go forth without anxiety; having traveled by sea with the merchant Lakṣmīdatta on his ship, you shall obtain that beloved maiden."
Delighted by those words, the king bowed to him and, traveling across various lands, rivers, and mountains, reached the ocean.
With its blossoming waves for eyebrows, white as a beautiful conch-shell, it seemed to gaze with its whirlpools for eyes out of the excitement of hospitality.
On its shore, he met with that merchant Lakṣmīdatta, who was about to depart for Suvarṇadvīpa, as had been foretold by the sage.
Having ascended the vessel with him alone, that king set out upon the ocean, bowing down as he beheld the footprints marked with wheels and other signs.
When the ship reached the middle of the ocean, that maiden emerged from within the waters, standing upon the trunk of a kalpa-tree.
As soon as the king beheld her, like a cakora bird gazing at moonlight, she began to sing in this manner, beautiful with the accompaniment of the lute.
Whatever seed of karma was sown by someone in the past, he surely reaps that; for it is impossible to alter what was done previously, even by means of ritual injunctions.

Therefore, wherever, in whatever manner, and whatever is destined to happen for someone by the conjunction of fate, he is led there and in that way toward its attainment, powerless; herein there is no delusion.
Reflecting on her as she sang thus, revealing the destiny of one destined for excellence, the king stood motionless for a moment, struck by the arrows of Love.
O Ratnākara, homage to you whose heart is true and unfathomable, by whom Hari was deceived when he was made to believe that his splendor had been concealed.
I have taken refuge in you, whose limits even the gods cannot reach, and who provide shelter to the winged mountains; grant me the fulfillment of my desired goal.
In this manner, as the king bowed and praised that ocean, the maiden sank there along with the tree.
Upon seeing her, the king threw himself after her along the path, as if to quench the torment of the fire of desire in that ocean.
Seeing that and thinking him lost beyond hope, the virtuous merchant Lakṣmīdatta became intent on giving up his life out of grief.
"Do not act rashly; there is no danger for you who are submerged in this ocean. This is King Yaśaḥketu, wearing the garb of an ascetic."
"He has come for the sake of this maiden; she was his wife in a former life. Having obtained her, he will once again return to the kingdom of Aṅga."
Thus, having been comforted at that moment by the voice arising from the sky, the caravan leader departed as he desired for the sake of accomplishing his goal.
King Yaśaḥketu, submerged within the great ocean, suddenly beheld a divine city and was filled with wonder.
It was resplendent with palaces featuring pillars made of radiant jewels, walls shining with gold, and windows adorned with lattices of pearls.
It was adorned with gardens that grant all desires, enriched by wish-fulfilling trees, and featuring stepped walkways and ponds bordered by slabs of various precious gems.
Although that city was prosperous, he entered every house one by one; yet, when it became deserted, he did not see his beloved anywhere at all.
Then, searching about, the king saw a single lofty palace of jewels; having ascended it and opened the door, he entered.
Having entered within, he beheld a certain man lying alone upon a couch of excellent jewels, his entire body covered by a garment.
With longing, he opened her face, wondering, "Could it be she?", and as soon as he did so, he beheld that very woman he had desired.
With the beauty of her moon-like face laughing as the darkness of her slipping blue garment faded away, she resembled the night descended into the underworld, bright with moonlight even by day.
And upon seeing him, she then experienced a certain state that is like the state of a traveler in the desert during the summer season upon seeing a river.
She too, opening her eyes and seeing him of auspicious form and marks suddenly arrived there, abandoned her bed in a state of agitation.
Having been offered hospitality, she bowed her face as if worshipping his feet with the placement of her lotus-like eyes in full bloom, and slowly spoke to him.
Who are you, and why have you entered this inaccessible subterranean realm? Why do you, whose body is marked with the insignia of royalty, observe the vow of an ascetic?
"O illustrious one, grant this if you have favor toward me. Having heard these words of hers, the king replied to her.
"O beautiful one, I am the King of Aṅga, known by the name Yaśaḥketu; and from a trustworthy source, I have heard that you were seen here in the ocean every day."
Then, having assumed this disguise for your sake and renounced the kingdom, I arrived here and entered the ocean following in your wake.
When he said to her, "Tell me, who are you?", she, feeling both bashful, affectionate, and joyful, replied as follows:
There is a glorious lord of the Vidyādharas named Mṛgāṅkasena; know me to be his daughter, Mṛgāṅkavatī by name.
Having left me all alone here in my own city, I do not know for what reason my father has gone away somewhere together with his citizens.
Therefore, having emerged from the ocean of my despondency with this empty dwelling, I have ascended the mechanical wish-fulfilling tree and sing of destiny.
When she had spoken thus, the king—remembering those words of the sage—was so enamored by her with his affectionate words that she was likewise filled with passion for him.
Overpowered by passion, she immediately accepted the status of wife to that hero, yet she stipulated one condition.
"O Noble Son, on the fourteenth and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights, for four days each month, I am not at my own disposal."
Wherever I may go during these days, you must neither question me nor forbid me, for there is a reason for this.
When she had thus stated her condition, the king said "So be it" and married that divine maiden according to the Gāndharva rite.
Then he sent her there, and she enjoyed the pleasure of union with him; for her manner of adornment was entirely different from that of love.

When the garlands had fallen from her hair, there was a series of nail-marks from the seizing of her locks; then, when the red dye on her bimba-like lips had been squeezed out, there were the marks of her teeth.
On her breasts, the rows of nail-marks were like broken strings of rubies; on her limbs, where the cosmetic ointments had vanished, there remained only the passion of the tight embrace.
Once, while the king was thus established in the bliss of that divine enjoyment, his wife Mṛgāṅkavatī spoke these words to him.
"You should wait right here while I go somewhere for the sake of my task; for today is that very fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kṛṣṇa which has arrived for me."
"Stay here, noble son; do not go to this crystal house, lest you fall into this pond and return once more to the world of mortals."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him, she departed from that city; the king also, having obtained his sword, followed her incognito, desiring to know her destination.
There the king beheld a Rākṣasa, dark as the night and with a gaping mouth like a cavern, approaching like the underworld incarnate.
That rākṣasa, having fallen down and let out a terrible roar, then cast Mṛgāṅkavatī into his mouth and swallowed her.
Upon seeing that, suddenly as if blazing with extreme rage, he [struck] with his great sword, dark as a snake that has cast off its slough.
Drawing his sword from its scabbard, the lion-like king rushed forward and severed the head of that charging demon, whose lips were bitten together in a snarl.
Then, by the blood of that king, which was vomited forth by the demon's headless trunk, the fire born of his wrath was extinguished, but not the fire born from separation from his beloved.
Then, while this king was blinded by the night of delusion and his course was ruined, [the light] suddenly burst forth as if piercing the body of a demon dark as a cloud.
Illuminating the circle of the quarters like a spotless form of the moon, that Mṛgāṅkavatī emerged alive with her limbs uninjured.
Seeing his beloved thus delivered from that peril, the king ran toward her in great agitation, crying out, "Come! Come!", and embraced her.
"Dear one, what is this? Is it a dream or an illusion? Thus questioned by the king, that Vidyādharī, remembering [the truth], spoke as follows.
"Listen, noble son: this is neither a dream nor an illusion; rather, such was the curse pronounced upon me by my father, the lord of the Vidyādharas."
For although my father had many sons, while he formerly lived here, he would never take food because of his excessive affection for me.
And I, being always devoted to the worship of Śarva in this secluded place, would come on the fourteenth and eighth days of both fortnights.
And once, on the fourteenth day, having come here, the day ended by chance while I was worshipping Gaurī for a long time with my juices.
On that day, waiting for me, my father—though hungry—neither ate nor drank anything; he remained angry toward me.
Then, at night, as I approached him with my face cast down in shame for my transgression, he—his affection swallowed by the power of destiny—pronounced this curse upon me:
Just as I am now seized by hunger due to my disregard for you, so too shall I be seized only on the eighth and fourteenth days of every month.
While you are here, absorbed in the joy of worshipping Hara, a Rākṣasa named Kṛtāntasaṃtrāsa will swallow you up outside the city.
"Having pierced his heart again and again, you shall emerge alive; you will remember neither the curse nor the agony of being swallowed."
"Once you have spoken these words of a curse, saying, 'You shall remain here all alone,' my father, having been gradually entreated by me, reflected and told me the end of the curse."
When the king named Yaśaḥketu becomes your husband, he will see you swallowed by the Rākṣasa and shall slay him.
Then you shall be released from the curse, having emerged from his heart; you will remember the curse and all your own sciences.
Having thus prescribed the end of the curse and abandoned me here alone, my father departed for the Niṣadha mountain and the world of mortals along with his retinue.
And while practicing in that manner, I dwelt here due to the delusion of a curse; now that curse of mine has been exhausted, and memory has returned to me in every respect.
Therefore, I shall now go to the Niṣadha mountain, to my father’s side; for this is our agreement: that at the end of the curse, we shall return to our own state.
"Stay here, or go to your own kingdom; you have freedom in this matter. When she had spoken thus, the king, filled with sorrow, made this request to her:
"Be gracious, O lovely-faced one; you must not go for seven days. Let us first dispel our longing here in the garden with diversions."
"You go now to your father's place; I too shall go to my own. To these words of his, that innocent girl agreed, saying, "So be it."
Then the king took delight there for six days with that beloved wife in the gardens, and by the ponds whose eyes were water-lilies amidst their waters.
As if making the sound "Do not go, leaving us behind! with the cries of swans and cranes, their wave-hands were tossed upward.
On the seventh day, he skillfully brought his beloved there to the house where that mechanical door-well, which leads to the world of mortals, was located.
There, having seized her by the neck and fallen into that pond, he emerged from the middle of the pond in his own city's garden together with her.
Seeing him there, accompanied by his beloved, the garden-keepers were delighted; they went to the minister Dīrghadarśin and told him.
The minister also, having approached and prostrated at his feet, saw that the king had been brought the desired woman; together with the citizens, he led the king into the inner apartments.
"Aha! How has this divine woman been obtained by the king—she who was seen by me like a flash of lightning in the sky, visible for but a moment?"
Whatever has been written for someone by the Creator in the lines of letters upon their forehead, that necessarily comes to pass for them, even if it be improbable.
Thus, while this chief minister and other people were meditating upon the wonder of attaining a celestial woman amidst the festivities of the king’s arrival.
Having seen that the king had returned to his own country, Mṛgāṅkavatī desired to attain the state of a Vidyādharī once the full seven days had passed.
And even when remembered, her science of flight did not manifest at that time; consequently, as if robbed of it, she fell into the deepest despondency.
"Why do you appear so despondent all of a sudden? Tell me, my dear," the king said to her; thus addressed by him, that daughter-in-law spoke as follows.
Although I am released from the curse, because I have remained here for so long out of affection for you, my magic sciences have been lost and that divine state has perished.
Hearing that, King Yaśaḥketu thought, "Ah, this Vidyādharī has been won by me," and thereupon he celebrated a great festival to its full extent.
Having seen that, the far-sighted minister went home at night; while lying upon his bed, he suddenly passed away from a ruptured heart.
Then, having experienced that grief, Yaśaḥketu himself, bearing the burden of the kingdom, remained for a long time united with Mṛgāṅkavatī.
Having told this story on the way, the Vetāla, remaining upon his shoulder, spoke again to King Trivikramasena.
Therefore, O King, tell me this: when such prosperity had been achieved for you, his master, why did the heart of that great minister suddenly burst?
Was it because his heart was bursting with grief at thinking, "Why have I not obtained a celestial woman?", or rather from the sorrow born of the king's arrival for one who desired the kingdom?
And if you do not tell this to me here, O King, even though you know it, your righteousness will perish and your head will instantly shatter into pieces.
Having heard this, King Trivikramasena said to the Vetāla: "Neither of these two things is fitting for that excellent minister of such virtuous conduct."
But what can be said now of that king who, out of mere passion for women, neglected his kingdom, yet is now even more infatuated with this celestial woman?
"Alas! Though I have acted for his benefit, a fault has instead increased all the more"—as that minister reflected thus, his heart burst asunder.
When the king had spoken thus, that illusory Vetāla returned once more to his own place; then the resolute-minded king, desiring to seize him by force, again ran swiftly after him.
The Twentieth Wave: Then King Trivikramasena, having gone back and reached the śiṃśapā tree once more, took that vetāla upon his shoulder.
And as he was approaching, the Vetāla spoke again to that king: "O King, listen; I shall relate to you a single tale in brief."
There is a city named Vārāṇasī, the dwelling place of Śiva; there lived a venerable brahmin named Devasvāmin, who was honored by the king.
That wealthy man had a son named Harisvāmin, and his wife was Lāvaṇyavatī, who was exceedingly excellent.
I believe that Brahmā, having attained mastery in the creation of celestial women such as Tilottamā, fashioned her with a beauty and loveliness beyond price.
Once, exhausted from amorous dalliance, Harisvāmin went to sleep with that beloved wife in a palace cooled by the rays of the moon.
At that time, a young Vidyadhara named Madanavega, traveling through the air at will, arrived by that path.
There he saw that Lāvaṇyavatī by her husband's side, sleeping with the excellence of her limbs clearly revealed as her garments had slipped away from the exhaustion of passion.
His heart captivated by her form and blinded by passion, he pounced upon her while she was still asleep, seized her, and departed through the sky at that very moment.
Then, awakening in an instant, the young Harisvāmin, her husband, rose up in agitation, not seeing that mistress of his life.
"Aha! What is this? Where has she gone? Is she angry with me? Or is she hidden there to test my mind, or perhaps to mock me?"
Thus, agitated by a flood of many such doubts, he wandered through the night, searching for her here and there among the balconies, palaces, and upper chambers.
Searching for her everywhere throughout the palace gardens, when he could not find her anywhere, he, tormented by the fire of grief, lamented with a voice choked with tears.
"Alas, O moon-faced one! Alas, O you who are fair as the moonlight! Alas, my beloved! Why have you not been spared by this night, which seems to hate your very virtues?"
This very moon, who—conquered by your beauty and fearing you as it were—once gladdened me with rays cool as sandalwood, now brings me no joy in your absence.
O beloved, now that an opportunity has been gained, he torments me with those very same [feelings] as if with blazing coals or with arrows smeared with poison.
As Harisvāmin was thus lamenting, the night passed away with great difficulty; but the agony of separation did not.
At dawn, the sun pierced the universal thick darkness with its rays; yet it was not able to pierce his blinding darkness of delusion.
Then, as if encouraged by the cakravāka birds who had crossed over the night, the sound of his piteous wailing increased a hundredfold.
Though being consoled by his kinsmen, the young Brahmin, inflamed by the fire of separation, found no composure without his beloved.
"She stood here, bathed here, performed her adornment here, and sported here"—saying this, he went from place to place, weeping.
"She is not yet dead; why then do you destroy yourself in this way? You shall certainly obtain her at some point, as long as you remain alive."
Therefore, take courage and search for that beloved; for there is nothing in this world unattainable for one who is steadfast and resolute.
Thus enlightened by the words of his kinsmen and friends, Harisvāmin finally, with great difficulty, regained his composure after some days through the support of his resolve.
And he thought: "Having given away my entire possessions to a brahmin, I shall now wander to sacred fords and exhaust the accumulation of my sins."

"Indeed, through the destruction of my evil karma, I may eventually find that beloved while wandering"; having reflected thus, he rose from his state as he was and performed his ablutions and other duties.
And on another day, he provided a feast of various foods and drinks for the twice-born at the sacrificial session, and moreover, he gave away his wealth without reserve.
Then, possessing only his Brahminhood as his wealth, he departed from his own country and went forth to wander among the sacred fords (tīrthas) out of a desire to find his beloved.
And as he was wandering, the lion of the summer season arrived for him—a lion whose face was the fierce sun and whose mane was its blazing rays.
And the winds blew with extreme heat, as if their warmth had been deposited by the breezes of sighs from travelers tormented by separation from their beloveds.
With their mud dried up and cracked, and appearing as if their very hearts were split asunder, the reservoirs of water appeared with the wealth of their waters entirely lost to the heat.
Resonant with the chirping of *cīrī* birds and their lower lips of leaves withered by the heat, the trees on the roads seemed to weep from the separation from the beauty of spring.
At that time, exhausted by the heat of the sun, by separation, by hunger and thirst, and by constant travel, he was withered, parched, and pale.
Seeking food, Harisvāmin, wandering about somewhere, reached the house of a Brahmin named Padmanābha who maintained a sacrificial hall for guests.
There, seeing many Brahmins eating inside, he stood leaning against the doorpost, silent and motionless.
Seeing him remaining in that state, his wife—the virtuous mistress of Padmanābha—was moved by compassion and reflected:
Ah! This thing called hunger is so heavy that it would bring no one to shame; for here stands some seeker of food at the door, with his face cast down.
Having traveled a long distance, he had bathed and was now exhausted by hunger; perceiving that he was therefore a worthy recipient for the gift of food, she—
The virtuous woman, lifting up with both hands a vessel filled with excellent rice, accompanied by ghee and sugar, brought it forward and gave it to him with humility.
And he said to him, "Go to the edge of some pond and eat this; this place is surrounded by Brahmins who are eating while remaining in a state of ritual impurity."
Saying "So be it," he took that vessel of food and, having gone not very far, placed it on the bank of a pond beneath a banyan tree.
Having washed his hands and feet at the pond and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) there, he approached that excellent rice-porridge with satisfaction, ready to eat it.
Just then, a hawk, having seized a black snake with its beak and its two talons, arrived from somewhere and perched upon that tree.
As that snake was being carried away by the bird, the bird seized it; then, its life having departed, poisonous saliva issued forth from its mouth.
Then she fell into that vessel of food situated below; and Harisvāmin, not seeing her, went there and ate that food.
Then, for him who was afflicted by hunger, as soon as he had eaten all of that delicious food, a sharp pain from poison arose.
Alas! When fate is perverse, what here does not turn upside down? For even my food, consisting of rice with milk, ghee, and sugar, has turned into poison.
Speaking thus, afflicted by poison and stumbling as he went, Harisvāmin approached the housewife of that Brahmin who was the spy and said to her:
"Poison has arisen from the food given by you; therefore, quickly bring some one to me who is an expert in neutralizing poison, otherwise you shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin."
Having spoken thus to that virtuous woman, who was distraught, asking "What is this?", Harisvāmin, his eyes rolling back, was deprived of life.
Then, although she was blameless and hospitable, that spy drove his wife out of the house, driven by the anger of one who had been falsely treated as a guest and murdered.
Having incurred the reproach of falsehood even for her most virtuous deed, that chaste woman, feeling humiliated, resorted to a sacred ford to perform austerities.
"Whose murder is this? Is it that of the snake, the hawk, or the one who gave them food? Thus there arose a dispute before the King of Dharma, but there was no final decision.
Therefore, O King Trivikramasena, tell me now: whose is that Brahman-murder? Otherwise, that former curse shall fall upon you.
Having heard this from the Vetāla, King Trivikramasena, restrained by the curse, broke his silence and spoke as follows.
That sin belongs to the serpent alone; for what fault is there in this helpless creature being devoured by its enemy?
Then, what was wrong with that hungry hawk as well, who, having brought his own prey that had arrived unexpectedly, was eating it?
How could there be any fault in either of those two—the husband and wife, or the giver of food—or even in one of them, since both are solely engaged in the practice of dharma?
Therefore, I consider that the guilt of Brahmin-murder belongs to that dull-witted man who, without investigation, should attribute it to any one of these.
When the king had spoken thus, the vetāla once again departed from his shoulder and returned to his own place; yet the steadfast king followed after him once more.
The Twenty-first Wave: Then King Trivikramasena went back to that śiṃśapā tree, reached the vetāla once more, and took him upon his shoulder.
And as that lord of the earth was setting out, the vetāla spoke to him again: "O King, you are weary; therefore, listen as I relate a wonderful tale to you."
There exists a city named Ayodhyā, which served as the capital for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in the form of Rāma, the bringer of destruction to the race of Rākṣasas.
In that city there was a king named Vīraketu, who, with his mighty arms, protected this earth just as a rampart protects a city.
While that king reigned, there was in this city a certain great merchant named Ratnadatta, who was the leader of a fleet of trading vessels.
To him, by his wife named Nandayantī, was born a daughter named Ratnavatī, acquired through the propitiation of the gods.
And that high-minded woman grew up in her father’s house, together with her innate qualities of beauty, grace, and modesty.
And when she reached the bloom of youth, not only did great merchants, but even kings, solicit her from Ratnadatta.
But she, being a hater of men, did not desire even Vāsava as her husband; intent on abandoning her life, she could not endure even talk of marriage.
Because of that, her father remained silent, distressed by paternal affection; and that rumor spread everywhere throughout that city.
In the meantime, it is said that all the citizens, being constantly plundered by thieves, assembled together and petitioned King Vīraketu there.
"O Lord, we are constantly being robbed by thieves here night after night; yet they are not seen by us. May Your Majesty know what is beyond this."
Thus petitioned by the citizens, the king ordered the night-watchmen to remain in disguise throughout the city in order to search for the thieves.
They too did not capture the thieves, for that city was being plundered; then one night, the king himself went out at his own will.
Wandering there alone with his sword grasped, he saw on one side a certain man walking along the top of a wall.
He possessed skill in various gaits with a silent placement of his feet, and he looked repeatedly over his shoulder with eyes trembling with apprehension.
"This is surely that thief who robs my city while wandering alone," thinking thus, the king drew near to him.
Then that thief, seeing the king, asked, "Who are you? The king replied to that thief, "I am a thief."
Then that thief, having seen him, said: "In that case, you are my equal and a friend to me; therefore come to my house for now, and I shall perform the duties of a friend toward you."
Having heard that, the king said, "So be it," and went with him to that house situated within an underground cavern deep inside the forest.
Richly endowed with every kind of enjoyment, illuminated by shining lamps, it was like a new Pātāla presided over by King Bali.
When the king had entered there and taken his seat, that thief then went into the inner apartments.
At that very moment, a certain maidservant approached the king there and said to him: "O illustrious one, how have you entered here into the jaws of death?"
"For this man is a lone thief; having escaped from here, he will surely commit a wicked act as a betrayer of trust. Therefore, depart from here with haste."
Having been addressed thus by her, the king departed quickly from there; having reached his own capital, he marshaled his armies during the night.
And having arrived with his army arrayed for battle, he blocked that opening of the underground chamber belonging to the bandit with forces tumultuous with the blaring of trumpets.
Then, perceiving that his house was besieged and having learned of the disclosure [of his identity], the brave thief, resolved upon death, went forth to battle.
Having gone forth into battle, he displayed superhuman prowess; he lopped off the trunks of elephants and cut through the legs of horses.
Wielding sword and shield, he alone carried off the heads of the soldiers; then the king himself rushed toward him, whose army had been destroyed.
That king, who was skilled in the science of swords, by means of a clever maneuver, snatched from his hand both the sword and the dagger.
Then the king, being unarmed and having laid down his weapons, struck down the thief on the ground with a wrestling match and captured him alive.
Having bound him along with his wealth, he led him to his own city; and in the morning, he ordered his execution by impalement upon a stake.
And from her palace, that merchant’s daughter Ratnavatī beheld the thief being led to the place of execution with the beating of drums.
Upon seeing him, though he was wounded and his limbs were smeared with dust, she, deluded by Māra, went to her father Ratnadatta and said:
"This man who is being led away to his execution—this very one has been chosen by me as my husband. Therefore, O father, protect him from the king; otherwise, I shall die following him."
Having heard that, her father said to her: "What is this you say, daughter? You who do not desire even kings as husbands, though they long for you."
"How can you desire this wicked thief who has fallen into calamity?"—though addressed by her father with these and other words, she did not waver from her resolve.
Then his father went quickly to the king and, even at the cost of all his possessions, begged for the thief's release from execution.
But the king did not release that thief, who had stolen everything, even for hundreds of millions of gold pieces; he was one whose ransom had been offered as his own body.
Then, when her father had arrived and turned away, that merchant’s daughter, having performed her ritual bath, prepared to die following him, even though she was being restrained by her kinsmen.
Having ascended his palanquin, she went to the execution ground of that bandit, followed by her weeping father, mother, and the people.
And at that moment, the executioners impaled that thief upon a stake; with his life-breaths failing, he beheld her thus arrived along with her kinsmen.
Having heard the account from the people, that thief shed tears for a moment and then, laughing, gave up his life while impaled upon the stake.
Then, having removed that corpse of the thief from the stake, the virtuous daughter of the merchant took it and ascended the funeral pyre there.
And at that very moment, the Lord Bhairava himself, having manifested his presence in this cremation ground while remaining invisible, spoke thus to her from the sky:
"I am pleased with this devotion of yours toward this very self-choosing assembly; therefore, O devoted wife, ask a boon from me."
Having heard that boon from the god, she bowed and made this request: "O Lord, may there be a hundred sons for my father, even though he is currently childless."
To this virtuous woman who had spoken thus—"By which means this son of no other shall not give up his life without me"—the god spoke again.
"May you have a hundred sons for your father; choose another boon as well, for one of such firm resolve as you does not deserve merely this much."
Having heard that, she then said: "If the Lord is pleased with me, then let this husband of mine live, and let him always be righteous."
"Let it be so! May this husband of yours rise up unhurt and alive; may the king be righteous, and may Vīraketu be pleased."
When Śarva, whose form was invisible, had spoken thus while stationed in the sky, that thief rose up there at that very moment alive, with his limbs uninjured.
Then the merchant Ratnadatta, his heart filled with wonder and joy, took his daughter Ratnavatī along with that thief, who was now his son-in-law.
Having entered his own palace together with his delighted kinsmen, he who had obtained the boon of a son celebrated a festival befitting his joy.
And the king, pleased by the news he had learned, summoned that sole hero Ekavīra at that very moment and appointed the thief Vīraketu as his general.
Then, having desisted from theft and married that merchant’s daughter, Ekavīra lived happily on the road, esteemed by the king.
Having spoken thus, the Vetāla, who was perched upon his shoulder, questioned King Trivikramasena, reminding him of the fear of the curse he had previously pronounced.
O King, tell me: having seen that merchant’s daughter standing there with her father, why did the thief weep and laugh while being impaled upon the stake?
Then the king replied: "The thief wept out of sorrow; therefore, I have not attained freedom from debt to this friend without cause, for I am his merchant."
And he laughed out of wonder, thinking: "How is it that this maiden, having rejected excellent kings, is enamored with this man? Oh, how strange is the heart of a woman!"

When the king had spoken these words, that supreme Vetāla, the master of illusion, departed by his own power from the monarch’s shoulder to his own abode; and the king, too, followed after him once more as before.
The Twenty-second Wave: Then, having gone back and once again reached the Vetāla at the śiṃśapā tree, Trivikramasena took him up and set out once more.
As the king was approaching with the Vetāla upon his shoulder, the Vetāla spoke to him once more: "O King, listen; I shall tell you this story."
In the land of Nepal, there was a city named Śivapura; there, in ancient times, lived a king whose name was Yaśaḥketu, truly worthy of his name.
Having entrusted the burden of government to his minister named Prajñāsāgara, he enjoyed worldly pleasures together with the queen named Candraprabhā.
In due time, a daughter was born to that queen by him, named Śaśiprabhā, whose radiance was like the moon, the eye of the world.
In due course, having reached the bloom of youth, she once during the month of Madhu went with her attendants to a garden to see a festival procession.
There, in one part of that place, he saw her intent on gathering flowers, with one breast revealed by her upraised creeper-like arms.
A wealthy man’s son named Manaḥsvāmī, a twice-born who had come on a journey, beheld her as she shone with a pair of tongs dripping from the stalks of flowers.
As soon as his mind was captivated by that sight, the youth—though he was the master of his own mind—became no longer its master, being utterly deluded by passion.
Is this the pleasure of the Mind-born God for the sake of his arrows, that she herself gathers here the flowers gathered by spring?
"What does this forest deity wish to worship, this Mādhava?"—while he was reflecting thus, the princess also beheld him.
The moment she beheld him, with his limbs like those of the god of love newly reborn, she—filled with longing—forgot her flowers, her limbs, and even herself.
While the two of them remained there, their hearts overflowing with mutual and fresh love, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! suddenly arose.
While the two of them were looking with their necks upraised, wondering "What is this?", there arrived [an elephant] out of anger aroused by the scent of another elephant perceived there.
An intoxicated elephant, having broken its hitching post and emerged, ran along crushing the trees by the road, with its driver fallen and its goad hanging down.
Then, while the attendants fled in terror, she ran toward the princess with haste, lifted her up alone with both arms, and—
The lord of her mind led her, who had been slightly embraced by his limbs and was agitated by fear, love, and shame, far away from the reach of the elephant.
Then, accompanied by her attendants who were praising that best of brahmins, she led him to her own palace, looking back at him again and again.
There she remained, distressed, remembering only him who had given her life, being cooked day and night by the smelting-furnace fire of love.
Then Manaḥsvāmī, following her from that garden, saw her enter his inner apartments and, filled with longing, reflected:
Without her, I cannot now endure to remain or to live; therefore, for me, the illustrious Mūladeva—the rogue who has attained perfection—is my teacher, my refuge, and my goal here.
Having reflected thus, when that day had somehow come to an end, he went in the morning to the presence of his teacher Mūladeva.
And he beheld him, ever united with his friend the Moon, traversing the path of wondrous supernatural powers, like the sky itself incarnate.
And having bowed to him, he announced his own desire; he too, smiling, agreed to accomplish it for him.
Then that master of rogues, Mūladeva, having thrown a yoga-pill into his mouth, assumed for himself the form of an old Brahmin.
Having given him the second pill, which was to be placed in the mouth, he transformed that Brahmin Manaḥsvāmin into the form of an exceedingly beautiful maiden.
Then that master of rogues, having taken up that disguise and gone there, made his request to the king, the father of his beloved, while he was in his assembly hall.
"O King, I have an only son; for his sake, I requested this maiden from afar and brought her here, but he has now gone somewhere."
I am going to search for him; therefore, let her be protected by you until I bring back my son, for you are the protector of the entire world.
Having heard that and out of fear of the curse, King Yaśaḥketu agreed and had his daughter Śaśiprabhā brought to him.
And he said to this daughter, "You must protect this girl in your own palace; you should provide her with food and a bed right by your side."
Having been told "So be it" by his parents, Manaḥsvāmī, in the form of a maiden, was led by that princess into her own inner apartments.
Then, after Mūladeva had departed as he pleased in the form of a brahmin, Manaḥsvāmin remained there in the form of a maiden by the side of his beloved.
And after some days, when she had fully attained the confidence and affection of friendship, [he saw her] one day emaciated by separation, her body tossing about upon the bed.
At night, staying near her bed in secret and disguised in the form of a maiden, that Manaḥsvāmī questioned the princess.
"O friend, O moon-like one, why is your radiance pale and waning day by day? Are you sorrowful like one separated from her beloved?"
Tell me, for what reason would there be a lack of trust in you, my affectionate and charming friend? From now on, I shall not eat at all if you do not speak to me.
Having heard that, the princess sighed and spoke softly: "Do you have no confidence even in me? Listen, friend; I shall tell you."
Once, I went to see a festival at the Madhu garden; there I saw a certain handsome young son of a Brahmin.

Possessing the splendor of the moon released from the clouds, it kindled the god of love at the mere sight of it; like the month of Madhu (Caitra), its forest was adorned with the sport of blossoming flowers.
And as these two eyes of mine, looking upward, began to act like cakora birds, they became drinkers of the nectar from the splendor of the moon of her face.
Just then, a great elephant, with rut-fluid streaming from its temples, suddenly arrived there without restraint, roaring like an untimely cloud at the end of the world.
In the confusion that ensued, when my attendants had fled, I, overwhelmed by fear, was lifted up and carried far away by that very same Brahmin’s son.
As if anointed with sandalwood paste, and likewise as if sprinkled with nectar, I know not what state I reached through the touch of his limbs.
And in an instant, having been forcibly brought here by my assembled retinue, I was cast down from heaven as if onto the surface of the earth.
From that time forth, even though I am awakened, I see my life-giving husband standing by my side, his union with me fashioned by those various mental resolves.
And while asleep, I behold him in my dream performing endearments, forcibly making me abandon my shame through kisses, embraces, and other such acts.
And yet, being unworthy and deluded by ignorance regarding his name and other such things, I do not attain him; thus, this fire of separation from the lord of my life consumes me.
Thus, his ears filled with the nectar of her speech, that lord of the mind, assuming the form of a Brahmin maiden, was filled with joy.
Considering that the time had come to reveal himself, he, who regarded his purpose as accomplished, drew out a pill from his mouth and manifested his true form.
And he said, "O tremulous-eyed one, I am that very person who was purchased by you for a sight in the garden and reduced to the state of a sincere slave."
Due to the momentary lapse in my praise of you, I incurred that affliction, the consequence of which has become this assumption of the form of a maiden by me.
Therefore, O slender-limbed one, endure this separation-pain of mine so that it may bear fruit; for beyond this point, Smara cannot tolerate even my own [existence].
Seeing her lord of life speaking thus so suddenly, the princess was instantly overwhelmed by affection, wonder, and bashfulness.
Then, for those two who had performed their Gandharva marriage through intense longing, the festival of love became exactly as that passion itself had envisioned it.
Then the successful Manaḥsvāmī remained there, assuming two forms: by day he was a maiden with pills, and by night he was a man without pills.
Then, as those days passed there, King Yaśaḥketu gave his own daughter to his nephew named Mṛgāṅkadatta.
She, named Mṛgāṅkavatī, endowed with the most precious wealth, was given in marriage to a twice-born man, the son of the great minister Prajñāsāgara.
At that wedding of her maternal cousin’s daughter, the princess Śaśiprabhā went to her uncle’s house, having been invited there.
Accompanied by that retinue of maidens, Manaḥsvāmin, the son of the Brahmin who had assumed the form of the lovely maiden, also went along with her.
Then, upon seeing him there assuming the form of a maiden, that minister’s son was reportedly struck by the powerful arrows of the hunter Smara.
Then, his mind stolen by that deceitful maiden, the minister’s son went to his own empty house accompanied by his wife.
There, absorbed in meditation on the beauty of her face, he was bitten by the great serpent of intense passion and fell unexpectedly into a state of delusion.
While the people there, abandoned by the festival, were bewildered as to what this could be, his father Prajñāsāgara, having learned of it, quickly approached him.
And though he was being comforted by his father, he, awakening from his delusion, spoke as if lamenting with madness, vomiting forth what was in his mind.
Considering him to be no longer under his own control while his father was utterly overwhelmed, the king also learned of this and arrived at that very spot.
Upon seeing her, the king instantly reached the seventh stage of love through intense attachment, and spoke to his ministers:
How can this Brahmin’s deposit be returned? This maiden is to be given to him; for without her, he will certainly meet his final end.
"If he is lost, this father of his—my minister—will perish; with his destruction comes the destruction of the kingdom. Therefore, tell me in this matter, what is the course of action?"
Thus addressed by that king, all those subjects spoke; they declared the king's own duty to be the protection of the dharma of the people.

They know that counsel is its root, and that counsel resides in the ministers; therefore, since the destruction of the root follows the loss of the minister, one must certainly guard against any injury to the Dharma.
Moreover, there would be sin for this twice-born minister and his son due to the killing; therefore, you must certainly protect him, lest there be a violation of dharma so close at hand.
The maiden entrusted to the minister’s son must be given to him; when the Brahmin returns at another time and becomes angry, he will take his revenge.
Having been addressed thus by his subjects, the king agreed, saying "So be it," in order to give that artificial maiden to the minister's son.
And having determined an auspicious moment, Manaḥsvāmin was brought from the princess’s quarters in the form of a maiden; he then spoke to the king.
If you give me away to another when I was brought here by one for the sake of another, let that be as you wish; you are the king, and both dharma and adharma belong to you today.
"I desire marriage under such a condition: that I must not be led by force to a single bed with my husband."
If he has not returned after wandering among the holy fords for six months, then know me to be dead, with my tongue cut out by my own teeth.
When these words had been spoken by that youth who bore the form of a maiden, the king enlightened the minister’s son, and he attained peace.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," and having quickly performed that marriage, they placed him in a single, well-guarded dwelling.
The fool, desiring to please his beloved, set out on a pilgrimage to holy sites, taking with him both that first wife Mṛgāṅkavatī and that deceptive wife.
And that Manaḥsvāmī, having assumed the form of a woman, dwelt there with Mṛgāṅkavatī in a single house, sharing the same bed and seat.
While he was thus situated, Mṛgāṅkavatī once at night spoke to him in secret within the bedchamber, while his attendants were sleeping outside.
"Tell me some story, my friend, for I cannot sleep. Having heard that, the young man, who was in the form of a woman, told her that story.
Long ago, when the royal sage named Ilā, born of the solar dynasty, attained womanhood—enchanting to the entire world—due to the curse of Gaurī;
Through the joy of seeing one another within the forest of a celestial garden, a union occurred with Budha, and Purūravas was born.
Having told that story, the rogue spoke again: "Thus it is, either by the command of a deity or through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs."
A man may sometimes become a woman, or a woman may at times become a man; even for the great, such unions born of desire come to pass.
Having heard this, the young and innocent Mṛgāṅkavatī, who had been separated from her husband by marriage, spoke with confidence due to their long cohabitation.
"Having heard this story of mine, my limb throbbs; this heart of mine seems to sink. Therefore, tell me, friend, what does this mean?"
Having heard that, the Brahmin in female form spoke to her again: "Surely, my friend, these signs of passion are unprecedented in you."
"I have experienced these things, but I shall not conceal them from you," he said; to him, Mṛgāṅkavatī replied slowly.
"O friend, you are as dear to me as my own life; since you know the proper time, why do I not speak? Indeed, by some means or other, there must be an entrance for the man."
When she had spoken thus, the disciple of the master of rogues, having discerned her intention, then said: "If it is so, then I shall tell you."
"I possess a Vaiṣṇava grace by which I may become a man at my own will during the night; therefore, for your sake, I shall today become a man."
Having said this, Manaḥsvāmī drew a pill from his mouth and showed her his beloved self, now exuberant with youth.
Then, with confidence expressed and all formal constraints cast aside, there arose between them a certain celebration of love, characterized by sentiments appropriate to the occasion.
Then that Brahmin remained there with the wife of the minister’s son; by day he was a woman, and by night he became a man.
Realizing that the minister’s son would arrive in a few days, he took her and fled from there at night, departing in secret.
And at this juncture in the conversation, Mūladeva, his teacher, having understood all of that, again assumed the form of an old Brahmin.
Accompanied by his friend Śaśin, who had taken the form of a young brahmin, he approached King Yaśaḥketu and, bowing low, spoke to him.
"I have brought this son; give me back my daughter-in-law. Then, having deliberated and fearing a curse, that king said to him:
"O Brahmin, I do not know where that daughter-in-law of yours has gone; forgive that. For the sake of my son's transgression, I give my own daughter to you."
Having spoken thus to that king of rogues, who was speaking with feigned anger and harshness while disguised as an old Brahmin, the monarch made his request.
To Śaśin, who was his friend and to whom he had given the designation of "son," he gave that daughter Śaśiprabhā according to the prescribed rites.
Then Mūladeva, taking the bride and groom exactly as they were, departed for his own abode, having no desire for the king's wealth.
Then, when Manaḥsvāmin had joined them, a great dispute arose between Śaśin and him both in the presence of Mūladeva.
Manaḥsvāmin said, "Let this Śaśiprabhā be given to me; for she was already married by me previously, through the grace of my preceptor."
The Moon said, "Who are you to her, you fool? She is my wife; for she was bestowed upon me by my father with Agni as witness."
Thus, due to the incident involving the princess who had attained power through illusion, there was no resolution between those two who were intent on their dispute.
Therefore, O King, tell me first: to whom does that wife belong? Cut through my doubt, for the agreement previously mentioned applies to you.
Having heard this from the Vetāla who was perched upon the top of his shoulder, King Trivikramasena replied to him:
I believe this princess is a fitting wife for the Moon himself, since she was openly bestowed upon him by her father according to the path of dharma.
But Manaḥsvāmin approached her through theft, according to the Gāndharva rite; for it is never at all right that a thief should have ownership over the property of others.
Having heard these words of the king, the Vetāla suddenly departed from his shoulder back to his own abode; the king, however, quickly followed after him.
The Twenty-third Wave: Then, having gone back to the śiṃśapā tree, Trivikramasena once more took the vetāla upon his shoulder and set out from there.
And as the king was approaching, the vetāla spoke to him again: "O King, listen; I shall tell you a noble story."
Here is the king of mountains named Himavat, the source of all jewels, who is the equal origin of Gaurī and Gaṅgā, the two beloveds of Hara.

And he whose back has never been touched by a coward, who stands tall with pride in the midst of the mountain-like kings of his lineage, is truly celebrated throughout the three worlds as one possessed of truth.
On its ridge there is that city named Kāñcanapura, which truly lives up to its name, shining as if it were a mass of rays deposited there by the sun.
In that excellent city of old, there was a glorious lord of the Vidyādharas named Jīmūtaketu, like Śatakratu on Mount Meru.
In the garden of his own house, he possessed a kalpa-tree inherited through his lineage, which was famous by a name true to its meaning as it granted all desires.
Having supplicated that deity, by his grace the king obtained a son who remembered his former births and was born from a portion of a Bodhisattva.
A hero in generosity, a great being who has compassion for all creatures, devoted to the service of his elders, he was named Jīmūtavāhana.
And when his son had attained youth, he, urged by virtuous men and by ministers on account of the prince's qualities, consecrated him as the crown prince.
And while Jīmūtavāhana was established in the position of crown prince, his father’s ministers, desiring his welfare, approached him and said:
O Lord, this Kalpavṛkṣa which exists for you, the granter of all desires and unassailable by all beings—this very tree is always worthy of your worship.
"For while he exists, even Śakra could not harm us, let alone anyone else. Having heard this, Jīmūtavāhana thought to himself:
"Alas! Having obtained such a celestial tree as this, why have our ancestors not attained any such fruit from it?"
By seeking even a few objects fit only for the wretched, both this man and the Great Soul alike bring themselves to contempt in the eyes of the world.
"I shall accomplish that desire which is in our hearts"; having thus resolved, the Great Being went into the presence of his father.
There, having satisfied his father—who was comfortably seated in private and pleased by every service he had provided—he addressed him with this request.
Therefore, you yourself know that all this within the ocean of existence, from the very body onwards, is as flickering as the agitation of waves.
Especially the twilight, which dissolves its light before long, and lightning and fortune—where and when have these ever been seen to be stable?
In this world, however, only service rendered to others is imperishable; for it gives birth to dharma and fame that bear witness through hundreds of future ages.
Therefore, dear father, for what purpose should such a wish-fulfilling tree as this be guarded in vain by us amidst these transitory enjoyments?
Or by whomsoever this was protected by such a grasping as "this is mine," where are those former ones now? Where is he? And who is he, or who belongs to him?
Therefore, O Father, by your command, I shall employ this wish-granting kalpa-tree for the sake of accomplishing the singular fruit of benefiting others.
Having been granted permission by his father with the words "So be it," Jīmūtavāhana then went and spoke to that wish-fulfilling tree.
O God, our desired wishes have been fulfilled by you for our ancestors; therefore, fulfill this one unique wish of mine.
Act in such a way that I shall behold this earth free from poverty; may prosperity be yours! Go, for you have been given by me to the world that seeks its welfare.
When Jīmūtavāhana had spoken thus with palms joined in reverence, a voice issued from that tree: "I have been released by you; I am born!"
In an instant, that wish-fulfilling tree rose up to heaven and rained down wealth upon the earth, so that there was no one left on this earth who was destitute.
Then, because of that intense compassion for all living beings, Jīmūtavāhana’s fame spread throughout the three worlds.

Therefore, all those born of his lineage, unable to endure it out of envy, [lamented] him who was now deprived of that wish-fulfilling tree which had made worldly suffering its own and destroyed all affliction.
Considering him as one who had his father still alive, they united and made a firm resolve; desiring to seize that kingdom, they equipped themselves for battle.
Seeing that, Jīmūtavāhana said to his father: "Father, when you have taken up your weapons, who else possesses such power?"
But who indeed, having ungrudgingly slain their kinsmen for the sake of this evil, perishing body, would desire a kingdom?
Therefore, what need have we for sovereignty? Having gone elsewhere, somewhere else, we shall practice only the Dharma, which brings happiness in both worlds.
"Let these wretched heirs, greedy for the kingdom, rejoice!"—to him who had spoken thus, his father Jīmūtaketu said:
"O son, if you yourself desire the kingdom for my sake, yet you abandon it out of compassion, what use is that to me, an old man?"
Thus, having been granted permission by his father and mother, Jīmūtavāhana, renouncing the kingdom, went to the Malaya mountain accompanied by them.
There, in a mountain cave with waterfalls covered by sandalwood trees, he remained, having prepared a hermitage and attending upon his father.
And there he obtained a friend known as Mitrāvasu, the son of Viśvāvasu, who was the king of the Siddhas residing in that place.
And once, while wandering there, Jīmūtavāhana entered a temple of the goddess Gaurī situated in a grove to pay her homage.
There he beheld an excellent maiden playing the lute, accompanied by her circle of friends and intent upon the worship of the Daughter of the Mountain.
