The deer stood motionless as if ashamed by the beauty of her eyes, while listening to the sweet sound of the lute in her song.
Bearing Kṛṣṇa as its star with Arjuna as its eye, it was like the Pāṇḍava army seeking to penetrate the very base of Karṇa.
As if desiring to behold the moon of her face through mutual rivalry, her two breasts stood facing each other as if never sated.

As the Creator fashioned her, he compressed her waist between his fingers, which were pressed together in a fist-like grip; thus, the beautiful slenderness of her middle was marked by the impression of his knuckles.
And by that glance, as soon as she entered the path of his vision, Jīmūtavāhana’s heart was instantly stolen away by that slender maiden.
She too, seeing that adorned garden which stirred longing and agitation, had resorted to it like the forest of Madhu out of a world-weariness born from the burning of the limbs of desire.
Overwhelmed by such passion, the maiden fell into a state of agitation, so that even her lute, like a friend, became distraught and its strings went out of tune.
Then Jīmūtavāhana asked her friend: "What is the name of your friend who is so blessed? What lineage has been adorned by her?"
Having heard that, the friend said: "She is named Malayavatī; she is the sister of Mitrāvasu and the daughter of Viśvāvasu, the king of the Siddhas."
Having spoken thus, that kind-hearted woman asked Jīmūtavāhana for his name and lineage, as well as that of the sage’s son who had come with him.
He spoke to Malayavatī with words softened by a smile: "Friend, why do you not offer hospitality to this lord of the Vidyādharas?"
When she said, "This guest has arrived who is worthy of worship by the whole world," the daughter of the Vidyādhara remained silent, her face bowed down with shame.
Then one of her friends, saying, "This modest girl has drunk too much; please accept this offering," presented him with a garland along with the guest-offering (arghya).
And Jīmūtavāhana, overflowing with love, took that garland and placed it upon the neck of Malayavatī.
She too, looking askance with a tender glance, fixed her gaze upon him as if it were a garland made of blue lotuses.
Then, having approached those two who were distinguished by their mutual exchange of words and their self-choice marriage, a certain maidservant spoke to that Siddha maiden.
"O princess, your mother remembers you; come back without delay. Hearing this, she drew herself away with great difficulty, as if pinned by the arrows of love.
With longing, she somehow turned her gaze from the face of her beloved back toward her home; Jīmūtavāhana also returned, bowing his head, to his own hermitage.
Then, seeing her own mother, Malayavatī, distressed by the separation from her lord of her life, went quickly and fell upon the bed.
Then, her eyes clouded as if by the smoke of the fire of internal passion, shedding streams of tears with limbs feverish from the heat of torment, she spoke.
Anointed with sandalwood paste by her friends and fanned with lotus leaves, she found no pleasure on the couch, nor in the lap of a friend, nor upon the ground.
Then, when the day had departed somewhere with the crimson twilight, the moon, laughing, seized the face of the East and kissed it.
Although urged by the god of love to send messengers and so forth, she was unable to do so because of her shame, having abandoned all desire for life.

And she passed that night, as difficult as one with the moon, like a lotus-pond whose swarm of bees has become bewildered; having reached a state of contraction within her heart, which was shrouded by a mass of delusion.
And at that moment, Jīmūtavāhana, though lying upon his bed, fell into the hands of the Flower-Bowed God, tormented as he was by the pain of separation from her.
Though his passion was newly awakened, his complexion turned pale; and though silenced by shame, he spent the night expressing the torment born of love.
And in the morning, filled with even greater longing, he went once more to that temple of Gaurī, where he had seen the daughter of the lord of the Siddhas.
There, his friend, the son of the sage, came up from behind and consoled him while he was overwhelmed by the fire of passion.
Just then, unable to endure the separation, Malayavatī herself emerged alone into that very desolate place and went there in secret to abandon her life.
Not perceiving her beloved, who was hidden by the trees, the young woman, with eyes full of tears, addressed Queen Gaurī.
"O Goddess, if by devotion to you my husband Jīmūtavāhana has not been obtained by me in this birth, then may he become mine in another birth."
Having spoken thus, she immediately fashioned a noose from her own upper garment upon the branch of an aśoka tree in the presence of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Alas, Lord Jīmūtavāhana! Why have you not protected me, even though you are renowned throughout the world for your compassion, O God?
When she had spoken thus and was about to place that noose around his neck, a divine voice uttered from the sky.
"Daughter, do not act rashly; Jīmūtavāhana shall indeed become your husband, a sovereign of the Vidyādharas and a universal monarch."
When the goddess had spoken thus, Jīmūtavāhana, having heard her words, approached his beloved who was filled with joy, together with his companions.
"Behold, this very boon granted by the Goddess has indeed become true for you!"—thus did he speak to that young girl while her friend, the son of a sage, looked on.
Speaking various words tender with affection, Jīmūtavāhana removed the noose from her neck with his own hand.
Then, as those two thought it was like a sudden shower of nectar, Malayavatī drew the earth with a bashful glance.
Arriving suddenly while searching, her friend joyfully said to her: "O auspicious friend, congratulations on your good fortune through the attainment of your desired goal!"
For this very day, O Great King, your father Viśvāvasu was addressed by Prince Mitrāvasu in my presence.
"O father, this son of the lord of the Vidyādharas, Jīmūtavāhana—who is honored by the world and who bestows the wish-fulfilling tree—has arrived here."
Because he is our guest, he is worthy of our honor; no other boon is like him. Therefore, let him be honored with this jewel of a maiden, Malayavatī.
When the king had thus expressed his faith, your brother Mitrāvasu went to the hermitage of this illustrious one for that very purpose.
"I know that your marriage will take place immediately; therefore, come to your own palace, and let this illustrious man also go to his own abode."
Having been addressed thus by her friend, the princess then slowly departed, joyful yet longing, repeatedly turning her neck back to look.
Jīmūtavāhana also went quickly to his own hermitage, and having heard the desired business from Mitrāvasu who had arrived there, he welcomed it with joy.
Remembering his past lives, he related to him his own previous birth, in which he had been his friend, and she had indeed been his sister-in-law.
Then Mitrāvasu, being pleased, informed his parents who were equally delighted; having gone to them, he, having accomplished his purpose, gladdened his own parents.
And at that very moment, he led Jīmūtavāhana to his own home and prepared the festive arrangements with a magnificence befitting his own supernatural power.
And on that very auspicious day, they celebrated the marriage of that lord of the Vidyādharas with his sister Malayavatī.
Then Jīmūtavāhana, his desires fulfilled, remained there together with his newly wedded bride, Malayavatī.
Once, wandering out of curiosity there on Mount Malaya with Mitrāvasu, he reached a forest on the shore of the ocean.
There, having seen many unstable heaps of bones, he asked that Mitravasu, "To which living beings do these collections of bones belong?"
Then his brother-in-law Mitrāvasu said to that compassionate one: "Listen to this account here; I shall describe it to you in brief."
In ancient times, it is said that Kadrū, the mother of the Nāgas, having defeated Vinatā—the mother of Tārkṣya—through a deceitful wager, reduced her to the state of slavery.
Out of that enmity, the powerful Garuḍa, even after releasing his mother, proceeded to devour the Nāgas who were the sons of Kadrū.
Then, constantly entering Pātāla, he devoured some of them, crushed others, while some perished of their own accord out of terror.
Seeing that, and fearing the total destruction of all beings at once, Vāsuki, the king of the serpents, established an agreement with Tārkṣya preceded by a formal request.
"O Lord of Birds, for the sake of food, I send one nāga after another here to this beach of the southern ocean every single day."
But you must not enter this Pātāla by any means; for what self-interest do you have if the Nāgas are destroyed all at once?
When this was said by the Naga king, Garuḍa, who perceives his own interest and possesses great prowess, accepted the agreement, saying, "So be it."
And from that time forward, that lord of birds ate one nāga every day, sent by Vāsuki, right there on the shore of the ocean.
Therefore, these heaps of bones belonging to the nāgas being devoured here, resembling mountain peaks, have increased over the course of time.
Having heard this from the mouth of Mitrāvasu, Jīmūtavāhana—a treasury of compassion and fortitude—spoke with inner sorrow.
Pitiable is that King Vāsuki, who, being a coward, day after day offers his own subjects as a sacrifice with his own hand to his enemy.
Though he possessed a thousand faces, how was it that even with a single mouth he was unable to say at first, "O Tārkṣya, eat me first"?
And how did he, devoid of strength and hardened by constantly hearing the wailing of the Naga women, entreat Tārkṣya for the destruction of his own kin?
Even Tārkṣya, the heroic son of Kaśyapa, who purifies through his abiding in Kṛṣṇa, commits such a sin; oh, how profound is the power of delusion!
Having spoken thus, that Great Being formed this aspiration in his heart: "May I obtain the essence here, even by means of this essenceless body."
Today, by giving myself to Garuḍa, I shall provide protection for the life of even a single nāga who is terrified and without kin.
While Jīmūtavāhana was thus reflecting, the chamberlain arrived from the presence of Mitrāvasu’s father to summon him.
"Go; I shall follow after you," Jīmūtavāhana said, and then he sent Mitrāvasu back home.
When he had departed, that compassionate man, wandering alone there intent upon his desired goal, heard from afar the sound of piteous weeping.
Having gone there, he saw a single young man of handsome form, distressed, near a high rocky surface.

He was returning at that very moment a woman who was weeping, having been brought back by a man like a royal officer who had abandoned her, as he was persuading the elderly woman with gentle entreaties.
Meanwhile, Jīmūtavāhana remained there in concealment, overwhelmed with compassion, listening and wondering who this person might be.
Meanwhile, that old woman there, oppressed by a heavy burden of sorrow, began to lament again and again upon seeing that youth.
Alas, Śaṅkhacūḍa! Alas, you who have encountered a hundredfold sorrows! Alas, virtuous one! Alas, sole thread of your lineage! O son, where shall I behold you again?
Child, once this moon of your face has set, how will your aged father endure, fallen into the blinding darkness of grief?
If even your body would suffer pain from the touch of the sun's rays, how will you be able to endure the agony born of being devoured by Tārkṣya?
Even though the world of the nāgas is vast, you were found by the Creator and the lord of the nāgas; why have you been chosen as my only son by one so unfortunate?
As she was thus lamenting, her young son said to her: "O Mother, why do you distress me so intensely, even though I am already afflicted by grief?"
Return home; this is your final salutation. For the time may come when Garuḍa arrives here.
Hearing that, the old woman cried out, casting her eyes of distress in all directions: "Alas! I am ruined! Who here will protect my little son?"
And at that moment, Jīmūtavāhana, who was a partial incarnation of a Bodhisattva, having heard and seen this, was overcome with intense compassion and reflected:
Alas, this ascetic nāga named Śaṅkhacūḍa has now been sent by Vāsuki for the sake of food for Tārkṣya.
And this is his mother, who has followed him here out of affection; she is old, having him as her only son, and she laments, distressed by grief.
If I do not protect this single, suffering elephant with this body that perishes utterly, then shame on my fruitless birth!
Having reflected thus and approaching her with joy, Jīmūtavāhana said to the old woman, "Mother, I shall protect your son."
Hearing that, the old woman Garuḍaśaṅkhinī, her fear aroused and trembling with terror, cried out, "O Tārkṣya, eat me! Eat me!"
Then Śaṅkhacūḍa said: "O mother, this is not Tārkṣya; do not be afraid! Where is this man, delightful like the moon, and where is that terrifying Tārkṣya?"

"Whom shall we embrace here?"—as if to see this, the eyes, resembling black antelopes, were cast about incessantly by the calamities as if by dice.
"Who is there whose fortune I shall not seize, even that of the Lord of Alakā?"—thus she seemed to proclaim through the sounds of the gamblers' quarrels.
Having entered it, he played dice with the gamblers in succession; and although he had lost his clothes and other such things, he lost further wealth as well.
When he did not give that wealth which was being sought, even though it was impossible [to produce], the court official seized him and beat him all over with clubs.
Then that son of the Brahmin, with all his limbs struck by the club, remained motionless like a stone, making himself appear as if dead.
When he had remained there for two or three days in that very manner, the enraged master of the gaming house spoke to his own gamblers in the hall:
"Since they have resorted to this state of being like stones, throw him somewhere; having taken that lifeless man to a blind well, I shall give you wealth."
Having been addressed thus by him, those gamblers then seized Candrasvāmin and, seeking a well, carried him a great distance into the forest.
There, one aged gambler addressed those others thus: "This man is practically dead; so what is the use of our throwing him into the well?"
"Therefore, having abandoned him right here, we shall say that he was abandoned in the well"; thus all of them accepted those words, saying, "So be it."
Then, after those gamblers had departed, Candrasvāmin rose up and entered a certain empty temple of Śiva there.
There, having recovered his breath somewhat, he reflected in his distress: "Alas! Having placed my trust in their deception, I have been robbed by gamblers."
Where then can such a person as I go, with my feet scorched by fire and covered in dust? For what indeed would my father, kinsman, or friend say upon seeing me?

As he was reflecting thus, weary and without clothing, the sun, having shed its heat, abandoned the sky and went to the mountain of setting.
And at that moment, an ascetic arrived there, his limbs smeared with ashes, bearing matted locks and a trident, like a second Hara endowed with great vows.
Having seen Candrasvāmin and asked, "Who are you?", and having heard his account from him, the ascetic spoke to him as he bowed humbly.
"You have arrived here at my hermitage as an unexpected guest, exhausted by hunger; therefore, arise, bathe, and take your portion of my alms."
Thus addressed by the ascetic, Candrasvāmin then said to him: "I am a Brahmin, O venerable one; how shall I eat your portion of alms?"
Having heard that, the perfected ascetic, who was fond of guests, entered his own small hut and called to mind the magic science that accomplishes one's desires.
When she had been recalled to mind and appeared before him, saying, "What shall I do?", he commanded her: "Perform the hospitality for this guest."
When she replied, "So be it," Candrasvāmin beheld there a golden city, complete with its gardens and its womenfolk, suddenly come into being.

There within, the youth beheld a certain preeminent young woman, beautiful in every limb, as if she had been fashioned by the Creator out of mere curiosity.

When that ascetic had spoken thus, by that very means, Candrasvāmin enjoyed those pleasures there every night through his favor.
And having gradually understood that power of knowledge, being impelled by destiny, he once propitiated that lord of ascetics and made this request.
If it is true, O Blessed One, that you have compassion for me who has come to you for refuge, then grant me this vidyā, the power of which is such as this.
To him who spoke thus with persistence, the ascetic replied: "This science is unattainable for you; for it is mastered only within the water."
And there, as the practitioner recites it, this net of illusion is quickly created for his delusion, by which he does not attain accomplishment.
For there he beholds himself born again as a child, and then as a youth who has taken a wife and likewise begotten sons.

But he who, having reached twenty-four years of age, has been awakened by his teacher’s knowledge, remembers his birth and understands that it was a manifestation of *māyā*, is a wise man.
Even under its influence, one enters the fire in that very same way; yet, having emerged from the water, he who has mastered the vidyā perceives the ultimate reality.
This knowledge does not belong to anyone else; for it succeeds only for the disciple. If it is bestowed upon an unworthy recipient, it perishes even for the guru.
Since the result is already established by my own success, what is the use of this grasping of yours? Should my success fail, even this of yours will surely perish.
Even when the ascetic had spoken thus, Candrasvāmin, being possessed by a planetary influence, said to him: "I shall learn everything; let there be no anxiety on your part in this matter."

Then, having led him to the riverbank, that observer of the great vow said to him: "My son, if while reciting the spell you see that illusion, then—"

Having spoken thus, that pure one, the best among those who observe vows, properly taught that science to Candrasvāmin, who was himself pure and had performed the ceremonial sipping of water.

"Indeed, taking this image of myself, which is made of gold and jewels and accompanied by a hundred villages, given by the King, I bestow it upon you both."
In this way, my debt to you will be discharged and your own purpose will be accomplished; moreover, both of you, with your poverty destroyed, shall obtain many sons.
When he had spoken thus, his parents suddenly said to him: "What is this that you say, my son? Are you perhaps agitated by the wind?"
Or have you been seized by a planet, that you prattle so strangely? For who would destroy a son for the sake of wealth, and what infant would give up his own body?
Having heard these words of his parents, the boy spoke again: "I do not prattle from a delusion of intellect; listen to my meaningful words."
This body, filled with unspeakable impurities, loathsome by its very nature, and a field of suffering, will surely perish before long.
Therefore, whatever merit is acquired by means of this which is so utterly insubstantial—that alone is called the essence within saṃsāra by those of refined intellect.
And what other supreme good deed is there than benefiting all living beings? Even in that regard, if there is devotion toward one's parents, what fruit is seen from the body [other than this]?
With these and other such words, that boy of firm resolve caused his grieving parents to accept his own desire.
And having gone, he brought that golden image from the king's servants and gave it to them along with the edict for a hundred villages.
Then, placing those very royal servants in front of him, he quickly set out for Citrakūṭa to be near the king, accompanied by his two parents.
Thereupon, King Candrāvaloka, beholding that boy whose splendor was unimpaired—as if he had obtained a protective jewel—rejoiced.
Having placed him, adorned with garlands and ointments, upon the back of an elephant, he led him along with his father to the abode of the Brahmarākṣasa.
There, having drawn a mandala at the side of that pipal tree and having offered oblations into the fire by the officiating priest with the prescribed worship, [he should proceed].
He appeared, letting out a loud burst of laughter while reciting his studies; reeling, intoxicated by the wine of blood, he yawned repeatedly and sighed.
With blazing eyes, he cast darkness upon the directions with the shadow of his body; Jvālāmukha was a Brahma-rākṣasa of most terrible appearance.
Then King Candrāvaloka, seeing him, bowed and said: "O Blessed One, that human offering has been brought by me for you."
Today is the seventh day since that vow of yours was made; therefore, be gracious and accept this offering according to the prescribed rite.
Thus entreated by the king, the Brahmarākṣasa looked upon the young Brahmin, licking the corners of his mouth with his tongue.
At that moment, the Great Being, though appearing as a child, rejoiced and thought: "By this gift of my own body, I have acquired a well-performed deed."
Therefore, let there be no heaven or liberation for me that is devoid of purposeful action; rather, may I have a body in birth after birth for the sake of the welfare of others.
Even as he was thus forming this resolution, the sky in an instant became filled with the celestial chariots of the hosts of gods, which were raining down showers of flowers.
Then, as that boy was brought before the Brahma-rākṣasa, his mother seized him by the hands and his father likewise by the feet.
Then, just as the king drew his sword and sought to kill him, that infant laughed in such a way that everyone there did likewise.
Together with the Brahma-rākṣasas, they abandoned their respective activities and, filled with wonder, stood with palms joined in reverence, bowing low and gazing at his face.
Having thus related this tale, varied and full of charm, the Vetāla spoke again to King Trivikramasena.
Tell me that, O King: what was the reason that he laughed then, even though he was but a child, at such a moment, alas, when his very life was at its end?
I have a great curiosity in this matter; if you do not tell me this, even though you know it, then your head shall split into a hundred pieces.
Having heard this from the Vetāla, the king replied to him: "Listen to what the intention was behind that laugh of the child at that time."
Whatever weak creature there may be, when danger has arisen, cries out for the sake of its life to its own father and likewise to its mother.
And upon his departure, one should worship the king, who was appointed for the protection of the distressed; or, in his absence, whatever deity is appropriate here according to the circumstances.
But for him, even though all this was gathered together in one place, it turned out otherwise; for his hands and feet were held back by his parents through their thirst for wealth.
And the king, intent on killing him himself in order to save his own life, had as his devourer there a divine *brahmarākṣasa*.
Such is the mockery of those deluded ones who, for the sake of this body—which is unstable, ultimately loathsome, and wounded by mental and physical ailments—pursue such ends.
Since even Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others are inevitably perishable, what kind of such obsession with the stability of their bodies could they possibly have?
Having seen this variety of delusion and having considered his own desire as accomplished, that young Brahmin laughed with wonder and joy.

Having spoken thus, as the king ceased speaking, that Vetāla suddenly returned to his own place from the monarch’s shoulder, vanished by means of his magic power. Yet the king followed after him again with unwavering resolve and speed; alas, the heart of the great is indeed as unshakeable as the ocean.
The Twenty-eighth Wave: Then, having gone back and reached the śiṃśapā tree once more, King Trivikramasena took that vetāla upon his shoulder.
As he was returning, the Vetāla spoke again to the king: "O King, listen; I shall tell you a story concerning one whose passion is intense."
There exists on earth another city called Viśālā, created by the benevolent Creator for the sake of the virtuous who have descended from heaven, just like the city of Śakra.
In that city there was a king known as Padmanābha, who delighted the circle of the virtuous, was illustrious, and had subdued the kingship of Bali.
While that lord of the earth reigned, there lived in that city a very great merchant named Arthadatta, who surpassed even Kubera with his wealth.
To him was born a daughter named Anaṅgamañjarī, who appeared like a reflection of a celestial beauty displayed upon earth by the Creator himself.
And she was given by that merchant to the son of a preeminent merchant named Maṇivarman, a resident of Tāmraliptī.
Because she was his only child, that merchant was exceedingly affectionate toward her; he did not send his daughter Anaṅgamañjarī from the house to be joined with her husband.
And that Maṇivarman became a hateful husband to that Anaṅgamañjarī, like a bitter and pungent medicine to one who is ill.
But that fair-faced woman was dearer to her husband than his own life, like the long-accumulated wealth of a miser obtained with great difficulty.
And once, on account of longing and other such reasons, that Maṇivarman went from his parents' presence to his own home in Tāmraliptī.
Then, as the days passed, the summer season arrived here, blocking the paths of those away from home with its arrows of sharp sunbeams.
The winds blew, thick with the fragrance of jasmine and trumpet-flowers, like the hot sighs of the quarters of the sky due to their separation from spring.
Lines of dust, stirred up by the wind, rose into the sky like messengers dispatched by the scorched earth to summon the arrival of the clouds.
Like travelers scorched by the fierce heat who long for the shade of trees, even the days passed away only after a long time.
The nights, white with the rays of the moon, reached an extreme state of weakness without the winter season that bestows the pleasure of a firm embrace.
At that time, that merchant’s daughter was like a sprout of the God of Love, white with an application of sandalwood paste and adorned with a fine silk garment wrapped around her body.
Once, while standing at a high window of her own house accompanied by a trusted female friend, she beheld a handsome young son of a Brahmin.
He saw the son of the royal priest, named Kamalākara, moving about like the newly arisen god of love for the sake of attaining pleasure.
Upon seeing that lovely form standing above him like the moon, that lake of lotuses, filled with joy, attained the state of a bed of night-lotuses.
Then, by the powerful command of Love, there occurred between those two youths that priceless mutual gazing, which was a spell for enchanting the mind.
With their modesty uprooted and their minds cast far away, the two of them, overcome by passion, were carried off by the whirlwind of the impulse of love.
And having seen her, Kamalākara was overcome by passion; with the help of his friend who stood beside him, he was somehow led back to his own home.
Anaṅgamañjarī, having learned his name, entered her chamber slowly with that friend of hers, feeling utterly helpless.
There, brooding over her beloved and afflicted by the fever of passion, she saw nothing and heard nothing as she rolled upon her bed.
When two or three days had passed, she, filled with shame and fear, became thin and pale, unable to endure the madness of separation.
Once at night, having abandoned all hope for union with her beloved who was so difficult to attain, she was drawn away as if by the moon, whose rays streamed through the window.
When her attendants were asleep, she went out at her own will and, intent on death, proceeded to the pond in the garden of her own house, which was overgrown with trees and creepers.
There, having approached the goddess Caṇḍikā—the family deity for whom her father had established a noble shrine—and having bowed to and praised her, he made this request:
"O Goddess, if I have not obtained Kamalākara as my husband in this life, then may he become mine in another birth as well."
Having spoken thus, the passionate woman fashioned a noose from her upper garment at the foot of an aśoka tree in front of that goddess.
Meanwhile, her trusted friend woke up in that dwelling; not seeing her there, she happened by chance to come to that garden while searching for her.
Seeing her there placing the noose around his neck in that manner, he cried out, "No! No! and rushing forward, he cut that noose of hers apart.
And Anaṅgamañjarī, seeing her own friend arrive with her bonds cut, fell to the ground, overcome with even greater sorrow.
Reassured by her friend and questioned by her in turn, she immediately explained the cause of her sorrow and spoke to her again.
"Friend Mālatikā, since union with my beloved is so difficult for me to attain, being dependent on my elders and others, there is no happiness for me beyond death."
Even as she was speaking thus, Anaṅgamañjarī, intensely inflamed by the fire of the arrows of the Bodiless One, fell into a swoon, unable to endure her despair.
Alas! The command of Smara is difficult to transgress, by which this friend of mine—who used to mock other undisciplined women—has been brought to such a state.
While she was lamenting in this manner, her friend Mālatikā gently comforted her with cool water, breezes, and other such means.
And for the sake of allaying her fever, he made a bed for her with lotus petals and placed upon her heart a necklace cool as ice.
Then, with tears in her eyes, Anaṅgamañjarī said to that friend: "Friend, this burning of mine does not subside even by means of necklaces and other ornaments."
Whatever may bring about peace, perform that by your own intellect; unite me with my beloved, if you desire my life.
When she had spoken thus, Mālatikā said to her affectionately: "Friend, the night has grown very long today; tomorrow morning, however, I shall come again."
"I shall bring your beloved here, having made an appointment with him right now; therefore, summoning fortitude for the time being, enter your own palace."
When she had spoken thus, Anaṅgamañjarī was pleased and, drawing a necklace from her own neck, gave it to her as a reward.
"Go now to your own home; depart in the morning for the sake of success. Having thus sent her friend away, she entered her own dwelling.
And in the morning, that friend of hers, Mālatikā, went unobserved by anyone to the house of that Kamalākara.
While searching there in the garden, she saw him at the foot of a tree, tossing restlessly upon a bed of lotus leaves moistened with sandalwood paste.
He was being comforted by a single friend who held the secret [of the remedy], with breezes from plantain leaves, while he himself was being consumed by the fire of love.
Thinking, "What might be the state of desire of this person to be converted? she remained there in concealment to ascertain his resolve.
Then that friend said to Kamalākara: "Cast your gaze for a single moment upon this delightful garden."
"O friend, divert your mind; do not fall into despondency. Hearing this, the Brahmin's son said to that friend of his:
How can I divert this mind of mine, whose inner disposition is desolate, now that it has been stolen away by that merchant’s daughter, Anaṅgamañjarī?
For my heart is empty due to Smara, and I have been made a quiver for his arrows; therefore, act for me in such a way that I may obtain that thief of my mind.
When this had been said by the son of the brahmin, Mālatikā, having revealed herself and being filled with joy, approached him and spoke, her doubts now dispelled.
"O fortunate one, I have been sent to you by Anaṅgamañjarī; I myself shall deliver her message to you with its meaning made perfectly clear."
What kind of refined conduct is this, that having forcibly entered her heart and stolen away the mind of the innocent girl, you depart with your true nature concealed?
And it is marvelous that she, who is so beautiful, will now desire to give even her body along with her life-breaths to you alone, O Manohara.
For she, tormented day and night, emits sighs that are like the rising of smoke from the blazing fire of Kandarpa within her heart.
Teardrops mixed with collyrium fall from her face again and again, like bees greedy for the fragrance of her lotus-like countenance.
"Therefore, if you so desire, I shall speak that which will bring welfare to both of you. Having been addressed thus by Mālatikā, Kamalākara replied:
"O blessed lady, this speech of yours causes me fear, yet it also brings me comfort, as it describes my beloved's distressed state while she remains steadfast in her devotion."
"Therefore, you are our only recourse in this matter; act as you see fit. When Kamalākara had spoken these words, Mālatikā said:
"Today, I shall secretly bring Anaṅgamañjarī to the garden of her own palace at night; you should remain there outside."
"Therefore, I shall cause you to enter within here by my own ingenuity; in this way, a union between you two will take place according to your desire."
Having spoken thus and gladdened that brahmin’s son, Mālatikā then departed; having achieved her purpose, she also brought joy to Anaṅgamañjarī.
Then, as the sun departed with the day somewhere, full of affection for the twilight, the face of the eastern quarter was beautifully adorned by the moon as its tilaka mark.
As if out of joy at the thought, "I have abandoned the lotus-pond and attained Fortune," the pure lily-pool laughs with its fully blossomed faces.
Having completed his adornments, Kamalākara, full of longing and filled with desire, went at his own will to the exterior of the garden gate of his beloved’s house.
And meanwhile, Mālatikā, by means of a stratagem, brought Anaṅgamañjarī—who had passed the day with great difficulty—to that garden.
And having seated her in the midst of a thicket of mango trees, he went out and brought Kamalākara into that very place.
And having entered, he beheld Anaṅgamañjarī standing amidst a thicket of trees dense with a mass of leaves, just as a traveler beholds the shade.
As soon as he approached her, she saw him, ran toward him, and—her modesty swept away by the force of passion—suddenly threw her arms around his neck.
"Where are you going? You have been caught by me!"—as she spoke these words at that moment, her breath became stifled by the weight of excessive joy, and she passed away.
And she fell upon the surface of the earth like a creeper broken by the wind; alas, how varied and treacherous is the course of the ripening of desire!
Seeing that terrible fall of the thunderbolt, Kamalākara immediately cried out, "Alas! Alas! What is this? and fell to the ground in a swoon.
Then, having regained consciousness in an instant, he embraced his beloved who was placed upon his lap, kissed her, and lamented many things one after another.
Thus, he was so violently oppressed by the excessive burden of suffering that his heart burst instantly with a loud crack.
Then, seeing that both of them had met their end while being lamented by Mālatikā, the night itself seemed to waste away as if out of grief.
In the morning, having learned from the garden-keepers about those two, their kinsmen arrived there, overwhelmed by confusion caused by shame, wonder, grief, and delusion.
For a long time he remained bewildered as to what ought to be done, his face cast down in grief; alas, wicked women are indeed a source of bitter disgrace to their families!
And at that moment, Anaṅgamañjarī’s husband Maṇivarman arrived from his father’s house in Tāmraliptī, filled with longing for her.
Having reached his father-in-law’s house and understood the situation as it truly was, he returned to that very garden, brooding with eyes blinded by tears.
There, seeing his wife dead even though she was accompanied by another, that lustful man, inflamed by the fire of grief, immediately gave up his own life.
Then, while the people there were wailing, all the citizens, having learned what had happened, arrived on the scene, agitated by the clamor and filled with astonishment.
Then, the goddess Caṇḍī, who had been previously invoked there by Anaṅgamañjarī’s father and was present nearby, was addressed by her own attendants:
"O Goddess, this merchant Arthadatta has always been devoted to you, establishing your image; therefore, show compassion for him in his distress."
Having heard this from the hosts, she, the refuge of all and beloved of Śaṅkara, commanded: "Let these three, their passion now stilled, live."
Then, by his grace, they all rose up in an instant as if awakened from sleep—alive and free from passion.
Then, having witnessed that marvel while all the people were filled with joy, Kamalākara departed for his own home with his face bowed in shame.
Arthadatta also, taking his daughter Anaṅgamañjarī who was bashful, went to his home with her husband, full of great joy.
Having spoken thus, that Vetāla told another story on the road during that night to King Trivikramasena.
"O King, tell me, among these who are deluded by passion, whose delusion is the greatest? For if you know and do not speak, that previously mentioned curse shall fall upon you."
Having heard this from the Vetāla, the king replied to him: "Of these, that Maṇivarman appears to me to be the most deluded by passion."
For if both of those others, whose states of love have ripened through the passage of time and who are mutually enamored, should give up their lives, so be it.
But Maṇivarman was utterly foolish; for upon seeing his wife dead from attachment to another man, instead of feeling anger at that time, he was filled with passion and gave up his life out of grief.
When the king had spoken thus, alas, the lord of the Vetālas departed once more from the seat of his shoulder to his own place; then the king also followed after him again.
The twenty-ninth wave: Then King Trivikramasena went back once more to the vetāla at the foot of the śiṃśapā tree, and having reached him, he placed him upon his shoulder.
And as the king was approaching, the Vetāla said to him on the road: "O King, you are virtuous and of noble character; therefore, hear an unprecedented tale."
Formerly, there was on this earth a king named Dharaṇīvarāha, who was the lord of the city known as Kusumapura.
In that kingdom, which was predominantly inhabited by Brahmins, there was a royal grant named Brahmasthala; therein lived a twice-born man named Viṣṇusvāmī.
He had a wife worthy of him, just as Svāhā is to the consumer of oblations; and from her, four sons were born to him in succession.
When they had completed their study of the Vedas and passed beyond childhood, Viṣṇusvāmin departed for heaven, followed by that wife of his.
Then all those sons of his, having been summoned there in a state of distress, with their entire property seized by their kinsmen, consulted among themselves.
"There is no way out for us here; why then do we not go from here to my maternal grandfather's house in the village named Yaṣṭhasthala?"
Having firmly resolved upon this very course, they set out, subsisting on alms-food; then, after many days, they reached their maternal grandfather’s house.

There, in the absence of their maternal grandfather, they remained in his house, receiving shelter from his maternal uncles; devoted to the practice of Vedic study, they lived there while partaking of food.
And in the course of time, those [sons] became destitute and fell into a state of contempt among their maternal uncles regarding food, clothing, and other necessities.
Then, to them who were brooding in secret, their spirits crushed by the insults flashing forth from their own kinsmen, the eldest brother spoke this:
"O brothers, what can be done? Fate ordains everything; it is not possible for a person here to do anything at any time."
Wandering about in agitation, I have today arrived at the cemetery; there I saw a man lying on the ground in a state of ruin, his limbs trembling with fear.
And seeing him, I thought, longing for that same state: "Blessed indeed is this man, who, having cast off the burden of suffering, has found such rest."
Having reflected thus and having made the resolve to die at that very moment, I suspended myself by means of a noose fastened to the top of a tree.
And while my breaths were still issuing from my nostrils as I lay unconscious, I fell here upon the surface of the earth with my bonds severed.
And having regained consciousness, I saw myself being quickly comforted by some compassionate man with the breezes from his garment.
"Friend, tell me: even though you are wise, toward whom do you feel such distress? For happiness comes from good deeds and suffering from evil deeds, and not from anything else."
If you feel aversion toward suffering, then practice virtuous deeds; for how can you desire the suffering of hell by means of self-sacrifice?
Having spoken thus and comforted me, that man departed for some unknown place; and I, having abandoned my resolve for death, have come here.
Thus, since death cannot even be obtained when one does not desire it during the performance of a rite, I shall now consume my body with austerity at a sacred ford.
To that eldest brother who had said, "By this means may I never again be a partaker of the suffering of poverty," the younger brothers replied:
O Noble One, how is it that even you, being wise, are afflicted by suffering on account of wealth? Do you not know that the course of riches is as fickle as an autumn cloud?
Even when brought under control and guarded with great effort, friendship with the wicked, a courtesan, and royal fortune—each inwardly devoid of affection—are stable for whom and at what time?
Therefore, a wise person should acquire some extraordinary quality through diligent effort, by which the deer of wealth are repeatedly brought under control, bound and dragged back by force.
Thus addressed by his brothers, the eldest regained his composure in an instant and said, "What kind of virtue ought to be acquired?"
Then, having deliberated, they all said to one another: "Having searched the earth, let us learn some form of specialized knowledge."
Having thus decided upon this place of rendezvous and announced it for their meeting, those four went each in a separate direction toward the four quarters.
When the time came, they met at the appointed place and said to one another, "Brothers, who has taught what?"
Then one among them said: "I have learned such a science by which, having obtained a fragment of bone belonging to any living being whatsoever,"
"I shall instantly produce for him the flesh appropriate for that moment. Having heard these words of his, the second among them spoke.
I know that upon that very fragment of bone where flesh has grown, I shall produce the hair and skin belonging to that living being.
Then the third one also spoke: "I know that I was right there as well, having been born with skin, flesh, and hair in order to create the limbs of those living beings."
And then the fourth spoke: "I believe that very living being, possessing the form of produced limbs, must be endowed with vital breaths."
Having spoken thus to one another, all four brothers set out for the forest toward a heap of bones in order to display their respective supernatural knowledge.
There, by the power of destiny, they came upon a fragment of the lion's bones; and not discerning its specific nature, they took it up just as it was.
And one [of them] then provided it with appropriate flesh; the second likewise produced its layers of skin and hair.
And the third [son] completed it with all the remaining limbs suitable for that purpose; and the fourth gave life to him who had become a lion.
Then there arose an exceedingly terrifying lion, its mass of manes bristling, its mouth crowded with fangs, and its sharp claws like goads.
Having run after them, the lion killed all four of those very creators; being satisfied, he then entered the forest.
Thus those twice-born ones perished through the fault of their lion-transformation; for having raised up a wicked creature, who could find happiness within themselves?
And thus, even a quality acquired with great effort, when fate is adverse, does not merely fail to lead to prosperity; rather, it results in calamity.
For when the root of destiny is unimpaired and watered with the water of wisdom, the tree of human effort generally bears fruit, its trencher being the method of right conduct.
Thus, on that night, having related this story from his shoulder by means of the Vetāla, King Trivikramasena was addressed once more by him.
"O King, among those four, who was at fault there in that lion-transformation, that he slew him? Tell me the rule established therein; that was your prior agreement."
Having heard this from the Vetāla, the king thought: "This one wishes to depart while I remain silent; let him go, for I shall bring him back again."
Having thus resolved in his heart, that lord of the earth replied to the Vetāla: "He who restores life to that lion shall be the sharer of their sin."
For those who, by the power of reasoning, have determined the production of flesh, skin, hair, and limbs without having perceived the specific living being, there is no fault on account of ignorance.
But by him who, seeing the form of a lion, being eager to manifest his magical power, surrendered his life-breaths—by him those acts of Brahmin-slaughter were committed.
Having heard these words of the king, that excellent Vetāla returned to his own abode; yet the illusory king once again followed after him from his shoulder.
The Thirtieth Wave: Then, having gone from that śiṃśapā tree once more, that best of kings, Trivikramasena, reached the vetāla.
And having placed him upon his shoulder, the silent man displayed various transformations; as soon as he had set off, that vetāla spoke to him:
"O King, although this is an improper matter, this obsession of yours is difficult to restrain; therefore, to dispel your fatigue, I shall tell you a story—listen."
In the region of Kaliṅga, there was a city named Śobhāvatī, which was like the city of Śakra in heaven—a dwelling place for those of virtuous deeds.
Whom the king named Pradyumna—renowned for his preeminent sovereignty and valor like the god Pradyumna himself—ruled with triumphant commands.
In that [city], discord was heard only in the strings of bows, the striking of hands upon drums, the yokes of chariots, and the sharpness of wisdom.
In one part of that city, a royal grant known as Yajñasthala was bestowed by the king; it became a brahman settlement (agrahāra) containing many twice-born men.
There lived a Brahmin named Yajñasoma, who had mastered the Vedas, possessed great wealth, maintained the sacred fires, and honored guests and deities.
When his youth had passed away, by means of hundreds of desires, only one son was born to him from a suitable wife.
And that boy of auspicious marks grew up in his father’s house, having been duly named Deva-soma by the twice-born.
And having reached the age of sixteen, he—having won over the people by means of his learning, discipline, and other virtues—suddenly met his death through fever.
Then his father Yajñasena, out of affection, embraced him as he lay lifeless; grieving together with his wife, he did not abandon him for a long time to be cremated.
O Brahmin, do you not know that the course of this gandharva-city of saṃsāra—though you are a knower of the high and the low—is as fragile as a bubble on the water?
Those who filled the earth with their armies, now reclining upon jeweled couches on the charming rooftops of palaces resounding with the music of singing.
With their limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and surrounded by excellent women, those kings, considering themselves equal to the immortals, sported in this world of mortals.
They too were left alone in the cremation grounds, followed by weeping spirits, lying upon funeral pyres where they were devoured by carnivorous beasts and consumed by fires.
With their outskirts encircled by jackals and devoured by Time, they could not be restrained by anyone; as for others there, what need is there even to mention them?
Then the assembled elders informed that brahmin, saying, "O learned one, embrace this deceased man and tell us: what will you do? and so forth.
Then, having somehow released him, he placed his son—who was lifeless and had been prepared with the funeral rites—upon a palanquin.
The kinsmen, accompanied by their weeping relatives who were struck by the slaughter, brought him to the cremation ground amidst a tumultuous clamor.
In the meantime, there was a certain aged ascetic, a Pāśupata yogin, who had made his dwelling in a small hut within that cemetery.
Carrying a body exceedingly emaciated by age and asceticism, it was encircled by veins as if out of fear of breaking.
Known by the name Vāmaśiva, his form was covered with hair as white as ash; with a mass of matted locks tawny like lightning, he was like another Maheśvara.
At that time, the ascetic there [addressed] that fool—vexed by his reproaches, deceitful, arrogant due to his meditation and yoga, and full of egoism.
Having heard that clamor of people outside from afar, he spoke to his disciple, who dwelt nearby and observed the vow of subsisting on alms:
"Arise, go outside, find out what it is, and return quickly! From where does this tumultuous noise come, never heard before in this cremation ground?"
When the teacher had spoken thus, the disciple replied to him: "I will not go myself; you go, for my time for alms is passing away."
Having heard that, the teacher said: "Fie upon you, fool devoted only to your belly! When half a watch of the day has passed, what business for alms is there for you here?"
Upon hearing this, that wicked disciple became enraged and said to the ascetic: "Shame on you, you decrepit old man! I am not your disciple, nor are you my teacher."
"I shall go elsewhere; carry this bowl yourself," he said, and rising, he departed, leaving his staff and water-pot behind.
Then, laughing, that ascetic emerged from his hut and went to the place where the young Brahmin had been brought for cremation.
And seeing him, whose prime youth was being mourned by the people, the yogi, himself afflicted by old age, resolved to enter that body.
Having gone quickly to a secluded spot and wept aloud with unrestrained throat, he then immediately danced with appropriate *aṅgahāra* gestures.
Then, desiring youth, that ascetic abandoned his own body and, through yoga, entered the corpse of the brahmin’s son in an instant.
At that very moment, as the funeral pyre was being prepared, that young Brahmin suddenly regained his life and rose up, stretching his limbs.
Seeing that, a cry arose there from the circle of kinsmen and from all the people: "By good fortune he lives! By good fortune he lives!"
Then, so as not to break his vow toward them all falsely, that lord of yoga, the ascetic who had entered within the body of the brahmin’s son, spoke to them:
Today, having spoken directly to me as he had departed for another world, Śarva granted me life and commanded that the Great Pāśupata vow be undertaken.
"I must go now and observe that vow in solitude; otherwise, my life cannot continue. Therefore, you all depart, for I am going."
Having thus addressed all those present there, the firm-minded ascetic sent them home, though they were overwhelmed by both joy and sorrow.
Having gone there himself and cast his former body into that chasm, the great yogi, having undertaken his vow and become young again, departed elsewhere.
Having thus related the story at night on the road, the Vetāla then spoke again to King Trivikramasena.
"O King, tell me: why did that lord of yogis weep while dwelling in another's body, and why did he then dance? I have a great curiosity regarding this."
Having heard this from the Vetāla, that king, the best among the wise, fearing a curse, broke his silence and spoke to him as follows:
Listen to what was the intention of that ascetic in that matter: "This body of mine, grown old over a long time, is the means for attaining perfection."
Thinking, "I am leaving today that which was cherished by my parents in childhood," that aged ascetic wept; for attachment to the body is indeed difficult to abandon.
"I shall enter a new body and achieve even more than this"—with such joy he danced; for who indeed does not desire youth?

Having heard these words of the king, the Vetāla, remaining within the corpse, once more departed for that śiṃśapā tree; the king too pursued him with even greater resolve, for the steadfastness of the courageous surpasses even the stability of the principal mountains at the end of an aeon, as they seek their goal again and again.

Disregarding that terrible sight, King Trivikramasena went back to that śiṃśapā tree and once again took hold of the vetāla upon it.
And as he departed, carrying him upon his shoulder as before, the vetāla spoke again to that king of men.
"O King, I am distressed, but you are not by these comings and goings; therefore, listen as I explain this one great question of mine."
There was once a certain local ruler in the Deccan named Dharma, a leader among the virtuous and born of many lineages.
He had a wife named Candravatī, born in the land of Mālava, who was of noble lineage and the crest-jewel among excellent women.
And to that king, by that wife of his, was born a daughter alone, named Lāvaṇyavatī, whose name was truly significant of her beauty.
And when that daughter was about to be given away in marriage, King Dharmabhūpati was uprooted by his kinsmen, who had joined together and were sowing dissension within the kingdom.
Then, having fled, he departed from that country at night with his wife and that daughter, carrying away a collection of excellent jewels.
Setting out at his own will toward Mālava, the dwelling place of his father-in-law, he reached the Vindhya forest that very night, accompanied by his wife and son.
As he entered it, the night departed as if shedding tears in the form of dew-drops, having thus escorted that lord of the earth on his nocturnal journey.
Then the sun, with its rays uplifted like hands, ascended the eastern mountain as if to ward him off, saying, "Do not go into this forest of thieves!"
Then, with his feet wounded by the thorns of *kuśa* grass, that king traveled on foot with his son and wife and reached a village of the Bhillas.
It was filled with men who robbed others of their lives and all possessions, devoid of righteous people, and difficult to traverse like the city of Death.
There, as soon as they saw the king from afar, adorned with clothes and ornaments, many Śabaras bearing various weapons rushed forward to plunder him.
Seeing them, King Dharma said to his daughter and wife: "The Mlecchas will soon touch you; therefore, enter the forest from here."
Thus addressed by the king, Queen Candravatī entered the heart of the forest out of fear, together with her daughter Lāvaṇyavatī.
There, the heroic king, bearing sword and shield, slew many Śabaras who were rushing toward him with arrows in their hands.
Then, commanded by their chief, the entire village fell upon him and killed the king alone, his skin wounded by blows.
When the army of bandits had departed, having taken the ornaments, she saw from afar that her husband was slain while standing within a thicket of forest trees.
There, Queen Candravatī, overwhelmed with distress, fled together with her daughter and entered deep into the dense forest.
There, even though the shadows had retreated into the trees along with the travelers—like roots of trees distressed by the heat of midday—they remained cool.
On one side of the lotus pond, at the foot of an aśoka tree, she sat down together with her son, exhausted and weeping, afflicted by grief.
Meanwhile, a certain great man living nearby arrived at that forest on horseback with his son for the sake of hunting.
And that man named Caṇḍasiṃha, seeing there the two tracks of footprints rising from the dust, spoke to his son Siṃhaparākrama.
If these two women of auspicious marks and fortune follow you and obtain you, then choose one of them as you please.
To him who had spoken thus, his son Siṃhaparākrama said: "She whose feet are so delicate appears to me as the one to be my wife."
For I know that she, being of very young age, is surely suitable for me; but this one, with her large feet, is fit for you, who are advanced in years.
Having heard these words of his son, Caṇḍasiṃha said to him: "What kind of talk is this? Your mother has indeed only recently departed to heaven."
"When such a virtuous wife has departed, where else could there be any attachment? Having heard that, the son also spoke to Caṇḍasiṃha.
"Father, do not say such a thing; for the house of a householder is empty indeed without a wife. Furthermore, have you not heard the verse spoken by Mūladeva?"
Where does a non-deluded man enter that fortress known as a "house"—which is unbarred—when his beloved, with her firm breasts and hips, stands watching the path?
"O father, I adjure you by my life: if you do not accept her as a second wife for my desire, you shall be cursed."
Having heard these words of his son and having agreed with them, Caṇḍasiṃha, accompanied by his friend, followed the trail of footprints and proceeded slowly.
And having reached that lake, he beheld Queen Śyāmā, who was adorned with a multitude of pearls like stars and illuminated by the moonlight.
Accompanied by her daughter Lāvaṇyavatī, who was as radiant as moonlight, she resembled the night sky at midday when it has taken refuge in the shade of a tree.
And full of curiosity, he approached her together with his son; she too, seeing him, rose up in alarm, suspecting him to be a thief.
"Enough with this fear, O Mother; these two are not thieves. They have gentle appearances and are well-dressed; they have surely come here for the sake of hunting."
While the queen, having been addressed thus by her daughter, was still wavering there, Caṇḍasiṃha dismounted from his horse and spoke to both of them.
"Why this agitation? We have come out of affection to see you both; therefore, being free from fear, speak with confidence—who are you two?"
When Manmatha had been consumed by the flames of the fire from Śiva’s eye and was thus distressed, Rati and Prīti entered this very forest as if they were [fleeing] there.

"How is it that your feet, worthy of the lap of a beautiful woman, have wandered upon this thorny ground?"—this thought causes pain in our hearts.
And this dust, rising from your feet and falling upon your faces, stirred up by the wind, makes our own faces lose their luster—how strange!
And as this ray of the fiercely burning sun falls upon this limb of yours, so delicate with flowers, it scorches us with its intense heat.
Therefore, tell us your own story, for our hearts are indeed pained; we are unable to look upon your stay in this forest infested with wild beasts.
When Caṇḍasiṃha had spoken thus, the queen of that pauper, overwhelmed with shame and grief, slowly related her own story to him.
Then, perceiving her to be without a master and consoling her along with her daughter, Caṇḍasiṃha took possession of them, winning them over with sweet words.
Having mounted her along with her daughter upon the backs of his two horses, he led her and her daughter to his own residence, which was as prosperous as the city of Kubera.
She too, as if driven by the karma of a previous birth, accepted him helplessly; for what can a woman do when she is unprotected, fallen into distress, and in a foreign land?
Then, because of her delicate feet, Caṇḍasiṃha’s son, Siṃhaparākrama, took that queen Candravatī as his wife there.
And Caṇḍasiṃha made that king’s daughter, Lāvaṇyavatī, his wife because of her large feet.
For previously, indeed, after seeing the two rows of footprints—one small and one large—he accepted the truth from them; and who can overstep that?
Thus, due to the exchange of their feet, the daughter and mother of those two became the wives of each other's father and son, and they were then born as mother-in-law and daughter-in-law.
In due course, sons and daughters were born to those two by their two husbands; thereafter, others among them were likewise born in succession.
Having thus reached them, Caṇḍasiṃha and Siṃhaparākrama remained there with Lāvaṇyavatī and Candravatī.

Having heard this from the Vetāla and reflecting upon it in many ways, when the king did not know the answer, he then departed in silence.
Then the Vetāla, seated upon his shoulder and dwelling within the body of the dead man, laughed inwardly and reflected:

Therefore, having today deceived that evil-minded one by means of a stratagem, I shall bestow his supernatural power upon this king, whose future is auspicious.
Having reflected thus, the vetāla then said to that king: "O King, in this cremation ground, terrible in the black night, by means of these comings and goings..."

"Let us carry this corpse away now; I shall depart from here. But listen to what I say for your benefit, and do it."
"That for whose sake you have brought this human corpse—the wicked monk shall summon me today and worship me within it."

"First, show me [the way] yourself; I shall do exactly that. Thus, O Great King, you should say to that ascetic.
Then, as soon as he has fallen upon the ground and offers you a salutation, you must cut off his head with your sword.
"Therefore, you shall obtain that mastery over the Vidyādharas which was desired by him; enjoy this earth as an offering to him."

"May you achieve success; go," having said this, the Vetāla emerged from the back of her shoulder and departed from that corpse-body.

They say that truth alone is unshakable and preeminent among you, the mountains of the lineage, since by it the welfare of others is accomplished through such disregard for oneself.
This indeed is said by the wise to be the greatness of the great: that they do not waver from what they have undertaken, even when their very lives are at stake.
Speaking thus, that mendicant, considering his purpose already accomplished, then caused the corpse to be lowered from the shoulder of the king.
Having bathed him, anointed him, and adorned him with a bound garland, he placed that corpse within the center of the maṇḍala.
With his body smeared with ashes, wearing matted hair and a sacred thread, and clad in the garments of the deceased, he remained for a moment absorbed in meditation.
Having caused that excellent Vetāla, summoned by the power of mantras, to enter the human corpse, the mendicant worshipped him in due order.
He offered him the arghya water from a skull-bowl as an offering vessel, using human teeth that were perfectly pure; then he gave flowers and fragrant ointment.
Having offered incense with human eyes and likewise an oblation of flesh, and having completed the worship, he spoke to that king who was at his side.
O King, here, having prostrated upon the ground with your eight limbs, perform obeisance to this sovereign of mantras, for whom the preparatory rites have been completed.
"By means of this, this bestower of boons will grant you the accomplishment of your desire. Hearing this and remembering the Vetāla's words, the king said to him:
"I do not know that; may your lordship show it to me first, and then, O Blessed One, I shall do exactly as you have instructed."
Then, just as that monk fell to the ground to show [the truth], the king severed his head with a stroke of his sword.
And he drew out the lotus of the heart torn from his belly, and gave that head and heart-lotus to that Vetāla.
Then, when the hosts of spirits had joyfully offered their applause, the Vetāla, being pleased, spoke to the king from within that human corpse:
"O King, that sovereignty over the Vidyādharas which was desired by the mendicant shall indeed be yours, but only after you have enjoyed the empire of the earth."
"You have been troubled by me; therefore, choose whatever boon you desire. To the Vetāla who had spoken thus, the king replied:

And where was our departure from Ayodhyā in order to attain that [state], and where was our mutual separation in the Vindhya forest due to the curse of the Nāga?
Then, for some among us, where was our gradual meeting, and where now is this separation, O friend, which brings about the abandonment of what is dear?
"For they have been seized by a spirit in this tree; without them, what is Śaśāṅkavatī to me, and what is life? Enough with these delusions!"
Having spoken thus, Mṛgāṅkadatta rose up there in the lake to cast himself into the water out of grief, even though Śrutadhi tried to restrain him.
At that moment, an incorporeal voice rose from the sky: "Do not act rashly, my son; for everything shall turn out well for you."
The god Gaṇapati himself dwells in this tree, and he has been insulted today by these ministers of yours out of ignorance.
For they were impure, having neither sipped water nor washed their hands and feet; afflicted by hunger and desiring fruit, they had climbed up into this dwelling.
Then, once they were touched there, they attained the very state of fruits; by the curse of Vighneśa, they went to whatever state their minds were directed toward.
Moreover, those other four ministers of yours who came by this same path likewise mounted upon it and attained the state of its fruit.
Therefore, propitiate this leader of the Gaṇas with austerities; through his grace, the accomplishment of all your desires shall come to pass.
Thus addressed from the sky by a voice that seemed to pour forth a shower of nectar, Mṛgāṅkadatta regained his resolve and desisted from abandoning his body.
Having bathed in the lake and worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas beneath that tree, he abandoned all food and, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise to him.

Victory to you, O Lord with the face of an elephant, who are being prostrated to by the entire world—including its mountains, forests, and the earth itself—as it bows down, weighed down by the crushing burden of your own majestic *tāṇḍava* dance.

Victory to you, whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by the three worlds including the gods, asuras, and humans; O treasure-store overflowing with various supreme siddhis, whose form resembles a water-pot!

Victory to you, whose blazing splendor is like twelve fierce suns risen simultaneously, and who bring about the untimely end of the world for the hosts of Daityas who are invincible even to Hara, Hari, and the Lord of the Gods!

Victory to You, O Dispeller of the afflictions of Your devotees, whose palm shines with the flame of fire held in the hand like an excellent axe, appearing as if it were the torch of a playful *nīrājana* rite!
O Gaṇeśa, you who were worshipped by Gaurī as well for the sake of her husband’s desired success in the conquest of Tripura—I have taken refuge in you; let there be salutation to you!
Having thus praised the Lord of Obstacles, Mṛgāṅkadatta spent that night without food on a bed of kusha grass at the foot of that tree.
In that very manner, devoted to the propitiation of Vighneśa, the prince spent eleven days with Śrutadhi as his attendant.
On the night of the twelfth day, Gaṇeśvara spoke to him in a dream: "Child, I am pleased with you; you shall regain your ministers, released from their curse."
And having gone with them and gradually found that Śaśāṅkavatī, you shall return to your own city and rule the kingdom of the earth.
Thus instructed by Gaṇeśvara at the end of the night, the awakened Mṛgāṅkadatta related that dream he had seen to Śrutadhi.
Having been welcomed by him, he bathed in the morning, worshipped Vināyaka, and performed a circumambulation of that tree where he had stayed.
Then, having descended from that tree together, all ten of those ministers, now called "fruits," fell at his feet.
Vyāghrasena, as well as Sthūlabāhu and Meghabala, and Dṛḍhamuṣṭi as the fourth—these six who were described here at the beginning.

Then, having suddenly encountered all those ministers together with a gaze agitated by emotion and a voice faltering with joy, the virtuous son of the lord of men looked upon each one repeatedly with exceeding affection, embraced them, and thereafter conversed with them.

Seeing their lord emaciated like the new moon and having performed austerities, they shed tears; and having heard the truth as declared by Śrutadhi, they praised him and did not consider themselves to be of any purpose.

Then, having regained his composure for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, Mṛgāṅkadatta joyfully performed a pleasant breaking of his fast right there in the lake together with his ministers, after they had bathed and attended to their other needs.

Thus ends the thirty-third wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The thirty-fourth wave: Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, having completed his fast and being well-rested on the shore of that lake, sat down together with those ministers of his.
Then, when those four of his own ministers arrived that day, he respectfully questioned them regarding the events of their time away from him.
Then that one named Vyāghrasena, from among them, said to him: "O King, please listen to our story; I shall describe it."
When, due to the curse of that nāga named Pārāvata, I fell far away from you and became deprived of my senses;
Then, having wandered through the forest at night, although I regained consciousness after a long time, I could see neither the directions nor the path, being shrouded in darkness.
And when that long night of painful hardship had passed, the Blessed Sun arose, gradually illuminating the quarters of the sky.
I thought, "Alas, what a pity! Where has our lord gone? And how will he fare here, alone and separated from us?"
"How shall I find him? Where shall I search? What is my recourse? It would be better for me to go to Ujjayinī; perhaps he might be found there."
"She must indeed go for the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī, for she is staying there"—with this hope, I slowly set out toward Ujjayinī.
Then, entering that difficult forest which was like a state of misfortune, he was scorched by the sun's rays as if by heaps of burning embers.
Somehow I reached a lake whose lotuses were like eyes, which seemed to engage in conversation through the sweet cries of swans and other birds.
Like a virtuous person who, by his very sight, removes all suffering, he extends the tips of his hands with waves of grace and possesses a serene and vast intention.
Having bathed there, eaten, and drunk the water along with lotus stalks, while I remained there, I saw these three arrive.
Then, having approached Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Sthūlabāhu, and Meghabala, we inquired among ourselves after your welfare.
And though we were all ignorant of this, fearing some evil, we resolved to give up our lives, unable to endure separation from you.
Just then, a young ascetic son of Dīrghatapas, named Mahātapa, arrived at that lake to bathe.
With his own flames matted together like braided hair, he was like Agni once more desiring to consume the Khāṇḍava forest; blazing with splendor, he took recourse in a body of Brahmanic nature.
Clad in a black antelope skin, holding a water-pot in his left hand, and bearing a rosary and a ring in his right hand.
Accompanied by deer that had come together to bathe in the mud dug up by their horns, he was joined by a few other young sons of sages who were his equals.
Upon seeing us prepared to leap into the lake, he approached us; for the virtuous are the kinsmen of all without cause, their hearts moistened with compassion.
And he said: "You must not commit evil deeds worthy of base men; for those who are blinded by suffering and cowardly fall indeed into the abysses of calamity."
But the wise, who have seen the true path and possess the stainless eye of discernment, do not fall into the pit; they reach what is to be reached and certainly attain it.
And you possess auspicious forms; you will surely attain well-being. Therefore, tell me: what is the sorrow that afflicts your minds? For my own heart is pained.
When the son of the sage had spoken thus, I immediately related my entire history to him from the very beginning.
Then, having been awakened by him with various words that revealed the future, we were dissuaded from abandoning our bodies, even though he was accompanied by his followers.
Then, having bathed, that young son of a sage led us, not very far from there, to his father’s hermitage, desiring to offer us hospitality.
There, even the trees—with their high branches and arms raised upward, standing upon the altars as if they had begun a penance—seemed to drink in the rays of the sun.
Having seated us in one place and offered us water for our feet, that son of the sage went to each of the trees of the hermitage and begged for alms.
In an instant, his alms-bowl was filled with fruits that had fallen of their own accord from those trees; then, taking it, he came into our presence.
And he gave us those fruits of divine flavor, by eating which we then became satisfied as if by nectar.
When the day had waned and the sun had fallen into the ocean, the sky was filled with celestial lights, as if by sprays of water splashed up by that very fall.
As if out of aversion to that very thing, the moon took refuge on the peak of the eastern mountain—a grove of asceticism—clad in bark garments washed white by the moonlight.
We went there to visit the sages who were seated together in one place in that hermitage, having completed all their respective duties.
Having prostrated and sat down, we were quickly asked by those great sages—who had offered us hospitality and spoke kindly—“From where have you come?”
Then, that young sage related to them the entire account concerning us, ending with our entry into his hermitage.
Then, a wise sage named Kaṇva spoke to us there: "O sirs, why have you, though being heroic men, fallen into such cowardice?"
Maintaining steadfastness in adversity, remaining free from pride in prosperity, and never abandoning one's zeal—this indeed is the vow of a virtuous man.
And the great ones, having crossed over even great hardships through fortitude and having attained great goals, have acquired the title of "Great."
This is the story of Sundarasena; hear now how he experienced such suffering for the sake of Mandāravatī.
Having spoken thus, that sage Kaṇva, while all the great ṛṣis and we ourselves were listening, related this story.
There is a country named Niṣadha, which adorns the face of the northern quarter; in that land, there once existed a city named Alakā.
In that city, the people were always happy, with every purpose fulfilled; the only thing that never ceased was the burning of the jewel-lamps.
In that city there was a lord of the earth named Mahāsena, whose name was true to his character; though born of Śaraja (the god of fire), he scorched his enemies with a fierce and terrible heat.
That king had a great minister named Guṇapālita, who was an abode of valor and a bearer of the earth's burden like another Śeṣa.
While the king was thus happy, having laid down his burden and destroyed his enemies, a son was born to him by the queen named Śaśiprabhā.
He who was named Sundarasena, though but a child yet not a child in his virtues, was chosen as his own husband by the goddesses of valor and beauty.
In this place, that prince had five heroic ministers who were equal to him in age and virtue, having grown up together with him since childhood.
Caṇḍaprabha, Bhīmabhuja, as well as Vyāghraparākrama, the hero Vikramaśakti, and Dṛḍhabuddhi was the fifth.
And all those great beings were endowed with strength and intelligence; they were of noble birth, devoted to their master, and even possessed knowledge of the cries of birds.
There, in his father's house, the prince lived together with them; though young, he remained without a wife and without a companion, as he lacked a suitable bride.
In this world, a man is honored for valor that does not retreat, for wealth earned by one's own arms, and for a wife who is a worthy match for his beauty.
Otherwise, what would be the use of even these three? Thus thought Sundarasena, that hero, together with his ministers.
And once, accompanied by his armies and those five companions, that prince went out from the city for the sake of hunting.
And as he was departing, a certain eminent female ascetic named Kātyāyanī, who had come from a distant land, saw him.
"Is this the moon accompanied by Rohiṇī, or is it the Love-god who brings no pleasure? Thus she reflected upon that superhuman form as she gazed at it.
And having learned from his attendants that he was a prince, she marveled, praising the Creator’s wondrous variety in creation.
Then, with a voice that was distant yet long-drawn out, she bowed down to the prince, saying, "O Kumāra, may you be victorious!"
But Sundarasena, not even hearing that, departed at that very moment with a mind preoccupied by the conversation begun by his own ministers.
Then, making herself heard loudly, that angry female ascetic said to him: "O Prince, why indeed do you not listen even to my blessing?"
"Whom on earth have I not honored—whether kings or princes—if such is this pride of yours arising from youth and the like?"
"You shall obtain as your wife that maiden Mandāravatī, the daughter of the lord of Haṃsadvīpa, who is the ornament of the world."
Therefore, I think that you will certainly not hear my words even from Mahendra and the other gods due to your arrogance; what then of wretched mortals?
Having heard her speak thus, Sundarasena, full of curiosity, called her to him and, bowing low, asked forgiveness from that female ascetic.
And he sent his servants to the house of his minister Vikramaśakti for rest, desiring to question him.
Then, having gone out and returned from his hunt, the prince performed his daily rites; he summoned her after she had finished her meal and questioned her.
"O Blessed One, please tell us: who is this maiden named Mandāravatī whom you have mentioned today? For our curiosity is indeed great."
Having heard that, the female ascetic said to him: "Listen, I shall tell you this: for the sake of visiting sacred fords and such, I wander this earth with its various continents."
Wandering about, I arrived at Haṃsadvīpa by chance; there, I beheld the daughter of King Mandāradeva.
Worthy of being enjoyed by the sons of gods and visible only to those of meritorious deeds, she who bears the name Mandāravatī is like the goddess Śrī herself in the Nandana grove.
Bearing a golden form that kindles the god of love upon being seen, she was created by the Creator as another lunar body composed of nectar.
On this earth, there is truly no one else who resembles her in beauty; I know that you alone emulate the perfection of her form.
"Those by whom she has not been seen, their eyes and their very birth are fruitless. Having heard this from the mouth of the female ascetic, the prince said:
"O Mother, how can we see her form as it truly is? Having heard these words of theirs, the female ascetic replied:
Out of passion, I carry her—painted upon a canvas at that very moment—inside a magic pouch; let this be seen as a marvel.
When she had spoken thus to the gratified prince, she drew [the figure] from the casket and showed it to him as it stood in the painting.
