And Sundarasena, gazing upon that maiden of wondrous form—even though she was depicted in a painting—stood motionless with joy.
At that moment, he sat with his limbs bristling with horripilation, as if pinned down by the dense arrows of the Flower-Bowed God.
Gradually, no longer hearing, speaking, or seeing anything at all, he became absorbed in that [state] and remained for a long time as if depicted in a painting.
Seeing that, the ministers said to that ascetic woman: "Noble lady, paint King Sundarasena here upon this canvas."
"Let us first observe your skill in painting portraits. Upon hearing this, she painted the prince on a canvas in an instant.
Seeing that it was so exceedingly similar, everyone there said this: "There is not even the slightest discrepancy between the painting and the Blessed Lady."
For the thought indeed arises regarding this painting: "This is the prince himself"; thus, the form of Queen Mandāravatī here does not contradict [the reality].
When the ministers had spoken thus, Sundarasena, having taken the two painted cloths, joyfully honored that female ascetic.
And having dismissed her—who had been living in one place—according to what was appropriate, he entered his inner apartment, carrying the portrait of his beloved.
Is this her face, or is it the moon whose stains have been washed away by her radiance? Are these her breasts, or rather the two consecration jars of the God of Love for his royal coronation?
Are these the waves of the ocean of her form—the three folds of her waist—or is this her hip, or perhaps the pleasure-couch of Rati?
Thus, contemplating Mandāravatī limb by limb as she appeared there in the painting, he remained prostrate upon his bed.
Remaining in that very state day after day, turning his back on food and other necessities, and overcome by the weight of the fever of love, he became [emaciated] in just a few days.
Having learned of this, his parents, Śaśiprabhā and Mahāsena, came and privately asked his friends the cause of his ill health.
And those companions of theirs told them everything exactly as it was, explaining how the daughter of the king of Haṃsadvīpa had become the cause of these events.
Then Mahāsena said to Sundarasena: "Son, why is this attachment of yours being concealed? It is indeed appropriate."
For that jewel of a maiden, Mandāravatī, is indeed worthy of you alone; and her father, King Mandāradeva, is my supreme friend.

"What kind of harassment can there be regarding a matter that is already settled by his messenger and appropriate? Having spoken thus to him and deliberated, they went to ask for that maiden from him."
That King Mahāsena dispatched an envoy named Suratadeva to Haṃsadvīpa for King Mandāradeva.
She gave him that portrait of Sundarasena, painted by the female ascetic on a canvas, which revealed the excellence of his beauty.
That messenger traveled swiftly and reached a city on the shore of the ocean belonging to King Mahendrāditya, known by the name Śaśāṅkapura.
Then, having embarked upon a ship, he reached that island of Haṃsa, and in a few days, he arrived at the palace of King Mandāradeva.
Announced by the doorkeepers, the messenger entered there, looked inside, and having presented a gift of wealth, spoke to the king according to what had occurred.
"O Great King, this was commanded to you by King Mahāsena: 'Give your own daughter to my son Sundarasena.'"
For she, known by the name Kātyāyanī, was indeed painted upon a cloth; that jewel of a maiden was brought here by the female ascetic and shown to me.
And because our desire was kindled by the likeness of his form, we had his portrait painted on a canvas; let the portrait of Sundarasena sent here also be viewed.
Moreover, this man, being unlike others in appearance, does not desire marriage without a wife who resembles him; and your daughter alone is her counterpart.
Having thus instructed him, he said: "This cloth was presented to me by the king; let it be viewed, and let the divine Mādhavī creeper be joined [to it] now."
Hearing these words of the messenger, the king joyfully had Mandāravatī and her mother, who were both asleep, brought before him.
Having opened it together with those two and seen that painted cloth, he abandoned his pride, thinking, "There is no one on earth equal to my daughter."
And he said: "If it is possible for this prince, then the creation of my daughter's beauty will have been fruitful."
For without him she does not shine, nor does he shine without her; for what is a lotus-pond without a swan, and what is a swan without a lotus-pond?
When the king had spoken thus, and while the queen was exceedingly full of faith, that Mandāravatī immediately became infatuated with passion.
With her wide-open eyes motionless, she stood fixed upon the painted canvas—like one possessed, like one asleep yet awake, and like one depicted in a painting.
Then Mandāradeva, seeing his daughter in such a state, accepted that gift and honored the messenger accordingly.
On another day, he dispatched that man as an envoy and sent his own Brahmin named Kumāradatta as a counter-envoy to King Mahāsena.
And having gone to that Lord of Alakā, he spoke to both of them: "Go quickly and say to King Mahāsena these words of mine."
"Out of friendship, I have already given my daughter; therefore, let it be said: should your son come here, or should the daughter be sent here?"
Having been given these instructions by the king, the two messengers then departed together by ship along the sea route with great haste.
Then, having reached Śaśāṅkapura by way of land, the two of them arrived at that prosperous city, which was like the city of Alakā.
Then, having approached and entered the royal palace as was appropriate, they beheld King Mahāsena, who had shown them due honor.
And they delivered that counter-message spoken by Mandāradeva to the king; and having heard it, he was pleased and honored them both.
And having inquired from the father’s messenger about the girl’s birth star, that king asked the astrologers for an auspicious moment for his son’s marriage.
And after three months, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika, they declared an auspicious moment for the marriage of the bride and the groom.
At that auspicious moment, the Lord of Alakā then dispatched his son for the marriage and sent word to Mandāradeva.
Having written it upon a letter for Kumāradatta, that other messenger named Candrasvāmin, and for himself, he placed it in their hands.
And those two messengers, having gone from there and delivered the letter exactly as it was, related everything before the lord of Haṃsadvīpa.
The king, having said "So be it," dismissed the honored Candrasvāmin, who was the messenger of Mahāsena, back to the presence of his own master.
When he had returned to Alakā, having determined the course of action to be taken, all those on both sides remained waiting for the auspicious moment.
Meanwhile, on Haṃsadvīpa, Mandāravatī had already conceived a passion for him long before she had even seen the painted canvas.
Having learned of that marriage hour, she, unable to endure even a moment's delay, became intensely eager for her beloved and was consumed by the fire of love.
A rain of glowing coals upon the body, even when anointed with sandalwood paste; a bed of lotus leaves that becomes a layer of scorching sand.
Alas, even the rays of the moon became like the blazing crests of a forest fire to her, whose heart was captivated by Sundarasena.
Maintaining silence, abstaining from food, and observing a vow of separation, she was questioned by her distressed and trusted friend and spoke thus with great difficulty.
"Friend, my wedding is far off, and I am unable to wait for that time without the son of the Lord of Alakā as my bridegroom."
The place is distant, the time is long, and the course of destiny is manifold; therefore, who here in this interval knows what will happen to whom?
Saying, "Therefore, I must surely die," Mandāravatī, distressed by separation, immediately fell into a critical state.
Having learned this from the mouth of her friend and having seen her in such a state, her father, together with his wife and ministers, held a consultation.
That King Mahāsena, the lord of Alakā, is our friend; and this Mandāravatī is unable to endure the passage of time here.
Therefore, let her shame be as it may; let her be sent right there, for staying near her beloved, she will endure the delay with fortitude.
Having reflected thus and consoled his daughter Mandāravatī, he placed her upon a ship together with her wealth and her attendants.
Then, on an auspicious day, she was sent from Haṃsadvīpa by way of the sea to her mother, who had performed the marriage rites according to tradition for the sake of the wedding.
Having bestowed his own minister, named Vinītamati, upon him, King Mandāradeva sent him off toward Alakā.
Then, for some days, as the princess Mandāravatī traveled upon the great ocean by means of the ship, she proceeded.
Suddenly, the thief-like cloud arose, thundering, emitting a fierce wind with a whistling sound and discharging a multitude of arrow-like rain-showers.
And in an instant, as if dragged far away by a powerful force like Fate itself, her ship, being battered by the wind, was shattered.
When that retinue had been drawn away along with Vinītamati, her entire treasury sank into the great ocean.
But the ocean, with its wave-arms, lifted that princess while she was still alive, carried her off, and then cast her down near the forest on the shore.
Where is a fall into the ocean, and where is being carried away by a towering wave into the forest? Alas, behold: nothing is seen to be impossible for that which is destined to be.
Then, in that desolate forest, she—terrified and overwhelmed upon seeing herself all alone—plunged once more into an ocean of sorrow.
Where have I set out for? Where have I arrived? And where is my retinue? Where is Vinītamati? What is this sudden change in my state?
"Where shall I, unfortunate as I am, go? Alas, I am ruined; what can I do? O cursed Fate, why was I brought out from the ocean by you?"
"Alas, father! Alas, mother! Alas, noble son, lord of Alakā! Since I am perishing without having reached you, look—why do you not save me?"
Lamenting in this way and more, Mandāravatī wept bitterly with tears resembling the pearls from a broken necklace.
And at that moment, the sage named Mataṅga emerged from a hermitage situated not far away in order to bathe in the waters of the ocean.
Accompanied by his daughter named Yamunā, who had been a celibate since childhood, that sage heard the sound of her weeping.
Approaching her out of compassion, he, accompanied by his son, beheld her like a doe strayed from the herd, casting her pained eyes in all directions.
"Who are you here in this forest, how did you come to be here, and why do you weep?"—thus the great seer questioned her with affectionate words.
Then, seeing him full of compassion, Mandāravatī, bowing low with shame, slowly comforted him and told him her own story.
Then, having made this vow, the sage Mataṅga said to her: "O princess, enough with despair; regain your composure."
The flood of afflictions oppresses you, whose limbs are as delicate as the śirīṣa flower; for do calamities ever consider whether one is fragile or not?
"You shall obtain your desired husband before long; therefore, come now to my hermitage, which is not far from here."

"Therefore, stay here in my own home together with this daughter of mine. Having thus comforted her and performed his ablutions, the great sage, accompanied by his daughter, led Mandāravatī to his own hermitage.
There she remained self-restrained, longing for union with her husband, accompanied by his son and diverting herself with service to that ṛṣi.
In the meantime, he remained constantly in Alakā, counting the days, looking forward to the day of his marriage with Mandāravatī.
In due course, Sundarasena also, who had been emaciated by long-standing longing, remained there being consoled by his own friends, Caṇḍaprabha and the others.
And as the day of the auspicious conjunction gradually drew near, the father, the king, made preparations for his departure toward Haṃsadvīpa.
Then, on an auspicious day, having performed the rites of departure, Prince Sundarasena set forth, making the earth tremble with his armies.
Proceeding by stages, accompanied by his ministers, he reached with joy that city of Śaśāṅkapura, which was an ornament upon the shore of the ocean.
There, having been met by King Mahendrāditya who was bowed low in humility, he entered along with his followers.
With the splendor of his form resembling a whirlwind, he reached the royal palace on his mounted elephant, like a wind entering a forest of lotus-ponds consisting of the city women.
There, having been received with honor by King Mahendrāditya, who had come forward to escort him, he rested for that day.
Or else, having crossed the ocean, may I reach that beloved woman, who is characterized by the bashfulness and timidity natural to a newlywed bride.
"And may I hear her crying out 'No, no! as she is being embraced"—with such longings as these, he passed that night.
In the morning, having stationed his own army right there in the city, he went to the shore of the ocean accompanied by Mahendrāditya.
There, together with that king, he himself boarded a single great ship filled with food and water, accompanied by his own ministers.
In the second carriage, the prince loaded his retinue, which had been necessarily reduced and made concise.
Then, once the ship was set free with its sails and banners fluttering in the wind, the two of them set out toward the south-western direction.
When two or three days had passed as they were traveling toward the ocean, a great and portentous wind suddenly arose there.
As if out of wonder, thinking, "Oh, what an unprecedented wind this is!", the rows of forests on the shores of the ocean began to sway violently.
And the masses of water from the ocean were repeatedly overturned by the wind, shifting from bottom to top, like worldly conditions through the passage of time.
Together with his cry, he offered jewels as a price to the great ocean; together with his effort, he cast aside the sail-cloth by means of the helmsmen.
While all, along with their hopes for life, were filled with agitation, heavy chains were fastened everywhere upon the rocks.
Tossed up and cast down by the waves like elephants bound in the ocean, those two ships reeled about as if engaged in combat.
Then Sundarasena, having seen that, moved from his seat due to the influence of his fortitude and said this to King Mahendrāditya:
"Due to my lack of merit, this sudden destruction has come upon you; therefore, I cannot bear to look upon it and shall cast myself into the ocean."
Having spoken thus, the prince quickly girded his loins with his upper garment and threw himself into the ocean there.
Seeing that, his five companions, Caṇḍaprabha and the others, together with Mahendrāditya, threw themselves right there.
Crossing the rivers with their arms, they were free from agitation; yet all of them were scattered here and there, tossed about by the force of the waves.
And in an instant, when the wind had subsided, the ocean became silent and still, resembling a virtuous man whose anger has been pacified.
And at that moment, Sundarasena, accompanied by Dṛḍhabuddhi, reached a small vessel that had been brought there from somewhere by the wind.
And he ascended it together with that one minister, as if onto another swing suspended between life and death.
Then, not knowing the direction and seeing everything as if it were composed of water, his manly courage having failed, he sought refuge in the gods.
Propelled by a gentle and favorable wind as if by fate itself, the ship reached the shore in three days.
Then, as that boat reached the shore, he, accompanied by his own self alone, simultaneously ascended both the dry land and the hope for life.
Having rested there, he spoke to Dṛḍhabuddhi: "Though I have crossed the ocean, I have gone even deeper than Pātāla."
From him [he obtained] Vikramaśakti, Vyāghraparākrama, Caṇḍaprabha, Bhīmabhuja, and likewise those ministers of such a kind.
Having now destroyed King Mahendrāditya, who was a friend without cause, and all others, what beauty is there for me in living?
When he had spoken thus, the minister Dṛḍhabuddhi said to him: "O King, take heart; I know that prosperity awaits us."
For just as we have, so too might they cross the ocean at some point; indeed, by whom can the course of destiny, which is difficult to discern, be determined?
While Dṛḍhabuddhi was speaking such various words as these, two ascetics arrived there for the purpose of bathing.
Seeing the prince thus despondent, those two virtuous men approached him, inquired about his situation, and spoke to him with compassion.
O wise one, even the gods who bestow happiness and suffering are not able to alter the power of past karma; it cannot be made otherwise.
Therefore, the wise person who wishes to abandon suffering should perform virtuous deeds; for that is the remedy for it, not grief, which only emaciates the body.
Therefore, abandon this despondency and protect your body with fortitude; for as long as the body exists, what human goal indeed cannot be accomplished?
"You possess auspicious marks, and surely prosperity awaits you. Having spoken thus and comforted them, the two sages led them to their own hermitage.
Then, waiting there for some days, Prince Sundarasena remained together with Dṛḍhabuddhi.
In the meantime, both his minister Bhīmabhuja and Vikramaśakti crossed the ocean with their arms and reached the shore separately.
And out of the hope that he too might one day emerge like us, the two of them, bewildered by suffering, entered a great forest while searching for him.
The two remaining ministers, Caṇḍaprabha and Vyāghraparākrama, as well as King Mahendrāditya, likewise crossed the ocean.
Distressed at not finding Sundarasena after searching for him, and sorrowful because their ship had been seized and wrecked, they went to that city of Śaśāṅkapura.
Then those two ministers, having learned the news there, went weeping with that army previously stationed there to their own city of Alakā.
When those who were not princes had arrived and were lamenting, that city became composed solely of wailing, with its people weeping aloud.
And King Mahāsena, together with his queen, having heard that news of his son, did not abandon his life-force; such was the power of his longevity.
And his ministers restrained him as he was intent on abandoning his body, along with the queen, by means of various words that demonstrated hope and logical reasoning.
Then, outside the city at the Svayambhū shrine, the king remained with his followers, performing austerities while searching for news of his son.
Meanwhile, King Mandāradeva in Haṃsadvīpa also learned the news of his daughter's and his son-in-law's fall into the ocean.
And he heard that his two sons-in-law and ministers had reached Alakā, while King Mahāsena remained established in asceticism, having renounced all hope for life.
Then that king as well, distressed by grief for his daughter and dissuaded from his attempt at death by various ministers upon whom he had entrusted the burden of state, [remained].
Accompanied by Queen Kandarpasenā, he went to the side of King Mahāsena in his city of Alakā, sharing in his sorrow.
"Once he has ascertained the news regarding his son, whatever he decides to do, I shall certainly do that very same thing along with him."
Having learned the news concerning Mandāravatī, King Mahāsena, overcome with even greater sorrow, met with him and lamented together.
Together with him, the lord of Haṃsadvīpa also remained there practicing austerities with his senses restrained, eating sparingly, and sleeping upon darbha grass.
When they had all been thus scattered here and there by the Creator, like leaves by the wind, he set out from his own hermitage.
By chance, Sundarasena reached the vicinity of that hermitage of the sage Mataṅga, where Mandāravatī was staying.
There he beheld a lake of clear water, its banks covered by trees bent down with many ripe fruits of various flavors.
Exhausted from that journey, having bathed there and eaten sweet fruits, Dṛḍhabuddhi went on with him as his companion and reached a river in the forest.
And as he was walking along its bank, past the side of a temple dedicated to a *liṅga*, he saw the daughters of sages busily engaged in gathering flowers.
In their midst, he beheld a maiden who was uniquely beautiful like the ruddy goose, illuminating the entire forest with her radiance as if with moonlight.
With her glances, she made the quarters of the sky appear like blooming blue lotuses, and with the placement of her feet upon the earth, she spread a forest of lotuses.
Who is this, worthy of being gazed upon by the thousand-eyed Indra—is she an apsaras, or is she the beauty of the forest with her sprout-like hands clinging to the flowers?
Surely this most wonderful body was fashioned by the Creator through the long practice of creating many celestial women.
"Ah! This [form] resembles that of my beloved Mandāravatī, whose appearance I have seen in a painting; could it indeed be she herself?"
How is this? Where is that Haṃsadvīpa, and where is this forest region? We do not know who she is, from where she comes, or why this beautiful woman is here.
Thus the prince spoke to Dṛḍhabuddhi, and Dṛḍhabuddhi, having seen that excellent maiden, then said this.
O Lord, this manner of hers—this arrangement of necklaces, waist-bands, girdles, and other ornaments—is truly something else entirely, even though they are made only of forest flowers.
Nor does such beauty or such delicacy as this occur in the forest; therefore, she must be either a divine being, a princess, or perhaps the daughter of some ṛṣi.
When Dṛḍhabuddhi said, "Let us both stand up for a moment to find out what is here," they both remained standing there, concealed by the trees.
Meanwhile, those hermit maidens, having gathered flowers, descended with that excellent maiden to bathe in that river.
While they were engaged in water-sports there, by the power of fate, that very same excellent maiden was seized by a crocodile that had come up.
Upon seeing that at that very moment, those maidens, terrified and overwhelmed, cried out in distress: "Save us! Save us, O forest deities!"
For here Mandāravatī, bathing unsuspectingly in the river, has been suddenly seized by a crocodile that came upon her; alas, she is perishing!
Upon hearing this, Sundarasena ran forward, thinking, "Could it be she, my beloved? and quickly slew that crocodile with his dagger.
Then, having quickly pulled her out from that [water] as if from the mouth of Death onto the bank, he comforted Mandāravatī.
Having crossed over her fear and beholding that handsome man, she thought: "Who is this great-souled giver of life who has come here through my good fortune?"
It is wonderful how very similar this is to that noble-born lord of my life, the son of the Lord of Alakā, whom I beheld in the painting.
"Could it really be him? Fie, fie upon my evil thought! May such a person as he, staying in a foreign land, never meet with harm!"
Therefore, it is not proper for me to remain now in the presence of another man; I shall depart from here, and may it be well with this great-souled one.
Having reflected thus, Mandāravatī said to her friends: "Having paid homage to this illustrious man, let us now depart."
Having heard that, the prince named Bahusādhāra—whose doubts had not yet been dispelled even by the mere hearing of the name—then [addressed] her friend.
There, Sundarasena asked one of them: "Tell me, auspicious lady, whose daughter is this friend of yours, and what is she like? For I am curious."
When he had asked this, the hermit maiden replied to him: "This is the daughter of King Mandāradeva, the lord of Haṃsadvīpa."
The daughter named Mandāravatī, a maiden being led to the city of Alakā to be given in marriage to Prince Sundarasena, was carried away.
Her vessel shattered in the ocean, she was cast upon the shore by the waves; it is said that after being brought here, she reached the hermitage of the sage Mataṅga.
When she had spoken thus, his friend Dṛḍhabuddhi, seeing Sundarasena agitated by both joy and despair, spoke to him as he was dancing.
"By good fortune, you are prospering today through the recovery of Queen Mandāravatī; for she is indeed this very person who was not even within the path of our imagination."
Having spoken thus, that friend informed the inquiring hermit-maidens of the entire account, delighting her friend in their presence.
Then, crying out "O noble son! Mandāravatī fell weeping at Sundarasena's feet.
He too embraced her and wept; and as the two of them wept there, even the logs and the blades of grass wept, moistened with compassion.
Then, having been quickly informed by those daughters of the sage, the sage Mataṅga arrived there accompanied by Yamunā.
Having thus comforted Sundarasena, who bowed at his feet, he led him, together with Mandāravatī, to his own hermitage.
On that day, having rested from those hospitable attentions and having attained peace, the great sage spoke to the prince on the following day.
"My son, I must now go to Śvetadvīpa for a certain purpose; therefore, you should go toward Alakā accompanied by Mandāravatī."
There, you should marry this daughter of the king and protect her; for she has been accepted by me as my own daughter and entrusted to you.
And for a very long time you shall rule the earth together with her; and before long, you shall regain all your own ministers.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him along with his daughter-in-law, the sage departed through the sky together with Yamunā, his daughter who was his own equal.
Then Sundarasena also, accompanied by Mandāravatī and with Dṛḍhabuddhi as his companion, set out from that hermitage.
Having reached the shore of the ocean, he saw a small vessel that had approached nearby, presided over by some young merchant.
And out of greed for the ease of the journey, he requested shelter from that merchant’s son, the husband of Dṛḍhabuddhi, who was nearby.
Seeing Mandāravatī, the merchant, deluded by love, likewise brought his vessel to the shore.
Then Sundarasena, having placed his beloved in front of him there on the bank, stood waiting until he himself desired to mount.
Then that rogue merchant, lusting after another's wife, gave a signal to the helmsman and quickly set the ship in motion.
And as Sundarasena was looking on, that vehicle of his, along with the weeping prince, became invisible in an instant.
Crying out, "Alas! Woe! I have been robbed by thieves," he fell down; and as he lamented there for a long time, he was addressed by Dṛḍhabuddhi.
"Arise and abandon this despondency; this is not the conduct befitting a hero. Come, let us go by this path to search for that thief."
"Even in the midst of terrible calamity, the wise do not abandon their resolve"—having been thus exhorted by that firm-minded one, Sundarasena somehow rose from the shore of the ocean and set out.
And as he proceeded, gradually lamenting, "Alas, my Queen! Alas, Mandāravatī!", he wept incessantly, tormented by the fire of separation.
Without food, accompanied only by his weeping and resolute-minded followers, he entered the great forest as if in a swoon, lost in utter delusion.
And there he did not take into account his friend's beneficial words; rather, being entirely absorbed by his beloved, he rushed hither and thither.

With blossoms for ornaments like those of a flower not yet closed, the creeper-vines appear as if they have come to meet their beloved who has fled from a thief—a merchant—now that they have fully bloomed.
"Has she, submerged in the lake out of fear, raised her face with its long-lashed eyes to look at me?"—thus [he thought] among the lotuses and the rice plants.
"What is she saying here? This charming-voiced girl is addressing me," [he thought] even amidst the warbling of cuckoos hidden by leafy creepers.
Thus, becoming bewildered at every step, he wandered for a long time with equal day and night, being scorched by both the sun and the moon as if they were alike.
Having somehow emerged from that forest, the prince of firm resolve, having lost his way, then reached a vast wilderness.
It was as difficult to behold as an army of bandits, fierce with uplifted swords, terrifying due to the presence of lions, and frequented by hosts of marauders.
As he was plunging into that place, which was difficult to traverse, full of many dangers, and without refuge, he encountered Pulindas with raised weapons, as if entering a state of misery.
By the command of Vindhyaketu, the lord of the Pulindas, the inhabitants of that region were being rounded up as human victims for sacrifice to the Goddess.
Foreign lands, the suffering of separation, humiliation from the base, lack of food, and the heat of the journey—such is the conflagration of the five fires.
Then the great sage created a sixth fire, a torrent of demons, in order to test the limit of that prince's fortitude.
Accompanied by only himself, he slew with a dagger those many bandits who were rushing toward him to seize him and showering him with arrows.
Having learned of that, the king dispatched another force led by Vindhyaketu; yet he, skilled in battle, slew even many more thieves than that.
Then, though he was accompanied by his companions, he—wounded, exhausted, and fainting—was bound by those Śabaras, led away, and cast into a prison.
There, the place was strewn with swarms of insects, fouled by the dwellings of spiders, and indicated the movement of snakes by their sloughs hanging from crevices.
In that place, where dust rose ankle-deep, where it was terrifying with rat holes gaping wide, and which was crowded with many terrified and afflicted people cast inside;
Just as if at the birthplace of hells, the two ministers first saw both of them standing there, bound and brought from elsewhere.
Those two, Bhīma and Vikramaśakti, who had crossed the ocean and entered that forest to search for their lord, spoke thus.
Recognizing them as they wept, the two fell at his feet; he too, recognizing them, embraced them around the neck, choked with tears.
Then, their suffering increased a hundredfold from seeing one another; they were addressed by other prisoners who remained there, seeking to comfort them.
What can be done with suffering? Is it possible to transcend one's past karma? Do you not see that death stands present for all of us alike?
"On the coming fourteenth day, these very people have been gathered by this King Pulinda for the purpose of being offered as animal sacrifices to the Goddess."
Therefore, why grieve? The course of destiny, which plays with living beings, is diverse; just as it has bestowed misfortune upon you, so may that very same power bestow fortune upon you.
Having been addressed thus by those held in captivity, they remained there bound; alas, how great is the heartlessness of calamities, even toward those in the midst of immense misfortune!
And when the fourteenth day arrived, they were all led by the king's command to the temple of Ambikā for the purpose of being offered as a sacrifice.
With tongues like flickering flames and mountains, with rows of teeth like bells, and with the severed heads of heroes clinging to it, it was as terrible as the very mouth of Death.
There, having seen that queen and bowed before her, Sundarasena, with a mind overwhelmed by devotion, praised her and made this request:
To her who, with her trident that shatters the arrogant daityas and rains down streams of weapons, has quelled the torment of the asuras, and who grants fearlessness to those who bow before her.
Extinguish [my suffering] with your gracious eye, raining down nectar; O Goddess, you have been seen by me who am consumed by the forest fire of misery—homage be to you!
Even as that prince was speaking thus, Vindhyaketu, the king of the Pulindas, arrived there to pay homage to the goddess.
Upon seeing and recognizing that Bhilla king, Sundarasena, bowed his head in shame and spoke privately to his own companions.
"Aha! This is that very lord of the Pulindas, Vindhyaketu, who approaches my father's side for the sake of service and frequents this great forest."
Therefore, let it be; we should not say anything here, for death is better for a man of honor than such a revelation of oneself.
While the prince was thus consulting with his friends, King Vindhyaketu addressed his own servants.
Show me that great hero, my mighty beast, by whom so many of my warriors have been slain while he was being captured.
Upon hearing that, Sundarasena—smeared with dried blood and grey with wounds—was brought before him by his servants.
Upon seeing him and recognizing him somewhat, that lord of the Pulindas, filled with apprehension, asked: "Tell me, who are you and from where have you come?"
Sundarasena replied to that lord of the Bhillas: "I am he; do whatever you wish, for what is the use of this to you?"
Then, having recognized him through their conversation, Vindhyaketu fell to the ground in a state of agitation, crying out, "Alas! Alas! in his distress.
Alas, Great King Mahāsena! Behold what kind of unworthy deed has now been committed by me, a sinner, despite your favors.
Since this son of yours, dear as your own life, has been brought to such a state, from where else could this Lord Sundarasena have come here?
Having embraced the prince in this manner, Vindhyaketu lamented so that everyone present there were moved to tears.
It was not much that you previously recognized this prince; what would you have done had the matter occurred later?
"What cause for despondency is there in this joy?"—thus was the Bhilla king consoled by those joyful companions of Sundarasena.
Then the king, having prostrated at his feet, honored Sundarasena with affection, for he had liberated all those human victims.
Having performed the worship and led him along with his companion to his own village, he gradually attended to him with wholesome remedies after bandaging his wounds.
And he asked, "O Prince, how indeed have you come here? For this is a matter of great curiosity to me; let it be told."
Then, after Sundarasena had related his own adventures, the Śabara king, his mind filled with wonder, said to him:
Where is the expedition for the sake of Mandāravatī, and where is the shipwreck in the ocean? Where is the arrival at Mataṅga’s hermitage, and where is the reunion with her there?
On one hand, there was the theft of that merchant's goods through his trust; on the other, your entry into the forest led to your imprisonment for the sake of a stolen smile.
And where is our recognition [of the truth], and where is our escape from the mouth of death? Salutations in every way to that Fate, whose methods are so diverse.
Therefore, you should not worry regarding your beloved; for as the Creator has fashioned this, so shall He quickly bring about that for you as well.
While the lord of the Pulindas was speaking thus, his own army commander, having arrived in haste and entered with joy, addressed him in this manner:
"Taking abundant wealth and an exceedingly beautiful jewel of a woman, some merchant accompanied by his followers has entered this forest."
Having learned of this, I went with my army and followers, seized him along with his wealth and women, and brought him here, where he now stands outside.
Hearing that, Sundarasena and Vindhyaketu reflected within themselves: "What could this merchant be, and what could this Mandāravatī be?"
When those two had said, "Let him and that woman be brought right here," the army commander ushered in the merchant and the lady.
Then, upon seeing them there, Dṛḍhabuddhi said: "This is that very Mandāravatī, and this is the merchant Durvarṇaka."
Alas, O Queen! Like a creeper scorched by the heat, how have you come to this state—devoid of your flower-ornaments, with your sprout-like lips utterly parched?
While Dṛḍhabuddhi was thus crying out, Sundarasena rushed forward and impetuously embraced his beloved by the neck.
Then those two lovers wept for a long time, as if washing away the stains of their separation from one another with the water of their streams of tears.
Then, having consoled them both, Vindhyaketu said to that merchant: "Why were the wife of that man, who trusted you, carried off by you?"
Then that merchant spoke with a voice faltering from fear: "I have done this in vain for my own destruction, yet she has been preserved."
By her own unassailable majesty, that high-minded woman could not even be touched by me, just like a flame of fire.
Moreover, having been brought to my own country, her anger appeased and herself propitiated, she became the intended bride for me, a sinner.
When the king had spoken thus and ordered his execution, Sundarasena then saved that merchant from death.
But his great abundance of wealth carried away that which was dearer to him than life itself; for day by day it is those whose wealth has departed who die, not those whose life-breaths have gone.
Thus, when Sundarasena had released that merchant, who was satisfied by the recovery of his life and had departed as he pleased, the wretch left.
Taking Mandāravatī, who was united with Sundarasena, King Vindhyaketu went to his own queen’s palace.
There, having given instructions to that queen and having honored Mandāravatī with baths, garments, and ointments, he likewise provided for him who had been bathed and adorned.
Having seated Sundarasena himself upon an excellent throne, he honored him with gifts such as pearls, musk, and other precious items.
And that king held a great festival for the union of the couple, in which all the Śabara women danced with joy.
Then, on another day, Sundarasena said to that king: "My wounds have healed and my purpose has been accomplished; therefore, let us depart from here now as you wish."
"We are going to our own city; therefore, father, quickly dispatch a messenger with a letter, conveying the news and announcing my arrival."
Having been addressed thus by the prince, that lord of the Śabaras dispatched a messenger with a letter containing exactly the same message.
As soon as that messenger reached the city of Alakā, King Mahāsena was there together with his queen.
Afflicted by the grief of not knowing Sundarasena's whereabouts, he prepared to enter the fire in front of the temple of Śaṅkara.
It is said that while he was surrounded by all the citizens who were lamenting, the Śabara messenger, having seen King Mahāsena, ran forward and announced himself.
Smeared with dust, bow in hand, his hair bound with the bark of creepers, dark-complexioned, he wore a loincloth made of bilva leaves.
"By good fortune you are prospering today, O Lord, since your son Sundarasena has returned from having crossed the ocean, accompanied by Mandāravatī."
"For he has reached the presence of our lord Vindhyaketu, O Lord; having sent me on ahead, he has set out to come along with him."
Having spoken thus, that messenger from the Bhilla king placed the letter at the feet of the king there, removing his grief.
Then, when all the people raised a clamorous shout of joy, the letter was read and the great wonder of what had occurred was understood exactly as it happened.
Having honored the messenger with gifts, King Mahāsena, casting aside his grief and holding a festival, entered the capital together with all his followers.
And then, on the following day, eager to be ahead of his son who was about to arrive, he set out accompanied by the lord of Haṃsadvīpa.
And his immeasurable fourfold army likewise trembled; the earth shook as if terrified by that unbearable oppression.
Meanwhile, Sundarasena also set out from that Bhilla village toward his own home, accompanied by Mandāravatī.
Accompanied by that Vikramaśakti, who had been released from prison, and also joined by his friend Bhīmabhuja, he was possessed of firm resolve.
Mounted on a horse with the speed of the wind, accompanied by Vindhyaketu and Pulinda armies, he made the earth appear as if composed entirely of them.
As he traveled, after only a few days on the road, he saw his father coming toward him with his retinue and kinsmen.
Then, having dismounted from his horse while being gazed upon with joy by the people, he approached and fell at the feet of his father along with his companions.
Beholding that son, he too—surging with waves of joy and exultation—could not contain himself within his own being, just as the ocean cannot contain the full moon of the night.
And seeing his daughter-in-law Mandāravatī prostrating at her feet, he considered himself successful and rejoiced in his lineage.
Then the king greatly rejoiced in those three—Dṛḍhabuddhi and the others—who were bowing down, as well as in his son’s ministers and Vindhyaketu.
Then Sundarasena also, having bowed to his father-in-law Mandāradeva who had been introduced by his father, rejoiced exceedingly.
And seeing those two ministers, Caṇḍaprabha and Vyāghraparākrama, who had arrived earlier, clinging to his feet, he considered all his desires to be fulfilled.
At that very moment, King Mahendrāditya also arrived there from Śaśāṅkapura, joyful at having heard the news with affection.
Then, together with all of them, that prince Sundarasena carried his beloved Mandāravatī, just as Naḍakūbara carried Rambhā.
Mounted upon his excellent vehicle, he went to his own abode, Alakāpuri—a place that is the repository of all prosperity and is filled with many Puṇyajanas.
And there, being showered with the blue-lotus eyes of the city women leaning from their windows, he entered his father’s capital together with his beloved.
Having prostrated there at the feet of his mother, whose eyes were clouded with tears of joy, the prince spent that day amidst a festival celebrated by all his kinsmen and servants.

Then, on the following day, at the auspicious moment indicated by the astrologers, the son of the lord of men took the hand of Mandāravatī—whom her father had offered to him—in that marriage long desired by her.
And his father-in-law, King Mandaradeva, who was childless, being delighted, gave him many highly precious jewels and even his own kingdom, which he intended to inherit after his own death.

And her father, King Mahāsena, performed a great festival in accordance with his desire and wealth—a festival that yielded inexhaustible cattle, released those held in bondage, and showered down gold and garments.

Then, seeing that Sundarasena had attained his life's purpose through his union with Mandāravatī, and observing the entire assembly of women singing and dancing, having indulged in the joy born of their wedding;
Honored by King Mahāsena, King Mandaradeva returned to his own realm; and that monarch Śaśāṅka, as well as Vindhyaketu, the lord of the great forest, likewise departed.

Then, after some days had passed, King Mahāsena, seeing that his son Sundarasena was endowed with excellent virtues and beloved by the subjects, established him in his own kingdom and departed for the forest.

Then King Sundarasena, having obtained the kingdom and having conquered the host of his enemies by the strength of his own arms, ruled the entire earth together with those ministers, his joy expanding from the attainment of Mandāravatī.
Having thus related this story to Mṛgāṅkadatta there on the shore of the lake, that minister named Vyāghrasena spoke to him further.
O Lord, that sage Kaṇva described this wondrous tale to us within his hermitage; and at the conclusion of the story, the compassionate man spoke thus to comfort us.

Those sons of his who, with resolute hearts, endure hardships that are most treacherous and difficult to overcome, attain in this way their supreme desires; but others do not, whose strength of being has dissolved and whose efforts are ruined.

Therefore, abandon this despondency; for that Mṛgāṅkadatta, your sovereign, having recovered all his ministers, shall rule the kingdom upon the earth for a very long time once he has united with Śaśāṅkavatī.
Thus addressed by that great seer, we took heart, spent the night there, and then departed from that hermitage; now, weary from the journey, we have reached this forest in due course.

"O Lord, scorched here by excessive thirst and hunger, we climbed this Gaṇanātha tree for the sake of its fruit and became fruits ourselves; today, through your ascetic power, we have been liberated."
Thus, this is our story brought about by the curse of the Naga during our separation from you; now that the curse has expired, go forth united with all of us for the accomplishment of your purpose.
Having heard this from his own minister Vyāghrasena, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having regained his fortitude through the prospect of winning Śaśāṅkavatī, passed that night.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The thirty-fifth wave begins: Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, having risen from the shore of that excellent lake, arrived together with all his assembled ministers.
Endowed with that wisdom acquired through learning, he bowed to that tree which conquers obstacles and set out toward Ujjayinī, desiring to win Śaśāṅkavatī.
Then they [beheld] those various forest regions, possessing hundreds of many cascades, their expansive stretches dark as the tamāla tree, like nights at the onset of the rainy season.
And other [forests], where kīcaka reeds were broken by wandering, fearsome, and rutting elephants, appeared like the city of Virāṭa with its trees resembling Arjuna in reverse.
The caves of the king of mountains were pure and filled with blossoming flowers; though they were inhabited by cruel creatures, they were also frequented by peaceful sages.
Having traveled by stages, that hero, the prince, accompanied by all his ministers, reached the vicinity of the city of Ujjayinī.
Then, having reached the river Gandhavatī and washed away his fatigue by bathing, he crossed it and, accompanied by his followers, arrived at the Mahākāla cremation ground.
And he beheld that place, strewn with various fragments of bones and skulls, formidable with human skeletons held aloft, and frequented by heroes.
It was crowded with many hosts of spirits, a place dear to sporting ḍākinīs, and blackened by the smoke of nearby funeral pyres, O Mahābhairava.
Having passed beyond that, he beheld the ancient city of Ujjayinī, protected by King Karmasena.
The main gate was guarded by protectors bearing various weapons, and watched over by numerous princes born of heroic lineages who were never seen to tire.
It was surrounded by walls shaped like the peaks of the king of mountains, difficult for strangers to enter, and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Beholding her to be so inaccessible from every side, Mṛgāṅkadatta, despondent, spoke to his own ministers.
Alas! For me, who am thus unworthy and have come with hundreds of afflictions, there is no entry here at all; what recourse is there, then, in not obtaining my beloved?
Having heard that, they also said to him: "O Lord, what does this seem to you? Is this great city to be achieved by force for all of us?"
A means must be sought here, and it will certainly be found; for how could this, which has been repeatedly instructed by the deities, have been forgotten?
Having been addressed thus by his ministers, Mṛgāṅkadatta remained for some days wandering about just outside that city.
Then Vikramakesarin meditated upon the Vetāla, who was already established [as his servant], from his bedchamber with the desire to summon the beloved of that [Vetāla] by means of its mantra.
He too was dark-complexioned, tall, with the neck of a camel and the face of an elephant; he had the feet of a buffalo, the eyes of an owl, and the ears of a donkey—such was the Vetāla.
Having arrived there, he was unable to enter; therefore he departed, for by the boon of Śambhu, such persons do not tread upon that city.
Then the Brahmin Śrutadhi, an expert in statecraft, spoke to Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was surrounded by his ministers, dejected, yet with a mind intent on entering [the city].

O King, though you are a knower of the principles of policy, why do you act as if bewildered and ignorant? For whose prowess is esteemed in this world if he does not perceive the distinction between himself and his enemy?
Indeed, at each of the four gates of every single city, there were two thousand elephants and twenty-five thousand horses.
And ten lakhs of chariots and foot soldiers remain armored day and night for the sake of protection; it is invincible due to the presence of heroes.
Therefore, for us few who have entered here so suddenly, this is merely the behavior of moths; it will not lead to the accomplishment of any purpose whatsoever.
Moreover, this city cannot be attacked by even a small army; for that conflict with one who possesses superior force would result in a battle between elephants and infantry.
By that young ascetic Tanmāya, who was a Pulinda king and a friend, he had been rescued from the terrible danger of the crocodiles in the Narmadā river.
And by that exceedingly powerful Mātaṅga king, his friend—the Piśāca of the Fort—who was devoted to their mutual alliance.
By that Kirāta king, who was his fellow-student in childhood, known by the name Śaktirakṣita, and who was endowed with great prowess.
Having assembled with all your forces, filling the quarters of the sky with your army, and being fully endowed with excellent allies, accomplish this desired objective.
And how have you forgotten this: that the king of the Kirātas remained there, awaiting the news of your messenger's arrival?
And Māyāvaṭu, having certainly arrived by the command of the Mātaṅga king, remained ready with him, for he had been made acquainted with the plan.
"Let us go to that fortress-residence of the lord of the Mātaṅgas, named Karabhagrīva, situated on the southern flank of the Vindhya mountains."
Right there, King Śaktirakṣita was summoned by his kinsmen; then, all of them joining together, they made auspicious preparations for success.
Having heard these meaningful words of Śrutadhi, which were approved by the wise, Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with his ministers, placed great faith in them, saying, "So be it."
And on another day, having paid homage to the sun—the kinsman of the virtuous, whose rising is firm, who reveals all directions, and who is the eternal traveler of the celestial path—[he departed].
Then he set out toward the southern slope of the Vindhya mountains, toward the abode of that lord of the Mātaṅgas, Durgapiśāca.
And his ministers were Vyāghrasena of terrible prowess, Guṇākara, Meghabala, and Vimalabuddhi.
Vicitrakatha, Sthūlabāhu, Vikramakesarin, Pracaṇḍaśakti, Śrutadhi, and Dṛḍhamuṣṭi followed him.
Together with them, he gradually traversed vast forests like his own extensive activities, and dense woodland regions like his own secret intentions.
Passing by lakes and taking shelter at the roots of trees on the banks during the night, he reached and ascended the Vindhya mountain, which was as lofty as his own mind.
Descending from its summit to the southern side, he gazed from afar upon the Bhilla villages, which were covered with elephant tusks and deer skins.
"Where in this world could there be a dwelling for that lord of the Mātaṅgas? How shall we find him?"—thus the prince reflected within himself.
Just then, he saw a young ascetic approaching; together with his ministers, he bowed down and questioned him.
"Do you know where the house of King Mātaṅga is here, O gentle one? For we must see Durgapiśāca."
Having heard that, the virtuous son of the ascetic spoke thus: "At a distance of only one *krośa* from here, there is a region called Pañcavaṭī."
And not far from that place was the hermitage of the sage Agastya, by whom King Nahuṣa—who had arrogantly cast down the gods from heaven—was effortlessly brought low.
There, having accepted forest-dwelling at his father’s command, Rāma dwelt for a long time with Lakṣmaṇa and followed by Sītā, attending upon that sage.
There, a headless trunk (kabandha), which portended the destruction of the Rākṣasa and was like the sun and moon, set out to attack Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
There, Rāma struck down the arm of Yojanabāhu, which was like the serpent Nahuṣa who had been turned into a python by the prayer of Agastya.
Where, even today at the arrival of the clouds, upon hearing the roar of the rain-clouds, they remember the sound of Rāma’s bow that filled the sky.
Beholding all directions empty, the aged deer, reared by Jānakī, look on with tearful eyes and do not take up mouthfuls of young grass.
As if to save the remaining deer from being slaughtered elsewhere, the golden deer, which brought about Vaidehī’s separation, carried Rāghava away to another place.
Where, in many great lakes abounding with the waters of the Kāverī, the ocean's water seems to be drunk and then vomited up by Agastya at every step.
Not very far from that hermitage, on a ridge of the Vindhya mountains, there is a fortress named Karabhagrīva, which is crooked and difficult to access.
There dwells that lord of Mātaṅgas, Durgapiśāca, who is powerful, of fierce prowess, and unconquered by other kings.
He was the lord of a hundred thousand archers, each one of whom was followed by five hundred warriors.
With those bandits, he plunders caravans, crushes his enemies, and enjoys this great forest, disregarding various kings.
Having heard this from the daughter of the sage and having taken leave of him, Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by his followers, departed quickly by that very same path.
And in due course, he reached the vicinity of that Karabhagrīva, the fortress of the king of the Mātaṅgas, which was crowded with Bhilla villages.
And there, not far away, he saw throngs of Śabaras here and there, carrying peacock feathers, elephant tusks, tiger skins, and the flesh of deer.
Behold those who live like animals, subsisting on forest fare; yet it is a marvel that they call even such a lord a "demon of a fortress."
There is indeed nothing that is without a king; alas, someone must surely exist among the subjects! This title "king" was created by the gods out of fear of the law of the fishes (*mātsyanyāya*).
Thus, having looked upon those Bhilla friends and speaking to them, Mṛgāṅkadatta sought out the path to the fortress of Karabhagrīva.
Then, as he first arrived there at the foot of the Nāyabaṭu tree, the scouts of the Śabara king beheld him, whom they had seen before.
Having gone immediately to that illusory woodcutter, they informed him of his arrival; and he too, accompanied by his army, went out to meet him.
Having approached and seen him, that king of the Pulindas, releasing his horse, ran forward and fell at the feet of the prince.
Having embraced him around the neck and inquired after his welfare, the king led him, along with his ministers, mounted upon a vehicle, to his own camp.
And then that lord of the Śabaras dispatched a doorkeeper to announce his arrival to that king of the Mātaṅgas.
And that king of the Mātaṅgas also arrived swiftly from his own country, a demon of a fortress who bore his name according to its true meaning.
With limbs as hard as a mass of stone, with foliage as dark as the *tāla* tree, and sinful as he is frequented by Pulindas, he was like another Vindhya mountain.
With a face made terrifying by a natural frown of three lines, he was as if marked by the Goddess dwelling on the Vindhya mountains with her trident to claim him as her own.
Though young, he has exhausted all [other] stages of life; though difficult to behold, he is Kṛṣṇa; and though subsisting on the feet of the mountain, he is served by none other.
Like a fresh cloud, he bore a variegated bow adorned with peacock feathers; like Hiraṇyākṣa, his body was wounded by a fierce boar.
Powerful like Ghaṭotkaca, he assumed a haughty and terrifying form; he was like the Kali age, in which the subjects are unrestrained and devoted to unrighteousness.
And that mass of troops, filling the surface of the earth, surged forth like the current of the Narmadā released from its confinement by Arjuna’s arms.
Is this a mass of rocks tumbling from Mount Añjana, or is it a premature torrent of clouds at the end of an aeon fallen to the earth?
Thus entertaining this suspicion, that multitude of Caṇḍāla troops advanced, darkening the faces of the quarters with their black shadows.
And having approached, that master Durgapiśāca, bowing his head to the ground from afar, paid homage to Mṛgāṅkadatta.
And today the goddess Vindhyavāsinī has become gracious to me, since you, born of a most noble lineage, have come to my home.
Having said, "Therefore, I am blessed; I have achieved my purpose," that king of the Mātaṅgas gave him a gift consisting of pearls, musk, and other such items.
The prince also greeted him with affection as was appropriate; then, right there, they all established their military camp.
That great forest was covered with elephants bound to hitching posts, horses stationed in the stables, and foot soldiers who had taken up their positions.
At that moment, as if reeling from the fortune of having attained the state of a city never before known since birth, she could not remain established in her own self.
Then, in that forest grove, having performed his auspicious ablutions and taken his meal, he sat comfortably in a secluded spot accompanied by his ministers.
While Māyāvaṭu was present, Durgapiśāca, in the course of conversation, spoke to Mṛgāṅkadatta with words tender with affection and humility.
"O Master, this boy Māyāvaṭu has been here for a long time; awaiting your command, he has remained with me."
Therefore, O prince, inform us now as to where you have been staying for so long and what you have done; let us be made aware of your affairs.
Having heard these words from the house of this Māyāvaṭu, that prince then spoke with Vimalabuddhi.
Having met Bhīmaparākrama together with Guṇākara, and having gone with Śrutadhi while searching for my other friends, I—
And Pracaṇḍaśakti has arrived, as well as this Vicitrakatha; and by way of the road, Vikramakesarī has also come from there.
Then, having reached the tree of Vighneśa on the shore of that excellent lake and climbed it for the sake of fruit, they were turned into fruits by its curse.
Then, having propitiated that Gaṇeśa with some effort, I was released; likewise, the others who were in that same state were also liberated by me there at the outset.
Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Vyāghrasena, Meghabala, and Sthūlabāhu—these four are his ministers.
Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Vyāghrasena, Meghabala, and Sthūlabāhu—these are his four ministers.
When all these had arrived together with me, I went to Ujjayinī; and since I was without an army, it was not appropriate for me to dispatch an envoy.
Therefore, having deliberated, we have come into your presence; now, my friend, you are our authority here for the sake of success.
When Mṛgāṅkadatta had thus related his own adventure, that Ugrapiśāca then spoke to him as he approached in the form of a young brahmin.
Be firm; how much work is this for us? These very lives have already been prepared for your sake.
"Let us bind that King Karmasena here and bring him away by force, and carry off his daughter Śaśāṅkavatī."
When the young Brahmin had been thus addressed by Mātaṅgarāja, Mṛgāṅkadatta spoke with affection and great respect.
What is not possible among you? For this very quality speaks for you: the steadfastness of character that carries out the task entrusted by a friend.
Having taken firmness from the Vindhya mountains, valor from tigers, and a mixed passion from the forest lotuses, you were fashioned here by the Creator.
When Mṛgāṅkadatta had spoken thus, "Deliberate on this and do what is appropriate," the Maker of Day (the Sun) rested upon the peak of the Setting Mountain.
Then they rested there for that night of three watches in dwellings prepared by the laborers within the military camp, each according to his rank.
In the morning, Mṛgāṅkadatta dispatched Guṇākara to bring his friend Śaktirakṣita, the king of the Kirātas.
Having gone there and related the events, that lord of the Kirātas arrived in just a few days accompanied by him and a very great army.
There were one hundred thousand foot soldiers, two hundred thousand horses, and ten thousand rutting elephants mounted by great heroes.
Eighty-eight thousand chariots followed that lord of the earth, their banners and umbrellas covering the sky.
And Mṛgāṅkadatta, having joyfully gone out to meet him and honored him, escorted the king, along with his friends and ministers, into the camp.
Meanwhile, all the other friends and kinsmen of Mātaṅgarāja, as well as those sent as messengers by Māyāvaṭu, arrived there.
And the ocean-like camp of Mṛgāṅkadatta’s army swelled, resounding with joyful shouts as hundreds of divisions converged, bringing delight to his heart.
There, that demon of a fortress honored those kings with pearls, musk, garments, loads of meat, and fruit spirits.
The lord of the Śabaras, Māyāvaṭu, provided for all of them the most excellent baths, ointments, food, drink, beds, and other necessities.
And Mṛgāṅkadatta ate together with all those lords of men, who were seated in their respective appropriate places.
He even fed that king of the Mātaṅgas at the front, from afar; for the task, the place, and the time are more important than the person.
Then, when the army of Kirātas and others who had newly arrived had rested, on the following day Mṛgāṅkadatta sat upon an elephant throne.
Having performed the appropriate honors for the assembly of kings in their respective places, he cleared the area of people and spoke to his friends, including the king of the Mātaṅgas and others.
Why is time being wasted now? Why do you not proceed quickly toward Ujjayinī with this entire army?
Having heard that, the Brahmin Śrutadhi said to the prince: "Listen, O King, I shall tell you here what is the opinion of those who know the science of policy."

One who desires victory must first understand the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; he should abandon that which is impossible to accomplish by any means as something not to be done.
That which is to be accomplished is the task; regarding that, the fourfold means are traditionally recorded as conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force.
Among them, each preceding one is superior and each succeeding one is inferior; therefore, the application of *sāman* is first joined here by the gods.
Indeed, while King Karmasena is free from greed, gifts do not lead to success; nor does sowing dissension, for he has no angry, greedy, or insulted subjects.
And when he is stationed in a difficult location and possesses superior strength, an expedition undertaken by kings against one who has never been conquered by others before brings about uncertainty.
The glory of victory in battles is unreliable even for the powerful; moreover, it is not fitting for one who seeks a maiden to cause the destruction of her kinsmen.
Therefore, let an envoy first be dispatched to that king using conciliation alone; if that fails, force will be employed when it arrives by way of necessity.
Having heard these words of Śrutadhi, they all there accepted them as true and praised his knowledge of the sequence of mantras.

Then, having deliberated together with those very men, he dispatched that best of brahmins, who was endowed with the qualities of an envoy and had previously been mentioned by them, as an attendant of the Kirāta king.
Mṛgāṅkadatta dispatched a messenger named Suvigraha to King Karmasena, carrying a letter and a verbal message.
Having gone to Ujjayinī, that messenger was announced by the doorkeeper and entered the delightful inner courtyard, which was filled with beloved horses and elephants.
Having entered the royal palace, he beheld King Karmasena seated upon his throne, surrounded by his ministers.
Having prostrated and sat upon a seat, he was questioned by the king about his welfare in due order; being welcomed by the monarch, he presented the letter to him.
Taking that [text], which had been spread out by the casting of mudrās by his minister, the one named Prajñākośa clearly recited it as follows:
Hail! From the slopes of the forest at the base of Karabhagrīva Fort, [comes this message] from the son of the Great King of Kings, the Lord of the city of Ayodhyā.
There, the illustrious Mṛgāṅkadatta—the ornament of the earth’s surface—stood with the kings bowing humbly before him, having approached him.
In Ujjayinī, the great king Karmasena respectfully and clearly sends this message from himself, who is like the moon in the ocean of his own lineage.
"You have that daughter; she must certainly be given away, so bestow her upon another. She is suitable for me, for she has been ordained as my wife by the gods."
"In this way, our state as kinsmen shall come to pass and our former enmity shall perish; otherwise, I shall rely solely upon my own arms in this matter."
When this letter had been read there, King Karmasena, filled with anger, spoke to his ministers, headed by the minister Prajñākośa.
They are always our adversaries because of that [self] which lacks self-knowledge; this very point has been taught by him as he observed this present disorder.
Previously, we were drawn in by our own self-interest; later, out of contempt, he was puffed up with pride and finally boasted of the strength of his arms.
"Therefore, no reply is appropriate for me; what need is there even to speak of a maiden? Go, messenger, and let your master do whatever he deems fit."
Thus addressed by King Karmasena, that twice-born messenger, Suvigraha, who was full of splendor, spoke these words in due order.
O dull-witted one, you are now becoming aware only after not seeing that prince; be prepared, for when he arrives, you will know the difference between yourself and the other.
When he had spoken thus, that royal assembly fell into an uproar; the king, enraged, said, "Go! You are not to be executed; what shall we do?"
Others there, biting their lips and crushing their own hands with their hands, said to one another: "Why do we not go and kill him this very moment?"
"What is the use of being angry at the words of this talkative boy? We shall see what he does," said the others with fortitude.
Some stood silent with faces reddened by anger, as if signaling their readiness to string their bows with the knitting of their brows.
Thus, while the assembly was still in a state of anger, that messenger of handsome form departed and went to the side of Mṛgāṅkadatta at his own camp.
Karmasena related that which had been said to him and his friend; and having heard it, the prince likewise ordered the expedition for his army.

Then, tossed by the onset of the powerful wind of his lord’s command, that ocean of an army—filled with men, horses, and elephants as its sea-monsters—rushed forward. Spreading satisfaction in the hearts of the kings who possessed allies, it caused a terrifying agitation among those men who were cowardly.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta set out slowly toward Ujjayinī for victory, making the earth muddy with the ichor of elephants and the foam of horses, and deafening the world with the sound of his trumpets.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth wave in the *Śāśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The thirty-sixth wave: Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by his friends and with his army arrayed for battle, crossed the Vindhya mountains and reached the frontier of Ujjayinī.
Having learned of this, King Karmasena, firm and accompanied by his army, equipped himself for battle and then marched out from the city before him.
As those two armies drew near and came within sight of one another, a battle that gladdened the hearts of heroes broke out between them.
That battlefield became like the abode of Hiraṇyakaśipu, crowded with cowardly demons who were broken and terrified by the roar of the Man-Lion.
Continuous, piercing, thick, and traveling through the sky, arrows fell upon the great warriors like locusts upon grain.
The heap of pearls arising from the frontal globes of elephants struck by swords shone like a necklace of the Goddess of Battle, broken apart in her fury.
With its teeth like the points of sharp spears, devouring horses, men, and elephants, that battlefield shone like the gaping mouth of Death himself.
The severed heads of those endowed with mighty arms leaped upward, as if taking a high spring into the sky to kiss celestial nymphs.
And there, at every step, headless trunks danced, as if out of joy at the battle with their illustrious lord, which had been made manifest.
And thus, for five days, that battle which brought an end to heroes continued, with rivers of blood flowing daily and abounding in heaps of corpses.
On the fifth day, in the evening, as Mṛgāṅkadatta was gathered in private with his ministers, the Brahmin Śrutadhi approached him and said:
While you were occupied with the battle, I went from here in the guise of a mendicant, entered Ujjayinī through its unguarded gates, and proceeded inside.
O King, listen as I tell you exactly how that which was sought was found by me, having become invisible even from close proximity through the power of my knowledge.
At the very moment King Karmasena went forth to battle, Śaśāṅkavatī, with her mother’s permission, departed from the house.
Having departed, she took refuge in the temple of Gaurī located within that city, in order to propitiate that goddess for the sake of her father’s welfare in battle.
Remaining there, she spoke in secret to a trusted female companion: "O friend, on my account this conflict has arisen with my father."
And once he has been overcome, he will hand me over to that prince; for kings do not account for their affection for their children when it comes to the sake of the kingdom.
And I do not know whether that prince is suitable for me or not; for I would rather desire death than an ugly husband.
I believe that even a poor husband who is endowed with beauty is better than one who is ugly, even if he were the sovereign of the entire circle of the earth.
"Go from the army, look at what he is like, and then return. You are indeed auspicious in both wisdom and name, Caturikā."
Thus addressed by her friend, she went to our camp with skillful artifice; and having seen you, O Lord, she returned and spoke to that princess.
What else, my friend? I know that even Vāsuki does not possess a tongue capable of describing the beauty of that prince.
Furthermore, I declare this: there is no other woman equal to you in beauty, nor is there any other man who is your peer.
I consider what I have said to be far too little; indeed, in these three worlds, there is no one such as him—not a Siddha, nor a Gandharva, nor even a god.
Thus, by her friend’s words, Śaśāṅkavatī’s mind was set upon you, and it was simultaneously transfixed by the arrows of Kāma.
From that moment on, desiring your welfare as well as that of your father, she remained engaged in asceticism, becoming emaciated both by her penance and by the separation from you.
Therefore, go there tonight in secret and, having carried her away from Gaurī’s hermitage, bring that princess back from that solitary place unobserved.
"Go from here to the house of this Māyābaṭu; after these kings have secured the rear against any provocation, they will come there together with me."
Let this battle cease; let there be no further destruction of the armies. May there be well-being for your bodies, as well as for the king, your father-in-law.
For this is indeed a desperate course, a battle in which one must surrender one's life; it is proclaimed by the wise that this is the lowest among all strategic means.
Thus addressed by Śrutadhi, Mṛgāṅkadatta mounted his horses there at night and set out secretly with his ministers.
And having gone there, he entered that city of Ujjayinī, which was left with only sleeping women and children, its gates closed and guarded by only a few drowsy sentries.
Then, well-identified by the tokens provided by Śrutadhī, it was made known that he was staying within the great garden named Puṣpakaraṇḍaka.
Illuminated by the rays of the moon, which at that time adorned the face of the eastern quarter, the prince went to that hermitage of Gaurī.
And while her circle of friends slept, exhausted from their service and other duties, Śaśāṅkavatī remained sleepless there and reflected:
Alas, for my sake, day after day, those various heroic kings and princes are being slain in the encounter between the two armies.
And that prince was indeed commanded in a dream by this very Goddess Ambikā: "He was my husband in a former life; he fought for my sake."
And having torn out his heart after discharging a succession of arrows, Kāma, who has attained his mark, took it and presented it to him.
But my father will certainly not give me, who am of little merit, to him; for today I have heard from a letter that it is due to former enmity and pride.
In the case of the moon on the left, what certainty can there be regarding the instruction of a deity in a dream? And even upon obtaining a beloved, I do not see any direction whatsoever in any way.
As long as I do not hear that anything has been done to my father in battle, why should I not abandon this hopeless self?
Having risen and gone before Gaurī, who stood by an aśoka tree, she, distressed, fashioned a noose with her upper garment.
Meanwhile, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having entered that garden with his companions and tethered his horse to a tree, went to the hermitage of the temple of Gaurī.
There, having beheld the princess from afar, Mṛgāṅkadatta was addressed privately by his minister Vimalabuddhi:
"Your Majesty, behold here this certain noble maiden who is raising her hand with a noose to kill herself; who indeed might she be?"
Upon hearing that and seeing her, the prince said: "Aha! Who is this? Is she Rati, or perhaps Bliss (Nirvṛti) personified?"
Is this the embodied radiance of the moon, or the mobile command of the God of Love? Or perhaps a celestial nymph? No, it cannot be so; for how could she possess such a noose?
Therefore, let us remain here for a moment, concealed by the trees, so that we may somehow clearly discern who she is.
Having spoken thus, while he remained there concealed with his companions, Śaśāṅkavatī, filled with agitation, addressed the goddess.
"O Queen, if, due to my past misdeeds, that prince Mṛgāṅkadatta has not become my husband in this life," she said.
By your grace, O Goddess Gaurī, may he be my husband even in another birth—O Blessed One, you who remove the suffering of those who have fallen into distress.
Having thus addressed the queen and bowed down to her, the princess, her eyes moist with tears, placed the noose around her own neck.
At that very moment, having awakened and being distraught by not seeing her, her friends began searching and quickly approached her side.
"Alas, alas! What is this you have begun, friend? Shame on your rashness!"—saying this very thing, they removed the noose from her neck.
Then, while that young woman remained there, ashamed and dejected, a voice arose from within the inner sanctum of Gaurī.
"Do not despair, daughter Śaśāṅkavatī; those words that were spoken by me to you in your dream, O fortunate one, shall certainly not prove false."
This very Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was formerly your husband, has indeed arrived in your presence; go with him and enjoy the entire earth.
Having suddenly heard these words, Śaśāṅkavatī slowly looked around her side with some trepidation to see what it was.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta’s minister, Vikramakeśarin, approached him and spoke, pointing with his outstretched hand.
"O Goddess, what Bhavānī has commanded you is indeed true; for this prince, drawn by the noose of love, stands here before you as your husband."
Having heard that, she then cast her gaze sideways and beheld her beloved, radiant and standing in the midst of his companions.
Surrounded by the planets like the moon descended from the sky, he was a showering of nectar for the eyes, surpassing all other objects of comparison for beauty.
Then, as she remained motionless like a pillar with her limbs bristling as if covered by the feathers on the shafts of falling arrows of the God of Love, [he spoke].
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, approaching her and making her abandon her shame, spoke words suited to the occasion, dripping with the honey of love:
"O lady of curved limbs, having been made a slave by your virtues and bound by them, I have been brought far away from my own country, kingdom, and kinsmen."
Therefore, [this is the fruit] of my dwelling in the forest, of sleeping upon the bare ground, of subsisting on fruits, and of enduring the intense heat of the sun.
O slender-limbed one, such is the fruit obtained from the hardship of your asceticism: that this body of yours has been seen, a rain of nectar for the eyes.
O fawn-eyed one, if you have any affection or regard for me, then grant a festival for the eyes to the women of our city.
May the battle cease; may it be well for both sides; and may my birth be rendered fruitful along with the blessings of my preceptor.
When Mṛgāṅkadatta had spoken thus to Śaśāṅkavatī, she then replied slowly, her eyes fixed upon the ground.
This person, purchased by your virtues, is already at your disposal; therefore, noble son, do whatever you deem to be for your welfare.
Thus, having been satisfied and consoled by her nectar-like words, Mṛgāṅkadatta, feeling fulfilled, praised and bowed down before that goddess Gaurī.
Having mounted the princess upon a horse behind him, he was followed by her companions who had likewise ascended the backs of horses positioned behind him.
Then, accompanied by ten heroic ministers with weapons in their hands, the prince set out at night, bearing his own arms.
And although those eleven were seen there, they could not be restrained by the city guards, for they were as unassailable as the wrathful Rudras themselves.
Having departed from Ujjayinī, they went to the house of Māyāvaṭu together with Śaśāṅkavatī, just as Śrutadhi had instructed.
While the guards there were bewildered, wondering "Who are these people? Where have they gone?", that princess gradually learned in Ujjayinī that she had been abducted.
To inform King Karmasena of this, the Great Queen quickly dispatched the city magistrate toward the royal camp.
In the meantime, at that camp, a spy approached King Karmasena during the night and informed him.
"O King, at the very hour of twilight today, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having secretly departed from the army with his ministers, has gone to Ujjayinī by means of horses."
"I have correctly understood that he intends to abduct Śaśāṅkavatī while she is staying at the temple of Gaurī; beyond this, the Lord himself knows."
Having heard this, King Karmasena summoned his own general and described everything exactly as he had heard it in private.
And he said: "Accompanied by five hundred excellent horses mounted by brave men, go quickly and secretly to Ujjayinī."
"Slay that wicked Mṛgāṅkadatta, or having captured him, bind him! Know that I am coming after you, with my army stationed at my back."
Thus addressed by the king, that general, equipped with the forces as commanded, set out for Ujjayinī at night, saying, "So be it."
On the way, he met the city magistrate and heard from him how the princess had been carried off by certain other heroes.
