Then the city superintendent returned and informed King Karmasena of everything exactly as it had happened.
Having understood that and reflected upon it, the king realized it was impossible; he desisted from the assault and passed that night in silence.
In Mṛgāṅkadatta’s army as well, the kings headed by Māyāvaṭu likewise spent that night prepared for battle, in accordance with the words of Śrutadhi.
In the morning, King Karmasena, having ascertained the facts and being wise, dispatched a messenger to the camp of Mṛgāṅkadatta to inform the kings.
"My daughter has already been carried off by Mṛgāṅkadatta through a stratagem; let it be so, for who else indeed could be such a suitable husband for her?"
Therefore, let him now come with you to my house, so that I may perform the marriage of my daughter according to the prescribed rites.
In this manner the king delivered his message through the mouth of the messenger; and then those kings, together with their learned ministers, placed full confidence in it.
And they said to the messenger: "In that case, let this lord of yours go to his own city, so that we may go there and bring back the prince."
Upon hearing that, and having been described in such a manner by that messenger who had gone there, Karmasena, together with his army, agreed and went to Ujjayinī.
Seeing that, those kings also, led by Māyāvaṭu and accompanied by Śrutadhi, set out toward Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Meanwhile, Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by Śaśāṅkavatī, reached that city of Kāñcanapura, the home of Māyāvaṭu.
There, having had due honors paid to him by the women of the inner apartments, he—his purpose accomplished, accompanied by his friends and his beloved—rested.
On another day, those kings, accompanied by their learned ministers, arrived there; as did that heroic lord of the Kirātas, Śaktirakṣita, together with his army.
That powerful King Māyābaṭu was also the lord of the Śabaras, a hero, and a Piśāca of the fortress; he was the commander of the Mātaṅga army.
Seeing Mṛgāṅkadatta united with Śaśāṅkavatī like a night-lotus with the moon, they all celebrated and congratulated him.
Having shown him the honor he deserved, they announced to him Karmasena’s message as well as his own admission into the palace.
Then, having established his camp which resembled a moving city, Mṛgāṅkadatta sat down together with all of them for consultation.
He asked the kings and his ministers, "Should I go to Ujjayinī for the wedding, or not? Let it be told."
That king is wicked; how could there be any well-being in going to his house? There is no business whatsoever to be done there, for his daughter has already arrived.
When the kings and ministers had spoken thus with one accord, Mṛgāṅkadatta then questioned that Brahmin Śrutadhi.
O Brahmin, why do you remain thus in silence like one who is indifferent? Is this indeed your own preference, or is it not? Speak!
Then Śrutadhi said: "If you will listen, I shall tell you; it is my opinion that we must go to the house of Karmasena."
For this was indeed communicated by him without guile; otherwise, how could that powerful man, upon the abduction of his daughter, abandon the battle and go home?
And what could he do even if he were to reach your house while accompanied by his army? For you would feel the same joy there as he would upon arriving with you.
Furthermore, he would be our ally through his affection for our daughter; yet, because he does not desire a marriage contrary to the law, he speaks thus according to the truth.
When Śrutadhi then said, "The journey there is appropriate for that," they all, placing faith in his words, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! regarding that matter.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta said to them, "Let all this be as you say; however, without my father and mother, marriage does not please me."
"Let someone go from here to summon our mother and father; once we have learned their intention, we shall do what is appropriate."
Having spoken thus and consulted with his own minister, the hero of terrible prowess dispatched him to the side of his parents while remaining right there himself.
Meanwhile, in that city of Ayodhyā, his father King Amaradatta learned from the people about him over the course of time.
Vinītamati falsely slandered Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta, thereby causing his banishment from the country.
Then, having slain that evil minister along with his lineage out of anger, he fell into a state of misery and hardship caused by the intense grief of his son's exile.
Having departed, the king stayed in a temple of Hari outside the city; he practiced austerities together with his wives in the place called Nandigrāma.
While he remained there for a long time, that man of terrible prowess, whose arrival had been reported by a spy, reached Ayodhyā with the speed of a wind-swift horse.
He beheld that city, distressed and deprived of the king's son, as if it had once again encountered the calamity caused by Rāma’s exile.
Then, surrounded by the citizens who were inquiring after the prince's welfare, he heard the news from their mouths and proceeded from there to Nandigrāma.
There he saw King Amaradatta, accompanied by his queen, whose body was emaciated by asceticism and who was filled with longing for news of his beloved son.
Approaching the king, Bhīmaparākrama fell at his feet; embracing him around the neck and having been asked for news of his welfare, he spoke with tears.
O King, that Śaśāṅkavatī, the daughter of King Karmasena, has been won by your son Mṛgāṅkadatta through his own prowess.
And for that man devoted to his father, a marriage with anyone other than the King and the Queen does not appear auspicious in any way.
Therefore, having been dispatched by him with the instruction, "Let [him] come right here," your son has sent me to inform you, bowing his head to the ground.
And he remained in Kāñcanapura, O King, in the house of the lord of the Śabaras, King Māyāvaṭu, awaiting you all.
"Now listen to the account," he said, and beginning from his departure from that country, he related the long and difficult story of his dwelling in the forest and his separation [from her].
He of terrible prowess recounted the entire account of his own master, including the battle with Karmasena, its conclusion through a treaty, and various wonders.
Having heard that, King Amaradatta, whose welfare was now assured, made a firm resolve and immediately ordered his own departure out of joy.
Then, mounted upon an elephant together with the queen, the kings, and his ministers, he set out with his force of elephants and horses, eager for his son.
And in just a few days, without delay, that king reached his son’s camp, situated within the territory of the Śabara chief.
And as soon as he learned of this, Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with all the kings and his companions, went forth before him, having long been filled with longing.
As soon as he saw them from afar, he dismounted from his horse and fell at the feet of his father and mother, who were mounted upon an elephant.
Embraced by his father’s body, he filled the space between his father’s arms with his own limbs, his heart with longing, and his eyes with tears.
The mother also, having embraced her son after a long time and gazing at him again and again, was unable to let go for a long while, as if fearing separation once more.
And those kings, the friends of Mṛgāṅkadatta, having been informed of that by him, then paid homage to their lord Amaradatta together with his queen.
That king and his queen, as a couple, out of affection for their many sons, welcomed those companions in times of distress.
Then, having entered the capital of Māyāvaṭu and beheld Śaśāṅkavatī there, he [recognized her] as his daughter-in-law bowing at his feet.
Having accepted the gift, Amaradatta, together with the queen and his daughter-in-law, went forth and took up residence in his own camp.
And having eaten there together with his son and all the kings, he spent that day happily amidst songs, instrumental music, and dancing.
And he considered himself a man of merit through that son, Mṛgāṅkadatta, who had already attained fame and was destined to become a universal emperor.
Meanwhile, King Karmasena, being wise, deliberated and dispatched a messenger here to Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Your Honor will not come here to Ujjayinī for the time being; therefore, I shall send my son named Suṣeṇa to this very place.
"He will give you his own sister Śaśāṅkavatī according to the prescribed rites; therefore, O sinless one, she must not be wedded by you through an improper rite."
"If there is compliance with our affection," thus that king instructed him, both in a letter and through the mouth of his messenger, to that prince.
When that message was heard by the prince in Rājasthāna, his father—the king himself—gave the reply to that messenger.
Who else but King Karmasena would speak such words? Since he possesses a noble mind and has a genuine affection for us, let him therefore send him from here.
"We shall act in such a way that the marriage of his son Suṣeṇa will bring him complete satisfaction."
Having spoken thus and dispatched that honored messenger with a reply, the king addressed his son Śruta-dhi and the other monarchs.
"Let us go now to Ayodhyā; there the marriage shall be celebrated with splendor, and there the hospitable reception for Suṣeṇa will be duly accomplished."
"Let King Māyāvaṭu wait here for Suṣeṇa; once he has arrived, the king shall subsequently proceed to Ayodhyā accompanied by him."
"We shall go once more ahead for the sake of the wedding preparations"—thus they all agreed to the king's words there.
Then on the following day, that lord of the earth, together with the queen, his armies, Mṛgāṅkadatta, and those kings and ministers, set out.
Having left Māyāvaṭu there until the arrival of Suṣeṇa, the two skillful men then departed together with Śaśāṅkavatī.
It was crowded with hundreds of waves consisting of throngs of galloping horses, and its quarters were filled by the waters of the surging infantry that were beyond counting.
The ocean of that army, deep and terrifying, surged forward, its hearing of other sounds drowned out by the tumultuous sound rising up.
And they made the earth, covered in dust, appear like the heavens, while the sky, filled with roaring elephants like thick clouds, appeared like the earth.
Traveling along the road in due course, the father and son reached the house of Śaktirakṣita, the king of the Kirātas.
There, he and his wife, together with their retinue, performed a grand worship with heaps of great jewels, gold, and fine garments.
Having taken food for one day and rested with their army, they then set out and reached their own city, Ayodhyā, in due course.
With the faces of the city women, shimmering as they leaned from the palace windows and blossoming with radiance, it was as if the city were filled with swaying lotuses in full bloom.
Their restless eyes, eager to behold the prince who had returned with his bride after a long time, were like trembling blue lotuses.
And they entered that city, which was filled with royal swans arriving from all sides and rippled by banners fluttering in the wind, like a lake on a windy day.
There the citizens rejoiced as the two were being offered blessings by the twice-born, praised by bards, and celebrated in song by the *cāraṇas*.
If the great ocean were to behold this daughter of Karmasena, he would no longer take pride in his own daughter Lakṣmī.
And even upon seeing the wealth of beauty possessed by Śaśāṅkavatī, the people were struck with wonder and did not say, "She is like Gaurī," nor "He is like Himavān."
And then, with the echoing sounds of great auspicious musical instruments, they seemed to announce to the quarters of the sky the arrival of a festival, as if making it known to the kings.
As if overflowing with passion poured outward, that entire city became filled with festive joy, as if dancing with vermilion.
On another day, when the astrologers had determined the auspicious hour for his son's wedding, King Amaradatta made preparations for that marriage ceremony.
His city was filled with various jewels arriving from all directions, such that it surpassed even the city of Kubera.
Then, shortly thereafter, a messenger of Māyāvaṭu arrived, announced by a joyful gatekeeper, and addressed the king there as follows:
The prince Devagata and King Suṣeṇa—both of them were stationed at the frontier of this Ayodhyā by Māyāvaṭu.
Upon hearing that, King Amaradatta immediately dispatched his own general, Suṣeṇa, along with his troops, into the presence of that [ruler].
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with his friends, went out from Ayodhyā to meet the prince who had arrived there with him, out of affection.
Having descended from their vehicles from afar and embraced one another around the neck, those two princes met and inquired after each other's welfare.
Mounted upon a single chariot out of love, they entered that city, presenting a great festival for the eyes of the city’s women.
And there, having seen the king and being highly honored by him, Suṣeṇa then went to the residence of his sister Śaśāṅkavatī.
Having risen there and embraced her as she shed tears, he sat down and spoke to that bashful princess.
"Your father says to you: 'Daughter, nothing improper has been done by you; for today I have learned this very thing from Ambikā in her dream concerning you.'"
"This prince Mṛgāṅkadatta has been designated as your husband; and for women, following the path of their husband is the supreme vow."
Thus addressed by him, that young woman, looking down at her own heart, cast aside her shame as she perceived: "Your desired goal is accomplished."
Then Suṣeṇa took that wealth which Śaśāṅkavatī had personally accumulated and presented it before the king for her.
Two thousand loads of gold for the purpose of making jewel ornaments, five well-fed young camels, and other vessels made of gold.
And he said this: "O father, that which was sent for her own sake shall be given to her in due order at the wedding altar."
Then all of them, having eaten and drunk there in the presence of the king, spent that day in contentment together with Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others.

On the following day, when the appointed hour for the wedding had arrived, while the king himself was busily occupied with joy, Mṛgāṅkadatta performed his ablutions and other rites in a manner befitting himself.
And there, the women adorned Śaśāṅkavatī, who was already captivated by her own beauty, solely out of adherence to custom.
Then, having emerged from the chamber of curiosity with the agitated Suṣeṇa, the bride and groom took their seats upon the altar blazing like fire.
In that [ceremony], he took the hand of the princess from Vyagrasuṣeṇa—hand which was beautiful with the splendor of a held lotus—just as Acyuta took the hand of Lakṣmī.
During the circumambulation of the fire, the face of Śaśāṅkavatī shone with a certain heat and smoke; though she was not angry, it became reddened and tearful like the moon.
And handfuls of parched grain scattered by her into the fire shone like the smiles of the Mind-born God, who was delighted by the success of his efforts.
And at that time, during the first scattering of parched grain, Suṣeṇa gave five thousand horses and a hundred elephants.
Two hundred and ninety female elephants were laden with loads of gold, as well as fine garments, excellent jewels, and ornaments of pearls.
Her brother bestowed upon her the wealth born of his conquest of the earth, and at each subsequent scattering of parched grain, he gave her twice as much in succession.
Then, while the sound of festive musical instruments resounded, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having completed the auspicious marriage rites, entered his own palace together with his newly wedded bride, Śaśāṅkavatī.

And his father, the king, by bestowing upon him as was fitting elephants, horses, jewels, ornaments, food, and drink, delighted his own subjects and citizens, from the circle of vassal kings down to the parrots and mainas.

And at that time, the excellence of that king’s generosity was recognized here by its very sufficiency: for the trees, laden with garments and ornaments, caused the illusion that they were the wish-fulfilling trees of the earth.
Then that king, together with Mṛgāṅkadatta, Śaśāṅkavatī, and the other kings, having eaten, spent that day in a drinking party along with Suṣeṇa.

Then, while the people in that house were engaged in dancing and singing after having eaten and drunk well, and while the sun—having exhausted its course and drunk up the essence of the earth—entered the cave of the western mountain, it set.
And beholding him departing somewhere, united with the twilight glowing with fresh passion, the splendor of the day, as if angry with jealousy, rushed after him with her girdle of trembling birds.

And she was seen gradually emerging like a night-woman going to meet her lover, her dark garment of shimmering darkness trailing behind her, with a face whose pupils were trembling as the god of love grew powerful within her.

Then the moon, rising as radiant as fresh vermilion and resembling the curved goad on the trunk of the elephant that is the mountain of sunrise, became the brother of the arched outer corner of the eye of an angry, long-eyed woman.
When the darkness had departed, the eastern quarter, its grace restored, bore a smiling face with that moon—acting as an ear-ornament for her sport—as a fresh sprout upon the creeper of Rati.
Having performed the evening rites, Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by his new bride Śaśāṅkavatī, entered at night the bedchamber for the night’s rest, which was furnished with a costly couch.

Then, by the moon-like face of that woman, which dispelled the darkness within, the interior was illuminated as if its painted walls were lit; thus, the excellent jewel-lamps were rendered superfluous.
And there, as she remained upon the bed, he turned toward his beloved and, embracing her, gradually removed her modesty with kisses and the biting of her lower lip.
And he experienced the long-desired bliss of her fresh enchantment—the essence of a mantra—uttering only a few syllables of "no, no, enough," while the broad, precious jeweled girdle slipped down.

At the conclusion of their love-making, he delighted in her moon-like face with its disheveled locks and half-closed eyes, and in her limbs, languid and slackened by exhaustion, with their ointments partially rubbed away.
Then, as if through the mere play of their enjoyment, that night was spent; yet their love, with its expanding flow of longing for the festival of sexual union, reached a state of further increase.
The night has passed; O Lord, arise now from this bed of dalliance that dispels the fatigue of lovemaking, for these breezes from the palace chambers blow, shaking the curls of the deer-eyed women.
Like pearls fallen from the laughter of the Night as she suddenly follows the Moon, the dewdrops of the dawn shimmer with clear luster, clustered upon the tips of the dūrvā grass.

Behold, O Prince, those bees who for a long time sported within the buds of the *kairava* lilies, drinking their nectar and dwelling comfortably inside them during the meeting with the moonlight; now that those flowers have closed and their beauty has vanished, the dark bees depart elsewhere. For whose prosperity is ever stable in times of adversity?

Upon merely beholding the night, whose lower lip was adorned by the rays of the sun, the Mind-born God (Kāma) made her body marked with the spotless moon as its tilaka, and likewise smeared it with the collyrium of extremely diminished darkness.

Thus, at dawn, having been released from his throat by the soft and sweet words of the bards, Mṛgāṅkadatta—his sleep dispelled and the fatigue of the end of lovemaking gone—suddenly abandoned his bed.

Having risen, he performed his daily duties, for which all the necessary arrangements had been made by his father; and once again, accompanied by his beloved, he spent many days in that same manner with great festivity.
Then King Amaradatta, his father-in-law, first bound a turban upon the head of Suṣeṇa, his son-in-law, who had been consecrated.
Out of great respect, that king gave him as a fitting reward a single elephant, horses, loads of gold, garments, and a hundred beautiful women.
Then he [confronted] the lords of the Śabaras and Kirātas, as well as Māyāvaṭu and Śaktirakṣita, together with their kinsmen and wives, and that king who was the commander of the Mātaṅga army.
He brought Durgapiśāca and those ministers of Mṛgāṅkadatta, along with Śrutadhi, together by bestowing upon them territories, cattle, horses, gold, and garments.
Then, having dismissed those kings led by the lord of the Kirātas to their own countries along with Suṣeṇa, King Amaradatta, finding solace in his son’s valor, ruled his kingdom with that happiness.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, too, having conquered his enemies and after finally regaining Śaśāṅkavatī, lived happily for a long time together with his own ministers, Bhīmaparākrama and the others.

Then, as time passed for that King Amaradatta, old age of its own accord approached the root of his ear; having enjoyed all royal splendors, it was as if it had become his very limb to say, "Truly, this is the time for tranquility, brought on by the ripening of years."

Then that lord of the earth, his mind dispassionate toward worldly enjoyments, addressed his own ministers: "Listen, I shall now describe to you that which I intend to do and which dwells within my heart."

Our youth has departed; now, with the messenger of Death, gray hair has seized us by the locks. When old age arrives, for those like me, the addiction to the thirst for base enjoyments is but a mockery, its vigor withered away.
That the grip of greed and passion increases in tandem with one's growing age is undoubtedly the vow of a base man; for it is born of a natural disposition that the virtuous have never learned.

Therefore, I have found on this earth a worthy ally in this Mṛgāṅkadatta, who has acquired fame by defeating the King of Avanti along with his royal retinue; he is superior in virtue, naturally beloved by his subjects, and possesses excellent companions.

Therefore, having entrusted this flourishing kingdom of mine to him, I shall resort to a sacred ford for asceticism; for the conduct of the high-minded, when beyond reproach by others, is truly beautiful when it accords with their age.

Having heard these well-considered words of the lord of the earth, his steadfast ministers, the citizens headed by the queen, and all others then indeed accepted them, saying, "So be it," in due order.

Then, on a day when the auspicious moment had been declared by the astrologer, that king, accompanied by the foremost of the twice-born, performed the festival of the royal consecration for his son Mṛgāṅkadatta in a secluded place.
Then the king’s palace seemed to reel with joy, crowded here and there by people rushing at the steward’s command, with groups of officials busily engaged, and with excellent bards and women dancing.
Abundant water from the sacred bathing place fell upon the head of Mṛgāṅkadatta together with his wife; meanwhile, streams of water flowed forth once more from the eyes of his two joyful parents.
When that new king, possessing the prowess of a lion, had occupied the throne, his enemies—bowed down by fear and anger—perceived the very ground as being no different from a royal throne.
Then his father, King Amaradatta, for seven days held a great festival, having prepared the royal highways and honored the assembly of kings according to their merit.
On the eighth day, having departed from the city with his wife and having turned back his son Mṛgāṅkadatta—who was weeping along with the citizens—he went to Vārāṇasī accompanied by his minister.

There, with his limbs bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, the king remained performing worship to the Destroyer of Tripura at the three junctions of the day; subsisting on fruits and roots, he lived like a sage together with his wife while practicing asceticism.

Then, having attained that vast and stainless kingdom—just as the sun reaches the expanse of the sky—that Mṛgāṅkadatta, his majesty spreading abroad, began to blaze forth, subduing the kings by the imposition of his tribute.

Together with Māyāvaṭu and others, along with his army, and accompanied by those ministers such as Śruta and Dhi, he conquered this earth with its continents and its four horizons, and ruled the circle of the world under a single umbrella.

And while that king reigned, the earth—though it had previously borne the sufferings of famine, bandits, foreign invasions, and other fears heard of in tales—now bore a constant state of joy and happiness, equal to the bliss found in the excellent sovereignty of Rāma-bhadra.

Having occupied that city of Ayodhyā together with those ministers, the sovereign emperor—whose lotus feet were worshipped by kings arrived from various directions—enjoyed for a long time, along with his beloved Śaśāṅkavatī, pleasures free from all thorns of distress.
Having thus related this story at the edge of the Malaya forest, the sage Piśaṅgajaṭa spoke to that prince Naravāhanadatta, who was suffering from the pangs of separation.
Therefore, my son, just as Mṛgāṅkadatta obtained Śaśāṅkavatī in the past by enduring hardships, so too shall you obtain that Madanamañcukā.
Thus, having heard this nectar-like speech from that lord of sages, Piśaṅgajaṭa, Naravāhanadatta took courage in his heart regarding the attainment of Madanamañcukā.
With his mind fixed upon her, he then took leave of that best of sages and wandered through Mount Malaya, searching for Lalitalocanā, who had previously led him away.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth wave in the Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And here concludes this twelfth lambaka, the Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka. Śrī!

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa; the thirteenth book, named Madirāvatī. This nectar of stories, it is said, formerly emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth when it was churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Lord of Mountains. Those who forcibly savor it—having attained success through the removal of obstacles—bear upon this earth the status of the gods themselves by the grace of Bhava.
First Wave: May that Lord of Obstacles protect you—he whom the series of worlds, as if bowing and rising, dances along as he dances during the twilights.
May the radiance of Śambhu’s forehead-eye bring you happiness—the radiance that graces the beauty of the red lac upon Gaurī’s feet as she applies her ornaments.
We pay homage to the Goddess Sarasvatī, the bee dwelling in the lotus-mind of the Lord of Poets, whose very form is the sound that brings joy to the connoisseurs of the heart.
Then, tormented by separation from Madanamañcukā, that Naravāhanadatta, the son of the Lord of Vatsa, remained among them.
Wandering among the foothills of the Malaya mountains and in the forests surrounding them, which were enchanting with honey, he found no pleasure anywhere at all.
Although she was delicate, the mango blossom pierced his heart with the arrows falling upon it, just as the vine of Cupid’s bow pierces the heart here on earth.
And though it was sweet, the cry of the cuckoo, harsh with words of reproach and threats of death, caused unbearable pain to his ears.
And the Malaya breeze, though cool, fell upon him like the fire of passion—tawny with the pollen of flowers—and burned his limbs.
Then, as if being driven out by those forests noisy with the humming of swarms of bees, he slowly left that region.
And proceeding by degrees, accompanied by the deity, he somehow reached the bank of a lake within a forest near the path leading to the Gaṅgā.
And there he saw two young sons of Brahmins, both of auspicious appearance, sitting at the foot of a tree, engaged in private conversation.
Seeing him, they both rose up and, bowing low out of fear of the God of Love, said: "Salutations to you, O Blessed One, whose weapon is the flower!"
"Speak, O God! Why do you wander alone from here, having abandoned your flowery bow? Where is that Rati, your companion?"
Having heard that, the son of the Lord of Vatsa spoke to those two brahmins: "I am not Kāma; I am a human being, but my Rati has truly perished."
Having spoken thus and related his own story, the king asked those two brahmins, "Who are you two, and what kind of tale is this of yours here?"
Then, one of those two young brahmins said to Vinata: "How can a secret be spoken in the presence of kings such as yourself?"
Nevertheless, because your command cannot be disregarded, I shall speak; listen. There is a city named Śobhāvatī in the region of Kaliṅga.
It has not been entered by Kali, nor touched by evil deeds, nor seen by a foreign kingdom; it is as if created by the Creator himself in such a manner.
He had a learned, wealthy, and highly ritualistic Brahmin named Yaśaskara; he had a wife named Mekhalā.
Of those two, I was born as their son when they were in the middle of their lives; thereafter, I was gradually raised and initiated by them.
Then, while the boy was reciting his lessons—which were exceedingly difficult for me to master—a famine arose in that region caused by drought.
Therefore, my father, taking me along with my mother, departed from there for the city named Viśālā, together with his wealth and his retinue.
In that dwelling of Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, where enmity had been abandoned, he then took up residence, having been granted shelter by his merchant friend.
And I, while pursuing the acquisition of knowledge in the house of my teacher, lived there among fellow students of my own age.
Among them, there was one friend of mine, a kṣatriya youth named Vijayasena, a virtuous son of a very wealthy kṣatriya.
Once, my friend’s sister, a maiden named Madirāvatī, came along with him to our preceptor’s house.

Out of fear, the entire retinue went to the royal palace and spoke, having set aside the terrified Madanamañcukā even as she was trying to restrain them.
Then King Mānasavega, accompanied by his own forces, rushed there and surrounded Naravāhanadatta.
Then the goddess Earth, his mother, quickly approached him and said to the king: "O son, this man must not be killed by you, nor by me."
For this son of the King of Vatsa, Naravāhanadatta, is no adulterer; he has come here to his own wife.
"By the power of my knowledge, I know that you are blinded by anger; do you not see that this man is our son-in-law, born of the lunar race, and worthy of honor?"
Having been addressed thus by his mother, Mānasavega, thinking "In that case, this man is my enemy," spoke to her with rising indignation.
Then his mother spoke to him again out of affection for her son-in-law: "My son, no unrighteous act can be committed in this world of the Vidyādharas."
"For here exists the assembly hall of the Vidyādharas, where dharma and artha are pursued; there, in the presence of its presiding members, cast the blame upon his head."
Therefore, whatever is done for him will appear beautiful; otherwise, the Vidyādharas would manifest their powers and the deities would not tolerate it.
Accepting these words of his mother out of respect for her, Mānasavega proceeded to bind him, intending to lead him to the assembly hall.
Unable to endure his bonds, Naravāhanadatta uprooted a pillar from the archway and slew many of the king's servants there.
From among them, having seized the sword of one who had been slain, that hero of divine prowess instantly struck down the others as well.
Then Mānasavega, by means of his own divine magic power, bound him along with his wife and led them to that assembly hall.
There, summoned by the great sound of the drum, the Vidyādharas gathered from here and there, just as the gods assemble in the Sudharmā hall.
Then a king named Vāyupatha, surrounded by his courtiers and Vidyādharas, arrived and sat down there upon a jeweled lion-throne.
As he was being fanned with chowries that seemed to shake off all unrighteousness, the wicked Mānasavega stood before him and spoke these words:
"Though he is a mortal, this man is a destroyer who has ruined my inner apartments and violated my sister; he is my enemy and must be executed today, for he truly desires no sovereignty over us."
Having heard that, the hero Naravāhanadatta was questioned by that courtier regarding the reply, and he spoke with confidence:
That is an assembly where there is an assessor; he is an assessor who speaks according to dharma; that is dharma where there is truth; and that is truth where there is no deception.
"I am bound by illusion and remain right here on the ground, whereas you are seated upon a non-existent seat and are liberated; what dispute can there be between us two in this matter?"
Having heard this, Vāyupatha seated him upon the ground and, according to justice, caused Mānasavega to be released.
Then, while everyone there listened, Naravāhanadatta spoke this reply in the presence of Vāyupatha:
"If I have obtained my own wife, Madanamañcukā, who was carried off and brought here by him, whose harem has been violated by me?"
If, having approached her because of her beauty, I have deceived her and become her brother's husband, what fault of mine is there in that?
"If I desire sovereignty, whose desire does not arise for something, somewhere? Having heard this and reflected upon it, King Vāyupatha then said:
"This high-souled one will be of great future prosperity; he speaks according to dharma. O Mānasavega, my dear friend, do not commit unrighteousness toward him."
When he had spoken thus, Mānasavega did not turn back from his unrighteousness, blinded as he was by delusion; therefore, Vāyupatha proceeded against his wrath.
Then, together with Mānasavega and his arrayed army, there arose a great agitation for that king who was devoted to righteousness.
For the wise, who perceive only what is right, sit upon the seat of Dharma and recognize—alas!—the weak as their own, whether they be strong or another.
Abandoning deceit, fight clearly with me; behold my prowess as I slay you with a single blow.
Thus Naravāhanadatta spoke to Mānasavega while looking at the celestial maidens there with curiosity.

And while those Vidyādharas were engaged in mutual strife there, suddenly from the very center of an excellent pillar situated within the assembly hall, a deity in a terrifying form indeed emerged with a loud crash.

Pervading the sky, dark as collyrium, and eclipsing the sun, with the rays of his eyes flashing like flickering streaks of lightning, and with rows of teeth shining like flocks of cranes descending, he was as fierce as a roaring cloud at the time of the great dissolution.

"There is no defeat for this rogue, even though he is a future Wheel-Turning King of the Vidyādharas"—saying this, the Lord, gladdening Mānasavega, dismissed him as he hung his head and took to the path of the wind.

Taking Naravāhanadatta by his two arms for protection, the Blessed One quickly brought him to the auspicious and excellent mountain Ṛṣyamūka; having established him there, he then indeed vanished from sight.
Then that agitation of the Vidyādharas in that assembly subsided among one another; and Vāyupatha, accompanied by them and his own other followers, departed from there just as he had come.
And that Mānasavega, placing Madanamañcukā before him—she who was overwhelmed by joy and despair—went dejectedly to his own city of Āṣāḍhapura.

Thus ends the second wave in the fifth book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave. I believe that Fate intends only for a man's ultimate welfare; it repeatedly and intensely tests his fortitude in both happiness and sorrow.
In foreign lands, at every step, he united Naravāhanadatta with various wives and then separated him from them once more.
Then, having approached Naravāhanadatta as he was staying on that Ṛṣyamūka mountain, his beloved Prabhāvatī spoke to him.
Indeed, because of the fault of being under the influence of intoxication, you were then taken by Mānasavega, who desired to do evil, to that assembly hall.
Having learned of that, I came at that very moment and, by means of the power of my magic science, created a grand display of divine manifestations and brought you here.
For even the vast array of spells of the powerful Vidyādharas does not prevail on this mountain, since it is a field of spiritual accomplishment (siddhakṣetra).
For this very reason, even my own power of knowledge does not succeed here; therefore, it is my sorrow that how you will subsist on forest food.
When she had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta remained there with her, awaiting the appointed time, as he meditated upon Madanamañcukā.
He bathed in the purifying Pampā lake near that mountain and partook of roots and fruits of divine flavor.
He drank the meritorious water of the pond, which was savory and fragrant with fruits fallen from the trees on the bank, and which was accompanied by the side-dish of venison.
He dwelt at the roots of trees and within the interiors of mountain caves, following the conduct of Rāma as he lived in the forests of that region.
And having seen those various hermitages of Rāma there, Prabhāvatī described to him the narrative of the Rāmāyaṇa for his amusement.
Here, Rāma, accompanied by Saumitri and followed by Sītā, dwelt in the forest at the foot of a tree where he had constructed a hut, together with the ascetics.
With Anasūyā as her unguent and Sītā perfuming the forest, she dwells here among the wives of the sages, wearing garments of bark.
In this regard, the Daitya Dundubhi was slain by Vālin in a cave; he was the cause of the enmity that existed previously between Vālin and Sugrīva.
For Sugrīva, believing through delusion that Vālin had been killed by the Daitya, went away in fear after blocking the entrance of the cave with mountain crags.
And Vālin, having broken through that gate and emerged, drove Sugrīva away, thinking, "He has imprisoned me here out of a desire for the kingdom."
Having fled, that lord of monkeys, Sugrīva, established his residence here on this ridge of Ṛṣyamūka together with those headed by Hanumān.
Then, having approached while Rāmadeva’s mind was deceived by the ruse of the golden deer, Rāvaṇa carried off the daughter of Janaka.
Then, seeking news of Sītā, that scion of Raghu formed an alliance here with Sugrīva, who himself was seeking the death of Vālin.
And there, to demonstrate his strength, he pierced seven palm trees with a single arrow—even those which the exceedingly powerful Vālī himself had only managed to split with great difficulty.
Having gone from here to Kiṣkindhā, that hero, having slain Vālin with a single arrow discharged with ease, bestowed his sovereignty upon Sugrīva.
Then, while Sugrīva’s followers, headed by Hanumān, set out in the four directions to obtain news of Sītā, [the following occurred].
Here, during the rainy season, Rāma dwelt together with the resounding clouds, which, with their falling streams of water, seemed to share his sorrow.
And when it was learned through great effort that Hanumān had crossed the ocean at the word of Saṃpāti, [Rāma] went forth accompanied by the monkey forces.
Having bound the ocean with that bridge and slain the enemy, the Lord of Laṅkā, he brought back the goddess Jānakī by way of this celestial chariot.
In this way, O noble son, you too shall attain prosperity; for fortunes come of their own accord to steadfast men in times of adversity.
While Prabhāvatī was speaking in this manner and so forth, Naravāhanadatta remained there, sporting with her here and there.
Once, while he was at Pampā, two Vidyādharīs, Dhanavatī and Ajināvatī, descended from heaven and approached him.
By means of those two, he was led from the city of the Gandharvas to Śrāvastī, where Bhagīrathayaśas was married by him.
When Prabhāvatī had joined her as a friend at Ajināvatī, Dhanavatī spoke thus to Naravāhanadatta:
"This daughter of mine, Ajināvatī, was previously promised by my word; therefore, marry her, for your time of prosperity is near at hand."
Out of affection for her friend, Prabhāvatī and Naravāhanadatta both welcomed these words of Dhanavatī, saying, "So be it."
Then Dhanavatī gave that daughter Ajināvatī to him, the son of the Lord of Vatsa, according to the appropriate rite.
And she brought to completion that auspicious marriage ceremony of her daughter, made beautiful by the magnificent divine preparations fashioned through her own supernatural power.
Then, on another day, she said to Naravāhanadatta: "My son, it is not proper for you to remain here for long in such a place."
The people of the Vidyādharas are illusory, and you have no business here; therefore, go now to your own city of Kauśāmbī together with your wife.
And I myself shall come there with my son Caṇḍasiṃha and with the lords of the Vidyādharas for your prosperity.
Having spoken thus, Dhanavatī ascended, making even the day appear as if filled with moonlight by the radiance of her white body and garments.
And Prabhāvatī and Jināvatī brought that Naravāhanadatta through the air to the city of Kauśāmbī.
Having arrived there at that garden, Naravāhanadatta was brought down from the sky and seen by his own attendants.
"This prince has arrived; by good fortune we are prospering!"—thus a cry arose there from the people on all sides.
Then, having learned of that, King Vatsa, together with Vāsavadattā, was filled with joy as if suddenly drenched by a shower of nectar.
Padmāvatī and her brides, Ratnaprabhā and the others, as well as Yaugandharāyaṇa and the other ministers of the Lord of Vatsa, quickly [arrived].
Kaliṅgasenā and her own ministers, Gomukha and the others, approached him as was fitting, like travelers to a lake in the heat of summer.
And they beheld him in the midst of those two wives of the Sudaśārha clan, seated like Kṛṣṇa between Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.
As if out of fear that their own limbs might shatter, they closed their eyes with tears of joy upon seeing those [limbs].
And Vatsarāja and the two queens, having at last embraced their son, were unable to let him go from their limbs, which felt as if they were bristling with thorns.
Then, while that great festival was proceeding with the sounding of musical instruments, there arrived the daughter of Vegavat, the wife of Naravāhanadatta.
Having descended through the path of the sky, Vegavatī, the sister of Mānasavega, arrived there, having perceived [her brother] through the power of her perfected vidyā.
Having prostrated at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, she, bowing at their feet, spoke to her own husband, Naravāhanadatta.
Having become weakened on your account, I mastered the sciences in the forest of asceticism; now, O auspicious one, I have returned once more to your presence.
When she had spoken thus, she was greeted with approval by her husband and the others, and she approached her two friends, Prabhāvatī and Ajināvatī.
While she was being embraced by those two and seated there in their midst, Mātṛjināvatī and Dhanavatī also arrived.
And those various lords of the Vidyādharas arrived together with her, surrounded by their armies which covered the surface of the sky like clouds.
Her son was the heroic Caṇḍasiṃha, possessed of mighty arms; likewise, his kinsman named Amitagati was endowed with great strength.
And that Piṅgalagāndhāra, the father of Prabhāvatī, was powerful; he too was Vāyupatha, the presiding lord of the assembly who had previously undertaken [the vow].
And that heroic King Hemaprabha, endowed with great strength, was addressed by Ratnaprabhā together with his son Vajraprabha.
The Gandharva king Sāgaradatta also arrived, accompanied by his daughter Gandharvadattā and Citrāṅgada.
Having arrived, they were duly honored by the King of Vatsa together with his son, and they sat down upon seats as was appropriate.
Then King Piṅgalagāndhāra addressed his son-in-law, Naravāhanadatta, who was standing in the assembly, saying: "Wait a moment."
"You are a universal monarch, created by the gods for all of us; out of the power of great affection, we have all come to you."
This Queen Dhanavatī is your mother-in-law, firm in her vows; she possesses divine knowledge and wears a rosary, a black antelope skin, and garments.
Exerting herself to protect you, she is like the Blessed Goddess herself, or like Sāvitrī, a perfected lore praised by the highest of the Vidyādharas.
"Therefore, there will be success in your undertaking; however, listen to what I say. Here on the Himalayas, there are two divisions of the Vidyādharas."
The northern and the southern [peaks] are situated on different levels of the mountain ridges; indeed, the northern one is beyond Kailāsa, while the southern one is on this side of it.
In that regard, for the sake of supreme sovereignty, this Amitagati now performed difficult austerities and completely satisfied Śaṅkara.
"Naravāhanadatta, that universal monarch, will fulfill your desire; having been commanded by him, he has come to you."
There resides a chief king named Mandaradeva, who is wicked-minded; though he is powerful, he is not invincible to you once you have acquired the vidyā.
But he who is in the middle of the south, known as Gairimuṇḍa, is a wicked-souled king who, through the power of his magic sciences, is exceedingly difficult to conquer.
And he is the greatest friend of his enemy Mānasavega; as long as he has not been won over here, this task will not be accomplished.
"Accomplish the supreme reality quickly, for the power of your knowledge is great"—when Piṅgalagāndhāra had spoken thus, Dhanavatī sang in reply:
"Thus it is, my son; as this king says to you, so shall it be. Having gone from here to the field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), [worship] the Lord for the sake of attaining the vidyā."
"Exert yourself in propitiation, for without his favor, how can excellence be attained? Moreover, these kings assembled here will protect you."
Then Citrāṅgada spoke thus once more: "Let this Vijaya be made the foremost of us all."
Then, having resolved upon this very course and performed the auspicious rites for his departure, he prostrated at the feet of his parents and his elders, who were bathed in tears.
Having been granted blessings by them, he ascended an excellent palanquin prepared by Amitagati’s wisdom, accompanied by his wives and ministers.
Then Naravāhanadatta set forth, obscuring the sky with his forces, which resembled the waters of the ocean tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon.
With the echoes of the army's roar reaching to the ends of the quarters, it was as if announcing to the sky-dwellers: "The universal monarch has arrived."
In an instant, he was led by those lords of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas, along with Dhanavatī, to that mountain of the Siddha-field.
There, having been instructed in his vows by the Siddhas, he performed austerities for the propitiation of Śaṅkara, bathing in the morning, subsisting on fruit, and sleeping upon the ground.
And those kings stood surrounding him, providing protection on all sides for the dwellers of heaven, remaining vigilant day and night.
There, the Vidyadhara maidens, filled with longing, made him appear as if he were covered by a black antelope skin through the radiance of their eyes as he performed his austerities.
At that moment, with eyes whose corners were intent upon him and hands placed upon their chests, the other women seemed to show him having entered into their hearts.
And seeing him, five other daughters of the Vidyādharas were scorched by the fire of passion and made a mutual agreement among themselves.
"This husband is to be chosen by us five friends simultaneously, and our marriage must likewise be performed without any division."
If one [wife] were to perform a marriage separately with him, then the others should enter the fire on her account, for she is a betrayer of her friends.
While those celestial maidens were thus agitated upon perceiving him, great portents suddenly appeared there in the penance grove.
A most fierce wind blew, uprooting the auspicious trees, as if saying, "In this manner shall the heroes fall here in battle."
As if out of fear that "what might happen here?", the earth trembled; as if terrified, the mountain ridges split apart to provide space.
"O Vidyādharas, protect, protect this lord with all effort!"—thus, as it were, the sky, free from clouds, uttered a terrible sound.
And Naravāhanadatta, amidst this tumultuous upheaval of portents, remained perfectly motionless, meditating upon the three-eyed Lord Śiva.
And those heroes—the lords of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas—stood ready in armor, guarding him while apprehensive of some misfortune.
Brandishing forests of sword-blades like whisks, they let out lion-roars, as if threatening portents that foretold the arrival of misfortune.
Then, on another day, suddenly, a host of Vidyādharas was seen in the sky, thick as the clouds at the end of an aeon and emitting a terrible roar.
"This Gaurimuṇḍa has arrived together with Mānasavega," Dhanavatī then said, recollecting her own magic science.
Then Gaurīmuṇḍa, together with Mānasavega, rushed toward those lords of the Vidyādharas and the Gandharvas who were bearing their weapons.
To him who was speaking thus—"Where is this mortal, and where are we? Therefore, O sky-dwellers, I shall today quell your pride," [the sage replied: "This is indeed for those who are partial."
Then Citrāṅgada, running forward in anger, attacked him, as did King Sāgaradatta, the sovereign of the Gandharvas.
Caṇḍasiṃha, Amitagati, King Vāyupatha, as well as Piṅgalagāndhāra—all these were lords of the Vidyādharas.
The great chariot-warriors, accompanied by their assembled armies, rushed toward that evil Mānasavega, roaring like lions.
Shrouded by the thick clouds of dust from the armies, with the flashes of weapons as streaks of lightning, and with blood falling like rain, that terrible storm of battle broke forth.
Citrāṅgadā and the others performed what was like a great sacrificial rite for the spirits, filled with the wine of blood and strewn with the offerings of the heads of their enemies.
Rivers of blood began to flow, crowded with headless trunks as their crocodiles, carrying weapons as their serpents, and having froth made of mingled fat.
Then Gaurīmuṇḍa, his army destroyed and himself facing death, called to mind the Gaurī-vidyā, which had been previously propitiated and was well-pleased with him.
And having manifested herself visibly, three-eyed and armed with a trident, she bewildered those great heroes who were the followers of Naravāhanadatta.
Then Gaurīmuṇḍa, having gained his strength, rushed forward roaring and fell upon Naravāhanadatta for a wrestling match.
Pierced by that wrestling, the master of illusion again remembered that true knowledge; by its power, he seized him by the arms and flew into the sky.
But Gaurīmuṇḍa was unable to kill that prince by the power of the Dhanavatī-vidyā; instead, he hurled him onto the Fire Mountain.
Mānasavega, too, taking those friends of his, Gomukha and the others, leapt up into the sky and cast them in all directions with utter disregard.
And those [jewels], having been cast up and guarded by the employed Dhanavatī, were split apart by the Rūpiṇī vidyā and established upon the surface of the earth.
"You shall quickly regain that lord, successful in his purpose and in good health"—having thus consoled them one by one, that Vidyā vanished from their sight.
Then, thinking "the conquest has been achieved by us," Gaurīmuṇḍa returned home with Mānasavega, each going by the way he had come.
"Naravāhanadatta will return to you with his purpose accomplished; there is nothing that can befall him as ill," thus spoke Dhanavatī.
Those lords of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas, Citrāṅgada and the others, having likewise cast off their delusion, have now departed for their own respective abodes.
Dhanavatī also, taking her own daughter Ajināvatī who was there with her co-wives, went to her own home.
Mānasavega also went to that Madanamañcukā and said to her, "Your husband has been killed; therefore, accept me."
"He shall be your slayer; no one can kill him, for he was created by the gods"—thus she replied to him, laughing even as she stood before him.
And as Naravāhanadatta was being thrown onto the Vahni mountain by his enemy, a certain divine man arrived and seized him.
Having protected him, he quickly led him to the cool bank of the Mandākinī; and when asked by him, "Who are you?", he comforted him and spoke to him.
"O Lord, I am the king of the Vidyādharas named Amṛtaprabha; I have now been sent by Hara for the purpose of protecting you."
And this mountain Kailāsa, the abode of him [Śiva], stands before you; having propitiated Śiva here, you shall attain your welfare without obstacle.
Having said, "Therefore come, I will lead you there," that best of Vidyādharas brought him there at that very moment, and after taking his leave, he departed.
Naravāhanadatta, having reached Kailāsa, propitiated Vināyaka, who was stationed there before him, through his ascetic penance.
Having been granted permission by him, he entered the hermitage of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain; emaciated by his observances, he saw Nandin at the gate.
After he had performed the circumambulation, Nandin spoke to him with compassion: "You have likely attained success, for your obstacles have now been pacified."
Therefore, remaining here, perform ascetic penance until you have propitiated the Blessed One; for spiritual accomplishments depend upon purification through austerity that destroys evil.
When Nandin had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta, meditating upon the God and the goddess Pārvatī, performed supreme penance, subsisting only on air.
And the Lord Śiva, pleased by his ascetic penance, granted him a vision and, together with the goddess Girijā, commanded him as he stood bowed before him.
Now become the universal monarch of all the Vidyādharas; may all the vidyās, surpassing all others, manifest for you.
By our power, you shall be invincible to your enemies; neither to be cut down nor to be pierced, you shall slay all your foes without exception.
But once you have been seen, the spells of your enemies will no longer prevail; therefore, go, for even the Gaurī-spell shall come under your control.
Having thus granted a boon together with Gaurī, Hara gave him a great lotus-like celestial chariot (*vimāna*) fashioned by Brahmā, fit for a universal monarch.
Then all those sciences appeared before him in embodied form, eager to carry out his commands, saying, "What do you command? What shall we do?"
Thus Naravāhanadatta, having received a multitude of boons from the Siddhas, bowed to the Supreme Lords and, with their permission, ascended that divine lotus-palace.
First, he went to that city of Amitagati known as Vakrapura, its path revealed by the sciences and celebrated in song by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Amitagati, having seen him from afar approaching through the sky in a celestial chariot, went out to meet him and, after he had offered his salutations, led him into his own home.
And there, in order to grant him the attainment of his own described supernatural powers, he joyfully gave to that Naravāhanadatta his own daughter, named Sulocanā, as a gift.
Then, together with her—who was like a second Fortune of the Vidyādharas obtained by him—the joyful emperor spent that day in celebration.

Thus ends the third wave in the fifth book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave: Then, in that city of Vakrapura, Naravāhanadatta—the newly installed emperor—was seated in his assembly hall.
On another day, having descended from the sky with a staff in hand, a certain man approached, bowed, and made this request:
"O King, know me to be the hereditary doorkeeper of the Cakravartin, named Paurarucideva, who has come here for the purpose of serving you."
Having heard that, he looked at the face of Amitagati; and when he was informed by him, "It is true, O Lord," he rejoiced in his appointment as chamberlain.
Then, having understood the situation through its power, Dhanavatī, along with her wives Vegavatī and the others, and her son Caṇḍasiṃha, [set out].
Likewise, King Piṅgalagāndhāra, accompanied by Vāyupatha, and Citrāṅgada, together with Sāgaradatta, were there.
Accompanied by Hemaprabha and others, they arrived with the sun obscured by their army, as if signaling beforehand their inability to endure the splendor of the enemy.
Having approached, they fell at the feet of that universal monarch; he too honored them with a welcome according to their merit.
Out of respect, he bowed at the feet of Dhanavatī; she too, being pleased, honored her son-in-law with blessings.
Then, having heard the account of the establishment of his own self as told by that lord, Caṇḍasiṃha and all the others felt extreme joy.
Then, seeing his wives seated by his side and Dhanavatī, that emperor asked, "Where are my ministers?"
"Having been hurled by the power of my mind, they were protected and established by me; now they have been shattered by you through the power of a spell," she replied to him.
Then, having commanded his personified Vidyā, he had them brought; and when they arrived, having inquired after his welfare and clung to his feet, he spoke to them.
"By whom were so many days spent, how, and where? O you, let each one of you tell me this wondrous tale."
Then Gomukha first related his own story in this way: "At that time, when I was cast away by my enemy, a certain goddess took me up in her hands."
Having comforted me and placed me in a distant forest, he vanished; then, distressed, I desired to cast off my body from a precipice.
"Do not do so, Gomukha; you shall see that lord Siddhārtha again. Thus did someone approach me and restrain me from my ascetic practice.
When I then asked him, "Who are you, and how do you know this?", he replied, "Come to my hermitage; there I will tell you."
Then, accompanied by him whose wealth of knowledge was indicated by the consciousness of my name, I went to that hermitage in the field of Śiva.
There, having been offered hospitality, he spoke these words to me: "I am a twice-born man named Nāgasvāmin, from the city called Kuṇḍina."
When my father had gone to heaven, I went to Pāṭaliputra and attended upon the teacher Jayadatta for the sake of learning.
Even while being instructed, because of my dullness, I did not understand even a single syllable; for that reason, all the students mocked me there.
Then, consumed by that humiliation, I set out for the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhya mountains; on the way, midway, I reached a city named Vakrolaka.
There, as I had entered her house for the sake of alms, the housewife gave me a single red lotus along with the alms-food.
Having taken that, when she saw me arrive at another house, the mistress of that house said, "Alas, what a pity! You have been claimed by a yoginī!"
"Behold, this woman has offered you her hand under the guise of a red lotus. Having heard that, as soon as I looked, I saw that it was not a lotus, but a hand.
Then, abandoning that [thought] and falling at her feet, I said: "O Mother, devise a means for me so that I may live."
Having heard that, she said to me: "Go from here three yojanas; there is a twice-born man named Devarakṣita in the village of Karabhaka."
In his house there is an excellent Kapila cow, who is Surabhi herself; she will protect you this night now that you have come to her for refuge.
Thus addressed by her, I fled in fear at the close of day and reached the house of that twice-born man in the village of Karabha.
Having entered there and seen that Kapilā, I bowed down and addressed her: "O Goddess, I have come to you for refuge, being terrified."
Meanwhile, that yoginī, threatening me along with her companions, came there through the air at night, seeking my flesh and blood.
Seeing that, Kapilā then placed me between her hooves and protected me by fighting all those yoginīs throughout the entire night.
In the morning, when they had departed, this Kapilā spoke to me in a distinct voice: "O son, I shall not be able to protect you today."
Therefore, go five yojanas from here to a forest sanctuary; there dwells a wise man named Bhūtiśiva, the foremost among the Pāśupatas.
"He will protect you, who have come for refuge, for this one night alone. Having heard that, I bowed to her and then set out from there.
Having quickly reached that Bhūtiśiva, I took refuge in him; and there at night, those same yoginīs came once again.
Then, having led me inside the inner chamber, Bhūtiśiva, standing at the door with a trident in hand, rebuked those yoginīs.
"O Brahmin, after defeating these [demons] and feeding me, Bhūtiśiva said to me in the morning: 'I am no longer able to protect you now.'"
"There is a village ten *yojanas* from here called Saṃdhyāvāsa; there lives a Brahmin named Vasumati—go to him."
"Then, having passed this third night, you shall be released. Having been told this by him, I bowed to him and set out from there.
As I traveled, the sun set midway due to the length of the road; and those yoginīs, coming up from behind, seized me in the night.
And as soon as they had taken me and were joyfully traveling through the air, other unprecedented yoginīs descended before them.
A fierce battle suddenly broke out with them; because of it, I fell from their hands into a very desolate region.
Then I saw there a single great palace; it seemed to say to me, "Enter," through its open door.
Having fled and entered there within, I, overwhelmed by fear, beheld a woman of wondrous form accompanied by hundreds of women.
Shining with radiance as if ablaze at twilight, she was like a great medicinal herb for protection created by the Creator out of compassion for me.
After I had comforted her for a moment, she questioned me and said to me: "I am a yakṣiṇī named Sumitrā; it is only because of a curse that I remain here in this state."
And for the sake of pacifying my curse, union with a human has been ordained for me; therefore, approach me without hesitation and enjoy me, free from fear.
Having said this, she quickly entered and, with baths, ointments, garments, food, and drink, she attended to me with joy.
Where is that fear caused by the ḍākinīs, and where is that happiness in that very moment? Alas, the sudden onset of pleasure and pain is inconceivable, even for Fate.
Then, I spent those days there happily with that yakṣiṇī; and then one day, she spoke to me of her own accord.
"O Brahmin, that curse of mine has been exhausted; therefore, I depart today. And by my grace, divine knowledge shall arise within you."
"You shall become an ascetic who enjoys the fruits of perfection and shall be fearless; while remaining here in this house of mine, do not look toward the middle city."
Having spoken thus, she vanished; then, out of curiosity, I ascended that middle city and there I saw a horse.
Therefore, having approached him, I was thrown by the horse and struck by its hooves; in an instant, I saw myself standing in this temple of Śiva.
From that time forward, I have remained here and have gradually attained perfection; thus, even though I am a human being, I possess knowledge of the three periods of time.
Thus, although the accomplishments of everyone here are abundant with afflictions, remain here; Śambhu will bring about the accomplishment you desire.
Having been addressed thus by that wise man, I remained for so many days in that hermitage, having conceived a hope for attaining your feet.
"O Lord, it is said that today, by Śarva, through the power of a boon granted in a dream, I have been brought here by some divine woman who took me away."
Having said, "Such is my story," Gomukha stood silent; then Marubhūti spoke before Naravāhanadatta.
Then, as I was being hurled by the force of my own mind, a certain goddess caught me in her hands, set me down far away in the forest, and vanished from sight.
Then, afflicted by suffering there and thinking of a means for death, I wandered about and saw a hermitage surrounded by a river.
Having entered there, I saw that ascetic seated upon a stone slab with matted locks; having bowed to him, I approached him.
"Who are you, and how have you come to this non-human land?"—when thus questioned by him, I described everything to him.
Then, having understood this, he said to me: "Do not kill yourself now; you shall learn news of your master here, and thereafter you will do what is appropriate."
While I remained there, having spoken thus out of a desire to hear news of you, celestial women came to that river to bathe.
Then that ascetic said to me, "Go, bring her garment; from one of these women who are bathing, you will learn news of that lord."
Having heard that, I did exactly so; and that bride followed after me, her clothes stolen and wearing only wet garments, with her hands placed over her breasts in the svastika gesture.
Having related the news of Naravāhanadatta, she was told by that ascetic, "Take these two garments," whereupon she replied:
Naravāhanadatta, remaining today on Kailāsa while propitiating Hara, will become the emperor of the Vidyādharas after some days.
When she had spoken thus, that divine woman became his wife through the power of the curse, owing to her familiarity with those stories.
Then that ascetic remained with that Vidyādharī; and by her word, I too stayed here, having conceived hope for my reunion with you.
After several days, having become pregnant and giving birth to that child, the celestial woman said to the ascetic, "The curse has been pacified for me through my union with you."
"If you still desire my company, then cook and eat these along with rice"; having said this, that ascetic flew up into the sky and departed.
Having said this, she departed; [the king] cooked her embryo together with rice, ate it, and followed after him, saying, "Eat this, and then you shall obtain me."
Although I was told this at first, I did not eat it, waiting for success; however, having obtained two grains of rice from the cooking pot, I ate them.
Because of that, wherever I spat, there it became gold; then, wandering about in a state of destitution, I reached a certain city.
While I was living there in that courtesan’s house with lavish expenditure using my gold, the procuress, wishing to test me, gave me an emetic by means of a trick.
As I was vomiting, those two grains of rice that I had previously eaten emerged from my mouth, shining like rubies.
As soon as they had gone out, those [gems] were seized and eaten by the procuress; thus the Golden Elixir was lost, having been stolen away by that procuress.
Since even today Śiva still bears the crescent moon and Hari still possesses the Kaustubha gem, I know that the fruit of these two falling within the range of a procuress is such as this.
Moreover, since this saṃsāra is so full of wonders and so full of deceptions, by whom and when could it ever be fully comprehended, any more than the ocean?
Reflecting thus, I became despondent; then, in order to attain you, I went to the temple of Caṇḍikā to propitiate that goddess through ascetic penance.
Having fasted for three nights, that goddess commanded me in a dream: "Your master has achieved his desire; go and see him."
"Having heard this, O King, I awoke in the morning and was brought to the feet of Your Majesty by some goddess; such is my story."
When Marubhūti had been thus mocked by the procuress, Naravāhanadatta laughed along with those who were at his side.
Then Hariśikha said: "O King, when I was cast away by my enemy at that time, some deity protected me and placed me in Ujjayinī."
There, distressed and desiring to cast off my body at the onset of night, I went to the cremation ground and constructed a funeral pyre with the wood found there.
Having lit that fire and approached me as I was worshipping the fire there, the lord of spirits known as Tālajaṅgha spoke to me.
"For what purpose do you enter the fire? Your lord is alive and waiting for you; when he has attained his own perfection, you shall be reunited with him."
Thus, even though he was cruel, he restrained me from death out of affection; for even stones attain a state of true softness when fate is favorable.
"Then, having gone there, I remained performing austerities before the gods; today, O Lord, I have been brought to your side by some deity."
When Hariśikha had spoken thus, and likewise by the others in turn, that King Naravāhanadatta [acted] according to the words of Amitagati.
Having urged Dhanavatī—who was worthy of honor, possessed of wealth, and worshipped by the Vidyādharas—you caused her to bestow all the sciences even upon those ministers of yours.
Then, when those ministers of his had become Vidyādharas, Dhanavatī said on an auspicious day, "Conquer your enemies now!"
That heroic universal monarch commanded his armies to begin their march toward the city of Gaurimuṇḍa, known as Govindakūṭa.
Then the army of the Vidyādharas, which obscured the sun in the sky, set forth, causing the illusion that the moon was being seized by an untimely Rāhu.
Naravāhanadatta himself ascended the pericarp of that lotus-palace, while his wives took their places upon the filaments.
Having placed his companions, Caṇḍasiṃha and the others, upon the leaves, he set out through the sky with them as his vanguard for the sake of victory.
While traveling, he stopped at the house of Dhanavatī when he had reached the halfway point; honored by her, he spent that day in the city named Mātaṅgapura.
Remaining there, he dispatched a messenger to summon the two lords of the Vidyādharas, Gaurīmuṇḍa and Mānasavega.
On another day, having left his wives there in Mātaṅgapura, he went to Govindakūṭa along with the kings and the sky-dwellers.
There, as Gaurīmuṇḍa and Mānasavega went forth to battle, Caṇḍasiṃha and the others intercepted them in front.
With the trees that were the noble warriors felled by the onset of battle, that Govindakūṭa mountain became one from which torrents of blood flowed.
With his tongue-like banner of a sword smeared with blood and shimmering, that time of battle yawned forth, desiring to devour the lives of the heroes.

That festival of battle became terrifying with flesh and blood, and the clapping of hand-drums played by intoxicated vetālas; it was a spectacle where headless trunks danced for the delight of the bhūtas.
Then, in this battle, Naravāhanadatta himself rushed in fury toward that Mānasavega who had come before him face-to-face.
And having rushed forward and seized him by the hair at that very moment, the universal monarch cut off the head of that evildoer with his sword.
Seeing him enraged and rushing there, Gaurīmuṇḍa seized him by the hair and threw him to the ground, his power of magic destroyed by that sight.
Having thrown him down and seized him by his two feet, Naravāhanadatta whirled him around in the sky and crushed him against a rock.
Thus, when Gaurimuṇḍa and Mānasavega had been slain by him, the remainder of their army fled in fear.
A rain of flowers fell upon the body of that universal monarch, and all the gods stationed in the sky exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then Naravāhanadatta entered the capital city of Gaurimuṇḍa together with all those kings of his own.
At that very moment, the lords of the Vidyādharas, accompanied by Gaurimuṇḍā and others, approached his command and, bowing down, accepted it.
Then, during the festivities following the conquest of the kingdom and the defeat of his enemies, Dhanavatī approached that sovereign emperor and addressed him.
"O King, Gaurimuṇḍa has a daughter named Trailokyasundarī; marry that maiden here, who is called Ātmanikā."
Having been addressed thus by her, the king had her summoned at that very moment, married her, and spent that day in happiness with her.
In the morning, having dismissed Vegavatī and Prabhāvatī, he had Madanamañcukā brought from the city of Mānasavega.
Her face blossomed wide, moist with tears of joy, as she beheld her husband standing at the mountain of sunrise, having destroyed the darkness of his enemies.
At the end of the pain of separation from Śūra, she attained a certain joy, like a lotus pond whose lotuses have blossomed with the water of the morning dew.
He too, having long yearned for all the sciences, joyfully bestowed them upon her; and she, having immediately attained the status of a Vidyādharī, took delight with him.
And he spent those days there with his wives, staying in the garden of Gaurimuṇḍa’s city, indulging in the pleasures of drinking and other diversions.
Then, having sent away Prabhāvatī, Bhāgīrathayaśas was also summoned by him, and he bestowed the vidyās upon her.
And once, both Vidyādharas approached the universal monarch as he sat in his assembly hall and addressed him appropriately.
"O gods, we two have come here from the other side of the sacrificial altar, at the word of Dhanavatī, in order to learn the conduct of the god Mandara."
There we saw that lord of the Vidyādharas, who had gone to an improper place; while our bodies remained concealed, he spoke thus concerning you both.
I have heard that Gaurīmuṇḍa and all the others were slain by Naravāhanadatta after he attained the sovereignty over the Vidyādharas.
"Disregarding that, we must slay this newly arisen enemy. Having heard these words from him, we have come here to speak.
Having heard this from the mouth of the spy, the assembly of Naravāhanadatta shone, agitated with anger, like a lotus pond struck by the wind.
Citrāṅgada’s two arms, shaken and extended again and again, seemed to seek instruction from the clanging of their bracelets on how to fight.
The necklace on the chest of Amitagati, as he breathed heavily in his rage, seemed to say again and again, "Arise, arise, O hero! as if speaking thus.
Striking the ground with his hand, Piṅgalagāndhāra produced a loud sound that, like the syllable *oṃ* used at the beginning of a ritual, seemed to pulverize his enemies.
Even on the face of Vāyupatha, a frown took root; provoked by anger, it was like a banner of fickleness raised for the destruction of his enemies.
Furious, wringing his hand with his hand, Caṇḍasiṃha seemed to say: "In this very way, I shall crush my enemies."
The arm of Sāgaradatta seemed to summon his enemy with a swelling sound born from the slapping of his hand that echoed through the sky.
But Naravāhanadatta remained unperturbed even in the face of anger; for indeed, the very quality of being unshakeable is the hallmark of the greatness of the great.

Then, having first accomplished the ritual for the "jewel" of the body of a world-empire-ruling monarch who traverses the heavens, he made the firm resolve to set out on an expedition there in order to conquer his enemy.
Then, having ascended that celestial chariot together with his wife and accompanied by his ministers, that universal monarch set out from Govindakūṭa.
And all those lords of the gandharvas and vidyādharas, together with their armies, surrounded him and moved like planets around the moon.
Then, with Dhanavatī leading the way, Naravāhanadatta reached the Himālaya mountains and arrived at a great lake.
With its white lotus as a raised parasol and its shimmering swans as fly-whisks, it was like a gift fit for an emperor that had been brought and presented to him.
With its wave-hands raised high and facing upward not far away, it seemed to repeatedly issue an invitation for the ceremonial bath that marks the successful attainment of universal sovereignty.
Addressed by Vāyupatha with the words, "O Universal Monarch, you must bathe in this lake," the emperor descended there to bathe.
"The bath does not succeed here for anyone who is not a universal monarch; yet today that status of yours as a universal monarch has been achieved," so spoke a divine voice from the sky.
Having heard that, the universal monarch entered into the midst of those waters and sported together with his harem, like the Lord of Waters in the ocean.
There he took delight in gazing upon his beloveds, whose eyes were as red as dawn from washing, whose hair-braids were loosened, and whose wet garments clung to their limbs.
The rows of birds flying up from this lake with a sound shone like the girdles of its glories coming forth to meet them.
And the lotuses, surpassed by the loveliness of the beauty of that bride’s lotus-face, sank into the water-waves as if out of shame.
And having bathed that very day on the bank of that same lake, Naravāhanadatta dwelt there together with his retinue.
There, having stayed with his wife and minister, engaged in playful conversation, that successful man set out from there at dawn, mounted upon his celestial chariot together with his army.
Then, while traveling along the path of the wind, he reached a city by the force of his course and stayed there for that very day, out of consideration for it.
There, he beheld a maiden he had seen before, the sister of Vāyupatha, named Vāyuvegayaśas, who was standing in a garden and longing for him.
She wandered through the gardens on the banks of rivers with golden sands; her face was like the full moon, and she was enchanting with her gentle speech.
With a white smile, burdened by the weight of her heavy hips, and graced with excellent limbs, she—her heart already filled with love for him upon seeing him arrive—then vanished from that spot.
Then Naravāhanadatta, feeling embarrassed as he realized she was averse to any other cause, returned to his own quarters.
There, Marubhūti, by virtue of Gomukha’s cleverness, having learned that account of the king’s conduct while staying with him, [related it].
The queens performed various jests against that emperor while Gomukha stood there abashed at Marubhūti’s lack of wit.
Then Gomukha, seeing the king abashed and having comforted him, went to that city, desiring to ascertain the mind of Vāyuvegayaśas.
Then Vāyupatha, seeing him as if he had suddenly arrived to behold the city, offered him hospitable welcome with joy and, leading him aside, said to him:
I have a sister, a maiden named Vāyuvegayaśas; she has indeed been declared by the Siddhas to be the future wife of a universal monarch.
Therefore, I wish to give her here as a gift to Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch; please accomplish this desire of mine.
"I have set out to come to your presence for this very purpose," said Vāyupatha; to him, the minister Gomukha replied:
"Even though our lord has set out for the purpose of conquering his enemies, nevertheless, you must make this request; I shall accomplish this for you."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him, Gomukha went and reported that the task was accomplished to Naravāhanadatta, without even having to make a formal request.
And on another day, the wise Gomukha came in person to Vāyupatha and addressed that matter to the king, saying:
"O Lord, you must not cause Vāyupatha’s request to fail; for he who is devoted to you says, 'Whatever this one says must be done by the master.'"
Then King Vāyupatha also agreed to that proposal; he brought his own younger sister and gave her to him, even though she was unwilling.
Being married against her will, she said, "I was given away by my brother by force; therefore, O Guardians of the World, there is no unrighteousness in me."
While she was speaking thus, all the women of Vāyupatha raised such a clamor that others could not hear her words.
Then, in order to discover the king’s intention regarding the words he had spoken, Gomukha wandered here and there to search for a suitable stratagem.
