Having wandered about, he saw in a secluded spot four Vidyādhara maidens who were prepared to enter the fire simultaneously.
When questioned by him regarding the cause, those slender-waisted women told him that it was a violation of their agreement committed by Vāyuvegayaśas.
Then Gomukha went and reported the matter exactly as it was to Naravāhanadatta in the presence of all the king's courtiers.
When the king was astonished upon learning this, Vāyuvegayaśas then said: "Arise! Let us go quickly to protect him."
"Noble son, I shall then explain the reason for those maidens. Having been addressed thus by her, the king went there together with everyone.
And she saw those maidens with blazing fires before them; and Vāyuvegayaśas, restraining them, spoke to the king.
This one is named Kālikā, the daughter of Kālakūṭapati; this second one is Vidyutpuñjā, born from Vidyutpuñja himself.
O King, this third one is Mataṅginī, the daughter of Mandara; O Lord, this fourth one is Padmaprabhā, the daughter of Mahādaṃṣṭra.
And on the fifth day, having seen you performing austerities at the field of the Siddhas, we, deluded by Māra, made a mutual pact.
This beloved husband is to be taken away by all five of us together; he must not be surrendered to him by any one of us who has become estranged.
If one [sister] should separately arrange her marriage with him, then fire must be entered by the others, having aimed it at that betrayer of her friend.
Fearing this very situation, I did not desire a separate marriage; nor, O noble son, is my person surrendered to you even now.
My noble husband and the world-protectors themselves are witnesses here, that even now this agreement has been transgressed by me according to my own will.
Therefore, noble son, please accept these friends of mine; O friends, this matter must be cultivated by you and not otherwise.
When she had spoken thus, the maidens rejoiced and embraced one another, having escaped death; and the king also rejoiced within himself.
Having learned of this, their fathers arrived there at that very moment and presented those daughters to Naravāhanadatta.
At that time, even those lords of the Vidyādharas, who were the foremost followers of Kālakūṭapati, accepted the command of his son-in-law.
Thus, having obtained these five together, Naravāhanadatta, the son of a great Vidyādhara, attained supreme majesty therein.
And he remained there for some days with them; then the commander-in-chief, Hariśikha, spoke to him as follows:
"O King, though you are a knower of the treatises, why do you act by transgressing political ethics? At this time for war, what is this indulgence of yours in the pleasures of desire?"
Where is this undertaking of a military expedition to conquer that Mandaradeva, and where are these many days spent here in recreation with the women of the inner apartments?
When Hariśikha had spoken thus, the great king said: "What you have said is fitting; however, I have no effort here whatsoever for the sake of enjoyment."
"For this union with a wife, which grants the acquisition of kinsmen, has been welcomed by me as the primary limb for the crushing of the enemy at this time."
To the king who had said, "Therefore, let these armies of mine move today for the sake of conquering the enemy," his father-in-law Mandara replied:

O King, that Mandaradeva is difficult to conquer; he possesses all the jewels that are the limbs of a universal monarch who has not yet attained his throne, and he dwells in a land far removed and inaccessible.
This place is guarded by the cave named Triśīrṣā, which stands at the entrance protected by the great hero Devamāya.
O Lord, that cave was entered by the Cakravartin Siddharatna, and that sandalwood tree is his Cakravartin-jewel.
"There is such a person on this earth; therefore, accomplish that for the sake of attaining your desired goal. For no one who is not a universal monarch comes near that tree."
Having heard this, Naravāhanadatta, fasting and observing his vow, went at night toward that sandalwood tree on Mount Mandara.
Though being terrified by most dreadful obstacles as he went, the hero was not afraid; he reached the root of that great tree.
Having seen that great jewel with its high-altar enclosures, he approached, ascended by means of the stairs, and paid homage to the sandalwood tree.
"O Cakravartin, I am this sandalwood tree accomplished for you; having been remembered, I shall remain present for you, so depart from here now."
From there, you will obtain Govindakūṭa and other jewels; after that, you will conquer Mandaradeva with ease.
Having been addressed thus by that incorporeal voice there in the night, he replied, "So be it," and having bowed to that divine tree, he attained his supernatural power.
Then Naravāhanadatta, the great lord of the Vidyādharas, being overjoyed, returned to his own camp by way of the sky.
Then, having passed that night, he related in the morning, in the presence of everyone in the assembly hall, the entire account of how the sandalwood tree had been produced during the night.

Having learned of this, his beloveds, his young ministers, and those trusted Vidyādharas such as Vāyupatha and others, along with Citrāṅgada and the rest of the Gandharvas who had accompanied him, were overwhelmed with joy; they praised the greatness of his fortitude, which was characterized by the power of courage, energy, and steadfastness, now that he had forcibly achieved such great success.

Having consulted with them, the king, traveling in a divine celestial chariot, then went to Mount Govindakūṭa itself to conquer the pride of Mandaradeva and to obtain the other jewels produced by the sandalwood trees.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the fifth book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And here concludes this fourteenth book, the Pañcalambaka. // Śrī //

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The fifteenth book, named "The Great Consecration. This nectar of stories, it is said, was churned from the ocean of Hara’s mouth by the Mandara mountain of his love for the daughter of the Lord of Mountains; those who forcibly taste it, having attained success through the removal of obstacles, bear upon this earth the dignity of the gods by the grace of Bhava.
May the Conqueror of Obstacles (Vighnajit) steal away your darkness, as if nourishing the stars with the spray from the hissing of his trunk raised high in a dance during the nights. The First Wave.
Then, while the emperor Naravāhanadatta was seated there in his assembly hall on Govindakūṭa, [the sage] arrived before him.
That Vidyādhara named Amṛtaprabha traveled by way of the celestial path, he who had previously protected him when he was cast by his enemies onto the Fire Mountain.
Having arrived and announced himself, he bowed down before the universal monarch; and having been received with hospitable honors that brought him joy, that Vidyādhara spoke to him.
There is a great mountain named Malaya situated in the southern direction; in a hermitage there dwells the great seer Vāmadeva.
"O Lord, he summons you alone for the sake of some business; it is for this purpose that I have been sent to you today."
"You are my lord from a previous life, and for that reason I have come here; therefore, come, let us go quickly to the presence of that sage for the sake of attaining success."
When he had spoken thus, he left his wives and armies right there with that Vidyādhara, saying "So be it" to them.
Flying swiftly through the sky and reaching Mount Malaya, Naravāhanadatta approached the sage Vāmadeva.
And he saw him, tall of stature and white with age, with sockets of eyes devoid of flesh, wherein the pupils shone like excellent jewels.

The Himalaya mountain, its thick matted locks of forest creepers swaying, was the abode of the jewels of the lords of Vidyādharas; it appeared as if it had come along with him for the sake of assisting in his success.
Then he paid homage at the feet of that sage, and the sage, having offered him hospitality, spoke thus to the king:
Although you were previously consumed by Kāma, you have been made a universal monarch over all the lords of the Vidyādharas by Śambhu, who was pleased with Rati.
"In this hermitage of mine, within a deep inner cave, there are jewels; perform those tasks as directed by me."
Indeed, Mandaradeva shall become your Siddharatna; for this purpose you have been summoned here by me at the command of Giriśa.
Having spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta, instructed in the ritual by that very sage, entered the cave with great joy.
Having conquered those various floods of obstacles therein, the hero beheld a rutting lord of elephants charging toward him with a roar like thunder.
Having dealt a blow with his fist to the mouth and placed his two feet between the tusks, that king, through his agility, mounted the intoxicated elephant.
"Excellent! O Universal Monarch, the great elephant-jewel has been acquired by you!"—thus a bodiless voice then arose from within the cave.
Then he beheld a sword resembling a great lord of mountains, and having descended, he seized it as one would grasp the mass of hair of the Fortune of Universal Sovereignty.
"Excellent, O subduer of enemies! Your precious sword has been perfected as a victorious weapon"—thus a bodiless voice arose once more within the cave.
Then he accomplished the jewel of moonlight, the jewel of lovely women, and the jewel of magic science known by the name "The Destroyer."
Thus, together with the first two, along with *sarasā* and sandalwood, there are seven [substances] suitable for use at the time of performing the rite, which bestow greatness.
Having accomplished the acquisition of the jewels, he emerged from the cave and reported everything that had been achieved to the sage Vāmadeva.
Then that sage spoke with affection to the universal monarch: "Son, you who have accomplished the great jewel of a universal monarch, go now."
Victory to that Mandara-deva who dwells on the northern side of Kailāsa; enjoy the powerful imperial glory of both those flanks.
Having been addressed thus by that sage, the universal monarch Amṛtaprabha, his purpose accomplished, bowed to him and then departed through the sky.
In an instant, he reached his own camp situated at Govindakūṭa, which was protected by his mother-in-law Dhanavatī of great power.
There, he was seen by his own Vidyādhara lords who were intent on the path, and he was joyfully greeted by their wives and ministers as well.
Then, having sat down, he related to those who questioned him his vision of the sage Vāmadeva, his entry into the cave, and his attainment of the jewels.
Then, there occurred a great festival where the divine musical instruments were silenced by grief, yet it was filled with dancing Vidyādharīs and people intoxicated by drink.
And on another day, he was [assailed] by a malefic planet situated in the house of enemies, while a benefic planet of equal strength occupied the house of the kaṇṭaka.
Having performed the auspicious rites under a lunar mansion endowed with every excellence, he ascended that celestial chariot fashioned by Brahmā, which had been granted by Śarva.
Then Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by his army and the ladies of his harem, set out through the air from that place in order to conquer Mandaradeva.
And those followers—those heroic lords of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas—remained surrounding him, both devoted and fearful.
Caṇḍasiṃha, together with his mother Sumedhas and Dhanavatī, was obedient to the command of the general Hariśikha.
The hero Piṅgalagāndhāra, as well as the powerful Vāyupatha, Vidyutpuñja, Amitagati, and he who is the lord of Kālakūṭa.
Mandara, Mahādaṃṣṭra, his friend Amṛtaprabha, and the hero Citrāṅgada, together with Sāgaradatta—these were also there.
These and others who were there, taking refuge with Gaurimuṇḍa, all together, endowed with their forces, pursued him as he sought victory.
Then, the sun, its radiance eclipsed by that army's splendor, sank somewhere in the sky shrouded by it, as if out of shame.
Then, having crossed Lake Mānasa, which is frequented by hosts of celestial sages, and having passed beyond Gaṇḍaśaila, the pleasure garden of the celestial women;
That universal monarch reached Mount Kailāsa, which possessed a luster as white as crystal, as if it were the very foundation of his own mass of glory.
There, on the bank of the Mandākinī, the wise Vidyādhara lord Mandara addressed him, who was seated there, with these charming words:
O Lord, please remain right here for now on the bank of the celestial river; it is not proper to proceed further ahead by bypassing Kailāsa.
For the knowledge of this abode of Hara perishes through transgression; one must go to its northern side by way of the Cave of the Three Heads.
And she is being sought after by the king under the name Devamāyā; since he is exceedingly arrogant, how can we depart without first conquering him?
When Mandara had spoken thus and Dhanavatī had approved, Naravāhanadatta remained right there for that day.
Remaining there, he dispatched a messenger to Devamāya with conciliatory words; however, through that peaceful approach, the messenger did not at all accept his command.
Then, on the following day, that lordly universal monarch set out toward Devamāya together with those various kings of his, all clad in armor.
Devamāya also, having learned of this, arrived with his army to fight, preceded by Varāha, Vajramuṣṭi, and many other kings.
Then a battle commenced there between those two armies on Mount Kailāsa, while the sky was covered by the celestial chariots of the hosts of gods.
With the terrifying downpour of hailstones that were the severed rows of many heads, and with the thundering roars of the heroes, that terrible onset of the battle-clouds took place.
When Caṇḍasiṃha slew Varāha, the commander-in-chief and foremost warrior of Devamāya, it was not at all surprising.
But it was truly marvelous that even Devamāya, though himself a master of illusion, was bound by Naravāhanadatta—who was no magician—and rendered unconscious in battle by his blows.
And once he was bound, that army, along with Vajramuṣṭi, Mahābāhu, Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra, and the others, was broken by the great chariot-warriors.
Then, when the gods stationed in their celestial chariots cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!", everyone rejoiced in that victorious universal monarch.
Then the great lord, having consoled him who had been brought bound, favored Devamāya with his grace and set him free.
He, along with Vajramuṣṭi and the others, bowed down and accepted the command of that Cakravartin, who was victorious through his own arms.
Then, when that battle had ceased and the day had passed, he arrived at the morning assembly hall and stood by the side of the universal monarch.
Being thus questioned by him who desired to enter, Devamāya explained that tradition of the Three-headed Cave exactly according to its true nature.
O Lord, in ancient times, on Mount Kailāsa—which was inhabited by the foremost of the Vidyādharas—there were two sides, the southern and the northern, with their empires divided.
Then, by Lord Śambhu, who was pleased by his asceticism, the one named Ṛṣabha was designated as the sole universal monarch over both banks.
Once, while crossing over Mount Kailāsa on his way to the northern side, he fell from heaven, his magical powers lost due to the wrath of Śiva who was situated below.
Then, having propitiated Hara once more with severe asceticism, Ṛṣabha requested of him the imperial sovereignty as it had been previously ordained.
"O Lord, I am not yet able to leap over Kailāsa; by what path could I do so? For I shall become the sovereign emperor on both sides."
Having heard that, the wielder of the Pināka bow, in order to pass to its northern side, pierced Kailāsa and created a great cave-opening there.
Then, pierced and distressed, Kailāsa addressed Śiva: "O Blessed One, this northern side of mine is inaccessible to humans."
"Now this cave has been made accessible even to them; therefore, act in such a way that this boundary of mine is not violated."
Thus addressed by Kailāsa, Hara stationed guards within the cave: the elephants of the quarters, venomous serpents with eyes like those of the world-elephants, and Guhyakas.
To his right, at the gate, is Mahāmāya, the Lord of the Vidyādharas; and to the north are Kālarātri and Caṇḍikā Aparājitā.
Having thus appointed the guardians of the cave and produced great jewels, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara established an ordinance there.
This land of Dvipārśva shall belong to the Cakravartin Siddharatna, as well as to the sky-dwellers together with their wives and their messengers.
And those kings who shall be his successors hereafter are permitted to enter this cave, but no one else whatsoever may go there.
When the Three-eyed One had thus commanded, Ṛṣabha then waged war out of pride against the gods while exercising imperial sovereignty, and was slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Such, O Lord, is the traditional account of this cave known as Triśīrṣa; moreover, this cave is inaccessible to others except for those like you.
And from time to time, in the lineage of that guardian of the cave’s entrance, Mahāmāya, this one was born as I, the Lord Devamāya.
"Born among the Vidyādharas, he is invincible by enemies in combat; and whoever shall conquer him here will become a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
"Therefore, he must be your master, and you must obey that lord"—thus did a divine voice speak to me at my birth.
Thus, I have been conquered by you, and you are one who has attained the jewels of perfection and possesses great power; you are our lord here, the sole universal monarch over both sides of Kailāsa.
"Having crossed this cave of Triśīrṣa, conquer the remaining enemies," said Devamāya; thus addressed, the Cakravartin replied:
"Let us go today; let us dwell for now at the entrance of the cave. Having made our preparations, we shall enter that cave tomorrow morning."
Having spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta went and stayed there at the entrance of the cave together with all those kings.
And he beheld that cave, its interior deep and devoid of light, like the birthplace of the darkness at the end of an aeon, where neither sun nor moon exists.
And on the second day, having honored her, he entered that celestial chariot, accompanied by his retinue and aided by excellent jewels that appeared as soon as he thought of them.

He [dispelled] the darkness with the jewels of moonlight, the venomous serpents with sandalwood, the elephants of the quarters with the jewel of his own elephant, and the Guhyakas with the jewel of his sword.
Having warded off other obstacles with various jewels, he emerged from that cave through its northern gate together with his army.
And having emerged from the interior of the cave, he beheld the northern side of Kailāsa, which resembled another world of living beings where there is no rebirth.
Then a voice arose from the sky: "Excellent! O Cakravartin, by the majesty attained through the power of the jewel, you have crossed over this cave."
Then Dhanavatī and Devamāya said to that lord: "O Lord, Kālarātri is always present at the door."
And she was previously produced by Viṣṇu during the churning for the nectar, as a means to tear apart the lords of the Dānavas who desired to seize the nectar.
This very cave has been designated by Śarva here to protect it, so that no one else may cross over it except for those like you who have been described.
"You are a universal monarch who has crossed over and attained the jewels; therefore, this cave must be worshipped by you, for it is worthy of worship for the sake of victorious accomplishment."
In this manner, as Dhanavatī and Devamāyā were speaking, that day of Naravāhanadatta’s came to an end there.
And the northern slopes of Kailāsa turned crimson with the twilight, as if foreboding the sprinkling of blood from the imminent battle.
The darkness, having gained strength, enveloped the king's camp as if remembering the bitterness of its defeat by the cave-dwelling.
Like sprouts of anger born from disrespect, dejection, and the night of doom, throngs of bhūtas, vetālas, ḍākinīs, and jackals wandered about.
In an instant, the entire army of Naravāhanadatta became unconscious, as if asleep; he alone remained unconfused.
Then, perceiving that display to be the manifestation of the wrathful Kālarātri, the Cakravartin honored her with flowers of speech.
Skilled in the movement of the wheels from the navel to the crown, you are the form of the *praṇava*; I bow to you, the life-force (*prāṇa-śakti*) that sustains all living beings.
Homage be to you, O Durgā, whose form inspires confidence in the three worlds with the streams of blood flowing from the throats of the Mahiṣas as you pierce them with your triple-pointed spear.
With a skull held in your whirling hand filled with the blood of Ruru, you dance as if holding the vessel for the protection of the three worlds; victory is yours!
With eyes turned upward, glowing like a lamp-vessel, and holding a skull-cup, you are indeed Kālarātri; O beloved of Bhava, you shine like the moon together with the sun, with a skull in your hand.
Thus praised, Kālarātri was pleased; however, he desired to worship her not with that [praise], but by the offering of his own head.
"Do not act rashly, my son; I am already accomplished for you, O hero. Let this army of yours return to its natural state, and may you attain victory."
Thus spoke that goddess to him as he held his sword; at that very moment, his entire army became like one awakened from sleep.
Then his wife, his friends, and all those Vidyādharas praised that sovereign power of this universal emperor.
Then the Hero, having performed the necessary rites such as taking food and drink as ordained, passed that night of three watches as if it were a hundred long years.
And having worshipped that Kālarātri in the morning, he then set out toward Dhūmaśikha, whose path was blocked at its head by the Vidyādharas.
A battle such as that took place between him, the universal monarch, and King Mandaradeva, who was his chief opponent.
There, the sky was composed of swords, the earth was made of the heads of heroes, and the speech consisted of the fierce cries of warriors: "Slay! Slay!"
There, having forcibly captured Dhūmaśikha in battle and brought him back, that universal monarch honored him and made him accept his command.
And on that day, he stationed the army right there in that city, like a fire whose mass of smoke-crests has been stilled after its fuel has been consumed.
On the second day, having learned from his scouts that Mandaradeva was approaching ahead of him to do battle, and having already understood the situation from those in front, he [prepared].
Then Naravāhanadatta, having resolved upon its conquest, set out toward it together with those lords of the Vidyādharas.
Having gone a short distance, he saw before him the army of Mandaradeva, accompanied by a multitude of many kings, having arrived and formed into a battle array.
Then, having arranged his counter-array and being surrounded by kings, Naravāhanadatta charged against the enemy's force.
Then the battle between those two armies commenced, resembling the surging, turbulent floods of the ocean overflowing its bounds at the time of universal dissolution.
Then those great chariot-warriors, Caṇḍasiṃha and the others, fought on one side, while the heroes headed by the king named Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra fought on the other.
Making the three worlds tremble and shaking the great boundary mountains, that battle unfolded like the onset of the winds at the end of an eon.
Then Mount Kailāsa followed the Lord of Gaurī, its one side red with the saffron-like blood of heroes, while its other side was white with sacred ash.
With the fierce brilliance of many solar discs rising from the blades of swords, that great battle was truly the time of universal dissolution for heroes.
Such was that battle that even Nārada and others, who had witnessed the combat between the gods and the asuras, were filled with wonder upon seeing it.
Thus, in that terrible battle, Caṇḍasiṃha rushed forward and struck Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra on the head with a fearsome mace.
Seeing her son fallen from the blow of the mace, Dhanavatī uttered a curse and, by the power of her magic science, rendered both armies unconscious.
And Naravāhanadatta, the emperor, was deprived of his strength; thus, Mandaradeva and he alone remained conscious.
Then, seeing Dhanavatī enraged and capable of destroying the world, even the gods situated in the sky fled in all directions.
Then, seeing that sole universal monarch Naravāhanadatta, Mandaradeva rushed toward him with his weapon raised.
Naravāhanadatta also, having descended from his celestial chariot and drawing his precious sword, quickly received him.
Then Mandaradeva, desiring victory through illusion, assumed the form of a rutting and fierce elephant by means of his own vidyā.
Seeing that, Naravāhanadatta, who was distinguished by his superior mastery of the sciences, assumed a very great lion-form through his own power of illusion.
Then, his body shattered and clearly having abandoned his lion-like form, that universal monarch engaged in battle with the god Mandaradeva.
Performing various and diverse movements of the limbs and gestures, those two, holding the tips of their jeweled weapons, shone like two dancers engaged in a performance.
Then Naravāhanadatta, as if seizing victory itself, took the sword from Mandaradeva’s hand by means of a clever stratagem.
And there, while his sword was still in its sheath and his dagger had been drawn, the emperor suddenly snatched that away from him as well.
Then, having seized Mandaradeva—who was fighting with his bare arms since he was unarmed—by the ankles, the king threw him down upon the ground.
And with his feet placed upon the chest of his enemy, the emperor began to sever the head of that foe by pulling it by the hair with his sword.
Then a maiden named Mandaradevī, the sister of Mandaradeva, approached him and, seeking to dissuade him, spoke thus:
"O King, seeing you established in the forest of asceticism, I have already designated you as my husband; therefore, do not slay this brother of mine, who is like a son to me."
Having been addressed thus by Sudṛśā, the steadfast Great King, casting aside his modesty, spoke to that Mandaradeva.
"I have released you; let there be no shame for you, O Lord of the Vidyādharas. For victory and defeat in battle are indeed fickle for the brave."
Thus addressed by the king, Mandaradeva said to him: "What is this life of mine now, protected in battle by a woman?"

Therefore, I am going to the presence of my father, who dwells in the forest for the sake of asceticism; you alone have been appointed here as the sovereign emperor over half the circle of both Vedas.
"This matter was previously indicated to me by my father," having said this, the proud man went to his father's side in the penance grove.
"Excellent! O Great Universal Monarch, having conquered your enemies, you have attained sovereignty," the gods stationed in the sky said at that time.
Then, when King Mandaradeva had departed, Dhanavatī restored her son and both armies to consciousness by means of her own power.
Thus, as if having woken from sleep, all the ministers and others, perceiving that their enemy was defeated, congratulated the victorious Naravāhanadatta.
Moreover, those kings belonging to Mandaradeva—such as Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra, Aśokaka, Raktākṣa, Kālajihva, and others—accepted his command.
Upon remembering the blow from that mace received in battle when he beheld Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra, Caṇḍasiṃha grew furious, brandishing his excellent sword which was gripped firmly in his clenched fist.

Enough with this battle here, my child; who could possibly defeat you at the front of the fray? However, by a stratagem, I myself created that illusion for a mere moment to protect both armies from destruction.
And so, speaking thus and pacifying her son from his great anger, Dhanavatī then brought joy to her entire army by means of her own supernatural success, together with the emperor Naravāhanadatta.

When he had attained the sovereignty over the northern regions of the Śarvācala mountain—a realm from which the tumult of battle had vanished as the enemy heroes were either conquered, humbled, or fled—King Naravāhanadatta, whose circle of friends remained unharmed, experienced supreme joy.

Then, accompanied by his beloved wife and his ministers, and joined by a multitude of eminent kings, that successful man spent the day drinking wine—which was like the very majesty of his enemies—amidst the high-sounding trumpets struck for the festival of victory over his foes, and graced by the beautiful dancing and singing of the celestial nymphs.

Thus ends the first wave in the Mahābhiṣeka-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave: Then, on the following day, having risen from that peak of Kailāsa, that emperor Naravāhanadatta set out accompanied by his army.
At the command of King Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra, Mandaradevī set out for the city named Vimala, which was being led by the vanguard.
And he reached that city, beautiful with its lofty golden walls, like Mount Kailāsa come to pay homage to Mount Sumeru.
And he entered that exceedingly profound place, resplendent with the glory of Acyuta, an abode of infinite jewels, like a sea without water.
There, having approached the sovereign who was seated in an improper place and surrounded by kings and sky-dwellers, the elders of the royal harem addressed him.
"Now that King Mandaradeva has been defeated by you and has departed, his queens, having heard of this, are seeking to enter the fire; the Lord knows this now."
Having been addressed thus by them, the emperor, warding them off from death, shared his favor with them like sisters by granting them dwellings and other gifts.
Thus, that emperor brought the entire host of Vidyādhara lords to a state where they were bound by the fetters of his affection.
And there, out of gratitude, he consecrated that previously designated King Amitagati in the kingdom of Mandaradeva.
And he entrusted those kings, Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra and the others, to that king, who was devoted and steadfast.
And there, embraced by the Fortune of the northern side of Kailāsa as if she were his newly-wedded bride, he sported for seven days in those gardens of great splendor.
Then, although he had attained the status of a universal monarch over the Vidyādharas and the rulers of both halves of the world, he became desirous of even more.
Though restrained by his ministers, he set out to conquer those regions situated in that direction—the abodes of the gods where the grounds of Mount Meru are insurmountable.
Exceedingly accumulated, even without the attainment of further distinction, those who possess brilliance do not remain still, like blazing forest fires.
Then the sage Nārada, having approached him, spoke thus: "O King, though you are a knower of policy, what is this exertion of yours toward an improper object?"
One who proceeds with pride and a lack of shame is defeated in what is unattainable, like this [Rāvaṇa] here, who through arrogance attempted to uproot Kailāsa.
For even Meru is difficult to scale here by the sun and the moon; yet sovereignty over the Vidyādharas was ordained for you by Śarva, not sovereignty over the gods.
For the Himalaya, the realm of the Vidyādharas, has been conquered by you; therefore, what business do you have on Mount Meru, the land of the gods? Abandon this stubborn obsession.
He who is the father of Mandaradeva, known by the name Akampana—he, dwelling in the forest, should be visited by you if you desire your own welfare.
Having said this, the sage Nārada, after taking leave of that universal monarch who had agreed, saying "So be it," departed as he had come.
Even the Cakravartin, though he understood his duty, was dissuaded by Nārada, as he recalled what he had heard from Devamāyā regarding the destruction of Ṛṣabha.
Having reflected thus by his own intellect, he turned back from there and went to see that royal sage Akampana, who was dwelling in a grove of asceticism.
And his penance grove was filled with great rishis established in yoga, seated in the lotus posture, as if it were the world of Brahmā.
There he saw that aged man, wearing matted hair and bark garments, Akampana, who was surrounded by ascetics like a great tree inhabited by birds.
Approaching there, he prostrated at the feet of the ascetics; and that royal sage, having offered him hospitality, spoke to him.
"O King, you have done what was right by coming to this hermitage; for had you passed it by, the great seers would have cast a curse upon you."
While that royal sage was speaking thus to the universal monarch, he remained there in the forest of asceticism, having taken up the vows of a muni.
Then Mandaradeva also came into the presence of his father, accompanied by his sister, the maiden Mandaradevī.
And Naravāhanadatta, seeing him, embraced him around the neck; for toward enemies who have been conquered and pacified, affection alone is appropriate for the wise.
Then, seeing Mandaradevī arrived together with her brother, the royal seer Akampana spoke to that sovereign.
"O King, this daughter of mine is Mandaradevī by name; and she has been declared by a divine voice to be the queen of a universal monarch."
When the royal sage had said, "Therefore, marry this girl who is offered by me," his daughter then spoke.
"In this place, I have four dear friends who are excellent maidens; one is a maiden named Kanakavatī, born of Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra."
The second daughter was named Kālavatī, born of Kālajihva; the third, born of Dīrghadaṃṣṭra, was known by the name Śrutā.
The fourth was the daughter of King Prota, named Ambaraprabhā; and I am the fifth among those daughters of the lords of the Vidyādharas.
Wandering about, we five, having previously seen this noble son in the penance grove, were filled with longing and made a mutual agreement.
"This husband must be obtained by us all equally; she who would treat him with partiality—alas, her very self must be destroyed by the others immediately on her account."
"Without those friends of hers, my marriage cannot take place; for how could women like me perform such a rash act of transgressing the bounds of propriety?"
When she had spoken thus with such maturity, her father Akampana summoned those four fathers of the Vidyādhara lords.
He related the matter to them exactly as it had happened, and they too, considering themselves to have achieved their purpose at that very moment, brought those maidens and sons to him.
Then, beginning with Mandāradevī, Naravāhanadatta married these other five women here in succession.
And there he remained with them for many days, bowing to the sages at the three junctions of the day, having prepared the festive equipment.
"O King, go now to Mount Ṛṣabha for the sake of the great consecration. When this was said by Akampana, Devamāya then replied to him:
"O King, you must act exactly in this way, for it was on that mountain that the former universal monarchs, such as Ṛṣabha and others, were consecrated."
Having heard that, while he was praising the auspicious Mandara mountain nearby, these words arose from the sky concerning the consecration of Hariśikha:
"O King, all [the ancestors] indeed received the Great Consecration on Mount Ṛṣabha in former times; you too should go today to that very place of the perfected ones."
Having been thus addressed by a divine voice and having bowed to the Ṛṣis of Sākampāna, Naravāhanadatta set out from there on an auspicious day.
And he reached the northern gate of the cave known as Triśīrṣa, together with all the lords of the vidyādharas, headed by Amitagati.
There, having entered that cave through the gate where Kālarātri was worshipped, the emperor emerged by way of the southern exit.
Having set out together with his armies for the palace of Devamāya, he rested there with his retinue at the king's request on that day.
While staying there on Kailāsa, he, accompanied by Gomukha, reflected upon Hara who was present there and went of his own accord to see him.
Having reached his hermitage and likewise beheld Surabhi and the bull, he bowed down and approached the gatekeeper, Nandin.
Having been granted permission by him through a gesture of circumambulation, he opened the door and, having entered, beheld the Bull-bannered God together with the Goddess.
Even from afar, he brought delight with the rays of the moon upon his crest, which seemed to have gone here and there as if to rival the radiance of Gaurī’s face.
He was playing with his beloved using dice that were like dice by their own will—restless yet brought under control, having been granted autonomy for the sake of their own function.
And having seen him, he fell at the feet of that bestower of boons and of the goddess, the daughter of the mountain, and performed two circumambulations.
It is fitting that you have come here; otherwise, there would indeed be fault for you. Now, however, your vidyās shall become eternally indestructible.
Therefore, my child, go to that field of accomplishment, Mount Ṛṣabha; there, quickly obtain the great consecration, for the time has arrived.
Having been thus commanded by the king, the Cakravartin replied, "So be it," and after bowing to him along with his wife, he went to the palace of that Devamāya.
"Where had you gone, noble son, that you appear so joyful? Have perhaps five other maidens met you here as well?"
Having been told the true facts by the goddess Madanamañcukā through such playful conversation, he remained there happily, gladdening her.
On another day, accompanied by the entire host of Gandharvas and Vidyādharas, he made the sky appear as if it contained two suns by means of his own radiant splendor.
Then Naravāhanadatta, having ascended an excellent celestial chariot together with his harem and his ministers, departed for Mount Ṛṣabha.
And he reached that divine mountain, where the trees—with their matted creepers shaken by the wind and their scattered flowers—seemed like ascetics offering a guest-offering.
There, those various lords of the Vidyādharas brought for him the requisites for the great consecration, suited to the power of their lord.

And at his consecration, all the Vidyādharas from every direction arrived with gifts in their hands—those who were devoted, those who were terrified, those who were conquered, and those who were respectful.
Then those Vidyādharas asked him: "O God, who here is to be consecrated to the position of Mahādevī on this half-seat?"
"When the king declared, 'Queen Madanamañcukā is to be consecrated by me as my equal,' those sky-dwellers immediately entered into meditation."
Then an incorporeal voice arose from the sky: "O Vidyādharas, this Madanamañcukā is no mortal woman."
For this Rati has descended here as the wife of your lord Kāma; she was not born from Madanavega and Kaliṅgasenā.

For this child was not born from a womb; indeed, the gods, having transformed him through their illusory power (māyā), deposited him there at that very moment when she had given birth to her own embryo.
The one born from her who was named Bharga was given by the Creator to Madanavega and placed at his side; he is known as Akasa.
Therefore, this Madanamañcukā is worthy of sharing half the throne with her husband; for in former times, Hara, pleased by her ascetic penance, granted this boon to her.
Having spoken thus, that voice ceased, and those Vidyādharas rejoiced and praised Queen Madanamañcukā.
Then, on an auspicious day, while the domestic priest Śāntisoma was busily engaged, there arose the sounds of auspicious musical instruments and the beautiful songs of celestial nymphs.
While the brahminical chants of the Brahmins pervaded the ten directions, Madanamañcukā stood at his left side as he sat upon the lion throne.
The great seers consecrated Naravāhanadatta with waters drawn from various sacred fords and brought in golden jars.
Wondrously, as the water purified by mantras fell upon his head, the deep-seated stain of enmity toward his enemies was washed away from his mind.
The goddess Lakṣmī, as if out of a sense of kinship with the ocean water used for his consecration, followed him and visibly enveloped his body along with it.
A continuous garland of flowers, released from the hands of celestial nymphs, shone upon his body as it fell of its own accord like the Ganges with its many streams.
Then the sun, adorned with the crimson hue of dawn as if by its own majesty, shone forth as it stood upon the horizon, having bathed in the waters of the ocean.
Wearing a garland of bound mandāra flowers, radiant with fine garments and ornaments, and having donned a divine crown, he bore the splendor of Śakra.
And Queen Madanamañcukā, having received her consecration, shone at his side with divine ornaments like Śacī beside Indra.
With the sounding of drums like thunderclouds and a rain of flowers falling from the sky, that day became a wondrous storm, surrounded by celestial women like flashes of lightning.
Then, in the city of the Lord of Nagas, not only did the excellent women of the Vidyādharas dance, but even the creepers shaken by the wind danced.
During this great festival, when the mṛdaṅga drums were struck by the wandering minstrels, even the mountain seemed to play music, as its caves resounded with echoes.
Surrounded by Vidyādharas reeling from intoxication with the taste of divine liquor, even that mountain appeared as if it were itself spinning from drinking.
The splendor of this consecration has been described by him, seeing which even Indra, while traveling in his celestial chariot during his own consecration, became humiliated.
Thus, having obtained the consecration as a universal monarch according to his desire, Naravāhanadatta then remembered his father with longing.
Having consulted together immediately with his ministers, Gomukha and the others, the sovereign emperor summoned the king and gave him this command: Vāyupatha.
"Naravāhanadatta remembers you with great longing. Having said this and related the news, he continued, "Go, and bring my father here."
"You should likewise bring his queens and ministers by means of that same speech. Upon hearing this, Vāyupatha said, "So be it," and departed through the sky.
And in an instant he reached Kauśāmbī, surrounded by seven crores of Vidyādharas, beheld with fear and wonder by the citizens.
And there he beheld Udayana, the King of Vatsa, together with his ministers and his queens, who had shown him due respect as was fitting.
Then, having sat down and inquired after his welfare, that lord of the Vidyādharas, being gazed upon by everyone with curiosity, spoke to the king.
Your son Naravāhanadatta, having propitiated Śaṅkara and having beheld him in person, obtained all the sciences that are difficult for enemies to conquer.
Having slain Mānasavega and Gaurimuṇḍa in the south, and having conquered Mandaradeva, the lord of half the altar, in the north.
Having attained the great status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all the vidyādhara kings who occupy half of both halves of the Vidyādhara realm and who uphold the sacred commands.
O King, having now arrived at Mount Ṛṣabha for the great consecration, he remembers you with longing, along with your queen, ministers, and others.
And I have been sent by him with the command: "Come quickly from here! For those possessed of merit behold their own lineage as exalted."
Having heard this from Vāyupatha, the King of Vatsa, filled with intense longing, assumed the grace of a peacock thrilled by the roar of a rain-cloud.
And having accepted his words, at that very moment, he ascended a palanquin through the sky by the power of those sciences.
Followed by Kaliṅgasenā and accompanied by his wife and ministers, he traveled on and reached that great divine mountain named Ṛṣabha.
And there he saw his son seated upon a divine throne, standing in the midst of the lords of the Vidyādharas and accompanied by many wives.
Seated upon the summit of the eastern mountain, adorned by the assembly of planets, he resembled the moon surrounded by a multitude of stars.
Sprinkled by the nectar-essence of beholding him, his heart uplifted, that king assumed a certain resemblance to the ocean at the rising of the moon.
Naravāhanadatta, too, seeing his father after a long time, rose up in agitation and, full of longing, approached him along with his retinue.
Then, embraced by his father and placed upon his lap, he was drenched once more, as it were, by a flood of tears of joy.
And Queen Vāsavadattā, having embraced her son for a long time, drenched him with breast milk flowing at the sight of him, thereby reviving her memory of his childhood.
And Padmāvatī, the ministers headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa, her paternal kinsmen, and her maternal uncle Gopālaka, all beheld him after a long time.
They drank in his nectar-like form with thirsty eyes, like cakora birds gazing at a sovereign who has been duly honored according to his merit.
Upon seeing her son-in-law and then her daughter, Kaliṅgasenā could not contain herself even within the three worlds, let alone within her own limbs.
And Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others, seeing their sons headed by Marubhūti, rejoiced as they had attained divinity through the favor of their lord.
Queen Madanamañcukā was adorned with divine ornaments, as were Ratnaprabhā, Alaṃkāravatī, and Lalitalocanā.
Karpūrikā, Śaktiyaśas, and Bhāgīrathayaśas, as well as the sister of Ruciradeva who possessed a divine form;
Vegavatī and Ajināvatī, as well as Gandharvadattā, Prabhāvatī, Ātmanikā, and likewise Vāyuvegayaśas.
Her four friends, Kālikā and the others, as well as Sulocanā, and furthermore five other excellent women, Mandaradevī and the rest.
There, the queens of the universal emperor Naravāhanadatta bowed at the feet of their father-in-law, the Lord of Vatsa.
In the same manner, they and Harṣa likewise honored Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī with blessings appropriate to the occasion.
When the Lord of Vatsa, accompanied by his inner apartments, had seated himself upon a fitting throne, Naravāhanadatta ascended his own great seat.
And Queen Vāsavadattā, beholding those nine daughters-in-law who were there at that time, rejoiced as she inquired after their lineages and names.
Beholding that divine splendor of Naravāhanadatta, the Lord of Vatsa and the others considered their lives to have achieved their purpose.
Then, while that great festival of the reunion with kinsmen was underway, the brave warder Rucideva entered and spoke.
"This drinking hall is ready; therefore, please come here. Having heard that, they all went to that beautiful drinking hall.
With its jeweled goblets of various kinds and its blossoming lotuses of diverse sorts, it was like a garden lotus-pond strewn with many scattered flowers.
The city was filled with matronly women carrying jars full of intoxicating wine, who created the illusion that the nectar produced by the arms of the Moon’s snatcher had been brought forth once more.
There, that wine—which breaks the shackles of shame for the women of the harem, which is the very life-essence of Love, and the minister of amorous play—was drunk.
Their faces, flushed with wine, shone like the red lotuses of lakes in full bloom under the fresh rays of the morning sun.
As if terrified by contact with them, the cups of wine, surpassed by the lips of the host of goddesses, concealed their own liquor through their own luster.
Even at a time when anger was imminent, the queens of Naravāhanadatta, though touched by intoxication, then had their eyes reddened and their brows knit in a frown.
Then they gradually arrived there at the dining hall, which was enchanting with various foods produced by the power of their magical knowledge.
It was strewn with cloths, enriched with vessels, and provided with curtains; it was like a stage for the arts of fortune, filled with various kinds of delicious flavors.
There, having taken their prescribed meals, they rested in their bedchambers once the sun, together with the twilight, had settled upon the western mountain.
And Naravāhanadatta, having divided his body in many ways by means of his magic science, remained present in the dwellings of all the queens.
In truth, he took his beloved Madanamañcukā—who possessed a moon-like face, was composed, and had tremulous pupils—and delighted in her as if taking the night itself.
The Lord of Vatsa also spent that night with his followers, enjoying celestial pleasures, as if he had attained another birth in that very same body.
Having awakened in the morning, they all likewise enjoyed various pleasures in the gardens, palaces, and other dwellings of the perfected masters of knowledge.

Thus, as many days passed while they were engaged in various diversions there, the joyful King of Vatsa, desiring to go to his own city, approached his son—the king of all sky-goers—and spoke thus to him as he stood bowed before him.

"My son, what conscious person would not take delight in these divine enjoyments? Or rather, what draws humans away from their love for dwelling in their own birthplace? Therefore, let us go to our own city; as for this glory of the Vidyādharas, you may enjoy it, for these lands are suited to one who possesses both divine and human nature."

"Furthermore, my son, we should be summoned again on a future occasion; for this is the fruit of our birth here, that we behold this moon-like face of yours, lovely and filled with the nectar-essence to be drunk by the eyes, and that we rejoice upon seeing your divine splendor."

Having heard these very sincere words of his father, the Lord of Vatsa, King Naravāhanadatta quickly summoned the lord of the Vidyādharas, Devamāya, and commanded him with a voice faltering from a weight of tears.

"Father is indeed departing for his own capital city, accompanied by his mother and joined by his ministers and others; therefore, dispatch ahead of him a full thousand loads of gold and jewels, to be carried by thousands of celestial beings acting as porters."
Thus commanded with affection by his master, Devasāya bowed low and said: "O giver of honor, I shall go to Kauśāmbī myself, accompanied by my followers, for the sake of accomplishing this."
Then the universal monarch gave Vāyupatha and Devamāya, along with their followers, as attendants to his father, who had been honored with garments and ornaments.
The Lord of Vatsa, having boarded a divine vehicle together with his retinue, turned back his son who had followed him from afar and departed for his own city.
Queen Vāsavadattā, her longing intensified a hundredfold by the circumstances of that moment, turned back her bowing son as he wept; gazing after him, she somehow managed to depart.
And Naravāhanadatta, followed by his ministers and having bid farewell to his elders, returned with his face bathed in tears to that very mountain, Ṛṣabhaka.

There, that universal monarch dwelt together with his childhood ministers headed by Gomukha, and with hosts of Vidyādhara lords; accompanied by his harem and joined by Madanamañcukā, he remained insatiable in the constant delights of divine enjoyments.
Thus ends the second wave in the Mahābhiṣeka-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And here concludes this fifteenth Lambaka, named Mahābhiṣeka. // Śrī //

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The sixteenth book, named Suratamañjarī. This nectar of stories, it is said, was churned from the ocean of Hara’s mouth by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Mountain King; those who forcibly taste it, having attained prosperity through the removal of obstacles, bear upon this earth the dignity of the gods by the grace of Bhava.

First Wave: May the Conqueror of Obstacles protect you—he whose decoration of vermilion on his cheeks flies upward like a *tāṇḍava* dance, as if he were vomiting forth the very majesty of the obstacles he has swallowed.
Thus it was for Naravāhanadatta, as he remained on that Ṛṣabha mountain together with his wives and his ministers.
Once, while he was enjoying supreme bliss, nourishing his happiness as he relished the highest glory of the sovereignty of the lords of the Vidyādharas, spring arrived.
After a long time, the beautiful moonlight of the one marked by the deer became serene; the earth, embraced by fresh green grass, became as if perspiring.
And the rows of trees on the mountain slopes, being repeatedly embraced by the nearby Malaya breezes, were trembling, bristling with horripilation, and full of sap.
The cuckoo, acting as the gatekeeper for the flower-bowed god of love, gazed upon the mango branch and seemed to silence the pride of the proud woman with its warbling.
Swarms of bees flew out from the flowering creepers with a humming sound, like rows of iron arrows released from the bow of the hero Māra.
Having thus observed that flow of honey at that time, the ministers Gomukha and the others made their report to Naravāhanadatta.
"Your Majesty, behold! This Mount Ṛṣabha has now become something else entirely, composed of flowers, its forest groves filled with blossoming madhūka trees."
With flowers struck against one another, they seemed to possess cymbals of bell-metal; shaken by the wind, they were as if singing to the humming of bees.
O King, behold the creepers, who have gone to the garden prepared for spring—the very abode of the God of Love—adorned with garlands of pollen.
Behold this mango blossom-cluster, its string of bees serving as a slackened bowstring; it appears like the bow-creeper of Kāma, who has rested after conquering the world.
Therefore, O King, come now to this beautiful garden on the bank of the Mandākinī and let us go to enjoy this spring festival.
Having been addressed thus by his ministers, Naravāhanadatta then went to the bank of the Mandākinī together with the women of the harem.
There he sported in the garden, which resounded with the songs of various birds and was adorned with cardamom, cloves, bakula, aśoka, and mandāra trees.
And having seated the great queen Madanamañcukā on his left side, he sat down upon a vast slab of moonstone.
Accompanied by other women of the harem and surrounded by various lords of the Vidyādharas, headed by Caṇḍasiṃha and Amitagati;
While enjoying the drinking hall there and engaging in various conversations, the emperor, having considered that season, spoke to his ministers.
The southern breeze is pleasant to the touch and gentle; the quarters are stainless; and at every step, the groves are in full bloom with sweet fragrances.
The songs of the cuckoos are sweet, as are the pleasures of drinking games; what happiness is there not in spring? Yet, in this season, separation from one's beloved is unbearable.
Let alone others; even among animals, the pain of separation here is bitter. Behold this cuckoo, exhausted by the pangs of parting.
For this female cuckoo, having searched for her lost beloved for a long time while crying out, remained at the mango tree unable to find him, clinging to it as if dead and silent.
To the emperor who had spoken thus, the minister Gomukha said: "It is true that at this time, separation is unbearable for all living beings."
For instance, O King, hear what happened in Śrāvastī; there lived a certain prince who was a village overseer and a servant of the king.
To him, named Śūrasena, there was a wife born in the land of Mālava named Suṣeṇā, who was a worthy match for him and dearer to him than his own life.
Once, when Śūrasena was summoned by the king and prepared to go to the royal camp, he was addressed by his devoted wife:
"Noble son, you ought not to depart leaving me all alone; for I shall not be able to remain here for even a moment without you."
Thus addressed by his beloved, Śūrasena said to her: "O slender one, do you not know why I am not going? I have been summoned by the king."
"For I am a prince who lives dependent on others, a servant. Hearing that, his wife, her eyes filled with tears, spoke to him.
If you must go, I shall somehow endure it, provided that you do not pass even a single day and arrive during the spring.
Having heard this, he also said to her finally with certainty: "My dear, even if it means abandoning my duty, I shall come on the first day of Caitra."
Having spoken thus, and having somehow obtained the consent of his beloved, Śūrasena went to the king’s camp.
His wife also remained there in expectation, counting the days while watching for the day that marked the beginning of spring as the limit for his arrival.
Then, as the days passed, the festival day of spring arrived, its sound of cuckoos resonating like the incantations that summon the god of love.
The sound of bees, intoxicated by the fragrance of flowers, was heard like the twang of a bow being drawn by Kāma.
Thinking, "This honey festival has arrived; surely my beloved will come today," on that day, that bride of Śūrasena [waited].
Having reflected thus, Suṣeṇā performed her ablutions, worshipped Smara, adorned herself with ornaments, and stood watching the path by which he would come.
When her husband did not arrive even at the end of the day, she, distressed by despair during that night, reflected:

"The time of death has arrived for me, but that husband of mine has not yet come; for what affection indeed can there be toward one's own kin among those who are solely devoted to the service of others?"
As she was thus reflecting, her mind fixed entirely upon him, her life-breaths departed as if being consumed by the forest fire of love.
Meanwhile, having somehow freed himself from the king, Śūrasena—eager for his beloved and unable to endure the delay—departed.
Having mounted an excellent young camel and traversed the long road, he arrived at his own home in the final watch of the night.
There he saw his beloved, adorned with ornaments but deprived of life, like a creeper with blossoming flowers uprooted by the wind.
As soon as he saw her, while he was overwhelmed and holding her in his arms, the life-breaths of that man, who was separated from her, departed in an instant along with his lamentations.
Seeing the couple thus fallen into calamity, the family deity, the boon-granting goddess Caṇḍī, restored them to life out of compassion.
Then, having regained their lives from that moment on, the two of them, seeing their mutual passion, remained inseparable.
O Lord, in this way, during the spring season, fanned by the Malaya breeze, for whose embodied beings is the fire of separation not unbearable?
When Gomukha had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta, while indeed reflecting upon those very words, suddenly became as if despondent.
For great-souled beings, whether they are in a state of distress or well-established, their inner selves indicate future good or evil even without an external cause.
Then, when that day had ended, the emperor, having performed his evening prayers, entered his bedchamber and rested upon his couch.
At the end of the night, in a dream, he beheld his own father being dragged away by a dark woman and led toward the southern direction.
Upon seeing that very thing, he became awakened; fearing some misfortune for his father, he meditated upon and questioned the vidyā named Prajñapti, who appeared before him.
"Tell me, what is the news concerning my father, the King of Vatsa? For it is because of him that I am anxious due to the sight of this evil dream."
Having been addressed thus by him, that Vidyā appeared in bodily form and spoke to him: "Listen, O King, to the account of what befell your father, the King of Vatsa."
While staying in Kauśāmbī, he suddenly heard from a messenger who had arrived from Ujjayinī that King Caṇḍamahāsena had perished.
From him alone he heard that Queen Aṅgāravatī had likewise followed him in death, and out of delusion he fell to the ground.
Having regained consciousness after a long time, he, along with Queen Vāsavadattā and his retinue, mourned for his parents-in-law who had gone to heaven.
In this fragile existence, who possesses stability? And that king is not to be mourned, whose son-in-law you are and whose son is Gopālaka.
Then Naravāhanadatta, having been awakened and raised up by his ministers who reminded him that he was their grandson, offered the water libation to his two fathers-in-law.
Then the Lord of Vatsa, his throat choked with tears, addressed Gopālaka, his brother-in-law, who was standing by his side, afflicted with grief out of affection.
"Arise and go to Ujjayinī; rule over your ancestral kingdom! For indeed, the subjects are waiting for you," so I have heard from the mouth of a messenger.
Having heard that, Gopālaka wept and said to the King of Vatsa: "O Lord, I am unable to go, leaving behind both you and my sister."
Nor do I venture, dear brother, even to look upon my own city now that it is empty; therefore, let my younger brother, who is its protector, be the king here with my permission.
When Gopālaka, speaking thus, did not desire the kingdom, he then dispatched Rumaṇvat as the commander-in-chief to the city of Ujjayinī.
The Lord of Vatsa, having received permission from his elder brother, consecrated that younger brother-in-law named Pālaka upon the throne of that kingdom.
Having perceived that everything is unstable, he became dispassionate toward sense-objects and said this to his ministers, Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others:
In this essence-less existence, all things are ultimately devoid of flavor; we have already ruled the kingdom, enjoyed pleasures, and conquered our enemies.
Thus we have seen our son attain the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas; now our own youth has passed away along with that of our kinsmen.
We have been seized by old age by the hair to be delivered to death, and our bodies have been overtaken by wrinkles as if by a kingdom of eunuchs.
Therefore, having gone to Mount Kālañjara, I shall cast off this impermanent body and attain here the eternal state as it has been described.
Having been addressed thus by the king, all those ministers deliberated upon it, and Queen Vāsavadattā, being of equal mind with them, spoke to him.
O Lord, by your grace, we too shall attain the highest state in the next world, just as you have attained it according to your own desire.
Thus addressed by those who were like himself, the king, having made his resolution, spoke there to Gopālaka, his brother-in-law and a man of great responsibility.
"Naravāhanadatta and you are both my equal sons; therefore, protect this Kauśāmbī, for the kingdom has been bestowed upon you by me."
When the Lord of Vatsa had spoken thus, Gopālaka said to him: "Whatever be your fate, that shall be mine; I do not venture to abandon you."
While speaking thus with persistence, he who was so fond of his sister was addressed by the King of Vatsa, who feigned a display of anger.
This very day you have become independent, following me in vain; for who indeed would heed the command of one who is falling from his own position?
Thus addressed harshly by the king, Gopālaka, weeping with his face cast downward, turned back from his resolve to go to the forest at that very moment.
Then the king, mounted upon an elephant together with Queen Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī, set out accompanied by his ministers.
As he departed from Kauśāmbī, the citizens followed after him—weeping aloud, their faces clouded with tears—including women, children, and the elderly.
Having somehow consoled them with the words, "May Gopālaka protect you," and having turned them back, that Lord of Vatsa departed for Mount Kālañjara.
Having reached it and ascended, he bowed to the bull-bannered god and took the lute Ghoṣavatī—the beloved of all seasons—into his hand.
Accompanied by those two queens at his sides and together with his ministers, headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa, he threw himself from the precipice.
Even as he was falling, that king, radiant and accompanied by his followers, ascended to heaven in a brilliant celestial chariot that had arrived for him.
Having heard this from the mouth of Vidyādharī Mukha, Naravāhanadatta cried out, "Alas, my father! and fell there upon the ground, unconscious.
Having regained consciousness, he lamented for his father, his mother, and his paternal ministers, together with his own officials whose fathers had also passed away.
O Goddess, even though you know the true nature of this cyclic existence—which is momentary and like a magician’s illusion—how is it that you are so bewildered?
And why do you grieve for your fathers, who are not to be mourned and have fulfilled their purpose, since you, the sole universal emperor of the Vidyādharas, are their son?
Thus exhorted by the lords of the Vidyādharas and by Dhanavatī, he offered water to his ancestors and questioned her once more regarding that science.
"Where is that cowherd, my maternal uncle, and what did he do? Then that science spoke again to the emperor.
Having gone to Mount Mahāpatha, after mourning for that King Vatsa and considering his sister to be unstable, he remained outside the city.
Having summoned his brother Pālaka from Ujjayinī, Gopālaka bestowed upon him even this kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
When his younger brother was established in the two kingdoms, he then departed for the forest of asceticism, proceeding with world-weariness to Mount Asita at the hermitage of Kaśyapa.
There, O Lord, your maternal uncle Gopālaka now remains among the sages, performing austerities while wearing bark garments.
Having heard this, Naravāhanadatta, eager to see his maternal uncle, went with his retinue to the Black Mountain by means of a celestial chariot.
Having descended there from the sky, surrounded by the lords of the Vidyādharas, he beheld that hermitage of the sage Kaśyapa.
It seemed to offer a glance through the delusions of many black antelope, and it seemed to perform the custom of welcoming with the warbling of birds.
With the rising columns of smoke from the Agnihotra sacrifices being offered, it was as if [the city] were showing the path of ascent to heaven for the ascetics.
Resorted to by many mountain-kings and hosts of monkeys, it was like an unprecedented netherworld situated above the earth, free from all darkness.
There in the midst, he beheld his maternal uncle, with matted locks and clad in tree bark, surrounded by sages like tranquility incarnate.
The cowherd, too, seeing his nephew approach, rose up, embraced him closely, and wept with tearful eyes.
Then, their grief renewed, the two of them lamented for their kinsmen; for whom does the fire of sorrow, fanned by the wind of seeing one's own people, not burn?
Then, seeing them distressed by that suffering even among the animals here, the sages Kaśyapa and others approached and comforted them.
Then, when that day had passed, at dawn, the emperor entreated that cowherd, saying, "Come, you shall dwell in my sovereignty."
Gopālaka also said to him: "My child, is this not enough for you, that you have seen me? If you have affection for me, then dwell right here in this hermitage during this arrived rainy season."
Having been addressed thus at that time by his maternal uncle, Naravāhanadatta remained on that Black Mountain in the hermitage of Kaśyapa, accompanied by Sāricchada.

Thus ends the first wave in the *Suratamañjarī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave: Then, once upon a time, his own commander-in-chief addressed Naravāhanadatta as he sat in the assembly hall on that Asita mountain.
"O King, today while staying upon my palace roof and guarding the troops, I saw a woman being carried away through the sky at night by a divine being."
Having found her crying out, "O son of a noble man!", she who had stolen away the very essence of his beauty, and perceiving her brought back by the moon, which was powerful at that moment;
"O wretch! Having abducted the wife of another, where will you go in the kingdom of King Naravāhanadatta, the protector?"
In the realm of the Vidyādharas, extending for sixty thousand yojanas, even animals do not commit unrighteousness; what then need be said of others?
Having spoken thus, I myself, together with my attendants, quickly ran forward, bound that man, and brought him down from the sky along with the woman.
And having descended, we saw that he was your brother-in-law, O Lord—the sky-farer named Ityaka, who is the brother of your Great Queen.
When we asked him, "Who is this woman born of Queen Kaliṅgasenā by Madanavega, and why do you carry her away?", he replied:
This is the daughter of Matangadeva, the lord of the Vidyadharas, born of Aśokamañjarī, and named Suratamañjarī.
This very woman, who had indeed already been given as a portion by my mother in speech, was then bestowed here upon another mortal by her own father.
"Therefore, if my own wife was recovered by me today, what fault is there on my part? Having said this, Ityaka ceased his speech.
"By whom were you married, noble lady, and how did you come to be with him? Thus was Surata-mañjarī questioned by me, and she then spoke.
In Ujjayinī there is a glorious king named Pālaka; he has a son, a prince named Avantivardhana, who possesses an auspicious name.
Therefore, having been married by him, I was sleeping on the palace roof today when I was carried off by this wicked man while my noble husband was asleep.
When she had spoken thus, both she and that Cetaka, who remained restrained, were established here by me; now the Lord is the authority.
Having heard this from the commander-in-chief Hariśikha, the emperor went with him to Gopālaka and related the matter to him, still filled with doubt.
Gopālaka also said, "My dear child, this was not known to me; I only now learn that she has been married by the son of Pālaka."
"Let the prince be brought from Ujjayinī along with his minister Bharataroha; then we shall know the true state of affairs."
Having heard those words of his maternal uncle, that cakravartin dismissed the Vidyādhara Dhūmaśikha, the younger brother of his maternal uncle.
He then had both of them brought into the presence of King Pālaka—the prince from Ujjayinī and that minister, his son.
When they had arrived and offered their salutations, he, accompanied by the cowherds, honored them with affection and respect, and questioned him regarding the matter at hand.
While Avantivardhana—resembling the moon at the end of night—was established there, as was his father Setya along with Suratamañjarī.
While Kaśyapa remained silent among those present at the path of Vāyu and others, the minister Bharatarohaka spoke thus to the rest.
"Listen from the very beginning, O King: once, it is said, all the people of Ujjayinī assembled together and made this petition to King Pālaka."
"Today, O Lord, there is a festival in this city called the 'Gift of Water'; if you have not properly heard the reason for it, let that be heard."
Formerly, your father Caṇḍamahāsena, in order to obtain an excellent sword and a wife, gratified the goddess Caṇḍī through ascetic penance.
She gave him her own sword and spoke thus for the sake of a wife: "After you have slain the asura named Aṅgāraka, you will soon obtain his daughter."
"You shall obtain a noble wife named Putrāṅgāravatī,"—having been thus instructed by that goddess, the king remained there with his mind fixed upon her.
In the meantime, whosoever became the ruler of the city in Ujjayinī was devoured night after night by some being.
Then Caṇḍamahāsena, wandering at will through the city at night to search for him, encountered a man committing adultery.
He severed his head, adorned with ornaments, with his sword; and as soon as his neck was cut, a certain rākṣasa approached and seized it.
Saying, "Surely he is here," at the command of the city governor, the king seized that rākṣasa by the hair and began to kill him.
Then that rākṣasa said: "O King, do not kill me falsely! He who devours the lords of cities here is someone else entirely."
When the king asked him, "Who is he? Tell me," the Rākṣasa replied again: "There is here an Asura named Aṅgāraka, whose abode is in Pātāla."
O scorcher of enemies, O Lord, he issues commands to the city governors at nightfall and forcibly carries off royal maidens from every side.
And he is providing an escort for his daughter Aṅgāravatī; when you see him wandering in the forest, kill him and be successful.
Having spoken thus, the king released that rākṣasa and went to his own palace; and on one occasion, he then went out for a hunt.
There he saw a massive boar with eyes blazing with anger, appearing like a mountain of collyrium rising up together with its cave-filled slopes.
"Could this not be a boar? Or perhaps it is that deceptive Aṅgāraka?"—thinking thus, the king struck that hog with his arrows.
Disregarding those very arrows and shaking off his chariot, he went and entered a vast opening in the earth like a boar.
The heroic king also entered right after him into that very place; there he beheld a celestial city, but he did not see the boar.
And sitting there upon the bank of the pond, he beheld a maiden surrounded by a hundred girls, like Rati herself in embodied form.
That maiden approached him and, having asked the reason for his coming there, spoke to him with tearful eyes, love having arisen within her as she gazed upon him.
"Alas! Where have you entered, that such a boar was seen by you? That demon named Aṅgāraka possesses a body of diamond and great strength."
Having now abandoned his boar form, he sleeps within; however, upon waking at the time for food, he will do you great harm.
And I, O fortunate one, am this Aṅgāravatī, his daughter; and fearing some misfortune for you, my life-breaths have reached my throat.
Thus addressed by her, the king, remembering the boon granted by the queen and feeling confident that his purpose would be accomplished, replied to her.
If you have affection for me, then do this at my word: go and weep at the side of your father when he has awakened.
"O lovely-eyed one, if someone should kill you while you are heedless, what would become of me?"—thus should he who asks for the reason be addressed by you.
"When this is done, there will certainly be welfare for me as well as for you. Having been addressed thus by the king, she departed, infatuated with passion.
Having sat down by the side of her father who had awakened, she wept; and when questioned by him, she explained to him the cause of her fear, which was born from his impending death.
Then that Daitya said to her, "Who indeed can kill me, Vajrāṅga? For this bow, which is in my left hand, protects my vital organ."
The king, remaining concealed, overheard those words; then that Daitya proceeded to worship Hara after having bathed.
Manifesting at that moment, the king, with his bow strung, challenged that Daitya—who had maintained a vow of silence—for battle.
That Daitya also, raising his left hand while his other was occupied, gave a signal to the king, saying, "Wait a moment."
At that very moment, the Daitya was struck in a vital spot by the king with an arrow that had achieved its mark, and he fell to the earth.
"If he who has struck me down when I was afflicted by thirst does not satisfy me with water year after year, then five of that counselor's [descendants] shall perish."
Having spoken thus, when that Daitya had perished, the king took his daughter Aṅgāravatī and came to this city of Ujjayinī.
And having married that queen, O gods, your father, the god, caused the offering of water for Aṅgāraka to be performed every year.
Everyone here celebrates a great festival known as the offering of water; that day has arrived today, so perform for him that which was performed by his father.
Having heard these words of his subjects, King Pālaka then inaugurated a festival for the gift of water in that city.
While that [ceremony] was underway and the people were intent upon it in a tumultuous uproar, suddenly an intoxicated elephant, having snapped its tethering post, rushed toward them.
Having overcome the goad and shaking off its driver, that elephant wandered through the city, slaughtering very many people in an instant.
Although the elephant-drivers, accompanied by the mahouts, and the citizens all ran forward, no one was able to restrain that elephant.
As the elephant wandered through it in due course and reached the quarter of the Caṇḍālas, a certain Caṇḍāla maiden emerged from there.
As if delighted that the moon had been conquered by her face—her enemy—she illuminated the earth with the splendor of a lotus clinging to her foot.
For one whose mind has withdrawn from other objects and remains motionless, it bestows rest upon the eyes, like sleep for the entire world.
That maiden, having struck that lordly elephant with her trunk as it approached directly toward her, then assailed him with those crooked side-glances.
Deluded by the touch of her hand, with his face bent down and pierced by her gaze, that elephant stood looking at her and did not move even a single step from that spot.
Then, having fashioned a swing for him with her own upper garment suspended between his tusks, that excellent maiden leaped up, climbed onto it, and began to play.
Seeing her afflicted by the heat, the elephant went beneath the shade of a tree; having witnessed this great marvel, the citizens there spoke thus:
"Aha! This maiden must surely be some divine being, for by her form and her surpassing power, she has even captivated the animals."
In the meantime, having learned of this, Prince Avantivardhana went out to see the spectacle and beheld that maiden.
As the prince was looking on, the deer of his heart, having run toward her—the snare of the hunter Madana—was captured.
She too, beholding him, her heart captivated by his beauty, took from the swing made of the tusks of a lordly elephant an upper garment that lay upon it.
Then, once the prince had mounted the elephant driven by the mahout, she went to her own home, looking back at him with both shame and affection.
Even Avantivardhana, though the commotion caused by the elephant had subsided, went to his own palace empty-hearted, his mind carried away by her.
There, tormented by the absence of that excellent maiden and having forgotten the festival of giving water he had begun, he questioned his friends.
"Do you know whose daughter she is, and what the name of that maiden is? Having heard this, his companions spoke to the prince.
"In this place, within a settlement of Caṇḍālas, there is a certain Mātaṅga named Utpalahasta; his daughter is Suratamañjarī by name."
Her body, though beautiful, was fit only for the singular fruit of being beheld by the virtuous; like a form depicted in a painting, it was not capable of being enjoyed.
Having heard that from his companions, the prince said to them: "I believe she is certainly not the daughter of a Mātaṅga; she is surely some divine being."
For such a form could not belong to the daughter of a Caṇḍāla; if she, possessing that beauty, were not my wife, what would be the use of life?
Speaking thus with his ministers, whom he could not restrain, the prince became exceedingly tormented by the fire of separation from her.
Then Queen Avantivatī and King Pālaka, his parents, having learned of that, became deeply distressed for a long time.
When the queen had said, "How could a son born of a royal lineage not desire an outcaste woman?", King Pālaka replied:
Since my son’s mind runs toward her in this way, that maiden must surely be some other *ātaṅginī* who is the cause of it.
