The minds of the virtuous declare what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, whether they are impassioned or dispassionate; and regarding this, O Queen, if you have not heard this story, then let it be heard.
Formerly, in the city named Supratiṣṭhita, there was a daughter of King Prasenajit named Kuraṅgī, who was exceedingly beautiful.
As she was departing from the pleasure garden, an elephant that had broken loose from its bonds rushed up and, with a bound, tossed her along with her carriage high above its two tusks.
While her retinue fled crying out toward that elephant, a certain young Caṇḍāla, sword in hand, rushed forward.
Having slain that great elephant with a sword-stroke as it was being castrated, that great hero liberated the princess.
Then, her heart captivated by his perfection of valor and beauty, she went to her own palace accompanied by her gathering attendants.
"He is my protector from the elephant, or my husband, or even death itself"—thinking thus, she remained there, afflicted by the pain of separation from him.
And that Caṇḍāla youth, having slowly returned to his own home, his heart captivated by her beauty, brooded upon her and was consumed with anguish.
Where am I, born in my final birth, and where is that princess? What kind of union could there be, and where, between a crow and a royal swan?
This is a mockery that I am unable either to speak of or to ignore; therefore, in this crisis, death alone is my refuge.
Having reflected thus, he went to the cemetery at night, bathed, prepared a funeral pyre, kindled the fire, and made this petition:
O Purifier, O Soul of All, by the offering of my very self as a sacrifice into you, may that princess become my wife again even in another birth.
To him who had spoken thus and was preparing to cast himself into the fire, Agni, appearing visibly before him, spoke with favor.
"Do not commit a rash act; she shall become your wife alone. For you were not a Caṇḍāla from the beginning; listen to what I tell you."
In this city there dwells an eminent brahmin named Kapilaśarman; in his fire-sanctuary, I reside visibly as the letter *sa*.
There, once, out of desire for her beauty, I made his daughter—who had reached marriageable age and whose blemishes had been removed by a boon—my wife.
At that very moment, O dear son, you were born from my seed; and out of shame, she cast you onto the street at that instant.
Then, having been obtained by the Caṇḍālas, you were reared on goat’s milk; thus, though born from the womb of a Brāhmaṇī, you are my own son.
Therefore, there is no impurity in you who have been born from my splendor; moreover, you shall indeed obtain that princess Kuraṅgī as your wife.
Having spoken thus, the Fire-god vanished; and he too, filled with joy, the artificial son of the Mātaṅga, having gained confidence, went to his own home.
Then King Prasenajit, urged by fire in a dream and having investigated the truth of the matter, gave that daughter to the son of the Fire-god.
"Thus, O Goddess, divine beings always remain hidden on earth; therefore, this Suratamañjarī must be some divine being indeed, and not one of low birth."
For that jewel of my son is surely something else entirely, and she is certainly his beloved from a previous birth, as described by the passion of his gaze.
While King Pālaka was speaking thus and we remained there, I related this story concerning the fisherwoman.
In former times, there was a king named Malayasiṃha in the city of Rājagṛha; he had a daughter named Māyāvatī, who was peerless in beauty.
Once, while she was sporting in the Madhu garden, she was seen by a certain young fisherman who was endowed with beauty and youth.
And Suprahāra, having seen her, fell under the sway of love; for destiny does not regard the distinction between what is possible and what is impossible.
Having gone to his own home and abandoned the catching of pāṭhīna fish and other such activities, he remained on his bed with his mind fixed solely upon that, having renounced all food.
When questioned further regarding the consequences, he explained his intention; he, in turn, spoke of that son to his mother named Rakṣitakā.
"Cast off your despondency, my son; take food with certainty. I myself shall accomplish this desired goal for you by my own skillful means."
Having spoken thus, once he had been comforted, had regained his confidence, and finished his meal, she took some delicious fish and went to the house of the King’s daughter.
There, having been pointed out by the maidservants, that fisherwoman Rakṣitikā entered from the side door and gave her that gift of fish.
And by giving this very thing day after day in that same sequence, she propitiated the princess, who was longing for her word.
"Tell me what you desire from me; I shall do it, even if it be difficult," the princess said then with affection to that fisher-woman.
Then that fisherwoman, having been granted safety, spoke to her in private: "O Queen, without you whom I saw in the garden, my son is wasting away."
Having shown him hope, I am saving him from the loss of life; if you have compassion for me, then restore my son to life by your touch.
Thus addressed by that fisherwoman, the princess, feeling both bashful and constrained, reflected for a moment and spoke to her as follows.
"Bring that son secretly to my palace tonight. Upon hearing this, the maidservant was delighted and went at once to her son.
And at night, having adorned herself as best she could according to her own means, she brought her son to that prince’s inner apartments.
There, the princess, having felt affection for him, took Suprahāra—who had long been eager for her—and placed him upon the bed.
And she comforted him, whose limbs were exhausted by the fire of separation, with the touch of her hand—cool as sandalwood—as she massaged them.
Like a fisherman’s son suddenly drenched with nectar, he too felt his purpose fulfilled; having rested for a long time, he was instantly carried away by sleep.
And while he was asleep, the princess went elsewhere and slept there; she, the daughter of a fisherman won over by stratagem, had thus prevented the disaster.
Then, as he was awakened by the cessation of that touch of her hand, he beheld his beloved slipping away from his grasp.
Like a treasure-pot found by a man who is utterly destitute and despondent, the life-breaths immediately departed from the fisherman’s son, who was now devoid of hope.
Having learned of that and returned, the princess reproached herself; at dawn, she resolved to ascend the funeral pyre along with him.
Then her father, King Malayasiṃha, having learned of this, came there; seeing that she was irresistible, he sipped water for purification and spoke these words.
"If it be true that I am a devotee of the three-eyed God of gods, then tell me, O Guardians of the World, what ought to be done by me as is appropriate."
When the king had spoken thus, a divine voice said this: "This daughter of yours was the former wife of this young fisherman."
Long ago, in a village named Nāgasthala, there lived a most virtuous Brahmin named Baladhara, who was the son of Mahīdhara.
When his father had gone to heaven, he was robbed of his wealth by his kinsmen; consequently, filled with world-weariness, he went to the bank of the celestial river together with his wife.
Standing there without food, intending to cast off his body, he saw fishermen eating fish and believed it with his mind due to hunger.
Then, when he had met his death there, defiled by his own mental constructs, his wife—whose resolve was pure—followed him while remaining steadfast in her ascetic penance.
This very twice-born man was born into a family of fishermen due to the fault of his own volition; and she, Sutaṃtapā, was his wife—she has been born as your daughter, O King.
Therefore, O King, let this blameless daughter of yours restore her former husband—who has lost half his life—to life by means of half of her own lifespan.
Indeed, through the power of this austerity and likewise by the greatness of that sacred ford, this son-in-law of yours, having become purified, shall become king.
Having been thus addressed by a divine voice, the king gave that daughter, along with half of his own life-span, to Suprahāra, who had been restored to life.
Having become a king through the jewels of land, elephants, and horses bestowed by him, that skillful Suprahāra remained there, having obtained the daughter of that [king] as his wife.
Thus, a connection from a previous birth generally leads to affection for embodied beings; moreover, listen to this story concerning one who was connected to him as his own son.
In Ayodhyā there was a king renowned as Vīrabāhu, who always protected his subjects without distinction, as if they were his own offspring.
Once, the citizens approached that king and informed him: "O Lord, thieves are plundering this city every night."
"Even while we are awake, they cannot be detected. Having heard this, the king stationed spies there during the night.
They too did not capture the thieves, nor was the disturbance pacified; therefore, the king himself set out at night to search for them.
Wandering everywhere alone with a sword in hand, he saw a man moving upon the top of the rampart.
Out of fear, he took short steps, his eyes flickering like those of a crow, and he looked about like a lion, repeatedly turning his neck.
It was marked by the rays of swords drawn from their scabbards, as if with ropes stretched out for the purpose of seizing the bright jewels.
Having seen him, the king thought: "I know for certain that this is a thief; surely my city is being plundered by this man who wanders alone."
Having reflected thus, the king approached that clever thief; the thief also asked him apprehensively, "Who are you?"
Then the king, who was burdened by many calamities, said to him: "I am a reckless thief; tell me, who are you?"
The thief also said, "I am a lone wandering robber with great wealth; therefore come to my house so that I may fulfill your desire for riches."
Having heard that, the king agreed, saying "So be it," and went with the bandit to that dwelling at the edge of the forest, which was constructed by being excavated into the surface of the earth.
It was presided over by excellent women, illuminated by many jewels, always providing fresh enjoyment, and resembling a city of serpents.
Then, once that thief had entered the inner sanctum, a certain compassionate maidservant spoke to the king who remained in the outer area.
Where have you entered? Come out quickly, you betrayer of trust! For this [man], fearing his own betrayal, might slay you as you wander alone.
Having heard that, the king went out and quickly returned to his own palace; then, having summoned the commander-in-chief, he came back once more accompanied by his army.
Having arrived and blocked that house, he caused his heroes to enter within, seized the thief who had plundered the store of wealth, and brought him out.
When night had passed, that thief, whose arrest had been ordered by the king, was led through the middle of the marketplace to the place of execution.
Seeing him being led away there, a certain merchant’s daughter, captivated by his appearance, immediately spoke to her father.
"O father, if this man who is being led to the execution ground with the drum beaten for him should not become my husband, then know me to be already dead."
Then, seeing that she was impossible to restrain, her father went to the king and begged for the release of that thief even at the cost of ten million pieces of gold.
The king also became enraged at that merchant, but not with the thief; he released him without delay and impaled the other upon a stake.
Then that merchant’s daughter, named Vāmadattā, taking the corpse of that thief, entered the fire out of her deep affection for him.
Thus, since those beings are dependent upon the connections of their previous births, what future entity could one transcend, or who could prevent what for whom?
Therefore, O King, this Suratamañjarī belongs to your son Avantivardhana, having been brought about by some prior connection from a former life.
Otherwise, how could this prince of noble birth have such an attachment here for that woman of the Mātaṅga caste?
Therefore, O Lord, let that Mātaṅga, her father Utpalahasta, be requested for his daughter; let us first see what he says.
Thus addressed by me, King Pālaka then dispatched messengers with blue lotuses in their hands to request that maiden from him.
And when entreated by those messengers, the Mātaṅga said to them: "This is my desire; however, [it must be one] who feeds me in my own house."
To him, I must give my daughter Suratamañjarī, along with eighteen thousand Brahmins who reside in the city.
Having heard those words of his, which were accompanied by such a solemn promise, those messengers returned and reported it exactly so to King Pālaka.
Considering this to be the cause, the king, having related the entire account, summoned the Brahmins in his city of Ujjayinī and spoke to them.
"Eat here in the house of this Mātaṅga, who holds a blue lotus in his hand; you eighteen thousand shall not desire otherwise."
Thus addressed by the king, those twice-born ones, terrified of the Caṇḍālas and bewildered as to what ought to be done, took refuge in Mahākāla and performed austerities.
"Eat food from his house without hesitation; for he is a Vidyādhara, not a Caṇḍāla, along with his family."
Thus instructed in their dream by that Śambhu, those brahmins rose, went to the king, related it to him, and spoke again:
"O King, let this man cook pure food elsewhere than in the Caṇḍāla settlement; then, with Utpalahasta here, we shall eat it."
Having heard that, King Utpalahasta built another house for him; pleased, he had pure craftsmen prepare food for him there.
When he had bathed and stood before me with a blue lotus in his hand and wearing clean garments, eighteen thousand Brahmins were fed there.
When they had finished eating, he approached King Pālaka in the presence of the kingdom, and bowing with a blue lotus in his hand, he addressed him.
There was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Gaurīmuṇḍa; I was his dependent, known by the name Mataṅgadeva.
O King, when this daughter of mine, Suratamañjarī, had been born, that Gaurimuṇḍa spoke these words to me in secret:
"This son of the Lord of Vatsa, named Naravāhanadatta, who is destined to be a universal emperor here on earth, is being spoken of by the gods as our own."
Therefore, as long as that Kaṇṭaka has not attained the status of a universal monarch, go by means of your own magic power and strike him down; do not delay.
Thus urged then by the wicked Gaurimuṇḍa, as I was traveling through the sky for that purpose, I beheld Maheśvara before me.
Enraged, that Lord uttered a roar of "hum" and immediately cursed me: "O wicked one, how can you desire to commit sin against a great-souled person?"
"Therefore, with this very body, accompanied by your wife and daughter, go to Ujjayinī and fall among the outcasts, O evil-minded one!"
When he shall feed eighteen thousand Brahmins residing in the city as the bride-price for the gift of his daughter.
"At some point, the end of that curse will come within your house; you must give your daughter to him who provides her dowry."
When Śambhu had vanished after saying this, I then fell [into a womb]; I was born as one named Utpalahasta among others, yet there was no confusion between me and them.
Today that curse of mine has been pacified through the grace of your son; therefore, I give this daughter of mine, Suratamañjarī, to him.
And now I depart for my own Vidyādhara realm, in order to serve Naravāhanadatta, the universal emperor.
Having spoken thus and entrusted his son, that Matangadeva, accompanied by his wife, rose into the air and came, O King, into the presence of your feet.
King Pālaka, having realized the truth, was delighted and then performed the marriage of his daughter with that Suratamañjarī.
And his son, Avantivardhana, having obtained that Vidyādharī as his wife, felt his purpose fulfilled by attaining more than he had ever desired.
And once, while that prince was sleeping with her in his palace, he woke at the end of the night and suddenly did not see his beloved.
Having searched for her and not found her, he lamented and suffered so intensely that even his father, the king, became utterly distraught upon hearing of it.
"This city is well-guarded; no stranger may enter it at night. Surely she has been carried off by some wicked being who travels through the sky."
While we were thus conversing and had gathered there at that very moment, your Vidyādhara Dhūmaśikha descended from the sky.
Therefore, this Prince Avantivardhana has been brought here by him; and I, having related the circumstances, sought him from King Pālaka.
This very Suratamañjarī is present here with her father; such is her story, and Your Majesty knows what follows from this.
When the minister Pālaka had spoken thus and ceased, O Bharatarohaka, the members of the assembly questioned Mataṅgadeva in the presence of Naravāhanadatta.
"To whom have you given this Suratamañjarī? Tell me! He replied, "I have indeed given her to Avantivardhana."
Then Cetyaka, questioned by them, "Tell us, why do you carry her away? replied, "She was first given to me by my mother's word."

"If you have a father, who is your mother? And as for that gift, who here is your witness? "Therefore, this woman is another's wife; you are a sinner! thus the members of the assembly spoke to him harshly.
Thus, when Ityaka had been rendered speechless by them and was forcibly restrained, the Emperor Naravāhanadatta, enraged by his ill-behavior, issued an order for his punishment.

"Forgive this one transgression of his here; for he is indeed your brother-in-law, the son of Madanavega. Thus entreated by the eminent sages, Kaśyapa and the others, the king, having rebuked him somewhat, finally released him.
Furthermore, he dispatched his own nephew Avantivardhana, along with his ministers, to his own city, accompanied by his wife and placed in the hands of Vāyupatha.

Thus ends the second wave in the Suratamañjarī book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave: In this manner, on that Black Mountain (Asitagiri), the virtuous Suratamañjarī was [rescued] from that brother-in-law who had been humiliated and driven away by him.
Having recovered him and presented Naravāhanadatta—who was standing in the midst of the sages—to his husband, the seer Kaśyapa addressed him.
O King, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a universal monarch like you, whose mind—while seated upon the throne of righteousness—is not under the sway of passion and the like.
Blessed indeed are those who always behold you as one of virtuous deeds; for even in such a universal sovereignty, there is not the slightest fault in you.
For in former times, other universal monarchs such as Ṛṣabhaka and others were seized by various kinds of defects; they perished and fell from their prosperity.
Ṛṣabha, Sarvadamana, and the third, Bandhujīvaka—all of them met their downfall from Śakra due to excessive pride.
The Lord of the Vidyādharas, Jīmūtavāhana, having arrived, was questioned by the sage Nārada regarding the cause of his attainment of the rank of a universal emperor (cakravartin).
He related the gift of the wish-fulfilling tree as well as the gift of his own body; by that proclamation of his good deeds, he fell from his high station.
And he who was the universal monarch named Viśvantara here, his son Indīvarākṣa having been slain by the king of Cedi; |||
Deprived of his fortitude by grief and delusion over his wicked son, he perished through that [woman] named Vasantatilakā, who brought about the destruction of his family.
O Indra among kings, having become a human being with a singular focus, he attained the status of a universal monarch among the Vidyādharas through his meritorious deeds.
Having enjoyed the wealth of imperial sovereignty for a long time without encountering any fault, he eventually abandoned it of his own accord out of dispassion and went to the forest.
Thus, the Vidyādharas are generally deluded by the attainment of their own status; blinded by passion and other afflictions, they do not remain on the proper path and fall.
You must constantly protect yourself from straying from the path of truth, and you must protect these subjects of the Vidyādharas from any transgression of dharma.
Thus addressed by Kaśyapa, King Naravāhanadatta, having placed full faith in his words, respectfully questioned him as follows.
O Blessed One, please describe to us how Tārāvaloka, while still a human being, formerly attained the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas.
Having heard that, Kaśyapa said: "Listen, I shall tell you: there was a king among the Śibis named Candrāvaloka."
That Lord had a beloved named Candralekhā as his chief queen; she was of a lineage as pure as the Ocean of Milk, and her conduct was as stainless as the Ganges.
And he had an elephant, a crusher of enemy armies, known on the surface of the earth as the great Kuvalayāpīḍa.
By the power of that [mantra], the king was not overcome by any enemy, even a powerful one; nor was he ever oppressed by anyone in his kingdom, which had the citizens as its masters.
And when his youth had passed away, a single son endowed with auspicious marks was born to that lord of the earth by Queen Candralekhā.
Named Tārāvaloka, he gradually grew up along with innate virtues such as generosity, righteousness, and discernment.

The great-minded one studied the entirety of the meaning of all branches of knowledge; there was not a single word or meaning he did not learn, yet he never failed to grant the desires of those who sought his help.
In due course, though young in years, he became an elder by his deeds; though resembling the sun in brilliance, he was exceedingly gentle in appearance.
He was as beautiful as the full moon with its complete collection of digits, and like Kandarpa, he inspired longing in the entire world.
He was born as one who had surpassed Jīmūtavāhana in his service to his father, and was marked by the clearly manifested signs of a great universal monarch (cakravartin).
Then, for the sake of that son, King Candrāvaloka brought from the lord of Madra a daughter named Mādrī.
And when he had completed his marriage, the great king, his father, gratified by the excellence of his virtues, consecrated him as the crown prince at that very time.
And there, having been consecrated as crown prince by his father according to his command, Tārāvaloka established almshouses for the distribution of food and other gifts.
And rising from his bed, he would always mount the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa to personally inspect those very vessels.
Whatever anyone requested, he gave that to them, even his own life; by this, the fame of that crown prince spread in all directions.
Then two twin sons were born to him by Mādrī; and their father gave them the names Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
And those two children grew up as the very embodiments of their parents' affection and joy, becoming even dearer to them than their own lives; and they were likewise so to their grandparents.
Tārāvaloka and Mādrī could not have had enough of gazing upon these two, who were bent like bows with their virtues fixed upon them.
Then, seeing Kuvalayāpīḍa the elephant and the two sons of Dātṛyaśas, the enemies of Tārāvaloka spoke to their own brahmins:
"Go to the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa and beg him from Tārāvaloka; if he so desires, he will grant him to you."
"Therefore, we shall seize the kingdom from him once he is deprived of it; he will not give it up, and thus his reputation for generosity will perish."
Having been addressed thus by them, those brahmins said "So be it," and having departed from there, they requested that [gift] from King Tārāvaloka, beginning with the heroic Dāna.
"What indeed is the purpose of this elephant being requested by these twice-born men? I know for certain that they have been employed here by someone."
Therefore, let it be that this best of elephants must first be given by me; for how can a petitioner go away with his desire unfulfilled while I am still alive?
Having reflected thus, Tārāvaloka gave that excellent elephant to those brahmins with an entirely unwavering mind.
Then, seeing that excellent elephant being led away by those twice-born ones, the citizens of Candrāvaloka went in anger into the presence of the king.
And they said: "This kingdom has now been abandoned by your son, who, having renounced everything, has adopted the dharma of a sage."
Behold, this great elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa—the very root of royal fortune, whose scent alone overcomes other elephants—has been given by him to supplicants.
Therefore, either send this son of yours to the forest for asceticism, or bring back another elephant, or we shall make someone else our king.
Thus addressed by those citizens, Candrāvaloka caused that very message to be heard by his son through the mouth of the doorkeeper.
Having heard that, his son Tārāvaloka said: "I have already given away my elephant; furthermore, there is nothing that I cannot give to those who ask."
But what use have I for such a kingdom as this, which depends entirely on the citizens? And what use have I for wealth that flickers like lightning and is of no benefit to others?

Having performed that, I shall practice such intense austerity that this mockery shall not befall me, whose enemies have been conquered by my arms.
Having spoken thus and having restrained that friend who was trying to stop him, Vidyuddhvaja departed for the forest to perform austerities, without informing his parents.
Then, having learned of this, his parents followed him out of affection and said to him: "Where is a mere child, and where is such painful asceticism? O son, do not act so rashly!"

We have conquered our enemies and possess a kingdom; indeed, there is nothing greater than that even in the three worlds. Why do you wish for more, wasting yourself in vain? Why do you cause us both such grief?
To his parents who were speaking thus, Vidyuddhvaja said: "Even in my childhood, I shall acquire divine weapons through the power of asceticism."
I do not know why this world-kingdom, which is free of enemies, is protected by armies perpetually armored, as if it were merely one's own city.
Having spoken thus with certainty and having bid farewell to his parents, the asura Vidyuddhvaja performed austerities for the propitiation of Viriñca.
Subsisting on fruits, then subsisting on water, then subsisting on air, that Daitya remained for three hundred years each in succession, foregoing all food.
Then Brahmā, observing that his asceticism was capable of agitating the world, approached him and granted those weapons, beginning with the Brahma-missile, to him who requested them.
This Brahmā weapon cannot be countered by any other weapon, except for the fierce Pāśupata weapon, which is beyond our reach.
"Desiring victory, you must not employ this at an improper time. Having said this, Brahmā departed, and that Daitya returned to his home.
Then Vidyuddhvaja, together with his father and all his forces who had come for that festival, set out with the desire to conquer Śakra.
Then Śakra, having learned of his arrival and having established a protective rite in Triviṣṭapa, was accompanied by his friend Candraketu, the lord of the Vidyādharas.
And the lord of the Gandharvas, known by the name Padmaśekhara, went forth at the head of the army with the world-protectors and the gods, desiring to fight against him.
Then Vidyuddhvaja arrived there, covering the sky with his forces; and Brahmā, Rudra, and the others also came to witness this battle.
Then the battle between those two armies commenced, darkened by the gloom produced when the sun was obstructed by the clashing of their mutual missiles.
The ocean of battle swelled, agitated by the wind of indignation and overflowing with hundreds of armies; it had rolling horses and elephants for its crocodiles.
Then, when the dual combats between the gods and the asuras had commenced, Vidyutprabha—the father of Vidyuddhvaja—also approached Śakra in a rage.
Then, as Śakra was being gradually overwhelmed by that enemy of the gods in a battle of missiles and counter-missiles, he hurled his thunderbolt at him.
Struck by the vajra, that Daitya fell there, deprived of life; then Vidyuddhvaja, out of anger, rushed toward Śatakratu.
When his life was in danger, he first hurled the Brahma-weapon at him; and other great asuras struck him with various other weapons.
Then, having meditated for a moment upon the Pāśupata weapon as commanded by Īśvara, Śakra worshipped it as it appeared before him and hurled it at his enemies.
That demonic army was consumed by that weapon of the fire of time; however, Vidyuddhvaja, because of his youth, was not killed but fell down unconscious.
For that weapon does not strike one who is young, one who is old, or one who has turned his back; then the gods, having achieved victory, all went to their own abodes.
Vidyuddhvaja, having been struck down, regained consciousness after a long time; lamenting, he fled and spoke to the remaining soldiers who had gathered together.

"Though we were victorious, we have been defeated today by this Brahmā-weapon that has been acquired in return; therefore, having gone to the battlefield and approached Śakra, I shall sacrifice my life."
"I shall not be able to go back to my own city while my father is still hated"—to him who had spoken thus, his aged paternal minister replied:

The Brahmāstra, though discharged at an improper time, was rendered sluggish by other weapons already loosed; indeed, it was thwarted by the great weapon of Īśāna, which could not be endured by other missiles.
"You ought not to provoke an enemy who has achieved great victory at an improper time; for by doing so, you would only cause his further growth and bring about your own destruction."

For the steadfast man, by protecting himself and waiting for the time when the enemy's strength is reached, and having taken retaliatory action against his wrath, enjoys fame praised by the whole world.
When he was addressed thus by the elder, Vidyuddhvaja said: "In that case, you go for the sake of protecting our kingdom; as for me, however—"
"I shall go and propitiate that very Śiva, the Lord of All," he said; and having spoken thus, he dismissed his attendants even though they were unwilling to leave.
Having gone there with five companions, the sons of Daityas, he took up residence at the foot of Kailāsa on the bank of the Gaṅgā to practice ascetic penance.
In the midst of five fires during the summer heat, and in water during the winter cold, he remained for a thousand years meditating on Śiva while subsisting on fruits.
The second [fast] consists of eating roots; the third, subsisting on water; the fourth, consuming air; and the fifth, being without food at all.
He did not think much of the lotus-born Brahmā, who had come for the sake of granting a boon; rather, he said, "I have seen the power of your boon; you may depart."
After he had remained for that same length of time without food, Śambhu himself appeared before him as a great smoke rising from his head.
When he was told, "Choose a boon," that Daitya said to him, "O Lord, by your grace, may I slay Śakra in battle."
Arise! There is no difference between one who is conquered and one who is slain; therefore, you shall conquer Indra in battle and dwell in his place.
Having spoken thus, the god vanished; and Vidyuddhvaja, considering his heart's desire accomplished, broke his fast and returned to his own city.
There, welcomed by the citizens and having met with that minister of his father’s who had performed arduous penance for his sake, he held a great festival.
Having summoned the hosts of the Asuras and arranged the preparations for battle, he dispatched a messenger to Indra, saying, "Be ready for war."
And the sky, rent by the thunderous roar of the armies, trembled as they covered it with their banners, as if portending the destruction of the dwellers of heaven.
Indra, too, perceiving that he had arrived having obtained the boon, became agitated; after consulting with the preceptor of the gods, he summoned the celestial armies.
Then, when Vidyuddhvaja had arrived, a great battle took place between those two armies, in which the distinction between one's own side and the enemy's could no longer be discerned.
The Daityas led by Subāhu fought with the Vāyus; those led by Piṅgākṣa fought with the Kuberas, and those led by Mahāmāya fought with the Agnis.
The Iron-bodied ones and others were subdued by the Sūryas; the Ākampanas and others by the Siddhas; the Daityas by other Vidyādharas; and the Gandharvas and others by yet others.
Thus there was a great battle between them for twenty days; on the twenty-first day, the gods were broken by the Daityas in combat.
And those [demons], being broken, fled and entered within Triviṣṭapa; then Vāsava himself, mounted upon Airāvaṇa, went forth.
And having surrounded him, the divine armies went forth once more, together with the lords of the sky-dwellers, headed by Candraketu.
Then, as the battle commenced in which the Asuras and the gods were being slain, Vidyuddhvaja rushed toward Indra out of wrath for the killing of his father.
As the lord of the Daityas countered his weapons with counter-weapons, the king of the gods repeatedly severed his bow with arrows.
Then, emboldened by the boon of Maheśvara, Vidyuddhvaja took up a mallet and rushed with speed toward Vāsava.
Leaping up and placing his foot upon the tusks of Airāvaṇa, he ascended the top of its frontal globe and struck down the driver.
And he dealt a blow with a mallet to the King of the Gods, and the King of the Gods quickly struck him back with a club.
Vidyuddhvaja struck him again with a mallet; Indra fell down, unconscious, upon the chariot of Vāyu.
Vāyu, with the speed of thought, carried Indra away on his chariot elsewhere; and Vidyuddhvaja, having leaped after him, fell to the earth.
"This is not the time; withdraw Indra quickly from the battle!"—thus did the goddess Sarasvatī speak aloud from the sky at that very moment.
Then, after Śakra had been driven away by Vāyu, Vidyuddhvaja, mounted upon his chariot, pursued him with the speed of that vehicle.
Then Airāvaṇa, enraged and unrestrained, rushed forward, crushing and routing the armies, and went toward where Śakra was.
Then, having abandoned the battle, even as Indra pursued him, the preceptor of the gods led the terrified Śacī to the abode of Brahmā within the celestial army.
Then Vidyuddhvaja, having achieved victory and found the city empty, entered Amarāvatī accompanied by his shouting armies.
Indra, having regained consciousness and seeing that it was no longer the right time, went back to that very abode of Brahmā together with all the immortals.
"Now, this is the power of the boon from Hara; do not grieve. You shall regain your own station," the Grandfather consoled her thus.
He gave him his own place called Samādhisthala, a site situated in a certain region of the Brahma-world that brings all happiness, for his residence.
There the lord of the gods dwelt together with Śacī and Āvaṇa; and at his word, the lords of the Vidyādharas went to the world of Vāyu.
The lords of the Gandharvas went to the invincible world of Soma; others, having abandoned their respective dwellings, went to other worlds.
And Vidyuddhvaja, having caused the drums of the gods to resound throughout the earth, seized and enjoyed sovereignty in the triple heaven without restraint.
In the meantime, at this juncture of the narrative, the lord of the Vidyādharas, Candraketu, who had long resided in the world of the Wind-god, thought to himself as follows:
"How much longer must I remain here, fallen from my own station? Even now, the power of our enemy Vidyuddhvaja’s asceticism has not yet been exhausted."
I have heard that my friend Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Gandharvas, has departed from the world of Soma to the city of Śiva for the sake of ascetic penance.
Whether or not His Majesty has shown him favor, I do not yet know; having learned that, I shall know what must be done by me.
While he was thus meditating, his friend, the king of the Gandharvas, who had obtained a boon, approached that lord of the Vidyādharas.
Embraced by Candraketu and offered a welcome, the lord of the Gandharvas was questioned regarding his own adventures and spoke as follows.
Having gone to Śivapura, I gratified Śambhu with my ascetic penance; and he commanded me, "Go, for a most excellent son shall be born to you."
Furthermore, you shall regain your kingdom and even the most excellent maiden; the hero who shall be her husband will be the slayer of Vidyuddhvaja.
"Having been thus commanded by Hara, I have come to tell this to you," said [the messenger]. Upon hearing these words from the lord of the Gandharvas, Candraketu spoke.
For my part, in order to pacify this suffering, Maheśvara must be propitiated; for without propitiating him, the desired accomplishments do not come to pass.
Having thus resolved, Candraketu went with his wife Muktāvalī to the divine field of the Trident-bearer for the sake of asceticism.
Having related his own excellent adventure to Indra regarding the destruction of his enemies, Padmaśekhara, filled with resolve, departed for the realm of Soma.
Then the Lord of the Gods, remaining there at that site of meditative concentration, having conceived hope for the destruction of his enemy, called to mind the Teacher of the Immortals.
When he had been remembered and appeared there, Padmaśekhara bowed humbly and, having honored him, spoke; Śiva, pleased by his asceticism, had thus commanded him.
"He is indeed the slayer of Vidyuddhvaja and will become his son-in-law; let there be an end to this evil deed of ours, though it has taken me so long."
O Blessed One, I dwell here in despondency, ill at ease due to the fall from my own station; therefore, I contemplate here the imminent danger that acts with such haste.
Having heard these words from Śakra, the preceptor of the gods said to him: "Granted that the depletion of his ascetic power has been brought about by the evil deeds of that enemy."
Therefore, this is our opportunity to employ our own efforts; come, let us speak to Brahmā, and he will tell us the means.
Having been addressed thus by his preceptor, Śakra, joined by him, went into the presence of Brahmā; and having prostrated before him, he related what was in his mind.
Then the Self-Existent One said: "Is this not my concern as well? However, that which was wrought by Śarva can only be averted by Śarva himself."
And that god is difficult to reach for a long time; therefore, let us go to him who is near to Hari, for he is non-different from his own self—he will tell us the means.
Having thus deliberated, Brahmā, Śakra, and that preceptor of the gods mounted their swan-vehicle and arrived at Śvetadvīpa.
There, every person—both in physical form and in mind—is identical with the Blessed One, possessing four arms and bearing the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace.
There, within a palace of great jewels, they beheld the god Hari, reclining upon the bed of Śeṣa, his feet served by Kamalā.
Having offered their salutations to him, they were honored by him according to their rank; and being greeted by the divine sages, they sat down there as was appropriate.
When asked about their welfare by the Blessed One, those gods informed him: "O Lord, what welfare can there be for us while Vidyuddhvaja exists?"
For the Lord surely knows all that we have done; this journey of ours was for his sake, and therefore the Lord knows what lies beyond that.
When they had spoken thus to the gods, Janārdana said to them: "What is it that I do not know? My established order has been shattered by that asura."
However, that which was done by the Lord himself, the destroyer of Tripura, can be undone only by him, and not by me.
From that very [source] shall come the destruction of that sinful Daitya; if you will hasten, listen as I tell you the means.
There is a divine field of Maheśvara named Siddhīśvara; there the god Hara is eternally present.
And this very Lord, appearing in the form of a linga with visible flames, previously spoke to Prajapati regarding that which was formerly hidden from the grasp of others.
Therefore, let us go there and entreat him through asceticism; he alone will pacify this affliction of the worlds.
Having been thus instructed by that god Viṣṇu, they all went to Siddhiśvara, traveling on the vehicles of Tārkṣya and the swan.
Untouched by old age, death, or disease, it is the sole abode of happiness; there, even the beasts, birds, and trees are composed of gold and jewels.
There, having worshipped the Linga of the Trident-bearer—which manifests different internal forms from moment to moment and assumes the appearance of various other jewels—[he remained].
Devoted to that goal, those four—Hari, Brahmā, Indra, and the preceptor of the gods—performed difficult austerities directed toward Hara.
In the meantime, Śiva, gratified by his intense asceticism, granted a boon to that lord of the Vidyādharas, Candraketu.
"Arise, O King! That great hero shall be born as your son, who will slay your enemy Vidyuddhvaja in battle."

He who had descended into the human world due to a curse, having performed service for the gods, [was reunited] with Padmāvatī, the daughter of the Gandharva king, through the power of her asceticism.
Furthermore, having regained his own station together with that very wife, he shall exercise the sovereignty of all the Vidyādharas for ten kalpas.
When the god had thus vanished after granting the boon, Candraketu, together with his wife, returned at once to the realm of Vāyu.
Then, pleased by their intense asceticism, Hara, beholding Nārāyaṇa and the others within the interior of the liṅga at Siddhīśvara, spoke to them as they stood there rejoicing.
Arise! Enough with this distress; I have been gratified by the Vidyādhara lord Candraketu through his ascetic penance on your behalf.
A heroic son named Śambhava, who is a portion of myself, will be born to him; he shall soon slay that Daitya Vidyuddhvaja in battle.
Then, having fallen into the human state by a curse for the sake of another divine purpose, he shall be rescued by Padmaśekhara, the daughter of a Gandharva.
Together with his wife named Padmāvatī, who was born from a portion of Gaurī, he will rule the empire of the sky-dwellers and shall come to me alone.
"Therefore, fulfill this desire of yours to some small extent. Having spoken thus to Acyuta and the others, Śiva vanished from their sight.
Then, the joyful Hari, Brahmā, and those two, Śakra and the preceptor of the gods, returned once more to those very places from which they had come.
Then the beloved Muktāvalī of that lord of the Vidyādharas, Candraketu, became pregnant and in due time gave birth to a son.
He was illuminating the quarters with his invincible splendor, like the newly risen sun rising to dispel the affliction of darkness.
And as he was born, a voice from heaven was heard by Bhāratī: "O Candraketu, this son of yours shall slay the asura Vidyuddhvaja."
"Know him by name as Muktāphalaketu, the subduer of enemies. Having said this to Candraketu, her voice ceased with a sense of festive joy.
A rain of flowers fell, and Padmaśekhara, having understood the matter, departed; Śakra and the gods who had remained hidden also went there.
Relating the account of Haraprasāda to one another, they experienced great joy and returned to their own respective abodes.
And that Muktāphalaketu, refined by all the formative processes (*saṃskāra*), gradually attained growth along with Ānanda among the gods.
Then, after some days had passed following the birth of his son, a daughter was also born to Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Gandharvas.
This daughter of the lord of the Gandharvas, Padmāvatī by name, shall become the wife of you, the enemy of Vidyuddhvaja and lord of the Vidyādharas.
When she was thus born, a voice rose up from the sky; thereafter, Padmāvatī gradually grew up there as a maiden.
She was radiant with a flood of loveliness that flowed like a wave, as if produced by the nectar born from the world of the moon.
That great-minded Muktāphalaketu also became a youth; filled with devotion to Śiva, he constantly performed austerities such as vows and fasts.
Once, while he was established in meditation and had fasted for twelve days, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Girijā, appeared before him in person and spoke.
"I am pleased with this devotion of yours; by my grace, all the missiles, sciences, and likewise all the arts shall manifest before you."
And take from me this sword named Aparājita, by means of which you shall exercise sovereignty, unconquered by adversaries.
Having spoken thus, that Lord gave him a sword and vanished; and that prince immediately became possessed of great power, strength, and valor through the divine weapon.
In the meantime, once upon a time, that great asura Vidyuddhvaja, while staying in the third heaven, engaged in water-sports in the waters of the celestial river.
He beheld her great body of water, brownish with the pollen of flowers, permeated with the scent of rut, and agitated by ripples.
Then, puffed up with pride in his own arms, he said to his followers: "Who is playing with water even over my head? Go and see!"
Having heard that, as they proceeded upward, those Asuras saw the bull of Śiva sporting in the water together with Indra’s elephant.
Having arrived, they said to that lord of the Daityas: "O Lord, the bull of Śambhu, accompanied by Airāvata, has gone up into the water and is sporting upon it."
Hearing that this water was mixed with the ichor from Airāvaṇa's temples and with his garlands, the asura, disregarding Śiva out of intoxication, became enraged.
Deluded by the ripening of his own evil deeds, he said to his servants: "Go, bind those two—Āvaṇa and Āvaṇa—and bring them here with oxen."
Then, as soon as those Asuras went there desiring to seize them, the two—Vṛṣa and Dvipa—rushed forward in anger and slew them.
The survivors of the slaughter went and reported this to Vidyuddhvaja; enraged, he dispatched against those two a very great army of asuras.
Having crushed that army, which met its destruction through the ripening of its sins, Vṛṣa went into the presence of Hara, while Airāvaṇa approached Indra.

Then Indra, having observed those actions of the son of Diti and having heard of the host of guards following Airāvaṇa, considered that enemy to have reached the hour of his destruction—even though he had previously shown contempt for the Blessed Lord, the husband of Gaurī.

Having reported this to the Lotus-born [Brahmā], Śakra then assembled with the Vidyādharas and others, along with the celestial armies; having mounted his preeminent divine elephant and performed the auspicious rites prepared by Śacī, he set forth to slay that enemy.

Thus ends the second wave in the *Padmāvatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave: Then, having reached heaven, Indra surrounded it with his forces, which were emboldened by the favor of Hara and had gained strength through the opportune moment.
Seeing that, Vidyuddhvaja set forth with his army fully equipped; as he was departing, then various ill omens occurred for him.
Lightning struck the banners, vultures circled above, great parasols were shattered, and jackals howled inauspiciously.
Disregarding those ill omens, that asura went forth; and then a great battle commenced between the gods and the asuras.
When the wielder of the thunderbolt asked, "Why does that Muktāphalaketu not yet arrive?", Candraketu, the lord of the sky-dwellers, then informed him:
Having forgotten it in my haste as I was coming, I did not tell him; but having realized this, he will surely follow after me very quickly.
Having heard this, the lord of the gods dispatched a swift chariot with Vāyu as its charioteer to bring that illustrious Muktāphalaketu.
And his father, Candraketu, dispatched an attendant who followed him in a chariot, along with an army, to summon him.
And Muktāphalaketu, having learned that his father had gone to the battle with the Daityas, prepared to go there himself along with his followers.
Then, mounted upon his victorious elephant and having had the auspicious rites performed for him by his mother, he set forth from the world of Vāyu, bearing the divine sword.
As he set forth, a rain of flowers fell from the sky; the gods beat their drums, and auspicious winds blew.
Then those hosts of gods gathered together and surrounded him; meanwhile, those who had fled and remained hidden out of fear of Vidyuddhvaja now emerged.
Traveling with that great army, he beheld on the way a vast mountain hermitage named Meghavana.
Not transgressing that command, he respectfully descended from the elephant, gathered divine flowers, and proceeded to worship the Goddess.
In the meantime, Padmāvatī, the daughter of Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Gandharvas, having attained youth, arrived surrounded by her female companions.

Having taken leave of his own mother, who was established in asceticism for the sake of her husband’s welfare as he had gone forth to battle, [he departed] from the world of the moon by means of a celestial chariot.
Seeking Śiva as her father’s kinsman and her desired husband, she went to that very divine abode of Gaurī for the sake of penance.
Not even now has any suitor been determined who stands ready for battle; moreover, for the sake of your father’s welfare, your mother has taken recourse to ascetic penance.
"But you, my friend, for whose sake do you wish to perform penance as a maiden? Having been addressed thus on the road by her friend, Padmāvatī spoke this.
O friend, for maidens, the father alone is the deity who grants all success; and as for the groom, he has certainly been determined by me to possess qualities that are not shared by any other.
He who was born from the lord of the Vidyādharas to slay Vidyuddhvaja—Muktāphalaketu has been designated by Śambhu as my husband.
I heard this from the very mouth of my father when he was questioned by my mother; and he will certainly go, for he has already set out for battle as my chosen champion.
Therefore, desiring victory for both my husband and my father, I shall propitiate the blessed Gaurī through the power of asceticism.
To the princess who was speaking thus, her friend said: "Even regarding a future matter, such resolve is indeed appropriate for you."
"May that which you desire be fulfilled," said her friend; and she reached a large, auspicious lake near the temple of Gaurī.
It was covered with radiant, blooming golden lotuses, as if they were dappled by the splendor radiating from her lotus-like face.
Having descended there, that daughter of the Gandharvas gathered lotuses for the worship of Ambikā, and while she was about to perform her bath, [the following occurred].
While that battle between the gods and asuras was thus proceeding, and while the demons were rushing forward, greedy for the prey, two rākṣasīs arrived by that same path.
With tawny, upward-pointing hair from which flames are vomited from a mouth made terrible by fangs, you have a massive body dark as smoke and breasts that hang from a protruding belly.
As soon as those two night-rangers saw the daughter of the Gandharva king, they swooped down, seized her, and carried her off toward the sky.
As long as the presiding deity of that celestial chariot restrains those two Rākṣasīs, and as long as her distressed retinue continues to cry out, [she will remain there].
Meanwhile, Muktāphalaketu, having performed his worship, emerged from the temple of the goddess; hearing the cry for help, he came to that very spot.
He saw her, possessed of radiant splendor, held by the pair of rākṣasīs like a flash of lightning caught amidst a mass of dark clouds.
Having rushed toward Padmāvatī, the great hero released her, striking those two Rākṣasīs with his palms so that they fell unconscious upon the ground.
And he beheld her, who flowed like a cascade of the essence of loveliness, graced by a waist made beautiful by the waves of the three folds.
She seemed as if fashioned by the Creator himself, who had attained the pinnacle of skill through the creation of the celestial nymphs, having concentrated therein the very essence of all beauty.
And having seen her, his senses dulled by the delusion of Kandarpa, he—though steadfast—stood for a moment there motionless, as if fixed in a painting.
When the agitation caused by the rākṣasīs had subsided, Padmāvatī, having recovered as if in a mere moment, also beheld that Muktāphalaketu.
He was a form that provided a festival for the eyes of the world and incited the passion of women, appearing as if he were fashioned by the Creator by uniting the moon and the god of love into one.
Then, her face covered in shame, she spoke privately to her friend: "May it be well with her; I shall depart from here, from the side of this strange man."
While she was speaking thus, Muktāphalaketu asked her friend, "What does this young woman say? to which that friend replied.
She too said: "This Sukanyā has been given as a blessing by your life-saver; she says to me, 'Come, let us go away from the presence of another man.'"
Hearing that, Muktāphalaketu spoke to her in agitation: "Who is she? Whose daughter is she? And to what man of auspicious deeds has she been given?"
Thus questioned by him, her companion said to him: "O fortunate one, this maiden named Padmāvatī is our friend."
Born from the self of Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Gandharvas, her husband has been ordained by Śambhu to be Muktāphalaketu.
The son of Candraketu, the lord of the Vidyādharas, beloved by the world, the ally of the king of the gods, and the destroyer of Vidyuddhvaja.
Desiring victory for her husband as well as for her father in battle, she has now come to this temple of Gaurī for the sake of performing penance.
Having heard this, the followers of Candraketu’s son delighted that princess, saying, "By good fortune, O Queen, he is indeed your husband."
Then, O Mother, it was fitting that those two—the maiden and the suitor—did not recognize one another within their own selves, which were filled with the joy of mutual discovery.
While the two of them remained there, gazing at one another with mutual affection through side-long glances, the sound of musical instruments was heard.
Then the army was seen, and the chariot joined by Vāyu; likewise, Candraketu’s doorkeeper arrived with great haste.
And those two, Vāyu and Pratīhāra, having abandoned their mounts with due decorum, approached Muktāphalaketu and spoke to him.
"The Lord of the Gods and your father are summoning you from the field of battle; therefore, mount this chariot and come quickly."
Then, although bound by his love for Padmāvatī, that son of the lord of the sky-goers ascended the chariot with those two on account of his weighty duty.
Having quickly fastened the divine armor sent by Śakra, he set out, repeatedly turning his neck to look back at Padmāvatī.
And Padmāvatī, beholding him as he had come from beyond the range of sight, saw that the two night-stalkers had been struck down by a single blow of his palm.
Thinking only of him, she bathed and worshipped Ambikā and Hara; from that time forward, she performed austerities right there for the sake of his welfare.
Reflecting upon that vision, which was auspicious, indicative of victory, and brought about by the gods and asuras, Muktāphalaketu also reached that place.
And seeing that hero arrive well-armored with his army, all those great asuras rushed toward him alone.
With their heads shattered by his shower of arrows, that hero offered a sacrifice to the deities of the quarters at the commencement of the festival of battle.
Seeing his army being slaughtered by that Muktāphalaketu, Vidyuddhvaja himself rushed toward him in a fit of rage.
As that Daitya was falling, he was struck with arrows by the diligent [hero]; thereupon, the entire Asura army rushed toward him from every side.
Seeing that, Vāsava, accompanied by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and gods, immediately rushed toward that army of Daityas.
Then there arose a tumultuous battle, with falling arrows, spears, javelins, clubs, and axes, in which countless soldiers were slain.
Rivers of blood flowed, with the bodies of elephants and horses as their crocodiles, the pearls from elephants' tusks as their sands, and the heads of great heroes as their stones.
That festival of battle became a source of joy for the headless trunks as they danced together with spirits intoxicated by the wine of blood and seeking flesh.
In that ocean of battle between the Daityas and the gods, the fortune of victory, as fickle as a great wave, moved from here for a moment and from there for a moment.
Thus the battle lasted for twenty-four days, watched by Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā as they stood in their celestial chariots.
On the twenty-fifth day, when both armies were nearly exhausted and the principal duels had commenced in that battle, [the following occurred].
And between that Śrīmuktāphalaketu and Vidyuddhvaja, a duel commenced, with one mounted on a chariot and the other upon an elephant.
The darkness-weapon [is neutralized] by the sun-weapon; the winter-weapon by the summer-weapon; the mountain-weapon by the thunderbolt-weapon; and the serpent-weapon by the garuḍa-weapon.
Having restrained the driver and the elephant of that Asura, Muktāphalaketu struck them down, each with a single arrow.
When he had mounted the chariot, Vidyuddhvaja resorted to his illusory power (māyā) because he had slain both the charioteer and the horses.
Becoming invisible to the entire army, he ascended to the sky and rained down rocks and various weapons upon the celestial host from all sides.
Then that Daitya burned with showers of fire the impenetrable net of arrows that had been released by Muktāphalaketu.

Then, having consecrated with mantras the Brahmā weapon—which was capable of destroying the entire universe—he, whose banner bore the emblem of a pearl, released it toward that enemy and his followers.
Struck by that weapon, the great asura Vidyuddhvaja, along with his army, was deprived of life and fell from the midst of the sky.
The remaining ones, including the sons of Vidyuddhvaja and others, fled together with Vajradaṃṣṭra and his followers out of fear, and went to the depths of the netherworld.
And the gods, following the sound, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! and honored the illustrious Muktāphalaketu with showers of flowers.
Then, once the enemy was slain, Śakra regained his kingdom and entered Triviṣṭapa; a great festival took place throughout the three worlds.
The Lord of Creatures himself arrived there, preceded by Śacī, and he fastened the most excellent crest-jewel upon Muktāphalaketu.
Indra, too, placed upon the neck of that prince—who was graced by victory and destined to bestow the kingdom—a necklace from his own throat.
And he seated him upon his own seat, while various blessings were bestowed by the gods who were filled with joy.
And having dispatched the warder to the city of the asura Vidyuddhvaja, he accepted his own city as a gift, intending to bestow it upon him at the proper time.
Then the Gandharva Padmaśekhara, wishing to give the maiden Padmāvatī to this prince, looked meaningfully at the face of the Lord.
And the Creator, having understood his intention, said to that lord of the Gandharvas: "There remains a certain task; therefore, endure for a little while longer."
Then, there occurred Indra’s victory festival, resounded by the songs of Hāhā and Hūhū accompanied by their own melodies, and by the dances of Rambhā and others.
When the joy of the festival had been witnessed and the Creator had departed, the slayer of Vṛtra honored the world-protectors and others, and dismissed them to their respective abodes.
And he dismissed that king of the Gandharvas, Padmaśekhara, after honoring him and his retinue, sending him back to his own city of the Gandharvas.
And Hari sent the honored Śrīmuktāphalaketu and Candraketu to his own city of the Vidyādharas for the festival.
And he, having removed all thorns from the world and followed by many kings of the Vidyādharas, then returned to his capital with his father-in-law, Muktāphalaketu.
And at that time, studded with excellent jewels and garlanded with silk banners and streamers, the city shone brightly when this victorious prince returned after a long absence along with his father.

And his father Candraketu, having immediately gratified the circle of his kinsmen and servants in the city, extended that magnificent festival of his son’s victory by raining down wealth, just as a cloud pours forth water.
And although that Muktāphalaketu had achieved even the fame of subduing Vidyuddhvaja, he found no delight in his own enjoyments without Padmāvatī.
Furthermore, with his heart being consoled by a friend named Saṃyata, who informed him of Śarva’s command and other matters, he passed those days with great difficulty.

Thus ends the third wave in the *Padmāvatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fourth Wave. In the meantime, that king of the Gandharvas, Padmaśekhara, entered his own city once more, where a vast and resplendent festival was being celebrated.
Having learned from the mouth of his wife that his daughter Padmāvatī was performing austerities at the hermitage of Girijā out of hope for victory over him, he had her summoned.
And as his daughter, emaciated by asceticism and separation, approached and fell at his feet, he spoke to her, bestowing his blessing.
O child, you have undergone great hardship through penance for my sake; therefore, [slay] that son of the king of the Vidyādharas, the destroyer of Vidyuddhvaja.
"Quickly obtain as your husband that illustrious Muktāphalaketu, the refuge of the world, the victorious one who was himself designated by Śambhu."
While Vinatā remained there with her face cast down after her father had spoken thus, her mother Kuvalayāvalī addressed the king.
How was that such asura slain in battle by that noble son, the prince who bestows fearlessness upon the three worlds?
Having heard that, the king described to her the prowess of that prince, including his battle with the gods and the asuras.
Then, Padmāvatī’s friend named Manohārikā also related the story of her effortless slaying of the pair of rākṣasīs.
Then, having learned of their mutual meeting and the affection between them, the king and the queen attained great joy regarding both his son and her daughter.
And they both said: "Who are those two Rākṣasīs belonging to him by whom the hosts of Asura armies were swallowed, just as the ocean was swallowed by Agastya?"
And by that gale of descriptions regarding her excellence in manly prowess, the fire of Padmāvatī’s passion blazed up even more intensely.
Then, having departed from her parents' presence, the princess ascended in an instant, full of longing, to the jewel-adorned palace within the inner apartments.
There, in that place where pearl lattices were fastened to pillars inlaid with jewels, and where there was a noble couch and a comfortable seat set upon a jeweled floor;
Though she remained in that place, delightful with its various divine enjoyments appearing at her mere thought, she suffered intensely from the fire of separation from her beloved.
And then, from behind him, he beheld a divine and magnificent garden, covered with golden trees and creepers, and filled with hundreds of jeweled ponds.
And having seen it, he thought: "How wonderful is this supreme city of ours, more beautiful even than the world of the Moon, the birthplace of my lineage!"
Yet I have not seen this crest-jewel of the Himalayas, where there is such a city grove that surpasses even the Nandana garden.
Therefore, having gone there to that secluded place, which is excellent, shady, and cool, I shall somewhat alleviate this torment of the fire of separation.
Having reflected thus, that young woman then slowly and alone, having skillfully descended from there, set out to go to the city garden.
Unable to go on foot, she was carried to that garden by birds that appeared through her own supernatural power to serve as her vehicle.
There, within a house made of plantain groves, he sat upon a bed of flowers while the sound of divine songs and other music was being heard.
She found no delight therein, nor did her passion subside; on the contrary, the fire of desire increased all the more in the absence of her beloved.
Then, eager to behold her beloved even as he appeared in a painting, she took up a painting board and colored pencils from the storehouse.
Since even the Creator is unable to produce another being equal to him, how could I, with my hand paralyzed by longing, paint his likeness?
"Nevertheless, for the sake of my own diversion, I shall paint him however I can. Having thus reflected, she began to paint him upon a wooden board.
Just then, her friend named Manohārikā, searching for her and distraught at not seeing her, arrived at that very spot.
Standing behind her, she saw the princess there alone in the bower of creepers, longing for him and holding a painted tablet.
"Let me see what this woman is doing here all alone. Having thought thus, her friend remained there concealed.
Meanwhile, Padmāvatī, her lotus-like eyes filled with tears, spoke thus concerning her beloved who was depicted in a painting:
Having slain the Asuras who were defeated by Indra through your mere conversation, how is it that you do not protect me from the Māras?
Even the wish-fulfilling tree fails to give, even the Sugata lacks compassion, and even gold turns to stone for one of meager merit.
And being surely ignorant of the fever of love, you certainly do not know my suffering; what can that wretched flower-arrowed god do for you, now that he has been defeated by the Daitya?
What more shall I say? Fate is adverse to me, since it seeks to cover my eyes with tears, desiring that I not behold you even in a painting.
Having spoken thus, the princess began to weep, with teardrops resembling large pearls falling from her broken necklace.
At that very moment, her friend Manohārikā approached her; the princess, having covered the painting, said to her:
"You have not been seen for so long; oh, friend, where have you been? Hearing that, Manohārikā said to her while laughing:
O friend, searching for you alone, I have wandered for a long time; therefore, why is this being hidden by you? It is a marvel that I have either seen it or heard of it.
Thus addressed by her friend, Padmāvatī, with her face bowed in shame, spoke to her while holding her hand, her voice faltering with tears.
"Friend, everything was already known to you; why is it being concealed? At that time, by that prince, I [was seen] in that hermitage of Gaurī."
Though she was rescued from the midst of the fire of the most terrible ogress, she has been cast into the submarine fire of passion, where the flames of unbearable separation rage.

Therefore, I do not know where I should go, to whom I should speak, or what I should do; nor do I know what recourse or means to rely upon, for my mind is attached to that which is difficult to attain.
To the princess who was speaking thus, her friend said: "O friend, this attachment of your mind is appropriate; it is well-placed."
Indeed, the union of you two is for the sake of mutual beauty, like that of the crescent moon and the matted-hair crown of Śarva.
And let there be no lack of fortitude in this matter; he will certainly not remain without you. Have you not observed him to be such as that?
Even women, greedy for beauty, desire the state of manhood upon seeing her; who then would not be desirous of you, since you possess such a form? How much more so, then, one who is your equal?
Is even Śarva a speaker of falsehood, by whom you two were told that you are a married couple? For who can maintain composure regarding a desired object that is not within reach?
Therefore, take heart; he alone shall soon become your husband. No one is difficult for you to attain, but you are difficult for everyone else to attain.
Having been addressed thus by her friend, the princess said to her: "Friend, although I know this, nevertheless, what shall I do?"
But this mind of mine, so attached to him, cannot endure for even a moment without that lord of my life; nor can it bear the god of love.
For as I remember him alone, my mind finds no peace for even a moment; my limbs burn with anguish, and my vital breaths seem to depart.
Speaking thus, deluded by infatuation, that princess, as delicate as a flower, fell into the lap of her companion.
Then, with the sprinkling of water, the tender leaves of plantains, and the fanning of breezes, that female friend gradually comforted her while shedding tears.
The lotus-fiber necklace, bracelets, moist ointment of sandalwood, and the bed of lotus leaves—these were the things that her friend prepared for her.
In contact with her, those [lotuses] too, being joined with her intense heat, became heated and, as if sharing her sorrow, grew withered.
Then the distraught Padmāvatī said to her friend: "Why do you distress yourself in vain? My anguish will not be appeased in this way."
"If you do that by which [the pain] is stilled, it will lead to well-being. To her, who had spoken thus and was distressed, her friend replied:
"What is there that I would not do for your sake? Tell me that, my friend. Having heard this, the princess spoke somewhat bashfully.
"Go quickly, dear friend, and bring that beloved of mine here; otherwise, there can be no peace for me, nor will my father cease his anger."
"On the contrary, he will give this very thing to me once he has come here. When she had spoken thus, her companion also spoke to her with enthusiasm.
"If this is so, then take heart; how small a task is this! O friend, here I go myself to bring back your beloved."
That supreme city of your father, the lord of the sky-dwellers, Candraketu, is known by the name Candrapura; be at peace—why do you grieve?
Having been thus consoled by her friend, the princess said: "Therefore, arise; may your path be auspicious; go with all speed."
And that hero, the lord of my life and protector of the three worlds, should be addressed by you with affection on my behalf, O friend: "My friend, he should be told these words of mine."
Why did you not protect me in that temple of Gaurī from the fear of the rākṣasīs, while I was being struck by the woman-killer Makaraketu?

O Lord, what kind of dharma is this for those like you who are capable of uplifting the world, that you remain indifferent during a time of calamity, even though the people previously relied upon you?
"Speak thus to her, O auspicious one, or as you yourself know best. Having spoken these words, Padmāvatī dismissed that female friend.
And she, having mounted the bird-vehicle that had appeared for her own success, set out toward the city of the Vidyādharas, captivating his mind.
And Padmāvatī, having gained a modicum of fortitude through hope, took her picture-board and entered her father’s palace.
There, having entered her own dwelling surrounded by female servants, she bathed, and having worshipped the Lord of Gaurī with devotion, she made this request:
O Blessed One, in these three worlds, without the favor of your will, no one's desire—whether great or small—is ever fulfilled here.
"If you do not give me that desired husband, the son of the noble Vidyādhara universal monarch, I shall cast off my body before you."
Having heard this declaration made by the one who bears the moon as his crest-jewel, the retinue, filled with both sorrow and wonder, spoke.
O Goddess, why do you speak thus, showing such indifference toward your own body? Is there anything in these three worlds that is truly unattainable even for you?
For even the Sugata, when entreated by you, would surely relinquish his self-restraint; thus, he alone here is truly virtuous who is sought after by you in this manner.
Having heard this, the princess, drawn by his virtues, said: "He alone is the sole refuge of the gods, including Indra."
By whom alone was the asura host destroyed, as darkness is by the sun; and he who is the giver of life to us—how could he not be sought after?
Speaking thus with longing, she remained there with the servant-women who had arrived, occupied solely with that very conversation.
In the meantime, that friend of hers, Manohārikā, also quickly reached Candrapura, the city of the lord of the Vidyādharas.
Having built the city of the gods, Viśvakarman, as if still dissatisfied, created this wondrous place of extraordinary splendor.
There, not having found Muktāphalaketu and searching for him, Manohārikā, remaining in the air, went to his city garden.
It possessed the inconceivable power of its perfected state, with trees made of radiant jewels, and clusters of blossoms of many different species arising from a single tree.
Beholding that place, beautiful with the songs of birds mingled with the sound of divine music and featuring stone slabs of various jewels, she took her delight.
And having been seen by the garden-keepers, who had assumed various forms of birds, they approached them with very clear speech and spoke pleasant words.
Having seated her at the foot of the Pārijāta tree upon a seat of emerald and gems, worship was performed for her with appropriate offerings.
Having accepted that worship, we reflected there: "Oh, how marvelous are the diverse powers of accomplishment belonging to the lords of the Vidyādharas!"
For them, such is the garden where enjoyments arrive in an inconceivable manner, where celestial women perform music, and where winged beings serve as attendants.
Having reflected thus and questioned those very garden-keepers, she reached a grove of trees other than the Pārijāta.
There she beheld Muktāphalaketu lying upon a bed of flowers sprinkled with sandalwood paste, looking like the very Kalpa tree itself.
Recognizing him as one she had previously seen at Gaurī’s hermitage, she thought to herself while remaining hidden: "I shall observe what illness he has."
While his friend Saṃyataka was thus consoling him with snow, sandalwood, and breezes, Muktāphalaketu said to him:
"Certainly, it was by Smara that glowing coals were placed upon the snow, the fire of chaff upon sandalwood, and a forest fire upon the wind."
"O friend, why do you thus exhaust yourself fruitlessly, while this [fire] spreads its heat on all sides, born from the torment of separation?"
Even with diversions such as the dances and songs of beautiful women, my mind is distressed in this garden, which indeed surpasses the Nandana grove.
But without that Padmāvatī, born of Padmaśekhara and lotus-faced, this fever from the arrows of Smara does not subside for me.
I do not dare to speak of this to anyone, nor do I find any firm resolve; yet there is only one means for its attainment that I know.
I am going to the sanctuary of Gaurī, where my beloved, having uprooted my heart with the arrows of her sidelong glances, carried it away.
In that regard, through union with the daughter of the first king, Śambhu, propitiated by my ascetic penance during our meeting, will provide me with the means.
Having said this, just as the prince desired to rise, Manohārikā, her heart filled with joy, revealed herself.
"Friend, congratulations! By good fortune, your desire has been fulfilled; I have come as a friend to that beloved woman to see you."
"Indeed, I saw her at Ambikā’s hermitage while standing by your side," Saṃyataka said to the prince out of joy.
Then, seeing his beloved’s friend, the prince fell into a certain state agitated by surging joy, wonder, and longing.
Having seated her nearby, he then questioned that woman—who was like a rain of nectar to his eyes—regarding the welfare of his beloved’s body.
Then she spoke thus: "O Lord, my friend's welfare is certain as long as you are her protector; however, at present, she is indeed suffering."
From the moment her heart was stolen by you upon being seen, she has been distracted ever since; she neither hears nor sees.
Having cast off her fine silken garment, she now wears a necklace of lotus fibers; abandoned by her couch, she rolls upon a bed of lotus leaves.
She who formerly could not endure even a mention of a suitor out of modesty—she has today reached this state without her beloved.
Thus, O best of the accomplished, her own limbs—now white with sandalwood paste drying from the heat of her fever—seem to be laughing at him.
Having said, "And thus she speaks to you," she recited for him those songs containing the message from Padmāvatī, which were composed by Manohārikā.
Having heard all that, Muktāphalaketu was freed from his distress; he greeted Manohārikā with joy and spoke to her.
As if sprinkled with nectar by your words, this consciousness of mine has been restored; breath has returned, fortitude has arisen, and exhaustion has departed.
And today my former good deeds have borne fruit, since even that daughter of the Gandharva king is so partial toward me!
How might I possibly endure the pain of separation? But how could she, whose limbs are as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, ever bear it?
Therefore, I shall go to that very hermitage of the Mountain-Daughter; there you must bring your friend, so that our union may take place today.
Go quickly, O auspicious one, and comfort that friend of yours; and take this which has been bestowed upon me by the Self-Existent One himself in his satisfaction.
"Give her this crest-jewel, which destroys all suffering; and this necklace, obtained by me from Śakra, is your reward."
Having spoken thus, he offered her the crest-jewel from his head; and that prince placed the necklace from his own neck upon her neck.
Then, having bowed to him with joy, Manohārikā set out from there, mounted upon her bird, toward her friend Padmāvatī.
And Muktāphalaketu, his fatigue dispelled by great joy, entered his own city in haste together with Saṃyataka.
She too, having reached Padmāvatī’s side, related to her that heart-stealing fever of love which Manohārikā desired for her.

He recalled those words, affectionate, tender, and sweet, exactly as he had heard them, along with that appointment for their meeting which had been mentioned in the hermitage of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Then he gave her that crest-jewel sent by him, and he showed her the necklace given as a reward by her.
Then Padmāvatī, having embraced that successful friend, honored her and forgot the pain of the fire of love.
Having tied that crest-jewel upon her topknot like bliss itself, she prepared herself to depart for the grove of Gaurī.
In the meantime, by chance, the sage Tapodhana arrived at that forest of Gaurī together with his disciple named Dṛḍhavrata.
And there the sage spoke thus to his disciple of firm vows: "In this divine grove, I have maintained meditative absorption for a moment."
"Standing at the door, you must not allow anyone to enter; I shall worship Pārvatī once I have completed my meditative absorption."
Having spoken thus, the sage stationed that disciple at the gate of the garden and, beneath the pārijāta tree, entered into meditative absorption.
Having arisen from his meditative absorption, he entered within to worship Ambikā; yet he did not speak of that to his disciple who was waiting at the door.
