Just then, Muktāphalaketu arrived there, having adorned himself and mounted a divine camel along with Saṃyataka.
And as he was entering that garden, he was stopped by that disciple of the sage, who said, "Do not, do not! My teacher is staying here in meditative absorption."
Thinking, "Perhaps my beloved has come here to this vast interior, while the sage remains in one corner," he became filled with eager longing.
Having passed out of the range of vision of this son of the sage, the prince, accompanied by his friend, entered that garden by way of the sky.
And as long as he looked at that, so long did he enter therein; for the disciple of the sage had gone to observe the completion of his teacher's meditative absorption.
He did not see his teacher there, nor did he see him with his companions; instead, he saw the illustrious Muktāphalaketu, who had entered by an unauthorized path.
Then that disciple of the sage, filled with rage, cursed the prince: "Because of this lack of discipline, go to the human state along with your companions."
"Since you have broken my concentration here and disregarded me, my guru," having thus pronounced this curse, he followed after his own guru.
And Muktāphalaketu, while his desire was nearly accomplished, fell into deep despondency due to the falling thunderbolt of the curse.
Meanwhile, Padmāvatī, eager for union with her beloved, arrived there mounted upon a bird, accompanied by Manohārikā and the others.
Seeing her who had come to the svayaṃvara and was yet separated from him by a curse, the prince fell into a painful state composed of both joy and sorrow.
And at that moment, as Padmāvatī displayed her lack of courtesy, her right eye throbbed and her mind trembled.
Then, seeing her beloved there looking distressed, the princess thought to herself, "Could he be troubled because I did not arrive before him?"
And when she had approached him with humility, the prince said to her: "My dear, our desire has been frustrated; even though it was accomplished, fate has thwarted us."
Hearing that, the prince, with agitation, described his own curse to her as she asked, "Alas! How was it broken?"
Then, distressed by the curse, they all went to their preceptor, the sage, who was staying in the temple of the goddess, to entreat him for an end to the curse.
Seeing them approach and bow down, the wise great sage spoke with affection to Muktāphalaketu.
"You have been cursed by this fool, who acts without foresight; you did nothing at all for me, for I rose up from there of my own accord."
In this matter, you must act solely as an instrument; for there exists a divine task that you must necessarily perform in your human state.
Upon seeing this very Padmāvatī by chance, you will become afflicted with love; then, casting off your mortal body, you shall be swiftly released from the curse.
With this very body, you shall again protect this mistress of life; for you are the protector of the universe, and you truly ought not to endure this curse for long.

Since even the Daityas, including children, the elderly, and others, were slain by the Brahmāstra when it was discharged by you, that slight trace of unrighteousness is the cause of your [condition] here.
Having heard that, Padmāvatī, with tears in her eyes, entreated the sage: "O Blessed One, may whatever be the fate of my noble husband now become mine as well."
"I shall not be able to remain even for a moment separated from this," said Padmāvatī as she made her request; to her, the sage replied:
This is not so; you must remain right here for now performing austerities, so that before long he shall be released from his curse and marry you.
Then, accompanied by this Muktāphalaketu, you shall rule the empire of the sky-dwellers and asuras for ten kalpas.
This crest-jewel, endowed with great power, has been produced from the water-pot of the Creator; when given to you, it shall protect you while you remain engaged in ascetic penance.
When the sage of divine vision had thus spoken to Padmāvatī, Muktāphalaketu bowed before him and made this request:
"O Blessed One, may I have unbreakable devotion toward you in my human existence. Padmāvatī then cursed that offending disciple.
When the sage had said, "So be it," Padmāvatī, being deeply distressed, cursed that offending disciple of his.
"Because you cursed my noble son out of folly, you shall become his very mount in this human world—capable of assuming any form at will and moving at pleasure."
Thus, when he had been cursed by her, the dejected king was then accompanied by that ascetic, his own disciple, as the sage vanished from sight.
Then Muktāphalaketu said to Padmāvatī: "I shall go to my own city; let me see what might happen there for me."
Hearing that, Padmāvatī, terrified of separation, fell instantly to the ground like a creeper broken by the wind, with her flowers and ornaments still upon her.
Having somehow consoled her as she wept, he, accompanied by his friend, departed from there with Muktāphalaketu repeatedly casting glances back at her.
And when he had gone, Padmāvatī, lamenting in great distress, spoke to her friend Manohārikā, who was trying to comfort her.
"Friend, I know that today in a dream I beheld the goddess Pārvatī; she even attempted to cast a garland of blue lotuses around my neck."
"Let it be; I shall give you more," she said, and then she ceased speaking. Thus, she has indicated to me this very obstacle to my attaining my beloved.
As she was thus lamenting, her friend then said to her: "This dream was shown to you at that time for the sake of consoling the Queen."
The Sage has spoken thus, and the command of the gods is likewise; therefore, take heart, for before long you shall have a reunion with your beloved.
By these words of her friends and by the power of the crest-jewel, Padmāvatī then established her resolve and remained in the hermitage of Gaurī.

And she performed penance at the three junctions of the day, worshipping the Lord here in union with Girijā; likewise, she treated the portrait of her beloved—which had been brought from her own city—with the same devotion as she did the deity.

"O you whose desired object is certain to come to pass, do not undergo the fruitless toil of asceticism!"—to her parents, who had learned the truth and were approaching her with tears to dissuade her, she spoke thus.
Now that my husband has suddenly fallen into the misery of a curse, ordained by fate, how could I dwell here in comfort? For the husband is indeed the supreme deity for women of noble family.

When this evil has been exhausted by my ascetic penance and Śambhu has become pleased, I shall soon be reunited with my beloved; for indeed, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished through austerities.
When Padmāvatī had thus spoken with firm resolve, her mother Kuvalayāvalī said to her father, the king:
"O King, why do you perform this painful penance in vain? Why distress yourself further? This must come to pass; there is a cause for it here, and I shall tell it—listen."
A daughter of the lord of the Siddhas named Devaprabhā, performing most arduous penance in order to obtain her desired husband, resided long ago in Śivapura.

Approaching her, he said, "Why are you not ashamed that, accompanied by me, you have gone to see King Padmāvatī? How is it that you do not suffer for this through your asceticism? and so he laughed at her.
"You laugh out of childishness, but you too shall perform penance that brings suffering for the sake of a husband"—saying this, she then cursed her with anger in the presence of the Siddha maidens.
Therefore, that hardship caused by the curse of Siddha’s daughter must necessarily be endured; who else is able to alter it? So let her do whatever she does.
Having been addressed thus by the queen, the Lord of the Gandharvas took his leave of her with some difficulty and departed for his own city, while his daughter remained prostrate at his feet.

She too, traveling through the sky every day, worshipped that Siddhīśvara who is served by Brahmā and the other gods; and there, in the hermitage of Girijā, Padmāvatī remained devoted to her observances and silent prayers, having been told in a dream by Hara: "Stay here."

Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Padmāvatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave. While Padmāvatī was thus engaged in asceticism for the sake of attaining him, Muktāphalaketu reached his own city.
Out of fear that his descent into human form was imminent due to the power of a Brahmin’s curse, the son of the lord of the Vidyādharas sought refuge with Śiva.
While worshipping him, she heard a voice from that inner sanctum: "Do not fear; indeed, you shall suffer no distress from dwelling in the womb."
In human form, you shall experience neither suffering nor a long stay; you will be born as a prince of great strength and prowess.
From the sage whose wealth is asceticism, you shall obtain the entire collection of divine weapons; and my attendant, known as Kiṅkara, shall become your younger brother.
Having conquered your enemies with his assistance and accomplished the task of the gods, you shall once again exercise sovereignty over the sky-dwellers, united with Padmāvatī.
Having heard these words, the prince remained there with firm resolve, as if awaiting the arrival of the fruit of that curse.
In this interval of the narrative, in the eastern direction, there was a city named Devasabha, which surpassed the assembly of the gods in splendor.
There, a universal monarch named Merudhvaja reigned as king; he was the ally of the King of the Gods whenever the war between the gods and the asuras broke out.

That high-souled one had no greed for fame, nor did he covet the property of others; his sharpness was found in his sword and not in his punishment, and his fear arose from sin rather than from an enemy.
Cruelty was found in his eyebrows during anger, yet not in his heart; roughness was found in his arm, marked by the scars of the bowstring, but never again in his speech.
He who, in battle, took pleasure in striking with weapons rather than in guarding his treasury; and he who placed his delight in the practice of dharma rather than in women.
Two thoughts were constantly present in the heart of that king: one was that not even a single son had yet been born to him.
And the second [reason] is that previously, after the great battle between the gods and asuras, those asuras who remained after being slain fled to the netherworld (pātāla).
Having departed from there, they repeatedly went to the netherworld (pātāla) after destroying his holy fords, temples, and hermitages from afar by means of deceit.
But that king did not find them, for they moved through the underworld and the sky; consequently, the radiant monarch felt distressed, even though he was without rival upon the earth.
Once, agitated by these reflections, he went to the abode of the gods in a noble chariot sent by Śakra, at the arrival of a bright day in the month of Caitra.
For at the beginning of every year, Śakra holds a universal assembly; King Merudhvaja used to go there constantly by means of that chariot.
But then, even though that place was filled with the dancing and singing of celestial women, and although he was honored by Śakra, the king sat there sighing.
Seeing that, the King of the Gods, who knew his heart, said to him: "O King, I know the sorrow you have; let it not remain yours."
A son named Muktāphaladhvaja, a portion of Śiva, shall be born to you; one will be an incarnation of a Gaṇa, and the second will be Malayadhvaja.

Muktāphaladhvaja, along with his younger brother, will obtain from the sage whose wealth is asceticism (tapodhana) the sciences (vidyās), a vehicle that assumes any form at will (kāmarūpa), and divine weapons (astras).
Having again obtained the great Pāśupata weapon, that invincible one, having slain the asuras, will bring both the earth and the netherworld under his control.
And you, accept from me these two sky-travelers equipped with great weapons, as well as the elephant Kāñcanagiri and likewise Kāñcanaśekhara.
Having spoken thus and given him the weapon-elephant, he was then sent off by the wielder of the thunderbolt; and Merudhvaja returned joyfully to his own city upon the earth.
But those asuras, having incurred blame through their deceit, did not attain the state of moving through the sky even after he had reached the refuge of Pātāla.
Then, having heard this from Śakra, the king, desiring a son, went on his divine mount to the hermitage of that seer whose wealth was asceticism.
Having approached that ṛṣi there and informed him of Śakra’s command, he said to him: "O Blessed One, instruct me quickly on the means to achieve this. He replied:
And for the sake of his wife's swift attainment of her desired goal, that sage prescribed for the king, together with his queen, the vow of propitiation to Śambhu.
By means of that vow, the lord of the earth propitiated Śiva; and the gratified Lord spoke thus to the king in a dream:
Arise, O King! You have reached [the time] for the destruction of the remaining Asuras; without delay, you shall obtain two unconquered sons in due course.
Having heard this, the king woke up at dawn, spoke to the sage, and after breaking his fast along with his wife, returned to his own city.
There, after a few days, that queen Merudhvajā, the great consort of King Merudhvaja, reached her season, being endowed with auspicious marks.
Having abandoned that Vidyādharī body by the power of a curse, Muktāphalaketu unexpectedly came to be conceived within her womb.
And that slender body of his remained there in his own city of Candrapura, preserved by his kinsmen and kept from withering by the power of his magic sciences.
There, in the city of Devasabhā, Queen Merudhvajā, having become pregnant, brought joy to her husband, King Merudhvaja.
And just as that queen became languid from the burden of her pregnancy, so too did her husband, the king, become full of enthusiasm.
And when the time had arrived, she gave birth to a son who resembled the sun—a child of fierce luster, like Kumāra born of Pārvatī.
And a festival arose not only throughout the entire surface of the earth, but even in the vault of heaven, as the drums were struck by the gods.
Then that sage, rich in asceticism and possessed of divine vision, came there in person to congratulate King Merudhvaja by good fortune.
Together with that sage named Śakra, the king, having performed a great festival, made Muktāphaladhvaja his son.
Then, after that sage had departed, at the end of a year, a second son was born to the king by that queen.
And the king gave him the name Malayadhvaja, together with that very same sage who had arrived out of joy.
Then that Saṃyataka, the son of the minister, was born from the curse; and his father gave him the name Mahābuddhi.
Then those two princes grew like lion cubs, together with that minister’s son, and gradually increased in splendor as well.
Then, when about eight years had passed, that sage rich in asceticism came and performed the initiation ceremony for those two princes.
And for another eight years, those two were trained by him in the sciences, the arts, and in all the great weapons.
Then, seeing those two youths, who were skilled in all weapons and combatants in the three modes of fighting, King Merudhvaja considered himself successful.
Then, as the sage desired to go to his own hermitage, he said to him: "O Blessed One, please accept this desired sacrificial fee now."
O lord of the earth, this alone is the desired sacrificial fee from you: that you, together with your son, shall slay the Asuras who destroy the sacrifice.
To the great seer who had spoken thus, the king replied: "Therefore, O Blessed One, you must now accept a sacrificial fee."
Therefore, commence that sacrifice; the Asuras will come to obstruct it, and at that time I too shall go there along with my sons.
O Sage, in former times, those Daityas, having committed an offense against you through deceit, flew up into the sky and, descending into the ocean, went to the netherworld (pātāla).
"But now I possess two sky-faring elephants given by Indra; with them, I shall reach those who travel through the air, even along with my sons."
Having heard that, the sage was pleased and said to that lord of men: "In that case, prepare for my sacrifice the necessary materials as is appropriate."
"Once I have gone as far as my fame extends throughout the world and commenced the sacrifice there, I shall send you this disciple of firm vows as a messenger."
Having assumed the form of a great, powerful bird unrestrained by desire, he shall become the vehicle for this Muktāphaladhvaja.
Having spoken thus, the sage departed for his own hermitage, and the king immediately dispatched all the necessary provisions after him.
And when that sacrifice had commenced and an assembly of gods and sages had gathered, the Dānavas dwelling in the netherworld became agitated upon learning of it.
Knowing this, that sage sent his disciple Dṛḍhavrata to the city of Devasabhā, where he had assumed the form of the king of birds as ordained by Śāstra.
Seeing that he had arrived there and remembering the words of the sage, King Merudhvaja readied those two divine elephants.
He himself ascended the principal of those two, the Golden Mountain (Kāñcanagiri), and he gave the Golden Peak (Kāñcanaśekhara) to his younger son.
And Muktāphaladhvaja, having taken up his divine weapons and being saluted by a multitude of bards, mounted that king of birds, Dṛḍhavrata.
Then those three heroes set forth on their aerial vehicles, having been granted blessings by the best of the twice-born, with their troops dispatched ahead of them.
When they had reached his hermitage, that sage, with a joyful mind, granted them the boon: "May you be impenetrable by all weapons."
And at that moment, the host of Dānavas arrived to destroy the sacrifice; seeing this, Merudhvaja’s army charged forward, roaring aloud.
Then a battle commenced between the Daityas and the humans; the Daityas, remaining in their own positions, oppressed the humans who stood upon the surface of the earth.
Then he, whose vehicle is a bird and whose banner bears a pearl, having rushed forward, cut and struck down the Daityas with a rain of arrows.
And seeing him seated upon the bird, blazing as if with splendor, the remaining Daityas fled, filled with apprehension for Nārāyaṇa.
And having gone to Pātāla out of fear, they reported that very same thing at that time to Trailokyamālin, the king of the Daityas.
Having learned of this, he quickly searched for him through his spies; and having discovered that Muktāphaladhvaja was a mortal, he became unable to endure being surpassed by a human.
Having assembled all the dānavas from the netherworld, the lord of asuras came to that hermitage to fight, even though he was being dissuaded by the birds.
Muktāphaladhvaja and the others remained there, fully attentive; as soon as they saw the lord of the Dānavas with his army, they rushed toward him.
Then, as that great battle between mortals and asuras commenced once more, the gods, headed by Rudra and Indra, arrived in their celestial chariots to witness it.
And at that moment, Muktāphaladhvaja beheld before him the great Pāśupata weapon, which had appeared instantly, possessing an invincible splendor.
Of immense proportions, with upward-flaming tongues of fire, three eyes, and four faces; having one leg and eight arms, he resembles the fire at the end of an aeon.
"Know that I have come at the command of Śaṅkara for your victory. Having spoken thus, the prince honored him and accepted his offer.
Meanwhile, from the sky, the army of Merudhvaja, standing below and already distressed, was further afflicted by various showers of missiles discharged by those asuras.
Then, in order to protect that [city], Muktāphaladhvaja, a versatile warrior, spread a web of arrows in its midst and fought with the asuras.
Seeing him, the sky-farer’s vehicle, accompanied by his father and brothers, that lord of the Daityas, Trailokyamālin, released the serpent-missile (pannagāstra).
As he emerged from there, Malayadhvaja struck down countless, terrifying venomous serpents with Garuḍas produced from the Gāruḍa-mantra.
Then, whatever weapon that lord of the Daityas and his son discharged, Muktāphaladhvaja effortlessly repelled each one of them.
Then, enraged, that enemy of the gods, his son, and the other Dānavas simultaneously hurled the Āgneya and other divine weapons at him.
Seeing those blazing weapons standing before him as the Pāśupata [weapon], all the missiles became terrified and in an instant turned away.
Then, while those terrified Daityas were fleeing as far as they wished, the hero Muktāphaladhvaja perceived their intention.
At that very moment, he bound a net of arrows above them and in the four directions—a net difficult to pierce, resembling a cage of adamant.
There, as those Dānavas were wandering about like birds, he, accompanied by his father and brother, struck them down with sharp arrows.
And the hands, feet, bodies, and heads of those Daityas fell down; their severed limbs flowed away as rivers of blood.
Then, when the gods had offered words of praise accompanied by a rain of flowers, Muktāphaladhvaja discharged the *mohana* (stupefying) weapon at those enemies.
He rendered those asuras, together with the king, who were bewildered and fallen to the ground, bound by nooses through the Vāruṇa weapon.
Then that sage, whose wealth was asceticism, said to King Merudhvaja: "This army of Asuras, which remains after being slain, must certainly not be killed."
For by accepting this very [weapon], you shall enter the netherworld; meanwhile, this lord of the Daityas, together with his sons and his ministers, shall be bound and led away.
Accompanied by great asuras, wicked nāgas, and chief rākṣasas, he should be stationed within a cave of the White Mountain near the assembly hall of the gods.
Thus addressed by the sage, Merudhvaja said to the Daitya warriors: "Do not fear; you are not to be slain by us, for he is with his brother."
"Follow now the command of this Muktāphaladhvaja!"—having been addressed thus by the king, the Dānavas joyfully accepted his word.
Then that king brought the Daitya king Trailokyamālin, together with his sons and the others, to Mount Śveta.
And he placed him, bound and guarded by the chief ministers endowed with the strength of many heroes, within that cave.
Then, when the battle had ceased, while the celestial beings released showers of Mandāra flowers and departed, a festival for the world commenced.
There, the victorious King Merudhvaja said to his two sons: "I am staying right here for the time being in order to protect the sacrifice."
"Go both of you to Pātāla with these soldiers of yours, accompanied by the multitude of Daitya celestial chariots and the remaining forces of the Asuras."
Having comforted the inhabitants of Pātāla and established them under your control, and having appointed leaders over them, you shall return here after taking possession of them.
Having heard this, the hero Muktāphaladhvaja, whose vehicle was a divine wish-fulfilling cow, and Malayadhvaja likewise quickly replied, "So be it."
Both brothers, together with their armies, entered Rasātala, accompanied by the Dānava host which marched before them in submission.
Having slain the guards and the adversaries stationed at various places, they there sounded the drum of fearlessness for the rest of the people.
And toward people who trusted and bowed down to them, these two took possession of seven netherworlds, filled with hundreds of cities made of various jewels.
And they enjoyed those delightful [gardens], which were filled with groves that granted every desire, and possessed stepped bathing-pools containing divine liquors.
There, the wives of the Dānavas and their daughters beheld those two of wondrous form within the trees, their bodies concealed by illusion.
And then, for the sake of her husband’s welfare while he was imprisoned, his wife named Svayaṃprabhā undertook austerities there.
And her two daughters, Trailokyaprabhā and Tribhuvanaprabhā, likewise began austerities for the welfare of their father.
And those two princes, having honored all the people there in Pātāla—who had attained peace and were established in well-being—with various pleasant gifts, [remained there].
Having appointed Saṅgrāmasiṃha and the other officials, they went to the vicinity of their father’s hermitage in the penance grove.
At that moment, the sacrifice of the sage reached its conclusion; the gods and the ṛṣis then began to depart for their respective abodes.
Then Merudhvaja addressed Śakra, who was well-pleased: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, please come to my city."
Having heard that, Vāsava took leave of the sage and went to the city of Devasabhā together with his beloved wife and that king along with his son.
And there, that king, the lord of two worlds, attended upon Śakra in such a way that he forgot his celestial happiness.
Then Śakra, being pleased, led that lord of the earth together with his son, mounted upon a divine celestial vehicle, to his own heaven, Triviṣṭapa.
There, having caused Merudhvaja—who was accompanied by Samaladhvaja—to rest in that place made beautiful by the pleasure of the music of Nārada, Rambhā, and others;
Having given Muktāphaladhvaja a pārijāta garland and a divine crown, Indra honored him and sent him home.
Having come here to the world of mortals and to Pātāla, those god-like kings, making their comings and goings between the two worlds, ruled as sovereigns.
Then Merudhvaja said to Muktāphaladhvaja: "O son, you two brothers have conquered your enemies; you are both young men."
Princesses are at my disposal, and I have sought them out; the time has come, so let the taking of a wife be performed.
When his father had spoken thus, Muktāphaladhvaja then replied: "Father, my mind is not yet inclined toward marriage."
"I shall now practice austerities to propitiate Hara; let this son of mine, Malayadhvaja, however, undergo marriage."
Having heard this, his younger brother Malayadhvaja said to him: "O noble brother, how can marriage be appropriate for me while you remain without a wife?"
"Or rather, if you do not remain in the kingdom, I shall indeed follow your path. When this was said by Malayadhvaja, the king replied:
Merudhvaja said to his eldest son Muktāphaladhvaja: "What has been spoken by this younger brother of yours is indeed appropriate."
But you speak what is improper; for while you are still in this very youth, what indeed is the time for asceticism? This is truly your time for enjoyment.
"O son, this evil obsession is not appropriate for the present time; let it be abandoned,"—even though he was addressed thus by the king, the eldest son remained there.
When he did not accept the marriage now with certainty, the king remained silent, waiting for the right time.
In the meantime, in the netherworld (pātāla), those two daughters of his, who were engaged in ascetic penance, spoke to Svayaṃprabhā, the wife of Trailokyamālin.
"O Mother, while we were only seven or eight years old, our father became self-restrained; why, then, has this loss of our kingdom occurred for us who have performed no meritorious deeds?"
This is now the eighth year that we two have been performing austerities, yet Hara is not pleased with us, nor has our father been released from his bonds even to this day.
Therefore, as long as there shall be no humiliation from our enemy, let us both offer this body, devoid of distinguishing marks, into the fire.
Having been addressed thus by her two daughters, Svayaṃprabhā spoke in this way: "Daughters, wait for now; for there shall be a reunion for us again."
For while I was established in asceticism, I remember that in a dream the god Śiva said to me: "Daughter, maintain your fortitude; your husband shall regain his kingdom."
Muktāphaladhvaja and likewise Malayadhvaja—these two princes shall become the husbands of your two daughters.
"Do not think that these two are mere humans; for one of them is a preeminent Vidyādhara, and the second is a member of my own retinue."
"Thus was I commanded by Īśvara at the end of the night; with this intention, I have endured this great hardship."
Therefore, I inform you of this matter concerning your lordly father; by his will, I shall strive for the accomplishment of your marriage.
Having thus comforted her two daughters, Queen Svayaṃprabhā spoke to an elderly woman of the inner apartments named Indumatī.
Go to the presence of the noble son at the White Rock Cave; falling at his feet, represent my words to him.
O Great King, I was created by the Creator from a different kind of wood; for even now I am not consumed by the blazing fire of separation from you.
"But my own self has not been abandoned by me, for I still hope to see you again. Having said this, you should report to me my dream-instruction from Śiva.
"Therefore, you must ask him regarding the marriage of my daughter; whatever he says, you must come and tell me, and I shall act accordingly."
Having spoken thus to Indumatī, she sent her away; and she, having departed from Pātāla, reached the well-guarded entrance of that mountain cave.
Having entreated the guards, she entered there and, seeing Trailokyamālin bound, she grasped his feet with tears in her eyes.
Being skilled in reading his mind, she gradually related to him her entire message from her wife; then the king spoke.
"Let that attainment of sovereignty which was foretold for us by Śarva come to pass exactly so; but what need is there to speak of the giving away of the daughters of Merudhvaja’s two sons?"
"I would rather perish right here than give my own son as a gift to these two human enemies while I am held in captivity."
Having spoken thus, Indumatī was then sent away by the king; she returned and related those words to her husband's wife, Svayaṃprabhā.
Then, having heard this, those two daughters of the lord of the Daityas, Trailokyaprabhā and Tribhuvanaprabhā, spoke to their mother, Svayaṃprabhā.
"Since fire alone is now our refuge due to the fear of our youth, O Mother, we shall enter it on this fourteenth day."
When those two had thus made their resolve, her mother as well, along with her retinue, then made a resolution for death alone.
And when the fourteenth day arrived, they all gathered at the sacred ford named Pāparipu and, having worshipped Hāṭakeśvara, performed their funeral rites.
On that very lunar day, King Merudhvaja arrived there with his son and his wife to worship Dhāṭakeśvara.
While traveling with his followers to that holy ford of Pāparipu for the purpose of bathing, he saw from afar smoke rising up from within the forest on its bank.
To that king, who was asking, "From where does this smoke arise here?", his own officials in charge of Pātāla, headed by Saṅgrāmasiṃha, replied.
O Great King, Trailokyamālin’s wife, Svayaṃprabhā, remained here engaged in ascetic penance together with her two daughters, who were still maidens.
Surely they are performing some ritual duty here today, such as the fire-sacrifice; or perhaps, exhausted by extreme asceticism, they are entering the fire.
Having heard that, the king went there with his two sons, his wife, and those officials to see him, having forbidden all other attendants from following.
And standing there in concealment, he beheld those two Daitya maidens together with their mother, worshipping a well-kindled funeral pyre.
With the outpourings of the abundant splendor of their faces, they seemed to fashion hundreds of lunar discs throughout all directions and even within the netherworld.
With their two golden jars of breasts, they performed, as it were, the consecration of Kāma for the conquest of the three worlds, using the flowing streams of water from their dangling necklaces.
She bore a broad expanse of hips bound with a girdle, like the forehead of the elephant of Smara marked by a garland of stars.
And their two masses of hair flowed like two serpents fashioned by the Creator to guard the treasury of all their beauty.
Having seen them, the king was filled with wonder and thought to himself: "Aha! The creation of the Creator is radiant, ever-new, and marvelous."
Therefore, neither Rambhā, nor Urvaśī, nor Tilottamā attains equality in beauty with these two daughters of the lord of the asuras.
While the king was thinking thus, that eldest daughter of the Daityas, Trailokyaprabhā, having worshipped the fire, made this request:
Ever since my mother told me the dream and its interpretation, from that moment on, I have indeed maintained the conviction that he is my husband.
"O Blessed One, may that very prince Muktāphaladhvaja, that treasury of virtues, become my husband once again in another birth."
In this life, although my father, while remaining in self-restraint, desired to give me to him, and although my mother wished to give me to him, I was not accepted by him.
Having heard that, Tribhuvanaprabhā likewise chose Malayadhvaja, the son of Hutāśa, as her husband in another birth.
Then King Merudhvaja, thrilled upon hearing that, and his queen, the Mahādevī, spoke to one another.
If these two sons of ours were to obtain these two wives, then the fruit resulting from the conquest of both worlds would be attained by them.
Therefore, before they throw themselves into this fire, why do we not approach and stop them, along with their mother?
Having deliberated thus with the queen, the king approached them and said: "Do not commit this rash act; for I shall surely pacify your suffering."
Having heard these words of the king, which were like a rain of nectar to the ears, and having beheld him, all those celestial women bowed down to him.
Although we were looking [at you] before, we were not noticed because we were concealed by illusion; today, however, we have been seen here by you, the Lord of the two worlds.

For those who have been seen by you, the end of our suffering will surely come before long; how much more so when a boon has been granted by Your Majesty himself in response to our entreaty with his own voice?
Therefore, having accepted seats, please accept the water for the hands and feet and other offerings; for you are honored by the entire world, and this is our hermitage.
When Svayaṃprabhā had spoken thus, the king said with a smile, "Let water for the feet and the guest-offering be given by you to these two sons-in-law."
Then, by his own power, the bull-bannered god said to them, "Let the guest-offering and other honors be presented by you today; let it be accepted."
Then Merudhvaja said, "I have now taken all this; you, however, must now desist from your efforts toward death."
"Enter and remain together in one of your own cities, O you who fulfill all desires; then I myself shall know how to ensure your welfare."
To the king who had spoken thus, Svayaṃprabhā said: "By the command of our lord, we have desisted from our resolve to cast off our bodies."
"But while our lord is confined in prison, how can it be right for us to remain in our own homes? Therefore, O King, we shall stay right here for the time being."
"As long as Your Majesty yourself shall uphold the boon granted to us, you shall liberate our lord, along with his sons and ministers."
Once liberated, he will become your subordinate and rule the kingdom; and by your will, he shall hand over the kingdom to you alone.
And he will establish such a binding agreement; meanwhile, we shall remain here together with the inhabitants of Pātāla.
"And take for yourself the jewels from our netherworlds. To her who had spoken thus, King Merudhvaja replied:
"I myself shall understand this; you must simply remember your own words. Having said this, the king bathed and worshipped Hāṭakeśvara.
And those two daughters of the Daitya king, their own perceptions being thus directed toward those two sons, became single-mindedly focused upon them.
Then King Merudhvaja, the virtuous one, having been prostrated to and entreated for liberation from Trailokyamālin by all the inhabitants of the subterranean realm (rasātala), [consented].
Shrouding the quarters with his own white umbrellas of glory, accompanied by his wife, sons, and servants, he emerged from that realm of the asuras and returned to his own city.
There, his son Malayadhvaja, brooding over that younger daughter of the Dānava king, spent the night afflicted by the fever of love, with eyes closed even though he was not asleep.

Even though he had heard of her from his father, the lord of the ocean, and although that youth Muktāphaladhvaja felt a firm and fixed passion for the daughter of the lord of the asuras—she who could provoke amorous agitation even in the minds of the great sages—he was not at all disturbed in heart by the elder sage, despite the latter having previously granted him a boon.

But Merudhvaja, having learned that his son had desisted from marriage, that Malayadhvaja was under the sway of passion, and that the great Asura was averse to giving his daughter in marriage, became anxious in his mind as he sought to devise a stratagem.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Padmāvatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Sixth Wave: Then King Merudhvaja, seeing Malayadhvaja thus overcome by the fever of love, spoke to his queen as follows:
If, O Pātāladṛṣṭa, your daughter were not to become the wife of my two sons, what would have been gained by me? What purpose would have been served?
Except for the youngest of those two, my son Malayadhvaja—his fire of desire concealed by shame—is being cooked by a process of intense heating.
And for that purpose, although I have already promised liberation to the wife of Trailokyamālin, it has not yet been swiftly performed by me even to this day.
"Released from bondage, he will never give his two daughters to my two human sons, due to his pride in their asura nature."
"Let us now speak of this matter to him with gentleness; this is the best course. Having reflected thus together with the queen, he gave orders to the doorkeeper.
Having gone to the cave of the White Mountain, speak with affection in my name to that lord of the Daityas, Trailokyamālin, who remains there bound.
O Lord of the Daityas, you have long been afflicted here by the turn of fate; therefore, now follow my words and bring an end to this suffering.
"Give your two daughters, who are enamored with my two sons, to them; then, having established confidence, you shall be released from here and regain your own kingdom."
Having spoken thus, the chamberlain was sent by the king; having gone there into the interior of the cave, he delivered that message of the king to the lord of the Daityas.
"I will not give my two daughters to mere mortals," he replied; having been answered thus, the chamberlain returned and reported it to the king exactly as it was.

Muktāphaladhvaja set out for that divine abode of Gaurī’s Lord; having reached it, he rejoiced as he beheld it exactly as it had been seen in his dream.

"He has surely gone somewhere today on the fourteenth day to worship Hara; therefore, let us wait for him right here for this day."

"Look at what kind of man this is—how similar he is to my beloved! It is a marvel; could it be that very same person? No, for this is surely not a human being."

Look, even this companion of yours appears to possess a resemblance to that Saṃyataka, who was indeed the dear friend of your beloved.

And that Muktāphalaketu, having previously attained the sovereignty of the Asuras from Indra, and having subsequently regained from his father that status as the emperor of the Vidyādharas, [proceeded].
Accompanied by Padmāvatī, as if with Nirvṛti incarnate, that man of merit enjoyed for ten kalpas the glorious happiness of a fully prosperous universal sovereignty over both realms.

Having perceived that all phenomena are tasteless in their ultimate end, and having finally taken refuge in the forest of the Lord of Sages, he attained the supreme light through the excellence of his asceticism and reached union with the Lord Dhūrjaṭi.

Having thus heard this story of the lakes from the pair of swans and having obtained wisdom from their mouths, King Brahmadatta—having attained his divine state—as well as his wife, his minister, and those two birds, all went to Siddhīśvara; there, casting off their bodies born of a curse, they all regained their own original status as attendants of Śiva.
O sages, having heard this story from Gomukha regarding my separation from Madanamañcukā, I diverted my mind with fortitude for a mere moment.
When Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch, had thus finished his tale, those sages at Kaśyapa’s hermitage, together with Gopālaka, were thoroughly delighted.
