Having become a hero born of the lunar dynasty, why indeed do you lose your senses? What lack of faith can there be toward the fixed command of the gods; what, then, is this attachment of yours to a wife?
Even meetings with those who seem impossible for men to encounter do occur in this world; for instance, I shall relate to you the story of Vikramāditya—listen.
In the land of Avanti, there exists a famous city named Ujjayinī, built by Viśvakarman at the beginning of the Yuga, which is the dwelling place of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva).
Like a virtuous wife, she was invincible; like a lotus pond, she was graced by beauty; like the wisdom of the wise, she was rich in righteousness; and like the earth, she was full of wonders.
In that city, there was a world-conquering king named Mahendrāditya, who, like Maghavan in Amarāvatī, was the slayer of the forces of his enemies.

In valor he was like the wielder of various weapons and missiles; in beauty, he was like the god of love; in generosity, his hand was ever open; yet in [holding onto] this [wealth], his fist was firmly clenched.
That lord of the earth had a wife named Saumyadarśanā, who was like Śacī to Indra, like Gaurī to Śambhu, and like Śrī to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The lord had a chief minister named Sumati, and a doorkeeper named Vajrāyudha who had served in that position for generations.
Together with them, that king, while ruling his kingdom and propitiating Hara, constantly observed various vows out of a desire for a son.
In the meantime, in that mountain cave inhabited by hosts of gods, which was beautiful with the laughter of Kubera, who rejoiced at his conquest of other quarters;
The gods, including Indra, distressed by the harassment of the Mlecchas, approached Purāri, who was accompanied by Pārvatī and residing on Kailāsa, the lord of mountains.
Having prostrated and sat down immediately thereafter, those immortals, having offered praises and been questioned regarding the purpose of their arrival, addressed the god in this manner.
O Lord, those asuras who were slain by you and those who were slain by Viṣṇu have now been born again today on the surface of the earth in the form of mlecchas.
They cause obstacles to arise, they destroy rites such as sacrifices, and they abduct the daughters of sages; what evil do these sinners not commit?
O Lord, the world of the gods is perpetually nourished by the earth-world, for the oblation offered by Brahmins into the fire serves for the satisfaction of the inhabitants of heaven.

And when the world of mortals is overrun by barbarians and devoid of the auspicious sound of *vaṣaṭ*, the world of the gods languishes due to the cessation of sacrificial portions and other offerings.
Therefore, devise a means for this matter and bring down some great hero to the surface of the earth who shall exterminate those barbarians.
Thus addressed by the gods, the Enemy of Tripura said to them: "Go; you need have no anxiety here; be at ease."
"I shall undoubtedly devise a means for this here before long," having said this, the Lord of Ambikā dismissed the gods to their own abodes.
When they had departed, the Blessed One summoned the group known as Mālyavat and, together with Parvatī, gave this command:
"O son, descend into human form and be born in the great city of Ujjayinī as the heroic son of King Mahendrāditya."
That king is indeed a portion of myself, and his wife is born from a portion of Ambikā; being born in their house, accomplish the purpose of the gods.
"Slay all the Mlecchas without exception, who are destroyers of the dharma of the three Vedas; and by my grace, you shall become a king, the lord of the seven islands."
Even yakṣas, rākṣasas, and vetālas shall remain under your control; and having enjoyed human pleasures, you shall return to us once again.
Thus commanded by the Conqueror of Cities, the Gaṇa Mālyavat replied: "Your command is not to be transgressed by me; however, what enjoyments are there in the human realm?"
Where there are the most unbearable separations from kinsmen, friends, and servants, and where there is the agony arising from the loss of wealth, old age, disease, and so forth.
Thus addressed by that host, Dhūrjaṭi replied to him: "Go, O sinless one; these sorrows shall no longer be yours."
"By my grace, you shall be happy at all times. Having been addressed thus by Śambhu, Mālyavat then became invisible.
Having gone to Ujjayinī, that best of Gaṇas was conceived in the womb of the queen of King Mahendrāditya during her fertile season.
And at that time, the Lord, whose crest was adorned with a digit of the Moon, commanded King Mahendrāditya in a dream:
"I am pleased with you, O King; therefore, a son shall be born to you, who will traverse the earth with its seven continents by his own prowess."
The hero will bring under his control even the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others, whether they dwell in the netherworld or roam the sky; he will slay the hosts of mlecchas.
For this very reason, he shall be known by the name Vikramāditya; and likewise, because of his hostility toward his enemies, he shall indeed be named Viṣamaśīla.
When the god had vanished after saying this, the lord of the earth woke up and, delighted, reported that dream to his ministers in the morning.
Then those ministers, filled with joy, reported to the king in due order that dream-vision of Hara which had resulted in the attainment of a son.
Then, having arrived, the maidservants of the inner apartments showed the fruit directly to the king, saying, "Śambhu gave this to the Queen in a dream."
Then that king rejoiced, being congratulated by his ministers, saying again and again, "Truly, a son has been granted to me by Śarva."
Then that queen became pregnant with one of intense splendor, like the eastern quarter at dawn bearing the orb of the rising thousand-rayed sun.
And she shone with the dark luster of her nipples upon her breasts, like the seal of breast-milk protection for a sovereign residing in the womb.
Then, in a dream, she crossed all seven oceans while being saluted by all the yakṣas, vetālas, and rākṣasas.
And when the time had arrived, she gave birth to a radiant son, by whom the lying-in chamber was illuminated as the sky is by the young sun.
And when he was born, the sky shone, laughing with showers of falling flowers and resounding with the noise of the celestial drums of the gods.
At that time, the city became as agitated by the joy of the festival as if it were intoxicated, possessed by spirits, or overwhelmed by a disturbance of the winds.
And at that time, while wealth was raining incessantly upon the king, there was no one who was not a follower of the Sugata, nor anyone who was not a sovereign.
His father named him Vikramāditya according to the word of Śiva, and King Mahendrāditya likewise named him Viṣamaśīla.
As other days passed there, a son was born to that king’s minister, Sumati, named Mahāmati.
To Kṣattṛ Vajrāyudha was born a son, Bhadrāyudha; and to Mahīdhara, the royal priest, a son Śrīdhara was born.
Together with those three ministers, that prince Vikramāditya grew here like the sun increases by means of its splendor, heroism, and power.
For him who had been initiated, the teachers served merely as the cause for his learning; rather, those sciences manifested themselves to him spontaneously and without effort.
Whatever science or art he employed, each and every one was perceived by those who knew them to be unsurpassed by him.
And seeing that prince fighting with divine weapons, the people became indifferent even toward stories of Rāma and other great archers.
His father brought back those beautiful maidens given by kings who had submitted after being attacked, as if they were other forms of the goddess Śrī herself.
Then, seeing that his son had reached youth and possessed abundant prowess, he consecrated him—who was beloved by the people—in the kingdom according to the prescribed rites.
King Mahendrāditya, though accompanied by his wife and ministers, went to Vārāṇasī in his old age and sought refuge in Śiva.
Having obtained his father’s kingdom, Vikramāditya also gradually began to blaze with royal splendor, like the sun in the sky.
As soon as he saw the string fixed upon his bending bow, even the kings, though their heads were already held high, bowed down in every direction as if out of respect for his training.
Possessing divine power, he brought even vetālas, rākṣasas, and other such beings under his control, and then properly instructed those who were treading upon the wrong path.
Adorning the quarters of the sky upon the surface of the earth, the armies of that Vikramāditya went forth like the rays of the sun.
Though he was a great hero, he was timid regarding the next world; though brave, he was not fierce-handed; and though a lord of the earth, he was beloved by women.
He was the father of those who were fatherless, the kinsman of those without kin, and the protector of the helpless; among his subjects, who was there that he did not become?
Surely the Creator took the White Island, the Ocean of Milk, Mount Kailāsa, and the Snowy Mountain as the models for his creation of his fame.
And once, when King Vikramāditya had entered the assembly hall, the doorkeeper Bhadrāyudha approached and addressed him.
When he was dispatched with his army for the conquest of the southern region, it was Vikramaśakti whom the King sent as his companion.
"O Lord, this messenger Anaṅgadeva has arrived and stands at the gate; he is accompanied by a companion, his face is joyful, and he speaks auspiciously."
When the king said, "Let him enter," the doorkeeper respectfully ushered Anaṅgadeva into his presence along with his companion.
Having entered and uttered a cry of "Victory! with a respectful salutation, the messenger sat down before him; then he was questioned by the king.
Is that king Vikramaśakti, the commander-in-chief, well? And are the other kings, such as Vyāghrabala and the rest, also in good health?
Regarding the other princes and the leaders in that army, I hope all is well with the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Thus questioned by the king, Anaṅgadeva spoke for the welfare of Vikramaśakti, his entire army, and all present.
The western region was conquered by Your Majesty, as were the southern lands, the Middle Country together with Saurāṣṭra, and the eastern direction including Vaṅga and Aṅga.
The northern region including Kaśmīra was made to pay tribute, as were those various difficult fortresses and islands that had been conquered.
The hosts of Mlecchas were slain, and the survivors were brought under subjection; those various kings entered the camp of Vikramaśakti.
And that Vikramaśakti, having joined with those kings, O Lord, is indeed staying here for only two or three more marches.
King Vikramāditya, being pleased with him who had spoken thus, rewarded the messenger with garments, ornaments, and villages.
Then the king questioned that excellent messenger again: "Anaṅgadeva, which countries were seen by you while traveling here?"
"O good man, tell me where and what curious thing was seen by you," the king said, and Anaṅgadeva proceeded to speak.
"O King, by your command, I went from here and reached, in due course, the vicinity of Vikramaśakti and that assembly of your army."
It was adorned by the glorious Hari, who was attended by infinite lords of serpents gathered together; it was as vast as the ocean, inhabited by winged mountains.
And having arrived there, I was received with great honor by that Vikramaśakti, who bowed down to me and said, "I have been sent by my lord."
While I remained there, observing the very form of Vijaya, an envoy belonging to the Lord of Siṃhala arrived.
"Anaṅgadeva, who has become the very heart of the king, stands near him"—this was told to me by messengers who have returned from your presence.
Therefore, send this Anaṅgadeva to my presence with haste; I shall tell him something auspicious regarding a certain matter of state business.
Thus that messenger, having come from Siṃhala, spoke these words of his sovereign in my presence to that Vikramaśakti.
Then Vikramaśakti said to me, "Go quickly; go to the presence of the Lord of Siṃhala and see what he says regarding you."
Then, together with that envoy of the Lord of Siṃhala, I went to the island of Siṃhala by ship along the path of the ocean.
And there I beheld a royal capital fashioned of gold, with palaces of variegated jewels, like the city of the gods.
And there I beheld that Vīrasena, the lord of Siṃhala, surrounded by his disciplined ministers like Śatakratu by the gods.
Having received me with respect and inquired after the welfare of my lord, the king allowed me to rest there with great hospitality.
On another day, that king, having entered the assembly hall, summoned me and, displaying his devotion toward you, spoke in the presence of his ministers:
"I have a daughter, a maiden who is the singular beauty of the mortal world; her name is Madanalekhā, and I give her to you, O King."
She is a wife suited to him, and he is a husband worthy of her; for this purpose you have been summoned by one who desires to recover his master.
And go with my messenger to speak to the master: "I shall send my daughter here immediately after you."
Having spoken thus, the king had his daughter brought there, who was adorned with an abundance of ornaments and possessed of beauty, grace, and youth.
Having seated her on his lap and shown her to me, he said, "This maiden has been given by me to your master; let her be accepted."
And having seen that princess, I was struck with wonder at her beauty; joyful, I said, "I desire her for the sake of the king."
And I thought: "Aha! Fate is never sated in its wondrous works; for even after creating Tilottamā, it has produced this most excellent woman."
Then, having been honored by that king, I set out from that island together with this messenger of Dhavalasena.
Having boarded the vessel, as we were traveling upon the ocean, we suddenly beheld a great sandbank in its midst.
In their midst, we saw two maidens of wondrous form: one with limbs as dark as the priyaṅgu flower, and the other with the stainless luster of the moon.
Adorned with garments and ornaments appropriate to their respective castes, they offered salutations with hands joined together, the sound of which was enhanced by the tinkling of jeweled bracelets.
They were dancing before a young play-deer, which was made of gold, adorned with jewels, and appeared to be alive.
Seeing that, we both, filled with wonder, said to one another: "Aha! What is this marvel? Is it a dream, an illusion, or perhaps a delusion?"
Where is there a sandbank in the middle of the ocean, and where are two such maidens there? And where is a living golden deer with limbs variegated with such jewels for them?
O King, while we two were speaking these words with wonder, a wind suddenly began to blow, tossing up the ocean.
Reflecting on that, our ship was shattered by the surging waves; and the people on board, being devoured by sea-monsters, sank beneath the waters.
And those two maidens, having approached us and taken hold of our arms, lifted us up and carried us to the sandbank before we had even reached the mouths of the sea-monsters.
As that bank was being filled by the waves, we two became overwhelmed; then, having comforted us, we were made to enter [the cave] by them, as if into the interior of a mountain cavern.
Then we beheld a divine forest of various trees; there was neither ocean, nor shore, nor fawn, nor maidens.
"Is this a marvel? Surely it is some kind of illusion," we said as we wandered there for a moment, until we beheld a great lake.
Like the disposition of the great, it was naturally pure, profound, and vast; like Nirvana personified, it quelled the torment of craving.
And there we saw a certain excellent woman, surrounded by her attendants, who had come to bathe and who appeared like the very goddess of the forest in person.
Having descended from her palanquin and gathered appropriate lotuses, she bathed in the lake and performed meditation upon the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva).
Just then, rising from the lake with us in amazement, Śiva in the form of a linga appeared visibly before her.
Having worshipped that lute made of divine jewels with various enjoyments suited to her own wealth, the beautiful woman took it up.
Following the southern path with its proper notes, rhythms, and words, she played that [instrument] while singing it correctly with great concentration.
Just as their hearts were drawn by hearing that [sound], the Siddhas and others who had come from the sky remained there motionless, as if they were painted.
Then, having concluded the musical performance for Śambhu, she performed his dismissal; and right there, the god submerged himself in the lake.
Then, having risen and boarded the vehicle with her attendants, that fawn-eyed woman began to proceed slowly from there.
Although we both repeatedly and with great effort asked, "Who is this woman?", none of her attendants gave an answer as we followed after her.
Then, wishing to demonstrate your power to this envoy of the Lord of Siṃhaladvīpa, I spoke to her aloud as follows:
"O auspicious one, you are bound by an oath upon the touch of King Vikramāditya's feet: if you depart without revealing your identity to me, you shall be a mere illusion."
Having heard that, she dismissed her retinue, descended from the vehicle, approached me, and spoke with sweet words:
"I hope that the lord Śrī Vikramādityadeva is well; or rather, what need is there to ask, O Anaṅgadeva, for everything is known to me?"
Indeed, it was by me alone that you were brought here after displaying this illusion; for the sake of that king, he is one who must be honored by me as my savior from great danger.
Therefore, come to my house; there I shall tell you everything—who I am, how the king is to be honored by me, and what his purpose is.

Having spoken thus, she who had gracefully released her vehicle proceeded on foot along the path; bowing low, that fair-faced woman led them to her own city, which was like unto heaven, adorned everywhere with various jewels and fashioned from gold, its gates guarded by heroic men bearing diverse weapons and assuming various forms.

There, in a secluded place, she honored us with baths, ointments, fine garments, and ornaments—by means of brides who were like personified successions of all divine enjoyments and perfections—and now she causes us to rest.

Thus ends the first wave in the Viṣamaśīla book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave. Having spoken thus to King Vikramāditya as he sat in the assembly hall, Anaṅgadeva began to relate this story once more.
Then, after we had finished eating, she, standing in the midst of her friends, said to me: "Anaṅgadeva, listen now; I shall tell you everything."
I am Madanamañjarī, the daughter of Dundubhi, the king of the yakṣas, and the wife of Maṇibhadra, the brother of the Giver of Wealth.
Thus, upon the banks of rivers, on mountains, and in delightful groves, I always lived happily with my husband.
And once, it is said, I went to Ujjayinī with my beloved to enjoy myself in a garden named Makaranda.
There, by chance at dawn, a certain wretched Kāpālika mendicant saw me, who had awakened after sleeping in the monastery cell.
That wicked man, fallen under the power of desire, went to the cremation ground and began to employ me as his wife through the performance of a fire sacrifice and the use of mantras.
Having understood that through my own supernatural power, I informed my husband; he, in turn, reported it to his elder brother, Dhanada.
Having gone there, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) informed the Lotus-born One (Brahmā); and that Blessed One, having meditated thus upon Brahmā, spoke to him.
It is true that Kapālin was intent on abducting your brother’s wife; for such is the power of those mantras used for the propitiation of Yakṣas.
But she, being drawn away by that spell, must cry out to King Vikramāditya; he will then protect her from that danger.
Having approached my husband, the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) spoke these words of Brahmā; and my husband told them to me, whose soul was terrified by an evil spell.
And at that moment, while performing a fire sacrifice in the cremation ground, that Khaṇḍakāpālika himself spontaneously drew me forth by means of a mantra perfected through successive stages.
And I, drawn by the mantra, fled in terror from there and reached a fearsome cemetery, abounding in bones and skulls, frequented by spirits.
There, I then beheld that wicked Kāpālika, who had offered oblations into the fire and was presiding over a mandala established upon a consecrated, upturned corpse.
And that Kāpālika, seeing me arrive, was deluded by pride; by some means he went to the river nearby to perform his ritual rinsing, as fate would have it.
At that moment, having forgotten the words of Brahmā, I thought: "Why do I not cry out to the king? He might perhaps wander here during the night."
Having reflected thus, I cried out loudly there: "Save me, O Lord, King Vikramāditya!"
O jewel that guards the waking world, behold this virtuous woman, a lady of noble family and the wife of Maṇibhadra, the younger brother of the Lord of Wealth.
"This Kāpālika is intent on destroying me, the Yakṣiṇī Madanamañjarī by name, the daughter of Dundubhi, within your kingdom."
Even as she was thus crying out, I beheld that king approaching with sword in hand, as if blazing with splendor.
And he said to me, "O blessed lady, do not fear; be at ease. O auspicious one, I shall protect you from this Kāpālika."
"Who indeed is capable of committing such unrighteousness in my kingdom? Having said this, he summoned a vetāla named Agniśikha.
And he, being summoned, approached the king while still blazing, with his hair standing erect like dust, and said to him: "What shall I do? Command me."
Then the king said, "This wicked Kāpālika, who has committed the theft of another's wife, must be killed by you and eaten."
Then Agniśikha, entering that corpse which was situated within the circle of worship, sprang up and rushed forward with his arms and mouth wide open.
And that Vetāla seized from behind the Kāpālika—who had rinsed his mouth and spat out the water—as he was intent on flight.
Having whirled him about in the air and swiftly dashed him against the ground, he crushed both his body and his desire together into powder.
Seeing the Kāpālin slain while the creatures were greedily craving his flesh, a fierce Vetāla named Yamaśikha arrived there.
Having approached, he seized that corpse of a Kāpālika; then the Vetāla Agniśikha, who had been there before, spoke to him.
"By the command of the illustrious King Vikramāditya, I have slain this wicked Kāpālika; who are you to him?"
Having heard this, Yamaśikha said, "In that case, tell me: what is the power of that king? Thereupon Agniśikha replied:
If you do not know his power, then listen as I tell it to you: in this city there was once a very resolute gambler named Dākineya.
Once, having had all his possessions stolen by gamblers through the artifice of dice, he was bound by them for the sake of recovering an excessive amount of wealth that had been lost.
Because he was not his own master and because he would not give, he remained there being beaten with those very clubs and other instruments, like a stone or as if dead.
Then, having led him away, all those sinful members of the assembly cast him into a great blind well, anticipating that he would find a remedy while still alive.
And there, that gambler, the son of a *ḍākinī*, having fallen into a very deep well, beheld two great men within the fire.
Seeing him fallen there and terrified, the two of them questioned him with gentle words: "Who are you, and from where have you fallen into this well? Let it be told."
Then, having related his own story to the horse, the gambler asked them both: "Tell me, who are you two, and from where have you come here?"
Having heard that, those two men standing in the pit said: "O good sir, we two are Brahmarākṣasas in her city, in the cremation ground."
And we two married right here in this city these two maidens: one the daughter of the chief minister, and the other the daughter of the chief merchant.
And no one was able to liberate the two maidens from our presence, not even a master of mantras possessing blazing spells on this earth.
Then King Vikramāditya, who was devoted to his father, learned of this and went to the place where those two maidens were staying together with their father's friend.
As soon as we saw that king, although we both desired to flee after leaving the two maidens, we were unable to go from there.
We saw all the directions blazing with his splendor; then, seeing us, that king bound us by means of his own power.
Seeing them thus distressed by the fear of birth and death, he commanded: "O you two sinners, dwell within this blind well for the duration of one year."
Therefore, you two who have been released must not act like this again; if you do so, I shall then punish you both.
Having thus commanded, we two were cast into this blind well by that King Viṣamaśīla; yet, out of compassion, we were not destroyed.
With eight days remaining until the end of our dwelling in this well, the term of our stay will be fulfilled; after one year from now, we shall both be released from there.
"If you give us these few days' worth of food, friend, we shall pull you out from that well and cast you outside."
"If you do not grant us food once we have agreed, then we shall certainly depart from here and devour you."
Having said this, those two brahmarākṣasas then agreed to the gambler's request, saying "So be it," and threw him out from the well.
Having emerged from the well and seeing that his goal could not be attained otherwise, he entered the cremation ground at night to sell his own flesh.
At that time, while staying there, I saw that gambler saying, "Let someone take it; I am selling human flesh."
When I asked, "I shall take it; what price do you seek?", he replied, "Give me your own beauty and splendor."
When I asked him again, "O hero, what do you intend to do with those two? that gambler related his entire life story and spoke as follows:
Therefore, having drawn those enemies along with the members of the assembly by means of your form and power, I shall give those gamblers as food to two Brahma-rākṣasas.
Having heard that, being pleased by his fortitude, I bestowed upon that gambler my own beauty and power for a period of seven days, after speaking these words to him.
Having dragged those wrongdoers out by means of those two and thrown them into the well one after another, he subjected them to being devoured by the brahmarākṣasa within seven days.
Then, after I had accepted my own form and splendor, that gambler, the son of a Dakini, spoke to me while overwhelmed with fear.
"Today, no food was given by me for those two on that eighth day; therefore, having emerged, those two Brahma-rākṣasas will devour me."
"Therefore, tell me what must be done by me in this matter, for you are my friend. To him who had spoken thus, I replied out of affection born from our long acquaintance:
"If that is so, then those gamblers were indeed devoured by those two Rākṣasas for your sake; therefore, I shall devour those two Rākṣasas once again on your behalf."
"Then show me those two friends," I said; and at that moment, saying "So be it," the gambler led me into their presence.
And while I was looking down into that well without hesitation, he gave me a half-moon blow and threw me into its depths.
Then, having fallen into the middle of a well and been seized by two rākṣasas who regarded me as food, a hand-to-hand struggle ensued between them and me.
When they were unable to overcome my strength of arms, they abandoned the fight and asked me, "Who are you?"
Then, after I had related my own story starting from the account of the Ḍākineya, those two showed me friendship and said to me:
Oh, what a state has been brought upon you two, upon us, and upon those gamblers by that wicked-souled gambler!
What trust can there be in those gamblers who possess only the science of deception, whose minds are untouched by friendliness, compassion, or kindness?
Impetuosity and recklessness are innate to gamblers; likewise, let the story of Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla be heard by you.
In this very city of Ujjayinī, he had previously been a gambler named Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, a fierce man whose name was truly significant.
As he was constantly losing at dice, those other players who were victorious gave a hundred cowries to the gamblers every day.
Having purchased wheat flour from that shop at the close of day, he kneaded it with water somewhere in a bowl and made cakes.
Having gone to the cremation ground and cooked them over the funeral pyre, she returned before Mahākāla and ate them, having anointed them with the ghee from his lamp.
And there, in the courtyard of the temple of the god Mahākāla, he always slept at night upon the ground with his arm used as a pillow.
Once, at night, while he was looking at the images of the circle of Mothers, Yakṣas, and others in that temple of Mahākāla, [the following occurred].
As they quivered through the presence of the mantra, this thought arose in his mind: "Why do I not employ a stratagem here by means of a logical device for the sake of my purpose?"
"If he succeeds, it is well; or if he does not succeed, what loss is there for me? Having reflected thus, casting aside those deities, he spoke for the sake of gambling.
"Come, sir, I shall play with you here; I myself shall be the arbiter, the thrower of the dice, and the one who immediately accepts what is won."
When they remained silent after being addressed thus by him, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla made a wager of various cowries and struck them down.
"If the gambler does not object, his defeat is accepted"—such indeed is always the standing rule for gamblers in every case of gambling.
Then, having conquered them and acquired much gold, he said to those deities: "Give me the wealth that was won, just as it was promised."
When those deities did not say anything at all, even though they were addressed repeatedly by that gambler, he then spoke out in anger.
If you remain silent while standing there, then that which is done for the gambler—who stands like a stone, having lost his wealth through what was not given—will be done for you as well.
I shall perform for you the tearing apart of your limbs with a saw as sharp as the tips of Yama’s fangs; indeed, I have no concern whatsoever.
Having said this, just as he was taking up a saw and rushing toward him, those deities gave him gold according to what he had earned.

And having caused that wealth to be taken away, he returned at night and in the same manner the next morning, he again seized the property from the group of Mothers by means of a fraudulent game of dice.
As he continued doing this every day, the goddess Cāmuṇḍā once spoke to those mothers whose minds were distressed.
"O goddesses who have the Mothers as their deities, this is the custom regarding gambling: he who says, 'I have come out from here because I was summoned,' cannot be challenged in the game."
"Therefore, when he calls out, dismiss him by saying that very same thing. Thus addressed by Cāmuṇḍā, those goddesses took this to heart.
When that gambler arrived at night and was summoned to the game of dice, all the deities said, "We have departed from this gambling match."
Thus rebuffed by them, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla summoned that very lord Mahākāla to play at dice.
Thinking that he had found an opening for a forced game of dice, the king reportedly said, "I am leaving this gambling match."

Alas, even the gods fear the wicked man who has not exhausted his faults, who acts with partiality, and who is devoid of regard for both the desirable and the undesirable, as if they themselves were powerless.
Then, having been defeated by the deceptive stratagems of Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla through his practice of gambling, he reflected thus in his distress:
"Alas! Having been defeated by the gods after learning their method of gambling, I now take refuge in this very Lord of the Gods."
Having reflected thus in his heart and having clasped the feet [of Mahākāla], Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla praised him and made this request:
I bow to you as you sit naked, with your cheek resting upon your knee, while the dice-won moon, bull, elephant, and hide were being cast by the Goddess.
While those gods bestow various such powers merely by their will, he is free from desire, possessing only matted hair, ashes, and a skull as his belongings.
O you of meager merit, how is it that you have become so full of greed toward me today, that for such a trivial reason you seek to deceive me? Alas!
Even the wish-fulfilling tree certainly does not fulfill the hopes of the unfortunate; for though you support the entire universe, O Bhairava, you do not support me, O Lord.
O Blessed One, O Sthāṇu, you ought to forgive even my transgression, for I have taken refuge in you with a mind overwhelmed by painful calamities.
You have three eyes, and I am just like you; there is ash on your body, and that is on mine as well. Just as you eat from a skull-cup, so do I; have compassion for me.
Having conversed with you, how indeed could I converse again with gamblers? Therefore, rescue me who am thus fallen into distress.
With these and other words, the gambler thus praised that Bhairava; meanwhile, the god, being thoroughly pleased, spoke to him directly.
"Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, I am pleased with you; do not be distressed. I shall grant you enjoyments; stay right here in my presence."
Thus, by the command of the god, that gambler remained there at that time, enjoying an abundance of pleasures brought about through his grace.
And once, having seen the Apsarases who had come there at night to bathe at the Mahākāla-tīrtha, that god commanded him.
"When all these celestial women have begun to bathe, you must quickly take the garments they have laid upon the bank and bring them back."
"As long as they do not give this Apsaras maiden Kalāvatī to you, do not release their garments."
Thus addressed by Bhairava, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla went and stole the garments of those women with eyes like those of celestial deer as they were bathing.
"Release, release our garments; do not make us naked!"—to those speaking thus, he replied with the power of Hari.
"If you give this maiden Kalāvatī to me, then I shall release these garments for you; not otherwise."
Having heard that and having seen him who was so difficult to overcome, and remembering Śakra’s curse upon Kalāvatī, they all accepted this.
Then, according to the prescribed rite, they gave that daughter of Alambuṣā, Kalāvatī, to him, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, who had abandoned his former dwelling.
Then, after the apsarases had departed, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla remained with Kalāvatī, his dwelling place having been created by the will of the gods.
And Kalāvatī went by day to attend upon the Lord of the Gods in heaven, and she always returned to her husband at night.
And at times, out of affection, she would say to her beloved: "O Śakra, by means of the curse that was the cause for my attaining you, it has been turned into a boon."
Having been asked by her husband, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, about the cause of that curse, the virtuous Kalāvatī, a celestial nymph, spoke as follows.

Having once seen the gods in the garden, I praised the enjoyments of mortals; yet, upon seeing the enjoyments of the twice-born gods, I censured them for providing pleasure only through the mere sight of them.
Having understood that, the king of the gods cursed me: "Go; you shall eat as food, for you have been wedded by a mortal; you shall experience those human pleasures."
Therefore, this union between us two has come about with mutual consent; tomorrow I shall arrive from the sky without delay, and let there be no anxiety in you.
"O beloved, Rambhā will indeed perform a new dance before Hari; we must remain there until its conclusion."
Then Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, doting with love for her, said: "I shall see that dance; lead me there in secret."
Having heard this, Kalāvatī said to her husband: "How is this appropriate for me? For the King of the Gods will surely be angry when he learns of it."
When he persisted in his insistence even after being told this, Kalāvatī then consented to take him [with her] out of affection.
In the morning, having concealed him within the lotus on her ear by means of her supernatural power, she brought Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla to the palace of Mahendra.
Seeing that city, whose gates were adorned with magnificent elephants and which was as beautiful as the Nandana grove, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla rejoiced, considering it to be a celestial realm.
And there, in the assembly hall of the enemy of Vṛtra, frequented by the thirty gods, he beheld the wonder of Rambhā’s dance festival, where throngs of celestial nymphs were singing.
He heard all kinds of musical instruments played by Nārada and others; for when the Supreme Lord is pleased, what is there in this world that cannot be attained?
Then, at the conclusion of the spectacle, a divine jester in the form of a goat rose there and began to dance with celestial gestures.
Seeing him and recognizing him, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla thought: "Aha! Here I behold that very goat-sacrifice victim from Ujjayinī."
Even here before Indra’s city, such a dancer of mockery appears; alas, this is some wondrous and inconceivable divine illusion!
While Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla was thus reflecting in his heart, at the conclusion of Chāgabhaṇḍa’s dance, Śakra returned to his abode.
Then Kalāvatī, delighted, brought Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla back to his own place, just as he had been resting upon her ear-lotus.
And on another day, seeing that Devabhaṇḍa had arrived in Ujjayinī in the form of a goat, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla spoke to him out of pride:
"Dance before me as you dance before Indra; otherwise, I shall not forgive you! O buffoon, show that dance!"
Having heard that, the goat was struck with wonder and remained silent, thinking to himself, "How is it that even this human knows me so well?"
When he was spoken to with persistence, the goat did not dance at all; thereupon, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla struck him on the head with clubs.
Then, having gone to Śakra, the goat reported everything exactly as it had happened with his head dripping with blood.
Even Indra, through his supernatural power, perceived it as clearly as if he were in heaven; he brought Kalāvatī from Rambhā’s dance to Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla.
And when that offender had witnessed the dance of the goat, Indra summoned Kalāvatī and cursed her as follows:
Out of passion, you have secretly brought here that man for whom you have brought this goat into such a state for the sake of his dance.
Therefore, go to the city of Nāgapura; in a temple built by King Narasiṃha, become a statue upon its pillar.
Having been thus addressed by Kalāvatī’s mother, Alambuṣā, Śakra, being entreated with difficulty, ordained this end to the curse.
When that celestial abode, completed over many years, perishes and becomes level with this earth, then the end of the curse will occur.
Thus Kalāvatī, with tears, related to Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla both Indra’s curse and its termination, having reproached him for his words.
Having given him his own ornaments, she vanished and entered a statuette atop a pillar in a temple within the city of the Nāgas.
Then Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, struck by the poison of separation from her, could neither see nor hear; he fell to the ground in a swoon and rolled about.
"Alas! Though I knew it was a secret, it has been revealed by me, a fool; for how can there be self-restraint in those like me who are naturally fickle?"
"Now this terrible separation has come upon me," he cried; having regained his senses with these words, the gambler lamented.
In an instant he thought: "This is no time for despondency; having summoned my fortitude, why do I not strive for the sake of ending her curse?"
Having reflected and deliberated thus, that rogue assumed the garb of a wandering ascetic—complete with a rosary, deerskin, and matted locks—and went to Nāgapura.
There, in the forest outside the city, he buried four jars adorned with beautiful ornaments, having fixed them in the ground in the four directions.
And at night, he buried a fifth [vessel] filled with great jewels within the city, on the ground of the marketplace of the foremost gods, at his own will.
Having done this, he remained there on the bank of the river, having constructed a hut; relying upon hypocritical asceticism, he practiced artificial meditation and recitation of prayers.
Performing three ablutions daily and eating alms-food after washing it with water upon a stone slab, he attained the renown of a great ascetic.
Since he did not come into the king's presence even though invited by the king after gradually reaching the path of his hearing, the king went to his side.
After they had stayed there for a long time conversing, as the king desired to depart in the evening, a jackal suddenly let out a cry from a distance.
Hearing that, the gambler in the guise of an ascetic laughed; and when asked, "What is this?", he replied, "What is the use of this?"
And when the king questioned him persistently, that deceiver spoke thus: "In the forest to the east of this city, beneath a cane thicket..."
"O King, there is a jar filled with precious ornaments; take it," thus was I told by this auspicious woman who understands the cries of birds.
Having spoken thus, he led the king, who was filled with curiosity, to that spot, dug up the earth, extracted the jar, and gave it to him.
Then, having received the ornaments, the king, his confidence restored, regarded that ascetic—who was free from desire—as truly wise and truthful in speech.
Having brought him to his own hermitage and bowed repeatedly at his feet, he went to his palace at night with his ministers, praising his virtues.
As the king approached him in this manner, the rogue, under the pretext of the bird's cry, caused him to procure three other jars of jewels from the other directions.
Then that king, the citizens, the ministers, and the women of the inner apartments became devoted solely to that ascetic; they were entirely absorbed in him.
Once, while being led by the king to inspect the temple, that wretched ascetic heard the cawing of a crow in the marketplace.
Then he said to that king, "The words of the crow were heard by you: 'Right here in this marketplace, O King, it stands buried in the ground before the deity.'"
"Why is that jar, filled with the seven precious gems, not taken? Thus was it said by the crow; "Therefore, come and take possession of it."
Having said this, that false ascetic led him there, lifted him out of the ground, and gave him to the king a jar filled with excellent jewels.
Then, out of excessive delight, the king himself took hold of that pseudo-knower by the hand and entered the temple.
There, having shaken off his weariness at the pillar, the wandering ascetic beheld that statue of a woman carved in relief, which had been entered by his beloved Kalāvatī.
And Kalāvatī, assuming the form of that statue, became distressed upon seeing her husband and began to weep there.
Seeing that, the king, accompanied by his followers, filled with wonder and despondency, asked Jñānābhāsa: "O Blessed One, what is this?"
Then that rogue, appearing dejected and bewildered, said: "Come to my own home; there I shall tell you this, even though it is something that ought not to be told."
Having spoken thus, he led the king to the capital and said to him: "This temple has been built by you in an improper place and at an inauspicious moment."
"Whatever has been done by you will become harmful to you on the third day; therefore, because of her sight of you, this statue of a pillar wept."
O King, if you have need of that body, then crush it completely this very day and quickly level this temple with the ground.
Since you are constructing a temple for the gods here at an auspicious place and a favorable moment, may all ill omens subside, and may there be well-being for you and your entire kingdom.
Having been addressed thus by him, the king, out of fear, issued a command to his subjects and had that temple leveled with the ground in a single day.
And in another place, he began to build a temple once again; alas, even lords are deceived by rogues through their guiles after having been inspired with trust!
Then, having accomplished his purpose, that gambler Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla abandoned the garb of a wandering mendicant, fled, and departed from there for Ujjayinī.
And Kalāvatī, having learned of this and being released from her curse, approached him on the road; delighted, she comforted him and went to heaven to see Indra.
Indra, too, was astonished; having learned of that illusion of the gambler from the mouth of the husband, he both laughed and was pleased.
Then Bṛhaspati, standing by his side, said to Śakra: "Gamblers are always like this, possessing such diverse illusions."
In a former age, there was once a gambler in a certain city named Kuṭṭinīkapaṭa, who was an expert in fraudulent gambling.
And when he had gone to the other world, the King of Dharma reportedly said to him: "O gambler, by virtue of your own sins, your residence in hell shall last for an eon."
For one day, however, your status as Indra exists by virtue of a gift from you; indeed, at some time, you gave even a single piece of gold to a knower of Brahman.
"Therefore, tell me first: which shall you enjoy first—hell or the state of Indra? Having heard that, the gambler said, "I shall enjoy the state of Indra first."
Then that gambler, sent by Dharmarāja to heaven, raised Indra up for one day and was consecrated in the kingdom by the gods.
Having attained the sovereignty of the gods, he summoned his friends, the gamblers, along with the courtesans, and by virtue of his lordship, commanded the deities in heaven.
"Having led us to all the sacred fords—whether celestial, terrestrial, or even those located throughout the seven continents—bathe us all instantly."
Having entered today itself all the kings upon the earth, bestow great gifts incessantly for our sake.
Thus commanded by him, the gods performed all of that at that very moment; having shaken off his sins through those merits, that rogue attained a stable state of lordship.
And his companions and courtesans whom he had brought to heaven also attained immortality through his grace, their sins having been destroyed.
On the second day, Citragupta informed Dharmarāja that the gambler had attained a stable sovereignty over the gods through his own intellect.
Then, having understood their virtuous conduct, the King of Dharma was struck with wonder, exclaiming, "Alas! We have been deceived by gamblers!"
"O wielder of the thunderbolt, such are these gamblers! Having said this, when the Guru had ceased speaking, Indra sent Kalāvatī as a messenger and brought Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla to heaven.
There, the king of the gods, pleased with his intelligence and fortitude, honored him, gave him Kalāvatī, and made him stand by his own side.
Then that wise Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, like a god, lived happily with Kalāvatī in heaven through the grace of Śaṅkara.
Such is the way of gamblers, both in their deceit and their recklessness; therefore, O Vetāla, what is the wonder in a gambler that he [acts thus]?
"You have been cast into this well by the Ḍākinī through her illusory power; therefore, come out, for we two, your friends, shall emerge from this pit."
Having been addressed thus by the two Brahma-rākṣasas, I emerged from that pit and, afflicted by hunger, encountered a Brahmin traveler in this city during that night.
And as I ran toward that Brahmin with the desire to seize him, he cried out to King Śrī Vikramāditya.
As soon as he heard this, the king, blazing like fire, came forth and cried out from nearby, "Ah, you sinner! Do not kill the Brahmin! and struck me down.
As he proceeded to cut off the head of the man in the painting, my throat began to bleed as it was struck by that [blade].
Then, clinging to his foot, I was protected by him even as I abandoned my life; such is the power of that divine King Vikramāditya.
"By his command, this Khandakapalika was slain by me; therefore, O Vetala, release this Yamaśikha, who is my prey."
Although addressed thus by Agniśikha, Yamaśikha, out of pride, struck with his hand the body of Khaṇḍakāpālika.
Then the illustrious Vikramāditya, revealing his own self there, drew a man upon the ground with chalk and severed its hand with his sword.
When his hand was cut off by him, it fell upon Yamaśikha; thereupon, abandoning that corpse, he fled away out of fear.
And Agniśikha devoured that corpse of the skull-bearer; and I, free from fear, witnessed all of that by the power of the king.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, that Yakṣa-wife Madanamañjarī spoke to me again concerning your power.
Then that king spoke sweetly to me: "O Aṅgadevī, leave the Kāpālika Yakṣas and go to your husband's home."
Then, having bowed to him, I have come here to my own home, reflecting on how to repay that favor of the king.
"In this way, my life, my family, and my husband were given to you by my lord; and when she is told of you, she will recognize my story."
And today it has been learned that the daughter of the King of Siṃhala, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, has been sent by him as a bride to be chosen by the king himself.
And all those kings, acting together with envy, resolved to seize her after killing Vikramaśakti, the vassal of that king.
Therefore, go to Vikramaśakti and inform him of this, so that he may remain attentive in providing a remedy for them.
And I shall make such an effort that King Vikramāditya, having slain those enemies, will achieve victory.
For this purpose you were brought here by me through my own power of illusion, so that you shall relate all of this to the king along with his vassals.
And I shall send such a gift to that lord of yours, so that by it I may offer even a small measure of recompense for his kindness.
While she was speaking thus, those two maidens whom we saw in the ocean, accompanied by a deer, arrived there.
One had limbs as white as the moon, while the other was dark as the priyaṅgu plant; they were like the Gaṅgā and Yamunā attending upon the Lord of Rivers.
When they were both seated, O King, I asked that yakṣī: "O Goddess, who are these two maidens, and what is this golden deer?"
Having heard that, O Great King, the yakṣiṇī spoke to me: "Anaṅgadeva, if you have curiosity, listen as I tell it."
Formerly, at the time of the creation of progeny by Prajāpati, two terrible Dānavas named Ghaṇṭa and Nighaṇṭa, who were invincible even to the gods, came forth as obstacles.
And Vidhātā, desiring their destruction, created these two maidens, whose beauty of form was unrestrained and intoxicating to the world.
Upon seeing these two great asuras carrying away that most wonderful [child] and fighting with one another, both of them went to their destruction.
Then Brahmā entrusted these two daughters to the Lord of Wealth, saying, "These two must be given by you to some suitable husband."
Dhanada gave these to my husband, his own younger brother; and my husband likewise gave them to me for the sake of a boon.
I have chosen Śrī Vikramāditya as the husband for these two; indeed, an incarnation of a god is the only fitting consort for them.
O maidens of such form, listen to this narrative of the deer: there is a beloved son of the Lord of Śacī named Jayanta.
Once, while being carried through the sky by celestial nymphs as a child, he saw princes playing on the ground below with young deer.
Then, out of childishness, deprived of his pet fawn, he went to heaven in a state of distress and wept before his father.
For his sake, Śakra had Viśvakarman fashion a deer made of gold and jewels, its life-breath infused by the sprinkling of celestial nectar.
Then Jayanta played with him and was well-pleased; and that young deer also remained there, sporting in the celestial realm.
At that time, Indrajit—the son of Rāvaṇa whose name was truly meaningful—having seized the deer, carried it from the sky to his own city, Laṅkā.
And when time had passed, due to the wrath arising from the abduction of Sītā, Rāvaṇa and Indrajit were slain by the two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
That wonderful deer made of jewels and gold remained in the palace of Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who had been consecrated in the kingdom of Laṅkā.
And once, during a festival, Vibhīṣaṇa brought me to his home and, out of affection for my husband's kinsman, gave me a deer as a mark of honor.
Thus, this divine young deer now dwells in my house; and I must present it as a gift to your lord.
While that yakṣiṇī was thus recounting the sequence of my story, the sun, the beloved of the lotus, went to its setting.
Then, after she had instructed us regarding the evening rites in her residence, both this envoy of the Lord of Siṃhala and I lay down to sleep.
Having awakened in the morning, they honored him and inquired after his welfare; then, he desired to ask us about the message from the Lord of Siṃhala.
Then, reflecting upon that manifestation of the Yakṣiṇī’s power, we two went quickly to the side of Vikramaśakti, filled with wonder.
And as soon as he saw him, having honored him and inquired after his welfare, he wished to ask about the message from the Lord of Siṃhala while they were still on the ship.
Meanwhile, those two divine maidens, possessing the forms described by the Yakṣiṇī, arrived there together with the young deer, surrounded by the Yakṣa army.
Seeing them, and suspecting them to be the illusion of evil spirits and the like, Vikramaśakti, out of doubt, asked me, "O Lord, what is this?"
Then, in due course, I described to him the matter concerning the Lord of Siṃhala, as well as the pair of Yakṣiṇī maidens and the deer's tooth.
Having heard from the mouth of the yakṣī that effort directed against kings is detested by all kings because of their unanimous consensus, I then spoke to her.
Then, having honored us and both those divine maidens, he, the vassal lord, being overjoyed, made his army ready for battle.
In an instant, the great roar of the army's musical instruments was heard here, O King; and in another instant, the vast force of the opposing kings along with the Mlecchas came into view.
As those two armies—our own and the enemy’s—rushed at one another out of anger upon seeing each other, a battle between the two commenced.
Then, by those yakṣas dispatched by the yakṣiṇī, our enemies' army was struck down—some by the yakṣas themselves, others by our own soldiers who had been possessed by them.
A terrible storm of battle arose, thick with clouds of dust from the armies, incessant with the strokes of sword-edges, and filled with the roars of heroes.
With the heads of our enemies falling as they were severed, the Goddess of Victory shone upon us as if she were playing with balls.
In an instant, those kings who had survived the slaughter, their armies shattered, bowed down and sought refuge in the camp of your vassal.
Then, O Lord of all the earth, when the four quarters containing the six continents had been consolidated and the barbarians had been eradicated by you;
Manifesting together with her own husband, that Yakṣiṇī spoke thus to King Vikramaśakti and to me:
Whatever service I have performed for you, my lord, must be reported to you; furthermore, he should be informed by my words as follows.
"You must marry these two maidens created by the gods; you should look upon them with favor, and this deer as well must be cherished."
Having said, "This is indeed my gift," the Yakṣī presented a heap of jewels and, together with her husband and her followers, vanished from sight.
On another day, that daughter of the Lord of Siṃhala, Madanalekhā, arrived with a vast retinue and great splendor.
Then, having come forward to meet him, Vikramaśakti, bowing with great joy, led him into his own camp.

There, having obtained a small amount of money through various means, I enjoyed myself for several days. Then, as I was returning home one evening, I saw a certain young man who appeared to be a prince. Seeing him, I felt compassion and asked him: "Who are you, and why do you wander alone in such a state? He replied: "I am a prince named Vīrabāhu, the son of King Siṃhabala of Siṃhala-dvīpa. And so, the Blessed One related to us the tale of how, in a former life, a certain merchant’s son had saved the life of a king who was being pursued by a tiger, and how, as a result of that act of merit, he had been reborn in a royal family and had now come to meet the Buddha. May you also, O King, find such merit in your own deeds. [End of Story] Then, having heard this, the King was filled with wonder and said: "O wise one, you have shown me the fruit of virtue. And I, having gained confidence, knew that it was so there, and I went accordingly; that clever old female ascetic also gave her consent to me.

There, while he was enjoying the festival of love with her, she was awakened at the end of the night by a maidservant staying in the house.
Then, having banished that maidservant out of anger, she, remembering her beloved whom she had seen in a dream, blazed with the fire of separation.
Seeing no way out and rendered helpless by love, she rose again and again from her bed, only to collapse once more with her limbs trembling.
Like one who was mute, as if possessed by a spirit, and as if stupefied by darkness, she gave no answer at all to her attendants when they questioned her.
Having been discovered by her father and mother and questioned with great persistence, she related that account of her dream through the mouth of a trusted female friend.
Then, comforted by her father, she made this vow: "I shall reach that fire within six months, unless otherwise."
"Five months have passed since today; who knows what will happen to her?"—such was the report concerning that matter which reached me throughout the city.
When Śambarasiddhi had thus spoken in consultation with him, and the king was delighted by his certainty regarding the matter, Bhadrāyudha addressed him.

Having gone there, they spoke to his father, the king, in that same manner; then that monarch, freed from sorrow and filled with joy, approached the king with humble reverence.
At that moment, the bard Śambarasiddhi, who was skilled in discerning the right occasion, raised his arm on high and recited this:

Victory to you, who have subdued the hosts of spirits by your own splendor; victory to you, the forest fire to the jungle of the Mlecchas! Victory to you, O Lord, the husband of the Earth, who regards the seven oceans as her boundaries!
Victory to you, whose exceedingly weighty commands are borne upon the bowed heads of all conquered kings! Victory to you, Viṣamaśīla, ocean of valor, Vikramāditya!
When the bard had spoken thus, King Malayasiṃha, realizing that Vikramāditya had arrived there, grasped his feet.
And having been offered hospitality by him, he entered his own palace together with her, Malayavatī, his daughter who had been released from death.
And that king gave his daughter to King Vikramāditya, considering himself to have accomplished his purpose through that son-in-law.
Just as in a painting, so in a dream; and just as in a dream, so too did he behold his beloved Malayavatī in person, resting upon his lap.
And Vikramāditya, for his part, considered that wonder to be the fruit of the celestial tree that is the grace of the Beloved of the Mountain’s Daughter.
Then, taking that bride Malayavatī—who was like personified bliss—he crossed the ocean, which was surging with waves as if it were his own long separation.
Being saluted at every step by kings with various gifts in their hands, Vikramāditya returned to his own city, Ujjayinī.
Beholding there that power of his, which made various wonders come true according to his will, who was not amazed? Who did not rejoice? Or who did not hold a great festival?

This story which was told to me by the traveler Devasena regarding this very matter, I shall now relate to you; let it be heard.
To me, who was grieving, "How have I been married by the king without due rites?", that kārpaṭika spoke thus to comfort me:
"Do not give way to anger, O Queen, for you are possessed of supreme faith; having restrained your excessive agitation, hear the story from its very beginning."
Once, while serving as a wandering mendicant under your lordship, I saw from afar in the forest a very large boar.
With a mouth formidable with fangs and a complexion dark as the *tāla* tree, he was like the personified dark fortnight devouring the digits of the moon.

There, that boar, which was even swifter than the horse Uccaiḥśravas, vanished from his sight somewhere.

Having entered there to pass the night, I saw a certain woman within; and I remained there, treated with hospitality by her.

Then, drawing my dagger with a frown, I, remaining fearless, said to her: "Have you ever seen such a man anywhere?"
Then, assuming a gentle form, she spoke to me without any change of expression: "I am a Yakṣī named Caṇḍī, and I am pleased with your fortitude."
"Therefore, tell me now: what pleasing service may I do for you? To her who had spoken thus, I, the Yakṣiṇī, replied:

Therefore, coming here every day to this forest region, I shall eat fruits and, having returned to Ujjayinī, perform service for you.
"Thus, O Queen, the king was informed by me; he considered it within his power and, with a gracious look, spoke to me, saying that I was a fit companion for him."

The Vetāla also said: "O King, I do not possess such power; powers are restricted in their scope—does water ever extinguish the fire of lightning?"
Then the king said, "In that case, friend, let us go to this village; perhaps some means might then become known to us from among the Bhillas."
Having reflected thus, the king went to that village accompanied by the Vetāla; there, seeing him adorned with ornaments, the thieves surrounded him.
And while they were raining down showers of arrows, those five hundred were devoured by that Vetāla Bhūtaketu at the king's command.

Having heard these words of the king, the general said: "Let this Devānuga show him to my son."

Where garments made of peacock feathers, necklaces of guñjā berries, and the flow of elephant ichor serve as the ornaments for women.
There, the commander’s wife herself performed service for him; her garments were perfumed with the fragrance of musk, and she was adorned with pearls and other ornaments.
Then, having bathed and eaten, the king saw his aged sons and that youthful commander-in-chief there, and he questioned him.

"I am a Brahmin named Candrasvāmin who formerly lived in Māyāpurī; once, at my father's command, I went to the forest for the sake of firewood."

"He will not eat me for now; therefore, it is better that I go by another path. By showing him this, I shall observe the disposition of this monkey."
Having reflected thus, I set out on that path; and that monkey went before me, looking back at me as he moved forward.
Having gone a long distance, that monkey climbed a jambu tree; and upon its back, thick with a network of creepers, I fixed my gaze.

Then, having climbed the tree and cut that snare of entwined creepers with my axe, I liberated that female monkey.

When he had eaten that, old age and disease departed from me along with my wife; thereafter, a calamity of famine arose there in our country.

At that time, there was a chief of the Śabaras here named Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra; taking up his weapon, I entered into service under him.

And by worshipping that Lord with a single meal a day, I further propitiated him; thus, though he was childless, he bestowed the kingdom upon me alone at the time of his end.
While remaining here, twenty-seven hundred years have passed for me, yet there is no old age for me because of eating that fruit.
Having thus related his own story, that king of the Bhills, Ekākikesarī, addressed the astonished monarch once more.
"By me, through the fruit of the monkey and other deeds, long life was achieved; therefore, today the full fruit of that has been attained: the sight of your feet."
Therefore, O Lord, I entreat you: let this favor shown toward me today by your coming to my home be brought to its full satisfaction.
A daughter has been born to me by my Kṣatriya wife through a god; she is peerless in beauty and is named Madanasundarī.
And that jewel of a maiden does not shine anywhere else except for you; therefore, I give her to you—marry her according to the prescribed rites.
"I am your slave, O Lord, and I have followed you with two hundred thousand bows. When he had thus petitioned him, the king agreed, saying, "So be it."
And at an auspicious moment, he married that daughter of his, who gave him hundreds of camels laden with burdens of pearls and musk.
Having stayed there for seven nights, the king then set out together with Madanasundarī and that army of Bhillas.
In the meantime, while the king had been carried away by the horse in that hunting forest, our army stood there distressed; then Bhadrāyudha, the Kṣattṛ, spoke to them.
Enough with despair; your lord will arrive before long. Nothing whatsoever can cause harm to one who possesses such divine power.
Do you not remember how he went down to Pātāla, married the Nāga maiden named Surūpā, and returned here all alone?
And having gone to the world of the Gandharvas, the hero returned from there, taking with him Tārāvalī, the daughter of the lord of the Gandharvas.
Having spoken thus, they were all comforted by Bhadrāyudha; they remained at the entrance of the forest, watching for the path of the king.

Mounted upon his horse, he entered that forest together with me and Vetāla, desiring to see the boar he had previously beheld.

O Queen, as that corpse was being torn open by the Vetāla who had run toward it, a handsome man suddenly emerged from its belly.
Just as the king, filled with wonder, asked him, "Who are you?", a forest elephant, resembling a moving mountain, arrived there.

And as the king was desirous of asking questions, that man emerged from the belly of the boar and said: "O King, listen; I shall tell you my own story."
"We two are divine youths; this one is named Bhadra and I am Śubha. While wandering about, we saw the sage Kaṇva absorbed in meditation."
"Out of playfulness, we assumed the forms of an elephant and a boar; having done so, we terrified the great seer out of delusion, and he cursed us."
"In the forest, you two shall become exactly such an elephant and a boar; when slain by King Vikramāditya, you will attain liberation."
"Thus, by the sage's curse, we two became an elephant and a boar; today we have been liberated by you. But this woman must herself tell her own story."
Touch this boar by the neck and the elephant by the back; for these two shall indeed become a divine sword and shield for you.
Having spoken thus, he vanished along with his companion; and the king’s boar and elephant, when touched by his hand, were transformed into a sword and a shield.
Then, being questioned about her own story, that woman spoke thus: "I am the wife of a merchant chief named Dhanadatta in Ujjayinī."
"While I was sleeping on the roof-terrace of my palace, this elephant came, swallowed me whole, and brought me here; yet there was no man within it."
"A man has emerged from my split belly along with me. To her, who had spoken thus, the king said to that distressed woman:

Having said this, he had her brought and handed her over to Queen Madanasundarī, who was departing by a separate path along with the Vetāla.

There is an island named Kaṭāha, the abode of all prosperity; there dwells a king named Guṇasāgara, whose name is true to his character.
To him, by his chief queen, was born a daughter named Guṇavatī, who, by her beauty, was a source of wonder even to the Creator himself.

"King Vikramāditya is a worthy suitor for this daughter of mine; therefore, I shall send her to him alone for the purpose of taking her hand in marriage."
Having thus deliberated, the king placed his daughter, along with her attendants and her wealth, upon a ship in the ocean and sent her forth.

These two princesses here, having crossed the ocean, are proceeding step by step; we have arrived here as their attendants.
"O Lord, as we reached this place, two very large boars rushed toward us; then we cried out in this manner."

When he had said this, as we were wandering about there, we saw on one side a pillar-statue of extraordinary beauty.

Reflecting thus, searching, crying out, lamenting, and weeping, I remained there without food, consumed by the fire of separation from him.

That beautiful woman, having risen of her own accord and unnoticed by others, followed after her husband with curiosity, remaining faithful to him.

Hearing that, Rūpavatī approached him suddenly and said this: "Eat me; for if this husband of mine is devoured, what refuge would I have?"
When the rākṣasa said, "Alms are your refuge," she replied to him: "O Great Being, who here will give alms to a woman such as I?"

There, because his life-force still remained, he recovered his breath and reflected: "Ah! This service has been rendered to me by that brahmin."
Or rather, was it not precisely because of his lawless stupidity that he did not say so, since he united his son with a wife by having him married off to another?
While he remained there, overwhelmed with anxiety, reflecting thus, the night arrived, during which the circle of sky-faring women roamed about.
Waking up during that fourth watch of the night, he heard a clamor in the sky and saw before him a handsome man who had fallen from the heavens.
After a long time, having perceived that he was unaltered, Kesaṭa, though terrified, asked him, "Who are you? Thereupon, that man replied.
"Tell me first who you are here; then I shall tell you mine. Having heard that, Keśaṭa described his own life-story to him.

On the bank of the river Veṇā, there is a city named Ratnapura; there I lived as a householder, a wealthy son of a twice-born man, known by the name Kandarpa.
Thus, at nightfall, seeking water, I descended into the river Veṇā; having slipped there, I fell and was carried away by the force of the current.
Having been carried a great distance by that night, at the arrival of day, I was placed by him in a grove of trees situated on the marshland by the force of destiny.
Having climbed up by hanging from a branch and rested near the bank, I saw there a large, empty temple of the Mothers.
Having entered it and seen the Mothers within, as if throbbing with splendor, I bowed to them with my fear stilled, and after praising them, I made this request:
O Blessed Ones, grant protection to me, who am wretched; for I have today come before you as one who has sought refuge.
Having thus made my request, as I rested there—exhausted by the torrent of the river—the day, my friend, gradually came to its rest.

Therefore, let him be taken and established wherever it may be well for him; we shall bring him back again, for he has sought refuge with us.
Having spoken thus, they took me through the air, adorned me, and placed me in the house of some wealthy brahmin in a certain city; then they departed.
There I saw that everything was prepared for the maiden's wedding—the altar was ready and the auspicious moment had arrived—but the groom’s party had not yet arrived.
Then, seeing me standing there in divine and excellent attire, all the people said, "At last, this boon has been obtained."
Then, having led me to the altar and brought his daughter there adorned, that brahmin householder gave her to me according to the prescribed rites.
"By good fortune, through the attainment of a husband of equal status, the beauty of this Sumanas has now borne fruit," the women said to one another.

And I do not know that city where I married Sumanā; nor do I know what will happen now.

Since she did not waver from her resolve even though being exhorted by us, Kandarpa, having tested her mind, approached her.
Seeing that he had arrived and recognizing him, the wise and noble-minded Sumanā fell at his feet and wept.

"Friend, I shall wear away this body by wandering among the sacred fords. Hearing that, Yajñasvāmin, who was standing there, said to Keśaṭa:

"Why indeed do you not marry me here this very day? Then, having placed her in the city garden, that evil-minded man went to the market to fetch the wedding requisites.

She did not escape at all until she was seen by the people; there, seized by those others, that mule was carried off.

Meanwhile, that circle of Yoginīs, supremely compassionate toward Kamadeva, conquered other Yoginīs and reached their own abode.
There, having recollected Kandarpa and realized through their own supernatural knowledge that his wife had been lost in the forest, they deliberated together.
The wise man Kandarpa shall himself attain his desire; however, his young wife, having been lost in the forest, will surely give up her life.
"Let us take her to Ratnapura and cast her there, so that she may dwell together with her co-wives in the house of Kandarpa’s father."
Having deliberated thus, those yoginīs went to that forest, comforted Sumanas there, and taking her with them, they brought her to Ratnapura.
When the night had passed, that noble-minded woman, wandering there in the city, heard these words being spoken by the people as they ran about.
This is Anaṅgavatī, the wife of the twice-born Kaṃdarpa; when her husband had gone away somewhere, she spent some time longing for his return.
That virtuous woman, not having found him, has now departed in despair; pursued by her two suffering parents-in-law, she is now intent on entering the fire.
Upon hearing this, Sumanas immediately went to that cremation ground and, approaching Anaṅgavatī, restrained her in this manner.

This Rūpavatī was being exhorted by her husband Keśaṭa to die; hear now the tumultuous outcry that arose because of it, and the account of what happened there.
Having spoken thus, that man related the curious account of Keśaṭa’s marriage and the Rākṣasa, which involved Rūpavatī, and then spoke again.
Then, having thus deceived Keśaṭa, that old Brahmin took Rūpavatī and departed from there for the sake of his son.
But Kesaṭa was not seen; having married her, it was unknown where he had gone. And Rūpavatī, not seeing Kesaṭa, spoke thus on the road:
"I do not see my noble son; why is he not here while everyone else is departing? Hearing that, the aged brahmin showed him his son and said:
"Therefore, daughter, look upon this man, your husband, who follows his own will. Then Rūpavatī, filled with rage, spoke to the old women standing there:

Speaking thus, having been deprived of food and drink out of fear of the king, she was led by that aged brahmin back to her father’s house.
There, lamenting her under the pretext of those twice-born men whom he had mentioned, her father said to her: "Who is he, my daughter? How is that husband of yours to be recognized?"
Then Rūpavatī said: "Father, my husband is that man named Keśaṭa, the son of a Brahmin called Deśaṭa from Pāṭaliputra."
Having said, "I have indeed heard this from the mouth of the Rākṣasa," she related the entire account of the husband and the Rākṣasa to him.
Then his father went there, and seeing the Rākṣasa lying dead, he gained full conviction and was truly gratified with that couple.
Having comforted his daughter with the hope of her eventual recovery, he sent her toward Pāṭaliputra to the side of Keśaṭa’s father, while he himself went to search for him.
Having gone there and returned before long, they spoke thus here: "That teacher of our master, residing in Pāṭaliputra, has been seen by us."
And when he was asked there, "Where is that son Keśaṭa of yours?", he replied with tears: "How could our son Keśaṭa be here?"
For even though his friend named Kandarpa arrived together with him, he departed from here for some unknown destination without saying a word, leaving me in the misery caused by Rūpavatī.
"Having heard these words of his, we have come here in due course. When the searchers had spoken thus, Rūpavatī addressed her father.
"O noble son, I have attained nothing; therefore I shall enter the fire. Bereft of my husband, father, how much longer indeed could I remain?"
When she, speaking thus, could not be restrained by him, Rūpavatī then went out today to die by fire.
Her two friends, both maidens, likewise went forth to die; one was named Śṛṅgāravatī, and the other was Anurāgavatī.
At that wedding, the young Kesaṭa was indeed seen by those two; with their hearts captivated by his beauty, they conceived of him as their husband.
When he was told by that man, "Such is this clamor of the people here," Kandarpa went to the vicinity of their funeral pyre.
Then, having quieted the clamor from afar and approached quickly, he spoke thus to that beautiful woman as she was worshipping the fire:
"Enough of this rashness, noble lady; Keśaṭa is indeed alive. He is your husband and my friend; know me to be Kaṃdarpa."
Having spoken thus, he related the entire account of Keśaṭa, beginning from his boarding the boat under the guise of an old Brahmin.
Then, her confidence established by their conversation, the joyful Rūpavatī entered her father’s house together with those two female companions.

Where Kesaṭa married your friend named Rūpavatī, there Kaṃdarpa resides, as does that very Rūpavatī.
Thus that man spoke, and the meaning of the letter was exactly so; and Kesaṭa described his own marriage to the father of Kandarpa.
Then, having celebrated a festival, on the following day his father dispatched a messenger to bring Kandarpa back, and he sent Keśaṭa to win back his beloved.
Keśaṭa also went together with that messenger to that country where Rūpavatī resided in her father’s house.
