Having met with Kandarpa, he married those two companions of Rūpavatī mentioned previously, being urged by her.
And Kesaṭa, taking with him Anurāgaśṛṅgāravatī and Rūpavatī, departed for his own country without having asked Kaṃdarpa’s leave.
Then Kandarpa, accompanied by his messenger, went to Ratnapura and was reunited with Sumanas and Anaṅgavatī, as well as their kinsmen.
Then, having reached their own respective countries and obtained Rūpavatī and Sumanas as their beloveds, Keśaṭa and Kandarpa remained there enjoying worldly pleasures.

Thus, those of firm resolve, though separated from their beloveds by adverse fate, once again attain reunion with them after having traversed difficult and piercing sorrows whose depths and limits cannot be measured.

Therefore, rise quickly, my friend; let us go. While searching, you too may eventually find your wife. Who knows the course of destiny? Even by me alone was my wife recovered alive, though she had been dead.
Having been thus encouraged and followed by my friend after he had told this story, I wandered the earth and reached this place; here, I beheld a lordly elephant together with a boar.

Having been disgorged by that elephant and then swallowed once more, I beheld with wonder my own helpless wife; and while searching for that elephant, which had long been seen and then lost, I have today, through my past merits, beheld Your Majesty here.
When the merchant’s son had spoken thus, King Vikramāditya had that wife—who had been obtained by the slaying of the elephant—brought before him and restored her to him.
Then that couple became joyful at their wonderful reunion, recounting their adventures to one another, their faces eloquent with praise for the illustrious Viṣamaśīla.

Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Viṣamaśīla* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Fifth Wave. Then King Vikramāditya questioned that very friend of the merchant’s son who had accompanied him, in this manner:

Thus addressed by the king, that friend of the merchant's son said: "If there is curiosity, O King, then listen; I shall tell you this."
I am Candrasvāmin, the son of a twice-born man, residing in the foremost agrahāra of Brahmasthala; and I have a beautiful wife in my home.
Once, when I had gone to the village on business by my father's command, a Kāpālika came there for alms and saw that wife of mine.
As soon as she saw him, she was seized with a fever and died that very evening; then my kinsmen took her away and placed her upon the funeral pyre at night.
When the funeral pyre was blazing, I arrived there from the village and heard the account of what had occurred from my own kinsmen as they wept before me.
When I had gone to the vicinity of the funeral pyre, that Kāpālika arrived, with a skull-topped staff dancing upon his shoulder and the loud sound of his ḍamaru drum resounding.
O Lord, when the funeral pyre was extinguished by the scattering of ashes, that woman of mine rose from the midst of the pyre with her limbs uninjured.
Taking up that skull-bowl which had been drawn after him by the Siddhi, he fled swiftly; and I, armed with bow and arrow, pursued him.
Having reached a cave on the bank of the Gaṅgā and set that khaṭvāṅga upon the ground, he spoke out of joy to the two maidens who were within it.
"Though you two have arrived, I did not enjoy them without her; today she has come into my hands, and thus my vow has reached fulfillment."
While he was speaking thus and showing my wife to those two, I threw that skull-topped staff of his into the Gaṅgā.
"O Kāpālika, you who wish to seize my wife shall not become Śiva!"—thus did I revile him, whose mastery of the khaṭvāṅga had been lost.
Then, not seeing his skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), that deceitful man intent on flight drew his bow and was struck down by me with a poisoned arrow.
Those heretics, who mock the Śiva scriptures by finding satisfaction solely in the accomplishment of evil deeds, fall in this manner—even though they have already fallen.
Then, taking my own wife, those other two women, and the two maidens, I returned home, causing wonder among my own kinsmen.
When questioned there regarding my own history, those two maidens said to me: "We are the two daughters of a king and a merchant-prince in Vārāṇasī."
When we were seized by this skull-bearer through his supernatural power, we have now been liberated from this sin by him alone, rendered stainless through your grace.
When they had spoken thus, on the following day I took them both to Vārāṇasī and, having related that entire account to them, I restored them to their own kinsmen.
And as I was coming from there, I saw this son of a merchant who was separated from his wife; having met with him, I have come here.
Behold how a fragrance wafts from my body, even though it has been washed, having been stained with the cosmetic unguent obtained from the cave of the Kāpālika.
To that brahmin, who said, "In this way, I have obtained my wife who had risen from the dead," the king paid his respects and sent him along with the merchant's son.
Then, having brought Guṇavatī, Candravatī, and Madanasundarī, and taking them along, he joined together with his own troops.
King Vikramāditya came to the city of Ujjayinī, and there he married Guṇavatī and Candravatī.
Then, remembering her as she stood among the statues on the pillars in the temple of Viśvakarman, the king commanded his doorkeeper.
Let a messenger be dispatched to Kaliṅgasena to obtain that maiden, whose likeness was seen by me in the statue on the pillar.
Thus commanded by the king, the chamberlain brought before him a messenger named Suvigraha and dispatched him with a message.
Having gone to the kingdom of Kaliṅga and seen King Kaliṅgasena as was appropriate, that messenger spoke to him thus:
"O King, His Majesty Śrī Vikramāditya commands you: whatever jewel exists upon this earth that you know of, let it come to us."
"You possess a jewel of a daughter; bestow her upon us, and by our favor, enjoy your own kingdom free from all thorns."
Having heard this, that King of Kaliṅga spoke in anger: "Who indeed is this Vikramāditya? Is he the one who gives us our commands?"
"Blinded by pride, he will seek a maiden as a bride-price and fall into ruin"—having heard this from Kaliṅgasena, the messenger replied:
Even as a servant, how can you, being thus ignorant of yourself, act with such insolence toward your master? O fool, do you wish to behave like a moth in the fire of his majesty?
Having spoken thus, the messenger returned from there and reported those words spoken by Kaliṅgasenā to King Vikramāditya.
Then that lord Viṣamaśīla, enraged, set out with his forces toward Kaliṅga, accompanied by Bhūtaketu and the Vetāla.
While the echoes of the army's roar seemed to say to that King of Kaliṅga, "Give up the maiden quickly," he reached that region in all directions.
Then, seeing him prepared for battle and having hemmed in that king with his forces, King Vikramāditya thought thus in his mind:
"As long as I do not have her daughter, I have no peace at all; how then can I kill my father-in-law? What reasoning can I apply here?"
Having reflected thus, the king, accompanied by Vetāla and unobserved due to his supernatural power, entered the bedchamber of the sleeping King of Kaliṅga at night.
"Are you sleeping after having quarreled with one of such treacherous character? Having awakened him there while he was terrified, that Vetāla spoke, laughing.
And having risen, the King of Kaliṅga, seeing that display of audacity and recognizing the king who was accompanied by the fierce Vetāla, [was struck with wonder].
"Now that I am under your power, O God, command me; what shall I do? he requested, bowing at his feet in fear.
"If you have need of me as your lord, then give me your daughter Kaliṅgasenā," the king replied to him.
"So be it," the Lord of Kaliṅga agreed to that; and the king, successful and accompanied by the Vetāla, returned to his own camp.
And on another day, O Queen, your father, the Lord of Kaliṅga, gave you to King Viṣamaśīla according to the prescribed rites and with great magnificence.
"Thus, O Queen, you were wed by the king with deep affection and at the risk of his own life according to the prescribed rites, not out of a desire for conquest over his enemies."
Having heard from the mouth of the pilgrim Devasena that my resentment was born of insult, O friends, I abandoned my anger.
In this manner, I was married by the King upon seeing the statue on the pillar, and Malayavatī was likewise married by him upon seeing her portrait.
Thus Kaliṅgasenā, the beloved of Vikramāditya, having recounted the power of her husband, delighted her co-wives.
And thus Vikramāditya, accompanied by all of them and by Malayavatī, remained established in his imperial sovereignty.
Then once, a certain prince named Kṛṣṇaśakti, who had been humiliated by his own kinsmen, arrived there from the Deccan.
Having arrived at the main gate, he adopted the vow of a mendicant attendant upon the king, accompanied by five hundred princes.
And even though he was being dissuaded by the king, he vowed, "I must serve King Vikramāditya for twelve years."
And as he remained there with his followers, waiting with certainty, eleven years passed for the prince at the main gate.
And when the twelfth year had arrived, his wife, who was staying in another land and pained by their long separation, sent him a written letter.
While the king was engaged in his heroic wandering at night, remaining hidden and listening, he had this letter read aloud to his wife by means of a lamp.
O Lord, in separation from you, these sighs of mine—hot, long, and trembling—issue forth incessantly; yet it is my breaths that depart, not my life.
Having repeatedly heard these words from that royal attendant as he spoke them, the king returned to his own capital and reflected:
"Alas, this distressed traveler, burdened by his wife, will give up his life after twelve years have passed, having failed to accomplish his purpose."
Thinking, "I must not allow him any delay," the king immediately sent a maidservant and had the kārpaṭika summoned.
Having had this edict inscribed, he thus commanded him: "O Bhadra, go to the northern direction by way of the Oṃkārapīṭha."
"There, by this decree, enjoy the village granted by me; you shall obtain it by going and asking for that place known as Khaṇḍavaṭaka."
Having spoken thus, that king gave him the royal edict; and that kārpaṭika, without informing his servants, departed in the night.
"What desire for victory can I have for a single village that brings only shame? Nevertheless, the command of my lord must be carried out. Thus dissatisfied, he proceeded on his way by stages.
Having gone from the Oṃkāra-pīṭha into a distant forest, he saw many maidens playing there, and then he questioned them.
"Do you know, sirs, where Khaṇḍavaṭaka might be here? Having heard this, they said to him, "We do not know it."
"Go ahead; our father stays about ten yojanas from here. O gentle one, ask him; perhaps he might know that village."
Having been addressed thus by those maidens, he went and beheld their father, that *rākṣasa* of terrifying appearance, who was a *kārpaṭika*.
"Tell me, my good lady, where is Khaṇḍavaṭaka here? He questioned her, and that Rākṣasa, deluded by his own fortitude, replied to him.
What business have you there? For that city has been empty for a long time; nevertheless, if you must go, listen: this road before you branches in two.
There, you should proceed by the left-hand path until you reach the gateway of Khaṇḍavaṭaka, which is captivating with its high ramparts.
Having been addressed thus by the Rākṣasa, he went and reached that gateway; he entered that divine city, which was both terrifyingly empty and yet charming.
Having entered the royal palace there, which was surrounded by seven courtyards, he ascended to the top of the mansion constructed of jewels and gold.
There, seeing a jeweled throne, he sat down upon it; and at that moment, a Rākṣasa approached with a cane in his hand and addressed him.
"O man, why are you seated here upon the king's throne? Hearing that, the steadfast mendicant Kṛṣṇaśakti replied:
"I am the lord here, and you are my subjects and householders, granted [this status] by King Vikramāditya through my edict."
Having heard that command and seen him, the Rākṣasa bowed to him and said: "O King, you are the doorkeeper here, and I am yours."
"The command of King Vikramāditya is indeed unbroken everywhere. Having said this, that Rākṣasa summoned all the subjects.
The ministers and the royal retinue arrived there, and that city was filled with a fourfold army.
Then, being saluted by everyone, that joyful kārpaṭika performed all the rites, beginning with his bath, according to royal custom.
Then, having become a king there, he reflected with astonishment: "Aha! What an extraordinary power this King Vikramāditya possesses!"
The marvelous and unprecedented majesty of that Lord’s profundity bestows even such a kingdom as this, while declaring, "It gives a mere village."
Thus, filled with wonder, he dwelt there ruling his kingdom; meanwhile, Vikramāditya also maintained those friends of his in Ujjayinī.
And after some days, that eager kārpaṭika approached King Vikramāditya to pay his respects, while the king’s army caused the very earth to tremble.
When he had arrived and prostrated at his feet, Vikramāditya said to him: "Go and restrain the sighs of my wife, for whom this letter was sent."
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇaśakti, filled with wonder, was sent away by the lord of the earth; accompanied by his friends, he went to his own country.
Having sent away his kinsmen and delighted his wife, who had long yearned for him, he then enjoyed supreme royal splendor, having attained more than his heart's desire.
Thus, King Vikramāditya, whose conduct was so marvelous, once beheld there a certain Brahmin with a single hair standing erect upon his head.
And he asked him, "O Brahmin, why are you such as this? Thereupon, the twice-born man related his own history to the king in this manner:
"O King, there was a Brahmin named Agnisvāmin in Pāṭaliputra; I am his son, Devasvāmin, born of that great performer of the Agnihotra sacrifice."
And I married a Brahmin girl from a distant land; because of her youth, she was kept right there in her father's house.
In due time, having mounted my horse with a single servant, I went to my father-in-law's house to bring her back while she was still in the prime of youth.
Honored by my father-in-law, I then departed from there with my wife, who had mounted her horse and was accompanied by a single maidservant.
And on the way, when my horse was weary, my bride alighted and, under the pretext of drinking water, went to the bank of the river.
While she was not returning for some time, I dispatched that servant who had been standing there with me to keep watch over her.
"He too has not yet arrived; meanwhile, I have gone there myself, leaving that maidservant behind to guard the mare."
When I went there and looked, I saw that my servant had been devoured by that wife of mine until he was reduced to mere bones, his face smeared with blood.
Terrified, as I was going toward my mare, she too was likewise devoured by that same maidservant of mine.
Having fled from there, I went away; yet even now, because of that terror, the state of having my hair and body-hair standing on end does not cease within me.
When that brahmin spoke thus, "Therefore, O God, my refuge is in you," Vikramāditya, by his command, rendered him free from fear.
"Alas! Shame! There is no trust to be placed in women, who are the very ground of recklessness. While the king was saying this, one minister spoke as follows:
"O King, such indeed are these ill-born women; have you not heard here what happened to the Brahmin Agniśarman?"
Right here there is a twice-born man named Agniśarman, the son of Somaśarman; he is as dear to his parents as their own life, yet he is a fool, untrained in all branches of knowledge.
A daughter of a twice-born man from Vardhamānapura was married by him; and because she was but a child, she was not abandoned by her wealthy father from his home.
And when she had reached her youth, her parents said to Agniśarman: "Son, why do you not bring that wife of yours even now?"
Having heard this and without taking leave of his parents, that dull-witted Agniśarman then set out alone toward his wife.
As he had departed from his home, a partridge appeared on his right, and an auspicious jackal howled to his right, portending success.
That fool also welcomed him, crying out, "Live! Live! And the deity presiding over the omen, having heard this, laughed unseen.
Having reached his father-in-law’s abode and as he was about to enter it, an unfavorable kapiñjala bird appeared on the left, and an inauspicious female jackal howled on the left.
Furthermore, he rejoiced, uttering "Jīva-jīva," and that deity presiding over the bird also reflected upon it.
"Ah! This fool rejoices in what is inauspicious as if it were auspicious; he brings about that very action by which his life must be protected, and therefore it is for me to preserve his life."
While that deity was thus reflecting, Agniśarman, filled with joy, entered the residence of his father-in-law.
When asked by his father-in-law and others, "Have you come here alone?", he replied to them all, "I have come to the house without having informed anyone."
Then, when the night had come, his wife, having performed her appropriate bathing and eating, approached him in his bedchamber, beautifully adorned.
And as he slept from the fatigue of the road, she went outside and approached her paramour, the thief, even though he had been impaled on a stake.
Embracing his body, she whose nose had been bitten off by his teeth fled from there in fear because of the spirit that had entered him.
Having gone there, she placed her unsheathed dagger at the side of her sleeping husband and, making her kinsmen hear, cried out thus:
"Alas, alas! I am dead, truly dead, because this husband of mine has done something so senseless—having risen up, he has cut off my nose!"
Having heard that, her kinsmen came, and seeing her with her nose cut off, they beat that Agniśarman with clubs and other weapons.
In the morning, having informed the king, he delivered him to the executioners for execution by the king's command, on the grounds that he was a betrayer of his innocent wife.
When he had been led to the place of execution, that deity who was his bird, having witnessed the entire sequence of events concerning his wife, reflected thus:
He has already obtained the fruit of the signless (animitta) through this very act; since he said, "Live, live!", I shall therefore protect him from execution.
Having reflected thus, that hidden deity spoke from the sky: "O executioner, this son of a brahmin is blameless; he must not be killed."
"Go between the teeth of the thief on the stake and look at his nose," she said, and then she related to him the events of that night involving her bride.
Then, having observed that nose situated between the teeth of the thief, the king was informed by the executioners through the mouth of the chamberlain on account of that very circumstance.
Having released Agniśarman from execution, he sent him home; but he seized that wicked woman and punished her daughters-in-law as well.
When the minister had spoken thus, "O King, such are women," King Vikramāditya agreed, saying, "So it is."
Then the rogue Mūladeva, standing before the king, said: "O King, virtuous women do not exist at all; what then is there to say of those who are unvirtuous?"
Are there not mango creepers even amidst poisonous vines? Listen, therefore, to this which was experienced by me myself.
I previously went to Pāṭaliputra together with Śaśin, considering it a field of urbanity out of a desire to behold its cleverness.
There, seeing a woman washing clothes at a certain lake on the outskirts, I asked her, "Where can travelers stay here?"
On these shores, the cakravāka birds dwell; in the water, the fish; and upon the lotuses, the bees. I have not observed a lodging for travelers here.
Having been thus answered with an indirect remark by the elderly woman, I, feeling embarrassed, entered the interior of the city together with Śaśin.
There, seeing a child weeping at the door of his house, Śaśin spoke as he stood before a vessel of hot milk-rice.
"Alas! This child lacks understanding, for he does not eat the first offering; he needlessly torments himself with weeping instead of the finest rice-milk."
Hearing that, the boy wiped his eyes and said with a laugh, "You fools do not know what advantages there are for me in weeping."
As the milk-rice cools, it gradually becomes more palatable; furthermore, it acts more effectively [as a laxative], and the phlegm (kapha) undergoes depletion.
"These are my virtues; I do not weep out of folly. You, however, are vulgar and foolish, for you do not understand my intention."
When this was said by that boy, both Śaśin and I, abashed by our own lack of cleverness and filled with wonder, withdrew to another place.
There too, we saw an excellent maiden who had climbed onto the trunk of a mango tree to gather its fruit, while her attendants remained at the foot of the tree.
"O auspicious one, give us also some mango fruits," we said; and thus addressed by us, that maiden spoke as follows.
"Should I eat mango fruits that are warm, or perhaps those that are cold? Having heard that, desiring to know this marvel, I spoke to that maiden.
"Let us eat these warm ones first, O beautiful one, and then others as well. Hearing this, she threw the mangoes onto the ground in the dust.
Having cleared them of all impurities by blowing upon them with the breath from our mouths, we ate them; then that maiden, along with her attendants, laughed and said:
"These mango fruits were previously given to you while they were still warm; yet, having blown upon them after giving them, you ate them."
"Take these cool fruits, without blowing upon them, onto your garments. Having said this, she threw the fruits onto the hems of our clothes.
Taking those [gems] from that place, we departed feeling quite embarrassed; then I spoke to my other companions and to Śaśin.
"This clever maiden must certainly be married by me; a remedy for this mockery must be made—otherwise, what would be the point of my artifice?"
Thus, having searched for her father’s residence according to my instructions, we went there on the following day, disguised by our altered attire.
While we were studying the Veda there, that twice-born man, the father of the maiden, approached us as we were reciting and asked, "Where have you come from? regarding Yajñasvāmin.
"We have come here from the city of Māyāpurī for the sake of learning"; having been addressed thus by us, that wealthy and best of brahmins then spoke.
"In that case, dwell right here in my house for these four months; show me your favor, for you have come from a distant land."
"O Brahmin, having heard this, we said: 'We shall obey your word, provided that at the end of four months you will grant us our request.'"
Thus addressed by us, that brahmin Yajñasvāmin replied: "I shall certainly give whatever it is for the sake of which you are searching, provided it is possible."
When he had thus promised, we remained in his house; then, when four months had elapsed, that brahmin was addressed by us.
"Let us go; give us that which we have previously mentioned and for which we pray. To him who asked, "What is that?", the Moon replied, pointing toward me: "It is he."
"Let this maiden be given by you to him who is our chief"; then that brahmin Yajñasvāmin, bound by his word, reflected.
"I have been deceived by these; let this be, for he is a man of virtue. Having reflected thus, that brahmin gave his daughter to me in due form.
And one night, laughing in the bedchamber, I said to that bride: "Do you perhaps remember those mangoes, both warm and cool?"
Having heard that and recognized me, she said to me with a smile: "In this very way are country folk mocked by city-dwellers."
Then I also said to her: "Stay here happily, O city-dweller; I, a rustic, shall go far away, having made a vow to leave you."
Having heard this, she also made a firm vow: "I must certainly capture you and bring you back by means of a son born from you."
When they had thus made their mutual agreement, she lay down with her face turned away; and while she was asleep, I placed my own ring upon one of her fingers.
Having departed from there and reunited with those companions of mine, I came to my own city of Ujjayinī, desiring to witness her cleverness.
That daughter of a Brahmin also, waking up in the morning and not seeing me, yet seeing the ring marked with my name, reflected:
"He has already departed, leaving me behind; thus he has fulfilled his vow. I too must fulfill my own vow, casting away all remorse."
"The name 'Mūladeva' is seen upon this ring; therefore, he is certainly that very same man known as the rogue Mūladeva."
"He is said by people to be residing constantly in Ujjayinī; therefore, having gone there by a strategic means, I must accomplish my desired objective."
Having thus resolved, she spoke this falsehood to her father: "Father, my husband has suddenly departed, leaving me behind."
"How can I remain here at ease when separated from him? Therefore, I shall go on a pilgrimage to sacred sites; I will weary this wretched body."
Having spoken thus, and having with great effort obtained permission from her father even though he was unwilling, she then set out with her wealth and her attendants.
Traveling by stages and assuming the highly precious attire appropriate for a courtesan, that woman, the peerless beauty of the world, entered the city of Ujjayinī.
And having made an agreement regarding what was to be done with her retinue, Sumaṅgalā gave the son of the Brahmin the name Vipraśātman.
"She is a courtesan named Sumaṅgalā, who possesses the ability to assume any form at will and enjoys great liberality; she has arrived here," so it was announced to him by his servants.
Then the preeminent courtesan of that place, named Devadattā, approached her and offered her a separate residence worthy of royalty.
There, my friend Śaśin, captivated by her fame, first spoke to her through the mouth of a servant, saying, "Let my fee be accepted."
Whoever would follow our word may enter here as a lover; we have no need for hirelings, nor for other men who are like beasts.
Having been addressed thus by Sumaṅgalā through her very mouth, Śaśin said, "So be it," and went to her palace at the onset of night.
Having reached that first gate and announced his presence, he was addressed by the gatekeeper: "Do as our mistress commands."
"Even though you have already bathed here, bathe once more; otherwise, there is no entry for you. Having heard that, Śaśin accepted the bath, saying, "So be it."
Then, while he was being confidently bathed by the female slaves following the application of oil and fragrant unguents, the first watch of the night passed away.
Having bathed, he then reached the second gate, where he was addressed by the gatekeeper: "You have finished bathing; therefore, first perform the rite of adornment."
When he had said, "So be it," his female servants performed their adornment until the second watch of the night had also passed away.
Then, having reached the third courtyard gate, he was addressed by the guards: "Eat first; enter the interior after that."
When he had said, "So be it," those female servants detained him with various kinds of food until the third watch had passed.
Then, having somehow reached the fourth door of the bedchamber, he was thus reviled there by the doorkeeper:
"Village lover, depart; do not suffer humiliation! Is this the time for a courtesan's new union in the final watch of the night?"
Thus insulted by him, like the moon whose luster has faded before Time personified, he departed from there just as he had come.
In this manner, other lovers were likewise deceived by that daughter of a Brahmin who, assuming the form of a courtesan, bore the name Sumaṅgalā.
Having heard that, out of mere curiosity, I made a round-trip journey as a messenger and went to her house at night, well-adorned.
There, I gratified the doorkeepers at each gate with gifts of wealth; then, without delay, I reached the door of her inner apartments.
When the time had come and I was liberated, I entered that house through the gatekeepers and beheld my beloved, unrecognized by the courtesans in their boudoir.
Having recognized me, she performed the customary rites of welcome and so forth; like a cunning courtesan, she attended upon me as I sat cross-legged on the couch.
Then, having spent the night with her, the peerless beauty of the world, I became bound by passion and was unable to leave her house.
She too, having conceived a deep passion for me, did not depart from my side at that time, until after some days she became pregnant, her nipples turning a dark blue-black.
Then, having composed a forged letter, that clever woman presented it to me, saying, "The king, my lord, has sent this letter; let it be read."
Then, having released it, I read the letter as follows: "From illustrious Kāmarūpa, the glorious King Mānasiṃha [writes]:”
She addresses Sumaṅgalā: "How is it that you have remained here so long? Come quickly, abandoning your curiosity for other lands."
When I had thus read the letter, she spoke to me as if in sorrow: "I am going; do not harbor resentment toward me, for I am dependent on another."
Having thus made this pretext, you departed for Pāṭaliputra; but I, though devoted to her, did not follow, for she was dependent on another.
And she, residing in Pāṭaliputra, in due time gave birth to a son; and as he grew, the child mastered all the arts.
And once, when he was twelve years of age, that boy, out of childish fickleness, struck a fellow slave of his own age with his foot.
Being struck, that slave, weeping in anger, said to him: "You strike me, you whose father is not even known!"
"Since you were born here and there while your mother was wandering in foreign lands,"—having been told this by him, he went and questioned his mother out of embarrassment.
"Mother, who is my father, and where does he dwell? Tell me! Then that mother, the daughter of a brahmin, looked at him for a moment and spoke to him.
"Your father, named Mūladeva, left me and went to Ujjayinī"; having said this, she related her entire life story to him from the very beginning.
Then that boy said to her, "Mother, I will go and bring that father back bound; I shall fulfill your promise."
Having spoken thus to his mother, the boy set out from there; and, possessing the token she had described, he reached this city of Ujjayinī.
Seeing me there playing with dice and certain of my identity by the signs, he went to the gambling hall and defeated everyone at the game.
Even in his childhood, he was a great deceiver who caused wonder in everyone; he gave to those who asked for it the wealth he had won from gambling.
Having come by her own artifice at night, she placed me lightly upon a heap of cotton and carried away my bedstead while I slept.
Then, having woken up, I saw myself upon the back of a cotton mattress; suddenly, I was filled with shame, laughter, and wonder.
Then, O King, having slowly entered the marketplace and wandering about, I beheld that very boy selling that same bedstead.
Approaching him, I asked, "How much will you give for this bed as its price? Thereupon, that boy said to me:
"O crest-jewel of rogues, this couch cannot be obtained for a price; it can only be obtained by describing unprecedented and marvelous accounts."
Having heard that, I then said to him: "I shall tell you something wonderful regarding the truth; if you understand it as being truly real, you may accept it."
But if you should say that it was untrue because of my lack of trust, then you would be born of an adulterer, and I would fall upon my bed.
Listen, my dear, as I tell you this wonderful account of that time: formerly, there was a famine in the kingdom of a certain king.
With the great torrents of water from the spray of his mounted elephants, the king himself performed the act of plowing upon the back of the beloved of the Boar.
Then, enriched by the grains that had been produced, that lord of the earth, honored by the people, brought an end to the famine for his subjects.
When I had spoken thus, that boy then laughed and said: "Clouds are the vehicles of the Nāgas; the earth is the beloved of the boar."
For she is said to be most beloved by Viṣṇu in his form as a boar; what wonder is there if grain is produced in her by the waters of the clouds?
Having said this, that rogue of a boy spoke again to me, who was filled with wonder: "Now I shall tell you something unprecedented."
If, having understood this, you accept it as true in accordance with reality, then I shall give you this bedstead; otherwise, you shall become my slave.
When I replied, "So be it," that rogue boy then said this: "O Lord of Rogues, long ago a certain boy was born here."
He who, as soon as he was born, shook the earth with the weight of his footsteps, immediately became grown and set foot in another world.
When that boy had spoken thus, not understanding his meaning, I said: "This is false; alas, there is no truth whatsoever in this."
Then that boy said to me: "When Hari was born in the form of a dwarf, did the earth not tremble under the tread of his feet?"
At that very moment, having attained growth, what position did he not establish through him? He has indeed conquered you in the celestial realm, and you have been made his slave by me.
All these people here in the marketplace shall be our witnesses regarding this wager; therefore, wherever I go, you must come with me.
Having said this, that wise boy grasped my arm with his hand; and all the people standing there likewise gave him their testimony.
Then, having seized me and bound me by a wager, he, along with his followers, led me to my mother’s city, Pāṭaliputra.
Then his mother, seeing him, said to me: "Noble son, I too have today fulfilled my own vow."
"He has been brought here, held fast by a son born of you yourself," having said this, the virtuous woman related the entire account in the presence of everyone.
Then all her kinsmen, having celebrated a festival, congratulated her—she whose desired goal had been accomplished by her own wisdom and who was cleansed of the family's infamy by her son.
Having achieved my purpose, I dwelt here for a long time with that wife and that son, and then returned to this city of Ujjayinī.
Thus, there certainly exist here on earth noble women devoted to their husbands; however, it is not the case that all women are in every respect of wicked conduct.
Having heard this story from the mouth of Mūladeva, King Vikramāditya, together with his ministers, was filled with delight.
Thus hearing, seeing, and performing these wonders, King Vikramāditya conquered and enjoyed the earth with all its continents.
Having thus related this tale of Viṣamaśīla, which is filled with unions and separations, the sage Kaṇva spoke again to me regarding my separation from Madanamañcukā.
In this way, the separations and reunions of living beings are inconceivable; therefore, O Naravāhanadatta, it will not be long before you too shall have a reunion with your beloved.
Take heart, O son of the King of Vatsa; together with your wife as your counselor, you shall for a very long time enjoy the status of a beautiful emperor over the Vidyādharas.

Thus, having gained fortitude through the words of the sage Kaṇva, and having passed the period of separation, I then gradually obtained my wife, the sciences, and the sovereignty of the sky-dwellers.
And that [knowledge], O great sages, I have already described to you in its entirety, exactly as it was obtained by me through the grace of Śambhu, the giver of boons.
Having thus related his own story to all the sages and to his maternal uncle Gopālaka, Naravāhanadatta delighted them in that hermitage of Kaśyapa.

Having spent those days there during the onset of the rainy season, and having taken leave of his maternal uncle and the sages dwelling in the forest of asceticism, he then departed with his wife and ministers, ascending a celestial chariot that covered the sky with its army of sky-goers.

Having reached in an instant his own mountain abode, Ṛṣabhaka, he dwelt there for the duration of a kalpa with Queen Madanamañcukā and Ratnaprabhā and the others, enjoying the happiness of sovereign rule in the midst of the lords of the sky-dwellers.

Thus was this *Bṛhatkathā* formerly narrated on the summit of Kailāsa by the Moon-crested Lord, out of zeal at the request of the daughter of the Snowy Mountain; thereafter, it attained incomparable renown on the surface of the earth through Puṣpadanta and others, who, having been born there due to a curse, assumed the forms of Kātyāyana and the rest.

"Whoever recites this well-told tale that has issued from my mouth, or whoever listens to it with devotion, or whoever preserves it, shall before long have his sins destroyed and, having become a perfected being, will surely attain the status of a true Vidyādhara and reach my own world"—thus did the beloved of the Mountain’s Daughter then grant this boon for this story.

Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Viṣamaśīla* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. This eighteenth book, the *Viṣamaśīla-lambaka*, is complete; and this *Kathāsaritsāgara* is also finished. The Author’s Praśasti: There was a king named Saṅgrāmarāja, a *pārijāta* tree in the ocean of the illustrious Sātavāhana dynasty. Having descended and been attended by various learned men, he transformed the region of Kaśmīra into a second Nandana grove.

To him was born a son, the illustrious Ananta, a universal monarch and a wish-fulfilling tree for his lineage, who was a singular mass of valor; whose footstool was polished by the luster of the rubies in the crowns of all the prostrating kings.

And at the threshold of his gate, the head of the king—its neck severed and its belly cast out—rolled about like Rāhu, who had come as a servant and attained satisfaction upon hearing the beautiful fame of the Conqueror, which surpasses that of the great discus of Hari.

Then that moon among kings took as his queen the daughter of the lord of Trigarta, the goddess Sūryavatī, who dispelled the darkness of her subjects like the sun and was worthy of universal homage like the dawn.
Like the sacred scriptures, they were served by hundreds of brahmins born in various lands; like the oceans, they bore jewels and were a refuge even for kings who were themselves sources of fear.
By that queen, Kaśmīra was adorned with magnificent monasteries constructed day after day, which—like wish-fulfilling trees—dispelled the suffering of those who approached them in need.

The celestial mansions, constructed on banks two cubits wide with flowing pure waters and white as lime-plastered palaces, bear a resemblance most strikingly to the peaks of the Himalayas encircled by the celestial river.

Though she has been given countless mountains of jewels, gold, great land-grants, black antelope skins, wealth, and thousands of cows, the Goddess—who indeed always sustains the entire universe—has neither been exhausted nor even supported by them.

The illustrious King Kalaśadeva—though he was the sole ornament of the circle of the earth, yet remained free from falsehood; though a friend to the virtuous, yet was composed of thick nectar; though inauspicious to the assembly of his enemies, yet was an incarnation of Śiva.

That city belongs to him, the excellent king named Śrī Harṣadeva, who was created by the gods as a new-born Agastya from a jar—steadfast, capable of bending all the lofty mountains and able to drink even the seven oceans.

For that goddess, whose constant efforts were bound to the rites of worshipping Giriśa, performing fire-oblations, and making various kinds of gifts, and whose fatigue was always spent in listening to the scriptures as prescribed—[he spoke] for some momentary diversion of her mind.

This compendium of the essence of the *Bṛhatkathā*—which consists of the nectar of various tales and is like a full moon for the ocean of the minds of virtuous people—has indeed been composed by Soma, the son of Rāmā, who is as delightful through his many virtues as the most excellent of Brahmins.
This Kathāsaritsāgara, composed by Soma of pure intellect with its exceedingly expansive waves of narrative, may it be for the joy of the hearts of the virtuous.
